Australian coral reefs face collapse risk by 2075: global assessment
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:38:12 CST
11:38:12 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Every shallow-water coral reef ecosystem in Australia faces an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, largely driven by projected ocean warming, according to a global assessment.
The assessment, led by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) researchers at Australia's University of Melbourne and over 250 researchers across more than 80 countries and territories, found that 96 percent of the world's assessed coral reef ecosystems are classified as critically endangered, including all 17 Australian coral reef ecosystems, according to a university statement released on Thursday.
Researchers identified climate-driven ocean warming as the most widespread and severe threat to coral reefs, with increasingly frequent marine heatwaves causing mass coral bleaching and widespread coral mortality.
The study evaluated coral reef ecosystems in 127 tropical and subtropical marine ecoregions, including Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in Southeast Asia and the western Pacific, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef and the Red Sea.
Mishal Gudka, a University of Melbourne research fellow and scientific lead of the assessment, said much of the risk is driven by projected changes that have not yet fully materialized, making this a critical window for conservation and climate action.
Despite covering less than 1 percent of the ocean floor, coral reefs support around a quarter of all marine species and provide habitat, food and breeding grounds for thousands of species, while supporting fisheries, tourism and coastal protection for millions of people, the researchers said.
The assessment warned that stronger local management and rapid decarbonization could help avoid coral reef collapse, but the window for action was rapidly closing. ■

Brazilian Amazon emits more carbon than it absorbs, study shows
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:37:31 CST
11:37:31 KST

SAO PAULO, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- In 2010-2024, Brazil's Amazon emitted an annual average of 1.17 billion tons more carbon dioxide than it absorbed, according to a study published on Thursday by the Sao Paulo Research Foundation.
The imbalance is adding to global warming and eroding the rainforest's role as the planet's most important tropical climate regulator.
The study, also published in the British scientific journal Nature, showed fires released approximately 1.47 billion tons of carbon dioxide annually, compared to an absorption capacity of about 300 million tons per year.
The research, led by specialists from Brazil's National Institute for Space Research (INPE), revealed that drastically reducing fires, eliminating deforestation, and restoring forests are essential to preventing the Amazon from reaching a "tipping point," the threshold beyond which it would lose the ability to sustain itself and recover as a tropical rainforest.
Brazil is home to 60 percent of the Amazon rainforest.
"The main conclusion of the research is striking: the problem in the Amazon is human activity. We are losing the rainforest because the region's development model has been based on destruction," said Luciana Vanni Gatti, coordinator of the Greenhouse Gas Laboratory at INPE and the study's lead author.
In an analysis spanning 46 years, the research team also detected an increase of 1.13 degrees Celsius in the average annual temperature and 1.81 degrees during the dry season. These changes reduce regional humidity and worsen conditions that favor fire spread and environmental degradation.
"This places immense stress on the remaining forest," Gatti said, explaining that the loss of forest cover reduces rainfall and raises temperatures, creating a feedback loop that fuels more fires and speeds up the deterioration of the remaining forest.
Scientists are investigating why the rainforest is absorbing progressively less carbon, and the extent to which this phenomenon is driven by a reduction in photosynthesis versus an increase in the decomposition of vegetation.
The Sao Paulo Research Foundation believes these results reinforce the importance of conservation and restoration policies for the Brazilian Amazon, whose role in carbon storage and the regulation of the water cycle is key to regional and global climate balance. ■

Brazil electoral prosecutors seek to fine Meta over alleged breach of candidate equality orders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:32:32 UTC
11:32:32 KST

Mariam Ashalem De Andres
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Brazil’s Electoral Prosecutor’s Office has sought to fine Meta over alleged non-compliance with court orders requiring equal treatment online of presidential candidates, the news website UOL reported Thursday.
The office said Meta failed to provide all required information on electoral content, political advertisements and measures to ensure equal treatment online of the two runoff campaigns.
It also raised concerns about the company's artificial intelligence tools, including a translation feature that allegedly changed the meaning of comments about a candidate.
Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva’s campaign cited the phrase “Flavio futuro presidiario,” meaning “Flavio, future prisoner,” which was translated as “Flavio future president,” according to UOL, referring to Lula's rival, Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
The case follows a complaint filed by Lula's campaign on Oct. 19 accusing Meta of violating court orders and favoring Bolsonaro's campaign, the Brazilian newspaper O Globo reported.
The campaign alleged that content published by Lula's coalition and its supporters faced restrictions while material supporting Bolsonaro received more favorable treatment.
The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) had ordered Meta to ensure equal treatment of political content across its platforms.
The office acknowledged that Meta had lifted restrictions on Lula's campaign account and suspended some unauthorized political ads.
However, prosecutors said other submissions were incomplete or insufficient to demonstrate full compliance.
The TSE will decide whether to impose a fine. Meta could face penalties of up to one million reais ($198,000) per day for non-compliance, according to UOL.
The case has renewed scrutiny of social media platforms' role in Brazil's presidential runoff and their responsibility to ensure that candidates receive equal treatment online.
The runoff is scheduled for Oct. 25, following the first round on Oct. 4, when Bolsonaro received 47.3% of valid votes, according to official results. Lula secured 45.2%.

US accuses Canada of election meddling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:30:18 UTC
11:30:18 KST

US accuses Canada of election meddling
The US has accused Canadian officials of attempting to interfere in American elections, citing politically targeted trade measures, anti-Trump advertising campaigns and meetings with Democratic politicians ahead of next month’s midterms.
In a fact sheet published on Wednesday, the US Embassy in Ottawa accused Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government of openly seeking to influence American politics.
“The Canadian government brushes off concerns about potential interference in US elections, even as its ministers and premiers openly describe plans to influence American politics in official documents and public appearances,” the embassy stated.
The document singled out Canadian Industry Minister Melanie Joly, citing her remarks about deliberately targeting Republican-leaning states with retaliatory tariffs in response to President Donald Trump’s trade policies.
“We’re making sure to put pressure on American businesses, in key Republican states to put pressure on the Trump Administration,” Joly said in March. “We’re being wise and strategic to put political pressure,” she added in August.
Washington also questioned Joly’s meetings with Democratic officials in Boston and Chicago in September, as well as an anti-tariff advertising campaign launched by Ontario Premier Doug Ford featuring former President Ronald Reagan criticizing protectionist trade policies.
The embassy also highlighted a recent appearance by Canadian Consul General Bernadette Jordan alongside two Democratic congressmen at a Vermont roundtable on trade tensions, just three weeks before the midterms. It also cited a Canadian government billboard campaign targeting 12 mostly Republican-voting states and Washington, DC.
The embassy also cited Liberal lawmaker Anthony Housefather’s campaigning for Democratic Representative Debbie Wasserman Schultz in Florida, and listed 11 Canadians who had been charged or sentenced in 2026 for illegally voting in previous American elections.
“All Canadians should refrain from attempting to participate in or influence US elections in any way,” the statement concluded. “Americans decide America’s elections.”
The accusations followed a warning from US Ambassador Pete Hoekstra, who said Washington was closely watching Canadian political activities ahead of the November 3 congressional elections.
“We’re monitoring it, we’re evaluating it and if some of it becomes election interference then America will respond to it,” Hoekstra said.
Ottawa has rejected the allegations. Carney insisted that Canada’s measures were intended to protect its workers and businesses from American tariffs, while Ford denied any interest in meddling in US elections. Joly defended her meetings with American politicians as normal diplomacy, pointing out that she had engaged with both Republicans and Democrats.
The dispute comes amid deteriorating relations between the neighboring countries, driven by Trump’s sweeping tariffs and repeated suggestions that Canada should become America’s 51st state.
In September, Carney revealed that his government had examined the possibility of US military action against Canada, describing the scenario as an “extreme tail risk” that nevertheless warranted contingency planning. Ottawa, meanwhile, has been seeking closer military and economic ties with Europe to reduce its dependence on Washington.

The artificial intelligence agent software market across Asia, Australia and New Zealand is set to expand more than 14-fold by 2030, according to research firm Omdia, as Chinese tech companies increasingly deploy automated tools across office and industrial operations.
During its annual event in Beijing on Thursday, Omdia forecast that regional market revenue, which included mainland China and Hong Kong, would reach US$11.2 billion in 2030, up from an estimated US$782 million this year. Over the same period, the agentic share of the region’s AI software revenue was projected to rise to 12.3 per cent from 1.7 per cent.
AI agents use models to autonomously plan and carry out multi-step tasks – such as data analysis, report writing and software operations – allowing users to delegate work that would otherwise require repeated instructions.

Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming who in the Ukraine-Starlink row?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:16:26 UTC
11:16:26 KST

(L-R) Elon Musk, Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s civilian casualties have surged while questions over who is responsible for limiting Kyiv’s access to Starshield remain unanswered. Composite: Reuters/Pool EPA/AP
(L-R) Elon Musk, Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Ukraine’s civilian casualties have surged while questions over who is responsible for limiting Kyiv’s access to Starshield remain unanswered. Composite: Reuters/Pool EPA/AP
Trump, Musk, Zelenskyy: who is blaming who in the Ukraine-Starlink row?
A war of words has erupted over who is responsible for the restrictions on Starshield access in Ukraine
A war of words has erupted between the Trump administration, officials in Kyiv and Elon Musk over who is to blame for limiting Ukraine’s access to Space X’s military-grade version of Starlink.
The restrictions to Starshield have rendered many of the drones used by Kyiv to strike behind the frontlines inoperable and hampered air defence systems that stop Russian attacks, according to Ukrainian officials.
Donald Trump said on Thursday that the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
Amid the diplomatic handwringing, civilian casualties in Ukraine have surged, and the question over who is ultimately responsible for limiting Kyiv’s access has remained unanswered.
1. Donald Trump
The restrictions came as relations between the US and Ukraine hit their lowest point since Russia’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago.
Donald Trump has accused Ukraine of driving up diesel costs for Americans through its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysis by the BBC found that the US-Israel war on Iran and resulting restrictions on oil exports from the Gulf have likely had a greater impact on global diesel supplies.
Trump initially denied any responsibility for the changes to Starshield, telling reporters last Friday: “I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” referring to Musk, SpaceX’s CEO.
Trump’s cabinet backed him up, with secretary of state Marco Rubio saying on Wednesday: “What I can tell you with certainty is the president of the United States nor anyone in our system ever requested that any changes to that system be made.”
Rubio, however, also made a comment that threw suspicion on to Musk, the world’s richest man.
The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk. That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that the US president had asked Musk to restore the service, with Trump later telling reporters the system was “back”.
He refused to comment on whether he had spoken to Musk, but appeared to suggest the ultimate power to limit the service rested with the SpaceX CEO. “I guess the bottom line, he put it back,” Trump said, referring to Musk.
However, John Cornyn, a Republican who is in his final weeks as the US senator for Texas, told US media that he didn’t believe Musk would have acted “without at least the acquiescence of the White House”.
2. Elon Musk
Musk has supported Trump’s calls for Volodymyr Zelenskyy to be replaced and has been highly critical of the Ukrainian president. However, he was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”.
Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.
Musk – one of the Republican party’s biggest donors and a Trump ally – continued to deny responsibility for the changes. However, on Tuesday the Wall Street Journal reported that Musk made the order to slow down Starshield, with the paper’s sources in disagreement over whether this was made in concert with Trump.
Vice-president JD Vance backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
So I don’t think this is about Elon. I think it’s fundamentally what is America’s policy in Ukraine and Russia going to be.
3. Volodymyr Zelenskyy
The Ukrainian president initially blamed the restrictions on “SpaceX and the United States”, saying on Wednesday last week that the move would “bring a lot of human losses … of course, people will die”.
Shortly after the systems failed, Zelenskyy said there were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in European Union countries and that they applied only to Ukraine. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
Zelenskyy said at the weekend that Musk’s SpaceX was ultimately responsible for suddenly limiting the speed at which Starshield worked in Ukraine. “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed ... And technically, SpaceX did it.”
Despite Trump’s insistence on Thursday that the service had resumed, a senior European official told the Associated Press that nothing had changed in the operation of Starshield.
Prior to Trump’s comments, Zelenskyy said full Starshield speed had still not been restored for Ukraine, adding that he hoped for talks with Rubio in the coming days.

Airbnb scraps guest checkout chores such as cleaning

Airbnb scraps guest checkout chores
October 23, 2026
Chores such as washing dishes, stripping beds and taking out the trash at the end of your Airbnb stay will soon be a thing of the past.
Under new rules unveiled this week, the short-term rental platform says hosts should only make "reasonable" requests of guests.
Airbnb said hosts are generally not allowed to "ask guests to complete tasks that require significant effort or time, or would typically be performed by a cleaner, including stripping the bed, taking trash offsite, or washing and putting away dishes."
Why did Airbnb introduce the new rules?
Checkout chores have been a contentious issue for guests, especially in cases where they are also charged cleaning fees.
Airbnb has previously admitted that such fees can create confusion between guests and hosts.
"Guests expect checkout to be relatively simple, and most want to avoid unexpected chores," Airbnb said in a message to hosts on the platform.
"Asking them to do things a cleaner should handle can negatively affect their stay and your reviews."
The new rules come amid growing protests against housing shortages in many European cities, with protesters arguing that short-term rentals such as Airbnb have pushed them out of their own cities.
In September, the European Commission proposed more restrictions on Airbnb and other short-term rental companies in tourist hubs.
What else do the new Airbnb rules for hosts say?
Guests can still be asked to leave dirty dishes in the sink, to gather used towels and separate trash and recyclables, for example.
Hosts can also require guests to put trash in animal-proof containers areas where bears are active or ask them to "limit shower time due to local drought-related water restrictions."
But hosts will no longer be allowed to ban guests from using amenities listed in the property description, such as air conditioners, nor will they be allowed to fine guests.
Instead, hosts must seek compensation for any damage from insurance that the platform provides.
The new policy applies to bookings starting on November 20.

metal pipe grid transforms personal rituals of control into participatory playground
what does it take to feel secure? south korean sculptor won ji lim transforms personal rituals of counting, checking, and seeking balance into participatory sculptural environment.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
Interactive playground by WON JI LIM EXPLORES rituals of control
Created by Chicago-based South Korean artist Won Ji Lim, Shifting Center (2026–ongoing) is a participatory sculptural installation that translates personal rituals of control, such as counting, checking, and aligning objects, into a physical, interactive environment. Measuring approximately 9 × 9 × 6 feet, the modular structure is constructed from metal pipes and connectors, forming a framework reminiscent of a playground jungle gym. The installation integrates suspended objects, woven membranes, transparent pockets, balancing mechanisms, and a series of rule-based activities that visitors can physically enter and navigate.
The artwork is a self-contained system, open to physical additions
The project by artist Won Ji Lim pairs structural framework with unstable or organic materials. Hog casing is tightly woven across sections of the metal frame, undergoing physical shifts as it stretches and dries over time to demonstrate the limits of fixed structural order. A suspended plumb bob set within a hand-woven square visualizes the process of seeking physical balance, while transparent pockets hold archived written thoughts that are photographed and re-integrated into the system to document the installation’s ongoing assembly. Additional interactive components include a converted baseball rebounder with a target graphic, numbered tags, and colored beads. Designed to be reconfigured over time, the modular installation functions as an evolving system where visitor movements continuously alter the spatial dynamics.

Ilhan Omar plans to move out of her Washington DC home after federal raid
Last week, US federal agents raided Omar’s home as part of an investigation into alleged immigration fraud.
US Congresswoman Ilhan Omar says she will move out of her home in Washington, DC, citing safety concerns following a recent raid of the property by US federal agents.
In an interview with MS NOW on Wednesday, Omar spoke for the first time about the raid, noting that the incident has made her feel unsafe there.
Last week, officers searched Omar’s home with what a Justice Department spokesperson described as a “judicially authorised search warrant”, adding that the raid was part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation”.
According to NBC News, which cited one person familiar with the matter, potential future charges against Omar may include conspiracy and making false statements in her immigration paperwork. Omar denies wrongdoing and accuses the administration of political intimidation.
Omar, who was born in Somalia and is a naturalised US citizen, said she is “confident in the fact that I didn’t do anything wrong”.
The progressive Minnesota Democrat has been a frequent critic and target of US President Donald Trump, who has on multiple occasions pushed for the prosecution of his perceived political enemies.
Earlier this week, Trump called the congresswoman “sick” and “dishonest” and slammed her birthplace as a “real s—house”.
For years, Omar, who is Muslim, has been the target of right-wing conspiracy theories about her immigration status, including allegations that she had married her brother.
The Minnesota congresswoman has repeatedly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies”.
Five-hour search
In the interview with MS NOW, Omar said she was rattled by the search weeks out from the November 3 midterm elections, which will decide control of the House and Senate. She is running for re-election in a deep blue district in Minneapolis and is expected to retain her seat.
Omar recalled waking up at about 6am to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali-language children’s book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.
Omar came with her family to the US at age 12, after they obtained asylum. She became a US citizen five years later, in 2000.
“It would be a huge undertaking to, I suppose, indict a 12-year-old for so cleverly conspiring to defraud immigration services to come to the United States. I’m sure there are a lot of smart 12-year-olds, but that seems like a leap,” she said in the interview.
The search drew sharp condemnation from congressional Democrats, who also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.
Omar said the agents were “intrusive but polite”, logging the items they took and putting back everything else in its place.

Europe has a big cheese problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

“How can you govern a country which has 246 varieties of cheese?” — Charles de Gaulle.
As cities across France are burnt and ransacked by protesters, it seems the French general was right. Paris now looks less like La Ville-Lumière and more like the aftermath of the Jack Daniel’s World Championship Invitational Barbecue in Lynchburg, Tennessee — the home of that particular spirit but not a place you can drink it, as it is a “dry” county (and they say Americans don’t do irony).
Advertisement
France has been having a bad time of late, and it’s not just because of riots, fires and looting — incidentally, if anyone wants 250 slightly singed Paris Saint-Germain football jerseys and several dozen boxes of apéricubes, please look for me on eBay.
The droughts and heat waves that battered Europe mean strict production rules for some of France’s most famous cheeses were loosened. Comté, Beaufort and Abondance — not a French kids TV series about three dairy-loving glove puppets but rather cheeses made out of milk from cows that graze in the mountains and carry the appellation d’origine protégée label — all suffered because of a lack of suitable grazing land, so farmers were allowed to temporarily change the diet of their cows (perhaps to Diet Coke and Mars bars).
And it’s not just France that’s having cheese problems.
Readers over the age of four may remember Italy as Europe’s version of the fun uncle who isn’t an actual uncle; wonderfully entertaining but also disturbingly unstable. Though Italy has been a bastion of calm of late (relatively speaking).
That appears to be coming to an end now, as a truckers’ strike has wreaked havoc on the production of buffalo mozzarella. The war in Iran has caused the cost of fuel to soar, so the truck drivers have pulled over to the side of the road, which means buffalo milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region, and the cheese cannot reach customers.
Italians, who never have any strong opinions on food (!!!!!!), are furious and hungry in equal measure, with an estimated €3 million of cheesy, milky goodness lost in just 24 hours.
Advertisement
The problem is that buffaloes are known to be unreasonable creatures that have to be milked regardless of whether dairies are open or closed, and strict production rules require their milk be turned into mozzarella within 60 hours.
A spokesperson for buffalo made a low rumbling sound. A spokesperson for bison said: “This has got nothing to do with us. We are two distinct types of animal.”
Thanks for all the entries. Here’s the best one from our mailbag — there’s no prize except the gift of laughter, which I think we can all agree is far preferable to cash or booze.

Spain wins landmark victory in decades-long dispute over lost energy subsidies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen speak on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly in New York on Sept. 22, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images
MADRID — The Spanish government has won a significant victory in a long-running legal dispute with international investors over its decision more than a decade ago to scrap renewable energy subsidies.
This week, a Belgian court overturned a ruling that ordered the Spanish government to pay investors nearly €76 million.
It was a major win for Spain, which has been fighting attempts to freeze its assets around the world from clean energy investors who claim they are owed at least €2 billion in subsidies.
Advertisement
The dispute dates back to 2013, in the middle of the European debt crisis, when cash-strapped Spain, then under a new conservative government, decided to remove subsidies for renewable energy. Investors who had poured money into Spanish renewables said this was a breach, as they had invested on the understanding they would receive the subsidies.
The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes ruled that Spain must pay the money, but the European Commission has told Spain doing so would constitute unlawful state aid.
The standoff has played out all over the world, with investors attempting to freeze Spanish assets in multiple jurisdictions. In June, U.S. investment fund Blasket Renewable Investments LLC issued subpoenas demanding documents from Adidas, Hilton Hotels, and other entities involved in Spain’s Football World Cup participation to help with its bid to freeze Spanish assets.
In the end, the team went back home with its assets intact, along with the World Cup.
Spain also has cases going on in courts in Australia, Germany and the U.S.
In 2023, a British court ordered an embargo on an international school in London owned by the Spanish state. The Belgian court’s original decision was one of the few examples where investors were successful, and the decision this week to overturn it will set a precedent for other challenges.
Advertisement
The case
Spain’s defense persuaded a Belgian court to lift an embargo imposed in 2025 on state-owned air-navigation company Enaire for €75.76 million, according to documents seen by POLITICO.
The case was also brought by Blasket, which bought the dispute from an investment fund called RREEF. The European Commission intervened in support of Spain.
RREEF, which was originally linked to Deutsche Bank, invested in Spanish wind and solar power under a 2007 regulatory framework that guaranteed subsidies for renewable energy. In 2013, amid the economic crisis, the government of then-Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy, of the conservative People’s Party, cut those subsidies to reduce electricity costs.
International investors turned to arbitration, arguing that the Energy Charter Treaty, an international agreement signed in the 1990s, guaranteed them fair and predictable treatment. The funds sought more than €10 billion in compensation, according to sources at Spain’s Environment Ministry.
The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, part of the World Bank, which handled most of the arbitration cases, ruled against Spain, though it reduced the amount sought in many cases. The total awards came to about €2 billion. In its 2019 ruling, the tribunal ordered Spain to pay RREEF €59.6 million, plus interest and costs.
Most of the claims, including RREEF’s, were sold to Blasket, which began seeking to enforce the awards. The funds have searched for Spanish assets that could be seized to satisfy the claims.
Advertisement
Spain says it cannot pay because the European Commission has determined that doing so would constitute unlawful state aid. The funds invested through companies based in Luxembourg, and the EU’s top court ruled that the Energy Charter Treaty did not apply to disputes between EU investors and EU member states; EU law governed instead.
In August 2026, the Commission opened infringement proceedings against Spain over a €23 million payment on an award involving a Japanese company, which was not based in the EU.
On June 17, 2025, Blasket secured a Belgian court order freezing €75.76 million belonging to Enaire, the state-owned company that manages air navigation in Spain. Enaire receives payments from Eurocontrol, the Brussels-based European organization that collects air-navigation charges from airlines and distributes the proceeds.
That arrangement made it possible to freeze Spanish public funds in Belgium. After a legal dispute, Spain deposited €75,759,538 on May 4, 2026.
The freeze was a high-profile win for investors pursuing Spain. They have secured other attachments in the United Kingdom and are engaged in ongoing U.S. court disputes over enforcement of the awards.
Spain appealed, and the European Commission intervened on its behalf. The Belgian state also argued that the attachment breached EU law. The Belgian court has now ruled in Spain’s favor, lifting the freeze and ordering Blasket to pay the legal costs.
That leaves Spain in a stronger position against international investors seeking to enforce the awards — at least within the EU.

====================================================================================================

‘Andy Time’: Why Burnham’s budget isn’t going to deliver a revolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

LONDON — When Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrived a few minutes late to a meeting with regional mayors on Thursday, his Cabinet ally Angela Rayner had a name for it. She joked they were on “Andy Time.”
The rest of Britain is beginning to learn what that feels like.
Burnham entered 10 Downing Street three months ago promising a “new economic model.” However, the prime minister’s first budget next Wednesday will ask voters to wait a bit longer for it.
Advertisement
John Healey, Burnham’s top finance minister, is expected to announce cuts to business regulation, new steps to move power out of Whitehall and targeted cost-of-living help as energy bills surge due to the wars in Iran and Ukraine.
But while London’s banking sector is resigned to a tax rise, Healey is broadly not expected to completely overhaul tax regimes that many in Burnham’s center-left Labour Party have long seen as unfair. These include business rates, which treat high street shops more harshly than out-of-town delivery warehouses; capital gains tax, which charges less on income from assets than from work; and council tax on homes, which is based on valuations from 1991.
Healey and his allies are already rolling out a pitch for lower-key changes to tax and spending than his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, insisting budgets are about more than their bottom-line “scorecard.” They point instead to thinning the “sludge” of business bureaucracy and helping “bloody-minded” entrepreneurs.
The reason behind this is about much more than war dragging on the British economy and keeping inflation high. Many radical reforms just aren’t ready yet.
Next Wednesday will mark just 100 days since Burnham took office, after a whirlwind special election that ended the Greater Manchester mayor’s decade-long absence from parliament.
Burnham’s much-touted “10-year plan” to rewire Britain’s public realm is far from finished; its publication date is edging closer to Christmas. And many granular details of his plan for reform — including higher defense spending, welfare reforms and ownership of the water sector — will only come at a multi-year spending review some time in 2027. Healey is still trying to decide when that will happen.
Advertisement
POLITICO spoke to 22 current and former government officials, MPs and people who speak regularly to Downing Street to map out Burnham and Healey’s strategy, most of whom were granted anonymity to speak frankly.
Several offered the view that Healey’s budget was designed to act as a stepping stone toward the 10-year plan and spending review, while not spooking the bond markets — which Burnham complained Britain was “in hock to” last year. That is despite Britain inching closer to a general election that the prime minister must call by summer 2029.
“They want it to be a non-event,” one person who speaks regularly to both 10 and 11 Downing Street said of the budget.
Expectation management
This narrative has already left Healey’s allies bristling.
People are “accusing us of not making decisions and kicking the can down the road when actually this budget is incredibly difficult,” said one government official. This person added: “This is the first budget of this country that will have come to the House of Commons for scrutiny while the war in the Middle East is raging and an illegal invasion of Ukraine continues by Russia. The idea that this is by any means small is quite difficult to stomach.”
A second U.K. government official argued the budget would be “as ambitious as possible within the political context.” But a third government official said they believed the budget would be more “steady as she goes” than finished solutions to Britain’s problems.
Advertisement
Ruth Curtice, a former Treasury official who is now chief executive of the Resolution Foundation, a think tank focused on living standards, added: “In some ways it’s quite surprising to have such a small budget, given we have a new prime minister and chancellor and quite a lot has happened in the world since the last one.”
The opposition Conservative Party is preparing to seize on this “deferral budget” theme. Tory strategists are ready to paint it as a cowardly act from an administration they claim prefers sweeping vision to hard decisions. “Why act tomorrow when you can act today?” said one shadow cabinet minister. “Have some balls!”
Cameron Brown, a former Tory special adviser in the Treasury, was more sympathetic. “There’s no need to crystallize any kind of savings or cuts now,” when the spending review is looming anyway, he argued. Brown predicted a “tight and concise” but “intellectually coherent” package: “[Healey] will have some buffer at the end, a nice little cost of living package, Labour MPs will be happy, he’ll target the bad people — gamblers and banks — and he’ll push things down the road a bit.”
A Labour official voiced concern that a cautious budget could lose the goodwill Burnham has built with the public — as happened to his predecessor Keir Starmer, who promised “change” in his 2024 manifesto.
And Reeves’ former Political Secretary Matt Pound urged “caution” on deferring too many decisions to the 2027 spending review. “The truth is that they could end up putting a monumental amount of pressure on that spending review,” he told POLITICO’s Westminster Insider podcast in an interview released Friday. “There are already a lot of pressures they will need to fund.”
Hard to get
“Energy” will be the key thread linking Healey’s messages for the budget, a fourth U.K. government official said — from “breathing space” help with bills to building a more resilient infrastructure network.
Advertisement
There will also be a “fiscal devolution roadmap” on budget day, setting out terms of how regional mayors can get more power and money and drawn up partly by Burnham’s new Manchester outpost, No. 10 North. Legislation to let them impose tourist taxes will be published in the coming weeks. And officials have talked behind the scenes about procurement and boosting Britain’s heavy industries; the budget needs to find almost £5 billion to plug a hole in a defense investment plan unveiled under Starmer.
Targeted cost-of-living measures appear likely to include scrapping “standing charges” on domestic gas bills, which cost the average household just over £100 a year. Burnham said Wednesday that he had asked Healey to look at the issue — though any help could be eclipsed by a predicted £276 rise in domestic bills this January.
The other message will be that the Treasury can do big, consequential things without raising taxes. Healey will make “a political argument that actually there are other types of budgets that you can have,” said the first government official quoted above, “busting through some of that sludge and ripping up a lot of that red tape.” Cash-strapped chancellors have reached for regulatory reform before, with mixed success.
MPs are looking closely at cost-of-living support. One backbencher in an affluent seat said any help had to be significant, because even their well-off constituents were struggling to take the holidays they wanted. Defense, by contrast, barely comes up on the doorstep: “There are hardly any votes in it, but it’s just something we have to do.”
There has been heavy engagement with Labour MPs, whose detachment from No. 10 helped force Starmer out in July. Treasury ministers Torsten Bell and James Murray are among those engaging while Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds handles tricky negotiations with Cabinet ministers, alongside No. 10 chief of staff James Purnell.
Healey has negotiated with Cabinet ministers and spoken to union leaders, banks and MPs — though not lobbyists. “No one can get to Healey,” said one. “It’s very smart. Let him do his job.”
Advertisement
Markets will look at the “headroom” — a snapshot of the buffer between Healey’s five-year plans and his self-imposed fiscal rules. The fourth official quoted above said Treasury officials have considered having only a small “headroom” buffer compared to the £21.7 billion left by Reeves, as it could be increased in future years.
Reeves’ former political secretary, Pound, warned against this, telling Westminster Insider: “If the headroom is so low that it’s clear that they can’t clear the defense investment plan, for example, or the wider defense pressures, then I think that that could then start to have a bit of a knock-on effect that would be quite negative.”
However, headroom is merely a snapshot, often out of date by the time it is published. It is likely to be buffeted further by any events in the Middle East arising from the U.S. midterm results on Nov. 3.
And as with all budget briefings, some opposition politicians believe there is an element of expectation management. Conservatives suspect that headroom will come out higher than predicted — which Healey can paint as a victory.
Time is ticking
Then it’ll all be over — and Westminster will immediately start preparing for the next step.
A date was never confirmed for Burnham’s 10-year plan (beyond the latter part of 2026), but some officials believe it has already slipped slightly from the original intention.
Advertisement
Downing Street and Cabinet Office officials remain determined to publish it in December, though some in Whitehall worry it might be delayed. “Knowing the things on the horizon and how big they are, I genuinely don’t see how you could make space for it,” said one official in another department.
While some Cabinet Office civil servants were first tasked to work on the plan in August, others only joined the team this month as it has grown, according to one person with knowledge of the staffing. Burnham’s ally Louise Haigh, the first secretary of state, is leading three “task forces” ahead of the plan on the cost of living, public control of utilities and the renewal of run-down high streets.
The 10-year plan won’t have all the answers, though. POLITICO reported this week that while it will contain a high-level vision, priorities and principles for the water industry’s future, much of the granular detail of how future ownership models will work is expected in the 2027 spending review.
One Labour figure who has spoken to the government about the water industry said they believed ministers will choose “different horses for different courses” — an array of ownership models for various firms depending on how stricken they are. A second Labour figure talking to the government said: “You can’t do this in two years.”
The Labour official quoted earlier in this story said they feared the 10-year plan would be a let-down. “These big plans governments are always throwing forward to have a habit of turning out quite thin,” this person said. “At which point we all realize there was never a big plan all along.”
There are other plans to come, including an imminent plan to reform the welfare system by the former Labour Cabinet minister Alan Milburn, and a white paper in December that is due to set out a timetable, legislation and borders for plans to move more power outside Whitehall.
Advertisement
Devolution is one area where Burnham has moved quickly, pleasing many regional mayors. But some officials in the union movement fear that Burnham’s initial focus on devolution risks taking up bandwidth that could have been spent on other issues. A fifth government official added that they were worried all the conversations between different public bodies could crowd out the push for growth. They said: “I sit on Teams calls that are 30 people, all from different arms of the state. Sometimes I think — ‘You do know none of us are making this money?’”
‘Rubber hits the road’
Then there is the 2027 spending review.
It will set out how the state allocates money across its arms for the next three to five years — turning these plans and the difficult trade-offs they require into reality.
The Treasury has previously confirmed it will set out the entire pathway to lift U.K. defense spending from 2.6% of GDP this year to 3.5% by 2035. It is also likely to address questions about Burnham’s pledge to create a state-funded national service for social care, funded by reducing the rise in the state pension.
There will be months of to-and-fro between Whitehall departments and a Treasury looking for cuts, efficiency savings or both to balance the books.
“The spending review is when the rubber hits the road,” said the fifth government official quoted above. “It’s already beginning. Departments are beginning to work out sacrificial lambs to offer up.”
Advertisement
Three people with knowledge of the conversations said Healey still hasn’t decided when in 2027 he wants to hold the spending review, though it is broadly expected no earlier than the summer. He has been privately musing with allies about the options.
Curtice said Healey’s options are essentially to hold a small fiscal event followed by a spending review next summer, or to hold a spending review with an annual budget simultaneously in fall 2027.
She added: “The big question we’ve posed for this budget — that we’re not necessarily expecting an answer to — is what is the spending total for the spending review that we know needs to come next year? Until we know the answer to that question, we don’t really know whether we can believe the path of tax and borrowing that is set out in the budget.”
Senior Conservatives argue the spending review will be so difficult that Burnham could call a snap election before it is due. He has insisted he will only force it in 2029.
Until then, much of the spending review work will fall to Reynolds. Her predecessor Darren Jones argued the existence of the 10-year plan and spending review meant it would be sensible for next week’s budget to be a little low-octane.
“The prime minister’s been clear that the 10-year plan is going to be the political strategy for the government,” Jones told POLITICO. “So I think it makes sense to do all of your public spending decisions after the publication of the 10-year plan. It would be odd if this October’s budget tried to deal with all the big trade-offs on defense, mayoral budgets, or more ownership of public utilities.
Advertisement
“So I think in many ways, actually the 10-year plan is more interesting this autumn in terms of the political strategy of the government.
“And then 2027 will be the year in which ministers will have to start thinking about how to implement that strategy operationally, including in public spending decisions.”
Much of that will fall to Burnham himself.
Crowdsourcing
Rayner’s joke about “Andy Time” was not without cause.
Unlike Starmer, Burnham gets into the weeds of an issue even if it derails his schedule. The prime minister chews things over with colleagues so much that some have joked they could just remove his Downing Street desk, said the third government official quoted above. By contrast, Starmer used to retreat to No. 10’s first-floor study to read away from the hubbub.
Burnham’s approach can lead to Downing Street making decisions late in the day. One former No. 10 official said: “A Prime Minister needs to do 80 things in a day and if that goes to 60, then you end up massively behind.”
Advertisement
The flipside is that ministers and officials know what their leader actually wants from them — even if they are left to work out the detail.
“It’s like we’ve woken up from a political coma,” one backbench MP enthused. “I know what the prime minister thinks,” added the third government official quoted above.
Aides used to complain that Starmer, by contrast, tried to be efficient but would end meetings without setting a clear political direction. “Keir was always a stickler for time, even if the issue wasn’t resolved,” as one former colleague put it.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, suggested this week that Burnham was failing to flesh out the detail behind his vision. “Talking about it is not making a decision,” she said of social care reform at prime minister’s questions. Burnham was visibly frustrated—insisting he was making the long-term decisions other politicians duck.
And for the prime minister’s allies and most of his MPs, the vibes remain good. The No. 10 environment is more relaxed and open. Junior ministers, in meetings over bacon sandwiches, feel they can share their views and be heard.
“There’s definitely still a buzz,” said the person who talks regularly to Downing Street, who was quoted earlier in this story. “But you don’t want to spend too much time buzzing while Rome burns. There’s a reality check that I feel is going to come imminently.”
Patrick Baker, Sascha O’Sullivan, Esther Webber and Emilio Casalicchio contributed reporting.

Serbia’s protesting students mount serious challenge to Vučić’s power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

Supporters of Serbia's student-led movement attend the final campaign rally of the student-backed election list in central Belgrade on Oct. 22, 2026, ahead of the country's snap parliamentary elections on Oct. 25. | Andrej Isakovic/AFP via Getty Images
Serbia’s Aleksandar Vučić has won every election he has contested since 2012, but on Sunday, a student-led movement stands a real chance of edging out his ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the country’s parliamentary elections.
A poll published Tuesday by New Serbian Political Thought, an independent pollster, put the Student List narrowly ahead of the Progressive Party, at 44.5% to Vučić’s 42.7% — the first time an opposition list has led a national poll ahead of an election in over a decade.
“Gen Z and students are rising up and fighting for a government that will invest in their futures instead of actively undermining us before we properly start our adult lives,” Kosta Golubović, a 21-year-old law student at the University of Novi Sad, told POLITICO.
Advertisement
The largest protest movement in modern Serbian history began in November 2024, when a freshly renovated railway station awning collapsed in Novi Sad, killing 16 people, including two young children.
Vigils for the dead turned into mass protests, fueled by government denials of wrongdoing that forced out the previous prime minister. Demonstrations drew huge crowds, peaking with a March 2025 rally attended by more than 325,000 people in Belgrade. Student protesters have been demanding early elections ever since.
A fraught campaign
New Serbian Political Thought’s editor Đorđe Vukadinović cautioned that the polling figures released by his outlet are a snapshot, not a projection, adding that he had considered not publishing the results at all given what he called “near-hysterical” attacks and reactions from the government to its previous findings.
Pro-government tabloids and senior Progressive Party figures have spent the election campaign tearing into independent pollsters, branding them “fake researchers.”
But for the Student List, the polling reflects months of concerted door-to-door canvassing to reach every corner of the country, as well as something Serbia’s established opposition parties may be short of after more than a decade of fighting SNS’s omnipresence in the country: the stubborn persistence of youth.
“We have the energy. We refused to accept that this was a lost cause or accept there were pro-SNS dead zones that we didn’t reach out to,” Golubović said, explaining that the Progressive Party was the only party that previously had the capacity to mount nationwide campaigns.
Advertisement
Vučić, who has been in power as president or prime minister for 12 years and stood down as president to run as a prime ministerial candidate in the forthcoming elections, has also taken his campaign on the road. At times, he has driven himself to election rallies in a black Škoda while singing folk ditties, all posted on his TikTok account, where he hosts live Q&A sessions.
Vučić’s penchant for gimmicky political ads has also come to the fore in the campaign. In one, he plays a restaurant waiter taking orders from a Serbian family. The grandfather asks for no sanctions on Russia, while the others ask for new highways, higher salaries and better pensions.
Aleksandar Vučić addresses his supporters gathered in a sports hall during the election campaign rally in Belgrade on Oct. 22, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
In another, he sits across from an empty chair bearing a photograph of the Student List’s lead candidate Ilija Srdanović and a cabbage-pickling stone, traditionally used in the Balkans to weigh down barrels full of sauerkraut in the fall — all part of his attempts to include folksy and everyman details in his campaign.
Looking the other way
Vučić’s Progressive Party has spent 14 years as the West’s awkward but indispensable partner in the Balkans.
Serbia, an EU candidate country, has refused to sanction Russia. Vučić flew to Moscow for President Vladimir Putin’s Victory Day parade last year. European leaders have mostly looked the other way, valuing a predictable Belgrade over a democratic one. As student protests grew, they were conspicuously slow to say anything.
In the past, the opposition were unable to mount sustained challenges to the ruling party — especially as Vučić’s power and control over the media and key institutions grew, explained Igor Novaković from the International and Security Affairs Center.
Advertisement
But the student-led movement is “heavily depersonalized,” said Novaković, and is focused on issues with broad electoral appeal. “They managed to create a single unitary platform which is mainly centered around issues related to the rule of law. All the issues that previously divided the Serbian electorate were not in the cards,” he added.
The government’s first line of attack against the growing political movement was to argue that students could not run a country. So the protesters built a list of hand-picked candidates, including doctors, engineers and professors — people who made their careers outside of politics.
“Many people are happy to hear that someone isn’t a politician but, say, a doctor,” Golubović said. “It isn’t hard to pitch the idea that an expert is going to help more than someone whose main skill is to talk into a microphone for 30 years straight.”
Crucially, the students have built a social media machine which, by their own count, includes some 900 influencers with a combined reach of more than 40 million followers.
The effect is visible on any ruling-party TikTok or X post, where the first dozen back-to-back comments, each with hundreds or even thousands of likes, repeat the campaign’s motto — “Studenti pobeđuju!” or the students will win.
If Student List is victorious in the elections, argues Novaković, it will face “a heavily entrenched system and bureaucracy, and that could be really demanding. The transition will not be easy.”
A win for Vučić and his party, meanwhile, would come with challenges of its own. “SNS and the government are heavily wounded,” he added. “Even if they don’t lose outright, they will face a period of weakened legitimacy and authority.”

Construction and assembly work has now been fully completed. The facility must still obtain a license and the necessary permits before it can begin operating.

Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:47:39 UTC
10:47:39 KST

Will ICE agents play a role in the 2026 US midterm elections?
Rights groups are worried that the agency at the heart of Trump’s immigration crackdown could sway the vote on election day.
Since returning to office for a second term, United States President Donald Trump has embarked on a campaign to root out and deport the country’s undocumented immigrants.
Spearheading that campaign is Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), a federal agency housed in the Department of Homeland Security.
Under Trump, the agency has grown substantially, boasting 22,000 officers and agents as of January, a staffing increase of 120 percent.
Thanks to recent spending packages, ICE is also considered the best-funded federal law enforcement agency in the US.
But the agency, founded in 2003, has come under increased scrutiny for its aggressive tactics and expedited hiring techniques.
Immigration agents, under the authority of ICE and other agencies, have been responsible for at least 25 shootings since the start of Trump’s second term, six of which have been fatal. At least 60 people have also died in ICE custody since January 2025.
That track record has made democracy advocates and human rights groups worried about ICE’s activities in the lead-up to the November 3 midterm elections.
Organisations like Human Rights Watch and the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) have voiced concern that the Trump administration could use ICE to intimidate voters.
The threat of encountering ICE agents could also keep some voters away from the ballot box, the groups say. One national poll, conducted in September by the University of California, San Diego, found that 40 percent of respondents expected ICE agents to be present near polling stations on election day.
Can ICE agents legally operate at or near polling stations?
Federal law prohibits the use of armed federal agents at polling stations. Some states have similar provisions.
The federal prohibition dates back to 1865. The law reads that it is illegal for anyone “engaged in the civil, military or naval service of the United States” to order or bring “any troops or armed men” to election sites.
There is, however, a loophole if such force is needed “to keep peace at the polls” or “to repel armed enemies of the United States”.
Another federal law prohibits members of the military from interfering with elections, and several other laws prohibit efforts to “intimidate” voters.
Those measures have been tested this year. During the primary elections for the midterms, there were at least two incidents – one in San Antonio, Texas, and another in Ventura County, California – where ICE agents reportedly conducted routine operations near polling stations.
In both cases, the ICE agents left after being asked to do so by local police.
How has the Trump administration used ICE agents before the election?
Though there are prohibitions against law enforcement near polling stations, advocacy groups say the Trump administration has nevertheless used ICE agents for election-related matters.
ICE has different offices under its control, one of which is Homeland Security Investigations (HSI).
In the months leading up to this year’s midterm elections, HSI has reportedly been ordered to prioritise its investigations of non-citizen voting, an illegal act. Only US citizens are allowed to vote in federal elections.
Starting in August, the Department of Homeland Security deployed HSI agents for “field investigations” in at least nine states to probe questions of voter eligibility.
Some have reportedly gone door to door, asking residents if they are citizens and if they plan to vote.
This week, a federal judge ordered the Department of Homeland Security to pause those investigations, citing the risk that a US citizen could be “wrongly swept up” and “subjected to intimidation”.
The judge also noted a “high likelihood of error” in how the federal agents were identifying alleged non-citizens.
Trump has pointed to non-citizen voting as support for his false claims of pervasive voter fraud.
Experts, though, say such fears are unfounded, with tiny numbers of non-citizens actually taking part in elections, despite Trump’s depictions of the issue as a widespread problem.
What has the Trump administration said about deploying ICE during the midterms?
Trump officials have refused to rule out using ICE agents to stop illegal voting, an effort that could extend to election day itself.
In May, Trump was asked by reporters: “For the midterm elections, would you send the National Guard or ICE to voting locations in November?”
Trump declined to answer directly. “I’d do anything necessary to make sure we have honest elections. We have to have honest elections,” he replied.
Other leaders in his administration have issued similar statements. In September, for instance, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin affirmed that ICE would not “patrol” polling stations, but he suggested its agents could be there for other reasons.
“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said.
Another member of Trump’s cabinet, Attorney General Todd Blanche, has questioned the uproar over the issue, framing it as misguided.
“Why is there an objection to sending ICE to polling stations?” he asked in March at a conservative conference. “Illegals can’t vote. It doesn’t make any sense.”
What has been the response from advocacy groups?
The Trump administration’s rhetoric has raised alarm with a number of rights groups, who fear an ICE presence on election day could dampen voter turnout.
On Tuesday, Human Rights Watch called on the Trump administration to order ICE agents not to deploy near polling stations or other midterm election sites.
“ICE officers’ abuses have already seriously affected US citizens who have been stopped, beaten, detained, deported and even killed,” said Philippe Bolopion, the executive director at Human Rights Watch. “Voters should not have to fear being caught in an ICE dragnet when they head to the polls.”
On October 16, the rights group Amnesty International issued a similar appeal.
“Eligible voters must have the meaningful opportunity to participate in elections without discriminatory and arbitrary barriers, intimidation by armed forces, or fear of harm when seeking to exercise their rights,” the group said.

Trump says Musk restored Ukraine’s Starlink access amid Russia war
The US president has declined to comment on the process that led Starlink to lift speed and access restrictions on Ukraine.

On Thursday, Trump declined to discuss a report from The Wall Street Journal that he had called Musk and instructed him to end restrictions on Ukraine’s connection.
The news outlet reported that Starlink services returned to normal following the call.
“I don’t want to comment on it, whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference, I guess. The bottom line, he put it back,” Trump told reporters when asked about the report.
On October 13, Ukrainian officials announced that sudden restrictions on Starlink services had left the country’s military scrambling.
Though the system came back online, connectivity has reportedly remained spotty.
Questions have persisted about where the decision to restrict access came from, with Musk and the Trump administration officials trading blame.
Trump has denied ordering restrictions on Ukraine’s access to Starlink.
“Well, I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” he said on Friday. “And from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said this week that decisions about Starlink’s speed and access belong to Musk.
“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” Rubio said on Wednesday.
But Musk has denied any responsibility, stating that Starshield, the military-grade version of Starlink, is “owned and controlled by the US government”.
“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said in a social media post on October 14, using the acronym for “president of the United States”.
The Starlink speed caps and restrictions have also raised concerns that Trump, or the president’s right-wing allies, might seek to leverage such technology to pressure Ukraine into complying with US demands.
Trump has had a contentious relationship with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, repeatedly calling him “difficult” in comparison to his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin.
Ukraine has been locked in a slow-grinding war with Russia since February 2022, after Putin launched a full-scale invasion of the Eastern European country.
While Europe has backed Ukraine’s defence against the invasion, Trump has suggested Ukraine itself could be to blame for the conflict.
In 2025, for instance, Trump blamed Ukraine’s ambitions of joining NATO. “ I actually think that that was the thing that caused the start of the war,” he said at the time.
More recently, Trump posted on Truth Social that it was Zelenskyy’s fault the war had not yet ended. “He doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did,” Trump wrote.
As the war continues, Trump has been criticised by Democrats and some members of his own Republican Party for easing US pressure on Russia.
Recently, his administration issued a series of announcements to buy Russian diesel and ease restrictions on Russia’s energy sector.
Those decisions come as Trump is struggling with the political fallout of high fuel prices caused by his decision to join Israel in launching a war on Iran.
He has also suggested he would be open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, which would be a first for the three leaders.

ABC staff targeted in sophisticated cyber attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:41:30 UTC
10:41:30 KST

ABC wipes staff devices exposed to new, sophisticated cyber attack
In short:
The ABC is wiping a small number of staff devices as a precaution but says it has found "no signs of compromise" from ads linked to a spyware campaign from an Israeli company.
Researchers uncovered an operation using online ads to infect devices, targeting Australian high-profile and sensitive organisations.
What's next?
More than two dozen other Australian organisations are part of a "significant cluster" of targets, but they have not yet been identified.
The ABC has wiped staff devices that were exposed to a new, sophisticated cyber attack carried out as part of a broader campaign to track and even hack into networks of some of Australia's most high-profile and sensitive organisations.
It can be revealed the ABC is among more than two dozen Australian government, critical infrastructure, universities and media organisations that researchers claim were targeted by an Israel-based company abusing the online advertising system.
The public broadcaster confirmed a "small number" of devices had been exposed but said so far it had not identified any impact from the attack discovered by researchers at The Citizen Lab.
"The ABC is aware of the Citizen Lab report that describes exposure to advertising that may contain spyware. There is no evidence of a resulting compromise," a spokesperson said.
'No evidence' ABC impacted by cyber attack
The ABC attack was part of a bigger campaign, dubbed "Adfection", revealed by Citizen researchers last week.
The Canadian-based group found evidence that company Discover-Tech exploited digital advertising technology from major platforms like those run by Google to deliver spyware that could infect devices merely by viewing an online advertisement and without clicking.
Researchers were able to confirm Discover-Tech's technique was used to infect devices at international news network Al Jazeera with spyware from another Israeli company, Candiru.
A spokesperson for the ABC confirmed that this had included the public broadcaster but had found no evidence so far of any adverse impact.
"Our review found that ads from this network were shown on a small number of ABC devices. We have found no evidence that any staff member has been identified or tracked," they said.
"For the small number of ABC devices identified, we have found no signs of compromise, and are wiping any still in service as a precaution. We take the privacy of staff and the protection of journalists' sources seriously."
New method of cyber attack exploits known risks of online advertising
Even if this infection is unsuccessful, researchers said, the same method also allowed the attackers to profile tens of millions of devices that were shown these malicious advertisements — measured by "impressions" — potentially giving information about their identities and online habits.
University of Queensland Professor Nicholas Carah, whose research focuses on digital advertising, said the attack was proof of the well-known risks about online advertising technology.
"On one level, it's horrifically surprisingly, but on another level it's like, well, yeah of course, online advertising is really useful infrastructure for doing something like this," he said.
Professor Carah said the report showed how bad actors could exploit existing characteristics of online advertising technology to thwart protections that were supposed to stop tracking for nefarious purposes.
"You can get an [internet protocol] address, or a mobile, then, hey, presto, you're able to identify those individuals," he said.
Greens leader and digital rights spokesperson David Shoebridge said the report's contents were alarming.
"When foreign zero-click adtech is aimed at our public broadcaster, and other sensitive government agencies, that of course raises serious questions about foreign interference," he said, adding that this shows the need for privacy reform and to include advertising in the government's proposed digital duty of care.
Australian government, critical infrastructure and media organisations targeted
While there were devices targeted across the world using Discover-Tech's techniques, Citizen Lab researchers noted a "substantial cluster of impressions in Australia, including on government and private-sector networks associated with critical infrastructure".
The researchers did not know who Discover-Lab or Candiru were carrying out the attacks on behalf of, if anyone.
The report singled out Australia's nuclear science agency, ANSTO, as being a hot spot in their data for the number of malicious ads shown. It did not specify the other organisations.
An ANSTO spokesperson told the ABC earlier this week it had not identified any impacts.
Australia's cybersecurity agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, declined to comment.
Researchers also claimed three Australian media organisations had seemingly been targets.
Media organisations and journalists are common targets for commercial spyware operations, alongside politicians, dissidents and human rights groups.
"The use of spyware against journalists is on the rise," international group Reporters Without Borders wrote late last year.
"Digital attacks often go unnoticed, so it is vital that journalists regularly check if their devices are compromised."

How Hong Kong can go from passive trade hub to regional control tower
Hong Kong’s challenge is to reposition itself as a regional supply-chain management hub linking diverse Asian production networks with Western markets
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Ningrong Liu is deputy vice‑president (international strategy) and professor of globalisation and business at City University of Hong Kong. 
This year has opened a rare window of relative calm in global commerce. On October 8, the World Trade Organization doubled its forecast for global goods trade growth, from 1.9 to 3.9 per cent. The easing of US-China and Europe-China tensions has given open economies some breathing space.
Hong Kong has seized the moment. Its exports rose 42.5 per cent year on year in the first eight months of 2026, with figures from August alone up 53 per cent, driven largely by AI-related equipment and high-value electronic components.
A deeper transformation lurks beneath the headline numbers. Hong Kong is no longer merely a passive trade hub. For decades, its role in global commerce was defined by its position as a buffer in geopolitical cross-currents. The traditional model of “Made in China, shipped via Hong Kong, consumed in the West” made the city a passage point rather than a decision point.
The question now is whether Hong Kong can reposition itself as a regional supply-chain management hub linking diverse Asian production networks with Western markets. Three structural shifts are creating this opportunity.

According to the publication, Rosneft has suffered significant losses from Ukraine’s campaign of strikes against Russian infrastructure. The company operates 12 oil refineries, accounting for about one-third of Russia’s total refining capacity. According to Bloomberg’s calculations, of the 15 confirmed drone strikes on Russian oil refineries in September, five targeted major Rosneft facilities supplying fuel to European Russia, the country’s largest consumer market.
Damage estimates reviewed by Bloomberg showed that the Ryazan oil refinery – one of the largest refineries supplying fuel to Moscow and surrounding regions – had been shut down for more than half the time since the first attack in May and, when operating, had been running significantly below full capacity. The refinery has come under repeated attacks as Rosneft sought to restore operations.
The Syzran refinery was either completely offline or operating at less than one-third of its nominal capacity for most of the past six months, while the company’s Tuapse refinery on the Black Sea coast has been offline since April, according to data analyzed by the agency.
The report says Rosneft managed to restore operations at some refineries within several weeks of being hit, but the facilities came under attack again when repair work had been completed or was nearing completion.
According to Rosneft officials, the need to repeatedly repair damaged equipment is complicating operations and driving costs to levels that cannot be sustained over the long term. Unnamed Bloomberg sources said some refineries were deliberately slowing repair work, stretching it out over weeks instead of a few days.
According to company plans reviewed by Bloomberg, measures to protect facilities with shipping containers, nets and steel cables have proved ineffective against swarms of UAVs. Damage is particularly difficult to repair when strikes hit complex secondary processing units, such as fluid catalytic cracking units, reformers and hydrocrackers, for which parts were previously supplied by Western manufacturers.
As reported by Ukrinform, a fire broke out at the Ryazan oil refinery in Russia overnight on October 15 following a drone attack.

Microsoft develops AI tool that can diagnose ‘sequentially’ like a doctor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:15:00 UTC
10:15:00 KST

Microsoft develops AI tool that can diagnose ‘sequentially’ like a doctor
- Microsoft researchers say an AI tool that diagnoses step by step was more than twice as accurate as general physicians in complex cases, according to a study in Science on 22 October.
- The system uses an “orchestrator” and a simulated panel of clinical experts to ask questions, order tests, and update its diagnosis like a doctor.
- It also cost less than human doctors in work-ups, and the team will next test it for emergency department triage with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center.
AI generated
Washington - Microsoft researchers say an artificial intelligence (AI) tool that diagnoses patients step by step, as doctors do, was more than twice as accurate as general physicians at solving complex medical cases, according to a study published in the journal Science on Oct 22.
The model identifies and coordinates the questions that should be asked of a patient, as well as the exams and tests that should be ordered, using an “orchestrator” that organises how AI will tackle a problem by employing a simulated panel of clinical experts collaborating to solve diagnostic cases, according to the report.
Existing medical AI models typically take an all-at-once approach that examines all of a patient’s symptoms, lab results and imaging studies to generate a diagnosis.
With the orchestrator coordinating the steps to reaching a diagnosis, the AI model first decides what to ask about the patient’s history and what is significant in the physical exam. Based on what it learns, it decides which tests to order, considers the results, and orders further testing as appropriate.
All the while, it is updating its working hypotheses and plans, the research leaders said in an interview.
Tasked with diagnosing more than 300 highly unusual and confusing medical dilemmas, the model employing the diagnostic orchestrator was more than twice as accurate at “working up” the patient and determining the diagnosis as general physicians using textbooks and the internet.
The tool also outperformed human physicians when presented with scenarios drawn from a major database of emergency room admissions.
Assessments comparing these types of older systems to human doctors usually use multiple-choice questions, the researchers said.
“AI has become very good at getting a 100% pass rate on those,” said Dr Dominic King, the corporate vice-president of the health unit at Microsoft AI, whose team is developing the new technology.
“But of course, that’s not real-world. No patient ever came to see me with a nice summary.”
The researchers also found that diagnostic processes cost less when the orchestrator designs the work-ups than when human doctors do.
“We’re not just measuring the accuracy of the systems. We’re also measuring how judiciously and carefully it goes through a diagnostic work-up,” said Harsha Nori, head of AI at Microsoft AI Health.
In a collaboration with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, the researchers will next test the tool’s ability to triage patients in emergency department waiting rooms. REUTERS
