Mixed reviews
Early reviews have praised the Duo’s design as well as its sturdy and barely visible hinge, a major feat for phones whose prominent creased screen has long been a drawback and potential deterrent for buyers.
But reviewers have said camera compromises including the absence of a telephoto lens and third-party apps that still need to be reworked for the new display size could disappoint some buyers. They have also said the Duo in its smaller, folded state is less handy for the litany of quick tasks that most users carry out each day on standard iPhones, with several prominent reviewers recommending against the Duo for many Apple customers.
“It’s been a lot of fun trying the Duo out for a week, but it feels like I’ve gotten to use an extraordinarily polished prototype – not a finished product that I’d want to buy and carry,” longtime Apple commentator John Gruber, author of the blog Daring Fireball, wrote in a review.
Tech commentator Marques Brownlee, popularly known as MKBHD, said in a YouTube review that “if you’re just a regular person who doesn’t do much more than texting, social media and browsing here and there, then it is probably a no. But if the US$2,000 doesn’t mean much to you, and you like the idea, after the learning curve and getting used to not having facial identification, it is a really fun phone.”
Tough to find
The limited supplies could disappoint Apple fans lining up in front of stores to buy the Duo.
Apple told Reuters that walk-in availability would vary by country, with limited stocks in the US, Australia, Canada, Mexico and much of Britain and Europe.
In China, France, Hong Kong, India and Japan, units would be available only for customers who had ordered online.
In the China-governed territory of Macau, where the iPhone Duo will be available for walk-in customers only, fans lined up hours in advance of the store opening, social media posts and media reports showed.
“Foldables have been an established category for years, but adoption has remained relatively limited compared with conventional smartphones. Apple’s entry could bring the format to a much broader audience,” said Francisco Jeronimo, vice-president at market researcher IDC.
IDC expects Apple will take 44% of the foldable value in 2026 on 31% of foldable units. By 2027, it will become the market leader in the category both in value and units shipped, IDC forecast.
“Apple has made a convincing case for this form factor,” Jeronimo said after spending a week with the passport-shaped Duo.
“Now comes the next test: turning excitement into availability, adoption and a lasting new chapter for the smartphone market,” Jeronimo said. REUTERS

Chinese astronomers find real 3-body system. It is not what Liu Cixin thinks
In a case of life imitating art, Chinese researchers have discovered an ‘extremely rare’ three-star system that is not science fiction
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Ling Xinin Ohio
In author and computer engineer Liu Cixin’s science fiction hit The Three-Body Problem, three suns throw a doomed world into chaos. Chinese astronomers say they have found a real three-star system that is far better behaved.
Using FAST, the world’s biggest single-dish radio telescope in southwestern China, the researchers found two dead stars and a “living” one locked in a steady cosmic dance about 7,000 light years from Earth.
One of the dead stars is a pulsar that spins more than 300 times a second, about as fast as the blades of a kitchen blender. It whirls around its partner, a white dwarf – the dim, burnt-out core of a smaller star – every eight days.

Thousands protest across Poland for access to free and legal abortions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:54:51 UTC
09:54:51 KST

Thousands protest across Poland for access to free and legal abortions
Demonstrators gathered on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court.
Thousands of people have protested in more than 20 towns and cities across Poland, calling for access to free and legal abortion services.
Demonstrators gathered on the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban imposed by Poland’s highest court.
Currently, abortion is only legal in Poland when a pregnancy results from a criminal act like rape or incest, or when it threatens the life or health of the mother.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s government promised to liberalise abortion laws ahead of its 2023 election victory, but divisions within the coalition have slowed progress.
The demonstrations come days after parliament passed two bills that would ease abortion restrictions in the mostly Catholic country, but are likely to be vetoed by Poland’s conservative President Karol Nawrocki.
Passing the draft laws now, a year before the next parliamentary election, is a case of “token gestures” rather than a genuine effort to reform abortion law, said Zofia Marcinek of the Abortion Dream Team, a reproductive rights activist group in Warsaw.
She said the liberal government knew the draft laws stand no chance of withstanding Nawrocki’s veto, and has merely tried to create the impression of taking action because it needs women’s support to win elections next year.
In the capital, Warsaw, about 1,000 protesters demonstrated in front of parliament despite rain.
“Over the last six years, nothing has really changed,” said 36-year-old Emilia Niemiec, who manages the AboTak abortion centre, which provides women with access to resources, including pills, and a space to be able to seek support or carry out a pharmacological abortion.
Abortion laws tightened
Restrictive abortion laws have been in place in Poland since 1993, with Polish women leading calls for the legalisation of abortion ever since. In 2016, nationwide demonstrations took place, with women donning black as a sign of protest.
But rather than being relaxed, Poland’s abortion laws were tightened further, banning abortions of foetuses with congenital defects in 2020 under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government.
Despite the laws, abortions remain common in Poland, with the overwhelming majority carried out by women at home using pills obtained from outside the country. Women who undergo abortions, including by taking pills, do not face criminal responsibility under Polish law. But people helping them, including doctors and family, can potentially be prosecuted.
Polish hospitals performed 573 abortions in the first half of 2026, compared with 452 in the whole of 2022 before Tusk came to power, according to data from the National Health Fund. But activists say tens of thousands of abortions happen yearly outside of hospitals.
Campaigners organising Thursday’s protests are claiming the Tusk government has betrayed Polish women – and that Tusk’s claims that women’s access to abortion has improved during his administration have actually complicated getting care for some women.
“The government’s promises act as a type of disinformation,” Marcinek said. “Women getting pregnant hear the prime minister say that everything is OK, that there is access to abortion, and then they end up in the hospital and see that is not the case. So they come to us when it’s very late and very complicated and expensive to help them.”

Venezuelans call for elections in first national protest in nearly two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:52:28 UTC
09:52:28 KST

Thousands of Venezuelans took to the streets on Thursday in the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years, demanding free elections and other political changes, with security forces present in notably small numbers.
The United States has been working closely with the interim government led by acting President Delcy Rodriguez since US forces captured President Nicolas Maduro in January. Both US President Donald Trump and Rodriguez, Maduro's former deputy, have said elections will be held, but have not set a date for either a legislative vote or a national presidential contest.
Opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado, who has been outside the country for nearly a year after living in hiding following a contested 2024 election, has said elections must take place by July 2027.
Her Vente Venezuela movement organized the protest, which took place in the capital Caracas and other cities, including Valencia, Maracay, San Cristobal and Maracaibo.
“Seeing this makes me happy because I know change is possible," said 18-year-old cosmetology student Leosmary Hernandez, as she gathered with hundreds of others in northern Maracay. "I’ve been through so many hardships, so many problems because of the dollar, and difficulties studying. I have high hopes for my country and for our next leader, president, Maria Corina."
Venezuela's socialist movement has been in power since 1999
"I went out to protest before, when things were much tougher, and I’m even less afraid today because I want my voice to be heard,” she added as music boomed around protesters waving Venezuelan flags.
Venezuela's socialist movement, in power since 1999 under late President Hugo Chavez and then Maduro, has in the past deployed security forces against protesters decrying political repression, dizzying inflation, poor public services and other problems in the economically battered country, including after the 2024 presidential election.
Security forces had minimal presence at protest sites on Thursday, and in many smaller cities demonstrators dispersed before dark.
The ruling Socialist Party called for its supporters to march from Caracas' Plaza Venezuela, the same place the opposition planned to gather two hours later, to a location near the presidential palace to commemorate Breast Cancer Awareness Month.
Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, known for his close ties to the security services, was pictured on state television attending the march, while the opposition supporters moved their protest to a nearby location.
Negotiations continue
US-backed talks between a faction of the opposition and the interim government, aimed at remaking the top court and the electoral council with an eye toward ensuring fairness at eventual elections, held their latest session this month, but changes could take significant time. The negotiations do not include Machado's political movement, though she has said she will not stand in the way of their progress.
Machado's proxy roundly won the 2024 election according to vote tallies released by the opposition. But the government, which never released full counts, backed Maduro, as did the country's legal and electoral institutions.
"We want presidential elections now. We want an electoral timetable to be announced now. We are not going to wait until 2028," said Maria Debora Marin, 57, who runs a clothing store in central Valencia, referring to rumors elections may only take place the year after next. "What we want is to move forward and finally get out of this nightmare."
Amid the arrests of some of her closest collaborators, Machado went into hiding. Her last public appearance in Venezuela was at protests to mark Maduro's third inauguration in January 2025, where she was briefly detained.
Machado has for years sought US support, aligning with hawks in the Trump team who argued that Maduro, through links to drug gangs, represented a direct threat to US national security. Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are facing drug and torture charges in the US. They have pleaded not guilty.
But Trump has repeatedly praised Rodriguez's management and her willingness to welcome US investors, saying last month it is too soon to consider elections.
Machado's desire to return home, especially after devastating twin earthquakes in June, has caused friction in Washington, with US officials asking her to delay her trip, Reuters has reported.
"We're in limbo," said recent graduate Rayeska Puesme, 18, as she attended the protest in Caracas, adding she had considered leaving because of a lack of opportunities. "The United States removed one big problem, which was Maduro, but the rest are still there."
"I feel in my heart that things are going to change, but I don't see when."
Demonstrators were also calling for the release of prisoners they say are held for political reasons.
Legal rights group Foro Penal, which represents opposition figures and others who have been detained, often on charges like treason, says there are still more than 320 political prisoners in Venezuela, despite releases that took place under an amnesty law backed by the legislature earlier this year. The government has repeatedly denied holding political prisoners and says the amnesty is generous.
US welcomes progress in Venezuela political reconciliation talks
The US State Department said on Thursday it welcomed the conclusion of a third round of political reconciliation talks between Venezuela's 2015 National Assembly and its interim government.
The State Department said the process "continues to strengthen democratic institutions" and "lay the groundwork for free, fair and credible elections" in the South American country.
The US continues to urge the immediate release of all political prisoners in Venezuela, State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement.

Former hostage Elkana Bohbot recalls how faith, family helped him survive Hamas captivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:52:24 UTC
09:52:24 KST

Former Hamas hostage Elkana Bohbot described how his determination to reunite with his wife and son, along with his religious faith, helped him survive captivity in Gaza, in an IDF podcast featuring Lt.-Col. (res.) Tamar Aviv, the officer who supported his family throughout his captivity.
"First of all, what kept me going there, more than anything, was the belief that I would see my son Re'em again, my wife and my family," he said.
Bohbot explained that he was determined not to give Hamas the satisfaction of seeing him give up.
"I would do everything I can to come back and show them what resilience and renewal really mean. To show them that we're here and we're going to stay here. There's nothing you can do about it.”
Bohbot also said he continued observing religious practices during captivity, starting each morning with prayers of gratitude for surviving another day and saying Kiddush on Friday night and Saturday.
"Even when the terrorist was right next to me, literally right next to me, I would quietly recite my Kiddush and preserve my identity. Absolutely," he said.
Elkana Bohbot recalls his first meeting with Tamar Aviv after his release
Describing the moments following his return from captivity, Bohbot recalled being surrounded by IDF soldiers and struggling to recognize the people around him, including Aviv.
"Only later, when she got into the helicopter with me, did I understand who Tamar was," Bohbot said. "My mother told me, 'Meet Tamar. She's been accompanying us for two years,' and it immediately clicked."
Aviv, who had spent more than two years supporting Bohbot's family, said the meeting marked the culmination of a deeply personal mission.
She explained that she initially knew Bohbot only through a photograph but gradually came to know him through conversations with his relatives and friends.
"It is no longer just a mission. It becomes something emotional. I don't actually know him. We've never met, but I have tremendous love for him, concern and anxiety," she said.
Aviv described the prayers and anticipation that accompanied the long period of uncertainty, saying her own religious faith had strengthened during that time.
"But the moment we received the report at Re'im that they had reached him and that he was, so to speak, with us, that was the moment I truly felt an enormous release of tension and overwhelming excitement," she said about the day he was released by Hamas.
The emotional toll of accompanying a hostage's family
Aviv said she had been responsible for supporting Bohbot's entire extended family throughout his captivity, including his parents, wife, son Re'em, siblings, and sisters-in-law.
Her role involved maintaining constant contact with relatives, arranging meetings with military and government officials, providing intelligence updates, and helping families manage everyday needs.
"Things happen along the way that we don't want the family to wake up in the morning and discover on the news," she said, explaining that she was responsible for updating relatives, even in the middle of the night.
Aviv described the emotional difficulty of becoming so familiar with someone she had never met, without knowing whether he would return.
"You're learning about someone who isn't here, and you don't even know whether he's ever coming back."
One of the greatest challenges, she said, was supporting Bohbot's young son, Re'em, who was growing up without his father.
She recalled a video Bohbot's wife, Rivka, sent her showing three-year-old Re'em sitting on his bed, looking at a picture of his father and pleading for him to return.
Aviv said she struggled to answer Re'em's questions about his father's absence while shielding him from the full reality of captivity.
"You sort of bend the truth," she said.

Wes Streeting warned that people needed to be more aware of emerging risks facing the UK and make plans to deal with them, the BBC reported.
Speaking at the UK Gun Hall Plant in Telford, where he announced that the country has resumed domestic production of tank gun barrels for the first time in two decades, he stressed that the public needs to be prepared for cyberattacks on businesses or supply chain disruptions caused by "hostile state actors or terrorists."
“But we’ll also need to take the country a step further and ask them are they prepared for increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks on our businesses, are they prepared for the eventuality that there may be disruption to essential supply chains caused by hostile state actors or terrorists?” he said.
It comes after Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle said last month that people should prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Nino event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean.
"How would we cope if the payment systems at the local supermarket went down?" Streeting said, adding that those are the sorts of "everyday challenges and threats" that people could well face.
"And it's right that we ask the country to be ready for those things and to ask everyone to do their bit," he added.
The government is launching a "be ready" campaign to provide advice to the public, including by gathering supplies and finding out how to volunteer to support communities during an emergency.
“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared, are they ready, do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves? Streeting said.

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The heads of state of the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) may reach a decision on Armenia’s membership at the upcoming session of the Collective Security Council on November 11, CSTO Secretary General Taalatbek Masadykov told TASS.
Speaking about Yerevan’s potential withdrawal from the organization, he said "it could happen if the issue is brought up at the meeting of the Collective Security Council." "Proposals are usually submitted either by the chairing country or by another country, that is, by the head of state, member of the Collective Security Council. What happens de facto aligns with Article 25 of the Collective Security Treaty Organization’s Charter, which stipulates that if membership dues are not paid and quota-based positions remain unfilled, there is no right to vote," Masadykov added.
"It would seem that Armenia is not taking part in the discussions. It would seem that they are not participating. However, an Armenian representative attends the weekly meetings of the Permanent Council, where the permanent representatives of the CSTO member states sit. The Armenian representative listens and, presumably, reports back about what we are discussing and what decisions are being reached, moreover, all issues that we discuss, and potential decisions," he noted.
The next session of the Collective Security Council of the CSTO will take place on November 11 in Moscow.
Earlier, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said in parliament that he favored Armenia’s expulsion from the CSTO and would be pleased if that happened. The country does not intend to step up its participation in the CSTO over the next five years, he said, adding that Armenia’s interest in the CSTO had run its course. At the same time, the Armenian prime minister gave a vague answer when asked what Armenia planned to replace its CSTO membership with - strengthening relations with Turkey and Azerbaijan or applying for NATO membership, which the country has not been invited to pursue.
In September 2024, Pashinyan said that Yerevan had frozen its participation in the CSTO because, he claimed, the organization had created threats to the republic’s sovereignty. In October 2024, Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said at an international security forum in Warsaw that Yerevan was assessing all the risks associated with a decision to withdraw from the CSTO. In December of the same year, the Armenian prime minister said that relations between Armenia and the CSTO had passed the point of no return.

Kenya launches emergency aid efforts as hundreds flee deadly clashes in Ethiopia

Andrew Wasike 
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
The Kenya Red Cross said late Thursday that it was scaling up emergency assistance for families fleeing deadly clashes between Ethiopia's Oromia and Somali regional states, with an initial humanitarian response targeting 1,000 households in northern Kenya.
"Our priority is to make sure every family arriving in Moyale is safe, sheltered and treated with dignity. Our volunteers and staff are on the ground and will continue to respond as needs evolve," Kenya Red Cross Secretary General Dr. Ahmed Idris said in a statement.
Marsabit County Commissioner Stanley Kamande confirmed that displaced Ethiopians had entered Kenya, with many seeking shelter among relatives and residents on the Kenyan side of the border.  
Hundreds of Ethiopians crossed into Kenya following violence in Moyale, a town divided by the international border, where gunfire erupted amid tensions between Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regions as the cause of the clashes remained unclear.
The Red Cross said many displaced families had arrived in Kenya's Marsabit County with few belongings and urgently needed shelter, food, clean water and medical assistance.
Working with county and national authorities, the humanitarian organization said it had begun establishing temporary shelters and distributing tents, blankets, sleeping mats, water containers and kitchen supplies.
It is also providing fortified porridge flour for young children, pregnant women and breastfeeding mothers alongside first aid and assistance to reunite families separated during the displacement.
The organization warned of urgent shortages of food, safe drinking water, sanitation facilities and health services, particularly affecting women, children, older people and people with disabilities.
The violence erupted in Moyale on the Ethiopian side of the border following tensions over the display of the Somali Regional State flag at a local administrative office in an area administered by Ethiopia's Oromia Regional State.
Oromia and the Somali Regional State are two of Ethiopia's federal regions, home predominantly to Oromo and ethnic Somali communities respectively. Both communities have longstanding ties to the border area.
The killing of a 13-year-old girl on Oct. 18 further heightened tensions before armed confrontations rocked with heavy gunfire broke out Wednesday night and intensified Thursday.
Residents reported heavy gunfire involving regional security forces, while local officials said the fighting had spread to Gumi Eldallo, Wachile and Arero districts in southern Ethiopia, according to Ethiopian local media stations.
Homes and trading centers were burned, disrupting commercial activities and forcing residents to abandon their properties.
The exact number of people killed or injured remained unclear, with no independently verified casualty figures available.
Moyale, approximately 780 kilometers (485 miles) north of Kenya's capital, Nairobi, and about 770 kilometers (478 miles) south of Ethiopia's capital, Addis Ababa, by road, is a major commercial crossing between the two countries.
The border town serves communities in both countries, with close family and trading connections making it an important route for people fleeing insecurity.
The Kenya Red Cross said it was conducting a rapid assessment to determine the most urgent humanitarian needs and would continue coordinating with government authorities and other partners.
The organization also said it was restoring family communication links to help displaced people reconnect with relatives.
Although the initial relief operation is expected to assist 1,000 households, the total number of people displaced within Ethiopia or crossing into Kenya has not yet been established.
The violence comes amid renewed conflict in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region, adding to concerns over civilian safety and humanitarian needs in the Horn of Africa.

Netanyahu helped Kushner hide $1 billion in UAE funds at Israel's central bank, book claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:37:19 UTC
09:37:19 KST

A secret network of bank accounts allegedly connected Jared Kushner, senior adviser to President Donald Trump, with powerful Gulf rulers and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during Trump's first term, according to allegations detailed in a forthcoming book by investigative journalist Matthew Cole, excerpts of which were published by Vanity Fair. 
The book claims that at least $2 billion was made available through financial arrangements spanning the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia and Israel, including an alleged $1 billion transfer to an account at Israel's central bank. Kushner's lawyer categorically denied the alleged arrangements.
The claims appear in Cole's book, Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East. According to Cole's account, Emirati leader Mohamed bin Zayed and Saudi Arabia's Mohammed bin Salman initially discussed establishing a fund exceeding $10 billion to advance political objectives important to the incoming Trump administration. The plan reportedly narrowed into several accounts allegedly giving Kushner access to foreign funds outside conventional U.S. government oversight.
One of the most significant allegations concerns approximately $1 billion that bin Zayed allegedly transferred to Israel through Azerbaijan in 2018. Citing a person briefed on the arrangement, Cole writes that Netanyahu encouraged Kushner to place the money in an account at the Bank of Israel, where it would appear to be associated with government funds rather than with Kushner personally. The source claimed the money was intended for Kushner's personal benefit, although the book excerpt does not establish how the funds were ultimately used.
The Bank of Israel does not operate personal accounts, and government accounts require authorization from two individuals to conduct transactions. According to Cole, Netanyahu wanted Kushner to inform him before any transfers, with messages allegedly conveyed through David Friedman, then the U.S. ambassador to Israel. One source claimed that significant sums were subsequently transferred through Cyprus. Friedman emphatically denied any knowledge of the alleged arrangement or involvement in transmitting messages, while Kushner's lawyer insisted that "there are no accounts and never were."
How Dutch intelligence allegedly uncovered the financial trail
Cole traces the alleged financial network to an extraordinary intelligence operation that began in late 2017, when the Netherlands' military intelligence service reportedly discovered that a hacker working for Russia's GRU military intelligence agency was preparing to travel to Britain. With British cooperation, Dutch intelligence officers allegedly persuaded the operative to provide access to a Russian intelligence server rather than face arrest. Investigators reviewing material on that server reportedly discovered screenshots from Kushner's iPhone, prompting an effort to determine how Russian hackers had compromised the device.
By early 2018, Dutch cyber specialists had allegedly found a vulnerability that allowed them to monitor images appearing on Kushner's screen as he used his phone. According to the book, the surveillance revealed that Kushner was accessing a UAE bank account that had received hundreds of millions of dollars through an Azerbaijani bank. The account, identified by Cole as Alpha, was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank and had allegedly received approximately $750 million beginning in 2017, with funding attributed to Saudi and Emirati sources.
The use of Azerbaijan was particularly significant, Cole argues, because certain banks there allegedly facilitate large foreign-currency transfers that obscure the original source of the funds. Rather than transferring Saudi riyals or Emirati dirhams directly to their destination, clients could reportedly use intermediary transactions that delivered equivalent amounts in U.S. dollars. For investigators examining the final transfer, the money could appear to originate from an Azerbaijani institution, concealing the financial arrangements behind it.
The Alpha account was allegedly held by the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, an Emirati government-funded charity, rather than by Kushner personally. Cole alleges that Kushner was made an authorized signatory, giving him potential access to the funds without formal ownership. The foundation, headed at the time by Dherar Belhoul Al Falasi, allegedly served another purpose: facilitating covert Emirati arms purchases and foreign operations. A confidential source cited by Cole described the charity as a vehicle that could reduce scrutiny of sensitive transactions. Kushner's lawyer denied that his client knew Al Falasi, had any connection to the foundation or possessed access to a UAE bank account.
According to Cole, the alleged financial arrangements developed alongside ambitious diplomatic plans involving Washington, Riyadh, Abu Dhabi and Jerusalem. Mohammed bin Salman was seeking to consolidate his position as Saudi crown prince, while bin Zayed wanted the Trump administration to abandon Barack Obama's nuclear agreement with Iran. Kushner, meanwhile, was pursuing an Israeli-Palestinian peace initiative and closer relations between Israel and Gulf states. The book alleges that access to the funds was connected to those overlapping political objectives, although the precise terms of any arrangement remain disputed.
Israeli security arrangements and questions of oversight
Cole's book also describes a third, separate account allegedly established during secret contacts between Israel and the UAE before the countries formally normalized diplomatic relations in 2020. Kushner reportedly helped negotiate an understanding under which Israel would assist the Emirates in defending against a major Iranian military attack. According to Cole, Abu Dhabi deposited additional money into an Israeli central bank account to finance such emergency assistance. The excerpt does not specify the amount involved or establish whether the funds were ever used.
Cole argues that the three alleged accounts effectively created an unofficial financial framework through which Kushner could pursue Middle East diplomacy with senior regional leaders. The arrangements, if substantiated, would raise questions about transparency and government oversight. Kushner was an unpaid senior White House adviser but remained a federal employee subject to financial disclosure requirements, including obligations associated with access to classified information. Cole says four former senior Trump administration officials, including national security advisers and a former CIA director, were unaware of presidential authorization for Kushner to access a foreign government account.
The book excerpt also examines potential legal implications. A former prosecutor who worked on Robert Mueller's investigation told Cole that any agreement to provide official influence in exchange for money could potentially violate federal bribery laws or foreign-agent registration requirements. Such an assessment depends on whether the alleged arrangements existed and what, if anything, was promised in return. The allegations presented in the book do not amount to a judicial finding that Kushner committed a crime, and his attorney denied any legal violations or undisclosed financial arrangements.
Kushner's counsel maintained that his dealings with foreign officials were conducted with Trump's approval and in the interests of the United States. Friedman separately rejected the allegations involving him as entirely false. The competing accounts leave major questions unresolved, including whether the reported bank accounts existed as described, who controlled the funds and whether any money was used for personal purposes. Cole's account, published in excerpt form by Vanity Fair, nevertheless places the alleged financial relationships at the center of the diplomatic efforts that preceded the Abraham Accords, raising questions about whether an undisclosed system of financial arrangements operated alongside official U.S. Middle East policy.

Macron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France
French President Emmanuel Macron has announced a crackdown on public demonstrations, ordering authorities to ban protests deemed “illegitimate” and restrict even officially organized marches as nationwide unrest over soaring living costs and deteriorating public services continues.
The restrictions, announced Thursday following an emergency meeting with intelligence chiefs and senior ministers, come ahead of another wave of demonstrations planned for Saturday, after some of France’s worst street violence in years.
Macron said local authorities would prohibit gatherings organized by individuals or groups deemed to lack legitimate authority, while demonstrations arranged by recognized organizations, such as trade unions, would be considered for approval but could be forced onto alternative routes.
“The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days,” Macron declared, insisting the measures were necessary to restore calm and protect businesses and public buildings.
“Last Saturday we had political and seditious acts by ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic,” he claimed, accusing organized radicals of orchestrating violence and looting.
The announcement significantly tightens restrictions on public gatherings in a country where the right to protest is constitutionally protected. Under French law, authorities can prohibit demonstrations on public-order grounds, although such decisions must be proportionate and can be challenged in court.
A Paris administrative court overturned a police ban on a student demonstration on Thursday, allowing thousands of protesters to gather despite official objections. The rally proceeded peacefully under heavy police presence, according to AP.
However, authorities have already prohibited Saturday’s demonstrations in central Lyon, where hundreds of businesses were ransacked last weekend. Similar restrictions have been imposed in Marseille, Nice and Toulon. In Paris, one authorized march has been diverted away from the city center, while another involving students and members of the Yellow Vest movement has been banned.
France has been gripped by escalating unrest since protests over teacher shortages and deteriorating school conditions spread into a broader movement against rising prices, inequality and cuts to public services.
Around 550,000 people joined demonstrations last Saturday, which descended into clashes with police, arson and widespread looting. Nearly 2,500 people have since been arrested, while approximately 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured, according to figures reported by French media.
Opposition leaders have blamed Macron’s policies and failure to maintain order for the crisis. National Rally leader Marine Le Pen described him as a president “without credibility or authority” who has “lost all touch with reality,” while left-wing leader Jean-Luc Melenchon accused his government of undermining public services over the past decade.
Even police unions have turned against the administration. Alliance Police Nationale announced plans to sue the state, accusing officials of abandoning officers during the riots and failing to provide adequate equipment and clear instructions.
Macron has also clashed with US President Donald Trump, who blamed France’s turmoil on uncontrolled immigration and radical groups. The French leader dismissed comments by foreign politicians about the unrest as “stupid” and “unacceptable.”
The president is expected to chair another emergency defense council meeting on Friday to decide whether further restrictions are needed ahead of Saturday’s protests.

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia is not preparing for war with Europe, while the statements about the "threat of the war" with Russia are "political schizophrenia," President Vladimir Putin told Vesti journalist Pavel Zarubin.
In its contacts with Washington, Moscow reached an agreement to be ready to resume Russia-US-Ukraine talks that will focus on ensuring the security of Russia and Ukraine once peace is achieved.
Moreover, Putin spoke about the situation in the Ukrainian army: the number of deserters there is half a million, if not more. The motivation of Ukrainian citizens is declining.
TASS has gathered the main statements by the Russian leader.
"Political schizophrenia" in Europe
Russia is not preparing for war with Europe, the president said.
"If we look at the political processes underway in Europe, we will see that the peoples of Europe don’t want to fight with Russia. I would like us to be heard: we don’t want [to fight with Europe] either," he said.
EU statements about the "threat of the war" with Russia are "political schizophrenia": "This [Donbass and Novorossiya’s decision to reunify with Russia], as is well known, became the reason or the pretext for some of our ill-wishers abroad - primarily, as we see today, in European countries - to launch an anti-Russian campaign in all directions. Now they are also constantly talking about a threat from Russia and the start of preparations for the war with Russia, which, in my view, is a kind of political schizophrenia," Putin said.
"This too shall pass," he added.
Ukrainian conflict and trilateral talks
Russia called for a peaceful solution to the Ukraine conflict from the very beginning, "from the very first days, in 2014," offering its help to facilitate a negotiated solution, but Kiev resorted to force instead.
The Russian leader also mentioned the Minsk agreements. "We have always sought to ensure that they could reach an agreement with the part of Ukraine that does not accept coup d'etat. However, they refused to do so," he said.
For its part, Russia does not want war, it’s Kiev that wants to go to war with Moscow, "let it have it," Putin stressed.
That said, the war against Russia in order to weaken it cannot be Ukraine’s national idea. "Certain countries of Europe, for example, or from other global regions want to wage war against Russia in order to weaken it. But is this really a national idea for Ukraine itself?" the president asked rhetorically.
Defeating Russia on the battlefield is impossible, and inflicting a strategic defeat on it is improbable, Putin emphasized, adding that it is "better to live in friendship" with Russia: "I think people who have sought to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia - and, unfortunately, such people still exist today - will come to terms with reality and understand that it is better to live in friendship with Russia. This is in the interests of their nations."
Regarding trilateral talks on Ukraine, Russia has reached an agreement with the US to be ready to resume them. They will focus on ensuring security of both Russia and Ukraine once peace is achieved, Putin stated.
According to the president, US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff said at the October 21 meeting that, when discussing issues related to ensuring "the future security of both Ukraine and Russia, it will be surely necessary to address the European security architecture as well." "Basically, I agree with that," Putin added.
Prior to the start of the Russia-US-Ukraine talks scheduled for November, Moscow will be monitoring the situation "in the coming days."
Russia remains ready to make agreements and seek solutions to the situation surrounding Ukraine, Putin said, adding that Russia has always called for settling the conflict peacefully. However, if Kiev wants a different solution to the conflict, that is its will. Moscow will continue the special military operation and achieve all its goals through it, the president noted.
Loss of motivation among Ukrainians and 500,000 deserters in Ukrainian army
Ukrainian citizens are being picked up off the streets like stray dogs and forcibly conscripted, which results in lower motivation among Ukrainians. "This is leading to severe consequences as troops' motivation declines. Yes, there are still formations made up of motivated nationalists. There are some. But it’s not always them fighting on the frontline. Those who have been forcibly rounded up are being thrown onto the frontline," Putin said.
The president pointed to the fact that the Kiev regime and its Western sponsors are treating Ukrainian citizens as expendable. "They [in the West] have always said they are ready to fight until the last Ukrainian is standing. And what about the Ukrainian authorities and their attitude to their own people? Do they share the approach of those abroad who want to fight with us and treat Ukrainians as expendable? They are their fellow citizens, after all," Putin noted.
Meanwhile about 500,000 servicemen have already deserted from the Ukrainian armed forces, but the real figure may be even higher, the Russian leader added. "Well, the figures are almost official: [there are] half a million deserters. Officially, over 300,000 criminal cases have been initiated, but in reality - and they are already talking about this almost publicly as well - it is 500,000, half a million," he said.
On territories lost by Ukraine
The lands lost by Kiev are not Ukrainian territory, those are historically Russian lands. Putin believes it is inappropriate for Kiev to speak of any territorial losses after Donbass and Novorossiya residents voted to reunite with Russia.
"The people who live there voted for, first, state independence, and, second - I would like to point out - for reunification with Russia," the Russian leader stated. "This is why I think it’s inappropriate to speak of any territorial losses. Still, it’s a debatable issue, and debates can go on indefinitely," he added.
Russians and Ukrainians genetically one people
Russians and Ukrainians are not merely close, they are genetically one people, Putin stressed. That said, the head of state expressed respect for the fact that a political division of the broader Russian nation occurred historically.
"Someone has a different opinion, fine," he admitted. "Alright, we agree, this is how the history of Russia shaped out, and such are the realities of today. But everything is negotiable."

Why Australians are being urged to spend 20 minutes outside
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:23:41 UTC
09:23:41 KST

In brief
- The annual Aussie Bird Count will close on 25 October.
- Australians are encouraged to step outside for 20 minutes, to record the birds they see.
One in six Australian birds are facing extinction, and conservationists are calling on Australians to help by counting them this weekend ahead of the annual Aussie Bird Count deadline on 25 October.
Each year during National Bird Week, Australian conservation charity BirdLife asks people to spend 20 minutes outside, observing, counting, and identifying the birds they see.
Participants log their results online or on a free app, where they can submit findings from as many 20-minute sessions as they please.
Since 19 October, more than 3 million birds have been counted, and the charity is now calling for last-minute submissions before the survey winds up on Sunday.
The initiative seeks to answer questions about Australia's bird populations, including "Which birds are Australians most likely to see?" and "Which species are part of everyday life in our suburbs, parks and gardens?"
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The Aussie Bird Count takes place in spring, during which birds are "more lively and visible", BirdLife says on its website, as thousands of migrant birds return to Australian shores.
"They begin nesting, breeding and flocking and generally appear more playful."
"For these reasons it is also National Bird Week, a tradition that started back in the early 1900s when 28 October was first designated by our predecessor, the Royal Australasian Ornithologists Union, as the first 'Bird Day'."
While the Aussie Bird Count is designed to be fun and accessible, BirdLife says, it also contributes valuable large-scale citizen-science data.
"Because tens of thousands of people take part across Australia at the same time each year, the Count provides a unique annual snapshot of the birds people are seeing in backyards, parks, schools and local neighbourhoods."
To participate, Australians are asked to sit in one spot outside and count the number of birds they see and which species they are.
The app includes a field guide to assist with identification, and people who can establish bird species by their calls without a clear sighting are encouraged to include those in their reports.
The 20-minute period is the set standard for BirdLife's survey, allowing the data to be more scientifically robust, which BirdLife says allows the data to be used in conservation efforts.
"If you wanted to count for one hour, you will need to submit three consecutive 20-minute counts."
More than 5 million birds counted last year
More than 66,000 Australians participated in the 2025 Aussie Bird Count, which recorded 5,014,889 birds across more than 150,000 reports.
More than 600 bird species were recorded, and the most commonly spotted was the magpie, which featured in one in every two reports.
The second-most commonly sighted bird was the rainbow lorikeet, which was also the most numerous bird counted, with regular sightings of colourful flocks adding more than 535,000 individual birds to the count.
"Because rainbow lorikeets are more social, hanging out in flocks, when we see them, we see more of them," BirdLife Australia’s national public affairs advisor Sean Dooley said in a statement.
The native noisy miner, the sulphur-crested cockatoo, and the magpie-lark closed off Australia's most commonly sighted birds.
A 'challenging time'
A landmark study in 2020 found that nearly one in six Australian bird species faced extinction.
Following the study, an action plan from BirdLife Australia and Charles Darwin University highlighted the increasing role of climate change as a key threat to bird populations, with unprecedented frequency and intensity of drought, fires and heat endangering species.
And this is the first year that the Aussie Bird Count occurs amid the threat to native wildlife posed by H5 bird flu, which arrived on mainland Australia in June.
The highly contagious strain of avian influenza can cause serious illness or sudden death.
The federal government's agriculture department has warned Australians to look out for sick birds that can’t stand, walk, or fly properly, have a droopy or puffed-up appearance, display breathing problems like panting or sneezing or have an unusual head or neck posture.
BirdLife said the count was occurring at a "challenging time" for Australia’s birds.
"Our birds need a bird-loving community now more than ever. We need them too, because watching birds brings us joy and gives us hope, which we all need right now."
It said that despite the threat the virus poses to birds, watching and enjoying them remains as safe as ever.
"We can all play our part by being mindful of the signs of H5 bird flu, especially in waterbirds, seabirds and birds of prey, and making sure we avoid any contact, record the location and details, and report what you’ve seen to the Emergency Animal Disease Hotline on 1800 675 888."

The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, wants to end more than 14 years of rule by Vucic’s rightwing populist Serbian Progressive party (SNS) in Sunday’s vote.
Civil society groups have said the campaign has been marred by intimidation, arrests and misuse of public resources.
“I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country,” Marija Nedeljkovic Radic, 47, said as she arrived for the students’ rally.
“Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible.”
Sunday’s vote comes after nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The tragedy, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of Slobodan Milošević in 2000.
The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, snowballed from demands for a transparent investigation into the tragedy into calls for an early election.
Waving “Students are winning” flags, chanting and blowing whistles, students and their supporters marched through Belgrade before converging on Slavija Square, the site of some of their biggest protests.
The Archive of Public Gatherings, an independent crowd-size monitoring group, estimated about 150,000 people gathered at the rally.
“We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours,” university professor Jugoslav Gasic – one of 250 candidates on the Student List – told the crowd, which chanted “Victory, victory!”
“You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!”
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade, serving as either prime minister or president.
Amid mounting pressure, Vucic announced the snap vote last month, setting up his biggest electoral challenge since his party took power in 2012.
Vucic, who addressed supporters at a sports hall in the capital on Thursday, has regularly accused the student movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
“Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it,” said the 56-year-old, who resigned to run for prime minister.
“Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!” he said before white ticker tape and balloons showered the crowd.
Many of the 250 candidates of the Student List running for the 250-seat parliament are drawn from academia or are deliberate political outsiders.
The movement has a broad platform, but at its core is a pledge to fight corruption.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling, and surveys have produced widely differing results.
Days before the vote, Serbian civil society groups warned that conditions for “free and fair elections” were lacking.
On Wednesday, Belgrade prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting “violence, riots and attacks” on election day.
Reports of threats and intimidation targeting student demonstrators have grown in recent months, but their rallies have remained largely peaceful since they began.
“I’ve been following this fight since the very beginning,” 35-year-old student rally attender Igor said.
“Today is the last rally, and it’s important that we all come here to send a message of love and peace and that we see each other on the 25th at the polling stations.”

Trump invokes Cold War-era Defense Production Act for oil production, refining

Trump invokes Cold War-era Defense Production Act for oil production, refining
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump determined on Oct 22 that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defence, a move that could open up US funding for fossil fuel projects.
In a presidential memo, Trump also invoked part of the Cold War-era Defense Production Act, allowing him to provide financial incentives for oil-related activities, pipelines and storage of liquid fuels.
Prices for crude oil and diesel have surged since the US and Israel attacked Iran in joint action at the end of February. Since then, the conflict has limited energy shipments globally, with Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries exacerbating the fuel shortages.
The surge in costs poses a risk for Trump in the Nov 3 elections, as his fellow Republicans try to maintain control of both chambers of Congress. The Reuters/Ipsos opinion poll that closed Oct 19 shows just 36% of Americans approve of Trump’s handling of the economy.
The memo said that without taking the actions, the US is not able to provide enough of those energy services in a “timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations”.
The memo did not mention specific projects that could be funded. The US averaged around 13.6 million barrels of daily crude production in 2025, making it the largest crude producer worldwide.
Last week, Vice-President J.D. Vance said the administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity of a Texas refinery owned by Delek US Holdings.
Trump signed legislation in 2025 that included US$1 billion (S$1.28 billion) in Defense Production Act funding for energy-related projects deemed critical to national security. REUTERS

UN Security Council reform should address over-representation of developed countries: Chinese envoy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:12:08 CST
09:12:08 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The ultimate goal of UN Security Council reform is to change the situation where developed countries are over-represented, a Chinese envoy said Thursday.
Security Council reform must focus on enhancing the representation and voice of developing countries, said Fu Cong, China's permanent representative to the United Nations.
"The Security Council, as the core of the collective security mechanism, must reflect the realities of international politics and give more developing countries and small and medium-sized countries with independent foreign policies the opportunity to take part in Security Council decision-making," he said at a UN General Assembly meeting on Security Council reform. "In particular, we must redress the historical injustice suffered by Africa and make priority and special arrangements for Africa's demands."
The ultimate goal, he said, is to change the situation where the composition of the Security Council is imbalanced between the North and the South, where a single bloc has long dominated, and where developed countries are over-represented.
Fu said there is a need to respect the consensus of member states and adhere to a package solution.
Security Council reform is a systemic project, and all five clusters of issues are indispensable. It must, therefore, be addressed through a package solution. Before the parties reach a clear consensus, any attempt to hastily adopt a "consolidated model," push for the launch of text-based negotiations, or even impose artificial timelines and take a "step-by-step" or "piecemeal" approach will only aggravate differences and disputes among the parties, which is not conducive to the long-term development of the United Nations and the common interests of member states, he said.
Fu said the intergovernmental negotiations (IGN) must be the main channel.
"The IGN is the only legitimate platform for member states to discuss Security Council reform, and its role is irreplaceable," he said. "China supports all parties in continuing dialogue and consultation on this platform to build consensus, and firmly opposes any attempt to launch an alternative platform."
China noted that an increasing number of member states have expressed interest in establishing regional, rotating seats on the Security Council. Compared with proposals to expand the current two categories of seats, this concept is fairer and more democratic. China hopes that member states will continue to hold in-depth discussions on new reform ideas, pool wisdom, and actively explore reform ideas that enjoy general support among member states, he said.
Within the IGN framework, China stands ready to continue to work with all parties, respect one another, and engage in candid exchanges and consultations on an equal footing, to ensure that Security Council reform moves in a direction conducive to the common interests of member states and the sound development of the United Nations' cause, and to make positive contributions to building a more just and equitable global governance system, said Fu. ■

U.S. stocks end mixed as AI spending jitters spark tech sell-off

2026-10-23
08:12:07 CST
09:12:07 KST

NEW YORK, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- U.S. stocks ended mixed on Thursday on renewed concerns around spending by artificial intelligence (AI) companies.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 11.89 points, or 0.02 percent, to 52,867.98. The S&P 500 sank 93.74 points, or 1.21 percent, to 7,663.43. The Nasdaq Composite Index shed 694 points, or 2.6 percent, to 26,008.86.
Six of the 11 primary S&P 500 sectors ended in green, with consumer staples and utilities leading the gainers by going up 3.11 percent and 1.98 percent, respectively. Meanwhile, communication services and technology led the laggards by losing 3.01 percent and 3 percent, respectively.
U.S. Treasury yields tumbled on Thursday as investors sought safety in government bonds. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield fell more than 17 basis points to 4.957 percent, its lowest in almost a month and its largest single-day drop of the year. The 30-year yield eased over 12 basis points to around 5.28 percent.
Oil prices surged on escalating Middle East tensions. Brent crude futures settled at 113.17 U.S. dollars a barrel, up 4 percent and the highest since May, while West Texas Intermediate crude rose 2.39 percent to 99.47 dollars a barrel. The gains followed more Houthi attacks on Saudi targets and reports that the United States and Israel are drawing up plans for strikes on Iran after the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections.
"It's a wonderful day on Wall Street," said Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser and market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest in Elmhurst, Illinois. "The only part of the market that is really suffering here is technology, which has been the golden child of the markets up until about June. Investors are starting to realize that there are some holes in the AI story."
On the corporate front, Meta Platforms sank about 7 percent despite reporting third-quarter revenue of 64.6 billion dollars, up 26 percent from a year earlier and above Wall Street expectations. Tesla fell over 3 percent after reporting adjusted earnings of 48 cents a share that beat expectations, but flat revenue of 28 billion dollars and a cut to its 2026 capital-spending forecast to about 20 billion dollars. SpaceX tumbled over 9 percent, more than erasing Wednesday's rally after its first profitable quarter.
Chip stocks were hammered. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index plunged nearly 6 percent, with Lam Research down 11.76 percent after warning that supply-chain constraints would delay shipments, while Intel, AMD, Micron and Nvidia each fell more than 4 percent. GE Vernova slumped 10.64 percent as Meta's spending outlook stoked AI financing worries, and CoreWeave dropped more than 10 percent.
On the economic front, the number of U.S. citizens filing new claims for unemployment benefits fell 6,000 to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 last week, near 57-year lows and below economists' expectations of 200,000, pointing to a stable labor market. The Conference Board's leading economic index was unchanged in September at 99.6.
With the Federal Reserve in its pre-meeting quiet period, attention turned to its Oct. 27-28 meeting, where traders largely expect policymakers to hold rates steady. ■

This photo taken on Oct. 22, 2026 shows a view of central London seen from the top of the 109-meter north-west chimney of Battersea Power Station in London, Britain. Located on the south bank of the River Thames in London, Battersea Power Station was built in two main phases between 1929 and 1955. At its peak, the coal-fired power station supplied about one-fifth of London's electricity, powering important buildings including Buckingham Palace and the Houses of Parliament.
The building, known for its four white chimneys, stood derelict for decades after electricity generation ceased in 1983. Following restoration and redevelopment, the former industrial landmark reopened to the public in 2022 as a mixed-use complex featuring shops, restaurants, offices, homes and leisure facilities. ====================================================================================================

France braces for fresh unrest as Macron restricts protests and Paris shopkeepers arm themselves
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:11:38 UTC
09:11:38 KST

French authorities continued preparations Thursday evening for a major day of nationwide protests planned for Saturday by groups opposing the country's economic conditions, exactly one week after the previous wave of demonstrations on October 17 descended into widespread violence. During those riots, crowds attacked police officers and government buildings and looted hundreds of shops and businesses across France.
President Emmanuel Macron announced that authorities would prohibit demonstrations organized by what he called "illegitimate" groups, referring to far-left organizations that the government blames for last weekend's unrest. Marseille and Lyon, France's second- and third-largest cities, have both announced blanket bans on demonstrations within their jurisdictions Saturday. However, activists may challenge the restrictions in court, arguing that they violate their constitutionally protected right to protest.
The calls for nationwide demonstrations are being led by France's main student union, UNEF, and members of the Yellow Vest movement, which emerged during protests against the rising cost of living and Macron's economic policies in 2018.
Fearing another outbreak of widespread violence, Macron's government has promised a "massive deployment" of police officers. The administration acknowledged that it had been inadequately prepared for the previous demonstrations, when nearly 1 million people took to the streets, far exceeding official estimates.
Some military personnel will also assist, including soldiers from Operation Sentinelle, the counterterrorism force deployed to patrol French cities following the wave of Islamic State terrorist attacks in France and elsewhere in Europe beginning in 2015. The soldiers will secure sensitive sites, freeing additional police officers to manage demonstrations and prevent looting.
Authorities in Paris also attempted to prevent demonstrations Thursday over concerns that they could turn violent, but a court overturned the police ban. Thousands subsequently gathered in the capital for a stationary protest rather than the march originally planned. No major incidents were reported. One sign carried by demonstrators read: "We don't need tear gas for our future to look bleak."
Meanwhile, Macron convened a special security meeting at the Élysée Palace, where he again accused far-left organizations of orchestrating last weekend's riots in an effort to create anarchy in France. "Last Saturday, we witnessed political and subversive acts by far-left groups whose objective is to bring down the republic," Macron said.
The president explained that the government's strategy for the coming days would be to reject demonstration requests submitted by "individuals or groups without legitimate authorization."
"The rules are simple, and I think they are simply a matter of common sense," he said. "The general recommendation is that no demonstrations take place in the coming days. For those who nevertheless wish to demonstrate, if they are trade unions, prefects will propose alternative routes." Macron was referring to routes considered less dangerous for business owners, many of whom fear further looting.
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin called for tough measures against anyone violating protest bans, including stripping offenders of their voting rights. He also proposed restricting social media access for people involved in violence, looting or attacks on police officers.
In recent days, relative calm has returned to Paris and other French cities, partly following the introduction of partial curfews. On Thursday evening, authorities in the capital announced an extension of the nighttime curfew covering the Place de la République area and the Les Halles district, from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. local time, until Monday morning.
The French Culture Ministry also announced that several of Paris' most prominent museums, including the Louvre and Musée d'Orsay, would remain closed Saturday. The Grand Palais, Picasso Museum and Musée de l'Orangerie will also close for the day.
The ministry instructed institutions under its supervision to take all necessary measures to ensure "visitor safety," "employee protection" and "the preservation of works of art." Organizers of Art Basel Paris, the international art fair, also announced that the event would be closed over the weekend.
Paris City Hall urged residents and visitors to "exercise the utmost vigilance" Saturday because of "the risk of further violence by rioters who have no connection to the social protest movement."
Shopkeepers across the capital are also preparing for renewed unrest. Last weekend's riots damaged 450 businesses in Paris alone, with 228 of them looted. Many owners have begun boarding up storefront windows with wooden panels in an attempt to protect their premises against break-ins and theft.
Along Boulevard de Magenta, which connects Gare de l'Est railway station with Place de la République, workers spent Thursday installing protective boards over shopfronts. There, as elsewhere in the city, the makeshift barriers have also become gathering points for efforts to support local businesses.
One poster urged residents to join a neighborhood WhatsApp group intended, among other things, to "prevent break-ins." Another called for donations to a fund supporting "Ali Hussein and his devastated team" after their shop was looted.
French news agency AFP reported that growing fears of further violence have also prompted many Paris business owners to purchase weapons for self-defense.
Yves Goulet, who owns a gun shop in Paris, told AFP that sales had "increased tenfold" since the riots and that he had already sold out of guns that fire rubber bullets. According to Goulet, shopkeepers are "arming themselves because they are terrified," while some customers told him they had been "trapped inside their stores with the looters."
Michael, a Paris optician whose name was changed to protect his identity, purchased pepper spray from another weapons shop. He said he bought it "in case looters enter the store," explaining that it would give him at least "some measure of protection."
Other business owners told AFP they hoped authorities would be better prepared this time and prevent another breakdown of law and order. "Last Saturday was a nightmare. I was afraid I would be killed," said hairstylist José Gedge. "But I refuse to believe for even a moment that this Saturday will look the same."
Gedge expressed confidence that authorities had "learned lessons" from the previous unrest. He spoke to reporters in front of his salon's glass door, which had been smashed by rioters and temporarily repaired with wooden boards that still allowed cold air to blow inside.
Emmanuel Renal, 60, who owns a paint and home improvement supply store near Gare de l'Est, remains traumatized by last weekend's events. Since Monday, he has been sleeping inside his shop, which is now half empty. "I doubt we'll be open next Saturday," he said. "I still don't understand why the looters came to steal paint and tools."
Last weekend's riots began after large demonstrations against the rising cost of living and deteriorating conditions in educational institutions. The protests were largely led by radical left-wing activists and included significant participation from immigrant communities.
Rioters attacked police officers and threw stones at them, assaulted passersby, set fire to garbage bins, cars and buildings, and looted or damaged approximately 3,000 businesses in Paris, Marseille, Lyon, Nice, Nantes, Limoges and numerous other cities.
More than 2,700 people were arrested during the unrest, and nearly 1,000 police officers were injured, some seriously. Macron and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu acknowledged intelligence and preparedness failures that left police overwhelmed by the scale of the violence.
The demonstrations that preceded the riots brought together high school and university students, trade unions and members of the Yellow Vest movement.
They followed weeks of student protests that began last month in schools in impoverished suburbs north of Paris, driven by teacher shortages and poor educational conditions. Those demonstrations were also marked by numerous violent incidents, and similar unrest subsequently spread to other European countries, including Belgium.
In France and abroad, some commentators have emphasized the involvement of immigrants and the children of immigrants from Africa, Arab countries and Muslim-majority nations in both the demonstrations and the violence.
Such allegations have circulated since the student protests earlier this month. U.S. President Donald Trump also claimed that the unrest was evidence of an alleged attempt by Islam to take over France.
Macron rejected those claims, calling them an "absolute lie," and has instead emphasized the role of far-left organizations in the riots.
Prime Minister Lecornu, along with right-wing figures in France, has accused Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of the far-left France Unbowed party, of allegedly fueling the violence as a show of political strength ahead of next year's presidential election. Polls cited in the report project that Mélenchon would reach the decisive second round against far-right leader Marine Le Pen but would then lose by a wide margin.

LIMA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori on Thursday announced a package of fiscal measures that includes an additional 18 billion soles (about 5.25 billion U.S. dollars) in funding for 2027 to address the effects of the El Nino phenomenon, boost infrastructure investment and protect the most vulnerable families.

Summer heat’s toll on Europe: 50,000 deaths and a $24.3b GDP hit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:08:00 UTC
09:08:00 KST

Summer heat’s toll on Europe: 50,000 deaths and a $24.3b GDP hit
- Europe’s summer heat caused about 50,000 deaths in cities, the highest on record. Imperial College London said nearly two-thirds were linked to climate change.
- Bloomberg Economics said extreme heat cut EU GDP by about 0.17%, or close to €17 billion. France, Germany and Spain all saw smaller economies.
- Heatwaves from May to September damaged homes, hospitals and transport. Experts warned that hotter years ahead will raise risks and strain vulnerable people and infrastructure.
AI generated
Europe’s summer of extreme heat caused an estimated 50,000 deaths in cities across the region – the highest number on record – and wiped roughly 0.17% from European Union GDP from April through September, or close to €17 billion (S$24.36 billion).
Those findings, from two separate studies, reveal the extent of Europe’s vulnerability to rising temperatures in what is likely to be one of the hottest years in modern history.
The estimated mortality toll comes from a study released on Oct 23, led by scientists at Imperial College London, which determined that almost two-thirds of the deaths linked to high summer temperatures would not have happened without climate change.
A recent study from Bloomberg Economics, meanwhile, measured the hit to Europe’s GDP at two-and-a-half times the average loss for the period over the previous decade.
The overall mortality level, triggered by a series of record-breaking heatwaves, was far higher than those in the next most deadly years.
The figure compares to about 29,000 heat-related deaths in cities in 2022 and about 28,000 in 2003, according to the research, which is due to be published in Nature Health next week.
“We had these repeated heat events that – even without the extra heat from anthropogenic warming – would’ve been dangerous, but with that extra boost from anthropogenic warming became really, really dangerous,” said Clair Barnes, extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial and the study’s lead author, in an interview.
European countries experienced extreme temperatures throughout the summer. Heatwaves began in May and continued into September, with temperature records broken by significant margins in many countries.
Average temperatures in Western Europe were nearly 3 deg C higher than the summer average between 1991 and 2020, with some days as much as 12 deg C higher.
Across the continent, vital infrastructure suffered. Wildfires destroyed homes, hospitals overheated, transport broke down and cooling systems in fridges and air conditioners failed.
French GDP was 0.2 percentage points smaller in the second quarter due to extreme heat, according to Ulrich Eberle, author of the Bloomberg Economics report. Germany’s economy was 0.1% smaller over the same period, while Spain saw a 0.05% heat-related GDP dent.
The study by Imperial and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine covered 854 cities in 30 countries across the EU, Britain, Switzerland and Norway, accounting for about 40% of the countries’ total population.
The number of heat-related deaths linked to climate change has risen over time, the study found, as fossil fuel emissions have pushed temperatures higher. Climate change accounted for nearly two-thirds of this summer’s excess mortality toll, up from about 40% in 2003.
Calculating heat deaths is challenging because people rarely die directly from heat exposure. Instead, high temperatures typically put extra stress on the body and exacerbate existing conditions, especially those affecting the heart or respiratory systems.
Measuring a person’s core temperature accurately can also be difficult outside of hospital settings. If someone has died alone at home, it is not always clear how or if heat played a role. As a result, heat-related deaths are not always recorded as such.
“We often see elderly patients become confused or have strokes or have cardiac-type events where heat may have made a significant contributing factor to the death,” said Andrew Hartle, an intensive-care consultant at Imperial College Healthcare NHS Trust, in a press briefing on Oct 21.
“A post-mortem won’t tell you whether somebody was hot or not.”
The Imperial study combines temperature records with previous findings that calculate the impact of heat levels on mortality, to estimate a death toll linked to the heat.
This method has previously been consistent with official statistics, many of which have not yet been released by government health authorities for the full 2026 summer season, the authors said.
“Clearly we need to support those most at risk, including the elderly, the unwell and those from poorer backgrounds, and to act to prevent the collapse of infrastructure that keeps vulnerable people safe in the heat,” said Toby Perkins, chair of Britain’s Environmental Audit Committee.
The year 2027 is expected to be even hotter than 2026. Global warming is now virtually guaranteed to exceed 1.5 deg C versus pre-industrial levels and the world must now focus on minimising its overshoot, the United Nations said on Oct 21.
