NORTHCOM Wraps Radar Test to Boost Arctic Early Warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:04:23 UTC
09:04:23 KST

U.S. Northern Command and multiple research organizations just wrapped up a joint, three-year experiment to test new radar technology that could enable the Northern Warning System to detect incoming threats at longer ranges across Alaska and northern Canada.
The Sept. 7-14 test event marked the conclusion of live-fly testing in the experiment series, which explored how existing radar infrastructure and emerging technology could complement current surveillance capabilities, according to an Oct. 19 release from Alaskan Command, a subordinate command under NORTHCOM. The Arctic air domain awareness experiment series focused on closing surveillance gaps across a region where vast distances, harsh weather and limited infrastructure present challenges for air surveillance.
The Air Force Research Laboratory and Defense Research and Development Canada also participated in the exercise alongside scientific organizations in the region. The Air Force and NORAD have relied on the AN/FPS-117 and AN/Transportable Phased Array System-77 radar systems to detect and track incoming threats out to 250 miles throughout the region.
The experiment paired an existing high-frequency transmitter, paired with a newly developed, low-cost receiver array, according to the release.
Initial results show the system was “successfully able to achieve full skywave (beyond line of sight) detections” of an E-3 Sentry from the 962nd Airborne Air Control Squadron, HC-130J Combat King IIs from the 211th Rescue Squadron, and KC-135 Stratotankers from the 168th Air Refueling Wing—aircraft that served as cooperative targets, providing known positions against which researchers could compare the experimental data, the release states.
Researchers used the University of Alaska Fairbanks’ High Frequency Active Auroral Research Program, or HAARP, facility and a receiver array in Cold Bay developed by MITRE to collect data on participating aircraft over the Gulf of Alaska and Bering Sea.
The effort supported a broader focus of Alaskan Command to improve how units detect and track aircraft across Alaska and its approaches and help commanders assess potential threats for homeland defense, the release states.
“Understanding what this technology can do in the Arctic starts with collecting data under real operating conditions,” Dr. Carolyn Stwertka, chief scientist for Alaskan Command, said in the release. “Working with operational units allows us to compare the experimental observations with known aircraft positions and assess where this approach could help address gaps in air surveillance.”
The experiment occurred as NORAD is building and deploying high-frequency systems to detect hypersonic missiles with over-the-horizon radar, modernizing the Northern Warning System and building a polar over-the-horizon radar network.
The Homeland Defense OTHR, which kicked off in 2022, is being funded by both the United States and Canada at an estimated $6-7 billion and $3.1 billion, respectively. Initial Operating Capability is slated for 2028-29, with Full Operational Capability targeted for 2031.
Meanwhile, the Air Force is looking to replace its Air Route Surveillance Radar-4, a three-decade-old radar warning system that protects the coastlines and borders of the United States and a few remote locations.
The ARSR-4 system, which was built in the 1990s, was designed to help operators distinguish aircraft or potential missile threats from other radar “clutter,” which is more prevalent at lower altitudes. The system has been very effective, but Air Force officials maintain that newer additions to the cluttered landscape, namely wind farms, can distort the radar’s ability to “see” clearly, according to a recent Air Force Life Cycle Management Center sources sought notice.

Kazakhstan’s Republic Day celebrated at official reception in Ljubljana
A formal reception was held in Ljubljana, the capital of Slovenia, to celebrate the Republic Day of Kazakhstan, marking the 36th anniversary of the national holiday and the 34th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the press service of the Kazakh Embassy in Slovenia.
The event became the first official state reception organized by the Embassy of the Republic of Kazakhstan in Slovenia, with the support of leading business partners. It represented an important milestone in strengthening Kazakhstan’s diplomatic presence and expanding its presence in South-Eastern Europe.
More than 200 distinguished guests attended the reception, underscoring its significance for Slovenia’s political, diplomatic and business communities. Guests of honour included former Slovenian President Danilo Türk, Mufti of the Islamic Community in Slovenia Nevzet Porić, Archbishop Metropolitan of Ljubljana Stanislav Zore, advisers to the President of Slovenia, government officials, parliamentary committee chairs, members of the diplomatic corps, representatives of state institutions and civil society organizations, business and industry leaders, cultural figures, members of the Kazakh diaspora, and residents and visitors of Ljubljana.
In a special video message, Slovenia’s Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Tone Kajzer, congratulated the people of Kazakhstan on their national holiday. He highlighted the strategic importance of Kazakhstan and Central Asia in Slovenia’s foreign policy, noting that the opening of Kazakhstan’s Embassy in Ljubljana had provided fresh impetus to bilateral relations. He also expressed confidence that political dialogue and trade and economic cooperation would continue to deepen, creating opportunities for major joint projects.
In his welcoming remarks, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Slovenia, Altai Abibullayev, emphasized the historical significance of Republic Day and its connection to the adoption of the Declaration of State Sovereignty. He also outlined Kazakhstan’s ongoing transformation and key socio-economic reforms aimed at building a fair, modern and technologically advanced state amid global change.
The Ambassador highlighted several important developments in Kazakhstan, including the referendum on the adoption of a new Constitution, elections to the Qurultay, the country’s new unicameral legislative body, and Kazakhstan’s international environmental initiatives. These included the national Taza Qazaqstan programme and the initiative proposed by the President of Kazakhstan to establish an International Water Organisation under the auspices of the United Nations. He also emphasized Kazakhstan’s contribution to strengthening the European Union’s energy security.
Speaking on bilateral ties, Ambassador Abibullayev noted that Kazakhstan and Slovenia were entering a new phase of enhanced partnership, supported by the historic visit of Slovenian President Nataša Pirc Musar to Kazakhstan.
Energy, digital technologies and artificial intelligence, transport and logistics, healthcare, green technologies, science, education and tourism were named as promising areas for further cooperation.
One of the evening’s major highlights was the official announcement of KMG International’s entry into the Slovenian market. The development marked an important step towards expanding practical cooperation between the two countries in the energy and investment sectors.
In recognition of Kazakhstan’s designation of 2026 as the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence, guests were also presented with innovative video content produced by the Embassy using advanced AI technologies. The presentation highlighted Kazakhstan’s technological ambitions and its commitment to promoting innovation on the international stage.
The reception in Ljubljana went beyond commemorating a national holiday. It demonstrated the strong mutual respect and trust between Kazakhstan and Slovenia, as well as their shared commitment to developing a sustainable, long-term partnership in an evolving geopolitical landscape.

According to Slovenian customs statistics, bilateral trade turnover in 2025 amounted to USD 215.6 million. During the first eight months of 2026, trade turnover reached USD 153.7 million.

Pentagon and Lockheed announce deal for 850 F-35 jets over 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
00:00:05 UTC
09:00:05 KST

The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin have announced a 10-year agreement for the production of 850 F-35 warplanes, underscoring Washington's long-term commitment to the high-tech stealth aircraft.
The two sides announced the deal on Thursday but did not specify a value for the agreement, which comes as the Pentagon seeks to strike multi-year deals to expand American weapons production and boost the US defence industrial base.
The announcement "cements (the plane's) role as the free world's key frontline fighter for years ahead," Lockheed Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet said on a call with investors.
F-35s — which Washington's forces have used in combat during the US-Israeli war on Iran — come in three versions that can cost more than $100 million per plane.
The "framework agreement," which the Pentagon said would "modernise and expand" the F-35 programme, still requires congressional approval and funding.
"We have fundamentally changed how we stabilise the American defence industrial base to produce at speed and scale," top acquisition official Michael Duffey said in the Pentagon's announcement.
"By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win," Duffey said.
The F-35, a joint project between the United States and a number of allies, is one of the world's most advanced military aircraft. There are more than 1,375 F-35s based around the world, according to Lockheed.
The deal, if approved, would give Washington a "predictable, affordable, and resilient" fighter jet programme, Lockheed said, pointing to billions of dollars in expected savings thanks to "long-term pricing and industry volume discounts."
'Greater certainty'
In exchange for the Pentagon's 10-year commitment, Lockheed Martin will fund $7 billion in projects supporting the F-35s, the Pentagon said.
"With the greater certainty that comes from the US government's transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain," Lockheed's Taiclet said in a statement.
"That's good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies," he added.
In addition to the F-35s themselves, the agreement also covers "initial spares, 10 years of modification kits and sustainment, and international customer orders," Lockheed said.
The United States recently announced the approval of a $24.3 billion sale of 48 of the stealth planes to Saudi Arabia last month.
Lockheed said the F-35 programme will support more than 315,000 jobs and generate nearly $80 billion in economic activity in the next 10 years, "strengthening the nation's industrial base and providing long-term stability for suppliers."
The company on Thursday announced better-than-expected earnings for the third quarter, once again benefiting from higher activity levels across all of its segments.
Lockheed shares surged more than seven percent in Thursday trading, closing at $590.2.

A Personalized Cancer Vaccine Lowers Melanoma Recurrence by 42%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:54:49 UTC
08:54:49 KST

Moderna and Merck reported on Oct. 22 that a customized cancer vaccine for people with late-stage melanoma can reduce the risk of cancer recurrence or death over two years by 42% compared to current treatment.
The results will be presented at the European Society of Medical Oncology meeting in Madrid on Oct. 24.
The study involved more than 1,130 people with Stage 2B to Stage 4 melanoma, all of whom had their tumors surgically removed. Some were then randomly assigned to have a cancer vaccine custom-made after their tumors had been genetically sequenced. They received that vaccine, called intismeran, once every three weeks for up to nine doses, along with Keytruda, a checkpoint inhibitor, every six weeks for up to nine cycles, for about a year. Others were randomly assigned to receive a placebo vaccine and Keytruda.
Intismeran, developed jointly by Moderna and Merck, represents a new way to harness the immune system in cancer, by training immune cells to recognize 34 specific proteins on tumor cells. The mRNA coding for these proteins, or antigens, are encased in a lipid particle in a similar way to Moderna’s COVID vaccine, which used mRNA from the COVID virus’ spike protein. Using this mRNA approach, once cells start making the foreign proteins coded for by the mRNA, the immune system sees them as intruders and mounts a response against them—and the latest data show that the approach works not just against viral proteins but also against those found on tumors.
Keytruda contributes a key part of the response by removing the brakes that keep immune cells from recognizing and attacking tumor cells because they originate from normal "self" cells.
“I was surprised by the fact that the results replicated the Phase 2 [study] so closely,” says Dr. David Berman, chief development officer at Moderna, referring to an earlier stage study the companies released in June that the combination lowered the risk of cancer returning or death by 49% over a year. That study also reported that the therapy lowered the risk of the cancer spreading to other sites by 59% compared to the checkpoint inhibitor alone. “This Phase 3 [study] included a much broader population, so the hypothesis was that the treatment effect would be harder to see. There was a lot of suspicion going in that these results would not be as good as those in the Phase 2. But the fact that they reproduced almost exactly what we saw initially in the Phase 2 blew my mind.”
The companies report that the effect seems to start six months into the therapy—an important insight in understanding how immune-based approaches may work in cancer. “We think it’s because the immune system takes time to be activated,” says Berman. That includes making sure that immune cells like T cells, which are critical to recognizing and controlling cancer, have time to learn to detect tumors. Berman says these results could also help to explain why only about 30% of cancer patients respond to the checkpoint inhibitors, a powerful new tool in cancer that allows immune cells to see tumors rather than thinking they are "self" cells and therefore not foreign. “This shows us that in a significant percentage of patients, the checkpoint inhibitors are not doing anything because the immune system hasn’t even been educated to recognize the cancer cells,” he says of the potential role that the mRNA-based intismeran may play. “That’s where we now need to focus—on how to better educate the immune system. It’s a big leap, a big piece of information, that there is now another way to educate the immune system to recognize cancer.”
Data on overall survival of people on the combination therapy isn’t available yet.
Moderna and Merck are studying the intismeran-Keytruda pairing in other cancer types in nine other studies, such as pancreatic and gastric cancer, as well as in three late-stage trials of non-small cell lung cancer. They are also exploring the role of using intismeran alone in an early study in lung cancer.
Traditionally, personalized therapies have not been practical as medical treatment because of their high cost and long timeline to develop. But Berman is confident that the bespoke process of making an individualized mRNA cancer vaccine for each patient is both scalable and potentially affordable. “We have scaled down the technical footprint and have plans to scale up [the program] to look at different tumors,” he says. “The nice thing about the [mRNA] system is that it’s purely enzymatic, so no cell cultures need to be grown.” Another advantage of using mRNA is its speed—scientists at Moderna can develop a customized vaccine based on a patient’s tumor within weeks—critical for any patient with cancer.

Two critical PHP vulnerabilities threaten websites worldwide. Here’s why Russia, where the language powers more than 90% of sites, faces particularly high risks.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:51:35 UTC
08:51:35 KST

Two critical PHP vulnerabilities threaten websites worldwide. Here’s why Russia, where the language powers more than 90% of sites, faces particularly high risks.
What happened?
On October 21, the team behind the PHP programming language said it had discovered two vulnerabilities. Both scored 9.2 out of 10 on the CVSS scale, a critical severity rating. The vulnerabilities allow attackers to run code remotely on a server without authentication. This could let them gain unauthorized access to files and databases, insert malicious code or alter a website’s content, redirect traffic to other sites, or use the server for DDoS attacks or spam campaigns.
The vulnerabilities have put almost 70% of all websites on the internet at risk of being hacked. That is the share of sites that use PHP, according to W3Techs estimates. The developers strongly recommend installing updates immediately. Updates are already available for PHP versions 8.2 and later.
What exactly is PHP?
PHP is an open-source scripting language created by Danish programmer Rasmus Lerdorf in 1995. It powers the server side of many websites and online services. Several groups now contribute to its development: the PHP Group, the official group of independent developers whose members include Lerdorf; the nonprofit PHP Foundation; and independent contributors.
PHP doesn’t have the best reputation among professional developers, though the reasons for that are rather odd. For example, it is easy for beginners to learn, which could be considered a good thing. But that also means a lot of bad code has been written in PHP. There is also a widespread view that it is unsuitable for complex systems, though that is not true. The language has long faced criticism for inconsistencies and illogical features resulting from its haphazard development.
Still, PHP remains more popular than its competitors. It was created specifically for web development, is simple to use, and has a huge ecosystem built around it. Many major websites, including Facebook, were originally built with PHP, and many continue to use it to avoid the enormous cost and effort of rewriting all their code.
So how do these vulnerabilities work?
Both vulnerabilities involve errors in how the server handles memory. Bugs in PHP’s code allow an attacker to trick the system into treating malicious data as safe.
- In the first case, the system processes a request incorrectly and crashes. When it tries to free that memory, a failure occurs that opens the server to remote control.
- In the second case, “leftover” data from a previous user is accidentally left behind in the server’s memory. This causes an error when a new request is processed, again allowing malicious programs to run.
How were the vulnerabilities discovered?
Researchers from two teams discovered the vulnerabilities independently. In August 2026, Calif researcher Ryan Austin found them using the GPT-5.6 Sol AI model. Separately, researchers at Wiz identified the same problems and reported them to PHP’s developers. They also used AI systems, including the Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol models, as well as their own tool, Wiz Atlas.
OpenAI said in a statement that the PHP development team spent two months working with partners at Wiz, Cloudflare, and other companies to fix the vulnerabilities. Their goal was to release an update before the problem became widely known and attackers began exploiting it on a large scale.
However, the PHP Foundation wrote on its blog that an external security audit had detected signs of one of the vulnerabilities back in 2024. At the time, a theory emerged that attackers could exploit an out-of-memory error. But the developers found no specific way to use it in a cyberattack and turned their attention to more obvious threats. Thai Duong, the head of Calif, told The Wall Street Journal that the problem had been present in the code for decades.
Are they really that dangerous?
OpenAI says the vulnerabilities are among the most far-reaching cybersecurity threats in recent years. Volker Dusch, a security engineer who works on the PHP project, agrees. He says this is the most serious problem the programming language has faced in more than 10 years.
Dusch believes the situation is comparable to Heartbleed, a bug in the OpenSSL cryptographic library that allowed attackers to steal servers’ private keys. That problem became public in 2014, when about half a million websites were vulnerable to attack — roughly 17% of all secure web servers.
Who is at risk?
It might seem that PHP vulnerabilities are a problem only for system administrators, but that isn’t the case. Attackers can target a vulnerable website and steal users’ personal data. They can also alter its content. Someone visiting a familiar website could then fall victim to a phishing attack or end up with infected software on their device.
Finally, critical vulnerabilities like these can affect websites’ availability. In this case, for example, some government agencies in Belgium, the United Kingdom, Denmark, the Netherlands, Finland, and France had to take their public websites and services offline temporarily. Agencies in more than a dozen countries took similar measures. Several other countries only recommended taking sites and services offline.
In Russia, Reg.ru, one of the largest domain registrars and hosting providers, reported temporary restrictions on file uploads because of the PHP problems. The television channel TV Rain also temporarily took its website offline.
But if the vulnerability has been fixed, what is there to worry about?
Just because an update is available doesn’t mean system administrators at every company and organization will install it promptly. According to Netcraft, there were almost half a billion websites worldwide as of July 2026. But only 216 million were considered active, meaning they were still being maintained and regularly updated. There is a high risk that people will visit a forgotten website and fall victim to a cyberattack.
Many website-building platforms use PHP, which complicates the problem. The most popular, WordPress, accounts for more than 58% of the market. In Russia, the closest equivalent is 1C-Bitrix, though it was designed primarily for corporate clients. The risks for Russians are even higher, since more than 90% of websites on the Russian internet use PHP.
Many websites also use older versions of PHP, such as 8.1 and earlier. Official support for these versions has ended, and moving to newer ones often requires rewriting old code. Although the developers made an exception in this case and released patches for older versions, installing them on servers could be difficult and take considerable time.

- Around 150,000 people rallied in Belgrade for the student-backed Student List before Serbia’s Oct 25 election, challenging Aleksandar Vucic’s SNS after more than 14 years in power.
- The movement grew from protests over the 2024 Novi Sad station canopy collapse, which killed 16 and fuelled anger over corruption, leading to calls for an early vote.

BELGRADE – Around 150,000 supporters of Serbia’s opposition student movement rallied in central Belgrade on Oct 22, seeking to oust the party of veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic in crunch parliamentary elections this weekend.
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, wants to end more than 14 years of rule by Vucic’s right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) in the Oct 25 vote.
It is the biggest threat Vucic has faced and civil society groups have warned the poll campaign has been marred by intimidation, arrests, attacks, misuse of public resources and a distorted media environment.
“I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country,” 47-year-old Marija Nedeljkovic Radic told AFP as she arrived for the students’ rally.
“Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible.”
Around 150,000 people gathered at the Student List rally in the evening on Oct 22 in Belgrade, the independent crowd size monitoring group the Archive of Public Gatherings said in a post on X.
The vote comes after nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The tragedy, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia’s largest protests since the fall of strongman Slobodan Milosevic in 2000.
The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, snowballed from demands for a transparent investigation into the tragedy into calls for an early election.
Waving “students are winning” flags, chanting, and blowing whistles, students and their supporters marched through Belgrade before converging on Slavija Square, the site of some of their biggest protests.
They filled the square and the surrounding streets, according to AFP reporters.
“We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours,” university professor Jugoslav Gasic, one of 250 candidates on the Student List, told the crowd who chanted “Victory, victory!”
“You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!”
The rally ended with the candidates stepping down from the stage into the crowd while holding the Serbian constitution in their hands before dancing a traditional folk dance with supporters.
Vucic defiant
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade, serving as either prime minister or president.
Amid mounting pressure, Vucic announced the snap vote in September, setting up his biggest electoral challenge since his party took power in 2012.
Vucic, who addressed supporters at a sports hall in the capital on Oct 22, has regularly accused the student movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
“Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it,” said the 56-year-old, who resigned to run for prime minister.
“Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!” he said before white ticker tape and balloons showered the crowd.
Many of the 250 candidates of the Student List running for the 250-seat Parliament are drawn from academia or are deliberate political outsiders.
The movement has a broad platform, but at its core is a pledge to fight corruption.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling, and surveys have produced widely differing results.
Political scientist Dusan Vucicevic from Belgrade University told AFP it was difficult to predict an outcome but expected students to win more than 40% of the vote, a result significantly larger than any opposition list since SNS came to power.
Threats, intimidation
Days before the vote, Serbian civil society groups warned that conditions for “free and fair elections” were lacking.
“This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government,” a joint statement by 24 organisations said.
“It is supported by documented findings from independent Serbian organisations working in different fields.”
On Oct 21, Belgrade prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting “violence, riots and attacks” on election day.
Reports of threats and intimidation targeting student demonstrators have grown in recent months, but their rallies have remained largely peaceful since they began.
“I’ve been following this fight since the very beginning,” 35-year-old student rally attendee Igor said.
“Today is the last rally, and it’s important that we all come here to send a message of love and peace and that we see each other on the 25th at the polling stations.” AFP

Here’s what Moderna’s latest mRNA cancer vaccine data actually show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:40:13 UTC
08:40:13 KST

Data from Moderna and Merck’s phase 3 clinical trial for an mRNA-based skin cancer vaccine leaked on social media on Thursday, prompting the pharmaceutical companies to release an early look at the results of the trial.
The results, which triggered Moderna’s stock to drop, are “really encouraging,” says Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, a nonprofit. This kind of mRNA cancer vaccine was “fiction” 10 years ago, she says. “It was thought to be very difficult to do.”
As Scientific American previously reported, the Moderna-Merck clinical trial includes two treatments: a personalized mRNA-vaccine called intismeran autogene, which works by instructing the body in how to identify and fight cancer, and pembrolizumab (sold as Keytruda), a drug designed to prevent cancer from “hiding” from our immune system, according to Merck.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The clinical trial included 1,137 cancer patients with “high risk” melanoma, a type of skin cancer. Together, the mRNA vaccine and pembrolizumab reduced the risk of cancer recurrence or death by 42 percent in people, after a median period of about two years, compared to people on pembrolizumab alone. On top of that, the dual treatment reduced the risk of cancer spreading to other parts of the body or death by 38 percent over just pembrolizumab, according to Moderna and Merck.
The findings don’t yet include overall survival, Knudsen notes. “Did people who got the vaccine live longer than people who didn't? And what was their quality of life?” she asks. Those results are coming. But the new findings are “really, really good milestones along the way,” she says.
“From the beginning, we believed mRNA technology could make it possible to develop cancer treatments uniquely matched to each patient’s tumor, Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in a statement. “These results reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer.”
The results have been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine, Merck and Moderna said. Now, the companies are “engaging with regulatory authorities” to seek approval for their mRNA vaccine.
Moderna and Merck did not immediately reply to requests for comment from Scientific American.

Ukraine simplifies underground construction for defense industry companies
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi announced this on Telegram, Ukrinform reports.
"The first measure involves engaging private businesses to build underground production facilities for defense needs. In practice, this means that, starting today, private companies can build such facilities and subsequently lease or sell them to companies directly involved in weapons manufacturing," the statement said.
The decision is expected to simplify the process and increase the number of available facilities, particularly amid the intensification of Russian attacks.
The second measure exempts components for weapons production paid for by international partners from import duties and VAT. In addition, inspection and customs clearance procedures for these goods have been simplified and shortened through the introduction of a "single window" system.
The Ministry of Defense provided further details on the decision to simplify underground construction for defense industry companies.
"The government has supported an important initiative that expands opportunities for attracting private investment in the development of underground production facilities and other infrastructure," the ministry said.
The changes give private investors access to a simplified mechanism for construction and obtaining permits. Developers will therefore be able to build protected production facilities using their own funds and, once construction is complete, transfer them to defense industry companies through sale, lease, or other arrangements for their use.
Construction timelines, terms of use, and transfer procedures will be determined by agreements between investors and defense companies. At least 25% of the floor space must be allocated specifically to the defense sector.
To use this mechanism, developers will need to conclude agreements with, among others, Defence City residents, state contract performers, and companies designated by the Ministry of Defense as critical to the defense industry.
"Russia is trying to destroy our defense production. In response, we must make Ukraine's defense industry more resilient. To achieve this, it is important to move production to protected facilities and preserve our manufacturers' unique capabilities. That is why we are now proposing a more flexible mechanism for attracting additional resources to such projects," Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said.
The Ministry of Defense stressed that the adopted changes would make it possible to attract non-budgetary funding for the development of protected defense infrastructure, accelerate the creation and expansion of production capacity, and simplify the relocation of defense industry companies.

Earthquake of magnitude 7 strikes China's Tibet, killing 16, Xinhua reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:36:45 UTC
08:36:45 KST

An earthquake of magnitude 7 struck China's southwestern region of Tibet at around 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, killing 16 people and injuring 32 others, state news agency Xinhua reported, citing Nagqu City's emergency management bureau.
As of 2:25 a.m. on Friday, 11 of the injured were in serious condition while 21 sustained minor injuries, Xinhua reported.
Local authorities have found at least two people injured in a village near the epicenter, with some houses in villages closest to the epicenter showing cracks, the state broadcaster said. The quake is the strongest to hit China since January 2024.
The epicenter was in a sparsely populated, high-altitude county in Nagqu, northern Tibet, at a depth of 10 km (6.2 miles). The average elevation within 5 km of the epicenter is about 4,864 meters (15,960 feet), China Earthquake Networks Center(CENC) data showed.
Videos released by local officially run media showed people leaving their homes and seeking shelter outside or in their cars parked on the street. One resident reported being awakened by the strong quake and heard the house squeaking in the tremor.
The quake was clearly felt in the local area, CENC said. The epicenter was around 400 km from the Tibetan capital of Lhasa.
Local fire and rescue teams have mobilized and are heading to the affected region, state media said.
Smaller tremors recorded in surrounding regions
A string of smaller tremors of around magnitude 3 and 4 have been recorded in surrounding regions following the magnitude 7 quake, CENC data showed.
In 2010, a magnitude 7.1 tremor struck Yushu in neighboring Qinghai province, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 people missing.

Over 65,000 Israelis abroad estimated to travel to vote in 2026 elections, new Fly&Vote survey says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:36:19 UTC
08:36:19 KST

Approximately 67,000 Israelis abroad plan to travel to Israel to vote in the upcoming elections for the 26th Knesset, according to a Thursday survey published by the Fly&Vote initiative, up from the previous estimate of 53,000 published at the start of October.
The initiative, which is operated by the AID Coalition, has recently been the focus of a Likud petition seeking to restrict its activities.
The survey, conducted between October 12 and 21 and involving approximately 23,000 Israelis living abroad, found that 79.6% of respondents intend to travel to Israel to participate in the elections. By comparison, only 14% said they had traveled to Israel to vote in the 2022 elections.
Fly&Vote cautioned, however, that the survey was voluntary and does not constitute a representative sample of all Israelis living abroad. It also noted that the estimate of 67,000 potential voters is based on an analysis of registration data from the initiative, rather than a count of travelers who have actually arrived in Israel.
According to the survey, most respondents (48%) are coming from the United States, 37% from European countries, 5% from Canada, and 2% from Australia and New Zealand. Other participants are traveling from South America, Asia, and South Africa.
Approximately 70% of respondents said that the initiative's activities influenced their decision to travel to Israel and vote, while another quarter said it had helped them obtain information and prepare for their trip.
Likud charges Fly&Vote backers with influencing voters
The findings come approximately two weeks after the conclusion of the legal battle Likud waged against those behind the initiative.
In a petition filed by attorney Ilan Bombach, Likud argued that assistance with securing flights and related services could constitute the provision of prohibited benefits to voters which may influence how they vote.
The proceedings concluded on October 6 with a settlement reached before Judge Noam Sohlberg, chair of the Central Elections Committee (CEC). The petition was withdrawn, but the initiative agreed not to subsidize airline tickets, offer discounts, or organize any additional flights beyond those that had already been offered.
It also agreed to limit related services, including transportation and accommodation.
Likud presented the agreement as a legal victory, while the initiative stressed that its activities had not been prohibited and that it would continue helping Israelis exercise their right to vote.
Unlike in many other countries, Israel does not allow most of its citizens living abroad to vote remotely. They must travel to Israel to cast their ballots in person.
Votes of Israelis abroad equivalent to approximately 1.7 Knesset seats
Yehonatan Bar Sadeh, president of the AID Coalition, said Israelis from around the world were taking time off work and their studies and spending hundreds or even thousands of dollars to travel to Israel. "The future of the State of Israel matters so much to them that they are taking time off work or from their studies," he said.
If the initiative's estimate is accurate and about 67,000 Israelis living abroad travel to Israel to vote, their votes would equal about 1.7 Knesset seats, based on an estimate of around 40,000 votes per seat in the upcoming elections.
However, this would not automatically translate into additional seats for any particular party or political bloc. The actual allocation of seats depends on the election results, the electoral threshold, and how votes are distributed among the parties.
Last week, Israeli law firm Erdinast, Ben Nathan, Toledano (EBN) sent a letter on behalf of the Choosing Israel organization requesting clarification from the Israel Airports Authority (IAA) on its preperations to operate without disruptions on Election Day.
The letter cited concerns that political actors could attempt to disrupt operations at the country's airports in an attempt to prevent citizens from voting and urged the airport to work to prevent such things from happening.
The IAA's recent response, as well as one from the Transportation Ministry's legal advisor, affirmed that the airports would remain open and fully functional in the days leading up to October 27, and on the day itself.
Udi Ezion contributed to this report.

New York City bans horse-drawn carriages from June 2028
NEW YORK – The New York City Council voted on Oct 22 to ban horse-drawn carriages from city streets and Central Park beginning in June 2028, ending a historic tourist attraction and longstanding industry.
Out of the city’s 51 lawmakers, 40 supported the Bill, which was backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who earlier in October said the horse-drawn carriage industry would come to an end. Seven council members voted against it and two abstained.
Support for the ban grew after the death this summer of Romanch Mahajan, an 18-year-old tourist from India. Mahajan was thrown from a carriage and died on June 17, when the horse bolted after the driver stepped away to take a picture of Mahajan’s family.
President Donald Trump, who has both attacked Mamdani and held cordial meetings with him, expressed scepticism about the ban.
“When there is a car accident in the area, of which there are many, they don’t stop cars from entering the Park. So why would they stop the Carriages? It was a Great Tradition. Another piece of History that’s gone. It will be missed!” Trump, whose business empire is headquartered in Trump Tower, minutes from Central Park, wrote on Truth Social.
The Bill requires the city to develop a transition plan for the workforce by April and to consider a programme to compensate carriage operators for their businesses and help with the disposition of their horses. Under the proposal, the horses could not be slaughtered.
The day before the vote, the Transport Workers Union, which represents carriage business owners and drivers, said that if the Bill is enacted, it will seek a temporary restraining order from a court “the minute the ink dries”, according to a letter sent to New York City Corporation Counsel Steve Banks.
“This may be the first time in City history that a previously licensed profession was banned,” the letter signed by principal attorney Arthur Schwartz said.
“The proposed Bill deprives the owner of all economically beneficial or productive use of their property.” REUTERS

Almost all shallow-water coral reefs now face extinction risk, study warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:32:13 UTC
08:32:13 KST

Almost all shallow-water coral reefs now face extinction risk, study warns
The world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of all coral reef systems as "critically endangered".
Almost all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse in the next 50 years, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) has warned in a new global assessment.
In a report released on Thursday, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96 percent of the planet’s coral reef systems as “critically endangered”, its highest risk category, with total extinction possible by 2075.
“The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems,” said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.
Corals are heat-sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world’s oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.
When a reef collapses, hard corals disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges. As a result, the reef no longer supports a diverse ecosystem that can include everything from tiny invertebrates to reef fish like grouper.
The emergence this year of a “super” El Nino, the natural warming phenomenon, also presents a risk to corals, Gudka said at a news conference at the UN’s COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
It’s the latest dose of bad news for coral reefs, which are critical sources for seafood and tourism and often serve as buffers against coastal erosion and storms.
Sometimes dubbed “rainforests of the sea”, they have some of the world’s richest biodiversity and support a quarter of marine species as well as coastal communities and businesses.
Most of the world’s famous reef systems – including the Great Barrier Reef in Australia, the Coral Triangle in the Western Pacific Ocean and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System and the Red Sea coral reefs – are critically endangered, according to the assessment.
Elevated risk of extinction
For its report, the IUCN used the “middle-of-the-road” scenario from the UN’s panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
Its analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 square kilometres.
A week ago, another IUCN study in the journal Nature found that nearly 44 percent of reef-building coral species face an elevated risk of extinction due to climate change. A year ago, a survey found that harmful bleaching of the world’s coral had grown to include 84 percent of the ocean’s reefs, the most intense of its kind in recorded history.
Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world “are not yet lost”.
“Coral reefs have shown a remarkable ability to bounce back from devastating bleaching events,” said Gudka. “Pockets of surviving, resilient coral reefs can still remain in the future, so we must do everything within our reach to set them up for success.”

The missiles are air-launched Joint Strike Missiles (JSM) made by Norway’s Kongsberg for the Nordic country’s F-35 stealth fighter jets and the ground-launched Anthem missile made by Covenant.
“The purpose of the acquisitions is to strengthen national and collective deterrence. These are weapons that are in demand by NATO and that contribute to Denmark's security,” Denmark’s Defense Ministry said in a statement on Thursday, adding that “they can both deter attacks from outside and strike back deep inside enemy territory if necessary.”
The JSM is a fifth-generation air-to-surface missile that fits in the internal weapons bays of the F-35A, allowing the aircraft to retain its stealth profile. The high-subsonic missile has a range of 350 kilometers and autonomous target recognition capabilities. It is in use by 15 other countries, including the United States, Germany, Norway, Romania, and Poland.
Covenant, which has operations in the US, Germany, and Israel, emerged from stealth last month. Covenant’s flagship system, Anthem, is built to deliver heavy payloads at extended ranges while remaining affordable enough to produce in large quantities. The company has disclosed relatively little about Anthem’s specific performance characteristics, including its precise range, payload, and unit cost.
According to the company, most of Anthem’s components are commercial‑off‑the‑shelf (COTS) parts, supported by long‑term agreements for critical parts. Covenant says this approach allows the missile to be produced quickly and reliably, even during wartime, by drawing on supply chains across allied nations.
“Covenant Industries is proud to partner with Denmark as it moves with urgency to strengthen European defense and NATO’s collective security. As a global defense company with a growing European industrial footprint, Covenant is committed to delivering affordable, long-range precision strike capabilities at scale. This agreement, signed through our German company, represents an important step in our commitment to producing Anthem in Europe, for Europe, supported by a sovereign European supply chain,” Abby Denburg, its president and CGO told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post.
Denmark’s Minister Defense Jeppe Bruus said that “the acquisitions are a significant step toward making Denmark better able to defend itself, strengthening NATO, and increasing our ability to strike back.”
Last year, Denmark said that it would be spending 58 billion Danish crowns ($9.20 billion) on European-made air defense systems, its largest arms purchase ever. A week later, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen made the announcement that it would be purchasing long-range precision missiles because the country “must be able to credibly deter attacks on Denmark and NATO, and it is not enough to just have strong air defenses.”
Reuters reported that the Russian embassy in Copenhagen said that Denmark's missile policy aims at confrontation with Moscow and warned of "inevitable disastrous consequences.”
"Copenhagen is enthralled by the dangerous illusions that purchasing offensive high-precision long-range weapons to pose a military threat to a nuclear power will help strengthen Denmark's security and defense," the embassy said.

Amid Starlink crisis, Finnish tech giants announce plan to help Ukraine build its own sovereign satellite system
The Finnish tech companies ICEYE and Nokia signed a letter of intent with Ukraine's Defense Ministry on Oct. 22, formalizing a partnership aimed at developing Ukraine's own satellite communications system.
President Volodymyr Zelensky first announced the deal earlier in the day during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's visit to Kyiv, calling the satellite agreement "important for our defense and for the resilience of Ukraine."
The agreement with Kyiv comes a few weeks after Nokia and ICEYE announced plans to collaborate on building "broadband low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications systems for governments." These systems will support national defense, emergency response services, and border security, among other applications.
Ukraine currently relies on a different broadband LEO satellite communications system: Starlink, a service run by U.S.-based company SpaceX. Starlink has proven essential for battlefield communications, mid-range drone strikes, and air defense.
But the system has also proven vulnerable, as Ukraine learned after a week of persistent disruptions to its Starlink services. While U.S. President Donald Trump claimed that full speed and functionality had been restored to Ukraine's Starlink, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the restrictions remained in place.
read also
The jointly developed systems that ICEYE and NOKIA want to create, however, would give nations ownership over their satellites, ground segment, and terminals, the companies said. Ukrainian forces on the front lines would therefore not lose access to mission-critical systems due to the shifting whims of foreign governments.
"Ukraine needs secure, sovereign, and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls," ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said in a press release announcing the deal with Kyiv.
"We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today."
Nokia Defense Chairman Mikko Hautala echoed the sentiment, saying the project would give Ukraine "control over the connectivity it depends on."
ICEYE describes itself as "the European leader in sovereign intelligence from space" and telecommunications giant Nokia as "a global leader in connectivity infrastructure."

Tibet earthquake kills at least 16 people, injures dozens: state media

Tibet earthquake kills at least 16 people, injures dozens: state media
October 23, 2026
A strong earthquake struck Tibet in southwestern China on Thursday night, killing at least 16 people and injuring 32 others, Chinese state media reported.
Hundreds of homes in the remote Himalayan region collapsed due to the magnitude 7.0 quake, Xinhua reported.
China's President Xi Jinpinghas ordered "all-out search and rescue efforts" to locate missing people, provide "prompt medical treatment for the injured" and called for "every effort to minimize casualties," Xinhua said.
The earthquake is the strongest to hit the region in the past five years, broadcaster CCTV said, and the most powerful to hit China since January 2024.
How severe was the earthquake in Tibet?
At least 339 residential buildings have collapsed, local government officials said, according to state media. Twenty livestock sheds were also destroyed.
Of the dozens injured, 11 were in a serious condition, the local media office said.
Disaster relief efforts were ongoing as officials assess the scale of the damage, the state news agency added.
Xinhua reported that power and communication lines to the area were also disrupted.
What do we know about the area where the earthquake struck?
The earthquake's epicenter is around 190 kilometers (120 miles) northeast of Nagqu, a city around 300 kilometers north of the Tibetan capital, Lhasa, the US Geological Survey said.
The mountainous area is sparsely populated.
The quake struck at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.
How often do earthquakes hit China?
Earthquakes are relatively common in China.
In January 2025, a quake near Mount Everest in Tibet's Tingri region killed at least 126 people.
In 2010, at least 2,698 people were killed when a magnitude 7.1 quake hit Qinghai province, which neighbors Tibet.

Twenty countries complete establishment of Ibero-American Network for Disaster Risk Reduction and Civil Protection and approve roadmap for the coming years
Spain
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:23:40 CEST
08:23:40 KST

PRESS RELEASE 158
Twenty countries complete establishment of Ibero-American Network for Disaster Risk Reduction and Civil Protection and approve roadmap for the coming years
- The new cooperation platform will strengthen the exchange of knowledge, capabilities and experience to improve emergency preparedness and response across Ibero-America.
- Member States have agreed to establish a permanent Technical Secretariat, a role to be performed by the General Secretariat for Civil Protection and Emergencies, and have formalised the handover of the rotating presidency to Andorra.
- They have also approved the Network's rules of procedure and defined its strategic guidelines for 2027–2030 and its first Action Plan, which will set the organisation's roadmap.
As of today, the Ibero-American Community has a new permanent cooperation mechanism to strengthen emergency prevention, preparedness and response. The national authorities of 20 countries have signed off on the definitive establishment of the Ibero-American Network for Disaster Risk Reduction and Civil Protection (RGIR), consolidating a joint, permanent cooperation initiative to strengthen resilience and comprehensive disaster risk management for the benefit of more than 670 million citizens. The Network has been established as a lasting forum for collaboration to share capabilities, knowledge and experience and coordinate efforts to address the natural, technological and human-induced risks affecting the region.
The launch of the Network marks the culmination of a process led by the General Secretariat for Civil Protection and Emergencies and the Ibero-American General Secretariat (SEGIB), with support from CAF – Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, and from the Spanish Agency for International Development Cooperation (AECID) and the Foundation for the Internationalisation of Public Administrations (FIAP), both under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, European Union and Cooperation.
The Network was established during the first meeting of the Ibero-American Conference of National Authorities for Disaster Risk Reduction and Civil Protection, held at the National School of Civil Protection in Rivas-Vaciamadrid (Madrid), as part of the official programme of activities for the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government.
This initiative responds to a shared reality in the region: Ibero-American countries' high exposure to natural, technological and human-induced phenomena that have significant human, economic and environmental impacts every year. In this context, regional cooperation is a means of strengthening societies' resilience and protecting citizens.
Objectives achieved and agreements reached
During the meeting, delegations approved the key instruments that will enable the Network to operate effectively with immediate effect. The most significant agreements include the approval of its rules of procedure, the adoption of its strategic guidelines for 2027–2030 and the endorsement of its first Action Plan. These documents will define the organisation's priorities for the coming years.
Member States also supported the establishment of a trust fund to finance cooperation, training, technical exchanges and institutional strengthening. This mechanism will receive support from the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean, which will be responsible for structuring and supporting the financial instrument that will ensure the sustainability of the initiatives promoted by the Network.
Handover of the presidency
The meeting also formalised the handover of the Network's Pro Tempore Presidency. Having led the establishment process and driven the organisation's preparatory work, Spain's General Secretariat for Civil Protection and Emergencies has transferred the presidency to Andorra's Department of Civil Protection and Emergencies, in accordance with the rotating model approved by member countries. The Principality will assume the presidency with effect from 1 January 2027.
Member States have also agreed to establish a Technical Secretariat as a permanent body supporting the Network, a role to be performed by the General Secretariat for Civil Protection and Emergencies. Its responsibilities will include coordinating the organisation's activities, following up on the agreements reached and developing the joint work agenda. The Technical Secretariat will also ensure institutional cohesion and continuity, acting as a link between successive rotating presidencies and overseeing the implementation of the agreements and objectives adopted.
Participants also approved the organisation's official visual identity, including the logo that will henceforth identify the Ibero-American Network for Disaster Risk Reduction and Civil Protection and accompanies this press release.
A new phase in Ibero-American cooperation
With the approval of its key governance instruments, the launch of a dedicated financial mechanism, the definition of the Technical Secretariat's role and the transition from a temporary to a rotating presidency, the Ibero-American Network for Disaster Risk Reduction and Civil Protection officially begins its work as a permanent platform for regional cooperation.
The establishment of the Network strengthens Ibero-American cooperation on disaster risk reduction and civil protection. With a consolidated governance structure, a joint work agenda and the commitment of its Member States, the organisation is embarking on a new phase aimed at developing shared solutions to the challenges affecting the region.

Palmer Luckey Made a Genetically Modified Military Dog Startup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:15:00 UTC
08:15:00 KST

A new startup launched today with the definitely not terrifying mission of creating genetically enhanced dogs for the United States military, law enforcement, and emergency first responders.
Warhound is the brainchild of Anduril’s Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences cofounder Ben Lamm. The startup has raised $200 million to “rebuild America’s domestic supply of elite working dogs” and reduce dependency on European dog breeders for military canines.
Lamm tells WIRED that Warhound is in the process of gene-editing its first batch of dogs. The startup has already collected blood samples from specific "top-performing” military, police, and first responder dogs in the United States, and its goal is to clone them. Breeds will be “mostly Belgian Malinois, some labs, and some shepherds,” he says. The company anticipates the first round of puppies to be born in early 2027.
The initial rounds of gene-editing will focus on eliminating common health conditions that impact these breeds, like hip dysplasia. Further down the line, Lamm envisions expanding to “really interesting things,” such as incorporating olfactory receptor genes from wolves to “enhance” the military dogs. (Colossal Biosciences is perhaps best known for its work on gene-edited wolves for its so-called Dire Wolf De-Extinction Project.)
Warhound, based in Texas, will also equip its canines with “Anduril’s advanced cybernetic Augments, software, and battlefield situational awareness,” according to a press releaseAsked if this means the dogs will be some kind of cyborgs, Lamm clarifies that the plan right now is to supply them with tools like “advanced body armor” rather than, say, embedding some sort of computer in their dog bodies.
“So no dogs with lasers?” WIRED asked Lamm.
“I can’t comment on what Anduril plans,” he says. “Dog safety and performance, and then helping continue helping to improve the human handler and dog bond, and working as a team—that is what the mission is.”
Neither Luckey nor Lamm will be involved in Warhound’s day-to-day, although Lamm is on the company’s board, he says. David Spirk, a former Department of Defense chief data officer who most recently worked at Palantir, is serving as chief executive, and investors include In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, and ARK Invest. Luckey is not an owner and does not have equity in the company, nor does Anduril; Colossal Biosciences does have an ownership stake.
Luckey and Lamm have been working on the project for over a year, Lamm says, and just recently decided to take the company out of stealth. “Someone said, ‘So it's like the Captain America dog program with the Ironman tech program on top of it,’” Lamm tells WIRED.
Everyone can agree that this is normal, and good, and that when the precision-designed beasts arrive on Earth, they will recognize that we are not the enemy.
The company plans to operate under the guidance of the American Humane Society.

Never be, never see: Metallica's cowardly silence on Palestine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:14:27 UTC
08:14:27 KST

Breadcrumb
Never be, never see: Metallica's cowardly silence on Palestine
During Metallica’s residency at the Sphere in Las Vegas earlier this month, frontman James Hetfield told concertgoers: “Metallica is not here, like some other entertainers, to influence you with their bullshit, OK?” He then declared: “We’re here to forget about all the outside shit, OK? Metallica’s agenda is love, energy and heavy music, baby!”
The remarks arrived less than a month after rapper Macklemore was removed from Ed Sheeran’s US tour following his onstage call for a free Palestine. Many interpreted Hetfield’s words as a swipe at Macklemore; NME raised that exact question.
Indeed, the timing matters. Musicians are facing professional consequences for speaking out about Palestine, and one of rock’s most influential frontmen was ridiculing the practice of addressing audiences about political causes.
Whether it was directed at Macklemore or not, Hetfield’s comments were particularly rich coming from a member of Metallica because for decades, the band has sold millions of records filled with condemnations of militarism, political repression, and institutional corruption.
For Palestine solidarity activists, this highlighted the contradiction between the band’s professed ideals of justice and their behaviour when it comes to Palestinian oppression.
A history of mixing politics and music
Metallica did not become famous by pretending the world beyond the concert hall did not exist. On their album Master of Puppets (1986), their track Disposable Heroes critiques young soldiers as expendable instruments of military command. Blackened imagines the planet's destruction, and the song … And Justice for All attacks a legal order distorted by money and power. The band’s own anniversary retrospective described the latter as music that confronts broken systems and serves as a “battle cry for change”. Its power lay precisely in making listeners face the world around them – not hide from it.
The politics are even less ambiguous in the track One, which tells the story of a soldier catastrophically wounded in war and trapped inside his own body. In an interview republished on Metallica’s official website in September 2026, Hetfield called it “the anti-war song.”
Discussing The Shortest Straw, which references McCarthyism and restrictions on artistic freedom, he said it was “more political than any of the other songs”.
Not only does this history make Hetfield’s attack on other entertainers hollow, but the fact that so many of their anti-war tracks were then performed on the night that their fans were urged to forget the outside world makes it all the more so.
There is no difference between condemning war through song lyrics and speaking out against it on stage.
Several band members have also openly expressed political opinions. For example, guitarist Kirk Hammett urged people to defend American democracy and reject Donald Trump’s rhetoric of “American carnage” in 2017. He used his considerable platform to criticise the new administration and called on his followers to respond.
Drummer Lars Ulrich also publicly opposed Trump’s proposed wall on the US-Mexico border, and invoked Metallica’s ability to bring people across national and cultural divisions.
And during a period of rising racial tension in 2017, Hetfield made his opposition to division and intolerance clear during a performance in Edmonton.
As has been the case with many artists over the past three years of the attacks on Gaza, Metallica's response to Russia's invasion of Ukraine has also highlighted much hypocrisy. Through the ‘All Within My Hands foundation’, Metallica gave an initial $100,000 and then a further $500,000 to World Central Kitchen’s relief effort for Ukrainians displaced by the war. The foundation even turned the campaign into a mobilisation of Metallica’s fanbase, using merchandise, auctions, fan-club activity and matching donations to raise more money.
By June, the band announced that the drive had met its $1 million target.
Apparently, it’s not “bullshit” when artists use their influence to rally support for Ukraine…
Palestine
Palestine was hardly a new political question for Metallica. Already, in 2009, the Palestine solidarity movement urged the band to cancel its scheduled concert in Tel Aviv, warning that performing would help normalise Israel’s system of occupation, apartheid, and dispossession of the Palestinian people.
Activists published an open letter which started with a passage from “...And Justice for All”, deliberately confronting Metallica with its own denunciation of corrupted justice.
Despite the mobilisation, Metallica went ahead with the show, choosing to disregard calls for a cultural boycott from Palestinian civil society. Its official concert archive confirms that the band played at Ramat Gan Stadium in Tel Aviv on 22 May 2010, which was their third time performing in Israel.
Little has changed, clearly.
In reality, Hetfiled's tone-deaf comments earlier this month only fuel hostility towards those who dare to speak out during a time of political repression, in Donald Trump’s America – which the band was once all too willing to publicly oppose – and around the world. And given that their fellow artists have been targeted and censored for speaking in support of Palestinian liberation and calling for an end to the killing, their message puts them on the wrong side of history.
As Antonio Gramsci argued, ruling groups maintain power partly by making their ideas seem like common sense. This helps explain the political significance of Metallica’s call for disengagement at a time when Israel’s genocide in Palestine demands urgent international attention. Hetfield’s vague agenda of “love, energy and heavy music” ultimately amounts to a refusal to stand for anything meaningful. And that refusal is itself deeply political.

Critically endangered Bangka slow loris documented after decades without scientific records
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
23:14:26 UTC
08:14:26 KST

Critically endangered Bangka slow loris documented after decades without scientific records
The Bangka slow loris, a venomous primate classified as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct) on the the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List of Threatened Species, has been documented across Indonesia’s Bangka Island, according to a new study published in the scientific journal Spixiana, Qazinform News Agency reports.
The findings are based on records of more than 90 slow lorises rescued by the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center between 2015 and 2025. Although the species had not been documented in scientific literature since the 1930s, local residents continued to find the animals in gardens, along roadsides and on power lines.
The study was co-authored by the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center, Timon Glaw of the Haus des Meeres Aqua Terra Zoo in Vienna and the Taman Safari Prigen Conservation Breeding Ark. Of the more than 90 animals rescued, 86 recovered and were released at seven sites on the island.
“We are glad to contribute to the scientific record to show that the Bangka slow loris is not lost, but the species is still very close to extinction,” said Langka Sani, director of the Alobi Wildlife Rescue Center.
Sani said the species’ natural habitat had shrunk significantly because of illegal tin mining and extensive land clearing for oil palm plantations.
According to the study, human settlements, roads and power lines also threaten the species, while slow lorises are targeted by the pet trade across their range in Asia.
“Bringing the Bangka slow loris back onto the scientific radar is only the first step,” said Glaw, one of the study’s co-authors. He called for population surveys, genetic studies and protection of the species’ remaining habitat.
The researchers recommend a conservation program to protect suitable forests and continue monitored releases. They also propose a conservation breeding program to learn more about the species’ biology and behavior.
Benji Barca, exploration program manager at Re:wild, said the rescue center’s records had helped bring the primate back into scientific view.
“A species can disappear from the scientific record without disappearing from the lives of the people who share its home,” Barca said.
The Bangka slow loris was first scientifically described in 1906 and recognized as a distinct species in 2013. Slow lorises are the only primates known to be venomous. They mix secretions from a gland on the inside of their upper arm with saliva, producing a bite that can cause pain and swelling.
Qazinform previously reported that a rare Central Asian river otter, listed in Kazakhstan’s Red Book of endangered species, had been captured on camera at Charyn National Park. The footage highlighted the role of wildlife monitoring in studying rare species and supporting conservation efforts.

King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit

The head of the Caribbean’s reparations commission has appealed to King Charles III as a “human brother” whose family he said had benefited from slavery to support reparations talks at next month’s Commonwealth leaders meeting in the Caribbean.
Speaking at a press conference ahead of the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm) in Antigua and Barbuda next month, professor Hilary Beckles urged the king to use his influence to advance slavery reparations talks between Britain and the Caribbean.
Beckles, the chair of the Caribbean Community (Caricom) Reparations Commission, said: “My personal appeal to King Charles III, not so much in his role as head of the Commonwealth, not so much in his role as the constitutional monarch of the United Kingdom … I’m appealing to Charles Windsor, a parent, a grandparent, a man today who reflects upon the history of his family, and he can see the enrichment that slavery has presented to his family.”
He declared that he believed the king was aware that the wealth he is passing on to his children and his grandchildren came from chattel slavery.
Referring to the king as “a man, as a human brother”, he urged Charles to ensure the Commonwealth, historically “the site of this crime”, becomes a “moral institution committed to human justice”.
Beckles’s appeal comes amid growing calls from Caribbean leaders and groups for Charles to formally apologise for slavery when he visits Guyana and the Bahamas next week ahead of Chogm, which he will attend in Antigua.
On Thursday, Commonwealth secretary-general Shirley Ayorkor Botchwey told Sky News that a formal apology for slavery from King Charles “wouldn’t hurt” and that the “time has come” for a serious conversation regarding reparations.
Eric Phillips, head of Guyana’s reparations committee and vice-chair of the Caricom Reparations Commission, joined the calls for an apology from the king.
“The king is a decent monarch based on his lifelong commitments to the world in which the environment for him is sacred. We Africans are also part of that sacred environment. As an enlightened monarch, I strongly believe King Charles will want to promote a conversation of decency that reflects his character and values,” he said.
“The citizens of the United Kingdom say, long live the king. We in Guyana say, long live the king, so he can apologize and call for reparations,” he added.
Last month, when Jamaican officials lodged a landmark petition to King Charles for legal advice on its claim for slavery reparations, which will be heard by the privy council in March, a palace spokesperson said Charles “has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today”.
But David Comissiong, the deputy chair of the Barbados National Task Force on Reparations, said he was concerned about a lack of unanimous agreement on commitments on reparations in a draft of the 2026 Chogm communique, which records agreements made by leaders.
Comissiong said a paragraph that referenced the commitment to dialogue made at the previous Commonwealth summit in Samoa and highlights subsequent developments at the UN, African Union and Caricom, was confirmed, but there was disagreement about a second paragraph mandating Commonwealth foreign ministers to advance discussions on historical harms from the transatlantic slave trade through “structured, inclusive, and good faith dialogue”.
“It is very peculiar, to say the least, that the second paragraph which speaks about the Commonwealth foreign affairs ministers coming together to engage in these discussions … has not been unanimously agreed upon,” he said.
Dorbrene O’Marde, chair of the Antigua and Barbuda reparations commission, said that campaigners are expected to raise the issue of reparations during the conferences’ major forums, and that discussions between governments are expected to take place at their meetings.
He said the reparations movement will launch a “Global Reparations Caravan”, described as an international movement combining reparations advocacy, demonstrations and culture, at a separate event on 3 November.
O’Marde added that, while there will be stringent security measures around the event, he expects physical demonstrations from groups who are “inflamed” by the blanket statements of no apology coming out of the UK.
“Blanket no apologies from both government and monarchy reek of gross insensitivity to the demands of the citizens of the Caribbean,” he said.
Beckles stressed that the absence of a dedicated official event at Chogm does not mean that reparations would remain peripheral to the summit. He described the meeting as “the Chogm of reparations” and the “first round of reparations negotiations”.
“This is the meeting of the Commonwealth in the Caribbean, and the number one item in the Caribbean as far as this gathering is concerned is reparatory justice,” he said.
“I can assure you that [for] everyone in the Caribbean right now, everyone who’s going to be at that meeting from the Caribbean, with an interest in the Caribbean, from Africa, and an interest in the global African movement, this will be the number one item on the table.”
