New wave of aliyah presents opportunities, challenges for real estate investors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:48:40 UTC
04:48:40 KST

The prospect of increased aliyah from North America and the rest of the world presents Israel with a challenge that requires both economic and practical preparation. Nefesh B’Nefesh’s forecast of more than 4,000 immigrants from North America in 2026 points to a significant movement, particularly at this challenging time for the Jewish people, both in Israel and worldwide.
The scale of aliyah in the coming years will depend, in part, on the ability to translate the willingness to immigrate into a realistic and viable plan for life in Israel. For many families, housing will be central to that decision. They will ask what they can afford to buy, what financial commitments they will need to undertake, and which community they can become part of.
At the heart of the challenge is the relationship between Israeli housing prices and the purchasing power of the capital these families have accumulated abroad.
The strengthening shekel places an additional burden on families whose assets and income are denominated in dollars. An apartment priced at NIS 3 million, for example, costs C$1 million at an exchange rate of three shekels to the dollar, roughly the rate today. At four shekels to the dollar, a rate seen less than three years ago, the same apartment would have cost C$750,000. That represents an increase of one-third in its dollar cost, even if its shekel price remains unchanged. A family that planned its aliyah around a particular amount of capital may discover a financing gap substantial enough to change its decision.
Homeownership abroad also requires a sober assessment. The proceeds available for purchasing a home in Israel are determined by the sale price after repayment of the outstanding mortgage, expenses, and any applicable taxes. At exchange rates on October 14, 2026, C$1 million is worth approximately NIS 2.16 million before these deductions.
By comparison, individual apartments with three bedrooms and a living room, classified in Israel as four rooms, are on offer at approximately NIS 3.2 million in Jerusalem, NIS 3.3 million in Ra’anana and NIS 2.7 million in Beit Shemesh.
These are asking prices for specific properties, but the gap they illustrate is substantial, particularly when families also need financial reserves as they establish themselves professionally and settle into their new lives.
Assessing housing affordability for new olim
My experience as chairman of "Amidar, Israel’s national public housing company", together with my deep familiarity with the Israeli real estate market and its established, trusted participants, has taught me to assess housing options in terms of affordability over time and the buyer’s overall circumstances.
In my current role as chairman of "Ofek Israeli", the national company for promoting aliyah and a subsidiary of the Jewish Agency for Israel and the World Zionist Organization, the connection between these fields takes on added significance. Immigrant families need housing options suited to their financial circumstances and their stage in the relocation process.
Rental housing with security of tenure, professional management, and clear contractual provisions for rent adjustments can allow a family to make aliyah, enter the workforce, and become familiar with its surroundings before purchasing a home. Alongside this, pathways to future ownership can be developed, subject to appropriate legal and financial structuring.
Broadening the geographical search is equally important. Examples of comparable apartments with three bedrooms in Karmei Gat, Karmiel and Beersheba have been offered at approximately NIS 2.05 million, NIS 1.65 million and NIS 1.45 million, respectively. Such a difference can substantially reduce the borrowing required to purchase a home.
For these alternatives to be attractive, a supportive social framework is also essential. Community aliyah can, for example, enable a rabbi or community leader to relocate together with members of the community. It can also bring families from different locations together to form a community in their country of origin before making aliyah as a group.
The experience of "Israela", founded by Shalom Vach, provides a foundation for organizing such groups and preparing communities in Israel to welcome them. Combining this approach with housing concentrated in one neighborhood can enable families to buy or rent close to one another, maintain networks of mutual support, and integrate into the surrounding Israeli community.
New aliyah wave creates opportunities for US real estate investors
This also presents an opportunity for American real estate investors. Acquiring a residential building or a group of apartments, in partnership with an experienced Israeli partner, can provide a range of housing options for a group whose needs have been assessed in advance. Such an arrangement may improve occupancy planning, reduce marketing costs, and support longer tenancies.
For American real estate investors who no longer wish to invest in New York, where Zohran Mamdani serves as mayor, or who are seeking to diversify their investments, an attractive opportunity is emerging in Israel: investing in properties that generate rental income and serve an identified source of demand, while strengthening their connection to the country. This can be pursued in partnership with reputable Israeli real estate companies with established track records.
The task ahead is to develop projects in which immigrant families can build their future, investors can assess financial viability, and Israel can expand its capacity to welcome new Olim.
The writer, Dr. Izhak Lax, is an attorney and chairman of Ofek Israeli.

Airbnb to ban hosts from requiring guests to clean before checkout

Airbnb to ban hosts from requiring guests to clean before checkout
Short-term rental platform Airbnb has updated its rules for property owners. Starting November 20, hosts will no longer be allowed to require guests to carry out time-consuming cleaning tasks before checkout, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Under the new rules, hosts will be prohibited from requiring guests to wash and put away dishes, strip beds or do laundry. They will also be barred from asking guests to take trash outside the property.
However, hosts may still ask guests to place used dishes in the sink, gather towels or sort waste into bins inside the property. Airbnb says cleaning tasks that require significant time or effort should remain the responsibility of cleaning staff.
The changes will also affect other house rules. Hosts will no longer be allowed to introduce additional requirements after a booking has been confirmed. All rules must be disclosed in the listing in advance.
In addition, hosts will be prohibited from imposing their own fines on guests or restricting access to amenities included in the booking.
Airbnb will continue to allow hosts to set rules on smoking, pets, events and quiet hours.
The company will also permit exceptions based on local conditions. For example, in areas facing water shortages, hosts may ask guests to limit the length of their showers.
For violations, Airbnb may issue warnings, add notices to listings or lower their ranking in search results.
The new policy will apply to bookings made on or after November 20, 2026.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agencyreported that European cities were tightening restrictions on short-term rentals, including properties listed on Airbnb.

Facade of Mexican university building draws on Gothic architecture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:45:28 UTC
04:45:28 KST

Facade of Mexican university building draws on Gothic architecture
Mexican studio Jonathan Corral Arquitectos has completed an educational building called the UAD Alamedas Tower, which features a faceted facade that takes cues from stained-glass windows found in Gothic cathedrals.
The building is part of the Universidad Durango Santander, or UAD, a private institution with campuses in several Mexican states.
For its Durango location, the university acquired a site overlooking Las Alamedas, a prominent, tree-lined promenade that stretches through the heart of the city.
Responding to this context was a key concern for the building’s designer, local studio Jonathan Corral Arquitectos.
“The project establishes its relationship with this setting through an intermediate condition – an architecture with a clear urban presence, whose scale and materiality engage with the existing landscape,” said the team.
Triangular in plan, the 7,987-square-metre building contains eight levels and a basement.
A variety of spaces are found in the building, including classrooms, studios, meeting rooms, auditoriums, offices, a cafeteria and a courtroom for mock trials, among other spaces. The school offers courses in law, architecture, medicine, sciences, communication technologies and gastronomy.
On the exterior, the building appears as multiple structures given the use of varying facade treatments.
Along the main elevation, which faces north, one portion is clad in grey fibre-cement panels, while another is lined with a black metal screen.
The central portion features a glazed elevator and a faceted curtain wall with dark mullions and triangular panes of glass – a design that draws upon Gothic architecture.
“The large glazed surface of the facade draws on the compositional logic of the Gothic stained-glass window, translating it into a contemporary urban scale,” the team said.
While the front elevation is meant to be transparent, the rear wall is more opaque. It has grey cladding and short, horizontal windows.
The main entrance is fronted by a broad stone staircase that doubles as a plaza. The building is elevated above grade to help protect from potential flooding, the team said.
Visitors enter a full-height atrium, ringed by walkways with frosted glass railings. The atrium is meant to establish “visual continuity” between the interior spaces and the adjacent promenade.
“From within, the urban landscape is framed by different levels and circulation routes, keeping the context a constant presence throughout the building experience,” the team said.
The lobby features a sunken plaza wrapped in black marble and a suspended staircase, which acts as a sculptural element.
The building’s structural elements were left exposed in many areas.
The building’s basement – which contains digital research and consultation space – has exposed concrete walls and flooring.
On the top level – which holds three auditoriums – a pine-lattice ceiling is meant to be “in dialogue with exposed structures and ducts, as well as steel railings”.
“Rather than concealing the logic of construction, the solution allows structure and program to share a common architectural expression,” the team said.
The building is topped with a rooftop terrace, where people can gather and take in views of the city.
Other university projects in Mexico include a business school by a team of architects in the city of Aguascalientes, which features courtyards and lush gardens, and a Tatiana Bilbao-designed biotechnology building in Mexico City that is composed of irregularly stacked glass boxes.
Project credits:
Design architect: Jonathan Corral Contreras Design team: Heriberto Díaz Ortega, Aida Uribe, Sergio Cisneros, Osvaldo Medina, Julio Rodriguez
Contractor: Forum Constructura, Martin Soriano Villanueva, Fernando Soriano Villanueva
Structural engineering: Jesús González Flores
Photography by Recording Architecture (unless stated otherwise)

He traveled to Russia for love, then ended up in prison for spying: 'They stole my life'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:45:26 UTC
04:45:26 KST

Two separate espionage cases came to light in Europe on Thursday against the backdrop of the ongoing war between Russia and Ukraine. In Germany, a Ukrainian national was arrested on suspicion of working for Russian intelligence and gathering sensitive information about Europe's defense industry and NATO military facilities. Meanwhile, a Reuters investigation revealed how Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB) allegedly staged the arrest of a young Romanian man convicted of spying for Ukraine, months after he had already been taken into custody.
German prosecutors said the Ukrainian suspect, identified as Vadim Y., was arrested in the eastern state of Brandenburg. According to prosecutors, he had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service through an intermediary since at least July 2025. His activities allegedly included gathering military intelligence on the production of armored vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as military personnel and facilities in areas intended to protect NATO's eastern flank.
German media reported that the suspect is 53 years old and lives in Eisenhüttenstadt, in eastern Germany. According to "Der Spiegel," one of his targets was a German armored brigade scheduled to be stationed in Lithuania as part of NATO's preparations against the Russian threat. The brigade is expected to become fully operational by the end of 2027, with approximately 4,800 soldiers and 200 civilian employees. Its deployment is one of Germany's flagship initiatives to strengthen the alliance's eastern flank.
Some of the information collected by the suspect was publicly available. However, German prosecutors said he also approached people working in Europe's defense industry in an effort to obtain additional details. According to the German newspaper "Bild," officers from the Federal Criminal Police Office arrested him following intelligence provided by Germany's domestic intelligence agency.
The suspect is expected to appear Friday before an investigating judge at the Federal Court of Justice, who will present the arrest warrant and determine whether he should remain in custody pending further proceedings. German authorities have not released additional details about his identity or the extent of the information he allegedly managed to pass to Russia.
'They took me out of prison and staged an arrest'
Alongside the arrest in Germany, a Reuters investigation published Thursday uncovered another case, this time involving Russia's accusations that a foreign national had been spying for Ukraine.
At the center of the investigation is David Adrian Kercso, a 23-year-old Romanian citizen who grew up in England and traveled to the Black Sea coast in 2024 to pursue a romantic relationship with a woman he had met online. His journey ended with his arrest, his transfer into the custody of Russia's FSB and a 15-year prison sentence for espionage.
In a video released by the FSB, a young man wearing a blue wool hat and carrying an Adidas backpack is seen walking along a path in a park. Suddenly, two security officers emerge from a van, tackle him and pin him to the ground. A voice in the background asks him in English for his name, while a gloved hand turns his face toward the camera. The young man identifies himself as David Adrian Kercso and says he is from Romania.
But a Reuters investigation found that the footage, presented by Russian state media as the moment of the suspect's arrest, was not filmed during his actual detention. An analysis of the video, compared with Russian court records, showed that Kercso had already been in custody for months when it was filmed.
His story began in late 2023, when he was living in Reading, west of London, and working for an electronics recycling company. Around that time, he met a woman named Valeria online. She lived in Abkhazia, a breakaway region of Georgia controlled by pro-Russian separatists since the early 1990s.
The two began a long-distance relationship, and in August 2024, Kercso traveled through Turkey to meet her. Family members said they met in the Russian city of Sochi before crossing into Abkhazia a few days later. He remained in the region for several months, but their relationship deteriorated, partly because he was running out of money, and he eventually decided to return home.
His mother, Julia Kercso, told Reuters that she had tried to prevent her son from making the dangerous trip. "I told him to not go there because it's very dangerous, because it's a war," " she said. "And he never listened to me yet."
Kercso was supposed to return to England on November 28, 2024, but he disappeared that day. He stopped answering calls and messages, leaving his family with no information about his whereabouts. In letters he later sent from prison, he claimed that he had been arrested in Abkhazia that same day.
About two weeks after his disappearance, on December 13, 2024, the separatist authorities in Abkhazia announced his arrest and released a video showing him being escorted by local security officers. In another recording, he appeared to confess to having contact with Ukrainian intelligence and receiving instructions to photograph military facilities in Abkhazia using a drone.
However, in letters sent to his family from prison, Kercso claimed the confession was false. He said his captors forced him to memorize a script they had dictated and promised that if he repeated it on camera he would be released and allowed to return home. Instead, after the recording, he was taken to the border and handed over to Russian FSB officers.
The day after the Abkhazian video was published, on December 14, Kercso appeared before a judge at a court in Sochi. Court documents examined by Reuters show that over the following four months, he made 10 court appearances, during which his detention was repeatedly extended.
Despite that documented custody, Russian authorities later released another video purportedly showing the moment of his arrest. In his letters, Kercso claimed that in mid-April 2025 FSB officers woke him shortly before dawn, removed him from prison and drove him to a nearby location in Sochi to film the staged arrest.
Reuters investigators identified the filming location in a park along the Matsesta River in Sochi by comparing details visible in the video, including streetlights, trees, a bridge and a wall, with satellite imagery and archival photographs. The green vegetation visible at the location indicated that the footage was filmed after the beginning of spring, rather than before his documented arrest in December.
Russian lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov, who is familiar with the case, told Reuters that staged arrest videos are not unusual in the activities of Russia's security services. He said that in dozens of previous cases, detainees who had already been held for months were taken to streets, forests and train stations to film dramatic footage supposedly showing their arrests.
'I was blinded by love and didn't see the warning signs'
Kercso claims that during his detention in Russia he was beaten, held in solitary confinement and tortured. Reuters stressed that it could not independently verify those allegations. The news agency was also unable to examine and verify the full body of evidence presented in the espionage case.
When Kercso was sentenced, the FSB announced that he had provided a Ukrainian intelligence agency with information about the locations of Russian air defense systems in Sochi during the summer of 2024. The Russian security service also released a video in which he appeared to confess to the charges, but Kercso maintains that this confession, too, was coerced.
"None of that happened, they stole my life for no reason and fabricated everything," he wrote in a letter from prison.
Since his arrest, Kercso has learned to speak Russian. He says he misses his family deeply and dreams of returning home. He now hopes to appeal his conviction.
"Now I know that coming here was a huge mistake," he said. "I was blinded by love and didn't see the warning signs."
The FSB did not respond to Reuters' questions, including why it had published footage purporting to show the arrest of a man who had already been in its custody for months.
The security service of the separatist authorities in Abkhazia, the Russian Embassy in London and the foreign ministries of Romania and Ukraine also did not respond. Reuters also attempted to contact Valeria, the woman with whom Kercso had been romantically involved, but received no reply.

Opinion | Who Wants to Be a Victim in the Wild West Bank?

====================================================================================================

China, Djibouti Express ‘Serious Concern’ Over Threats to Red Sea Shipping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:45:00 UTC
04:45:00 KST

Djibouti’s Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar is visiting China from October 19 to 25. On October 21, he held a meeting with his counterpart and host, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi. According to a spokesperson from China’s Foreign Ministry, “They had an in-depth exchange of views on the Horn of Africa situation and the safety of shipping lanes across the Red Sea.”
The Red Sea is under siege – a major concern for Djibouti, which sits on the Horn of Africa, at the junction between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden.
For most of 2026, the world has been focused on another crucial waterway: the Strait of Hormuz, a transit route for around one-fourth of all global crude oil shipments and one-fifth of the world’s LNG. Israel and the U.S. began strikes against Iran on February 28; Iran retaliated in part by shutting down shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Traffic through the strait has been constrained ever since.
In response, Saudi Arabia began rerouting some its oil via pipeline to the Red Sea. Saudi oil shipments on this route jumped nearly fivefold, going from 1 million to 4.9 million barrels per day. But new attacks by the Houthis, Iran-backed militants that occupy much of Yemen, are now jeopardizing that shipping. Starting in September, the Houthis began a concerted effort to seize control of the Bab al Mandeb Strait, the body of water between Yemen and Djibouti and a crucial chokepoint for shipping via the Red Sea.
While Yemeni government forces have taken back much of the territory, the threat to shipping remains high. A Washington Post article, citing “Iranian officials and diplomats in the region,” said that Iran saw the weeks before the U.S. midterm elections on November 3 as a “critical window” for weakening U.S. President Donald Trump. Iran is accordingly stepping up attack in the Strait of Hormuz – and may have the Houthis do the same in the Red Sea.
That leaves regional states like Djibouti to reckon with the fallout.
China, as the world’s largest exporter, has a direct stake in the outcome as well. Wang and Omar not only discussed the shipping threat during their talks but issued an entire joint communique on the subject.
Unfortunately, there’s not much new in the document. It serves more as a vehicle for both countries to express their concerns than an attempt to offer concrete solutions.
Djibouti and China agreed that “the recent escalation of tensions in the Red Sea poses a serious threat to the global economy, particularly to economic activities in the Horn of Africa region, including trade, investment, energy, and food security.” But they also made it clear that the onus is on other countries to solve the issue. “Both sides believe that easing tensions in the Middle East is key to resolving the security challenges in the Horn of Africa and the Red Sea,” the statement declared. In other words, this is ultimately a problem for Israel, Iran, and the United States to tackle.
The joint statement called on “all parties” involved to “take concrete actions through dialogue and diplomacy to address the serious challenges facing the Middle East, the Red Sea, and the Horn of Africa, preventing the escalation or further complication of regional tensions.” There’s no indication that either China or Djibouti will take new steps to facilitate that “dialogue and diplomacy.”
“The Horn of Africa must never be used as a geopolitical arena, and the flames of war in the Middle East must never be brought to the Horn of Africa,” the statement avowed. How China or Djibouti plan to prevent exactly that outcome is left unsaid, other than Djibouti’s enthusiastic backing for China’s vague and largely unactionable peace plans for both the Middle East and “African hotspots.”
The reason for China’s concern is obvious. The Red Sea is a vital shipping link for Chinese exports to Europe, especially with the Strait of Hormuz looking increasingly unstable. That was highlighted during President Xi Jinping’s visit to Egypt in early September. Egypt controls the Suez Canal, which links the Red Sea to the Mediterranean – and Europe. China has already plowed over $5 billion into the Suez Canal Economic Zone in Egypt.
On the southern end of the Red Sea, China also has a lot invested in Djibouti specifically. The state-owned firm China Merchants Group helped build Djibouti’s Doraleh Multipurpose Port project, to the tune of $590 million. Separately, CMG has a 23.5 percent stake in the Port of Djibouti.
China also funded and built the Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway, to give landlocked Ethiopia another trading route for its exports. And let’s not forget that Djibouti hosts China’s first overseas military facility, whose stated purpose is to provide logistics for Chinese anti-piracy patrols in the region.
During their talks, Wang told Omar that China will “support” Djibouti “in building itself into a regional hub for trade, logistics, and connectivity.” But Djibouti’s ambitions – and China’s billions in investments – have little hope if the Red Sea is closed to shipping by militant attacks.

Wallaroos great inspired by mantra 'you can't be what you can't see'

Retiring Wallaroos great Emily Chancellor inspired by mantra 'you can't be what you can't see'
In short:
Emily Chancellor says making the Wallaroos more visible was a career goal.
Chancellor will play her 42nd and final Test this evening.
What's next?
The Wallaroos face Scotland at Canberra Stadium in the last Test of their 2026 season.
As Emily Chancellor runs out for her final Test, she will know she has fulfilled one of her ambitions as a Wallaroos representative.
Upon making her Test debut in 2018, Chancellor wanted to help increase the visibility of the Wallaroos among young fans.
Even though she followed rugby growing up, the Wallaroos were not on her radar as the women's game lacked adequate support and promotion.
Chancellor only began playing as a 21-year-old university student, admitting earlier this week "rugby wasn't an option" during her childhood.
At Canberra Stadium this evening, there will be young girls among the spectators eagerly watching the Wallaroos play Scotland.
They will be cheering on their heroes and dreaming of playing for the national women's rugby team, proving Chancellor has taken giant steps in accomplishing her mission.
"You can't be what you can't see," Chancellor told ABC Sport on the eve of her Test farewell.
"I feel like that is something that has driven me so hard; to want to keep playing and pushing the image of the Wallaroos to a wider audience.
"I feel like I've had a positive impact on that over the last eight years. I love seeing the kids in the crowd, with their parents, excited.
"What excites me is that there has been so much growth when I look back over the last eight years, considering where I was when I was a kid and the visibility of the game in the women's world [at the time].
"It's come so far. I'm really proud of where we've got to and how many young girls are turning up to games."
Tight bond
After 42 Tests, Chancellor will leave the game as a Wallaroos great.
The 35-year-old appeared in two World Cups and captained the team during the 2025 season.
A stellar domestic career with the NSW Waratahs and stints playing club rugby in the UK and Japan are also among her most cherished experiences.
Aside from her on-field achievements, nothing means more to Chancellor than the tight bond she enjoys with her Wallaroos teammates.
She describes the close-knit squad as a "sisterhood".
"We're all struggling or thriving with the challenges rugby faces, particularly in the women's space," said Chancellor, who will start at openside flanker against Scotland.
"Be it pay, the lack of professionalism, or the striving for both of those things, I think that bonds you together massively."
'Limitless' future
The Wallaroos's semi-professional status has made it difficult for the squad to compete with the likes of England and New Zealand, both of which benefit from having full-time programs.
The Wallaroos are in the process of becoming full-time in the build-up to the 2029 World Cup, which will be hosted by Australia.
Chancellor believes the team's opportunities will be "limitless" when this is finally achieved.
"You see how much natural ability the girls have, how much we do with so little in terms of game time at the moment," she said.
"I get excited by what Rugby Australia did with the Aussie women's sevens team when they went full-time.
"A bit more hard work and time together … wow, I think it will be exciting."
Chancellor will be enjoying retirement once the next World Cup rolls around, but her commitment to the Wallaroos's cause shows no signs of diminishing.
The drive to increase visibility of the Wallaroos and women's rugby will remain.
"We've still got a long way to go, and I don't plan on letting up on that goal of making it as visible as possible when I step away from playing," she said.

External evaluators find flaws in OpenAI’s AI monitoring system in pilot review

External evaluators find flaws in OpenAI’s AI monitoring system in pilot review
- METR and Redwood Research found flaws in OpenAI’s AI monitoring system during a July 21 to Aug 11 pilot review. They said an exploit could hide hundreds of agent actions from monitoring.
- The evaluators also found a possible way for OpenAI’s Codex agents to bypass security limits and use users’ full permissions. OpenAI said it has patched the issues in production safeguards.
- The review gave outside researchers deep access to OpenAI’s internal code, documents and staff. The groups said future evaluations should be more transparent, while OpenAI said the findings will shape later research.
AI generated
NEW YORK - AI safety evaluators METR and Redwood Research found several new vulnerabilities in OpenAI’s internal system, including an exploit agents could have used to keep hundreds of their actions from being monitored, in a pilot review earlier this year.
The exercise, conducted from July 21 to Aug 11, gave outside researchers “a deep level of access” to OpenAI’s internal infrastructure for so-called embedded evaluations, the safety nonprofits said on Oct 22.
METR and Redwood said they each sent one researcher, tested an arrangement giving access to OpenAI’s internal code, documentation and some technical staff. Both were accompanied on site and used OpenAI-issued devices that “never left the premises”.
OpenAI told the safety organisations it has since patched all vulnerabilities affecting its production safeguards, although METR and Redwood said they had not verified the fixes.
AI labs, experts and the Trump administration have touted independent evaluation by outside reviewers as a way to safely advance the technology without slowing its development.
However, AI companies are worried that evaluator staff working inside the companies’ walls could take proprietary information to rivals, Reuters reported earlier this month.
While OpenAI received a full 61-page internal report, METR and Redwood said they agreed to publish only a broad summary publicly, and gave OpenAI the right to redact sensitive information.
Unlike in some previous evaluations, they could not independently disclose those redactions, but said they expected greater transparency in future evaluations.
The researchers also identified a potential way for OpenAI’s Codex agents to bypass security restrictions and act with their users’ full permissions.
The evaluators assessed the monitoring system as it existed on and before July 21, and noted that OpenAI was expanding the system during the exercise.
OpenAI said the “findings helped strengthen safeguards as we expanded the system and will help shape future research collaborations with METR and other third-party evaluators.” REUTERS

Why Kyiv is skeptical of Trump’s renewed peace negotiations with Russia and Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:38:56 UTC
04:38:56 KST

On October 20, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and representatives of European countries in Oslo, where he presented his proposals for a peace settlement to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
Speaking at a press conference after the talks, Zelensky said Ukraine and the West had “clear ideas about how to achieve peace.” One was to arrange a three-way meeting between President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Zelensky himself “to resolve issues that only leaders can address.”
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who also attended the meeting, said the talks had yielded “real progress on two levels”: in the short term and “in the broader context.” He said the discussion focused on key issues: air defense, energy facilities, and the possibility of a partial ceasefire.
Sources told Axios that participants in the Oslo meeting focused on developing a framework agreement to end the war that they could propose to Russia.
Axios reported that the parties made “meaningful progress” and reached “a full mutual understanding at the working level” on the next steps. Sources also told Axios that Jared Kushner, the U.S. special envoy for peace and the president’s son-in-law, again asked Ukraine at the meeting to stop striking Russian oil refineries.
The following day, Witkoff flew to St. Petersburg, where he met with Putin. Afterward, Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said Moscow was ready to resume three-way talks involving the United States in November.
The Oslo meeting drew little enthusiasm in Kyiv, a source close to the Ukrainian president’s office told Meduza.
The main problem is that Russia continues to insist on recognition of its control over occupied Crimea and the Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions — including areas it does not control.
“For us, this [new round of U.S. talks with Ukraine and Russia] changes nothing, because there’s a consensus here: Ukraine will not give up its territory,” Meduza’s source said:
We’re ready for a ceasefire along the line of contact right now — with security guarantees from the United States [a bilateral agreement between Washington and Kyiv modeled on Article 5 of the NATO treaty]. But Putin doesn’t want to freeze the conflict along the line of contact.
In an October 21 interview with Fox News, Zelensky said he was ready for a ceasefire along the current front lines, provided that further negotiations followed and Ukraine received security guarantees. He was responding to a journalist’s question about a possible peace agreement that would freeze the current front lines and leave “75% or more” of the country’s territory under Kyiv’s control.
In early October, Russia and the United States reached a deal on Russian diesel fuel supplies to U.S. and global markets. In the middle of the month, sources told The New York Times that the Trump administration had proposed to Ukrainian and European officials, including Zelensky, that they resume trade in Russian gas as part of negotiations to end the war. The newspaper reported that Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are promoting the idea.
Meduza’s source declined to say how Kyiv had received the proposal.
In mid-October, the Ukrainian military command reported that drones equipped with Starshield, the military counterpart to Starlink terminals, had begun losing their connections at speeds above 160 kilometers per hour. The military said this had caused several operations to fail.
Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov said that “this cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” referring to the conflict between Zelensky and Trump. The Wall Street Journal reported that relations between Zelensky and Trump were at their “lowest point” since their Oval Office clash in early 2025.
According to Meduza’s source, Starlink in Ukraine does indeed start malfunctioning at 120 kilometers per hour and “no longer works” above 130 kilometers per hour, even though drones need to fly that fast to strike military targets. He declined to explain why this was happening.
In mid-October, Kyiv said that during several Russian strikes, the Ukrainian military had received no attack data from the U.S. satellite system that provides early warning of ballistic missile launches. The United States gave Ukraine access to the system at the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Meduza’s source close to Zelensky’s office confirmed that, at one point, Kyiv had not been receiving U.S. intelligence on “some Russian missile launches.” “Now we can see everything again,” he said.
He said Trump was trying to pressure Ukraine through these actions.
Western media previously reported that the idea of restricting connections based on speed came from SpaceX owner Elon Musk, who proposed it to Trump. Musk denied this.
Meduza’s source close to the president’s office believes that “indirectly, all of this [Trump’s policies] is pushing Zelensky toward a soft capitulation”:
The Americans are pushing Kyiv to accept that it’ll inevitably have to do this, so it’s better to discuss how to [capitulate] at less cost to Ukraine, in exchange for some sort of security guarantees, rather than discuss Ukraine’s terms [for a ceasefire]. They’re offering us investment, reconstruction… It’s hard to say where all this will lead.
Russian comments on American efforts to restart negotiations have also reflected some uncertainty. After Putin’s meeting with Witkoff, a correspondent for Vesti asked Ushakov whether the war was nearing an end. His answer could be read two ways: “I don’t know how much closer we’re getting, but that’s where things are heading.”
Meduza’s source in Kyiv said Russia had stepped up its attacks on Ukraine as news of the talks emerged:
In places that used to be relatively quiet — Vinnytsia, Lviv, and Lutsk — attacks have become about 10 times as intense. They’re sending 20 to 30 jet-powered drones there every day. They’re already hitting central Kyiv with Iskander missiles carrying cluster warheads.
The Russians will probably step up their terror attacks on the government district. They’re already hitting bridges. It’s already like Aleppo. For some reason, the Russians keep believing this will get results and Zelensky will agree to terms that amount to capitulation. But people won’t accept that, and neither will the government.
After Witkoff’s departure, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles on the night of October 21–22. One person was killed in Kyiv and more than 20 were injured. Commenting on the attack, Zelensky said it showed there had been no “real changes in [Russia’s] attitude toward everything that is happening.”
Ukraine, in turn, launched drone strikes on several Russian regions that same night, including Moscow and the surrounding Moscow region. Two people were injured in New Moscow.
Meduza’s source believes that despite U.S. pressure and Russia’s intensified attacks on Ukraine, Zelensky “will keep trying to salvage something from even the worst situation until the very end” — “that’s just who he is.”
Volodymyr Fesenko, head of Ukraine’s Penta Center for Applied Political Studies, sees the resumption of talks as a positive development in itself: “Bad negotiations with little chance of success are better than no negotiations.”
Fesenko called Russia’s agreement to resume three-way meetings a tactical move and “a continuation of its efforts to court Trump.” In his view, Russia’s willingness to participate in this format does not, in itself, mean there is any substantive discussion yet about ending the war:
If the Trump administration keeps using its current approach (continually making concessions to Russia upfront and trying to draw it into peace talks with more gifts — what Witkoff is doing), this strategy has no chance of success. Unfortunately, it will only fuel the war.
In Fesenko’s view, the main problem with the current negotiations is the lack of “clear signs that Russia is actually ready to negotiate an end to hostilities.” He believes the Kremlin will not engage seriously in negotiations until Moscow understands that it cannot win the war:
Ukraine is short of air defense systems, and Russia’s advantage in ballistic missiles gives it the upper hand in the air war. Putin hopes to break Ukraine this winter by using airstrikes to destroy its energy infrastructure and economy. If Ukraine makes it through the winter, and if the imbalance in the air war can be reduced at least somewhat, the chances of real negotiations will improve.
Commentary from Meduza’s Explainers desk
Ukraine and Russia have long accused each other of having no real desire to end the war. Both Kyiv and Moscow insist that the war can end only on their own terms.
- Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said he is ready to negotiate only after Ukrainian forces leave the Donbas — either voluntarily or as a result of a Russian military operation. The Kremlin has not publicly stated its official position on the territory of the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions, which are listed as Russian regions in Russia’s Constitution. However, according to leaks to Western media, at the Anchorage summit, Putin and Trump discussed dividing the two regions along the current line of contact. “Once Ukrainian troops leave the territories they hold, the fighting will stop. If they don’t leave, we will achieve this by force,” Putin said in November 2025. The Kremlin’s official position has not changed since then.
- Kyiv insists that the only possible basis for a ceasefire is freezing the current lines of control along the front, including in the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. Zelensky believes Russia will not be able to seize by force all the territory that remains under Ukrainian military control.

Israel’s Ben-Gvir shares AI videos mocking Gazans as ‘donkeys’ and sending them to Paris
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.

Issued on:
Israel’s far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir is using AI-generated videos to mock Palestinians and push political messages ahead of the country’s election, including videos magically transporting Gazans to Paris or calling them "donkeys" for choosing to stay. One video has sparked an online spat with France. AI is playing a growing role in the campaign, with parties using deepfakes, bots and AI-generated content, raising concerns about disinformation and the technology’s influence on voters.
With Israel’s general election looming, several Israeli politicians have been using AI-generated content as campaign videos. Among them is far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, who has recently shared AI-generated videos mocking Palestinians in Gaza and depicting a fictional journey transporting a Gazan to Paris.
One video portrays Gaza in 2030 as a ghost town, with homes, schools and infrastructure destroyed. A donkey then appears alongside a message from Ben-Gvir’s party: “You’d have to be a donkey to stay in Gaza.”
The video appears to reference Ben-Gvir’s so-called “voluntary emigration” plan, which advocates encouraging Palestinians to leave the enclave and move abroad.
Another AI-generated video shows an elderly Palestinian man sitting among rubble, wearing a traditional keffiyeh. After rubbing a magic lamp, he summons Ben-Gvir and asks for help leaving Gaza. The man is then transported to Paris, where Ben-Gvir tells him: “Here, you’ll feel right at home.”
The video comes amid comments by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu about protests in France. Netanyahu claimed that Muslim migrants were responsible for unrest in the country and warned that, if Israel did not stop Hamas in Gaza, “you’ll see them on the streets of Paris”.
The claims linking the French protests to Muslim migrants have no substantiated evidence, and have previously been examined by Truth or Fake on FRANCE 24.
A public spat with France
Ben-Gvir’s Paris video prompted a response from the French Foreign Ministry, which addressed him through its official “French Response” account on X.
“Imagine having a magic lamp and wasting your wish on Ben-Gvir. Even magic can’t lift his ban from entering France,” the ministry wrote. The message referred to France’s decision to bar Ben-Gvir from entering the country last May, following his treatment of activists aboard a Gaza-bound aid flotilla.
Ben-Gvir responded with another AI-generated video, in which he speaks French and accuses France of welcoming the consequences of its support for a Palestinian state.The video includes an AI-generated image of a devastated Paris, with Palestinian flags across the city and a keffiyeh draped over the Eiffel Tower.
The exchange comes amid a wider wave of misleading and AI-generated imagery attempting to connect unrest in France with immigration, Muslims and Palestine, despite the protests having domestic political and social causes.
AI reshapes Israel’s election campaign
Ben-Gvir’s videos are part of a broader trend in Israeli politics, where AI-generated content is playing an increasingly prominent role ahead of the election.
Political analysts have described the upcoming vote as the first “AI-driven election”, with major parties using the technology in a variety of ways.
An analysis by Deutsche Welle’s fact-checking team found that leading Israeli political parties had incorporated AI into their campaigns. Posts by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party used AI in a quarter of the content analysed.
Israel’s Election Commission requires AI-generated or AI-modified campaign content to be labelled, though aside from that, there's not much regulation regarding AI's use in the election race.
However, concerns extend beyond the use of synthetic images and videos. AI-powered robocalls have also been used to contact voters and ask about their voting preferences, offering a cheaper and more conversational alternative to traditional automated messages. Meanwhile, networks of bots and fake accounts have been found amplifying the campaigns of Netanyahu and Ben-Gvir.
The technology could also influence how voters make their decisions. According to figures cited in DW's reporting, around a quarter of Israelis say they intend to turn to AI for help deciding how to vote, raising questions about how chatbots generate political responses and whether online campaigning can influence their answers. DW's analysis found that Israeli government promotional material was already being published online with the stated aim of influencing how AI chatbots respond.

The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government said Thursday that it intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by Yemen’s Houthi group toward Najran in southwestern Saudi Arabia, near the border with Yemen.

The coalition also reaffirmed Saudi Arabia’s commitment to Yemen’s security and stability and its opposition to attempts to exploit Yemeni tribes or drag them into conflicts.
The incident comes amid renewed military escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition since July, with both sides exchanging attacks.
Earlier Thursday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed that the group had launched four missile and drone attacks against targets in Saudi Arabia over the previous 48 hours, including facilities in Riyadh, Dammam, Yanbu and Abha.
Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognized government against the Houthis since March 2015.

Republican Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine has denounced a controversial ad featuring the estranged mother of Dr. Amy Acton, taking sides with the Jewish Democratic candidate for governor and former member of his Cabinet over her Republican rival, Vivek Ramaswamy.
At a gathering with reporters at the Ohio Statehouse, DeWine — recalling the painful experiences of rape victims he dealt with as a county prosecutor and state attorney general — called the ad “deeply, deeply troubling.”
“It’s wrong to run this ad,” he said. “And, even at this late time — my wife, Fran, saw the ad just run this morning on TV — I would just urge the Ramaswamy campaign to take this down.”
The term-limited DeWine’s remarks place him at odds with Ramaswamy, whom he has endorsed. The biotech entrepreneur and 2024 presidential candidate has taken responsibility for the 60-second video and is spending $4 million to broadcast it online and on TV.
If elected, Acton would become the first woman and the first Jewish person to serve as governor of Ohio. Last month, an armed assailant charged toward Acton during a campaign stop at a central Ohio city fair. 
DeWine stops short of pulling his endorsement
But the governor stopped short of pulling his backing of the Republican for now. DeWine recalled a previous line of attack by the Acton campaign had mentioned Ramaswamy’s mother and said that also was wrong — “family members have always historically been off limits” — though he noted it was never used in a multimillion-dollar ad campaign.
That critique from the summer cited an investigative report into Geetha Ramaswamy’s role at a pharmaceutical company run by her son, who Acton and Democrats described as “hiring his own mother to manipulate clinical trial data.”
The Ramaswamy campaign called those claims “slanderous” and said he’s being held to a different standard than Acton and other Democrats who have attacked Republicans’ families.
“Governor DeWine is correct that the first and only candidate to attack the mother of her opponent in this race was Amy Acton,” spokesperson Connie Luck said in a statement, adding: “We refuse to accept the media’s double standards.”
Ohio Republicans divided over the ad
By chiming in, DeWine has entered the fray of a growing rift among Ohio Republicans over the advertisement — as both the governor’s race and a race for U.S. Senate appear far tighter than expected in a state Donald Trump won handily three times. The video features Acton’s birth mother, Donna Arthur, calling her “a liar” and insinuating she has mental health issues.
Acton, Ohio’s COVID-19-era health director, has made no secret of facing homelessness and abuse as a child. Arthur lost custody of her children after their stepfather, Arthur’s husband, was indicted on a charge of rape involving Acton. Acton’s campaign on Tuesday posted a video of her brother, who supported her backstory about living in a tent and being abused.
Republican Vice President JD Vance, an Ohio native son, expressed disgust during an Ohio campaign swing Wednesday with Republicans “whining” about the ad as low and in poor taste. But Republican U.S. Sen. Jon Husted, DeWine’s former lieutenant governor — running in a tight retention race against Democrat Sherrod Brown — has said he would not have run the ad, as has Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose, who is running for state auditor.
Another influential Ohio Republican, former U.S. Rep. Jim Renacci, posted a lengthy essay on X overnight, suggesting that “the floor may have just fallen out from under the Republican campaign for Ohio Governor” and urging every Republican to distance themselves from it.
Amid the turmoil, Ohio Republican Party Chairman Alex Triantafilou posted what sounded like a warning, or a threat.
“The final days of a tough campaign are always the best time to find out who is really with you and who just posts and pretends,” he wrote. “Yes—we are keeping score.” The quote was followed by a winking-eye emoji.
Ad has faced bipartisan rebukes, support in conservative media
The ad is also dividing Republicans nationally.
Nikki Haley, who sparred with Ramaswamy during the 2024 Republican presidential primary over the personal nature of his attacks, called him “a bad guy” in a social media post Tuesday. “It’s a shame he continues to get away with it,” she wrote.
At the same time, Media Matters for America, a left-leaning media watchdog group, has reported that many within the national conservative media are promoting and praising the ad. Ramaswamy’s campaign manager, Jonathan Ewing, characterized it as “a campaign-ending moment for Amy Acton.”
Wayne Allyn Root, of Gateway Pundit, called it “absolutely hilarious” and Daily Wire host Michael Knowles described it as “brilliant.”
Police and court records show Cledith Arthur was arrested and charged with the rape of Acton in July 1978, when she was 12, after her biological father lodged a formal complaint against him. The abuse allegedly happened from December 1976 to April 1978. Cledith Arthur failed to show for a court appearance and became a fugitive.
Donna Arthur remained married to him until his death in 2004.

At least 4 Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza

At least four Palestinians were killed and several others wounded Thursday in Israeli airstrikes and gunfire across the Gaza Strip, Palestinian medical officials said, as renewed attacks threatened to further undermine an already fragile cease-fire agreement.
The deaths were reported in separate incidents in Gaza City, Khan Younis, central Gaza and the northern Jabalia area, while Israeli forces continued shelling residential neighborhoods and areas sheltering displaced families.
In Gaza City, an Israeli drone struck a vehicle in the southwestern Tel al-Hawa neighborhood, killing at least one Palestinian and wounding others, including one person who sustained serious injuries, medical sources told Anadolu Agency.
The Interior Ministry said the attack killed a noncommissioned officer from its drug control police department and wounded another officer as they returned from an assignment.
Images from the scene showed emergency crews attempting to extinguish flames engulfing the vehicle as residents gathered nearby.
In the northern Gaza Strip, Israeli gunfire killed a Palestinian near the Jabalia refugee camp, according to medical sources. Initial reports differed on the victim's age, with one identifying the person as a girl and another as a woman.
In southern Gaza, an Israeli drone struck a motorcycle in Khan Younis, killing a Palestinian man and injuring two others, medical officials said.
Another Palestinian man was killed in a separate Israeli strike near the Nuseirat refugee camp in central Gaza, bringing the reported death toll from Thursday's attacks to at least four.
The Israeli military said it had targeted Hamas militants in Khan Younis, Nuseirat and Gaza City but was unaware of the reported shooting in Jabalia.
The military's account could not be independently reconciled with Palestinian reports of the casualties.
Israeli artillery fire also struck a school sheltering displaced Palestinians in Khan Younis, wounding four members of the same family, according to Palestinian medical and local sources.
A medical source at Nasser Hospital said a man, his wife and their two children were admitted with injuries of varying severity after a shell hit a tent in the courtyard of Mustafa Hafez School.
The school had been serving as a shelter for Palestinians displaced by the prolonged Israeli military offensive.
Witnesses also reported heavy gunfire from Israeli military vehicles targeting areas near residential buildings and tents housing displaced families east of Hamad City in Khan Younis.
In Gaza City, Israeli forces carried out additional attacks on residential properties early Thursday.
Witnesses said an Israeli helicopter struck an evacuated apartment in the Rimal neighborhood, while a drone targeted an empty house in the Nasr neighborhood that had already sustained damage in previous Israeli bombardment.
Israeli forces also continued demolishing residential buildings in the eastern Tuffah and Shujaiya neighborhoods.
Residents reported hearing two powerful explosions overnight and early Thursday as demolition operations continued.
Israeli artillery also shelled areas near the Al-Sanafour junction east of Tuffah, accompanied by heavy gunfire from military vehicles positioned nearby.
The latest attacks come amid growing tensions over the implementation of the U.S.-brokered cease-fire agreement that took effect on Oct. 10, 2025.
Palestinian authorities have repeatedly accused Israel of violating the agreement through continued airstrikes, artillery attacks and gunfire across the enclave.
According to figures reported by Palestinian authorities as of Wednesday, Israeli attacks since the cease-fire began had killed 1,538 Palestinians and wounded 5,498 others.
Israel, meanwhile, has accused Hamas of attempting to rebuild its military capabilities and carrying out attacks in violation of the agreement.
Hamas has denied the accusations, rejecting claims that it has sought to launch new attacks or rearm, and has accused Israel of undermining the cease-fire through continued military operations.
The Israeli military has intensified strikes in recent weeks, further raising concerns about the durability of the truce.
Israeli authorities say four Israeli soldiers have been killed since the cease-fire took effect.
Although the agreement was intended to pave the way for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, negotiations over key provisions have made little progress.
Disagreements over the disarmament of Hamas and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the territory have prevented the sides from reaching a comprehensive arrangement for the next stages of the agreement.
The continued hostilities have also complicated efforts to restore essential services and rebuild civilian infrastructure devastated during more than three years of war.
Since October 2023, Israeli military operations have killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 others in Gaza, according to Palestinian authorities.
Local authorities estimate that approximately 90% of the enclave's civilian infrastructure has been destroyed or damaged during the offensive.
Israel launched its military campaign following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, which killed approximately 1,200 people, according to Israeli figures.
Despite the cease-fire, recurring Israeli attacks and the lack of progress on unresolved political and security issues continue to leave Gaza's population facing widespread displacement, destruction and uncertainty.

White evangelical support for Trump slips but still strong as midterms near

Unknown Publisher

04:31:47 KST

White evangelical support for Trump slips but still strong as midterms near
A new poll finds white evangelicals still outpace other demographic groups in supporting Trump, as he rallies the Republican base.
United States President Donald Trump’s support among white evangelical Protestant voters remains strong but has slipped since he retook office in January 2025, according to a new poll.
A survey released this month by the news agency Reuters and research firm Ipsos found that Trump’s support among the group had tumbled to 63 percent, down from 77 percent at the time of his second inauguration.
The shift comes as Trump’s approval rating drops to an all-time low of 31 percent.
White evangelicals are considered a key Republican demographic, and the decline could prove significant during the midterm elections on November 3, when the right-wing party will seek to defend its majorities in Congress.
Democrats remain widely favoured to take control of the US House of Representatives in the election. Their chances of flipping the Senate too are increasing amid widespread discontent over affordability and the US-Israeli war on Iran.
But experts say Republicans are counting on their base to counter signs of a Democratic surge at the polls.
On Wednesday, Trump campaigned in South Carolina, located in the southern “Bible Belt”, where exit polls found six in 10 Republican voters were white evangelicals in the 2024 presidential primary.
Trump carried the state by nearly 18 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election, but polls have shown Republican Senate candidate Darline Graham holding only a narrow lead over Democratic challenger Annie Andrews just two weeks ahead of the midterm vote.
As with many of his campaign appearances, Trump focused his South Carolina speech on several social issues that resonate with conservative Christians, including policies related to transgender people. During the rally, he referred to Andrews with an anti-transgender slur.
“She’s a fanatical transgender activist,” Trump said at a different point in his speech, despite Andrews skewing moderate on the issue within the Democratic Party. “How the hell do you run in South Carolina? Am I in a different state?”
Long a key demographic in Trump’s coalition, white evangelicals accounted for nearly a third of Trump’s winning coalition in 2024, according to a Public Religion Research Institute (PRRI) survey and a validated-voter analysis by the nonpartisan Pew Research Center.
The US president has been able to maintain support from key evangelical leaders despite a series of scandals at odds with the conservative values they espouse. Trump has faced allegations of sexual misconduct and extramarital affairs, which he denies.
All told, about 80 percent of white evangelical voters cast their ballots for Trump in the 2024 general election. The demographic makes up about 13 percent of the overall US population.
Beyond states like South Carolina, evangelicals in the Midwestern states of Iowa and Kansas, as well as the Southern state of Texas, could be key to the Republican Party maintaining its hold on the US Senate.
Christian faith leaders are challenging Republicans in several top races, including Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist Church pastor, in Kansas, and James Talarico, a Presbyterian seminarian, in Texas.
Both Hamilton and Talarico represent mainline Protestant denominations, not evangelical ones.
White evangelicals’ voter trends are distinct from other evangelical groups. For example, Black Protestant evangelicals, a vanguard of the US civil rights movement, have remained a key Democratic voting bloc.
Still, support for Trump among evangelicals remains strong compared with other demographic groups.
It remains unclear if shifting attitudes towards Trump would affect conservative turnout during the midterm elections, in which the US president is not on the ballot.
The Reuters news agency noted that white evangelicals were the only demographic it tracks that surpassed 60 percent support for Trump in the final stretch of the midterms.
The drop in support among the group was less pronounced than for Trump’s overall approval rating, tumbling 14 percentage points compared with a 16-point decline among Americans overall.

WHO warns ‘more complex’ Ebola outbreak now present in 3 African countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:31:27 UTC
04:31:27 KST

WHO warns ‘more complex’ Ebola outbreak now present in 3 African countries
Health officials are investigating where Nigeria’s first patient, confirmed this week, was infected.
The World Health Organization (WHO) says the Ebola outbreak that emerged in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is growing more “complex”, with cases now present in countries in East and West Africa.
This comes as health authorities investigate where Nigeria’s first case, which was confirmed this week, originated, raising questions about whether the patient crossed paths with Kenya’s first patient at a Ugandan airport.
“We are facing a more complex outbreak landscape,” Mohamed Janabi, regional director for WHO in Africa, told an online media briefing on Thursday.
Nigeria reported its first case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that was announced in DRC in mid-May and has since killed more than 4,000 people there.
Kenya, DRC and Nigeria all have active or recent cases of the Bundibugyo strain, while Uganda had cases earlier in the year but has since been declared Ebola-free.
The Nigeria patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja. Authorities in Uganda said she had travelled to eastern DRC before transiting through Uganda. But the WHO and Africa’s top health agency said on Thursday they had not received confirmed information that the woman travelled to the DRC.
A Swiss government statement to the Reuters news agency also said the patient is believed to have contracted the disease while travelling in Uganda.
Wessam Mankoula, the head of Emergency Preparedness and Response at the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), said on Thursday that both the first Nigerian case and the first Kenyan case had left Entebbe on October 3, and that a possible encounter between them was under investigation.
Ugandan authorities rejected the suggestion that she was infected in the country. Government spokesman Alan Kasujja told the AFP news agency that it was “preposterous” to link Uganda to the case simply because she had holidayed there.
However, Mankoula said there was no validated information that she had been to DRC, and Jean Kaseya, the Africa CDC director general, said the same. Pavel Ursu, the WHO representative in Nigeria, said the information given to the organisation included no travel outside Uganda.
Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response manager, said on Thursday the source of her infection was still unknown as health authorities were working to piece together her travel history.
Investigators were looking at which Abuja health facilities she visited between the onset of symptoms and her hospitalisation 48 hours later, he added.
An increase in numbers
Kenya’s Ministry of Health confirmed its first case earlier this month and had reported eight more since. Patrick Amoth, the Health Ministry’s director-general, said officials had traced all 135 contacts of the first case.
Nigeria is now tracing 44 contacts, and Mankoula said more had since been identified but did not give a new number.
The current outbreak is the deadliest in DRC’s history, according to the country’s health authorities. It has killed more than 4,000 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases since May.
Neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 confirmed cases, including 15 imported from the DRC, and two deaths, before it was declared Ebola-free in August.
The Africa CDC has warned of an “extremely serious threat”, with the fatality rate in DRC approaching 50 percent.

Quick hits: Bavuma hides from Smith implosion as Boland outgrits batters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:30:31 UTC
04:30:31 KST

Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while nightwatchman Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha.
Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Head passes 100 but can't go on
Travis Head began day five needing 13 runs for a gritty, fighting century.
And after a two-hour rain delay, the punchy southpaw reached three figures with relative ease, bringing up the milestone with two leg-side boundaries against South African destroyer Marco Jansen in the sixth over of the day.
His celebrations were understandably muted given the state of the game, with his helmet staying in place as he raised his bat and a grin not even threatening to peek through his grill.
It was just Head's second overseas ton after his effort in the 2023 World Test Championship final at the Oval against India, and first against a team on its home patch.
But Head was unable to set up for the long haul his team so craved, with the Australian departing just after the first drinks break, chopping on while attempting a cut shot that was never there.
Head was out for 121 and Australia was 5-209.
2. Boland shows batters how it's done
By now, Australian cricket fans should know better than to doubt Scott Boland.
But even the most optimistic of those watching back home surely wouldn't have expected the nightwatchman to outlast both Head and Steve Smith, take his innings deep into the day and soak up a staggering 166 deliveries.
There were a couple of streaky moments, sure, but Boland made his luck more than he rode it, defending with the kind of authority and simplicity his more celebrated batting teammates were so desperately lacking throughout the Test.
He even played a few memorable shots, including an immaculate straight drive back past South Africa spearhead Kagiso Rabada.
But finally, in the second over after tea, Boland's marathon vigil was over, with Wiaan Mulder producing a jagging peach to have the brave nightwatchman bowled through the gate for a new Test best of 40.
3. Bavuma can't watch as Smith throws it away
It was the moment — and didn't Temba Bavuma know it.
The South Africa captain just couldn't watch as Steve Smith top-edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer high into the blue Gqeberha sky, turning his back completely as Matthew Breetzke raced back and settled under the ball.
It was a rash, ugly shot from Smith, and certainly not one befitting of a man tasked with saving a Test match.
But for a moment, it looked like he was going to get away with it.
Having just-about settled underneath the ball, Breetzke juggled once and then twice before securing the wicket that was destined to end the Australian resistance.
Smith, perhaps still struggling with his neck issue from day four, was out for 3 and Australia was 6-255.
4. Mulder does damage after tea
With four wickets still in reserve, Australia reached tea still with a sniff of pulling off one of the great escapes.
But in removing Australia's best two batters, the Proteas had already done the hard part, and there would have been no panic as they readied themselves for the game's final stanza.
And in the opening exchanges of what was being sold as a marathon, 44-over evening session, all-rounder Mulder struck not once, but twice.
First, he ended Boland with that divine off-cutter; then he produced something similarly inspired to send the newly-arrived Pat Cummins packing for 4.
At 8-262, it was all beginning to unravel.
There was only one thing that could save the Aussies now ...
5. South Africa beats descending gloom
All of a sudden, things were beginning to darken in Gqeberha.
With ominous clouds gathering on the outskirts of the oval and ground staff poised to pounce at the boundary rope, the South Africans were in a race with the elements.
Two wickets were needed.
Well aware of the descending gloom, Bavuma threw the ball to his premier spearhead.
And Rabada delivered in the first over of his spell, bowling Mitchell Starc with the tailender attempting an ugly and wholly unnecessary slog.
But with the skies continuing to intimidate, we were treated to surely one of the most farcical drinks breaks in Test history.
Those five lost minutes, however, were not enough to save the Australians.
The heavens never did open, and number 11 Josh Hazlewood was promptly caught behind the wicket, confirming a chastening innings and 31-run defeat for Australia and a richly deserved series-levelling triumph for the South Africans.

Monet’s Iris fetches €50 million at Paris auction

Monet’s Iris fetches €50 million at Paris auction
- Claude Monet’s “Iris” sold for €50 million in Paris, the highest auction price ever for art in France. It had been kept in the Schlumberger family home and was known only from a black-and-white photo.
- The painting was bought by Jeanne Schlumberger and was made in Monet’s later years. Sotheby’s said the sale marked the centenary of Monet’s death, with Paris exhibitions honouring him.
- Three Paul Cezanne works were withdrawn before the auction after a deal to return them to Aix-en-Provence. Christie’s also sold 26 works for €41.6 million, including Monet, Renoir and Picasso pieces.
AI generated
PARIS - Iris, a monumental painting by Impressionist Claude Monet, sold for €50 million (S$70 million) including buyer fees in Paris on Oct 22, becoming the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction in France.
The 1.60m high and 1.8m wide work had never left the billionaire Schlumberger family’s mansion in Paris and was known only through a black-and-white photograph.
It was acquired by Jeanne Schlumberger (1889–1983), according to Thomas Bompard, co-head of the Modern and Contemporary Art Department at Sotheby’s France.
Iris had been estimated at between €22 million and €30 million, “the highest valuation ever given to a painting offered at auction in France,” Sotheby’s noted when presenting the sale.
It was painted by Monet in his twilight years.
Alongside Iris, three other canvases by Monet were included in the sale, among them “Saule Pleureur” (Weeping Willow), valued at €9 million to €12 million.
The sale comes in the year marking the centenary of Monet’s death on Dec 5, 1926, which is being commemorated by two Paris exhibitions – Monet, Painting Time and Stories Of Landscapes, From Monet To Hockney.
Three paintings by Paul Cezanne classified as “national treasures” were withdrawn from the sale a few hours before the auction began “with a view to their return to the artist’s hometown, Aix-en-Provence,” Sotheby’s said.
It followed an agreement between the current owners and the city of Aix-en-Provence, which, with the support of the French culture ministry, is considering acquiring these works.
Another Paris auction by Christie’s on Oct 22 saw 26 works being sold, including two Monet paintings – “Bord des falaises a Pourville”, which went for €12.7 million and “Trois pots de tulipes”, which sold for €3.1 million.
A work by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, “Jeunes filles au bord de la mer,” fetched €5.8 million, while “Nature morte au gruyere” by Pablo Picasso sold for €3 million.
The total amount of Christie’s sale was €41.6 million, buyers fees included. AFP

The hardest part of ending Russia's war is making sure it cannot start it again. As the peace talks have escalated ahead of the US elections, Ukraine is weighing three options for its postwar security.
Among them are NATO membership, direct US guarantees modeled on NATO’s Article 5, and a European “Coalition of the Willing” backed by Washington, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy says, according to UNIAN. But none of them have been agreed to yet.

Three guarantees, none of them signed

Why Zelenskyy says even Russia should want Ukraine in NATO

Star actor who appeared in the films "Top Gun" and "Alien" has died
Kyiv • UNN
Actor Tom Skerritt has died at the age of 93 from natural causes. The Emmy winner became famous for his roles in "Alien," "Top Gun," and "The Fencer's Outpost."
Veteran actor Tom Skerritt, best known for his roles in "Top Gun," "Alien" and the television series "Picket Fences," has died, UNN reports.
According to the actor’s family, the Emmy Award winner died on Wednesday of natural causes.

Skerritt’s Hollywood career spanned six decades, and his major breakthrough came with a role in the 1970 war comedy "M*A*S*H."
