Multipolarity and peace take centre stage at 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:23:30 UTC
04:23:30 KST

The emergence of a multipolar world, Europe’s future role and approaches to ending the war in Ukraine have dominated the opening day of the 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum in Istanbul.
Political, business and academic figures from more than 30 countries gathered at Ciragan Palace on Thursday to discuss how to navigate the changing global order without fuelling further conflict.
Discussions repeatedly returned to the need for dialogue and a new balance of power among the US, Russia, Europe and other global and regional powers.
Türkiye prioritises stability amid global uncertainty
In his opening remarks, Turkish Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said conflicts, supply chain disruptions and rising commodity prices were putting mounting pressure on the global economy.
Türkiye’s response centres on maintaining macro-financial stability and strengthening its resilience to external shocks, he said.
Ankara would maintain a data-dependent, restrictive monetary policy, rebuild fiscal buffers and accelerate its green transformation to reduce reliance on imported primary energy, Simsek added.
He also highlighted Türkiye’s diplomatic role amid growing geopolitical tensions, saying the country benefits from “stability, peace and prosperity” in surrounding regions and continues to invest in mediation and dialogue.
US faces era of 'permanent rivalry'
Speaking at a special session of the forum, Thomas Graham, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and former senior US official on Russia policy, argued that Europe would have to play a central role, while describing the changing international system as an unprecedented challenge for Washington.
"For the first time in history, the United States faces a multipolar order from which it cannot withdraw," Graham said.
The US could no longer dominate the international system as it had during earlier periods, he said, arguing that Washington instead had to adapt to an era of "permanent rivalry" with other major powers.
That would require avoiding direct conflict, particularly given the destructive capacity of modern weapons, while maintaining enough cooperation to address transnational challenges.
Graham said the objective should be to establish regional equilibria in Europe, the Middle East and East Asia that could ultimately underpin a broader Eurasian balance.
He rejected the idea that Washington, Moscow and Beijing could determine the future of the rest of the world among themselves, saying Europe remained a critical part of any such arrangement.
Türkiye's role in emerging multipolar order
Necmeddin Bilal Erdogan, chairman of the Ilim Yayma Foundation, placed Türkiye's growing regional role within the same shift toward a more multipolar international system.
Erdogan said regional actors should be encouraged to take greater responsibility for their own security and future, arguing that those living in a particular region ultimately bear the greatest consequences of instability there.
Türkiye, he said, had sought to play such a role through efforts concerning Syria, Iraq and the Caucasus and its ability to maintain dialogue with competing sides.
Erdogan called for dialogue channels to remain open despite conflicts and political disagreements, saying prejudices and double standards in international affairs were eroding trust between countries.
He argued that both Türkiye and Russia were part of the broader European space and that losing sight of such historical and geographic realities amid current conflicts would make prospects for peace more difficult.
He also linked the debate over international security to wider questions about technological and economic development, questioning the purpose of advances in areas such as artificial intelligence if they failed to contribute to peace, human welfare and greater equality.
'Without Europe there can be no peace'
Romano Prodi, former president of the European Commission and former Italian prime minister, recalled a dramatically different atmosphere in Russia-Europe relations two decades ago, saying cooperation between the two sides had once appeared capable of reaching much further.
The war in Ukraine had since made the divide extremely difficult to overcome, he said, while a succession of conflicts from Ukraine to Sudan, Gaza and Iran had created an increasingly dangerous international environment.
"It is time to change," Prodi said, arguing that Europe had been marginalised amid contacts between Russia and the US, partly because of its own internal divisions and weaknesses.
But excluding the continent from a future settlement would be a mistake, he said.
"Without Europe there can be no peace," Prodi said, stressing the bloc's economic weight, technological capabilities and experience in overcoming historical conflicts.
Referring to discussions about a potential understanding among major powers, Prodi used the analogy of a "little Yalta," suggesting that the world could be moving toward negotiations in which major powers establish new rules for managing relations.
He cautioned, however, that a potential US-Russia energy understanding alone could not resolve broader international problems and that any durable arrangement would also require Europe's participation.
Approaches to ending Ukraine war
The discussions also focused on possible paths toward ending the war in Ukraine.
Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special representative for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries and CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, said Moscow was seeking a permanent end to hostilities and a stable European security architecture rather than temporary ceasefires.
"It's not about temporary ceasefires. It's not about temporary solutions," Dmitriev said, arguing that an interim arrangement could eventually lead to renewed hostilities.
He said recent US-Russia discussions had been positive in this regard and praised efforts by the Trump administration to balance the interests of Russia, Ukraine and Europe in search of a lasting settlement.
Graham said permanent peace could not realistically emerge from a single agreement but would have to develop through a longer process.
"To demand permanent peace as a condition for a ceasefire actually is a call for continued warfare," he said.
He said negotiations could first establish principles and parameters for a future settlement, followed by a ceasefire that would allow detailed talks to continue in a less volatile environment.
Such an outcome would require concessions from both Russia and Ukraine and active European participation, he added.
Dmitriev urges renewed Russia-Europe economic ties
Beyond the Ukraine negotiations, Dmitriev argued that economic ties could eventually help rebuild relations between Russia and Europe.
He said there was "no question" that Russia wanted to and would cooperate with Europe, while criticising European efforts to increase defence spending and rejecting claims that Moscow posed a threat to the continent.
Dmitriev also urged European business leaders to press policymakers more forcefully over restrictions on access to the Russian market and the economic consequences of reduced Russian energy supplies.
In separate remarks during the discussion, he argued that the resumption of broader Russian energy supplies to Europe was ultimately "economically inevitable."
He also said Russia-US economic cooperation could expand beyond energy, pointing to potential collaboration in areas including fertilizers.

Bulgaria: Journalist Hospitalized After Assault by Security Detail Protecting Radev’s Speaker of Parliament (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:20:44 UTC
04:20:44 KST

Journalist Sonya Koltuklieva was hospitalized after a National Protection Service (NSO) officer forcefully threw her to the ground as she tried to question Parliamentary Speaker Mihaela Dotsova outside the headquarters of Prime Minister Rumen Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria party in Sofia, according to footage circulated on social media and reports by the news agency PIK.
The incident occurred on Hristo Botev Boulevard shortly after Radev held an emergency press briefing about a critical European Parliament declaration concerning his policies toward Moscow. Journalists had gathered outside the party headquarters to ask Dotsova about the repeated postponement of parliamentary hearings into pardons granted by Iliaana Yotova while she was vice president.
Koltuklieva asked Dotsova why she had derailed the hearings twice. The Speaker did not respond and quickly entered her official vehicle. As Dotsova shut the door, the PIK reporter approached, filming with her phone and attempting to open it to continue asking questions.
"Why are you afraid? Come out and talk to us," Koltuklieva said.
Video footage shows an NSO officer pushing the journalist away with considerable force and throwing her onto her back. Witnesses nearby shouted in protest, demanding to know what the security personnel were doing and calling them brutes.
Dotsova drove away in her official limousine with its lights and siren activated, without checking on Koltuklieva or offering assistance. Neither the security personnel nor anyone at the party headquarters came to the journalist's aid as she lay motionless on the sidewalk in front of horrified passersby. An ambulance subsequently took her to the Military Medical Academy.
According to PIK, Koltuklieva suffered a concussion, a broken collarbone and a dislocated shoulder. Earlier reports had also indicated a suspected concussion and shoulder dislocation.
The video quickly spread across social media, attracting tens of thousands of views and comments. Journalists condemned the officer’s actions as unacceptable.
The incident prompted the NSO to order an immediate investigation after reviewing footage published by PIK and other media outlets. The Service also notified the competent Military Prosecutor’s Office.
In its statement, the NSO called for respect for the privacy and security of people under its protection, while saying its personnel must respond in accordance with the law to attempts to breach that protection. The Service’s leadership said it had taken the necessary steps to establish the full circumstances of the incident and warned that the strictest measures would follow if officers were found to have acted contrary to the requirements of the situation.
The assault has also drawn strong criticism from politicians across the political spectrum. Atanas Atanasov, leader of Democrats for a Strong Bulgaria (DSB), called for Dotsova to resign in a Facebook post, citing the physical injury inflicted on a journalist and the Speaker’s failure to show concern for her condition.
"Such callousness and inhumane behavior are incompatible with the position of Speaker of the Parliament," Atanasov wrote.
Former Prime Minister Boyko Borissov also called for Dotsova’s resignation in a Facebook post, condemning the use of force against a journalist asking questions.
"A disgrace! This job is not for amateurs! Shoving and clearing away anyone who asks a question?! Resignation!" Borissov wrote.
Asen Vassilev said the incident showed a complete loss of perspective and urged voters to use Sunday’s vote to demonstrate that the state did not belong to those in power.
Kornelia Ninova described the assault as shocking and unacceptable, accusing Dotsova of leaving Koltuklieva on the sidewalk and walking away without concern. She called for the Speaker’s resignation and criticized Radev and his associates, saying the incident illustrated what could happen to people who asked uncomfortable questions or opposed the government.
Ivaylo Mirchev from Democratic Bulgaria condemned the NSO officer’s use of force, saying that a person could not be knocked to the ground and then abandoned. Although he said he strongly disagreed with Koltuklieva and her journalistic methods, he stressed that this did not justify the treatment she received.
Mirchev called the NSO’s response unacceptable and urged President Iliana Yotova to demand an explanation and hold those responsible accountable. He said the Service should defend the state against hostile attacks rather than protect people in power from questions.
Bozhidar Bozhanov, Yes Bulgaria, also denounced the officer’s conduct, describing it as disgraceful and saying the most serious failure was leaving an injured person on the ground before driving away. He said the issue was not the reporter’s opinions but basic decency and the professionalism of the security service.
Bozhanov called for an immediate and unequivocal response from the NSO director, Yotova, who oversees the Service, and the Speaker of the National Assembly.
The incident is the second reported confrontation involving security personnel protecting figures from Radev’s administration. The first took place in Strumyani this summer, when civic activist and journalist Gergana Petrova was detained after trying to ask the prime minister questions.

‘It’s all God’s creation’: farmers continue a ‘Jewishly inspired’ agrarian tradition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:18:11 UTC
04:18:11 KST

Wendy Rhein is trying to round up the sheep hanging out among the hazelnut and walnut trees of her Chutzpah Hollow farm in Tryon, North Carolina.
“Hi, Brea. Come on down. I hear you,” Rhein calls to the bleating queen of the flock. If the Barbados black belly ewe moves, the rest will follow.
Brea, a bottle-fed lamb named Hadassah and their flock mates bound down the hill when Rhein rustles a box of kosher tea biscuits. The small treat reveals something different about this farm. Rhein is remarkable for several reasons: she’s a female farmer in a male-dominated industry and a single mother who had no farming experience when she launched her farm at age 52. She’s also Jewish.
Rhein, who also works as vice-president of a faith-based advocacy organization, is part of a renewed interest among Jews in farming as an expression of their religion, culture or values. Shani Mink, co-founder of the Jewish Farmer Network, often hears “Jewish farmer – isn’t that an oxymoron?” Mink’s organization serves about 1,800 farmers, most of them first-generation agriculturalists, and offers conferences, classes and farm-to-table Shabbat dinners.
There is no solid estimate of the number of Jewish farmers in the country; the US Department of Agriculture’s census of the farming workforce doesn’t collect data on religion. But as Mink points out: “Jews have been farmers from time immemorial. The Jewish tradition is an agrarian tradition” – evidenced by how many holidays, such as the autumn harvest celebration Sukkoth, are tied to the agricultural calendar.
The Jewish Agricultural Society, chartered in 1900, helped people facing persecution in eastern Europe relocate to US farmland, where they could gain skills and independence. By 1933, more than 100,000 Jews earned some or all of their living from farming, according to Gary Moore, professor emeritus at North Carolina State University. But as the US population shifted away from agricultural work, many Jewish people moved into cities and suburbs. Some are returning to rural environments and family roots to farm, inspired by principles of their faith and building better food systems.
Rhein grew up in Detroit, the daughter of a man who was raised on a dairy farm he couldn’t wait to leave. In contrast, she loved the idea of raising livestock and being closer to her food sources; she challenged herself to prepare every ingredient she and her two sons consumed, down to the ketchup, while living in a high-rise with a kitchen “the size of a postage stamp” in Washington DC. When the pandemic hit, she started to search for land and research a new venture selling starter flocks of sheep.
Her brother, who lives about 45 minutes away in Asheville, showed her properties for sale over FaceTime. “I did not step foot on to this land or into this house until the day of our closing,” she said. Now she owns a 10-acre property.
Despite rising Jewish interest in land stewardship, Mink noted that most Jewish growers are “the only Jewish person in their farming community or the only farming person in their Jewish community”. In Rhein’s case, the nearest synagogue is almost an hour away. For her, that means “how I practice being a Jew on a day-to-day basis is how I farm and how I am attached to and care for this land”.
Rhein donates 10% of everything she raises to a local food bank, a reflection of pe’ah, a Talmudic concept that describes giving part of the harvest to the needy. She prays over every duck, chicken and sheep she slaughters so her family may eat.
“It’s all God’s creation,” she said. “It is a gift that we get to be part of it. We are stewards. We are not owners.”
But she also differs in her interpretation of some principles. The concept of bal tashchit focuses on limiting waste, so she keeps a pig to eat food scraps – a controversial decision for some Jews who don’t eat pork due to kosher dietary practices, many of whom disagree with her choice online.
“I am very clear this is not a quote-unquote ‘Jewish farm’,” Rhein said, “but I do consider us to be a Jewishly inspired place.”
Blending traditions and futures
A number of Jewish farming organizations focus on both community building and skills building. The Sacred Slaughter Institute trains students to become a shochets, ritual slaughterers of kosher meat; the butchering process calls for prayer, a highly sharpened knife and a single clean cut to lessen tza’ar ba’alei chayim, or animal suffering. Elsewhere, at the 20-acre non-profit Adamah Farm in Falls Village, Connecticut, Jewish people in their 20s and 30s come for three-month farming fellowships. Located at the Isabella Freedman Jewish Retreat Center, Adamah sells vegetables and herbs through membership in its community-supported agriculture (CSA) model.
Adamah Farm co-founder Shamu Sadeh said the work “is a process of reinvigorating Judaism and the Jewish community with an ecological perspective, and of reinvigorating the ecological environmental community with people who feel spiritually connected”. Graduates work in food rescue programs, food policy, environmental groups and Jewish social services, among other fields; a small percentage are farmers.
Rabbis Shoshana and Philip Ohriner run the 16-acre Ma’alot Farms in Los Gatos, California, with grants from community organizations and foundations. The farm nurtures hundreds of varieties of produce, from olives and broccolini to marionberries, a type of blackberry. Almost everything is given away to people facing food insecurity, including kids in afterschool programs and seniors with nutritional needs.
Ma’alot’s marketing doesn’t refer to Judaism. Still, “you cannot step on to Ma’alot Farms without feeling our Judaism permeate everything”, Philip Ohriner said, “from the way in which we care for our staff and provide a living wage for them and benefits, to the ways in which we seek to share our abundance to feed the hungry, to seek to bring equity and justice more fully into our world.”
At Ekar Farm, located at an eldercare community in Aurora, Colorado, executive director Jason Plotkin offers intergenerational gardening programs and donates about 20,000lb of organic produce annually to groups including Hope Communities, which serves refugees, and Spirit of the Sun, an Indigenous-led organization. The farm grows epazote, Thai hot chilies and bitter melon among its crops based on requests from recipients. Plotkin grew up Jewish but wasn’t religious. “I actually have learned more about my Jewish identity working for Ekar,” he said, “than what I brought into it.”
Non-profit farms exemplify the idea of tzedakah, or charity, a requirement in Jewish tradition. Small-scale for-profit farms strive to be community partners in their own ways.
Zalman (Robbie) Friedman operates a subscription and delivery service for local kosher meat from Robariah Farms in South Deerfield, Massachusetts. A certified shochet, he tends to about 1,000 birds, including meat chickens, egg layers and turkeys. About a quarter of his customers aren’t Jewish but appreciate Robariah’s regenerative farming practices. His birds have plenty of room to move and dine on fresh pasture every day thanks to mobile coops. “We raise a slower-growing variety that’s very active on the grass,” he said.
The laws of kashrut, or keeping kosher, outline how to slaughter an animal but are less specific about its care, Friedman said. “Why can’t it be done in a way that also honors the life of the animal, which is also a very important Jewish value and Jewish practice?”
Jewish guidance can show up even in crop selection. Ian Yosef Hertzmark grows ancient grains such as emmer, einkorn, spelt and Persian wheats, among other crops, on the 32-acre Migrash Farm in Baltimore county, Maryland. He plants ancient grains in the fall to be yoshon, or “old”, taking root before Passover (the Torah forbids eating chadash, or “new” grain). Hertzmark finds fulfillment in having “a relationship with land in an observant and seasonal context”.
Rhein agrees. She feels “more self-aware, more confident, more alive and whole as a human being here, doing this, than I ever felt living in Manhattan … This way of life – attaching yourself to land and animals and seasonality – is a constant sense of joy.”

Albania's student protests are only getting bigger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:18:00 UTC
04:18:00 KST

Albania's student protests are only getting bigger
October 22, 2026
The fallout from the October 13 protests was still visible when students and faculty from the University of Tirana gathered outside the Education Ministry in Albania's capital on Tuesday to express their continued discontent. Smashed windows have yet to be replaced; the walls are still black with soot from fires that broke out during the protests.
Albania has seen nearly five months of peaceful anti-government protests, sparked initially when plans were made public that Jared Kushner — a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump — and associates intended to build a luxury hotel complex within a nature reserve.
Since then, anti-government and anti-corruption protests have escalated. Now, college and high school students clash with police forces almost daily, with the fiercest clashes so far occurring last week.
Protesters denounce corruption, mismanaged universities and the rising cost of education in Albania — and call for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in office since 2013.
Wearing a black hooded jacket and a scarf across her face to conceal her identity, a woman who asked to be called Sara because she fears repercussions for speaking to the press told DW that protesters "communicate via text messages — that's the only way."
She cut the interview short as some protesters began flinging stones at the Education Ministry. Police pushed demonstrators and journalists out of the way, using water cannons to disperse the crowd.
"Social media is the most important public space today — more so than physical spaces," Besmir Semanaj, a prominent Albanian cybersecurity advocate told DW. "Young Albanians no longer organize through traditional structures such as political parties, associations or public appeals. Instead, they organize themselves where they spend much of their daily lives: on their cellphones."
"The most important communication channels include Instagram, WhatsApp groups for academic-year cohorts, departments and dormitories, Telegram channels for general announcements, and TikTok for sharing videos," Semanaj said. He added that people who are especially concerned with security use the Signal messaging app.
"This is a horizontal organizational structure, without individual 'leaders' and without a central command structure," Semanaj said. "That is exactly why the government is having such a hard time understanding and controlling the situation."
Semanaj said the Telegram messenger app had proven particularly useful for protesters. "Telegram channels allow you to reach tens of thousands of people at once," he said. "Notifications are sent out within seconds, and external control is more difficult to establish than on traditional platforms."
Rama: 'Hybrid war'
Rama has called the youth uprising a "hybrid war." He said protesters thought they could "make Albania a better country through TikTok and without even being able to string together more than seven coherent words." Though not all are terrorists, he said, he believes that "they are hostages to a certain mindset, a new ideology that has only one goal: to destroy, to turn everything upside down, to raze everything to the ground."
Over nearly five months, Rama has accused various "true" masterminds of organizing the anti-government and anti-corruption protests. He has alleged that the governments of Greece, Russia and Iran are stirring up dissent.
Most recently, Rama said it was "antifa" — or a decentralized movement of global antifascists — that had stoked anti-government and anti-corruption sentiments in Albania. "These are young people who have been radicalized and ideologically indoctrinated and who are acting under the pressure or influence of a new, dark force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, a force that the President of the United States has designated as a terrorist organization: Antifa," Rama claimed.
Redion Qirjazi, a security affairs researcher who focuses on violence prevention and conflict resolution, told DW that Rama's claim was not likely to prove true. "That is a serious accusation — one that requires equally compelling evidence," Qirjazi said. "To date, no verifiable evidence has been presented to prove the existence of an organized Antifa structure in Albania, let alone its involvement in coordinating the protests."
Qirjazi said Rama's reference to Trump's calling antifa a terror group was problematic. "Antifa is not a unified international organization with a centralized structure or leadership," he said, "but rather an umbrella term for various movements and groups united by the fact that they are, at their core, anti-fascist."
Sara said she rejected the "terrorist" label that Rama had attempted to slap on her and her fellow protesters. "There are groups that are willing to use violence — that's true — but I have nothing to do with them," she said. "As soon as I see violence, I walk away; I'm against it."
Is Rama deflecting?
Arlind Qori, the chairman of the Together Movement, a social-democratic opposition party with just one seat in Albania's parliament, said youths had taken to the streets out of dissatisfaction with the status quo rather than any particular ideology. "Young Albanians are outraged by the current socioeconomic conditions: the poverty, the fact that many of their parents have emigrated because they couldn't support their families, the decline of the education system, the lack of postgraduation prospects," Qori said. The students' central demand is for Rama to resign, he added "not a socialist revolution."
"People aren't demanding anything radical," Qori said. "They merely want a corrupt head of government to resign — that's a fundamental and moderate demand. But Edi Rama continues to meet this demand with police violence and arrogance."
Qirjazi said Rama's allegations of foreign interference could be a strategy. "When a government faces protests and public discontent, linking demonstrators to extremism and foreign influence may serve to divert attention away from the actual causes and toward a national security narrative," he said.
"This can serve several political purposes: to delegitimize the protesters, to weaken their support among the public, and to justify a tougher crackdown in the name of law and order," Qirjazi said.
Semanaj said this was a common pattern in governments' efforts to dismiss dissent. "Protests are portrayed as acts of violence," he said. "Young people are cast as manipulated, and their legitimate concerns — conditions at universities, tuition fees, corruption and a lack of prospects — vanish from the news agenda."

Lina Attalah: Mada Masr journalist sent for trial in Egypt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

04:17:00 KST

Lina Attalah: Mada Masr journalist sent for trial in Egypt
October 22, 2026
Egypt's Supreme State Security Prosecution sent Mada Masr journalist Lina Attalah to stand for trial, the independent Egyptian news website said Thursday.
One of Madr Masar's co-founders, Attalah serves as the site's editor-in-chief. The website, which publishes in both Arabic and English, frequently features critical reporting related to Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's government.
What do we know so far?
Prosecutors questioned Attalah for six hours on Wednesday in New Cairo, Mada Masr said.
She is accused of running a website without a license and the publication of false news "with the aim of disturbing public peace." Under questioning, the latter allegation was dropped from the charge sheet in the trial referral.
The trial has been referred to a New Cairo misdemeanors court and is slated to begin on October 27.
Hassan al-Azhari, Mada Masr's legal counsel, said there was "haste" in the trial referral and said the trial beginning next week signals "unjustified urgency."
Al-Azhari said Attalah could face a financial penalty of between 1 million to 3 million Egyptian pounds (around €16,000 to €48,000; $18,000 to $54,000) if convicted.
Mada Masr said the organization has sought a license from the Egyptian government to run its news website since 2018 — the same year Egypt passed and ratified a law to regulate the press.
Egyptian authorities have been unresponsive over the past years to Mada Masr's attempts to procure a license, with Mada Masr later finding out in 2022 that its request was rejected. The site filed a lawsuit in 2022 and found out in 2023 that the rejection was due to missing documents.
The proceedings against Attalah come after Egyptian authorities arrested six journalists last month for independent fact-checking and investigative website Matsadaash (Egyptian Arabic for "don't believe").
Press freedom groups condemn actions against Attalah
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) expressed alarm about Attalah's referral to trial.
"Egypt is weaponizing its media law to punish independent journalism and intensify one of its worst crackdowns in years, which began with the arrest of the six Matsdaash journalists," the CPJ's director for Middle East and North Africa Sara Qudah said. "It is long past time for Egypt to end this campaign and allow independent media to report freely."
Reporters without Borders (RSF) had earlier said it was alarmed by prosecutors' questioning of Attalah.
According to RSF's World Press Freedom Index, Egypt ranks 169 out of 180 countries, with many of the country's biggest news outlets either state-owned or controlled by wealthy businessmen who submit to the will of the government.
Egyptian President el-Sissi came to power in a 2013 military coup against Islamist President Mohamed Morsi. Since then, el-Sissi has cracked down and blocked websites such as Qatar's Al Jazeera and The New Arab on allegations of supporting the Muslim Brotherhood.

Kyiv denies reports that Trump, Musk have restored Starlink speeds in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:17:00 UTC
04:17:00 KST

Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional comments from U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukraine's military Starlink service is still operating at a speed cap of 161 kilometers per hour, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 22.
The official's statement contradicts claims quoted by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), which reported on Oct. 22 that Starlink functionality was back to normal in Ukraine following a phone call between SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump called Musk on Oct. 21 to request he lift restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield service, the military application of the Starlink program, according to the WSJ. Following the call, sources reportedly told the outlet that Starlink was functioning more normally — though some Ukrainian officials said it wasn't fully restored.
But when asked about these claims, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent they were "all false."
"Overall, nothing has changed anywhere," the official said. The 161 kph speed cap remains in place, severely limiting key military operations, including mid-range strikes and high-speed drone interceptions.
Trump was evasive about whether or not he called Musk, but also claimed that Starlink was back up and running as usual in Ukraine in comments to reporters.
"Yeah, I don't want to comment on it, whether I called, or whether somebody else called, it doesn't make a difference," Trump told a journalist when questioned about the WSJ story.
"The bottom line, (Musk) put it back."
Ukraine has been trying to sort out the reasons behind the restriction — and restore service to its previous speed level — ever since Starlink was disrupted without warning on Oct. 14. While fingers have been pointed at SpaceX, the White House, and a Trump-Musk alliance, no one has claimed responsibility for the move.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that Trump had a hand in the change, saying on Oct. 18 that "no one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed."
Zelensky spoke with Rubio again on Oct. 20, as Starlink disruptions persisted. Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 22 that he was waiting for a response from Rubio as to whether Starlink communications could be restored to speeds of up to 400 kph.
Rubio promised to get back with him within 48 hours, Zelensky said, but definitive answers may take longer.
"Maybe something will become clear by morning," the official who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said.
"For now, the main interesting aspect of this is that there are absolutely no explanations for what's happening. Even though this is a top-priority system."
CORRECTION: A previous version of this story said it was reported that Musk called Trump to discuss Starlink. The WSJ reported that Trump phoned Musk. The error has been corrected.

Trump's Pentagon breaks world? Just historic globe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:12:00 UTC
04:12:00 KST

Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth asked aides to retrieve a globe linked to legendary World War II General Dwight Eisenhower, only for them to break it, a report said Thursday.
The large orb fell while being carried by untrained staff, resulting in the loss of a large chunk of the world near Antarctica, The Washington Post said.
The Post reported that historic items are typically moved around the Pentagon premises by trained curators. However, Hegseth's office had dispatched its own team.
Photographs published by the Post showed the hole in the Antarctica area and an accompanying plaque identifying it as one of two nearly identical, historic "Eisenhower Globes" in the Pentagon's possession.
The Army acknowledged the damage in a statement to the Post. Army spokesperson Christopher Surridge said the globe was damaged during an "attempted move" on Feb. 3. Aside from the hole, "the spherical portion of the globe was detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate," Surridge was quoted.
After the report, a Defense Department official provided the Post with a brief, unattributed statement acknowledging the mishap.
"Accidents happen," it said. "We are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired."
President Donald Trump's secretary of defense has focused on promoting a muscular image for the U.S. military, starting by attempting to restore the Department of War name, which was dropped in 1947 for the Department of Defense.
Hegseth, who rose as far as major during an Army National Guard career before becoming a Fox News host, regularly does televised exercise routines with troops. He has ordered mandatory testosterone screening for male military staff over 30.
He is currently overseeing the eight-month war against Iran, which Trump has promised repeatedly to bring to a rapid conclusion.
Eisenhower led the U.S. war effort against Nazi Germany, commanding the D-Day landings that launched the phase of conflict leading to Adolf Hitler's defeat.
A five-star general, he was then elected president in 1952, taking the helm of the White House as the Cold War gathered pace. He was often photographed posing alongside elaborate globes.

UN says settler attacks, Israeli restrictions block Palestinians from olive harvest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:11:59 UTC
04:11:59 KST

Rabia Iclal Turan
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The UN said Thursday that recurrent attacks and Israeli access restrictions are preventing Palestinians in the occupied West Bank from safely harvesting their olive crops.
Spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told a media briefing that Acting Special Coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov traveled to Jenin with diplomats from 13 member states to learn about challenges linked to the olive harvest and the prolonged displacement of Palestinian communities.
“In the village of Arraba, they heard from farmers growing olives about recurrent settler attacks, which, combined with Israeli access restrictions, are undermining food security,” said Dujarric. “Our humanitarian partners briefed the delegation on efforts to protect olive pickers, including by accompanying them to the groves and providing legal aid to challenge Israeli-imposed access restrictions.”
Dujarric said that Alakbarov indicated that “the harvest season should be a time of celebration, with up to 100,000 Palestinian households depending on olives for their livelihoods, but many Palestinians are being prevented from gathering their crops safely.”
“He said that crimes committed against them must stop, and the perpetrators must be held to account by the Israeli authorities,” said Dujarric.
“At a clinic in the city of Qabatiya, diplomats met with Palestinians who, since early 2025, have been prevented from returning to Jenin Camp by the Israeli authorities, where many of their homes have been destroyed,” he said.
Alakbarov “stressed that more funding is needed so that humanitarian organizations can help the displaced Palestinians and urged Israeli authorities to enable their safe and dignified return,” said Dujarric.
The visit came days after Israeli occupiers attacked a delegation that included European diplomats and Catholic Church officials near the town of Taybeh, east of Ramallah, according to the Palestinian Foreign Ministry.
Israeli Army Radio reported that seven masked attackers surrounded a diplomatic car and smashed a window of a Belgian consular vehicle, and that Israeli troops and police did not arrive for three hours.
The Israeli military described the attack as a “serious violent incident,” but said the delegation had not coordinated the visit in advance, and that no troops were present at the scene.
Occupier attacks have intensified since the olive harvest began earlier this month, with the Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission reporting 40 attacks and violations against farmers, farmland and olive crops in a single day last weekend.

21 years on, double life term for Jammu terror attack that killed baby, 2 others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:02:53 UTC
04:02:53 KST

The court ordered that the fines be paid to those injured in the July 2005 terror attack
JAMMU: A Jammu court has imposed two life sentences and fines of Rs 2 lakh on Mohammed Sharief, a terrorist who gunned down three members of a family, including a six-month-old infant, in Ramban district’s Gool area over 21 years ago.In his order on Wednesday, principal sessions judge Ramban Ajay Kumar Gupta rejected defence arguments that the attack had taken place more than two decades ago when Sharief was young, his long incarceration and possibility of rehabilitation.Besides the life sentences, the court imposed two separate terms of 10 years on Sharief under various sections pertaining to murder and arms act offences. “All sentences shall run concurrently, while the period already spent in custody shall be set off in accordance with law,” the judge said.The court ordered that the fines be paid to those injured in the July 2005 terror attack and directed J&K State Legal Services Authority to provide compensation to heirs of the deceased and the survivors.Judge Gupta rejected defence arguments about the testimony of two injured eyewitnesses, saying they were reliable and corroborated by medical and other evidence. Defective investigations or delay in recording statements could not automatically result in acquittal when credible evidence otherwise established the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the judge said.
Public prosecutor Wajid Ahmed pressed for maximum punishment under law, contending that the murder of three innocent family members, including the baby, and the use of an AK-47 rifle warranted a stringent sentence.The court considered aggravating and mitigating circumstances and held that although the crime was extremely grave, the case did not warrant the death penalty under the rarest of rare principle.

Indonesia records over 333,000 acute respiratory infection cases as fires rage in several regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:00:02 UTC
04:00:02 KST

Saadet Gokce
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Indonesia has recorded 333,470 cases of acute respiratory infections (ARIs) linked to forest and land fires in several regions, the Health Ministry said Thursday.
The ministry's director of environmental health, Then Suyanti, said that daily cases remained high, with 4,522 new cases reported, according to state-run news agency Antara.
She said the latest Air Pollutant Index showed that air quality in several areas had reached hazardous levels, particularly in six provinces prioritized for fire management: Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra, West Kalimantan, South Kalimantan and Central Kalimantan.
Suyanti said exposure to wildfire smoke, which contains fine particulate matter such as PM2.5, carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide and other organic compounds, can cause health problems. including ARIs, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, eye and skin irritation and other systemic health effects.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto said Thursday that if foreign-backed companies are responsible for recurring forest and land fires, those businesses could lose their operating permits, and revoked concessions could be reassigned to younger Indonesians.
"Regarding forest fires, there are indications that many foreign companies bear responsibility. They have held concessions for over a decade, yet some have committed violations three, four, or even a dozen times --some as many as 19 times," Prabowo said, adding that their permits should be revoked if they commit two violations.
Separately, thousands of students and others demonstrated in Samarinda, the capital of East Kalimantan, demanding the government declare forest and land fires a national disaster, according to iNews.
Indonesia is experiencing an unusually prolonged dry season, with El Nino contributing to conditions favorable for wildfires.

Russia's "Fishing" Boats May Be Hunting Undersea Cables Instead of Fish, NATO Official Warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:56:35 UTC
03:56:35 KST

- Category
- World
Russia's "Fishing" Boats May Be Hunting Undersea Cables Instead of Fish, NATO Official Warns
Russian fishing trawlers have made more than 500 suspicious movements above critical undersea communication cables connecting Britain with Europe and the US, potentially mapping infrastructure for future sabotage, The Telegraph investigation published on October 21 revealed.
The outlet analyzed 4.5 years of vessel-tracking data from Global Fishing Watch. The investigation identified 17 Russian fishing vessels repeatedly operating at low speeds near important telecommunications cables in the North Atlantic.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
"Some of these ships have never seen a single fish on their deck," an unnamed NATO official told The Telegraph, suggesting that some vessels may be operating under the cover of commercial fishing.
The investigation documented suspicious activity north of Scotland, where Russian trawlers spent 337 hours near the Atlantic Crossing 1 telecommunications cable, including 322 hours in April 2023 alone.
One vessel changed direction ten times while following a 25-kilometer section of the cable. According to The Telegraph's analysis, the same ship approached nine separate undersea cables connecting Western Europe with the US over four years.
Other vessels reportedly operated near the Hibernia Express, Shefa-2, Amitié, and Google's Grace Hopper cables.
Naval experts explained that fishing trawlers could use sonar equipment and remotely operated underwater vehicles to map seabed cables. Such information could help Russian intelligence identify vulnerable sections for potential sabotage.
Royal Navy chief General Sir Gwyn Jenkins has warned that Russia is increasingly probing undersea infrastructure. The Telegraph noted that disrupting these connections could affect banking, healthcare, transportation, and international communications.
However, the vessel-tracking data do not establish that the identified trawlers engaged in espionage or damaged cables.
Russia's interest in undersea cables has extended beyond fishing fleets to its specialized deep-sea forces. In spring 2026, British, Norwegian and US forces confronted submarines from GUGI, Moscow's Main Directorate of Deep-Sea Research, that were rehearsing a previously unknown weapon designed to sever cables near Svalbard without leaving traceable evidence.
The drill targeted the two fiber-optic lines linking Svalbard to mainland Norway, and the Russian vessels withdrew without damaging any cables. In April 2026, Britain also disclosed a covert operation near its waters involving an Akula-class submarine and two GUGI deep-sea vessels that threatened energy pipelines and data cables.

====================================================================================================

EU Sanctions Envoy Pushes for Action Against Rusal’s Irish Alumina Refinery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:56:00 UTC
03:56:00 KST

Material produced in a major metals refinery in Ireland is “undoubtedly” going into Russia’s weapons supply chain, the European Union’s Sanctions Envoy David O’Sullivan said on Thursday, adding that “there is a very real issue to be addressed.”
The comments, made at the Institute for International and European Affairs (IIEA) in Dublin, come seven months after OCCRP and partners published an investigation showing that the Aughinish Alumina refinery in western Ireland was indirectly supplying Russian weapons producers.
As much as half of the alumina from the Aughinish refinery was shipped to smelters owned by its parent company, United Company Rusal, and used to produce aluminum. The metal was then sold to a trading company supplying dozens of EU-sanctioned Russian weapons manufacturers, OCCRP’s investigation showed.
Weapons made by these firms have leveled entire city blocks in Mariupol, struck a children’s hospital in Kyiv, and blown open an apartment building in western Ukraine, according to EU sanctions listings, Ukraine’s military intelligence, and the London-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
Aughinish Alumina's sales to Russia — which have increased since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — are entirely legal under EU trade rules. That is because although EU exports of finished aluminum are banned, shipments of the intermediate material alumina are not, partly as a result of lobbying years ago by Ireland, where Aughinish Alumina is an important employer.
OCCRP’s investigation sparked controversy in Ireland and internationally, and led to growing pressure to sanction EU alumina exports. The Irish government launched its own investigation, which reached an ambivalent conclusion, saying that a lack of data made it “difficult to ascertain where Russia is sourcing its tools and weapons from.” It shared its findings with the EU Commission in July.
O’Sullivan was less cautious in his assessment.
“The alumina goes to smelters in Russia, who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex,” he said. “I've read the government report. I personally, I think there's no doubt the investigative journalists got it right.”
O’Sullivan did not say whether the EU would eventually ban alumina exports to Russia.
“I think there is a very real issue to be addressed. We just have to find the best way of doing it, which doesn't have unhelpful collateral consequences,” he said, noting that Aughinish Alumina also supplied smelters in Europe.
In July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a visit to Dublin that “Every ton of raw material that ends in Russia is used against us. I do hope whatever we are doing now, we are cutting every possibility, every sphere for Russia to build up, to militarize itself.”
Aughinish Alumina has said that its material is not used to make weapons, and that almost all the alumina it sends to Russian smelters is solely used to produce aluminum for onward export out of Russia.
OCCRP’s original investigation was published in partnership with iStories, the Irish Times, KibOrg, De Tijd, The Guardian, and Delfi.

====================================================================================================

Why the EU avoids tackling Big Soccer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:54:27 UTC
03:54:27 KST

FIFA President Gianni Infantino attends the FIFA World Cup 2026 Round of 32 match at Monterrey Stadium on June 29, 2026 in Guadalupe, Mexico. | Carl Recine/Getty Images
BRUSSELS — The EU’s influential competition regulators have taken on some of the planet’s most powerful companies, from Google to Gazprom. But they are steering clear of opening a case against the world soccer governing body, FIFA.
A complaint lodged by the European Leagues professional soccer association in October 2024 accused FIFA of abusing its dominant position by imposing its international match calendar on other sporting stakeholders. It argued that FIFA’s dual role as a governing body and the organizer of its own competitions creates a conflict of interest, through which it enriches itself. The leagues broadened the complaint last month to cover the women’s game — but the Commission has yet to open formal proceedings.
Brussels has left the European Leagues complaint in the “freezer,” one senior EU official with knowledge of the file told POLITICO.
Advertisement
The episode underscores the Directorate-General for Competition’s long-running reluctance to open investigations into sports federations, which current and former European officials say is due to sport's special status in EU law — the treaties recognize its social and educational role — but also a deliberate policy choice to swerve potentially controversial cases in an emotionally charged sector.
Now, pressure is building against the competition department over the languishing European Leagues complaint, after a cross-party group of EU lawmakers urged the Commission to use its antitrust powers to rein in FIFA.
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, obtained by POLITICO and copied to competition chief Teresa Ribera, MEPs called for action. Bruno Gonçalves and Hannes Heide (both from the Socialists and Democrats) and Bogdan Zdrojewski (from the conservative European People’s Party) asked the Commission to take formal action, including in relation to the complaint lodged by the European Leagues, which represents 53 men’s and women’s professional football leagues across the continent.
The MEPs say the governing body’s application of the calendar “raises concerns about FIFA’s use of regulatory powers to advance FIFA’s own commercial interests,” and that those powers “must be exercised through transparent, objective, non-discriminatory and proportionate procedures, with effective safeguards against conflicts of interest.” The EU’s top court set that test for sports bodies in its landmark 2023 Super League ruling.
“FIFA is both referee and promoter of the show,” Gonçalves told POLITICO. “We have to make sure the referee doesn’t put business before people.”
Representatives for the European Leagues pressed their case in a meeting with Competition Commissioner Teresa Ribera’s Cabinet in late April, but their overtures have so far been fruitless.
Advertisement
“The thinking has always been, on the one hand, that sports has a special status, so it is not a market comparable to others that normally are scrutinized by the competition directorate,” said one former senior EU official, who was granted anonymity to discuss a sensitive file in order to protect relationships.
“But also, sports cases get very political and the Commission feels that member states tend to take the side of the federations so it’s hesitant to pick this fight up,” the former official added.
The Vestager principles
Over the last 15 years, Brussels has opened blockbuster investigations into Gazprom’s behavior in Central and Eastern European gas markets; whether Google illegitimately hindered the development and market access of rival mobile operating systems; and Apple’s rules for app developers.
But the Commission’s caution on sports is long-standing.
When then-competition chief Margrethe Vestager ordered the International Skating Union in 2017 to drop rules threatening speed skaters with lifetime bans for joining money-spinning rival events, she said the decision didn’t mean the Commission was “trying to be the referee in every dispute about sport.”
Many disputes, from doping penalties to deciding the precise scheduling of games, have “little or nothing at all to do with competition rules,” Vestager said at the time. National courts and competition authorities, she added, are “usually well placed to deal with competition disputes involving a sport federation.”
Advertisement
Those principles have since come to guide how the Commission’s competition department decides which sports disputes to take on. There is no shortage of candidates, with controversies in sports including tennis, padel and sailing, as well as soccer.
Any investigation would test recent case law. A pair of July rulings on FIFA’s agent rules went largely the governing body’s way. In those cases, the Court of Justice of the European Union accepted that federations can impose restrictions if they pursue legitimate aims proportionately.
Ben Van Rompuy, a competition law professor at Leiden University who helped bring the original ISU complaint, said there would likely be “little appetite” in Brussels to take up the leagues' case.
When the ISU complaint reached the Commission, courts had said little about how competition law applied to sport. Since then, “we’ve had an abundance of such guidance,” and “national enforcement in front of the courts seems to work,” Van Rompuy said. That leaves less reason for the Commission to step in. The leagues have also sued in a Brussels court, which suggests “they themselves believe that the national courts could protect their rights.”
Measured against the Commission’s own criteria for prioritizing complaints, the case looks weak, Van Rompuy said. Its impact on the EU’s internal market is “extremely limited,” he added.
FIFA declined to comment on the European Leagues complaint and the EU lawmakers' letter.
Advertisement
Commission spokesperson Ricardo Cardoso said international sports bodies have “a primary responsibility” for organizing global events, and that sport is mainly a matter for national governments, with the EU playing a supporting role.
When sports organizations act as undertakings, the EU legal term for entities carrying out economic activity, they are subject to the rules of competition, Cardoso said. He added that the Commission constantly monitors markets for possible breaches, and that “if any complaint is filed, the Commission will assess according to standard practice.”
Public and political criticism of FIFA has reached fever pitch over the last 12 months due to the governing body’s cozy relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration and an ultimately aborted plot this summer to sell off parts of the World Cup tournament to private investors.
According to the letter from EU lawmakers, FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s commercial sell-off scheme “exposed serious shortcomings in transparency, accountability and institutional decision-making.”

Space Force Picks Six Companies for Commercial Reserve Fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:52:34 UTC
03:52:34 KST

The Space Force has selected six commercial space domain awareness companies to support military operations with both steady-state and surge capacity, as part of the service’s new Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve.
Officials have been working since 2022 to establish a fleet of commercial satellites and other assets to provide capabilities like satellite imagery, space domain awareness, and communications during peacetime that can be surged on demand. The concept is not unlike the Air Force’s Civil Reserve Air Fleet, which leases aircraft capacity from commercial airliners for use during a conflict.
Last year, the Space Force announced it would pilot the CASR program with four unnamed companies who specialize in identifying and tracking objects in space—also called space domain awareness. The service awarded them 90-day contracts worth a combined $1.1 million, and in the ensuing months conducted a series of wargames and training events to better understand how to integrate their capabilities and services into its operations.
These new contracts announced Oct. 22 are meant to operationalize that capability and create a pool of CASR companies specifically focused on SDA. Those firms include:
- Anduril
- Intrack
- Slingshot
- LeoLabs
- EOS, an Australian firm
- Northstar, a Canadian firm
Space Force officials explained to reporters Oct. 21 at AFCEA’s annual Space Industry Days conference that the six companies initially tapped for CASR are firms that operators already trust today and would turn to should something happen on orbit that requires more visibility or object tracking capabilities. According to Lt. Col. Brandon Galindo, all of the companies in this initial cohort currently work with the Joint Commercial Operations Cell, a Space Force hub that integrates commercial space data and services and shares it with joint international partners.
“What we heard from the operational community is that … if something were to happen on orbit, debris or some breakup scenario, these are the companies on the commercial side that we would really depend upon,” Galindo said.
That said, the initial cohort of space domain awareness companies isn’t meant to be static. Col. Tim Trimailo, director of the Commercial Space Office said other companies will have a chance to onboard in the future.
“This is not a chalk line that we’ve snapped that says you can never get into CASR for the space domain awareness mission,” he said during. “It’s a living program. So, we’re always looking for new entrants, new opportunities, new companies that have proven themselves and that are trusted partners to be part of CASR.”
While these are operational contracts, Trimailo said the initial dollar values—which he didn’t disclose—are fairly low. As the Space Force gets a handle on how much demand there is for the capabilities from operators within combatant commands, it will look at options to adjust funding.
Galindo echoed that sentiment, describing the program’s work to establish the reserve as an iterative process that will include regular updates within each mission area as well as opportunities to add new mission areas under the CASR umbrella. He also noted that contract terms and strategies will vary by company and by mission.
“It’s not cookie cutter,” he said. “Each mission area is so unique, the companies within a mission area are unique. And we love that, because then we can assemble the best companies that offer something unique and we can put them together.”
The Commercial Space Office has started to look at what its next CASR mission will be and is considering commercial satellite communications, launch, and telemetry, tracking, and command—which would leverage the Space Force’s existing Joint Antenna Marketplace—as potential options.

Putin slams European warmongering as ‘political schizophrenia’
Repeated claims by European officials that Russia poses a threat of war to their countries amount to “political schizophrenia,” President Vladimir Putin has said.
He made the remarks on Thursday while speaking to Russian journalist Pavel Zarubin after participating in the Union of Theatre Workers congress at the Bolshoi Theater in Moscow.
Putin strongly denied the repeated allegations that Moscow has been gearing up for war with Europe in any fashion, dismissing them as a part of the ongoing “anti-Russian campaign” on the continent. 
“They now go so far as to constantly speak of a ‘Russian threat’ and even discuss preparations for a war with Russia – which, in my view, amounts to a kind of political schizophrenia. But I hope that it will pass,” Putin stated.
The Ukraine conflict has clearly demonstrated that Russia cannot be defeated on the battlefield, the president argued, adding that the idea of inflicting a “strategic defeat” on the country was “simply not realistic.” Putin expressed hope that those still entertaining such a scenario would “come to recognize the realities of modern life.” 
“They will hopefully realize that it is better to live in harmony with Russia – a path that truly serves the interests of their own peoples. If you look at the political processes currently underway in Europe, it becomes evident that the European peoples have no desire to go to war with Russia,” the president stated.
In fact, Russia does not want to fight Ukraine either, Putin said, pointing at the shared past and the longstanding ties between Russians and Ukrainians. Still, Kiev itself chose war in 2014, when it opted to fight the people of then-Ukrainian Donbass, who had rejected the Maidan coup, the president said, adding that Ukraine has also rejected Moscow’s repeated attempts to mediate that conflict.
“If the current Ukrainian leadership wishes to fight, then let them fight. But why do they expect everyone else to foot the bill and supply them with weapons? I suppose they have their arguments – likely rooted in past promises of help. But it seems that the ‘help’ was intended to last until the very last Ukrainian,” Putin said.
The Russian president also touched upon the territorial issues between Moscow and Kiev, pointing out that the loss of formerly Ukrainian regions should not be treated as such, since they were never Ukrainian in the first place.
“It is not their territory, it is a part of historic Russia,” he stressed, adding that local residents voted to secede from Ukraine and reunify with Russia.
Russia remains ready to resolve the Ukraine conflict through diplomacy, Putin said, reiterating Moscow’s willingness to resume trilateral talks with Washington and Kiev.
“The purpose of these negotiations will be to discuss how to ensure the security of both Ukraine and Russia following the conclusion of peace agreements, specifically, definitive, long-term agreements, rather than a mere temporary cessation of hostilities,” the president said, adding that the discussions should involve a wider all-European security architecture.
Moscow announced it was ready to resume the trilateral talks following Putin’s meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov subsequently said the next round could take place in Abu Dhabi around mid-November.

One year of Ukrainian arms exports, and industry has questions: how much army gained, where Berlin office is, who joins joint ventures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:50:33 UTC
03:50:33 KST

Ukraine now builds far more weapons than it can afford to buy. A year ago, it promised to sell the surplus abroad and turn the proceeds back into its own army. However, 12 months later, that promise has barely materialized: a state fee of up to 30% is pricing Ukrainian arms out of foreign markets, and no one can say how much the army has actually gained, said Ihor Fedirko, executive director of the Ukrainian Council of Armorers.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the resumption of controlled weapons exports in October 2025, resting it on four promises: 1) sell what Ukraine makes beyond its own needs, 2) channel part of the proceeds into a special fund for the army, 3) open export offices in Europe and the US, and 4) establish joint ventures abroad.
The surplus is real: Ukraine's defense output is projected to reach $55 billion in 2026, far beyond what the state can finance. A year on, Fedirko checked each promise in turn.
1) Export of surpluses: rules that strangle businesses
On 1 July 2026, the government approved rules for controlled arms exports. They shortened the maximum application review period from 90 to 30 days, but also introduced an export fee: 20% for finished products and technologies, and 30% for components. For finished products exported under the special procedure, the contract value must be at least $334,000.
In September, the Ukrainian Council of Armorers, together with other associations, proposed a zero rate, no advance collection of the fee, refunds for deals that fall through, and simplified test shipments. The industry was promised that its amendments would be taken into account and that the resolution would be rewritten.
Even in early October, however, the rules still needed work. According to Fedirko, the new mechanism has effectively not started working. Whether it can bring in additional funds for defense depends on how acceptable the export terms are to manufacturers.
Fedirko says, though, that judging by current decisions, the state intends to keep the export fee.
“The industry is ready to discuss its contribution to defense financing. But the rate must be economically justified,” he says.
2) Procurement for the Ukrainian military: balance is only being established
He adds that the Ukrainian Council of Armorers intends to push for a rate significantly lower than 20%, one that would let companies fulfill contracts and invest in production.
With such high rates, Fedirko says, the competitiveness of Ukrainian weapons on foreign markets is in question, as is the ability to send even small test batches to potential buyers.
“The fundamental requirement is post-payment: after the contract has actually been fulfilled and the manufacturer has been paid. A company should not pay the state in advance a share of income it has not yet received,” he says.
Trending Now
He added that, given all this, the real export figures remain unclear, as does how much exports have actually brought the military.
“The military and manufacturers must feel the benefit of exports. I sincerely hope that next year will bring much better results,” he says.
In addition, on 12 October, the Ukrainian Parliament passed bill No. 15400 in the first reading. It provides for crediting the export fee to a special fund directed to the Ministry of Defense: 50% for the procurement, modernization, and repair of weapons and equipment, and 50% for the pay of Armed Forces personnel.
The bill has not yet been adopted, but Fedirko says he expects “final adoption and launch of the mechanism.”
3) Export offices: offices in Germany and Denmark
On 3 November, the Ukrainian government named the first cities for export offices: Berlin and Copenhagen. On 15 December, it again spoke of preparing an office in Berlin. In reality, Fedirko says he does not know the office’s status, and it likewise remains unclear how companies can apply to it and how many contracts it has helped close.
4) Joint ventures abroad: There are concrete results in this area
According to Fedirko, eight joint ventures have been created, five of which are already supplying products to Ukraine. He stresses that this is the result of work by Ukrainian companies, foreign partners and the state, and that it deserves recognition.
As early as February 2026, the authorities spoke of plans to create ten joint ventures in Europe within a year. At the same time, they announced Quantum Frontline Industries in Germany, with a planned annual capacity of 10,000 drones for Kyiv.
Beyond the number of ventures and deliveries, however, it is important to understand how other manufacturers can join the Build with Ukraine program.
“Who accepts applications, by what criteria are decisions made, and what support does a company receive?” Fedirko asks.
In other words, joint ventures are already delivering results, but the rules of participation and the state support mechanism must be clear to companies that want to develop production abroad.

Up to 70% of Russia’s import payments handled outside banking system via intermediaries

03:49:21 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, October 22. /TASS/. Russian companies conduct up to 60-70% of their import payments outside the banking system through various intermediaries, Vice President of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs (RSPP) Alexander Murychev said at the Russian Industrialist International Forum.
"We process the bulk of payments - up to 60-70% in the import segment - through payment intermediary arrangements. In other words, outside the banking system. This shows that the role of intermediaries has increased significantly recently," Murychev said.
He stressed that the architecture of international settlements has undergone fundamental changes over the past four years. By 2025, complex functional systems for foreign trade settlements had emerged.
"In 2025-2026, businesses moved toward widespread adoption of all available foreign trade settlement arrangements. According to aggregated industry data, the monthly volume of cross-border payments by Russian businesses stabilized at the equivalent of $12-14 bln in 2024-2025," Murychev said.
He noted that amid changing conditions for foreign economic activity, businesses need a systemic solution rather than temporary adjustments. "At the RSPP level, we have identified the following priorities. First, creating our own payment infrastructure under the control of a Russian bank. Second, developing infrastructure controlled by major importers and exporters. Third, developing barter arrangements, with mandatory simplification of accounting and taxation at the legislative level," Murychev said.
He also identified other priorities, including developing insurance for foreign trade transactions, increasing the settlement capacity of Russian banks’ foreign branches, and establishing a legislative framework for the use of digital financial assets in foreign economic activity.
TASS is the forum’s general information partner.

Norwegian auction house withdraws sale of SS-looted Torah fragment following Israeli outcry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:48:58 UTC
03:48:58 KST

A Norwegian auction house canceled the sale of a valuable parchment fragment from a Torah scroll, following intervention by Israel’s Foreign Ministry.
On Sunday, Valkyrie Historical Auctions listed on its auction itinerary a “Very Old Piece of Jewish Torah Roll Plundered by German SS Soldiers During Shoah.”
In the item description, the auction house wrote that the fragment was sent to a relative as a souvenir. This piece is handwritten in calfskin and shows signs of damage, probably from a fire. The fragment is said to have been used by an SS soldier as wrapping paper to mail a package to an address in Germany. The soldier’s field unit and the address to which he sent the package are still partially legible in the handwriting. The estimated sale price was listed as $1,500-$2,000.
Valkyrie Historical Auctions is a web-based platform auctioneer offering authentic historical items to collectors and museums worldwide. It specializes in historical artifacts from World War II and Holocaust-related material.
One thousand two hundred and fifty items were for sale in Sunday’s auction, ranging from postcards to private notebooks and photo albums.
Foreign Ministry outraged by sale
The news that the item was for sale sparked outrage from Israel’s Foreign Ministry, which called the sale “a Nazi celebration in Oslo.”
“It is a parchment sheet from a Torah scroll that was desecrated, looted, and defaced by the SS and was even used as wrapping paper by SS soldiers. At the same time, the Norwegian government is expected to cancel its financial support for visits by Norwegian students to extermination camps. Auctions of sacred texts looted by the Nazis: ‘In.’ Visits to extermination camps: ‘Out,’” the ministry said, calling on the Norwegian government to put “an immediate stop to this moral obscenity.”
Recently, in its national budget proposal, the Norwegian government suggested ceasing funding for school trips to World War II concentration camps.
However, following the end of the auction, the item was listed as sold for $8,500, with an additional 25% buyer’s premium payable to the auction house, bringing the total to $10,625
A spokesperson for Valkyrie Historical Auctions told Norwegian media outlet Verdinytt that the Torah parchment had been withdrawn from sale just 10 minutes before the auction was due to begin, due to the Israeli Foreign Ministry’s strong reaction.
Regarding why it was listed as “sold,” the spokesperson said that the auction house had no practical way of removing the item from the auction on such short notice before it began, and had instead placed its own bid that was so high that nobody would outbid it.
Scroll set to be donated to nonprofit in California
Allegedly, the scroll will be donated to RUTH – Remember Us The Holocaust, a nonprofit organization in San Diego, California.
“We are currently working with some organizations in the United States that display Holocaust-related artifacts in public spaces and preserve them for educational purposes. We believe that such an institution is a far more appropriate place for this piece than a private sale,” a spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry told Verdinytt.
On Elpeleg, a Norwegian-Israeli activist, told The Jerusalem Post that he hopes the same approach will be taken with all other personal belongings that once belonged to Jewish victims of the Holocaust.
“These items should be returned to their rightful owners or their descendants. Where that is not possible, they should be donated to the Jewish Museum in Oslo,” he said.
Elpeleg also said it is important that museums around the world dedicated to Holocaust education be given priority when purchasing historical artefacts from World War II, so that these objects can be used to educate future generations, preserve historical memory, and honor the victims of the Holocaust.
The Jerusalem Post reached out to the auction house for comment.

Ahead of the elections, the High Court of Justice ruled Thursday that party representatives serving on polling-station committees or as observers cannot digitally count voters who have cast ballots and relay those totals in real time to the parties they represent.
The 2-1 decision follows a September ruling barring those representatives from reporting which identifiable voters had voted. The latest dispute concerned whether they could instead send numerical totals without identifying anyone.
Justices Khaled Kabub and Ruth Ronnen comprised the majority, with Justice David Mintz dissenting. The court issued its operative decision on Thursday and said its reasons would follow.
The ruling came on a petition by the Israel Democracy Guard organization challenging permission granted by Dean Livne, acting director-general of the Central Elections Committee, the body responsible for administering Knesset elections.
In an October 14 clarification issued following a request from Likud attorney Ilan Bombach, Livne said polling-station committee members and party observers could use digital tools to count voters and send numerical information to their parties, provided they did not identify the voters.
High Court restricts voter tracking by political parties
Parties generally use turnout information to direct their efforts to get supporters to the polls. Earlier reporting systems, including applications such as Elector, enabled campaigns to compare information from polling stations with their own databases and contact likely supporters who had not yet voted.
The legal dispute began with restrictions imposed in August by Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg, chairman of the Central Elections Committee (CEC). After Likud challenged his decision, the issue went before the full committee, which voted in September to allow the reporting practice to continue under restrictions.
On September 17, the High Court unanimously overturned that permission. It held that party representatives at polling stations perform public functions and lack legal authority to pass identifiable voter information to their parties for campaign purposes. The court also found that the practice infringed voters’ privacy.
The new petition argued that removing voters’ names did not resolve the separate question of whether officials working inside polling stations could collect information for party headquarters.
The organization maintained that its role was to administer and oversee voting, and that a legitimate interest in encouraging turnout did not authorize it to transmit information obtained in that role.
The state and Likud defended Livne’s clarification, arguing that numerical reporting was different from identifying individual voters and could help parties encourage participation.
They maintained that the clarification did not change the existing legal position and had been issued with Sohlberg’s approval.
The dispute also concerned who should provide turnout figures. Under an arrangement previously established by Sohlberg, the CEC was to publish turnout data for each ordinary polling station at least four times during Election Day.
That official reporting mechanism differs from the continuous updates Livne’s clarification would have allowed party representatives to send directly to their headquarters.
