People power in the suburbs exposes the fragility of the AI boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:47:44 UTC
03:47:44 KST

analysis
NEXTDC slump and Firmus float flop signal investor doubts over AI boom
A small data centre operator with three sites being briefly valued at $44 billion, more than Woolworths.
A neighbourhood dispute over power poles that wipes $3 billion off a listed company's value in a single day.
And trillion-dollar global infrastructure build-out getting a wake-up call from the suburbs.
The fragility of the AI boom has been on full display in recent weeks.
An industry that has ignored the concept of "social licence" is colliding with people committed to their communities. And investors are feeling the financial consequences.
Australia ringing the alarm on AI valuations
It's a long way from West Footscray to Wall Street.
But as information has come to move in milliseconds, the titans behind trillion-dollar deals in our AI-boom economy may have spent time looking up "WeFo" on Google Maps, reading about plans for Tasmanian data centres, and wondering: is this where it started to unravel?
Let's step back.
Shares in data centre operator NEXTDC fell 42 per cent in a single day after the company revealed that delays in getting power to a proposed expansion of its massive complex in inner-west Melbourne meant its future earnings would be cut by a third.
Those delays were due to an act of civil disobedience.
When power company Jemena's crews dug holes in Sanderson Street, Yarraville, a suburb next to West Footscray, residents who had warily watched the approach of industrial-scale power poles took action, leaving cars and bins in the street to block the workers' access.
Unable to get equipment in position, the Jemena crews filled in the holes they had prepared, left and have not been back.
That quiet act of suburban defiance not only stopped infrastructure meant to provide the juice for the next stage of NEXTDC's West Footscray data centre, it resulted in the company's very bad day on the stock exchange on Wednesday.
Firmus hit a similar hurdle.
The AI data centre company wanted to list on the stock exchange with an initial public offering (IPO) that would have valued it at about $44 billion.
It would have been one of the five biggest floats in the world this year, the biggest in Australia since Telstra went from being government-owned to listed on the markets.
But it fell apart. For one reason, and then a lot of them.
The key reason was that large investors didn't think the company was worth what it thought it was. They refused to buy it at $11 a share, which would have made it one of Australia's 20 largest firms, more valuable than toll road operator Transurban and supermarket giant Coles.
But the others are important, too: growing community opposition to power and water-hungry data centres and the transmission lines needed to feed them; fears about the job-killing nature of artificial intelligence; the collision of election cycles in the US and Australia with voter unhappiness about economic instability and uncertainty.
AI not dead, but hitting resistance
The idea of social licence is that it's the ongoing acceptance and approval of an organisation's activities by people affected by them and society at large.
Whaling has lost its social licence. Very few countries now kill whales.
AI and data centre companies, spawned from the "move fast, break things" ethos of the tech sector, rapidly evolved from medium-sized warehouses in industrial areas to massive facilities closer to homes.
They became the physical manifestation of people's fears about AI. At the end of their street.
Standing outside NEXTDC's massive facility, the behemoth is undeniably dystopian. Devoid of any visible staff, the entirely black box rises vastly above the single-story brick and weatherboard houses on the other side of the street.
Protests in Europe and the US tuned leaders to the bad vibes coming from constituents. They didn't see the benefits of facilities that drove up power bills, drained precious water resources, and seemed to be in the business of making masses of people unemployed. The number of jobs in data centres, post-construction, is minimal.
But don't expect the sector to go away. As analysts at Morningstar detail, NEXTDC's assets, "both current and planned, are still in great demand". In addition, community concerns over the centres may increase costs and force new ones further away from built-up areas:
"However, this will affect all developers, will likely be factored into new contracts, and will likely make existing data centres even more valuable."
A single-street power pole dispute that costs $3 billion
There's a reason NEXTDC's difficulties are getting attention. It exposes the fragility of the AI boom, already unfolding on a scale the world has rarely seen.
Filip Tortevski, senior analyst at Wealth Within, calls it the "first serious warning shot" as investors weigh if this is an isolated incident or the beginning of something much bigger.
"What's concerning isn't simply the $140 million in revenue affected by electricity delays," they write.
Loading...
"It's the potential chain reaction nobody was pricing in. NEXTDC has acknowledged that delayed customer billing could affect its ability to draw on $6.7 billion in available debt facilities. It has also warned that the delays could affect property valuations, with the financial impact still unknown.
"Think about that. A delay in connecting electricity can potentially affect revenue, financing flexibility and asset values simultaneously."
UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce helps manage $175 billion in assets.
Before the Firmus float was pulled, he wished the company well and explained why the fund wouldn't invest a cent in it.
"It all comes down to valuation. We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation. At the current valuation, it's priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation."
Priced to perfection. The amount the company is valued at requires every single plan to run perfectly, in every element.
Many of our large AI and data centre companies appear to rest on the same belief.
This is a world of storms and natural disasters. Of electricity pole installation. Of technologies from labs we hadn't heard of three months ago. Of changes in government. Of residents who don't feel heard. Of shipping delays. Of construction challenges.
Our world is a lot of things. Perfect it is not.

This implant burns up excess blood sugar with electricity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:43:34 UTC
03:43:34 KST

A new wireless implant could burn up excess sugar in the blood, letting people with type 2 diabetes live healthier lives without having to completely rely on medication.
Traditional drugs used for diabetes such as insulin, metformin and glucagonlike peptide 1 (GLP-1) agonists all treat the condition by effectively forcing the body to keep glucose levels under control—but these treatments are prone to side effects and many involve taking a fixed quantity of medication regularly despite blood sugar changing with mood, sleep and meals. Automated insulin pumps can adjust dosing to a patient’s blood sugar in real time, but they still deliver drugs that can linger in the body.
“We wanted to have a completely new principle,” says Martin Fussenegger, the study’s senior author and a bioengineer at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich. For a new study in mice, published in Science, he and his team abandoned drugs altogether by developing a below-the-skin implant that chemically eliminates glucose from the blood on its own rather than triggering the body’s own mechanisms in order to do so.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The device, called ECHO, which stands for electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization, looks like a little flat rectangular chip, roughly the size of a USB stick. It contains a graphite wafer that carries an electric current, embedded with branching structures of gold nanoflakes that are studded with even smaller spheres of platinum. These structures work as a catalyst—a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process. The implant is operated and powered wirelessly, and when voltage is applied, the surface oxidizes glucose into an easily processed metabolite called gluconate. The mouse subjects’ bodies burned roughly a fifth of the resulting gluconate for energy, and the rest was flushed out through the kidneys.
Blood carries important molecules similar to glucose such as fructose, galactose and lactose, but the implant successfully targeted glucose specifically. Fussenegger admits the researchers don’t yet know why it is so successful, although that likely relates to the particular combination of gold and platinum. “We have no functional or structural explanation for that. We did not design for it,” Fussenegger says. “The specificity is, I would say, a lucky strike.”
In diabetic mice with obesity, the implant brought blood glucose levels under control within an hour when turned on, and repeated treatment held it there for six weeks. The mice also showed reduced triglycerides—a type of fat associated with disease risk—and lower body weight.
The team also tested the implant while connected via a smartphone to a commercial continuous glucose monitor, which relayed blood sugar readings that allowed the smartphone to turn the implant on and off as needed. For two weeks, this closed-loop system ran with no human involvement.
Many glucose-focused implants under development rely on capsules containing engineered cells that secrete therapeutic proteins—these tend not to last because they get sealed off by scar tissue in the body. But for ECHO, the mice’s tissue showed no signs of inflammation around the implant, no scarring and no leached metal. Implants removed after six weeks still worked, and some remained active even after three months under the skin, according to the study.
“Six weeks of operational stability is already well beyond the current technology,” says Luisa Torsi, a chemist at the University of Bari Aldo Moro in Italy, who was not involved in the study. “The crucial next steps are to establish long-term tissue compatibility, sustained catalytic activity and safe, effective glucose removal at the scale required for human treatment.”
A mouse has roughly two milliliters of blood, whereas humans typically hold five liters—ECHO would need to scale up to function at that level. Fussenegger is confident about that task, however. As part of the study, the team circulated sugary fluid through a five-liter flask—a stand-in for human blood volume—and the implant cleared it just as efficiently.
Because the device is small and sits just under the skin, Fussenegger expects the implantation procedure in humans would require a minor incision rather than complex surgery. “If it’s possible to do this maybe every three months or up to a year, and then ‘I can forget my diabetes,’ I think people would be happy,” he says.

Attorney-general urged to step in as court data breach concerns grow
In short:
The Coalition and the Greens are calling on the Attorney-General to set up an independent audit after several court data breaches.
New emails reveal Federal Court CEO Sia Lagos was notified of a 2014 breach.
What's next?
The Federal Court said it was reviewing a report into the latest data breach. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner is also looking into the issue.
An integrity crisis in Australia's court system has deepened, prompting calls from the Coalition and the Greens for the Attorney-General to step in and set up an independent audit.
Revelations that highly sensitive court data was accessed in India on at least two occasions has sparked national security fears.
Now, internal court emails have revealed the Federal Court CEO was notified in 2016 of the first data breach — an incident for which no action was taken.
However, a spokesperson for the Federal Court said its CEO, Sia Lagos, had no recollection of having been notified of the data breach by the then-deputy principal registrar.
Security concerns were first raised in 2014 by former Auscript national manager, Paul Cutbush, who made Public Interest Disclosures (PID) to both the family court and the Federal Court as well as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) about the offshoring of sensitive data.
In an email from then-Deputy Principal Registrar of the Federal Court John Mathieson to Mr Cutbush in 2016 he stated:
"I have notified Ms Sia Lagos, who is Acting Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar of the Federal Court, in Mr Soden's absence, as I am required to do so, of the decisions and determinations I have made under the [Public Interest Disclosure] Act."
A spokesperson for the Federal Court of Australia said it was "not accepted that there has been a failure to act" in either the data breach earlier this year or the historical incident.
"Ms Lagos did not have any recollection of a procedural notification she had received almost 10 years earlier concerning the Family Court of Australia and matters pre-dating the present administrative entity," the spokesperson said.
"Beyond that single notification, Ms Lagos had no involvement in the management of this matter."
Neither the Federal Court, nor the family court acted on the disclosures made to them by Mr Cutbush in 2014. The family court responded two years after the disclosures were made, classifying the breach as "minor and inconsequential" in emails seen by the ABC.
The family court has denied any current executives had knowledge of the first breach despite Mr Cutbush's disclosures.
Last week, Mr Cutbush said the most recent data breach was a "slap in the face" after his concerns were ignored in 2014.
Auscript was responsible for court transcription services in 2014 before VIQ Solutions took over around 2020.
A second data breach occurred earlier this year when VIQ was managing transcription services and the company was shutdown shortly after.
Cases heard in the Federal Court include critical human rights matters, industrial relations cases, taxation law and matters involving multi-million-dollar corporations while the Federal Circuit and Family Court hears migration cases, and matters involving child sexual abuse, domestic violence and property settlements.
It is unclear how many files were accessed in India during either of the offshoring incidents.
'Warning signs ignored by court leadership': Greens
A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said the courts were "responsible for their own operation and management" — a position ridiculed by the Opposition.
Shadow Attorney-General Michaelia Cash said the latest developments strengthened the need for a full independent audit coordinated by the Attorney-General.
"I again call on the Attorney-General to take control of this matter and organise a whole-of-government response," she said.
"We need to know what has occurred and how widespread this issue is. It is not good enough for the Attorney-General to keep her head in the sand."
Greens Leader Senator David Shoebridge took aim at the court's leadership.
"It's almost impossible to believe that we are now facing another round of obfuscation from the Federal Court," he said.
"These data breach issues date back to 2014 and it appears that at least some senior staff members of the court have known this.
"This requires a prompt and public explanation from the court.
"Family court transcripts hold some of the most private and painful moments in people's lives, and twice now that material has gone offshore while the warning signs were ignored by the leadership of the court.
"The Attorney-General keeps saying the responsibility is solely with the court, but the fact is the listed entity is under her administrative authority so she also has a clear role here.
"The Attorney-General should order a forensic audit across every agency in her portfolio that used Auscript and VIQ transcription services to provide people with real certainty about what on earth happened with their sensitive court data."
The Federal Court said it was currently reviewing a report by CyberCX into the latest data breach.
A privacy complaint has also been passed on to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) regarding the offshoring of Australian citizen's data.
The Federal Court said it had provided information to the OAIC and the family court said it would "fully cooperate" with the OAIC or any other government inquiry.

Christa Pike’s IV team warned vein might be ‘blowing’ before failed execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:42:14 UTC
03:42:14 KST

The Tennessee execution team tasked with setting an intravenous line in the arms of the death row prisoner Christa Pike through which she could be injected with a lethal dose of pentobarbital repeatedly warned that her vein might be “blowing”, before they went ahead with the procedure, her lawyer has revealed.
Members of the intravenous (IV) team used up to 10 needles as they sought to establish a line through which Pike could be killed with a massive dose of the sedative. About 20 minutes into the attempt, they began discussing among themselves whether the prisoner’s vein “might be blowing”.
Two unidentified members of the team began poking the site through which they were trying to set up the line, and both agreed that they couldn’t tell whether they had succeeded in finding the vein. “One of them said something like: ‘It’s either blood or blown, I need to know,’” the lawyer’s new account says.
The potentially critical new details of how Tennessee’s execution team failed to kill Pike, 50, on 30 September are contained in the most detailed account yet given by Pike’s lawyer Randy Spivey.
In a declaration that was released as part of separate legal proceedings, Spivey gave a minute-by-minute chronology of Pike’s ordeal, which he personally witnessed in the death chamber.
The account suggests that the IV team was racked by doubts even before the pentobarbital began to flow, as they struggled to find a vein for almost an hour. The search began at 6.35pm that evening, and was completed at 7.24pm, at which point the team left the chamber assuming everything was going according to plan.
But Pike remained alive, making snoring and choking sounds.
The execution was eventually called off, and after 10 days in hospital Pike was returned to prison in Nashville. She is the only prisoner in modern times to survive a full dose of a lethal injection drug.
Though she can now talk and walk, her long-term prognosis is still unknown. The gruesome events of her failed execution have prompted nationwide soul-searching about the death penalty in the US, and forced the Republican governor of Tennessee, Bill Lee, to call off all executions in the state pending a review.
Spivey’s blow-by-blow chronology gives agonizing new details about the lengths to which the IV team went to find a vein, as well as their profound anxieties about whether they were doing the right thing. A person on the IV team named by Spivey as “member two” first expressed the fear that Pike’s vein might be blown at 6.53pm.
The team then discarded the 20-gauge needle that they had been using, saying: ‘“It’s not long enough. What is the longest you’ve got?”
Three minutes later, at 6.57pm, member two repeated it “might be blowing”. Spivey reported: “Member two and IV team member 3 inspected the insertion site and poked it. Both said that they ‘can’t tell’.”
Despite the uncertainty, the IV team agreed among themselves that they had established a line just two minutes later, only to discover that it was not, in fact, properly working. “I need to work again,” member two said, pulling the needle out of Pike’s left arm. “It appeared to be severely bent,” Spivey records.
At 7.08pm member two called on the team to think again. “Let’s regroup,” he said. They began checking Pike’s right arm again, and poking around the insertion site. At 7.13pm, member two told Pike directly that they “have it”, and the injection of pentobarbital that they thought would kill her was set to begin.
The revelations of so many doubts and foiled efforts to find a line, including the critical fears that her vein might have blown, lend added weight to one of the most prominent theories that have emerged for how the execution failed and Pike survived. Had the drug entered her bloodstream at such a extreme dose she would almost certainly have died, but if her vein burst, the pentobarbital would have been diverted into her arm tissue, causing her severe injuries but falling short of killing her.
As Spivey noted in his chronology, at 7.34pm Pike cried out: “I feel like my arm is about to bust. It burns.”
Spivey’s detailed minute-by-minute account is attached as an exhibit in a new legal motion filed on behalf of Tony Carruthers and other death row prisoners. Tennessee attempted to execute Carruthers on 21 May, but he too survived after the execution team failed to find a vein in more than 30 minutes.
Carruthers’s lawyers have asked permission from the Davidson county chancery court to file a supplemental complaint challenging Tennessee’s lethal injection protocol. They made an initial complaint in March 2025 in which they warned that the prisoner could face a torturous death by pentobarbital poisoning because the team administering the lethal drug were “incompetent, insufficiently trained, insufficiently dedicated to doing their jobs, and/or insufficiently attentive”.
As such, they warned, the execution ran an unacceptable risk of violating constitutional protections against cruel and unusual punishment.
The failed executions in May, and Pike’s subsequent failed execution in September, bear out the lawyer’s advance warnings, the new motion asserts. “The specific failures that Mr Carruthers and Ms Pike endured were predicted, in detail and at length,” the new motion states.
Kit Thomas, an attorney for the death row plaintiffs, said: “Instead of addressing the problems in the 2025 Protocol when we identified them last year, the Tennessee Department of Correction and the Attorney General’s Office doubled down on secrecy and refused to make changes. The result was just as we predicted: extreme pain and suffering for our clients, in botched execution attempts that also inflicted lasting harm on victims’ families, corrections staff, and media witnesses, among others.”
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of her friend Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 at the time of the murder, and spent the next almost three decades in solitary confinement.

They were already afraid. The Helen Haines attack reminds us why

IN BRIEF
- Many Australian women are feeling unsafe and traumatised by the news of the attack on Helen Haines, experts say.
- The federal MP was attacked in Wangaratta on Monday and remains hospitalised and in a critical condition.
WARNING: This article contains distressing content and references to violence against women.
When Marie, whose name has been changed for privacy reasons, heard about the attack on Indi MP Helen Haines, she was shocked.
"How is this possible?" Marie told SBS News. "It's really confronting. Her life is irrevocably changed."
Police allege Haines was run down by 43-year-old Brendan Nugent outside her electoral office in Wangaratta, Victoria, on Monday afternoon. He has been charged with multiple offences including harming a Commonwealth official and drug charges. His motive is unclear.
She sustained serious injuries, has had both legs amputated and remains in hospital in a critical condition.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Marie, who is in her late 40s, is a survivor of gendered violence.
She said the increasing rate of violence against women being reported by the media is "retraumatising".
The psychological impact has forced the Canberra mother to delete her social media accounts and limit socialising.
"I don't feel safe in public anywhere anymore," she said, adding that she feels increasingly unsafe around men.
According to a 2024 survey from The Man Box, one in four Australian men aged between 18 and 45 admitted to having used physical and/or sexual violence against an intimate partner.
Marie said that, when she's alone with men, this statistic is firmly in her mind.
"I get into a lift at work, and if there are a group of men in the lift, I think 'it's one in four men – how many of them have assaulted a woman?'"
"I know it's not all men, but it's always a man [involved in such attacks]."
'A level of fear that women just live with'
Australian Sex Discrimination commissioner Anna Cody believes many women have been impacted by the attack on Haines.
"We see ourselves in Helen Haines, we see our vulnerability. [We have] that sense of 'it could be us'," she told SBS News.
"We know that women experience high levels of violence and there has been an escalation in the online and real-life expression of hatred towards women, the resentment towards women, and those messages have gained momentum in the last two years."
Cody described Haines as a "compassionate, strong, fierce, and really effective parliamentarian".
"I'm hopeful that this can be a reckoning point where we realise that speaking hatefully about any group, or any person, does translate into actual physical violence."
The Trauma Recovery Centre's head of programs and founder of Doctors Against Violence Towards Women, Karen Williams, told SBS News that Australian women are "rightly" feeling unsafe.
"The reality is that it isn't actually safe for women. You don't want to gaslight people into thinking they shouldn't feel unsafe," she said.
"These things are happening on a significant level. It's not a one-off, occasional thing ... These are not small risks; they're real.
"We are powerless against it really ... There is a level of fear that women just live with and regard as normal."
She said the news of Haines' attack could exacerbate that fear for many women.
"Community is meant to be a place where you feel safe... but events like what's happened with Dr Haines make people think our community itself is not safe," she said.
"Dr Haines is someone who should have the resources and protections, and even she isn't safe from violence."
While media reporting of violence against women can be triggering and retraumatising for some, Williams said it's "the only sort of information or education women are getting on the risks they're exposed to".
"Everything we ever hear about is only through the media," she said. "They have a very important role in explaining to people that these risks do exist because they do."
No 'real deterrent' for violence against women
Williams believes reducing violence against women requires a "huge systems change" that begins with having "deterrents to harming women".
"There isn't a real deterrent. You can hurt women and get away with it ... and [perpetrators] know they can get away with it," she said.
She said that, until there is a "deterrent", people would "keep harming women".
For those experiencing distress, Williams recommends focusing on basic needs: physical exercise, eating well and creativity.
"We know from research that having physical capabilities does actually help, so getting out there and exercising and moving ... training your body to feel like you have some control over your body, feeling autonomous and empowered," she said.
"Music and creativity are also really important things for a person trying to regulate their nervous system."
Marie has started gardening, alongside seeking professional support and counselling, grounding techniques and leaning on her support network.
"I want to be able to present, and I want to be able to enjoy my life again because I don't feel like I've had any capacity to do so."

A $3 billion downgrade could send a ripple through a surging Australian industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:40:36 UTC
03:40:36 KST

When energy provider Jemena announced on Wednesday that it had paused the installation of new 22-metre-tall concrete power poles needed for a nearby data centre, it triggered a chain reaction.
One of the country's biggest data centre operators, NEXTDC — which was forced to delay a planned expansion of its M3 data centre in West Footscray, Melbourne — quickly saw its market valuation drop by around $3 billion.
The plunge was equivalent to about 42 per cent of the company's value, which could send fears through a surging sector still reeling from the failed float of one of its other biggest players.
Luke Laretive, CEO of Seneca Financial Solutions, said fear of "a significant downgrade" to NEXTDC's future earnings and a "contagion-type vibe" had spooked the share market.
"Are [data centre operators] going to be in a position now where ... despite having insatiable demand, they're unable to actually build these facilities in locations that have access to power, water, a community that's happy to have them nearby and are still close enough to the businesses and the people that want to use them?" the investment adviser told SBS' On The Money.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Some of the community around NEXTDC's West Footscray facility seemingly aren't happy to have it nearby. Local residents have previously expressed fears about the amount of diesel stored on the site and raised concerns about noise pollution.
The installation of the power poles required to meet the facility's significant electricity needs has also sparked community anger, with some residents of a nearby suburb using their cars and bins to block equipment deployed for the electricity network upgrade in September.
"Has NEXTDC lost its social licence to operate here, or have data centre providers more generally lost their social licence to operate?" Laretive asked.
Data centres and social licence
Less than two weeks earlier, data centre operator Firmus Technologies withdrew its application for public listing on the Australian Stock Exchange — a move that had been touted as the biggest since Telstra's 1997 float.
Firmus Technologies operates a data centre in Melbourne and is currently building another in Tasmania, with plans for at least two more — despite facing some community backlash.
A month before cancelling its public listing, Firmus announced several-year sponsorship deals with the Tasmania Devils AFL teams, Cricket Tasmania, and Tasmania JackJumpers and Jewels basketball teams, raising concerns of 'sportswashing'.
Olivia Shen, director of strategic technologies at the University of Sydney's United States Studies Centre (USSC), thinks the social licence for data centres could be in the process of being lost across Australia.
"The build-out has been incredibly fast and incredibly rapid," she said.
"And I think at the local level, communities are just feeling quite blindsided by all this development, and especially where it's happening on very large scale in areas where they're not used to this kind of development."
This sentiment conflicts with government messaging that, according to Shen, is more focused on a "narrative that these data centres are incredibly important public facilities for AI development".
That narrative may not be cutting through, with the USSC's 2025 annual poll finding that 67 per cent of Australians "want to prioritise the regulation of AI even at the cost of innovation".
"These Australians are basically saying that even if it slows innovation, we want to progress at a bit of a slower pace rather than having these technologies being shoved down our throats and being told that they're actually good for us," she said.
However, Shen said people should be careful in making broad generalisations about the entire industry.
"Not all data centres are the same, not all of the technologies they use are the same from one operator to another, and the impact on the community really, really depends on the local conditions of that community," she said.
A data centre reliant on a polluting energy plant planning to build next to rural farmland used for cattle production will have a different impact to one hoping to build in a quiet suburb in the city.
Laretive, meanwhile, suggested data centre operators "learn from the likes of the BHP's and the Rio [Tinto]'s of the world" for community engagement.
"They are a real participant in the community, and they're not just there kind of soaking up resources," he said, referencing jobs created by mining companies.
Fears history is repeating itself
The Western Downs Digital Park is a $32 billion proposed data centre in Queensland. AI giant Anthropic signed a lease for the first of four planned buildings, but the site has not yet received approval.
Luke Munn, an Australian Research Council future fellow with the University of Queensland, and Joanna Horton, a postdoctoral research fellow, are studying the proposed site.
"I think what we've seen in the last couple of years is a kind of increasing recognition from the public that there's an infrastructure and a material footprint around the AI boom," Munn said.
Horton said the community have been "really pushing back against the proposed development".
A petition to stop the project already has 23,496 signatures — the most support for any active e-petition on the Queensland parliament website.
"It has been a hotspot for gas extraction, which has been a really big 'boom and bust' industry for the region," she said.
It's left residents concerned about history repeating, with new jobs being created only to disappear before too long. Another concern is natural resource extraction and water use, which critics have said could have a significant impact on the drought-prone region.
Horton said locals are also taking action, with the Environmental Defenders Office, a non-profit community legal centre, reporting a 250 per cent increase in inquiries related to data centres since January of this year.
"I think that shows that all over Australia really are seeing data centres as a) something that they're not sure about that they have very real concerns about, and then b) something that they actually want to take action and push back on," she said.
Munn added that some companies now saw potential community opposition as a more important factor than geography or energy supply when choosing potential sites for data centres.
Is the data centre bubble starting to pop?
Shen doesn't think challenges faced by companies like Firmus are necessarily a sign that Australia's data centre boom is over, but she sees it as a warning that not every data centre company will see its investment pay off.
"There are firms jumping on this data centre bandwagon that are probably not going to be the best firms," she said.
"This is complex physical and digital infrastructure, and I don't think every single investor in a data centre is necessarily going to make their money back."
She says it could be a good thing if it encourages "more level-headedness with people investing in the right places".
Laretive said the NEXTDC case likely doesn't say too much about the demand for AI, but he still urges caution for investors.
"We need to be careful about evaluations and the amount of the future that we price into today's numbers and today's market capitalisation."

Trump called Elon Musk to ask him to lift restrictions on Ukraine’s military-grade Starlink service, WSJ reports
Donald Trump called Elon Musk and asked him to lift restrictions on the military version of Starlink in Ukraine, sources told The Wall Street Journal.
Trump expressed frustration that the system still had a speed cap of about 160 kilometers per hour, the newspaper’s sources said. The restriction left some Ukrainian attack drones and interceptor drones ineffective against Russian attacks. The Journal reported that Trump and Musk spoke after it published a report saying Musk himself had ordered the restrictions on Starlink in Ukraine.
U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the system began working “more normally” shortly after Trump’s conversation with Musk.
Ukrainian drone commanders on the front line said the Starlink restrictions had been lifted, according to Oliver Carroll, a journalist for The Economist. “They are still doing tests but ‘this looks to be the case,’” Carroll wrote.
On October 14, the Ukrainian military reported encountering restrictions on Starlink satellite communications terminals — specifically, their military version, Starshield. Drones lost their connection when flying faster than 160 kilometers per hour.

Meet Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE's candidate for UN Secretary-General
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:38:53 UTC
03:38:53 KST

- i24NEWS
- Middle East
- The Gulf
- Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE's candidate for UN Secretary-General?
Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE's candidate for UN Secretary-General?
Lana Nusseibeh defended the Abraham Accords just weeks before they were signed, saying that previous attitudes toward Israel hadn't achieved anything
Lana Nusseibeh grew up between the UK and Abu Dhabi, where her father Zaki worked as a senior advisor to Sheikh Zayed Al Nahyan, the father of the current President of the UAE.
The Nusseibeh family originally comes from Jerusalem, where they are one of two families who guard the keys to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The Nusseibeh family have reportedly held this role since the conquest of Jerusalem by the Rashidun Caliphate in the 7th century.
Zaki Nusseibeh was also educated in the UK where he attended Queens' College, Cambridge, graduating in 1967. Unable to return to Jerusalem after the Six-Day War, he opted to move to Abu Dhabi, quickly becoming a central figure in the state's media around the time of independence in the 1970s.
Lana Nusseibeh followed in her father's footsteps to Queens' College, Cambridge for her undergraduate degree. She graduated from the School of Oriental and African Studies with a master's degree in Israeli and Jewish studies.
She began working for the UAE government in 2006, working to promote the "mobilisation of women voters." She subsequently served in the policy planning department of the Emirati Foreign Ministry.
In 2013, she was appointed as the UAE's ambassador to the UN, a role she held for over a decade. During that time, Nusseibeh succeeded in getting the UAE elected to the UN Security Council for the 2022–2023 term, for the first time since 1986.
The Abraham Accords were signed while she was ambassador to the UN. While her direct involvement remains unclear, she was a clear supporter of the move. She defended the Accords just weeks before they were signed, telling the Emirati newspaper The National: saying "The empty chair policy [of not being engaged with Israel] has not led to the fruition of peace that we were hoping for."
Notably, she hosted Israel's then-UN Ambassador Gilad Erdan at the UAE's mission, with discussions focusing on the COVID-19 global pandemic.
She also served during the initial stages of the war in Gaza, where she spearheaded the passage of UNSC Resolution 2720 in December 2023, which pushed for the reopening of border crossings into Gaza to allow for humanitarian aid.
Nusseibeh was promoted to minister of state for foreign affairs, a role in which she was responsible for handling relations with the European Union.
Nusseibeh announced her candidacy on Wednesday, promising where she promised to focus on reinvigorating the organization around its core purpose and ensuring results.
Following the announcement, she will need the Security Council's approval, requiring at least nine of its 15 members to vote in her favour and no veto from any of the five permanent members: the United States, the United Kingdom, France, Russia and China. She would then face a vote in the UN General Assembly.
She may face some opposition, as, according to the traditional regional rotation of UN secretaries-general, the post should go to a candidate from either Latin America or Eastern Europe, as no secretary-general from Latin America has been appointed since 1991, while no Eastern European has ever held the post.

Promised a better life, New Zealand voters are asking what went wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:37:41 UTC
03:37:41 KST

Māori and Pacific communities weigh what it takes to stay before New Zealand election
Families living in campervans, workers spending their house deposits and communities watching loved ones leave for Australia.
As New Zealand heads to the polls, voters are asking what happened to the promise of a better life.
For generations, New Zealand has offered a simple promise: work hard, look after your whānau, your family and build a future here.
But for many, that promise is getting harder to keep.
About 350,000 people, including non-New Zealand citizens, are estimated to have left New Zealand over the past three years, with almost half of them moving to Australia.
For those who stay, frustration over the rising cost of living is spilling onto the streets. In August, hundreds of people marched on parliament in protest at soaring bills from Tiaki Wai, the Wellington region's water provider. The average annual bill is now almost $NZ2,390 ($2,000).
Ahead of the November 7 election, Māori and Pacific communities, which are among those hardest hit by unemployment and homelessness, are asking whether politicians can give them a reason to stay.
Katherine Taniwha's family knows how to build a home.
She is a rigger. Her husband David is a crane driver. Their son Eli builds houses.
Now all three live in a campervan while Katherine, 62, undergoes treatment for blood cancer. She says she takes her chemotherapy tablets at night to sleep through the side effects.
David has had to cut back his working hours so he can take his wife to appointments and weekly tests.
As their savings dwindled, Katherine says they sought housing assistance but were told David's campervan counted as their home.
"They said, 'You don't qualify. David has an RV. That's your home,'" Katherine says.
The family has lived in the campervan for more than two years. David says he has sometimes had to borrow money just to get to work and put food on the table.
"We don't really have that much to stretch out anymore," he says. "I almost have to beg for some money at work just to help me get to work or help put a little bit extra on the table for my wife and son."
For Katherine, it's a situation she has come to accept.
"This must be how it is now," she says.*
Their story is not unique.
At the 2023 census, about 112,500 people were severely housing deprived across New Zealand, a figure some housing organisations say has only grown, with Māori and Pacific people disproportionately affected.
"By almost every measure, things have gone backwards quite significantly in the past three years," Paul Gilberd, from Community Housing Aotearoa, says.
Katherine wants politicians to see that reality for themselves.
"Get your hands dirty. Don't say you're doing your best, 'cause your best isn't enough apparently," she says.
The promises and the politics
Loading...
New Zealand is home to about 5.4 million people. Unlike Australia, voting is not compulsory, although enrolling is.
At the last election in 2023, about 2.9 million voted, just over 78 per cent of those enrolled.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is seeking another term for his National-led coalition with ACT and New Zealand First.
Labour, now led by Chris Hipkins after he succeeded Jacinda Ardern in 2023, hopes to return to government, potentially with support from the Greens and Te Pāti Māori.
But New Zealand's electoral system works differently from Australia's.
Voters get two votes: one for their local MP and another for a political party. The party vote largely determines how many seats each party wins, making coalition negotiations central to who governs.
One of the system's most distinctive features is its seven Māori electorates: voters of Māori descent can choose to enrol in these electorates, where they elect their own local MPs, or join the general electoral roll. Both groups also cast a party vote.
About two-thirds of New Zealand's Pacific population lives in Auckland, many in the south, making it a key electoral battleground and a familiar stop on the campaign trail, despite traditionally being a Labour stronghold.
At Johnnie Timu's Brown Pride gym, there's frustration with politicians who turn up during elections but struggle to connect with the people they're trying to reach.
"They always come out in community, but they make a big racket out of it," Johnnie says.
He wants politicians to build trust beyond election season.
Finding work remains a pressing concern.
Unemployment reached 5.6 per cent in the June quarter, with unemployment among people with a Pacific background double that at 11.6 per cent.
For Haora Hema, who lives down in Wellington, the economic downturn has come at a high personal cost.
He spent five years as a principal adviser helping the public service work with Māori and the Crown, before his team was disbanded last year.
His partner, who has a PhD and worked on a programme supporting Pacific leaders, also lost her job, leading the couple to start spending their house deposit just to get by.
"The reality is the job market is smashed," he says.
They pulled their children out of sport and swimming, and slept beside a single heater during winter to save on electricity.
The family wonders if they'll ever own a home.
Beyond financial issues, Haora says he is also worried about how Māori issues have become a source of political division.
"My wish is that people understand that Te Tiriti and Māori stuff is not about division: it's about how we exist here in a harmonious way," he says.
Te Tiriti o Waitangi, or the Treaty of Waitangi, is New Zealand’s founding agreement between Māori chiefs and the British Crown, signed in 1840. Its place in modern New Zealand remains a source of political debate.
National minister Paul Goldsmith says the previous Labour government's spending and public service expansion were unsustainable.
"It's not fair to make future generations pay for uncontrolled spending today," he says.
He points to forecasts of stronger growth and jobs. Haora is still waiting for that recovery.
"What is the vision for our country?" Haora says.
A reason to stay, a reason to leave
Loading...
In Waihi, a gold-mining town a couple of hours' drive from Auckland, mining offers some a reason to stay.
Chloe Witika, a young Māori woman who spent some time growing up in Australia, returned to New Zealand to be near her parents.
She works as a purchasing officer at the local mine.
She says Māori workers are a rare sight in the industry, but sees mining as a source of opportunity and hope, despite economic trade-offs.
"The pay is so low in New Zealand," she says, when asked about life in comparison to Australia.
"However, my mind has changed: home is everything for me, and to be able to work in a mining industry in New Zealand with my family is all I ever wanted."
When it comes to politics, she says she's still undecided on how to vote.
The government sees mining and infrastructure projects as a way to boost the economy, introducing controversial fast-track laws to speed up approvals for priority developments.
But the changes, which allow some projects to follow a streamlined approval process, have sparked opposition from communities, including around Waihi.
Neville Williams, a spokesman for a Māori collective opposing the mining development, says the approval process left too little room for their concerns.
"That's just some of the duality and the conflict that our people suffer from when confronted with a taniwha like gold mining — it divides, and it separates," he says.
For Chloe and Neville, both Māori, the debate exposes different views about what a future at home should look like.
Despite differences of sentiment or feeling though, Neville urges communities to vote.
"I want [Maori communities] to have hope, and to use their vote," he says.
But across the country, the question of staying or leaving is increasingly familiar, as more New Zealanders watch family, friends and colleagues make the move to Australia.
Back at the gym, Johnnie says several people he knows have moved to Australia this year, seeking secure work and better opportunities for their children.
For families like Johnnie's, New Zealand was once the destination. His own family's journey began in Samoa.
"They done all they could in Samoa and moved to New Zealand," he says.
"Now most of the families here have felt like they've done all they could in New Zealand, now move to Australia."
It's a move he admits he's considered himself, for his children's future. But despite the uncertainty, he remains optimistic.
"Regardless who's in power, we're gonna figure it out — we're gonna learn to survive."
A home worth coming back to
At South Auckland's 275 Markets, Savele "Fitz" Refiti sees neighbours helping each other through hard times.
"Coming together, we can stretch our dollar," he says.
"The village mentality has always worked for us."
But helping each other only goes so far.
Whoever forms the next government faces bigger questions about jobs, housing and whether families can afford to stay together.
For a country that has long promised opportunity and a better life, the challenge is not just stopping people from leaving, but giving them something to stay for.
Labour finance spokeswoman Barbara Edmonds knows that pull personally: her daughter plans to move to Australia after graduating.
"My job, as both a mother and as finance spokesperson, is to ensure that children like my girl will want to come back home," she says.
It's a dilemma facing families across New Zealand: how to build a future for the next generation, without losing them to somewhere else.
But for Katherine and David, the future is a more immediate concern, as the family fights for housing while receiving cancer treatment.
As voters prepare to decide who will lead their country, David hopes the next government will see the people struggling to get by.
"Open your eyes. See who needs help," he says.

====================================================================================================

Raiding super to pay medical bills leaves trail of 'financial damage'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:35:08 UTC
03:35:08 KST

Australians raid $1.4b from superannuation for medical costs as regulators warn of 'predatory' tactics
In short:
Australians withdrew $1.46 billion from their superannuation on compassionate grounds in 2025-26, with the vast majority used for medical costs.
There was a 13-fold increase in the amount withdrawn for dental treatment.
Regulators are cracking down on predatory practitioners who inappropriately help people access their superannuation.
Australians withdrew a record $1.46 billion from their superannuation last financial year on compassionate grounds, prompting regulators to sound the alarm over "predatory" sales tactics being used by health practitioners.
The amount of money taken from retirement nest eggs for compassionate reasons like medical treatment has skyrocketed in recent years, up about 220 per cent since 2018-19.
Consumers Health Forum (CHF) CEO Elizabeth Deveny said it reflected a health care system that had become increasingly unaffordable.
"When people are hit with a health bill on top of the cost-of-living crisis, it's understandable people reach for the only tools available to them," she said.
"Increasing numbers of Australians are having to choose between living in pain now or being poor in retirement."
Under the Australian Tax Office (ATO) early release rules, Australians can apply to withdraw money from their retirement funds on compassionate grounds, such as medical or funeral expenses.
Australians withdrew about $1.46 billion from their superannuation on compassionate grounds in 2025-26, with the vast majority of that — about $1.42 billion — used for medical costs including dental work.
Super Members Council CEO Misha Schubert said compassionate release provisions were an important safety net, but were designed to be used only in extremely rare circumstances.
"We're deeply concerned to see the scale of the financial damage that's being done often to very vulnerable Australians," she said.
Almost 65,000 applications for compassionate release of super were approved in 2025-26, which the ATO said was a 5 per cent decrease from the previous year.
ATO Deputy Commissioner Ben Kelly said while that drop was promising, some businesses were still trying to exploit the system.
"Our message to individuals and medical practitioners is clear, compassionate release of super should only be considered as a last resort," he said.
Total compassionate release of super applications
Source: ATO
'Concerning trend' from health practitioners
For the early withdrawal of super to be approved on medical grounds, two medical practitioners need to verify it is necessary to alleviate pain or mental illness, or to treat a life-threatening illness or injury.
The ATO has been working with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) to crack down on a "concerning trend" of health practitioners, like dentists, encouraging people to withdraw their superannuation inappropriately for services, such as cosmetic dental procedures.
"We are concerned by predatory sales tactics that use social media and internet advertising to attract patients for high-cost treatments they do not need or cannot afford," AHPRA CEO Justin Untersteiner said.
Over the past year, the ATO has ramped up compliance and fined practitioners a total of $1.5 million for making misleading statements so patients could secure early superannuation access.
One practitioner was fined around $30,000 for writing a medical report that relied on false clinical information, including an incorrect classification of the patient's condition.
A GP found to have engaged in professional misconduct while helping a patient access almost $20,000 of her superannuation for cosmetic liposuction was one of two health practitioners referred to tribunals by regulators, amid almost 100 related complaints between 2019 and April this year.
Ms Schubert said consumers needed stronger protections, calling for a ban on any advertising that promotes access to early super withdrawals.
"We're calling for this to be a real moment for the parliament and lawmakers to step in to protect vulnerable Australians to make sure that they have that strong nest egg of their retirement savings secured for them in retirement," she said.
What type of treatments was money withdrawn for?
Dental was again the most popular reason for someone to withdraw their superannuation on medical grounds, with $892 million taken out in 2025-26.
That is a 13-fold increase since 2018-19, when about $66 million was approved for release.
Public health researchers and the peak industry body have told the ABC the dramatic increase in early superannuation withdrawals for dental treatment pointed to "historical neglect" of the public system.
Dr Deveny said some providers were exploiting those gaps in care.
"It's completely understandable if you're living in constant dental pain, that you'll do whatever it takes to fix it… I think we need to be careful not to blame people for doing that," she said.
Early super withdrawals for IVF have more than doubled in the past eight years, from $36.2 million in 2018-19 to $76.4 million last financial year.
Ms Schubert said Australians needed to understand the long-term impact of raiding their nest eggs, saying withdrawing $20,000 of superannuation could ultimately cost someone $93,000 by retirement because they lose the compound interest they could have earned.
Financial Services Minister and Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said the government would continue to monitor the issue, including whether further measures were needed to protect patients.
"Australians should not be pressured into accessing their superannuation for unnecessary medical or dental procedures."

Luxury tax or relocation — what Meta did to keep Zuckerberg in California

Meta Platforms has reached an agreement with Mark Zuckerberg for him to continue living in California. This came after the CEO warned that he was considering leaving the state where the company is headquartered if voters next month support a proposal to introduce a wealth tax, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Meta said on Wednesday that under the terms of the agreement, Zuckerberg will receive non-voting shares. He will be able to sell them to cover potential tax liabilities amounting to billions of dollars if the proposal is approved. In return, he undertakes to remain a resident of California (or of whichever state Meta's headquarters are located in at that time) for eight years.
Zuckerberg, who according to Forbes is the world's sixth-richest person, told Meta that he was considering changing his primary residence to somewhere outside California. The reason was "Proposition 40" — an initiative dubbed the "California wealth tax." It could create enormous tax liabilities for him, potentially forcing him to sell voting shares to pay them.
According to political analysts, it is not yet known whether "Proposition 40," which provides for the introduction of a one-time 5% tax on billionaires residing in the state, will be approved. About 250 billionaires live in California, with combined fortunes exceeding $2 trillion.
Zuckerberg, whose fortune is estimated at approximately $240 billion, will be able to immediately sell 20% of the Class C shares he receives (representing 10% of his total economic stake in the company). This will allow him to pay the potential tax without losing control through voting rights.
The company also announced on Wednesday that in January 2027 it will issue a new type of non-voting Class C common shares (effectively carrying out a two-for-one stock split). This is being done to finance acquisitions and retain leading specialists while preserving Zuckerberg's control over the company.

‘London and I are a perfect match.’ Journalist Vladimir Raevsky talks about his adopted city for Meduza’s new series of questionnaires with Russian émigrés.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:29:40 UTC
03:29:40 KST

‘London and I are a perfect match.’ Journalist Vladimir Raevsky talks about his adopted city for Meduza’s new series of questionnaires with Russian émigrés.
A new installment of our “Emigrant Questionnaire” series! Our first questionnaire was completed by Monetochka, who lives in Vilnius, and the second by Elmira Drau, a 32-year-old English teacher in Yerevan. This time, journalist Vladimir Raevsky tells us about life in London.
What’s your name?
Vladimir Raevsky.
Where do you live, and how long have you lived there?
I’ve been living in London for three years now.
What do you love most about your new country?
Do you know why British writers so often come up with worlds within worlds? Like in “Harry Potter,” for example, or “The Chronicles of Narnia.” I think it has something to do with Britain being a world of its own within the wider world. And once you find yourself in it, it’s exactly where you want to be.
London and I are a perfect match. We’re compatible in every way. Nothing here pisses me off, I like everything, I find everything fascinating. And I can never quite figure it all out.
The first time I went down into the Tube, I looked around: two dudes in turbans sitting here, some Africans over there, Slavic women with foot-and-a-half-long nails over here. And right then I knew I was where I belonged. This is exactly the kind of society I want to live in — with lots of different people, all sharing a sense of friendliness, openness, curiosity about one another, and a rejection of violence.
No one here has ever tutted when I’ve bumped into them (which I do constantly) or rushed me when I’ve tried to tap my door key instead of my card on the Tube (it’s happened more than once). I feel completely at home here.
What was hardest to get used to in your new country?
I always always laugh it off and say my biggest complaint is that you need an adapter to plug a European plug into the outlets here. Or that cell reception is bad indoors. That British people have loudspeakers implanted in their throats as children and don’t realize it. That’s about the level of my beef with London. There’s nothing here I really dislike.
That said, London is an expensive, difficult city. You can’t say life here is easy. There are cities where all you have to do is show up and live: find a comfortable balance between work and the rest of your life, live in a way that makes you happy and comfortable. London is demanding. It makes you stand up straight and get moving.
It’s very hard to survive here if you’re just tired and doing nothing. You can’t afford to be tired here. You have to keep moving and working. You have to be focused, active, involved, willing to take the initiative. Sociable, extroverted. I think that makes things somewhat difficult. It’s a bit like the gym. Would someone in their right mind walk up and lift some heavy damn thing? Well, probably not. But you have to do it. And it’s the same here.
What’s your favorite place in your new city?
The British Museum — admission is free. I love popping in for 15 minutes to remind myself why the Parthenon Marbles should stay here forever.
What’s your favorite local food?
Boiled eel, pork cracklings, overripe cucumbers (I’m joking, of course — it’s all inedible, but someone has to give that answer, right?).
Have you taken up any new hobbies since moving abroad?
Tramping through mud in rubber boots among thickets of thistles, looking around and exclaiming, “It’s so beautiful!”
My wife and I have friends here who gave up drinking completely about three years ago. The way they tell it, it used to go like this: you’d go to the pub on Friday, get up to all kinds of trouble, have a hangover the next morning — the whole weekend revolved around drinking. Then they stopped drinking and had nothing to do. So they started going on little hikes every single weekend — literally every weekend, except when they were on vacation or sick. Just because they had nothing to do. And it turned out to be a great replacement for hanging out at the pub.
There’s a group chat where they organize these little hikes. Usually you get on a train at one of London’s stations, and an hour or an hour and a half later you’re somewhere amazing. You walk along the coast, or over some hills, or up to a castle. And you’re out there for two to four hours.
Once, we spotted a great route in an Instagram reel. It looked so beautiful: along the coast, over hills, through thickets. We went there in November or February — some pretty horrible month. All the plants were bare, and everything squelched underfoot. We ended up getting lost and finding ourselves in these hellish thorn bushes that clung to us from every side. It felt like we’d wandered into some forest out of “Harry Potter” that was attacking us and stabbing us with thorns. We finally came out with our clothes torn and thorns all over us. Our shoes were caked in mud. We looked at each other and said, “God, this is wonderful.”
That evening, we’d been invited to a housewarming party in a big, very beautiful house. And we showed up in these clodhoppers, covered in mud, and said, “We’ve been on a hike.” And everyone understood.
Have you managed to make new friends? How?
Most of our social circle here speaks Russian. They’re people from different countries: Russia, Ukraine, Lithuania, Belarus. And we have some English-speaking friends. Or, if not friends, then just people we enjoy meeting up and spending time with.
For example, once before Christmas, we went to the pub for a beer with friends of friends. One of them was my friend’s husband, Chris. A couple of months later, he invited me to Burns Night — a party celebrating Robert Burns’ birthday, where we ate haggis and sang Scottish songs.
At one point I asked if I could say something and told them that, surprising as it might seem, Robert Burns was very popular in Russia — thanks to a man who loved his work and translated a lot of it, brilliantly. That was Samuil Marshak. I told them a little about Marshak and said, “Let me recite a Burns poem in Russian, and someone here can do it in English.” And I recited “My Heart’s in the Highlands,” which every Russian knows from school. It made quite an impression. It was exotic: as if people in, say, Albania loved Lermontov, or people in Cameroon read Yesenin.
Do you have enough money to live in your new country? How do you deal with financial problems?
I think the only people in London with “enough” money are the ones who made it under Queen Victoria.
So you have to deal with financial problems by earning money. You have to hustle a lot. But I moved here from Israel, so I was already somewhat prepared for life in an expensive country. Though in Tel Aviv, it’s impossible to understand what you’re paying all that crazy money for.
Here, on the whole, you can live on any budget. Okay, you won’t shop at some expensive supermarket — but the cheaper one won’t be unpleasant, and you won’t feel excluded. Or, say, if you have plenty of money, you buy theater tickets in, let’s say, the fifth row of the orchestra. If you don’t, you get early-bird tickets, or enter ticket lotteries, or go to free classical concerts at churches, or figure something else out.
You really can live here even if you don’t have much money — and not feel like you’re somehow less than everyone else because of it.
What do you do to learn the new language?
I make reels in English and try to be funny in them… And I try to do everything I do in my native language: make friends, talk to people in the pub, write things, comment on people’s Instagram posts.
You constantly have to work on your English — especially here. On the one hand, it’s a universal language, and you feel like you can read, write, conduct interviews, do anything in English. But in London the bar immediately goes up: people here have been speaking this language for centuries, writing books and poetry in it, picking up on all sorts of nuances. So however well you know the language, you still feel you have to keep learning.
But of course, it’s paradise compared with living in a country where you don’t know the language. You can read anything. You can go on any website. You can talk to anyone. You have no trouble reading anything at an exhibition or in a newspaper. That’s an enormous privilege.
If you have children, would you want them to become locals?
They’ll have Hobson’s choice (google it).
How do you cope with intense homesickness? Do you get homesick at all?
What I miss most is snow, but last winter it snowed in Scotland, and I walked around in it to my heart’s content. And somewhere deep down, I was glad it wasn’t going to last five months.
Do you feel you’re losing touch with your home country? Is it possible to keep that connection?
We’re in touch…
First, I have friends and other people close to me in Russia — we’re literally in touch. We can message each other, send reels or memes, talk on the phone. Fortunately, that connection hasn’t been broken.
And second, there are things happening in Russia that worry me enormously. Everyone has an issue that’s personal to them — for me, it’s political prisoners. I have several friends who are in prison. And I stay in touch with them, their loved ones, their lawyers.
I think this is a good moment to remind people that you can write to Russian political prisoners. And don’t let the fact that they’re there and you’re somewhere else stop you. They’ll be happy to get a letter from anywhere.
Are you happy living abroad?
Very!

Type 45 extension not part of the plan, committee told
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:29:05 BST
03:29:05 KST

The Ministry of Defence does not want to extend the life of the Type 45 destroyers and would rather spend the money on new technology, with £1.5 billion set aside in this Parliament to initiate hybrid Navy projects, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Air Marshal Tim Jones, Deputy Chief of the Defence Staff for Force Development, was giving evidence alongside Wes Streeting, the Secretary of State for Defence.
Jesse Norman, the Conservative member for Hereford and South Herefordshire, asked about the timing of the Type 45 replacement. Jones said: “As you know, the Type 45s are due to start going out of service from 2035. At the moment, we have started investment in a hybrid Navy alternative for that. You probably heard the First Sea Lord talking quite passionately about his vision for a hybrid Navy. The early investment that we are doing is to get those projects up and running so that, by the time the Type 45 starts going out of service, we have a hybrid replacement for that capability coming into service.”
Asked whether the current ships would have their lives extended, Jones said: “We don’t want to extend the Type 45. Rather than extending older platforms that cost a lot of money to run, we would rather spend the money focusing on new technology. That is what the First Sea Lord wants, and that is what we are aiming to do.”
Pressed on whether a capability gap could open before the hybrid Navy is established, Jones said: “We have almost 10 years to get the Type 45 replacement up and running. We are in a world where we are seeing innovation moving quickly and the market being disrupted by start-ups and new tech companies.”
Norman asked for reassurance that adequate capability would cover the gap and more by the time the class is retired, and Jones said: “We will.” Asked whether the replacement would be comparable or better, he said: “It should be better, because new technology will come online, and the aim is to do that in a more effective way. As to when the transition happens in detail, that is what we are working through at the moment. We do not want to extend Type 45. It is clearly an option, but it is not part of our plan.”
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, told Andrew Bowie, the Conservative member for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine, in a written answer in July that detailed planning for the transition between Type 45 and the hybrid Navy maritime air defence capability would be done with industry, “which will determine whether a Type 45 extension is implemented”, and that “a final decision is not expected until 2027-28.”
Answering James Cartlidge, the Conservative member for South Suffolk, in August, Pollard said the Defence Investment Plan contains “a specific funding line within this parliament to conduct a study” covering “whether a life extension will be required”, and that this “will be assessed in 2027-28”, as this publication reported at the time. Jones did not mention the study to the committee, and Norman was pressing on exactly the transition it exists to examine.
On funding, Jones said: “We have £1.5 billion in this Parliament set aside for initiating hybrid Navy projects, and that project team is standing up now.” He described it as a start, and said it is by no means the limit of investment.
He told the committee that the Royal Navy is “already almost on contract for an uncrewed surface vessel; the competition is in the final stages, and the results of that will be announced soon. That vessel will be in the water next year, so we are getting on with it.”
The Royal Navy operates six Type 45 destroyers, which provide the fleet’s area air defence through the Sea Viper system. The Defence Committee reported this week that it is not persuaded the Hybrid Navy allocation will be sufficient to develop, procure and integrate its five planned classes, which include a crewed Common Combat Vessel to replace the Type 45.
Streeting told the committee that innovation always involves risk and that politically “we need to be more comfortable than we sometimes are with carrying risk.” He described the First Sea Lord’s hybrid Navy concept as “genuinely world-leading” and said counterparts are actively tracking it.

Germany leads push against EU’s ‘associate membership’ label for Canada
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:28:35 UTC
03:28:35 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivers a speech in the hemicycle of the European Parliament in Strasbourg on September 17, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Germany, France and at least six other EU countries are pushing against “associate membership” as the name for closer EU ties with Canada, six diplomats involved in the negotiations said.
The label is one of the main sticking points in talks over a joint declaration setting areas of deeper cooperation between Brussels and Ottawa ahead of the EU-Canada summit in Montreal on Oct. 29-30, the six diplomats and two EU officials told POLITICO. They were granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive negotiations.
The diplomats said the objections center on the wording of “associate membership,” not the broader goal of closer ties.
Advertisement
Five weeks after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen first proposed Canada becoming an “associate member” of the EU in her State of the Union speech — to the surprise of both Ottawa and EU capitals — and one week out from the summit itself, the disagreements show the term remains a political and messaging hurdle.
The EU "is really keen to have close cooperation with Canada," said Bernd Lange, chair of the European Parliament’s trade committee. But, he added, he too would avoid using the term "associate membership," as it leaves too much room for confusion with other forms of EU partnerships, such as association agreements.
Germany is pushing hardest to remove the label from the draft declaration, five of the EU diplomats said, while France, Italy and Belgium were among those expressing skepticism about the phrasing.
The central concern among the capitals that object to the term is that the EU is labeling the relationship before agreeing what it would mean. They argue the name should have been defined before negotiations with Canada began, four diplomats said, with two others adding that the objecting capitals are annoyed that von der Leyen proposed the label without first consulting national governments.
“We’ve definitely put the cart before the horse,” one diplomat said. “We’re announcing something and then figuring out how to flesh it out.”
A representative for the German Permanent Representation to the EU declined to comment.
Advertisement
The European Commission will engage with skeptical capitals and work on acceptable language, an EU official said, adding that they believe the countries’ doubts stem from not yet understanding what the proposal means in concrete terms.
There is no disagreement over the aim of strengthening an already close relationship, including economic and defense cooperation, international engagement and institutional links, the official stressed. “What matters is what we do, not what we call it.”
What’s in a name?
The label aims to describe the EU-Canada relationship as closer than Brussels’ partnerships with other countries, without making Canada a member of the bloc, one of the diplomats said. Canada cannot become a formal member, as the EU’s founding documents limit that status geographically to Europe.
The distinction matters because existing arrangements with European neighbors, including the U.K., Switzerland and countries in the European Economic Area, center largely on access to the EU’s internal market. Canada, on another continent, is not seeking the same model or the four freedoms of movement, the diplomat said.
The idea is to identify practical areas for cooperation first, then decide whether new treaties or formal negotiations are needed, the same diplomat said.
Work on six priority areas is expected to begin after the summit, with progress reviewed after six months and then a proper stock-take one year later at the next EU-Canada summit, which will be held in Europe.
Advertisement
The stock-take would consider whether Canada has moved closer to the EU by becoming a full member of Horizon Europe and Erasmus, is building undersea cables and stockpiling critical raw materials with the EU, and is exploring pension-fund investment. If Canada meets those criteria, it could become the EU’s first associate member, the diplomat said.
The diplomat described the idea as an experiment, adding that “Canada might be the only one” to ever get associate membership of the EU.
The plan reflects changing calculations on both sides. Canada has long depended heavily on trade with the United States, but tariffs and political pressure from Washington have sharpened concerns about that reliance. Prime Minister Mark Carney wants to diversify trade and modernize the country’s infrastructure, including energy links that largely run north to south.
For the EU, a closer partnership with Canada is part of a broader effort to build relationships as pressure from the United States, China and Russia grows. The summit is intended to give the partnership a more distinctive political framework.
The declaration is still being revised, with EU ambassadors due to discuss it again on Monday. One of the EU officials cautioned that several parts of the declaration still had comments outstanding.
Another controversial element concerns energy cooperation, with Austria pushing back against any mention of deepening nuclear ties, while France, Romania, Slovakia and some other countries support its inclusion.
A spokesperson from the Canadian mission to the EU did not respond to POLITICO's request for comment.

Ukraine Expands Satellite Cooperation With Finland as Starlink Doubts Linger
