Ukraine signed seven agreements with Finland, including deals to expand Kyiv’s use of Finnish satellite capabilities through Nokia and ICEYE after recent Starlink disruptions exposed how much of the country’s defense hinges on a single private provider that can restrict service with no prior warning.
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the agreements in a statement on Thursday, Oct. 22, after holding discussions with the government of Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo. The documents, signed at the Ukrainian-Finnish Business Forum, outlines possible cooperation in defense production, rail transport, energy and housing construction, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We agreed that we will make greater use of Finland’s satellite capabilities,” Zelensky said. “This is important for our defense and for Ukraine’s resilience.”
The total estimated value of today’s agreements is nearly €300 million (roughly $337 million).
Finland donates locomotives to Ukraine
Among the agreements, Finland committed to hand over 10 Dv12 diesel locomotives and spare parts to Ukraine’s state railway operator, Ukrzaliznytsia, free of charge.
Rail transport has become one of Ukraine’s most vital lifelines, with the country’s airspace closed to civilian flights from February 2022. Ukrainian citizens heavily rely on trains for travel, and the railway also carries critical cargo, including food shipments, across the country, making it a frequent target for Russian forces.
Vance: Starlink Use Depends on US Policy Toward Kyiv, Moscow – Not Musk
According to Koretskyi, Finland has become the first country to donate locomotives to Ukraine free of charge.
Earlier this week, Estonia has confirmed it will send a substantial number of locomotives to Ukraine. Although Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha did not provide additional information on the shipment, he said on Tuesday, Oct. 20, that during talks with Estonia, he had “outlined our urgent needs to strengthen Ukraine’s defense and resilience ahead of winter, with a particular focus on Russian strikes against our railways”
The appeal for railway help initially came mid-September, when Sybiha urged allies to provide Ukraine with replacement locomotives after a Russian strike hit a railway infrastructure just kilometers from the Polish border in Volyn region, in what may have been a deliberate attack on a train carrying diplomats.
Western allies were asked in particular to assist in finding locomotives compatible with the 1,520-milimeter railway gauge Ukraine uses, as well as provide funding to accelerate the procurement of new ones.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in 2022, Russia has damaged or destroyed more than 500 locomotives, with over half of those losses recorded this year alone, according to Sybiha’s estimates.
Mykola Kalashnyk, Ukraine’s Minister for Restoration, Infrastructure and Transport said on Aug. 23 that Russia has attacked Ukraine’s railway infrastructure at least 1,534 times so far in 2026.
Joint drone production and gas storage also explored
Ukrainian drone manufacturers are also exploring expanding joint production with Finnish companies on Finnish soil, Koretskyi said.
Separately, employers’ associations from the two countries plan to establish a Ukrainian-Finnish Industrial Council, while another project focuses on industrial housing construction.
The two governments also agreed to share experience in protecting critical infrastructure and discussed Ukraine’s need for mobile shelters.
Meanwhile, Kyiv invited Finland to join its War Risk Insurance Fund.
“We expect Finnish companies to become key investors and long-term partners of Ukraine,” Koretskyi said. “Together, we can create products, technologies and businesses that will be competitive in Ukraine and across Europe.”
Ukraine’s large unused gas storage capacity and developed gas transmission system were on the agenda as well, with the two sides discussing how they could help Europe build strategic non-commercial gas reserves.
The discussions come as the EU works to cut off Russian gas entirely.
According to the European Commission, the EU’s dependency on gas imported from Russia has fallen from 45% of total imports to 12% in 2025, while all imports of Russian coal have been banned under EU sanctions.
“The remaining 35 billion cubic meters of Russian gas still imported to the EU annually will be out of our markets in less than two years,” the EC said on its official website.
In January 2026, EU member states gave final approval to a law banning Russian gas imports by late 2027, despite opposition from Hungary and Slovakia, both of which remain heavily reliant on Russian energy.
Under the law, imports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) will end by the end of 2026, and pipeline gas by Sept. 30, 2027. According to The Baltic Times, Brussels built the ban on trade and energy legislation rather than sanctions, which require unanimity, so that it could not be blocked by Budapest and Bratislava.
Europe looks beyond Starlink
The agreements with Finland come as Ukraine and its European partners search for alternatives to Starlink, the satellite service operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, speed restrictions were imposed on Starlink terminals without prior warning, crippling Ukraine’s drone operations. The limits disrupted several types of drones Ukraine uses to defend itself against Russian attacks, including interceptor drones deployed against jet-powered Shaheds.
The connectivity was lost on terminals moving at roughly 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) or faster, while Ukraine needed the operating speeds to reach at least 450 kilometers per hour (280 miles per hour).
The restrictions coincided with a reported week-long suspension of US intelligence sharing, which left Kyiv without allied warnings of Russian ballistic missile attacks.
Zelensky has accused those responsible of deliberately restricting the service during Russian attacks, saying the disruption weakened Ukraine’s defenses and, by doing so, endangered civilians.
After meeting senior US envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo on Tuesday, Oct. 20, Zelensky confirmed the intelligence sharing had resumed. He added that progress on Starlink restrictions and Patriot interceptors could come within 48 hours.
Separately on Thursday, US Vice President JD Vance said Musk should not be at the center of the dispute over restrictions on Ukraine’s satellite service, framing the issue instead as a matter of US policy toward Russia’s war.
“Well, I think that fundamentally Elon Musk runs a private corporation, and I think it’s completely understandable that he doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the US government effectively directing him on what to do,” he said, leaving unanswered who ordered the restrictions.
Both Musk and the White House denied responsibility for the restrictions, while pinning the blame to the other.
Meanwhile, the European Union is negotiating Ukraine’s access to its secure satellite communications program that could expand the system with commercial services in early 2027.
Currently, Europe has no ready-made replacement that Ukrainian troops can immediately attach to their drones and political pressure to develop alternatives is growing.

EU will ‘inevitably’ restore economic ties with Russia – Putin aide (VIDEOS)

Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, made the remarks on Thursday at the 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum in Istanbul. 
The Russian official hailed Trump’s readiness to restore dialogue with Russia and reverse a “very dangerous situation where top nuclear powers don’t communicate.”
He said the recent Russia-US diesel deal could lay the groundwork for broader cooperation between Moscow and Washington, potentially paving the way for further agreements on energy and fertilizers. Under the deal, Russia has agreed to release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and additional supplies thereafter.
Commenting on Europe’s problems, including high energy costs and mass migration, Dmitriev accused European politicians of “using Russia as a boogeyman” to distract from more fundamental issues, warning that they have come to believe their own narratives and are unwilling to correct their mistakes.

Ukraine could face a second wave of migration after the war: demographer explains who will leave and why
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:20:32 EEST
03:20:32 KST

Ukraine could face a second wave of migration after the war: demographer explains who will leave and why
Kyiv • UNN
Ella Libanova predicts a new wave of male migration after travel restrictions are lifted. The population of the government-controlled territory has fallen to 28.5 million.
After the war ends and martial law is lifted, Ukraine may face a new wave of migration, this time involving men. Ella Libanova, director of the Mykhailo Ptukha Institute for Demography and Quality of Life Studies of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, said this during the 10th Ukrainian Women's Congress on October 22, UNN reports.
The reason may be the lack of a sufficient number of jobs offering decent pay, as well as Ukrainians' desire to reunite with their families abroad.
Details
According to the demographer, the possible consequences of the end of the war and the lifting of restrictions on men traveling abroad are currently causing the greatest concern. Libanova explained that after service members return to civilian life, Ukraine may prove unable to provide them with jobs and salaries that meet their expectations.
When men are allowed to leave the country, when they return from the front, we will not be able to offer them jobs they consider достойні, or salaries they consider acceptable. And then the question arises: where will Ukrainian families reunite—in Ukraine or outside it? I am very afraid that a second, so-called male migration wave will emerge
In the scientist's view, such a development is quite likely. At the same time, it will depend to a large extent on the decisions of the service members themselves who return from the front, as well as on the opportunities Ukraine will be able to offer them.
Ukraine may lose up to another 600,000 men
Libanova had previously warned of the risks of additional migration after the war ends. In particular, in August 2026, she suggested that after martial law is lifted, another 500,000 to 600,000 Ukrainian men could leave to join their families abroad. In her assessment, one of the determining factors will be the economic situation in Ukraine, above all the possibility of finding stable employment, securing housing for one's family, and earning a competitive salary.
At the same time, the demographer does not expect Ukrainian refugees to return en masse immediately after the war ends. She emphasized that the decision to return would depend on the security situation, housing conditions, and employment prospects.
Ukraine's population has fallen to 28.5 million
During the Ukrainian Women's Congress, Libanova also reported that, according to the latest estimate by the Institute of Demography, the population in the territory under Ukraine's control stood at approximately 28.5 million people as of mid-2026. This is 500,000 fewer than the previous estimate of 29 million. According to the scientist, the main reason for this decline was population migration, rather than losses resulting solely from hostilities.
Context
According to the latest Eurostat data, as of August 31, 2026, 4.43 million people who had left Ukraine because of russia's full-scale invasion held temporary protection status in European Union countries. The largest numbers of Ukrainians granted such protection were in Germany—nearly 1.3 million, Poland—more than 939,000, and the Czech Republic—more than 398,000.
Adult women accounted for 43.6% of all temporary protection beneficiaries, men for 27.3%, and minors for 29.1%.
Reminder
Libanova previously said that approximately 31.5 million people live in the territory of Ukraine under government control. Demographic losses caused by the war amount to 10 million, of whom 4.5 million have gone abroad; one-third of them are teenagers under 18.

Hegseth’s staff damaged Eisenhower’s World War II-era globe during Pentagon move: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:19:21 UTC
03:19:21 KST

Diyar Guldogan
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s staff damaged a historic globe associated with Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower during an attempt to move the artifact to Hegseth’s Pentagon office, according to a report published Thursday by The Washington Post.
Photographs obtained by the newspaper show a gash several inches wide near Antarctica on the globe, which reportedly fell onto its base during the relocation attempt on Feb. 3.
It is one of two 30-inch floor globes housed at the Pentagon that are said to have been used by Eisenhower during World War II. The artifacts have been maintained by successive generations of army leaders, according to people familiar with the history and a plaque dating them to the 1930s, the Post reported.
Hegseth’s interest in the globe’s historical significance prompted his staff to request that one of the artifacts be moved to his office, according to the newspaper. But rather than using the Pentagon’s customary process for relocating historical items under the supervision of trained curators, Hegseth’s staff sent its own team to handle the move, the Post reported, citing those familiar with the incident.
The team lost control of the globe, causing it to crash onto its base and puncture its fragile outer shell, according to the report.
The army acknowledged the damage in a statement to the Post. Army spokesman Christopher Surridge said the globe was damaged during an “attempted move” on Feb. 3. Aside from the hole, “the spherical portion of the globe was detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate,” Surridge was quoted.
The army’s office responsible for the artifact had expected to consult specialists at the US Army Center of Military History about safely transporting the globe and documenting its relocation, according to two people familiar with the matter.
But those experts had been furloughed during a partial government shutdown stemming from a congressional dispute about aspects of the Trump administration’s immigration policy. With the specialists unavailable, Hegseth’s staff decided to move the globe themselves, the Post reported.
After the Post published its report, a Defense Department official provided the newspaper with a brief, unattributed statement acknowledging the mishap.
“Accidents happen,” it said. “We are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired.”

96% of world's coral reefs face critical risk of collapse, IUCN warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:18:00 UTC
03:18:00 KST

96% of world's coral reefs face critical risk of collapse
October 22, 2026
Nearly all of the world's shallow-water coral reefs face an extremely high risk of collapse by 2075, with climate change being the greatest threat, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Thursday.
In the first systematic survey of the world's 127 tropical and subtropical coral reef systems, the IUCN said 96% were critically endangered, which is its highest risk category.
Shallow-water reefs are colorful coral ecosystems found at depths of up to around 40 meters (131 feet), and are home to a high level of biodiversity.
Among the reefs affected are Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in the western Pacific and Southeast Asia, the Mesoamerican Reef System and the reefs in the Red Sea.
"Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide," the IUCN said when it presented the study at the United Nations' COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
What are the threats to the reefs?
Worldwide, shallow-water reefs cover around 188,000 square kilometers(73,000 square miles).
Their corals are highly sensitive to temperature changes. This means when the water gets too warm, the corals expel the tiny algae living in their tissues, which provide much of their nourishment.
This then leads to coral bleaching and can ultimately lead to their death.
Overfishing is another major threat. In particular, the overfishing of parrotfish and groupers affects reef ecosystems since these fish help maintain ecological balance.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and increasingly severe storms also contribute to reef degradation.
When hard corals disappear, their structures are often replaced by algae, rubble and sponges, leaving less diverse ecosystems that do not sustain as many species. Affected animals include reef fish, mussels, sea turtles, and sharks.
Can the reefs still be saved?
"The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems," according to Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.
The study uses a climate scenario developed by the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, which expects global warming of around 2.7 degrees Celsius (4.86 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
Despite the bleak outlook, the IUCN said most reefs had not yet been lost. Without projections of future climate change and based on the changes over the past 50 years, only 24% would qualify as critically endangered.
"This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring," Gudka explained.
"The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people," he added.
IUCN Director General Grethel Aguilar said it was "not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover."
"We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them," she said.

Israel frees suspects in two settler attacks as West Bank pogroms intensify
Israeli court releases nine settler suspects over West Bank attacks as investigations into recent assaults continue.
Israel has released nine of the 10 Israeli settler suspects arrested over attacks on a US journalist and European diplomats in the occupied West Bank, placing them under house arrest.
An Israeli court in Jerusalem ordered the release late on Wednesday, according to Honenu, a law firm that represents Israeli settlers.
Israeli police said one suspect remained in custody and that the investigation into the violent incidents was continuing.
Masked settlers were filmed last week assaulting Heidi Levine, a Washington Post photojournalist covering a Palestinian olive harvest who was taken to hospital and underwent surgery on a finger.
In a separate attack earlier this week, masked settlers assaulted French, Belgian and Polish diplomats and a French mayor in another part of the West Bank.
The suspects had been detained after the United States called for a crackdown on settler violence. France, Belgium and Poland also urged Israel to act.
“In the vast majority of attacks against Palestinians, no arrests are made at all,” said Yonatan Kanonich, head of research at the Israeli rights group Yesh Din. “In cases that receive media coverage … the police arrest several settlers and release most of them shortly afterward.”
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said in a post on X Thursday that the situation in the occupied Palestinian territory was “out of control”, with Palestinians continuing “to suffer daily attacks by Israeli settlers” and journalists and diplomats also being attacked.
Guterres called for “a credible political path towards lasting peace”.
Separately, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission on Thursday said it documented 17 West Bank pogroms by Israeli forces and settlers against Palestinian farmers and their land during the olive harvest.
The commission recorded 409 attacks in October, 317 of which were by settlers and 92 by Israeli forces.
Nablus recorded the most attacks, 166, followed by Salfit with 91.
The commission said the attacks included assaults on farmers, preventing them from reaching their land, theft of crops and agricultural equipment, damage and burning of olive trees, as well as arrests, threats at gunpoint and live fire.
Ali Hassan Bazzari from Burqa died of wounds from settler gunfire while picking olives on October 7, the commission reported.
On Thursday, settlers set fire to olive trees near Imatin, east of Qalqilya, while Israeli forces forced farmers to leave and detained a farmer and several of his workers, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Near Yabad, west of Jenin, settlers stole 17 bags of harvested olives and equipment, local sources said.
Citing a local Palestinian official, Wafa reported that around Jenin, Israeli forces closed transport roads and most village gates, preventing farmers from reaching land in Barta’a.

Ex-prosecutor’s killing puts Guatemala’s crime-politics nexus back in focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:16:41 UTC
03:16:41 KST

Ex-prosecutor’s killing puts Guatemala’s crime-politics nexus back in focus
GUATEMALA CITY, Oct 22 - Former Guatemalan anti-corruption prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa was one of the country's most high profile voices denouncing alleged links between politicians and business leaders and the country's increasingly powerful organized crime groups.
Over the weekend, he was shot dead on a soccer field, a killing that former officials and diplomats consulted by Reuters said has heightened concerns over organized crime's influence in the Central American nation.
The killing of an outspoken former prosecutor who had publicly challenged powerful interests shocked the country and revived debate over criminal networks’ penetration of state institutions.
"This is a threat against human rights defenders. This is a threat against activists for democracy," said Frank La Rue, a human rights advocate, who attended the wake for Solorzano Foppa on Monday, which featured portraits of the slain lawyer with his family.
For many Guatemalans, it recalled the 1998 assassination of Bishop Juan Jose Gerardi, beaten to death two days after presenting a report documenting atrocities from the country’s civil war, and stirred fears that violence could again be used against prominent critics of powerful interests.
Experts said criminal networks have strengthened their influence in recent years as anti-corruption efforts and institutions tasked with combating impunity have weakened, issues likely to loom over the June 2027 election as Guatemala chooses President Bernardo Arevalo’s successor.
Authorities have not established a motive for Solorzano Foppa's killing. But officials and diplomats said the case has fueled concerns about criminal groups’ ability to intimidate or silence critical voices.
More than 100 former prosecutors, judges, journalists and human rights defenders have left Guatemala in recent years, according to some international human rights organizations, after denouncing corruption or alleged links between state structures and criminal networks.
This week, following Solorzano Foppa's killing, a high-profile lawyer who also railed against political corruption said he has received death threats. On Wednesday, Arevalo denounced the threats against the lawyer, Edgar Ortiz.
"Guatemala cannot return to being a country where defending democracy can cost one peace, freedom, or their life," Arevalo wrote on social media.
'RED LINE CROSSED'
Corruption has been a major institutional challenge in Guatemala for decades. From 2007 to 2019, the UN-backed International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) helped investigate corruption and organized crime networks within the state, including cases that led to the resignation and subsequent prosecution of then-President Otto Perez Molina and his former vice president, Roxana Baldetti.
Since CICIG's departure in 2019, human rights groups, prosecutors and international observers have denounced setbacks in the fight against corruption. President Arevalo, who took office in 2024 promising to tackle the problem, has acknowledged difficulties advancing reforms and dismantling structures accused of corruption.
In videos posted on Facebook, TikTok and Instagram, and seen by Reuters, Solorzano Foppa alleged links between Barrio 18 leader Aldo "El Lobo" Ochoa, who is serving combined prison sentences of more than 1,600 years, and people close to the leadership of the National Unity of Hope (UNE) party, headed by former first lady Sandra Torres. Reuters could not independently verify the allegations.
UNE told Reuters in a statement that "those allegations were never proven and should not be presented as established facts."
Solorzano Foppa, a former head of Guatemala's SAT tax administration agency, also alleged ties between criminal networks, political figures and sectors of the judicial system, though the accusations did not result in judicial proceedings.
Officials have not identified who ordered the killing. The Organization of American States and the United Nations have called for a thorough investigation.
The Public Prosecutor's Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. On Sunday, following the murder, it said in a statement that "in order to guarantee due process, it will not disclose additional details about the evidence gathered or the specific lines of investigation."
A former government official, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said insiders had turned to Solorzano Foppa with information they felt unable to expose themselves, making him an outlet for allegations from within the state. His killers "left no trace," the former official said, complicating the investigation.
Guatemala's criminal networks range from gangs and drug traffickers to structures involving former officials and members of the security forces. Analysts say some have retained influence over state institutions, while armed groups like Barrio 18 and Mara Salvatrucha (MS-13) remain involved in extortion and territorial control.
They include the so-called CIACS, or Illegal Clandestine Security Apparatuses, networks linked to former security structures that experts say retain political and economic influence. Guatemala is also a major drug-trafficking corridor to the United States, with groups associated with Mexico's Sinaloa Cartel and Jalisco New Generation Cartel operating through local criminal networks.
"Many of us fear that a red line has been crossed," said Stephen McFarland, former US ambassador to Guatemala from 2008 to 2011. "A return to political assassination as a way of settling scores and protecting the ambitions and money of certain people." REUTERS

UEFA Conference League: FC Kairat fall to Panathinaikos at home

The match proved dramatic for the host side.
Rafael Urazbakhtin’s side got off to a slow start. Hesitant choices and static positional play from the Almaty team allowed the visitors to take complete control early on.
Vicente Taborda opened the scoring in the sixth minute, and Cyriel Dessers doubled the Greek side’s lead in the 24th minute by calmly converting a penalty kick. The teams went into halftime with the score at 2-0.
The second half began similarly. Just a minute after the restart, Dessers completed his brace. In the 57th minute, Greek substitute Kings Kangwa extended the lead to four.
A critical lack of pace forced Kairat’s coaching staff to take radical action in the 64th minute.
Fresh legs entered the pitch at the same time: Lev Kurgin, Ismail Bekbolat, and Damir Kasabulat replaced Luís Mata, Marc Gual, and Jaakko Oksanen.
After the triple substitution, the Almaty club tried to step up the tempo and push play away from their goal. Nevertheless, the Greek giant expertly neutralized the game by retaining possession. Moreover, Elmin Rastoder capped off the scoring for Panathinaikos in the 75th minute, 5-0.
In the 79th minute, Kairat managed a consolation goal, with youth prospect Ismail Bekbolat outmaneuvering the Greek club’s defense and goalkeeper to score.
The match ended in a 5-1 defeat for FC Kairat.
In the Conference League phase, Kairat has one point after two matchdays, earned during an away draw against Latvia's Riga FC.
As reported in August this year, the Kazakh club suffered a 3-0 away defeat to Belgian side Anderlecht in the second leg of the UEFA Europa League qualifying playoffs.

Ukrainians face a fine of up to UAH 1,530 for collecting firewood in the forest: what is prohibited and how to legally gather timber
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:11:30 EEST
03:11:30 KST

Ukrainians face a fine of up to UAH 1,530 for collecting firewood in the forest: what is prohibited and how to legally gather timber
Kyiv • UNN
Unauthorized collection of firewood, brushwood, and fallen trees is prohibited in Ukraine. Fuel can be legally purchased through forestry offices or official sellers.
On the eve of the heating season, which promises to be difficult because of severe frosts in winter and likely disruptions to gas supplies (the result of targeted missile-and-drone attacks by the Russian Armed Forces), Ukrainians are increasingly considering alternative sources — coal and firewood.
It would seem that in rural areas, obtaining firewood should not cause any difficulties. One might simply travel to the nearest forest and take fallen trunks or branches left after logging. But far from everything found in the forest may be taken to one's homestead to heat a stove or a "potbelly stove." After all, in Ukraine, illegal logging carries fines and, in some cases, criminal liability.
How to act lawfully and avoid being left without firewood in winter is explained by UNN.
Fine of up to UAH 1,530: what Ukrainians may be punished for in the forest
The Forest Code distinguishes between general and special use of resources. Mushrooms, berries, and nuts may generally be collected for personal use without a permit. However, different rules apply to the harvesting of timber. Fines are предусмотрені for illegal felling or damage to trees, as well as for transporting or storing illegally felled timber.
In particular, citizens face a fine of up to UAH 1,530 for repeated violations of rules related to illegal tree felling. Moreover, payment is required both for cutting down live trees and for transporting or storing illegally felled timber.
Under Article 65 of the Code of Ukraine on Administrative Offenses, illegal felling or damage to trees and shrubs is punishable by a fine of between UAH 510 and UAH 1,020. If a person commits the relevant violation again within a year after an administrative penalty has been imposed, the fine increases to UAH 1,020–1,530.
Can dry branches and brushwood be collected in the forest without a permit
In Ukraine, the law prohibits independently collecting dry branches, brushwood, and other wood in the forest for heating a home. As explained by the State Environmental Inspectorate (SEI), brushwood is also considered timber. According to the Instruction on Maintaining Electronic Timber Records, it includes thin trunks, treetops, branches, and twigs less than four centimeters in diameter and up to six meters long.
It is also prohibited to take logging residues left after forestry operations without authorization. They are classified as forest resources and are subject to registration. Exceptions apply only to territories where hostilities are currently taking place or have taken place. A special procedure for the free collection of such branches applies there.
SEI specialists advise Ukrainians to contact the local forestry office before collecting branches for heating and clarify whether this is permitted in a particular area. Such an inquiry will help avoid fines and administrative liability and make it possible to legally obtain alternative fuel.
Why fallen trees cannot be taken for firewood independently
In Ukraine, it is prohibited to take fallen, dried-out, or damaged trees from the forest without authorization for use as firewood. Even if a tree fell as a result of strong winds, a storm, or snowfall, it remains a forest resource. Therefore, the law does not permit using it for personal needs.
As explained by the SEI, dead and fallen trees are not considered ownerless. Decisions on their removal, sanitary felling, and subsequent use of the timber are made by forest owners or permanent forest users. Even if a tree has fallen onto a forest road, blocked passage, or poses a danger to people, this still does not grant the right to cut it up independently. In such a case, the relevant forestry office or another authorized service must be notified.
What fines apply in Ukraine for illegal timber harvesting in 2026
In 2026, illegal timber harvesting in Ukraine carries administrative liability and, in certain cases, criminal liability. The penalty depends on the nature of the violation, whether it is repeated, and the damage caused to forestry.
In particular, the following fines may be imposed for violating timber harvesting rules:
-  from UAH 510 to UAH 1,020 — for citizens for the first violation; 
-  from UAH 1,020 to UAH 1,530 — for a repeat violation within a year, if the person has already been held administratively liable for the respective actions; 
-  from UAH 2,550 to UAH 5,100 — for officials for the first violation; 
-  from UAH 10,200 to UAH 15,300 — for officials for a repeat violation. 
In addition, Article 64 of the Code of Ukraine on Administrative Offenses establishes liability for violating the prescribed procedure for harvesting and removing timber. Such actions carry a fine of UAH 102 to UAH 238 for citizens, and UAH 170 to UAH 272 for officials.
The offender may also be required to compensate for the damage caused to the forest. The amount is calculated separately depending on the nature of the damage, the number of trees, their diameter, and other circumstances.
If illegal felling, transportation, storage, or sale of timber causes substantial damage, liability may arise under Article 246 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. In particular, Part One of this article provides for a fine of UAH 17,000 to UAH 25,500, probation supervision for up to three years, restriction of liberty, or imprisonment for the same period. Under aggravating circumstances, the punishment may be more severe.
Who is allowed to collect firewood free of charge
During martial law, a special procedure applies to residents of territories where hostilities are or were taking place. Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 861 allows, under certain conditions, the free collection of logging residues for household needs. It should be noted that these conditions will remain in effect for six months after the termination or lifting of martial law.
However, this right does not apply to all communities. The sites must be safe, and their list, as well as the days and hours for collection, is approved by the regional defense council.
Only logging residues may be collected: separating a tree trunk from its stump and using gasoline-powered or electric saws is prohibited. Going into the forest without authorization, especially in potentially mined areas, is dangerous.
How to legally procure timber for heating a private house
First of all, people should contact the nearest forestry office or permanent forest user to find out whether the lawful collection of timber is possible in a particular area and what conditions have been established for it.
After that, it is necessary to obtain a document authorizing the harvesting of firewood — a logging ticket or forest ticket. However, it should be remembered that this does not give the right to simply come to the forest and cut down the first tree one sees for personal needs.
Where Ukrainians can legally purchase firewood for the winter
For residents of the vast majority of Ukraine's regions, the simplest lawful way to supply a private house with fuel for the winter remains purchasing ready-made firewood from forestry offices, forest districts, or official suppliers.
Thus, the state-owned enterprise "Forests of Ukraine" sells firewood through forest districts and the official online store Drovaye drovae.gov.ua. To place an order directly at a local unit, a passport and the taxpayer registration number are usually required. The buyer is issued an invoice, and after payment, the pickup of the timber is arranged. Up to 15 cubic meters of firewood can be purchased here per year. The availability of the required species, price, and delivery conditions should be уточнено at the конкретному forest district.
When purchasing from private sellers, it is advisable to verify the origin of the timber and keep the contract, receipt, or another document confirming the purchase.
What to do if a person is stopped with collected firewood
If a person is stopped in the forest while collecting or transporting firewood, the main thing is not to panic and to find out the reason for the inspection. State forest protection officers have the right to check documents for timber, inspect it, and stop vehicles within the scope of their authority. If the firewood was purchased legally, the person should show documents confirming this—for example, a payment receipt, a consignment note, or an invoice from the seller.
It may happen that forestry officials conclude that the timber was harvested illegally and draw up an administrative report. Before signing it, the document should be read carefully. In particular, check whether they have correctly written the personal details, the location of the incident, the circumstances of the violation, and the article under which they intend to hold the person liable.
If a person does not agree with the accusations, they may write this directly in the report and provide their own explanations. They may also refuse to sign, explaining the reason. However, such a refusal does not mean that the case will automatically be closed.
If a fine is nevertheless imposed but the person considers it unfounded, the decision may be appealed. Usually, there are 10 days to do so from the date it was issued.
Reminder
Earlier, UNN wrote about who can receive a subsidy for firewood and coal and how to apply for it.

In war between Russia and Ukraine, United States is first to surrender, but Americans still stand with Ukraine
Demonstrators rally in support of Ukraine in downtown Chicago, Illinois, on March 2, 2025. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
The Kyiv Independent Opinion Desk
Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent? Send it to letters@kyivindependent.com — your letter may appear in our Letters section.
Mark Cary, United States member
I vividly remember when the Soviet Union collapsed. I was in my second year in college studying the history, ideology, and global influence of this dictatorship in an academic concentration called "Soviet and Eastern European Studies."
In 1989, the world felt joy and hope when the Berlin Wall fell. Once that dam broke, the end was inevitable.
Then came the horror of the murderous Soviet crackdown in Lithuania in 1991 as they tried in vain to hold on to their empire.
In December of 1991, Ukraine, Russia, and Belarus dissolved the Soviet Union, and 15 new countries were born.
The world was changed for the better, or so we thought.
Many factors contributed to this moment. All empires inevitably crack and begin to rot. The disastrous war in Afghanistan exacerbated the economic strain created by decades of military expenditures. The Soviets could no longer provide basic needs while simultaneously competing against Reagan's buildup and his willingness to challenge them at every turn.
Glasnost and Perestroika, Gorbachev's dual efforts to modernize Soviet society, backfired when the people got a taste of what could be.
In the West, we felt we "won" the Cold War. We spoke of a "peace dividend," and the United States assumed the position of the world's only superpower.
Some people called this "the end of history."
While we cheered, took a victory lap, and hoped to help guide these new emerging democracies, we failed to understand that there were those like Vladimir Putin for whom the Cold War never ended.
In 1999, a dictatorship in the fascist, imperial mold returned to Russia. Many in the United States recognized this threat; most did not.
Perhaps we weren't vigilant enough. But never in my life did I expect to see my country, led by the republican party, eagerly stand on the side of tyranny and imperialism. The party of Reagan now helps resuscitate and support an empire that we spent years, blood, and treasure trying to defeat.
What I am witnessing now in my United States is unconscionable.
Donald Trump has always had deep ties to the dark underbelly of Russia. His sons brag about the financing they receive from shady Russian oligarchs. He has selected pro-Russian politicians to cabinet positions. He has stated that he trusts the FSB over his own intelligence services.
I don't want to believe conspiracies that he was compromised by the KGB on his all-expenses-paid trip to Moscow in 1987. However, in light of his history of deference to Russian President Vladimir Putin and his now intentional switching of sides in the war between good and evil, right and wrong, democracy and tyranny, it is hard not to.

and it may appear in our Letters section.
The truth is actually worse than that.
The truth is that a malignant narcissist with no values and a transactional view of policy is grasping at straws to deflect blame for his disastrous decisions.
Ukraine is an easy mark. From his shallow promise to "end the war in 24 hours" to his hatred of Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, he sees no problem leaving Ukraine to fend for itself with only a disorganized and unprepared Europe to defend it.
Ukraine is being sacrificed at the altar of cynical political expediency.
I am sick, angry, frustrated, and tormented at this. I fear for the mental and physical health of my friends throughout Ukraine as they weather hour after hour of unrelenting attacks. We don't know what to say, how to comfort or ease both the pain of war and betrayal.
I am consumed by hatred, not only for Putin, but for the smug cabal of traitorous and ignorant Americans willing to abandon the values and principles that our country was founded on, and that we have defended throughout our history.
But I want my Ukrainian friends to know that you still have very broad and determined support in the United States.
"In the war between Russia and Ukraine, the United States is first to surrender, but Americans still stand with Ukraine" — these are the words I saw on the posters of protesters and in comments about our new embrace of Russia.
We still remember the feelings we had when we watched freedom come to Eastern Europe, and we understand that what our government is doing is objectively wrong.
Those of us who have committed to helping you will not stop. This is not only the right thing to do for Ukraine, but it is also an act of resistance by decent Americans against the creeping fascism and moral vacuousness that our leaders represent.
Stand strong, and we will always stand with you.

Egypt calls for Yemen talks as parliament weighs military support to Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:06:38 UTC
03:06:38 KST

Egypt calls for Yemen talks as parliament weighs military support to Saudi Arabia
Oct 22 - Egypt advocates exploring "every opportunity" to resolve the Yemen conflict diplomatically, its foreign minister said, ahead of a parliamentary vote next week on authorising the armed forces to support Saudi Arabia against the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Any direct involvement of the Egyptian military, one of the region's largest, would raise the stakes in the conflict between the kingdom and the Houthis, an increasingly destabilising front in the spreading US-Israeli war on Iran.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called on Saturday for an urgent parliamentary session to authorise military involvement supporting the kingdom. After a closed session on Sunday, lawmakers postponed the vote until October 26 to allow more deliberation.
Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh on Wednesday to deliver a letter to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman from Sisi, who said Egypt's support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders rather than attacking Yemen.
What kind of support Egypt will ultimately provide remains unclear.
EGYPT HAS LIMITED ROLE IN SAUDI-LED YEMEN COALITION
Abdelatty said on Thursday that Egypt underlined the need to "explore every opportunity for the possibility of reaching political solutions" ensuring a full Houthi withdrawal from territory seized during the group's advance in September near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a critical chokepoint at the Red Sea's mouth and gateway to Egypt's Suez Canal.
"So that we can move on the political path that we always emphasize, and also side by side in support of the defensive path for the kingdom," Abdelatty told a press conference.
Clashes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government have intensified since the group's push towards Bab el-Mandeb on the Red Sea further strained global oil supplies. The militia has since attacked Saudi airports and oil facilities.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, is a vital strategic and economic partner for Egypt, providing billions in aid, central bank deposits and energy supplies under Sisi.
The war in Yemen, which has caused a humanitarian crisis, started in 2014 when the Houthis drove the internationally recognised government out of the northern capital, drawing Saudi-led military intervention.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in March 2015 mainly as a naval partner, sending warships to secure Red Sea shipping lanes while pledging air support. It also deployed around 800 ground troops but played only a limited combat role.
A US-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted attacks.
While Cairo has voiced support for Riyadh since the resumption of hostilities, it has avoided direct combat. It did not join the Mecca mutual defense pact linking Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, though it says membership remains under consideration.
The Saudi crown prince sought military assistance from the United States, but President Donald Trump did not agree to the US striking Houthis, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters in September. Washington told Riyadh that it would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, they added.

IDF denies Trump halted Iran strike, warns of dangerous miscalculation: 'Attack was never on the table'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:06:11 UTC
03:06:11 KST

Senior IDF officials say U.S. President Donald Trump did not block an Israeli strike on Iran, contradicting reports that Washington had intervened to prevent a renewed military confrontation ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
"Trump did not stop us from attacking Iran because an attack was never on the table. There was an increase in alert levels and heightened military readiness, in line with American preparations," the officials said. According to them, there is no reason to strike Iran before the elections unless Israel detects preparations by Tehran to launch an attack.
However, alongside the military preparations, senior defense officials are concerned about statements coming from Israel's political leadership. At a time when the IDF is trying to maintain a high state of readiness without triggering an escalation, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz continue to speak publicly about the possibility of an attack.
On Wednesday, Netanyahu said Iran was "once again trying to develop its bombs of death," while Katz said Thursday that "Bennett, Lapid or Golan will be responsible for any terrorist attack or strike." The military is uncomfortable with such statements. Commanders have no control over the messages issued by political leaders, yet they will be responsible for managing any consequences on the ground.
Iran, meanwhile, is also listening. Public statements about a possible Israeli attack could prompt Tehran to raise its own alert level and prepare for retaliation. Israel could then interpret those Iranian preparations as a warning sign and respond by increasing its readiness further, creating a potentially dangerous cycle of action and reaction. In such circumstances, a misunderstanding of the other side's intentions could lead to an escalation that neither country necessarily intended. That is precisely the danger of miscalculation.
Preparations within the Israeli Air Force are continuing. According to published reports, dozens of fighter jets participated this week in a training mission simulating an attack on Iran, flying as far as the vicinity of the Iranian border.
Such exercises are part of routine operational preparations intended to maintain the Air Force's capabilities, assess enemy vulnerabilities, identify effective flight routes and preserve the element of surprise. While they demonstrate continued readiness, they do not, in themselves, indicate that a decision has been made to launch an attack before the elections.
Trump: Iran is 'fabricating fake attacks'
For now, Trump appears unwilling to launch an attack on the Islamic Republic, at least before the November 3 U.S. midterm elections. In a new social media post Thursday, the president did not threaten military action. Instead, he accused Iran of "fabricating fake attacks."
"Iran is doing everything it can to drive up oil prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections," Trump claimed. "They are even making up fake hits, mines, and everything else, because more oil is now passing through the Strait of Hormuz than even before the conflict began."
Iranian state television claimed Thursday that seven oil tankers had been struck or hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz overnight. If confirmed, the incidents would apparently represent the largest number of vessels damaged in the strait in a single day since the war with Iran began on February 28.
Citing a statement from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' navy, the Iranian report said four tankers had come under attack and three others had struck naval mines. It also warned that the Revolutionary Guards could target U.S. military bases in the region if Washington attempted to facilitate tanker traffic through alternative routes in the strait.
Lloyd's List Intelligence, a company specializing in shipping data and analysis, said tanker operators willing to risk the passage have been transporting oil from Gulf states through the strait at night. The vessels reportedly use a route near Oman's coast protected by the U.S. military, with their tracking systems and mobile phones switched off. The oil is subsequently transferred to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman before being shipped to customers in Asia.
Iran unveils what it calls a 'suicide drone production line'
Alongside its warning that American military bases could be targeted, Iran's state broadcaster released footage carrying another implied threat. The video purportedly showed what it described as the Iranian military's "suicide drone production line," unveiled for the first time. Iranian army commander Amir Hatami appeared in the footage, which authorities claimed featured the country's most advanced drone.
The developments follow a Financial Times report published Wednesday claiming that Trump had blocked an Israeli attack on Iran ordered by Netanyahu for the weekend of October 10, nearly two weeks ago.
According to the report, the IDF had prepared for several days of fighting against Iran, with planned targets including civilian infrastructure such as power stations, nuclear facilities and other sites associated with the Iranian regime. The operation, which Netanyahu had reportedly pushed for, was ultimately halted because Trump opposed a resumption of hostilities before the U.S. midterm elections. Netanyahu has denied the report, while senior IDF officials now say no such attack was planned. 
Meanwhile, the New York Times reported overnight that the U.S. and Israeli militaries have developed detailed plans to resume strikes on Iran after the American midterm elections, including a "short and intense" operation. According to assessments cited in the report, a three-day assault could inflict enough economic damage on Iran to push it back into negotiations.
Iranian officials, however, said they were aware of the American and Israeli military plans and were developing new targets and tactics of their own.
Among the potential targets threatened by Iran are data centers and undersea internet cables. Iranian officials have also warned that any renewed confrontation "will not be short."
Peyman Salehi, a political commentator in Tehran, said that if Iran were attacked, "some of its response plans would include striking major oil refineries in Saudi Arabia, including facilities belonging to the national oil company Aramco, because such a move would lead to an immediate and sharp increase in oil and energy prices."
"The war has made it clear to us that the best leverage against Trump is to drive up oil and energy prices, because that would hurt the American people," he added.

New norms to limit fuel leaks, protect EV batteries in rear-end crashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:06:07 UTC
03:06:07 KST

In a notification, road transport ministry has also made the automotive standard, AIS-192, mandatory. (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Govt has tightened norms for protection of fuel systems and electric power drive systems, with all new vehicles manufactured from April 2029 onwards required to comply with the new standards, a move that will prevent fire in rear-end collisions.In a notification, road transport ministry has also made the automotive standard, AIS-192, mandatory for Event Data Recorder (EDR) from Oct 2029 if it is installed in any car. The EDR feature is not mandatory for all cars, and it remains an optional feature. EDR records crash details, which help establish what happened immediately before and during a collision. It is similar in purpose to an aircraft’s flight-data recorder or black box.In the case of standards for fire safety, the revised automotive industry standards (AIS)-101 specify that after a rear-impact crash test, liquid-fuel systems must not develop more than slight leakage and continuous leakage must not exceed 30 grams per minute. The key safety requirements include the fuel system not allowing a fire to be sustained following the impact. In the case of electric vehicles, the battery and its securing mechanism must remain in position during and after the impact test.
This standard lays down requirements for protecting occupants from electrical hazards, including the high-voltage circuit being automatically disconnected after a collision.The ministry has notified revised vehicle safety standards, including updated frontal and side-impact crash protection requirements, with implementation for new models scheduled from Oct 2027 and for all models from Oct 2028.It has also revised requirements for protecting pedestrians and other vulnerable road users. The updated standard will apply to new models from Oct 2028.

Energy secretary appears to U-turn on opposition to tougher migration rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

03:04:58 KST

The energy secretary has been forced to clarify that she backs Shabana Mahmood’s migration policy, after earlier joking that she had not been able to “lie” about supporting a key element of the changes.
Miatta Fahnbulleh made the original remarks to a journalists’ event in Westminster, referring to an “awkward” Sky News interview in which she repeatedly refused to say she was in favour of plans to make foreign workers wait 15 years to get permanent residency.
She told the event: “I made three promises to myself when I came into politics. The first was never lie, which has created some awkward moments, including being interviewed by Sophy Ridge yesterday.”
The implication that she could not bring herself to lie about supporting the changes appears to have gone down badly among colleagues in government, although No 10 refused to be drawn on whether they requested her to issue a clarification.
Fahnbulleh posted a statement on social media on Thursday evening saying: “Today I made what was meant to be a lighthearted, self-deprecating remark. I didn’t get it right and it hasn’t come off as I intended.
“I fully support our home secretary and the government’s position on migration reform. As I said earlier this week, it’s absolutely right that people should have to make a contribution to this country in order to earn citizenship.”
The clarification represents a twist in the cabinet split over the issue of the migration changes, with Fahnbulleh and Angela Rayner among those not keen on elements of the original plan.
Mahmood, the home secretary, is consulting on plans to increase the period before foreign workers can claim indefinite leave to remain (ILR) from five to 15 years, backdated to apply to anyone arriving from 2021 onwards.
She has previously hinted that her plan to make it harder to claim permanent residence could be watered down by exempting care workers from the new rule.
However, there were reports on Tuesday that she was holding firm against making changes. A senior ally told the Times that she had the prime minister’s support, saying: “Andy has been on Shabana’s side throughout this row over ILR. He is holding the line.”
This week it was reported that Fahnbulleh appeared to criticise the plans on her Peckham constituency website in a post about a community discussion that was later removed. She was quoted as saying: “If we continually prolong the time people have to wait for settlement, we can also prolong the process of building cohesion.”
And earlier this year, Rayner, the housing secretary, publicly criticised the plans, while dozens of Labour MPs oppose the changes.
One of the leading opponents, Mike Tapp, a former immigration minister who clashed with Mahmood over the policy, said the home secretary should “read the room” in relation to the strength of feeling about the changes.
“It’s important we do the right thing. If people have come to the country and genuinely worked in the sector, they shouldn’t be punished and should have the right to apply for settlement after five years as they expected,” he said.
MPs campaigning for changes to Mahmood’s policies believe they have a chance of convincing Andy Burnham to exempt care workers, given reforming adult social care is an issue close to his heart. However, the Home Office has said that would lead to an exodus of foreign workers from the sector when they are no longer bound by the terms of their visa.
No 10 stressed on Wednesday that Mahmood was “carefully considering” more than 200,000 responses to a consultation before finalising the planned changes.
Asked whether tweaks to the home secretary’s revamp – including no longer applying the policy retrospectively – could be ruled out, Burnham’s press secretary said: “We set out proposals for consultation. We’ve consulted on what the transition arrangement should look like for people already in the UK who have not received settled status.
“The home secretary is leading a thorough piece of work to ensure we get this right and have the right arrangements in place.”
Earlier this week, a Home Office spokesperson said: “This government has announced reforms that mean settlement must be earned and not automatic. We are currently considering responses to our consultation on elements of these reforms.”

Ukraine war latest: Ukrainian troops infiltrate Russian rear near Kupiansk through 15 kilometers of gas pipelines

Ukraine war latest: Ukrainian troops infiltrate Russian rear near Kupiansk through 15 kilometers of gas pipelines
Key developments on Oct. 22:
- Ukrainian troops infiltrate Russian rear near Kupiansk through 15 kilometers of gas pipelines, Khartiia says
- Ukraine to gain access to NATO procurement system for weapons, ammunition, Financial Times says
- Ukrainian military intelligence reveals new Russian cruise missile 'Filin'
- Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage of military communications near major Moscow data center
- Deadly Russian missile strike on Kyiv used cluster warheads, hours after Putin-Witkoff meeting
Ukrainian troops infiltrated the rear of Russian forces near Kupiansk in Kharkiv Oblast after moving about 15 kilometers (9 miles) through underground gas pipelines, Ukraine's National Guard’s 2nd Khartiia Corps said on Oct. 22.
The operation, code-named "Veles," was carried out by the 2nd Khartiia Corps together with other Ukrainian units, according to the corps.
Khartiia commander Brig. Gen. Ihor Obolienskyi said Ukrainian forces had studied how Russian troops were using underground routes and anticipated that they would try to exploit major gas pipelines running through Kharkiv Oblast.
"The Russians intended to use the gas routes to penetrate the rear of our forces. So we went underground ourselves," Obolienskyi said.
According to Khartiia, Ukrainian troops moved through the pipelines before combining the underground advance with operations above ground, including drone strikes.
The corps said more than 30 Russian soldiers were captured during the operation and that Russian forces suffered more than 100 casualties. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify those figures.
Obolienskyi said the aim was both to stop Russian troops underground and to undermine tactics they had been using on the ground and from the air.
"We anticipated the enemy's actions and mastered the tactics of conducting combat operations underground," he said.
Russian forces have used gas pipelines on several occasions to move troops covertly around the Kupiansk sector. In January, Ukrainian troops said they had stopped a Russian assault involving about 50 soldiers attempting to advance through the Soyuz gas pipeline.
More recently, Khartiia said, Russian troops retreating near Kupiansk used civilians as human shields, leading a group that included children and elderly people to the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk pipeline and forcing them inside the pipe toward Russian-held territory. Ukrainian troops said they did not open fire, because civilians were present
"When the battlefield became transparent, the war went underground," the corps said when it first announced the operation on Oct. 21.
read also
Ukraine to gain access to NATO procurement system for weapons, ammunition, Financial Times says
Ukraine will be able to purchase weapons, ammunition, and other military equipment through NATO's centralized procurement agency, potentially giving Kyiv faster and cheaper access to defense supplies, the Financial Times reported on Oct. 22.
Ukraine is entering a partnership with the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), which handles procurement and logistical support for alliance members and partners, according to the Financial Times.
"It provides Ukraine with the ability to have a more structured framework to leverage a broad range of capabilities that we offer: procurement expertise, support services, and access to established industrial base," Jacqueline Borsboom, NSPA's director of support to operations, told the Financial Times.
The arrangement might allow Ukraine to use NATO's existing procurement system and supplier network rather than negotiating each purchase independently.
The NSPA also held an event in Kyiv last week attended by about 150 Ukrainian companies, explaining how manufacturers could register as eligible suppliers and compete for contracts, according to the Financial Times.
The new mechanism is separate from the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), under which NATO allies and partners fund purchases of U.S.-made weapons and ammunition for Ukraine. More than $6 billion in military equipment has been funded through PURL since the initiative was launched in July 2025, according to NATO.
The agreement comes as Kyiv seeks to diversify and stabilize its access to military supplies amid growing uncertainty over U.S. support.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has reported disruptions to some U.S.-provided capabilities, including intelligence sharing and the Starshield satellite system used by Ukrainian forces. President Volodymyr Zelensky said after talks in Oslo this week that efforts were underway to resolve those issues.
read also
Ukrainian military intelligence reveals new Russian cruise missile 'Filin'
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) announced details of a new Russian cruise missile called "Filin" and released a 3-D model of the missile alongside a list of components and electronics on its website on Oct. 22.
Russia began using the missile at the end of summer, HUR said, calling it a continuation of a Russian trend to build "inexpensive air attack means with jet propulsion and ground-based launch."
The missile is 3.5 meters long with a wingspan of 3 meters, ablte to carry either 50 kilogram or 100 kilogram warheads, HUR said. It can fly both at ultra-low altitudes and up to 6 kilometers (about 3.7 miles) high, at a top speed of 800 kilometers per hour (about 497 miles per hour), across a distance of 1,200 kilometers (about 745 miles), according to the agency.
Some parts of the missile are apparently 3-D printed, HUR said, while the electronic component base of the onboard equipment is similar to other Russian missiles, but stands out for the increased share of Chinese components. Besides Chinese components, the agency also said the "Filin" included 35 U.S.-made components.
The onboard equipment is manufactured by PLAZ LLC, which is also involved in producing the Harpiya drone, HUR said, while the engine is the Russian-made R500, produced by Reynolds LLC.
Russia uses cruise and ballistic missiles to strike at Ukraine, and increasingly at the country's energy infrastructure. On Oct. 22, Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others.
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," President Volodymyr Zelensky commented on the attack.
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles.
read also
Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage of military communications near major Moscow data center
Agents of the Ukrainian partisan group Atesh said they disrupted Russian military communication lines around IXcellerate, one of Moscow's largest commercial data center operators, to interfere with Russian air-defense coordination and help Ukrainian drones reach their targets, the group said on Oct. 21.
"We are disabling the enemy's channels, disrupting command and control, and helping UAVs reach their targets," Atesh said.
The group claimed Russia's Defense Ministry uses infrastructure linked to IXcellerate for military communications and air-defense command systems, while concealing that traffic within civilian server networks.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim, and Atesh did not provide details on the extent or duration of the disruption. There has been no public confirmation from Russian authorities or IXcellerate that military communications were affected.
IXcellerate operates several data centers across Moscow and describes itself as a leading commercial data center operator in Russia. Its facilities host telecommunications and other digital infrastructure used by banks, retailers, and business customers.
The partisan group has previously claimed sabotage operations against Russian military and defense-linked infrastructure inside Russia, including attacks on railway and energy facilities.
read also
Deadly Russian missile strike on Kyiv used cluster warheads, hours after Putin-Witkoff meeting
Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight on Oct. 22, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others, according to Ukrainian officials, only hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff visited Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office reported these numbers in the morning, saying Russia had struck across Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, Svyatoshynskyi and Dnipro dsitricts in Ukraine's capital.
Among the injured are four children, one of whom has been hospitalized, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said.
"Last night, the Russians used, among others, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads against Kyiv. The peculiarity of these missiles is that they explode in the air, hitting the target, and hit everything around within a diameter of 400 meters," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," Zelensky commented on the attack earlier.
During a meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff lauded Putin — wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Ukraine — as a "humanitarian."
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 181 drones, including 87 jet-powered ones, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 32 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight others.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that the Iskander missiles carried a K5 cluster munitions warhead.
"This warhead explodes above the ground and is specifically designed to cause maximum damage to people and equipment in an area of 400 by 400 meters," Beskrestnov said.
"This strike was not carried out with a military purpose. The goal was to destroy part of the old city and injure as many people as possible," he added.
Zelensky said one of the missiles struck Pechersk, in Kyiv's historic center, in an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Sviato-Vvedensky Monastery. Buildings belonging to the monastery, residential buildings, shops, cafes and other civilian infrastructure were damaged, he said.
"There was not even theoretically any military facility nearby," Zelensky said. "It was a deliberate choice of weapon, a deliberate choice of the area of use, a deliberate attempt to inflict as many casualties and as much damage on civilians as possible."
Zelensky reported two people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast as a result of the attacks.

Rwandan, Chinese academics urge strong research collaboration to tackle environmental challenges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:01:06 CST
03:01:06 KST

KIGALI, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Academicians, researchers and officials have called for strong research collaboration, increased investment in scientific research and the application of homegrown knowledge to address environmental challenges and promote sustainable development in Rwanda and across Africa.
The call was made on Thursday, during the International Conference on Environment, Energy and Development held in Kigali, the capital of Rwanda, under the theme, "Resilient Earth: Water, Ecosystems, Energy and Sustainable Development."
The conference was co-organized by the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography (XIEG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the University of Lay Adventists of Kigali (UNILAK) and the Sino-Africa Joint Research Center (SAJOREC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Olivier Habimana, head of the department of Digitalization and Research at the Rwanda's Higher Education Council, said Rwanda needs locally generated scientific knowledge to achieve its development ambitions, particularly in water management, environmental protection, renewable energy and climate resilience.
"That ambition cannot be achieved through borrowed knowledge alone. Instead, it requires homegrown science," Habimana said, urging universities and research institutions to strengthen collaboration with government agencies, industries and local communities.
He noted that research must go beyond academic publications to inform policy decisions, generate practical solutions and benefit communities. He also highlighted the need to increase investment in research and development and strengthen links between academia and industry.
At the conference, Jean Ngamije, vice chancellor of UNILAK, urged researchers to pursue evidence-based solutions and expand scientific cooperation among Rwanda, China and other African countries.
"I call upon our researchers to pursue scientific evidence and strengthen collaboration," Ngamije said, emphasizing the importance of turning research findings into practical interventions that improve people's lives.
According to Duan Weili, deputy director of XIEG, the ICEED series has been successfully held in Kigali six times since its inception in 2013. Over the past decade, this conference has grown from a regional academic platform into an important space for dialogue, bringing together peers from China, Africa, and beyond.
"East Africa is facing multiple pressures from water security, ecosystem degradation, and climate-induced disaster risks," Duan said, noting that this year's conference is highly relevant and timely.
Speaking at the event, Wang Shengwei, deputy director of SAJOREC, called for stronger cooperation in student training, academic exchanges and capacity-building to advance biodiversity conservation and ecosystem restoration.

Feature: When a Ghanaian college student meets with Chinese traditional face-changing art
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:00:34 CST
03:00:34 KST

Austin Elikem Afiawo, a final-year Chinese language and linguistics student at the University of Ghana, speaks during an interview with Xinhua in Accra, Ghana, on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Seth/Xinhua)
by Justice Lee Adoboe
ACCRA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Amid the sweeping green oasis that rises gently over the Legon Hill in the northern part of Accra, Ghana's capital, lies the 11.4-square-kilometer University of Ghana, the country's premier higher-education institution.
As a typical ivory tower, the university is made up of different schools, departments, and institutes, including the Confucius Institute. Here, many young Ghanaians come to study the Chinese language and culture.
Among the current crop of students is 20-year-old Austin Elikem Afiawo, a final-year Chinese language and linguistics student at the university, who loves to spend time at the Confucius Institute working on his Chinese language and cultural studies.
For young Afiawo, his academic journey, including structured classroom work and writing test papers, is also interspersed with cultural activities such as Chinese dance, stage performances, music, and drawing, among others.
One specific Chinese art form that the Ghanaian student has taken keen interest in and has been mastering is "Bian Lian," the traditional Chinese Sichuan Opera's face-changing performance.
Afiawo, then a first-year student, attended a cultural performance at the Confucius Institute. But this turned out to be a moment that would transform him from being part of the audience to a key cast member in cultural performances at the institute.
"I watched one gentleman, Jesse Twumasi-Ankrah, on stage in a blue costume just changing faces. I was really shocked and got interested in it. So, I decided to approach him after the program and ask him how he did it," he told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Twumasi-Ankrah, then a senior student, began teaching Afiawo the basics of the face-changing performance, and Afiawo gradually started perfecting the art. Later, other teachers of the Confucius Institute at the University of Ghana (CIUG) also joined in to train him.
Being new to the stage craft, the young student found the performance initially difficult to learn and cope with. But gradually, he mastered the art and has established himself as a face-changing art performer in Ghana.
"The first difficulty is that, while people think the performance is just about changing faces, the real challenge is the costume. Putting on the costume is a very difficult part of the performance," he said.
According to him, "The costume with several masks is very heavy. It puts a lot of stress on you. So those are some difficulties we face."
"I remember my very first performance, which was here at the Confucius Institute. I was very nervous, being the first time I stood in front of a large audience to perform, and one mistake can destroy the entire performance," he said.
To manage his stage fright, Afiawo avoided eye contact by looking above the audience's heads and pretending he was alone in the auditorium, which helped him enjoy his act.
Afiawo has since mastered the art and is able to perform during events organized by the three Confucius Institutes in the West African country and other events organized by Chinese organizations in the country.
Chinese Director of the CIUG Liu Baijun spoke highly about Afiawo's enthusiasm. "He's very active in CIUG activities. He always comes to the Confucius Institute and learns some Chinese culture."
"Face-changing is a tradition in China. Maybe it's quite strange for some of the foreigners, but for Austin, he likes it very much," Liu said. "He practices face-changing in his spare time, and his skill has improved a lot."
One of the values Afiawo has learned through performing the face-changing art is endurance, as the heavy costume he puts on to perform on stage causes him to sweat a lot in Ghana's warm, humid tropical weather. Furthermore, the need to pile up different masks in the costume, which he keeps changing on stage to portray different looks, requires enduring discipline.
"But after every performance, we realize that no matter the struggle we go through, we can actually pull through," added the Ghanaian student.
Afiawo expressed gratitude to the CIUG for the enormous support he continues to receive from them, both for his academic work and training in stage performance.
Liu noted that more and more Ghanaians are eager to learn the Chinese language and culture in recent years. The CIUG will introduce more Chinese culture, not only traditional but also the latest Chinese technology, to the Ghanaian people. ■
