RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's presidential runoff, scheduled for Sunday, Oct. 25, will pit incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against Flavio Bolsonaro in a closely fought contest that could shape the country's policy direction over the next four years and influence Latin America's political balance.
Lula, of the Workers' Party, is seeking to overcome a first-round deficit against Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party candidate and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro won 47.03 percent of valid votes in the first round, against Lula's 45.16 percent. Neither secured more than 50 percent of valid votes, the threshold required to win outright.
A Quaest poll released on Wednesday put Bolsonaro at 45 percent and Lula at 44 percent, with the gap within the poll's two-percentage-point margin of error. The survey interviewed 2,154 people between Oct. 17 and 20.
Both campaigns are courting supporters of eliminated candidates and voters who stayed home in the first round, when abstention reached 21.08 percent.
Lula has stepped up his digital campaigning, drawing on younger politicians and influential online supporters. Since Oct. 7, he has posted selfie-style videos urging supporters to take their campaign onto the streets and speak directly to voters.
Bolsonaro has consolidated support among conservative politicians and business leaders while seeking a more moderate public image, emphasizing policy proposals and steering clear of controversies that could alienate undecided voters.
At their televised debate on Sunday, Lula pledged to sustain economic growth, strengthen public security and defend Brazil's sovereignty in international affairs. He also proposed a public security ministry to coordinate federal, state and municipal action.
Bolsonaro emphasized tougher measures against organized crime, including classifying criminal factions as narco-terrorist organizations and expanding prison capacity. He also pledged to reduce public debt, support debt restructuring for businesses and individuals, and improve public healthcare by bringing in specialists and adopting advanced technology.
The contest has also moved into the courts. Bolsonaro's campaign filed a case on Tuesday seeking to disqualify Lula's ticket, and Lula's coalition filed a similar request against Bolsonaro's ticket on Wednesday. The allegations remain subject to judicial examination.
The congressional results will also shape the next government's room to maneuver. The Liberal Party won 121 of the Chamber of Deputies' 513 seats, compared with 88 for the Workers' Party-led federation.
The Liberal Party is set to hold 28 of the Senate's 81 seats starting in 2027, making it the largest party bloc, although it will still fall short of an outright majority. Whichever candidate wins the presidency, building support across party lines will be important to advancing his legislative agenda.
Beyond these domestic challenges, the outcome could influence Latin America's wider political direction.
Zhou Zhiwei, a researcher at the Institute of Latin American Studies of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said Brazil's election offers an important window into the region's changing political landscape.
Conservative forces have gained momentum across Latin America over the past year or two and demonstrated their strength in Brazil's first-round contests, he said.
A rightward turn in Brazil could further weaken the Latin American left, while Lula's re-election would give it a significant boost, Zhou said.
For both candidates, the immediate challenge is to turn support into votes. Their ability to reach beyond committed followers and bring voters to the polls could prove decisive. ■

====================================================================================================

Older adults with depression tend to have smaller volumes of a specific part of the hippocampus brain region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:00:23 UTC
03:00:23 KST

An analysis of more than 2,000 cognitively healthy older adults found that those with depression tended to have a smaller volume in one part of the hippocampus, a brain region central to memory and one of the first affected by Alzheimer’s disease. The association did not appear to be explained by amyloid and tau, two proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease. The paper was published in Translational Psychiatry.
Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia in older adults. It gradually disrupts memory, thinking, behavior, and everyday functioning. The disease is accompanied by characteristic changes in the brain, including abnormal clumps of amyloid protein, called plaques, and twisted strands of tau protein, called tangles, along with the loss of nerve cells.
Research suggests that depression may also play a role in the risk of Alzheimer’s disease. People who experience depression during their lifetime appear to have a higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease later on. One possible connection between the two conditions involves the hippocampus, which is central to memory and is among the first areas affected by Alzheimer’s disease.
Depression has likewise been associated with changes in the structure of the hippocampus, although previous studies have produced inconsistent findings. Part of the difficulty may be that the hippocampus is not a single uniform structure but consists of several smaller regions (called hippocampal subfields) that can be affected differently by depression and Alzheimer’s disease. Antidepressant medications may also play a role, as some evidence suggests that they could protect against hippocampal shrinkage, while other findings raise questions about their effects in older adults.
Study author Danielle Luu of the Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute at the University of Southern California and colleagues set out to examine how depression and antidepressant use relate to the volume of hippocampal subfields in older adults without cognitive problems. They also wanted to know whether Alzheimer’s-related factors, including amyloid and tau buildup and the APOE4 gene variant, which raises Alzheimer’s risk, play a role in these relationships.
The researchers considered two possibilities for antidepressants. The medications might be linked to larger subfield volumes by relieving depressive symptoms. Alternatively, they might be linked to smaller volumes, either because of unknown harmful effects on the brain or because doctors are more likely to prescribe them to people with more severe depression.
The researchers analyzed data from the Health and Aging Brain Study-Health Disparities, which recruited Hispanic, Black, and white older adults through the University of North Texas in Fort Worth. The analysis included 2,009 cognitively unimpaired adults between 50 and 90 years of age, with an average age of about 65.
Of these participants, 630 were classified as having depression, either because they scored 10 or higher on the Geriatric Depression Scale or because they reported having been diagnosed with depression by a health care provider. The remaining 1,379 participants were classified as not depressed.
Participants underwent high-resolution MRI scans of the hippocampus and reported whether they used antidepressant medications. The researchers used the scans to calculate volumes of three hippocampal subfields: the CA1, the subiculum, and a composite region that included the CA2, CA3, and the dentate gyrus (CA23DG). Subsets of participants also underwent PET scans measuring amyloid (684 people) and tau (386 people) in the brain.
Participants with depression tended to have a smaller CA23DG, but depression was not associated with the volume of the CA1 or the subiculum. The association was small and held after the researchers accounted for body mass index and physical activity, as well as tau levels and APOE4 status. When amyloid was added to the analysis, the association was no longer statistically significant, but its size was similar, which the authors attribute to the smaller number of participants with amyloid scans.
The severity of current depressive symptoms and the age at which depression began were not associated with the volume of any subfield. In exploratory analyses, the link between depression and smaller subfields appeared stronger in men than in women, but the authors interpret this cautiously because the formal test of a sex difference was not statistically significant.
Among participants with depression, those who used antidepressant medications tended to have smaller CA1 and CA23DG volumes than those who did not. These associations weakened to borderline levels after the researchers accounted for body mass index and physical activity. When antidepressant use and depression were included in the same analysis, the link between depression itself and a smaller CA23DG faded, while antidepressant use remained associated with a smaller CA23DG.
The authors suggest that the medication findings may reflect what is known as indication bias, meaning that people with more severe depression may be more likely to be prescribed medication in the first place. Antidepressant users reported fewer current depressive symptoms than non-users, suggesting the medications were relieving symptoms, but the researchers did not have information on how severe participants’ depression was before treatment or how long they had taken medication.
“It is important to study AD [Alzheimer’s disease] in the context of mental health, since rates of depression rise with age. Moreover, it is crucial to investigate how depression and antidepressant medication use affect the hippocampus, a region of the brain that is heavily impacted by AD. Understanding the relationship between depression and the development of AD is important for exploring preventative measures against brain atrophy and dementia,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the neural underpinnings of depression in older adults. However, it should be noted that the design of this study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results. Depression diagnoses and medication use were self-reported rather than drawn from medical records, and the analyses involving amyloid and tau were based on smaller subsets of participants.
The researchers did not compare different types or doses of antidepressants. They note that the possibility that the medications themselves affect hippocampal structure should be tested in randomized controlled trials.
The paper, “Depression and hippocampal subfield volume in older adults,” was authored by Danielle Luu, Alicia M. Twisselmann, Victoria R. Tennant, Brandon J. Hall, Arjun Mahajan, Audrey Kim, Jamie Terner, Marylan L. Davison, Koral Wheeler, Christopher R. K. Ching, James Hall, Matthew T. Borzage, Leigh Johnson, Arthur W. Toga, Sid E. O’Bryant, Kristine Yaffe, and Meredith N. Braskie for the HABS-HD Study Team.

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said on Thursday that the initialed peace agreement with neighboring Azerbaijan could be signed in 2027-2028, state news agency Armenpress reported.
In response to a question about the deal at a news briefing, Pashinyan said Yerevan needs to continue working with Baku.
On Aug. 8, 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Pashinyan initialed an agreement and, along with Trump, signed a joint declaration at a summit in the White House, aiming to end decades of conflict, with commitments to cease hostilities, reopen transport routes, and normalize relations.
In this context, Pashinyan was quoted as saying that the implementation of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a transit corridor project linking Azerbaijan with its autonomous Nakhchivan exclave through southern Armenia, is also important.
“Of course, one has nothing to do with the other, but we are now beginning to implement the TRIPP project,” Pashinyan said.
Pashinyan said he does not rule out holding snap parliamentary elections to adopt a new Constitution, and that they will publish draft of the new document "in the near future," launch discussions, and submit it to parliament.
"We will try to persuade our opposition colleagues that this is a very important and fundamental issue, one that concerns determining and resolving the question of the continuity of the Armenian state. We will try to persuade them. If that does not work, we will pursue other scenarios, including holding snap elections," he said.
Earlier in the day, Pashinyan said they are entering the implementation phase of the TRIPP project. At a working visit to the southern most Syunik province, he said a development company for the project will be established in the near future.
"We are now essentially in the final stage of establishing the company, and once it is established, the work carried out, including as our contribution, will be transferred to the company," he added.

Twelve officers and non-commissioned officers from the Senegalese Gendarmerie completed a specialized training course in Rome at the Carabinieri Command for the Protection of Cultural Heritage (TPC).
                                    
Established in 1969 as the world’s first unit specializing in this field, the Command shared its expertise with its Senegalese counterparts in preventing and combating the illicit trafficking of cultural property.

What's next?
Crossbench colleagues plan to raise increases to regional health funding and MP security measures when parliament resumes on Monday.
Independent MP Helen Haines privately lobbied the prime minister for urgent rural health funding just five days before she is alleged to have been mowed down outside her electorate office by a man whose lawyer says is suffering from mental and chronic health conditions.
ABC News understands Ms Haines handed Anthony Albanese an annotated copy of the Forgotten Health Spend: A Report on the Expenditure Deficit in Rural Australia 2026 in a special crossbench catch-up with the prime minister last Wednesday to highlight a growing $2.7 billion expenditure gap between metropolitan and regional areas.
Sources with knowledge of the meeting who spoke with the ABC on the condition of anonymity said the health funding disparity between the cities and bush had been raised.

A spokesperson for Mr Albanese said the prime minister often met with independent members of the crossbench and had done since 2022.
"Members are free to raise any issues and we follow up," they said.
Haines, a former nurse and maternal health expert, has long campaigned for additional support for regional services, using her maiden speech to call for timely access to mental health care that "should not be reliant on your postcode nor your ability to pay once your 10 Medicare-funded services run out".
That reality is acutely felt in her hometown where local council health data shows Wangaratta records 23.7 registered mental health clients per 1,000 residents, almost double the Victorian average of 11.9.
She remains in a critical but stable condition at The Alfred hospital in Melbourne after having both legs amputated.
Court appearance and parliamentary security
Brendan Nugent, who is alleged to have deliberately struck the MP twice using his four-wheel drive, is facing charges of dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.
His lawyer told Wangaratta Magistrates' Court on Wednesday that Mr Nugent had mental health concerns and a neurological condition.
Monday's horror incident has become a flashpoint for parliamentarian security, with a special briefing from ASIO, AFP and Department of Home Affairs officials on Wednesday warning that high-office holders were facing a spike in violent threats driven by personal grievances or by motives that "aren't always rational".
The attack is driving renewed calls for better mental and rural health services in areas such as Haines's tight-knit community.
Her crossbench colleagues are expected to raise the issue when parliament returns on Monday.
Friction over document
It comes as Mr Albanese downplayed a document created by his office against Ms Haines in September after she called out a $6m grant to the prime minister's local golf course.
The file, seen by the ABC, is titled: In the past two years — the member for Indi has asked for more than $1.8 billion worth of funding for projects she's selected.
It lists possible questions journalists could pursue regarding funding requests Ms Haines had made on behalf of her local community, including whether she had received undeclared gifts.
Mr Albanese told ABC Radio today the document was not a personal criticism of the MP.
"Let's be very clear because apparently it's been published somewhere. It's a list of funding asks from Helen Haines, just showing that people of integrity stand up for their electorate," he said.
"No personal criticism of Helen. Helen is a strong advocate for her electorate. She's advocated for funding for projects in her electorate."

A New Ice Age Was Beginning. Then Humans Started Burning Fossil Fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Burning fossil fuels may have stopped the Earth from entering another ice age, a new study suggests. The research, published Thursday in the journal Science, uses samples of ancient vegetation and rock records to analyze the growth—and sudden retreat—of an ice cap that is the last vestige of an ice sheet that once covered much of North America.
The findings shows the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers parts of Canada’s Baffin Island, started growing a few thousand years ago before rapidly reversing course beginning in the 1960s as carbon pollution ramped up.
“A question that’s in the popular consciousness is, have we caused enough global warming to stop the next ice age from happening?” says Andrew Wickert, an associate professor of environmental science at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, who was not involved in the research. The new research shows that “even as we were just starting to ramp up emissions, we’ve already done enough damage to cause the major North American ice sheet to already start retreating. That’s significant.”
The planet regularly goes through phases where ice extends down from the high latitudes—what we colloquially call "ice ages"—due to natural shifts in the Earth's rotation and orbit, known as Milankovitch Cycles. Those are followed by interglacial periods where ice retreats toward the poles.
The last ice age ended 12,000 years ago. At its peak, what's known as the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered all of Canada and extended as far south as New York and the Midwest. It retreated to form the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers an area the size of Delaware on Baffin Island.
Unlike glaciers, which can move, the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the bedrock, preserving the vegetal record of what grew around it under the ice. That quirk allowed the scientists leading the new study to glean information about how much it has grown—and shrank.
To determine when it first reached its modern size, they used an exposure dating technique to calculate roughly how long rocks several meters from the glacier’s edge had been exposed to the sky. Using measurements of Beryllium-10, an element that forms on the surface of exposed rock, the authors calculated that the ice sheet first reached the size it is today around 3,600 years ago.
Next, they wanted to see how much the ice cap had regrown from that point. To do this, they turned to the humble denizens of the tundra in front of the glacier: mosses and lichen.
“After the ice cap retreated, mosses eventually colonized this newly exposed land,” says Nicolás Young, a paleoclimatologist at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory at Columbia University and lead author of the new paper. “These mosses are living there, and things are normal—then, eventually, the ice cap starts to re-expand. The ice covers the moss, and kills it.” The traces of the dead moss are preserved in newly reexposed land, allowing Young and his team to piece together a timeline of how the ice has moved across the landscape.
Thanks to these records, Young and his coauthors estimate that the glacier started growing again around 2,000 years ago. This may have signaled the start of another glaciation period.
But starting in the 1960s, the ice cap has done something that wouldn’t correspond with another ice age: It started getting smaller again. The team used historic aerial photos that showed that the ice has reversed course, retreating significantly back from its new margins. The Barnes Ice Cap’s edges have retreated an average of 4 meters per year since the 1980s. That coincides with a period of rapidly increasing carbon emissions, which has caused ice to go into retreat worldwide. The ice cap offers a particularly stark example, though, given the growth prior to the 1960s.
“Modern retreat of this glacier has reversed 2,000 years of net expansion—that’s a pretty decent chunk of time,” Young says.
Meredith Kelly, a professor of earth sciences at Dartmouth, says the data gathered in the study is “awesome” and that the study shows a “clear pattern of what the ice cap was doing.” However, Kelly says that she would like to see a comparison of some of the data to other sites around the world to more fully grasp how, exactly, the Earth was moving into its glaciation period before the effects of human-caused warming kicked in. While we have a broad understanding of what kicks off periods where ice can grow, the exact mechanisms are still something that require more research.
The evidence presented in this paper, Young says, could also validate a decades-old hypothesis that has long been held up by climate deniers as “evidence” climate change is a hoax. In the early 1970s, scientists gathered for a meeting at Brown University to discuss hypotheses of when the next ice age might happen. (Young says that two of his coauthors on this paper were at that meeting.) The scientists concluded that a glaciation period was so imminent that they sent a warning letter to President Richard Nixon.
“I think this study actually helps show that scientists were right about a pending glaciation,” Young says. “
Media coverage of the meeting, as well as a colder period of weather in the 1970s, have long been pitched by climate deniers as “proof” that global warming isn’t actually happening. It very much is, though, and the new research actually adds to the evidence.

Portuguese and Spanish unions discuss 'Iberian general strike'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:59:44 UTC
02:59:44 KST

Several Spanish trade unions have already called a general strike for 11 November, but the leader of Spain's biggest union CCOO says a joint strike with Portuguese unions is now being considered.
Portuguese and Spanish trade unions are in talks over a possible "Iberian general strike", Unai Sordo, secretary-general of Comisiones Obreras (CCOO), said on Thursday in an interview with the programme "Los Desayunos" produced by Spanish broadcaster RTVE and the EFE news agency.
According to Sordo, Portuguese unions are considering calling a general strike on 11 November, the same day as a planned walkout in Spain involving the country's two main trade union confederations, CCOO and the General Workers' Union (UGT).
The aim, Sordo explained, is to organise an "Iberian general strike", although he stressed that the plan depends on a decision by Portuguese trade unions.
'Saramago strike'
"It is up to the Portuguese to decide whether, in the end, we join forces in a mobilisation across the Iberian Peninsula that would also be historic", the CCOO secretary-general said.
Sordo also caustically referred to José Saramago, the Portuguese Literature Nobel laureate, who spent nearly two decades living in Lanzarote in the Canary Islands and maintained close ties with progressive movements.
"If they hold [the strike] in Portugal, we are going to call it the Saramago strike", Sordo concluded.
The general strike in Spain on 11 November has been planned for several weeks and is scheduled to take place 18 days before snap elections called by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, after parliament rejected government measures aimed at tackling the housing crisis.
Both countries have seen protests over housing affordability and the rising cost of living. Inspired by demonstrations that began in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square in late September, thousands of protesters camped overnight in central areas of Portuguese cities, including Porto and Lisbon.
Demonstrators in both countries are demanding decent, affordable housing, with many arguing that having a job is no longer enough to afford rent in major cities.

Unsafe water, burning eyes and kerosene slicks: residents demand answers on River Taff leak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:58:51 UTC
02:58:51 KST

Oily slicks of kerosene still appeared to be leaking into the River Taff this week, several days after a breach of thousands of litres was spotted by members of the public.
The breach into the Welsh river was identified last Friday, after people reported strong chemical odours emanating from it. Natural Resources Wales (NRW) officers arrived on site soon afterwards to identify the source of the pollution and were assisted by the south Wales fire and rescue service, which placed absorbent mats and booms to contain as much kerosene as possible.
Residents along the Taff were advised to keep windows and doors closed last week, after it emerged that thousands of litres of kerosene from a GE Aerospace site in Nantgarw, Rhondda Cynon Taf had entered the river. Four kilometres (2.5 miles) of waterway were affected, according to NRW.
GE Aerospace is a US multinational company that designs and builds military and commercial aircraft systems and engines. Its site in south Wales is among the world’s largest maintenance, repair and overhaul facilities for commercial aircraft engines, employing more than 1,350 people. In 2017 GE Aerospace was the recipient of £5m in funding from the Welsh government, intended to support innovation and sustainability in the aerospace sector.
Despite early estimates of a volume of about 25,000 litres of kerosene spilled, NRW was unable to confirm what quantity entered the river, and could not comment on possible enforcement action while its investigation was under way and it gathered information.
Public Health Wales advised that the community should avoid all contact with contaminated areas along the busy stretch of river, which runs parallel to many popular trails on both banks, including the Taff trail. People near the river had been complaining of sinus problems and headaches.
“Kerosene vapours may be mildly irritating to the respiratory system. Our current assessment is that people who can smell kerosene may experience temporary irritation, particularly if they are exposed for prolonged periods,” said the health body.
Sarah Llywelyn, who lives in a riverside home in Glan Y Llyn downstream from the GE Aerospace facility, was among those who reported the leak to NRW.
“The smell was absolutely unbelievable. My eyes burned as soon as I opened our door into the garden. I knew it must have been huge because of the smell, and it’s a fast-flowing river – it was essentially unsafe from the point of contamination to Cardiff Bay. We moved here because of the river. What I want more than anything is for lessons to be learned. This should never happen again.”
A visit by the Guardian to the site found oily slicks still leaking into the Taff five days after the incident began. NRW believes that the pollution has now been stopped from entering the river.
An NRW spokesperson said: “Fuel that entered the drainage system before the leak was stopped by the operator could remain within parts of that network and whilst containment measures help reduce and capture pollution, they are not always able to separate all fuel from flowing water. Our work to investigate this incident and assess environmental impacts is ongoing.”
Prof Steve Ormerod, from Cardiff University’s Water Research Institute, confirmed that the photos of the leaks appeared to show the kerosene still entering the waterway through the bunding (a secondary storage system, usually to catch overflows). “The Taff has been recovering from its grossly polluted past,” he said. “So this incident is a potential setback to clean water species such as salmon, dippers and kingfishers that have been recolonising the river.
“Kerosene is a mixture of paraffins, naphthenes and benzene-like chemicals that risk direct toxicity to aquatic organisms, reductions in oxygen transfer across the water surface, and suffocation through impaired gill function in fishes or insects. Effects on feather waterproofing are also likely in the birds that have no choice but to enter the water to feed. Overnight rain was insufficient to raise river levels and flush the Taff, so kerosene will still be lurking in backwaters and eddies along the river.”
Gerwyn and Jordan Lewis from Ynysgau farm, directly opposite the site of the main spill into the river, said they were advised by NRW that the river was unsafe for animals to drink from due to kerosene pollution, meaning that areas of the farm with access to the river could not be safely grazed.
“We simply cannot take the chance of our animals becoming seriously ill or dying. Our winter feed stocks could now be depleted at an alarming rate, leaving us facing the possibility of having to purchase substantial additional feed at considerable expense.
“We also operate a tourism business comprising campsite pitches and glamping accommodation, a sauna and cold plunge facilities, all beside the affected river.”
A GE Aerospace spokesperson said: “The safety of our employees, neighbours and environment remains our top priority. We are continuing to work closely with Natural Resources Wales to address a fuel spill that occurred during repair work at our site on Friday 16 October. The source was identified and isolated on Friday, and containment and clean up are ongoing, with specialist teams working both on and off site.”

Iran says seven ships hit in Hormuz Strait, warns US of wider response

Iran says that seven oil tankers have been struck and sustained damage in the Strait of Hormuz, the largest single-day toll for the waterway since the United States and Israel started their war against Iran on February 28.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said in a statement on Thursday that four of the vessels were transferring oil when they were targeted and caught fire overnight. The other three were disabled after striking mines.
The claims could not be independently verified, and the report did not provide details about possible casualties or the tankers’ flags.
The IRGC also warned that it could strike US bases across the Middle East if Washington moves to help tankers transit other parts of the strait.
“The US military must know that if this trend continues, the conflict will extend to its bases in the region,” the IRGC said in a statement on its Sepah News website. “This is a serious warning.”
Iran claims control over Hormuz, a strategic shipping route through which one-fifth of the world’s oil supplies passed before war broke out. It regularly attacks ships that attempt to navigate the strait without its authorisation.
But the US military has been escorting vessels through the waterway in increasing numbers, with Iran responding by stepping up attacks.
US President Donald Trump said on Thursday that “Iran is doing everything they can to drive up the price of oil prior to the US Midterm Election”.
In a post on his Truth Social platform, he added: “They are making up fake hits, mines, and everything else because more oil is coming through the Hormuz Strait now than it did even prior to the beginning of the conflict.”
A US Central Command spokesperson, speaking anonymously to Al Jazeera, also called Iran’s mine claims incorrect.
The spokesperson said US forces have cleared the international shipping lanes of mines and that Iran is using missiles and drones.
The strait remains open, the spokesperson said, with 95 percent of vessels getting through.
The attacks, the spokesperson added, show Tehran’s “desperation” under the US blockade, which cuts Iran off from the resources it needs to rebuild the military capabilities the US has said it destroyed.
Americans want ‘relief’ from war costs
“The number of ships and tankers attacked every single day is increasing, and Iran is saying it is continuing to do this because they are not going to allow any change in that situation,” said Al Jazeera’s Mohamed Vall, reporting from Tehran.

Vall said there is also talk in Tehran about an imminent escalation in the war, with the Iranians expecting the US to attack even before US midterm elections in early November.
“The IRGC army chief has boasted that Iran is more ready than anytime before, and has produced enough weapons and equipment to wage a symmetrical war against the United States,” he said.
Reporting from the US White House, Al Jazeera’s Kimberly Halkett said: “Striking Iran does not appear to serve any Republican interests”, adding that pre-election polls tell the same story for Trump’s political party.
“What we’ve seen in surveys in recent months, and as of today, is that most Americans want relief from their tax money going to pay for any potential war with Iran that is ramped up,” Halkett said.
“There is real frustration over the rising cost for everyday Americans, given the rising fuel prices that have occurred as a result of this conflict … As a result, the US president is having to make the case.
“The pressure is on the president, and it’s not just from the opposition party,” she said. “It is also from within the Republican Party as well.”

Jewish Federations to hire 100 professionals to combat rising antisemitism across North America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:57:04 UTC
02:57:04 KST

The Jewish Federations of North America (JFNA) announced Wednesday an expanded community response to rising antisemitism, including plans to hire 100 new professionals for frontline advocacy and community relations.
The new roles will concentrate on local and state advocacy, K-12 and higher education, and interfaith and intergroup partnerships, joining existing teams to counter hate manifesting across civic life.
JFNA is carrying out this hiring effort through its Frontline initiative. Backed by more than 25 funders, the $35 million initiative distributes targeted grants to 120 local federations while providing professional training, shared tools, resources, and expert guidance.
Highlighting the urgency of the initiative, JFNA reported that antisemitic incidents have surged following the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks on Israel, with physical assaults reaching record highs last year and Jews targeted in 64 percent of religiously motivated hate crimes. Furthermore, polling cited by the organization indicates that 65 percent of Jews in the US believe the country has a significant amount of antisemitism, compared to 45 percent in 2020.
Rising US antisemitism prompts Jewish Federations to expand advocacy network
JFNA stated these personnel will function as a community defense line in municipal meetings, healthcare environments, school boards, and educational curricula.
Detailing the broader aims of the program, Shira Hutt, Executive Vice President of JFNA, said, “Federations have been deeply engaged in the work of community relations and civic engagement for decades. Today, we require new strategies and increased resources to address the dramatic rise of antisemitism that is permeating every facet of civic life. Federations are on the ‘frontlines’ of this work every day.”
Hutt added: “Frontline is a game-changing initiative that will equip Federations with the talent, support, and resources they need to confront the increasingly complex and growing challenges they face, whether in government, in educational institutions, in media, or our other civic spaces.”
Beyond personnel additions, the Frontline program funds several targeted engagement projects. These include year-round training sessions, the Project Halo messaging hub for data-driven strategic guidance regarding security and Israel advocacy, and the Student to Student high school initiative.
The Student to Student program operates in 50 communities to foster connections with non-Jewish teens and has reached more than 60,000 students over the past three years, with nearly half of those engagements occurring in the preceding year. Additional investments back the One Mitzvah A Day mobilization platform, which has grown to reach a daily distribution list of 25,000 individuals.
Julie Platt, Chair of Frontline and immediate past Board Chair of JFNA, said, “In the aftermath of October 7, our community was very disappointed to see that many people we thought were our allies stayed silent. We learned the hard lesson that our civic engagement efforts must be more focused, more targeted, and more outcomes-based, and that is exactly what Frontline is designed to do.”
She added, “Only through deep, sustained, and strategic engagement can we ensure that antisemitism is neither tolerated nor normalized, and that our communities remain safe.”
The Frontline effort mirrors the operational model established by LiveSecure, a $130 million security initiative launched in response to the 2018 Tree of Life synagogue shooting in Pittsburgh. In 2018, fewer than 20 communities maintained professionally managed security programs that met necessary standards; since then, LiveSecure has expanded that national infrastructure to more than 140 communities within four years—a systemic scale-up that JFNA now aims to replicate across its advocacy and civic relations networks.

What happens when ideology becomes more important than the people? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:56:52 UTC
02:56:52 KST

A Jewish town is attacked. Agitators have just entered. Suddenly, three SUVs pull in. They have Palestinian license plates. Keffiyehs around their necks. One man holds a selfie stick. A Jewish resident tells them to stop. Asks them the purpose of their visit. Requests they turn around.
What is the appropriate response when the driver hesitates?
That happened to me this week. Except I was in the car. It wasn’t a Jewish town. It was Arab. We weren’t wearing keffiyehs, but our drivers wore kippot. Israeli flags hung from our rear-view mirrors. When the Arab resident politely asked us to turn around, we answered with questions.
Except I didn’t know. I assumed we’d only go to Area C. I wasn’t in the car that spoke to the Arab resident. I didn’t hear what he said. I only saw frantic gesticulations. I felt only fear, dread, and confusion.
This week I was invited on a tour to Area C in the West Bank. I was told we’d see the mansions the Palestinian Authority was building and that we’d have an experienced field coordinator who had IDF approval.
Suddenly, I found myself entering an Arab village in a convoy of three cars. A resident asked us to turn around. I never heard the conversation. When a crowd surrounded us, I assumed he intended harm.
When we finally escaped under threat of attack, our story went viral instantly. A Knesset candidate was the victim of aggression! This must prove settler violence is a hoax!
Even my first video reflected that same assumption. I, too, had already begun interpreting what happened through a narrative I thought I understood.
I never heard the Arab resident ask us to leave.
It was only in the coming hours when the adrenaline subsided. When everyone began to post videos of the incident. That I began to piece together what actually happened.
And what happened?
I was a victim of a terror attack. A mob encircled me. Boulders were thrown at my car. It missed my car’s window by centimeters. I thought I was going to die. I’ve woken up in middle of the night screaming. But I garnered no sympathy.
Both sides asked, “Why were you there?” And they are correct. Why was I there?
Imagine agreeing to a trip based on the itinerary you were given, only to find yourself somewhere you hadn’t understood you would be going. To be met with violence, fear, and terror. And when you share your experience, you’re told you should have expected it.
Nobody sympathizes with you. You can barely sympathize with yourself.
Caught between competing narratives
The right says you deserved it for calling it the West Bank. The left says you deserved it for agreeing to go. The world says it should have been worse because you’re a Jew. But you’re only there because your friend told you it was an opportunity to learn.
And suddenly, you’ve never been more confused.
Because what if three SUVs entered a Jewish village with Palestinian license plates?
Everyone tells influencers that they have a responsibility. You must document. You must show. And when we’re pressured to do just that, we’re told we risked our lives for attention.
But who actually benefits from the attention we bring?
What happens when the narrative becomes more important than those who experienced it?
Thirty-one years ago, Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated by a Jew who opposed the peace process he championed. Rabin was also one of the architects of the Oslo Accords. A contributor to the current reality in the West Bank. The confusion between Area A, Area B, and Area C. A division he thought would finally bring peace.
But people were afraid. Afraid for the Jewish future. Afraid of what this division of land would bring.
An area of land so misunderstood that I agreed to go on an educational trip to hear a new perspective. The trip was described as an opportunity to see the “Palestinian Authority’s efforts to… advance a de facto state in Area C.”
A scary reality. A reality that deserves to be shown. A reality influencers are pressured to portray – the truth.
But what is the truth?
Does the truth change based on the ideology of the people delivering it?
How far will an ideology go to deliver its message?
And what happens when you didn’t consent to be the messenger?
Thirty-one years later, is the legacy of the Jewish state still stained by those that can’t separate an ideology from the person delivering it?
The writer is an accidental hasbara content creator. Originally from New York, she graduated from Columbia with a degree in biomedical engineering before making aliyah and enlisting in the IDF after October 7. She now hopes to follow in the footsteps of her great-grandfather, Ben-Gurion’s private doctor, and practice medicine in the hospitals he helped create.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited the Leviathan natural gas platform on Thursday alongside Energy and Infrastructure Minister Eli Cohen, highlighting the role of natural gas as a strategic national asset and a major source of state revenue, according to a statement from the Prime Minister's Office (PMO).
Since the Leviathan gas field began operations in December 2019, the project has generated NIS 32 billion in revenue for the state treasury, the statement said. Cumulative state revenues from Israel's natural gas and oil sector are projected to exceed NIS 350 billion, according to the PMO.
A significant portion of the sector's expected revenue comes from energy export agreements with neighboring countries, particularly Egypt. In December 2025, Israel approved a natural gas export agreement with Egypt worth approximately NIS 112 billion, highlighting the resource's economic and diplomatic significance.
The agreement is expected to generate approximately NIS 58 billion in revenue for the Israeli treasury.
The PMO highlighted the impact of domestic natural gas production on household energy costs, claiming that it has saved Israeli families thousands of shekels annually. According to the statement, energy prices in Israel are more than 20% lower than those in the European Union and other Western countries.
Israel is continuing efforts to identify additional natural gas reserves and expand its energy infrastructure, including to meet growing electricity demand from artificial intelligence data centers.
Leviathan gas field exceeds original production capacity expectations
In May, The Jerusalem Post reported that Israel's largest natural gas field, Leviathan, exceeded its previously announced annual production capacity, reaching 15.8 billion cubic meters (BCM) from earlier projections of 14 BCM, according to partner Ratio Energy.
During Thursday's visit, Netanyahu and Cohen also received a security briefing from the commander of the Israeli Navy's Haifa base on efforts to protect the offshore platform.
The Leviathan gas field was temporarily shut down for more than 30 days following the launch of Operation Roaring Lion against Iran on February 28, amid concerns that the platform could be targeted. Operations resumed in early April.

Paraguay's central bank under pressure over politically connected lender

Paraguay's central bank under pressure over politically connected lender
ASUNCION, Oct 22 - Paraguay's central bank and its president face mounting calls to resign as scrutiny intensifies over how they supervised a fast-growing digital bank with political ties.
Senators from the ruling party and the opposition have urged President Santiago Peña to remove the central bank's top leadership, despite it being credited with helping Paraguay secure investment-grade status.
The case is testing the reputation that has helped Paraguay become one of South America's emerging destinations for foreign capital, much of it from neighboring Brazil.
In recent weeks, authorities have repeatedly tried to calm financial markets after it emerged that ueno bank faced regulatory scrutiny of its business and an administrative investigation. The bank uses lower case in company statements.
In written statements to Reuters, Paraguay's central bank defended its governance structure, saying regulatory and supervisory processes operate independently and in accordance with established legal procedures.
Ueno said it would continue to "fully cooperate" with the central bank and maintained that the preliminary administrative proceeding did not constitute a finding of wrongdoing.
Ueno has scaled rapidly from a niche local fintech player to a mid-tier bank, in line with digital platforms like Monzo and Nubank. It says it has 3 million customers and manages roughly $800 million to $850 million in public funds.
Details of the preliminary probe appeared in a central bank report sent to the Senate this month. The report aimed to dispel doubts about loans issued by ueno to related companies, but it ended up fueling more questions from lawmakers, the banking association and other business groups.
"The replacement of the Central Bank authorities must take place," ruling-party Senator Gustavo Leite said in an interview with Reuters. "The people at the Central Bank have lost credibility."
Opposition Senator Rafael Filizzola said the financial system was "suffering" and filed another request for information on ueno, which experienced a major selloff of its global bonds. Fitch Ratings changed the outlook on the company's securities from stable to negative last week.
Paraguay's Banking Association, which represents 14 private lenders including Brazil's Itau, published a statement on October 18 reiterating that the central bank's response to the senate was "incomplete."
POLITICAL TIES
The case is politically sensitive. Paraguay's central bank president, Carlos Carvallo, previously worked at ueno and served as its president until August 2023, the company confirmed in a statement to Reuters. Peña, a former economist, was a business partner of the group that owned the bank until March 2025. Ueno said Peña never had a relationship with the bank itself as a shareholder or investor.
Much of the pressure for answers has come from lawmakers of the ruling Colorado Party, amid an internal dispute over the party's presidential nomination for the 2028 general elections.
In a written response to Reuters, the central bank said there was no conflict of interest, saying Carvallo had "recused himself" from all decisions related to ueno bank.
Paraguay’s presidency did not respond to a request for comment.
In remarks to local media in early October, Peña described the situation as an "overflow" of a technical matter that was taken into the political arena and had done "tremendous damage to the image of the entire country."
The ueno case has put a spotlight on stability in Paraguay's grain-exporting economy that won investment-grade credit ratings from Moody's in 2024 and S&P Global last year.
The IMF expects growth of 4.5% this year, almost double the regional average. REUTERS

'Post' sees letter requesting West Bank trip coordination despite IDF denial - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:56:26 UTC
02:56:26 KST

The incident on Wednesday in which the IDF detained a US congressional nominee and around 90 foreign volunteers, including senior members of Rabbis for Human Rights (RHR), as they attempted to assist Palestinians in harvesting olives in the West Bank, was a highly complex situation, IDF sources told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.
Given extensive recent reports of Jewish extremists harassing Palestinians and preventing them from completing their harvests, the activists sought to assist in the olive harvest.
Claims from both sides involved were subjected to careful examination. One issue that remains unclear is the status of communications between the sides before the incident.
RHR initially said that they had sent letters requesting to coordinate their visit with the IDF Chief’s office and with the IDF Central Commander, to the IDF head of COGAT, to the Samaria Brigade Commander, and to the Etzion Brigade Commander, but had received no response.
Letter requesting to coordinate visit seen by 'Post'
The IDF and the Foreign Ministry initially said that RHR had failed to coordinate its visit to the West Bank area and that the area was a prohibited zone.
However, on Thursday evening, the Post received a copy of the letter sent by Rabbis for Human Rights to the IDF. The letter is undated, but the organization said that it was sent to the IDF on August 25, nearly two months in advance of the visit.
At press time, the military had not clarified whether or not it had received the letter.
Earlier on Thursday, IDF sources had expressed that they were unaware of such a letter.
Further, they indicated that the IDF receives many letters and sometimes may not see or respond to all of them on time.
If the RHR had indeed sent such a letter to the IDF, and the military simply had not read it in time due to being overwhelmed with paperwork, this would neutralize one of the main justifications for its detention of the activists seeking to assist the Palestinian olive harvesters.
Yet there is another complex series of arguments regarding the incident.
RHR said that the village they visited was in a Palestinian area and, as such, did not require coordination with the IDF.
Faced with this claim, the IDF sources explained to the Post that 90% of the area where the olives were harvested was open and did not require coordination with the military, but 10% did require such coordination.
Regarding the visit, IDF sources argued that a large part of the problem – which had prevented a slower and more careful assessment of the situation – was the very large number of foreign visitors and the fact that they had come within some 50 meters of a Jewish village known to have provocative and aggressive members.
In other words, when the IDF arrived in the area, some two hours after the olive harvesting had begun, they were seriously concerned that even if the RHR group was peaceful, the extremists from the nearby Jewish village would attack them, given the size of their group.
Of course, RHR and the Palestinian harvesters could respond that it was the IDF’s job to protect them and allow them to do their harvesting; not to forcefully evacuate them – let alone detain them – to avoid provoking extremists into breaking the law.
IDF sources did not have a satisfactory answer to that question, saying that the soldiers on the ground had not known that US Congressional candidate Brad Lander (D-NY) was present or understood much about the group when they arrived.
Rather, IDF sources said that since a series of provocative incidents involving Palestinians, Jews, and foreign visitors have taken place and since there was no registered coordination, the military assumed that the visitors were provocateurs who had to be detained and removed from their proximity to potential Jewish extremists, in the interests of avoiding a potentially large-scale and deadly incident – in light of recent occurrences.
Later, when the IDF officials realized who Lander was, they immediately released him. Further, they said, they released almost all the detainees within a matter of hours.
While the military’s narrative of the incident was not particularly favorable, IDF sources said that the broader olive harvesting situation was very favorable.
They said that a huge area of Palestinian West Bank olive harvesting had been properly coordinated with the IDF in the last week and a half.
The IDF said that over 100 olive harvest trips had been coordinated with the IDF without any problems. The military added that 22,500 tons of olives were harvested, and 5,600 tons of olive oil were packaged, worth around NIS 225 million.
The Foreign Ministry said that one quarter of the entire area had already been harvested.
However, the letter from RHR to the IDF noted data indicating that there had been a 63% increase in Jewish crimes against Palestinians during the first half of the year. The military had not allowed harvesting in the specific area in question.
Lander was specifically released with a warning, he recalled in a statement.
“I’ve been released from IDF custody with a ‘warning,’ apparently because of my public profile (I told them I wasn’t even a congress member yet, just a nominee),” he wrote. “But several dozen rabbis and participants harvesting olives with me are still in detention. For harvesting olives. They should all be released immediately,” he said, adding that “Palestinians face far worse consequences every day.”
Rabbis for Human Rights activists detained in West Bank
RHR said that the volunteers had worked in the village of Nahalin near Bethlehem, accompanying Palestinian farmers to groves during the olive harvest.
RHR leadership said that their work in the West Bank was peaceful, and that it was the organization’s policy to comply with IDF orders.
“We came to accompany farmers to land they had been unable to access for three years, and after two hours of peaceful olive harvesting, large numbers of troops arrived and closed off the area. No one could have known about this order in advance.
“Instead of protecting people working their land, the army is keeping them away from it and detaining those who came to accompany them for identification,” acting HRH Executive Director Anton Goodman said.
“The fact that Israeli and American rabbis are compelled to stand alongside Palestinian farmers to help them harvest their olives and protect them from settler violence is a damning indictment of the Israeli government. The fact that these same rabbis are detained by security forces, rather than the authorities protecting the farmers and taking action against those perpetrating the violence, is nothing short of a disgrace,” Yizhar Hess, vice chairman of the World Zionist Organization, said.
Meanwhile, the IDF and the Foreign Ministry view the entire incident as planned and designed to be more of a public relations incident than focused on helping with the olive harvest, which they say is generally proceeding well, despite some increased Jewish extremist violence.
Corinne Baum contributed to this report.

Stephen Hubbard's son: 'It’s tragic when family members are torn apart' by Russian captivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

Stephen Hubbard's son: 'It’s tragic when family members are torn apart' by Russian captivity
Stephen Hubbard (C-L), a 74-year-old retired U.S. schoolteacher who was freed after being imprisoned in Russia following his capture in Izyum, Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine, is seen with his family heading home in a photo shared on Oct. 21, 2026. (@SEPeaceMissions / X)
For years, Father Joseph Coleman had little ability to influence what happened to his father, Stephen Hubbard, an American retiree imprisoned in Russia after being captured in Izium, a city in Ukraine’s Kharkiv Oblast occupied by Russian forces in 2022.
Hubbard, 74, was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison after a closed trial in Russia. Russian prosecutors accused him of fighting for Ukraine as a mercenary, a charge his family has disputed. For Coleman, who lives in Cyprus and had not seen his father in years, the news of his release brought a long-awaited chance to see him "free and well."
“Two or three weeks ago, I was under the impression that all efforts were not going to be successful. Therefore, when I was told on Friday or Saturday that he would most likely be released, as they say, hope was rekindled,” Coleman said in an interview with the Kyiv Independent.
“Typically, I’m reserved until they say wheels up,” Coleman said. There had been another possibility of freedom in early 2025, he recalled, but it had fallen through. When the confirmation finally came, he said, he felt “overwhelming relief, joy.”
Coleman acknowledged that his father may have suffered mistreatment in captivity, though he said he could not be certain. “Many tragic things happen in war,” he said. “Was he mistreated? Some people say yes. I don’t know. I wasn’t there. Some evidence points to that, but I wasn’t there.”
Despite his concerns, Coleman said Hubbard appeared healthier than he had expected and was in high spirits. Still, he acknowledged that the years in Russian captivity may have left emotional scars that are less visible.
“He looks good, especially considering what he’s endured,” Coleman said. “You know, there’s always some probably emotional trauma that’s hidden that he’ll have to work out.”
For now, Coleman is not pressing his father to recount what happened behind bars. He said he had not asked Hubbard about his experiences in Russian custody and would leave it to his father to decide whether — and when — to speak about them. Hubbard has always been a reserved and private person, Coleman said, and he would not be surprised if some parts of the ordeal remained untold, even to his family.
“He'll tell me if he wants to and when he wants to,” Coleman said. “I wouldn't even be surprised if he never tells me the whole story.”
While Coleman said his father has no plans to return to Ukraine, he hopes to one day travel to both Russia and Kyiv on a religious pilgrimage. For Coleman, an Orthodox Christian, the journey would be about faith rather than politics — a chance to visit sacred sites and the relics of saints that have drawn pilgrims to the region for centuries.
“As an Orthodox Christian, it was always my hope and dream to do a pilgrimage to Russia, both to Russia and actually even Ukraine, Kyiv,” Coleman said. “But not for political reasons in any way, just strictly spiritual or religious reasons.”
read also
Questions about his father’s imprisonment
Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher from Michigan, had moved to Ukraine to live with a Ukrainian woman. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, he remained in the country.
“Things kicked off, and he didn’t leave,” Coleman said. Coleman said he believed his father’s continued presence in Ukraine had made him a target. A Russian court later convicted him of being a mercenary and sentenced him to 82 months in prison.
Coleman said his understanding was that “Ukrainians put him on a list of volunteers and because of that piece of quote-unquote evidence the Russian government accused him of being a mercenary."
“Witkoff’s pathetic fawning over this KGB thug betrays American values & security.”
Coleman objected to describing Hubbard as someone who had volunteered to fight for Ukraine, saying that the characterization was misleading and could have consequences for him and his father. He knew little more about the circumstances, other than that the woman had since moved to Cyprus with her daughter.
Coleman also pushed back on reports describing his father as pro-Russian, saying that Hubbard’s connection to the Russian Orthodox tradition was religious rather than political.
“He is a part of the Orthodox Russian tradition,” Coleman said, explaining that his father had entered the Orthodox faith through that tradition and had participated in Russian-tradition Orthodox churches in both the United States and Japan. Hubbard was not officially a member of any Russian Orthodox Church, Coleman said.
Despite the uncertainty surrounding his father’s imprisonment and the negotiations that secured his release, Coleman expressed gratitude to those he believed had played a role. He named “God and Donald Trump and even President Putin.”
Asked about the Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war still held by Russia, as well as Ukrainian children taken from their families, Coleman said he believed families should be reunited.
“I think it's tragic when family members are torn apart and they should be reunited,” he said. “But beyond that, like I said, I have no political power.”
An unexpected meeting with Witkoff
Coleman was not directly involved in the negotiations that led to his father’s release. Much of the campaigning on Hubbard’s behalf in the United States had been undertaken by his aunt, Tricia, who lives in Florida.
Coleman, meanwhile, was thousands of miles away in Cyprus, where he said he struggled with his inability to help.
“To be honest with you, in Cyprus, I felt a little helpless not being able to do anything at all,” he said. “I’m a priest, so mostly I was focused on prayer.”
He nevertheless met U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff at Witkoff’s home in Florida. Coleman said he rarely followed American political news and did not recognize Witkoff when he arrived.
“When I showed up at Steve’s house, we jumped out of the car, and there was a man with a golf club, and I didn’t even recognize him,” Coleman said.
“I told him later, I said, ‘I apologize, I didn’t recognize you,’” he recalled.
Witkoff’s role in the release drew criticism after he publicly praised Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian.”
“WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” Republican U.S. Senator Thom Tillis wrote in an X post directed at the U.S. envoy. “You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian.’”
read also
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal also criticized Witkoff’s remarks.
“Witkoff’s pathetic fawning over this KGB thug betrays American values & security,” Blumenthal wrote. “He should cite Putin’s humanitarian greatness to the prisoners he’s tortured & killed, the children he’s kidnapped, the Ukrainians whose country he’s bombing.”
Blumenthal co-authored legislation with the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham imposing sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia and Iran. Trump signed the measure into law in September but later waived many of its provisions.
Trump denied that the United States had made concessions to secure the American’s freedom.
The U.S. “gave nothing in exchange” for the release, Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that “we’re getting closer” to settling the war.
Asked by a reporter how waiving of sanctions did not amount to giving Russia something in return, Trump replied, “You are a stupid person.”
The exchange took place as Trump spoke to reporters en route to a rally in South Carolina, where he was campaigning for Republican candidate Darline Graham, the late Senator Lindsey Graham’s sister. He spent two years pushing legislation to sanction Russia. Asked about his sister’s reaction to the prisoner release and the decision waive sanctions, Trump dismissed the question, saying, “You don’t know anything, fake news CNN.”
“The other important thing, very important, is that we are negotiating with Russia right now on Ukraine. We are maybe close to a deal for the first time in a long time. When you are close to a deal, you are having very delicate negotiations. You don’t put sanctions on it,” Trump told reporters.
Coleman said he did not believe sanctions are helpful.
“I think that sanctions don’t really help in the long run,” he said, adding, “I’m not really politically minded. I don’t actually even know how a sanction benefits or hurts someone, to be honest with you.”

Another 11 Ukrainians return from temporarily occupied territories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:56:00 UTC
02:56:00 KST

Another 11 Ukrainians return from temporarily occupied territories
According to Ukrinform, Dmytro Lubinets, Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner for Human Rights, reported this on Facebook.
“Another 11 Ukrainian citizens have returned to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government! For some of them, the journey was particularly difficult because of their health conditions, the need for medical care and the need to arrange a safe departure,” he said.
According to the Ombudsman, those who managed to leave included a married couple for whom the journey home effectively began twice.
“The woman had previously managed to leave the occupied territory. However, her husband became seriously ill and was admitted to intensive care. She returned to be by his side and, after his condition improved, once again arranged for them to leave. Today, they returned to Ukraine together,” he added.
The Ukrainian Parliament Commissioner stressed that this year, cooperation with the International Committee of the Red Cross in Ukraine has been significantly strengthened in efforts to return civilians who need assistance leaving the occupied territories.
“I am grateful to them for their cooperation, as it is now systematic. Measures to return citizens take place weekly or every two weeks, depending on the lists compiled, people’s circumstances and the possibility of arranging a safe route,” he said.
In parallel, cooperation is also underway with another important partner, Caritas Ukraine, which has been helping since early 2025 not only with the return itself but also afterward – with onward transportation, temporary accommodation, financial, social and psychological support, as well as other immediate needs.
“The Office of the Ukrainian Ombudsman is effectively the only state institution that systematically organizes the return of citizens from temporarily occupied territories via the humanitarian route Mokrany–Domanove. We work with people who often have no way to leave on their own and coordinate assistance at every stage of their return. The scale of this work is significant. As part of measures to relocate people and reunite families in various areas, 818 people received assistance in 2023–2026,” Lubinets emphasized.
Overall, according to him, 24,953 people, including 2,054 children, returned to Ukraine through the Mokrany–Domanove border crossing between May 24, 2024, and October 15, 2026. This year alone, 11,815 people returned, including 802 children.
These data have been recorded since 2024, following the Ombudsman’s Office becoming involved in work at the border.
“The direct presence of our staff at the Mokrany–Domanove border crossing plays a special role in this work. An employee of the Ombudsman’s Office works there, advising citizens on their rights and helping resolve urgent issues after they cross the border,” he explained.
This makes it possible not to limit the work to processing appeals remotely, but to identify people’s needs directly on site, help them contact relatives, arrange onward transportation and coordinate interaction with government agencies and humanitarian partners.
“The defining feature of this work is that assistance is provided first and foremost to those who cannot return on their own. These include elderly people, persons with disabilities and serious illnesses, people with limited mobility and bedridden individuals, children and families with children. Assistance is also needed by citizens facing persecution or the threat of forced mobilization, people who have been unlawfully detained and those left without money, housing, family support or proper documents,” Lubinets concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, according to Lubinets, the most difficult category to return is Ukrainian civilians detained or convicted by the occupation authorities on charges of “high treason” or for assisting the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

02:55:00 KST

Iran warned Wednesday that U.S. political assets and infrastructure belonging to countries involved in any renewed war against Tehran could become targets of retaliation if Iranian officials are assassinated or civilians killed, according to a senior security official cited by the semi-official Fars News Agency.
The Tehran-based official said Iran assumes that the U.S. and Israel will launch another attack and considers Washington’s diplomatic gestures "unreliable.”
The official said this perception had intensified following remarks by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Athens, which Tehran interpreted as giving a historical and civilizational justification for Washington’s war against Iran.
According to the official, Iranian political and intellectual leaders have increasingly concluded that US Middle East policy is directed by Israel, which they believe is preventing Washington from pursuing a diplomatic solution.
The official claimed that Israel takes priority in U.S. President Donald Trump’s regional policies.
Iran already considers itself at war with the U.S. and views Washington’s economic and naval blockade, along with restrictions on Iranian airspace, as a continuation of the military aggression that began on Feb. 28, the official said.
He added that growing pressure from different segments of Iranian society was pushing authorities toward "decisive action” to break the blockade under what Tehran considers its right to self-defense.
According to the official, Iran has instructed various operational units that, in the event of another large-scale conflict involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, it would consider U.S. political assets and the infrastructure of countries participating in the war as "legitimate targets.”
The warning comes amid heightened tensions between Tehran and Washington over the U.S. naval blockade and restrictions on maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
The US and Israel launched military strikes against Iran on Feb. 28, triggering a wider regional conflict. Despite subsequent diplomatic efforts, disagreements over the blockade and security arrangements in the strategic waterway have continued.
The warning also follows an Israeli media report on Wednesday that dozens of Israeli fighter jets flew close to Iran’s border earlier this week, with U.S. sources suggesting the operation may have been intended to provoke an Iranian response.

Turkish parliament passes law on liquidation of certain investment funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:53:02 UTC
02:53:02 KST

Adem Balta, Gazi Nogay and Gokhan Ergocun
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Turkish parliament passed legislation Thursday establishing procedures for the liquidation of certain investment funds and the recovery of assets unlawfully removed from their portfolios.
The law applies to funds ordered liquidated by the Capital Markets Board of Türkiye (CMB) on Sept. 17, whose liquidation had not been completed by the law's publication date.
Under the legislation, liquidation will be carried out by designated institutions under the supervision of the CMB, with proceeds added to the funds' liquidation assets after necessary expenses are deducted.
The law allows interim payments of up to one million Turkish liras ($20,150) to eligible investors in funds designated by the CMB, subject to their net investment amounts and other conditions.
Investors whose net investment amounts are below one million liras may receive payments up to those amounts, while payments to those with higher balances will be capped at one million liras.
Individuals and institutions found by the CMB to have engaged in specified market abuse, insider trading or market manipulation involving the affected funds will be barred from receiving payments from their liquidation assets or recovery accounts.
The legislation makes portfolio management companies that established or managed the funds primarily responsible for losses, with other parties held liable under specified conditions if the losses cannot be recovered from those companies.
The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (SDIF) will be authorized to pursue the recovery of losses from responsible parties identified by the SPK and may be appointed as trustee over certain assets.
Assets seized or confiscated in connection with the affected funds may be returned to the funds or transferred to recovery accounts under the procedures set out in the law.
Recovered funds will be distributed to investors through designated liquidation institutions or, where liquidation has been completed, through the Investor Compensation Center (ICC) in proportion to their fund holdings.

====================================================================================================

Our digital lives increasingly depend on data centers. How do we secure them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:49:58 UTC
02:49:58 KST

When Alexander Olshansky received a call in September telling him that the data center hosting his company's infrastructure in Kyiv had been destroyed by a Russian attack, he made a beeline for the scene.
“As I was driving up to the data center, I saw a column of black smoke, a block cordoned off by the police and fire trucks,” recalls Olshansky, president of the Ukrainian domain registration and Web hosting provider MiroHost. The data center was damaged, but Olshansky’s employees had been sheltering elsewhere when the attack happened.
Despite the facility’s destruction on September 23, just around one in 20 of MiroHost’s customers were affected. The company had reserved enough computing capacity in Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia to back up its Ukrainian infrastructure in the event of an attack.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Other data centers haven’t fared as well. In October Ukrainian drones struck three data centers operated by the Russian technology giant Yandex, disrupting services and damaging artificial intelligence infrastructure. Earlier this year Iranian drones damaged Amazon Web Services facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, causing Web outages across the region.
What is inarguable is that, like them or not, data centers are increasingly important parts of our lives, and as such, they’re increasingly seen as fair targets in war. How they are secured is a matter of national—and even international—importance.
“I would say 2026 is going to be the first year of drone strikes taking out data centers being a thing,” says Doug Madory, head of international Internet analysis at the cybersecurity company Infoblox. “I just don’t think that anybody had anticipated this as a risk to interrupt service.”
Because of their vital role in the economy, data centers are designed with multiple layers of security. These include restricted access to the site, constant surveillance and backup power systems. In the event of fire, suppression equipment keeps flames at bay. But those defenses are mostly focused on stopping bad actors from getting inside or on keeping services running when equipment fails—not on withstanding attacks from the air.
“Most data center security standards in the industry focus on physical access restrictions,” says Connor Martin, an international affairs fellow in national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. But protecting facilities against drone or missile strikes is a different challenge—and one the sector must start focusing on. Data centers can seem like sitting ducks from the air because they’re massive, cavernous buildings containing enormously expensive equipment in often remote areas. They “can’t pick up and move,” Martin says.
Still, some protection is possible without going as far as installing missile defenses at key data center locations. Peter Judge, senior research analyst at the Uptime Institute, says operators can build shields around vulnerable equipment such as generators and air-handling units and use overhead netting or screens to hinder aerial surveillance. Yet more sophisticated systems might combine radar, cameras and radio sensors to identify approaching drones or aircraft.
But if a craft is spotted, what can actually be done is trickier. Aviation laws typically prevent jamming drone signals—scrambling their radio signals—or bringing them down without authorization. Some newer drones don’t transmit radio control signals at all.
For his part, Olshansky isn’t convinced physical protection is viable in a war zone anyway. “No fire suppression system is designed for a direct hit by a bomb, missile or drone,” he says.
Truly protecting such a facility could mean burying it deep underground, which isn’t feasible. Instead, the industry’s best approach may be in redundancy—distributing services across multiple facilities so that when one is destroyed, another can take over. It works, as MiroHost showed, but it also costs more: Olshansky says his company effectively doubled its available computing capacity to prepare for an attack.
Madory points out that cloud providers already offer ways to distribute workloads across different geographic regions. The problem is that many customers don’t bother because of the additional cost and technical complexity. “In theory, you could be resilient, but in practice, a lot of stuff is not,” he says.
The recent attacks could change where companies choose to build their data centers, Martin says. The Gulf states have invested heavily in attracting those kinds of instalments, but their proximity to regional conflicts could make future projects harder to justify. Larger countries such as the U.S. and China, meanwhile, have more opportunities to build facilities far from potential conflict zones. But even then, there are no guarantees. As Olshansky says, “It is always better to have two copies of something than just one, even if it is highly protected.”

Millions in cheese revenue lost as protest hits Italy’s buffalo mozzarella output

A truckers’ protest in southern Italy has halted the production of the famed buffalo mozzarella, causing an estimated loss of €3 million (US$3.37 million) in just 24 hours as the milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region and the finished cheese cannot reach customers, an official said.
The week-long strike by truck drivers over the high cost of diesel driven up by the Iran war has also blocked deliveries of other basic goods to supermarkets and left fuel pumps empty in much of southern Italy.
