The disruption is particularly damaging to buffalo mozzarella because the production of the protected cheese depends on a tightly timed supply chain.

Nestlé exceeded sales expectations — how it managed to do so and what about its assets in Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:45:46 EEST
02:45:46 KST

Nestlé exceeded sales expectations — how it managed to do so and what about its assets in Russia
Kyiv • UNN
Nestlé’s organic sales rose by 4% in the third quarter, exceeding analysts’ forecasts. The company excluded its Russian assets from its reporting.
Nestlé reported stronger-than-expected organic sales growth in the third quarter. This sent shares in the Swiss food producer up by around 1.5%, as the business transformation process led by CEO Philipp Navratil gathers pace, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Navratil, who took up the post in September 2025, has taken charge of a conglomerate facing subdued consumer spending and the consequences of the introduction of U.S. tariffs. At the heart of his strategy is real internal growth — that is, an increase in sales volumes. The strategy also involves reducing Nestlé’s presence in segments such as ice cream, bottled water and vitamin brands.
"I am pleased with our progress," Navratil said. "But I am not fully satisfied. We still have a lot to do to fully unlock the potential of the business."
Nestlé shares, which have risen by more than 7% since the start of the year, reached a three-month high.
The company reaffirmed its full-year 2026 organic sales forecast, expecting growth of between 3% and 4%. The actual quarterly figure was 4%, exceeding analysts’ forecast of 3.4%.
Real internal growth reached 2.8%, beating expectations of 1.5%, while growth driven by higher prices came to 1.1%, compared with a forecast of 1.9%. This was the first quarter since 2024 in which Nestlé’s organic sales growth was driven primarily by higher volumes rather than price increases.
In a review, Vontobel analysts said that volume-driven growth "inspires confidence and provides further confirmation that Nestlé is successfully implementing its growth priorities."
"The recovery is becoming increasingly convincing, although the true test remains the consistency of the results," they added.
Barclays analyst Warren Ackerman noted in a commentary that ahead of 2027, "pricing remains the main topic of discussion." There are some doubts about profitability levels next year, as consumers are forced to cut spending while production costs rise. Chief Financial Officer Anna Manz sought to dispel concerns that price increases had been lower than expected, noting that prices rose moderately in 2026 compared with the significant increases in 2025.
"We will raise prices as much as possible without harming consumer reach in the medium term," Manz said. "Given the inflationary environment, we are likely to see further price increases in 2027."
In addition
Nestlé also said it had excluded its Russian subsidiary from its consolidated financial statements after Moscow effectively seized the business last month. This was part of mounting pressure on European companies amid Europe’s support for Ukraine.
The owner of the Maggi and Nescafé brands played down the overall impact of the loss of its Russian assets.
According to Manz, the Russian business, which accounted for around 2% of the group’s total sales, has no longer been included in consolidated financial results since the end of September. This does not affect organic sales growth, sales volumes or pricing.
At the same time, Manz said, Moscow’s seizure of the assets affects reported sales, operating profit from the core business and free cash flow starting in the fourth quarter. She added that the write-down of net assets would worsen the net debt figure by approximately 900 million Swiss francs ($1.1 billion) in 2026.
Nestlé said it was removing Russian assets worth 1.6 billion francs from its balance sheet overall, while also recognizing non-cash expenses of around 1.4 billion francs related to accumulated foreign-exchange differences.

Romania to speed up development of Black Sea capabilities after cargo ship attacks
BUCHAREST, Oct 22 - Romania will accelerate its development of surveillance capabilities and equipment to counter mines and drones in the Black Sea after a series of drone attacks on commercial ships off its coast, its top defence council said on Thursday.
At least seven cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with some 30 sailors reported dead or missing. Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down two of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters on Saturday.
NATO said on Tuesday it will send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea.
• Romania's top defence council said latest ship attacks are direct consequences of Russia's aggression beyond Ukraine's borders.
• Threats to freedom of navigation and critical energy projects in the Black Sea pose a security crisis for Romania.
• The current risks require concrete measures to protect human lives, maintain free access to national ports, and ensure the security of energy facilities in the Exclusive Economic Zone.
• The top defence council said it will accelerate the development of capabilities for maritime surveillance, countering naval mines and intervening against drones illegally breaching national airspace and waters.
• Authorities will practice to improve the efficiency of their operational response.
• Romania will seek to improve cooperation with fellow NATO members Bulgaria and Turkey with whom it shares the Black Sea.
• "The Council members also analyzed ways to intensify coordination within NATO. This includes strengthening the deterrence and defense posture on the Eastern Flank and identifying new measures to respond to threats in the Black Sea region." REUTERS

‘Longer we wait, worse it gets’: Struggle of Gaza’s breast cancer patients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:40:24 UTC
02:40:24 KST

‘Longer we wait, worse it gets’: Struggle of Gaza’s breast cancer patients
Breast cancer patients in Gaza face delayed diagnoses, medicine shortages and limited access to scans and treatment, leaving many fearing their condition is worsening.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip – Hiba Musbah has already been through seven rounds of chemotherapy for the breast cancer that is plaguing her body. Next week will be the eighth.
But the 36-year-old mother of three, from eastern Deir el-Balah, says her condition has continued to deteriorate as she waits to travel outside Gaza for further treatment.
“I can no longer take care of my children as I used to. My son is the one who helps me,” she told Al Jazeera. Her husband Motaz, who has a heart condition, has had to take on more responsibility as her health has worsened, caring for their three children – Mohammed, 13, Jaber, 10, and Ahmad, eight.
Musbah first noticed lumps around her right breast in January 2024, a few months after the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. At the time, she initially ignored them because she was displaced and the war was intensifying. Her mother eventually insisted that she seek medical attention.
Doctors confirmed it was cancer, but despite needing urgent surgery, it took two months for Musbah to be operated on, with the delay caused by Israeli military attacks around the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, where she was being treated.
“The situation was difficult, with the bombardment and the tanks,” she said. “I delayed the operation because of the war. The last time, I nearly died from tank fire, so I postponed the operation.”
Her chemotherapy was initially also delayed for seven months because medicines were unavailable at Nasser Hospital.
Musbah’s experience reflects the reality facing hundreds of women with breast cancer in Gaza, where Israel’s war and blockade have severely weakened the health system’s ability to diagnose and treat the disease.
Shortages of medicines and medical equipment, broken diagnostic machines, the absence of radiotherapy and difficulties leaving the Gaza Strip for specialised care have turned the fight against cancer into another struggle amid Gaza’s deepening health and humanitarian crisis.
Surgery, chemotherapy and the cost of waiting
The lack of access to diagnostic equipment is now another source of anxiety for Musbah. She explains that she needs a new computerised tomography (CT) scan to assess how her condition has progressed, but has been unable to obtain one because the equipment is unavailable at public hospitals.
A private hospital has a scanner, she said, but the examination costs about 150 shekels ($48), which she cannot afford. The waiting time for an appointment can also exceed three months.
“I am now suffering from pain in my back and leg, and I have not had a scan for three months because the equipment is unavailable,” she said. “My doctor told me he was concerned that the disease might have spread through my body, but I still do not know.”
Musbah now struggles to walk and move one of her arms, and experiences pain in her shoulder, legs and eyes, as well as damage to her hair and nails during treatment.
“If I had received treatment early, things would not have reached this point. My condition has become much more difficult because my treatment was delayed,” she said. “Cancer patients also need good food, fruit, meat, fresh produce, but we cannot afford everything we need.”
According to Musbah, she has been waiting for around two years to leave Gaza for treatment after receiving a medical referral. But Israel, which controls all entry and exit from Gaza, has yet to give her security approval to travel.
“I want to travel, receive treatment and get better,” Musbah said. “I want to regain my health and return to the way I was before.”
Growing crisis
According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, the Gaza Strip recorded about 360 new breast cancer cases annually before the war, compared with 250 in 2024 and around 260 in 2025.
The ministry has warned that these figures may not reflect the true number of cases because screening and early-diagnosis services have largely collapsed, potentially leaving hundreds of patients undiagnosed.
In a statement on October 1, the ministry said repeated breakdowns of mammography machines and shortages of laboratory supplies had severely restricted early detection in Gaza. Chemotherapy, hormonal and targeted therapies were also unavailable or critically scarce, while radiotherapy was completely unavailable.
The ministry said surgery for advanced tumours had also been halted because of a lack of specialised medical capabilities.
The shortage of diagnostic equipment adds another obstacle for women who suspect they may have cancer.
Dr Iman al-Haj Ahmad, an obstetrician and gynaecologist at Hikmat al-Jamei Health Centre in Deir el-Balah, understands these barriers both as a doctor helping women seek diagnosis and as a breast cancer patient herself, having been diagnosed in May 2025.
“I had to search until I found a place where I could get a mammogram,” al-Haj Ahmad said. “I kept thinking about ordinary women who don’t have the medical knowledge or connections that I have. If it was this difficult for me, how much harder must it be for them?”
Before the war, women could seek an initial examination at a primary healthcare centre and be referred to hospitals for mammography, ultrasound scans, and further tests.
Now, al-Haj Ahmad said, imaging services are limited, some cancer specialists have left Gaza, and tests needed to confirm a diagnosis are not always available through public health services. Some patients have to pay privately.
Al-Haj Ahmad waited about a month for surgery, eventually undergoing the operation at Nasser Hospital with a visiting Jordanian medical team while the hospital was operating under dangerous conditions.
Chemotherapy and severe food shortages later took a heavy toll on al-Haj Ahmad’s health. She said she lost about 20kg (44lb), her immune system weakened significantly, and doctors had to pause chemotherapy temporarily.
Al-Haj Ahmad is now receiving hormonal treatment while waiting to travel abroad for radiotherapy. Her referral for treatment abroad had been pending since September 2025.
Despite her own illness, she continues to examine women and refer suspected cases to the surgery department at Al-Aqsa Hospital. She also encourages women with a family history of breast cancer to be especially attentive to changes in their breasts.
“Early detection is especially important in Gaza because treatment options are so limited,” she said.
Pink October
It has been a year since the “ceasefire” began in Gaza, although Israeli attacks continue, bringing the death toll from the war up to more than 74,400 Palestinians.
October is the global Breast Cancer Awareness Month – also known as Pink October. Health workers in Gaza are participating in the international initiative, with staff at Hekr al-Jameh Health Centre in Deir el-Balah trying to reach women through healthcare visits and targeted awareness sessions.
It’s part of a Pink October campaign they’ve called “pink blooms from among the rubble”, which teaches women about breast cancer, demonstrates breast self-examination, and offers psychological support to those affected by the disease.
Sabreen al-Buhaisi, who supervises Hekr al-Jameh’s primary healthcare services, said the centre had screened between 700 and 800 women during the campaign. Seven or eight cases were referred to hospital surgical departments for further assessment.
But identifying women who may have cancer is only the first step. Al-Buhaisi said free mammography was available at a limited number of hospitals, where women face long waits for appointments. Private screening is too expensive for many families.
“The financial cost is very high for women. Our people cannot afford these expenses,” she said.
Still, al-Buhaisi urged women to continue examining their breasts despite the difficult circumstances the vast majority live in.
“Even displacement and living in the camps should not stop you from examining yourself,” she said. “Take five minutes of your time. It can make a big difference in your treatment journey.”
Amid these hardships, Musbah continues her fight against time.
She says she has repeatedly followed up on the travel arrangements, but remains unable to leave, with no clear explanation for the delay.
The evacuation process is coordinated between the World Health Organization and Gaza’s Ministry of Health, but they have to then submit patients’ files to Israel for security screening and approval.
“I have been waiting for two years,” Musbah said. “And I still haven’t travelled.”

'LeBron James disrespects our country': Trump lashes out at NBA star
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:38:50 UTC
02:38:50 KST

What was supposed to be a celebratory season opener for LeBron James with the Philadelphia 76ers quickly turned into a political and public controversy. Shortly before Tuesday's game against the New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden, the 41-year-old NBA star was filmed appearing to practice a golf swing and then his shooting motion as the U.S. national anthem played inside the arena. The video quickly spread across social media, drawing angry reactions and prompting criticism from President Donald Trump.
Trump launched a scathing attack on James, accusing him of disrespecting the country. "While listening to our National Anthem, LeBron James disrespects our Country! I said right from the beginning that he’s no good, a TOTAL DISGRACE. LeBron James should apologize to all of those Great American Warriors and Heroes who died for the American Flag, and all that our Country stands for!" Trump wrote on his social media platform Truth Social.
The backlash on social media was swift. Fox News host Laura Ingraham responded sarcastically, writing, "Classy, as always." Matt Wallace, whose account was among those sharing the video, wrote, "This isn't a protest. This isn't a statement. It's just disrespect." Clay Travis, founder of the sports media outlet OutKick, also criticized James for apparently practicing his golf swing during the anthem, adding that he was already "looking forward to his retirement."
However, the video does not establish that James intended to protest or disrespect the national anthem. According to reports, neither James nor the 76ers has publicly responded to the controversy. The online debate has largely centered on viewers' interpretations of his movements rather than any explicit statement or gesture of protest by the player.
This is not the first time James' pregame routine has drawn criticism. In December 2025, while playing for the Los Angeles Lakers, he faced similar backlash after footage appeared to show him making golf-swing motions before a game against the Sacramento Kings. Sports radio host Craig Carton criticized the behavior at the time, saying, "Don't do it during my national anthem."
On the court, however, Philadelphia had the final word. The 76ers defeated the Knicks 106-100, spoiling the home team's championship ring ceremony. James finished his debut with 14 points, nine rebounds and seven assists, helping Philadelphia open the season with a victory.

Türkiye, Canada seal strategic partnership to advance economic, defence ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:36:25 UTC
02:36:25 KST

Türkiye and Canada have launched a strategic partnership aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation in trade, investment, energy, defence, security, and technological development.
The announcement followed a meeting between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday at the Presidential Complex in Ankara, where Erdogan welcomed Carney with an official ceremony.
The leaders held bilateral talks, followed by discussions between their delegations and a joint news conference.
'Canada-Türkiye partnership is essential'
In a joint statement on the partnership, the leaders said: "In an increasingly complex global security environment, rising geopolitical uncertainties, and evolving humanitarian challenges, a strong and resilient Canada-Türkiye partnership is essential, providing a foundation to mitigate shared threats and capitalise on new opportunities.”
Building on 83 years of diplomatic relations, the partnership aims to expand political dialogue, boost economic growth and trade, advance technological development, and strengthen shared security objectives, it said.
Both countries are NATO allies and reaffirmed their commitment to human rights, individual liberties, democracy, and the rule of law.
The leaders also launched a three-year action plan built around four pillars: trade, investment, and innovation; energy and climate cooperation; defence and security; and government-to-government dialogue and people-to-people ties.
Trade, investment, and innovation
Under the first pillar, Canada and Türkiye agreed to work toward successfully concluding a bilateral free trade agreement and expanding trade and investment in priority sectors, including energy supply, defence production, aerospace, and artificial intelligence.
They also committed to ratifying the Canada-Türkiye Air Transport Agreement, strengthening cooperation between trade and export agencies, including on projects in third countries, and promoting collaboration between their innovation ecosystems.
Energy and climate cooperation
The two countries pledged to advance cooperation across the energy sector, including liquefied natural gas, civil nuclear energy, renewable energy, clean technologies, and the resilience of critical energy infrastructure.
The plan also calls for encouraging investment, facilitating dialogue among nuclear sector stakeholders, strengthening sustainable mining and critical minerals supply chains, and expanding cooperation on climate resilience and environmental protection.
The leaders welcomed a joint statement on energy cooperation agreed upon by their respective energy and natural resources ministers.
Canada also welcomed Türkiye's role as host and president of next month’s COP31 UN Climate Change Conference in the southern city of Antalya, starting on November 9.
Ottawa expressed its readiness to work closely with Türkiye's presidency to ensure a successful conference.
Defence and security
The leaders pledged to deepen bilateral and multilateral defence cooperation, including through NATO, building on a recently signed statement of intent on defence cooperation.
They agreed to strengthen efforts to support peace and security in the Euro-Atlantic region and beyond, including in Ukraine, the South Caucasus, and the Middle East, particularly Gaza.
The statement also welcomed the conclusion of a memorandum of understanding on defence sector partnerships between Global Affairs Canada and Türkiye’s Defence Industries Secretariat.
The agreement is intended to facilitate expanded defence industry partnerships and advance discussions on further cooperation in areas of mutual interest.
The leaders also emphasised the importance of initiating a dialogue on strengthening mutual legal assistance in criminal matters and extradition.
Political dialogue and people-to-people ties
Under the fourth pillar, the countries agreed to establish an annual Canada-Türkiye Strategic Dialogue while continuing annual meetings of the joint economic and trade committee, as well as political-military and counterterrorism consultations.
They also pledged to strengthen cooperation on consular matters and migration, explore measures to facilitate travel and mobility, and promote cultural exchanges and engagement with their respective diasporas.
The two leaders agreed that their foreign ministers would oversee implementation of a three-year action plan with the goal of deepening bilateral relations, promoting international security, and building prosperous green economies.
Carney expressed appreciation for the Turkish government's warm hospitality during his visit, described in the joint statement as the first visit by a head of government between the two countries.
Türkiye also welcomed an invitation for Erdogan to visit Canada at a mutually agreeable time.

Foreign national beaten to death by a mob in South Africa

Unknown Publisher

Foreign national beaten to death by a mob in South Africa
Police say a 50-person mob in Durban killed a man amid a wave of anti-migrant marches.
A mob has beaten a foreign national to death during a protest in the South African port city of Durban, amid a wave of anti-immigrant tension.
Police said the group approached the man as he stood by the side of a road in Durban’s central business district.
The victim was allegedly assaulted by a group of about 50 people and was declared dead at the scene, a police statement said.
Police did not reveal the nationality of the man or details of the march.
They said the victim was in his 30s or early 40s, and they were still trying to identify suspects in the attack.
Anti-migrant marches
Durban has been at the epicentre of months of protests against foreign nationals, with looting and violence erupting after an anti-migrant march in the city two weeks ago.
Demonstrations calling for government action against African migrants who entered the country illegally began in June, with some escalating into violence.
Nigeria, Mozambique, Malawi and other countries have said some of their citizens have been killed in xenophobic attacks in South Africa.
South African authorities disputed some of those claims, saying that some deaths were linked to criminal activity.
Tens of thousands of migrants have left South Africa in recent months in one of the largest mass exoduses in years to avoid the violence.
The government also said that many were deported for not having the required papers to be in the country.
South Africa is Africa’s largest economy and migrants have moved to the country for opportunities. But communities in South Africa say there are not enough jobs and public services are overburdened.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has denounced anti-migrant violence but acknowledged that weak border control systems allowed undocumented migrants to travel to and stay in the country.
Government figures show there are about 2.4 million foreign nationals living among South Africa’s population of 62 million.

Italian: A “Brilliant” Language—Italian Language Week in the World Takes Place in Paris
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:32:55 CEST
02:32:55 KST

The Italian language and culture take center stage in Paris during the 26th edition of the Week of the Italian Language in the World, with two events organized by the Italian Embassy and the Italian Cultural Institute: on October 20, at the Institute, the theatrical monologue “A Night Journey Around My Bedroom,” based on the work by Xavier de Maistre in the Italian translation by Paolina Leopardi and performed by Giuseppe Nitti; on October 21, at the Embassy, the event “Italian Treasures in France: The Art of Manuscripts and Miniatures,” organized in collaboration with the Bibliothèque nationale de France (BnF) and the Treccani Italian Encyclopedia Institute.
                                    
Promoted annually by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation through its diplomatic-consular network and the Italian Cultural Institutes, under the High Patronage of the President of the Republic, the initiative is one of the key events in Italian cultural diplomacy. The 2026 edition, dedicated to the theme “Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, and Creating with Italian,” aims to highlight the Italian language as an expression of creativity, knowledge, and innovation. The main speakers at the event hosted by the Embassy were Prof. Carlo Ossola, President of the Treccani Italian Encyclopedia Institute, and Gilles Pécout, President of the Bibliothèque nationale de France, in a discussion moderated by journalist and writer Fabio Gambaro, founder of Italissimo, a festival dedicated to Italian literature in France.
                                    
Before a large audience composed of representatives from the Italian and French literary, academic, cultural, and institutional worlds, the discussion explored the richness of the Italian manuscript tradition and the art of illumination, focusing on the circulation of works and knowledge between Italy and France and on the role of cultural institutions in the preservation and promotion of a shared heritage. The highlight of the evening was the *Romuleon*, a precious manuscript by Benvenuto da Imola preserved in the BnF’s collections, recently reproduced in facsimile by Treccani as part of the “Tesori svelati” series. The publication is the result of a significant scholarly collaboration between the two institutions, bringing together historical research, artistic expertise, artisanal skill, and technological innovation to reproduce the characteristics of the original manuscript with the utmost fidelity.
                                    
In his introductory remarks, Ludovico Serra, Chargé d’Affaires at the Italian Embassy in Paris, emphasized the central role of culture in bilateral relations: “May this event further contribute to interpreting culture as a living and essential dimension of relations between our countries: a space for mutual understanding and dialogue that we have the privilege of continuing to cultivate together.” The symbolic value of the work was highlighted by Prof. Ossola’s words: “Who wouldn’t want to be an heir to the history of ancient Rome? All of Europe has claimed this legacy, and this *Romuleon*, written by Benvenuto da Imola and illuminated in Bourges in Jean Colombe’s workshop, is the most distinguished embodiment of Humanism and European consciousness.” For his part, President Pécout emphasized the deep ties that unite the two countries from a literary and linguistic perspective: “With Flaubert’s Emma Bovary, who ‘wanted to learn Italian,’ the Italian language no longer belongs solely to the world of scholars in France. From the study of Italian manuscripts in the King of France’s library to the study of Italian in the schools of the Republic, the adventures of Dante’s language speak to the richness of the French perspective on Italy.”
 The Italian Cultural Institute in Paris also accompanied the celebrations for Italian Language Week Around the World with a program that, from September through December, explores the many expressions of our language through literature, theater, cinema, and music. Among the events was a lecture by historian Alessandro Barbero on October 12, dedicated to St. Francis of Assisi and the *Canticle of the Creatures*, one of the earliest examples of Italian literature in the vernacular. The program also featured monologues adapted from the works of Alberto Moravia and Elsa Morante, performed by Lucia Lavia and Arianna Scommegna, respectively, to a large and deeply moved audience, as well as a presentation of Denise Pardo’s novels, attended by the author and writer André Aciman. Upcoming events include an international conference and a performance dedicated to Carlo Collodi and Pinocchio, as well as tributes to Mario Soldati, Carlo Fruttero, Pier Vittorio Tondelli, and Emilio Salgari’s *Sandokan*, in a theatrical adaptation.
                                    
“Parisians love Italian—not only as a means of enjoying our culture, but also as a language with an important history and rich in regional variations, such as Neapolitan and Venetian, the languages of Eduardo and Goldoni. This love is evidenced by the more than one thousand students of all ages enrolled in our courses,” stated the Institute’s Director, Antonio Calbi, who then continued: “For SLIM, we chose to highlight a female voice—that of Paolina Leopardi, sister of the more famous Giacomo—who produced a highly effective translation, infused with touches of lyricism and irony, Xavier De Maistre’s *A Nighttime Journey Around My Bedroom*, written by the general and writer in his room in Turin. A precious literary gem that once again bears witness to the friendship between the two countries, even in the literary sphere, and in which actor Giuseppe Nitti has excelled with great skill.”
The events organized by the Embassy and the Italian Cultural Institute confirm the central role of linguistic and cultural promotion in Italy’s international activities and attest to the vitality of Franco-Italian cultural cooperation, embodying the continuity between tradition and innovation.

Umbria on Thursday approved a law on
medically assisted suicide, the fifth Italian region to do so.
                                    
The Legislative Assembly of Umbria has approved a citizens'
initiative bill titled "Provisions for regional healthcare
assistance regarding medically assisted voluntary death through
the self-administration of a lethal drug."
The outcome of the vote was met with prolonged applause in the
chamber. The President, Stefania Proietti, did not participate
in the vote.
                                    
Last month Veneto became Italy's fourth region to approve a law
regulating end-of-life situations, after Tuscany, Sardinia and
Emilia-Romagna, and the first run by a centre-right
administration.
                                    
The right-to-die Luca Coscioni Association have helped several
people to commit assisted suicide in Italy since a landmark 2019
ruling by the Italian supreme court that stated assisted suicide
is legal in some cases.
                                    
Before that it took the terminally ill people who wanted to end
their lives to the Dignitas Clinic near Zurich.
                                    
The supreme court ruling laid down strict markers on cases in
which assisted suicide is legitimate and called on parliament to
end a legislative vacuum at the national level on end-of-life
issues.
                                    
So far it has failed to do so.

Warning: This article contains profanity and descriptions of sexual violence.
Irina, a St. Petersburg resident, has accused an officer at Police Station No. 14 in the city’s Frunzensky District of abuse, beatings, and sexual violence.
It began on October 10, when she filed a police report alleging rape. According to Irina, the day before, she had agreed to visit a man she had met a while earlier through the Daivinchik dating bot. She had occasionally messaged with him, mostly about soccer. Two other people were at the apartment: the host’s brother and a friend of his. Two of the men are police academy cadets, including the man she accuses of rape.
The men and Irina “drank, chatted, and played cards.” “Everyone got pretty drunk, including me,” Irina wrote on Telegram. She said she had no money for a taxi home, so she decided to stay until public transportation started running.
Irina alleges that the host took advantage of her incapacitated state and had unprotected sex with her, without her affirmative consent. “He took advantage of the situation — basically, the fact that I was so drunk I could barely move or say anything,” Irina wrote.
Then, she said, the host took her outside, said, “The stop’s over there. Bye,” and went back inside. Irina went home and slept all day, then went to the police the following day to report the rape. The police accepted her report, although one female officer told her that “it was her own fault, that she should have had the sense to avoid getting into situations like that.” Irina said she spent at least two hours at the station. An acquaintance who had accompanied her was sent home after being told, “This is going to take a while.”
Irina returned home, but about two hours later, the police called and told her she needed to come back to add to her report and undergo a medical examination. According to Irina, the officers refused to let her wait until the next day and came to pick her up and take her to the station.
Mediazona reported that leaked data links the phone number used to call her to Nikita Severov. Phone directory apps list him as an investigator in the Admiralteysky District.
Irina alleges that one of the officers at the station began abusing her. He repeatedly made her strip down “to her socks,” grabbed her by the hair, threw her to the floor, jumped up and down on her, slammed her head “against whatever was there,” and “touched her all over while hitting her.” He threatened to “fuck” her, suggested they “sleep together,” forced her to her knees and moved her face toward his crotch, and said that “all girls like pain.” According to Irina, the officer said that “the Investigative Committee wouldn’t believe her, and neither would anyone else.”
At one point, Irina said, the man she accuses of rape was also brought to the station. He, too, was hit several times, and the officer said, “Two fuckheads couldn’t settle something, and now I’ve got to sit here all night dealing with it.” According to Irina, the officer demanded that they “reconcile,” after which the man she accuses of rape offered her money. She refused.
Other officers watched, including Nikita, whose surname Irina did not give in her post. “He said I was ruining the guy’s life and that he would kick me to death right there,” Irina told Mediazona.
She told the outlet that when she arrived at the station, she was told she would be speaking with the station chief. On Telegram, Irina wrote that the officer who abused her “didn’t introduce himself.”
According to Irina, the abuse lasted four to five hours. She published tracking data from the 2GIS app showing that she was at the police station from 12:42 a.m. to 5:45 a.m.
Afterward, Irina hurriedly left St. Petersburg and flew to Kamchatka, where her family lives. She published her first Telegram post about what had happened while she was already on her way. In Kamchatka, Irina sought medical attention and was diagnosed with a closed traumatic brain injury and bruising of the soft tissues of her head. She also reported the incident to the Investigative Committee’s office in Yelizovo, Kamchatka Krai. According to Irina, investigators there told her they would “send everything to St. Petersburg, since that’s where it happened.”
In another post on October 21, Irina indicated that before going to the police, she had told someone she had been in contact with for two years about the rape, and he “decided to take advantage of the situation and started trying to extort money from that guy.” Irina maintains that she stopped the extortion attempts, but the police learned about them. (Her post indicates that the officers examined the messages on her phone, including those she sent after her first visit to the station.) According to Irina, the police deleted the messages in which she tried to dissuade her acquaintance from extorting money, but an archived copy of the conversation survived. When she told this person that she had been beaten because of his extortion, Irina said, he cut off contact with her.
As of publication, no official inquiry into St. Petersburg’s Police Station No. 14 had been announced. Journalists from the news outlet Bumaga reached the station chief by phone. He said the Investigative Committee was looking into what had happened overnight on October 10–11. The station chief categorically denied any involvement in the abuse of Irina. Investigative Committee officials in Yelizovo told Irina that the committee’s St. Petersburg office had taken an interest in the case and that she had been summoned for an interview.
In comments to Mediazona, the Team Against Torture, which helps victims of police violence, described the abuse Irina reported as “the height of cruelty.” “We can’t remember the last time we saw violence this severe in St. Petersburg or elsewhere in Russia,” the human rights advocates said.

Cyprus police are investigating the financial and tax affairs of Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich

Cyprus police have launched an investigation into the financial and tax affairs of former Chelsea football club owner Roman Abramovich following the publication by The Guardian and its media partners of a report on the management of the Russian billionaire oligarch’s sprawling business empire, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
During a hearing before a parliamentary committee in Cyprus, a senior police official said that law enforcement officers were examining events that took place between 2003 and 2006; the investigation is expected to last several months.
This followed an investigation by The Guardian, The Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC into the management of the Russian billionaire oligarch’s sprawling business empire.
The report alleges that Abramovich’s aides — including employees of the Cyprus office of international auditing firm Deloitte — may have falsified documents describing the structure of his offshore assets.
According to the findings of the investigation, these actions — including the alleged backdating of key documents relating to assets worth billions of pounds sterling — may have helped Abramovich’s companies evade taxes and conceal assets.
The involvement of the Cypriot police became known during a regular meeting of the parliamentary committee on institutions, values and the commissioner for administration, reports CIReN, The Guardian’s Cypriot partner in the investigation.
Andreas Anastasiades, deputy director of the Crime Fighting Department, said that after the report was published, the police began gathering evidence. According to him, the investigation is likely to last six months, although he noted that the considerable amount of time that has passed since then complicates the process.
He also added that the police would contact the relevant state authorities to assess the available materials.
The Guardian approached representatives of Abramovich and Deloitte in Cyprus for comment.
The former owner of Chelsea had previously denied any wrongdoing, saying that he relied on advice from professional experts. Deloitte’s Cyprus office previously stated that the company "operates in accordance with all applicable laws" and also noted that it no longer had access to the relevant documents due to the passage of time.
The Guardian’s findings on Abramovich’s finances are based on material from a data leak known as "Cyprus Confidential." The trove, consisting of more than 500,000 documents, was initially obtained by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists (ICIJ), after which it was analyzed by various organizations, including The Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC.

Thousands of student movement supporters rally as Serbia heads to poll

02:31:00 KST

Tens of thousands of supporters of Serbia's opposition student movement gathered in central Belgrade on Thursday, as the country's longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic rallied across town at the dueling final events ahead of pivotal parliamentary elections.
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, is seeking to end more than 14 years of rule by Vucic's right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) when the country votes on Sunday.
It is the biggest threat Vucic has faced to his hold on power, and civil society groups have warned the election campaign has been marred by intimidation, arrests, attacks, misuse of public resources and a distorted media environment.
"I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country," 47-year-old Marija Nedeljkovic Radic told Agence France-Presse (AFP) as she arrived for the students' rally.
"Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible."
The vote comes after nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The tragedy, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia's largest protests since the fall of Slobodan Milosevic, accused architect of genocide in the Balkans, in 2000.
The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, snowballed from demands for a transparent investigation into the tragedy into calls for an early election.
Waving "Students are winning" flags, chanting and blowing whistles, students marched through Belgrade before converging on Slavija Square, the site of some of their biggest protests.
By early evening, thousands had arrived, and crowds were still growing.
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade, serving as either prime minister or president.
Amid mounting pressure, he announced the snap vote last month, setting up his biggest electoral challenge since his party took power in 2012.
Vucic, who addressed supporters at a sports hall in the capital on Thursday, has regularly accused the student movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it," said the 56-year-old, who resigned to run for prime minister.
"Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!" he said before white ticker tape and balloons showered the crowd.
Many of the 250 candidates of the Student List running for the 250-seat parliament are drawn from academia or are deliberate political outsiders.
The movement has a broad platform, but at its core is a pledge to fight corruption.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling, and surveys have produced widely differing results.
Political scientist Dusan Vucicevic from Belgrade University told AFP it was difficult to predict an outcome but expected students to win more than 40% of the vote, a result significantly larger than any opposition list since SNS came to power.
Days before the vote, Serbian civil society groups warned that conditions for "free and fair elections" were lacking.
"This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government," a joint statement by 24 organizations said.
"It is supported by documented findings from independent Serbian organizations working in different fields."
On Wednesday, Belgrade prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting "violence, riots and attacks" on election day.
Reports of threats and intimidation targeting student demonstrators have grown in recent months, but their rallies have remained largely peaceful since they began.
"I've been following this fight since the very beginning," 35-year-old student rally attendee Igor said.
"Today is the last rally, and it's important that we all come here to send a message of love and peace and that we see each other on the 25th at the polling stations."

The Guardian view on AI safety: the push for global regulation must advance | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:30:45 UTC
02:30:45 KST

Organisations around the world scrambled on Thursday to fix critical flaws in PHP, the software that powers much of the web. The vulnerabilities could allow attackers to take control of affected servers. Some websites were taken offline as a precaution while fixes were installed. The paradox is that while AI helped researchers uncover the flaw, it also threatens to accelerate the ability to exploit it. Amazon said that it had detected an attempt before the public disclosure of the PHP flaws.
What the episode highlights is AI’s central role in security – and not always for the right reasons. OpenAI’s models have also been responsible for two alarming hacks this year – a security breach of an Australian health department website and a raid by a swarm of AI bots on Hugging Face, an AI services platform. Citing those incidents, the AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, warned that a similar cyber-attack on the UK is “likely, if not inevitable”.
Britain is not uniquely vulnerable. In some respects it is more advanced than many countries in grasping the scale of the challenge. The London-based AI Security Institute is internationally recognised as an authority in a rapidly evolving field. A cybersecurity bill to protect critical digital infrastructure is going through parliament.
As Mr Narayan concedes, national governments face limits in protecting their citizens from a global threat. Having Donald Trump in the White House makes the international challenge harder. The US president has rejected calls for international negotiations on AI regulation. He is even dismissive when the bosses of US technology companies recognise the need for external monitoring and ask for statutory guardrails on their own activities.
Mr Trump takes the view that America’s lead at the most advanced frontier of AI is a national strategic asset that would be compromised if other nations, and China in particular, were allowed to set the pace of advancement. In the president’s eyes it is a race for global supremacy and only losers urge caution. “Whoever wins AI, wins,” he has said. That is a disturbingly reckless approach to technology that, in some of the more apocalyptic prognoses, has the potential to destroy humankind. Even in more circumspect scenarios, the risk of some catastrophic incident or severe economic shock caused by the malicious or accidental use of AI is growing at a rate that more responsible leaders than Mr Trump cannot afford to ignore.
Andy Burnham has said that he intends to put AI at the top of the agenda when the UK holds the G20 presidency for the first half of next year. In his speech at the Labour party conference earlier this month, the prime minister compared his role to the global leadership position that Gordon Brown took on as the chair of the G20 in early 2009, coordinating a response to the financial crisis.
But the world looks very different in 2026. Mr Burnham’s convening power will not move a US administration that treats historic allies and multilateral institutions with contempt. That is not a reason to abandon the ambition. The drive to build some global regulatory architecture has to advance. If Mr Trump cannot be moved by care for humanity, this week’s PHP emergency should remind him that America’s technological lead offers no protection from disruption. Shielding US citizens and businesses from such turmoil requires international cooperation that a race for AI supremacy puts at risk.

An artist's answer to finding a place for uncomfortable feelings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:30:00 UTC
02:30:00 KST

The first time Clare James arranged funeral flowers was for her friend's 10-year-old son Harper, who was killed, along with his father, when a tree fell on their car in 2019.
Impelled by the urge to give the children in the room something to look at beyond their friend's coffin, she created a wild and twisting semi-circle of branches, flowers, moss, pebbles and fungi. Woven into the installation were Harper's toys, and guests were invited to light a candle and place it among the pebbles when they arrived.
"So, that was the first one. I just did that because I was worried about how the kids would get through such a funeral," Clare says.
That same year, Clare, an artist based in Victoria's Yarra Valley, created a similar installation in her backyard. Using flowers recycled from a wedding — floristry has been her long-time side hustle — she built a flowery alcove, an altar upon which to lay the grief that doesn't find a home at a funeral.
"For relationships broken, parents that had to leave, pets who died, bodies that no longer work, regrets that haunt, wilderness lost, rivers poisoned, animals slaughtered and the endless amount of grief out there which need a place to be acknowledged," she said at the time.
Growing up with anxiety disorder, Clare says her thoughts get caught in a loop and "things that have upset me or worried me in the world I've not found it easy to let go of". For once, until the flowers wilted and the candles melted, this altar gave her thoughts a place to rest.
The Place for Lost Feelings
In 2022, she built a similar installation for the public. With her sister, artist Kate James, she created The Place for Lost Feelings in an old hall in Healesville. "While we were building it, we got the giggles a few times going, 'Do you think anyone will come?'" Clare says.
But she had a hunch that she wasn't the only one searching for this place, or this experience, outside of organised religion. A church is a place she says she wouldn't feel safe or comfortable.
The two sisters weren't quite ready for what happened next.
"People came from so far and wide and people came with extraordinary grief," Clare says. They came to mourn, to remember and forget, to confront death.
One man in his 50s, diagnosed with terminal cancer, arrived with his wife and his two best friends. When it was their turn to enter the space, the man lay down in front of the installation and they sat with him, Clare says. Later, he told her "it was the first time he actually accepted his mortality".
In the comments book, someone wrote: "It's not like we were hungry for this; we were starving." Clare says it struck her as a "profound thing to say and feel about this little pop-up flower thing".
Clare's installations reflect a high-end floristry movement that has emerged over the past two decades. A slave to the vase no more, bold installations of traditional cut flowers, branches, grasses and edible plants scrunch and twist up walls, creep along ceilings, and hang in defiance of gravity. They scream with life, and they're not cheap. They appear at well-heeled weddings, events and restaurants.
For Clare, giving everyone the chance to experience such a luscious installation at a free event is part of the appeal. Fresh flowers and candles are "there for the most important celebrations in our life", she says. And there's something about their fragility, their ephemerality, which make them the perfect medium for these artworks.
Tomorrow, Clare will open the doors on the second iteration of The Place for Lost Feelings in Healesville. For two days, people will have the opportunity to spend five minutes alone in the space and light a candle. As they exit, two trauma response workers will be available to check in with people.
A new understanding of grief
The event was meant to occur in March, but as Clare was preparing it, her husband Mark suffered a massive stroke. Since then, grief has gained new meaning for her.
There is a "new, profound grief that I feel, and that Mark feels, for everything that he has lost", she says. "The things that we together have lost is huge, and the level of his brain injuries is just so life changing." There is also gratitude that things could have been worse.
"I said to my sister the other day, 'Oh my God, I need The Place for Lost Feelings,'" she says. "I'll go in there and sob for myself and for Mark."
At the same time, she doesn't understand what it's all for: "It doesn't bring back your child, it doesn't make your body better, I don't understand, yet, what it is that makes it feel alright."
After we speak on the phone, Clare texts me photos of the flowers she was looking at in her garden while we talked. There are Granny's Bonnets in different shades of purple, an orange tree bursting with blossom, and a delicate flower, the colour of mango, turning its face to the sun. Brief glimpses of beauty that will return to the soil.
The Place for Lost Feelings, supported by the Margaret Lawrence Bequest and Yarra Ranges Council, is a free event open from 3pm - 6:30pm for people without bookings at The Healesville Living And Learning Centre on October 24 and 25.

====================================================================================================

Europe’s dangerous winter of discontent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:28:10 UTC
02:28:10 KST

Europe is angry.
Rents are soaring. Energy prices are rising, fueling pain at the pump and inflation. Growth is stagnating. And borrowing costs are climbing in France, Italy, Spain and Greece, meaning cash that could have been used to rebuild schools, subsidize housing or compensate drought-stricken farmers must now go toward repaying creditors.
The societal consequences of this spiraling cost-of-living crisis are already surfacing, from rioting and looting in France on the sidelines of peaceful protests to blocked supply chains in Italy and giant campouts in historic Spanish plazas. Authorities in Paris and Rome are deploying extra security forces to prevent similar scenes from playing out in the coming days.
But fixing the underlying issues driving people to the streets appears to be difficult for Europe’s cash-strapped governments.
“No other generation has known, over the past 50 years, as many challenges,” said French Green MP Pouria Amirshahi, one of the co-chairs of a newly formed parliamentary committee tasked with investigating to what extent the government mishandled Saturday’s protest.
With temperatures plunging and the energy crisis showing no signs of easing, a European winter of discontent is hovering on the horizon — while major elections, some featuring confident nationalist-populist parties, loom across the continent.
Continental discontent
The situation in France — where on Saturday, students who had been blockading schools for weeks to pressure the government to better fund education joined forces with hundreds of thousands of people protesting the rising cost of living — is particularly concerning for the EU’s overall stability given the country is the bloc’s second-largest economy.
But it’s not unique.
“In terms of cost of living, the situation in France is not so much different from the rest of Europe,” said German economist Carsten Brzeski, ING’s global head of macro research.
The eviction of an 87-year-old pensioner from her home in Madrid last month triggered demonstrations across Spain over rental protections and housing prices, which between 2015 and 2025 rose by 80% while salaries increased by only 30%. Protesters in Portugal, where house prices have nearly tripled since 2015, driven up by tourist demand and digital nomads, followed suit.
Albanians have been peacefully protesting since May against alleged widespread government corruption and a proposed luxury resort linked to U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner. But the situation turned violent last week when students entered the fray, airing grievances including poverty and the cost of living, a lack of investment in education and health — and calling for the entire political class to resign.
Thousands of students and teachers took to the streets on Wednesday in Athens and around 50 other Greek cities, demanding more state funding for education, safe school buildings and affordable housing. Serbian students are out in force as well, turning the largest protests the country has ever seen into de facto political rallies ahead of parliamentary elections on Sunday.
Youth movements have also called for protests in Germany, where small-scale gatherings over educational funding cuts have already taken place in Berlin and Hanover.
Over the weekend, students marched in several northern Italian cities to protest low wages and the cost of living. Flashes of violence, similar to those in France and Albania, were seen as well, with masked groups looting stores, throwing stones at police and setting fire to street furniture. Italian public broadcaster RAI, citing a police report, put the number of protesters at around 10,000 across several cities.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her government responded by enacting stringent new security measures, including sending 500 troops “to defend” Milan.
“Demonstrating is a right, devastating our cities is not,” Meloni said.
Marie Hyland, a researcher at Eurofound, the EU’s agency for improving living and working conditions, said the cost-of-living crisis was “undermining” the social contract between generations, as young Europeans face the prospect of falling short of their “implicit expectation” of being as prosperous as their parents.
Amirshahi, the French MP, is among the growing number of his government’s critics who accuse ministers of letting things get out of control by failing to engage with the student movement early on, noting that it took weeks for the French education minister to meet with student protest leaders.
“The initial demands were very simple and practical. Toilet paper in restrooms; ceilings that hold together, having teachers,” he said.
Amirshahi, who took part in last weekend’s protests in his Paris constituency, said “all European democracies should watch with vigilance” what’s happening in the country as it faces what he described as an attempt to crush popular revolt by force.
“The situation in France is on edge,” he said.
Online contamination, real-life concern
Social media has played a key role in the growth of protests and the deeply polarized political debate surrounding them. According to social monitoring platform Visibrain, more than 2.2 million tweets about the protests were posted Saturday, three times the number of messages shared during the peak of the Yellow Vests crisis in late 2018.
The French government summoned key platforms Tuesday to discuss the proliferation of content seen as glorifying street violence after live footage of looting and rioting was shared on video platforms such as TikTok.
Online activism also helped movements spread across borders. In the Italian city of Bologna, protesters chanted viral slogans heard during French high school protests. Instagram pages have picked up France’s call for a new protest on Saturday, while Telegram groups keep members updated on the political situation in both countries. In Albania, some protesters said their counterparts in Spain had sent them money for supplies like masks and purified water to fend off the effects of tear gas.
On the airwaves, far-right parties in France, Spain and Portugal have moved to capitalize on the anger on the streets by blaming traditional, centrist political forces for failing to address ordinary citizens’ needs.
French presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, the 2027 election front-runner, is trying to convince voters that she and her far-right National Rally party are the only political force that can restore law and order. Jorge Martín Frías, an MEP from Spain’s far-right Vox party, argued that Europe’s mainstream politicians had “committed the sin of pride and forgotten the common people.”
The French government and right-wing politicians have accused far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, an early supporter of student protests, of fueling the unrest to his political advantage. Mélenchon strenuously denies the allegations — as do some of his adversaries — and the first post-riot presidential poll showed little change in voter intentions.
In any case, Italy’s situation, where the right-wing Meloni faces youth protests in the north and truckers and farmers block motorway exits over fuel prices in the south, shows leaders across the political spectrum are facing similar issues.
In Spain, most surveys have the conservative People’s Party on track to win enough seats to form a coalition government with far-right Vox in the country’s upcoming snap elections, which Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called after lawmakers rejected a long-delayed package of housing measures he put forward in response to the protests.
But Spaniards are likely to remain exasperated with politicians, according to Valeria Racu, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenants’ Union, which has helped spearhead the protest movement.
“Whoever governs, this is not going to stop,” after the November election, she said, arguing that the demonstrators had achieved more in a few weeks of protests than Sánchez’s left-wing government had in eight years in power.
Housing activists intend to drive that message home on Nov. 11, during Spain’s first general strike in 15 years.
“Politics is returning to where it always should have been: the streets and the people,” Racu said.
Eyes on Germany
All eyes are now on falling temperatures and rising energy prices, which are poised to weigh heavily on household budgets.
Phuc-Vinh Nguyen, head of the Energy Centre at the Jacques Delors Institute, said social movements were to be expected as the mechanisms put in place by governments to shield households from rising energy prices linked to the Iran war are expiring.
No country appears immune, with Germany appearing to be one of this winter’s most vulnerable.
“Germany is among the countries to watch because [its] gas reserves are at historically low levels,” Nguyen said.
That means German households are likely to see their heating bills hit hard by surging prices, and tensions in the gas market are also likely to ripple through electricity markets and neighboring countries, Nguyen said.
Brzeski, the German economist, agreed.
“There is an issue that is now voiced more loudly in France, but it is very similar to the situation in other European countries,” he said, pointing to a stagnating economy and affordability issues.
“The biggest difference between France and Germany is that, at the moment, Germany has fiscally deeper pockets,” to soften the impact, Brzeski said. “But what is currently happening in France can easily happen in a couple of years from now in Germany.”
Aitor Hernández-Morales reported from Madrid and Alice Taylor reported from Tirana. Nektaria Stamouli contributed reporting from Athens and Una Hajdari contributed reporting from Belgrade.

The Guardian view on England's north-south divide: Burnham must deliver more than devolution | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:25:45 UTC
02:25:45 KST

Andy Burnham’s call to abandon “40 years of neoliberalism” rests partly on the damage that he says it has done to northern England. A new study – published in the Lancet this week – adds weight to his argument. It found that for adults aged 25 to 49, death rates in the north were 13% higher than in the south in 1981. By 2024, that gap had more than tripled to 42%. What happened in the four decades that left younger adults in northern England with so much worse chances of survival?
The answer lies in the lives and jobs that people have, and the homes they can afford, as well as the state of the public services, like the NHS, that they rely on. Deindustrialisation stripped secure employment from many communities in the north of England – as it did in Scotland and Wales. Austerity then weakened support systems. These reasons also underscore Mr Burnham’s analysis that Britain’s economic model and concentration of power in London have failed its regions.
The question for the budget is what will it do about these inequalities. The north has substantial levels of deprivation, lower rates of pay and fewer healthy years of life for its people. Among people under 75, the Lancet study found that mortality in northern England was 26% higher than in the south. To close these gaps means helping poorer households with the rising cost of essentials and sending more resources to deprived areas. Investment in, say, early years education and council budgets would help to deal with the social conditions underlying ill health.
Reducing regional inequalities requires redistribution – not just devolution alone. Giving a poorer area more control over an inadequate budget does not increase the cash it can spend. Mr Burnham’s idea to let mayors retain locally raised taxes may help. But without a way to ensure each region gets enough resources to meet their needs, such a policy might simply preserve existing disparities. Researchers at Manchester and Liverpool universities and Health Equity North divided England into two roughly equal populations along a line from the Wash to the Severn Estuary. Closing the north’s health gap, they claim, could add £18bn a year to its economy.
Regional policy plays a complementary role to redistribution by aiming to change where wealth is produced. However, in a recent paper, Steve Fothergill of the Industrial Communities Alliance warned that “the UK has moved away from a long‑established framework that explicitly sought to promote jobs and growth in its less prosperous places … the UK now deploys a weaker set of tools for regional economic development than at any point since the mid-twentieth century”. Mr Burnham needs to reverse this trend.
The chancellor, John Healey, says that he wants a budget for “bloody-minded entrepreneurs”. But a richer northern England would not necessarily be a healthy or more equal one. During the 19th century, when Manchester became known as “Cottonopolis”, Friedrich Engels – bemoaning the city’s “disgraceful unhealthy slums” – was shocked to be told by a local businessman: “And yet there is a great deal of money to be made here.” Bringing investment and good jobs to economically weaker regions matters. But whether the resulting prosperity translates into secure incomes, decent homes, good public services and longer lives is just as important. Mr Burnham’s ambition needs to meet twin challenges: where wealth is created and what life it lets people enjoy.

Tuesday Labs debuts "droid butler" Voxel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:24:56 UTC
02:24:56 KST

Tuesday Labs debuts “droid butler” Voxel
New York technology company Tuesday Labs has debuted its first semi-autonomous robot Voxel Series-1, designed to help with household chores and to avoid the appearance of an “uncanny valley” humanoid robot.
Voxel Series-1 (Voxel) performs tasks such as watering plants and sweeping crumbs, which it currently achieves with a combination of autonomous intelligence and teleoperation.
The robot is counter-height and covered in a colourful matte plastic shell with primarily “cuboid” body parts, LED eyes and 1-DOF grippers for hands. Tuesday Labs founder Rosalind Shinkle told Dezeen that initial designs were informed by home objects such as lamps, chairs and briefcases.
Working with former Pixar character designer Alonso Martinez, Shinkle said the finalised Voxel is a combination of “exceptional capability and charming character”.
“We deliberately didn’t build a humanoid,” Shinkle said. “We wanted to stay far from the uncanny valley, and far from robots that fill a human-shaped space in the home.”
“Instead, we made Voxel relatively small and cuboid, to signal his role in your life: a droid butler, not a human butler.”
“We know we don’t want him to feel almost-human, and we know we don’t want him to feel like a toaster,” she continued. “A believable character needs every element sitting at roughly the same point on that human–toaster spectrum.”
Shinkle said five key principles drove the design of Voxel, including easy integration into the home, a maximalist appearance, simplicity, luxury and playfulness.
Part of the strategy was also “affordance matching”, or that, when Voxel is perceived by a human, its capabilities can be inherently understood.
“When someone looks at a robot, they should be able to roughly predict what he’s capable of,” Shinkle said. “If you correctly match perceived and actual affordance, you can avoid that constant feeling of disappointment when a humanoid robot isn’t quite as good at doing things as a human.”
Voxel’s plastic shell and finishes are meant to keep it relatively lightweight, but Shinkle said the external design should also communicate its quality.
Like another home robot that is currently in production, Neo by 1X Technologies, Voxel’s initial customers are “early adopters” who opt in to help informally train the robot’s autonomous software at home.
“We’re starting with a limited number of robots for early adopters who are excited to experience and help shape this technology,” she said.
“Voxel’s estimated price is $20,000, so he will be a luxury product. But our ambition is much bigger – as the technology improves and production scales, we want to make household robots accessible to far more people.”
Shinkle said her own distaste for household chores was part of what drove Voxel.
“Robots will soon be a part of our homes,” she said. “I set out to build the robot that I would actually want to live with.”
“Also, I hate cleaning my apartment, and I’d much rather spend my time building something that solves that problem once and for all.”
Voxel is powered by a rechargeable battery and will charge in an at-home docking station as part of “his normal routine”.
Tuesday Labs is based in New York City and was founded in 2025 by Shinkle, who previously worked as an engineer at Boston Dynamics. The studio is focused on creating “robots that feel natural and delightful to live with”.
The combination of advanced technology and autonomous intelligence has made the creation of robots more possible than ever at this point in history.
This has allowed the field to diversify, and technology companies and studios have released a varity of different types of robots in recent years, including all the cute robots from CES 2025 and five that were displayed at Carlo Ratti’s architecture biennale.
Other recent home robots that debuted include Neo by 1X Technologies and CLOiD by LG.

The far-right activist Tommy Robinson has told his harassment trial that he used private investigators to track down journalists who had written about his alleged role in the 2024 riots, and had photographs taken of their homes “to put pressure” on them.
Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, denied in court that his actions, which included sharing photos of the wife and daughter of one of the journalists, were designed to intimidate and bully.
“I’m not coming to beat [them] up … they know that,” he said, referring to messages and telephone calls, including a voicemail message left for the editor of the Daily Mail after Robinson had paid to get his personal number.
Robinson is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber, in 2024. He denies the charges.
Robinson, 43, gave evidence and was cross-examined on Thursday, when he claimed he “felt it was totally reasonable” to publish a photo of Dirnhuber at his home because he was “in a race against time” to get the Mail to remove a photo of his ex-wife, which the Mail published in a story about him being in Cyprus, with the headline: “Stoking race riots from his sunbed”.
However, he conceded that when he sent messages to the journalists, spoke to one on the phone, and left a message on the voicemail of the Mail’s editor-in-chief, Ted Verity, he had not asked for the Mail to remove the image.
Robinson said he believed he was “restrained” in the voicemail he left for Verity, in which he said he would make him and his family famous, and went on to say he told the journalists involved that he would get their addresses because he was “using it as a play card”.
The prosecutor Ben Holt asked him about Dirnhuber and his partner having to leave their home as a result of threatening emails he allegedly received, and about Young’s family having also considered leaving their home.
“The entire situation, I wish didn’t happen, I wish that none of that had happened,” said Robinson. “I was unfortunately in a situation where I was panicked.”
Referring to the journalists and how they felt about messages he sent to them, he told Southwark crown court: “They know I’m not going to come and beat them up. They know that.”
Holt continued: “They are scared of you, Mr Lennon,” to which came the reply: “They are not scared of physical violence from me.”
Robinson was also asked about messages and online posts directed at the journalists by others after he had started using his own X account to tweet about them, including one post from an X user who told Dirnhuber they would beat the “fuck” out of him.
Asked by Holt if he appreciated that messages such as this had been “generated” by his own output, Robinson said: “I don’t agree with any of these messages … I don’t know who sent these messages. I don’t know, I don’t know, I don’t know.”
Robinson had been in Cyprus in early August 2024. At the time, violence was breaking out across England in the wake of the murder of three girls in Southport. He told the jury he was with “my ex-wife, my three children and three other families and their children”.
In the witness stand, Robinson claimed he had not “stoked” the riots, but tried to calm things.
The first day of the trial was told on Monday that journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after Robinson deployed “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics”.
