Why Russia wants peace between Iran and the Gulf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:23:21 UTC
02:23:21 KST

Why Russia wants peace between Iran and the Gulf
On October 18, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov visited Manama, where he attended the ninth ministerial meeting of the Russia-Gulf Cooperation Council strategic dialogue and held separate talks with the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. The following day, he traveled to Tehran to meet with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and President Masoud Pezeshkian.
In Manama, discussions centered on de-escalation in the Persian Gulf, maritime security, and Russian proposals for a collective security framework, while bilateral meetings provided an opportunity to clarify individual countries’ positions. Lavrov and his Kuwaiti counterpart stressed the need to reduce tensions quickly and agreed that a political and diplomatic settlement is the only viable way forward. In Tehran, regional affairs featured alongside Russian-Iranian cooperation, with Moscow reaffirming its commitment to economic and investment agreements despite the deteriorating security environment.
Diplomacy between the Gulf’s two shores
The trip aimed to prevent a new divide between Iran and the Arab monarchies from becoming entrenched, as the consequences of the US-Israeli aggression against Iran are affecting the security of the entire region. Yet rebuilding trust also requires acknowledging that the Gulf states have their own grievances against Tehran over strikes on their territory and threats to maritime routes.
During the Manama talks, Arab representatives explicitly said they hope Moscow would use its relationship with Iran to convey their concerns. Discussions also covered Yemen, maintaining the ceasefire in Gaza, humanitarian access, and the resilience of energy and food supply chains – the various and interconnected sources of instability plaguing the Middle East.
In Tehran, Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow’s support for restoring security and shipping conditions to what they were before the US-Israeli military operation began. Iran, which sees the attack as the primary cause of the current crisis, likewise stated its commitment to resolving disputes through diplomacy. Agreement on broad principles, however, does not yet amount to agreement on the specific obligations that the parties must accept.
Russia could mediate efforts to de-escalate tensions and mitigate the deterioration in relations between Tehran and the Gulf monarchies, since it maintains close ties with Iran while developing political, economic, and energy cooperation with the Arab states. These relationships allow Moscow to relay messages, identify the scope for compromise, and facilitate direct dialogue, which can easily give way to competing ultimatums during a crisis.
However, this two-way access does not mean Moscow can dictate what its partners actually decide, and its closeness to Tehran may raise questions among Arab participants. The effectiveness of Russian mediation will ultimately depend on whether the parties themselves are willing to negotiate, acknowledge one another’s concerns, and take practical steps to address them.
Inclusive security as an alternative to permanent crisis
In Manama, Lavrov once again presented Russia’s updated concept of collective security in the Persian Gulf as a potential contribution to a lasting settlement. The proposal continues a longstanding initiative rather than a document developed solely for this visit. As early as June, he reported that updated proposals had been circulated to regional capitals and that Moscow was receiving initial responses.
The approach rests on the premise that the Arab monarchies and Iran must take part in a shared framework, because attempts to secure one group of states by isolating another reproduce the causes of confrontation. Confidence-building measures and regular contact are intended to reduce uncertainty gradually, while the Gulf countries and their immediate neighbors should have the decisive voice in shaping the regional order.
An earlier Russian concept circulated at the United Nations in 2019 already envisaged a gradual normalization of conditions, respect for sovereignty, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the development of collective security mechanisms. The current proposals can be assumed to carry over the same spirit, even if specific provisions have changed or been updated.
Moscow has argued that the region needs an inclusive security system of its own, free from external military intervention and imposed political arrangements. This does not rule out international assistance, however, as Russian diplomacy allows for support from outside actors, including members of the UN Security Council, provided that it serves the interests of regional states.
The practical value of this model will depend on whether broad principles can be translated into agreed procedures for preventing incidents, protecting civilian infrastructure, and keeping maritime routes open. These arrangements could provide the first steps towards a more stable order, whereas an attempt to resolve every political disagreement at once could obstruct even limited measures to ease tensions.
Why expensive oil does not make war good for Russia
Western media and expert debates, including those focused on Middle Eastern politics, frequently portray Russia as a beneficiary of the war, arguing that disruptions to Gulf supplies drive up energy prices and create opportunities for Russian exporters.
A short-term price benefit is certainly possible, but to assume that war gives Russia a strategic advantage is analytically unsound, because the country’s national interests are not limited to a single source of export revenue. Additional income from commodity sales says little about the cost of damaged partnerships, postponed investment, and worsening conditions for long-term projects.
The Middle East matters to Russia as a political and economic partner, and stable relations depend on predictable institutions, transport routes, and financial transactions. A prolonged war raises shipping and insurance costs, complicates infrastructure agreements, and forces partners to divert resources from development toward immediate security needs.
This is evident in Russia’s cooperation with Iran, where its projects require a stable operating environment. In Tehran, Lavrov spoke of Russian specialists gradually returning to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, as well as prospects for cooperation in hydrocarbon production and transportation. A protracted war creates additional risks for these activities, and higher oil prices cannot remove them.
Moreover, a sustained energy shock can weaken the global economy, while the resulting decline in demand limits exporters’ initial gains. Even if some consequences of a Middle East war can benefit Russian suppliers in the short term, claims that Moscow wants endless war in the region are superficial at best. Russia’s strategic interest lies in the region’s long-term stability, which would allow it to preserve partnerships, markets, and opportunities for economic engagement.
Regional autonomy in a changing world order
The transformation of the world order and the erosion of Western hegemony give Middle Eastern states greater scope to pursue independent policies, but a redistribution of international influence does not in itself resolve regional disputes. If dependence on external guarantees is merely supplemented by new competing patrons, while mechanisms for direct dialogue remain weak, the Middle East will continue to serve as an arena where local conflicts intersect with rivalry among major powers.
Regional autonomy requires that neighboring states agree on rules for coexistence, even when their foreign policy priorities and perceptions of threats differ substantially. A durable system will require mutual respect for sovereignty, a rejection of imposed military solutions, and recognition that lasting security cannot be built on another state’s permanent vulnerability.
Russia can support this process by providing diplomatic channels and helping identify a workable sequence of agreements, but only the countries of the region can build a peaceful future. External mediation delivers results when it supports an existing willingness to compromise, while even substantive initiatives can remain on paper if that willingness is absent.
Lavrov’s visits to Manama and Tehran highlighted an opportunity to connect urgent de-escalation with discussions about a more durable regional order. Seizing this opportunity will take time and difficult political decisions, because the parties will need to constrain their own use of force, rebuild damaged trust, and accept reciprocal obligations. Moscow can mediate this process, but its outcome will depend on the desire and readiness of the Gulf states and Iran to reach an agreement.

Türkiye's Central Bank lowers policy rate to 36% after 5 consecutive holds

Türkiye's Central Bank lowers policy rate to 36% after 5 consecutive holds
Türkiye's central bank cut its benchmark policy rate by 100 basis points to 36%, in accordance with market expectations, after holding rates steady for five consecutive meetings, Anadolu Agency reports.
The bank's Monetary Policy Committee, headed by Governor Fatih Karahan, lowered the one-week repo auction rate from 37%.
It also reduced the overnight lending rate from 40% to 39% and the overnight borrowing rate from 35.5% to 34.5%.
According to the committee, despite monthly fluctuations, recent inflation figures and leading indicators confirm a slowdown in the underlying inflation trend.
Economic activity data and the limited pass-through of supply shocks to domestic prices suggest that domestic demand remains weak, it added.
However, elevated energy prices stemming from ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to pose an upside risk to the inflation outlook.
The committee said it is closely monitoring how geopolitical developments influence inflation through costs, economic activity, and expectations.
“The tight monetary policy stance, which will be maintained until price stability is achieved, will strengthen the disinflation process through demand, exchange rate, and expectation channels,” it said.
Future rate decisions will take into account realized and expected inflation, as well as its underlying trend, to maintain the tightness needed to support the projected disinflation path in line with interim targets.
The size and timing of policy steps will be determined prudently on a meeting-by-meeting basis, with a focus on the inflation outlook.
“In case of a significant and persistent deterioration in the inflation outlook, monetary policy stance will be tightened,” the committee said, reiterating its attention to upside inflation risks.
Additional macroprudential measures will support monetary transmission if unexpected developments emerge in credit and deposit markets, while liquidity management tools will continue to be used effectively.
Earlier, it was reported that Türkiye expects 4.2% economic growth in 2027.

02:22:52 KST

Andy Burnham has said he will not “abandon the responsibility” of fighting the climate crisis after the government approved the Jackdaw gasfield, pledging to block new North Sea licences and keep Britain on track for net zero by 2050.
The comments are the prime minister’s most forthright yet on net zero, after many MPs have privately cast doubt on the authenticity of his commitment to tackling the climate crisis.
The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, insisted that she alone would make a decision on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield – a decision sources say she is minded to block.
Burnham has been under pressure from industry and political opponents, as well as some Labour MPs, to water down Labour’s manifesto promises on new oil and gas licences and the net zero targets.
“There has been much speculation about what this announcement means for Britain’s commitment to addressing the climate crisis. I want to be clear that our determination is unwavering,” the prime minister said in an article for the Guardian.
He said he was conscious of the “acute global instability” affecting energy security and wanted to treat oil and gas workers with more dignity.
Burnham said that would not stop the government from abiding by its climate targets, saying he was “personally committed to confronting” the challenges of the climate crisis.
“Britain has just emerged from its hottest summer on record, during which we had nurses collapsing on hospital wards, bus drivers working in intolerable conditions and families losing everything to wildfires,” he wrote.
“More extreme weather is forecast in the months ahead. The climate crisis is no distant threat. It is here, on our doorstep, affecting people’s lives and livelihoods. I am personally committed to confronting it, and I will not abandon the responsibility we have to future generations.”
Meanwhile, Fahnbulleh doubled down on her insistence that she would not be influenced by other departments on whether to approve the Rosebank oilfield, setting up a potential standoff with the Treasury.
The chancellor, John Healey, has said he expects “oil and gas” revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, but Fanhbulleh said “only I can make that decision”, insisting that she bore the legal responsibility to ensure the UK did not violate its climate commitments.
Dismissing speculation that Burnham, or his chancellor, would make the final call, she said: “[It] sits heavy for such a big controversial decision because, in the end, only I can make it. And if it is overturned by other colleagues, all that means is we’re going to be overturned in the courts. So we will do the process and we will do it properly.”
Fahnbulleh said she was “really concerned” and “quite sad” about the breakdown in consensus about the climate crisis. She said: “I think it’s a sad place where Reform has gone and got to. But I’m even sadder about the Tories because they know better, and they’ve had a long tradition, including Boris Johnson, of working cross-party on climate action.
“It has been really painful and tragic to watch that consensus burn at a time when we’re seeing the impact of climate change this summer.”
The climate crisis was having a real impact on communities, she added. “It’s people’s livelihoods, it’s their jobs, their communities. Even if you don’t care about climate – care about that, you’ve got to take action.”
Reflecting on the decision to approve the Jackdaw gasfield, Burnham said he wanted to make the transition to a greener future “on our terms”, saying that meant giving oil and gas workers a path to new jobs and using homegrown rather than imported gas.
“At a time of acute global instability, it makes sense to responsibly use our resources here at home. Gas from this field will begin heating our homes and powering our businesses this winter.”
He said he had been moved by the plight of oil and gas workers in Aberdeen, adding that it was an industry that had suffered from deindustrialisation “with too little thought given by politicians to the places left behind. I will not be so careless with people’s lives.”
Fahnbulleh echoed the prime minister’s words, saying the private sector had invested £100bn in clean energy in the last two years. “It’s a huge opportunity for parts of our countries that have been left behind,” she said. But that investment had to have a real-world impact, she added. “When you say jobs are going to be created, don’t say it. People need to see it.”
Burnham said the energy wealth fund that was being created to convert North Sea oil and gas tax revenues to clean energy programmes was long overdue – “something that, frankly, should have happened more than 40 years ago”.
It comes as Burnham announced that military planes and helicopters would fight wildfires for the first time, ahead of a major wildfire summit with fire chiefs, local leaders and experts.
The RAF’s chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft will fight fires and help crews across the UK tackle blazes on remote moorland, steep hillsides and other hard-to-reach terrain.
“Heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs,” said the prime minister.

Vance: Starlink Use Depends on US Policy Toward Kyiv, Moscow – Not Musk

US Vice President JD Vance said on Thursday, Oct. 22, that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk should not be at the center of the dispute over restrictions on Ukraine’s satellite service, framing the issue instead as a matter of US policy toward the war in Ukraine.
Vance spoke to reporters before departing for a rally in North Platte, Nebraska, a day after senior US special envoy Steve Witkoff held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Well, I think that fundamentally Elon Musk runs a private corporation, and I think it’s completely understandable that he doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the US government effectively directing him on what to do,” Vance said.
“So I don’t think this is about Elon,” he continued, leaving unanswered who ordered the restrictions – a decision for which both Musk and the White House denied responsibility while pointing to the other.
Vance turns criticism on European leaders
Asked by a reporter whether he supported Republican calls for an investigation, Vance turned to European governments instead of answering directly.
He said it was ironic that countries with nothing comparable to SpaceX’s technology had spent years targeting the company with regulation and licensing restrictions, now relying on the company.
Currently, the EU is negotiating Ukraine’s access to its secure satellite communications program that could expand the system with commercial services in early 2027.
Russian Shahed Drone Strikes Private Home in Zhytomyr, Injuring 8, Including 2 Children
“Now they’re all running to SpaceX saying, ‘Please do what we need you to do,’” he said, arguing that the situation proved a point that US President Donald Trump has long made; that European countries rely on American technology, businesses and military power.
At the same time, Vance claimed that “European political leaders love to bash the US allies that they depend upon so much.”
The remark comes amid European criticism of Trump’s abrupt Oct. 9 diesel deal with Putin, which eased US sanctions on Russian fuel and effectively cleared the war for over 4.8 million tons of Russian diesel to reach the global market.
While Europe has sanctions imposed on Moscow since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Trump has waived new sanctions on Russia which he signed into law just three weeks before striking a deal with the Kremlin leader.
On Monday, Oct. 19, a member of Trump’s Republican party, US Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, warned that anyone who tries to restrict Ukraine’s use of Starshield will face accountability, including a full investigation, public hearings and steep budget cuts.
Fitzpatrick also pledged to introduce bipartisan legislation, the “Roland Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,” blocking all purchases of Russian oil.
‘A tall mountain to climb’
One of the reporters pointed out that Ukraine has repeatedly agreed to negotiations, while Russia has not, and asked what gives Vance confidence that the current peace negotiations, led by Witkoff, will be different.
Vance claimed that both countries have agreed to join the negotiating table, adding that “the reason why we haven’t struck a peace deal is because they’ve [Kyiv and Moscow] just been too far apart on some of the details of that negotiation.”
According to him, Witkoff re-engaged the process.
“I mean, the nature of these things is you take a swing at it, you see how much progress it can make, and you’re back at it. And sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn’t,” he said, praising Witkoff and Trump’s administration for taking on difficult work, knowing that they “have a tall mountain to climb.”
So far, the Kremlin rebuked every proposition for a direct meeting with Ukraine, as well as proposals for a ceasefire.
In September, during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York, 51 countries issued a joint statement supporting Ukraine and urging Russia to accept an immediate ceasefire.
During the same summit, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, who represented Putin, said that the Kremlin will not pause its “special military operation” even during negotiations. He also blamed Europe for “engaging in their shenanigans,” saying Ukraine would have kept its 1991 borders if they hadn’t.
At Witkoff’s request during their three-hour meeting on Wednesday, Oct. 21, Putin said he would be willing to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the US in November.
During the same visit, Witkoff praised Putin as a “humanitarian” for releasing an American prisoner held in Russia, drawing sharp criticism from both Republicans and Democrats.
Starlink dispute deepens rift between Kyiv and Washington
The Starlink (Starshield) controversy is just one of the latest strains in diplomatic relations between Ukraine and the US.
Tensions began when Trump announced the controversial diesel deal while the Ukrainian delegation was in Miami with US officials, hoping for a breakthrough in Russia’s war.
Kyiv later said it had been warned that Washington could restrict intelligence sharing if Ukraine kept striking Russian oil refineries. Around the same time, Trump also called for Ukraine to elect a new president, claiming Putin was easier to negotiate with.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Ukrainian military units lost connectivity on terminals moving at roughly 160 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour) or faster, without prior warning. The disruption crippled several types of drones Ukraine uses, including interceptor drones used against Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds.
On Oct. 14, Musk claimed that limits on the military Starshield service were set by the US military, and ultimately the president himself, while Trump denied involvement.
“I don’t know if it was somebody, because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said.
Since then, reports have pointed in both directions. While Reuters reported on Oct. 15 that the order originated inside the White House, The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, Oct. 20 that Musk ordered the restrictions himself.
On Oct. 21, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Musk determines Ukraine’s access to Starlink under a private commercial contract.
The episode has even drawn criticism from within Trump’s own party. Besides Fitzpatrick, Republican Senator Thom Tillis and Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen led nine senators in asking the Pentagon’s inspector general on Oct. 15 to investigate the disruptions.
Following a meeting with Witkoff in Oslo, Norway, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 20 that US intelligence sharing with Ukraine for early warnings of Russian attack is working again, adding that Ukraine could see results within the next 48 hours on Patriot interceptors and Starlink restrictions.

Ben-Gvir calls for Israeli takeover of Gaza, Palestinian emigration in rare foreign media interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:21:15 UTC
02:21:15 KST

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for Israel to occupy the entire Gaza Strip and encourage Palestinians to leave both Gaza and the West Bank, outlining his vision for a larger Israeli state in a rare interview with the American magazine TIME ahead of next week's national elections.
Ben-Gvir, who frequently speaks to Israeli news outlets, gave his first interview with foreign media since taking office in 2022. The leader of the far-right Otzma Yehudit party said Israel must expand its territory to ensure its survival and argued that encouraging Palestinian emigration would strengthen the country rather than deepen its international isolation.
"If Israel wants to continue to live and not be destroyed, we have to capture all of Gaza," Ben-Gvir told TIME. "We have to promote voluntary emigration. Gaza could be a Riviera. It’s a beautiful place. But we can’t have one Hamas member there."
The magazine described Ben-Gvir as a combative far-right figure who was once considered too extreme to serve in the IDF. It said he hopes to emerge from the elections with greater leverage over Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, potentially making another Netanyahu-led government more dependent on far-right parties advocating Palestinian emigration and Israeli sovereignty over Gaza and the West Bank.
"I want Netanyahu to be prime minister. He’s a leader. I prefer him a million times over Eisenkot," Ben-Gvir said, referring to former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu's main political rival.
TIME described Ben-Gvir as wearing a white shirt and white skullcap and speaking in halting English. At one point, the minister reportedly beat his chest while explaining his political ambitions.
"What will really help Netanyahu be right wing is if I, Ben-Gvir, will be a senior minister and it’s a full right-wing government," he said.
'Gaza was always ours'
Ben-Gvir argued that Israel should seek to expand its territory, describing Gaza as historically belonging to the Jewish state.
"Gaza was always ours," he said. "Israel is a tiny country. We have to be wider, broader."
He also portrayed Hamas as a threat extending far beyond Israel.
"Hamas are terrorists who don’t just want to destroy Israel. They want to destroy the whole world," he said.
His proposals would represent a dramatic departure from longstanding international positions on the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which generally envision Gaza and the West Bank as part of a future Palestinian state.
Israel withdrew its soldiers and settlers from Gaza in 2005, though it has continued to control key aspects of the territory's access and borders. Proposals to reestablish Israeli control and facilitate the departure of Palestinians have drawn international criticism, particularly over concerns that displacement under conditions of war and military occupation could amount to forced transfer.
TIME noted that Ben-Gvir offered no clear explanation of which countries would agree to accept large numbers of Palestinians or how their departure could be considered voluntary under the conditions he proposed.
Asked whether removing Palestinians from Gaza would deepen Israel's international isolation, Ben-Gvir rejected the concern.
"I think that the stronger we are, we won’t be isolated," he said. "Israel is isolated when it’s weak. If we help the population leave Gaza, we can be very strong."
Calls for Israeli sovereignty over West Bank
Ben-Gvir extended his proposals to the West Bank, territory Israel captured from Jordan in the 1967 Six-Day War and which Palestinians seek as the core of a future independent state.
He called for disarming Palestinian Authority security forces, accusing them of preparing for attacks against Israel.
"We need to take away the weapons for the Palestinian Authority," he said. "As of now, they are training in Jericho. They’re not training to direct traffic, are they? They want to do another Oct. 7."
The Palestinian Authority exercises limited self-rule in parts of the West Bank under agreements reached with Israel in the 1990s. Its security forces have also engaged in security coordination with Israel, though the relationship has been strained by repeated violence and political disputes.
Ben-Gvir said he would encourage the millions of Palestinians living in the West Bank to leave while pursuing the extension of Israeli sovereignty over the territory.
"We want sovereignty in Judea and Samaria, where we also want voluntary emigration," he said, using the biblical names commonly employed in Israel for the West Bank.
"Just so we understand, we want voluntary emigration—not kicking anyone out. People will choose the option to leave."
The distinction between voluntary departure and forced displacement has become central to international criticism of proposals to relocate Palestinians, particularly when such plans are advanced alongside military operations or restrictions on civilian life.
Ben-Gvir defends Netanyahu over Oct. 7 failures
Ben-Gvir also defended Netanyahu against accusations that the prime minister bears primary responsibility for the security failures preceding Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel.
TIME described the Otzma Yehudit leader as one of the most prominent voices on the Israeli right seeking to shift responsibility for the failures away from Netanyahu and toward the military and intelligence establishment.
"Even if he’s not perfect, and even if he made mistakes, and he indeed made mistakes, what screwed him up on Oct. 7 was our intelligence," Ben-Gvir said.
"The army, the intelligence, the Shin Bet. They are all to blame. Netanyahu is not clear of blame, but there are many people who are more at fault than him."
The Oct. 7 attack, in which Hamas-led terrorists killed about 1,200 people and abducted roughly 250 others, exposed major failures in Israel's military preparedness and intelligence assessments, prompting demands for accountability across the country's political and security leadership.
Ben-Gvir insisted that his support for Netanyahu was not unconditional.
"I’m not backing him; I’m not his crony on everything," he said. "I think he’s much better than Eisenkot. I want to be next to him. I want him to be very strong. I want to pull him to the right."
Defends Jewish prayer at Temple Mount
The interview also addressed Ben-Gvir's policies at Jerusalem's most sensitive religious site, known to Jews as the Temple Mount and to Muslims as the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound.
TIME reported that under Ben-Gvir's tenure, Israeli police have increasingly permitted Jewish worship at the site, describing the policy as a deliberate provocation toward the Arab world and noting condemnations by Jordan and the Palestinian Authority.
The hilltop compound is Judaism's holiest site and Islam's third-holiest. Under the longstanding arrangements governing the site, Muslims are permitted to pray there while non-Muslims may visit under restrictions but are not permitted to worship.
Changes to those arrangements have repeatedly triggered diplomatic disputes and fears of broader violence.
Ben-Gvir defended his approach as a matter of religious equality.
"It used to be an apartheid up there and Jews could not pray," he said. "That could not happen in any normal country. I returned justice to the Temple Mount."
Jordan, which retains a special custodial role over Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem under its peace treaty with Israel, has repeatedly opposed changes to the compound's established arrangements.
Ben-Gvir reflects on Kahanist past
TIME also examined Ben-Gvir's political history, including his longstanding admiration for Rabbi Meir Kahane, the founder of the extremist Kach movement.
Kahane, who advocated the expulsion of Arabs from Israel, was elected to the Knesset in 1984. His party was later barred from Israeli elections because of its racist platform, and Kach was subsequently designated a terrorist organization by Israel.
Ben-Gvir told TIME that he continues to admire Kahane, although he said he no longer supports some of his mentor's most extreme positions.
"I went to his yeshiva. He did a lot of good things. He protected Jews. He was murdered sanctifying God’s name," Ben-Gvir said.
"Not everything that he did do I fully agree with. In the past, I thought we should kick out all the Arabs from the land of Israel. Now I think there can be some."
Ben-Gvir said his acceptance of Arab residents depended on their loyalty to Israel as a Jewish state.
"I accept that there are some Arabs who live here. And I have no problem with part of them. Those who recognize the State of Israel as the Jewish state. Those who are loyal to the Jewish State," he said.
The magazine also revisited Ben-Gvir's association with Baruch Goldstein, an Israeli extremist who killed 29 Muslim worshippers at the Ibrahimi Mosque, also known as the Cave of the Patriarchs, in Hebron in 1994.
According to previous reports cited by TIME, Ben-Gvir and his future wife, Ayala, visited Goldstein's grave on their first date. For years, Ben-Gvir displayed Goldstein's portrait in the living room of his home.
TIME also noted that Ben-Gvir became a lawyer representing settlers and Jewish activists accused of extremist violence and accumulated criminal convictions, including for incitement to racism and supporting a terrorist organization.

Women protest across Poland over stalled abortion law reforms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:18:30 UTC
02:18:30 KST

Since 1993, Poland has allowed abortion only in cases of severe foetal abnormalities, risks to the mother's health or life, or pregnancies resulting from rape or incest.
Thousands of people took to the streets of Warsaw and more than 20 other Polish cities on Thursday to demand abortion rights, marking the sixth anniversary of a near-total abortion ban introduced following a ruling by Poland's highest court.
The demonstrations were held under the slogan "Red card for abortion". Participants carried red cards and banners opposing the current abortion laws, with slogans including "Abortion ban kills women" and "Women's hell continues".
The protests came just days after parliament approved two bills aimed at easing abortion restrictions in the predominantly Catholic country. However, both measures are expected to face a veto from conservative President Karol Nawrocki.
People accuse Prime Minister Donald Tusk's liberal government of failing to deliver on its promise to reform the country's strict abortion laws.
Zofia Marcinek of the Warsaw-based reproductive rights group Abortion Dream Team described the legislation as a series of "token gestures" rather than a genuine attempt at reform, arguing that the government was aware the bills were unlikely to survive a presidential veto.
She accused the government of trying to win back women's support ahead of next year's parliamentary election by appearing to take action on abortion rights.
What the two abortion bills propose
Poland's parliament voted on Tuesday to ease the country's strict abortion laws, which are among the most restrictive in the European Union.
The first bill, proposed by Tusk's Civic Coalition (KO) and the Left, would partially decriminalise abortion and remove criminal penalties for assisting someone in obtaining one, an offence currently punishable by up to three years in prison.
The second bill, introduced by the more conservative coalition partners Poland 2050 and the Polish Peasants' Party (PSL), would overturn the effects of a 2020 Constitutional Tribunal ruling that banned abortion in cases of severe foetal abnormalities.
The first bill passed with 217 votes in favour, 213 against and three abstentions, while the second was approved by 233 votes to 203, with one abstention.
Where the protests took place
Alongside full decriminalisation, protesters are demanding access to legal abortion up to the 12th week of pregnancy, full access to the "morning-after" pill, and action by local authorities to disperse illegal protests held outside hospitals in Warsaw and Gdańsk and the AboTak clinic in Warsaw.
Demonstrations took place in 26 Polish cities as well as in London. Organisers announced another protest for Sunday.

“He states that there are four people in the cell, they smoke, and of course it is like a gas chamber,” she described.
Under the sentence, Ananiev is expected to spend the first four years in prison and the remainder in a high-security penal colony. He was also fined 600,000 rubles ($7362).
Sviatnenko described the 18-year sentence as “mockery of a human being” and stated that his defense team is preparing an appeal. She also called the case against Ananiev and the other defendants fabricated, according to Suspilne Crimea.
Olha Skrypnyk, head of the Crimean Human Rights Group, noted that rights organizations had repeatedly appealed to international institutions and governments, including the OSCE, UN bodies, and the US administration, seeking help securing the release of Ananiev and other civilian detainees held by Russia.
“Volodymyr Ananiev is the oldest among Crimean political prisoners,” Skrypnyk told Suspilne Crimea. “Given his age and health condition, this sentence is simply a sentence for him. In essence, it is death.”
Russia occupied and annexed Crimea in 2014, a move is widely recognized internationally as illegal, turning the peninsula into a heavily militarized territory where dissent, independent media, and pro-Ukrainian activism have been systematically suppressed. Russian authorities have used raids, arbitrary detention, imprisonment, forced disappearances, and laws against the so-called “discrediting” of the Russian military to target activists and residents, with Crimean Tatars among the most heavily persecuted groups.
UNITED24 Media has previously reported how repression has intensified under occupation, with hundreds of criminal cases opened over alleged espionage, treason, terrorism, and sabotage.
Human rights advocates have documented 64 cases involving elderly Crimean political prisoners as of October 2026, including 49 men and 15 women, according to the Crimean Tatar Resource Center.
Ananiev and 71-year-old Halyna Dovhopola are the oldest among them. Dovhopola, a pro-Ukrainian activist from Sevastopol, was detained by Russia in 2019 and later sentenced to 12 years in prison on treason charges.
The sentence comes amid a wider pattern of Russian prosecutions in occupied Crimea involving alleged Ukrainian intelligence ties. Earlier in October, Russian prosecutors sought a combined 152 years in prison for eight Crimeans accused of belonging to a Ukrainian intelligence network, while defendants alleged torture, threats, and coerced testimony.

Russia Hid a Buk-M1 in the Trees—Autumn Gave It Away to Ukrainian Drones
Ukrainian drone operators have struck a Russian Buk-M1 surface-to-air missile system on the Huliaipole axis, where Moscow has been moving additional air defenses forward to counter increasingly active Ukrainian aviation, Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Response Corps of the Air Assault Forces reported on October 22.
The strike was carried out by operators from the 433rd Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Footage released by the corps shows the Russian Buk-M1 being detected and hit after it was positioned in the area to help protect Russian rear positions from Ukrainian airstrikes.
During a subsequent mission, the drone crews also located and struck another camouflaged air-defense target, although the exact type of system has not yet been identified.
Russian forces have been attempting to conceal their air-defense equipment inside tree lines, but Ukrainian troops say the changing season is increasingly working against them as vegetation thins and large military systems become easier to detect from the air.
“The occupiers carefully camouflage their air defenses in forest belts. However, autumn is not working in their favor: the greenery is gradually disappearing, and hiding expensive equipment is becoming increasingly difficult. Coordinated interaction between units under the operational command of the 7th Air Assault Corps and effective intelligence sharing are producing results,” the corps said.
The Buk-M1 is a medium-range air-defense system designed to engage aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles, and other aerial targets. Its deployment on the Huliaipole axis reflects Russia’s effort to strengthen protection of rear areas as Ukrainian aircraft continue striking military targets behind the front.
But moving such systems closer to the battlefield also exposes them to Ukrainian reconnaissance and strike drones—especially as the natural cover Russian crews rely on begins disappearing with the onset of autumn.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces identified and struck a Russian Buk-M3 medium-range surface-to-air missile system valued at approximately $45 million.

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Yangtze River governance shows progress, offers insights for regional cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:08:05 CST
02:08:05 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Along the Yangtze River in Yichang, central China's Hubei Province, steel frames that once supported sand-and-gravel conveyors now hold swings, while a former industrial building has been transformed into an art gallery.
The structures stand in Lighthouse Square, a riverside public space created on the site of a former port, where phosphate ore, sand and gravel were once loaded and unloaded.
Chen Yuanyuan, a local resident who now volunteers to patrol the riverbank, recalls when dust was so thick that residents kept their windows closed. Today, the restored waterfront has become a popular spot for daily walks and environmental education.
Since 2018, Yichang's riverbank restoration project has removed 15 docks, relocated 35 enterprises and 113 households, restored vegetation across 87 hectares and rehabilitated eight kilometers of Yangtze River shoreline.
Along the Yangtze River, shoreline restoration is accompanied by broader efforts to improve water quality, control pollution and restore aquatic habitats across the basin.
FROM LOCAL RESTORATION TO BASIN-WIDE GOVERNANCE
China's efforts to protect the Yangtze River have improved water quality and supported the recovery of native species, although restoring a healthy river ecosystem will require a substantially longer period of time.
The Ministry of Ecology and Environment rated the Yangtze River basin's water quality as excellent in the first quarter of 2026. Across the wider Yangtze River Economic Belt, the proportion of monitored sections meeting Grade I to III water quality standards has risen from 67 percent in 2015 to 96.5 percent.
Habitat restoration has helped create conditions for the recovery of endangered species. In April 2025, researchers recorded natural spawning and successful hatching of Yangtze sturgeon in a restored spawning ground in the Chishui River, a tributary of the upper Yangtze River.
Researchers released 20 adult sturgeon into a restored habitat of about 8,000 square meters, where a natural spawning ground had been created. The species had not reproduced naturally since the early 2000s and was declared extinct in the wild by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2022. The recent successful spawning and hatching mark an important step toward rebuilding a wild population.
In 2018, the southwestern Chinese provinces of Yunnan, Guizhou and Sichuan established a water environment compensation fund for the Chishui River basin, creating the first cross-provincial ecological compensation mechanism in the Yangtze River Economic Belt.
The three provinces jointly contributed 200 million yuan (about 30 million U.S. dollars) under the initial agreement, with compensation allocations linked to water quality at designated monitoring sections. A second-round agreement signed in 2023 increased annual funding to 300 million yuan for the 2021-2025 period.
In the Yunnan section of the Chishui River, water quality at the exit monitoring section had remained at Grade II for five consecutive years as of the end of 2024, while the number of recorded fish species in the section had risen from 36 in early 2020 to 43.
At the basin level, the Yangtze River Protection Law, which took effect in March 2021, provides a legal framework for ecological conservation, pollution control and resource management. Under the river chief system, officials at different levels are responsible for waterway protection, with mechanisms in place to clarify responsibilities across administrative boundaries and coordinate action among upstream and downstream areas.
According to Li Xiaokai, senior water resources management specialist at the World Bank, China's approach to Yangtze River governance features integrated management of the basin as an ecological and economic system, coordination across government levels and sectors, and the integration of ecological protection with economic development.
The World Bank-supported Yangtze River Protection and Ecological Restoration Programs, which cover three provinces in the middle reaches of the river basin, place institutional development at their core, recognizing that sustainable outcomes depend as much on governance systems as on infrastructure investments, said Li.
LESSONS FOR REGIONAL COOPERATION
Despite differences in geography and development contexts, China and many countries across the Asia-Pacific face similar challenges in river governance and ecological protection, Li said. One major challenge is institutional fragmentation.
River basins rarely conform to political boundaries, and responsibilities for water resources, environmental protection, agriculture, energy, transport and land management are often divided among multiple agencies. Decisions made in one sector or jurisdiction can therefore have unintended consequences elsewhere in the basin, said Li.
In the Lancang-Mekong basin, China has provided year-round hydrological information from two upstream stations to the Mekong River Commission (MRC) since November 2020, supporting river monitoring and upstream-downstream coordination on flood and drought risks. The country has proposed further cooperation on urgent notifications, wider data sharing across the basin, and joint work on flood forecasting and drought response to strengthen upstream-downstream coordination in addressing flood and drought risks.
Sun Jingrui, an associate professor at Yunnan University, said the Yangtze River governance experience shows that fish recovery depends on a governance system capable of sustaining the costs of conservation, rather than on fishing restrictions alone.
Fish protection must be treated as both an ecological issue and a matter of food systems and livelihoods, Sun said. Measures to reduce fishing need to be accompanied by alternative sources of income and food, vocational training and social security for affected communities.
This is particularly important in the Lancang-Mekong basin, where fish resources are closely linked to food security and community culture, especially in downstream countries. Differences in countries' enforcement capacity, development priorities and dependence on fisheries mean that a uniform, long-term fishing ban across the entire basin would be difficult to implement, Sun said.
Fish recovery also requires restoring river connectivity and protecting the habitats needed for fish to complete their life cycles. A paper co-authored by Sun found more than 10,000 small river barriers in the lower Mekong, disrupting connectivity along fish migration routes.
Sun suggested introducing seasonal or area-specific fishing restrictions during key migration and breeding periods, prohibiting destructive fishing methods, improving fish passage around barriers and adjusting dam and sluice operations where feasible. Protecting key habitats, including spawning grounds, deep pools and floodplain nursery areas, is another priority, Sun said.
"Truly sustainable conservation must give affected people the means to make the transition with dignity," said Sun. ■

COMESA leaders call for stronger regional integration, intra-African trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:08:03 CST
02:08:03 KST

HARARE, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Regional leaders on Thursday called for stronger integration and increased intra-African trade to boost economic growth at the 25th Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) Heads of State and Government Summit held in Mount Hampden on the outskirts of Zimbabwe's capital, Harare.
Held under the theme of "One Market, One Future: Advancing Inclusive Industrialization, Investment and Regional Integration in COMESA," the summit brought together regional leaders and senior government officials across its 21 member states to discuss trade, investment, industrialization and economic integration.
In his acceptance speech upon taking over as COMESA chairperson, Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa urged the 21-member regional bloc to harness its resources and investment potential to accelerate modernization and industrialization.
"Our common market must enable enterprises to produce at scale, facilitate cross-border movement of factors of production and reach new customers. The future we envision requires every member state to contribute to, and benefit from, our collective progress," said Mnangagwa.
He called for measures to address persistent non-tariff barriers, infrastructure gaps and policy misalignments, urging member states to simplify border procedures, embrace digital trade systems and adopt innovative financing models for long-term infrastructure development.
Mnangagwa underscored the importance of climate change mitigation, environmental sustainability and regional cooperation in strengthening food security, while calling for greater local processing of natural resources to promote sustainable economic development.
"The message to the region is that the natural endowments of Africa must industrialize our economies, create jobs and broad-based empowerment which improves the quality of life for our peoples," said Mnangagwa.
Outgoing COMESA chairperson, Kenyan President William Ruto, said regional integration is essential for the bloc's member states to navigate growing global fragmentation.
"The global order is shifting. Geopolitical tensions are rising. Protectionism is returning. Supply chains are breaking. Competition for critical and strategic resources is intensifying," Ruto said.
In this regard, he urged African countries to increase intra-African trade, build resilient regional value chains, reduce reliance on exporting raw materials and focus on adding value to their resources, adding that COMESA could strengthen Africa's position in global trade by negotiating as a unified market.
On regional stability, he said COMESA should strengthen its capacity to prevent conflict, stressing that peace, security and good governance were essential for achieving prosperity. "Because there is no prosperity without peace, no peace without security and no security without good governance, we continue to strengthen our capacity to prevent conflict," he said.
COMESA is a regional economic community working to promote regional integration through trade, investment and infrastructure development. ■

IOM warns Somalia floods could displace 874,000 people
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:07:53 CST
02:07:53 KST

MOGADISHU, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Imminent flooding could displace nearly 874,000 people in Somalia over the next three months, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) warned Thursday.
Heavy rainfall and rising rivers now threaten communities already struggling with drought and repeated displacement, the UN migration agency said in a statement, urging international support for preparedness and early action.
"There is still time to reduce the impact, but that window is closing. We urgently need funding to help people protect their homes and livelihoods, reach safer ground where necessary, and avoid another cycle of displacement," said Manuel Marques Pereira, chief of mission for IOM in Somalia.
New projections by IOM and the Danish Refugee Council estimate that 874,319 people could be displaced between October and December, with flooding driving 92 percent of that displacement.
The warning comes as Somalia enters its rainy season, which is forecast to bring above-normal rainfall driven by strengthening El Nino conditions.
According to IOM, signs of flooding are already emerging across the country.
The Jubba River at Dollow is approaching flood levels, while the Shabelle River at Jowhar is rising toward the top of its banks.
Heavy rainfall in Baidoa has already damaged homes, forcing families to flee several neighborhoods.
Despite the mounting crisis, IOM said it has secured just 14.4 percent of the 16.62 million dollars needed to respond to the impending El Nino floods.
The severe funding shortfall jeopardizes critical relief efforts aimed at supporting over 517,000 vulnerable people across flood-prone areas of Somalia, it said.
IOM said rising floodwaters threaten to wipe out crops, devastate livelihoods, contaminate water supplies, and cut off access to healthcare and essential services, further deepening crisis levels in communities already battered by successive climate shocks.
According to IOM, while it is working with Somali authorities and local partners to strengthen early warning systems, map evacuation routes, and prepare emergency aid, acute funding shortages are bottlenecking critical response efforts.
"Without immediate resources, plans to build safe relocation sites and deliver emergency shelter, clean water, sanitation, and healthcare remain severely constrained," IOM said.
IOM called for urgent international support to scale up early action before rising floodwaters displace hundreds of thousands more families. ■

WINDHOEK, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has cut its 2026 economic growth forecast to 2.3 percent from 3.1 percent following weaker-than-expected first-half performance, Finance Minister Ericah Shafudah said Thursday.
Presenting the 2026/2027 mid-year budget review in Parliament, Shafudah projected growth of 2.6 percent in 2027, 3.0 percent in 2028 and 3.3 percent in 2029, supported by mining projects, strong uranium and gold prices, and a recovery in consumption as inflation and interest rates ease.

Shafudah said mining revenue remained the main source of weakness, underscoring the need to diversify the economy through agriculture, downstream value addition, services and renewable energy.
Public debt is projected to reach 201.7 billion Namibian dollars, or 68.7 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), in 2026/2027. Interest payments are forecast at 15.4 billion Namibian dollars, equivalent to 17.5 percent of revenue, while the budget deficit is projected at 5.5 percent of GDP.
Furthermore, the government also plans to allocate 179 million Namibian dollars to contain and manage the foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, she noted
Namibia's economy grew by 1.7 percent in 2025, down from 3.8 percent in 2024. The International Monetary Fund has urged the country to accelerate structural reforms to support private-sector-led growth and address persistent unemployment, poverty and inequality. ■

UN chief calls for efforts to stop expanding conflicts
China
Unknown Publisher

01:07:33 CST
02:07:33 KST

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres speaks during a press encounter at the UN headquarters in New York, Oct. 22, 2026. Guterres called Thursday for an end to widening conflicts and stronger protection for civilians, warning that wars are spreading their economic consequences far beyond the battlefield. (Xinhua/Shang Xuqian)
UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- United Nations (UN) Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called Thursday for an end to widening conflicts and stronger protection for civilians, warning that wars are spreading their economic consequences far beyond the battlefield.
"Today, conflicts are not only intensifying. They are expanding," Guterres told reporters. "In climate, we know El Nino as a disturbance in one part of the planet that disrupts weather patterns and upends lives thousands of kilometers away. We are now witnessing an El Nino of war."
Conflicts are fueling one another, with consequences spreading farther and faster, he warned.
Guterres said attacks against civilians and civilian objects are prohibited under international law and must stop. But the effects of war extend beyond battle zones, disrupting energy markets, shipping lanes, supply chains and financial systems.
He warned that these shocks were hitting an already deeply unequal world, where some people could absorb higher prices while others had to choose between food and heating, and where poorer countries faced difficult choices between servicing debt and investing in health and education.
Guterres called for an end to fighting, including in the Middle East, and urged respect for international law, civilian protection and freedom of navigation, while giving diplomacy room to succeed.
Speaking ahead of a planned visit to Egypt on Friday, Guterres reiterated his call for peace.
"We need to stop the widening of war, protect civilians and create the political space for diplomacy and peace," he said. "People everywhere want security. They want dignity. They want governments and international institutions to deliver." ■

Roundup: Ebola spread raises regional alarm in Africa, urging coordination
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:07:17 CST
02:07:17 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Africa is facing "a more complex outbreak landscape" as Ebola spreads across borders and persistent surveillance gaps cast doubt on whether recent signs of a slowdown can be sustained.
Despite a temporary decline in transmission in some affected areas, gaps in contact tracing and delays in diagnosis have heightened concerns that undetected infections could fuel further spread, elevating the ongoing Ebola outbreak to a regional public health threat.
As the outbreak widens, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) are calling for stronger regional coordination to contain transmission and prevent further cross-border spread.
CROSS-BORDER SPREAD RAISES ALARM
Africa CDC data shows five countries, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria and France, have reported Ebola cases linked to the current outbreak since May.
"Ebola does not wait. It follows movement, exploits gaps, and tests the strength of our health systems," WHO Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi said Thursday during an online press briefing.
"Today, the test is no longer confined to one place... We are facing a more complex outbreak landscape," Janabi said, calling for stronger regional vigilance and collective action.
The DRC remains the epicenter, accounting for 9,704 confirmed cases, including 4,687 deaths as of Tuesday, with a case fatality rate of 48.3 percent, according to a situation report released Wednesday by the DRC health authorities. The outbreak has affected eight of the country's 26 provinces and 66 health zones.
Beyond the DRC, Kenya has confirmed nine cases, including one death, while Nigeria reported its first imported case on Tuesday.
All eight secondary cases in Kenya had been detected among previously identified contacts who were already under quarantine, suggesting that the known transmission chains remained traceable, said Wessam Mankoula, head of the Continental Incident Management Support Team for the Ebola response at Africa CDC, at an online press briefing Thursday.
Kenya has identified 135 contacts, with 118 currently in quarantine, Mankoula said.
In Nigeria, the confirmed patient, a woman who arrived from Uganda on Oct. 3, developed symptoms four days later but was not diagnosed with Ebola until Oct. 20.
The WHO's latest regional situation report released Tuesday showed that the prolonged interval between symptom onset and confirmation raises concerns about possible undetected exposures and secondary transmission, requiring urgent retrospective investigation and intensified surveillance.
Mankoula said the source of the patient's infection remained unknown, with Nigerian and Ugandan authorities conducting joint investigations into her travel and exposure history.
On Tuesday evening, following Nigeria's confirmation of its first Ebola case, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya warned that the outbreak had become the most geographically widespread Ebola epidemic on record, with infections reported across Central, Eastern and Western Africa.
FRAGILE SLOWDOWN MASKS PERSISTENT TRANSMISSION
Despite recent signs of easing transmission in some affected areas in the DRC, health authorities warned that the outbreak remained far from under control.
The WHO's latest regional report showed that Ebola infections in the DRC have rebounded after a brief decline.
"The most recent seven-day moving average indicates a modest upward trend, suggesting renewed intensification of transmission," the WHO Regional Office for Africa said in the report, highlighting the outbreak's "widening international dimension and the growing complexity."
Beyond the fluctuating case numbers, health authorities identified persistent weaknesses in early detection, contact tracing and access to treatment as major obstacles to controlling the outbreak.
Africa CDC data showed only about 12 percent of confirmed cases in the DRC have been identified among previously known contacts, meaning that nearly nine in ten infections are being detected outside established contact-tracing networks.
"This means there are ongoing chains of transmission that we are not detecting," Mankoula warned.
Africa CDC announced Wednesday that it would convene an extraordinary virtual meeting of African health ministers on Oct. 28 to coordinate efforts against the escalating outbreak.
The epidemic was declared in the DRC on May 15 and designated a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO two days later. The Africa CDC subsequently declared it a public health emergency of continental security.
The current Ebola outbreak has become the largest and deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

The constant need for repairs is driving costs to levels that cannot be sustained in the long run, the outlet’s sources said. As a result, they said, some plants have deliberately slowed repairs, stretching work that would normally take a few days into weeks.

Cast and cane behind bars.

Photo: alexander.kynev / Instagram
The Moscow City Court has rejected an appeal against the arrest of political scientist Alexander Kynev, who faces large-scale drug distribution charges. Kynev, who was severely beaten during his detention, appeared at the hearing by video link with his leg still in a cast, Mediazona can report from the courtroom. He will remain in custody until at least November 24.
Kynev, 51, is a leading expert on Russian regional politics and elections and the author of the 2025 book “Who Governs Russia’s Regions and How”. The Justice Ministry designated him a “foreign agent” in February 2026; despite that, he chose to stay in Russia and provided coverage of the Duma electoral campaign.
Moscow’s Perovsky District Court sent him to pre-trial detention on September 25, just two days after he posted a summary of his four-month monitoring of the State Duma elections. The charge carries 10 to 20 years in prison. He denies the charges, but further details of the case remain unknown.
Days after the arrest, the human rights project Slovo Zashchite reported that Kynev had been diagnosed with two tibia fractures, citing a source in the prison service’s medical unit who described the injuries as “the result of torture.”
At the appeal hearing, Kynev told the court he could hardly move. To reach the room where the video link was set up, he said, he had to climb stairs over and over across a cold floor, his leg “effectively in a cast.”
His lawyer Vera Goncharova called his continued detention “inhumane.” “If Kynev does not receive medical care soon, he will be left disabled,” she said, adding that the injuries were sustained during the arrest and that complaints had been filed. A discharge summary submitted by the defence shows that Kynev was treated in a surgical ward for a closed fracture from September 25 to October 8. He was discharged in “satisfactory condition,” walking on his own “with the support of a cane.”
The judge questioned Kynev about how he came to be injured. He said he was detained in his apartment by officers who did not identify themselves. “I felt fear and shock, not understanding who had come for me,” he said. “They threw me to the floor. I remember the rest very poorly.” Asked whether he had done anything before that, Kynev said he had not. “Just stood there? And they took you and threw you down? Your position is clear,” the judge replied.
Another defence lawyer, Arseny Levinson, said Kynev had not resisted (prompting a quick rebuttal from the judge: “And you were there?”) and that the delay in treating him risked “irreparable harm” to his health. Levinson also told the court that Kynev’s foreign travel passports had been seized during a search, though this is not reflected in the case file. The defence noted that Kynev has no criminal record, owns an apartment in Moscow and has no property abroad, and asked for a non-custodial measure.
The prosecutor called the original ruling lawful. After a brief recess, judge Natalya Nikishina left the arrest in place.
On October 14, Kynev was transferred from the hospital wing of “Matrosskaya Tishina” to Moscow’s SIZO-4, “Medved.” In a letter shared by journalist Gleb Yarovoy, Kynev wrote that he would remain in a cast for about three more weeks but could not really walk because he had no crutches. Rights advocates have documented beatings, extortion and inadequate medical care at the “Medved” facility for years.

'The future of Hungarian Jewry’: Budapest opens synagogue run entirely by teens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:02:08 UTC
02:02:08 KST

In a Budapest synagogue that has stood for more than 150 years, the next generation is now taking the lead. The Hungarian capital’s Jewish community has reopened the historic Wagon Drivers’ Synagogue as a space exclusively for teenagers, in what may be the world’s first teen-run synagogue.
Established in 1870, the building served as the central synagogue for the Orthodox community following the Communist era, until its closure in 2014. It has now reopened after extensive refurbishment and is designated exclusively for teens up to the age of 18.
The officer holders, board leaders, and event organizers are all local teens. The “oldest” regular worshiper at the sanctuary is youth community emissary Rabbi Tzami Bassman, an American-born and extremely jovial rabbi and Chabad emissary in his early 30s.
It will be operated moving forward by the C-Teen youth organization, with full funding and logistical support from the Association of Hungarian Jewish Communities (EMIH).
The Jerusalem Post visited the synagogue on Monday in Budapest. The inside of the building is beautifully decorated and still smells of fresh paint.
Rabbi Bassman took time out from helping a 12-year-old boy with his bar-mitzvah preparation to speak with the Post.
Opening ceremony drew 200 teens
At the opening ceremony, just before Rosh Hashanah, there were 200 teens present, he said.
“It was really, really incredible. We had a teen blow the shofar, a teen carrying the Torah, and teens cutting the ribbon. It was special and moving.”
During the ceremony, President of the Budapest Orthodox Rabbinate Rabbi Baruch Oberlander highlighted that it is critical for young people to be active leaders and decision-makers, not merely passive participants in communal life.
“These young people represent the future of Hungarian Jewry,” he said. “It is deeply moving to see that they are not satisfied merely learning and participating, but are eager to assume active responsibility for shaping Jewish life.”
Just two weeks after the opening, Bassman said there was a minyan of teens for Kol Nidrei. They also constructed a sukkah in the courtyard.
Now, every Thursday night, the synagogue hosts a learning program comprising 70 to 80 teens, Bassman said. It also includes Hebrew, Hungarian, and Russian classes, the latter because many members of the Budapest community are those who fled Ukraine during the war.
On Friday nights, Bassman said, they can expect between 30 and 50 teens.
The demographic is wide, he added, although the teens are “primarily not religious.”
“Some teens are familiar with davening [“praying”] and things like that, but primarily these are teens that come from non-religious families.” Many do not attend one of the Jewish schools in the city.
Several of the teens and their parents learned about the synagogue from social media – where Bassman and his wife are active – or met Bassman on one of his Chabad-mobile visits to the local stores.
Eventually, he said, there will be a kitchen and a lounge area with couches and games.
Bassman is most looking forward to growing Friday night Shabbats, which have only just started.
“I’m looking forward to growing them and making them really, really special,” he told the Post. “We’re really just at the beginning, and we have lots of ideas, lots of plans. With God’s help, it will be amazing.”

====================================================================================================

The West Bank must not hold Israel’s European security ties hostage - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:01:47 UTC
02:01:47 KST

Israel supplies the postcodes the EU uses to deny settlement goods preferential tariffs.
Under a 2004 technical arrangement, Israeli origin certificates identify production sites, distinguishing settlement goods from exports made in Israel without either side conceding sovereignty.
Israel has not annexed the West Bank as a whole. The Supreme Court holds that territory under military administration lies outside the state, with commanders deriving authority from the law of belligerent occupation, not sovereignty.
Pre-1967 local law and military orders govern; even settlement councils derive authority from orders incorporating Israeli municipal law.
Israeli legislation does not apply automatically: the Knesset renewed regulations in 2023 that apply specified laws to Israeli residents personally, not territorially.
The Central Bureau of Statistics counts West Bank Israelis in the national population but classifies Judea and Samaria separately from Israel’s six districts.
Under Oslo, Israel transferred defined civil and policing powers in Areas A and B to the Palestinian Authority, retained specified security responsibilities, and reserved borders and settlements for final-status negotiations.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal court, identified duties in its 2024 advisory opinion to distinguish dealings with Israel from those involving the West Bank, east Jerusalem, and Gaza and withhold assistance sustaining what it deemed an unlawful Israeli presence there.
It imposed no blanket ban on defense procurement from sovereign Israel. Tariff preferences, settlement-import bans, and defense-supplier exclusions require distinct legal bases.
Ireland instructed its defense ministry not to buy Israeli military equipment; its tender rules allow it to reject Israeli and other third-country bids on defense and security grounds.
Germany’s Israeli Arrow 3 achieved initial operational capability, enabling ballistic-missile interception beyond the atmosphere. These are national choices, not an EU arms embargo.
Europe was Israel’s largest regional defense market in 2025, accounting for 36% of a record $19.2 billion in signed export agreements. Those contracts sustain research, industrial capacity, and the IDF’s force buildup.
Europe needs Israeli defense capabilities; Israel needs European technology, components, and industrial capacity.
By October 2026, British and Canadian arms manufacturers had asked Israeli firms to identify production sites, raw materials, and subcontractors beyond the Green Line, the pre-1967 armistice line.
A settlement-made component does not determine the origin or legality of a system assembled in sovereign Israel, but can trigger contractual or regulatory scrutiny. Prime contractors, financiers, and insurers may exclude suppliers rather than verify compliance.
A seal costing a few hundred dollars can jeopardize a multimillion-dollar defense contract; replacing it in a missile, aircraft, or communications system may require months of requalification, disrupting Israeli production and delaying deliveries to European forces.
Under the US military-aid agreement, spending American assistance on Israeli production is being phased out by 2028, steering orders towards US plants and risking Israeli jobs and wartime industrial capacity. That is a strategic mistake.
Settlement-origin exposure calls for the reverse: move production into sovereign Israel or qualify alternative suppliers without sacrificing domestic capacity.
Israel’s security is the objective; a supplier’s location is a means. If relocation preserves military capability, expertise, wartime capacity, IDF supply, and operational freedom, it is a supply-chain decision.
Restrictions on equipment that may be used in Gaza are different: export controls govern supply; the laws of war govern use. Israel must obey those laws, but cannot submit its lawful defense to foreign approval or sacrifice essential capabilities for a contract.
Keeping production in the West Bank, despite a viable alternative, is a political choice the government may make, but must own its cost, not disguise it as military necessity.
Defending Israel's sovereignty
Beyond procurement, Israel’s 2021 Horizon Europe research agreement excludes territories brought under Israeli administration after June 5, 1967, without prejudicing its position on their status.
The EU’s 2011 data-adequacy decision, retained after its 2024 review, permits certain civilian personal-data transfers but recognizes only Israel as defined under international law.
Both exclude east Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, where Israel has applied its law. The adequacy decision does not authorize operational police-data exchanges.
Europol, the EU’s law-enforcement agency, has a 2018 arrangement with Israel permitting strategic exchanges and liaison, not routine transfers of suspects’ personal data or investigative records.
A draft initialed in September 2022 covered terrorism, organized crime, and cybercrime, but excluded use of European information in territories brought under Israeli control in 1967, subject to exceptions for imminent threats to life and criminal investigations.
The Council Legal Service, the EU Council’s legal advisers, objected to those exceptions under EU and international law, citing Palestinian self-determination and policing powers transferred under Oslo.
Israeli intelligence protects Europe against threats unrelated to Israel or Jewish communities. In 2018, an Israeli diplomat confirmed that the Mossad, Israel’s foreign intelligence agency, helped Denmark thwart an Iranian plot to assassinate a dissident.
Israeli reports also credited the agency with helping French, Belgian, and German authorities foil a bombing at an Iranian opposition rally near Paris, and linked its warning to Danish raids against suspected jihadist cells in 2019.
In November 2025, Austrian investigators seized five handguns and 10 magazines from storage in Vienna, allegedly intended for attacks on Jewish and Israeli institutions.
The following month, Italian authorities uncovered an alleged €7 million Hamas-financing scheme involving charities.
Israeli intelligence aided the Italian investigation, which was coordinated with Dutch authorities through Eurojust, the EU agency supporting cross-border prosecutions.
These operations relied on national, case-specific channels, not routine EU-Israel data transfers. Eurojust agreements permit systematic exchanges of case information and evidence, as well as the appointment of liaison prosecutors.
A warning can cross a border. A prosecution needs a lawful chain of evidence.
The European Commission proposed talks in 2020 subject to territorial exclusion; the Council authorized them in 2021. By September 2026, the EU had signed agreements with Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Lebanon, but not Israel.
National channels may warn of imminent threats from the West Bank; a Europol agreement cannot automatically authorize using EU-origin personal data there. Any lawful emergency procedure must be agreed beforehand.
The EU and Israel should conclude separate Europol and Eurojust agreements, backed by one Israeli law binding every recipient of European personal data, including security agencies and onward recipients, to agreed territorial, purpose, retention, and onward-transfer restrictions under independent oversight.
Both must comply with EU and international law, including fundamental-rights and data-protection safeguards. Exceptions require mutual consent and prior authorization where applicable; emergency procedures, if lawful, need independent oversight and auditing.
Israeli law alone cannot resolve EU legal objections. Israel retains its final-status positions and lawful powers over independently obtained intelligence.
To distinguish the West Bank from sovereign Israel is to defend Israel’s sovereignty, not condemn it.
Secure, negotiated borders are an Israeli strategic interest: they establish jurisdiction, delimit security responsibilities, and anchor enduring partnerships.
The writer is founder & principal of Line of State, an international strategic practice for strategic affairs, government relations, and public power. He previously served as vice president of external relations at Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and as chief of staff to its chairman.
