UN expert urges Indonesia to reconsider involvement in Trump's Gaza board

Breadcrumb
UN expert urges Indonesia to reconsider involvement in Trump's Gaza board
Indonesia should reconsider its involvement in US President Donald Trump's Gaza peace plan because it is being shaped by Israel and the US and lacks a Palestinian voice, the United Nations special rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories told Reuters on Thursday.
The "Board of Peace," of which Indonesia is a key troop-contributing member, was unveiled by Trump in January to address global conflicts typically handled by the United Nations. The world's largest Muslim-majority nation has also pledged troops to be deployed to Gaza as part of an international stabilisation force.
Francesca Albanese, a prominent human rights lawyer known for her vocal criticism of Israel, said in an interview in Jakarta that Indonesia has historically supported the Palestinian cause, but joining the board was dangerous.
Indonesia's Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that Board of Peace discussions remained on hold, reiterating its earlier position.
Albanese has drawn the ire of a number of Western capitals. The US has imposed sanctions on her, and others, including her own native Italy, have called for her resignation.
"I understand (Indonesia's) good intentions. I still think that it's very dangerous, because it risks to normalise a very abnormal mechanism," she said.
Albanese said that, legally, Israel could not have a role in determining the future of Palestinians.
Rights experts have criticised the board for not including a Palestinian representative even though it is meant to supervise the temporary governance of a Palestinian territory.
The Board of Peace did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside US business hours.
Indonesia, which backs a two-state solution and has repeatedly condemned Israeli violence, has drawn criticism from domestic Muslim groups for agreeing to join the board, which also counts Israel as a member.
President Prabowo Subianto has vowed to quit if it does not bring benefits to Palestinians, his office has previously said, adding that joining the board would allow Indonesia to push for cessation of violence.
Albanese said Indonesia risked compromising its close ties with Palestinians. "It's very risky to do so when the rules are set by Israel," she said.
Albanese recommended Jakarta join the Hague Group of countries, which includes South Africa and Indonesia's neighbour Malaysia and seeks to uphold international law and processes, including in the International Criminal Court over Israel's actions.
Trump's Gaza plan has stalled. A 2025 ceasefire secured the release of the remaining captives held by Hamas and hundreds of Palestinian detainees, but efforts to disarm Hamas and secure an Israeli withdrawal have faltered, while Israeli forces continue near-daily attacks in Gaza.

Ukraine Destroys Elusive North Korean Koksan Supergun in Operation Vivaldi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:20:20 UTC
01:20:20 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Destroys Elusive North Korean Koksan Supergun in Operation Vivaldi
Ukrainian drone operators from the 3rd Army Corps destroyed a North Korean-made Koksan self-propelled artillery system in the Donetsk region during Operation Vivaldi, according to footage released by Ukraine’s 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade on October 22.
The strike was carried out by operators from the brigade’s Fatum unit, which published a new compilation showing attacks on Russian equipment and personnel.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Hellish autumn notes of ‘Vivaldi.’ Operators of Fatum from the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade burned a North Korean Koksan self-propelled gun, as well as several vehicles. In addition, quad bikes and buggies were destroyed, along with enemy infantry moving on them. The pilots of the Troika continue to erase the enemy,” the brigade said.
The Koksan is North Korea’s longest-range conventional tube-artillery system and one of the most unusual weapons Pyongyang has supplied to Russia. Western intelligence first identified the system in 1979 near the North Korean city of Koksan, which later gave the artillery piece its commonly used Western name.
The original M1978 Koksan can reportedly strike targets at ranges of up to roughly 40 kilometers with standard ammunition and as far as 60 kilometers with rocket-assisted shells. Its rate of fire is relatively slow at around one to two rounds every five minutes, but its long reach allows it to operate well behind the immediate front line.
The weapon’s gun is mounted in an open configuration, providing little protection for its estimated four-to-six-person crew.
The earlier model also requires a separate vehicle to carry ammunition because of the size of the weapon and its shells, while the later M1989 variant can carry around 12 rounds onboard.
The Koksan has combat history dating back decades. North Korea supplied the system to Iran, where it was used during the Iran-Iraq War and gained a reputation as an effective long-range counter-battery weapon.
Earlier, Ukrainian drone operators destroyed four North Korean–made M1989 Koksan self-propelled artillery systems deployed by Russian forces.
The mission was carried out by the 412th Nemesis Regiment, which used both bomber drones and FPV drones to strike the weapons.

23 US Lawmakers Urge Trump to Unlock Starlink for Ukraine to Target Russian Missile Launchers
Twenty-three members of the US House of Representatives, including 16 Democrats and seven Republicans, urged President Donald Trump on October 21 to help Ukraine gain access to Starlink inside Russia to locate and target Russian missile launchers.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
This was reported by The Hill on the same day, citing a bipartisan letter sent to Trump and obtained exclusively by the outlet. The lawmakers called on the president to persuade SpaceX owner Elon Musk to lift restrictions preventing Ukraine from using Starlink to locate missile launch systems on Russian territory.
“If Ukraine cannot reliably intercept Russian ‘arrows,’ it must be able to shoot the ‘archer,’” the lawmakers wrote in their appeal to Trump.
The signatories argued that expanding Ukraine's access to Starlink would help protect civilians from Russian missile attacks while increasing pressure on the Russian leader Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the war.
The seven Republican signatories included Representatives Joe Wilson of South Carolina, Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania, Don Bacon of Nebraska, Max Miller of Ohio, Carlos Gimenez of Florida, Jeff Hurd of Colorado, and Andy Harris of Maryland.
Sixteen Democratic lawmakers also endorsed the request, demonstrating bipartisan support for expanding Ukraine's ability to strike Russian missile launch infrastructure.
The lawmakers emphasized that Ukrainian authorities had already approached Musk about securing an exception to existing restrictions. They argued that Trump's direct intervention could resolve the issue and enable Ukrainian forces to use the satellite network against launch sites inside Russia.
The initiative also reinforces efforts by Republican Senator Roger Wicker, chair of the Senate Armed Services Committee, who led a congressional delegation to Ukraine the previous week. Republican Representative Dan Crenshaw, who participated in the visit, separately advocated expanding Ukrainian access to Musk's satellite network.
Earlier, Ukraine has faced new restrictions on Starshield, SpaceX’s military-grade satellite service. On October 14, Ukrainian forces were forced to cancel drone missions after moving terminals began losing connectivity, with some aircraft experiencing outages at speeds of around 110–120 km/h.

The Netherlands has temporarily closed its embassy building in Egypt’s capital Cairo to the public amid demonstrations outside the premises, the mission said on Thursday.

“As a precautionary measure, the Netherlands Embassy building in Cairo is closed to the public until further notice,” it said.

The discussions followed the circulation of videos on social media showing an Egyptian national holding signs criticizing Egyptian authorities in the presence of Dutch police officers.
During the call, Abdelatty also requested clarification regarding the detention of an Egyptian citizen in the Netherlands and called for his prompt release.

13 far-right militants' convictions upheld for Fascist salutes at Ramelli march
Court of Cassation rejects appeals, four-month sentences confirmed
ROME,
22 October 2026, 18:18
ANSA English Desk
Share
Link copiato
- ALL RIGHTS RESERVED
The supreme Court of Cassation on Thursday rejected the appeals and finalized four-month suspended prison sentences for 13 far-right militants who performed Fascist salutes during an annual march in Milan on April 29, 2018 commemorating Sergio Ramelli, an 18-year-old member of the neofascist youth group Fronte della Gioventù (Youth Front) who was killed by the far-left group Avanguardia Operaia in 1975. Ramelli was brutally attacked with iron bars and wrenches in March 1975 and died 47 days later. His case remains a prominent event from Italy's Anni di Piombo (Years of Lead) of rightist and leftist terrorism. The defendants were charged with engaging in a fascist demonstration, in violation of Article 5 of the Scelba Law banning the reconstitution of Mussolini's Fascist Party.
There have been contradictory rulings on Fascist salutes in Italy in recent years with them often going unpunished if adjudged merely commemorative.

Poland paired with County Donegal for Ireland's EU presidency
Poland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:17:10 CEST
01:17:10 KST

Poland paired with County Donegal for Ireland's EU presidency
As part of the County Pairings Programme, which matched each of Ireland's 26 counties with an EU member state, the north-western County Donegal, a home to just over 161,000 people, was paired with Poland until the end of December.
Thanks to the initiative of the Irish authorities and the efforts of the Polish Embassy in Dublin, the pairing has helped raise awareness in Ireland of Pawel Strzelecki, a largely forgotten Polish hero of the Great Irish Famine. The unveiling of a commemorative plaque at a school in Donegal brought the achievements of the Polish explorer, geographer and philanthropist to the attention of local residents for the first time in 178 years.
In Poland, Strzelecki is best known for naming Australia's highest mountain Mount Kosciuszko in 1840, in honour of the Polish national hero Tadeusz Kosciuszko, whom he admired throughout his life. Strzelecki was the first Pole to undertake a scientific expedition around the world, travelling through both the Americas, the Pacific region, Australia and Tasmania. He also played a remarkable role in Irish history.
During the Great Irish Famine, Strzelecki worked on the island as a volunteer for a British humanitarian organisation. By introducing an innovative food distribution system centred on schools, he helped save the lives of as many as 200,000 children, both Catholic and Protestant.
The Polish explorer and philanthropist visited famine-stricken Ireland twice, working without pay out of a deep sense of compassion and duty. His efforts focused on three counties: Donegal, Mayo and Sligo.
Remembering Strzelecki sheds light on a different chapter in Ireland's history, highlighting the compassion and dedication of a Polish volunteer who devoted himself to helping Irish families through one of the darkest periods in the country's past. His legacy stands as a powerful testament to the solidarity that can transcend national, religious and political divides. (PAP)

The army’s 4th Infantry Division said in a statement that its forces had recaptured the Bakouri and Akleili areas following military operations that inflicted heavy losses in personnel and equipment on opposing forces.
The division said its troops were continuing operations to pursue rival forces, secure the two areas and consolidate control.

In a separate statement, Sudanese army spokesman Asim Awad said air defenses had shot down a “hostile strategic drone” near Bakouri on Thursday morning.
Awad said the military had tracked the aircraft since it crossed into Sudan from Ethiopia, without identifying the party operating it.
On Monday and Tuesday, the army announced that it had repelled attacks by the RSF and allied SPLM-N forces on the Al-Baraka and Sali areas in Blue Nile state.
The state has witnessed escalating clashes in recent weeks between the army and the allied forces.
Sudan has been engulfed in fighting between the army and the RSF since April 2023 over disagreements concerning the integration of the paramilitary group into the military. MEPs call for Yemen's Houthis to be added to EU terrorist list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:16:04 UTC
01:16:04 KST

A non-binding European Parliament resolution urges a freeze on all the Yemeni group's funds, as the EU struggles to counter the threat to civilian maritime traffic in the Red Sea.
The European Parliament on Thursday approved a resolution calling for Yemen's Houthis to be added to the EU’s list of terrorist organisations.
The call follows an escalation in recent weeks of attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Iran-backed group, which prompted the UK to pledge defensive missions to protect Riyadh, while the EU struggles to increase its naval presence in the Red Sea to shield commercial vessels from possible attacks.
The non-binding text, adopted by a large majority of MEPs in a show of hands, urged the freezing of all funds and economic resources belonging to the Houthis and their facilitators.
Inclusion on the EU terrorist list mainly entails financial restrictions — freezing all bank accounts and property held in EU countries, and banning EU individuals and companies from financing the listed group.
The final decision rests with the EU member states, which must approve any new listing unanimously.
The European Parliament justified its request by condemning the Houthi naval blockade of Saudi Arabia and their attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial shipping in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb strait, which are severely disrupting maritime traffic and driving up energy prices in the region.
The resolution describes the attacks as flagrant violations of international law, stressing that many Yemeni civilians have been killed and displaced, and that the country’s humanitarian crisis has deepened since the latest attacks.
The group formally known as Ansar Allah, which has been at war with the internationally recognised government of Yemen since 2014, launched a blitz offensive along the Red Sea coast in July to take control of the vital waterway crucial to the world's energy and cargo shipping.
A counteroffensive by the Saudi-led coalition saw much of the gains made by the Houthis reversed, but the group still poses a threat to international vessels traversing the strait that links Europe and Asia.
The Houthis have pledged safe passage to all ships bar those linked to Saudi Arabia, while continuing their attacks against energy infrastructure and airports across the neighbouring kingdom.
MEPs also stressed the crucial role of Aspides, the EU naval mission in the Red Sea, and urged member states to provide additional naval and air assets.
The mission currently has three ships from Italy and Greece, with two more pledged by Belgium and the Netherlands. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has said at least 10 are needed.

More than 100 countries have banned the use of cluster bombs under the Convention on Cluster Munitions, an international treaty that was adopted in 2008. The munitions spread smaller "bomblets" over a wide area that can hit civilian locations indiscriminately.
Russia, like the United States, did not sign on to the treaty.
Russia's Defense Ministry said, meanwhile, that air defenses downed 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, and that two people were reported injured, The Associated Press reported. More than 600 drones were fired toward Moscow between late Wednesday and early Thursday, according to Mayor Sergei Sobyanin.
The developments came after Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was quoted by Russian news agencies as saying Moscow would study proposals on the Ukraine war brought to St. Petersburg by Witkoff, but that the talks would take a long time.
"Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack," Zelenskyy said. "This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening."
Twelve regions came under attack from Russia overnight, according to Zelenskyy, who said one attack hit Pechersk, Kyiv's historic center, and damaged monastery buildings, homes, shops, cafés and other civilian infrastructure.

Aerial attacks in Sudan have led to an increase in civilian casualties in recent weeks, with hundreds of people reportedly killed in strikes believed to have largely involved armed drones, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said Thursday.

It also underlined that attacks that fail to distinguish between targets or cause excessive civilian harm are prohibited, while all practicable measures must be taken to protect civilians.
The ICRC said hospitals receiving its assistance treated more than 2,700 patients with weapon-related injuries during the first half of 2026.
It urged all parties to consider the potential consequences for civilians when deploying armed drones, particularly in populated areas.

01:13:00 KST

BRUSSELS, Belgium — Restrictions against Russian refineries and oil export terminals loom large in a new set of EU draft sanctions listings, first presented to EU ambassadors on Oct. 21 and seen by the Kyiv Independent.
The EU's diplomatic arm, the EEAS, "proposed 117 additional listings targeting sectors which raise revenue for Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, such as the financial sector, energy sector, and the Russian shadow fleet," an Irish Council Presidency spokesperson told journalists.
The draft document lists 12 individuals and 105 entities, which, if adopted, would subject them to a transaction ban with the EU and a freeze on any assets they hold in the bloc. Being a sanctioned entity can also make it hard to do business with companies in third countries, which don't want to risk their own commercial ties with the EU.
A key focus of the latest proposed sanctions listings is Russia's oil processing, refining, and exporting capacity, with 31 listings spanning the breadth of Russia, from St. Petersburg to Sakhalin.
The EEAS' proposal of those listings is especially timely, coming barely two weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump agreed to import diesel — itself a refined oil product — from Russia.
That deal, and the U.S.' wider attitude change to Ukraine, led to widespread condemnation from EU leaders when they met in Brussels on Oct. 15-16.
"We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender," said the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas, who oversees the bloc's sanctions.
The other listings included 52 banking and financial institutions, two entities that process Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), and a steel company operating from Russian-occupied territory in Donetsk Oblast.
The EU has also sanctioned entities in several third countries that have been helping Moscow evade sanctions, 12 in the United Arab Emirates alone, and other listings for companies based in Oman, Singapore, Hong Kong, and the Seychelles.
Also likely to be of interest are some of the 12 individuals sanctioned by the EU, which have ties to e-commerce platforms Ozon and Wildberries, which have been trading in products that help Russia's military effort, as well as Moscow's internet search engine Yandex.
All three companies have been targets of successful Ukrainian military strikes.
Finally, the EU is preparing to apply sanctions to a further 15 companies belonging to Russia's military-industrial complex, and to remove one entity in a third country because "the entity has ceased the activity which led to its inclusion in the list and has committed to refrain from any such activity in the future," reads the EU's draft legal text.
The next step is for the listings to be scrutinized by sanctions experts appointed by the 27 EU countries. After that, the list returns to ambassadors for approval, and then to ministers for a final vote.

Voters prioritize costs and Iran over investigating Trump for next Congress, AP-NORC poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:12:14 UTC
01:12:14 KST

Breadcrumb
Voters prioritise costs, Iran over investigating Trump for next Congress, poll finds
Regardless of the outcome of the 3 November election, a new AP-NORC poll shows voters from both major political parties want the next Congress to focus on making life more affordable and ending the war in Iran, while fewer are looking for an emphasis on President Donald Trump — whether it's investigating him or supporting his agenda.
The results suggest that voters are ready for Congress to tackle core issues, despite Trump’s centrality in the midterm campaign.
About 8 in 10 registered voters, including a large majority of Republicans and Democrats, say lowering the cost of living should be one of the highest priorities for the session coming up, the survey from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research finds.
Justin Campbell, a 31-year-old Democrat from Brookhaven, Mississippi, said he wants the government to focus on helping people like him rather than wealthy people.
“I’m not a millionaire and probably won’t ever be," he said. "I prefer policy that helps me instead of someone I’ll never be.”
Most voters also want Congress to prioritise ending the war with Iran, with roughly 7 in 10 saying this should be a top focus. Substantially fewer voters, about 4 in 10, want Congress to make investigating the Trump administration a high priority, and only about 2 in 10 want Congress to prioritise supporting the Republican president's agenda.
But the poll also indicates that there are deep divisions within the parties on what to focus on, with moderate Democrats and Republicans differing sharply from voters on the left and right wings of their parties.
Most Democratic voters who identify as supporters of democratic socialism are hoping for a Congress that will investigate the administration, and many want to end military aid to Israel, while MAGA Republicans are interested in Congress supporting Trump’s agenda.
Moderates in both parties, are much more likely to want Democrats and Republicans to find common ground.
Lowering the cost of living and ending the Iran war overshadow a wide range of other issues as voters consider priorities for the next Congress.
While most registered voters say reducing costs and ending the war should be among the highest priorities for Congress, only about half say reducing the budget deficit and finding common ground between the two parties should be high priorities. About 4 in 10 want investigating the administration and passing new laws regulating artificial intelligence to be high priorities.
Fewer, about 3 in 10, prioritise ending military aid to Israel, and only about 2 in 10 want a focus on supporting Trump's agenda.
Though most registered Democrats want Congress to investigate the administration, that falls behind the larger priorities of lowering costs and ending the conflict with Iran. About 6 in 10 registered voters who identify as Democrats call investigations into the administration “one of the highest priorities.”
Arthur Brown, a 71-year-old Democrat in Magee, Mississippi, wants to see the next Congress work on making the economy stronger and prices lower. He feels less urgency about holding Trump accountable, mostly because there will be only two years left in Trump’s term. He thinks it’s more important to try to turn the economy around.
“They should just focus on, you know, trying to tackle these problems,” he said. “Eventually down the road, justice will come.”
For Republican voters, bolstering Trump's goals also falls behind lowering the cost of living, ending the war in Iran and reducing the budget deficit.
In a strikingly tepid show of support for the president, only about 4 in 10 Republican voters say the next Congress should make supporting the administration's agenda one of its highest priorities.
House Democrats have begun planning an ambitious 100-day agenda for what they would do if they win control of Congress in November. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York has said the party's top priorities include making life more affordable and conducting vast oversight of the administration.
But there are potential schisms in the party awaiting Democrats if they win a governing majority. The Democratic Party has reckoned in primary campaigns with a growing wing of democratic socialists. Their progressive stances on some issues have divided the party — including on whether to continue military aid to Israel, whether to compromise with Republicans and how strongly to investigate the administration.
About three-quarters of Democratic voters who identify as supporters of democratic socialism say one of the top priorities should be investigating the administration, compared with slightly less than half of Democrats who say they're not democratic socialists.
Democratic socialists are also more likely to want Congress to end military aid to Israel and less likely to say it’s a top priority to find common ground between the two parties.
Campbell, the Democrat in Mississippi, identifies as a democratic socialist and wants Congress to hold the administration accountable.
“It feels a little cliche to just say roll back the past two years, but honestly, mostly just roll back the stuff he’s done the past two years," Campbell said.
MAGA Republicans
Republicans are broadly aligned on what they want the next Congress to do, regardless of whether they identify with the “Make America Great Again” movement — except when it comes to Trump.
At least half of MAGA and non-MAGA Republicans want leaders to lower costs, end the Iran war and reduce the federal budget deficit.
Richard Longo, a 74-year-old Republican in Lake Forest, California, wants to see the president’s agenda pursued in the next Congress but is especially worried about balancing the budget.
“You’re not going to balance the budget in one year, but you have to have a plan," Longo said.
But while about 6 in 10 MAGA Republicans want Congress to prioritize supporting the administration's agenda, only about 2 in 10 Republicans who are not supporters of MAGA say the same.
Lisa Ostlund, a 46-year-old from Wayland, Massachusetts, who identifies as a MAGA supporter, wants to see the next Congress prioritize Trump's agenda. She doesn't support everything Trump does, but she credits his policies with her recent ability to find housing after struggling with homelessness for several years.
“You got to care about your American people," Ostlund said. "He definitely doesn’t say it right, but you do have to put them first.”

JERUSALEM, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Chinese automaker BYD Auto has launched its new electric bus model in Israel, its local official importer said Thursday.
Dozens of buses of the B12e03 model, capable of carrying up to 105 passengers, are expected to be delivered to public transportation operators across the country by the end of 2026, said a statement from Shlomo Motors.
The 12-meter-long bus is built on an entirely new electric platform and features BYD's Blade lithium iron phosphate battery, with a capacity of 491 kWh and a driving range of up to 600 km on a single charge, the statement said.

The design also strengthens the bus floor, lowers its center of gravity, and improves dynamic performance. Two additional battery packs are installed on the reinforced roof.
Besides, electronically controlled shock absorbers adjust to road conditions for better comfort and handling, the statement said.
BYD first supplied Israel's public transportation system with its K9 electric buses back in 2013. ■

Ukraine, Britain and Latvia will track Ukrainian grain stolen by Russia
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:10:45 EEST
01:10:45 KST

Ukraine, Britain and Latvia will track Ukrainian grain stolen by Russia
Kyiv • UNN
The three countries will launch a joint grain verification scheme based on isotope and chemical analysis. It will help identify illegally exported produce.
Ukraine, Latvia, and the United Kingdom will introduce a joint mechanism for verifying the origin of grain, which will help identify agricultural products illegally taken by Russia from Ukraine’s temporarily occupied territories. Isotopic and chemical analysis will be used for this purpose. The Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food of Ukraine reports this, UNN writes.
Details
On October 21, the countries signed a trilateral memorandum of understanding on the Grain Verification Scheme (GVS).
The document provides for joint verification of the origin of agricultural products and the creation of an evidence base regarding their possible illegal appropriation and removal from the occupied territories.
Grain samples will be examined using isotopic and chemical analysis, after which they will be compared with a reference database of products whose geographical origin has been confirmed.
The checks will cover wheat, corn, barley, and sunflower seeds. The results obtained will make it possible to identify suspicious batches and may be used as evidence of the illegal removal of Ukrainian agricultural products.
"The Grain Verification Scheme will make it possible to scientifically confirm the origin of grain and create additional opportunities to counter illegal trade. Every attempt to legalize stolen Ukrainian grain must receive an appropriate response," emphasized Taras Vysotskyi, Minister of Agrarian Policy and Food.
The memorandum also provides for authorized bodies of the three countries to access the GVS system, exchange scientific data, and coordinate the work of laboratories.
The parties will appoint responsible representatives, hold technical consultations, and coordinate actions in the event that batches of agricultural products of questionable origin are identified.
The agreement continued the negotiations between Ukraine and Latvia, which took place on September 25, 2026, in Riga.

US State Department questions promotion candidates about Trump voting history: Report
Unknown

Berk Kutay Gokmen
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The US State Department has reportedly asked career diplomats seeking promotions whether they voted for President Donald Trump in the 2016, 2020 and 2024 elections, The Washington Sun reported Thursday.
Senior agency officials indicated that support for Trump could determine eligibility for mid-level and senior Foreign Service positions, according to the report.
Candidates were also reportedly warned that their campaign donation records would be reviewed and contributions to Democratic candidates could cause them to be disqualified.
The report cited six current and former State Department officials, three of whom said they had spoken directly with individuals who faced the questions.
The reported practice has drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats, who have raised concerns about political loyalty becoming a factor in federal employment decisions.
“The Committee has been following allegations that the Trump Administration is making political affiliation a factor in employment for some time now,” Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, told the newspaper.
“These are critical national security positions and individuals should be chosen for their experience and ability, not their political loyalty,” she said, adding that lawmakers were working with other committees to investigate the allegations.
US federal law prohibits government officials from making personnel decisions based on political affiliation.
The State Department declined to comment directly on the reported questions but defended its staffing and promotion approach.
“Fidelity means upholding the Constitution and the law and executing policy with loyalty to the American people and their interests,” a spokesperson told the newspaper.
The spokesperson said the principle was not about “partisan behavior” but about implementing the president’s foreign policy agenda.
The spokesperson added that Secretary of State Marco Rubio has prioritized merit and “demonstrated performance on behalf of administration priorities” when promoting career employees into leadership roles.

Palestinian youths shield US journalist from Israeli settlers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:10:09 UTC
01:10:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Palestinian youths formed 'protective shield' for US journalist against Israeli settlers
A US photojournalist working for The Washington Post has recounted how Palestinian youths helped save her during a brutal attack by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank that left her seriously injured.
Heidi Levine was attacked by a group of settlers last Friday while covering the olive harvest near Abu Falah, north-east of Ramallah, alongside Palestinian villagers, journalists and activists.
She said local Palestinians formed a “protective shield” to help protect her from the attackers.
“The Palestinian youth put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing,” Levine told British newspaper The Guardian on Wednesday.
She described the scene as being “like a biblical battle”.
The Guardian cited witnesses who said Palestinian youths drove the settlers back, allowing US journalist Jasper Nathaniel and other reporters to reach Levine and help her to safety.
Levine said the violence escalated after Israeli forces arrived at the scene.
A group of masked Israeli settlers had appeared on a nearby hilltop, watching the Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying the harvesters.
“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said.
“Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw tear gas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.”
Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds after being knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by the masked settlers.
She said she was kicked and struck with sticks “probably more than a hundred times”, even after attempting to play dead.
The photojournalist also said she feared she could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye had she not managed to keep her face towards the ground during the beating.
Despite her injuries, Levine said she intended to resume reporting from the occupied West Bank once she had recovered.
“My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
Meanwhile, fellow US journalist Jasper Nathaniel, who helped rescue Levine, wrote on his website that the young Palestinians had been instrumental in saving her life, stressing that they were “prepared to defend the community against the invaders”.
Nathaniel added that “had the shabab (young men in Arabic) not stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead”.
“It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s,” he wrote.
Levine also condemned Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office for questioning accounts of the assault in a statement posted on the social media platform X, which referred to an “alleged attack”.
The statement further claimed that some footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.
"That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why," Levine told The Guardian.
"They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me."
Levine, who is Jewish and has lived in Israel for four decades, said Israeli President Isaac Herzog had personally called her to apologise for the attack. She quoted him as saying the settlers responsible were "not representative of who this country is".
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee also condemned the assault as a “despicable act of terror” and called for those responsible to be prosecuted.
Israeli police have since arrested 10 suspects following the incident in Abu Falah.
However, an Israeli court released four suspects in the assault on Levine on Wednesday and placed them under house arrest, citing insufficient evidence to keep them in custody.
Asked whether she expected her attackers to face justice, Levine rated her confidence at “two out of 10”.
“I am not very hopeful,” she told The Guardian. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it.”
Israeli settlers have intimidated Palestinians harvesting olives in the occupied West Bank for decades.
However, this year has seen a sharp escalation in violence, alongside widespread theft of crops, according to Palestinian witnesses, rights groups and the United Nations.
Israeli rights group Yesh Din reported on Wednesday that it had documented 125 physical attacks on Palestinian olive harvesters during the 24 days since the season began, alongside 168 incidents of crop theft. Israeli military forces were present in at least a quarter of the cases.
Yesh Din warned that settler violence was "part of a campaign of ethnic cleansing, paving the way for the annexation of the West Bank without its Palestinian population".
UN bodies, with support from countries around the world, have repeatedly affirmed that Israeli settlements in territory occupied during war are illegal under international law governing military occupation.

What Russians are told — and not told — about Ukrainian strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:09:47 UTC
01:09:47 KST

What Russians are told — and not told — about Ukrainian strikes
A woman rides on a bus as smoke rises from the area of Gazprom Neft’s Moscow oil refinery in Moscow, Russia, on Sept. 20, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
Andrii Sukharyna
Head of analytics at Join Ukraine
On the night of Sept. 12, Ukrainian drones attacked Taganrog. Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) reported hits on an FPV drone production facility, two drone storage sites, a Pantsir air defense system, and a radar.
Local authorities, as usual, listed something else: 16 commercial buildings, five cars, a football club, and a Svetofor store.
Regional social media channels summed it up in a single sentence about "drone debris" that set a store and several non-residential buildings on fire.
Under a post by a Rostov community on VKontakte, one commenter clarified: "One big-box store selling aircraft tires has been burning since 4 a.m. and is still burning."
They were referring to a military airfield where, judging by satellite imagery, fuel tanks caught fire.
Three days later, missiles struck the city.
Ukraine's General Staff reported explosions and a fire at the Atlant Aero plant, which manufactures Molniya strike drones. Russian authorities listed broken windows, a gas pipe, a grocery store, and an Ozon warehouse. The regional communities we monitor published 178 posts about the two strikes on Taganrog. Only one identified the target. Atlant Aero was not mentioned once.
The case of Taganrog offers a clear picture of how Russia's audience is structured. It is divided into segments, each seeing a different war.
Most people get their news from television and local online communities: television remains the main source of information for 61% of Russians.
Those interested in the war also read pro-war bloggers, known in Russia as Z-war bloggers. The smallest group reads independent media run by Russians abroad.
A month ago, using Novorossiysk as an example, we wrote that Russians do not see strikes on military targets. In September, we expanded our monitoring beyond 1,000 regional communities on Telegram and VKontakte to include more than 40 major nationwide channels, giving us a broader picture.
The first group gets the authorities' version.
On Sept. 9, the Ukrainian Navy said a Neptune missile had hit the Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk.
Of 246 regional posts about that night, only one mentioned ships, while nearly 100 posts reported deaths: according to Russian authorities, four people were killed in the city.
Regional Russia knows about the civilian deaths, but not the frigate.
On Sept. 22, Ukraine's General Staff reported a strike on a base near the village of Tsymbulovo in Oryol Oblast, from which Russia launches jet-powered Geran drones.
Over the following month, the village's name did not appear in any of the thousand communities we monitored, including those in Oryol.
The shutdown of the Moscow oil refinery after a Sept. 20 strike, reported by Reuters, appeared in just six of 407 posts. The state-run channels in our sample, Solovyov and Komsomolskaya Pravda, simply repeated official statements in nine out of every 10 posts.
This feed creates the impression that air defenses shoot down hundreds of drones and debris falls on residential buildings.
Readers of Russian military bloggers know much more.
On Sept. 12, the Voyennyy Osvedomitel channel identified a military airfield as the likely target in Taganrog. On Sept. 18, it published a satellite image of damaged Atlant Aero workshops.
Overall, military bloggers identified the target in nine of 16 posts about Taganrog.
On the Moscow oil refinery, Z-blogger Fighterbomber wrote: "Let me remind you, this is the most heavily protected oil refinery in the country. Perhaps even in the world. I predict it will be attacked more than once."
But this knowledge is one-sided. The same channels report Russian strikes on Ukraine far more frequently and in greater detail.
Some 92% of reactions to such posts are positive. And Voyennyy Osvedomitel presented the strike on Tsymbulovo as a story of resilience: the shelters are sturdy, and the launchers are cheap to replace.
Independent media and those run from abroad provide the most comprehensive coverage of the strikes: they identified the target in 14 of 20 posts about Taganrog. Yet they have the smallest audiences.
In our sample, a typical military blogger's post about a strike on Russia receives 73,000 views, compared with 14,000 for a post by an independent media outlet.
Everything changes when a strike hits close to home.
The official account then clashes with what people heard during the night, and they start asking questions.
Under a post about Taganrog, people write: "Your Telegram channels say it wasn't just the store" and "When will they finally learn to tell the truth?"
In Oryol, a woman asked the governor about nighttime explosions during a live broadcast. She heard an explanation about a "piece of a drone" and recounted it in the comments: "Short and clear. Yes, that piece fell with such a bang that almost the whole city heard it."
The same community debunked a deepfake in which the governor supposedly admitted that the region lacked air defenses. The comments under the debunking post read: "This fake is telling the truth" and "I'd vote for the fake."
In Salekhard, the capital of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, people reasoned this way after a gas plant in Novy Urengoy was hit: "How did it happen that the attack was repelled, the drone was turned into debris, and the facility it attacked is on fire? So the attack wasn't repelled, and this wasn't debris. It hit exactly what it was supposed to hit."
The numbers reflect this pattern, too. In communities based in the region that was hit, 34% of substantive comments question the effectiveness of defenses and the official figures. Another 23% describe what people saw and heard themselves or ask their neighbors about it.
They do not always find the right answers.
Novy Urengoy lies nearly 3,000 kilometers (about 1864 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and drones reached the city for the first time. The neighboring Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug banned the publication of anything about drones that same day.
The most popular comment about the strike in our databases reads: "It's been obvious for a long time that they aren't being launched from Ukraine."
Where the authorities stay silent, Russians find their own answers, and they are not always right.
Ordinary Russians in the regions know little about this war. They are told about downed drones and damaged buildings, and as long as the explosions are far away, that is enough.
Questions emerge when a strike hits their own city. In September, Yamalo-Nenets appeared on our map for the first time, and communities in 24 regions posted about the strike.
Questioning the authorities does not necessarily mean wanting the war to end. In the aftermath of the month's largest attack, the one on Moscow, 59% of substantive comments blamed the authorities and air defenses, while 16% blamed Ukraine and the West. Yet only one in 12 called for the war to end.
To sum up, here is what ordinary Russians were not told in the news in September: a strike drone factory and a military airfield in Taganrog; a frigate carrying Kalibr missiles in Novorossiysk; a launch base for jet-powered Geran drones; the shutdown of the capital's main oil refinery; and a gas plant in Yamalo-Nenets.
Russians in the regions continue to be shielded from learning by accident that the war is not going as victoriously as Putin claims. The results are rather underwhelming.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

WATCH: Fueled by a life's mission, Netanyahu asks Israelis for time to 'finish the job' in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:09:46 UTC
01:09:46 KST

It was 2:14 a.m., and Benjamin Netanyahu wanted to know whether we were tired.
He had just turned 77. Members of his staff were dozing on couches and chairs. Netanyahu was alert, focused, and apparently in no hurry to end the night. We admitted that we were probably more tired than he was.
“You’re not the first to say that.”
A little earlier, his staff had surprised him with a birthday celebration: krembos, the chocolate-covered marshmallow treats; along with chocolates and gummies; and an individual tiramisu for the prime minister. He ate it with evident enjoyment.
Outside, aides had been searching for “the chair,” the one he preferred sitting in. Even at this hour, the small machinery of looking after a prime minister kept turning.
Some of those around him had spent years at his side. They brought drinks, attended to him, and spoke with the conviction that he would win again. They believed Israel needed him. Netanyahu himself would give us a less comfortable assessment of the race.
How did it feel to be 77? “Feels fine. If you know what you’re about, and you have good health and a lot of energy, and a purpose.”
That word, “purpose,” came up repeatedly during the next half-hour. So did Iran, US President Donald Trump, and the danger Netanyahu saw in handing the country to someone else. With the October 27 election approaching, he was asking voters to let him finish work that he regards as the reason for his political life.
His partnership with Trump was central to that request. We wanted to know how his case would hold up when the American president was someone else.
Netanyahu: Iran does not want me elected
Could Iran attack before the election? Could Israel strike first?
Netanyahu said military intelligence and the Mossad had delivered “clear warnings” that Iran and its proxies were considering ways to influence the vote.
“They don’t want me elected.”
He suggested rockets or drones could be used to puncture Israelis’ confidence in the military campaign’s achievements. “If they do, it’ll be a big mistake because we’ll respond with force and might they cannot even imagine.”
People on his team, speaking on background, separately told us that current senior defense officials had contacted Netanyahu to say he needed to win because Israel’s enemies would see his defeat as their success. They also described serious security threats in the near future. That account of private conversations has not been independently verified.
Netanyahu moved quickly through the destruction of enemy capabilities and the killing of their leaders. October 7 was the starting point of his account of Israel’s recovery; the failures that permitted the attack under his government received little attention.
Iran still had capabilities, we pointed out. He acknowledged that it did. For as long as its present leadership survived, he argued, it would try to rebuild its nuclear and ballistic missile programs.
“My purpose is to break Iran’s murderous regime, remove the threat from our heads, and have multiple peace treaties.”
Finishing the job, by that definition, would require an outcome extending far beyond another successful strike.
Netanyahu says he can withstand a post-Trump US, expand Arab ties
Trump’s recent endorsement was quite an item for Netanyahu’s campaign literature: the American president wanted him reelected.
Netanyahu said the decision had surprised him. The motivation had not. He described a president who saw Iran as a danger to American cities and believed he had one reliable partner in confronting it.
We raised Vice President JD Vance’s refusal to offer an endorsement of his own. Vance had also made clear he was not opposing Netanyahu. Still, the question reached beyond this election. What would happen to the relationship when Trump left office?
Netanyahu’s answer began with the remaining opportunity under Trump, then moved to the possibility of a less friendly administration. He disliked that formulation.
“That’s really laundering words,” he said.
“What happens if you have a hostile administration? Who will withstand the pressures? Who will stand up to them? And I think the answer in both cases is the same.”
He meant himself. Experience with Washington, he argued, qualified him to make the most of Trump’s friendship and to resist a successor’s demands. Palestinian statehood was the example he returned to, describing it as the prospect of an Iranian terror base overlooking Israel’s population centers.
“You’re not going to withstand the pressure by succumbing to it, because then you’re finished.”
An Israeli government elected now will have to prepare for an America whose politics are already changing. Netanyahu placed considerable weight on the character of the man sitting across from the American president. He spent more time explaining how he would withstand American pressure than how he would broaden American support.
He did identify three tasks: strengthen the existing American base of support, fight the information war, and widen Israel’s international partnerships. India was one example. In the Middle East, he said, more Arab governments were interested in relations with Israel after seeing it act against Iran.
We tried to get the names. “Since it’s just the three of us, so who are we talking about? Which countries?”
“Well, we’re definitely talking about more than two.”
He gave us a number. Later, it grew to “many more than two.”
He traced the beginnings of the Abraham Accords to his confrontation with former president Barack Obama over the Iran nuclear agreement, recalling calls from Arab officials impressed by his willingness to challenge Washington.
Trump’s presidency had helped turn those contacts into agreements. Further military action against Iran, he argued, had made Israel still more attractive as a partner.
We challenged his suggestion that Arab leaders were untroubled by his coalition partners. Their reservations, we said, were expressed privately too.
“Most of them couldn’t care less.”
He went further: “And they couldn’t care less about the Palestinian issue, and they said, ‘We have to say it, but we don’t mean it.’”
That is his account of their private words. Their public position remains quite different: Saudi Arabia and other Arab governments reaffirmed support for Palestinian statehood in a joint statement on October 16.
Qatar, Qatargate, and Netanyahu’s defense against allegations of influence
Qatar brought the discussion of Israel’s standing abroad uncomfortably close to home.
We asked whether it should again mediate on matters involving Israel. Netanyahu had accused Doha of spreading hatred of the Jewish state; Israel had nevertheless relied on its role in hostage negotiations.
He maintained that Israel used Qatar because the United States did. He then accused it of driving antisemitism and anti-Zionism in American universities and on social media. “Qatar was one of the engines of our vilification, only one.”
This led him to cite his late father, Benzion Netanyahu, the historian of the Inquisition and modern Zionism. He recalled asking him whether America offered Jews an exception to the recurring dangers of European history.
“There are no exceptions if certain things happen,” he remembered his father replying.
Netanyahu described social upheaval and resentment exposing a visible minority to danger. “The Jews are prominent and weak,” he said, “and that’s a very dangerous place to be in a society.”
His father’s warning still shaped his explanation of America. Israel’s strength, he argued, gave Jews the means to prevent the physical destruction that had so often followed their vilification. He saw the current hostility as a historical danger that better public diplomacy alone could not resolve.
Then he returned to Qatar, offering a military action as his answer to suspicions about his own position.
“They accused me of being pro-Qatar; I attacked Qatar.”
Israel’s September 2025 strike in Doha targeted Hamas leaders. It did not answer the question we put to him next: What about the allegations concerning people in his own circle and their connections to Qatar?
“Except that the judge said there was nothing there.”
He continued: “The judge said it’s a witch hunt. Basically that’s what he said.”
He did not identify the judge or ruling. 'Qatargate' remains under investigation. The affair concerns allegations that aides, including Yonatan Urich, promoted Qatari interests while working for Netanyahu. They deny wrongdoing. Netanyahu has given evidence to police but has not been named a suspect.
Netanyahu argued that others who had worked with Qatar were now attacking him over it. “This is one hoax,” he said, before describing a campaign video mocking successive television controversies as manufactured storms.
“The idea is to divert attention and to mask the real issue in this election.”
He did not say whether Israel would use Qatar as a mediator again.
Who gets to join Netanyahu’s next government - and on what terms?
Netanyahu wants to build his next government with his present partners. On one possible appointment, however, he was explicit. Asked about Itamar Ben-Gvir’s ambition to become defense minister, he said: “I think the next defense minister should be from Likud.”
“But it’s going to be our government. We decide what the policy is.”
The conduct of the present government raised a different test of control. We pressed him on extremist settler violence against Palestinians, pointing to criticism from US Ambassador Mike Huckabee, hardly an unfamiliar face among Israel’s friends.
Netanyahu argued that international coverage distorted the scale of the violence compared with terrorism against Israelis. We persisted: “Huckabee knows that, but not everyone does, right?”
“No, I understand that, believe me.”
“We know you do,” we replied.
“You don’t have to explain it to me. I don’t want vigilantism.”
He rejected extremist Jews who have been taking the law into their own hands. The acts were wrong, he said, did “enormous damage to Israel abroad,” and harmed the reputation of the wider settlement community. He spoke about families killed by terrorists and the sons that those communities had lost in military service.
“That’s why I put the Shin Bet onto this and continue to do that.”
When we asked about bringing opponents into a broader government, the conversation turned to the courtroom.
“Why not have a unity government? Would you agree to sit with him?” we asked, referring to Gadi Eisenkot, the former IDF chief of staff.
Netanyahu said his opponents had ruled him out because of his corruption trial. “The trial’s collapsed.”
He spoke about what he and his family had endured, the conduct of investigators, and former attorney-general Avichai Mandelblit’s testimony. We returned to the political question.
“You would offer them a hand?”
“No, first of all, let me finish this because this is important.”
His objection was to proposals barring an indicted politician from serving as prime minister. Such a law, he argued, would hand prosecutors the power to decide who could govern, removing that choice from voters. He termed it “Iranian Bolshevism.”
Then came a demand concerning the trial itself: “It should be ended right now, and we should start an immediate criminal investigation against those who led it.
“You cannot do this to any citizen, and I’m a citizen, but also you cannot try to destroy democracy with the abuse of state power.”
The trial continues. Netanyahu faces fraud and breach-of-trust charges in three cases, and bribery in Case 4000. He denies wrongdoing. The allegations concern gifts from businessmen, discussions with newspaper publisher Arnon Mozes about favorable coverage in return for steps against rival Israel Hayom, and regulatory favors for Bezeq in exchange for intervention in Walla’s coverage.
Mandelblit, testifying for the defense, has acknowledged investigative steps beyond his approvals while defending his authorization of the investigations and the basis for the bribery charge.
Eventually, he answered the coalition question. If he secured a majority of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, he would form a government and establish its principles. Others could then accept them and join.
“First principle, no Palestinian state, period.”
He added Israel’s identity as the Jewish nation-state, with minority rights respected; an active security doctrine; a free-market economy; and expanded peace agreements. A broader coalition could follow victory, on terms that he would set.
Explaining his security doctrine, he searched for an English rendering of tachbulot, or stratagems. “My English isn’t that good.” He invoked King James’s translators and the 70 wise men of Alexandria. Biblical translation was one difficulty he was willing to concede.
Victory itself was less certain. We pointed out that polls also showed him struggling to assemble a majority.
“I think right now it’s an even tie. That’s what I see in the big numbers.”
Netanyahu says he wants 'five more terms' as Israel's prime minister
We returned to the birthday. If he won, would this be his last term?
“Oh no, I’m gonna have five more terms.”
He had a proposal for those who described him as worn out or physically inactive. “I invite them to come to the gym with me.” There was a condition: “But they’ll have to do the same thing.”
He recalled a commentator predicting, after his defeat in 1999, that he would not merit a footnote. The commentator was still around, he said; we pointed out that Netanyahu was too. He has had considerable practice reading his political obituaries.
“I don’t need the job. I don’t need the job,” he said. “I’m fueled by a mission.”
He described preventing Iran from acquiring the means to destroy Israel as the work of his adult life. Again came the question he wanted voters to ask: “Who will finish the job?”
It was 2:45 a.m. Netanyahu thanked us for our tenacity. His staff had celebrated another birthday and were expecting another victory; his own assessment still left the election in the balance. After we left, he continued working.
He had turned 77 in the middle of a working night. How much longer he would serve was now a question for the voters.■

A cold weather front will move across Bulgaria on Friday. The lowest temperatures will range from 8°C to 13°C, 8°C in Sofia.
Rain is expected during the day in Central and Eastern Bulgaria, with locally heavy showers accompanied by thunderstorms. The rain will ease across the country by the afternoon. Cloud cover will begin to break up and clear from the west during the morning, giving way to mostly sunny conditions. Moderate northwesterly winds will blow, temporarily becoming strong in northeastern areas. Maximum temperatures will range from 15°C to 20°C, around 15°C in the capital city.
Cloudy and rainy weather is expected along the Black Sea coast. Daytime highs will range from 18°C to 23°C. The seawater temperature is 17°C-18°C. Sea state 2–3 on the Beaufort scale.
In the mountains, it will be mostly cloudy, with rain and snow above 2,000 metres. In the afternoon, cloud cover will break up, giving way to mostly sunny weather. Moderate northwesterly winds are expected. Maximum temperatures will reach around 12°C at an altitude of 1,200 metres and around 5°C at 2,000 metres.
On Saturday, cloud cover will decrease across the country. Fog is expected in low-lying areas and valleys before noon. Northwesterly winds will weaken and shift to the south-southeast. Daytime temperatures will rise slightly, while morning lows will drop to between 1°C and 6°C, reaching 10°C to 12°C in Eastern Bulgaria.

What makes Bulgaria attractive to foreign investors?

What makes Bulgaria attractive to foreign investors?
A straightforward tax system and the quality of public institutions are among the key considerations for entrepreneurs looking to do business in Bulgaria
Thursday 22 October 2026 17:49
Thursday, 22 October 2026, 17:49
PHOTO AI generated
Font size
Foreign direct investment in Bulgaria more than doubled in the first eight months of 2026, reaching €3.829 billion, according to preliminary figures from the Bulgarian National Bank (BNB). This represents an increase of 100.5% compared with the same period last year, although the figures may still be revised.
Most of the investment came from profits reinvested by foreign-owned companies operating in Bulgaria. These amounted to €3.095 billion, up from €2.816 billion a year earlier.
But what makes Bulgaria an attractive place for foreign investors?
Joining the eurozone is an advantage, although not necessarily the deciding factor, according to Prof. Todor Yalamov, Deputy Dean of the Faculty of Economics and Business Administration at Sofia University St Kliment Ohridski.
"I wouldn't say the eurozone is a factor that will attract investors, but it is a useful addition to the other advantages because it reduces transaction costs and currency risk," he told Radio Bulgaria.
Prof. Todor Yalamov
PHOTO Sofia University St Kliment Ohridski
"A much more important factor is the simplicity of the tax system. You don't need expensive tax consultants to navigate it. In many European countries, you can pay low taxes only if you have good tax advisers. Otherwise, you end up paying high taxes.
Another advantage, according to Yalamov, is Bulgaria's low corporate tax rate of 10%, which is particularly attractive to smaller investors. Even the 15% minimum effective tax rate applicable to qualifying large corporate groups with annual consolidated revenue of at least €750 million is highly competitive.
He believes the flat-rate tax system and the country's social security contribution thresholds offer another competitive advantage.
"The flat tax is a more important factor, along with reasonable social security contribution thresholds compared with the rest of the European market. With the same labour costs for an employer in France or Germany, an employee in Bulgaria would take home more money. This helps companies attract staff and gives Bulgaria an advantage for certain investors."
Not everyone, however, sees rising wages as good news.
"Others who came here solely because labour was cheap have started leaving as wages have risen," he added.
Yalamov points to the growing number of Italian-owned restaurants in Sofia as an example of businesses that can earn more in Bulgaria than they might in their home country. Different investors, he explains, are attracted by different advantages.
PHOTO magnific.com
"Many Greek companies have moved not just their registered offices but also their actual production facilities to Bulgaria. They did so not because labour was cheaper, but because of financial stability. That is another reason Bulgaria is an interesting investment destination."
Yet the discussion about investment tends to overlook another important aspect: Bulgarian companies investing abroad.
Such investments, Yalamov argues, also contribute to Bulgaria's economic growth, employment and competitiveness. Companies cannot continue expanding indefinitely without entering foreign markets.
"Fortunately, many Bulgarian companies are investing abroad. And some of what is recorded as foreign investment in Bulgaria is actually Bulgarian capital. If you look closely at corporate ownership databases, you'll find that some businesses classified as foreign are in fact Bulgarian."
He mentions fintech companies operating worldwide, businesses trading in petroleum products and oils, and pharmaceutical firms. One company from Veliko Tarnovo has even established a textile factory in Florida.
"Learning through investment in foreign markets is extremely useful for the next generation of companies that have taken, or want to take, the same path," Yalamov said.
PHOTO Bulgarian Investment Agency
This raises another question: what prompts Bulgarian companies to invest overseas?
One obvious answer is access to markets.
In the early years after 1990, some foreign investors entered Bulgaria simply to secure a place in the market before their competitors did. This was particularly true in food production, sanitary products and certain services. Today, however, attention is increasingly turning towards foreign entrepreneurs who choose Bulgaria as the place to establish their businesses.
"According to traditional economic theory, investment is the most important thing. Nowadays, however, entrepreneurship seems to matter more than investment, because it is more often driven by innovation and aimed at new markets.
"In other words, attracting entrepreneurs who establish their companies in Bulgaria could prove more valuable than attracting a conventional investor who simply moves here the production of something previously made in Italy."
Yalamov recalls the Italian garment factories that relocated to Bulgaria. Some eventually closed, leaving workers without opportunities to retrain.
Ultimately, attracting investors is only part of the challenge. Keeping them in Bulgaria depends not just on competitive taxes but also on the quality of public institutions and how effectively the state functions. These, Yalamov argues, are among the factors that determine whether foreign businesses choose to stay for the long term.

Pro-Israel lobby AIPAC drops endorsements amid US backlash
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:07:39 UTC
01:07:39 KST

Breadcrumb
Pro-Israel lobby AIPAC drops endorsements amid increasing US unpopularity
The powerful pro-Israel lobby AIPAC has announced it will stop directly funding and endorsing US congressional candidates, marking a major shift in its electoral strategy amid growing public opposition to Israel over its genocidal war in Gaza.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) announced the decision on Wednesday, saying it would end formal candidate endorsements and direct contributions through its political action committee while continuing to spend heavily on elections through its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP).
The move comes as AIPAC faces growing criticism, particularly among Democratic voters, with a leading Palestinian advocacy figure telling The New Arab that the decision amounts to an admission that the lobby's support has become politically toxic.
"They're admitting themselves that their endorsement is a net negative for anyone that they would endorse," Hamid Bendaas, communications director at the Institute for Middle East Understanding (IMEU) Policy Project said.
The decision marks a significant change for one of Washington's most influential lobbying organisations, which established its political action committee and super PAC in 2021, expanding its electoral involvement.
In a letter to members, AIPAC said it would concentrate on mobilising individual donors and developing new fundraising methods, while insisting its objectives remained unchanged.
"Our mission and strategy remain the same," AIPAC spokesperson Deryn Sousa said.
Federal Election Commission filings show that AIPAC contributed nearly $25 million to candidates and political committees through September, while UDP spent more than $53 million on independent electoral expenditures.
Unlike traditional political action committees, super PACs can spend unlimited amounts supporting or opposing candidates, provided they do not coordinate directly with campaigns.
The announcement comes amid sharply deteriorating American attitudes towards Israel following its genocide in Gaza and wider military actions across the Middle East.
An April 2026 Pew Research Center survey found that 60 percent of Americans held an unfavourable view of Israel, including 80 percent of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents.
Polling published by the Chicago Council on Global Affairs in October found that American favourability towards Israel had fallen to its lowest level since the organisation began measuring attitudes towards the country in 1978.
The changing political climate has complicated AIPAC's efforts to support candidates, particularly in Democratic primaries.
In Michigan, AIPAC's super PAC spent heavily attempting to defeat Abdul El-Sayed, a critic of Israel, during the Democratic Senate primary.
El-Sayed nevertheless secured the nomination against Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who received substantial backing from pro-Israel interests.
UDP has subsequently intervened against El-Sayed in the Senate election campaign, where he faces Republican Mike Rogers, departing from AIPAC's traditional emphasis on maintaining bipartisan support.
Bendaas said the intervention was particularly significant given AIPAC's longstanding preference for influencing primaries rather than general elections.
"They usually stick to primaries, and they stay out of general elections because they want to stay bipartisan," he said.
Such interventions risk alienating Democratic voters whose overriding priority is defeating Republican candidates, regardless of their views on Israel.
Nevertheless, AIPAC's withdrawal from endorsements does not mean it is abandoning its ability to influence elections.
Its super PAC will continue operating, while supporters will still be encouraged to contribute to candidates backing its policy objectives.
Bendaas described the decision as a survival strategy intended to preserve AIPAC's financial influence while distancing candidates from an increasingly unpopular association.
"This is a move that's going to ensure that AIPAC stays relevant and continues to have an influence because they're going to continue to spend money through their SuperPAC," he said.
He also argued that AIPAC could increasingly rely on less transparent electoral spending, including committees whose financial backers may not become publicly apparent until after voting.
The restructuring comes as growing numbers of Democratic candidates reject AIPAC's support, challenging an organisation that has historically enjoyed considerable influence over both major parties.
For Bendaas, the most consequential aspect of the decision may be the loss of AIPAC's formerly privileged position in American politics.
"AIPAC is now just kind of one of those lobbies. But they're still a powerful one," he said, comparing the organisation to other wealthy lobbying groups seeking to influence elections.
"That kind of sheen and that feeling of no one should try to challenge us I think is gone probably forever."

MELITOPOL, October 22. /TASS/. The Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (NPP) has received a 10-year operating license for power unit No. 6 from Russia’s Federal Environmental, Industrial, and Nuclear Supervision Service (Rostekhnadzor), valid until October 21, 2036. This establishes a legal framework for the plant’s continued safe operation, the NPP said.
"The Zaporozhye NPP has received an operating license for power unit No. 6 from Rostekhnadzor. The license was issued for 10 years, until October 21, 2036. <…> Licensing establishes a legal framework for the plant’s continued safe operation. However, obtaining the license does not in itself mean that electricity generation will resume. Any change in the power unit’s operating mode will require a separate decision and compliance with all necessary safety requirements," the plant said on its Max channel.
The plant noted that this marks another stage in its systematic efforts to obtain the necessary permits in accordance with Russian nuclear energy regulations.
Power unit No. 6 is the third unit at the Zaporozhye NPP to receive a Russian operating license. Rostekhnadzor previously issued licenses for power unit No. 1 in December 2025 and power unit No. 2 in February 2026. The plant has also obtained licenses to operate radiation sources and its dry spent nuclear fuel storage facility.

Israeli attacks in Gaza kill four, including a young girl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:06:55 UTC
01:06:55 KST

Israeli attacks kill four as famine risk looms in Gaza
Gaza hospitals report four dead in 24 hours, as the death toll since the October ‘ceasefire’ rises to 1,538.
Israeli attacks across Gaza have killed four Palestinians, including a child, in the past 24 hours as the Israeli military continues to seize more territory inside the enclave.
This comes amid warnings from a rights group that Gaza could face another famine as Israeli restrictions on incoming goods leave residents struggling to obtain food.
The deaths on Thursday included a young girl who was killed by Israeli gunfire in northern Gaza near the Jabalia refugee camp, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
Al Jazeera’s Hani Mahmoud, reporting from Gaza City, said a strike on a vehicle in Gaza City’s Tal al-Hawa neighbourhood killed one person and seriously injured another.
A separate strike killed a man on a bicycle in the southern city of Khan Younis.
Meanwhile, the Gaza Health Ministry reported that a fourth person had died on Thursday of wounds sustained earlier in an Israeli strike.
Along with the deadly attacks, the Israeli military continues to grab more land inside Gaza. Close to two million people live in what remains of the shrinking territory, which is littered with thousands of tonnes of rubble and debris.
“Israel is expanding their control inside Gaza,” Mahmoud explained, noting that Israeli troops have been “taking more land since the ‘ceasefire'” and expanding from northern Gaza inward to the centre and westward.
“People cannot return to their homes, and most buildings in the areas Israel controls have been left in ruins,” the reporter said.
Al Jazeera’s maps have shown that nearly two-thirds of Gaza is under Israeli military control or subject to access restrictions.
At least 1,538 Palestinians have been killed and 5,498 injured since the “ceasefire” took effect in October last year, according to the Gaza Health Ministry.
Israel has killed more than 74,400 Palestinians in Gaza since October 2023.
Renewed famine risk
The deadly strikes come as Palestinians across Gaza face an escalating food crisis, which has been renewed by Israeli border closures and severe funding shortfalls targeting international relief operations.
The Geneva-based human rights group, Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, said on Thursday that its teams observed increasingly empty markets and soaring food prices, warning that Gaza could face another famine.
It accused Israel of “deliberately depriving” Palestinians of adequate nutrition as part of its ongoing genocide.
According to the rights group, after Israeli authorities suspended commercial goods deliveries to Gaza on October 13, it announced on October 19 that some imports would be allowed to resume. However, the group said the decision brought little relief, as shipments remained heavily restricted and fresh fruits and vegetables were denied entry.
The World Food Programme (WFP) announced this week that severe funding shortages have forced it to slash food assistance to Gaza by one-third, leaving an estimated 500,000 vulnerable residents without essential monthly support as winter approaches.
According to the United Nations, the supply of fresh food and basic staples has rapidly evaporated due to Israeli restrictions on commercial entry points and aid crossings.
Reporting from Gaza City, Al Jazeera’s Maram Humaid described a sudden and dramatic disappearance of basic sustenance, leaving local markets empty and families increasingly desperate.
“Food disappeared suddenly – no vegetables, no fruit, no meat, no eggs, no bread – prices skyrocketing,” Humaid reported.
“Today, we didn’t have breakfast until noon, after my husband spent hours looking for bread and any kind of fresh vegetables. He came back with just a few loaves. We’re back to canned beans.”
With no electricity or operational refrigeration across the ruined enclave, households are unable to store fresh provisions even when available.
“Stockpiling seems more limited this time,” Humaid noted. “The shortages started with flour and fresh produce, which people can’t store for long, especially with no refrigerators or electricity. Prices of other goods have gone up, but many people can’t afford to stock up. Others are simply exhausted and have lost hope. I’m one of them.”
Beyond physical deprivation, the psychological toll on residents forced to navigate overcrowded shops with dwindling inventory has reached a breaking point.
“It’s the whole experience – the panic and fear that come with shopping to stock up. You find yourself looking at every food item as if it might be the last time you’ll ever see it, saying goodbye to it. Everyone around you is gripped by the same panic, and the shops are unbelievably crowded,” Humaid said, adding that the experience is one many feel they “can’t go through all over again”.

Necva Tastan Sevinc
