Denmark’s Defense Ministry said Thursday that it is acquiring two types of long-range precision missiles to strengthen its defenses and NATO’s collective deterrence.
The acquisitions include the Joint Strike Missile, manufactured by Norway’s Kongsberg for use on Danish F-35 fighter jets, and the land-launched Anthem cruise missile from the American company Covenant.
The ministry said the weapons use advanced navigation technology to strike targets precisely over long distances, enabling Denmark to deter attacks and, if necessary, retaliate deep inside enemy territory.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said the acquisitions followed recommendations from the chief of defense.
“The acquisitions are a significant step towards making Denmark better able to defend itself, lifting our share of the burden in NATO, and at the same time we are sending a strong signal that we have the ability to strike back,” said Bruus.
The ministry described the missiles as capabilities sought by NATO that would contribute to Denmark’s security.
It did not disclose the value of the acquisitions, the number of missiles or a delivery timetable.

Indian pilots take a spin in upgraded Su-30 jet in Russia (VIDEO)
Indian and Russian air force crews practiced joint drills in Russia’s Chelyabinsk region as part of the wider inter-service Indra-2026 military exercise.
The Russian Aerospace Forces and the Indian Air Force (IAF) teams engaged in joint operations in Su-30SM fighter jets during the drill. The focus of the operations was on actions against small, low-flying targets and destroying carriers of short- and medium-range aerial weaponry.
The personnel also performed air combat maneuvers at medium and low altitudes, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Thursday.
The Su-30SM is a modernized version of the Su-30MKI model, the IAF’s workhorse fighter jet. It has been modified with Russian-specific avionics, radar, and communication systems and has extreme agility.
The IAF is also running its own program to upgrade and make its Su-30MKIs more lethal and survivable, under the ‘Super Sukhoi’ program, at the state-backed Hindustan Aeronautics Limited.
The $7.5 billion modernization program aims to upgrade an initial batch of 84 Su-30MKI fighter jets, with plans to eventually expand to over 200 more aircraft, extending the fleet’s service life through 2055.
Russia’s Rosoboronexport agency earlier highlighted that the modernization program can be performed with significant involvement from the Indian defense industry, while the facilities involved in the manufacturing of the Su-30MKI can be used for co-manufacturing of the Russian fifth-generation Su-57E fighter jet, if India decides to go ahead with Russia’s proposal.
The Indian and Russian crews also conducted exercises with Mi-8 army aviation helicopters.
The exercise’s aim was to build operational capabilities in deploying special forces units and for search-and-rescue operations in hazardous and difficult terrains.
The maritime phase of the drills took place in the Gulf of Peter the Great near Vladivostok over the weekend and involved the Russian Pacific Fleet corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov and the Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri
The land exercises will end on Friday, with troops practicing joint command and control and operations against simulated armed groups.

Pokemon cards stored in British attic for 15 years sell for $2M

Halis Sunnetci
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
A collection of rare Pokemon trading cards kept in a British attic for 15 years sold at auction for £1.56 million ($2.09 million), far exceeding its estimated value of £250,000, according to British media reports.
The collection belonged to an anonymous retired decorator from Woking, Surrey, who accumulated 42 sets of Pokemon cards from 1999 to 2009, kept one, and offered the remaining 41 for sale.
The auction, held Wednesday and organized by Ewbank's in Surrey, attracted bidders from around the world.
The most valuable lot was a Legendary Collection master set featuring a rare Charizard card, which fetched £130,000, including buyer's fees.
Another set, Skyridge, which the collector originally purchased for around £300, sold for £97,500, including fees.
The man began collecting Pokemon cards in the late 1990s after his son became interested in trading them at school. He purchased complete sets from a seller in Malaysia on eBay and stored them in his attic after his son lost interest.
He discovered their potential value only after reading a newspaper report about a single Pokemon card selling for more than £6,000.
Ewbank's described the sale as the most valuable trading-card auction in UK history and suggested it could also be a European record.
James Spooner, head of trading cards at Ewbank's, said advance bids had already reached £825,000 the day before the sale.
Andrew Ewbank, who conducted the auction, described the international interest as exceptional.
"The buzz was incredible, especially because the collectors could not believe how good this collection was – extensive, untouched, complete, and with just about every rarity you could hope for," he said.

Italy and Spain lift border controls after months of tension over Ceuta
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:04:21 UTC
01:04:21 KST

Italy and Spain lift border controls after months of tension over Ceuta
More than 70,000 people irregularly crossed from Morocco into Ceuta in late July, triggering border security concerns in the EU bloc.
Italy and Spain have agreed to lift border controls on each other’s citizens, ending a three-month standoff triggered after a mass surge of migrants and asylum seekers entered the Spanish enclave of Ceuta.
The Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi and his Spanish counterpart Fernando Grande-Marlaska spoke on the phone and agreed not to extend their suspension of the European Union’s open-border Schengen arrangements, an Italian statement said on Thursday.
“The decision, reached after a careful assessment of the situation, will be accompanied by enhanced information-sharing measures to ensure the full security of the common Schengen area,” the ministry added.
The decision followed a meeting between Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez on the sidelines of a European Council meeting.
Italy’s right-wing government first suspended its open-border arrangements with Spain on July 31, saying it wanted to make sure no migrants entering the North African enclave of Ceuta could travel to Italian territory.
Madrid responded by taking similar action against Rome, describing the Italian measures as “unjust, contrary to European Union interests, and discriminatory to the population of Spain”.
Ceuta migrant surge
The tit-for-tat border closures happened after upwards of 70,000 people swam around barricades and entered Ceuta from neighbouring Morocco on July 30 and 31, fuelling tension in the Spanish territory.
Most returned to Morocco within hours, but thousands, including unaccompanied minors, have remained for weeks in often dire conditions.
“We thought our government was going to do something in the short or medium term, but we’ve been here for two months, and these people haven’t been sent back,” Ceuta resident Ruben Gonzalez said.
The Spanish government’s handling of the mass crossing of migrants into Ceuta has complicated Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s bid for re-election in November.
Sanchez was already facing criticism for his government’s decision to open a path to legal status for hundreds of thousands of undocumented foreign residents.
After the Ceuta incident, Far-right Vox and centre-right PP parties accused him of being soft on immigration and put the issue at the centre of their campaigns in the run-up to next month’s elections.

🔴Live: Authorities in Lyon and Marseille ban all protests Saturday

Local prefects on Thursday banned all protests in France’s second- and third-largest cities Marseille and Lyon for Saturday in an attempt to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence and looting on the margins of demonstrations over the cost of living and education funding. Read our liveblog to see how the day's events unfolded.
This liveblog is now closing. Thank you for being with us today!
Pittsburgh Steelers cancel fan event in Paris due to unrest
A planned Pittsburgh Steelers fan event scheduled for Sunday in Paris has been canceled due to the recent unrest there.
The Steelers and New Orleans Saints are scheduled to play the NFL’s first regular-season game in Paris on Sunday at Stade de France.
“Following recent events in the Bastille neighborhood, and after careful consideration, we felt it appropriate not to move forward with the planned Steelers House fan event in Paris,” a message posted to X read.
2,700 detained amid riots and looting in France, justice minister says
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people have been taken into police custody in connection with riots and looting.
“There have been 2,700 people taken into police custody since Saturday in connection with these riots and looting,” Darmanin said in an interview with French news channel LCI.
Macron to receive representatives of high school students on Friday
Nighttime curfews imposed in parts of Paris until Monday, police say
Nighttime curfews have been imposed in parts of Paris until Monday morning, police said.
The curfews will be in force between 11pm and 6am, and concern the areas around Place de la République and Les Halles in central Paris -- which were both subject to widespread damage over the weekend.
French TV and radio watchdog Arcom urges ‘accurate and balanced’ coverage of protests
Arcom, the French regulator for broadcast media, has urged the country’s TV and radio stations to ensure “accurate and balanced” coverage of the current protests, saying it had received around a dozen complaints in the past few days.
One of the complaints concerned remarks made by a guest on CNews, a television channel frequently accused of promoting far-right views, who claimed that rioters had been seen carrying automatic guns – an allegation that was rejected by police.
Another complaint related to a commentator on radio station France Info who wrongly claimed that far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon had “never clearly condemned the October 17 violence”.
Paris's Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums closed on Saturday
The Louvre Museum – one of the world’s most visited – and some other Paris museums, like Musée d’Orsay and Picasso, will be closed this Saturday due to the risks to visitors, security staff and artwork amid the protests, the culture ministry said.
Protests banned in Marseille on Saturday
Authorities have banned all protests Saturday in France’s southern city of Marseille, and suspended public transport on that day, to try to prevent a repeat of rioting during fresh demonstrations planned.
The prefecture for the Rhone region covering the city gave the orders “for the obvious reasons of security”. It also expanded a curfew for minors in the city centre, which will also apply to adults for Saturday and Sunday nights.
Heavy police presence around Paris student protest
Paris shop-owners arm themselves ‘in case looters come’
In a Paris gun shop, sales of legal weapons have “gone up 10 times” ahead of this weekend’s protests.
Shop-owners “are arming themselves because they’re very afraid”, Yves Gollet, who owns the shop told AFP, adding he was already sold out of flash-balls, a weapon that fires non-lethal rubber projectiles.
In another Paris gun shop, a customer, who did not wish to be identified, said he had bought pepper spray, “in case looters come into the store” he owns, which sells eyeglasses.
Art Basel Paris says to shut this weekend due to protest risk
Art Basel Paris, the biggest annual art fair in the French capital, said it would shut this weekend, two days early, due to the risk of protests.
In a message to visitors, organisers said that "in light of potential demonstrations across Paris this weekend, and in the interest of safeguarding our visitors, exhibitors, partners, staff, and artworks", the show would finish on Friday evening, instead of Sunday as originally planned.
Several thousands to protest against National Rally congress in Orléans Saturday, ‘radical elements’ expected
Between 20,000 and 30,000 anti-far right activists are expected to protest against the National Rally’s (RN) party congress in Orléans on Saturday.
Regional Prefect Hugues Moutouh said that the demonstration is expected to attract between 2,000 and 3,000 “radical elements”.
In run-up to mass protests and riots, pro-Russian accounts amplified French anger, NGO finds
Research carried out by the Alliance4Europe NGO suggests that pro-Russian networks manipulated information online in an effort to exacerbate anger in France ahead of last weekend's massive protests and subsequent unrest. After analysing more than half a million posts across various social media platforms, the group says it was able to track the campaign back to the start of September. FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney speaks with Omri Preiss, Managing Director at the Alliance4Europe.
More than 200 people sent to prison over weekend unrest, justice minister says
French courts have jailed 217 people after convicting them in fast-track trials linked to last weekend's rioting, the justice minister said Thursday, hailing the judiciary's "extremely firm" response.
Speaking outside the Fleury-Merogis prison on the outskirts of Paris, Gerald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been detained since Saturday.
More than 1,000 of them had appeared in court, he said, of whom "217 people have been imprisoned... and this figure is continuing to rise a lot".
Darmanin told reporters that of the 217 sent to jail "half had no criminal record", adding that "in general these are men aged between 18 to 25".
French PM Sébastien Lecornu meets with leaders of political parties amid unrest
French PM Sébastien Lecornu holds a meeting with the leaders of political parties after unrest this weekend across the country. The aim is to prevent potential violence during the next protests, including on Saturday as the "Yellow vests" movement called for a new mobilisation. Details by FRANCE 24's Luke Shrago.
REPLAY: French President vows to prevent violence ahead of protests
French President Emmanuel Macron spoke to the press on Thursday after a meeting with security chiefs. He said that "illegitimate" protests would be banned in coming days, while those from organised groups such as unions would be offered alternative paths for the marches to protect businesses.
What is happening in France? Unpacking the recent waves of protests
Laura D. Keesman, an assistant professor of sociology based in Amsterdam, analysed recent French mobilisations and the government's police response. After weekend of unrest and riots, the government acknowledged that the security response had fallen short and promised a stronger approach ahead of a new wave of protests.
City of Paris urges residents to exercise ‘extreme caution’ on Saturday
Paris city hall has issued a statement urging Parisians to exercise “extreme caution” during the protests that are planned in the French capital on Saturday.
An estimated 450 businesses were damaged in Paris in the unrest that broke out over the weekend, and roughly half of them were looted. Cars, bicycles, and rubbish bins were also torched and vandalized.
"Starting Thursday, the city is taking several preventive measures in public spaces, stepping up the deployment of municipal staff over the weekend and urging residents and shopkeepers to take a few simple precautions," the city said.
It recommended bringing rubbish bins, bicycles and outdoor furniture indoors "from midday Saturday".
Ahead of the planned demonstrations, city hall said it had begun "clearing public spaces, as far as possible, of equipment and materials that could be used to cause damage, particularly barriers and movable construction site equipment". Street litter bins are being emptied and glass recycling containers removed, it added.
Trials underway for October 17 vandals and looters
Many of those arrested for looting and vandalism during the October 17 rallies are already being tried. While some say they did not understand that it was theft to pick up goods that lay strewn outside the broken shop windows, others claim to have been accidentally trapped inside the stores they were caught in. FRANCE 24's David Rich tells us more about the court hearings.
Paris police have banned a student protest scheduled for Thursday, citing the organisers' “inability to prevent violence and vandalism”, a police source told AFP.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu will on Thursday meet with the mayors of some of the cities that were worst hit by the riots over the weekend, including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.

Pentagon, Lockheed Agree on 10-Year Framework for Buying F-35s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:02:40 UTC
01:02:40 KST

The Pentagon and Lockheed Martin on Oct. 22 announced a framework agreement to buy F-35 Joint Strike Fighters for the next 10 years.
But the deal, touted by the Pentagon as “landmark” and a first of its kind, depends on Congress granting the military authority to enter into such a multiyear agreement.
Under the deal, Lockheed will build 156 of the fifth-generation jets per year for both the U.S. and international customers, across lots 21 through 30. The U.S. military will buy at least 850 of those 1,560 aircraft over the decade covering the agreement, as well as procurement of initial spare parts and modification kits, the Pentagon and Lockheed said in statements. The deal also covers sustainment of the global F-35 fleet.
Details such as pricing and schedules have yet to be hammered out. It’s also unclear how many of each F-35 variant will be produced, and how many will go to individual services like the Air Force, Navy, and Marine Corps.
“We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale,” Michael Duffey, undersecretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment, said in the Pentagon’s statement. “This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win.”
Lockheed Martin has also agreed to invest at least $7 billion of its own money into projects to support the F-35 program.
“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” Lockheed President and CEO Jim Taiclet said in the company’s statement. “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain.”
While the Defense Department touted the agreement’s ability to create “a stable, long-term procurement signal to modernize and expand” the F-35, it also noted in its statement that actually executing the agreement “remains subject to congressional authorization and appropriations.”
Congress is currently considering granting the Pentagon the authority to enter into multiyear procurement contracts for the F-35 and F-15EX fighters as part of its work on the 2027 defense policy bill. Lawmakers have also yet to pass a budget for fiscal 2027, leaving the agreement unfunded at the moment.
With all that legislation still pending, the Oct. 22 announcement is only a framework and not finalized.
Lockheed said if Congress does grant the multiyear procurement authority and the necessary appropriations in the next few months, it will work with the F-35 Joint Program Office to finalize the contract terms, pricing, and schedules through a formal award.
Lockheed said having predictable, multiyear procurement plans for the F-35 would save billions of dollars “through long-term pricing and industry volume discounts.” And the agreement will allow the program to combine data from a variety of sources into integrated analytics, that will provide more visibility into parts inventory and readiness metrics and allow “transparent, data-driven decision making.”
The deal will also allow Lockheed to enter into long-term contracts with suppliers to buy raw materials and critical parts in bulk, which the company predicted would improve F-35 mission-capable rates. Currently, those deals are made on an annual basis, which Lockheed said “has historically strained the industrial base.”
In an earnings call with investors Oct. 22, Taiclet said at least 60 percent of an F-35’s content comes from its suppliers, including major suppliers such as Northrop Grumman and BAE Systems, which make the center and aft sections of the jets’ bodies, respectively.
“We want them to have production stability, just as we would like to have it,” Taiclet said.
Taiclet said one of Lockheed’s biggest costs comes from suppliers providing components late, or at poor quality, and he predicted this agreement will help correct those problems.
Taiclet told investors that Lockheed and its suppliers will be under a fixed-price escalation contract, in which set prices increase under certain economic conditions.
“We’ll all collectively—if we do well and perform well, and those investments pay off that we make—we will get to retain those profits under the fixed-price-with-escalator concept,” Taiclet said. “Before, we would have to give back, with price and operating profit, any improvements we invested in internally. So that is going to apply to the production system. Even if it stays at 156, it’ll be a much healthier production system for industry, and a more predictable production system for government.”
And combining aircraft production with the purchase of spare parts and modification kits in the same contract will also yield volume savings and cost predictability, Lockheed said.
“Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” Lockheed Martin Aeronautics President OJ Sanchez said in the company’s statement. “This, in addition to the investments Lockheed Martin is making to the global spares pool, will directly translate into higher mission-capable rates and a more resilient supply chain—critical capabilities the warfighter needs to meet today’s mission and prepare for tomorrow’s threats.”
During the earnings call, Taiclet reiterated Lockheed’s desire—first voiced in April 2025, after the company lost the Air Force’s F-47 contract to Boeing—to add sixth-generation technologies into the F-35, which he previously referred to as making a “Ferrari” F-35. Taiclet said this could achieve 80 percent of a bespoke sixth-generation aircraft’s capabilities, at half the cost.
Lockheed’s primary F-35 factory is in Fort Worth, Texas.

Saudi oil boss issues global supply warning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:01:52 UTC
01:01:52 KST

Saudi oil boss issues global supply warning
The US-Israeli war on Iran has caused an “unprecedented” shock to global energy markets, removing some 3 billion barrels of oil supply, Saudi Aramco CEO Amin Nasser has warned.
The war launched in February effectively shut the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial oil and LNG artery, sending crude prices up roughly 50%. Despite Gulf exports recovering to a reported 80% of pre-war levels, renewed attacks on vessels have kept markets on edge, with Brent hitting a five-month high above $112 this week. Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and shipping have compounded the crisis, threatening another vital trade chokepoint, the Red Sea’s Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
In an interview with Al Arabiya Business aired on Thursday, Nasser said the nearly eight-month crisis had deprived global markets of an estimated 3 billion barrels of oil.
“The impact of this crisis on energy markets is unprecedented,” he said. “We have lost around 3 billion barrels since it began. And bear in mind that the Gulf accounts for roughly 20% of global oil demand.”
The figure is equivalent to nearly a month of global oil consumption and reflects cumulative supply losses caused by disrupted shipping, reduced production and logistical bottlenecks.
With global oil inventories already below their five-year average when the war erupted, prices could have soared past $200 a barrel, Nasser warned. He credited emergency reserve releases, China’s sharp cut in seaborne oil imports and Saudi Aramco’s East-West pipeline, which bypasses Hormuz, with averting an even more severe price shock.
Nasser warned, however, that even an end to the crisis could bring fresh pressure on oil markets, as recovering consumption and a rush to replenish depleted reserves will likely fuel another demand surge.
“Once things return to normal, we expect additional demand of around 3 million barrels per day – about 2 million from consumption growth and another 1 million just to replenish the reserves countries have drawn down during the crisis,” he said, noting that the added demand could keep markets under strain long after shipping routes reopen.
Fresh escalation fears
Meanwhile, fears of another escalation are growing as US-Iran talks remain deadlocked. Reports on Wednesday claimed Washington was quietly pulling troops from bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait, evacuating some diplomats and their families from Saudi Arabia and preparing similar withdrawals elsewhere. Similar precautions were taken ahead of the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
The moves follow US President Donald Trump’s rejection last month of Tehran’s proposal to reopen Hormuz in exchange for lifting the US blockade of Iranian ports, easing oil export restrictions, unfreezing Iranian assets and ending regional hostilities, including Israeli operations in Gaza and Lebanon.
Washington and Israel have since reportedly discussed another major offensive, potentially soon after the November 3 US midterms. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has also openly threatened fresh strikes on Iran, even without US backing.

Shas rabbi warns voters backing rival parties will have 'no place in the afterlife'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:01:09 UTC
01:01:09 KST

A senior rabbi in the ultra-Orthodox Shas party has warned that Jews who vote for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud or another political party will have no place in the afterlife, escalating a fierce battle for religious voters ahead of next week's national election.
Rabbi Moshe Maya, the oldest member of Shas' Council of Torah Sages and a former lawmaker who served in the Knesset in the 1990s, made the declaration as the party sought to prevent supporters from defecting to other parties on the political right.
"Anyone who votes for Likud or another party has no share in the world to come," Maya said, invoking the Jewish religious concept of Olam HaBa, or the world to come, commonly associated with the afterlife and spiritual reward.
The remarks underscored the increasingly heated rhetoric among the ultra-Orthodox parties as they compete for votes with Likud and other right-wing factions.
Shas, which primarily represents Sephardic and Mizrahi ultra-Orthodox Jews, has traditionally relied on the authority of prominent rabbis to mobilize its electorate. Religious endorsements and rulings play a significant role in the party's election campaigns, particularly among voters who regard rabbinical guidance as binding.
Former chief rabbi renews attack on Ben-Gvir
In a separate speech in Jerusalem, former Sephardic Chief Rabbi Yitzhak Yosef, another influential Shas religious leader, warned that a victory by the opposition bloc would bring severe restrictions on the ultra-Orthodox community.
"If the left comes to power, it will create difficulties," Yosef said. "What we have now will be nothing by comparison. It will be many times worse. You cannot imagine the decrees that will come."
Yosef claimed that an opposition leader had proposed expanding compulsory military service to include religious women, in addition to ultra-Orthodox yeshiva students.
"One of the leaders of the left said, 'We are not finished. We will also introduce the conscription of women, not just yeshiva students, but women into the army,'" he said.
"That is something one must die rather than transgress," Yosef added, invoking a principle in Jewish religious law under which certain prohibitions must not be violated even at the cost of one's life.
Military conscription has long been one of the most contentious issues in Israeli politics. Most ultra-Orthodox men have historically received exemptions or deferments while studying in religious seminaries, an arrangement that has faced growing legal and political challenges.
The issue has become especially divisive amid the military's manpower needs and demands for a more equal distribution of the burden of national service.
Yosef also reiterated a religious ruling he issued earlier this week prohibiting his followers from voting for National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose far-right political movement competes with Shas for support among religious and nationalist voters.
"It is forbidden to vote for him," Yosef said. "Anyone who votes for him is as though he himself ascended the Temple Mount. A person's agent is considered equivalent to the person himself."
The Temple Mount, known to Muslims as the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound, is the holiest site in Judaism and the third-holiest in Islam. While Ben-Gvir has advocated Jewish prayer rights at the site, many leading ultra-Orthodox rabbis prohibit Jews from entering the compound because of religious restrictions concerning ritual purity and the location of the ancient Jewish temples.
Yosef's remarks reflected that longstanding religious disagreement with Ben-Gvir, whose visits to the site have repeatedly generated controversy.
The former chief rabbi also accused Ben-Gvir of failing to intervene against police violence toward ultra-Orthodox demonstrators.
"Look at how the police beat the ultra-Orthodox," Yosef said. "He is the minister responsible for the police. Has he said a word?"
Yosef alleged that Ben-Gvir benefited politically from confrontations between police and ultra-Orthodox protesters because they could weaken support for Shas representatives.
"He is happy about it because people will get angry with our representatives and his support will rise," Yosef said.
He further questioned Ben-Gvir's contributions to ultra-Orthodox religious institutions.
"Has he established a single religious school? A ritual bath? A synagogue?" Yosef asked.
Addressing young religious voters, particularly Sephardic yeshiva students considering supporting Ben-Gvir, he added: "How is that even a consideration?"
Ultra-Orthodox parties devise new voter-tracking system
Meanwhile, United Torah Judaism, the other major ultra-Orthodox party, is preparing an alternative voter-monitoring operation following a Supreme Court ruling barring polling station committee representatives from transmitting real-time information about voter turnout to party campaign headquarters.
The practice has been a central component of ultra-Orthodox election campaigns, particularly in tightly knit religious communities where parties use turnout information to identify supporters who have not yet voted and encourage them to cast ballots.
The court's restrictions prevent party representatives serving on official polling station committees from digitally transmitting such information in real time.
United Torah Judaism is now preparing a separate monitoring operation designed to collect information outside the official election administration system.
Under the plan, a registration booth will be placed at the entrance to each polling station, outside the restricted area reserved for election officials and voters. Workers will record the identities of people entering to vote, with the information subsequently transferred to party headquarters without passing through the official polling station committee.
Agudat Yisrael, a Hasidic faction within United Torah Judaism, is preparing an additional system.
Party officials said they would establish dedicated tents at clusters of polling stations, staffed by married yeshiva students engaged in full-time religious study.
After casting their ballots, voters will be asked to visit the tents and report that they have voted using a designated digital platform.
To encourage participation, the faction has launched a campaign under the slogan, "If you voted but didn't report it, you didn't vote."
The initiative is being led by Jerusalem Deputy Mayor Tzachi Brim.
The arrangements are intended to preserve the parties' ability to monitor turnout and mobilize supporters despite the court-imposed restrictions on information sharing by official polling station representatives.

Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:01:00 UTC
01:01:00 KST

Are the French police the most violent in the EU?
October 22, 2026
Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.
The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups, not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.
France's protests grow
More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.
Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.
The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.
More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.
Weapons made for war?
The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.
Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests. In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.
"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."
Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.
What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.
"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.
Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material."
French police: the 'most brutal' in the EU?
The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.
"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Roche.
He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.
"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."
Confrontation vs. de-escalation
Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.
Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.
"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."
When can police officers use force?
According to international standards set by the United Nations, use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.
French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.
However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."
The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.
DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.
"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."
Experts are critical of the police's actions.
"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."
Less oversight than in the UK and Denmark
The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.
Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.
"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."
Edited by: Carla Bleiker

Disney’s multiplatform Super Bowl plan frustrates ABC affiliates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:50 UTC
01:00:50 KST

Disney knows that business, like football, is a contact sport. Sometimes the hits come in-house from feuding among executives. Sometimes they come in court, from battling the Federal Communications Commission.
And sometimes, Disney, which owns ABC, takes hits from its own affiliates.
ABC station owners are irritated with Disney's recent decision to air the Super Bowl on many different platforms, including Disney+, ESPN2, NFL Network and ESPNU. The game is already airing on both ABC and ESPN. The aggregate of the different platforms may drop advertising revenue associated with broadcast viewership by up to 35% compared to last year, according to a station group CEO who asked not to be named because the data is private.
Disney has the broadcast rights to this season's Super Bowl. ABC hasn't had the Super Bowl since 2006. Disney got back in the Super Bowl rotation when it struck its most recent media rights deal with the NFL in 2021.
The Super Bowl is a major moneymaker for ABC stations. Some of these are owned by Disney, but the vast majority are part of local station groups owned by companies such as Sinclair, Nexstar and Tegna.
Fox said last year that Super Bowl ads generated more than $800 million in gross revenue across all platforms. The math for the main broadcast network is simple. There are about 85 30-second spots during a standard game. At $8 million a pop on average, that's $680 million.
Most advertising campaigns are national, but some brands buy big markets only. That allows smaller markets to sell advertising locally.
An average primetime audience is around eight million viewers. So, if the Super Bowl gets 15 times the audience, advertising rates increase in lockstep. Super Bowl LX, held in February, had 125.6 million viewers.
About 3% of a typical local affiliate station's annual advertising revenue comes from the Super Bowl when the game is on its air, according to a person familiar with the matter. The number can be much higher for the owned-and-operated big market stations, which typically take in about $10 million in advertising revenue from the Super Bowl, according to a source familiar with the matter.
Local affiliate stations pay the owners of the broadcast networks — Disney for ABC, Comcast for NBC, Fox for Fox and Skydance for CBS — a so-called reverse retransmission fee for the right to carry network programming.
There's a standard process to retransmission fee discussions. Disney pays billions for live sports and then asks its affiliates for money to help pay for them. The affiliates then negotiate with the pay-TV providers and charge them retrans fees.
This is why the broadcast affiliates are steaming. For decades, the Super Bowl was exclusive to broadcast TV. Getting access to the Big Game was a big part of that fee.
For years, media companies have made the Super Bowl available for both broadcast and streaming audiences. Still, this year, Disney has taken a wrecking ball to the broadcast exclusivity of the past.
Disney's different options
Given the game is an ESPN production with ESPN's primary "Monday Night Football" announcing crew — Joe Buck and Troy Aikman — it's reasonable to assume the cable network will get a fair amount of viewership for the game.
Disney is also putting the game on Disney+ — a streaming service that's never been about sports. Airing the Super Bowl on a streaming service isn't new. NBCUniversal's Peacock, Fox's Tubi and Skydance's Paramount+ have streamed the game in the past. But those services allow for geofenced dynamic advertising insertion (DAI), allowing local affiliates to sell commercials to a streaming audience. Disney+, which doesn't typically air live ABC sports programming, doesn't have DAI.
Disney is also airing so-called "alt-casts" of the game on ESPN2 (Eli and Peyton Manning will do their typical "ManningCast"), ESPNU ("Super Bowl LXI Field Pass with The Pat McAfee Show"), and NFL Network ("Super Bowl LXI Playbook with Next Gen Stats").
Disney is even airing a "Star Wars"-themed alt-cast on Disney Channel and Disney XD. The "Star Wars" alternative broadcast will also be on Disney+.
The commercials that run nationally will be the same on all platforms, according to a Disney spokesperson. The "Star Wars" alt-cast will be ad-free.
Disney wants to synergize its platforms to maximize viewership — and collect the ad revenue.
"The Super Bowl is the year's most-watched telecast, and our broad distribution across ESPN, ABC, and Disney+ will give fans everywhere more ways than ever to enjoy the game," according to a statement provided by a Disney spokesperson. "Making marquee live events available via streaming is a well-established industry practice. Fox and NBC have recently offered the Super Bowl on Tubi and Peacock, and we've similarly streamed 'The Oscars' on Hulu and 'Dancing with the Stars' on Disney+, for example. There's nothing unprecedented about this approach as we are meeting the modern consumer where they are."
Still, the totality of it all will certainly lower broadcast viewership. One station group CEO estimated local advertising revenue associated with the game may fall 35%. That executive declined to be named because the analysis is private.
"Any time you fragment distribution, you're destroying value for each of the individual platforms," a station group CEO told me, who asked not to be named for fear of potential retribution. "I don't have a problem with what Disney is doing — I have a problem that there's no acknowledgement that we're losing money."
Affiliate board involvement
This issue of lower broadcast Super Bowl viewership, and associated advertising revenue, is of so much concern that it's currently being discussed at the affiliate board — an elected body of executives across the TV broadcasting industry who act as liaisons between local stations and their parent network (Disney/ABC, in this case).
It's unclear exactly how affiliates may be compensated, if at all.
The decline in traditional TV viewership is pushing Disney to broaden its coverage to new platforms and new audiences that don't watch cable or broadcast TV.
Station executives want Disney to lean in to what continues to be a profitable, albeit declining, business. Several of those executives told me privately they think Disney is doing itself and the broader linear TV ecosystem a disservice by not banding together with affiliates to keep viewers on broadcast platforms.
"Our ABC affiliates are important partners and we always take that into careful consideration when making these decisions," said a Disney spokesperson. "We've successfully navigated similar situations in collaboration with the governing board many times before, and this is no different."
The chairman of the ABC Television Affiliates Association Board of Governors declined to comment.

Second attack in 2 days

Eight residential houses were damaged, Bunechko reported in a statement on social media, confirming that no casualties were reported.

German AfD party asks government about UFOs, aerial phenomena
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:30 UTC
01:00:30 KST

Ayhan Simsek
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Germany’s right-wing AfD party has asked the government whether public institutions are reporting incidents of unidentified aerial phenomena, and whether any findings exist on the topic.
The parliamentary question, signed by the party’s co-chairs Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, follows recent US Pentagon reports, congressional hearings involving pilots and officials, and scientific work by NASA.
In the inquiry, lawmakers asked which ministries or offices are responsible for receiving and evaluating reports of unidentified aerial phenomena and since when records have been kept. They also inquired whether specific terms and definitions such as “UAP” or “UFO” are used and whether standardized federal guidelines exist for public officials.
The Defense Ministry replied to the parliamentary question on behalf of the government, and the response was published on the parliament’s website this week. “There is no information available regarding unidentified aerial phenomena,” the ministry said, adding that the government uses no specific terms or definitions such as “UFO,” “UAP” or “unidentifiable contacts.”
The ministry said monitoring of German airspace is handled by the interior, transport and defense ministries, while tracking objects near Earth in space is the job of the research, technology and space and defense ministries. Officials added that there are no special reporting channels for pilots, air traffic controllers and other personnel to report sightings of unidentified objects in the air or space.

Higher progesterone is linked to blurrier brain signals for emotional control, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:22 UTC
01:00:22 KST

Young women with higher natural levels of the hormone progesterone tend to show less distinct brain activity patterns when they must override their automatic emotional impulses, according to a new neuroimaging study published in Psychological Medicine. The findings suggest that progesterone may blur the neural signals that help the brain regulate emotional actions. Reduced precision in a frontal brain region also accounted for an indirect statistical pathway linking higher progesterone to worse recent mood.
In everyday life, people naturally gravitate toward positive or rewarding things and pull away from threats or unpleasant situations. Psychologists refer to this automatic habit as approach-avoidance behavior. Overriding these instincts, such as stepping toward an angry person or walking away from something appealing, requires active emotional control.
This regulatory process relies heavily on the lateral frontal pole, a brain structure located at the very front of the cerebral cortex just behind the forehead. A 2020 neuroimaging study indicated that the lateral frontal pole plays a key role in overriding automatic impulses when people have to make these kinds of emotional choices. When this region fails to properly guide behavior, people tend to struggle with emotional regulation, as seen in a 2023 study covered by PsyPost showing that highly anxious individuals have difficulty recruiting the lateral frontal pole and must rely on other brain regions instead.
Scientists have also found that sex hormones can influence these exact brain circuits. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2023 indicated that high levels of the hormone testosterone are associated with reduced activity in the anterior prefrontal cortex during emotional control in adulthood. Far less is known about how the female ovarian hormones estradiol and progesterone shape these regulatory networks.
“Historically, neuroscience research has disproportionately focused on men, partly because hormonal fluctuations across the menstrual cycle were considered a source of unwanted variability,” study author Macià Buades-Rotger, an associate professor of clinical psychology and psychobiology at the University of Barcelona, told PsyPost. “As a result, we still know surprisingly little about how naturally occurring changes in ovarian hormones influence the brain and behavior.”
“At the same time, the relationship between female hormones and emotions is surrounded by sexist stereotypes and assumptions that often have little scientific basis,” Buades-Rotger added. “I was interested in moving beyond these simplistic narratives to investigate what hormones actually do in the brain, particularly how they might influence the mechanisms that allow us to control our automatic emotional responses.”
Both estradiol and progesterone fluctuate naturally throughout the menstrual cycle, and shifts in these hormones are frequently tied to changes in emotional well-being. The authors of a 2020 review argued that progesterone can act like a double-edged sword: one of its chemical byproducts has proven useful for treating depression after childbirth, yet the hormone may trigger negative symptoms in women with premenstrual syndrome or premenstrual dysphoric disorder, a severe form of premenstrual mood disturbance. Meanwhile, a 2019 neuroimaging study of naturally cycling women found that during the cycle phase when progesterone is high, frontal and striatal regions tended to be more active during mental tasks.
Most earlier brain imaging studies looked only at whether entire brain regions became more or less active overall in response to hormones. Buades-Rotger and his colleagues wanted to look deeper by examining whether estradiol and progesterone relate to fine-grained patterns of brain activity during emotional control, and whether those patterns connect to recent mood.
To investigate this in a preregistered study, the researchers recruited 116 healthy, naturally cycling women between the ages of 18 and 35. None of the participants were using hormonal contraceptives or had a history of neurological, hormonal, or recent psychiatric disorders. Before entering the brain scanner, each participant provided a saliva sample (stimulated by chewing gum) so the researchers could measure their current levels of estradiol and progesterone.
Participants also completed questionnaires measuring their typical emotion regulation habits and their mood over the preceding seven days. The mood survey assessed feelings of friendliness, vigor, fatigue, anger, tension, and depression, which the researchers combined into a single overall mood score. All testing sessions took place between 4 p.m. and 7 p.m. to minimize natural daily fluctuations in hormone levels.
Inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging scanner, which tracks brain activity by measuring changes in blood flow, the women completed a 240-trial approach-avoidance task. During the task, they viewed photographs of actors displaying happy or angry facial expressions. Depending on the instructions for each block of trials, participants pressed buttons to either “approach” a face, which made the image grow larger as if looming closer, or “avoid” a face, which made the image shrink as if receding.
In half of the trials, the instructions matched natural human instincts: approaching happy faces and avoiding angry ones. In the other half, the instructions went against those instincts, requiring participants to approach angry faces and avoid happy ones. After excluding six participants with unusually high error rates, the researchers analyzed the behavioral responses of 110 women.
As expected, overriding automatic emotional tendencies took more effort. When participants had to approach angry faces, their average reaction time was 0.782 seconds with an error rate of 1.52 percent, compared to 0.663 seconds and a 0.55 percent error rate when approaching happy faces. Similarly, avoiding happy faces took an average of 0.762 seconds with a 1.36 percent error rate, compared to 0.684 seconds and a 0.64 percent error rate when avoiding angry faces.
Next, the researchers examined the brain scans of 106 participants, after excluding four additional women who moved too much in the scanner. Instead of just measuring overall blood flow in a given brain area, the team used a machine learning technique called multivoxel pattern analysis. A voxel is a tiny three-dimensional unit of brain tissue, similar to a three-dimensional pixel.
The computer algorithm looked at the detailed grid of activity across thousands of voxels during odd-numbered trials and tried to predict which task condition the participant was performing during even-numbered trials. If the computer could accurately tell whether a participant was overriding their instincts or following them based on a region’s activity pattern, it meant that brain area was distinctly encoding the rules of emotional control.
The algorithm had to sort each trial into one of the four task conditions, so guessing would be right 25 percent of the time. Activity patterns in several regions allowed it to beat that chance level, including the lateral frontal pole, the striatum (a cluster of neurons deep beneath the cortex that helps manage movement and reward), the central insula (a region involved in processing internal bodily states and emotions), the primary visual cortex, the cerebellum, and the periaqueductal gray (a brainstem area involved in threat responses). The amygdala, a threat-processing region the researchers had planned in advance to examine, did not distinguish between the conditions. The algorithm mainly succeeded at telling instinct-opposing trials apart from instinct-matching ones, while often confusing the two conditions within each type.
When the researchers combined the brain data, hormone levels, and mood scores for the 101 participants who had complete data across all measures, they found a consistent link with progesterone. Women with higher concentrations of salivary progesterone showed lower classification accuracy in both the lateral frontal pole (r = −0.25) and the striatum (r = −0.26). In other words, in women with higher progesterone, the brain activity patterns representing emotional control in these two regions were less distinct and harder for the algorithm to tell apart.
“In everyday life, we constantly encounter situations in which our automatic emotional reactions conflict with what we actually need to do,” Buades-Rotger explained. “Imagine needing to ask a grumpy colleague for help: your instinct might be to avoid them, but achieving your goal requires approaching them instead. Our findings suggest that higher progesterone levels may make the brain’s representation of these competing emotional demands less clear, potentially making it harder to distinguish when to follow an instinctive reaction and when to override it. This could be one way in which natural hormonal fluctuations subtly influence how we navigate emotionally challenging situations.”
Sharper activity patterns in the lateral frontal pole were also associated with better mood over the past week (r = 0.26). Even without a direct correlation between progesterone and mood reported in the study, a preregistered mediation analysis found a small indirect pathway: higher progesterone was linked to less distinct frontal patterns, which were in turn linked to worse recent mood. The model explained 7.1 percent of the variation in mood scores, and a reversed version that swapped the roles of progesterone and the brain patterns produced a weaker effect that was not statistically significant.
Contrary to the researchers’ initial expectations, estradiol levels were not linked to brain decoding accuracy or to mood. In addition, neither estradiol nor progesterone correlated with how quickly or accurately participants pressed the buttons during the behavioral task. When the researchers divided participants into early and late stages of the menstrual cycle based on self-reported cycle length, they found higher progesterone in the late phase as expected, but cycle phase by itself was not linked to differences in mood, task performance, or brain decoding accuracy.
“What surprised me most was the absence of comparable effects for estradiol,” Buades-Rotger noted. “Both estradiol and progesterone are known to influence brain function, and we had good reasons to expect that either hormone might be associated with how emotional control is represented in the brain. Instead, the associations we identified were specific to progesterone. This does not mean that estradiol has no role in emotional regulation, but it suggests that the two hormones may influence these processes through different mechanisms.”
The authors suggest that progesterone may make brain activity patterns more diffuse across frontal and striatal circuits. While this blurring of emotional signals might make it harder to actively regulate mood and impulses, the researchers note that a slight blunting of emotional representations could be helpful in other ways, such as reducing sensitivity to physical pain during the second half of the menstrual cycle.
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these findings. Because the researchers collected only a single saliva sample and brain scan from each woman at one point in time, the study cannot prove that higher progesterone directly causes changes in brain patterns or mood. In addition, the 101 participants included in the correlation analyses fell short of the preregistered target of 120, leaving the study with 71 percent statistical power to detect effects of the observed size. Tracking the same individuals across multiple days of their menstrual cycles in future studies will be necessary to separate temporary hormonal states from stable personal traits.
“One important misconception would be that higher progesterone necessarily makes women more emotional or less capable of controlling their behavior,” Buades-Rotger emphasized. “That is not what our study shows. We examined statistical associations between naturally occurring hormone levels, patterns of brain activity, and mood in healthy young women; we did not experimentally manipulate progesterone or demonstrate that these neural differences cause changes in emotional behavior. It is also important to remember that hormonal effects vary considerably between individuals, and many women experience little or no noticeable mood changes across the menstrual cycle.”
Methodological factors may have also introduced measurement noise that masked potential effects of estradiol. The researchers used chewing gum to help participants produce saliva, which is known to alter measured concentrations of steroid hormones, and salivary estradiol is a poor marker of menstrual cycle phase. In this sample, estradiol did not differ between the early and late phases of the cycle, while progesterone did. Finally, the pathway linking progesterone, frontal brain patterns, and mood accounted for just over 7 percent of the variation in mood among participants, meaning most of the differences in how participants felt were explained by other factors.
“The associations we observed were relatively modest, which is unsurprising given that mood and emotional regulation depend on many interacting biological, psychological, and environmental factors,” Buades-Rotger said. “Progesterone is certainly not a master switch that determines how someone feels or behaves. The significance of our findings lies primarily in identifying a potential brain mechanism linking hormonal variation to mood, rather than demonstrating a large or immediately noticeable effect on everyday behavior.”
Looking ahead, the researchers hope to test these hormonal pathways more directly over time. “An important next step would be to follow the same women across different phases of the menstrual cycle to determine whether changes in progesterone are accompanied by corresponding changes in neural representations of emotion control,” Buades-Rotger said. “Pharmacological studies that experimentally manipulate progesterone levels or the activity of its neuroactive metabolites would provide a more direct test of causality. Ultimately, understanding these mechanisms could help explain why some women are particularly sensitive to hormonal fluctuations, including those who experience premenstrual dysphoria, and potentially inform future approaches to treatment.”
“I think our findings also illustrate the value of looking beyond conventional measures of brain activation,” Buades-Rotger concluded. “This allowed us to investigate how information about emotional control is represented in the brain. More broadly, the study highlights why hormonal state should be taken seriously as a meaningful source of variation in neuroscience, rather than simply treated as a nuisance variable.”
The study, “Endogenous progesterone blurs frontostriatal representations of emotion control in healthy young women,” was authored by Macià Buades-Rotger, Rosamunde Hendricks, Beatrice Roncarati, Marta Calderón-García, Kaja Bergmann, and Francisco José Pérez-Cano.

The One Question AI Could Not Answer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:10 UTC
01:00:10 KST

The One Question AI Could Not Answer
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Why Children Need More Than Screens to Master the Future
Hong Kong is moving decisively into the age of artificial intelligence in education. The government has committed significant funding to digital education, supporting schools in purchasing AI tools, digital resources and related training. The message from policymakers is clear: our children must learn to master technology.
They are right. But true mastery requires much more than screen time.
To master AI, children must first master something far older, subtler and more profound themselves.
Artificial intelligence can calculate, translate, summarise, generate images and simulate conversation at astonishing speed. Used well, it can support learning and open new possibilities. But AI cannot replace the experiences through which children become grounded, confident, imaginative and fully human.
This is why, at Garden House Waldorf School, our approach to education begins not with the screen, but with the child.
The Senses Are Not Optional
Children do not become fully human through information alone. They become human through experience.
The evidence on screen time is alarming. Studies tracking children aged two to five have found that as screen time increases, so does emotional fragility, irritability, difficulty calming down, and an inability to complete tasks. These patterns persist across age groups from six to seventeen. Children with high screen exposure struggle to remain calm when faced with challenges. Their curiosity declines. The risks of anxiety and depression escalate.
These behaviours are not signs of dysfunction. They are signals of confusion — of a child who has lost their internal compass. The problem is not merely the screen itself. It is everything that screen time displaces: physical activity, imaginative play, face-to-face interaction, and the rich sensory engagement that builds resilience.
For those of us living in cities, there is another urgent concern. A landmark study involving over 300,000 children found that for every additional hour of daily screen time, the risk of myopia increases. At four hours per day, the risk roughly doubles. In parts of Asia, myopia rates have surged from modest levels in the 1970s to 80 or even 90 percent today. The eye is designed for flexibility — alternating between distant horizons and nearby objects. Locked onto screens for hours, it loses that adaptability.
The Sensory Imbalance of the Digital Age
Consider the online meetings that have become part of our daily lives. They engage at most two senses: vision and hearing. The sense of warmth — that tangible experience of human presence — is entirely absent.
This is the deeper risk of the AI era. A mode of perception dominated by vision and hearing will only intensify, leaving the lower senses — touch, smell, taste, life sense, balance and movement — chronically underdeveloped. AI excels at recognising words. But it operates on a dangerous assumption: that understanding words is equivalent to understanding thought, and that understanding thought is equivalent to understanding another human being. Everything becomes confined to the literal, with no warmth to complete the circuit.
There are people who "know" each other through social media, yet find themselves completely lost when meeting in real life. They possess information about one another, but they lack the sensory experience of one another. Their sensory pathway is incomplete.
Wisdom Cannot Be Downloaded
None of this means that technology is bad, nor that AI should be kept out of education forever. Children must eventually learn to understand it, question it and use it wisely.
But the key word is wisely.
The question for our age is not whether children will use AI. They will. The question is whether they will bring to it a fully developed humanity — bodies that are awake, senses that are alive, hearts that can feel, and minds that can judge.
That is the one question AI could not answer. It can only be answered by how we choose to educate our children.

Navy drone project kept quiet to protect advantage
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:00:07 BST
01:00:07 KST

Project HORUS is supporting an urgent operational requirement, and the Ministry of Defence will not specify the platforms involved, the length of the contract or the timing of a procurement decision in order to protect operational advantage, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, tabled three questions on the project, asking what platforms are being used by the Royal Navy under Project HORUS, what the length is of the contract for the capability provided, and by when a procurement decision will be made to replace the capability currently under contract.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, gave the same answer to all three: “Project HORUS is supporting an urgent operational requirement and so the MoD would not wish to specify specific platforms or procurement decisions at this stage, so as to protect operational advantage.”
An urgent operational requirement is the mechanism Britain’s forces use to buy equipment outside the normal procurement cycle when an operation needs a capability quickly, and it carries its own funding route and an abbreviated approvals process. Equipment bought that way is usually in service within months, and the mechanism was used heavily during Iraq and Afghanistan for protected vehicles, counter-explosive equipment and surveillance systems.

PHP security crisis prompts websites worldwide to push updates for critical vulnerabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:58:11 UTC
00:58:11 KST

Mert Davut and Emir Yildirim
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The widely used PHP programming language was found to have two critical security vulnerabilities affecting digital infrastructure worldwide, prompting organizations across the globe to implement updates.
The “PHP2Shell” vulnerability stems from errors in code and memory management, which allow remote code execution on compromised systems without entering a username or password.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation and the National Security Agency both warned the public about these newly discovered vulnerabilities.
Websites providing citizenship services were taken down in the Netherlands, while similar measures for prefectural websites came to the fore in France.
Countries including Denmark, Norway, Finland, Japan and South Korea issued cyber crisis alerts and implemented immediate updates.
Türkiye’s Cybersecurity Directorate instructed public institutions and private organizations to migrate their PHP infrastructure to secure versions, while nationwide security scans and technical monitoring are underway.
Probes into Türkiye’s e-Government Portal yielded no issues compromising the security of the digital services offered, authorities said.
These security vulnerabilities pose a theoretical risk to websites that contain sensitive information, and the mere existence of these security flaws does not necessarily mean personal data has been compromised.
Everyday users of the internet and online applications are urged to stay vigilant and practice basic digital security measures, while businesses and institutions are urged to determine which internal systems use PHP and identify which version is active, experts said.
An official security patch has already been released, but it is up to organizations to identify affected systems and update their PHP installations to a secure version.
Experts also advised blocking all international web traffic to domestic systems and enterprise applications that do not need global access and allowing traffic only from trusted and authorized IP addresses.

US judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in $10bn lawsuit against BBC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:57:31 UTC
00:57:31 KST

Donald Trump has been ordered by a US judge to cooperate with the discovery process mandated for his lawsuit against the BBC and to sit for a deposition by 11 December – or else he could be subject to sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the $10bn lawsuit.
The lawsuit stems from a Panorama documentary aired by the BBC that spliced together two comments made nearly an hour apart by Trump during a rally on 6 January 2021, before the US Capitol riot. The BBC has acknowledged that this specific edit was misleading, but Trump has gone on to claim, falsely, that the BBC did not just edit his speech but used AI to insert words into his speech.
While the broadcast was not readily available to view in Florida, Trump’s team has argued that he was personally damaged by the broadcast under Florida’s Unfair and Deceptive Trade Practices Act.
During a lengthy hearing dealing with a variety of discovery issues, federal magistrate judge Enjoliqué Lett on Thursday also rejected a request by Trump’s legal team to prevent the seven-hour-long deposition from being videotaped, though it will only be accessible to attorneys in the case.
Lett agreed with contentions from the BBC’s lawyers that Trump’s team had not been sufficiently forthcoming in handing over internal documents relevant to the case ahead of an 18 December deadline for discovery.
“We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance,” attorney Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, argued in a Miami courtroom.
The documents that Trump’s team have turned over have primarily been either pulled from the internet or provided by the BBC itself.
“It strains credulity that a thorough search has been done in order to determine that all of these requests have been responded to,” Lett told Alejandro Brito, Trump’s Florida-based attorney. “The court is not satisfied that anyone is doing a thorough job.”
The judge gave the plaintiffs 30 days to produce the relevant documents. While she acknowledged that the discovery process can be “burdensome” on both parties, she said that “failure to do so could result in sanctions, including possible dismissal of the suit for failure to prosecute the case and engage in meaningful discovery process”.
Of the Trump team’s obligation to adequately participate in the discovery process, the judge said: “This is the last opportunity to do so.”
After discussing the discovery process, the judge turned to the BBC’s request to compel the president’s team to agree for a deposition, after a previously scheduled date – 16 October – was cancelled for what Trump’s counsel said were “other matters of national importance”. While the BBC noted that Trump was actually campaigning in Georgia on that day, leading Tobin to conclude that the plaintiff’s team had transmitted “fake news”, Brito said the president was “involved in a host of things” on a daily basis that the BBC’s legal team “has no idea” about.
While Lett said she was obligated to adhere to the discovery schedule mandated in the case, that timeline could be extended by district court judge Jeffrey T Kuntz. Tobin, representing the BBC, said his side was willing to push back the timeline for Trump’s deposition if Kuntz adjusted the discovery schedule.
Lett once again threatened sanctions – including dismissal – if Trump’s team did not comply with her deposition order.
“The lesson for the day is that no plaintiff is above the law, and no plaintiff is above the orders of the court,” Tobin said.
In a filing on Wednesday, Trump’s team said he would be willing to sit for a deposition during the second or third week of January.
During the hearing, Lett also allowed the BBC’s subpoena to Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida club, to go ahead, despite protests from Trump’s attorney that the business was separate from the president.
Brito, Trump’s attorney, contended that the president does not run the club. “The president’s occupation is the president of the United States,” he said. “It has nothing to do with Mar-a-Lago as far as his occupation.”
Tobin, representing the BBC, vehemently disagreed. “To say that Mar-a-Lago is not tied to this president or his reputation ignores the fact that he hosts [Ukrainian president] Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he hosts the president of Ireland, [Russian president] Vladimir Putin – he uses Mar-a-Lago as a location to publicize his reputation as a symbol of his personal power, so it is inextricably intertwined. His business successes are a measure of his reputation.”
In issuing the ruling, the judge agreed that the club “falls within the scope of discoverability”.
“I think it is intertwined with his profession and therefore any harm that may be alleged under his professional trade and occupation would be reflected with how he conducts business with Mar-a-Lago, at least for discovery purposes,” she added.

Turkish seafood exports to China nearly triple, led by salmon and tuna

Firat Ozdemir and Emir Yildirim
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Türkiye’s seafood exports to China nearly tripled, surging 190% year-on-year in January-September and totaling a little over $18 million after the signing of new bilateral trade deals between the two countries last October, according to the Aegean Exporters’ Association.
The protocol on inspection and health requirements for wild-caught and farmed aquatic products was established, paving the way for easier entry of Turkish seafood into the Chinese market.
The total volume of Turkish aquatic exports to China jumped 153% to 1,588 tons this year.
The exports were led by salmon, whose revenue rose 93% to nearly $5.5 million, while its shipping volume rose from 433 tons to 861 tons.
Tuna followed, generating $4.5 million in revenue and reaching 291 metric tons, following zero exports to China during the same period last year.
Meanwhile, sea cucumber sales surged 138% and generated $3.7 million in revenue, while frozen snail exports rose 133% to $1.9 million.
Ufuk Atakan Demir, president of the Aegean Seafood and Animal Products Exporters' Association, told Anadolu that the figures since the establishment of last year’s protocols have encouraged the expansion of Turkish aquaculture.
Demir stated that rising sales led to new opportunities for Turkish producers and exporters to form long-term trade relations in China, urging the industry to promote their products and strengthen their relationships with Chinese buyers to sustain the momentum.
