U.S. Army to test robot supply vehicles in Hawaii
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:54:30 UTC
00:54:30 KST

- The U.S. Army selected nine finalists for an autonomous sustainment competition focused on resupplying troops across contested Pacific island chains.
- Finalists will demonstrate their ground and air delivery systems to soldiers at the Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center in Hawaii Nov. 4–15, 2026.
The U.S. Army has selected nine companies as finalists in a competition to find autonomous ground and air vehicles that can resupply troops spread across Pacific islands, and their systems will go before soldiers in Hawaii next month.
The competition, called G-TEAD USARPAC ACE 27-01: Autonomous Sustainment, is run by the Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate with U.S. Army Pacific and the Army FUZE xTech program. The finalists will take part in a live Soldier exercise scheduled for Nov. 4–15, 2026, at the Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center in Hawaii, the U.S. Army’s main combat training center for the Pacific.
Eight of the nine finalists are competing with ground delivery systems, and one with an air delivery drone, according to the competition page. The ground entries are Ark Robotics’ M4 unmanned ground vehicle, BlueSky Innovations’ Jekyll US, Cyborg Autonomy’s modular tracked robot, Dataspeed’s TWEEDLE attritable wheeled dolly, Hypercraft’s Razorback, which also provides tactical power, Raptor Defense Company’s PIT VIPER personal combat vehicle, Stridar’s Siderunner Pro and Swarmbotics AI’s FIREANT, designed for the last tactical mile of resupply. Phenix Solutions is the sole air finalist with its Ultra 2XL heavy-lift drone.
The Army framed the problem around the vulnerability of traditional supply lines in a Pacific conflict. Resupply between islands currently depends on high-value crewed ships and aircraft that would face serious risk in contested waters, while moving supplies on land puts a heavy physical load on soldiers. The service wants unmanned air, ground and surface systems that can carry different payloads over a range of distances, managed by software that routes supplies automatically and lets small teams control groups of vehicles.
The competition was open to three capability areas: attritable air delivery systems, attritable autonomous surface vessels able to carry one to four standard shipping containers, and autonomous ground delivery systems. Attritable means cheap enough to be lost in combat without major impact. The finalist list includes ground and air entries.
Entries had to meet demanding baseline requirements. Systems needed to be mature enough for testing in a realistic environment, be fieldable within 180 days of a contract award, work with the Army’s command and logistics networks, and keep operating when GPS and communications are jammed or degraded. They also had to show safe behavior around soldiers, including obstacle avoidance and emergency stops, and alert operators when a sensor or software fault occurs.
Each finalist receives $25,000, and those whose systems are successfully integrated into the November exercise will receive another $25,000. After the exercise, the Army plans to select up to five winners for an additional $150,000 each, with winners scheduled to be announced on Nov. 15.
The competition offers up to $1.5 million in cash prizes in total. From Nov. 30, 2026, through March 31, 2027, selected participants can submit proposals for follow-on prototype agreements worth up to $2 million, giving the Army a path to put the best-performing systems into units’ hands.

Macron bans ‘illegitimate’ protests in France as he tries to get a grip on unrest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:54:13 UTC
00:54:13 KST

Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend.
Speaking after a meeting with intelligence officials and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed.
Protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but they might have to use alternative routes.
The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.”
Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the republic”.
“The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.
An initial police ban on a student protest planned in Paris for Thursday was overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for the day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted.
Authorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze.
Authorities in Marseille, Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at the Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre.
However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said.
France’s main student union, UNEF, has also called for rallies on Saturday. Businesses in central Paris and other cities had already begun boarding up their windows and hiring private security in preparation for violence, French media reported.
The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 174 of the 2,500 people arrested since last weekend’s rioting had been remanded in custody and more than 900 were being prosecuted. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big-city mayors later in the day.
The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Élysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations.
The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high-school pupils around the country.
Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections, which will choose Macron’s successor.

Ben-Gvir arms more West Bank settlers ahead of Israeli elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:54:12 UTC
00:54:12 KST

Breadcrumb
Ben-Gvir arms more West Bank settlers ahead of Israeli elections
Far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has approved the expansion of gun licence across 11 additional illegal settlements and outposts in the occupied West Bank, despite warnings from Israeli security officials of a potential wave of settler attacks against Palestinians following next week's elections.
The decision, reported by Israel's Channel 14 on Thursday, comes as the Israeli military, Shin Bet security service and police face mounting criticism over their failure to contain settler violence, with security officials warning that extremist groups could attempt to seize more Palestinian land if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu loses power.
Ben-Gvir's move will allow residents of 11 more settlements and outposts in the northern occupied West Bank to apply for firearms licences, provided they meet the criteria set by Israel's National Security Ministry.
"We are continuing the arming revolution and expanding this reform to include the new settlements we have established in the northern West Bank," Ben-Gvir was quoted as saying by Channel 14.
The extremist minister pledged to continue expanding the programme, which his ministry claims is intended to strengthen security within settlements and enable residents to respond to attacks.
The expansion comes amid a campaign of settler violence against Palestinians, including assaults on farmers, land seizures and attacks aimed at forcing residents from their homes.
Yossi Dagan, head of the Northern West Bank Settlements Council, welcomed the decision, arguing that settlers who had served in Israeli combat units or military reserves needed weapons to defend their families and settlements.
He described the northern occupied West Bank as a "strategic defensive line" for Israel.
Fears of settler violence after Israeli elections
The expansion comes just days before Israel's 27 October parliamentary elections, with Israeli security officials warning that extremist settlers could launch a coordinated campaign of attacks against Palestinians if Netanyahu's governing bloc loses power.
According to Haaretz, which cited sources familiar with military assessments, far-right activists could seek to establish new illegal outposts, seize Palestinian land and attack residents in an attempt to prevent a future government from dismantling illegal settlements.
The concern is that extremist settlers may refuse to accept a change in government and instead attempt to impose new realities on the ground before any incoming administration can act.
The growing availability of firearms among settlers could further complicate efforts to evacuate illegal outposts, potentially increasing the risk of armed resistance to any future government seeking to remove them.
Israeli military officials are reportedly reinforcing troop deployments in the West Bank and seeking additional Border Police personnel in areas where violent settler groups operate.
Yet sources familiar with the security assessments have acknowledged that the army, Shin Bet and police are struggling to contain attacks, particularly when settlers strike several locations simultaneously.
"Anyone who tells you there is control is lying. The army, Shin Bet and police have lost control of the area," a security source familiar with the situation told Haaretz.
"They are running from one location to another chasing rioters. The problem is that no real effort is being made to regain control."
The remarks reflect growing frustration within Israel's own security establishment over the authorities' failure to stop settler terrorism, despite knowing where violent groups operate and the identities of prominent perpetrators.
Military officials have reportedly questioned why no effective preventive plan has been developed, rather than relying on forces to respond after attacks have already taken place.
Israeli security chiefs meet but take no action
Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir convened a meeting on Tuesday with senior security officials to discuss the escalating attacks and the risk of further violence surrounding the elections.
Despite the warnings, the meeting ended without significant new decisions, according to sources familiar with the discussions.
Officials within the military's Central Command reportedly criticised the absence of representatives from Netanyahu's office, Defence Minister Israel Katz and the National Security Council, arguing that the situation required direct political intervention.
One source described the meeting as little more than an exercise in recording a security assessment, with no meaningful steps agreed to prevent further attacks.
The failure to act comes as Katz has discontinued the use of administrative detention against Israeli settlers, removing a measure previously available to security forces dealing with extremist violence.
Instead, the military, Shin Bet and legal authorities are reportedly preparing exclusion orders that would bar individuals involved in incitement or attacks from entering the West Bank.
Security officials have acknowledged, however, that such orders would do little to prevent other settlers from establishing illegal outposts, seizing Palestinian farmland or carrying out attacks.
Ben-Gvir's drive to arm settlers
Ben-Gvir has made expanding access to firearms a central policy since becoming national security minister in early 2023, easing licensing requirements and widening the categories of Israelis eligible to carry weapons.
The programme accelerated following the start of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, alongside an intensification of Israeli military raids and settler attacks across the occupied West Bank.
On 21 January 2026, Ben-Gvir approved the addition of 18 settlements in the occupied territory to the list of locations whose residents could apply for firearms licences.
According to Israeli newspaper Israel Hayom, more than 200 cities, towns and other localities had been included in the expanded eligibility programme during 2026.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law, which prohibits an occupying power from transferring its civilian population into occupied territory.

The UK resumed domestic production of large-caliber weapons on Thursday for the first time in two decades, with Rheinmetall UK beginning manufacturing at its Telford gun hall and strengthening the country’s defense industrial base.
The facility, opened by Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, Chief of the General Staff Gen. Sir Roly Walker, and Rheinmetall AG CEO Armin Papperger, manufactures gun barrels for tanks and breeches for 120mm and 155mm weapon systems, including the RCH 155 and future artillery platforms.
The gun hall supports 100 highly skilled jobs, with the workforce expected to expand as production increases. The project also seeks to strengthen domestic supply chains through long-term partnerships with British small and medium-sized enterprises.
“Britain is back in the business of making the weapons that our Armed Forces need to defend the nation against our adversaries,” Streeting said in a statement. “From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action.”
Rheinmetall UK took over the facility in Autumn 2025 and brought it into full production within eight months, restoring a sovereign manufacturing capability for the British Armed Forces.
Streeting said the project demonstrated how defense investment could drive economic growth.
“One hundred skilled jobs in world-class manufacturing and the return of large-calibre weapon production to UK soil for the first time in twenty years – this is what defense as an engine for growth looks like,” he said.
The development is expected to support the long-term expansion of Britain’s domestic defense manufacturing capabilities and regional economic growth.

15:53:22 UTC

Police in Cyprus have opened an investigation into the financial and tax affairs of the former Chelsea FC owner Roman Abramovich following a report by the Guardian and media partners.
In a committee hearing in the Cypriot parliament, a senior official in the island’s police said they were looking into events between 2003 and 2006, with the investigation likely to last several months.
It comes after an investigation by the Guardian, the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC into the management of the billionaire Russian oligarch’s sprawling business empire.
The report found that aides of Abramovich – including staff at the Cypriot outpost of the global accountancy firm Deloitte – appeared to have falsified paperwork mapping his offshore businesses.
Their actions, including the apparent backdating of key documents concerning billions of pounds in assets, appear to have helped businesses owned by Abramovich to dodge tax and disguise assets, the investigation found.
The involvement of the Cypriot police emerged during a regular meeting of a Cypriot parliamentary committee on “institutions, values and the commissioner for administration”, according to CIReN, the Guardian’s Cypriot reporting partner.
Andreas Anastasiades, assistant director of the crime combating department, said police had begun gathering evidence after the report and expected the investigation to last six months, although he said the amount of time that had elapsed would make the investigation more difficult.
He said police would also consult the relevant authorities to assess the available material.
The Guardian approached representatives of Abramovich and Deloitte Cyprus for comment.
The former Chelsea FC owner has previously denied any wrongdoing and said that he relied on the advice of professional experts. Deloitte Cyprus has previously said that it “acts in compliance with all applicable laws” and that it could no longer access the relevant material because of the time that had elapsed.
The Guardian’s findings in relation to Abramovich’s finances were based on the Cyprus Confidential leak of more than 500,000 documents, first released to the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists and analysed by organisations including the Bureau of Investigative Journalism and the BBC.

FIFA launches tender of 2030 men's World Cup U.S. media rights, plans to choose winner by end of year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:52:16 UTC
00:52:16 KST

The FIFA men's World Cup U.S. television rights are formally up for auction.
FIFA is launching its tender offer Thursday for the 2030 U.S. media rights with an option for potential partners to also buy rights for the 2034 World Cup. FIFA wants bids in by Nov. 19.
YouTube, Netflix, Amazon and Disney are all interested, CNBC reported in July. Rights could sell for between $1.5 billion and $2 billion, some media executives predicted at the time. FIFA hasn't sold U.S. men's World Cup TV rights since 2011.
Fox paid $425 million for the 2026 World Cup, which broke U.S. ratings records. Matches averaged 13.5 million viewers — up 166% from 2022.
The 2030 World Cup will take place in Spain, Portugal and Morocco.
FIFA would prefer to sell the English and the Spanish-language rights packaged together to one media partner – a departure from previous deals. For this past World Cup, NBCUniversal's Telemundo owned the Spanish rights while Fox owned the English rights. That led to some tension between the broadcasters and FIFA, as Peacock carried the Spanish-language rights for a less expensive price than Fox One, which streamed the games with English announcers.
FIFA Chief Business Officer Romy Gai said it's too early to gauge what price is realistic for the 2030 World Cup. FIFA is willing to listen to offers where just one media company buys the entire package or a joint offering – potentially between a streamer and a traditional broadcaster.
"We want to be flexible," said Gai in an interview. "We expect a big number of participants, both from the linear side and from the streamer side, but we want to listen to what is relevant for them, and then we can build up the best case together."
While the 2026 World Cup took place in the U.S., Canada and Mexico — allowing matches to be played during U.S. afternoons and nights — the 2030 World Cup will have a significant time difference. The 2034 World Cup will be played in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh is seven hours ahead of New York.
The time zones may make it difficult for games to be played during U.S. primetime hours. That will play a role in how much media companies are willing to spend on both tournaments, but Gai doesn't expect the time zone challenges to play too much of a role in the bidding.
"I'm sure that we will have every day matches that will be available in the right time zone for the U.S.," Gai said. "We expect it to have an impact [on the bidding], but not as big as you think."
If a streaming service wins the rights, FIFA will ensure that a certain number of matches are available for free, either by forcing the streamer to sublicense certain rights or by putting some games on a free version of the service, if such a thing exists.
Netflix has already acquired the 2030 World Cup rights in Spain. That deal allows a free-to-air broadcaster to show at least one game each day.
After Nov. 19, when bids are due, a contingent from FIFA will come to the U.S. around Thanksgiving and begin speaking with media companies in person, Gai said. At that point, FIFA could narrow down the field and ask for one more final bid – or it could just choose a winner.
FIFA intends to select its next media partner before the end of the year, said Gai.

Ukraine's population had shrunk to 28.5 million by mid-2026

Source: Ella Libanova, Director of the Ptukha Institute for Demography and Quality of Life Studies at the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine, during the 10th Ukrainian Women's Congress, as reported by Ukrinform
Quote from Libanova: "Just a few days ago, we completed our assessment of the mid-year population figures – 28.5 million. We have lost half a million. This is not so much due to deaths as because people are leaving."
Details: Migration, both internal and external, remains the main driver of demographic change in Ukraine. Libanova believes that a new wave of migration should be expected after the war ends, when men are likely to leave to join their families living abroad.
Quote: "In terms of migration, I am not [so much] concerned about what is happening now as about what will happen after martial law is lifted: when men are able to leave, when they return from the front."
Details: Libanova suggested that it is likely Ukraine will not be able to offer them a job and salary that they would consider decent.
Quote: "Then the question will be: where will Ukrainian families reunite – in Ukraine or abroad? I'm very much afraid that there will be a second wave of what you might call 'male' migration. This is highly likely."
Background: In July 2026, the State Statistics Service and the Institute of Demography jointly estimated the population of Ukrainian-controlled territory at 29 million people. The estimate was based on data from mobile operators and state registers.

The First Day of Italophony at the Italian Permanent Mission to NATO
Italy
Unknown Publisher

17:51:30 CEST
00:51:30 KST

On October 15, 2026, the first Day of the Italian-Speaking Community at NATO was held in Brussels at Villa Manlio Brosio. The initiative, organized as part of Italian Language Week Around the World, marked the birth of an Italian-speaking community within the North Atlantic Alliance, bringing together those who, regardless of nationality, share a knowledge of and passion for the Italian language and culture.
                                    
The evening, attended by international officials and fellow Italians serving at NATO, was inspired by the theme chosen for this year’s edition, “A Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, Creating with Italian,” celebrating the Italian language as an expression of creativity and innovation, but above all as a tool for dialogue and cultural exchange. As Ambassador Alessandro Azzoni emphasized, it is precisely in the ability to build relationships that language meets diplomacy. In this spirit, the evening offered a journey through various expressions of Italian culture: an exhibition of historical documents on Italy’s participation in the founding of NATO, made possible thanks to the contribution of the Farnesina Historical Archives; artworks and installations presented in collaboration with the Italian Cultural Institute in Brussels and the painter Marco Angelini; and a performance by soprano Luna Grafin von Hardenberg, accompanied by Maestro Lionel Barms, featuring works by great Italian composers, including Puccini and Bellini.
                                    
The first Day of the Italian-Speaking Community at NATO thus marked the beginning of a process aimed at strengthening a community of Italian speakers within the Alliance, promoting the language as a shared heritage and a tool for building relationships in an international and multicultural context.”

For many years, the French authorities created social problems themselves, then unleashed terror against their fellow citizens, primarily children, Russian Permanent Representative to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) Dmitry Polyansky said at a regular meeting of the organization’s Permanent Council.

The issues include chronic underfunding of educational institutions, uncontrolled migration, overcrowded classrooms, dilapidated school buildings and unsanitary conditions. It was precisely on this ‘fertile ground’ that social protests erupted. For years, Paris had been fleecing its own citizens to benefit the corrupt Ukrainian regime. Now it could think of nothing better than to unleash terror against its fellow citizens, primarily children," he said.
"Today, human rights advocates compare the consequences of the use of excessive force to injuries sustained in combat," the Russian permanent representative continued. More than 200 teenagers had been injured as a result of excessive force, while over 6,500 people had been detained, the vast majority of them minors, he said.

UK plans tougher penalties for damage to undersea cables, pipelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:48:47 UTC
00:48:47 KST

Aysu Bicer
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The UK government has proposed tougher prison sentences and unlimited fines for those who intentionally damage critical undersea infrastructure, citing growing security threats, including suspicious Russian activity in British waters.
A White Paper published on Thursday outlines plans to modernize legislation dating back 140 years to strengthen the protection of undersea telecommunications cables, energy pipelines and electricity interconnectors.
Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical undersea energy and telecommunications infrastructure could face prison sentences of up to 14 years, alongside tougher financial penalties.
The plans would also introduce new security and resilience requirements for subsea telecommunications companies, obliging them to identify and manage risks to their networks.
The government would gain additional powers to direct telecommunications providers to take protective measures against threats such as sabotage and espionage. The proposals also include safeguards for fiber-optic sensing technology, which can detect activity at sea but may pose national security risks if sensitive data is compromised.
“Undersea cables are the hidden backbone of modern Britain, carrying the data we rely on every day to message friends and family, do our banking, and run our businesses,” Telecoms Minister Ian Murray said in a statement.
He added: “We intend to modernise those laws with tougher penalties, stronger requirements on industry and new powers to protect our national security, making sure the UK’s critical infrastructure is fit for the threats of today and tomorrow.”
According to the government, undersea fibre-optic cables carry around 99% of the UK’s international data, while subsea pipelines provide 74% of its gas supply. Electricity cables also support energy imports from Europe and connections to offshore wind farms.
Energy Minister Michael Shanks also said the legislation would strengthen deterrence and help prevent, detect and respond to threats against the country’s energy supply.
The publication of the White Paper marks the start of a 12-week public consultation seeking views from industry, experts and the public.

CEC impeachment: Speaker Om Birla says fresh motion against Gyanesh Kumar will be examined as per rules

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said if the opposition brings any fresh impeachment motion against the country's top poll officer, it will be examined according to rules and procedures.
Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said any fresh motion seeking the impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar would be examined in accordance with parliamentary rules and procedures, as opposition protests demanding the poll panel chief’s removal intensified over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The opposition has made two attempts to remove Kumar, with notices in the first attempt rejected by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Notices submitted in the second attempt are still pending in the Upper House.“If any fresh notice comes, we will see and examine it accordingly under rules and procedures,” Birla told a press conference, responding to a question on the possibility of another impeachment motion against the CEC.Protests against Kumar have intensified over the past fortnight, with opposition parties demanding his resignation over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls. The agitation gathered momentum after The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, alleging that these were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.
Under the Constitution, the CEC can be removed only through a parliamentary process similar to that prescribed for the removal of a Supreme Court judge. The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, also provides for the CEC or an Election Commissioner to resign by submitting a written resignation to the President.The removal process is governed by constitutional provisions and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. Once a removal motion is admitted in either House of Parliament, the Speaker or the Rajya Sabha Chairman constitutes a three-member committee to investigate the charges. The panel comprises the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge, a chief justice of a high court and a distinguished jurist.
If the committee finds the charges unsubstantiated, no further action is taken. If it finds the allegations proved, the motion is taken up for consideration in Parliament. Removal requires each House to pass an address supported by a majority of its total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, in the same session.The opposition’s attempts to remove Kumar have brought the Election Commission’s handling of the SIR under renewed scrutiny, with the possibility of another motion now hinging on the formal parliamentary process and the admissibility of any fresh notice.

Japanese troops test-fire air defense missiles at New Mexico range
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:47:27 UTC
00:47:27 KST

- Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force has been conducting live-fire air defense training since July 2026 at Shizunai, Rokkasho and other ranges in Japan.
- At McGregor Range in New Mexico, its Type 03 medium-range missile units are firing alongside Japan Air Self-Defense Force Patriot units.
Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force has been carrying out live-fire air defense training since July 2026 at ranges in northern Japan and in the United States, where its medium-range missile units are firing alongside Japan Air Self-Defense Force Patriot batteries at McGregor Range in New Mexico.
The Ground Self-Defense Force, Japan’s army, said on X that units at home are firing at the Shizunai range in Hokkaido, the Rokkasho range in Aomori Prefecture and other sites. The training covers the force’s layered short-range air defense weapons: the Type 81 short-range surface-to-air missile, the Type 93 close-range surface-to-air missile and the Type 87 self-propelled anti-aircraft gun.
Those systems cover the lowest and closest layers of Japan’s ground-based air defense.
The Type 93 mounts short-range missiles on a light utility vehicle, while the tracked Type 87 carries twin 35 mm cannons to engage aircraft, helicopters and other low-flying targets at close range.
In New Mexico, the Ground Self-Defense Force is firing the Type 03 medium-range surface-to-air missile, known in Japan as Chu-SAM, in coordination with Air Self-Defense Force Patriot units. Built by Mitsubishi Electric, the Type 03 replaced the U.S.-designed HAWK missiles Japan had used since 1965 and has a range of about 50 km (31 miles), with the system designed to hit aircraft, air-to-surface missiles and cruise missiles directly.
The Type 03 has a long history at the New Mexico range. Japanese forces fired it in a live training exercise for the first time at McGregor Range in late 2006, after six earlier test launches at nearby White Sands Missile Range.
McGregor Range, part of the Fort Bliss training complex, offers the open airspace and distances needed for live missile firings that are difficult to arrange in Japan. The Air Self-Defense Force has held annual Patriot live-fire training there since 1963, and recent iterations have included combined live firing with Ground Self-Defense Force anti-aircraft units, bilateral firing with U.S. Army Patriot units and, in 2025, counter-drone training.
Pairing the two services lets Japan’s army and air force practice defending against air threats as a single network, with the medium-range Type 03 and the longer-range Patriot covering different layers of the airspace.
The Ground Self-Defense Force said it will continue firing training at home and abroad to further strengthen its air defense capabilities.

Georgia on Democrats’ minds: Powering up the Black vote to counter Trump's meddling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:43:57 UTC
00:43:57 KST

Georgia on Democrats’ minds: Powering up the Black vote to counter Trump's meddling
ATLANTA, Georgia – President Donald Trump's push to redistrict congressional maps and a Georgia state election law disproportionately affecting African Americans are aimed at diluting the power of the Black vote. Six decades after Atlanta was at the heart of the civil rights movement that granted Blacks in the southern states the right to vote, the community is fighting back.
The Sunday service at Atlanta’s historic Ebenezer Baptist Church, where the late Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. was a senior pastor, is picking up steam, with the congregation punctuating their assent to the preachers and speakers on the pulpit with fervent “Yeahs!”, robust “Okays!” and the occasional “Amens!”
The church on Auburn Avenue in the US National Historic Landmark District of Sweet Auburn in western Atlanta has been at the forefront of African American socio-political engagement. Its preachers voiced visions of equality during the racially segregated era in the Southern states, provided services – such as education – that were denied to the community, and preached a “social gospel” that fueled the 1960s civil rights movement.
The pulpit-to-politics tradition carries on to this day with the Baptist church’s senior pastor, Rev. Raphael Warnock, who was elected to the US Senate in 2020, becoming the first African American to represent Georgia, and the first Black Democrat from a Southern state, to be elected to the upper house of Congress.
Watch moreUSA: Who is Senator Raphael Warnock?
With just weeks to go before the November 3 midterm elections, this Sunday sees Warnock on a roll as he leads the service.
“Alright, come on up. We need everybody to vote,” he proclaims.
“Yeah!” responds the congregation with a chorus of applause.
“A vote is a kind of prayer, for the world we desire for ourselves – and our children,” Warnock continues in the rhythmic, expressive cadence of southern preachers.
And with that, Georgia’s senator hands over the podium to Marc Morial, head of the National Urban League, a civil rights organisation that has served the Black community since 1910.
“The eyes of the nation are on the state of Georgia,” Morial tells the packed church. “When Georgia elected your pastor as its United States senator in the year 2020, many people across the nation had said that was an impossible feat. It could not be done. But Georgia made history,” he notes.
Democrats have had Georgia on their minds over the past few years as it has flipped from a reliably Republican “red” state to an uneven purple with the growth of liberal, educated suburban communities, including a “brain gain” influx of college-educated Black people returning to thriving Southern metropolises such as Atlanta from the rest of the country. But in order to maintain the hues of blue, Democrats need their traditional voter base to come out and vote.
Two years after Donald Trump won Georgia in the 2024 presidential election, and with the Republicans holding Congress, Democrats also have to stem the tide of legislative attempts to dilute the power of Black voters. As the US heads to the polls in the 2026 midterms, studies and editorials warn that the country is “on the cusp of eviscerating Black power”.
Six decades ago, the Ebenezer Baptist Church’s star preacher, Dr. King, launched a civil disobedience campaign to grant African Americans in the southern states their fundamental constitutional right to vote resulting in the landmark 1965 Right to Vote Act. The struggle has changed, but not ended, and Georgia is on the frontlines of the battle. It’s also a fight that has, once again, been largely left to the community to shoulder.
‘Jim Crow in the 21st century’
At the C.T. Martin Natatorium and Recreation Center in Adamsville, a predominantly Black neighbourhood in western Atlanta, early voting kicked off on October 13 in the spacious gymnasium serving as a polling station. A steady stream of voters lined up along walls plastered with election information and warnings such as, “It is illegal to carry a firearm”, into polling stations. Georgia’s early voting slot in the 2026 midterms runs from October 13-30, leaving the last weekend before the November 3 election day free of voting activity.
Outside, in the parking lot of the sprawling premises, a DJ belted out soul music in what was billed as a “get out the vote party”. On the sun-drenched lawn, the hosts of a community collective podcast interviewed politicians, activists and local celebrities emerging from the polling station with “I voted” stickers. At another stall, Deborah Scott, head of Georgia Stand Up, a grassroots NGO, hands out bottles of water, cookies and flyers with voting information.
“Democracy is on the line. And in this democracy fight, it's all going to start and end right here in Georgia,” she says with an infectious smile. “Georgia is going to show the rest of the country that when you organise, mobilise and work with the Black community, you can actually win. Even if they're underfunding it, even if they're not showing us love, we will show our people love.”
“Get out the vote” campaigns are strictly non-partisan initiatives where volunteers abstain from mentioning political parties and preferences.
In Scott’s case, the “love” – or lack of it – refers to a law, the 2021 Election Integrity Act, originally called the Georgia Senate Bill 202, and frequently called “SB 202” across the state.
The act was signed into law by Georgia’s Republican Governor Brian Kemp the year after the state elected two charismatic Democratic senators – Warnock and “Star of the South” Jon Ossoff – to the US Senate, and voted for Joe Biden in presidential race in 2020. Republicans say the law makes it “easier for citizens to vote and harder for anyone to cheat”. From the White House, Biden described it as “Jim Crow in the 21st century”, referring to the racial segregation laws in the southern states before the 1960s civil rights movement.
The law has been the subject of legal challenges by civil rights groups and many court rulings by justices attempting a compromise. Shortly after it passed, the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against Georgia alleging that the law is racially discriminatory. But in March 2025, two months after Trump took office for a second term, the Justice Department dropped the lawsuit, stating that it falsely accused Georgia of intentionally suppressing Black votes.
Among its many sections, the law prohibits the handing out of food and water to voters standing in line within 150 feet of a polling station. Scott believes the measure disproportionately affects minority communities. “SB 202 discriminates against black and brown people because only black and brown people were giving water to people who were waiting in lines. Our lines were longer than any other community. People were waiting in lines five, six, ten hours and they could not vote. People were passing out. We couldn't even give them a chair,” she said.
At the C.T. Center, the “get out the vote” party is safely 150 feet away from the polling rooms, but in smaller stations in densely populated neighbourhoods, it presents a challenge, says Scott. “They did that because they don't want democracy. We want democracy. So we said we're still going to do it, we're just going to do it further away. We want people to come and get their water and information before they even get in line,” she explains.
The shadow of 2020
Getting out the vote is critical to Republicans and Democrats in Georgia, a state that went for Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024.
After his 2020 defeat to Biden, Trump falsely claimed he won Georgia even after three vote recounts showed the Republican candidate had lost to Biden by 11,779 votes.
The state was under the media spotlight after Trump made an extraordinary phone call to Georgia’s secretary of state, Brad Raffensperger, a Republican. The transcript of the call, which was leaked to the press, showed Trump ordering Raffensperger to “find” enough votes to hand him Georgia. Raffensperger declined.
Six years later, the impact of the Georgia alleged meddling case continues to resonate on the 2026 midterms campaign trail. In February, the FBI raided election offices in the state’s battleground Fulton County to seize sensitive voting records from 2020 in what critics called an unprecedented “instance of the federal government directly interfering in a state election”.
Ossoff, who is seeking re-election in November, was quick to slam the raid. During a visit to an Atlanta Black church, the Democratic “Star of the South” accused Trump of ordering the raid to suppress the Black vote. “The power of Black voters, and the fact that the power of Black voters ejected him from office, may outrage him more than the defeat itself. And so he tries to delegitimise your exercise of power. With elections approaching, he tries to suppress it,” said Ossoff.
Watch moreMidterms 2026: Georgia's Ossof-Collins showdown lies at the heart of the battle for US Senate
Gerrymandering battlefield lines
The suppression of the Black vote has a long history in the American South, particularly in the “Deep South”, the subregion of Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, Mississippi and South Carolina, that has a distinct historic and cultural identity.
In Georgia, African Americans make up around 30% of the state’s estimated 11 million population, comprising a critical Democratic vote base. “For any Democratic candidate running for office, given the fact that Blacks are overwhelmingly Democratic in their partisan orientation, they absolutely need high voter turnout amongst African American voters – assuming that they vote predictably Democratic – in order to really have a chance at being able to win office,” explained Andra Gillespie, a political scientist at the Atlanta-based Emory University.
But over the past few years, there has been a concerted Republican push, spearheaded by Trump, to redraw congressional districts. Last year, Trump pressed Texas legislators to pass new districting maps to gain more seats for the Republicans in the House of Representatives, where the GOP holds a narrow 220-215 majority. In April, the US Supreme Court, in a landmark ruling, struck down a majority Black congressional district in Louisiana, opening the door for more redistricting and prompting three Southern states to draw new maps.
A Bloomberg News study of congressional maps, published on October 20, found that the gerrymandering – or manipulation of electoral district boundaries to give one political party an unfair electoral advantage – “are having an outsized impact on Black voters, who are more likely to have been shifted into new congressional districts in order to create more safe seats for Republicans ahead of the US midterm elections”.
In Georgia, Republicans in the state legislature earlier this year attempted to follow the Deep South states of Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee in redrawing congressional maps. But the plan was shelved ahead of the November midterms for fear of a voter backlash against the party.
Standing on the C.T. Center lawn after casting her ballot, Shirley Clarke Franklin, a former Atlanta mayor and a veteran Democrat, credited Georgia’s progressive politicians for the pushback. “African Americans in Georgia, especially our leadership, stood up against redistricting when it was raised in our legislature. And our legislature, which is dominated by the party that wanted to do redistricting, backed down,” said Franklin, referring to state Republicans. “So, the organisational skills of Georgians, the history of fighting for our rights, serves us well in difficult times.”
The pushback may have succeeded for the moment, but analysts believe Republicans will attempt to put the issue back on the agenda after the midterms.
Gillespie notes that this year’s gubernatorial race between Republican billionaire Rick Jackson and Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms to replace Republican Governor Kemp – whose term ends in January 2027 – could play a key role.
“Redistricting is definitely not off the table,” says Gillespie. “The timing of it will depend on who becomes governor of Georgia. It's highly likely that the governor [Republican Brian Kemp] will call a special session in November or December to address redistricting so that he can sign that into law if Keisha Lance Bottoms wins and before a new legislature comes in [in January 2027]. There might be less urgency to do that if Rick Jackson is elected governor.”
The ‘gift’ of the vote
Cruising westward on Atlanta’s Martin Luther King Jr. Drive in a car loaded with cartons of his self-published book, “All Power Back to the People,” Scotty Smart is upbeat about the power of his vote.
“If we vote in this election, we have the ability to fight back and slow down some of the things that are happening across the country,” says the young Black activist.
But minutes later, Smart bristles when asked about the Black male vote for Trump in 2024. “That's a false narrative put out by certain media platforms that like to chastise Black men,” he maintains. “In 2024, Black men overwhelmingly voted Democrat. But the emphasis is always put on that one small demographic.”
He has a point. A Pew Research Center voter analysis found that approximately 77% of Black men voted for Kamala Harris, while 21% voted for Trump. Among Black women, approximately 92% supported Harris, and 7% supported Trump.
After two years of Trump’s second presidency and the Iran war exacerbating the cost of living crisis, Smart believes the Black vote will overwhelmingly stick with the Democrats in the midterms. “Truckers are ready to go on strike because the diesel prices are so high, people are upset because food is so expensive. It's gotten so bad that people are finally seeing the effects” of Trump’s policies, he notes.
Standing outside the Ebenezer at the end of the Sunday service, Kamilah Aminah Jones, a psychotherapist and licensed ecclesiastical minister at the historic church, chokes up as she draws from the past to explain her responsibility, as a citizen, to vote in the latest elections.
“It's a gift. It's really a gift. And I'm getting emotional,” she pauses briefly to collect herself before continuing. “I'm getting emotional just thinking about that … It’s a promise that my ancestors possibly prayed for, not just prayed for, there was blood, sweat and tears to have that opportunity. And I stand in that now. I have a voice. It's something I can never take for granted.”

Abdul El-Sayed appoints Jewish liaison amid tight Michigan Senate race
US Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has hired a Jewish liaison as he seeks to win over Jewish voters amid his continued criticism of US-Israel ties.
He is currently running in a closely contested Senate race in Michigan ahead of the November midterm elections.
Veteran political consultant Lenore Goldman, who has worked with Jewish organisations such as the Jewish Community Federation of San Francisco, as well as the One Fair Wage movement, which campaigns for higher minimum wages in the US, was selected by El-Sayed.
Goldman confirmed her appointment in an interview with the Jewish Telegraphic Agency (JTA) on Wednesday.
Goldman told the news outlet that she had been working with the campaign since September, although El-Sayed’s team had not publicly announced her appointment.
The development follows local reports in August that the campaign was seeking to hire a liaison to Michigan’s Jewish community.
El-Sayed backs ending all US military assistance to Israel amid its genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023.
During the final televised debate in Michigan’s Senate race on Wednesday, Republican candidate Mike Rogers alleged that some “Jewish Democrats” were “literally afraid” of El-Sayed.
“We’re doing exceptionally well with Jewish Democrats who are literally afraid,” Rogers said during the debate in Detroit.
“I’ve talked to ones with tears in their eyes about the future of their kids and grandkids, because [of] the anger and division that he is laying out on the street.”
In his closing statement, Rogers further claimed that Jewish voters were among several groups of Democrats switching their support to him because they considered El-Sayed “too extreme”.
Rogers, a vocal supporter of Israel, was then accused by El-Sayed of being “bought off” by special interests, including pro-Israel lobbying group AIPAC.
El-Sayed cited a recent New York Times report that the group’s super PAC intended to spend $9 million to support Rogers.
AIPAC announced on Wednesday that it would stop endorsing candidates and making direct campaign contributions through its PAC, while its affiliated super PAC would continue independent election spending.
Rogers responded by accusing El-Sayed of being “bought off by the Muslim Brotherhood” and alleged that his campaign had received funding from the Palestinian group Hamas.
Amid attempts to conflate El-Sayed’s criticism of Israel’s actions in the Middle East with antisemitism, Rogers also targeted his opponent’s ethnicity and Muslim faith.
The accusations followed repeated Islamophobic attacks from Republicans, including President Donald Trump, over alleged family ties between El-Sayed and the Egypt-founded Muslim Brotherhood.
“If you are going to go to the United States Senate, we need to know: Are you for America or are you for these terrorist groups overseas?” Rogers said.
El-Sayed, who has denied any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, condemned the remarks as a “shameful” attack.
“To bring into question my commitment to the Constitution is really beneath you. I am proud of America. I’m proud to be an American. I’m proud of our Constitution that guarantees all of us the right to pray as we choose to pray,” he said.
If elected, El-Sayed would become the first Muslim to serve in the US Senate.
A Marist public opinion poll released on Wednesday showed El-Sayed leading Rogers by 50 per cent to 48 per cent among likely voters.

France hands out swift verdicts in fast-track justice after riots

15:41:55 UTC

France hands out swift verdicts in fast-track justice after riots
- French courts are using fast-track justice after weekend riots, handing out swift jail terms and suspended sentences to restore order.
- Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 2,500 were arrested and 917 prosecuted, calling the response a sign of “great firmness”.
- Lawyers say the process is rushed and harsh, with one calling it “state repression” and warning judges face pressure for tougher penalties.
AI generated
PARIS – French courts have swiftly handed out verdicts, including orders to serve jail time, in fast-track justice for defendants accused over the rioting that erupted on the sidelines of protests at the weekend.
The government says the accelerated legal processes are needed to restore order after some of the worst urban violence in recent years on Oct 17.
But courts are also overwhelmed, while some lawyers say the scale of the hearings reeks of state repression.
Mathilde B, a student, 19, and 20-year-old Francois D, who said he wants to be a mountain guide, had come to Paris on Oct 17 from Auxerre, a city south-east of the capital.
But police found a knuckleduster and flick knife in the young man’s bag and discovered the pair had discussed “guerrilla warfare” and “beating up riot police” on social media.
Mathilde B received a five-month suspended prison sentence; but Francois D was sent to jail immediately as part of an eight-month sentence, with two months to be served in custody.
Tristan Lawless, a lawyer at the bar in Melun south of Paris, said he was defending a client for whom prosecutors had demanded a five-month sentence with immediate custody.
He said the trial was taking place “on the basis of a 50-page case file that, in my view, was put together in haste, with reports that are often vague and lacking detail”, and alleged his client had been beaten in custody.
‘Pressure on judges’
Speaking on Oct 21 in the southern city of Marseille, which saw some of the worst violence, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said that out of some 2,500 people arrested nationwide at the weekend, 917 were being prosecuted, a number he hailed as a “truly impressive figure”.
“The holding cells are full,” he said, referring to the units where people are held ahead of trial, adding this was proof of “our great firmness”.
One of the most longstanding and hyperactive members of the government, Darmanin, a former interior minister, is taking a high profile as Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s Cabinet seeks to show it is in control.
Once seen as having presidential ambitions himself, he is a leading supporter of former centre-right premier Edouard Philippe, who is seen as one of the few candidates capable of defeating far-right front runner Marine Le Pen in 2027 elections.
“We’re here to firmly oppose what we see as an attempt by Gerald Darmanin to make the justice system more punitive,” said Paris lawyer Romain Ruiz, a member of the “Colere noire” (Black anger) collective, which is highly critical of the judicial system.
He accused Darmanin of “putting pressure on judges in pursuit of harsher penalties” and “publicly celebrating the imprisonment of young people”.
“We will never accept that the justice system should become an arm of repression.”
‘Perhaps unprecedented’
Manuel, a 21-year-old cook from central France with no prior criminal record, said he had come to Paris “on a whim” to celebrate his birthday with a friend.
But police who stopped him on Oct 17 close to the starting point of a demonstration found several glass bottles, some rags, and a lighter – what the prosecutor described as “the perfect kit” for a Molotov cocktail. He was sentenced to two months in prison and another six suspended.
Souleymane, a 19-year-old from Ivory Coast without valid residency in France, was arrested in northern Paris while allegedly trying to steal a scooter after storming a corner shop. Convicted three times previously, he was sentenced to eight months in prison and taken into custody.
Julien M, 27, a video artist from south-east France, is accused of hurling a traffic cone which just missed a policeman. He vowed that the protest would be his last and the court set him free under judicial control until a trial at the end of November.
In comments on Oct 20 in the northern city of Lille, also badly hit by rioting, Darmanin said 150 people had already been sent to prison, a colossal figure in a country where short sentences are often served outside of prison with electronic tags.
“People with no previous criminal record are being sent to prison. This is extremely unusual, perhaps even unprecedented, for offences involving damage to property,” he added. AFP

US Accuses Russia Of 'Deliberately Reckless' Move With Military Satellite Flyby
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:40:45 UTC
00:40:45 KST

US officials publicly accused Russia of threatening a Finnish-operated commercial satellite that provides imagery and intelligence to Ukraine and other nations, calling the move “deliberately reckless.”
In response to the accusations, made during a United Nations debate on October 21, Russia broadly described US claims as "absurd" and accused Washington of its own “aggressive military space ambitions.”
The back-and-forth came days after a Russian military satellite known as Kosmos-2612 moved “dangerously” near to ICEYE-X36, a satellite registered in the United States and operated by a Finnish company called ICEYE.
The Russian satellite came “exceptionally close” -- within 200 meters, by some estimates -- something that space officials and amateur satellite watchers said was extremely unusual.
"This was not a routine conjunction or 'fly by,'" LeoLabs, an aerospace intelligence company, told RFE/RL. "The behavior is consistent with sophisticated rendezvous and proximity operations."
ICEYE-X36 carries a radar technology that can gather detailed terrestrial images, even through cloud cover. The Finnish company in January signed a contract with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry to provide intelligence.
Kosmos-2612 “exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite,” Brian Hardesty, an adviser to the US Delegation to the Conference on Disarmament, said during a meeting in New York of the UN First Committee, a body that debates arms control and disarmament issues. “These behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation."
“The decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless,” he said.
Russia’s representative who could not be immediately identified, did not directly address the assertion.
"We call on member states to give the proper response to the aggressive military space ambitions of the United States," he said.
He also referenced comments made last month by the secretary of the US Air Force, the top civilian official for that military branch.
Speaking to a conference outside of Washington, Troy Meink’s comments that Washington has in fact deployed actual weapons in space -- “on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the Joint Force against hostile adversary action” -- caused a jolt among policy experts.
Other longtime space watchers, however, said, the announcement merely stated publicly what had already been obvious for some time.
“The United States did not suddenly weaponize space by acknowledging that it possesses these capabilities,” wrote Mallory Stewart, a former top arms control secretary at the US State Department. “An arms race in space has been under way for years.”

Pete Hegseth has reportedly given DHS permission to test ‘heat ray’ for use at US-Mexico border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:40:41 UTC
00:40:41 KST

Pete Hegseth, the US secretary of defense, reportedly signed a memo last month permitting the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to test a non-lethal “heat ray” for potential use at the US southern border.
The “heat ray”, known as the Active Denial System, is a military-grade weapon that shoots an energy beam causing “a sensation of intense heat on the surface of the skin”, according to a 2009 National Defense University case study on the weapon.
The sensation “creates an intolerable sensation and reflexive movement” such as ducking or running.
In a memo, first obtained by CNN, Hegseth authorized a “temporary loan” of the Active Denial System to the DHS for seven months beginning in September. The DHS can request further use of the Pentagon system if needed.
A spokesperson for Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said in a statement it was “continually evaluating new technology, especially technology that can save lives while simultaneously enhancing national security effectiveness”.
When asked for comment, the Pentagon referred the Guardian to the DHS, which shared the CBP statement.
It is unclear what the DHS plans to use the Active Denial System for exactly, but the memo permits the department to use it for potential operations at the US-Mexico border.
The US military initially brought the system to Afghanistan nearly 20 years ago, but it was quickly returned home without ever being used, the Washington Post reported.
Previously, CBP officials reportedly considered using the Active Denial System in areas with a large number of illegal crossings or for crowd dispersal, but it was never deployed.
When used, the Active Denial System can produce an invisible beam of 95 gigahertz that penetrates about 1/64th of an inch into the skin, causing a burning sensation. (The system is technically not a “heat ray” because it uses millimeter waves, not infrared, Forbes reported in 2020.)
Pentagon officials have compared the feeling to a blast of heat when opening a hot oven, according to CNN. The feeling is temporary, lasting between 10 and 15 minutes.
In 2012, the Marine Corps announced that the system was compliant with international legal obligations of the US, and officials said they felt “comfortable” that it was safe.
The new memo, seen by CNN, states that the DHS will be solely responsible for the system’s “employment, use and development of tactics, techniques and procedures”. It also states that no Department of Defense personnel shall operate it.
During the first Trump administration, officials sought to use the Active Denial System, first in 2018 to stop migrants from crossing the border, the New York Times reported. Later, in 2020, the administration also sought it to control protests in Washington DC after the killing of George Floyd, the Washington Post reported.

U.S. orders 60,000 attack drones from nine companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:40:05 UTC
00:40:05 KST

- The U.S. Department of War is preparing orders for 60,000 small attack drones from nine companies after the Drone Dominance Program’s Gauntlet II.
- Perennial Autonomy and Neros topped the Deep Strike and Close Quarters Battle categories, each receiving the maximum initial order of 8,000 drones.
The U.S. Department of War is preparing orders for 60,000 small attack drones from nine companies after the second round of its Drone Dominance Program, with Perennial Autonomy and Neros each set to receive the maximum initial order of 8,000 units.
The Defense Innovation Unit, which runs the program with the Test Resource Management Center, said orders are now in the works following Gauntlet II, a month-long flyoff held in August 2026 at Fort Carson, Colorado. Perennial Autonomy took the top spot in the Deep Strike mission area with 80.1 points, while Neros led the Close Quarters Battle category with 88.1 points, according to the program’s published leaderboard.
“Congratulations to all the winners. Now, it’s time to deliver,” the Defense Innovation Unit wrote in announcing the results.
The orders are split evenly between the two mission areas, with 30,000 drones in each, and scale with each company’s ranking. In Deep Strike, Hyperscale placed second and is in line for 7,000 drones, followed by Neros with 6,000, Skycutter with 5,000 and Swarm Defense Technologies with 4,000. In Close Quarters Battle, ORQA US placed second with 7,000, followed by XTEND with 6,000, Vector with 5,000 and ModalAI with 4,000. Neros is the only company to place in both categories, bringing its combined allocation to 14,000 drones, and final quantities will be set when contracts are awarded.
Gauntlet II tested the drones on a find-fix-finish mission, meaning locating a target, confirming it and striking it. Deep Strike lanes required drones to hit targets from 15 km (9.3 miles) away, while Close Quarters Battle lanes tested performance in confined spaces such as buildings, with part of the testing repeated at night. Additional lanes evaluated controlled strikes and electronic warfare performance, with the drones flown against counter-drone systems designed to jam or defeat them.
Companies were scored on more than flight results. The final rankings combined Gauntlet II performance with evaluations from military operators who flew the systems and an assessment of each company’s ability to produce drones at scale and secure its supply chain.
The second round raised the bar considerably on range. Gauntlet I, held at Fort Benning, Georgia, in February and March 2026, sent 25 companies through testing that included strikes at about 10 km (6.2 miles), and the Defense Innovation Unit said only 24% of drones in that round reached 10 km. That first round produced orders for about 30,000 one-way attack drones worth roughly $150 million, with London-based Skycutter topping the leaderboard and Neros in second place.
The program grew out of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s July 2025 memo on military drone dominance, which called for every U.S. Army squad to be armed with small one-way attack drones by the end of fiscal 2026. The Department of War plans to spend about $1.1 billion across four phases of the program, which is designed to build a U.S.-based industrial base for low-cost expendable drones. Officials said in testimony earlier this year that Phase II would exclude systems using motors or batteries from so-called covered countries, a requirement aimed at Chinese components.
Several of the Gauntlet II winners have already shared details of their orders. Vector said it received orders for up to 5,000 drone systems along with its high-voltage electronic safe and arm device, which lets operators arm drones with different munitions, and XTEND said it delivered 120 STRIKER systems for testing, as The Defence Blog reported when the Close Quarters Battle scores were released.
Officials plan to follow Gauntlet II with Gauntlet 2.5, focused on bomber drones that drop munitions, and Gauntlet 3 is scheduled to begin about six months after Gauntlet II.

ChatGPT adds PIN and Face ID chat locks
Unknown

ChatGPT adds PIN and Face ID chat locks
According to the company’s official guidance, locked conversations disappear from regular chat history, pinned chats and standard conversation searches.
“This can help keep sensitive conversations out of view when you share your screen or use a shared device,” OpenAI said.
Users can access protected conversations through Projects > Locked chats by entering a four-digit account PIN. Supported mobile devices also offer Face ID, Touch ID or device unlock.
To protect an existing conversation, users select “Lock chat” from its options menu and create or enter their PIN.
The feature is rolling out across Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu plans, although some conversation types are ineligible.
Locking a conversation does not add end-to-end encryption or change data retention and model-training settings.
OpenAI also cautions that resetting a forgotten PIN permanently deletes locked conversations and content protected solely by that PIN. Changing a known PIN preserves them.

Families of more than 4,000 Azerbaijanis still missing since the first Karabakh war brought their demand for answers to the EU institutions, hoping that the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan, after decades of suffering on both sides, could finally clarify the fate of their relatives.
Azerbaijani families of missing persons demanded support from EU institutions in Brussels during their demonstrations this week in front of the European Parliament and European Commission headquarters, as they continue to seek the truth about the fate of over 4,000 loved ones still missing since the first Karabakh war.
Organised by the Garabagh Missing Families Public Union, the families asked for help in their quest to establish the fate of their relatives, which include children, women and elderly people, who remain missing since the first war that ended in 1994, urging the EU institutions to pressure Armenia into disclosing archive information and the locations of mass graves.

The families said that Armenia has not disclosed any information about the missing persons, but they hoped that the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan can now shed light on the fate of their loved ones and achieve closure.
The rally participants wore white jackets, each with a picture of their loved one, their date of birth and a question mark, symbolising their unknown fate.
"My husband Azad Jabbarovwent missing in Khojaly and for 34 years we know nothing about him," said Farida Jabbarova, a participant at the rally.
"And here, I represent him and more than 4,000 people who went missing and require justice for them and to receive information."
The demonstration displayed personal items of those missing, including passports, photos and clothes.
According to Konul Behbudova, head of the Garabagh Missing Families Public Union, 328 missing persons were identified with DNA examinations and the remains of 273 victims were handed over to their families, but the fate of thousands is still unknown.
"These territories are contaminated with mines and unexploded ordinance, that's why it's difficult to find them," Behbudova said.
"Our goal is to find the places were these people were buried and find any information about their fate, to get their remains and be able to burry them and to have a place in the cemetery to visit them," Jabbarova said.
The plight of the Azerbaijani families is now part of the wider peace process and reconciliation between Armenia and Azerbaijan after decades of tragic wars over Karabakh which brought immense suffering to both nations, with thousands of casualties and refugees on both sides.

Top 9 horror films worth watching on Halloween
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:37:15 EEST
00:37:15 KST

Top 9 horror films worth watching on Halloween
Kyiv • UNN
A selection of nine horror films featuring mysticism, psychological tension, and supernatural threats. Among them are "The Witch of Konotop" and classic horror movies.
Scary stories come in many forms: some frighten us with otherworldly creatures, others keep us on edge until the very last minute, while some make us reflect on human fears. Over the decades, horror has evolved from classic monsters to psychological thrillers and unusual experiments with the genre. UNN has compiled a selection of the top 9 films that will create a chilling atmosphere and help set the mood for an evening of horror.
Rosemary’s Baby
In Roman Polanski’s film, an ordinary young woman’s life gradually turns into an unsettling story with mystical overtones. Rosemary begins to suspect that the people around her are hiding something dangerous, and that the events happening to her have a much darker explanation than they initially seem to. The film stands out for its atmosphere of constant anxiety and its skillful use of ambiguity. Rather than immediately revealing the source of the fear, the director leaves viewers room for doubt and speculation. It was this approach that made the film a notable example of supernatural horror.
The Ring
Journalist Rachel Keller begins investigating the mysterious deaths of four teenagers. Shortly before their deaths, they had all watched a strange videotape and then received a phone call warning them that they had only seven days left to live. A fifth girl, who witnessed her friend’s death, lost her mind. Rachel’s niece was among the victims, so the journalist decides to find out what the mysterious recording conceals. She finds the tape and watches it, but soon receives the same call, accompanied by a horrifying prediction of her own death. Together with a friend who works as a video engineer, Rachel tries to uncover the recording’s origins and stop the unknown threat. However, the danger also spreads to her family: the journalist’s son accidentally watches a copy of the video, after which he begins to be haunted by terrifying visions.
The Babadook
Amelia raises her son Sam on her own after the death of her husband, who died on the child’s birthday. The woman tries to cope with everyday difficulties, but the boy’s behavior becomes increasingly strange. Sam is convinced that a terrifying creature named the Babadook has moved into their home. Gradually, fear enters the lives of the entire family. However, the film is not only about a mysterious monster. Through Amelia’s story, the director shows a mother’s exhaustion, her inner tension, and the difficulty of living with constant responsibility for a child. "The Babadook" combines supernatural horror with psychological drama.
The Cabin in the Woods
A group of young people sets out to spend the weekend in a remote cabin in the woods. At first, everything resembles the familiar plot of a classic slasher, in which a group finds itself far from civilization and encounters danger. However, it soon becomes clear that events are unfolding in a completely unexpected way. The film plays with the familiar rules of horror movies and turns well-known genre conventions into part of an unexpected story. It has typical characters, a creepy location, and situations reminiscent of dozens of other horror films, but the creators use these elements to reinterpret the genre.
Paranormal Activity
A young couple moves into a house where unexplained things begin to happen. The woman says that she has felt the presence of an unknown entity since childhood. Her partner decides to set up a camera to record everything that happens at night. The film is shot in the found-footage style: viewers observe events through camera recordings, creating an impression of reality. Oren Peli worked on the film in his own home, and the production budget was approximately $15,000. After its release, the film became a major commercial success and launched an entire franchise.
The Witch
The events unfold in 17th-century New England. A Puritan family is expelled from the community and settles near the forest, hoping to start life anew. But the peace does not last long: the youngest child disappears without a trace, and strange things begin happening in the house. Gradually, distrust and fear grow among the family members. The mother is overcome by despair, the father begins to doubt, and their eldest daughter, Thomasin, is suspected of witchcraft. The film creates tension through its gloomy atmosphere, historical setting, and the conflict between religious beliefs and inexplicable events. It is a slow-burn horror film in which fear gradually builds, while the boundary between superstition and the supernatural remains uncertain.
The Witch of Konotop
The beautiful Olena has left her witching past behind for love and a peaceful life. However, the full-scale invasion destroys her plans: while trying to leave the combat zone, the woman loses her beloved, who is killed by Russian occupiers. What she has endured changes Olena. She returns to her true nature and uses supernatural powers to take revenge on those who took the most precious person in her life from her. The film reimagines the image of the Witch of Konotop in the context of the modern war. The film stars Tetiana Malkova and Taras Tsymbaliuk. For director Andrii Kolesnyk, it was his feature-film debut. Real captured military equipment was also used during filming.
Annabelle
John and Mia are preparing to become parents. To please his wife, the husband gives her a vintage doll to add to her collection. But that very night, their home becomes the site of a brutal attack: members of a Satanic cult break into the house. After this event, the couple encounters inexplicable phenomena connected with the doll. A dark entity is behind them, turning the family home into a place of constant fear. "Annabelle" combines the theme of occultism with a story about a threat to a young family. The doll itself plays a particularly important role in creating the eerie atmosphere, with its stillness only intensifying the sense of danger.
Other
In the mid-1940s, Grace Stewart lives with her two children in an old mansion on the island of Jersey. She is waiting for her husband to return from the war, though there has been no news of him for a long time. Her children cannot tolerate sunlight, so strict rules apply in the house: the windows must be covered with curtains, and the doors must be kept tightly shut. The usual order is disrupted when her daughter Anne tells her about an unfamiliar boy whom she supposedly saw in the house. The girl claims that he lives there with his family. At first, Grace does not believe her, but eventually she begins to notice strange things herself. The film gradually reveals a story in which the secrets of the old mansion intertwine with fear and very unexpected plot twists.
Mama
After the mysterious disappearance of their father, two young sisters, Victoria and Lily, are left alone in an abandoned house in the forest. Several years later, the girls are found and taken in by their uncle Lucas and his girlfriend Annabel. The children gradually adjust to their new life, but they behave strangely and constantly mention a mysterious "Mama" who, according to them, cared for them throughout all the years they were alone. Eventually, the adults begin to notice strange phenomena in the house... It constantly scratches at the walls and makes strange noises. At first, the new parents believe it is either the children’s imagination or emotional trauma, but in the end it becomes clear that it is their dead mother, who has returned from the other world to look after the children.

Greece, Egypt in talks to extend maritime zone further east
Oct 22 - Greece and Egypt are discussing extending their Exclusive Economic Zone eastwards towards Cyprus after eastern Libya's parliament ratified a disputed maritime agreement with Turkey earlier this week, Greece's foreign minister said.
Greece, Egypt and Cyprus have long opposed the Turkey-Libya maritime accord, arguing that it infringes on their own maritime claims in the eastern Mediterranean.
Any extension of the Greece-Egypt agreement would be fully in line with international law and the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis said on X.
Gerapetritis and Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty also reaffirmed their opposition to eastern Libya's ratification of the 2019 maritime memorandum between Turkey and Libya, saying they remained committed to international law and UNCLOS.
Greece and Egypt signed an agreement in 2020 delimiting an Exclusive Economic Zone in the eastern Mediterranean. REUTERS
