Hundreds of Ethiopians flee into Kenya after border town fighting
ISIOLO, Kenya, Oct 22 - Hundreds of Ethiopians have fled into Kenya following fighting in the border town of Moyale, Kenya Red Cross and local government officials said on Thursday.
Fighting broke out on Wednesday and gunfire could still be heard a day after in parts of the town on the Ethiopian side of the border, residents said. The settlement straddles the frontier and also extends into Kenyan territory.
It was not immediately clear what had started the fighting in parts of the town in the south of Ethiopia's Oromiya region. Officials there were not immediately reachable for comment.
"We have hundreds of people from Ethiopia, mainly children and women," the commissioner from Kenya's Marsabit county, Stanley Kamande, told Reuters.
"Many are staying with relatives and well-wishers in several villages at Moyale side Kenya," he added.
The Kenya Red Cross said it was conducting an assessment to work out how many people were affected and what their needs were.
"No camp is ready to host those displaced but we shall most definitely work on it," Red Cross official Ibrae John said.
The fighting broke out hundreds of miles away, on the other side of Ethiopia, from a conflict in the northern Tigray region between government forces and a rebel alliance led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front. REUTERS

Hendel: Reservists/Economic Party may not the biggest, but it will be most important - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:35:06 UTC
00:35:06 KST

The Reservists or the New Economic Party will be the most important party in the election even if it is not the largest, its leader Yoaz Hendel told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.
“We may not be the biggest party, but we will be the most important, because we are in nobody’s pocket,” Hendel said.
The party, he explained, will only join a coalition of Zionist parties, and isn’t ruling any of them out based on whether they are or are not current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“If a government comprising Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu, and [Naftali] Bennett were formed tomorrow morning, I would be part of it,” he added. “I’m not in the ‘anyone but Bibi’ camp.”
Hendel distinguished between his opposition to Netanyahu’s leadership and his willingness to join a government that includes him. His coalition decisions, he argued, would depend on its partners and policies rather than the prime minister’s presence alone.
“I make no secret of wanting to persuade everyone not to vote for Bibi. I make no secret of believing he bears responsibility for October 7,” he said. “But Netanyahu is not the central issue in my outlook.”
Reservists-Economic chair says his party will decide coalition for 2026 election
His refusal to sit with the haredi (Ultra-Orthodox) parties would also exclude a partnership with Likud if Netanyahu insisted on bringing them into the coalition.
“I won’t sit with the haredi parties. If Likud can’t part ways with them, I won’t sit with Likud,” Hendel said.
Hendel presented his party’s position outside the two rival blocs as the source of its potential influence, arguing that neither camp could form a government without it.
“Without the Reservists/Economic Party, there is a zero percent chance that either bloc will form a government. Zero, not even one percent,” he said.
That prediction underpins his argument for supporting a smaller party: Rather than strengthening an existing bloc, he wants voters to give his party the leverage to demand a different coalition.
“Every vote for our party influences Israel’s future. Every vote for the blocs keeps us stuck,” he said.
Hendel described a constituency spanning voters on the right who support settlement but oppose draft evasion, and voters in the center and on the left who reject cooperation with Arab parties that have not recognized Hamas as a terrorist organization.
“We want to hold the deciding vote,” he said.
Asked whether pressure on parties hovering around the electoral threshold could persuade him to withdraw, Hendel rejected the premise that other political leaders should determine how his supporters vote.
“That’s a quarter of a million Israelis who have the right to choose what they want to do,” he said. “Nobody can tell them what they should do.”
He criticized both Winter’s alignment with Netanyahu and the haredi parties and what he characterized as Eisenkot, Bennett, and Avigdor Liberman’s membership in an opposing bloc dependent on Arab parties.
“The moment you say you will only go with Netanyahu and the haredi parties, you are in the ‘only Bibi’ bloc. That means you won’t address conscription,” he said of Winter.
“There is no chance of recruiting soldiers when you’re with Goldknopf and Goldknopf is your partner.”
Hendel said he had repeatedly urged Winter to break that partnership, describing his own party as Winter’s “natural political home.”
Asked what would make parties such as Ra’am or Shas acceptable partners, Hendel said his objection was not to Arab or haredi citizens.
“I have nothing against haredim or Arabs,” he said. “I hope that one day there will be a haredi party of people who enlist and serve, and that one day there will be an Arab party of people who serve and see themselves as part of Israel.”
He linked that position to demands for core curriculum studies, the teaching of Zionism, and Israeli flags in publicly funded classrooms. Families rejecting that framework should fund their children’s education themselves, he argued.
“Every Israeli citizen will do something for the country, and anyone who doesn’t will receive nothing.”
Hendel backs Zelekha on economic demands
Hendel’s coalition conditions also extend to the economic agenda of his political partner, Yaron Zelekha of the New Economic Party.
“Both issues weigh heavily on reservists,” he said. “It isn’t only conscription. The cost of living hurts them badly, too.”
He also cautioned that easing the burden on existing reservists would take time. Training an infantry soldier takes approximately eight months, he said, while reducing annual reserve service to 30 days under current conditions remained a “pipe dream.”
Asked what he would change about his earlier conduct in politics, Hendel acknowledged making “plenty of mistakes,” pointing to the cycle of elections and dissolving Knessets, arguing that remaining in politics could not be an end in itself.
“Politics brought us to October 7, and politics has to get us out of it,” he said.
Hendel said his experience commanding reservists taught him that leadership depends on persuasion rather than simply issuing orders - an approach he said also shaped his partnership with Zelekha.
“Ultimately, what matters isn’t your rank but your level of commitment,” he said. “The same applies to politics.”

US House committee investigation exposes antisemitism, political indoctrination in public schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:34:26 UTC
00:34:26 KST

A congressional investigation released on Wednesday has detailed widespread antisemitism and political activism within American K-12 public schools and major teachers' unions following the October 7, 2023 attacks against Israel.
The majority staff report, called “Antisemitism in K-12 Schools” and published by the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, stated that antisemitic incidents in US schools increased by 135 percent in 2023, prompting congressional inquiries into several major school districts and labor organizations.
Committee Chairman Tim Walberg said, “Parents send their children to school to learn reading, writing, and math—not to be taught to hate Israel or embrace radical political causes. Yet that’s exactly the kind of material our investigation uncovered. Jewish students deserve to feel safe in their classrooms, and parents deserve to know what their children are being taught. Schools that receive taxpayer dollars must be held accountable when they fail to protect students from antisemitism.”
Investigations opened into California, Pennsylvania, Virginia schools
Under Chairman Walberg’s leadership, the committee opened investigations into Berkeley Unified School District (BUSD) in California, the School District of Philadelphia (SDP) in Pennsylvania, and Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia.
The committee selected school districts of varying size and geographic location after receiving numerous reports of antisemitic incidents. The committee noted that its inquiry into Fairfax County remains ongoing.
As part of the wider inquiry, the committee conducted a transcribed interview with Philadelphia Superintendent Dr. Tony Watlington on September 18, 2026, and also investigated the nation’s largest teachers union, the National Education Association (NEA), over allegations of antisemitism.
The committee released documents obtained through its investigations into Berkeley, Philadelphia, and the NEA while continuing its inquiry into Fairfax County.
Focusing on the SDP, the report examined the ninth-largest school district in the US, which comprises 330 schools. The district entered into a federal civil rights resolution agreement with the US Department of Education in December 2024 to address the handling of antisemitic harassment following a sharp rise in incidents after October 7, 2023. According to the congressional report, the investigation found that district curricula promoted ideology justifying violent resistance and legitimized radical groups that incite antisemitism.
Curriculum writers portrayed all resistance as righteous
For example, investigators detailed that a world history curriculum unit covering resistance movements directed students to honor a movement of their choice, listing the Gaza Great March of Return as an option, and opened by teaching that the fight to decolonize in India was not always peaceful.
The report noted that teachers were told to examine the works of Frantz Fanon, whose writings argue that decolonization is inherently violent and who is frequently cited by anti-Israel activists to justify the October 7 attacks.
The congressional report stated that the Philadelphia district’s materials also relied on resources from the Racial Justice Organizing Committee, noting that leaders of the group declared that all resistance is righteous and that there are no two sides to ‘apartheid, occupation, and genocide’.
In lessons using these materials, the report found that Philadelphia students were asked to color-code aspects of their identities as dominant or oppressed. These lessons categorized males, white people, and Christians as dominant, and black people, LGBTQ people, immigrants, and non-Christians as oppressed.
Furthermore, investigators outlined that district curricula introduce far-left activism and terms like “intersectionality,” “ally,” and “social justice” as early as the third grade. The report added that curricula recommended children’s books introducing pronouns such as “ey/em” and “ze/zir”.
According to the report, investigators established that district employees responsible for writing curricula fomented antisemitism online and among colleagues. This included the director of social studies curriculum, Ismael Jimenez, who the report noted had repeatedly rationalized violence against Jews.
The report stated that other curriculum writers maintained that all resistance is righteous. Additionally, investigators documented that the district has repeatedly partnered with the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) Philadelphia. The report highlighted that a representative previously suggested that curricular materials be reviewed for bias by qualified Muslim educators, and that Superintendent Watlington’s transition team included the group’s former executive director.
During his September 2026 interview with the committee, Superintendent Watlington stated that the social studies curriculum complied with district policies and did not indoctrinate students. He added that the district would standardize its curriculum by using national experts and that the social studies curriculum director was undergoing termination proceedings.
In Berkeley Unified School District, consisting of 20 schools in California, investigators examined extensive antisemitism complaints lodged by parents and students since October 7, 2023. These complaints occurred alongside the district’s adoption of liberated ethnic studies.
The report found that BUSD collaborated with the Liberated Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum Consortium, paying over $111,000 for curriculum writing and consulting since August 2023. According to the congressional findings, this collaboration resulted in lessons littered with antisemitic resources and activist ideology.
Berkeley’s ninth-grade Arab American Studies unit featured an ancestor acknowledgment of Helen Thomas. The report stated that the unit defended her remarks, which told Jewish people to leave the Middle East and go home to Poland and Germany, by framing the controversial statements as constructive activism, asserting that she was engaged in what is termed “good trouble” and that her comments had been taken out of context.
The congressional report noted that BUSD’s ethnic studies units cover topics like the seven pillars of colonization, including killing cultures and exploiting land, and feature specific lessons arguing that Asian people have been weaponized as pawns to serve a white supremacist agenda.
Leadership rationalized Hamas attacks
Berkeley elementary and high school teachers also collaborated on teaching guides that featured the alphabet book P is for Palestine. The book includes selections such as ‘I is for Intifada’. The guides recommended organizations such as the Middle East Children’s Alliance (MECA) and the Arab Resource and Organizing Center (AROC).
Berkeley high school teachers approved an Israel and Palestine lesson set that the report stated whitewashed terrorism and portrayed the phrase "from the river to the sea" as a call for freedom and peace. The committee noted that teachers warned colleagues that the curriculum could not be shared directly with families.
Furthermore, investigators documented that district staff and students raised money through bake sales and bracelet sales for MECA. The report highlighted that the Network Contagion Research Institute (NCRI) identified this organization as having fiscal and personnel ties to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), a US-designated foreign terrorist organization.
At the NEA, representing more than three million educators and administrators, investigators found that antisemitism surged following October 7, 2023. This surge culminated in a 2025 delegate vote to ban Anti-Defamation League (ADL) materials.
According to internal NEA documents cited in the report, the union was already not working with the ADL because of the watchdog’s efforts to combat contemporary antisemitism. Internal memos criticized the ADL for denigrating the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement.
The report also detailed that the NEA’s Center for Racial and Social Justice (CRSJ) advised against implementing a resolution by the union’s Jewish Affairs Caucus (JAC) to combat antisemitism because it utilized the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition.
Union staff wrote in a briefing document that the definition had been used by racist and nationalist actors as cover. Additionally, internal documents showed union leaders were advised to avoid action language regarding historical events in the Middle East because history is hotly contested.
Leadership was also explicitly advised that keffiyehs should be allowed at association gatherings as a sign of support for Palestine. The report confirmed that the union pledged thousands of dollars to Rethinking Schools and the Zinn Education Project.
According to the committee, these organizations published statements after October 7 rationalizing Hamas terrorist attacks by pointing to US and Israeli colonialism.
The committee concluded stating that political activism has increasingly displaced educational neutrality across American public education. This has created an environment where antisemitism is minimized, excused, and permitted to flourish.
The committee stated that “public schools should educate students, not enlist them in political causes.” The report added that “parents should be able to trust that schools will educate their children without subjecting them to radical ideology.”
The report stressed that “Jewish students are entitled to the same protection from discrimination and harassment as every other student, regardless of whether hostility toward them is expressed in overt antisemitic terms or cloaked in political rhetoric.”
The committee vowed that it “will continue to use its oversight authority to examine these issues, consider appropriate legislation, and hold federally funded institutions accountable for compliance with federal civil rights law.”

IDF intelligence continues to provide Saudi Arabia with exceptional capabilities to assist its military operations against the Houthis through US mediation, a defense official confirmed on Thursday.
The assistance is being provided in accordance with Israel's national interests and directives from the political leadership, the official said, emphasizing that the Shi'ite-Sunni confrontation reflects developments taking place beneath the surface across the Middle East.
According to the official, Sunni countries are watching the escalation led by the Houthis against neighboring Saudi Arabia, with encouragement and support from Iran, and understand that they could be next.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, is concentrating its efforts on launching powerful attacks against an extensive range of targets in Houthi-controlled areas, seeking to degrade critical military capabilities, including infrastructure.
"Two main points need to be made about this. First, it serves Israel's interests quite well because it wears down the military strength of an Israeli enemy that is preparing and planning to harm us in the future. In addition, we are monitoring and observing methods of operation and tactics, and learning a great deal from what is happening there, including about weapons that are not necessarily manufactured by the Houthis," the official said.
IDF helps Saudi Arabia combat Houthis
The defense official added that the relentless attacks against the Houthis are eroding their capabilities and forcing them to expend considerable effort.
"The Houthis are accustomed to building up their forces, not employing them on this scale. They are a serious enemy, well structured for the long term, but this presents them with a significant challenge. It is no coincidence that they operate sequentially rather than simultaneously against their enemies."
The official further said that the pressure on Saudi Arabia is reshaping alliances and relationships across the Middle East, creating new opportunities.
"The question here is who will intervene on Saudi Arabia's behalf. There is apprehension among countries, but we assess that there will be intervention. Everything remains open, and it is not too late for that to happen."
Meanwhile, the IDF is completing preparations across the sea, air, land, and electromagnetic spectrum domains for a potential Houthi attack as part of a multi-front scenario involving Iran, Hezbollah, and Shi'ite militias operating from Iraq.
The preparations include not only the integration of new technologies and sensors, along with improved connectivity within the IDF and between organizations, but also coordination with the US military.
The US military has a clear interest in protecting Israel's home front because thousands of American troops, aircraft, and US military systems, including air defense systems, are stationed in Israel.

Lockheed lines up deal for 850 U.S. F-35s over 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:32:33 UTC
00:32:33 KST

- The U.S. Department of War and Lockheed Martin agreed on a framework for 850 U.S. F-35s over 10 years, covering Lots 21 through 30.
- The deal keeps production at 156 aircraft a year and moves to a formal contract once Congress grants multiyear authority and funding.
The U.S. Department of War and Lockheed Martin have agreed on a framework for a 10-year F-35 production and sustainment deal that covers 850 aircraft for the United States, along with spare parts, modification kits and international orders across production Lots 21 through 30.
The framework keeps F-35 production at 156 aircraft a year and folds three things that have traditionally been bought separately into one long-term plan: new jets with their initial spares, a decade of modification kits, and fleet sustainment. The next step runs through Congress: once multiyear authority and the associated funding are granted, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will finalize contract terms, pricing and delivery schedules in a formal contract award.
“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” said Lockheed Martin Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet. “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain. That’s good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies.”
The 850 U.S. aircraft over 10 years work out to an average of 85 jets a year for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps, with the remainder of the 156-a-year production rate going to international partners and foreign customers. The United States plans to buy a total of 2,456 F-35s across its three services.
Until now, the F-35 has been bought in lot-by-lot contracts that often took years to negotiate. The most recent deal, covering Lots 18 and 19, was finalized on Sept. 29, 2025, after a handshake agreement the previous December, and covers 296 aircraft worth about $24.3 billion. Long-lead funding for parts for Lot 20 and Lot 21 aircraft has already been awarded, and Lot 21 is now the first lot included in the new framework.
A multiyear arrangement lets Lockheed Martin and its suppliers commit to larger, longer orders for raw materials and parts. The company says that approach will produce volume discounts, lower unit prices and savings for taxpayers estimated in the billions of dollars over the life of the program, while giving the government more predictable costs.
Readiness is a central part of the plan. The framework links aircraft production with purchases of spare and modification parts and adds integrated analytics that tie budget decisions to readiness results and give real-time visibility into parts inventories. Lockheed Martin says replacing the annual contracting cycle with long-term supplier contracts will cut turnaround times for parts and repairs and raise mission capable rates, the share of the fleet ready to fly its assigned missions.
“Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” said OJ Sanchez, president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics.
The company estimates the program will support 317,000 U.S. jobs and generate about $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade. International customers would share in the benefits through economies of scale across the global fleet and its shared sustainment network.
More than 1,375 F-35s are now in service around the world, operating from 42 bases, including in 13 countries that fly the jet from home soil, and the fleet has passed 1 million flight hours. Lockheed Martin delivered a record 191 F-35s in 2025.
The F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will move to a formal contract award for Lots 21 through 30 once Congress grants multiyear authority and the associated appropriations, which the companies expect in the coming months.

Save $150 on the Apple Mac Mini M4, but There’s a Catch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:30:31 UTC
00:30:31 KST

Apple’s Mac Mini M4 has become a popular mini-yet-mighty desktop computer for running local agentic AI 24/7—so much so that it’s been out of stock for months. But with the introduction of the new Mac Mini M6, the older M4 is no longer as scarce (there was no M5 Mac Mini), and the base model (256-GB hard drive, 16-GB unified memory) is on sale for $649—$150 off MSRP and $250 cheaper than the M6.
It’s a good deal for a computer that is plenty powerful for most people, and some M4 Mac Mini configurations can even handle AI tasks. But—and it’s a big but—shoppers should be aware that the M4’s original base price was $599 when it launched in 2024. However, with Apple raising prices on hardware across the board this year, driven by chip and memory shortages, the M4 ended up costing $799. In comparison, the new M6 starts at $899.
Depending on how you look at it, it’s either a discount or a hard pill to swallow, knowing that it used to be much cheaper. If you’ve been eyeing a new Mac Mini and don’t need the better performance of the M6, you’re unlikely to get a lower price than this M4.
Older but Still Capable
The M4 Mac Mini may no longer be Apple’s most powerful tiny computer—that title now belongs to the M6 and M5 Pro models—but the M4 is still an incredibly strong and efficient processor. When it was discovered that it could easily run agentic AI locally, people gobbled up the Mac Mini as the affordable computing option.
Of course, for intensive tasks like AI or video editing, you really need more than 16 GB of memory; those who bought it for AI purposes loaded it up with 32 GB of RAM. For most users, however, this base-specs machine is more than capable. While the M6 system on a chip is extra powerful due to having more CPU and GPU cores, Neural Accelerators, and higher memory bandwidth, the M4 Mac Mini isn’t lagging far behind. For things like web browsing and general productivity, you won’t see much of a difference in performance.
If you need the performance, we recommend the newer M6. But for most people, the M4 Mac Mini is more than sufficient for everyday computing, and you're unlikely to find a better deal than this one.

Compte rendu du Conseil des ministres du 22 octobre 2026.
PROJETS DE LOI
ACCORD ENTRE LA FRANCE ET LES FIDJI CONCERNANT LA COOPERATION EN MATIERE DE DEFENSE ET LE STATUT DES FORCES
Le ministre de l’Europe et des affaires étrangères a présenté un projet de loi autorisant l’approbation de l’accord entre le Gouvernement de la République française et le Gouvernement de la République des Fidji concernant la coopération en matière de défense et le statut des forces.
Cet accord, signé à Nouméa le 6 décembre 2023 par le ministre des armées de la République française et le ministre des affaires intérieures et de l’immigration de la République des Fidji, instaure entre les deux pays une coopération structurée dans le domaine de la défense et régit le statut des forces françaises aux Fidji et inversement celui des forces fidjiennes en France en cas de séjour ou de transit. Cet accord fixe un cadre juridique solide et pérenne à la coopération entre les deux pays en matière de défense dans des domaines tels que l’armement, la formation et la fourniture d’aide humanitaire.
Cet accord s’inscrit ainsi dans la stratégie française dans l’Indopacifique et participe au renforcement de notre relation bilatérale avec la République des Fidji, pays avec lequel la France entretient notamment une coopération en matière de maintien de la paix et de réponse aux catastrophes naturelles à travers les forces françaises déployées dans le Pacifique.
CONVENTION DE PARTENARIAT ENTRE LA FRANCE ET L’ORGANISATION INTERNATIONALE DE POLICE CRIMINELLE – INTERPOL (OIPC-INTERPOL) RELATIVE AUX MODALITES DE REALISATION DU PROGRAMME IMMOBILIER GLOBAL DU SIEGE D’INTERPOL A LYON ET AUX ENGAGEMENTS ET RESPONSABILITES DU GOUVERNEMENT FRANÇAIS ET D’INTERPOL
Le ministre de l’Europe et des affaires étrangères a présenté un projet de loi autorisant l’approbation de la convention de partenariat entre le Gouvernement de la République française et l’Organisation internationale de police criminelle – INTERPOL (OIPC-INTERPOL) relative aux modalités de réalisation du Programme Immobilier Global du siège d’INTERPOL à Lyon et aux engagements et responsabilités du Gouvernement de la République française et d’INTERPOL, signée à Marrakech le 27 novembre 2025 et à Lyon le 15 décembre 2025.
INTERPOL a établi son siège à la cité internationale à Lyon en 1989. A la suite d’une croissance continue des effectifs et des activités d’INTERPOL, le siège existant nécessite une opération immobilière d’envergure.
La convention de partenariat définit ainsi le cadre juridique, opérationnel et financier d’un programme immobilier global, répondant aux besoins fonctionnels et opérationnels d’INTERPOL, et des engagements et responsabilités respectifs des Parties. Ce programme comprend des travaux de rénovation du siège existant, financés par INTERPOL, et des travaux d’extension et de restructuration, financés par la France à hauteur de 61,2 millions d’euros, dont 43,2 millions d’euros de l’Etat. La convention de partenariat permettra de pérenniser l’implantation du siège d’INTERPOL à Lyon en créant des conditions de travail modernisées et adaptées à l’ensemble des agents d’INTERPOL, avec une ouverture des nouveaux locaux prévue en 2031.
Elle renforce l’attractivité du territoire national pour l’installation d’organisations internationales.

US President Donald Trump has failed to reach an agreement with Russian ruler Vladimir Putin on halting strikes against Ukraine's energy infrastructure. However, Trump is trying to shift the blame for this failure onto President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, he said on The Diary of a CEO podcast.
His words came amid Russia's four record waves of ballistic missile attacks, after US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian." Previously, US officials cut Kyiv off from US intelligence and lowered a speed cap on Starlink to pressure Ukraine into stopping strikes on Russia's oil refineries that bring Moscow revenue for its war.
Trump pins the problem on Kyiv, not Putin
Zelenskyy explained the behavioral pattern behind Trump's recent actions and statements. At first, Putin rejected his proposal for a ceasefire. Then, the US president blamed it all on him, explaining to his people that world fuel prices are rising because of him, which is not true at all, said the Ukrainian leader.
He pointed to the blocked Strait of Hormuz shipping chokepoint, not Ukraine’s refinery campaign, as the driver of higher prices.
He also noted that the volumes of diesel allowed by the US are insufficient to lower global oil prices.
Even so, Zelenskyy said he keeps a working relationship with Trump. What he will not accept is being cast as the villain in Russia’s war: by his account, the US president is rewriting the context, turning Ukraine’s leader into the target for a problem that starts in Moscow.
Earlier, experts said the diesel deal was unlikely to meaningfully lower diesel prices. For Putin, the agreement itself was a win.
A former senior State Department official says it hardly matters whether the fuel arrives, because Putin “has already achieved the result he wants,” with Trump believing he has a pre-election card that could move markets.

What would make neonatal units safer for babies? | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:27:59 UTC
00:27:59 KST

I support Mark McDonald’s submission that the Thirlwall recommendations will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS (17 October). We often hear of hospital scandals where trusts are intent on preserving their reputations, internal inquiries go nowhere, defensive clinical staff deflect blame on to others, non‑disclosure to patients of errors and “lessons learned” rhetoric that is quickly forgotten. There is also an industry of ambulance-chasing lawyers. None of this is conducive to a no-blame, honest, open culture in healthcare. The Thirlwall recommendations of more surveillance will make it worse.
There is an alternative. Most of my professional life as a hospital consultant, clinical director and deputy chief medical officer has been spent in New Zealand, whose publicly funded NHS is the same model as the UK’s – but with a major difference. In the 1970s, New Zealanders lost their right to sue for damages for medical accidents or injury through the public court system with the Accident Compensation Act. This got rid of the grievance culture and ambulance-chasers, and the system provided remedial care for any injury. In the 80s, after a huge scandal regarding medical investigations, the Cartwright inquiry ushered in the creation of the independent Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC) and overriding principles of patient safety, interests and consent.
All complaints – from patients, public and staff – about any health facility, organisation or practitioner go first to the office of the HDC for investigation. If the HDC deems it necessary, it goes to the various professional disciplinary bodies or to the Medical Council of New Zealand. HDC reports on complaints are publicly available.
In 2005, the government passed its “no fault, no blame” legislation. This brought in a duty to report “any risk of harm to the public from authorities responsible for patient safety”. This freed clinicians to engage with any compensation cases with openness. The system has its critics, but overall works well.
 
Dr Pamela S Melding 
 
St Helens, Merseyside
Mark McDonald’s column is a breath of common sense. The Criminal Cases Review Commission is still considering Lucy Letby’s convictions, yet Lady Justice Kathryn Thirlwall has constructed a programme of reform on the assumption that the central conclusion of the case is beyond question. Meanwhile, barely enough time has passed for reflection on what would actually make neonatal units safer.
Thirlwall’s answer appears to be surveillance, suspicion and blame: cameras in cots, encouragement to report colleagues and an explicit retreat from the “no blame” culture developed precisely to make organisations safer.
But what makes a hospital safe? Is it a nurse wondering whether a colleague is about to report them, or a nurse confident enough to admit that they have made a mistake? Is it a doctor practising defensively, or one willing to report a near-miss before it becomes a tragedy?
Destroy candour and you destroy one of the most powerful tools of patient safety. A frightened workforce will hide mistakes, keep quiet about doubts and practise defensively. Patients will pay.
 
Mark Hanson
 
Hitchin, Hertfordshire
In March this year my daughter was born and died in the neonatal intensive care unit seven days later. I believe her death was preventable and one key mistake was made that resulted in her death. But I don’t blame the consultant who made (what I consider to be) the error. She was doing the best she could in a difficult situation.
What I find concerning is the follow-up from the trust’s management. They have bent over backwards to try to hide their tracks rather than discussing it openly and using it as an opportunity to learn and ensure other babies don’t suffer a similar fate. The response has been so heavy-handed that it’s an insight into the fear and blame culture doctors face, which I find so concerning. Mistakes are an opportunity to learn.
 
Name and address supplied
 Mark McDonald makes many good points. But sadly he overlooks the role that patients and families play in their healthcare and safety. The NHS needs staff who can speak up without fear. But it also needs patients who are listened to, informed, supported and involved. Some of the most important safety signals come not from systems, but from the people experiencing care. If there is one lesson from the Lucy Letby case, it is that patients and families must be recognised as partners in identifying risk, seeking answers and driving improvement.
 
Paul Whiteing
 
CEO, Action Against Medical Accidents

Romanian Man From England Jailed 15 Years in Russia After Online Romance Led Him to Abkhazia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:27:04 UTC
00:27:04 KST

- Category
- World
Romanian Man From England Jailed 15 Years in Russia After Online Romance Led Him to Abkhazia
A Romanian citizen raised in England was sentenced to 15 years in prison in Russia on espionage charges, following what Reuters exposed as a staged FSB arrest video filmed months after his actual detention, Reuters reported on October 22.
David Adrian Kercso, now 23, was accused by Russia’s Federal Security Service of passing information about Russian air-defense systems in Sochi to Ukrainian intelligence.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The FSB released footage purporting to show Kercso being arrested in a park in Sochi. However, Reuters analysis of the video and Russian court records showed that he had already been in Russian custody for several months when the footage was recorded.
The first public announcement of Kercso’s detention came from pro-Russian separatist authorities in Abkhazia, a breakaway region of Georgia, after he disappeared on November 28, 2024.
Two weeks later, Abkhazian security authorities released video showing Kercso in custody and confessing that he had been in contact with Ukrainian intelligence and had been instructed to film military sites with a drone.
Kercso later wrote to his family that the confession had been dictated to him by his captors and that he had been told he would be sent home if he memorized and repeated the statement on camera.
Instead, he was transferred to Russia and appeared before a judge in Sochi on December 14, 2024. Court records reviewed by Reuters documented 10 appearances over the following four months as his detention was repeatedly extended.
Kercso wrote that the FSB filmed the staged arrest scene in mid-April 2025, after taking him from jail early in the morning to a park along Sochi’s Matsesta River.
Reuters found that the visible vegetation and location details were consistent with his account and showed the footage could not have been recorded before his documented detention began.
“We have seen this in dozens of cases where individuals detained months earlier are taken to a city street, a forest, or a train station so that a staged arrest video can be filmed,” Russian lawyer Evgeny Smirnov told Reuters.
Kercso also alleged that he was beaten, tortured, and held in isolation after being transferred to Russia. Reuters could not independently verify those claims.
When he was sentenced, the FSB stated that Kercso had transmitted the location of Russian air-defense systems in Sochi to Ukrainian intelligence during the summer of 2024.
Kercso rejected the accusation and stated that his later confession to the FSB had also been coerced.
“None of that happened, they stole my life for no reason and fabricated everything,” he wrote.
Kercso’s family believes he traveled to the Black Sea region after beginning an online relationship with a woman from Abkhazia. His mother stated that she had warned him not to go because of the war.
“Now I know that coming here was a huge mistake,” Kercso wrote from prison. “I was blinded by love and didn’t see the warning signs.”
Kercso’s case is not the only recent example of a Western national facing serious consequences after going to Russia. One such case is Texas resident Derek Huffman, who moved there with his family in 2025 under Moscow’s “shared values” visa program, then joined the Russian military and was reportedly sent near the front line despite initially expecting a non-combat role.

Carers can’t live on 51p an hour | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:26:59 UTC
00:26:59 KST

For 13 years, I have cared for my lovely 101-year-old adoptive mum who requires round-the-clock care. I feel blessed to care for her and have no regrets. But love does not pay the bills.
Carer’s allowance is £86.45 a week for 2026-27. Spread across 168 hours, that is roughly 51p an hour. As a sole carer, I have no downtime. I still work part-time as a self-employed therapist when Mum’s health allows, but when she is poorly, my work stops while the bills continue.
I do not claim carer’s allowance as the frequent paperwork required to report changes in my self-employed earnings is difficult to manage alongside my caring responsibilities.
Last winter, our electricity bill exceeded £400 a month because Mum needs heating round the clock. This is the reality of caring in a cost of living crisis. I worked hard to buy and pay off my own home. But it had no downstairs bedroom or bathroom, and was unsuitable for Mum. I had to rent it out, hoping one day to live there. Eventually, caring and the costs of maintaining the property forced me to sell, and I faced a capital gains tax bill.
I do not blame HMRC for applying the rules. I question whether government policy takes sufficient account of people whose caring responsibilities force them to make difficult decisions about their homes. Unpaid carers save society enormously, often at the expense of their own earnings, pensions and financial security. We need more than praise: we need practical support and a system that recognises the real cost of caring. Loving someone should not mean years of essential care leave you financially vulnerable.
 
Emma Sainsbury
 
Author, Love, Laughter and the Hidden World of Unpaid Carers

Situation in occupied West Bank &#8216;simply out of control,&#8217; UN chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:26:52 UTC
00:26:52 KST

The situation across the occupied West Bank has deteriorated beyond control as escalating attacks seek to drive Palestinian communities from their land, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned on Thursday, Anadolu reports.
“In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians continue to suffer daily attacks by Israeli settlers. The clear goal is to drive communities off their land,” Guterres told reporters.
He said the situation in the occupied territories is “simply out of control” as occupiers also target journalists and diplomats.
On Gaza, the UN chief pointed out that essential humanitarian assistance remains “severely restricted” ahead of winter, compounding obstacles facing the Security Council-backed roadmap to resolve the conflict.
Guterres stressed that the World Food Program “urgently” requires $450 million to feed populations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, noting that the sum equals approximately 90 minutes of global military expenditures. He appealed to international donors to step up while urging an end to the occupation to achieve a viable two-state solution.
‘El Nino of war’ and economic strain
Guterres compared modern conflicts to the climate phenomenon El Nino, and cautioned that cascading hostilities are reverberating through international energy markets, shipping corridors, and financial systems.
READ: Israel uses occupier violence to ‘ethnically cleanse’ Palestinians from West Bank: Amnesty
He linked widespread street protests over inflation, food, and fuel directly to the fallout of expanding global wars. “War does not create all these inequalities, but it feeds and exploits them,” Guterres said, emphasizing that while street violence is unacceptable, authorities cannot allow disorder to obscure the legitimate cost-of-living grievances of peaceful protesters.
Regional diplomacy, Sudan, and Yemen
Turning to Yemen, Guterres described continued Houthi attacks against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia as “totally unacceptable,” urging restraint amid mounting displacement in Yemen.
Guterres said he will travel to Egypt to advance regional de-escalation, underscoring Egypt’s essential diplomatic role as a mediator in the war between the US and Iran, alongside its neighboring stakes in the wars in Sudan and Libya.
He also demanded that neighboring and distant nations halt weapons supplies to factions in Sudan that are “killing civilians in an absolutely devastating way.”
Disregard for international law
Guterres dismissed concerns about institutional damage to the UN from violations of international law, declaring that the real crisis is the suffering of ordinary civilians whose survival is threatened by war-induced inflation and violence.
“The problem is not for the United Nations. The problem is for the people that is suffering dramatically everywhere,” he said.

Russia Hits Central Kyiv With Cluster Missile

Do Stormont politics stifle the non-sectarian parties? | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:25:52 UTC
00:25:52 KST

Your editorial on the dysfunction in Northern Ireland politics (15 October) does not mention the main cause: the denial of basic democratic rights to the people by the Labour party.
The party national executive committee refuses to run Labour candidates in any Northern Ireland election, whether to district councils, the Stormont assembly or the Westminster parliament.
This means people here, including affiliated trade unionists, are denied the basic democratic right to vote for our Labour government, which is setting our taxes and winding us up for war.
This undemocratic stance by Labour is not an act without consequences. By suppressing cross-community Labour party electoral politics, it forces the electorate into their ethnonational blocs and incentivises the sort of communal sectarian politics and stalemate that we are well used to.
 
Boyd Black
 
Secretary, the Labour party in Northern Ireland
It is undoubtedly true, as your editorial says that “Northern Ireland’s voters currently do not have the politics they deserve”. However, there are problems with your assertion that the current model of power-sharing “designed to reassure nationalist and unionist communities remains indispensable”. In fact, it plays a part in maintaining the current “cycle of dysfunction”.
I have family in Northern Ireland who would prefer to vote for parties that do not fit into this category, but doing so under the current rules would be pointless. They are part of a growing number of voters who do not primarily identify as being part of either “community”.
However, even if parties such as the Alliance, the Greens, People Before Profit were to win a majority at Stormont, they would under the current rules not be allowed to form an administration. In fact the current system reinforces sectarian division by stipulating that only those parties self-identifying as nationalist or unionist can “power-share”. Ireland needs real change. The current system cannot deliver it.
 
Declan O’Neill
 
Oldham, Greater Manchester

French MPs reject $4B revenue measure in social security budget

Necva Tastan Sevinc
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
French lawmakers on Thursday rejected a measure expected to raise €3.7 billion ($4.1 billion) for the social security system, undermining the government's efforts to narrow its deficit, the BFMTV broadcaster reported.
The provision in the 2027 social security financing bill would have reduced employer contribution relief for companies paying profit-sharing or employee share ownership bonuses.
MPs subsequently rejected Article 7, which contained the measure, following three days of debate marked by votes reducing projected revenue or adding spending.
“You're killing this Social Security Financing Bill,” said Socialist lawmaker Jerome Guedj, accusing fellow MPs of jeopardizing efforts to restore the system’s finances.
Lawmakers from President Emmanuel Macron’s camp and the right supported amendments that removed the provision, which opponents considered harmful to businesses.
Labor Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou warned about the financial effect of lawmakers’ proposals.
“We're no longer talking about the 15 million or 100 million we were discussing yesterday, we're talking about billions of euros,” he said.
Green lawmaker Sandrine Rousseau raised the prospect of a no-confidence motion, accusing opponents of abandoning previously agreed compromises.
The government wants to reduce the social security deficit from an expected €21.8 billion in 2026 to €12.7 billion in 2027.
Rejection of the entire revenue section would prevent lawmakers from proceeding to examine the bill’s spending provisions, according to the report.

Turkish army gets more Tayfun ballistic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:24:21 UTC
00:24:21 KST

- Türkiye delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to its Land Forces Command, following earlier deliveries in May and June 2026.
- The Tayfun Block 2 has a range of more than 500 km and a reported accuracy of under 10 meters.
Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence has delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to the Turkish Land Forces Command, adding to a missile force that began entering service only five months ago.
The delivery was reported on Oct. 22, 2026, and in line with previous handovers, the ministry kept the number of missiles classified. The new batch is at least the third known delivery this year: the ministry announced on May 20, 2026, that Tayfun Block 2 missiles had been accepted into the Land Forces inventory for the first time, and a second batch followed on June 25.
Tayfun, Turkish for “typhoon,” is the longest-range ballistic missile Türkiye has developed on its own. Roketsan, the state-owned missile maker, describes the Block 2 as having a range of more than 500 km (310 miles) and designed to strike high-value targets deep behind enemy lines, including air defense systems, command and control centers, aircraft hangars and other critical military facilities.
The missile is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and 610 mm (24 inches) in diameter, with a launch weight of 2,300 kg (5,070 pounds). It is fired from a wheeled transporter-erector-launcher, a truck that carries, raises and launches the missile and holds two rounds, which allows crews to move quickly between firing positions.
Roketsan says the Tayfun Block 2 lands within 10 meters (33 feet) of its target, measured as circular error probable, the radius within which half of the missiles fired are expected to land. It uses coordinate-based guidance, meaning it flies to a fixed point programmed before launch, and the company says it is highly resistant to GPS jamming and can operate day or night in poor weather. The missile carries a pre-formed fragmentation warhead, which breaks into a pattern of fragments on detonation.
Türkiye first test-fired Tayfun in October 2022 from Rize-Artvin Airport on the Black Sea coast, when the missile flew 561 km (349 miles) in 456 seconds before striking a target area off Sinop. That distance was roughly twice the 280 km (174-mile) range of Roketsan’s earlier Bora missile, previously the longest-range ballistic missile in Turkish service. Further test firings followed in May 2023 and in later years as the program moved toward serial production.
Roketsan has continued to expand the family alongside the Block 2 deliveries. In July 2025, the company unveiled the much larger Tayfun Block 4 at the IDEF defense fair in Istanbul, a missile about 10 meters (33 feet) long and weighing roughly 7,200 kg (15,900 pounds), which Roketsan presents as a hypersonic ballistic missile system. In July 2026, Roketsan released footage of a Tayfun Block 3 striking an unmanned boat at sea, which the company said was the first time a Tayfun had been used against a naval target and the first use of a seeker on the missile.
With three batches delivered since May, the Tayfun Block 2 is now steadily building up inside the Turkish Land Forces, while the Block 3 and Block 4 versions continue through development and testing at Roketsan.

Chief of the General Staff's speech at the opening of Telford Gun Hall
United Kingdom

Chief of the General Staff's speech at the opening of Telford Gun Hall
The Chief of the General Staff, General Sir Roly Walker's speech at the official opening of Telford Gun Hall.
Secretary of State, ladies and gentlemen, it is an absolute privilege to be here at Telford today. This marks the return of large-calibre gun barrel manufacturing to the United Kingdom. This is a capability that sadly has been absent from these shores for decades.
I say sadly because Great Britain has a proud history of producing its own artillery. For centuries the Royal Arsenal at Woolwich was synonymous with excellence in this technology, and it produced artillery that shaped the outcomes of conflicts from the Napoleonic Wars through the World Wars and into the Cold War.
That arc of history reminds us that whilst armies, navies and air forces can win the battles, it takes nations to come together to win wars. The world today has brought that lesson sharply back into focus. Modern warfare consumes equipment and ammunition at extraordinary rates. In Ukraine, we know that both sides fire tens of thousands of rounds of artillery ammunition every day. And that generates a weight of fire and levels of lethality across the battlefield that drones alone cannot replicate.
So, to be ready to defend against attack, we must be prepared to replace and repair those fighting systems at the rate of their consumption. But industrial capacity cannot be conjured in a crisis. It must be built before the conflict.
And this facility represents an important step, a really important step in that direction. It supports the modernisation of our land forces whilst also rebuilding the skills and industrial capacity on which our future fighting power depends. It is also an incredibly strong signal of intent, a commitment to the partnership between governments, industry, and the armed forces to build the national arsenal that underwrites our national security and allows the nation’s soldiers to protect all that we hold dear.
So, in many ways, this is for them, for those soldiers, and on their behalf, today’s and tomorrow’s that I say thank you for doing what you’ve done.

Livestock virus claims first human victim in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:22:57 UTC
00:22:57 KST

Livestock virus claims first human victim in France
The world’s first documented human infection with the Shamonda virus has been reported in France, where a hospitalized patient later died, according to the health authorities.
The insect-borne disease, which has circulated among livestock for decades, was previously believed to be incapable of infecting humans.
In a joint statement on Thursday, the French Health and Agriculture Ministries confirmed that the patient, who had a severely weakened immune system, died in early October after being hospitalized in Lyon.
“Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans,” the ministries said, according to AFP. They described the infection as the first confirmed detection of the pathogen in a person.
The patient developed severe neurological complications that the authorities believe were linked to the infection. However, investigators have still not established conclusively whether the virus was responsible for the death.
Officials suspect that the patient contracted the virus through the bite of an infected midge in eastern France, where the pathogen has recently been detected in cattle. The circumstances of the infection remain under investigation.
Despite the unprecedented case, the French authorities said there is currently no indication of a wider threat to public health. They stressed that the patient was severely immunocompromised and that no other human infections have been identified.
The Shamonda virus belongs to the orthobunyavirus group and was first identified in Nigeria in the 1960s. It is transmitted by tiny biting insects known as Culicoides midges and has been detected in livestock in Africa and Asia.
The virus has recently emerged among European cattle, triggering concern among the veterinary authorities. In France, infections have been reported across dozens of departments, with affected animals suffering fever, diarrhea, weakness, and falling milk production, according to the French agricultural authorities.
Other viruses that have crossed from animals to humans include HIV, Ebola, and bird flu. The Covid-19 pandemic was caused by a virus widely believed to have originated in bats.
The European Center for Disease Prevention and Control has confirmed the unprecedented human case and is working with the French authorities to assess its implications.
Health officials are continuing epidemiological and laboratory investigations to determine how the patient became infected and whether other cases may have gone undetected.

Türkiye aims to strengthen energy, climate diplomacy through next month's COP31 UN Climage Change Conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:22:52 UTC
00:22:52 KST

Gulsen Cagatay and Halis Sunnetci
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
As Türkiye prepares to host next month's 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31 or COP31 Türkiye), it aims to strengthen its role in energy and climate diplomacy, help turn global climate targets into concrete action and harness its renewable energy potential through international partnerships.
COP31, scheduled for Nov. 9-20 in Antalya, will provide an opportunity to highlight Türkiye's diplomatic capabilities, position in the energy transition and climate policies on the international stage.
Türkiye will hold the COP31 Presidency and lead the Action Agenda, while Australia will serve as President of Negotiations.
Türkiye's approach to the summit focuses on turning existing climate commitments into achievable and measurable outcomes through dialogue, consensus and action.
Priority areas include electrification, the clean energy transition, green industrialization, the circular economy, climate-resilient cities and climate finance.
The COP31 Presidency has announced initiatives aimed at increasing electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, reducing energy intensity in buildings by at least 25% and cutting the rate of growth in global waste generation by half.
Turning climate commitments into bankable and investment-ready projects is also a central part of the agenda.
 
Renewable energy potential supports cooperation
Türkiye's solar and wind energy potential provides a foundation for partnerships that could emerge from COP31.
Expanding renewable energy capacity, strengthening electricity grids and accelerating electrification are among the country's energy transition priorities.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar has announced that Türkiye aims to increase its installed renewable energy capacity to 120 gigawatts by 2035, with work underway on more ambitious targets for 2040.
COP31 is therefore expected to offer opportunities to advance Türkiye's clean energy investments through international financing, technology transfer and partnerships.
 
Geographic location enables regional energy cooperation
Situated at the crossroads of Europe, the Middle East and Asia, Türkiye is strategically positioned to connect energy sources with consumer markets, creating opportunities for cooperation in climate diplomacy.
Its location along international trade and energy routes allows the country to develop regional partnerships in electricity interconnections, renewable energy investment, energy efficiency and low-carbon industry.
Making better use of this potential to meet climate targets will require increasing the share of renewables in the energy system, upgrading electricity grids and accelerating the transformation of energy infrastructure.
 
International partnerships, green industry gain prominence
Global Energy Association President Murat Dilek told Anadolu that expanding Türkiye's manufacturing capacity for renewable energy equipment, particularly wind turbines and solar panels, offers significant opportunities for green industrialization and for strengthening the country's role in energy and climate diplomacy.
Increasing domestic manufacturing capacity would support renewable energy investment, while Türkiye's strategic position connecting Europe, the Middle East and Asia could help the country play a greater role in regional supply chains, Dilek said.
He added that these developments would improve Türkiye's competitiveness in the global clean energy market.
"Türkiye's diplomatic success in this process will be measured not only by the establishment of dialogue between countries, but also by the transformation of the targets set out in Antalya into concrete partnerships and viable projects," Dilek said.
"To turn this potential into lasting gains, Türkiye needs to implement its national climate targets, accelerate clean energy investments and facilitate access to climate finance," he said, adding: "By boosting domestic manufacturing and technological capabilities, reducing environmental impacts and strengthening international partnerships, Türkiye can demonstrate its potential not only as a diplomatic actor in the COP31 process, but also as a manufacturing and technology hub contributing to the global green transition."

Michael Wynne, Fired as SECAF Alongside CSAF Moseley, Dead at 82
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:21:43 UTC
00:21:43 KST

Michael Wynne, the 21st Secretary of the Air Force died Oct. 17. He was 82 years old.
Wynne was Secretary from 2005 to 2008, a stretch of time when the U.S. military was struggling to quell insurgencies in Iraq and Afghanistan and the Army was struggling to simultaneously man occupation forces in two theaters. Roadside bombs and insurgent attacks were killing U.S. troops, and the Air Force was under intense pressure to support its sister service with increased intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance coverage and manpower and force cuts to ease the Army’s burden.
The Air Force was also fighting to protect its modernization efforts at the time, especially the F-22 Raptor program, which was less than halfway to its objective of 750 planes, new tankers (which would ultimately become the KC-46), and a future bomber (which would eventually yield the B-21).
In 2006, an Air Force B-52 took off from Minot Air Force Base, N.D., and flew to Barksdale Air Force Base, La., its crew unknowingly carrying nuclear weapons on board, a so-called “bent spear” incident. The discovery kicked off an investigation, recriminations, self-examination, and subsequent organizational, procedural, and cultural changes across the nuclear community.
The incident added to the tension between the Air Force and then-Secretary of Defense Robert Gates, who saw the service and particularly then-Chief of Staff Gen. T. Michael “Buzz” Moseley as recalcitrant in their pushback over budget, manning, and modernization. Seeing Wynne and Moseley as a close knit tandem, Gates fired both in June 2008, beheading the service—the first-ever simultaneous removal of a service chief and secretary.
Military Roots
Wynne hailed from a military family and followed his father’s footsteps to attend the U.S. Military Academy at West Point, graduating at the height of the Vietnam War. Among his 578 classmates, 30 died in Vietnam and about 100 others were wounded in fighting in Southeast Asia.
Instead of joining the Army, however, Wynne followed his older brother into the Air Force, reporting for Active Duty in August 1966.
“The day I reported for Active Duty, the report of my brother being shot down was announced,” Wynn recalled in a 2005 interview with the Washington Post. Maj. Patrick Wynne, a 1963 graduate of the U.S. Air Force Academy, had trained as a pilot, and was assigned to the 555th Tactical Fighter Squadron in Thailand. After only four months in country, his F-4C Phantom was shot down over Vietnam on Aug. 8, 1966. He was declared missing in action, and remained so until 1977, when his remains were identified and later returned to the United States. He is buried at the Air Force Academy.
The younger Wynne served seven years in the Air Force, his final tour as an assistant professor of astronautics at the Air Force Academy.
Wynne then went to work for General Dynamics. For the next 26 years, he worked as an executive there, save for a three-year stint with Lockheed Martin after Lockheed acquired GD’s Space Systems Division. His work during in those years spanned General Dynamics’ F-16 and M1A2 tank divisions as well as space systems, including work on the Atlas, Titan, and Centaur launch vehicles.
In 2001, Wynne joined Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld’s Pentagon leadership team. Following the election of President George W. Bush, Wynne was confirmed as Principal Deputy Undersecretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics, the start of a seven-year run in public service. In 2003, he was made Acting Undersecretary and he remained in that role until June 2005. Among his tasks at the time were leading the Pentagon’s preparations for the 2005 Base Realignment and Closure plan, which sought to “rationalize” the Defense Department’s far-flung bases and increase cross-service cooperation.
The 2005 BRAC results proved disappointing. Projected to save the Pentagon more than $25 billion annually by 2011, the plans failed to deliver due to higher-than anticipated construction costs, inflation, and incorrect assumptions. Instead of savings, the changes yielded a net cost increase, even when spread out over 20 years.
As Air Force Secretary, Wynne opposed efforts to consolidate and adopt joint basing, having come to embrace the Air Force’s explanation that many of its units operate and fight from their home bases rather than deploy to forward theaters.
“The Air Force has a very different concept of operations,” he would tell Air Force Magazine in 2008, weeks after his departure. Putting Air Force bases under the control of other services would undermine combat effectiveness, he said, adding, “I’d probably get fired again over my objection to the way the joint basing is happening.”
More than that, Wynne was a visionary, said Richard Andres, a professor at the National War College worked with Wynne in government. Wynne’s ideas presaged numerous future defense initiatives, Andres said: “His vision of linking sensors and weapons across military domains anticipated today’s Joint All-Domain Command and Control. He was first to champion cyberspace as a warfighting domain and brought data transparency and decision dashboards into Air Force management. He understood early that America’s military advantage would depend as much on connecting information and people as on building superior weapons.”
Wynne also butted heads with Gates over the F-22. While Gates suggested the Air Force could give up the “exquisite” F-22 because the then-fledgling F-35 was scheduled to join the fleet in 2014, Wynne disagreed.
“The notion of the F-22 [is] … similar to the F-35—we need to get rid of that,” Wynne said in his 2008 debrief with Air Force Magazine. The F-35, rather, “complements the F-22, but the F-22 is clearly an air superiority and air dominance weapon. The F-35 is a multinational, multirole, [air-to-ground] versatile airplane.”
When Gates dismissed concerns about future conflict as “next-war-itis,” Wynne didn’t give in. “He was willing to put his position on the line. He understood that the demands of the wars we were fighting could not excuse neglecting the wars we might have to fight next.”
In the months leading up to his dismissal, Wynne and Andres spoke weekly, including about the possibility that Gates would fire him, Andres recalled. “He understood the risk,” Andres said. “He cared more about what the nation needed than about keeping his job.”
Gates took over as Secretary about a year after Wynne had been moved to the Air Force. At the time, USAF was bearing a heavy burden for the Army. In a 2006 C-SPAN interview, Wynne tried to justify a planned cut of 40,000 Airman, suggesting that technological advancement made it possible to do “trimming in advance of new systems coming on and planning for the future right now.” But he acknowledged that having 5,000 Airmen doing Army jobs in Iraq was not sustainable.
“At some point in the future, it doesn’t work in the math—the Army has to pick up combat service support,” he said.
The Air Force’s pursuit of a new tanker aircraft, a protracted and contentious effort that preceded him and would continue to drag on for years, was another challenge during Wynne’s tenure. As Secretary, he pressed for a single tanker aircraft rather than splitting the order between Boeing and Airbus platforms, as some urged. But after departing the Pentagon, he reconsidered, seeing value in it. He also came to regret not requiring that tankers become network nodes, an extra role for which they might have been well-suited.
And while many in the Pentagon failed to appreciate the Air Force’s contributions to the war in Iraq, Wynne became a strong advocate, noting that the 2007 “surge” of forces in Iraq was not merely an Army ground operation. “We surged 400 percent in the number of sorties and 1,000 percent in the pounds of ordnance dropped,” he said in a press conference on his final day in office. “What happened? I would tell you that what happened was the realization that we could get connectivity between the ground commanders and the air component—that there was true situational awareness available.”
Still, on June 5, 2008, Gates decided he wasn’t getting what he wanted out of Air Force leadership. Wynne and Moseley were en route to a Corona meeting of Air Force leaders at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, when Gates dropped the bombshell, dismissing both.
The stated reason was the failures of Air Force leadership to safely steward the security of nuclear weapons, but it was no secret Gates and the Air Force were at odds on a range of issues, and few believed the public explanation. From the number of “orbits” flown by surveillance drones over Iraq and Afghanistan to support troops operating on the ground to Gates objections to “next-war-itis” and the Air Force’s focus on high-end stealth fighters and the threats of a rising China in the Pacific, the two sides were out of sync.
Moseley, in an interview, recalled his close working relationship with Wynne as “a privilege and a gift.” The two tried to meet daily and they shared a perspective both in terms of their duty and vision for the service. They also became friends.
“Mike Wynne and I had the best relationship of any that I’ve seen with 13-plus secretaries I worked with,” Moseley said. Wynne was well versed in the workings of the Pentagon hierarchy, the needs of each of the services, and how to get things done, the former chief said. “But he also understood the theater logistics, the technology to address the new world, and he understood the acquisition process better than anybody.”
Together, they worked to lay out and explain their priorities, the need for increased resources—estimated then to be $20 billion annually to modernize, in order:
- Tankers
- Search and rescue
- Satellites that could be protected from cyber and maneuver attack
- F-35s to replace the F-16
- A new bomber
They laid out that plan shortly before the firing in a Pentagon meeting with Gates and other officials. Mosely recalled that afterward Wynne declared the presentation a success.
“I think that meeting went well,” Wynne told him, draping an arm around Moseley’s shoulder as they walked the Pentagon hallway. “But I think we’re both dead.”
Wynne may have been the only one who saw it coming.
When the decision came down to fire them, both were at Scott Air Force Base, en route to Dayton for a planned Corona meeting of Air Force leadership at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio. Moseley was ordered back to Washington, where Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Adm. Mike Mullen delivered the news. In Dayton, Wynne was told to stand by for an unscheduled visit from Deputy Secretary of Defense Gordon England, who was flying in. No reason was given. Was England coming to discuss Moseley’s successor, someone wondered. “No,” Wynne said. “He’s coming for me.”
As the Corona meeting unfolded, Moseley called Wynne from Washington to say he was being relieved. Reporters began to call before England even arrived, adding to Wynne’s convictions. CNN might have been first to report the firings. Defense News Editor Vago Muradian, a rare press gallery guest at the Corona gathering, got his story out online on Defense News and Air Force Times. At the Pentagon, frustrated reporters gathered outside the press secretary’s office looking for answers; inside, staff was still trying to piece together what happened.
Two weeks later, Wynne departed the Pentagon at an official ceremony presided over by Gates, with Moseley at his side. What had been a very public firing was glossed over for public consumption as Gates pinned a medal on Wynne’s chest. Having Gates preside was Wynne’s idea, said retired Maj. Gen. Daryl Burke, Wynne’s military aide at the time. It was a challenge: Gates would either have to refuse or honor Wynne for his public service.
At the ceremony, Wynne expressed love for the service. “But it is the people of the Air Force that make the Air Force,” he added, “so in loving the Air Force, we love the people.”
Burke recalled how Wynne advised him to stand away as they awaited England’s arrival. Burke insisted he would stand with Wynne regardless, but Wynne was trying to ensure that Burke wouldn’t be damaged by association in the future by being seen as too closely associated with a politically unpopular boss. Wynne subsequently worked behind the scenes to find Burke a next assignment that would keep his career on track. In doing so, Wynne demonstrated both caring for his Airman and a savvy hand on the tiller for navigating Pentagon politics.
Lt. Gen. David Deptula, now dean of AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, was on the Air Staff at the time, recalling that Wynne kept working on the issues he believed in up to the very end—in particular, his opposition to joint basing.
“Secretary Wynne was a leader of uncommon integrity, genuine kindness, and extraordinary loyalty,” Deptula said. “He never confused holding a position of authority with the responsibility to do what was right. I witnessed his character firsthand when, even after learning he would be removed as Secretary of the Air Force, he continued working tirelessly to strengthen the service he loved. He put principle above position, loyalty above personal ambition, and the nation’s security above all else. In a famous action, when SECDEF Gates told Secretary Wynne to fire Chief of Staff, Buzz Moseley… Wynne refused. So, Gates fired both. The Air Force and our nation are better for his service, and I am better for having known him. He will be greatly missed.”
Robbin Laird, a military analyst and prolific writer who worked for Wynne during his Pentagon tenure, wrote admiringly of the former secretary in a remembrance, citing what he called the Wynne Doctrine: “If you are ever involved in a fair fight, it is the result of poor planning.”
“It is easy to hear it as swagger. It was the opposite,” Laird wrote. “A fair fight is one whose outcome is in doubt. When the outcome is in doubt, young Americans pay for that doubt with their lives. Mike believed a leader’s first duty was to make sure it never happens. That meant technology, organization, the unglamorous work of logistics and sustainment, and the discipline to think years ahead of the adversary.”
Michael Walter Wynne was born in Clearwater, Fla. He is survived by his wife Barbara and four married daughters.

Russian forces detained Hubbard during the occupation of Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast in the early months of the full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2024, a Russian court convicted him of serving as a mercenary in the Ukrainian military, an accusation his family and lawyer disputed.
Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian" while commenting on Hubbard's release.
The area where Stativko lives was likely targeted overnight not only with conventional cruise and ballistic missiles, but also with cluster munitions, which scatter smaller explosive charges upon detonation, causing more widespread damage across a larger area.
Andrii Saulevych, manager of the local coffee shop Khlibna Kraina, also felt the impact of Russia's missile attack firsthand. The cafe's windows were completely blown out, but by 8 a.m. local time, it was already serving coffee to customers again.
"We put a piece of ourselves into every coffee shop," he said. "It's deeply upsetting to see everything destroyed like this."
"Humanitarians don't act this way. This is something else. This is anti-humanitarian," Saulevych added.
Another resident of the district, teacher Yaroslav Bahai, spent the morning waiting in line for humanitarian aid instead of preparing his lessons. The windows in his apartment had been blown out, and shrapnel had pierced straight through his kitchen refrigerator. His family was fortunate to survive the attack unharmed: they had taken shelter in the hallway with their children when the missiles struck.
Bahai said the war has significantly changed the way he teaches. His school cannot accommodate all its students in the bomb shelter, while the constant air raid alerts that have plagued the capital in recent months have made learning increasingly difficult, even online.
"I used to give children an assignment asking who they see themselves becoming in five years. Now they say it's hard for them to even imagine what tomorrow will look like," he said.
Bahai and his family have no plans to leave Kyiv for now, despite the approaching winter, which could be one of Ukraine's most difficult since 2022 due to continued Russian attacks and damage to the country's energy infrastructure. Bilous, however, is considering leaving the capital. Although reluctant to abandon her home, she said she can no longer cope with the constant sense of danger, which only continues to grow.
A fragment of a Russian missile landed right next to her house, shattering all the windows.
"I thought I was going to die," Bilous said.
"Such a 'gift' arrived in Kyiv after the (Witkoff-Putin) meeting. Who was it from? Putin? Witkoff? Trump?"
