Pete Hegseth’s staff break priceless historic globe he requested for office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:04:44 UTC
00:04:44 KST

A priceless pre-second world war globe coveted by the US defence secretary Pete Hegseth for his office in the Pentagon was damaged by his staff in a botched attempt to relocate it, army officials have admitted.
Photographs published by the Washington Post on Thursday show the shattered 30-inch Eisenhower globe, said to have been used by Dwight D Eisenhower, the 34th US president, as he plotted the D-day landings as allied supreme commander.
The fragile item was broken when Hegseth’s aides eschewed the services of specialist movers, then dropped it after deciding they would transport it themselves, the Post said, citing sources familiar with the February incident.
A US army spokesperson, in an email to the newspaper, conceded the damage occurred during “an attempted move”.
“The spherical portion of the globe was detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate,” the spokesperson said.
One photograph shows fragments of the globe below its wooden frame on a blue hallway carpet. A second shows an inches-wide gash in the bottom of the globe, with its base punched through.
According to the Post’s sources, Hegseth took a liking to the globe, one of two similar artifacts dating to the 1930s and housed in the Pentagon, and asked for it to be placed in his office.
The defence secretary has a well-documented fascination in the history of war, and has boasted of instilling a “warrior ethos” in the US military since his January 2025 confirmation.
The globe’s historical significance was attractive to him, the Post’s report noted, and aides moved quickly to enact the relocation.
Such was their haste, the sources said, that instead of waiting to engage specialist movers who would have packed the globe with precision and care, they dispatched their own team.
“They lost control of the artifact and dropped it, sending the globe crashing on to its base and impaling the fragile shell near Antarctica,” one of the sources said, blaming an “apparent lack of patience”.
Ultimately, the globe was not relocated, and is now undergoing repair.
An account of a successful 2022 relocation of an Eisenhower globe, between two army facilities in Alabama, appears on the website of specialist movers Craters & Freighters, which highlights the level of expertise and care necessary for such an undertaking.
“Since the globe is considered priceless, we knew its value was much greater than financial, and that our team was heavily relied upon for a safe delivery,” the article said, describing how the company designed and precision-built protective crating.
An spokesperson for the “war department”, as the US Department of Defense has rebranded itself during Donald Trump’s second term, dismissed the significance of the incident in a statement to the Guardian.
“An accident occurred while staff were transporting a replica of the Eisenhower globe as part of its relocation,” the official’s statement said.
“Accidents happen, we are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired. It is unsurprising that the Washington Post is once again dedicating time to another inconsequential non-story.”

Romanian prosecutors send hard-right lawmaker to trial for suspected hate speech
BUCHAREST, Oct 22 - Romanian prosecutors on Thursday sent one of the country's most prominent hard-right politicians, AUR vice-president and lawmaker Dan Tanasa, to trial on charges of inciting hate speech and discrimination against foreign workers.
Tanasa is a senior figure in the opposition hard-right Alliance for Uniting Romanians (AUR), Romania's second-largest party, which currently leads opinion polls.

Like other countries in central and eastern Europe, European Union member Romania relies on non-EU workers, many from South Asia, to fill labour shortages in sectors including hospitality and construction.
Tanasa was not available for comment. AUR called the prosecution an attack on free speech.
"If simply opposing immigration policy can become a crime then the problem is not Dan Tanasa," it said in a statement.

‘We shouldn’t exist’. Writer Linor Goralik on literary resistance, reaching Russian teenagers, and the Soviet dissident movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:01:14 UTC
00:01:14 KST

‘We shouldn’t exist’ Writer Linor Goralik on literary resistance, reaching Russian teenagers, and the Soviet dissident movement
Shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, poet and writer Linor Goralik founded the Resistance and Opposition Arts Review (ROAR), a literary almanac featuring antiwar essays, poetry, audio works, and artwork. A few months later, she launched News 26 (Novosti 26), an independent media outlet for teenagers in Russia. Meduza spoke with Goralik about how both projects have managed to operate during the war. The interview was conducted in English by journalist Sarah Chatta and translated into Russian by journalist Ksenia Mironova as part of a Pulitzer Center-supported series on efforts to resist literary censorship in Russia.
The following interview has been lightly edited and abridged for length and clarity.
— Tell me about ROAR.
— ROAR is an almanac that’s published bimonthly online. We try to be a space for voices that speak freely against the Russian regime and against the war in Ukraine. And this is horrible. We shouldn’t exist. We’re a magazine that wants to shut down. We want to stop. When we began, we thought that it would run for two or three issues, and now we’re on issue 22. [ROAR has since released issue 24.] It’s exhausting.
— How is your work different from, say, the Soviet dissident publication A Chronicle of Current Events (“Khronika”)?
— It’s very different from Khronika. And I know this for sure because I once interviewed its founder, Natalya Gorbanevskaya. Khronika’s main focus was informing people about repressions. There are now so many of our colleagues [doing that work]. We, and others, try to do the literary work.
— The Kremlin didn’t start censoring literature in Russia immediately after the full-scale invasion. What made you realize so early on that a project like ROAR was needed?
— I was told that it was a stupid idea. But it was in the air. It was very clear to me that this was going to happen. It was very clear that people who wanted to speak out against the war, those who wanted to write against the war, would not be safe in Russia. It was absolutely obvious that they needed a safe place to speak.
— What’s the submission process like?
— It is very simple. We have an email address. I look at submissions every other day and decide what’s good and what’s not, and that’s it. We have a team, but the decision about whether to publish a piece in the almanac is mine.
— How do you decide?
— Intuitively. My decision is based on two things: what seems to me to be of high literary quality and what seems to me to be an important political message. That’s it.
— Can you tell me more about your team?
— At its peak, ROAR had about 200 people, not including authors. The team includes editors, translators, and proofreaders. Not all 200 people work on every issue, but dozens of people work on each one.
— How many members of your team live in Russia?
— I don’t know, because the team manages itself. I do nothing. I choose the submissions, and I put them in a database. Our editor-in-chief and my very close friend, Maria, takes it from there and edits them. Then she distributes the work among other editors and proofreaders. As soon as a piece is ready, the editors and proofreaders put it in the database, and the layout team starts putting it on the site.
At the same time, the English team starts translating the texts. The head of the English team, Maya, finds translators for each piece. As soon as the translators finish a piece, she passes it to the editors, then to the proofreaders, and then to the layout team. They put it on the site. Then all I do is push the “publish” button.
— Who reads ROAR?
— We have about 2,500 subscribers on our Telegram channel, but we have zero understanding of who’s reading us because of VPNs. So, mainly, we work in the dark.
I wrote an article once about the 2011-2012 protests. I did maybe 25 or 30 interviews, and one of the things people kept repeating was that one of the most important things they did — beyond the protesting itself — was showing that people who protest exist.
That’s why events like the Berlin Bebelplatz festival are extremely important. They help people see that they’re not working in the dark. It boosts morale.
— You mentioned interviewing Soviet dissident Natalya Gorbanevskaya. Did that conversation help you when you were creating ROAR?
— It wasn’t only talking to Natalya, it was the whole history of the Soviet dissident movement. They were publishing almanacs. They were publishing magazines. It was like a basic instinct. The moment you can’t speak freely — do it.
But I didn’t do it for literature. I didn’t do it for authors, and I didn’t do it for the texts. I did it for me, because I had this feeling that I had to do something. Many of us felt extremely helpless. We felt enraged. We felt horrified. And this was an attempt to do something. I did it for myself.
— A few months after launching ROAR, you created a media outlet for teenagers in Russia called News 26. How did you come up with the name?
— I’m a marketing consultant by profession, so I wanted it to be very simple and recognizable. As for the number, I just chose it randomly, but we have two explanations we give when people ask. One is that in 2022, the oldest members of our audience, the 16-year-olds, would be able to vote in 2026. Another is that 12 plus 14 is 26 — and our target audience was 12- to 14-year-olds. But it has nothing to do with reality.
— Do these publications generate any revenue?
— Zero. They don’t make any money at all. All these years, it was volunteer work. Then, last year, we received our first grant for News 26. I wouldn’t tell you how much the News 26 team gets, because it’s very little. But they get something. We received our second grant this year, also small, but very significant for us, and we are very grateful. At least we have some resources now.
— Do you know if people in Russia read News 26?
— They most definitely do. Telegram is [de facto] banned, but they keep reading it and writing to us.
We have about 5,500 subscribers on Telegram, but that means nothing. It could be a readership of 10,000, it could be a readership of 1,000. We see that every post is read by about 2,000 people, and our TikTok videos sometimes reach 50,000 views. But again, today it’s 50,000. Tomorrow it’s 1,000. We never know. And now, with the widespread use of VPNs, we see nothing.
We have an anonymous bot on Telegram, and people write letters to us there. Every day starts with the thought: “Please no letters, please no letters,” because those letters are very scary.
— What makes them so scary?
— They’re letters from children who read News 26. We have a volunteer psychologist who helps us answer the letters and navigate complex issues.
For example, a teenage girl living in a small town near the border with Ukraine wrote that if the war came to her home, she planned to run away and hide because she didn’t think the adults would protect her.
I went to Katya, our volunteer psychologist, and I asked her, “Is this person stable?” And she said, “The scariest thing is that this letter is completely rational. The person analyzed the situation, understood the circumstances, and made a decision. She asked for help.” It was horrifying.
You can’t take too long to respond, because they feel abandoned. So you have hours, maybe days. And I thought maybe we could write two things. First, being alone on the streets is the worst thing for a teenage girl to do during a war. Second, I thought that what this girl needed was some feeling of control over what’s happening in her life. So I suggested some self-defense lessons. And I was dying of fear that she would never reply, but she did. She said that she thought it was a great idea.
— How many letters do you receive?
— Not many. Maybe two a month. Maybe three a month. But I’m afraid of these letters. Sometimes [the teenagers] write just to write: “I hate everything. I hate Putin. I want to donate to Ukraine — how do I do this?” or “I’m gay. I know that I live in hell, and I will live in hell for years. I will never hold my lover’s hand in public, and I’m writing to you just because I have to say it somewhere.”
Parents also write to us to tell us how much [News 26] means because it becomes a part of the conversation in the family. There are also some people who tell us that this is the only news that they can read, because it’s very simple, clear, calm.
So we do this project because we believe it helps some people in some way. For us, that’s enough. We don’t have this ambition to save thousands. We hope to help even five people.

Syria arrests Assad-era brigadier general over civilian attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:42 UTC
00:00:42 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria arrests Assad-era brigadier general over attacks on civilians
Syrian authorities have arrested a former brigadier general accused of ordering attacks on civilians under Bashar al-Assad's regime, alongside five other suspects, as the country's new government continues efforts to prosecute those implicated in atrocities during the civil war.
Brigadier General Abdul Hakim Wanous, former chief of staff of the 35th Special Forces Regiment, was detained by military police in the central province of Hama on Wednesday, according to local judicial authorities.
Wanous is accused of ordering artillery attacks, carrying out arbitrary arrests and participating in military raids and operations targeting civilian areas in the Damascus countryside and the Ghab Plain in Hama province.
Ahmed al-Sheikh Khalil, head of the transitional justice prosecution office in Hama, said the former officer was suspected of involvement in serious violations and crimes against humanity committed during the Syrian uprising.
The five other detainees, whose identities have not been disclosed, are also suspected of involvement in abuses against civilians under the former government.
Judicial authorities said preliminary investigations were continuing before the suspects are referred to Hama's specialised transitional justice investigation chamber.
Hama's attorney general, Mohammed Ahmed al-Naasan, stressed the importance of pursuing those implicated in abuses through legal proceedings that ensure accountability, justice for victims and compensation for those affected.
The arrests come amid a broader campaign by Syria's new authorities to locate former military and intelligence personnel accused of atrocities during Assad's rule, which ended in December 2024.
In a separate operation on Wednesday, security forces reportedly detained around 12 former regime officers and personnel in the Masyaf area of Hama province.
A security source told Lebanese newspaper Al-Modon that the operation involved internal security and counterterrorism units, and targeted former regime personnel who had previously undergone security reconciliation procedures after Assad's overthrow.
The detainees are suspected of continuing to gather intelligence on behalf of Assad loyalist networks despite having formally regularised their status with the new authorities.
Al-Modon also reported the arrest of Younes Mohammed, a former prison official accused of involvement in abuses against detainees at the Balouna prison in Homs and the notorious Saydnaya prison near Damascus.
Mohammed was reportedly arrested in Qadmus, in Tartous province, after security forces tracked him to a business he was operating under his wife's name. The allegations against him have not been independently verified.
Earlier this month, Hama authorities referred 30 suspects accused of crimes including murder, kidnapping, sexual violence and extortion to the transitional justice authorities following investigations in the Salamiyah area.
The arrests form part of Syria's attempts to confront the legacy of decades of repression under the Assad family, particularly the widespread detention, torture and killing of civilians during the civil war.
Following Assad's overthrow, the government of President Ahmed al-Sharaa established a National Commission for Transitional Justice in May 2025 to investigate crimes committed by the former regime, support victims and pursue accountability.
Syria began its first public trial of senior Assad-era officials in April 2026, including Atef Najib, a former intelligence chief and cousin of Bashar al-Assad, whose treatment of detained teenagers in Daraa helped ignite the 2011 uprising.
In August, a Damascus court convicted Najib and several other former regime figures, including Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher, who were tried in absentia, over crimes committed during the uprising.
However, human rights organisations have raised concerns about the capacity of Syria's judicial system to prosecute the vast number of alleged perpetrators while ensuring fair trials and protecting witnesses.
Human Rights Watch has warned that gaps in the country's legal framework, alongside questions over judicial independence and due process, could undermine accountability for crimes committed during the conflict.
The organisation has also called for investigations into abuses committed by all parties to the civil war, rather than limiting prosecutions to former government officials.

Russia intensifies pressure on occupied Ukrainians without Russian passports, military intelligence says

Russia intensifies pressure on occupied Ukrainians without Russian passports, military intelligence says
Russian security forces carried out a new round of raids across occupied Ukrainian territories in early October, targeting residents who have refused to obtain Russian passports, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) said on Oct. 22, as Moscow continues a long-running campaign of forced passportization.
The raids were conducted jointly by Russian police and the Federal Security Service (FSB) during the first 10 days of October as part of an operation dubbed "Illegal-2026," according to HUR.
Ukrainians without Russian passports are classified by occupation authorities as "foreign citizens" and subjected to Russian migration law, HUR said.
According to the agency, residents can face pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, expulsion from occupied territory, dismissal from work, and property seizure.
In occupied Luhansk Oblast, Russian authorities have also checked documents held by minors as part of the campaign, HUR said. Parents whose children do not obtain Russian passports have allegedly been threatened with fines, imprisonment, and the loss of parental rights.
HUR described the operation as another tool in Russia's broader effort to pressure Ukrainians into accepting Russian citizenship and push those who refuse out of occupied territory.
Russia has pressured residents of occupied Ukrainian territories to take Russian passports since 2014, tying access to employment, social services, property rights, and other aspects of daily life to possession of Russian documents.
Russian occupation authorities already carried out earlier phases of the "Illegal-2026" operation. In June, occupation officials said more than 300 administrative cases had been opened and more than 40 people expelled during a 10-day phase of the campaign.

Carney, Erdogan launch ‘strong and resilient’ Canada-Turkiye partnership
On trade, investment and innovation, leaders will work towards conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan have announced the launch of a Canada-Turkiye Strategic Partnership, backed by a three-year action plan.
“In an increasingly complex global security environment, rising geopolitical uncertainties, and evolving humanitarian challenges, a strong and resilient Canada-Turkiye partnership is essential, providing a foundation to mitigate shared threats and capitalise on new opportunities,” said a statement by the two leaders on Thursday.
This comes as Carney is on a two-day visit to Turkiye, seeking to forge a new partnership as Canada looks to reduce its dependence on the United States.
The partnership’s three-year action plan rests on four pillars: trade and investment; defence and security; energy; and ties between people, the statement said.
On trade, investment and innovation, the two leaders agreed to “work toward successful conclusion of a Canada-Turkiye Free Trade Agreement”, it said. They will also expand bilateral trade and investments in priority sectors, including energy supply, defence production, aerospace, and artificial intelligence (AI).
On defence and security, the leaders “underlined their intent to deepen bilateral and multilateral cooperation”. They also agreed to “strengthen cooperation in support of peace and security in the Euro-Atlantic region and beyond including Ukraine, South Caucasus, and the Middle East, in particular Gaza”.
Meanwhile, energy ministers from both countries will work on areas such as liquefied natural gas, nuclear energy and critical minerals.
‘Launching a new era’
Speaking to reporters in Ankara alongside Carney on Thursday, Erdogan said the two countries “hope to increase our trade volume, which currently stands at around $3bn, to $5bn initially and then to $10bn through the steps we will take”.
He said the two sides had agreed to begin free trade agreement negotiations before the end of the year to boost trade and investment, adding that elevating Turkiye-Canada relations to the level of a strategic partnership would not be merely a symbolic step on paper.
Canadian and Turkish leaders will convene next month in Ankara for the first round of trade talks, the joint statement said.
“We have today overcome the disconnect that had persisted between Turkiye and Canada for many years. Now, we are launching a new era between Turkiye and Canada,” Erdogan said.
Relations between the two countries will expand “for generations to come”, Carney said alongside Erdogan.
“Our goal is not self-sufficiency; it is collective resilience, and that’s why Canada is building deeper partnerships with reliable partners that create new opportunities for us both, and in Turkiye, we have an exceptional partner,” he added.
Carney is on the first bilateral visit by a Canadian prime minister to Turkiye, although he travelled to Ankara in July to attend the NATO summit.
He was scheduled to meet Erdogan and other officials before travelling to Istanbul for talks with Turkish business groups as the two countries seek to deepen trade ties.
The Canadian prime minister has sought to diversify partnerships and reduce reliance on the US amid an escalating trade war with US President Donald Trump, marked by US tariffs on Canadian goods, followed by retaliatory measures from Canada, as well as Trump’s statements questioning Canadian sovereignty.

Alberta welcomed migrant workers. Now, it wants to restrict their rights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:29 UTC
00:00:29 KST

When Vanesa Ortiz came to Calgary from Mexico, she found herself in a city gripped by winter. Outside the airport, it was -15C (5F).
“I would come to understand that this was not an extreme cold,” she said. “But in the moment it was terrifying.
But she also found in those first moments an immense warmth. She was welcomed by elderly volunteers in white cowboy hats, and Ortiz soon felt that Calgary was a place she could one day raise a family. And yet when the teacher reflects on that moment a decade ago, she worries that the opportunities she had to put down roots could be soon closed to others.
This week, Alberta held a referendum, asking residents to weigh in on the province’s relationship with Canada – and the extent to which the province should restrict some newcomers’ access to healthcare, education and social support. It also asked about the need for constitutional reforms.
While unofficial results show both the separation and constitutional questions will fail, the ones on immigration are likely to succeed.
“I love Calgary and I love Alberta,” said Ortiz. “But when I hear people asking whether people should get access to these services – I mean, that was my daughter’s education. That was my family’s healthcare.”
The referendum amplified the grievances of fringe separatists, but it also exposed a central tension in Alberta’s approach to immigration. Even as the oil-rich province seeks newcomers to fill shortages in the job market, the provincial government wants to limit services available to some of those same workers.
The governing United Conservative party blames the rapid population growth for overcrowded and underfunded hospitals and schools. But critics say the proposed solution – restricting access to healthcare, education and social supports – could leave workers and their families more vulnerable without fully addressing the underlying causes of the crisis.
The referendum asked if the government should introduce a law ensuring only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and “individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status” can access healthcare and education. Another asked if newcomers should have lived in Alberta for 12 months before qualifying for certain social support programmes and allowing the province to charge some temporary residents fees for healthcare and education.
Earlier in the year, the Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, blamed the immigration policy of Justin Trudeau’s Liberal government for the resource strains in classrooms, emergency rooms and social support systems. And in a social media post, Smith said: “For every $1 of taxes a guest worker generates, taxpayers are covering $10 in services. This is not sustainable.”
Canada’s federal government has since trimmed immigration targets and placed restrictions on its temporary foreign worker program amid criticisms it was being abused by large companies. But the western province’s economy relies on workers from abroad to fill jobs in sectors, like agriculture, food services and tourism, where employers struggle to recruit or retain enough staff.
Ortiz, who works with the non-profit Asociación de Mexicanos en Calgary, worries mounting skepticism towards migrant workers will push workers into the shadows and make them more vulnerable to labor exploitation.
“I can’t imagine the scale of the harm that a policy like this might create,” she said, noting that thousands of farm workers in the province don’t receive healthcare.
Ortiz has seen views shift on immigration in recent years and says the results of the referendum reflect a population that is “squeezed” economically.
“Scapegoating non-permanent residents is not going to lower the cost of living. That’s not going to fix our classrooms. They keep essential services open. In many cases, they are frontline workers. And now they’re being treated as disposable.”
For some residents, the proposals represent a sharp reversal from Alberta’s earlier efforts to attract newcomers. The UCP government invested in recruitment and expanded its provincial immigration nomination targets to address labour shortages. But as a growing number of Albertans sour on immigration, the government position has shifted.
Ximena González, a Calgary-based writer, said when the provincial government began its campaign to bring in more people, it “wanted more workers to exploit”, noting that most workers come from abroad on temporary permits.
“Now, the message feels more out in the open: ‘We wanted you to come, to exploit you. And now, we don’t need you any more – so we will punish you.”
The provincial government has claimed that temporary residents, who make up almost 6% of Alberta’s total population, contribute roughly $150m in tax revenues but cost the province more than $1bn annually in health, education and other social services.
But González argues that there is no data to back that claim.
Economist Gillian Petit notes that temporary residents also remit taxes to the federal government, which helps fund Alberta’s healthcare, meaning those residents probably contribute far more than the province acknowledges. If they contribute less in total tax dollars than other Albertans, it is because they earn less than the median resident. They are also less likely to use healthcare and education resources than the average Albertan.
“In all honesty, if I were a temporary resident and had to choose whether or not to stay, I wouldn’t,” said González, who came to Canada 16 year ago as an international student. “I would not feel wanted, and I don’t want to be treated like a third-class citizen.”
She says that media fixation on Alberta’s fringe independence movement meant the other questions in the referendum received little scrutiny and left voters uninformed.
“The media failed to help people to make an educated vote – instead of just voting based on racism.”
Economist Jim Stanford said hundreds of thousands of residents skipped over those questions on immigration, choosing to only answer the one on separation.
“This cannot remotely be interpreted as a mandate for the government to crack down on immigration,” he said, adding the province didn’t have the power to “unilaterally” act on these proposals. “This was a symbolic ideological exercise and gives a cast of legitimacy to some of these very rightwing nativist sentiments that are bubbling in the far right of Alberta politics.”
During a series of town halls over the years led by the government, more extreme views on immigration were clear. One resident received cheers after suggesting a policy of mass deportations and another said immigrants “harm” children and suggested she might seek asylum in the US.
For Ortiz, the government’s about-face reflects a “betrayal” of the workers who have helped build the province.
“We’re asking people if we should remove the right to access healthcare and education from taxpayers who are, quite literally, building our communities,” she said. “But I also worry that what gets lost in this debate is these people. They are not just labour. They work, study and raise their children here. They need to know they deserve the chance to build a life with dignity and with respect to feel safe and to feel welcome.”

Astronomers challenge dating of Van Gogh’s Starry Night
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:28 UTC
00:00:28 KST

It was long assumed to be a product of Vincent van Gogh’s rich imagination – but scientific sleuthing now suggests The Starry Night may be based on a real dawn sky.
Researchers say the celestial bodies depicted in the famous painting match the sky the Dutch artist may have seen on about 22 July 1889, a month later than the usual date given for the work.
At that time, Van Gogh was living at an asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where he had admitted himself after a series of mental health crises.
The June date rests on a letter Van Gogh wrote to his brother Theo on about 18 June, describing “a new study of a starry sky” and on a mental breakdown in July, thought to have left him unable to paint for weeks. However, the authors of the new paper argue that the idea of the sky being imagined also rests on the assumption that the celestial arrangement of the painting did not match what would have been seen in southern France in June.
Moving the date to July, they say, means the moon, Venus and a star cluster called the Hyades that are shown in The Starry Night could have been seen by Van Gogh from his window at the asylum, making the painting an exaggerated reality rather than pure fantasy.
To make their discovery, researchers in South Korea identified a ridge south-west of the asylum and matched an earlier sketch by Van Gogh to the real landscape.
The sketch showed he drew a surprisingly narrow slice of the scene. “I was standing where Vincent had stood 130 years earlier,” said Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, the study’s first author and an astronomer at Kyung Hee University in Yongin, South Korea.
The team used astronomy software to recreate the dawn sky for every day in June and July 1889. In the painting, the moon sits above Venus, so they looked for dawns where this occurred and both fitted inside the narrow frame. Only three dates qualified, and 22 July was the closest match, with a thin crescent moon, Venus and the Hyades arranged as in the painting.
“To bring the question into science, which needs quantitative data we had to measure the degree of resemblance between the star patterns in the painting and the real sky, using shape geometry and statistics,” Kim said.
The study is published in the journal Scientific Reports. However, the researchers acknowledged the results were not conclusive, with Kim noting that Van Gogh may have combined the skies of several days.
The Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, which was not involved in the research, said its experts had established that Van Gogh painted The Starry Night in June 1889. It said the painting was made on a roll of canvas he received in early June, and on 2 July Van Gogh sent his brother Theo a drawing based on it. The museum also said the artist had a severe breakdown on about 22 July that left him unable to paint for more than a month.
“Van Gogh was not concerned with exact likenesses,” a museum spokesperson said. “The positions of the celestial bodies depicted can therefore not form a reliable basis for dating the work.”
Donald Olson, professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at Texas State University, was also not convinced by the study because the positions of Venus and the Hyades cluster in the painting do not match their calculated position.
He added: “The authors’ assumed narrow field of view, essential for their theory that the stars of the Hyades fill most of the canvas, is inconsistent with the much wider field of view required to encompass Starry Night’s round hills and cliffs.”

Dreadnought reactor still on schedule, minister says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:00:11 BST
00:00:11 KST

Ministers have confirmed that good progress is being made in developing and manufacturing the Rolls-Royce PWR3 reactor for the Dreadnought class submarines, and that reactor components remain on course to support the first boat entering service in the early 2030s as planned, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what progress he had made on delivering the Rolls Royce PWR3 reactor for Dreadnought.
Luke Pollard replied: “Good progress is being made in developing and manufacturing the PWR3 reactor for the Dreadnought Class submarines. The Ministry of Defence continues to work closely with Rolls-Royce Submarines to ensure delivery of the reactor components in time to support Dreadnought entering service in the early 2030s as planned.”
PWR3 is the first wholly new British submarine reactor design since PWR2 entered service in the Vanguard class in the 1990s, developed by Rolls-Royce Submarines at Derby with design input drawn from American practice under the Mutual Defence Agreement. The plant is intended to run for the life of the boat without refuelling, which removes the mid-life refuelling docking that Vanguard required and changes the availability arithmetic across a four boat force.
Rolls-Royce has doubled its Derby site under a contract worth around nine billion pounds covering reactors for both Dreadnought and SSN-AUKUS, and has been recruiting at a rate the company has not managed since the Cold War. Reactor components are among the longest lead items on any submarine, so they drive the build schedule at Barrow.
Dreadnought replaces the Vanguard class on continuous at-sea deterrent patrol, four boats carrying Trident D5 missiles, with the first entering service in the early 2030s after a programme the National Audit Office has repeatedly flagged for schedule and cost pressure. The Vanguards are already serving well beyond their design lives, and patrol lengths have stretched past six months as a result.

The Price of Faustian Bargains with Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

For the past week, President Donald Trump and his aides have traded accusations with Elon Musk, the CEO of SpaceX, over who restricted Ukraine’s access to a military-grade version of Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite network product that Ukrainian forces depend on to intercept incoming Russian projectiles and target Russian launchers.
Musk blamed Trump and the U.S. military for the decision, writing on X, “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS.” Trump insisted that his administration did not disrupt Ukraine’s access to the network. Secretary of State Marco Rubio argued that decisions about Ukraine’s access to the network were in the hands of SpaceX and Musk and not the White House. The Wall Street Journal and CBS News reported that the decision had been Musk’s.
On Mar. 9, 2025, Musk had promised that, whatever his disagreements with U.S. policy toward Ukraine, “Starlink will never turn off its terminals. We would never do such a thing or use it as a bargaining chip.” Critics have raced to blame Musk alone, casting him as the puppeteer behind the throne, the first business titan to achieve what William Randolph Hearst, Marcus Alonzo Hanna, and J.P. Morgan only aspired to: a latter-day Cornelius Vanderbilt, who is reputed to have scoffed, “Law? What do I care about the law? Hain’t I got the power?”
That gets the story backward. Musk’s businesses are uniquely dependent on the blessings of Washington: a fifth of SpaceX’s revenue comes directly from federal agencies, its satellites require federal authorization to launch and operate, and the possible merger of Tesla and SpaceX will live or die by the decisions of federal regulators.
Confronted with a White House that appeared determined to squeeze Ukraine, whatever its public denials, Musk faced a familiar choice for anyone dependent on political patronage: capitulate, resist, or retreat into ambiguity. He chose ambiguity, revealing the limits of his power. The wealthiest man in the world still answers to someone else.
The finger-pointing creates a haze of ambiguity, giving both men plausible deniability. The apparent aim is to force Ukraine into a settlement by depriving it of the means to resist: a way to secure a quick, short-term peace and lower oil prices at the expense of Ukrainian sovereignty and international law.
But that calculation mistakes capitulation for stability. Rewarding President Vladimir Putin of Russia could encourage him to test NATO’s resolve in the Baltic states, Poland, Finland, or Sweden, raising the risk of a direct confrontation with the alliance. It would also signal to other U.S. adversaries that sufficient pressure can fold Washington’s commitments.
For now, Trump could claim to have brokered peace between Russia and Ukraine, even if the peace he delivers is the silence of a defeated country. Musk can evade responsibility by presenting himself as merely one supplier among many across the defense industry whose failures have weakened Ukraine’s defenses. He could point to weapons manufacturer RTX, whose Patriot interceptors are so scarce that Ukraine reportedly ran out of them this month, or to delays in delivering F-16s manufactured by Lockheed Martin that were promised two years earlier.
Faustian bargains
Beneath the public quarrel lies a familiar pattern: surrender political independence and retain the freedom to accumulate extraordinary wealth. The historians who have studied Putin’s Russia most closely would recognize the pattern instantly. Timothy Snyder has written that Russia’s oligarchs “were tamed, but not by a neutral state.” Rather, “Putin himself became the head oligarch, the boss of bosses.” Anne Applebaum echoed the insight and described Putin as making himself “godfather to all of the other oligarchs.”
Putin laid out the terms of that bargain on Jul. 28, 2000, when he met with 21 of Russia's richest men in the Kremlin, less than three months after his inauguration. The message was simple. The fortunes they had amassed in the chaos of the 1990s were theirs to keep, as long as they stayed out of politics entirely. Keep your distance from power, and the state would leave you alone.
Those who refused the deal faced immediate reprisals. Boris Berezovsky and Vladimir Gusinsky, whose television networks refused to bend the knee, were driven into exile within the year. Gusinsky’s NTV was seized by state-controlled Gazprom. Mikhail Khodorkovsky, then Russia’s richest man, funded opposition parties and lectured the Kremlin on corruption. In Oct. 2003 he was pulled off his plane at a Siberian airport and arrested. He spent a decade in prison and watched his oil company, Yukos, dismantled and its assets transferred to state-controlled companies.
Those who accepted the deal are the ones who got rich, and they have never been richer. Forbes counted a record 155 Russian billionaires this year, the fourth straight year that number has grown, with a combined fortune of $696.5 billion—up 11% from the previous year, even as Putin’s war against Ukraine entered its fifth year. Their collective wealth reportedly now exceeds the bank term deposits of the rest of Russia’s population: 155 oligarchs with fortunes greater than the savings of roughly 146 million ordinary Russians.
“Oligarchies are unstable,” Snyder has observed. “Members disappear.” For those who might have forgotten the terms of Putin’s bargain, an instructive reminder came in 2023, when Yevgeny Prigozhin, the head of the Wagner Group, did the one thing the bargain forbade: he challenged the Kremlin’s authority. Prigozhin seized a military headquarters in Rostov-on-Don and sent his forces toward Moscow. His column advanced to within 125 miles of the capital before he agreed to stand down under a deal brokered by Aleksandr Lukashenko, the Belarusian dictator.
Putin publicly called the mutiny treason, then appeared to forgive him. Two months later, on Aug. 23, 2023, Prigozhin’s private jet crashed north of Moscow, killing everyone aboard. The Kremlin denied involvement, the U.S. intelligence concluded that the plane had been blown up, and The Wall Street Journal later reported that the operation had been ordered by Putin’s Security Council chief. Putin’s eulogy, delivered the next day, described Prigozhin as a man who had “made serious mistakes in life.” No oligarch in Russia needed the rest of the sentence spelled out.
Prigozhin’s fate is only the most spectacular entry on a longer, murkier list. Since the invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, at least 85 Russian businessmen and officials have reportedly died in unexplained or violent circumstances, many of them figures in the energy industry. Among the dead are three Lukoil executives: board member Alexander Subbotin, who died in May 2022 after a visit to a “shaman” outside Moscow; chairman Ravil Maganov, who fell from a sixth-floor window that September; and vice president Vitaly Robertus, who was found dead in his office in March 2024.
In April 2022, two former energy and banking executives were found dead alongside their families. Vladislav Avayev, a former Gazprombank vice president, was found shot dead in his Moscow apartment with his wife and 13-year-old daughter. Sergei Protosenya, a former Novatek executive, was found hanged at a rented villa in Lloret de Mar, Spain, with his wife and daughter stabbed to death inside. Catalan police concluded that Protosenya had killed his family, then himself. His son rejected that finding, insisting that his father had been in good spirits and had no reasons to kill them and himself.
Transneft vice president Andrei Badalov fell from a 17th-floor window in July 2025. The Moscow Times has counted 18 such fatal falls from windows since 2002. Three days later, Russia’s transport minister, Roman Starovoit, was found shot dead in his car hours after Putin fired him. Another transport official died of supposedly acute heart failure the same day.
A shadow over America
Putin’s Russia offers an extreme and grotesque example of the bargain. Yet some critics see an emerging American version, in a far less violent form. Snyder and Applebaum have warned that Western billionaires risk repeating the mistakes of Russia’s oligarchs under Boris Yeltsin, believing they can manage a strongman for profit, only to discover that he is managing them.
Musk spent more than $277 million to help elect Donald Trump, took a desk in the West Wing, and ran the Department of Government Efficiency like a man who believed he was co-president. When that arrangement flamed out in May 2025, he tried to exercise independent political power by turning against Trump, calling his signature legislation, the Big Beautiful Bill, a “disgusting abomination.” Musk threatened to form a third political party and then briefly launched one. He even taunted Trump about Jeffrey Epstein, posting that the president “is in the Epstein files.”
After Trump publicly mused about terminating his contracts, Musk quickly retreated. He deleted the posts, and conceded that they “went too far.” He returned to the fold, shook Trump’s hand at Charlie Kirk’s memorial, accepted the National Medal of Science from him this month, and became the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterms, giving at least $366 million to Republican groups. He has grown vastly richer in the process: SpaceX’s June IPO made him the world’s first trillionaire, while the company remains the U.S. government’s dominant launch provider, with competitors such as Blue Origin winning only a fraction of the contracts.
Musk’s retreat illustrates the bargain: surrender the freedom to oppose the president and preserve the ability to enrich yourself. By that measure, Musk’s political defeat has come with an extraordinary financial windfall. He won by losing. The throttling of Starlink in Ukraine appears to fit this pattern. Last week, after Trump demanded that Ukraine stop striking Russian refineries and Kyiv did not comply, its access to a military-grade version of Starlink was restricted and responsibility disappeared into a haze of accusation and denial.
The costs of such Faustian bargains fall on everyone excluded from them. In Russia, soldiers die at the front by the hundreds of thousands while politically compliant billionaires accumulate obscene fortunes. In Ukraine, drone operators lost contact with their interceptors in mid-flight last week while Russian missiles were in the air; the consequences of a disrupted connection are immediate and potentially fatal. Other customers face the question: can a contract with Starlink be relied upon?
In America, democratic government rests on the principle that neither political office nor private places anyone above the law. Businesses must be free to challenge a president without fearing retaliation, and their owners must remain accountable for their conduct. Those protections help distinguish America from an authoritarian dictatorship like Putin’s Russia.
The Starlink saga does not suggest that America has become Russia. But it raises a troubling question: is political obedience becoming the price of commercial success in America? Putin’s oligarchs struck that bargain in 2000 and have been collecting on it ever since. Whether Americans accept a version of it will depend on how forcefully our institutions and business leaders defend our freedom to say no.

Police enquiries have uncovered indications that some of the minors housed in the property may have suffered physical assaults, including injuries caused by dog bites. Investigators are also seeking to determine whether both minors and adults were subjected to labour exploitation and forced to carry out various tasks, with their vulnerability being exploited.
Large police deployment in the El Príncipe neighbourhood
The operation required a significant police deployment because of the complexity of the area where the property was located and the potential danger posed by the organisation under investigation. According to the National Police, several of its members have extensive criminal records.
Inside the property, officers found 54 men, ten women and ten unaccompanied foreign minors. The detainee is suspected of offences involving the facilitation of irregular immigration, violations of workers' rights, causing injury to a minor and the labour exploitation of minors.
Police step up operations after migrant camps cleared in Ceuta
The operation comes against a backdrop of increased police activity in Ceuta, following the clearance of the settlements on Benítez beach and El Trampolín. The dismantling of these camps is thought to have led some of the migrants who had been living there to move to other parts of the city, including the El Príncipe neighbourhood.
In response to this situation, the National Police are maintaining surveillance and operational deployments both around and inside the neighbourhood.
The operation also targets the logistical infrastructure of the organisation under investigation, which allegedly housed large numbers of people while preparing to arrange their irregular transfer to mainland Spain.
The investigation was conducted in coordination with various police units along the Andalusian coast and central services, in collaboration with the public prosecutor's office to combat migrant smuggling.

Britain must outproduce its adversaries, says Streeting
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:57:16 BST
23:57:16 KST

Britain must be able to manufacture critical defence components at home in sufficient quantities, increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase, and sustain its armed forces through a prolonged conflict, according to the Defence Secretary.
Wes Streeting was speaking at the official opening of the UK Gun Hall at Telford, the Rheinmetall facility that returns large-calibre weapon production to Britain.
He said: “But those armaments do not get produced by waving a magic wand. Nor in the event that this country finds itself in a war fighting state, can that capability and capacity in industry be conjured up.”
He said: “To make sure we can deter and, if necessary, defeat, our adversaries, Britain must have the capacity to manufacture critical defence components at home and in sufficient quantities. We must have the capacity to increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase. We must have robust supply chains to back them up, and we must have the wider industrial resilience to sustain our armed forces through prolonged conflict.”
On the balance between technology and mass, Streeting said: “Despite the advent of drones and data of AI and autonomy, it is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm, though we must. We must also outproduce them too, because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field capability fastest.”
He referred to remarks made at the event by the Chief of the General Staff, saying: “As the Chief of the General Staff just said, we are making daily discoveries about the changing nature of the conflict in Ukraine. Yet, as was also pointed out, for all of the technological advances we’re seeing on the battlefield, what you might call more traditional weaponry still has its place in modern warfare.”
On the facility itself, Streeting said: “And so what we’re opening the doors to here is more than a manufacturing plant. We’re opening the doors to something much greater and much more ambitious. And that is readiness and resilience. For the first time in decades, artillery gun barrels will be produced in Britain. They will be made using British steel from Forgemasters. As we’ve heard, their production will create one hundred jobs here and hundreds more across the supply chain right across the country.”
He added: “Gun Hall will also support the next generation of equipment for the British Army, helping to deliver the firepower that will make us warfighting ready by 2030.”
The Telford facility will manufacture 120mm and 155mm weapon systems, including those supporting Challenger 3 and future artillery platforms, with a peak capacity of up to 245 barrels a year across both calibres and more than fifty breeches annually. Rheinmetall turned an empty building into an operational manufacturing capability in eight months, with breech production beginning in May and barrel production in June.
Streeting also set out the case for combining domestic production with allied integration, saying: “And this factory is a reminder that stronger domestic industries and deeper allied integration are not contradictory. Done right, each strengthens the other.”
He said: “The defining test is not where every single component of a piece of kit or equipment was made. It is whether our combined industrial base can give our armed forces what they need, when they need it, because an alliance that can mobilise its armies must also be able to mobilise its industries.”
The Defence Committee reported this week that general munition stocks are among the capabilities European NATO members lack in sufficient numbers, and that the unglamorous enablers of warfighting capacity including logistics networks and ammunition stockpiles have withered through decades of underinvestment across the alliance.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that there is no current requirement to procure new 105mm barrels for the L118 Light Gun, and consequently no plans to restore domestic production of that calibre. This publication has reported on the wider effort to rebuild Britain’s ability to manufacture large calibre guns.

Netanyahu promises Iran regime change: Can Israel topple Tehran government?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:55:59 UTC
23:55:59 KST

Netanyahu promises Iran regime change: Can Israel topple Tehran government?
Israel can inflict devastating damage on Iran, but analysts question its ability to overthrow Tehran’s government.
Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said that overthrowing Iran’s government remains Israel’s “primary objective”, as he faces declining support in the polls before national elections next week.
His remarks came after conversations with United States President Donald Trump on Sunday and a visit to Israel by Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. But Netanyahu offered no indication that Washington had agreed to join another offensive against Iran, let alone a campaign to bring down Iran’s leadership.
While Israel has the firepower to inflict serious damage on Iran, analysts told Al Jazeera, it lacks a clear strategy for translating military gains into the overthrow of Iran’s government. Air strikes alone are unlikely to achieve that objective, while a ground invasion would demand a far greater military commitment, they said.
A renewed offensive would also mean confronting a state that has already survived two rounds of attacks and retains the means to retaliate – both against Israel and its Gulf neighbours who are hosting US military assets. US backing, meanwhile, remains uncertain, with experts questioning Washington’s appetite for renewed fighting as it is yet to find a credible prospect of forcing Iran’s government to surrender to its demands.
Does Israel have the firepower?
Israel’s ability to attack Iran is not in doubt, experts say. Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera that its offensive weapons stockpiles, and “aerial refuelling” capabilities give it a substantial advantage. “Israel could again establish air superiority and strike Iranian targets,” he said.
But while Israel can inflict serious damage, analysts are sceptical that it can accomplish regime change.
Netanyahu has portrayed Iran’s leaders as a major threat since his first term as prime minister in 1996. Addressing the US Congress that July, he said, “The most dangerous of these regimes is Iran, that has wed a cruel despotism to a fanatic militancy.”
Nearly 30 years later, US participation in the June 2025 war, and again in the campaign launched on February 28 this year, delivered the military intervention Netanyahu had long sought. The overthrow of Iran’s government, however, did not follow. Netanyahu himself acknowledged the limits of airpower in March, saying, “You can’t do it only from the air.”
“There has to be a ground component, as well,” he added, without explaining what that would involve.
Caglar Kurc, an assistant professor at Abdullah Gul University in Kayseri, Turkiye, said bombing could weaken Iran’s military but not necessarily eliminate its ability to fight back. “Airpower can degrade military capabilities but cannot fully destroy offensive capabilities,” he told Al Jazeera. “Well-hidden systems would survive.”
Overthrowing the government, Kurc said, would require a willingness to deploy troops and remain on the ground for years. Israel can also no longer assume that covert methods used in earlier attacks would prove equally effective again.
Coningham described intelligence assets as “use and burn” because deploying these methods risks exposing networks that Iranian security services will investigate and disrupt.
Israel still has “human intelligence assets on the ground”, he said, while “cyberattacks” could also form part of another campaign. But using those capabilities risks revealing and sacrificing them, making the prospect of a tangible military gain an important consideration.
Covert operations and cyberattacks, in his assessment, do not offer a clear route to overthrowing Iran’s government. Coningham was similarly sceptical that Kurdish or Baloch armed groups could provide the ground force needed to challenge the state. In March, the Trump administration was said to be actively discussing providing arms to opposition Kurdish groups, according to CNN, which cited Kurdish and US officials. But this never progressed.
“Kurdish groups lacked the military capabilities to take on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC),” he said.
Iran can still retaliate
Iran also does not need to match Israel aircraft-for-aircraft to make another offensive very costly, experts say.
Sidharth Kaushal, a senior research fellow at RUSI, told Al Jazeera that the “Iranians likely retain sizeable stocks of missiles,” even if damage to their targeting systems may constrain their effectiveness.
“The actual antiship missile stockpiles likely remain large, both because they are comparatively easy to make, and Iran has in-housed much of the production of older Chinese ASCMs, and Iran’s southern mountains provide natural shelters against air attack,” Kaushal said.
Coningham said that, for Israel, sustaining its defences would be more difficult, with previous exchanges having drawn down interceptor stocks.
Repeated attacks also impose a financial burden, as Israel will be intercepting relatively inexpensive Iranian drones with far more costly defensive weapons. Over a prolonged exchange, that imbalance could place further pressure on Israel’s interceptor supplies, while Iran retains the capacity to mass-produce more cheap weapons for a lot longer.
Would Washington join another attack?
Analysts consider this unlikely, pointing to diverging political interests between Tel Aviv and Washington, with Trump facing pressure to avoid renewed escalation before the US midterm elections.
The Financial Times reported this week that an Israeli proposal for renewed strikes had failed to secure Trump’s approval, although it suggested disagreement about immediate action rather than Washington ruling out future attacks altogether.
Without Trump’s participation, Coningham said, Israel would lack US capabilities for striking deeply buried facilities. These include the 30,000-pound GBU-57 bunker-busting bombs that US B-2 bombers dropped on Iran’s Fordow and Natanz nuclear facilities in June 2025. Designed to penetrate deeply buried targets, the weapons gave Washington an offensive capability Israel could not match on its own.
Coningham also suggested that, if Israel were to attack without US support, Iran might concentrate its retaliation on Israeli territory while avoiding US targets and disruption to the Strait of Hormuz.
Such an approach would seek to punish Israel without drawing Washington directly into the fighting, potentially further isolating a country already widely ostracised by the international community amid its genocide in Gaza.
But analysts say the central obstacle that could ultimately prevent Israel from attacking Iran is the gap between its ability to destroy military targets and its capacity to force political change within Iran.
“You cannot change a regime unless you are prepared to deploy troops and stay in the country for some years. Israel cannot control Iran. The United States would not engage in another regime change, which could take decades,” Kurc added.

Staff sought in Antarctica to count penguins — what the job entails and how much it pays
Kyiv • UNN
The UK Antarctic Heritage Trust is offering a six-month position at Port Lockroy station with a salary of up to £2,096 per month. Physical fitness, residence in the UK, and the right to work are required.
The British UK Antarctic Heritage Trust is looking for staff to work at the former Port Lockroy research station in Antarctica. They will be responsible for monitoring a penguin colony, running a museum and gift shop, and working at the southernmost post office in the world. The salary is up to £2,096 — approximately €2,400 per month, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
The job lasts six months and requires serious physical fitness. Staff will have to carry 20-liter water containers, lift boxes weighing up to 15 kg, clear snow, and unload boats near slippery cliffs. The station has no running water, mobile phone service, or medical assistance. Showers are usually taken once a week, and staff have to live in a shared dormitory.
Duties include counting nests, eggs, and chicks. This data helps researchers track changes in the colony's population and assess the impact of tourism. In addition, staff welcome visitors from cruise ships, run the museum, and process mail by hand.
Port Lockroy is a former British research base founded in 1944. Today, it is a popular stop for Antarctic cruises: in summer, up to two ships carrying tourists may arrive there every day. The team itself lives in historic buildings that are preserved in their original form.
There is an important restriction for applicants: candidates must be at least 18 years old, reside in the United Kingdom, and have the right to work there.

Saudi Aramco evacuates HQ for first time since Yemen war resumed
Saudi Aramco reportedly ordered employees to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely on Thursday, amid escalating Houthi attacks on oil facilities across Saudi Arabia.
Reuters, citing six sources familiar with the matter, reported that it was the first time since the resumption of the war in Yemen in September 2026 that the Saudi oil giant had instructed staff to leave its main headquarters.
Aramco did not respond to the news agency's request for comment.
Bloomberg separately reported that the evacuation followed an alarm at the company's headquarters, citing people familiar with the situation.
The cause of the alarm was not immediately known, while neither Aramco nor the Saudi Energy Ministry responded to Bloomberg's requests for comment.
The evacuation comes just over a week after Aramco's headquarters was targeted in an attack on 13 October, which reportedly caused damage to several floors of the complex.
Reuters, citing three people familiar with the incident, reported at the time that the strike caused extensive damage and sparked a fire that spread across multiple floors.
Bloomberg reported that the attack struck a tower within the office complex, damaging approximately three floors.
However, the Saudi Energy Ministry said in a statement on Tuesday that the attack had caused only a limited fire and resulted in no injuries or deaths.
Strategic oil operations centre
Aramco's Dhahran headquarters houses a major operations centre responsible for monitoring and coordinating the company's vast oil and gas infrastructure.
The facility helps oversee onshore and offshore oilfields, refineries, export terminals and thousands of kilometres of pipelines.
Its operations coordination centre plays a central role in monitoring production and distribution networks, coordinating activities and responding to disruptions.
According to Aramco's 2017 annual report, the Dhahran operations centre monitors the company's distribution network to ensure continuity and respond to operational problems.
Dhahran, located between Dammam and Khobar in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, is home to Aramco's main administrative, operational and research facilities.
The company also established a research and development centre in the city in 2000.
The surrounding Eastern Province is the heart of Saudi Arabia's oil industry, containing some of the kingdom's most important energy facilities.
These include the giant onshore Ghawar oilfield and the offshore Safaniya field, as well as major crude processing and export infrastructure.
At Abqaiq, Aramco operates its largest crude oil processing and stabilisation facilities, while Ras Tanura is home to a major oil export port and terminals.
An extensive pipeline network connects the oilfields to processing, refining and export facilities, while the East-West Pipeline transports crude from the Eastern Province to Yanbu on the Red Sea coast.
Houthi attacks target oilfield and airport
Thursday's evacuation followed Houthi attacks on Saudi energy and transport infrastructure the previous day.
On Wednesday, Houthi forces targeted the Shaybah oilfield and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, in the latest escalation of attacks against the kingdom.
Saudi authorities said the airport attack killed two people and injured eight others.
Airport operations subsequently resumed, with air traffic returning to normal.
Bloomberg, citing the Saudi Energy Ministry, reported that the attack on the Shaybah oilfield had not affected production.
The latest incidents have raised concerns over the security of Saudi Arabia's critical energy infrastructure as the conflict with the Houthis intensifies.
Aramco, one of the world's largest oil producers, operates an extensive network of facilities that are central to Saudi Arabia's economy and global oil supplies.
The evacuation of its main headquarters marks a significant precautionary measure amid the continuing attacks, although there was no immediate indication that Thursday's evacuation had disrupted oil production or exports.

Wreckage of Soviet World War II fighter plane, pilot's personal items found buried underground in Hungary
The wreckage of a World War II-era Soviet jet was discovered in rural Hungary, along with some of its pilot's personal items, according to the Hungarian Museum of Military History and local media.
Excavators unearthed the Soviet Yakovlev Yak-1 fighter aircraft from about 17 feet underground in the central Hungarian village of Törtel, which is located about 50 miles southeast of Budapest, museum officials said. István Kocsis, a member of the research association who led the investigation into the wreck, said excavations in the area began in September.
Several portions of the plane were relatively intact when archaeologists recovered them from the crash site. The relics included what officials identified as a piece of the red star insignia printed on all Soviet military properties at the time, which they said was "in relatively good condition."
Part of the aircraft's fuselage was also recovered, displaying the jet's side number, in addition to the pilot's personal belongings. Among them was a book containing the pilot's signature, which experts at the museum are currently working to restore, the museum said.
Some of the best-preserved pieces of the wreck will be exhibited by the military museum, once its archaeology department has finished carrying out restoration procedures and logged records of their obervations.
Although scientists and archaeologists alike are still working to learn more about the decades-old debris, they were able to trace the wreckage back to a particular wartime crash that took place in November 1944, Hungarian local media reported. While opposing each other over Törtel, German Lt. Peter Düttmann and Soviet Lt. Alexander Semyonovich Andrianov's aerial duel ended with Düttmann shooting down the Soviet aircraft. Although Andrianov escaped by parachute, he later became a prisoner of war, according to the news site Hungary Today.

American Airlines forecast deeper losses this year and said it will slow its capacity growth next year as record revenue failed to help the airline recover from a spike in fuel costs.
American said Thursday that it expects to lose between $1 and $1.60 a share, on an adjusted basis in 2026. In July, it forecast adjusted full-year earnings per share between a loss of 65 cents and a profit of 65 cents.
The Fort Worth, Texas-based airline is the fourth major U.S. carrier to cut its forecast for 2026 due to a jump in jet fuel following the start of the Iran war. Rising jet fuel prices have driven up airfare more than 20% from last year, according to airline reports and federal data. Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines also slashed their outlooks this month.
Jet fuel is airlines' biggest expense after labor, and the spike has added billions to costs this year. American's fuel bill was up 67.5% in the third quarter alone, from last year to $4.64 billion.
"American delivered record third-quarter revenue and the strongest year-over-year revenue growth in my career, with premium performance leading the way," American CEO Robert Isom said in a news release.
Confidence in 2027 profitability
Despite the lower expectations for deeper losses in 2026, Isom said on an earnings call Thursday that he has "great confidence" that the company will return to profitability next year.
The CEO has been under pressure to boost profits at the carrier, which has dramatically trailed profitable rivals Delta and United. American has been investing in new lounges and revamped cabins with more premium seats and said this year that it plans to add seat-back screens again to its narrow-body fleet.
Earlier this month, the airline named a new network chief. It was the latest move in a management shake-up that has included new hires in its operations department and its commercial team. Last year, American brought in a new commercial chief, industry veteran Nat Pieper.
International and premium-travel demand has remained especially robust, executives said. Late last month, American said it would deepen its partnership with Alaska Airlines as the Seattle-based carrier would join American's trans-Atlantic and trans-Pacific joint businesses.
The airline is also closing in on an order for new wide-body airplanes, executives said. CFO Devon May told CNBC on Thursday that the airline has considered the Boeing 787 Dreamliner, Airbus A330 and Airbus A350.
American forecast it will lose between 50 cents and $1.10 a share, adjusted, in the fourth quarter, with revenue expected to be up as much as 22.5% from a year earlier and capacity up between 5.5% and 6.5%.
Here is what American reported in the third quarter compared with Wall Street estimates compiled by LSEG:
- Loss per share: 28 cents adjusted vs. 35 cents expected
- Revenue: $16.34 billion vs. $16.22 billion expected
For the third quarter, American had a net loss of $269 million or 41 cents a share, compared with $114 million, or 17 cents a share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, American reported a loss of 28 cents a share. Revenue jumped 19.3% from a year earlier to $16.34 billion.
