Indian diaspora could pay price for West’s immigration backlash, warns Sushant Sareen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:40:00 UTC
23:40:00 KST

Sushant Sareen sees the immigration debate as part of a wider crisis facing Western societies.
US President Donald Trump has blamed immigration for the recent unrest in France and urged President Emmanuel Macron to close the country’s borders, reigniting a wider debate over migration, integration and the future of Western societies.But the backlash could also hurt Indians who have built successful lives abroad through legal migration, strategic affairs expert Sushant Sareen has warned.
“The law breakers don't care anyways but it's the guys who follow the law who will also get crushed,” Sareen said in an interview on Faultline, hosted by Ananya Dasgupta.Trump has described France’s unrest as a consequence of immigration and warned that Europe risks decline unless it tightens its borders. Macron, however, has rejected attempts by foreign leaders to blame migrants for the violence, pointing to the exploitation of France’s domestic tensions for political gain.
Why Indians could pay the price
Sareen said the Indian diaspora had established a reputation for success in countries such as the US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand.“The Indian diaspora wherever it went it made a success of itself,” he said.However, he argued that this reputation could come under pressure as anti-immigration sentiment grows.
Referring to Canada, Sareen alleged that criminal activity involving some members of the Indian community, including people he linked to Khalistani networks, had damaged the image of the wider diaspora.His concern is that Indians unconnected with such activities could also face the consequences of a broader backlash against migrants.
Is the West paying for its own mistakes?
Sareen sees the immigration debate as part of a wider crisis facing Western societies. He argued that governments had failed to manage integration and address tensions around migration, leaving established political and social models under strain.“Multiculturalism has collapsed,” he said, describing what he sees as the failure of the Western approach to managing cultural diversity.Yet Western economies continue to need migrant workers, particularly as populations age and employers face labour shortages. Sareen said governments must rethink their immigration systems, including how long migrants can stay and what rights they should have.For Indians hoping to study, work or settle abroad, tougher visa rules could complicate future plans. Those already settled overseas could also face uncertainty if immigration becomes a proxy for wider anxieties about jobs, identity and cultural change.
The contradiction is that Western countries need foreign talent even as political pressure to restrict immigration grows.For India, the stakes extend beyond visa policies. If the West responds to its immigration crisis by treating migrant communities as a single group, law-abiding Indians who have contributed to their host countries could find themselves paying the price.Watch Faultlinewith Ananya Dasgupta and Sushant Sareen as they discuss the France crisis, the West’s immigration trap, the growing backlash and why Indians could pay the price.

Germany arrests Ukrainian man accused of spying for Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:36:06 UTC
23:36:06 KST

Germany arrests Ukrainian man accused of spying for Russia
Military has raised the threat level of Russian sabotage against German troops and facilities.
A Ukrainian national has been arrested in Germany on suspicion of spying for Russia, German authorities have said.
Germany’s federal prosecutors confirmed in a statement on Thursday that the man, identified as Vadym Y, was arrested in the state of Brandenburg 85km (53 miles) west of Berlin.
Prosecutors said the suspect had been in touch with the Russian secret service via an intermediary since at least July 2025.
The suspect had gathered military intelligence on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as military personnel and defence installations at locations designed to secure NATO’s eastern flank, prosecutors added.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who is currently meeting with regional leaders in Montenegro for the EU-Western Balkans Summit, said he was “not surprised” by the news of a suspected Russian spy.
The arrest comes after German authorities blamed Russia for drone attacks that officials said are part of Moscow’s “shadow war” on the country.
Germany’s armed forces on Wednesday raised the threat level of Russian sabotage against their troops and facilities to “significant” for the first time – the second-highest level on their internal threat scale, German news reports noted.
The move followed the discovery in mid-September of a crashed drone carrying high explosives near the Wunstorf airbase in Lower Saxony, German news sites WDR and Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported.
The drone resembled another unmanned aircraft – also laden with explosives – used in a failed attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August. Unlike the Leipzig incident, which authorities said targeted civilian cargo aircraft, investigators believe the Wunstorf drone targeted military aircraft, according to an internal military document seen by German media.
The report also noted a pattern of suspected Russian reconnaissance across Germany, including drones flown over a missile defence site in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, and a camouflaged camera found filming a strategically important railway station in Minden, in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
Martin Jaeger, head of Germany’s BND spy service, told lawmakers this month that Russia’s undeclared “shadow war” against Germany and its allies was escalating further and has “taken on a new, more dangerous character”.
“Germany is at risk of being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia,” he told an intelligence oversight committee at Germany’s parliament, the Bundestag.
Moscow denied involvement and has maintained it is not involved in sabotage or hybrid attacks on European nations.

Ilhan Omar home raid, Haines attack: Inside rise in violence on officials

United States Congresswoman Ilhan Omar has been forced to move out of her Washington, DC residence because of safety concerns after her home was raided, amid growing threats of violence against politicians.
Last week, US federal agents searched Omar’s home with what a Justice Department spokesperson described as a “judicially authorised search warrant”, adding that the raid was part of an “ongoing federal criminal investigation”.
According to NBC News, which cited one person familiar with the matter, charges against Omar may include conspiracy and making false statements in her immigration paperwork.
For years, Somalia-born Omar, who is Muslim, has been the target of right-wing conspiracy theories about her immigration status, including allegations that she had married her brother.
The Minnesota congresswoman has repeatedly denied the allegations as “disgusting lies”.
She has drawn the particular ire of US President Donald Trump, who views her as a thorn in his side and has threatened to deport her.
Omar came to the US in 1995 at age 12 and was naturalised as a US citizen in 2000. Since January 2019, she has served as a congressional representative for the state of Minnesota.
But on Wednesday, she told the US news outlet MS NOW that following the raid on her Washington apartment, she could no longer live there.
“Because our address has been public and with the death threats that I deal with, it’s no longer going to be feasible to be in that house and have my kids visiting off and on, having people track them,” she said.
The raid on Omar’s home comes as violent attacks on politicians have grown more frequent.
She, herself, has been physically assaulted. In January this year, Omar was sprayed with an unknown substance by an assailant while calling for the abolition of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency at a town hall meeting in Minneapolis.
On Monday this week, Australian independent MP Helen Haines, who has championed climate action and advocated for improved working conditions as a lawmaker, was hit by a car outside her electorate office, resulting in the amputation of both of her legs.
Australian police said it was a “targeted attack” and warned of growing “online extremism” and recorded a rise in abuse, threats and intimidation targeting lawmakers.
‘Dangerous escalation’
The violent attack on Haines was particularly shocking. Her attacker, identified as Brendan Nugent, 43, allegedly drove past her before turning his car around and veering towards Haines, pinning her against her car.
Australia’s Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the driver then reversed before ramming her again.
Sofia Collignon, a reader in comparative politics and director of the Mile End Institute of Research at Queen Mary University London, said instances of physical violence, such as the attack on Haines, are still “relatively rare in terms of numbers”.
“It’s very upsetting to see that more and more people in public life are paying a very high price for doing something that is a public good,” Collignon told Al Jazeera.
Abuse online often comes before physical attacks, however.
She said that women – and, in particular, women of colour in politics – are facing high levels of abuse on social media, and this is taking a worrying toll.
“We are seeing from research that this is having an effect on how they [women] behave in politics, or whether they change the way that they campaign, change the type of issues that they advocate or sometimes completely refrain from participating on social media,” she said.
According to a 2023 report by the Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), which assessed 12 years of data on attacks against Italian politicians, “marginally elected women are approximately three times more likely to experience an attack” than marginally elected men.
The Princeton School of Public and International Affairs Bridging the Gap initiative, which tracks political violence in the US, found that there has been a “dangerous escalation in the political violence risk environment in the US, including a series of high-profile assassinations and aggressive federal immigration operations”, in 2025
“Incidents of threats and harassment spiked, and leading community safety practitioners reported that the demand for de-escalation support surged to new heights,” it added.
In the case of Omar, Trump has repeatedly targeted the congresswoman since his first term of office over her Somali origins.
He has called her a “sick person”, an “extremist”, and “garbage”, among other inflammatory language.
Other Muslim or progressive congresswomen have also been subjected to Trump’s rhetoric. In February, he wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform that Omar and Palestinian American congresswoman Rashida Tlaib should be sent “back from where they came from”.
But Trump himself has also contended with political violence. In 2024, during his campaign rally, Trump was shot in the ear by a spectator attending the rally.
Then, Trump ally Charlie Kirk was killed in 2025 by a man named Tyler Robinson, who said he had carried out the attack because he had “enough of his [Kirk’s] hatred”.
‘Fierce political polarisation’ to blame
Online threats of attacks on politicians have led to real-life killings for some time.
In 2016, British MP Jo Cox was killed in her constituency while campaigning to remain in the European Union ahead of the referendum by a man named Thomas Mair, who had shouted: “This is for Britain.”
In 2021, Conservative British MP David Amess was killed by a man named Ali Harbi Ali, who claimed that he had targeted the representative over his vote for air strikes on Syria.
In 2026, former Conservative MP and spokesperson for the far-right Reform UK party, Ann Widdecombe, was killed by a man named Joshua Kerry, who has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for “acts of terrorism”, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
Collignon said she believes social media has “lowered the bar” for bad-faith actors to threaten politicians, which explains the increase in the volume of threats.
“For example, what people consider to be acceptable ways of referring to politicians or to talk to them are more and more aggressive. They can find it acceptable to use more aggressive terms, partly because of the polarisation in politics,” she said.
“It’s not an issue that we observed only on the right or on the left, but we observe it very often on the fringes of the spectrum. They find that it is acceptable to use unacceptable language or behaviour in the pursuit of their political goals. So that means intimidating a politician is something that they kind of condone.”
According to an Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) 2026 annual report, local officials faced a “persistent and evolving threat of violence in 2025” in an analysis of 2,653 incidents of violence that targeted local officials globally.
The data show that the recorded incidents worldwide have spread from 88 countries and territories in 2025 to 97 in 2024.
“Over the past five years, ACLED records at least 13,900 incidents in 138 countries and territories,” said the report. “Local officials often become lightning rods for broader societal grievances. Large-scale protest movements in recent years have directed their frustration and anger at local authorities, viewed as the nerve endings of a failing or corrupt state.
“Especially in Europe and the United States, a pernicious mix of fierce political polarisation and unchecked competition for political dominance exposes politicians, and especially local elected officials, to a growing trend of harassment, abuse and violence.”
Clionadh Raleigh, ACLED CEO, told Al Jazeera that while public officials can be challenged and voted out, “violence against them should never be ignored or excused”.
“Political violence is not exclusive to the left or right, and both extremes show greater openness to violence. These attacks are not simply isolated threats to individuals, but part of a wider pattern of political intimidation,” Raleigh said.
A 2026 report by the Inter-Parliamentary Union, a global international organisation of national parliaments, revealed that of the 519 parliamentarians who participated in research across five national case studies and joined a global survey, 71 percent of all respondents reported having “experienced violence by the public, whether online, offline or both”.
“Violence is heavily concentrated online, with between 65 percent and 77 percent of MPs across the case studies reporting online abuse,” it found.
However, Collignon said the line between online threats of violence and being physically assaulted has become increasingly blurred.
“Let’s say that I check my social media accounts at home, a place where I should feel safe,” she said. “But then, if my phone is showing me constant abuse, threats of violence, very nasty behaviour, then I am receiving all of these attacks in my living room.
“We currently are operating in a space where lines are blurry, and I think we shouldn’t be thinking about online violence as something that just happens in the digital sphere. It’s something that has consequences for the individual in their daily lives, and the way in which they are involved in politics.”

Cortisol: can the level of the stress hormone really be lowered with the help of foods
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:34:10 EEST
23:34:10 KST

Cortisol: can the level of the stress hormone really be lowered with the help of foods
Kyiv • UNN
Individual foods cannot reliably lower cortisol. A balanced diet, sleep, and consulting a doctor in case of symptoms are more important.
Bananas, chocolate, nuts, and magnesium—social media is increasingly recommending these foods and supplements for lowering cortisol, which is called the stress hormone. At the same time, its level depends not only on diet. Dietitian Oleksandr Kushch told UNN journalist in more detail whether food can influence cortisol production, what symptoms may indicate hormonal disorders, and when it is worth consulting a doctor.
Why the body needs the stress hormone at all
Cortisol is often associated with the negative consequences of stress, but in fact, this hormone itself is necessary for the normal functioning of the body. It is produced by the adrenal glands. According to the doctor, cortisol is involved in regulating metabolism, helps the body respond to exertion, and has a natural daily rhythm.
The adrenal glands are small caps located at the upper poles of our kidneys. Despite their small size, they produce many hormones. Cortisol has a specific rhythm: its level usually rises in the morning when we wake up. This is a normal physiological process that helps the body become active
Can cortisol be regulated with food
Oleksandr Kushch explained that nutrition does indeed affect the overall condition of the body; however, no individual food can reliably normalize cortisol levels or eliminate the consequences of chronic stress. Much more important are a complete diet, an adequate amount of protein, and a balanced intake of essential nutrients.
Nutrition certainly has an impact, but it is not as obvious as some people think. First and foremost, it is important to have a balanced protein-rich diet. The quantity of protein is not the only factor that matters; its quality, that is, its amino acid composition, is also important. The body needs all the essential amino acids that it cannot synthesize on its own
Eating together may reduce the risk of depression and dementia – BBC29.08.26, 03:56 • 15207 views
Sources of complete protein include, of course, eggs, fish, meat, dairy products, and certain other animal-derived products. Incidentally, a plant-based diet can also meet protein needs through legumes, soy, nuts, seeds, and grain products, provided there is sufficient variety. By contrast, “antidepressant food”—that is, desserts, pastries, candies, and so on—does not actually work very well against stress.
I recommend compensating for stress not with sweets, but primarily with protein-rich foods. It is important for the diet to be balanced and provide the body with the necessary amino acids. There is no single food that contains a special substance and can independently solve the issue of cortisol regulation
Bananas, nuts, and even dark chocolate can indeed be part of a complete diet, as some of these foods contain magnesium, fiber, and other nutrients. However, there is insufficient evidence that consuming even such beneficial and healthy sweets reliably lowers cortisol levels for them to be considered means of hormonal correction.
The normal functioning of the adrenal glands requires a whole complex of vitamins and trace elements. These include B vitamins, magnesium, zinc, and other minerals. However, it is impossible to single out one trace element responsible for the functioning of the entire system. Overall, a balanced diet is important
Why sleep is more important than individual foods
One of the key factors that truly affects the daily rhythm of cortisol is sleep patterns. Sleep deprivation, an irregular schedule, and night work can disrupt circadian rhythms, causing a person to experience fatigue, daytime sleepiness, and increased activity in the evening. Therefore, attempts to compensate for the consequences of constant sleep deprivation with vitamins or menu changes may be ineffective.
The issue of cortisol cannot be separated from the issue of sleep. There are certain biological rhythms according to which our body functions. If a person regularly stays up until two or three in the morning, works night shifts, or constantly disrupts their schedule, this can affect their well-being and hormonal rhythms
In addition, Oleksandr Kushch emphasizes that light from screens, especially in the evening, can also suppress the production of melatonin—a hormone involved in regulating the sleep–wake cycle. Therefore, to make it easier to fall asleep and sleep better, the doctor advises reducing the brightness of lighting in the evening or limiting the use of gadgets before bed altogether and maintaining a consistent rest schedule.
It is very important to establish a healthy sleep routine. Before going to bed, you should put away your gadgets, as blue-spectrum light can affect the production of hormones that regulate sleep. Therefore, I advise not focusing solely on nutrition, but working comprehensively on your daily routine and the quality of your rest
Can the adrenal glands become exhausted due to chronic stress?
On social media, one can often encounter the term "adrenal fatigue syndrome," which is used to explain fatigue, sleep problems, and a lack of energy. However, the dietitian explained that in evidence-based medicine, this term is not considered a recognized diagnosis, and the symptoms themselves may in fact have many other causes.
I would not say that the adrenal glands simply become exhausted and therefore produce a lot of cortisol. The endocrine system works like an orchestra: if the functioning of one link is disrupted, this can affect other processes. The causes of hormonal disorders can vary, including diseases of the adrenal glands themselves, so it is important to consider the situation comprehensively
When does elevated cortisol require examination?
Oleksandr Kushch noted that constant fatigue, sleep disturbances, mood changes, and fluctuations in blood pressure may be reasons to consult a doctor; however, on their own, they do not confirm an elevated cortisol level, since its concentration is affected by the time of day, physical exertion, stress, and even the circumstances in which the laboratory test is performed. If hormonal disorders are suspected, the doctor determines which examinations are needed, taking into account the person’s symptoms and medical history.
Cortisol is produced throughout the day, and its level changes. Therefore, a single test does not always provide a complete picture if the time the sample was taken and the clinical situation are not taken into account. It is difficult to interpret the results independently, so examinations should be conducted on a doctor’s recommendation
Do dietary supplements help lower cortisol levels?
Magnesium, B vitamins, and other nutrients are important for the normal functioning of the nervous system, but the doctor explained that there is insufficient reason for everyone without exception to take them in order to lower cortisol. According to him, supplements may genuinely be appropriate in cases of a confirmed deficiency or other specific indications; however, of course, they do not replace the diagnosis and treatment of endocrine diseases. Particular caution should be exercised with products advertised as "universal stress hormone blockers."
There are various vitamin and mineral complexes and supplements used to support the nervous system. But the needs of the specific individual must be taken into account, rather than simply taking everything indiscriminately. If there are problems with blood pressure, sleep, or other alarming symptoms, it is important to determine their cause
Thus, nutrition is indeed an important component of overall health, but there is no magic product that can normalize the stress hormone on its own. The best strategy is to provide the body with sufficient protein and other nutrients, establish a healthy sleep routine, and avoid self-medication. And if hormonal disorders are suspected, only a medical professional should determine the cause and treatment approach.
ATTENTION! This material is intended for informational purposes only. If you are concerned about health problems, consult a doctor.

Ukraine's population falls to 28.5 million, according to Institute of Demography
Ella Libanova, director of the Institute of Demography and Quality of Life Research, made this statement during the 10th Ukrainian Women’s Congress, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“Just a few days ago, we completed our assessment of the population as of mid-year (2026)—28.5 million. We’ve lost half a million people. This is not so much due to deaths as it is due to emigration,” Libanova said.
According to the researcher, migration—both internal and external—remains the main factor driving demographic dynamics at present.
At the same time, Libanova believes that after martial law is lifted, Ukraine may face a new wave of migration, particularly as men return to their families abroad.

Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:33:06 BST
23:33:06 KST

Why a student protest movement is challenging 12 years of Vučić rule in Serbia
- Published
Rallies have been taking place across Serbia on Thursday, the final day of campaigning ahead of a snap election billed as a referendum on the country's future.
After two years of student protests, Serbians vote for a new parliament on Sunday in elections that threaten populist leader Aleksandar Vučić's 12 years in power.
The main threat to Vučić's dominance in Serbian politics comes from a two-year-old student movement, but there are concerns surrounding the fairness of the vote.
Why is this student movement so important?
They have no obvious leaders and are not used to politics, but the "Student List-Students Win" movement has attracted anti-government voters across Serbia.
The Student List is fielding candidates from across Serbian society - and as he joined students marching towards Belgrade, lead candidate and cardiologist Ilija Srdanović said history was being rewritten: "The energy is unstoppable."
It all began on 1 November 2024, when the concrete canopy collapsed outside Novi Sad train station, in Serbia's second biggest city, killing 16 people.
The tragedy was seen as emblematic of corruption and negligence in Serbia. Critics linked the station's fatally flawed renovation to a president who had closely associated himself with the project.
What started as weekly student protests demanding justice on university campuses and city streets soon became a national movement, often at a local level, that encompassed far more sections of Serbian society, including farmers, actors and judges.
The Serbian Progressive party (SNS), founded by Vučić, was shaken and within weeks the prime minister resigned. Belgrade saw one of its biggest ever protests in March 2025, and while the leaderless student movement increased in strength, they organised themselves through student assemblies or plenums.
At the last election in 2023, Vučić's SNS was challenged by a loose coalition of pro-EU parties, that later fell apart. This time he faces a far clearer threat from a student movement that has shunned the mainstream opposition parties.
- Anger lingers in Serbia after train station tragedy 
  - Published1 November 2025
Who is Vučić and how popular is he?
Vučić has spent two terms as president and cannot seek a third term, so he is now leading his party with the aim of returning to the post of prime minister, which he left in 2017.
The right-wing populist leader has doubled down on unfounded allegations that his opponents are not so much students and professors, but "mighty great powers" seeking to overthrow Serbia. And he has vowed an end to what he sees as the politicisation of schools and universities.
Vučić has steered a careful path with the West, continuing to back Serbia's candidacy for the European Union, while refusing to impose sanctions on Russia for its full-scale war in Ukraine. Several government ministers attended the Belgrade funeral of war criminal Ratko Mladić, prompting EU anger at his "glorification".
Helena Ivanov of the Henry Jackson Society, a foreign policy think tank, says the students have been able to mobilise the masses in a way traditional opposition parties have not been able to - and this is Vučić's biggest challenge since he came to power.
"He's been running in all elections Serbia has had since the introduction of multi-party election system - so obviously defeating him isn't going to be easy, but this time around President Vučić isn't going to have an easy time either," she told the BBC from Belgrade.
- Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections 
  - Published27 September
How do Serbia's elections work?
Serbia has a parliament with 250 seats and there is just one national constituency under proportional representation.
Voting runs from 07:00 (06:00 GMT) and ends at 20:00 on Sunday.
There are 6.45 million registered voters and anyone over the age of 18 gets the right to choose which party's list of candidates to vote for.
Sunday's vote involves 18 lists but only seven of them are fielding the full 250 candidates. MPs are elected according to how much support the list receives if it wins more than 3% of the vote.
Several opposition parties have pulled out in favour of the Student List.
Who are the student leaders and what do they stand for?
Far from being students themselves, the candidates are made up of teachers and university professors, actors and doctors, farmers and scientists.
They still have no leaders, but top candidate Ilija Srdanović is a cardiology professor in Novi Sad, while others include ex-basketball star Dejan Bodiroga, renowned actor Tihomir Stanić and former National Bank of Serbia governor Dejan Šoškić.
Under an 11-point programme, external, the student movement wants to:
- eradicate corruption by forming a police unit to arrest those responsible for it
- purge officials in the internal affairs ministry of anyone who broke rules on cracking down on protesters, or anyone linked to organised crime
- reform Serbia's skewed media scene and free the public broadcaster of political control
- stop recruiting party loyalists to head public enterprises
Vučić and the SNS party deny corruption and seeking to influence the media.
How fair will the vote be?
European observers are monitoring Sunday's vote, but even beforehand the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) has spoken of a "tense and divisive electoral climate" and a "referendum-like atmosphere".
Serbia's election commission says elections are free and the ballot is secret. However, independent watchdog CRTA has warned of a campaign that has seen threats and physical violence, external, and opposition activists subjected to surveillance.
In a report ahead of the vote, it said instead of ensuring equal conditions for candidates, "a range of institutions, from ministries to local governments, became involved in electoral engineering".
Serbian media has seen almost three-quarters of TV coverage devoted to government representatives, the watchdog complained, and alleged that ministries and local governments had become caught up in "electoral engineering".
Some 160 attacks have been recorded on media and journalists in Serbia this year, says the European Centre for Press and Media Freedom.

Brazil picks its path: What’s at stake in the election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:32:54 UTC
23:32:54 KST

Brazil picks its path: What’s at stake in the election
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is once again fighting for his political future, in a runoff election against Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro. After a dirty campaign, voters will decide on Sunday whether Brazil maintains its leftward trajectory or lurches to the right.
Bolsonaro defeated Lula in the first round of this year’s presidential election, beating the incumbent left-winger by 47.03% to 45.16% on October 5. With neither candidate winning an outright majority, ten runners-up were eliminated and a runoff called for October 25.
Who are the candidates?
Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, more commonly referred to as ‘Lula’, has been a mainstay in Brazilian politics since the 1980s. After serving two terms as president from 2003 to 2011, he was sentenced to nine years in prison in 2017 for alleged involvement in a corruption and money laundering scheme within the state-run oil company Petrobras.
Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court struck down his conviction in 2021, and Lula returned to politics the following year, defeating Jair Bolsonaro by a margin of just 0.11%. In power, Lula has increased government spending to tackle poverty, handed subsidies to industry, and hiked taxes on the wealthy. Meanwhile, his government has deepened trade and diplomatic ties with Russia, China, and the rest of the BRICS group, while criticizing US intervention in Latin America.
“Brazil,” he said in a speech at the UN General Assembly last month, “does not fit into anyone’s back yard.”
A senator since 2019, Flavio Bolsonaro is the eldest son of Jair Bolsonaro, who was placed under house arrest last year after the Supreme Federal Court found him guilty of attempting to overturn his 2022 loss to Lula. A social conservative, Flavio Bolsonaro has promised to slash government spending, deregulate industry, crack down on crime, and rein in the power of the judiciary. If elected, he has promised to pursue amnesty for his father.
Bolsonaro favors closer relations with the US, and has said he would join US President Donald Trump’s military campaign against Latin American drug cartels. He has signaled he would “consider leaving” BRICS, accusing the organization of “provoking the United States by proposing that the dollar should no longer be the currency for international transactions.”
Should Bolsonaro win, he would fall into a growing camp of right-wing leaders in Latin America, including Presidents Javier Milei of Argentina, Abelardo de la Espriella of Colombia, Jose Antonio Kast of Chile, and Nayib Bukele of El Salvador.
What are the key issues?
Crime is the dominant issue in this election, with 28% of respondents telling CNN Brazil that “violence” is the main problem facing the country. Bolsonaro, who has pledged to designate drug trafficking gangs as terrorists, relax restrictions on police violence, and build a network of high-security prisons modeled on El Salvador’s CECOT facility, enjoys a 10-point polling advantage over Lula on this issue, according to a Bloomberg survey.
CNN Brazil identified “corruption” as the second issue atop voters’ list of concerns. Bolsonaro also leads Lula on fighting corruption, according to Bloomberg, albeit by a smaller margin of 4%.
Bolsonaro is currently a subject in two money laundering probes, but he has fired off corruption accusations at Lula, citing the involvement of Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes in one of these investigations. Moraes, a close political ally of Lula and the man responsible for jailing Bolsonaro’s father, was accused of taking bribes from the banker at the center of the probe.
Economic concerns are the third most pressing issue for voters, according to the CNN poll. Lula has made his economic record a central pillar of his campaign, pointing to Brazil’s rising wages, falling unemployment, and modest economic growth during his tenure. The president enjoys a narrow lead over Bolsonaro when it comes to tackling poverty and inequality, but Bolsonaro is seen as a stronger candidate when it comes to taming inflation and reducing Brazil’s national debt, according to Bloomberg’s poll.
Who’s interfering in the election?
The election has descended into a bitter battle over foreign interference, censorship, and dirty tricks. Earlier this month, Lula’s campaign accused Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta of intervening against him by throttling his posts and preventing him from boosting his advertisements on Instagram. Days before the first round of voting, Meta also blocked the Lula campaign’s advertising account on Facebook, preventing it from running new ads.
Meta claims that technical problems were to blame, and insists that any allegations of favoritism are “simply false and unsupported by the facts.” Whatever the explanation, Meta’s platforms are vital to both Lula and Bolsonaro, as other social media platforms – among them Google, TikTok, and X – have banned political advertising in the runup to the election.
Brazilian Attorney-General Jorge Messias has accused the US of election meddling, pointing to the White House’s awarding of a $1 million grant to right-wing groups “countering lawfare and censorship in Brazil” – essentially groups opposing Brazil’s Supreme Federal Court.
“Disagreements between governments are inherent to international relations,” Messias wrote on X earlier this month. “What cannot be tolerated is for foreign political interests to seek to interfere in the functioning of Brazilian institutions or to influence, directly or indirectly, choices that belong exclusively to the Brazilian people.”
Bolsonaro’s supporters view the court as a political instrument in the hands of Lula. Justice Moraes ordered the mass suspension of social media accounts over the spread of so-called “misinformation” in the runup to the 2022 election, with the overwhelming majority of accounts suspended being pro-Bolsonaro ones.
One day after the first round of voting this year, Moraes issued an arrest warrant for Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo, who lives in the US. Eduardo Bolsonaro had lobbied the Trump administration to campaign for his father’s release from house arrest.
Bolsonaro has accused Lula of using the machinery of state to boost his campaign. Bolsonaro’s lawyers have called for Lula’s disqualification over his use of the government’s Gov.br system to promote his social programs, his use of government databases to obtain citizens’ contact information in order to send campaign messages, and his use of public funds to produce campaign videos.
What do the polls say?
Lula and Bolsonaro are neck-and-neck in the polls, with every major survey taken up to this month within a margin of error. According to a Quaest poll released after a televised debate between the candidates on Sunday, Bolsonaro leads the leftist incumbent by 45% to 44%. Another poll by PoderData places both candidates in a 50-50 dead heat.
Although the race is too close to call, one historic constant is likely troubling the Lula campaign: since Brazil introduced presidential runoffs in 1989, no candidate has ever won a runoff after losing the first round. However, the first-round gap between Lula and Bolsonaro this month was the smallest in Brazilian presidential election history, at just 1.87%.
With his family persecuted – as he sees it – by Lula’s judiciary, the election is deeply personal for Bolsonaro. For Lula, who is 80 years old, this runoff may be the last of his political career, and the last chance to preserve the leftist state and multipolar foreign policy he’s spent decades building. Whoever wins, this election will be watched in Washington, Moscow, and beyond.
When will we know the result?
Polls close in Brazil at 5 PM Brasilia Time (10 PM Central European Time) on Sunday, and results will begin to emerge around an hour later as ballots are counted. A winner will likely become obvious within hours – in 2022, Lula’s victory was confirmed less than three hours after polls closed.
For more on the election and analysis of the results, stick with RT.

The European Parliament on Thursday awarded its 2026 Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought jointly to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and its senior officials, recognizing their work in upholding international law and justice, Anadolu reports.
“The European Union is founded on respect for multilateralism and international institutions. By awarding the Sakharov Prize to the International Criminal Court and its officials, Parliament recognizes the important work carried out by the Court to uphold international law and justice,” said EP President Roberta Metsola, announcing the winners to the full assembly.
The parliament highlighted the ICC investigations, prosecutions, trials, and issuance or authorization of arrest warrants for serious international crimes, including genocide, war crimes, and crimes against humanity.
“The Court plays an essential role in the global fight against impunity,” said an official statement.

Lawmakers have repeatedly called on the European Commission to activate the EU’s blocking statute to protect ICC officials from the extraterritorial effects of sanctions and safeguard the court’s independence.
The parliament also stressed that all EU member states are parties to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC, and are obligated to implement its decisions.
Established in 1988, the Sakharov Prize recognizes individuals and organizations defending human rights, democracy, and the rule of law.
The award ceremony will take place in December in Strasbourg.

The Bet on America With Bloomberg Opinion
Unknown

The European Parliament honored the court that issued an arrest warrant for Putin: who was awarded the 2026 Sakharov Prize
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:29:53 EEST
23:29:53 KST

The European Parliament honored the court that issued an arrest warrant for Putin: who was awarded the 2026 Sakharov Prize
Kyiv • UNN
The European Parliament honored the ICC for defending international law and justice. For Ukraine, the decision strengthens support for the investigation of war crimes.
On October 22, the European Parliament announced the laureate of the 2026 Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought. The award was presented to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and its officials for defending international law and justice.
UNN explains the history of the prestigious award, its laureates, and why this year's Sakharov Prize is important for Ukraine.
Sakharov Prize 2026: who became the laureate and what they received the award for
European Parliament President Roberta Metsola announced the decision to award the prize to the ICC during a session in Strasbourg. The deputies greeted the decision with a standing ovation.
The European Union is founded on respect for multilateral cooperation and international institutions, and the prize recognizes the court's important work in protecting international law and justice. The European Parliament supports the principle of independent investigations into the most serious crimes
ICC President Tomoko Akane, for her part, expressed gratitude for the honor, emphasizing that it had taken on special significance at a time when the institution and its staff were facing unprecedented challenges. She called for support for the court's independent and impartial work.
It should be noted that the decision to present the award to the ICC coincided with the imposition of U.S. sanctions on the court. Washington introduced the restrictions several hours after former ICC judge Navi Pillay received the Nobel Peace Prize.
What is the Sakharov Prize, and why is it considered one of Europe's most prestigious awards
The European Parliament has presented the Prize for Freedom of Thought since 1988. It is named after physicist and Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, who advocated for human rights. It is the European Union's highest distinction for work in the fields of human rights, democracy, and freedom of expression. It may be awarded to both individuals and organizations. Candidates are nominated by political groups or at least 40 Members of the European Parliament. After three finalists are selected, the final decision is made by the Conference of Presidents, which includes the president of the European Parliament and the leaders of the political groups. Laureates may receive financial support of 50,000 euros.
International Criminal Court: what the organization does and why it was honored in 2026
The ICC began operating in 2002 under the Rome Statute. It is a permanent international court that considers individual responsibility for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and, under special conditions, the crime of aggression. It intervenes when national courts are unwilling or unable to properly investigate such crimes.
Unlike the International Court of Justice, which resolves disputes between states, the ICC brings cases against specific individuals, including military and political leaders. At the same time, it has no police force of its own: the arrest of suspects depends on the cooperation of states.
Who else was nominated for the Sakharov Prize in 2026
The finalists were selected on October 19 by the European Parliament's Foreign Affairs and Development committees. In addition to the ICC, Tanzanian opposition politician, lawyer, and human rights defender Tundu Lissu was included on the shortlist. He is being held in custody on charges of treason, for which the death penalty is possible.
The third nomination went to Iranian sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi as symbols of those persecuted by the Iranian authorities. Taraneh was sentenced to death in connection with the protests, while Romina was given a lengthy prison sentence. Members of the European Parliament condemned the politically motivated sentences and demanded that they be overturned.
Of the six nominees, physician Hussam Abu Safiya, El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele, and the Israeli organization Standing Together did not make it to the final.
The Sakharov Prize and Ukraine: why the European Parliament's decision is particularly significant
For Ukraine, everything related to the ICC's activities is important primarily because it was this international institution that issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova, the Commissioner for Children's Rights. They are suspected of war crimes related to the unlawful deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children from occupied territories to Russia.
In 2024, the ICC also issued arrest warrants for Russian commanders Sergei Kobyلاش and Viktor Sokolov, and later for Sergei Shoigu and Valery Gerasimov. The cases concern, among other things, alleged crimes committed during strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
In addition, as of January 1, 2025, Ukraine became a full-fledged party to the Rome Statute. Therefore, the ICC's work is important for investigating crimes committed on the territory of Ukraine.
It is important to understand that the Sakharov Prize does not change the court's jurisdiction or ensure the immediate detention of suspects. However, this international award undoubtedly strengthens political support for the institution from which Ukraine expects justice.
The political context of the award: U.S. sanctions against the ICC and the position of the European Union
On October 9, 2026, the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump extended sanctions to the ICC as an institution, following earlier restrictions against individual judges and prosecutors. Washington explained its position by citing its rejection of the court's jurisdiction over Americans and the ICC's actions concerning U.S. allies. One of the causes of the conflict was the arrest warrants issued in 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.
The sanctions regime provides for restrictions on financial transactions and cooperation with U.S. companies. At the same time, some transactions were authorized for a 180-day transitional period. The ICC called the sanctions an attempt to obstruct independent justice.
The European Union criticized Washington's decision and said it was ready to support the court. The European Commission is discussing, among other things, the use of a so-called blocking statute, which could protect European companies from requirements to comply with certain foreign sanctions. As of October 22, no decision had been made to activate this mechanism. The award does not replace practical protection for the court.
Who received the Sakharov Prize previously, and which of the laureates were Ukrainian
Ukraine's history with the prize is embodied in two European Parliament decisions. In 2018, it was awarded to Ukrainian director Oleh Sentsov, who was then imprisoned in Russia. In 2022, the award was given to the "brave people of Ukraine" for resisting Russia's full-scale aggression and defending freedom and democracy.
Among the laureates of the prestigious international award were also Nelson Mandela, Malala Yousafzai, the Iranian movement "Woman, Life, Freedom," and Jina Mahsa Amini (2023). In 2024, the prize went to Venezuelan opposition figures María Corina Machado and Edmundo González Urrutia. The 2025 laureates were journalists Andrzej Poczobut from Belarus and Mzia Amaghlobeli from Georgia.
When will the 2026 Sakharov Prize be presented, and what does the award mean for the future of international justice?
The 2026 Sakharov Prize award ceremony is scheduled for December 16. It will take place in Strasbourg during a plenary session of the European Parliament.
For Ukraine, the significance of this event lies primarily in confirming European support for the principle of individual accountability for the gravest international crimes. Whether solidarity will become practical assistance will be shown by the subsequent decisions of the EU and the parties to the Rome Statute.
A reminder
Two journalists, Andrzej Poczobut and Mzia Amaghlobeli, imprisoned in Belarus and Georgia, received the 2025 Sakharov Prize. They were recognized for freedom of thought and speaking out against injustice while being imprisoned on fabricated charges.

Nunchuck-wielding man storms Australian minister's office as attacks on female lawmakers spark alarm
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:29:30 UTC
23:29:30 KST

A man was charged on Thursday with threatening an Australian lawmaker’s staff with nunchucks days after another legislator was critically injured when a man repeatedly hit her with a car.
Nunchucks are a controlled weapon used in martial arts consisting of two or more batons joined by a cord, rope or chain, according to Western Australia state law. Nunchucks can only be carried in public in the state for use in legitimate sports, training or martial arts instruction.
The incidents are heightening concerns about female politicians’ safety and security in a country where lawmakers are highly accessible to the public.
Man charged with entering lawmaker's office with nunchucks
Prosecutors said in a Perth court on Thursday that John Lawrence Smart, 56, was screaming when he entered Western Australian state government minister Hannah Beazley’s electorate office in suburban Perth on Wednesday, demanding to see her while holding above his head two pieces of wood tied together.
Beazley wasn’t in the office at the time. Two staff members remained safe behind a security barrier in the office and no one was hurt.
“It was confronting,” Beazley posted on social media.
Smart said from the prisoner’s dock that he had been holding claves, not nunchucks. Claves are typically wooden sticks used as a percussion instrument.
Magistrate Heidi Watson refused to release Smart on bail, saying he posed a potential risk to himself and the public. She ordered Smart to be medically assessed while in custody. He had previously been involuntarily admitted to hospital with schizophrenia.
Smart did not enter pleas to charges of being armed, or pretending to be armed, in a way that may cause fear and with making an unlawful threat.
There was no allegation that Smart's alleged behavior was connected to the driver who hit federal lawmaker Helen Haines with his car in the east coast state of Victoria on Monday.
Haines' alleged attacker, Brendan Nugent, appeared in a court on Wednesday on charges including intentionally causing serious injury. He did not enter pleas and remains in custody.
Police are still searching for a motive.
Haines, a 65-year-old independent lawmaker, remained in critical condition on Thursday in a Melbourne hospital where surgeons have amputated both her legs, a health department statement said.
Australians worry attacks threaten tradition of accessible politicians
Both the Haines and Beazley incidents have raised concerns about the safety of female politicians, who account for a growing proportion of lawmakers in Australian parliaments. Just under 50% of federal lawmakers and a majority of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s Cabinet are women.
Australian lawmakers are some of the most accessible in the world and political violence has traditionally been rare. But there are fears that increasingly toxic public debate driven by social media creates additional risks for elected women.
Albanese said the fact that the threat to Beazley came so soon after the alleged attack on Haines was “just heartbreaking.” Beazley is the daughter of Albanese's former federal colleague, Kim Beazley.
“We can have debate and disagreement, but do it in a way without descending into the sort of violence that we have seen in too many parts of the world,” Albanese told Australian Broadcasting Corp. “It’s certainly not who we are as Australians.”
Albanese attended an online security briefing this week for women lawmakers in his center-left Labor Party. Security agencies addressed misogynistic threats directed at them.
Male and female federal lawmakers agree that women are facing the worst of the online abuse.
“Of course people are concerned. They’re anxious,” Albanese said. “There has been a normalization of behavior that can be very aggressive in a way that wasn’t happening a couple of decades ago.”
Governor-general abused on social media
Governor-General Sam Mostyn, who is only the second woman to ever serve as the British monarch’s representative in Australia, said that she was abused on social media for speaking at a press conference on Wednesday alongside Haines’ husband Phil Haines.
“Like any woman who has stepped up into any position across any part of our society, there is a unique and pernicious form of attack that comes our way,” Mostyn told ABC.
“Women across the country know that there are certain things that are reserved for women in that attack that go to our gender and they are often vicious and just despicable,” she added.

Jobless claims near the lowest since the 1960s as low-fire trend continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:28:10 UTC
23:28:10 KST

Employers continue to hold onto workers even as hiring remains weak, sending weekly jobless claims to around their lowest levels in records that stretch back nearly six decades.
Initial filings for unemployment insurance slipped to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 17, the Labor Department reported Thursday.
That marked another leg lower in the low-fire trend, with the total just off the 189,000 reported for the week of July 18 that was the lowest since September 1969. Claims have averaged 212,000 over the past year, and the four-week moving average is down to 197,750.
Those numbers come against an uncertain backdrop for the labor market.
Nonfarm payrolls rose by just 29,000 in September and have averaged a gain of just 69,000 a month in 2026. The unemployment rate rose to 4.2%, an increase largely due to a sharp spike in labor force participation. Layoffs have remained modest, declining by 61,000 in August, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics data released Sept. 29.
Over the prior 12 months, the layoff rate measured as a share of the total workforce fell to 1%, down 0.2 percentage point during the period. Job openings were relatively flat during the period.
"Despite extremely pessimistic views expressed in consumer confidence surveys regarding the economy overall, countless headlines describing job cuts from a variety of businesses, and the phantom job-stealing power of AI, the claims data suggests that labor market conditions are stable," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a client note.
The data comes during the reference week that the BLS uses to calculate the payrolls growth number. The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6.
Federal Reserve officials gather next week to issue their latest decision on interest rates. Policymakers in recent days have characterized the labor market as a source of general strength and focused more of their attention on the nettlesome inflation problem that has kept the pace of price increases well above the central bank's 2% target.
Markets expect the Fed to hold off on a rate hike in October but then to institute another quarter percentage point increase in December.
Correction: The October jobs report will be released Nov. 6. An earlier version misstated the month and date.

Why Libya’s embrace of Turkey’s maritime deal reshapes the Mediterranean alignment - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:26:48 UTC
23:26:48 KST

Libya’s eastern parliament approved a maritime boundary deal with Turkey on Tuesday, appearing to bolster Turkey’s claims to part of the Eastern Mediterranean.
The deal dates from 2019, when Turkey sought to exploit Libya’s divisions by laying claim to a maritime boundary that would ostensibly link Libya and Turkey via a maritime border off the coast of Crete. This clearly overlaps with Greek claims.
However, it is at the heart of Ankara’s Mavi Vatan, or Blue Homeland policy, which asserts that Turkey claims a maritime zone that negates Greek claims to waterways between its islands.
Turkey is not going to take over these waters anytime soon. It also isn’t likely to be engaging in any kind of energy exploration off the coast of Crete. Libya is a divided and poor country. Therefore, the deal is more about symbolism. Turkey gets support from Libya, a country that can’t exercise its claims anyway.
This move increases tensions with Greece. However, Ankara may think that it can get some kind of concessions in the future. Either way, it means that any energy company that might want to explore a block of ocean off the coast of some Greek islands that overlap with Ankara’s claims may be wary of doing so. Thus, by asserting claims, Turkey can cause trouble and not have to do much more.
Increased tensions in eastern Mediterranean
When the deal took place in 2019, the Libyan government in Tripoli, which was called the Government of National Accord, was suffering setbacks on the battlefield against the Eastern/Tobruk-based administration aligned with General Khalifa Haftar’s Libyan National Army (LNA).
After the deal, Turkey rushed support to Tripoli. Forces arrived, along with Turkish drones. Haftar’s army was defeated in a battle at Watiya airbase in 2010.
“It has been fighting for more than a year to capture Tripoli, seat of the Government of National Accord (GNA), which is recognized by the United Nations and has moved onto the front foot in the war since January with military help from Turkey,” France24 noted at the time. “The LNA, under Khalifa Haftar, is supported by the United Arab Emirates, Russia and Egypt.”
Since 2020, Libya’s frontlines have been mostly a stalemate. The Trump administration has been hoping for a deal in Libya. Le Monde noted in September that “after 15 years of keeping a low profile on Libya, Washington now wants to reconcile the rival authorities in the country’s east and west by brokering a power-sharing agreement negotiated among a handful of local warlords.
Far from calming the nation, this initiative has triggered a frantic reshuffling of power dynamics and exposed the fragility of alliances on both sides.”
The Libya deal with Turkey in 2019 was designed to give Ankara a reason to back Tripoli. This was successful, and Ankara got a foothold in Libya, and the Libyan government was able to push back Haftar’s forces.
However, why has the deal been revived now? Having the eastern Libyan parliament embrace the deal would appear to mean that Libya is now unified on this policy. The decision has angered several other countries.
Egypt has condemned the decision. Greece and Israel have also condemned it. “Israel strongly condemns the decision of the Libyan House of Representatives to ratify the Maritime Jurisdiction Memorandum between Turkey and Libya. This agreement infringes upon the sovereign rights of our close allies in the region. Regretfully, once again we see Turkey working to destabilize the Eastern Mediterranean region.”
The Libya Observer notes that “the EU, Greece, Egypt and Israel have rejected the Libyan House of Representatives’ ratification of the 2019 maritime agreement with Turkey, arguing that the deal violates international law and infringes on the sovereign rights of other countries in the Eastern Mediterranean.”
Why did Libya decide now is a good time to make the decision?
With so many condemnations pouring in, why would Libya decide now is a good time to discuss this issue?
On the one hand, the new focus on the maritime claims could open up a new front in Turkey-Israel tensions. Turkey and Israel already have tensions over Syria and potentially over Somalia after Israel recognized Somaliland. Turkey has signed on to a new pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan. Meanwhile, it also has a deal with Indonesia, Qatar, and Pakistan to develop defense industrial production.
However, the tensions with Egypt and Libya over the deal also seem to create a challenge. Turkey and Egypt have been patching up their relations over the last several years. This comes after the countries were at odds over the toppling of Egyptian President Mohammed Morsi in 2013. In fact, when the deal was first announced in Libya in 2019, it appeared that Ankara and Cairo were involved in a proxy war in Libya. These days, Egypt is very close to Saudi Arabia and is considering backing it against the Houthis. Turkey and Riyadh are also allies. How will the deal potentially create tensions between Cairo and Ankara and thus create challenges for Riyadh?
There are other issues at stake. Israel’s Prime Minister recently laid out a national security doctrine. In his speech on October 18, he showed a map of the region. The map appeared similar to one created by the Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, which is associated with the Social Democratic Party of Germany. The map shows Israel aligned with the UAE, a member of the Abraham Accords. The map has raised eyebrows because of the alliances it appears to sketch out for Israel. “Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu unveiled a map of the wider Middle East showing his country and the UAE aligned with a paramilitary in Sudan, accused of committing genocide, and separatists in Libya, Yemen, and Somaliland,” Middle East Eye noted. Middle East Eye is hostile to Israel and usually sympathetic to Turkey and Qatar. Nevertheless, it makes a point about Libya that is worth considering.
If Israel was close to the eastern Libyan government in the past, then why would the eastern Libyans agree to the Turkish maritime deal? Has this angered their friends in Cairo also? What is afoot? Is it just strange timing?
It will take time to see what happens with this latest maritime controversy. It could fade, just as the 2019 deal did. That deal led to some increased tensions in the Eastern Mediterranean. However, it eventually seemed to be put on ice. Israel has increased its investment in its navy. It acquired new Sa’ar 6-class corvettes and submarines. Israel is now building five new Reshef-class vessels designed to replace the Sa’ar 4.5 ships. Israel and Greece are also growing closer. Greece is procuring a number of Israeli air defense systems as part of the billion-dollar Achilles Shield program. Meanwhile, Morocco is also seeking to acquire Israeli defense systems. Clearly, this shows that Israel has more influence in the Mediterranean.
What comes next with the Libyans. The US might get the Libyans to unite. The US has also pushed for a ceasefire in Sudan. There are other issues in the Horn of Africa. Ethiopia and Eritrea have tensions, and there are rebel groups in Ethiopia.
With so many new initiatives in the region, such as the Saudi-Turkey-Pakistan deal and the new Qatar-Indonesia-Turkey-Pakistan deal, the Turkish-Libya maritime deal is merely one more stepping stone for countries seeking to invest in a new regional order. This comes amid concerns about the US role in the region in the future. With reports that the US and Israel are preparing a new round of strikes on Iran and the US potentially withdrawing some diplomatic staff and moving around military assets, many things are in motion. For instance, NBC noted that the “US military has quietly been scaling back its troop presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days.” This appears to affect troops stationed in Jordan, Qatar, and Kuwait.
What happens next in the Eastern Mediterranean is anyone’s guess. The last decade has shown that despite many agreements and even talk of new energy corridors and pipelines, it takes time for any new initiative to take shape. As long as Israel and Turkey have tensions, and also Greece, Libya, Egypt, Turkey, and Cyprus do not agree, there can’t be a lot of energy development or new pipelines in these areas where conflicting overlapping claims take place. No one is going to invest in expensive pipelines when they could end up being attacked, for instance.
The Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and also the Iranian-backed militias attacking the East-West pipeline in Saudi Arabia already show how vulnerable energy trade routes are to cheap drones. The countries of the Eastern Mediterranean know this.

İstanbul Photo Awards 2026 exhibition opens in Rome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:23:32 UTC
23:23:32 KST

The second exhibition of the İstanbul Photo Awards 2026, organized by Anadolu, opened on Thursday in Rome, bringing more than 50 award-winning photographs from the international competition to Italian audiences.
After the first exhibition in Ankara, the show opened at Il Portale Ostiense, an exhibition and event venue. The opening ceremony drew distinguished guests from the diplomatic, media, cultural, artistic and business communities.
Attendees included Anadolu CEO Serdar Karagoz; Elif Comoglu Ulgen, Türkiye's ambassador to Rome; Fahrettin Altun, Türkiye's ambassador to the Vatican; Issa Kassissieh, Palestine's ambassador to the Vatican; Ermek Omuraliev, Kyrgyzstan's ambassador to Rome; Ammar M. Dawood, charge d'affaires at Iraq's Embassy to the Vatican; Mustafa Kemal Beyazbayram, representative of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) in Rome; Yahya Bostan, Anadolu’s academy and publications coordinator; and Rodolfo Cardarelli, international marketing director of Italian news agency ANSA.
Addressing the ceremony, Karagoz said Anadolu was pleased to bring the exhibition to Rome, one of the world's most important cities for its history and art.
He noted that people have used art for centuries to tell their stories and leave their mark on history, and photography continues this tradition today.
"Photography records the era we live in, shows the world as it is and helps us understand the lives of others. That is what makes photography so important," he said.
Emphasizing the role of photographers in bringing stories to light, Karagoz said: "Through İstanbul Photo Awards, we aim to make stories visible and share different aspects of the truth with the world.
"We want to support photographers who have the courage to show the world as it is, and the determination to bring these stories to the world."
Karagoz said approximately 22,000 photographers have submitted more than 207,000 photographs to İstanbul Photo Awards since its launch in 2015.
"Just this year, we received 19,000 photographs from all over the world. These figures show how İstanbul Photo Awards has evolved into an important international competition," he said.
He stressed that photography was about more than taking pictures, describing it as a way to document history and reveal the truth.
Photographs, he added, help people understand why events matter, while the responsibilities of photojournalists become particularly significant in wars and genocides.
Karagoz said the 2026 contest's international jury had selected a photograph from Gaza as the Photo of the Year.
The photograph, taken by Palestinian photographer Haitam Imad for EPA, is titled Gaza, No Hope. It shows a two-year-old girl named Sham Qudeih at Nasser Hospital in Gaza.
"She was struggling with severe hunger and illnesses. At the time, she weighed only 4 kilograms. Her condition laid bare the terrible human cost of the war in Gaza," he said. "After the photograph was taken, the little girl was brought to Naples, Italy, for medical treatment. We are very happy to learn that she is now recovering."
Karagoz said Sham's story represented the suffering of many other children in Gaza who continued to endure dire conditions.
"Little Sham had the opportunity to receive treatment, but many more children in Gaza are still suffering. We need more stories of hope from Gaza. Above all, we need to see the genocide in Gaza come to an end.
"Until that day comes, I will continue to report the facts, show the situation on the ground and tell the stories of civilians in Gaza.
"Because the world has the right to know what is happening in Gaza: civilians losing their lives in Israeli attacks, children struggling with hunger and disease," he said.
Karagoz emphasized that the world must recognize the scale of the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza, and ensure that these realities are never forgotten.
He also thanked ANSA, Anadolu's partner in Italy, Ambassador Comoglu Ulgen, Ambassador Altun and the exhibition's sponsors for their support in bringing the photographs to international audiences.
Türkiye's ambassador to Rome Comoglu Ulgen said Anadolu was holding an exhibition of this kind in Rome for the first time, and expressed hope that it would become a regular event.
"I believe this will not be the last exhibition here. I hope this exhibition will mark the beginning of a process that will now become a tradition," she said.
Noting that İstanbul Photo Awards exhibitions had previously been held in several major capitals around the world, Ulgen said bringing the exhibition to Rome at this particular moment was significant for both Turkish and Italian audiences.
"The opening of this important exhibition in Rome today, at this very moment, is extremely exciting for every Turkish citizen living in Italy, as well as for Italians, photography enthusiasts and those who follow news photography," she said.
Ulgen described Anadolu as an institution with a longstanding place in the history of Türkiye, which will celebrate its 103rd anniversary next week.
Founded during the period when Mustafa Kemal Ataturk was leading the struggle for Türkiye's independence, the agency continued to develop under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, becoming a news organization regarded as a reference not only in Türkiye but also across the wider region, Europe and the world, she said.
Recalling her time as ambassador to South Africa, Ulgen shared a message she had received from a Black South African man in reference to a speech by Erdogan at the UN General Assembly.
"People are suffering all over the world. Regardless of our religion, skin color or eye color, the tears that flow from our eyes are always the same color," the message said.
Reflecting on the shared human suffering represented in the exhibition, Ulgen said: "Here, in this room, I see that we all feel that pain. Whether tears flow from our eyes or we hold them inside, we all share the same pain."
Altun, the Turkish envoy to the Vatican, said he was delighted to host İstanbul Photo Awards and bring a part of Istanbul to Rome.
"It is a particular pleasure for me to host İstanbul Photo Awards here and witness a piece of Istanbul being brought to this magnificent city," he said.
Describing Istanbul and Rome as cities of memories shaped by great empires, peoples and cultures, Altun said the exhibition once again brought the two cities together through photography. "Tonight, once again, Istanbul and Rome meet through photography," he said.
Altun said the photographs invited visitors to pause, look more carefully and reflect deeply on the world they inhabit. "What we are opening today is not just an exhibition; we are opening a window onto our world," he said.
He described looking as a matter of choice and photography as a means of making that choice visible and accessible. The images on display covered a wide range of subjects, including Gaza, Syria, Ukraine, the environment, sports and the debris humanity has left in outer space.
Referring to the selection of a photograph about Gaza as this year's Photo of the Year, Altun said its power lay in its ability to place human beings at the center of geopolitics.
"This is a remarkable photograph. I believe its power comes from something very simple: It places the human being at the center of geopolitics. Geopolitics shows us borders, while photography shows us the people beyond those borders," he said.
Altun said the international community had a greater responsibility to look at what was happening in Gaza.
"What we see in Gaza is an unmistakable human tragedy in which human life is systematically placed under siege, hunger is turned into a tool of genocide and civilians are killed on a massive scale. That is why these images are not merely records of suffering; they are also documents bearing witness before history.
"The image of a two-year-old child in her mother's arms takes us beyond statistics, strategies and geopolitics and brings us back to individual human life," he said.
Altun added that photography could restore a human dimension to the way people viewed the world, emphasizing the importance of recognizing the work of photojournalists.
Following the speeches, Aykut Unlupinar, Anadolu's director of visual news, and Baris Seckin, Anadolu's Rome correspondent, guided guests through the exhibition and provided information about the winning photographs from 2026.
The exhibition in Rome will remain open to visitors through Oct. 30.
Turkcell is the competition's communications sponsor this year, while the Turkish Cooperation and Coordination Agency (TIKA) supports overseas events and Turkish Airlines (THY) provides partial transportation sponsorship.

Hacking attempts surge as websites race to patch PHP issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:22:54 UTC
23:22:54 KST

In short:
Cloud services firm Cloudflare says hacking attempts surged in the hours after two vulnerabilities with PHP were made public.
PHP is a programming language used widely across the internet.
What's next?
Global agencies, including the Australian Signals Directorate, are urging websites to urgently patch their code.
Millions of hacking attempts have been made since critical vulnerabilities were discovered in a key piece of internet software used by more than two-thirds of websites.
Governments and major websites have rushed to patch two critical issues with PHP, a widely used computing language, after they were reportedly discovered by AI.
Australia's own cyber security agency, the Australian Signals Directorate, is among agencies around the world to issue urgent warnings for websites to implement a new patch.
In some instances, governments have taken websites offline as a precautionary measure.
The emergency shutdowns of banking, airline, rail, tax and government services from Tokyo to Helsinki mark one of the most dramatic tests of the decades-old programming tools that keep the web running, exposing how deeply governments and companies depend on code that few people understand.
Cloud services firm Cloudfare said since the two vulnerabilities were made public, hacking attempts had surged into the millions.
"In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it," Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince said in a post on X late on Wednesday, US time.
"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now."
The developers of PHP released fixes for vulnerabilities that had lurked in the software for years until they were uncovered using AI, urging users to "update immediately".
"I've not seen anything like this in a long, long time," Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella said at an event in Germany on Thursday, local time.
He said the incident showed the importance of building software that can be maintained securely as systems grow more complex.
"It was a long day and a long night, I know, for all the IT and security folks."
Several Asian governments ordered cybersecurity inspections related to the PHP vulnerabilities.
China's industry ministry urged organisations and users to inspect systems and upgrade to the latest secure version of PHP.
It also recommended strengthening cybersecurity monitoring and changing accounts, passwords and keys where necessary.
South Korea raised its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures, citing concerns over an increased risk of hacking attacks.

Roche CEO slams Europe for failing to reward innovation
