Zehra Nur Celik
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The president of Luxembourg’s Chamber of Deputies said Thursday that Türkiye’s advances in the defense industry could pave the way for closer cooperation between the two countries.
Speaking at a joint news conference in Ankara following bilateral and interdelegation meetings with Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus, Claude Wiseler said: “Türkiye has a very strong defense industry.”
“We know that Türkiye has made very significant progress in this regard. Therefore, I believe there could be important partnerships in communication and information sharing when it comes to defense policies,” he said.
Noting that relations between Türkiye and Luxembourg could be further strengthened, Wiseler said the two countries were marking the 80th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations.
Highlighting bilateral cooperation, Wiseler said: “We have always been partners, of course. We have always discussed issues, held talks and maintained contact. However, given the current geopolitical situation in the world, this cooperation and relationship now need to gain new momentum and move to a new level.”
“That is precisely why we are not looking for new partners. You are already a longstanding partner for us, but we want to take this partnership to another stage, to a different level,” he added.
 
Luxembourg supported Türkiye’s EU membership bid from outset
Kurtulmus, for his part, said: “Luxembourg has been one of the European countries friendly to Türkiye that has supported its EU membership process from the very beginning. Therefore, I consider it my duty to thank them openly once again.”
Stating that Türkiye has always maintained that diplomacy should be the primary avenue for resolving all regional problems, Kurtulmus said Türkiye had continued to play a strong mediating role in the Russia-Ukraine war from the outset.
“We have also stated that the war launched by the US and Israel against Iran has already turned into an endless spiral of tension, from which neither the two countries, nor regional countries, nor the world will benefit in any way,” he said.
Kurtulmus said they also discussed Israel’s aggressive stance in the region, which it has maintained for a long time, its actions affecting countries across the region and, in particular, its “inhumane actions” against the Palestinian people.
“We expressed our strong appreciation for Luxembourg’s decision last year to recognize the State of Palestine and conveyed our congratulations and thanks,” he said.
Kurtulmus said another issue of regional importance was developments between Azerbaijan and Armenia.
“We focused our discussions on the vital importance of this normalization process, with Türkiye’s involvement, in ensuring lasting peace in the Caucasus and thereby establishing secure connectivity between East and West, and between Asia, the Caucasus and Europe,” he said.
Speaking about the Memorandum of Understanding on the Delimitation of Maritime Jurisdiction Areas between Türkiye and Libya, Kurtulmus said: “This agreement was not concluded against any third country.”
“It is an agreement that will safeguard the sovereign rights of Türkiye and Libya in their maritime jurisdiction areas in the Mediterranean,” he added.

State Budget for 2027 will begin to be considered in Verkhovna Rada next week

State Budget for 2027 will begin to be considered in Verkhovna Rada next week
Kyiv • UNN
During the next plenary week, the Verkhovna Rada will consider the 2027 budget and a number of laws to fulfill commitments to the EU and the IMF. The anti-corruption strategy may be withdrawn due to a lack of votes, putting €18 billion from the EU at risk.
The Verkhovna Rada will begin considering the State Budget for 2027 during the next plenary week; the agenda also includes a number of international commitments. This was reported on October 22 by Olha Vasylevska-Smahliuk, a member of parliament from the Finance Committee, on social media, UNN reports.
Details
"The next plenary week will be no less international-commitment-focused than the previous one," the MP noted.
According to Vasylevska-Smahliuk, the preliminary agenda includes:
-  Draft Law No. 13478-1, second reading — restoring competitive selection procedures and improving the procedure for entering, serving in, and terminating civil service. Ukraine Facility, EU. Critically important;

-  Draft Law No. 15269, second reading — improving the corporate governance of the Deposit Guarantee Fund for Individuals. IMF;

At the same time, MP Yaroslav Zhelezniak from the same committee said: "They sent us the agenda for the next plenary week. And then immediately a new one... No votes — no UAH 18 billion in the budget from the EU."

Energy ministry calls for billions in nuclear fusion investments to compete globally
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:56 UTC
23:06:56 KST

Israel's Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure published a strategic report on Thursday detailing Israel's opportunity to enter the global nuclear fusion industry, a sector the ministry claims could become one of the world's major energy sources in the coming decades and develop into a market worth hundreds of billions of dollars.
Multiple countries and private companies have been looking towards nuclear fusion as the energy of the future, using reactors to generate energy by smashing hydrogen isotopes together, a process that does not emit greenhouse gases or produce the level of nuclear waste that the current system of nuclear fission used in typical nuclear power plants does.
Since 2021, over $14 billion has been invested in the nuclear fusion industry, including approximately $4.5 billion in the past year alone.
According to the report, the first commercial fusion plants could be connected to electricity grids during the 2030s, developing into a global market worth hundreds of billions of dollars between 2040 and 2050.
Major technology companies including Microsoft and Google have already signed agreements with companies to purchase electricity from future fusion plants.
Israel already home to fusion research, development
Israel's expertise in several technologies essential to the development of fusion reactors, including high-power laser systems, power electronics and radio-frequency (RF) technologies, artificial intelligence and simulations, advanced materials, and robotics, provides it with an advantage and the potential to enter the industry as a supplier of critical technologies, expertise, and components, the ministry said.
Israel is also home to the Israeli Institute for Nuclear Fusion and Hot Plasma, which supports research in the sector and which the ministry is proposing to expand through investment in scholarships, workforce training, and academic research, at an estimated cost of NIS 50 million to NIS 100 million over five years.
Additionally, multiple companies within Israel are developing related technologies, including nT-Tao, which is developing a compact fusion reactor, and FusionMantle, which focuses on developing components for fusion reactor cores.
Energy ministry poses pathways to fusion development
The ministry proposed three different options for the national development in order to increase investment and development of nuclear fusion technologies within Israel, ranging from NIS 50 million to NIS 2 billion over five to ten years.
The first focuses on expanding Israel's academic research by investing in scholarships, workforce training, and academic research at an estimated cost of NIS 50 million to NIS 100 million over five years.
The so-called 'infrastructure-focused package' involves an estimated investment of 500 million to NIS 1billion over five to seven years in areas where Israel holds a competitive advantage, and would include new funding programs through public-private partnerships and making research infrastructure accessible to academia and industry.
The ministry's final and most comprehensive package involves an investment of NIS 1 billion to NIS 2 billion over seven to ten years to develop a complete national fusion ecosystem. A national coordinating authority would be established, major research facilities would be upgraded, academic training programs would be developed, and the ministry would look towards the possibility of establishing an experimental fusion reactor in Israel through an international partnership.
According to the ministry's report, Israel must take action in the coming years, or it will miss the critical window in which global supply chains are being established, and it will be significantly harder to enter the industry.

====================================================================================================

‘We’re all in the same boat,’ Ark researcher tells ‘Post’ at Turkey’s Durupinar site - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:56 UTC
23:06:56 KST

The Jerusalem Post visited the Durupinar formation last week, the boat-shaped mound in eastern Turkey that is possibly the resting place of Noah’s Ark, to see what a first round of drilling conducted by Noah’s Ark Scans (NAS) has turned up.
The Post’s visit came after the close of NAS’s most recent season of fieldwork at the site, during the week of Parashat Noah, when Jews around the world read the story of the Flood and the Ark.
But the story of the Ark does not belong exclusively to the Jewish people: It appears in the Torah, the New Testament, and the Quran, and the composition of the team working at the site reflects this.
For Adv. Ohav Cohen, that is the point: “At a time when nations and religions seem more divided than ever, this project brings together Jews, Christians, Muslims, and researchers from across the world in pursuit of a shared history,” he said.
Cohen, an Israeli lawyer and researcher working with NAS, told the Post. “Whatever we ultimately discover, there is something profoundly meaningful about people of different faiths working side by side, united by a story that belongs to all of humanity.”
“After all, if we are all descendants of Noah, then we really are all in the same boat,” he quipped.
NAS, led by Andrew Jones, documents the ongoing work at Durupinar. In May 2026, the Turkish government approved the group’s request to begin invasive study of the site, a major milestone after decades of surface-level analysis.
Working under Prof. Cenker Atila of Sivas Cumhuriyet University’s Archaeology Department, the team began core drilling in July. When the season ended in September, samples taken from within the formation were sent to several universities, including Bar-Ilan University, for testing, with a final report expected next spring.
The man who kept coming back
For Jones, the fascination with Durupinar goes back more than 30 years. Raised in a Christian home and drawn to “anything Bible-related,” he first heard about the formation in middle school.
Sitting on the sidelines of the 8th International Symposium on Mount Ararat and Noah’s Ark at Agri Ibrahim Cecen University, Jones told the Post that his interest in the site quickly grew beyond idle fascination, leading him to reach out to explorers who had studied it, such as Ron Wyatt and David Fasold.
Jones’ first visit to Durupinar was in 1997, following a trip to Turkey with a friend while in college. “It felt abandoned. There were no trees around it at that time,” he said. “It was this very lonely boat shape on the side of the mountain.”
The visitor’s center, built in 1987, was a bare cinder-block building run by a chain-smoking Kurdish caretaker who “offered us chai and no information about Noah’s Ark, nothing,” Jones noted.
He subsequently visited the site on three additional occasions between 1997 and 2000.
After a break of 13 years, Jones returned in 2013 with a tour group and reconnected with the Kurdish guides he had met on earlier trips. They asked whether he wanted to pursue something scientific, since little was happening at the site.
“Some tourists were going there; but again, it was kind of like it was in 1997. No one cared about it,” he said.
He returned to Turkey twice in 2014. On his second trip, ERT scans conducted at the site produced “really good results.”
“That got us all excited, since the last time anything was done on the ship [was in] the late 1980s,” Jones said. “That was kind of the start of the current effort because that got everyone excited.”
Further scans in 2019, utilizing ground-penetrating radar (GPR), LiDAR data collection, and thermal cameras, win conjunction with the Science Channel, showed what Jones described as an unnatural pattern of anomalies. The COVID pandemic closed borders in 2020. Following the death of his parents, Jones decided to move to Turkey to be closer to the site and learn the bureaucracy involved in excavating it.
In 2022, NAS renovated the site’s visitor center. Today, it is paneled with wood flooring and large-scale posters showing the results of the 2014 and 2019 scans covering the walls. A 3D scale model of Durupinar built using GPR data taken from the site sits in the center of the space.
During the visit, the Post was shown several marine fossils that had been previously found at and around Durupinar.
In 2024, soil scientist William Crabtree tested 88 soil samples taken from both within and outside of the site. He found that soil from inside the formation had more organic matter, more potassium, and a pH about one unit lower than soil from the outside.
But without a Turkish university partner, NAS could do nothing more than surface-level testing until Atila, a classical archaeologist from Turkey’s Sivas University, connected with Jones online.
On behalf of NAS, Atila appealed to the Turkish Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry for permission to conduct an invasive study of the Durupinar formation, providing a detailed, multi-step outline of the planned testing.
“We had core drilling to 75 meters down, everything geophysical I could think of,” Jones said. “All these are very expensive things to do. But I just threw it all in and said, ‘Let’s see what they approve.’”
According to Jones, the only question the ministry asked was regarding the requested depth of the core drilling. The 75-meter mark, he explained, was due to the estimate that bedrock rested at 70 meters below the surface.
“We wanted to core the deepest we’re allowed to,” Jones said. “To see what we can see all the way down.”
The ministry approved the plan two weeks later, Atila told the Post, with no changes made to any of the requests and plans.
What the drills found
The partnership between Atila and Jones produced results that the team says are worth pursuing, though no one is claiming to have found proof.
During the recent season, the team drilled 12 holes inside the formation and four outside it, going as deep as some 20 meters in places. By Jones’s account, none struck bedrock, which he said would have been the sign of a natural rock formation.
“We didn’t hit any solid rock layer across the site,” he said, adding: “I think that it’s in our favor.”
Notably, Jones mentioned, the drill bit had broken after hitting an unidentified object. Before breaking, the bit had been “through rock pretty fine… if we hit a boulder or something, we go right through it, back into the soil.”
Jones affirmed that NAS would be able to drill a slightly wider hole during its next season, in order to retrieve the broken bit.
To critics claiming that the drilling hadn’t gone deep enough, Jones replied that the team is expected to continue drilling during its next season, in the summer of 2027.
Alongside core drilling and collecting soil samples, the NAS team conducted new radar scans using BakhtarRadar, a subsurface imaging system developed by engineer Khosrow Bakhtar, chief scientist at Bakhtar Research and Engineering LLC.
Preliminary findings from the scans appear to show linear features, angular intersections, layered structures, and possible voids beneath the formation. Researchers interpret these features as possible corridors, compartments, and multiple internal levels similar to the biblical description of the ark.
The radar team had come from the United States, Atila said, but due to heavy rain and other constraints, had only seven days to work on the site. He noted that the team is expected to return in 2027.
Regarding the voids beneath the formation, Atila was careful not to overstate the results.
“I don’t want to say absolutely,” he said. “It’s a corridor. Maybe it can be a geological hole.”
He explained that he is planning future fieldwork at the site, attempting to understand whether the “hole” belongs to the Ark or to a geological formation.
Pieces of what may be petrified wood were also found at the site and sent to Sivas for carbon dating and identification, Atila added. The team is now awaiting the soil analysis, final radar, and carbon-dating results.
Cohen said: “As a lawyer, I have spent years examining evidence and understanding the importance of the bigger picture. In a courtroom, no single piece of circumstantial evidence necessarily proves a case, but the cumulative weight of independent findings can become extraordinarily compelling.
“That is precisely what fascinates me about this site. If this is not Noah’s Ark, we may be looking at one of the most remarkable coincidences in history. At some point, the sheer number of converging clues demands an explanation.”
But not everyone has welcomed the work being conducted at Durupinar.
Jones told the Post that not long after beginning fieldwork at the site in July, the local governor halted the dig for nearly a week after both the governor’s office and the Turkish Culture and Tourism Ministry received numerous phone calls questioning the work being done.
According to Jones, the callers questioned officials over why foreigners such as NAS were allowed to work so close to the Turkish-Iranian border and warned that they might do something illegal or damaging to the site.
The pause was lifted after the governor consulted with individuals familiar with the work happening on the ground, and the team was able to carry on under their original permit.
Jones recalled Atila telling him, at the time, that he’d never seen anything like it.
“This is the first time I’ve seen people so interested in the work that they want to stop us,” Jones recalled him saying. “They all become archaeologists suddenly.”
Jones said he could only guess at the motives behind the complaints, among them jealousy from other teams searching for Noah’s Ark in other locations or a Turkish dislike of foreigners working in the area.
Scientific objections to the claim of Durupinar being the resting place of the Ark, however, are less personal and focus more on the geological appearance of the site.
Such theories include the idea that its ship-like shape was formed by mud flowing around an upright piece of bedrock, that a solid limestone boulder originating near the Iranian border was over the years shaped by glaciers and weathering, and that the formation is actually a syncline (folded rocks).
All three theories, Jones noted, depend on having solid rock underneath, of which the team’s drilling found no evidence.
“We’re not forcing the results,” Jones said. “If we core drilled and hit a rock layer across the whole site, yeah, we’d be like, okay, it’s most likely natural. But we didn’t.”
Paperwork for a second season of work has already been submitted, Jones said.
While the initial permit presented by Atila and approved by the Turkish government covered far more than the team is currently able to undertake, there are several methods Jones wants to seek additional approval for, such as seismic imaging, magnetometry and microgravity, and possibly muon imaging, a technique used at the pyramids of Egypt to detect voids.
At the end of the two-year process, the team will decide on how to proceed based on the sufficiency of the data collected, Jones explained.
Digging would be the last stage of excavations, should analysis results come back positive and NAS is able to get it approved. If Durupinar is the Ark, Jones said, it would be the oldest man-made object documented by biblical chronology, making it extremely fragile, and any highly invasive work will have to be done carefully.
For Cohen, though, the case for pressing on goes beyond curiosity.
“I believe we have a moral, historical, and perhaps even spiritual obligation to investigate this site as thoroughly as possible,” he told the Post.
“We are potentially standing before something that could fundamentally change our understanding of human history.
“With every new clue, every radar scan, and every sample examined, the responsibility to pursue the truth only grows stronger. Whether this ultimately proves to be Noah’s Ark or not, walking away without exhausting every scientific possibility would be a disservice to future generations.”
For Jones and Crabtree, the discovery could mark a significant point of unification worldwide.
“If we can prove beyond a shadow of a doubt that this is Noah’s Ark, the whole world will feel it in their heart, whether they’re an atheist, a Christian, a Muslim, a Jew,” Crabtree told the Post.
Jones added, “We live in a world that’s divided, but the story itself can provide that type of unity to people, and hopefully those who want it can see it in the story, and in the site itself here.”

Peace absent from Israel's 2026 elections as West Bank tensions continue to rise -analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:55 UTC
23:06:55 KST

There’s a short video clip that’s been circulating on Israeli social media channels in recent days showing a massive crowd of jubilant young Israelis at a music festival singing along on repeat to “The Song of Peace.”
The scene, using an anthem forever associated with assassinated prime minister Yitzhak Rabin and the peace momentum that surrounded him in the 1990s, feels ironic today. As Israelis prepare to vote on Oct. 27, peace - the idea at the heart of the song and that was once at the heart of the political debate in Israel - is strikingly absent this time around.
More than three years of war have reshaped the country, but few candidates are offering a vision for relations with the Palestinians, let alone a path toward resolving the conflict.
Meanwhile, rising settler violence in the West Bank and mounting international pressure to resolve the decades-old intractable conflict with a two-state solution are making the costs of that political silence increasingly difficult to ignore.
“Objectively, this is just not the main issue in this election,” Prof. Gideon Rahat, a political scientist at Hebrew University of Jerusalem, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency in a recent interview.
Future character of state, security a focus in Israel 2026 elections
In contrast to the years leading up to Rabin’s assassination in 1995 - and even those that followed - the divisions in this election have little to do with the question of peace with the Palestinians.
Rather, said Rahat, they are more about the fundamentals, the future character of the state and security. For the past four years, the government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has sought to overhaul the country’s judiciary, while a burgeoning ultra-Orthodox population has avoided compulsory military service even though Israel has been fighting a relentless war on seven different fronts.
And while there has been an attempt by Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party to frame the debate as one between right-wing and left-wing, pro-and-anti-Palestinian statehood, Rahat said this was misleading.
Most of the parties in the opposition, those seeking to oust Netanyahu and the current government, are a mix of center-right and right-wing parties. Only one Jewish party in the bloc, the Democrats, appears open to addressing the Palestinian issue.
Rahat pointed out that Hamas’s attack on Israeli civilian communities in southern Israel and at a music festival had served to harden even those who previously thought a peaceful solution with the Palestinians might be possible.
Surveys published in recent years had already shown that support for a Palestinian state, or even a process to reach some kind of solution, had been steadily decreasing even before Oct. 7.
According to Tel Aviv University’s Peace Index, which has published regular data on Israeli attitudes toward peace with the Palestinians since the first Oslo Accords were signed in September 1993, in July this year only 29% of the Jewish public in Israel now supports any form of negotiations with the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinian leadership governing the Palestinians in the West Bank.
Broken down into right-wing vs. left-wing voters, the divisions on the issue of the peace process still appear to be sharp, with only 7% of those who identify as right-wing saying they support negotiations, compared to 83% of those on the left. Yet this is somewhat misleading, as overall, the percentage of people who identify with views traditionally associated with Israel’s peace camp and the left has been steadily shrinking.
After a historic low turnout for the two traditional left-wing parties, Labor and Meretz, in the 2022 election, the two factions joined forces to form The Democrats, now led by former IDF general Yair Golan. And while the Democrats believe in pursuing separation from the Palestinians through a diplomatic and regional process, Golan has refrained from talking about the position throughout the election campaign.
Additionally, former prime minister Yair Lapid, who heads the center-left Yesh Atid Party and has stated in the past that he supports a two-state solution for Israelis and Palestinians, has cooled on the idea.
He has teamed up with former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who is emphatically against the concept of two democratic states side by side, and is saying that the Hamas attack had postponed the possibility of Palestinian statehood at least for now.
“I don’t think the idea is dead. I think it will be delayed significantly because we need to find ways to secure the safety of our people,” Lapid reportedly said in an interview to a London-based Saudi Arabian newspaper in December 2023.
On the issue of settlements in the West Bank, recent surveys show that the majority of Israeli Jews support the concept. A poll published by the Israel Democracy Institute this month shows that around 55% of Israeli Jews support the policies of various governments to allow, and even encourage, the establishment of settlements. Only 32% think that settlement expansion was not correct, the research found.
While the question of peace with the Palestinians - and the possibility of a nation-state for them in Gaza or the West Bank, which many Israelis refer to by its biblical name of Judea and Samaria - is not being discussed on the political level, violent events in that contested area are becoming increasingly hard to ignore.
West Bank attacks undermine peace process
On Friday, Heidi Levine, a photojournalist with The Washington Post, was brutally attacked by masked settlers, as shown in video footage. And on Saturday, a group of European diplomats said they were similarly attacked. Both incidents took place as Palestinian farmers harvested their olive crop.
An influential rabbi associated with far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir had issued an edict that Jews were permitted to attack Palestinians and take their olives to “demonstrate our ownership of the land.”
Palestinians, Rabbi Dov Lior, the former chief rabbi of Kiryat Arba, wrote in a decree, had “stolen land in their hands,” and that it really belongs to Jews.
The phenomenon of Israeli settlers attacking Palestinians is not new, but, according to human rights organizations and the United Nations, it has increased in frequency since Oct. 7. Ben-Gvir, who oversees the Israel Police, has struggled, along with the military, to maintain law and order.
The violence has resulted in multiple deaths. Several governments imposed sanctions on individuals and organizations linked to settler violence. Netanyahu continues to insist that it is only a handful of disorderly youths who are responsible for the disorder.
The increasing violence has drawn condemnation from Netanyahu’s rivals and even some who support him.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief, whose party Yashar leads the opposition bloc, described the attacks, in a post on X, as “Jewish terrorism, under the auspices of the Israeli government.”
He said it was “burning away the little legitimacy the state of Israel still possesses.”
Avigdor Liberman, a former defense minister under Netanyahu who is now running as part of the opposition bloc, also criticized the violence, saying it was “wiping out Israel’s last bastions of support in the United States and around the world.”
“Bibi is putting out statements in English, but the defense minister and the national security minister are doing nothing to stop this madness,” Liberman wrote on X, referring to Netanyahu by his nickname.
“In the end, the damage is first and foremost to the State of Israel and the settlement enterprise. This just proves that Bibi doesn’t care about the country - he only cares about staying in power,” he wrote.
Israeli journalist Amit Segal, known for being pro-Netanyahu, wrote on X that the violence had caused great damage to Israel’s standing among its greatest friends.
Ilana Shpaizman, a senior lecturer in the department of political studies at Bar-Ilan University, said that the flare-up in violence was putting the Palestinian issue back in the spotlight in Israel and beyond.
“For many years or even decades Israeli policy in the West Bank was carried out quietly … It wasn’t like people didn’t know what was going on, but they tried to promote it as quietly as possible to maintain legitimacy to the settlement project,” she said, adding, “When we look at what has happened over the last couple of days, not only has the international community condemned it, but also Israeli politicians.
“People are starting to realize that this government’s support in the West Bank has become very dangerous,” Shpaizman said.
It’s not just Netanyahu, she said - the so-called “change” government that was in office between 2021 and 2022 also failed to address the Palestinian issue.
Shpaizman said Netanyahu was known for being indecisive and reluctant to address the Palestinian issue, and Bennett and Lapid’s slogan was to address only the issues they could solve and leave the tougher question of peace with the Palestinians for later, after other domestic rifts were resolved.
But she said the Palestinian issue is the most explosive and “cannot be ignored for a long period of time.”
Rahat said the rising tensions in the West Bank and the increasing international pressure, which will likely rise if Netanyahu’s government retains power, could end up forcing a solution, or at least putting the Palestinian issue back on the agenda.

Who made Gaza hospitals and homes targets? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:35 UTC
23:06:35 KST

In a Gaza neighborhood, beside a playground built with UNRWA money and flying a Hamas flag, sacks of rice and flour stamped with United Nations markings were stacked into a fighting fortification like sandbags.
Next door, according to an IDF commander who fought there, stood a Hamas training compound and a kindergarten. Inside the kindergarten, troops found weapons and photographs of small children in Hamas uniforms. A tunnel shaft had been dug into the kindergarten’s yard. When Israeli forces moved in, two Hamas gunmen emerged from that shaft and hit them with an RPG. Five soldiers were wounded.
This was the same war in which Israel stood accused, in newsrooms, at the United Nations, and in The Hague, of starving Gaza by design. In that compound, the food had arrived. Hamas used it for cover.
The scene comes from NAZA: The Real Story, the reply to NAZA, the Guardian-produced documentary by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor that took the Special Jury Prize at Venice. Three Israelis made the counter-film in under two weeks with their own money: Lt.-Col. (res.) Roi Danino, attorney and reservist Ariel Averbuch, and director Hagay Gutman.
A film made that fast has rough edges. But it puts IDF soldiers and officers who fought in Gaza on camera, and it backs their accounts with footage of Hamas weapons and military infrastructure in hospitals, mosques, and schools.
I wrote here last month about how NAZA recast Israel’s lawful collateral damage calculations as something nefarious. This piece concerns the half of the story it ignores. The Guardian’s documentary asks how Israel decided whether to strike. It never asks who decided where the target would be.
The war against Hamas
The answer is on the map, where the terrorist leaders who launched these wars of choice were finally found.
On September 27, 2024, Israeli jets killed Hassan Nasrallah in Hezbollah’s headquarters, a bunker beneath apartment towers in Beirut’s Dahiyeh suburb. He chose that spot knowing what the footage of any strike on him would look like.
On May 13, 2025, an Israeli strike killed Mohammed Sinwar, Hamas’s military chief in Gaza, along with its Rafah Brigade commander, Muhammad Shabana. Troops later found the compound directly beneath the emergency room of the EU-funded European Hospital in Khan Yunis. Hamas built its command center under that ER.
Mohammed Sinwar was no bystander to his brother’s war. He helped plan the 2006 abduction of Gilad Schalit, part of the template for October 7. He was central to building the Rafah tunnel network, where Hamas hid fighters, weapons, and hostages under a city that sheltered more than a million displaced Gazans.
He spent his last months underground, under a hospital, betting Israel would not find him or strike the building above him. Israel found him and aimed at the bunker, not the wards. Gaza’s Health Ministry still reported 28 dead. It did not say who built the bunker or how many of the dead were Hamas operatives, and it never mentioned Sinwar or Shabana. Its tolls don’t distinguish its fighters from civilians.
Sinwar’s brother Yahya, the architect of the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led invasion and massacres, died on October 16, 2024, in Rafah’s Tel al-Sultan neighborhood, inside a family home whose owner had evacuated months earlier.
Nearby, seven weeks before, Hamas executed Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Carmel Gat, Eden Yerushalmi, Ori Danino, Alex Lobanov, and Almog Sarusi in a tunnel whose shaft opened inside a child’s bedroom in another family’s home, its walls painted with Snow White and Mickey Mouse.
An apartment block, a hospital, a family’s home. Each was chosen in advance by men who understood that their neighbors’ bodies were their best armor.
Hamas imprisoned its hostages with the same logic. Noa Argamani, Almog Meir Jan, Andrey Kozlov, and Shlomi Ziv were rescued in June 2024 from family apartments in Nuseirat in central Gaza. Noa Marciano, 19, was murdered by a Hamas-affiliated doctor inside Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
Sharon Aloni Cunio said she and her three-year-old twins, Emma and Yuli, were held in a Khan Yunis hospital. The bodies of Shani Louk, Amit Buskila, Itzhak Gelerenter, and Ron Benjamin were recovered from a tunnel reached through a shaft inside a house in Jabalia. Emily Damari said after her release that Hamas held her in UNRWA facilities.
Criticism of 'NAZA'
The Guardian asks viewers to trust 24 interviewees whose names and faces they never see. Everything above rests on names, dates, and addresses any reporter can check. The record of where Hamas put its leaders and captives requires no trust at all.
NAZA treats every civilian death, and even every calculation meant to avoid one, as an entry in the ledger against Israel. It never opens Hamas’s books. Who dug the shaft in the kindergarten yard? While others pushed the starvation libel, who stacked UN bags of rice into a wall? The film never asks, and a documentary that will not ask obvious questions has stopped documenting.
International law requires asking these questions. Hamas chose this war on October 7, then built its strategy around erasing the line the law of war exists to draw. That law requires fighters to distinguish themselves from civilians and treats feigning civilian status as perfidy.
Hamas fighters stored their uniforms after October 7 and fought in civilian clothes, a choice no military makes for comfort.
The law forbids using civilians to shield military targets. Hamas put shafts in kindergarten yards, weapons in schools, anti-tank missiles under a children’s rug, and a command center beneath an emergency room. Under the Fourth Geneva Convention, a hospital used for acts harmful to the other side loses its protection.
International law bars armed groups from using anyone under 18 in hostilities and makes using children under 15 a war crime. NAZA: The Real Story shows children carrying weapons to Hamas fighters in broad daylight.
The same law obliges Israel to verify its targets, estimate the civilian toll before every strike, and call off any attack whose expected harm would be excessive relative to the military gain. NAZA presents Israel’s legal compliance as confession. And the law holds the side that hides behind civilians responsible for what follows. Collateral damage requires collateral, and Hamas put it there by design.
Hamas built its war so that every Israeli strike would leave civilian bodies, and every casualty would become an indictment of Israel. But that strategy works only with media accomplices. Abraham, Szor, and the Guardian did that job, and Venice gave them a prize for it.
Micha Danzig is a contributing opinion writer for The Jerusalem Post and other Jewish publications, as well as an attorney, former IDF soldier, and former New York Police Department officer.

UK lawmakers say letters from Palantir were intended to intimidate critics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:26 UTC
23:06:26 KST

Aysu Bicer
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
British lawmakers who criticized US tech firm Palantir in parliament have received letters from company executives, which they described as attempts to intimidate critics, Novara Media reported Thursday.
Former Labour Party leader Jeremy Corbyn and Labour and Cooperative Party MP Rachael Maskell received letters from Palantir’s UK CEO Louis Mosley on June 3, detailing their parliamentary remarks about the company and offering meetings.
“I am in no doubt as to why Palantir is writing these letters to MPs to intimidate its critics into silence,” Corbyn told Novara Media, adding that the tactics would not deter him from opposing involvement in public services by the company, which faces controversy over both its co-founder’s views and its work for Israel.
Maskell, who represents York Central, said the correspondence would not change her approach toward the firm, which holds contracts with Britain’s National Health Service (NHS), the Defense Ministry, and police forces.
“Clearly there is a reason as to why Palantir has paid close attention to the scrutiny that MPs have brought to this company,” she said.
Independent MP Shockat Adam also received an email from Palantir’s UK public affairs lead following critical social media posts about the company’s involvement in the NHS and its now-ended contract with the Leicestershire Police.
Adam called on Palantir executives Peter Thiel, Alex Karp, and Louis Mosley to explain their roles before Parliament, saying the public has a right to know how the company’s software was used across public services and the armed forces.
A Palantir spokesperson said the letters aimed to correct inaccurate claims about the company, adding that it would continue responding if politicians repeated what it described as falsehoods.
Labour MP Clive Lewis separately criticized a letter from Palantir’s UK senior vice president, former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, warning that the company was monitoring his activities related to Palantir.
US-based Palantir has long been controversial in many countries, partly because co-founder Peter Thiel, a supporter of the Trump administration, has repeatedly voiced skepticism about traditional democratic systems.
The company has also faced criticism from rights groups over reports that it provided AI-enabled systems, including targeting and data-analysis support as well as critical data infrastructure, to the Israeli military for operations in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran.
Recently, the company and London Mayor Sadiq Khan’s office have withdrawn allegations against each other in a legal dispute over a £50 million ($65 million) police technology contract, heading off a High Court trial scheduled for January.
Palantir sued the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC) in June after Khan intervened to block a proposed two-year contract for the Metropolitan Police to use artificial intelligence to process intelligence in criminal investigations.
Khan’s intervention followed concerns about the company’s work with the Israeli military and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The mayor previously said Londoners wanted public money to go to companies that “share the values of our city.”
The agreement comes one month after former Labour Party deputy leader Tom Watson was hired as a full-time lobbyist by Palantir. The company had raised concerns that excluding it from public contracts over objections to its leadership’s values could undermine its ability to operate in the UK.

Due to traffic congestion on the Southern Bridge in Kyiv, additional Kyiv City Express services will run — the schedule has been released
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrzaliznytsia has scheduled additional Kyiv City Express services via the Northern and Darnytskyi bridges. Intervals between services from the right bank\r\nwill be reduced to 15 minutes.
Due to traffic complications on the capital’s Southern Bridge, additional Kyiv City Express services have been scheduled, UNN reports, citing Ukrzaliznytsia.
Details
According to Ukrzaliznytsia, the additional trains will run along the semicircular route Kyiv-Demiyivskyi - Vydubychi - Berezniaky - Darnytsia - Rusanivka - Livoberezhna - Mykilska Slobidka - Voskresenka - Raiduzhnyi - Pochaina and back. Thus, Kyiv residents will have additional connections via both bridges – the Darnytskyi and the Northern.
The first additional service from Pochaina (transfer from the Blue metro line) toward Troieshchyna will depart at 16:56, while the service from Vydubychi (transfer from the Green metro line) toward Berezniaky will depart at 18:02.
Thus, starting at 16:40, intervals between services from the right bank to the left bank will be as short as 15 minutes.

Germany Arrests Ukrainian Suspected of Spying for Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:06:00 UTC
23:06:00 KST

Germany has arrested a Ukrainian man suspected of spying for Russia on military supplies and planning.
The man, identified as Vadym Y., was arrested in the German state of Brandenburg after starting to work with Russian intelligence via a middleman in July 2025, according to DW on Thursday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Russian independent outlet Astra claims the man is 53.
The man allegedly gathered intelligence on “the production of armored vehicles, ammunition, and explosives, as well as information on personnel and military facilities at locations intended to secure NATO’s eastern flank,” according to the German Federal Prosecutor’s Office.
The suspect reportedly gathered intelligence via open-source channels and solicited help from “individuals from the European arms industry.”
“Some of the information was publicly available; for other information, the accused specifically recruited individuals from the European arms industry,” the office’s press release says.
The court is set to decide on the man’s pre-trial detention on Friday, it adds.
“Significant” espionage threat level
Berlin raised the sabotage level from Russia against its military to “significant” for the first time on Thursday.
The classification, reportedly triggered by a crashed drone carrying high explosives near the Wunstorf air base in mid-September, is the second-highest level on the internal threat scale of the German military.
Russia’s New Filin Missile Uses US, Chinese Electronics
In September, Berlin said Russia was responsible for the attempted drone attack at the Leipzig airport in August.
An explosives-laden drone was also discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used for military supplies at the airport in eastern Germany, a key hub for NATO and Kyiv.
In September, Berlin said it has uncovered 165 suspected sabotage cases and 747 suspicious drone incidents nationwide during the first eight months of the year. In April, German authorities also arrested a Ukrainian and a Latvian national on suspicion of preparing sabotage activities.
European agencies have attributed the cases to heightened Russian sabotage attempts to disrupt Europe’s support for Ukraine.
Berlin also approved plans to close the Russian House, a prominent state-run cultural institution in Berlin, amid concerns that Moscow could use the facility to cover intelligence operations, though the closure would not occur until July 2027, when the contract expires.

Documents
Details
If consultation is to be undertaken on an amendment to the regulations or the implementation of new regulation, the MAA will issue an NPA. The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback. Feedback is important to further develop the IA.
Comments or enquiries on any NPA are to be sent to DSA-MAA-MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk by the date stated in the NPA. Please use the NPA Response Form template provided below to return your consolidated comments.
After the comments closure date, the NPA will be removed from the website.
NPA comment response sheets contain the collated MAA responses to individual NPA publications.
In the final preparation for publication similar Regulated Community comments have been consolidated into one response.
Some of the MAA responses to the Regulated Community comments may have been superseded by further internal review prior to the official publication of the new issue.

The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback; feedback is important to further develop the IA.

Tom Cruise to receive 2027 American Film Institute Life Achievement Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:04:01 UTC
23:04:01 KST

Halis Sunnetci
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Hollywood star Tom Cruise will receive the 52nd American Film Institute (AFI) Life Achievement Award, the organization's highest honor for a career in cinema, AFI announced Wednesday.
The 64-year-old actor and producer will be honored at a gala ceremony at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles on April 24, 2027.
"Tom Cruise is a global icon," said Kathleen Kennedy, chair of the AFI Board of Trustees.
"As an actor and producer, he brings an extraordinary commitment to everything he does. What I especially admire is his deep belief in movies and their ability to bring people together," she added.
Cruise, whose career spans more than four decades, has starred in major Hollywood productions including, Top Gun, Mission: Impossible, Jerry Maguire, Rain Man and A Few Good Men.
His films have grossed nearly $13 billion worldwide, according to AFI, with Top Gun: Maverick remaining his highest-grossing release.
He has received four Academy Award nominations, including three for acting and one for producing Top Gun: Maverick, which was nominated for Best Picture.
Cruise also received an honorary Oscar at the Academy's Governors Awards in 2025.
The honor comes weeks after the release of Cruise's latest film, Digger, directed by two-time Oscar-winning filmmaker Alejandro G. Inarritu. The Warner Bros. satire has struggled at the box office, grossing approximately $42 million worldwide despite a reported production budget exceeding $160 million.
Established in 1973, the AFI Life Achievement Award recognizes individuals whose careers have made significant contributions to cinema.
Previous recipients include Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, Nicole Kidman and Eddie Murphy, who received the honor in 2026.

Ukraine receives 252 bodies in swap with Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:03:33 UTC
23:03:33 KST

Ukraine has received the bodies of 252 people in an exchange of war dead with Russia.
Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War announced the repatriation on Thursday, while Russian lawmaker Shamsail Saraliev told the RBC news outlet that Moscow received 25 bodies in return.
The exchange of prisoners and war dead remains one of the few areas of cooperation between the two sides.
"As a result of repatriation measures, the bodies of 252 deceased have been returned to Ukraine," the Ukrainian headquarters said, adding that police and other officials would carry out identification procedures.
Police and other officials would "carry out all the necessary procedures to identify the repatriated deceased", it said.
It thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for help facilitating the exchange, posting pictures on social media of several large white trailer trucks parked back to back, as workers in white, hooded jumpsuits emblazoned with the ICRC logo stood nearby.
The I Want to Live foundation, which is affiliated with Ukraine's Intelligence Directorate and involved in managing Russia's prisoners of war, meanwhile said "the remains of Russian servicemen were repatriated".
Among them was the body of a Sri Lankan citizen, the organisation said, adding that he was sent to Russia since he was considered under international law as a combatant in the Russian army.
The exchanges of remains between the two sides take place regularly.
Earlier this month, Ukraine's military intelligence chief Kyrylo Budanov estimated that more than 26,000 bodies and human remains had been repatriated to Ukraine through exchange operations.
Most of them are still awaiting identification.
According to official announcements from both sides, Ukraine has received the remains of 5,300 people since the start of the year, while Russia has received fewer than 300.
The war, Europe's deadliest conflict since World War II, has claimed tens of thousands of lives since Russia launched its military offensive in February 2022.

Czech president: Europe must close “gap” and play more active role in Ukraine peace talks

Czech president: Europe must close “gap” and play more active role in Ukraine peace talks
Czech President Petr Pavel made this statement during a panel discussion at the Berlin Global Dialogue conference in Berlin on Thursday, according to a Ukrinform correspondent.
“I personally believe that our American allies do not necessarily represent European interests in the best way. That is precisely why I am firmly convinced that Europe must become more actively involved in the negotiations, have a clear vision of what the outcome should be and what the limits of the negotiations are, and propose alternatives that will make it possible to conduct the negotiations,” Pavel said.
According to him, Europe needs to develop a common position on ending the war and the future security architecture in order to become a full-fledged participant in the diplomatic process.
“Currently, these are merely negotiations between three parties—the United States, Russia, and Ukraine—in which Europe is not represented. I consider this a gap,” the Czech president noted.
At the same time, he acknowledged that European countries still lack a sufficiently coordinated vision for the continent’s future security architecture: “We do not have a single, clear European position. We have certain positions within the EU, but the EU does not represent all of Europe.”
In his view, without a strong, unified position, neither Russia nor the United States will regard European countries as full-fledged partners in negotiations.
At the same time, the Czech president emphasized that diplomatic contacts with Moscow are necessary, but they must be based on specific conditions and results. He also pointed out that Moscow is currently not showing any willingness to pursue a genuine peaceful settlement.
“They have not yet expressed any willingness to engage in peace talks, with one exception—Ukraine’s surrender and President Zelensky’s resignation. This is impossible for Ukraine. It is impossible for us on principle,” Pavel noted.
He also suggested considering future negotiations not only in the context of ending the war in Ukraine but also within the broader postwar architecture of European security.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 20 in Oslo, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky held talks with U.S. Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff, with the participation of Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gar Støre. European representatives also joined the preparatory consultations.
The parties discussed issues related to territory, security guarantees, and Ukraine’s postwar reconstruction. The following day, Witkoff traveled to Russia to continue diplomatic contacts.
On October 21, a meeting took place at the Konstantinovsky Palace in St. Petersburg between U.S. Presidential Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian dictator Vladimir Putin.
After the meeting, Witkoff stated that discussions on ending the Russian-Ukrainian war would continue in the format of trilateral talks at the technical level.

A communications edge helped Ukraine win Operation Vivaldi. US throttling of Starlink is now wearing it down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:01:49 UTC
23:01:49 KST

- Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi may have begun as early as March
- The counteroffensive seemingly inflicted more damage on a pair of Russian field armies than previously thought
- But the gains could be fleeting if a new speed cap on Ukraine's military Starlink terminals stays in place
The Ukrainian 3rd Army Corps' Operation Vivaldi—its secretive counteroffensive east of Sloviansk in northern Donetsk Oblast—started earlier than first reported, and by the time it ended on 14 October it had cost the Russians more than 8,000 troops, by the 3rd Army Corps' count.
It was a major Ukrainian victory in one of the most important sectors of Russia's 56-month wider war on Ukraine. But it could prove to be a temporary win, one the Russians may be able to partially reverse, if the administration of US President Donald Trump continues to throttle Starshield, the military version of Starlink that Ukraine's drones and commanders rely on.
The Ukrainians' former command and control advantage, largely attributable to once-reliable Starlink and Starshield access, was pivotal as Operation Vivaldi played out in the Donbas region in stages starting in March. That advantage shrank practically overnight on 14 October, when a new speed cap began cutting off Ukraine's Starshield terminals whenever they moved faster than about 160 km/h (100 mph).
The 3rd Army Corps attacked east of Sloviansk and north of Lyman as early as March, analyst and mapper Clément Molin concluded after scrutinizing official videos and interviews the Ukrainian defense ministry recently released. "The operation began much earlier than initially thought," Molin wrote.
The timing was probably no accident.
In early February, SpaceX, working from a Ukrainian defense ministry whitelist, switched off the thousands of stolen and smuggled Starlink terminals the Russians had been using.
That had the effect of grounding many Russian drones and blinding many Russian commanders. Taking advantage of the Russians' confusion, Ukrainian troops attacked in several key sectors: in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk Oblasts in the southeast, and east of Sloviansk in northern Donetsk.
The Donetsk attack expanded into a full-blown counteroffensive under conditions of strict secrecy as the 3rd Army Corps probed for weaknesses along the flanks of the Russian 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies, then overextended along the axis between the Zherebets River in the east and the outskirts of the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban conglomeration in the west.
The Russians had been threatening to lay siege to Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, the last two big free cities in Donetsk Oblast, from two directions: the north and the south. Operation Vivaldi eliminated the northern threat—and at great cost to the Russian 20th and 25th CAAs.
Drones lead
Aerial drones and unmanned ground vehicles led the attack, taking the Russians by surprise. "For an offensive operation, the Ukrainians sustained relatively few casualties compared to previous engagements," Molin explained. "Conversely, the defending Russian forces suffered significantly higher losses, largely due to the rapid encirclement of at least three regiments, not all of which managed to escape the area."
It's unclear how many casualties the Russians suffered, but they might number in the thousands. The 20th and 25th CAAs were particularly fragile because the 3rd Army Corps and supporting drone units had been bombarding their supply line with so-called "middle strike" drones.
Trending Now
But many middle strike drones rely on civilian-style Starlink satellite terminals or the more rugged, better-performing Starshield. Now that the 3rd Army Corps has wrecked Russia's 144th Motor Rifle Division, which the Institute for the Study of War assessed on 20 October has effectively ceased to exist as an organized fighting force, and pushed the Russian survivors back to the far bank of the Zherebets River, the Ukrainians are probably "consolidating their gains and adopting a defensive posture," according to Molin.
But that defensive posture, protecting Sloviansk from a northern attack, depends on reliable communications and responsive drones. On 14 October, a new speed cap hit Ukraine's Starshield terminals, cutting the link on any drone flying faster than about 160 km/h. Who ordered it is disputed. Sources told Reuters the order came from inside the White House, and that Pentagon leaders were told the service needed to be slowed.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk himself ordered the slowdown, and that he and Trump discussed it soon after it became public. While Trump has denied ordering the speed limit, it's worth noting that the American president has become more overtly friendly toward Russia as his Republican Party looks likely to lose control of the US Congress in the November mid-term elections.
The speed limit renders many of the faster middle-strike drones unflyable. As a result, "Ukrainian drone strikes have diminished significantly following yesterday's crippling of Ukraine's Starlink/Starshield connections, Russian sources report," the military history account ChrisO_wiki wrote on X on 15 October, the day after the speed limit took Ukrainian operators by surprise.
Russia is back at Dobropillia a year after it failed there. Now it’s the southern jaw of a pincer on Donbas’s last big free cities
A reduction in middle strikes on Russian supply lines could help Russian field armies recover from recent setbacks, including their retreat back across the Zherebets River. And if the communications confusion resulting from the partial loss of Starlink/Starshield connectivity persists, it could give the Russians the same kind of opportunity the Ukrainians had back in the spring.
An opportunity to go back on the attack—and an Azov communications engineer warned Euromaidan Press in February that the shoe might be on the other foot.
That's the worst-case scenario for the Ukrainians now that Operation Vivaldi has ended. The best case is that they get full Starlink and Starshield access back—or find command and control alternatives—and duplicate, in other sectors, the same success they enjoyed in northern Donetsk.
"Now that the northern flank of Donbas is secured, at least for some time, the focus will concentrate on the southern flank," Molin predicted.
Starlink crackdown cripples Russians—but American engineer warns Ukraine is just as vulnerable

- Russia is losing the Black Sea grain war it started. Its answer is to sink civilian ships off Romania and Bulgaria
- Russia is back at Dobropillia a year after it failed there. Now it’s the southern jaw of a pincer on Donbas’s last big free cities

The US Is Losing to China in the Battle of Global Influence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:01:00 UTC
23:01:00 KST

Global influence is frequently a topic for conference panels, talk show pundits, and earnest think tank recommendations, but this nebulous measure of soft power has real-world impact for national security, economic strength and political power.
Today, this battle is unfolding rapidly, region by region, country by country, through security and commercial partnerships, emerging regional groupings, newly established diplomatic outposts, and academic partnerships.
As conflicts erupt and new trade and political alignments emerge, it’s clear: China is building a dense network of relationships across all pillars of influence while the United States continues to weaken the institutions it traditionally used to compete. The United States should do more than watch China’s intensive investment in building global influence – in diplomacy, in academic and cultural exchanges, in economic partnerships, and in national security pacts.
Influence is hard to gauge – and even harder to count on. Even the closest of diplomatic partners have sovereign interests and political differences. Historical relationships, either through war-hardened alliances or postcolonial reckonings, can shape perception and sway alignment. However, China’s transactional approach inherently reflects its genuine disregard for human rights, democratic aspirations, and welfare of citizens in other countries. This is China’s weak point, which the United States can leverage to regain lost ground.
Diplomacy: You Must Show up
The work of diplomacy is accomplished behind the scenes, by building connections, negotiating agreements, and advocating for businesses. The work of a diplomat is to know the government officials and trade contacts before you make an ask. This allows diplomats to build the trust required to get to agreement before a crisis happens or an ask is made.
China is succeeding at one of the first rules of diplomacy: showing up.
The Lowry Institute’s Global Diplomacy Index paints a clear picture. China has 274 diplomatic posts globally, compared with the United States’ 271. The strategic advantage is even clearer in Africa – where China has 60 to the United States’ 56 – and in East Asia, where China has 44 to the United States’ 27. While the numerical difference is small, the trend is concerning.
Beijing leverages its growing diplomatic presence as a strategic asset, populating its embassies with commercial, educational, and political professionals. It is gradually making inroads even with the United States’ longtime partners. Just this month, China’s President Xi Jinping traveled to Egypt, where Beijing and Cairo signed an array of agreements, from linking Egypt’s national development plan to China’s Belt and Road Initiative to a pledge to increase trade and investments in their own currencies, moving away from the U.S. dollar.
For the United States, the trend is going the other way, and that’s worrying. Despite a slate of recent nominations, 93 out of 196 ambassadorial slots remain vacant, according to the tracker maintained by the American Foreign Service Association. And while in many cases there are able professional diplomats serving as chargés d’affaires in these roles, a confirmed ambassador signals seriousness to host governments.
The State Department has also taken steps to close a number of smaller consulates and shrink operations at other embassies. While there is absolutely a strong case for prioritizing engagement, streamlining operations, and improving efficiencies, the narrative that the United States is retreating from the world continues to spread.
Academic opportunities and cultural exchanges are important forms of diplomacy and a path to increasing the United States’ global influence. Engaging with the next generations of global talent is a critical investment or opportunity, and China understands this.
At the 2024 Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC), Xi announced 60,000 government scholarships for African students. In addition to opportunities for students, FOCAC commitments will see some 20,000 African regional and city leaders receiving training in China every year, along with African journalists sent to China.
These programs are far from boondoggles: They enmesh these emerging officials, journalists, and business leaders into Chinese institutions and professional networks. And despite warnings from the United States, China has now established over 500 Confucius Institutes around the world. These institutes are purported to facilitate Chinese education and people-to-people exchanges, but effectively serve as propaganda arms of the Chinese government.
The United States has extraordinary assets of its own, including an open and free democracy, the best universities in the world, and an innovation economy. Traditionally, U.S. government-supported exchange programs showcase all three.
From the International Visitor Leadership Program (IVLP), which identifies rising stars in business, government, security, and media and brings them to the United States to showcase America’s story to world-class State Department programs, including the Fulbright, Gilman, Boren, and Critical Language Scholarships, these programs engage professionals at key junctures in their professional careers.
A scholarship or an exchange isn’t simply tuition assistance. These academic and cultural programs create alumni who may become government and business leaders in their countries. According to the State Department’s own accounting, over 500 IVLP alumni alone have become heads of state or government since the program’s founding in 1940. Another 12 have won Nobel Prizes, and thousands more have served as elected officials, government ministers, and community and business leaders.
The United States can benefit from having these leaders as counterparts; they leave these programs with firsthand knowledge and appreciation of America’s economic strength, tech savvy, entrepreneurship, pluralism, and values.
These programs continue, albeit after some stutters in funding in 2025. Yet there are deep proposed reductions in the 2027 fiscal year’s budget. And there is a long-term cost to making such programs unpredictable. China is rapidly expanding its networks, while the United States is offering uncertainty into its own powerful equivalents.
Economic Strength: Building Partnerships, Not Transactions
This isn’t a new trend. Pundits have warned for more than two decades that Beijing is approaching traditional U.S. partners with something tangible to offer.
Through its Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), as well as smaller bilateral and regional deals, China has smartly offered financing backed by its government for desperately needed infrastructure projects linked to access to African and Western Hemisphere markets.
At the most recent FOCAC summit in 2024, Xi announced approximately $51 billion in financial support to Africa over a three-year period. At the 2025 China-Community of Latin American and Caribbean States (CELAC) Forum, Xi pledged a credit line of more than $9 billion for Latin America, as well as additional bilateral infrastructure investment. According to China’s own accounting in its 2025 BRI Investment Report, agreements that are part of BRI reached over $213 billion in 2025, up 75 percent from the previous year, with about 150 countries participating.
The United States can compete. The Lobito Corridor, which links Zambia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Angola, provides U.S. support for a critical rail and infrastructure network spanning mineral production to port facilities. Through a $533 million loan from the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), the United States both invested in these countries’ economic development and leveraged this financing with an eye to long-term regional security through employment, investment, and regional integration.
However, while the United States has (and uses) smart tools like the DFC and Millenium Challenge Corporation, it has stopped some other initiatives. Driven by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), the 2025 reprioritization of foreign assistance sidelined early-stage economic development efforts, such as programs for emerging entrepreneurs, small business, and agriculture – including dedicated programs to encourage women in these fields. These and other opportunities were once administered through the now-shuttered USAID and State Department programs. The 2025 foreign assistance restructuring halted these incubator projects worldwide, ending a values-based and long-term approach to economic growth.
While reform of U.S. assistance was absolutely necessary, the geopolitical cost is clear. When the United States – with its commitment to human rights, democracy, rule of law, and anti-corruption measures – withdraws from a relationship, it is often China that surges to occupy the space.
Today, faced with the immediate challenge of global leadership in artificial intelligence (AI), the United States must be more than the leader in a technology footrace with China. The U.S. global role and responsibilities will require sustained investment in innovation, talent, infrastructure and trusted partnerships so the United States can continue in setting global standards that shape how AI is developed, governed and deployed. The United States can build on its standards of openness and accountability while ensuring that these emerging technologies reflect both U.S. interests and U.S. values.
Reclaiming the High Ground
China is intensifying its investment in its initiatives, building a worldwide network of infrastructure, finance, commercial, and political relationships. The United States absolutely has best-in-class competitive alternatives, but Washington must invest in and deepen those ties.
Many countries, especially across the Global South, see benefits to relationships with both China and the United States, but U.S. strength has traditionally meant that it is the first choice for security relationships, cultural and educational exchanges, and business partnerships. China’s approach has significant and public weaknesses, including debt controversies, debates over its political influence, and allegations of exploitation and human rights abuses in partner countries.
But Washington has its own work to do to right the soft power ship. The United States possesses enormous advantages in its world-class academic institutions, technology, alliances, and the sheer love of ordinary U.S. culture. We must remember, though: the United States didn’t become a superpower by looking backward.
The United States must maintain its influence – and its values of freedom, opportunity, accountability, and compassion – by continuing to show up.

Danish retail chains have their stores ransacked amid ongoing riots in France

14:00:45 UTC
23:00:45 KST

Several Danish retail chains, including Pandora, Normal and Flying Tiger, have reported damage to their stores as protests over living costs and school conditions escalate into riots across France.
The companies confirmed the incidents to Danish business newspaper Børsen, with Normal reporting damage to 11 stores in Paris, Marseille and Toulouse.
Normal CEO Jakob Frølich Maarbjerg said the affected stores had suffered damage to their facades.
“We closed all stores before the unrest broke out, but there are still French employees who have experienced the situation up close, and we are taking good care of them,” he said.
Jewelry retailer Pandora reported damage to three stores in Paris and Lyon, while Flying Tiger confirmed that one of its stores in Lille was affected.
Fashion group Bestseller, which owns brands including Jack & Jones, Selected and Vero Moda, also reported material damage to two stores.
The company told Ritzau that it had activated emergency procedures and was monitoring developments in cooperation with its local operations.
Meanwhile, Danish furniture retailer Jysk said its stores had escaped damage, partly because most are located in smaller French towns.
Hundreds of thousands of people participated in demonstrations across France over the weekend.
The protests began peacefully but later turned violent, with widespread looting and vandalism.
According to the Paris Chamber of Commerce, approximately 2,000 shops were ransacked nationwide, including 300 to 400 businesses in the capital.
France’s Interior Ministry reported nearly 2,400 arrests and injuries to almost 1,000 police officers and gendarmes.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez acknowledged that police had lost control in several cities during the unrest.
Following the riots, second-hand marketplace Vinted removed numerous listings suspected of containing stolen goods, CNN reported Tuesday.

Lyon bans demonstrations after riots and widespread vandalism

Unknown Publisher

23:00:40 KST

Authorities in Lyon, France’s third-largest city, have banned all demonstrations scheduled for Saturday following riots and widespread vandalism during protests last weekend.
The French news agency AFP reported the decision.
In a statement, the prefecture of the Rhône region, where Lyon is located, said: “As a result of the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to ban all demonstrations in the city of Lyon this Saturday”.
A prefect is a senior government official responsible for administering a region or department in France.
Demonstrations have also been announced elsewhere in France for the coming Saturday. Last weekend, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets across the country. Protests that began peacefully over issues including the cost of living and conditions in schools escalated into riots, clashes with police and widespread vandalism.
In Lyon, Mayor Gregory Doucet said chaos had reigned for several hours during the protests. Between 150 and 200 shops were looted, and a tourist office was set on fire.
Nationwide, around 2,000 businesses were damaged. In Paris alone, between 300 and 400 businesses were vandalized, according to the French capital’s chamber of commerce.
France’s Ministry of the Interior said nearly 2,400 people were arrested during the demonstrations, while just under 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez subsequently acknowledged that police had lost control in several French cities during the unrest.
The demonstrations prompted Nunez to offer his resignation to President Emmanuel Macron. Macron refused to accept it, citing the need for “continued leadership of the police effort”.

International Criminal Court wins EU human rights prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:00:35 UTC
23:00:35 KST

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has been awarded the Sakharov Prize, the European Parliament’s annual award recognizing individuals and organizations that defend human rights and freedom of thought.
The European Parliament announced the award in a statement.
The ICC is an independent international court based in The Hague, the Netherlands. It investigates and prosecutes individuals accused of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes.
“With the awarding of the Sakharov Prize to the International Criminal Court and its representatives, the European Parliament recognizes the court’s important work to uphold international law and order,” European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said in the statement.
The court is also known as the war crimes court. The award comes shortly after former ICC judge Navi Pillay received the Nobel Peace Prize earlier in October.
“The court plays a crucial role in the global fight to end impunity. Through international criminal law, it seeks to hold those responsible accountable for their crimes and help prevent the crimes from happening again,” the European Parliament said.
The ICC has 125 member states that have signed the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the court. It can issue arrest warrants, and member states are generally required to arrest and surrender wanted individuals who enter their jurisdiction.
Among those sought for prosecution by the court is Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity in connection with the war in Gaza. Israel is not a member of the ICC, and neither is the United States.
The ICC’s actions have contributed to tensions with the US government under President Donald Trump, which has long opposed the court’s authority over nationals of countries that have not joined it.
The United States has imposed sanctions on ICC officials, including judges and prosecutors. It most recently imposed sanctions against the court after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to a former ICC judge earlier in October, according to the source.
Washington’s opposition is linked in part to the ICC’s arrest warrant for Netanyahu. The court has also previously investigated alleged crimes by US soldiers in Afghanistan.
Trump imposed sanctions on ICC officials during his first term in office. Those sanctions were lifted under President Joe Biden.
The Sakharov Prize is awarded annually by the European Parliament and is named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov.

“This means that we continuously simplify the organization, invest in new competencies, and move resources to the areas where we create the greatest value for our customers.
“It is a natural part of running and developing a large company.”
The latest cuts follow two previous rounds of job reductions in 2026.
In February, Danske Bank announced that it would cut 420 positions across the organization. At the time, the bank said it wanted to adapt to customer needs, invest in technology and advisory services, and become more digital.
Three months later, a further 262 positions were affected. The bank gave broadly similar reasons for those cuts.
Both earlier rounds primarily affected employees in Denmark.
Breum acknowledged the impact of the latest decision on employees.
“Decisions like these affect people,” he said in Thursday’s press release.
“For the colleagues who are affected, it is a difficult situation. Therefore, it is important that we implement the changes responsibly and give our affected colleagues the support and respect they deserve throughout the entire process.”
All employees affected by the latest cuts have been notified.
Danske Bank says on its website that it has more than 20,000 employees across its international operations.
