Denmark to get 51 emergency supermarkets stocked for major crises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:00:17 UTC
23:00:17 KST

Shoppers across Denmark will be able to buy essential groceries and household supplies during power outages, cyberattacks and other emergencies under a new initiative by Salling Group.
The Danish retail giant, which operates Bilka, Føtex and Netto, plans to establish 51 emergency-ready supermarkets nationwide by 2027.
The stores will be equipped to operate for at least 48 hours without electricity or external communication systems, ensuring access to basic necessities during major disruptions.
According to Salling Group, the network will include 17 Bilka stores, 32 Føtex stores and two Netto locations.
The stores will be distributed so that up to 80 percent of Denmark’s population lives within 50 kilometers of one.
Each location will maintain emergency stocks of 50 essential products, selected according to Danish authorities’ recommendations for household preparedness.
These include oatmeal, protein bars, canned meatballs in curry, rice cakes, tuna, beans, chickpeas and other foods with long shelf lives.
Nonfood essentials such as batteries, wet wipes and diapers will also be available.
Customers will be able to pay offline using almost all physical payment cards and digital cards stored on smartphones.
Salling Group recently partnered with payment provider Nets to help maintain card transactions during system failures.
CEO Anders Hagh said establishing the emergency stores remains a top priority, with preparations progressing toward the 2027 target.
Meanwhile, competing retailer Coop, which operates Brugsen, SuperBrugsen, 365discount and Kvickly, has not decided whether to establish similar stores.
Coop’s chief risk officer, Ulrik Mester, said the company was discussing crisis preparedness with authorities, including Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed (SAMSIK), Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security.

Danish krone loses value against major currencies in 2026
The Danish krone has lost value in 2026, making Danish goods and services cheaper for customers in several foreign markets while making some holidays abroad more expensive.
The krone’s effective exchange rate, a weighted average of its value against the currencies of Denmark’s most important trading partners, has fallen by 2.7 percent since the start of the year. The figures come from a compilation by Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry.
“The weakening of the krone’s value makes Danish goods and services cheaper for customers abroad, which makes it easier for export companies to secure new orders,” Sørensen said.
“It is in both the US, China, Norway, and Japan where the exchange rate means that they now have to pay less money to buy our products,” he added.
The Norwegian krone has risen 12.9 percent against the Danish krone over the past year, while the Chinese yuan has gained 9.8 percent. The US dollar and Japanese yen have each risen 4.8 percent.
However, not all currencies have strengthened against the Danish krone. The Swedish krona and Indian rupee have lost value, making goods from those countries slightly more expensive for Danish importers.
Exchange rates also affect the cost of holidays abroad. When a foreign currency strengthens against the Danish krone, Danish travellers get less for their money.
“For those who love a trip to the snow, a trip to Norway has become significantly more expensive solely as a result of the strengthening of the Norwegian krone,” Sørensen said.
“The weakening of the Swedish krona and low inflation in Sweden, on the other hand, make a ski vacation much more economically affordable in Sweden compared to Norway,” he added.
The Turkish lira has recorded the largest decline among the currencies in the compilation. It now costs 9.7 percent less to buy Turkish currency than it did at the start of the year.

Fake meat ban email tricks 1,200 Danish regional employees in phishing test
A warning about meat disappearing from workplace canteens prompted 1,200 employees in Denmark’s Capital Region to click a suspicious link in an internal cybersecurity test.
The exercise, reported by TV 2 Kosmopol, was designed to assess how well employees recognize phishing attempts, in which scammers impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into clicking links or sharing information.
Of the 13,000 employees who received the fake email, approximately 9 percent clicked the link.
The message claimed that meatballs and roast beef would be removed from workplace canteens and that some would switch to entirely vegan menus, excluding meat, dairy and eggs.
Employees were invited to click a link to find out how the changes would affect their local canteen.
However, the sender’s email address contained a small but important difference: it ended in “reqionh.dk” rather than the Capital Region’s actual domain, “regionh.dk”.
Anna Aaskilde Laursen, the region’s head of security, explained that the email deliberately targeted something employees cared about.
She told TV 2 Kosmopol that emotionally charged messages can prompt people to react without thinking, making it important to pause before clicking.
Laursen confirmed that the 1,200 employees who clicked the link would face no consequences.
Instead, the region intends to use the results to improve its preparedness for genuine cyberattacks.
Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security warns that phishing emails can be difficult to recognize because criminals often imitate official logos and use convincing language.
The agency recommends checking senders’ email addresses carefully and, when uncertain, contacting the supposed sender by telephone to verify whether a message is genuine.

New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.

The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.
“The development in the labor market matches well with the general economic development. Activity is increasing, and it is therefore not surprising that more people are entering employment,” Sørensen said.
There are multiple reasons for the increase in employed people.
One of the main reasons is foreign labor, according to Jesper Grunnet-Lauridsen. He works as chief analyst at 3F, Fagligt Fælles Forbund, which is the United Federation of Danish Workers and the largest trade union in Denmark.
“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.
Energinet to prioritize addressing public service queries as power grid capacity runs short
Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.
The payment company Nets has lost a court case against Konkurrencerådet, the Danish Competition Council, which serves as the public competition authority in Denmark.
The ruling was delivered Wednesday by Sø- og Handelsretten, the Danish Maritime and Commercial Court.
Nets had asked the court to set aside a decision made by the Competition Council. That decision concluded that Nets abused its dominant position in the market for payment solutions between the years 2012 and 2016.

The legal process has taken several years. Alongside the civil lawsuit, police have also run an investigation into Nets. The criminal case was put on hold to wait for the result of the civil case, and it has not yet gone to trial.

The court noted that the delay is needed because the text of the ruling may contain business secrets that cannot be made public.
Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.

Plans to tighten Denmark’s senior pension rules dropped after political opposition
The government has abandoned proposed changes to Denmark’s senior pension scheme after failing to secure support from parties behind the existing agreement.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen announced the decision Tuesday following a meeting with the parties involved.
The changes were part of the government’s proposed 2027 budget and were expected to save 200 million DKK in 2028, 500 million DKK in 2029 and 800 million DKK in 2030.
Under the proposal, applicants would have needed to prove that their ability to work was limited to 15 hours a week or less across all types of jobs, rather than just their most recent job.
This would have made qualifying for senior pension more difficult. In 2026, a single person receiving senior pension gets 22,053 DKK per month.
The scheme was introduced through a political agreement in 2019. Its signatories include the Danish People’s Party, the Social Democrats, the Socialist People’s Party, the Moderates and the Social Liberal Party.
Changes to the agreement require approval from all participating parties during the parliamentary term.
Several center-right parties opposed the proposal, while the Red-Green Alliance also rejected changes.
“We respect the agreements we have. It has not been my intention to terminate any agreement,” Halsboe-Jørgensen said.
“On the contrary. The fact that I called the colleagues from the other parties together today was precisely an expression of the fact that I actually wanted to discuss it with them, and that I respect that the agreement we have with each other gives all of them a veto right against changes in this area,” she added.
Dropping the proposal leaves a gap in the government’s budget plans.
Halsboe-Jørgensen said spending priorities would need to change but did not specify where the missing funds would come from.

About 14,000 higher education students living with their parents would lose their entire state education grant under the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
Another 8,000 students in the same group would receive lower payments, Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said in a parliamentary response.
Denmark’s state education grant is commonly known as SU.
An estimated 31,800 higher education students living at home received SU in 2025.
The government proposes ending payments for students whose parents have a combined annual income above 710,077 DKK. This corresponds to an average monthly income of 29,583 DKK for each parent in a two-parent household.
Payments would gradually decline for students whose parents earn between 419,589 and 710,077 DKK annually. The lowest monthly grant would be 500 DKK before disappearing entirely above the upper threshold.

Minister calls for talks after report finds major employment losses due to stress
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr will convene labor unions, employer organizations and other groups for talks on preventing work-related stress.
The first roundtable discussion will take place Friday following a new report from the Danish Economic Council’s independent economic advisers.
The report estimates that severe work-related stress reduces Denmark’s labor supply by between 16,000 and 39,000 people.
More than one in 10 people affected by severe stress do not return to employment, while more than one in three disability pension recipients receive the benefit after a stress reaction, according to the report.
“Stress makes us poorer,” Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party said. “This applies both to the individual person who becomes ill with stress and their family, but it also matters for our society.”
Chief Economic Adviser Jakob Roland Munch said severe stress has long-lasting effects on people’s connection to the labor market.
However, the report found no evidence that the number of severe stress cases has increased during the past 15 to 20 years.
Dyhr said Denmark must place greater emphasis on preventing stress instead of responding only after people become ill.
The government’s proposed 2027 budget includes 50 million DKK for a prevention fund intended to help people remain healthy and employed.
Dyhr said the government wants stronger evidence about which preventive measures work before deciding how to prioritize future efforts.
The European Commission has made security the main focus of its new Arctic strategy as Russia and China expand their activity in the region.
The approach marks a significant shift from the European Union’s 2021 strategy, which concentrated primarily on international cooperation, climate and environmental protection.
“As Russia and China increase their presence and ambitions, the Arctic has become a frontline in the global power competition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The Commission fears the Arctic could become a major source of conflict with Russia after the war in Ukraine ends.
The strategy proposes expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity and strengthening protection of northern maritime borders and critical undersea infrastructure.
The EU’s 27 countries collectively have about 10 icebreakers, compared with an estimated 40 operated by Russia.
The Commission also proposes creating a maritime security center to monitor activity in the Arctic.
A separate Arctic cable center would monitor, protect and repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. It could later track ships belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which transports sanctioned oil and gas.
Western intelligence services also suspect that Russia has used shadow fleet vessels in hybrid attacks.
The strategy contains no spending figures and must now be discussed with EU governments.
Kallas said Arctic security was a European concern because Denmark, Sweden and Finland are Arctic countries and more than 500,000 EU citizens live in the region.
Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.

Denmark’s housing market is showing signs of slowing after a strong start to 2026, according to transaction figures from property portal Boligsiden.
A total of 7,709 homes were sold in September, 12 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
Housing transactions during the first nine months of 2026 were three percent below the corresponding period in 2025.
Apartment sales have fallen most sharply. Eight percent fewer apartments have been sold nationwide this year, while Copenhagen has recorded a decline of 23 percent.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said rising mortgage rates could partly explain the slowdown.
Fixed-rate mortgages have recently fluctuated between four and five percent, compared with 3.5 percent at the beginning of the year.
Higher prices for gasoline, natural gas and electricity are also reducing the money households have available, he said.

Sales of houses and terraced homes are also below last year’s level. Holiday home sales, by contrast, have increased by 4.5 percent.
Boligsiden communications director Birgit Daetz said the increase indicates that many households remain financially secure because holiday homes are traditionally purchased during periods of economic strength.
Rising property values and the possibility of rental income may also make such purchases more affordable, she said.

More than half of surveyed Danish teachers feel stressed every week
More than half of teachers in a new union survey said they experience stress daily or weekly, with most attributing it to their working conditions.
The survey by Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, included responses from 1,901 public school teachers and kindergarten class leaders.
Sixteen percent said they felt stressed at work every day, while 36 percent experienced stress weekly and 23 percent monthly.
Nine in 10 of those experiencing stress said workplace conditions were responsible.
“We are facing a working environment problem in the public schools, while at the same time many teachers choose to leave,” union chair Gordon Ørskov Madsen said.
More than one in three respondents said they had taken sick leave from teaching because of stress.
Teachers identified classroom disruption, insufficient preparation time, heavy workloads and difficulty obtaining help for pupils with special needs as major pressures.
Some also reported that parents expected them to resolve conflicts between pupils that occurred outside school.
Nana Vaaben, an associate professor at University College Copenhagen, said teachers can experience moral stress when they know pupils need help but lack the authority to provide it.
Respondents identified fewer teaching hours, more preparation time and better support for pupils with special needs as the measures most likely to reduce stress.
The union plans to raise those proposals in upcoming negotiations with the government and other labor market parties.

Copenhagen begins separate collection of used diapers for recycling
The City of Copenhagen began installing separate waste bins for used diapers in residential courtyards and municipal day-care centers Monday.
Diapers previously had to be placed with residual waste and were incinerated. They will now be processed at Denmark’s first diaper treatment facility.
“There is a major climate benefit in recycling the diapers instead of incinerating them,” Climate, Environment and Technology Mayor Line Barfod of the Red-Green Alliance said.
The city estimates that between 85 and 94 percent of diaper waste, including liquids and feces, can be converted into new materials.
Cellulose and the contents of the diapers will become biofiber used to produce biogas, electricity and district heating.
Plastic components can be recycled into products such as car interiors. Superabsorbent polymers can become binding material for the construction industry.
Collection will expand to municipal nursing homes, senior housing and other city institutions in February 2027.
Residents of detached houses and members of allotment garden associations will also be able to join the program next year. The scheme is expected to be fully implemented in 2029.
The bins will accept diapers for children and adults, incontinence pads, paper-based cloths and wet wipes without plastic or bamboo. Menstrual hygiene products are excluded.
Diaper waste must be placed in an ordinary plastic trash bag sealed with a tight knot.
Study finds misogynistic TikTok content can appear within minutes
Young male TikTok users can encounter misogynistic content within minutes, even when they do not actively search for it, according to a Danish study.
Researchers from the Center for Digital Pedagogy and Analyse & Tal created eight fictional profiles representing men ages 16 to 19 interested in fitness, dating, investing and gaming.
After the profiles interacted with videos about those subjects, researchers allowed them to scroll automatically for one hour.
Content associated with the “manosphere” appeared after an average of three minutes. In one case, it appeared after 21 seconds.
The manosphere refers to online communities and content that degrade women or support restricting their rights and opportunities.
Researchers also examined one year of viewing data provided by 29 men ages 15 to 22. They identified an average of five to six manosphere videos in each participant’s weekly feed.
The researchers said this was a minimum estimate but emphasized that the 29 participants were not representative of all young men.
Employment and Equality Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen of the Social Democrats called for stronger social media regulation and more discussion in schools and homes.
TikTok said it takes the findings seriously.
“We proactively remove 98.1 percent of the videos that violate our rules on hate and hateful behavior,” Nordic communications director Lukasz Lindell said.
TikTok said it was also working to diversify recommendations and interrupt repetitive content patterns.

Electricity’s share of Danish energy use rises to 23.4 percent
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, an increase of 1.5 percentage points from the previous year.
Green Power Denmark, an industry organization representing the Danish energy sector, said the increase was driven mainly by electric vehicles and the district heating sector’s use of electric boilers and heat pumps.
The organization said growing electrification is gradually reducing Denmark’s reliance on oil and natural gas.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is happening in the Middle East and American politics,” Green Power Denmark chief executive Kristian Jensen said.
He said Danish energy prices remain affected by developments abroad because the country still relies on prices set by global markets.
Denmark’s electrification rate rose by only 3.8 percentage points in total from 2016 through 2024, making the 1.5-point increase in 2025 significant.
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of total energy consumption by 2035.
Jensen said achieving that target would require industrial companies to replace natural gas with electricity and heat pumps.
He pointed to iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, as examples of industries already using heat pumps.
Such changes could reduce companies’ carbon dioxide emissions and energy costs while improving their competitiveness, Jensen said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available.

Guldimund and Saveus won P3 Lytterhittet – the listeners’ choice award – for their song “Vil du noget?”.
Zar Paulo received P3 Live, an award recognising an artist who has distinguished themselves on Denmark’s live music scene. The award returned this year after previously being presented in 2001 and 2009.
Danish-Faroese artist Friða Saiya won P3’s Næste, a new award that has replaced P3 Talentet and highlights emerging artists.
Criticism over lack of women
This year’s P3 Guld also faced criticism before the ceremony over the gender balance among its performers.
Twelve men and two women were scheduled to perform during the evening.
Ditte Christiane Jensen, head of editorial at DR Ung, defended the lineup in a written response to Ritzau.
“Talent, creativity and artistic quality are not about gender,” she said.
“This year’s lineup was put together based on the artists and bands that have left a significant mark on the music year and in P3’s universe.”
Source: Ritzau
Trump: Greenland deal biggest real estate deal ever
The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.
US President Donald Trump has described a new defence and security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as potentially “the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made”.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.
“It is probably the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made.”
Trump was campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
His comments come after months of tension over Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has repeatedly said that the United States wants control and ownership of Greenland, arguing that the island is crucial to American national security.
Two new US military bases
The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new security and defence agreement on Greenland at the end of September following lengthy negotiations.
The agreement was signed at the United Nations in New York shortly after Trump addressed the UN General Assembly.
It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
Trump’s comments came as Republicans campaign to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Democrats are currently polling more strongly in the race for the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains more uncertain.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.

The Cornell 7 and the Problem with Writing as Punishment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:00:04 UTC
23:00:04 KST

Justice is elusive, and there are few clearer examples of this than when people who commit acts of sexual violence are given rote tasks as a means of atonement.
Recently, the “Cornell 7” case has inspired new conversations about what accountability and atonement involve. When college administrators investigated a report of sexual violence, some of the alleged perpetrators were reportedly assigned to write “reflection papers,” along with other punishments. The writing assignments drew such ire that Cornell issued a statement stating that "none of the individuals charged were offered the opportunity to write essays as a sole consequence of their involvement."
I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, which started when I was 11 years old. Abuse from my step-father went hand-in-hand with punishment. He knew how much I loved words, reading, and writing, and began to use them to discipline me.
Our household was governed by an elaborate set of rules. We were not allowed to speak during dinner without permission. We were required to stand while playing board games. Our bedrooms were inspected every evening, and our beds had to be made with hospital corners.
Any infraction could result in punishment. One of the preferred methods was to require me to write an essay outlining what I had done wrong and how to correct my misdeeds. If I didn't wash the dishes carefully enough, I would have to write an essay about why I needed to take better care when cleaning up after dinner.
Other times, I was ordered to write the same sentence hundreds of times.
If I complained about dinner, I had to write 100 times, “I will appreciate my mother’s cooking.”
If I made fun of one of my siblings, I had to write 250 times, “I will not make fun of my brother.”
And if I resisted attempts to assault me, the punishment could be a thousand repetitions of “I will listen.”
I was being punished for trying to protect myself from the person who was abusing me. In doing so, I learned that writing the correct words was not the same as believing them. I could produce an essay explaining what I might have done wrong and promise to be better, but it didn’t mean that I believed that I misbehaved. It meant that I understood what was required of me. The punishment was complete when the writing was complete, but whether I had learned anything was beside the point.
More than 50 years later, I find myself wondering what we believe an essay can accomplish when it is assigned in response to allegations of sexual violence. Cornell’s disciplinary proceedings have resulted in different sanctions for different students, including expulsions and suspensions. “Reflection papers” were among the educational requirements imposed on some students.
But what, exactly, can an assigned essay demonstrate?
An essay can be thoughtful and persuasive; it can express regret, recognize harm, and promise change. But how do we know whether the person who wrote it believes any of what is written? What happens when completing an assignment becomes a substitute for demonstrating genuine understanding or changed behavior?
I have spent my adult life writing, teaching, and interviewing people about their lives. I believe in the ability of language to help us understand ourselves and one another, and I know how easily language can be used to conceal the truth.
My abuser understood the power of words, and used them to dictate the terms of my obedience. He controlled what I was allowed to say. He warned me that no one would believe me and threatened violence against those I love if I spoke out. I believed him, and I remained silent and ashamed.
I was required to write about my smallest infractions while being forbidden, through fear, to speak about the most terrible thing happening in my life. And the person who demanded that I explain my wrongdoing was the person committing the most serious wrongdoing of all.
This is why the relationship between language and power matters so much to me. The person with authority often gets to decide what constitutes an acceptable explanation, a credible account, or a sufficient expression of remorse.
Jane Doe, the young woman at the center of the Cornell case, reported the incident to university police in 2024. Since then, the timing and content of her disclosures have become subjects of intense public scrutiny. Public debate has focused in part on differences between her initial statements and her subsequent allegations.
I cannot speak for her, and our experiences are different. But I understand how fear can determine what someone is willing to reveal, even when she desperately needs help.
There is something troubling about how much we expect words to prove in cases of sexual violence. We scrutinize the accounts of those who report abuse, searching for inconsistencies. Now we are asking those found responsible for misconduct to demonstrate understanding through written reflection.
I believe writing can lead to meaningful change. But an essay is evidence that someone has completed an assignment. It cannot establish whether that person understands the harm they have caused or whether their behavior will change.
Why are we putting so much faith in the words people are required to write, while questioning the words that others struggle to say?

Swiss franc is once again becoming a safe-haven currency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:59:25 UTC
22:59:25 KST

Swiss franc is once again becoming a safe-haven currency
After a few months in which the Swiss franc was not in particularly high demand, it has recently been rising sharply once again. This is primarily due to the weakness of the euro. Political developments in France are weighing on the single currency.
Early on Thursday afternoon, the Swiss franc even fell below the 92-rappen mark against the euro once again. This took the franc to its highest level since early July.
At the start of the month, a euro was still costing almost CHF0.95 rappen. The franc has also strengthened significantly against the US dollar recently. Most recently, a dollar cost CHF0.82, whereas at the start of the month it was at times still trading at almost CHF0.84.
+ The world’s strongest currency is also super-competitive
The main reason for the slight weakness of the franc a few weeks ago was the widening interest rate differential between the eurozone and the dollar zone. While the Swiss National Bank (SNB) was able to keep its key interest rate at zero thanks to persistently low inflation, both the European Central Bank (ECB) and the US Federal Reserve (Fed) had recently raised their interest rates.
Sentiment has completely reversed
However, sentiment has now reversed completely within a short space of time. What is causing financial market participants particular concern is the high and still-rising level of debt in France, the ongoing political uncertainty accompanied by unrest, and next year’s presidential elections. As a result, yields on French government bonds are now higher than in former problem countries such as Greece or Italy.
For ten-year government bonds, the yield spread over comparable German bonds has even reached its highest level in 15 years at just under 1.7 percentage points. As France is the second most important EU country after Germany, there is a great deal of uncertainty.
Will the euro soon fall below 90 rappen?
Market participants are understandably unsettled. The ongoing protests are not exactly inspiring confidence, according to a foreign exchange commentary by Valiant Bank this week. This is less due to the images of rioting than to the demands – some of which are justified – the fulfilment of which would entail high costs.
As the problem is unlikely to vanish into thin air any time soon, it is reasonable to assume that inflows into the Swiss franc will increase again and that the franc will regain its role as a safe haven. As during the euro debt crisis, the euro/franc pair is thus increasingly serving as a barometer for risks within the eurozone, according to a commentary by the private bank UBP.
Despite short-term interest rate differentials that remain favourable for the euro, the downside risks are likely to persist in the coming weeks and intensify as we look towards 2027. In the medium term, exchange rates of just under CHF0.90 per euro are even possible, according to the private bank’s analysts.

Bundeswehr Conducts Its First Exercise to Deploy Reinforcements to Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:59:23 UTC
22:59:23 KST

The Bundeswehr is conducting the Brave Blue exercise in Estonia for the first time, during which it is practicing the strategic deployment of additional forces to the Baltic states in the event of a crisis or war.
This was reported by the Estonian broadcaster ERR. The exercise began on October 16 and will continue through October 27 in cooperation with the Estonian Defense Forces.
The Bundeswehr’s 4th Logistics Regiment is participating in the exercises. German troops are practicing the deployment of personnel and equipment to Estonia simultaneously by land, sea, and air.
According to Lieutenant Colonel Benjamin Eberhardt, commander of the 4th Logistics Regiment, heavy equipment was transported by ferry, some vehicles traveled overland, and service members arrived by plane.
The Bundeswehr has not disclosed the number of troops and vehicles involved, nor the exact routes taken by the convoys.
During the exercises, German troops are setting up command posts and testing communications and logistics support systems. Separately, they are studying the terrain and the mobility of military equipment in the marshy terrain typical of Estonia.
The 4th Logistics Regiment’s main activities are taking place in the western part of the country. The Estonian Defense Forces have provided the German military with their bases to house personnel, while units conducted reconnaissance of the area outside these bases.
Brave Blue is an annual German exercise during which support for Bundeswehr units deployed in the Baltic states in crisis or wartime situations is practiced. Previously, such exercises were held in Lithuania and Latvia, and in 2026, Estonia hosted them for the first time.
During Brave Blue 26, participants are also practicing procedures for the entry of allied forces into Estonia, the operation of designated reception points, and the deployment and management of logistics areas.
The Estonian Defense Forces note that host-nation support must ensure the rapid movement of allied units to designated areas. This support includes transportation, accommodation, food, fuel, and other logistical services.
The current exercises are also intended to prepare German logisticians for larger-scale exercises planned for next year in Lithuania and Latvia.

Situation in occupied West Bank 'simply out of control,' UN chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:58:49 UTC
22:58:49 KST

Yasin Gungor
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The situation across the occupied West Bank has deteriorated beyond control as escalating attacks seek to drive Palestinian communities from their land, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned on Thursday.
"In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians continue to suffer daily attacks by Israeli settlers. The clear goal is to drive communities off their land," Guterres told reporters.
He said the situation in the occupied territories is "simply out of control" as occupiers also target journalists and diplomats.
On Gaza, the UN chief pointed out that essential humanitarian assistance remains "severely restricted" ahead of winter, compounding obstacles facing the Security Council-backed roadmap to resolve the conflict.
Guterres stressed that the World Food Program "urgently" requires $450 million to feed populations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, noting that the sum equals approximately 90 minutes of global military expenditures. He appealed to international donors to step up while urging an end to the occupation to achieve a viable two-state solution.
'El Nino of war' and economic strain
Guterres compared modern conflicts to the climate phenomenon El Nino, and cautioned that cascading hostilities are reverberating through international energy markets, shipping corridors, and financial systems.
He linked widespread street protests over inflation, food, and fuel directly to the fallout of expanding global wars. "War does not create all these inequalities, but it feeds and exploits them," Guterres said, emphasizing that while street violence is unacceptable, authorities cannot allow disorder to obscure the legitimate cost-of-living grievances of peaceful protesters.
Regional diplomacy, Sudan, and Yemen
Turning to Yemen, Guterres described continued Houthi attacks against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia as "totally unacceptable," urging restraint amid mounting displacement in Yemen.
Guterres said he will travel to Egypt to advance regional de-escalation, underscoring Egypt's essential diplomatic role as a mediator in the war between the US and Iran, alongside its neighboring stakes in the wars in Sudan and Libya.
He also demanded that neighboring and distant nations halt weapons supplies to factions in Sudan that are "killing civilians in an absolutely devastating way."
Separetely, Guterres's spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters that he is visiting at the invitation of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and is expected to arrive in Cairo early Saturday.
Over the weekend and on Monday, Guterres will meet senior Egyptian officials, including Sisi and Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, as well as Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy, Dujarric said.
“Egypt has been actively engaged in these efforts, working with regional and international partners,” he said, adding that the talks will also cover the situation in Sudan and Gaza.
Disregard for international law
Guterres dismissed concerns about institutional damage to the UN from violations of international law, declaring that the real crisis is the suffering of ordinary civilians whose survival is threatened by war-induced inflation and violence.
"The problem is not for the United Nations. The problem is for the people that is suffering dramatically everywhere," he said.

Saudi Arabia launches 2026-27 archaeology season in AlUla, Khaybar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:55:49 UTC
22:55:49 KST

Saudi Arabia launches 2026-27 archaeology season in AlUla, Khaybar
Research to focus on early human presence, ancient Arabian kingdoms, pilgrimage routes, water management, inscriptions, according to Royal Commission for AlUla
Lina Altawell
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
ISTANBUL
Saudi Arabia has launched its 2026-27 Archaeology Season across AlUla and Khaybar, focusing on research, excavation and conservation in one of the most significant archaeological landscapes in the country’s northwest.
The Royal Commission for AlUla (RCU) said in a statement on Monday that the season builds on previous years of archaeological research, excavation, documentation and conservation and is aimed at advancing knowledge of the region’s history while developing Saudi expertise in archaeology and cultural heritage.
According to the state news agency SPA, the program combines fieldwork, specialized studies, digital documentation, conservation, community engagement and capacity building.
The commission said this year’s research will focus on early human presence, ancient Arabian kingdoms and oasis communities, travel and pilgrimage routes, environmental history and water management, inscriptions and written heritage, material culture and ways of life.
At Hegra in AlUla, researchers will study the ancient settlement center, including plant and animal remains and archaeological finds, to provide greater insight into life at the site across different historical periods.
In Dadan, the second phase of the Dadan Archaeological Project will build on a previous five-year project, focusing on funerary and residential areas to better understand the development of one of AlUla’s major ancient centers, according to the commission.
Research in Khaybar will examine the relationship between people and the oasis across different periods, including the Neolithic era and Islamic periods, as well as sedimentary records, ancient environments and natural resources that influenced human settlement and cultural change, it added.
The commission also said that studies in southern AlUla will examine historic pilgrimage and trade routes, including forts, railway stations and other archaeological remains linked to travel networks that connected the area with surrounding regions.
Written heritage is another major component of the program. More than 25,000 inscriptions have been documented in AlUla, providing an important record of northwestern Saudi Arabia’s history, languages and cultural interactions, it said.
Specialized studies will also examine animal remains, ceramics, water systems, oasis water management and material culture to shed light on everyday life in past societies.
Saudi university students will take part in fieldwork, laboratory analysis, specialized studies and digital documentation under the supervision of Saudi and international experts.
The program also includes community activities linking archaeological research with local knowledge through museum and laboratory experiences and visits to archaeological sites.
The commission said the initiative forms part of its broader efforts to preserve AlUla’s cultural heritage and strengthen AlUla and Khaybar as centers for archaeological research, cultural exchange and heritage-led development, in line with Saudi Vision 2030.

NVIDIA unveils new AI factory design, robotics and safety tools at Berlin conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

NVIDIA unveils new AI factory design, robotics and safety tools at Berlin conference
Speaking at the three-day conference in Berlin, Huang said Europe was entering a new industrial revolution driven by AI. NVIDIA has committed nearly $10 billion to Europe’s technology ecosystem and works with more than 12,000 partners across the region, he said.
Huang described AI as a five-layer system, spanning energy, computing infrastructure, AI factories, models and applications. He argued that Europe must produce AI rather than simply consume it.
One of the main announcements was NVIDIA DSX POD, a reference design for AI factories built with NVIDIA Vera Rubin computing systems. Partners can assemble and test the facilities inside modular containers before delivery. Once a site has the necessary utilities, deployment could take as little as 14 days, down from six months.
NVIDIA also said its DSX AI Factory Platform can reduce water consumption for cooling by up to 100% and deliver the same AI output with up to 30% less power.
New tools for safer AI agents
Huang presented AI agents as a new computing platform. Unlike systems that only answer questions, agents can reason, use tools, access information and carry out tasks.
However, their ability to access files, networks and other resources creates security risks. NVIDIA introduced the OpenShell Reference Architecture for Safe AI Agents, designed to control agent permissions, isolate their activities and monitor their actions.
AI moves into factories, hospitals and vehicles
NVIDIA demonstrated how its Agent Toolkit can combine company data, AI models and specialized tools to support work across industries.
At Lila Sciences, agents help researchers explore potential treatments for B-cell lymphoma through virtual experiments and automated laboratory work. At Siemens, they help prepare products for manufacturing by testing plans in digital twins. At Dassault Systèmes, engineering agents use simulations to identify problems and refine vehicle designs.
In healthcare, NVIDIA and Siemens Healthineers are developing AI enabled adaptive radiation therapy. The system combines AI agents, digital twins and live imaging to adjust radiation targeting as a patient's body and tumor change during treatment.
In the automotive sector, NVIDIA said Volvo Cars was adopting its Hyperion computing platform and Alpamayo software for automated driving. Volkswagen, Jaguar Land Rover and Mercedes-Benz are also preparing vehicles compatible with Hyperion. Mobility partners, including Bolt, Lucid and Einride, are showcasing selected autonomous driving applications.
New humanoid robot platform and personal AI computers
Huang announced Agile ONE SN, a reference humanoid robot built on NVIDIA Isaac GR00T technology. Expected to become available in 2027, the platform features 31 degrees of freedom and aims to reduce researchers' setup time from weeks to days.
The system builds on NVIDIA's tools for collecting robotics data, training models in simulation and running robot software. Partners including Agility Robotics, Figure, KUKA and NEURA Robotics are also using NVIDIA's physical AI technologies.
Huang closed the keynote by demonstrating RTX Spark, a compact computer designed for local AI workloads. The machine delivers one petaflop of performance and 128GB of memory, specifications he compared with NVIDIA's DGX-1 system delivered to OpenAI in 2016.
He showed how an AI agent could train small Microduck robots by creating a simulated course, running training jobs in the cloud and evaluating the results on RTX Spark before deploying them to physical robots.
Four Microducks then appeared onstage, demonstrating movements learned through simulation.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported on NVIDIA’s Rev Lebaredian discussing the potential of digital twins in Kazakhstan and the challenges of implementing the technology.

“I continue to believe that Putin has things on Trump. I continue to believe that he is holding photos, videos, whatever it might be,” she said, without presenting evidence to substantiate the allegation.
She also pointed to Trump’s opposition to releasing files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, arguing that their eventual disclosure could shock even some of his supporters.
“So, honestly, I think it’s wannabe dictator. It is, you know, money, money, money. And it is, you know, let’s keep Putin happy so he doesn’t dump what he has,” Clinton said.
Report: Shahed Factory Gets Putin-Style Air Defenses
When Swisher asked whether she still stood by her description of Trump as Putin’s puppet, Clinton replied: “He is a willing Putin puppet to help Putin.”
She warned that Russia’s ambitions extended beyond Ukraine and linked Trump’s foreign policy to what she described as a desire among authoritarian leaders to divide the world into spheres of influence.
“Putin’s not going to stop with Ukraine,” Clinton said, arguing that Trump appeared to envision a world in which the United States controlled the Western Hemisphere, Putin controlled Russia and Europe, and Chinese leader Xi Jinping controlled the rest.
Hillary Clinton revisits 2016 warning about Trump and Putin
Clinton’s remarks echoed her exchange with Trump during the second presidential debate in October 2016, when Trump said, pointing at her, that “Putin, from everything I see, has no respect for this person.”
“That’s because he’d rather have a puppet as president of the United States,” Clinton replied during the debate.
She went on to accuse him of refusing to acknowledge Russian cyberattacks against the United States, encouraging espionage against Americans and supporting Putin’s political objectives.
“You are willing to spout the Putin line, sign up for his wish list, break up NATO, do whatever he wants you to do,” she said at the time.
Nearly a decade later, Clinton argued that events had borne out her warnings about Trump’s relationship with the Kremlin.
Bill Clinton accuses Trump of abandoning Ukraine
Meanwhile, Bill Clinton criticized Trump’s Russia policy during a campaign appearance on Oct. 20, his first appearance of the 2026 midterm election campaign.
He was campaigning for Florida Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly at the Koinonia Worship Center.
Bill Clinton accused Donald Trump of mistreating US allies and abandoning Ukraine while moving closer to Putin. The former US president said:

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting's speech at the opening of Telford Gun Hall
The Defence Secretary spoke on British industry and sovereign production capacity at the official opening of Telford Gun Hall.
Ladies and gentlemen, our dear friend, the German ambassador, Shaun Davies, the local member of Parliament, who is Telford’s greatest champion on the national and international stage, it really is a huge privilege to be with you all to open the new UK Gun Hall today. Special thanks are due to Armin, to Rebecca, to everyone from Rheinmetall, not just for laying on this great event, but also for your long-standing investment in Britain and the jobs and communities which that investment supports.
I think the fact that we’ve got such an array of leaders and representatives from across government, industry and the military speaks to the critical importance of this new facility, and I want to start by sending every single word you heard about the importance of what we’re marking today.
As someone who loves our country’s history, it’s not lost on me that we’re a stone’s throw away from the birthplace of British industry, and a part of our country that’s synonymous with engineering and manufacturing.
So it feels especially fitting that we’re here to celebrate how we are renewing and reigniting that unique industrial strength. Today is a vote of confidence in our country, a statement of intent on our mission to reindustrialise Britain and create good, well-paid jobs across our country, and proof that we are rebuilding the capabilities of our armed forces.
And so what we’re opening the doors to here is more than a manufacturing plant. We’re opening the doors to something much greater and much more ambitious. And that is readiness and resilience. For the first time in decades, artillery gun barrels will be produced in Britain. They will be made using British steel from Forgemasters. As we’ve heard, their production will create one hundred jobs here and hundreds more across the supply chain right across the country.
Gun Hall will also support the next generation of equipment for the British Army, helping to deliver the firepower that will make us warfighting ready by 2030. And on top of all of this, this facility stands as a symbol of the deepening defence industrial relationship between the United Kingdom and our friends in Germany.
All of this adds up to a new era of hope and opportunity for this town, this region, and our country as we face up to a new era of threat and jeopardy.
As the Chief of the General Staff just said, we are making daily discoveries about the changing nature of the conflict in Ukraine. Yet, as was also pointed out, for all of the technological advances we’re seeing on the battlefield, what you might call more traditional weaponry still has its place in modern warfare.
But those armaments do not get produced by waving a magic wand. Nor in the event that this country finds itself in a war fighting state, can that capability and capacity in industry be conjured up.
To make sure we can deter and, if necessary, defeat, our adversaries, Britain must have the capacity to manufacture critical defence components at home and in sufficient quantities. We must have the capacity to increase production and replenish stockpiles when threats increase. We must have robust supply chains to back them up, and we must have the wider industrial resilience to sustain our armed forces through prolonged conflict.
Despite the advent of drones and data of AI and autonomy, it is not enough to simply out-innovate those who would wish us harm, though we must. We must also outproduce them too, because advantage increasingly belongs to those who can manufacture at scale and field capability fastest.
And that’s what Rheinmetall here in Telford will help us to achieve. Here is also where our ambition to turn defence investment into jobs, skills and growth in every postcode becomes reality. The threat environment requires us to deliver the biggest sustained increase in defence investment since the end of the Cold War.
And I’m acutely aware that investment in defence comes with trade-offs and choices in other areas of government spending, and at a cost to the taxpayer. So investment in defence will only command lasting public support if people can see not only how that investment strengthens our national defence, but also if they can see how it improves their lives, how it makes sure that we have a Britain that is worth fighting for.
That means bringing opportunity to every corner of the country. Almost seventy percent of defence investment is already spent outside London and the South East, and we’re setting out shortly how people and communities in every nation and region of the UK will feel benefits and do feel benefits from the defence dividend.
Here in the West Midlands, the defence economy is worth £1.8 billion and directly support around 8,000 jobs, with Rheinmetall at the forefront. Defence can also help us to tackle the moral emergency of more than a million young people out of work or education or training.
So it’s not just about spending more, although spending more is necessary. Every pound we invest in defence should be judged by what it does for Britain. Does it strengthen our industrial base? Does it push the frontier of innovation? Does it create skilled work, especially for young people? Over the next decade, this facility will emphatically answer yes to all those questions.
And as it does, it will inject more than £400 million into the UK economy. That’s precisely what I mean when I say that the Ministry of Defence can also be a ministry for growth and a ministry for opportunity, not simply spending more, but investing more wisely, backing the people, places and businesses that strengthen our national security and drive our national renewal.
Every country across the NATO alliance faces similar challenges in the headwinds of rising threats and tighter finances. As we confront that reality, we need to avoid healthy competition becoming self-defeating rivalry and protectionism.
And this factory is a reminder that stronger domestic industries and deeper allied integration are not contradictory. Done right, each strengthens the other.
On so many fronts. UK and German interests align – nowhere more so than when it comes to our defence and security. We are the two biggest economies in Europe, the two biggest investors in defence, so it makes sense that we should come together in common purpose. Our partnership matters not as an end in itself, but because of what it allows our countries to deliver together.
The defining test is not where every single component of a piece of kit or equipment was made. It is whether our combined industrial base can give our armed forces what they need, when they need it, because an alliance that can mobilise its armies must also be able to mobilise its industries.
This has Armin alluded to, is what lies behind the Trinity House agreement that deepens defence cooperation between our two countries. By working as one, we can build manufacturing capability home so that we can deliver faster and ultimately strengthen NATO, which is in all our interests.
In this new age of insecurity, we need to spend more and better, and we are. We need to prepare more, and we are, with better training and more kit and equipment in the hands of our armed forces. And we need to produce more, and we are. We are right here in a region rich in industrial heritage, honouring its past by investing in its future. The threats we face are real, and they are closer to home. We need to step up and together we are.
So thank you very much for being here and for the amazing work that’s gone into this incredible facility. Thank you.

Major rail works to disrupt traffic on Israel's busiest highways
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:54:37 UTC
22:54:37 KST

Major infrastructure work by Israel Railways is expected to disrupt traffic on two key highways in central Israel this weekend, with lane reductions and traffic diversions planned along the Ayalon Highway and Route 531, ynet has learned.
The work, scheduled from Friday evening through Saturday, will affect motorists traveling through the Tel Aviv metropolitan area and the Sharon region to its north. Although neither highway will be completely closed, the temporary traffic arrangements could cause significant congestion.
Israel Railways has not issued a special public announcement about the disruptions as the work does not involve full highway closures. However, authorities responsible for the affected roads have been formally notified, and the changes have been incorporated into the Waze navigation app.
The construction is part of a nationwide project to extend railway station platforms, allowing them to accommodate newer, longer trains and increase passenger capacity as demand for rail travel grows.
Under the approved traffic arrangements, crews will carry out the work by reducing the number of available lanes and diverting vehicles around construction zones rather than shutting down entire highways.
Where and when traffic will be affected
On the Ayalon Highway, also known as Highway 20, work will begin Friday at 8 p.m. and continue until Saturday at 8 a.m.
The highway is one of Israel's busiest transportation arteries, running through the Tel Aviv metropolitan area and connecting major cities and employment centers along the country's central coastal plain.
Northbound traffic will be affected along two stretches: between the Shiv'at HaKochavim interchange and the HaMa'apilim area, and between the HaHalakha and KKL interchanges.
Southbound motorists will face changes along three stretches: between Shiv'at HaKochavim and HaMa'apilim, between HaHalakha and KKL, and between the Mevo Ayalon and Komemiyut interchanges.
Work on Route 531, a major east-west highway serving communities in the Sharon region north of Tel Aviv, will last longer. It is scheduled to begin Friday at 8 p.m. and continue until Saturday at 4 p.m.
Traffic arrangements will affect both eastbound and westbound lanes along the section between the Kfar Saba and Hod Hasharon railway stations.
Drivers traveling through either area are advised to allow additional time and consult navigation apps for updated routes.
Years of construction strain central Israel's roads
The latest disruptions come amid persistent traffic congestion across central Israel, where motorists have faced frequent delays over the past year as several of the country's largest transportation infrastructure projects advance simultaneously.
Among them is the construction of a fourth railway track along the Ayalon corridor, a major project intended to increase rail capacity through the Tel Aviv metropolitan area, where the existing tracks form a critical bottleneck in the national railway network.
Israel Railways is also carrying out an extensive electrification program to replace diesel-powered rail services with electric trains, while separate projects are expanding the Tel Aviv light rail network and preparing infrastructure for the planned metropolitan subway system.
Together, the projects have brought construction crews to major transportation arteries on an almost nightly basis, requiring recurring lane restrictions and temporary changes to traffic patterns.
Although much of the work is scheduled overnight to minimize disruption, construction frequently extends into periods of lighter daytime traffic and the early morning hours, creating bottlenecks and heavy congestion even when roads would ordinarily be relatively clear.
The overlapping projects have compounded the challenges facing drivers in the densely populated Tel Aviv metropolitan area, where major highways already carry substantial commuter traffic.
With another round of construction scheduled this weekend, motorists are being urged to prepare for possible delays, exercise patience and use navigation apps to check traffic conditions before setting out.

Hong Kong elderly urged to stay indoors as air pollution spikes to serious levels

Severe haze in Hong Kong over the past two days has prompted a government warning of serious health risks, with experts urging the elderly and vulnerable to stay indoors until sunset.
Air quality health risk levels at some of Hong Kong’s roadside monitoring stations rose on Wednesday and Thursday, with experts attributing the surge to elevated ozone levels caused by sunlight and high temperatures and warning that conditions were likely to persist over the next few days.
On Wednesday afternoon, the Air Quality Health Index issued by the Environmental Protection Department reached a “serious” health risk level at its Tuen Mun station, where it remained for two hourly readings.
The pollution persisted on Thursday, with Central/Western, Southern, Tsuen Wan, Tuen Mun and Sha Tin stations recording “high” health risk levels at 4pm. An hour later, the Southern station reached a “very high” level.

Elections in Israel: candidates and issues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:53:39 UTC
22:53:39 KST

Parliamentary elections are scheduled to take place in Israel on the 27th of October. These will be the first elections since the 2023 attack by the terrorist group Hamas and the subsequent wars in the Gaza Strip and Iran, as well as the conflict with the Houthis and the group Hezbollah, reports the BBC.
Many consider these to be the most significant elections in Israel's history—ones that will have an impact on the entire world. Current polls indicate that incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a fierce challenge from Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of the Israel Defense Forces.
Eisenkot’s popularity stems in part from his military background and his relatively recent entry into politics; he founded his own party only last year. Eisenkot’s son was killed in Gaza during the early months of the war, and Eisenkot himself served on Israel’s war cabinet until 2024, when he resigned due to disagreements regarding the conflict. His campaign is built on calls to hold those responsible for the errors that led to the October 7, 2023, attack accountable.
Other opposition leaders include Avigdor Liberman and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett. Both are representatives of the right wing who take a firm stance on security and advocate for continued Israeli control over the occupied West Bank. Another prominent figure is Yair Golan, from the political left, who, by contrast, advocates for an Israeli withdrawal from the West Bank. Despite these differing views, he could potentially form a government together with Eisenkot.
Netanyahu’s current government is the most radically right-wing in Israel’s history.
 To remain in office, he will have to rely on some of his existing far-right partners. Some hold radically nationalist views—for instance, calling for the annexation of the West Bank and the removal of Palestinians from Gaza, a move tantamount to the forced displacement of a population.
Two Arab parties are also running in the election (Arabs make up approximately one-fifth of Israel’s population). In theory, these parties could play a decisive role in determining who forms the government. At the same time, only one of the major Jewish parties has not ruled out the possibility of cooperating with the Arab parties.
The Israeli parliament has 120 seats, meaning a party must secure at least 61 to hold a majority. Israel uses a proportional representation voting system, which means that governments are always coalitions of multiple parties. Consequently, it can take several weeks or even months after an election for a new government to be formed.
Security is the primary issue during the election period. Netanyahu’s rivals have sharply criticized the failures that led to the Hamas attack, in which nearly 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage to Gaza. Nevertheless, Netanyahu has continued to portray himself as "Mr. Security," pointing to several strategic victories achieved since 2023.
Military service has also become a subject of intense debate.
 Historically, ultra-Orthodox Jewish men engaged in full-time religious study were exempt from conscription. However, since the start of the war, this policy has become highly controversial.
The reform of the judicial system has also been widely discussed. Netanyahu’s government continues to push for sweeping reforms—measures that had already sparked widespread protests even before the Hamas attack in 2023. Critics argue that the planned reforms would undermine the independence of the judiciary and threaten democracy. As in many other parts of the world, the cost of living is also on the agenda.
On the evening of election day, at 10:00 PM local time, Israeli broadcasters will announce the results of exit polls. While these will provide some insight into the voting outcome, the picture remains unclear, and current polls suggest that predicting a winner is difficult. Initial results are expected on October 28, while the official results are scheduled to be announced on the 4th of November.
Following consultations with party leaders, Israeli President Isaac Herzog will invite one of them to form a government. This process can be lengthy and may even prove unsuccessful. If the party leaders are unable to form a government, fresh elections are held. Between 2019 and 2022, elections took place five times in Israel because the parties were unable to reach an agreement.
