Trump’s tariffs loom over Maine Senate race between Collins and Jackson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:53:23 UTC
22:53:23 KST

PORTLAND, Maine — The same week President Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on imported steel, the domestic supplier of the wire mesh Mark Brooks uses to make lobster traps in Maine hiked prices by 20%.
When diesel prices began rising as the U.S. war with Iran escalated, Brooks started paying freight surcharges on his materials and saw sales slow as lobstermen tightened their belts. And when Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney slapped 50% tariffs on U.S. lobster traps in September as retaliation for Trump's own duties on Canadian goods, the roughly $2 million in annual shipments Brooks typically sends over the northern border dried up virtually overnight.
"It's basically the worst business climate for us that I've ever seen in 40 years," said Brooks, a third-generation lobster-trap manufacturer and supplier, who along with his siblings runs Brooks Trap Mill and its seven locations across Maine. "We've eaten as much cost as we can to try to keep our prices down, but we just can't eat any more than we have already."
Few states have been as vulnerable in the U.S.-Canada trade war as Maine, which sends more than 40% of its exports to the U.S.'s northern neighbor. Those challenges are also piling on top of cost-of-living issues that were already spiraling, especially relating to things like home heating oil, on which Maine depends more than any other state. As a result, tariffs specifically — and affordability concerns more broadly — are center stage in this year's "toss up" Senate race between GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Troy Jackson, a former president of the Maine Senate.
Polls show the economy is at the top of the list of voters' concerns this election, in Maine and nationwide. More than 90% of respondents in a Suffolk University poll this month of likely Maine voters rated the state's economy as "fair" or "poor," while a majority said the state is on the wrong track and 57% gave Trump an unfavorable rating.
The key question here is whether that dissatisfaction will translate into votes against Collins, or whether she will be able to separate herself from an unpopular piece of Trump's and the Republican Party's agenda. 
"That's one of the big issues in this campaign: How independent is Susan Collins from Donald Trump?" said Jim Melcher, a political science professor at the University of Maine at Farmington.
Across the country, Republican candidates in competitive seats have been working to find ways to distance themselves from the White House.
In Michigan, GOP candidate Mike Rogers has criticized the Canada tariffs and called for a quick end to the Iran war. In Iowa, Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for Senate, came out against Trump's decision to temporarily lower tariffs on imported ground beef, which she said would hurt U.S. cattle ranchers. And GOP Senate hopefuls in New Hampshire, Alaska, Ohio and Nebraska have all expressed concerns over Trump's decision to allow imports of Russian diesel, reversing course weeks after signing legislation to expand sanctions on Russia.
But Maine presents the ultimate test of whether voters this year will distinguish between the president and the rest of his party. Collins, long known and praised for her independent streak, is the lone GOP incumbent running for reelection in a state that voted against Trump in 2024. And polls show the race is tight, with Jackson leading by an average of 2 percentage points in polls compiled by FiftyPlusOne.
'We shouldn't be in a trade war with Canada'
Both Collins and Jackson have sharply criticized the tariffs, which are deeply unpopular here: Seven in 10 likely Maine voters say duties on Canadian goods are bad for the state, while only 12% called them "a good thing," according to a CNN poll last month.
But the candidates disagree over who bears responsibility for the economic damage, and who could better do something about it.
Collins has repeatedly pushed back against the Trump administration on duties and was able to secure exemptions from the Canada tariffs for some key items, including concrete, wood pulp and road salt. Jackson argues that Congress should have been able to prevent the tariffs altogether, and that Collins, for all her seniority in Washington, should have been able to do more to help her state.
"The bottom line is Troy and I both would have voted against the Canadian tariffs," Collins said in an Oct. 13 debate, the third of four held between the two candidates. "But I have been able to negotiate and get certain items removed from the tariff list — Troy would have gotten nothing."
"I'm not going to give Sen. Collins credit for taking things off the list, when we should have never had a list," Jackson replied. "We shouldn't be in a trade war with Canada."
"Troy spent most of his life working along the Canadian border, so he knows how important this relationship is to Maine's economy, and he sees Trump's tariffs for what they are: a tax on Maine families and small businesses," Maggie Amjad, Jackson's campaign spokesperson, said in response to CNBC's request for comment about the effects of tariffs and the Iran war.
"There's a fundamental difference between Senator Collins and Troy Jackson: she delivers results; he would get nothing," Blake Kernen, Collins' campaign spokesperson, told CNBC. "They both would have voted against the tariffs, but Senator Collins secured exemptions and delivered for Maine."
The lobster industry escaped the worst of the Canada tariffs, after Ottawa made a last-minute decision to leave lobster off its retaliation list. Collins' team says that move, too, was partly due to her influence: She met with Canada's ambassador in Washington to discuss lobster and seafood exclusions, and released a statement afterward warning that tariffs "would have caused tremendous harm to Maine's lobstermen."
But lobster fishermen say nearly everything else they use on the boat every day is still getting more expensive. The traps that Brooks makes are selling for $180 now, versus $130 two years ago. The diesel fuel that runs the boats is up 67% statewide over the past year, according to AAA. The rope, much of which is imported from India, and the bait, which largely comes from Europe, is also more expensive due to the combination of tariffs and higher fuel costs.
"Everything we do in this business costs more money right now," said Steve Train, a lobsterman who hauls 400 lobster traps a day out of Casco Bay. "These tariff wars are not helping us."
Train faults Trump for the tariffs and criticizes him for "bypassing Congress" to "issue executive orders to do things that cause us a problem." But he credits Collins for the work she has done to help the lobster industry. A registered independent, he says he will split his vote between the parties this election, but one vote will be for Collins.
"She has been like a guardian angel for the lobster industry for many years," he said. "I can't oppose her because she's in the same party as somebody I don't like."

Gaza’s Health Ministry warned Thursday that hospital electricity generators could stop working after stocks of operating oil were completely exhausted amid Israel’s continued blockade of the enclave, Anadolu reports.
The ministry said in a statement that engineering teams are working under difficult conditions to monitor the generators and keep electricity supply to critical hospital departments.
“Generators have been running for thousands of continuous hours without sufficient oil or maintenance, bringing them to the final point of mechanical danger,” the ministry said.
“If generator engines burn out because of the lack of oil, they could become permanently unusable even if supplies become available later,” it warned.
The ministry renewed its call for urgent intervention, saying the issue was no longer limited to securing operating oil but also involved protecting the remaining generators from complete failure.
On Wednesday, the ministry said stocks of oil needed to operate hospital generators had run out, adding that more than 2,500 liters (660 gallons) are urgently needed each month to prevent the remaining generators from breaking down amid Israeli restrictions on the entry of operating and maintenance supplies.
The ministry warned that the continuing shortage threatens the shutdown of life-saving medical departments.
In September, it said 70% of hospital generators had already gone out of service because of shortages of fuel, oil and spare parts caused by the Israeli blockade.
READ: Gaza hospitals face risk of power outages as generator oil runs out
Separately, Gaza’s Social Development Ministry warned Thursday of “catastrophic humanitarian consequences” threatening displaced Palestinians after most bakeries stopped operating amid Israeli restrictions on flour and essential food supplies entering the enclave.
“Continued restrictions on flour and supplies needed to operate bakeries amounted to an extension of the systematic starvation policy and the use of food as a weapon against civilians,” the ministry said.
“The restrictions are causing the collapse of the last line of food defense for vulnerable families, children and women who depend heavily on humanitarian aid and international relief organizations,” it added.
The ministry attributed the bakery shutdowns to Israel holding up flour shipments and preventing the entry of supplies needed to keep them operating, describing the restrictions as a violation of international humanitarian law and the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Hospitals in Gaza have relied heavily on generators to power operating rooms, intensive care units, neonatal incubators, ventilators, and dialysis machines since Israel cut electricity supplies to the enclave in October 2023.
Gaza’s sole power plant stopped operating on Oct. 11, 2023, after running out of fuel, causing a complete electricity blackout, while power lines, cables, and distribution networks suffered widespread destruction during the war.
Damage to the electricity network has prevented hospitals from reconnecting to the grid, forcing them to depend on generators for prolonged periods.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:50:18 UTC
22:50:18 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Russia’s international reserves stood at $723.2 bln as of October 16, 2026, down $0.3 bln over the week, according to materials published by the Bank of Russia.
"International reserves changed only slightly over the week, standing at $723.2 bln as of the end of October 16, 2026," the regulator said.
As of October 9, the reserves totaled $723.5 bln.
International reserves are highly liquid foreign assets held by the Bank of Russia and the Russian government. They consist of foreign currency assets, special drawing rights, the reserve position in the International Monetary Fund, and monetary gold.
Western countries imposed sanctions on the Bank of Russia after Russia launched its special military operation in Ukraine. In addition to freezing Russia’s gold and foreign exchange reserves, they banned all transactions related to the management of the Central Bank’s reserves and assets, as well as transactions with any legal entity, organization, or body acting on behalf of or at the direction of the Central Bank.

The film was directed by Hungarian filmmaker Krisztina Goda and produced by Andy Vajna, an American of Hungarian origin who was among the more than 200,000 people who left the country following the Soviet crackdown.
                                    
“It is right to remember, even on Italian soil, the tragic events of 1956,” stated Ambassador Alessandra Schiavo, “because the uprising in Budapest was the first in a series of courageous revolts by the peoples of Eastern Europe against Soviet rule. It is important to do so, not only to pay tribute to the thousands of victims and preserve their memory, but also to reflect on the wound inflicted on our continent by the outcome of World War II. It was a historical wound that left Europe divided in two. A wound that led to further bloodshed, lasting until 1989 and the fall of the Berlin Wall, and that caused political divisions even within Western countries.” “It is a wound,” the Ambassador continued, “that still challenges our consciences today, four years and eight months after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and while many peoples around the world still suffer as a result of repression or conflict.”

Putin appoints 5 new government members in Russian Cabinet reshuffle

Unknown Publisher

Elena Teslova
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday signed decrees appointing five new members of the government's Cabinet following their approval a day earlier by the lower chamber of parliament, the State Duma, the Kremlin said.
Under the decrees, Anton Siluanov was appointed deputy prime minister and finance minister, while Andrey Nikitin became deputy prime minister.
Irina Okladnikova was appointed deputy prime minister and chief of the government staff, Oleg Kozhemyako became deputy prime minister and presidential envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District, and Dmitry Yadrov was appointed transport minister.
The reshuffle also introduced a new position of deputy prime minister and finance minister, increasing the number of deputy prime ministers from 10 to 11.
Siluanov, who has headed the Finance Ministry since December 2011, was relieved of his previous position as finance minister following his appointment to the new post.
Putin also dismissed Dmitry Grigorenko as deputy prime minister and chief of the government staff. Sberbank said its supervisory board would consider his appointment as the bank’s deputy chair on Nov. 10.
According to Sber, Grigorenko is expected to oversee strategic projects, including cooperation with the government and regional authorities on digitalization and the use of artificial intelligence in the public sector.
Yury Trutnev was also dismissed as deputy prime minister and presidential envoy to the Far Eastern Federal District. Putin appointed him as a presidential aide.
Nikitin previously served as transport minister, a position he had held since July 2025. Yadrov headed the Federal Air Transport Agency, known as Rosaviatsiya, since September 2023.
Okladnikova previously served as first deputy finance minister, while Kozhemyako was governor of Primorsky Krai. During his career, he has also headed three other of Russia’s Far Eastern regions.
The newly restructured Cabinet is scheduled to hold its first meeting on Thursday, according to the government press service.
According to expert assessments, the reshuffle is aimed at strengthening the Cabinet’s economic bloc amid rising Western sanctions on Russia.

Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC)
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:48:46 BST
22:48:46 KST

Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC)
The Defence Serious Crime Command investigates serious crime committed by people subject to Service law, in the UK and overseas. Investigations are carried out independently of the single Service chains of command.
Introduction
The Defence Serious Crime Command (DSCC) investigates serious, complex and major crime where the person alleged to have committed the offence is subject to Service law, in the UK and overseas.
Anyone can report a crime to the Service Police. You do not need to be a member of the Armed Forces. If you are unsure whether an offence comes under Service Police jurisdiction, you can still contact the Service Police for advice.
The DSCC operates independently of the Royal Navy, Army and Royal Air Force chains of command. This means investigations and policing decisions are made independently of an individual’s Service chain of command.
Serious and complex crime
We investigate serious and complex crime where the Service Police has jurisdiction.
Investigations are conducted impartially and based on the evidence available. Victims and witnesses are kept informed about the progress of an investigation and the support available to them.
Major crime
We investigate major crime and other cases which require specialist investigative skills and resources.
Global policing
Our role extends beyond the UK. We investigate crime reported to have been committed by people subject to Service law overseas.
Investigations remain independent of the single Services’ chains of command regardless of where they take place.
Public protection and safeguarding
We work to protect vulnerable people and prevent harm.
Public protection and intelligence support the identification and management of risk and inform investigative activity.
Support for victims and witnesses
If you are a victim or witness of serious crime, committed by a person subject to service law, information and support is available to you throughout the Service Justice process.
The Victim Witness Care Unit (VWCU) provides specialist support and information to victims and witnesses.
Location
The DSCC Headquarters is based at Southwick Park, Fareham. The DSCC also operates from locations across the UK and overseas.
Reporting a crime
If you or someone else are in immediate danger in the UK, or you need support right away, call 999.
Contact the Service Police
To report a crime, whether in the UK or overseas, or to speak to the Service Police in a non-emergency:
- call the Service Police Crime Bureau on 02392 285 170 or 0331 145 7630
- attend or call a local Service Police station - the Service Police Crime Bureau will be able to provide location and contact details
Crimestoppers
If you are in the UK, you can contact Crimestoppers by:
- calling 0800 555 111 at any time of day or night
- completing the online information form on the Crimestoppers website – the form is completely secure and designed to protect your anonymity
If you are serving abroad, you must use the online information form to contact Crimestoppers. This will ensure your anonymity.
Fraud defence confidential hotline
Call the Fraud defence confidential hotline on 0800 161 3665 (UK) or +44 1480 44 638 (overseas).
Contact the DSCC
Defence Serious Crime Command
Southwick Park
1st Floor
Overlord Building
PO17 6EJ
Make a complaint
To make a complaint about the DSCC or VWCU, contact the Professional Standards Department at People-DSCC-PSDMailbox@mod.gov.uk
Service Police Complaints Form - GOV.UK
Make a Freedom of Information (FOI) request
Please visit the Ministry of Defence homepage, where guidance can be found under ‘make an FOI request’.

====================================================================================================

Prepare for more website shutdowns in the age of AI – but human inaction is the real culprit | Chris Stokel-Walker
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:46:26 UTC
22:46:26 KST

Parts of the internet are going dark. In the Netherlands, government websites, including its digital ID login service, have become unavailable. Finland has taken public services offline, and Wikimedia, the organisation behind Wikipedia, has switched off some of its systems too.
This sounds like the results of a cyber-attack. In most instances, however, the people running the sites deliberately switched them off because the alternative – keeping them online – was too risky. The future is here, and suddenly much of our digital infrastructure is looking very fragile.
The websites were turned off because of two serious security vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language that is used by about 70% of websites that we can track. Those vulnerabilities in effect gave hackers an open window through which to climb and loot everything within. That could mean an attacker getting into an online shop, stealing customers’ addresses and passwords, or changing its checkout page to harvest card details. The UK’s National Cyber Security Centre advised organisations that were unable to update immediately to consider taking their systems offline.
It’s very tricky to get people to care about something quite so techy. PHP is a tricky abbreviation – even explaining what it stands for (PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor) is complicated, because it’s recursive. And how it helps the web work is also difficult to explain: a good analogy is it’s like the back-of-house team in a restaurant: your browser puts in an order, and PHP handles the cooking and delivers the meal. In any case, what matters is that you’ve almost certainly used websites powered by it this week.
I’ve been reporting on scares like these in our digital architecture for more than a decade, and the underlying problem barely changes. In 2014, I wrote about Heartbleed, a vulnerability in OpenSSL, the software that helps keep communications across the internet secure. It was up to two men named Steve – working for OpenSSL on a shoestring budget and shouldering an awful lot of responsibility – to keep us from disaster. Twelve years later, it feels like we’re still having the same conversation.
Heartbleed wasn’t the end of it. In 2021 I reported on a dangerous flaw in Log4j, a seemingly mundane tool that records what happens inside computer systems. Then three years later we had XZ Utils, a tool for shrinking file sizes used on Linux computers into which someone had deliberately planted a backdoor. In each of these incidents, small teams working for the public good recognised the problem, acted, and averted disaster. Each one of these incidents underscored how we rely on a handful of under-resourced individuals to keep vital parts of the web secure.
The PHP Foundation made that point itself this week. Its developers first identified the issue that could bring the internet to a halt in 2024, but it was seen as too expensive and too tricky to fix. The foundation has since admitted the delay was a “structural failure” owing to poor resource levels.
This is where AI comes in. In August, researchers working with Calif, OpenAI and Wiz identified how easily the PHP issue could be exploited by using AI tools. And hackers quickly did too. Cloudflare’s chief executive, Matthew Prince, said his company had seen millions of attempts to exploit it already.
Automated systems powered by AI can hammer away at weaknesses in an instant, bombarding their human guards with reports that they have to sift through. Researchers documented about 48,000 vulnerabilities across the internet in 2025. We’ve already passed 84,000 in 2026, with more than two months of the year still to go. That’s one every five minutes. Not every one will be as serious as this latest one, which scored 9.2 on a 10-point scale used to measure these things. But we’re facing an onslaught.
Which all makes for an uncomfortable reality: we’re going to have more days like these. AI makes it inordinately cheaper to find weaknesses in vast volumes of old code, and repairing them is difficult. A 2025 review by the UK government found that about 28% of central government technology was classed as “legacy” – meaning out of date – while some organisations couldn’t even estimate how much old software they had. In April, ministers admitted they couldn’t give a comprehensive account of what had since been fixed or retired.
So we need to fix that. Companies need to know what software they’re using, including the obscure elements they rely on, and who’s responsible for fixing it. That documentation is boring work, which is probably why it’s overlooked. But we’re in a different world now, and it needs to be done. Paradoxically, AI can help with it. But companies and the organisations protecting us also need adequate funding.
There are some things to be optimistic about. The OpenSSL Foundation, the not-for-profit company that fell victim to the Heartbleed vulnerability in 2014, received more than €400,000 from Germany’s sovereign tech fund last year to bolster its resources. The PHP Foundation has hired more staff and is using AI to help triage what’s important and what’s not. And a number of organisations deployed fixes before the current issue went public.
But more is needed. The solution is the same one we keep talking about, but rarely actually do anything about: the big tech companies making billions from software they get for nothing (because of its open-source nature) should contribute properly to maintaining it. Governments ought to do the same, rather than hoping a handful of exhausted developers will keep things ticking over indefinitely.
I’m growing sick of reporting on, and explaining why, the internet repeatedly breaks. I’ve covered Heartbleed, Log4Shell and XZ Utils – and am now documenting the fallout from PHP. I don’t particularly want to keep doing it. Yet I fear unless we start properly valuing those who keep our internet safe, I will be.
- Chris Stokel-Walker is the author of TikTok Boom: The Inside Story of the World’s Favourite App

Mohammed Sami, Ikram Kouachi and Sahin Demir
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Yemeni army launched airstrikes on Houthi missile launchers and weapons depots in Taiz province in the country’s southwest on Thursday, according to state television.
Yemen Satellite Channel said the attacks hit several Houthi positions, including missile launchers, radars, military communications systems and weapons depots in the western, southern and eastern parts of Taiz.
Also, Yemen’s Interior Ministry said Thursday that Houthi shelling caused extensive damage to a mosque and a school in Taiz province.
In a statement posted on US social media company X, the ministry said Houthi forces fired shells at a mosque and a school in Al-Najd village in the Mashra’a Wa Hadnan district, south of Taiz.
The ministry reported significant material damage but did not specify whether there were any casualties.
The official Saba news agency, citing a local source, said several shells struck the Omar al-Tayyar Mosque and School in the village.
There was no immediate comment from the Houthis on the claims.
Separately, the Yemeni army announced Thursday that two officers and an unspecified number of soldiers were killed in clashes with Houthi forces in Taiz.
In a statement, the army’s 35th Armored Brigade mourned Col. Mahfouz al-Jaradi, the brigade’s training officer, and Capt. Mamoun al-Jaradi, along with other soldiers whose names were not disclosed.
The brigade said they were killed during fighting on the Al-Aqroud front in southern Taiz, without providing further details.
Taiz has seen rising escalation since July amid fighting between government forces, backed by a Saudi-led coalition, and Houthi fighters.
Meanwhile, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed Thursday that the group had carried out four military operations targeting sites in Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles and drones over the past 48 hours.
In a statement posted on US social media company X, Saree said the attacks targeted the Saudi Defense Ministry building in Riyadh, King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu and Abha International Airport.
He claimed that the strikes directly hit their targets, disrupted operations at Dammam airport and caused a fire at the Aramco facility in Yanbu.
Saree also claimed that Saudi forces had carried out more than 2,900 airstrikes and missile attacks over the past 100 days, killing or injuring more than 562 people.
Since Oct. 5, Yemeni government forces have been conducting Operation "Dawn of Yemen," which Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said aims to regain control of state institutions from the Houthis and recapture the capital Sanaa.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

Algeria boosts defense ties with former rival
Algeria and Niger have signed a military cooperation agreement following talks between defense chiefs in Algiers, the Algerian Ministry of National Defense announced on Wednesday. The deal marks another step in the restoration of ties between Algeria and its Sahel neighbors following a diplomatic rift last year.
The agreement was signed at a meeting between Algeria’s chief of staff, Lieutenant General Said Chengriha, and Niger’s defense minister, Lieutenant General Salifou Modi, who arrived in the country leading a military delegation. The two sides discussed strengthening bilateral military and security cooperation and addressing shared challenges.
Chengriha reaffirmed Algeria’s willingness to consider proposals aimed at improving cooperation. “I also wish to reaffirm to you our readiness in the People’s National Army to study any Nigerien proposal that would enhance military and security cooperation,” he said.
Modi praised the level of coordination between the two countries’ armed forces across multiple areas. The meeting concluded with the signing of a cooperation protocol, although the ministry did not disclose specific provisions of the agreement.
The move follows a broader rapprochement between Algeria and the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), comprising Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso, which began earlier this year.
Relations deteriorated in April 2025 after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near their shared border, claiming it violated Algerian airspace, prompting all three AES members to recall their ambassadors. Bamako rejected the accusation and said the aircraft was destroyed over Mali.
Algeria and the three Sahel states fully restored diplomatic ties earlier this year. In recent months, cooperation between Algiers and Niamey has expanded. In August, Algeria deployed four Su-30 fighter jets, along with military transport and refueling aircraft, to support Niger following a failed military mutiny at an airbase in Niamey. In February, the two states agreed to restart work on the long-delayed Trans-Saharan Gas Pipeline, a project designed to transport Nigerian gas through Niger and Algeria to Europe.

Zelensky pointed to sanctions approved by the US Congress as one tool Trump could use to pressure the Kremlin.

“The biggest compromise we are already making is a ceasefire. Let’s just stop this war,” he said.
Zelensky added that he had repeatedly urged Trump to understand the scale of the concession Ukraine was prepared to make by agreeing to halt the fighting without first resolving every territorial issue. Zelensky stated:
“I have tried to tell the US President many times: just understand us. It is a huge compromise – simply holding the lines where they are right now.”

We beat the Trump administration in court. Now we’re going to the ICC to hold the U.S. accountable for the Gaza genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:44:15 UTC
22:44:15 KST

Over the course of the last three years, my family has lost 49 family members in Gaza. Their bodies were torn apart by shrapnel, crushed by falling buildings, and mutilated by bullets and munitions made and provided by the United States of America. Now, the U.S. is trying to dismantle the International Criminal Court, the only international court that can criminally prosecute U.S. officials for aiding and enabling genocide, by sanctioning the Court and attempting to intimidate anyone, including U.S. citizens, from working with them. So, in response, I joined others to sue this administration in order to take them to the very court they’re trying to destroy.
I’m a Palestinian-American organizer, and I helped establish Taxpayers Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG), which recently partnered with Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN) to sue the Trump administration so we can continue much-needed legal and advocacy work. Over the course of over a year, TAAG worked with an international legal team to prepare evidence against top U.S. officials for aiding and enabling the genocide of my people, but up until now, we haven’t been able to submit our evidence to the ICC because of this administration’s attacks and sanctions on the court and its judges.
Thankfully, that will now change after we successfully challenged the Trump administration in court. On October 13 we won a preliminary injunction that blocks this administration from being able to target our groups for working with sanctioned parties, clearing the way for us to proceed to the ICC. For the first time since the genocide started, I am beginning to see a glimmer of hope that justice will be found for the dozens of family members I have lost in Gaza.
The Trump administration’s war on the ICC
Long before the Trump administration sanctioned the entirety of the International Criminal Court (ICC) on October 9, it first enacted Executive Order 14203 in February of 2025. This executive order granted administration officials the ability to sanction foreign nationals for supporting the ICC’s investigations into U.S. and Israeli parties guilty of committing war crimes and their complicity in genocide. Under this Executive Order (EO) , the Trump administration also sanctioned leading Palestinian human rights groups al-Haq, al-Mezan, and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights (PCHR), as well as the UN Special Rapporteur for the Human Rights Situation on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, Francesca Albanese, along with other ICC officials.
What many people don’t know is that the EO that allowed the administration to sanction these parties doesn’t only go after foreign nationals, it also makes it a federal offense — punishable by a $1 million dollar fine and/or 20 years in prison — for anyone, including American citizens, who provides or receives a “service” to or from a sanctioned party. This provision of the EO is exactly why TAAG and DAWN took this administration to court: Our lawsuit argued that the EO violates our First Amendment rights as American citizens to speak, associate, and engage in Palestine-related human rights advocacy with these parties. As a founding member of TAAG, I can tell you firsthand how these sanctions have prevented us and organizations like DAWN from being able to continue our work sharing evidence and advocacy ideas with people like Albanese and ICC officials, because the definition of “service” is so broad and undefined — the US can interpret it as being anything that confers a benefit to the recipient.
In an October 9 video of Marco Rubio announcing the actions against the ICC, he tries defending the administration’s actions by calling the ICC a “rogue court,” which the U.S. is “not subject to the jurisdiction of.” But Rubio leaves out a fundamental principle of international law: A country does not have to join the ICC for its nationals to fall within the Court’s jurisdiction.
If a country that is not a State Party to the Rome Statute commits a war crime on the lands of a country that is a state party, the perpetrator of that crime can be investigated. Given that Palestine is a State Party to the Rome Statute, and that Gaza (and the West Bank) are classified as Occupied Palestinian Territories by the United Nations, the ICC has every right to investigate and prosecute the United States and Israel for the insurmountable war crimes committed against my family members and thousands of other innocent civilians.
It is clear that the only “protections” this administration are seeking are for the citizens responsible for aiding and abetting war crimes, which after three years, we have plenty of evidence of. Anthony Aguilar, a retired US special forces officer and whistleblower who resigned from his work with the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF) aid distribution centers in Gaza, has gone on record saying he saw the Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) shooting at crowds of Palestinians, and in an interview with the BBC says he saw Israeli and American military forces of the GHF using an “indiscriminate and unnecessary force against a civilian population, an unarmed, starving population.”
Rubio consistently mentions the idea of “protecting American citizens” from investigations by the ICC, but the citizens he is referring to are the ones committing the war crimes he doesn’t want investigated. What about American citizens whose families have been killed with U.S.-supplied weapons? Who protects our right to seek justice?
In sanctioning the entirety of the ICC, the Trump administration is not only trying to cripple any attempt to hold them accountable for their war crimes, but they’re also telling American citizens like myself that if you dare to seek justice for the family members you’ve lost, we’ll imprison you.
The struggle for accountability moves forward
Now that the courts sided with us in our lawsuit, we are finally able to prepare for the next steps ahead.
With the injunction in place, TAAG is now moving forward to finalize its evidence submission and plans to imminently send this to the ICC. We are also rallying support, within the US and beyond, for human rights organizations and advocates for the ICC to act responsibly upon this massive collection of evidence, in hopes that more parties take appropriate legal actions where possible. We fundamentally believe that grassroots movements like ours, and so many throughout the world, are the ones who must step up where our leadership has failed, and build the democratic, popular power capable of ensuring that legal action against genocide is taken and enforced.
We also hope that our actions inspire more American citizens to speak up against this administration and the priorities of our government. I helped found Taxpayers Alliance Against Genocide because I’m sick of our tax dollars being used against my own family in Gaza, while our communities here in the U.S. suffer from a lack of housing, education and healthcare. Those of us within TAAG recognize that we have a duty as American citizens to hold our nation accountable for the war crimes they commit, not just in Gaza but all over the world. We will not rest until we’ve exhausted every avenue to seek justice and accountability for these war crimes. We will continue collecting evidence, and pursuing every available legal avenue, moving forward with our crucial evidence work for a prospective submission to the ICC and advance our efforts to hold U.S. officials accountable for crimes against humanity. We will not be intimidated into abandoning our work, our families, or the principle that no one is above the law.

ETH research team creates robots with real muscles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:41:56 UTC
22:41:56 KST

ETH research team creates robots with real muscles
A research team at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology ETH Zurich has created robots with real muscles. They can jump, swim, walk and grasp objects.
Until now, muscle tissue grown in the laboratory often contracted so weakly that movements were barely visible to the naked eye, as the ETH explained in a press release on Thursday.
The research team therefore adopted a new approachExternal link. For the first time, they designed the living muscle tissue from mouse cells and a soft hydrogel scaffold together on a computer from the very beginning. An algorithm determined the shape that would allow the muscle contraction to achieve the greatest mechanical leverage. The scaffolds were then produced using 3D printing.
According to the university, the resulting actuators, which are around 1.5 centimetres long, deform up to eleven times more than previous systems with a comparable amount of muscle. When jumping, a robot lifts itself about five millimetres off the ground – equivalent to a third of its body length. A running version achieves 6.2 millimetres per second and, relative to its size, is faster than any previously known running bio-robot.
However, there is still a long way to go before they can be used outside the laboratory. The muscles currently rely on a nutrient solution to survive.
The researchers emphasise that, for future, larger systems, the development of an artificial vascular system for the transport of nutrients and oxygen is absolutely essential. The study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

The view from Russia: The Ukraine conflict is entering its final phase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:40:18 UTC
22:40:18 KST

The view from Russia: The Ukraine conflict is entering its final phase
Andrey Sushentsov, dean of the Faculty of International Relations at MGIMO and a member of the Scientific-Expert Council under the Security Council of the Russian Federation, discusses why Western Europe is so afraid of a direct confrontation with Russia, how the US is shifting the burden of the Ukraine crisis onto the EU, why the “pyramid of trust” surrounding Kiev is crumbling, and when the Ukraine conflict might come to an end.
His interview, first published in Russian by TASS, was translated and edited by the RT team.
America sails away, Europe gets the bill
Evgeny Kuznetsov: You have noted that the US is seeking to extricate itself from the Ukraine crisis by shifting the burden onto Western Europe. If Washington does indeed distance itself, are these Europeans prepared, politically and economically, to assume the role of Ukraine’s principal “security guarantor”?
Andrey Sushentsov: The US strategy in the Ukrainian crisis initially reflected its archetype as a maritime power employing a “continental sword” in its confrontation with a major continental power. This involves a neighboring country with military resources, which the maritime power supports in order to weaken its rival.
Ukraine was well suited to this role, as a large state with substantial armed forces, motivated to confront Russia. But the limitation of such a strategy is that you can’t fully control the behavior of the “sword.” Nor is it entirely resource-efficient, there’s a limit to the resources that can be allocated to it, and if no turning point is reached in the confrontation, further support yields no additional gains in effectiveness.
The Americans realized early on that many of their interests in this crisis had been achieved and prepared to withdraw. They did what a maritime power usually does when it decides to turn its attention elsewhere as they sailed back to their own region. The main difference between a maritime power and a continental power lies in the freedom to choose where to deploy military forces. A maritime power can choose where to deploy them and launch strikes across various parts of the world’s oceans. This is usually carried out in the form of raids, as large-scale expeditionary campaigns rarely prove successful. The US decided it was time to leave.
But they didn’t want the withdrawal to be accompanied by the collapse of the Ukrainian regime. The US incorporated its withdrawal and the reorientation of its priorities towards East Asia into its policy towards its NATO allies. It handed over responsibility for supporting Ukraine to them and assumed the role of “moderator” as a negotiator who, rather than being the instigator of the crisis, is steering it towards a resolution. US strategic documents state an interest in bringing the Ukraine crisis to an end.
Yet the US behaved treacherously toward both Ukraine and its European allies, saddling them with this burden without warning. The Western Europeans lack military resources, technological capabilities, strategic thinking, and awareness of their own interests comparable to those of the Americans, qualities that enable them to weigh up causes and consequences, to discern what is achievable and what is not by military means, and to identify where their bloc’s interests lie in this crisis.
These Europeans currently have a financial instrument of considerable weight at their disposal, in essence, the only one they can draw upon. They are using it wastefully, given the domestic debt of most major European states is approaching or exceeding 100% of GDP. They can’t obtain external compensation for their military expenditure, and there’s no hope of a Ukrainian victory.
If there were any hope, they would be counting on recouping their losses through Russian resources, through new deals with Russia on new terms. None of these hopes is being realized.
Moreover, due to a lack of strategic experience, lost as a result of American patronage and the nuclear umbrella, these Europeans are beginning to deny their own geography. To deny that Russia is on the continent alongside them.
Geography is a constant, an immutable part of the foreign policy system. Governments and historical circumstances may change, but geography remains unchanged.
The course towards a long-term confrontation with their largest neighbor, a source of many benefits for the Western European economy, which they have now lost, demonstrates the narrowness of their vision. Domestic political processes in the EU suggest that, following the Americans’ example, it is time for these Europeans to reflect on what their interests are, which of these are achievable in the course of the Ukraine crisis, which are not, and what the possible trajectory might be. So far, the Western Europeans haven’t made any good moves.
When there are no good moves, it is better to pass a turn and stop making mistakes. So far, as our President [Vladimir Putin] put it, it looks like a series of mistakes, one after another.
Big spending, little strategic power
Evgeny Kuznetsov: Won’t they get tired of playing this game?
Andrey Sushentsov: Western Europeans states don’t possess the full strategic autonomy enjoyed by Russia and the US, and are not entirely capable of acting collectively from a unified position. Every major decision requires the consensus of nearly 30 countries.
The European Commission doesn’t have a very substantial budget of its own but relies on the budgets of the nation states. Despite the single currency, debt is measured separately for each country.
There is no unified army. It’s a far cry from even the most loosely organized confederation. They would carry strategic weight if they were capable of acting in unison, but there’s no sign of this. Western Europeans are terrified of being directly drawn into a military crisis with Russia. Speculation about sending troops into Ukraine always ends with the caveat that this will only happen once a lasting peace and a ceasefire have been achieved.
In part, their enthusiasm is fueled by what they perceive to be the relatively low cost of supporting Ukraine and this proxy conflict. They have no qualms about Ukraine. They are indifferent to what will become of it, its borders or its population. They express rhetorical outrage, flock to summits, pose for “family photographs,” and make categorical statements. But in essence, this is a gathering of onlookers who are not directly involved in the military crisis.
The tool at their disposal is debt financing at Ukraine’s expense, amounting to nearly $500 billion. An astronomical sum which has failed to deliver the strategically necessary results, whilst worsening their own position. All that money has gone up in smoke.
Russia as the glue holding Europe together
Evgeny Kuznetsov: The EU is not abandoning its plans to impose ever more restrictions on Russia. Incidentally, Brussels has also added you to its sanctions list. At the same time, some European leaders are calling for dialogue with Russia. Is that possible at present?
Andrey Sushentsov: Western Europeans are using the Ukraine crisis as a platform for unity, to become a more cohesive entity. Their strategic lack of autonomy, the prominent role of the Americans, and their internal fragmentation mean that the only platform for solidarity is an anti-Russian one.
The relevance varies from country to country. For Southern Europe, it’s not so obvious. For Spain, despite its anti-Russian government, Palestine and the Middle East are more important. The Baltic states and Northern Europe have an alarmist and militaristic outlook. Some share a border with us. The people in charge are a peculiar lot; one can expect all sorts of things. But no one wants to involve their armed forces in the Ukraine crisis, as North Korea has done on our side.
They are using Ukraine to strengthen their own agency and take steps towards coordinated action. These steps are not particularly effective. However, joint plans are being drawn up and substantial funding is being allocated.
One unresolved issue is the restructuring of the Western European defense industry; it’s fragmented and produces around 15 different types of main battle tank with guns of varying calibers. Standardization is a major and difficult challenge. A catalyst is needed. In other words, they are, to some extent, tackling an internal challenge.
Peace alongside Russia – or a strategic dead end
Evgeny Kuznetsov: Do the NATO Europeans want to sit at the negotiating table with Russia, representing a “united Europe,” in order to compensate for their strategic lack of autonomy?
Andrey Sushentsov: Their tactics for establishing agency include providing financial aid to Ukraine, the theft of Russia’s gold and foreign exchange reserves, the withholding and disposal of revenues, and an attempt to share the blame for this crime amongst everyone. If it’s a crime, then it’s a collective one, so that no single country is held solely responsible. And they are resolving many technical issues.
The US doesn’t resolve such issues, nor does Russia. We can afford to take strategic, autonomous, purposeful and consistent action. These Europeans take a step back, a step forward, two steps back; they look over their shoulders and seek consensus.
It’s in Russia’s interests to invite them to the negotiating table only if it is clear that these Europeans prioritize a stable world on the continent, based on the principle of “peace alongside Russia,” rather than against Russia. The “peace against Russia” approach is inherently unstable and a dead end for Western Europe. It dooms them to fall behind, to strategic defeat, and to never becoming a true player on the world stage. The more internal contradictions there are within the bloc regarding priorities, the more fragile it becomes, and the Russian question is gradually becoming precisely such an issue.
Ukraine’s ‘pyramid of trust’ is crumbling
Evgeny Kuznetsov: You said that the “pyramid of trust” surrounding Ukraine will soon crumble. When will this finally happen?
Andrey Sushentsov: From the Russian perspective, the logic behind this crisis is that we are waging a war to wear down our opponents and deplete their resources. We are targeting their rear lines and breaking their “continental sword.”
We are demonstrating that their strategy is irrelevant; its objectives are unattainable. And the resources they are expending will, over time, be needed in ever-greater quantities. The existing ones are becoming obsolete, as are the systems for utilizing them on Ukrainian territory. They need to be replenished and rebuilt.
Building infrastructure is extremely costly; in wartime conditions, it is simply impossible. In time, Western countries themselves will realize the unviability of this strategy. The opposition within those countries is already openly voicing its outrage and stating that this is a dead end.
[Friedrich] Merz’s visit to Kiev was heavily criticized by the entire opposition, at a time when Germany’s national debt is rising, the chancellor travels to Kiev and once again promises money and resources, essentially at the expense of the German people. The scale of the resources being invested is becoming so significant that the question arises as to what justifies it. What are Berlin’s objectives, what is it achieving, and what is it failing to achieve?
There are increasingly insistent calls for the Ukrainian leadership to take a realistic view of the situation and understand what is achievable and what is not. The “pyramid of trust” is crumbling. One after another, the parties involved are adopting an increasingly detached stance on this issue.
Their primary and secondary hopes have not been realized. Now they are almost left high and dry. We must admit, it was a mistake.
No one wants to take responsibility for it. It has not only a political but also a financial dimension. Who should be held to account for the hundreds of billions of euros spent on a strategically futile venture that has antagonized Russia and undermined security on the continent?
That is why we are talking about a short-term historical perspective. It may come to an end in the coming months, or perhaps in the coming years. But we are not talking about a decade-long war. The point is that this will still remain a crisis with its own distinct phases, and we are currently in the final phase of its resolution.

Regions Calling: More Questions Than Answers After Latest Black Sea Oil Spill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Hello and welcome to Regions Calling, your guide to developments from beyond the Russian capital by The Moscow Times.
In this week’s edition, we are putting the spotlight on the southern Krasnodar region, home to Russia’s vast Black Sea coast, which is reeling from the environmental fallout of a Ukrainian drone attack on a Liberian-flagged Aframax Rio tanker — while officials have offered few details.
For more of the latest news from the regions, subscribe to our biweekly email newsletter here or on Substack.
The Spotlight
On the evening of Oct. 6, apocalyptic photos of a thick plume of smoke rising from the burning sea against a bright dusk sky flooded the Russian internet.
These images showed the result of one of Ukraine’s most successful drone attacks on the energy infrastructure along Russia’s Black Sea coast as the 247-meter, Liberian-flagged Afromax Rio oil tanker had been hit off the shore of the resort city of Sochi.
Environmental specialists were quick to sound the alarm over the fire's potentially catastrophic consequences, saying its ecological impact could exceed that of the massive 2024 spill near the resort city of Anapa, which left beaches coated in heavy fuel oil and mobilized thousands of volunteers.
Two weeks after the attack, as locals find oil-covered birds and pollution builds up along the coast, there are still more questions than answers.
‘Who is responsible?’
“I would be a bad expert if I were to outline the [exact environmental] consequences right now,” one prominent environmentalist told The Moscow Times. “Why? Because it is not known how much oil has spilled as a result of this attack. And that is the main problem.”
Though regional authorities initially denied that the attack had caused an oil spill, Krasnodar Governor Venyamin Kondratyev warned of a potential emergency in Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk one week after the attack.
The regional Emergency Situations Ministry also said it “detected minor oil spills” along the shoreline near Novorossiysk last week, but denied they were linked to the Aframax Rio.
The environmentalist, who requested anonymity for safety reasons, said officials’ reluctance to publicize details of the attack’s environmental impact comes amid mounting evidence of a spill and contradicts Russian legislation that “prohibits classifying information about the environment and environmental pollution.”
The Afromax Rio was towed to Novorossiysk, Russia’s largest Black Sea port, the day after the attack — a move decried by prominent local environmental campaigner Tatiana Tribat, who pointed to the already heavy environmental burden borne by the city.
Satellite images analyzed by Greenpeace showed the damaged vessel leaving an oil slick that covered around 25 square kilometers by Oct. 8.
Independent environmental monitor Prozrachny Mir also dentified an oil slick stretching along the coast from Novorossiysk toward the town of Arkhipo-Osipovka some 70 kilometers (43 miles) south in images dated Oct. 10.
Meanwhile, residents of Novorossiysk, Sochi and smaller coastal towns along the tanker’s route have reported finding oil-covered birds and traces of pollution washing ashore.
“Every day we receive reports [of contamination] from Yuzhnaya Ozereevka, Limanchik, Dyurso and elsewhere. If it wasn’t the Aframax Rio that fouled the coastline, then who is responsible for the pollution?” Tribat told a local newspaper.
A cleansing fire
For coastal residents who remember the Anapa disaster, the images were causes for concern. Yet evidence available from local media and volunteers “suggest that the spill from Afromax Rio was, in fact, significantly smaller” than that disaster, the environmental expert told The Moscow Times.
The Anapa spill happened in December 2024 when two Russian-flagged oil tankers were damaged during a storm, releasing over 9,000 tons of heavy fuel oil, known as mazut, into the Black Sea. Pollution from the spill stretched from annexed Crimea to Georgia, though Russia’s Krasnodar region was hit the worst.
“What we see now is incomparably smaller coastal pollution,” the Russia-based expert said.
“Back then, hundreds — even thousands — of birds were affected. In this instance, the number is in single digits. Back then, about 60 kilometers [37 miles] of coastline was covered in…a continuous strip of fuel oil,” he said.
Though the Afromax Rio can carry up to 100,000 metric tons of oil — nearly 10 times the combined load of the two tankers that caused the 2024 Anapa spill — this leak’s less pronounced impact on the environment is likely the result of the apocalyptic fire documented in the initial images.
“Of course, burning oil pollutes the air, then the combustion products…fall into the sea,” the expert said. “But this amount of damage and consequences are incomparable to what would have happened if all that oil poured out unburnt into the sea.”
The ghost of Anapa
Authorities reopened beaches affected by the 2024 Anapa spill this summer, but the disaster is far from over.
Images analyzed by satellite imagery monitor Sky Eye in July identified a fresh oil slick coming from the sunken bow of the Volgoneft-239 tanker in the Kerch Strait.
Meanwhile, authorities have long denied any ongoing leaks coming from the wreckage — sometimes in statements accompanied by photos of divers emerging from inspections covered in oil.
The consequences of the Afromax Rio spill could be shorter-lived, as some reports suggest authorities have already started pumping the remaining oil out of the tanker.
But the ongoing war in Ukraine, which has seen an escalation in maritime drone activity in recent months, means that a new oil disaster threatening the Black Sea’s ecosystem could be just around the corner.
“In recent months, Ukraine has significantly intensified its attacks on civilian vessels [in Black Sea], including tankers. While there do not appear to have been any major spills…some level of pollution has nonetheless occurred,” the expert said.
“And yet no damage from a military strike can compare to a disaster caused by negligence of officials and vessel operators, corruption and the like — which is precisely what led to the 2024 accident,” he said.
Photo of the Week
Authorities in the Far East port of Vladivostok removed a statue of Nobel Prize-winning writer Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn from the city’s central embankment on Tuesday to relocate it to the city outskirts.
Vladivostok city hall had ordered the Soviet dissident’s statue to be relocated earlier this year after deeming its presence among the warships “inappropriate.”
But just a day later, the 2.5-meter-tall monument reappeared on the embankment after it was found to be too large for its new location. It is unclear if the authorities will proceed with the plan after this week’s mishap.

A Ukrainian national has been arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia. According to federal prosecutors, he allegedly gathered defence-related information.
A Ukrainian national was arrested in Brandenburg on Thursday on suspicion of spying for Russia, the Federal Public Prosecutor's Office in Karlsruhe has announced.
The suspect is alleged to have used contacts within the European defence industry to obtain sensitive information. According to the Federal Prosecutor General's Office, Vadym Y. had been in contact with a Russian intelligence service via an intermediary since at least July 2025.
In connection with the war between Russia and Ukraine, he is said to have obtained militarily relevant information for the service from within Germany. This included, among other things, information on the production of armoured vehicles, ammunition and explosives, as well as personnel and military facilities at sites used to secure NATO's eastern flank.
While some of the information was publicly accessible, the suspect is said to have deliberately obtained other details by approaching individuals working in the European defence industry.
Investigation for acting as an intelligence agent
The Federal Public Prosecutor's Office is responsible for cases that affect Germany's national security and involve suspected espionage on behalf of a foreign power.
The case comes at a time when German security authorities are issuing increasingly stark warnings about suspected Russian espionage and sabotage activities.
Other suspected espionage cases in Germany
As recently as April 2026, Euronews reported on the arrest of a man in Berlin who is alleged to have passed information on Germany's military support for Ukraine, defence companies and military convoys to a Russian intelligence service. Potential targets for sabotage operations are also said to have been involved.
Another case concerns a 53-year-old Ukrainian from Attendorn in North Rhine-Westphalia. According to a ruling by the Federal Court of Justice made public in October, he is accused of having monitored another Ukrainian in a refugee shelter on behalf of Russia's domestic intelligence service FSB and of having passed on information about that person's contacts via Telegram. In this case, charges have now been brought for acting as an intelligence agent.
The cases differ in their specific allegations. However, they illustrate that investigations by German authorities cover both the gathering of military information and the surveillance of individuals who might be of interest to Russia.
Presumption of innocence applies
In the current case in Brandenburg, the investigation is still ongoing. The precise background to the alleged gathering of information and any possible additional accomplices remain to be established. Until a final conviction is reached, the presumption of innocence applies to the accused.

Russia kept sneaking troops through gas pipes behind Ukrainian lines. Now Ukraine has gone more than 15 km underground to do the same to Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:38:50 UTC
22:38:50 KST

Ukraine's Defense Forces advanced more than 15 km through underground utility tunnels into Russia's rear on the Kupiansk axis in Kharkiv Oblast, the Khartiia Corps of Ukraine's National Guard reported on 22 October. The corps called it Operation Veles. The underground advance was paired with attacks on the surface and drone strikes, hitting Russian forces from two directions, the corps told Militarnyi.
Russian troops have repeatedly crawled through gas pipelines around Kupiansk to get behind Ukrainian lines, even after Ukraine reported confident control of the city in February. This time, Ukraine went underground itself. The operation took away Russia's chance to get into Kupiansk's rear, the corps said.
The corps reported more than 30 Russian soldiers captured and Russian losses of more than 100. Militarnyi, citing the unit, put the number of Russian troops killed at over 100.
Khartiia studied how Russian troops moved through pipes before going underground itself, the corps commander, Brigadier General Ihor Obolenskyi, said.
"We watched how the enemy works underground and studied how they do it. The Russians intended to use gas pipelines to get into the rear of our troops. So we went underground ourselves. We anticipated the enemy's actions and mastered the tactics of underground combat," he said.
For the operation, troops trained physically and psychologically to fight in confined spaces, sappers and engineers prepared the underground route, and special communications, navigation, silent logistics, and life-support systems were put in place, Khartiia told Militarnyi. The operation was named after Veles, the Slavic pagan god of the underworld.
Khartiia's brigade, the R.U.H. assault regiment, the Lava drone regiment, the Achilles drone brigade, and units of Ukraine's military intelligence, including the Freedom of Russia Legion and the Russian Volunteer Corps, took part, the corps said.
Russia has used pipelines to infiltrate before
By September 2025, Russian forces had used pipelines to move troops behind Ukrainian lines three times, Ukrainian monitoring project DeepState reported on 12 September 2025. The first was in Avdiivka, the second near Sudzha, and the third near Kupiansk, where groups crossed the Oskil River through a gas pipe.
Near Sudzha in March 2025, Russian special forces walked through a pipeline that until recently had carried Russian gas to Europe, the Associated Press reported. A pro-Kremlin blogger claimed they covered about 15 km and that some spent several days inside.
Russian troops kept using the pipeline near Kupiansk this year. On 27 September, Khartiia's reconnaissance drones recorded Russian forces leading nine civilians, including children, elderly people, and a person on crutches, through the gas pipeline out of the Kupiansk community. Men of military age in civilian clothes walked alongside them, and the corps believes they were Russian soldiers using the group as cover to withdraw. Ukrainian troops held fire because of the civilians, the corps said, adding that the case has been documented for a war crimes investigation.
Why the war is moving underground
Drones, constant surveillance, and AI-assisted targeting have made the battlefield surface transparent and deadly, argue John Spencer, chair of urban warfare studies at West Point's Modern War Institute, and Col. Drew Craig, principal military engineering staff officer at NATO's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. In an August analysis, they write that soldiers in Ukraine describe a "death zone" of some 30 km, where moving above ground can draw an attack within minutes. When firepower makes the surface too dangerous, armies have historically gone underground, as they did in World War I and Vietnam, and more recently in Gaza and Lebanon.
"Armies that cannot survive above ground must adapt below it," the authors write.
Fighting in tunnels brings its own requirements, the authors write: detecting the enemy by sound and vibration, and specialized unmanned systems that cannot rely on GPS or stable radio links. Long stretches underground also take a severe psychological and physical toll on soldiers.
Western militaries are not ready for this, Spencer and Craig write. No NATO partner maintains even general capabilities for large-scale underground warfare, and US and British efforts focused mainly on detecting and clearing tunnels rather than occupying and operating in them.

UK must prepare for infrastructure attacks by hostile states, says Streeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:38:22 UTC
22:38:22 KST

Every Briton is being urged to stock up to nine litres of bottled water and three days’ worth of food in new government guidance designed to ensure that households can survive a weather, cyber or other serious emergency.
The Be Ready campaign is aimed at persuading people to stock up with supplies to last 72 hours, amid growing official concern about the impact of the climate crisis, technological dependency and hostile state threats.
Dan Jarvis, the security minister, said that “those who can follow this advice should follow this advice”. It amounted to “simple steps to be ready for everyday emergencies” as part of a wider, community-oriented effort “to improve our resilience as a nation”, he said.
Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, added that Britain also needed to prepare for the threat of “state-sponsored terrorism” by Russia or other hostile powers targeting everyday infrastructure.
“Terms like ‘hybrid warfare’ and ‘grey zone threats’ do not accurately capture or convey to the general public what I prefer to describe as ‘state-sponsored terrorism’,” he said.
“So in the face of those threats, which are not hypothetical but real, and not somewhere else but increasingly here, we have to step up and take seriously our national resilience as well as our national defence.
“It’s really important that we ask households and businesses, are they prepared? Are they ready? Do they know how they would respond in the event of everyday challenges that might manifest themselves?”
People are advised to keep a ready supply of blankets and cash at home plus a first aid kit, a torch with batteries and a wind-up FM radio. Three litres of water per person per day should be stored for drinking – and more is needed for cooking and washing, the guidance adds.
The government had indicated in August that UK citizens would be told to stock up on tinned food but the Be Ready campaign from the Cabinet Office is more specific. It will be followed up with an advertising campaign on social media and radio.
Stocking up for three days is considered to be a realistic and practical proposal for households and would bring the UK in line with France, the Republic of Ireland and the Netherlands in advising people how to prepare for serious disruption.
Ministers timed the launch of the campaign to come before the winter storm season after a series of intense storms that have battered the UK in recent years. Tens of thousands of homes were left without power in the Midlands, the south-west and Wales after Storm Goretti hit in January, with winds reaching nearly 100mph.
There is also concern about the potential impact of the “super El-Nino”, a global phenomenon that could lead to 2027 being the hottest year ever recorded and uncertain weather patterns, affecting global food supplies and energy systems.
The guidance emerged as 32 UK government websites were taken offline in a precautionary measure in response to the discovery of a security vulnerability in the PHP programming language used by millions of websites around the world.
Britain’s National Cyber Security Centre sent out 50,000 alerts to affected organisations, in a reminder of the high degree of dependency that modern societies have on the internet and other critical technologies.
Spain and Portugal were suddenly left without power for several hours in April 2025, in a cascading failure triggered by voltage instability in the network. About 55 million people were affected in the incident, the worst blackout in Europe in recent memory.
People also need to consider how to respond to hybrid warfare attacks by Russia or other hostile states, including cyber-attacks that could knock out payment systems used by businesses or cause supply chains to collapse, Streeting said.
The minister was speaking at a new tank gun barrel factory in Telford in the West Midlands. The factory, owned by the German manufacturer Rheinmetall, is part of efforts to accelerate rearmament in the face of Russian military threats, but Streeting also emphasised that the public should be prepared for hybrid warfare, or sabotage actions that stop short of outright war.
Russian spy ships have been tracked by the Royal Navy monitoring undersea pipelines and cables that connect the UK to the continent of Europe and elsewhere, raising concerns they could one day be attacked, though this would represent a major escalation by Moscow.
European states have become increasingly vocal about the threat of sabotage efforts by enemies, particularly Russia, which can cause disruption or even directly threaten safety. These efforts have included an explosives-laden drone found next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport in August, and a series of explosions and fires at defence facilities.
Britain has only rarely embarked on public information campaigns, with governments of both parties reluctant to be accused of scaremongering. A 1980 campaign advising people on how to survive a nuclear war, Protect and Survive, advised people how to build a bomb shelter at home and retain enough food for 14 days.

Finns Party unveils €8b cuts list, spares small pensions
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

The Finns Party on Thursday presented its cuts list for the next parliamentary term, amounting to eight billion euros in cuts, plus a further one billion in other measures, including taxes.
The package is the party's plan for meeting the 'debt brake' that the majority of parliamentary parties agreed upon earlier this year. The next government will decide the actual savings in coalition talks after next April's parliamentary elections.
The savings would hit areas such as immigration, social security, the wellbeing services counties and development aid, while small pensions would be spared.
Taxes and pensions
The new levies include a higher tax on data centres as well as a sugar tax. The party would also impose an index brake on pensions above 2,000 euros a month in 2028-2031, with pensions below this threshold spared.
Immigration
"We will address immigration significantly, especially by reforming social security," Finns Party leader Riikka Purra said, adding that the party still wants to make the entire social security system citizenship-based at some point in the future.
The party would also raise income thresholds, restrict social security, end humanitarian immigration, and abolish the refugee quota and municipal integration compensation.
Government and agencies
The party would eradicate Sitra, the Finnish Innovation Fund, which would free up some one billion euros. Purra said this is a capital transfer, not a saving, and the money would go to growth measures and reforming basic education.
"In the spirit of Sitra, the sum would be used for the future of Finns. In other words, for growth measures and especially for reforming basic education," Purra said.
The Ministry of the Environment and the Natural Resources Institute Finland (Luke) would be merged into other state administration, and the National Agency for Education abolished, saving 10 million euros.
Public broadcaster Yle would lose 200 million, and its index linkage would be removed.
Development aid
Parliamentary group leader Jani Mäkelä said development cooperation would end entirely.
"New commitments will be ended and existing commitments will be terminated as far as is possible, however, within the coming parliamentary term."
Support for Ukraine, crisis aid and disaster relief would be unaffected.
