A man passes by the building of Türkiye's central bank in Ankara, Türkiye, on Oct. 22, 2026. Türkiye's central bank cut its benchmark policy rate by 100 basis points to 36 percent on Thursday, resuming monetary easing for the first time since January as inflation continued to cool. (Mustafa Kaya/Handout via Xinhua)
ANKARA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Türkiye's central bank cut its benchmark policy rate by 100 basis points to 36 percent on Thursday, resuming monetary easing for the first time since January as inflation continued to cool.
The latest cut follows a previous 100-basis-point cut to 37 percent earlier this year.
The bank said in its statement that "despite monthly fluctuations, recent inflation figures and leading indicators confirm the deceleration in the underlying trend of inflation."
Yet it cautioned that "elevated energy prices due to ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to pose an upside risk to the inflation outlook", signaling a careful approach to future policy.
Türkiye's annual inflation eased to 29.73 percent in September, marking a fourth straight month of slowing price growth. The relief, analysts say, provides some support for businesses burdened by high borrowing costs.
Despite this progress, economic challenges persist. The government recently raised its year-end inflation forecast from 16 percent to 28.4 percent, citing the economic fallout of the conflict in the Middle East.
As a major energy importer, Türkiye has struggled with persistently high inflation in recent years, though annual inflation has fallen substantially from its peak of 85.5 percent in late 2022. ■

Reviewing internal documents from Germany's armed forces, Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported that this is the military's second-highest threat classification.
"We are noting that we face a significant sabotage threat overall for [Germany's armed forces]," said a defense ministry spokesperson, according to Reuters.
Germany's reclassification of Russian threats comes as experts warn Russia is testing how far it can push Europe without triggering open war — from drones crossing NATO airspace to sabotage and cyberattacks across the continent. Europe has strengthened its defenses since 2022, but key gaps remain, including in air defense, communications, intelligence, and joint command, experts say.
On Oct. 5, Martin Jaeger, head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, told lawmakers that Germany is in a "shadow war" with Russia and risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Moscow.

Across China: From embroidery to tourism, SW China's Yunnan turns ethnic traditions into opportunities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:26:05 CST
22:26:05 KST

KUNMING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- On a warm afternoon, 63-year-old Yi woman Pu Lianying sat in a community workshop, embroidering pink peonies onto black velvet and chatting with friends. Occasionally, tourists stopped by to browse embroidered decorations displayed on a table.
The workshop is in Lianjiang Community in Eshan Yi Autonomous County, Yuxi City, southwest China's Yunnan Province, where residents of different ethnic groups, including Yi, Hani and Hui, live side by side.
In 2021, several old residential compounds were combined into a modern community with improved public spaces and facilities. The local women's federation helped establish a Yi embroidery workshop, giving residents a place to socialize while keeping traditional craftsmanship alive.
Yi embroidery, a traditional skill passed down through generations of the Yi ethnic group, is on China's national intangible cultural heritage list. The workshop brings in recognized inheritors to teach residents, who can choose from traditional designs and smaller contemporary products. Last year, Eshan County sold 40,000 Yi embroidery products, generating about 5 million yuan (about 744,000 U.S. dollars) in income for local residents, said Bai Xuemei, head of the county women's federation.
"I enjoy coming here to embroider and chat with my friends," Pu said, pointing to a half-finished traditional cloth used by Yi women to carry babies. Last year, she sold 10 pieces, earning 1,600 yuan per piece.
The community's efforts to improve residents' lives extend beyond the embroidery workshop.
Li Tianrong, a Han official who heads the subdistrict office administering Lianjiang Community, has learned the Yi language to communicate more easily with elderly residents. The community canteen regularly serves braised beef, a favorite among Yi residents, as well as other popular dishes for older people.
Revenue from renting out community-owned shops helps subsidize the canteen, where residents can enjoy a hearty meal for just 14 yuan. Older residents receive discounts and can even have meals delivered to their homes.
From helping residents preserve traditional crafts to making daily life more convenient, communities across Yunnan are finding various ways to meet local needs and boost livelihoods. Home to 26 ethnic groups, the province is turning traditional skills into specialty products and tourism experiences.
In Jinglai Village in Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture, near the China-Myanmar border, local residents are working with businesses to bring traditional crafts and arts to a wider audience.
One attraction is slow-wheel pottery, a traditional Dai craft on the national intangible cultural heritage list. Unlike modern electric wheels, the hand-operated wheel turns slowly, requiring artisans to shape the clay through repeated tapping and careful adjustment. The finished pottery retains visible layers of clay, giving it a distinctive rustic appearance.
"Our pottery-making skills have been passed down through generations. My mother made the pots and jars we used at home," said Yu Xianglun, a Dai inheritor of the craft. "Now that our pottery has a market, the craft will not be lost."
Visitors can also try traditional sugar-making by pushing a long bamboo pole around a wooden pivot to squeeze juice from sugarcane. Some are eager to drink the fresh juice before it is boiled down into sugar.
Jinglai Village has brought together over 20 traditional artisans who demonstrate more than 10 crafts, including bamboo weaving and traditional liquor brewing. The scenic area provides monthly subsidies of 1,500 to 3,000 yuan to help artisans continue their work.
This approach is helping preserve cultural traditions while boosting tourism. From January to September in 2026, the village received more than 100,000 visitors and generated over 1.85 million yuan in total tourism revenue, said Yan Wenxiang, Party chief of Jinglai Village.
Across Yunnan, cultural traditions are closely intertwined with everyday life, as people from different ethnic groups live side by side, share experiences and build bonds while maintaining their customs.
Liu Zhen, a guide at the Yunnan Nationalities Museum, knows this firsthand. Born in the 1990s, she grew up in Dehong Dai and Jingpo Autonomous Prefecture, where different ethnic groups live side by side.
For Liu, ethnic diversity was not abstract but part of daily life. Her wardrobe held traditional Yi and Hani clothing, and she joined Jingpo friends in dancing at their festivals. When her legs ached after exercise, her father would take her to a Dai neighbor for herbal remedies.
Today, Liu brings that childhood familiarity with different cultures to her work at the museum. She invites visitors to dance to traditional music, experience local festivals and enjoy well-known Dai songs.
When visitors ask which ethnic group she belongs to, Liu has a ready answer. "I belong to the Chinese nation, a big family where 56 ethnic groups love and care for each other." ■

UK teachers' union slams IHRA definition push in schools
The leader of the UK's largest education union has strongly criticised a recommendation for schools across England to adopt the controversial International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition of antisemitism, warning that it risks silencing legitimate criticism of Israel and stifling classroom discussions about the Gaza genocide.
Daniel Kebede, general secretary of the National Education Union (NEU), condemned the proposal as the "wrong approach", arguing that the contested definition could further restrict freedom of expression on Palestine by blurring the distinction between antisemitism and criticism of Israeli government policies.
His criticism followed the publication of Sir David Bell's independent review into antisemitism in schools, which recommended that educational institutions adopt the IHRA definition, despite longstanding concerns from civil liberties groups and academics about its implications for political speech.
The government has accepted all 27 recommendations in the review, with Education Secretary Lucy Powell announcing plans to write to educational institutions urging them to adopt the definition.
In a statement on Wednesday, Kebede warned that the recommendation could exacerbate the very problems it was intended to address, leaving teachers uncertain about how to discuss Israel's actions in Gaza without facing accusations of antisemitism.
"The IHRA’s contested framing risks blurring the line between antisemitism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government and the genocide in Gaza, leaving teachers with uncertainty when they need clarity," Kebede wrote.
"A young person’s opposition to the Gaza genocide and scrutiny of the Israeli government are not, in themselves, antisemitic."
The IHRA definition has faced sustained criticism over its accompanying examples relating to Israel, which opponents argue risk conflating anti-Zionism and legitimate criticism of Israeli state policies with antisemitism.
Many have warned that its adoption by public institutions can create a chilling effect on freedom of expression, particularly when discussions concern Israel's occupation of Palestinian territories, its treatment of Palestinians and its military campaign in Gaza.
Kebede warned that promoting the definition in schools could deepen this chilling effect, discouraging teachers from addressing the Gaza genocide and preventing pupils from engaging openly with one of the most contentious political issues of recent years.
He also raised concerns that restricting classroom discussions could push young people towards unsafe online spaces to explore issues they feel unable to raise at school.
"Recommending the IHRA definition risks tightening the chilling grip already stifling classroom discussion of the Gaza genocide. Schools need practical support to confront antisemitism, not a contested framework that risks shutting down legitimate discussion," Kebede said.
He also rejected suggestions that teachers were failing to uphold their responsibilities when addressing politically sensitive issues.
"This report will not tackle antisemitism. It wrongly calls into question the professionalism of teachers. The existing rules on impartiality in the classroom are very clear and teachers take that responsibility very seriously."
While welcoming "a strengthened focus on antisemitism" and acknowledging an increase in antisemitic incidents following the outbreak of the Gaza war in 2023, Kebede urged the Department for Education to "go a step further" by strengthening efforts to tackle all forms of racism.
His intervention highlighted concerns that adopting a disputed definition could undermine efforts to combat antisemitism by creating confusion over the boundaries between racial or religious hatred and legitimate political expression.
Government backs contested definition
The Bell review sets out 27 recommendations aimed at tackling antisemitism in schools, including calls for education unions to establish robust policies and procedures and ensure their members receive adequate training to recognise and respond to antisemitic incidents.
It also recommends that allegations of antisemitism involving trade union officials, representatives or members be addressed consistently under existing union policies on racism and prejudice.
Bell said reports from Jewish organisations and teachers highlighted concerns that some activities within education unions had become increasingly "politicised" on issues including the Israel-Palestine conflict.
However, the recommendation to promote the IHRA definition has brought renewed attention to longstanding objections that its examples concerning Israel could be used to police political speech rather than simply identify antisemitic prejudice.
The controversy centres on the risk that teachers and pupils could feel pressured to avoid legitimate discussions of Israeli government policies for fear that their comments might be interpreted as antisemitic.
Addressing the House of Commons, Powell defended the government's response to the review.
"All children and teachers should be able to go to school or college free from fear," she said.
She added that schools and colleges would receive further support on discussing "controversial and sensitive" issues and geopolitical events in an informed and impartial manner.
Bell, who led the independent review, also acknowledged the importance of allowing pupils to discuss Israel's military campaign in Gaza without experiencing "prejudice or hatred".
In an interview with the Press Association, he said it was "not good enough" that some teachers and pupils felt conversations about the conflict were "too difficult to touch" when the subject arose in classrooms.
He decided against recommending an outright ban on teachers and pupils wearing political symbols or flags, describing such a measure as "unworkable" and "untested legally".
However, he suggested that individual schools and colleges could use existing staff and pupil codes of conduct to establish rules governing what could be worn.
Education leaders, rights groups divided over proposals
Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders (ASCL), told The New Arab that the review had offered "clearer guidance and practical support for schools and colleges".
He said it could help teachers navigate discussions about complex and divisive political issues.
"Antisemitism, like all forms of discrimination, is utterly unacceptable and abhorrent," he told The New Arab.
"Unfortunately, there are differing views on what may or may not constitute antisemitism and what is a legitimate expression of views over the conflict between Israel and Palestine."
He added: "Schools and colleges are often caught in the middle of divisive issues and find themselves having to navigate between strongly held opinions on either side of an argument."
Di’Iasio stressed that "schools and colleges already robustly protect children and young people from all forms of racism, bullying, and harassment".
He said they complied with strict legal obligations prohibiting the promotion of partisan political views and added that "they take this responsibility extremely seriously".
Meanwhile, Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said that while it was commendable that the review aimed “to strengthen safeguarding, training and reporting” across the education sector, concrete action was needed to tackle all forms of racism.
Echoing the NEU’s position, Jakens said the latest proposal to adopt the IHRA definition across schools in England was “the wrong answer”.
“Protecting Jewish pupils and protecting free speech are not in conflict. We need both,” he told The New Arab.
“Amnesty and more than 100 organisations have warned that this definition has been used to stifle debate and silence people speaking up for Palestinian rights.”
Citing Amnesty International UK's latest report, published on Tuesday, which documented cases of UK universities allegedly suppressing pro-Palestinian solidarity among students and academics, Jakens warned that “schools must not go the same way”.
The report highlighted restrictions on expressions of solidarity with Palestinians, including chanting, clapping and wearing keffiyehs. Amnesty UK also documented repercussions faced by university students and academics, including suspensions, campus bans and threats to their visa status.
"Young people are already seeing these issues on their phones every day, on platforms that are failing to tackle hate. If they can’t ask questions at school, they’ll find answers in the darkest corners of the internet instead, and that is exactly where antisemitism thrives," Jakens told TNA.
"The answer to hate is education, not silence.”
Editor's note: This article has been amended to include comments from Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK's director of campaigns at 18:00 on Thursday, 22 October 2026.

Macron was right, and the scapegoats were chosen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:25:27 UTC
22:25:27 KST

Emmanuel Macron’s phrase landed like a cracked whip in the stale air of Western politics. “As unacceptable as they are stupid.” The target was not immigration policy, but a lie — the claim, amplified by Donald Trump and a chorus of right-wing figures, that Muslim migrants had set France alight. The protests that swept Paris, Lyon and Marseille were not a civilisational invasion.
They were a cry about grocery bills, overcrowded classrooms and a state that had cut 4,000 teaching posts while fuel prices climbed. Macron’s fury was therefore more than a defence of immigrants. It was a rejection of the most durable political technology of the age: the conversion of economic failure into cultural panic.
The mechanics are almost elegant in their cynicism. When wages stagnate, and public services buckle, the scapegoat is not the tax code or the corporate margin. It is the most visible minority. Trump told Macron to “close your borders and take control before it is too late”. The facts said otherwise.
More than half a million people marched — students, trade unionists, farmers — against the cost of living and the decay of public provision. The violence was real, but the culprits were not a religious category. They were a political economy that has spent four decades redistributing risk downward while protecting wealth upward.
The digital architecture of 2026 has made this old manoeuvre infinitely more potent. AI-generated images of an elderly couple “stripped and robbed,” of a Palestinian flag atop the Eiffel Tower, of “hordes” storming French streets, accumulated millions of views in hours. Macron named the mechanism precisely: foreign leaders, some mid-election campaign, “naively repeat AI-generated content or spread narratives that certain circles are clearly trying to promote”.
The grammar of the “Muslim threat” is centuries old; the delivery system is new. What once required a pamphlet or a tabloid now requires a prompt and an algorithm optimised for outrage.
READ: Macron says France to deploy forces to protect Saudi oil export port
Against this manufactured panic sits an empirical reality that is almost impolite to state.
The OECD finds that 77 per cent of immigrants across its member states are economically active, and that migration attenuates labour shortages in ageing societies.
Bruegel’s 2025 analysis is blunter still: with fertility rates unlikely to rebound, “continuingly high positive net-migration levels” are the only route to mitigate the economic effects of ageing, and inward migration can deliver a positive net contribution to public finances.
In Spain, the net annual fiscal contribution of the average immigrant has been estimated at some €1,600 more than the native-born, while costing the treasury 32 per cent less. The scapegoat, in other words, is subsidising the very state that is being told to fear him.
France’s security apparatus tells a more troubling story about how the panic is institutionalised. The FSPRT file — the register of suspected Islamist radicalisation — contained some 15,800 individuals as of late 2024. The database does not measure crime; it measures risk, and risk is a category that expands to fill the political demand for it. When a state can see a population through the lens of pre-emptive suspicion while remaining structurally blind to the socioeconomic composition of a protest, it has perfected a form of strategic unknowing.
The Muslim is legible as a suspect, illegible as a citizen with a grievance. That asymmetry is not a bug in the liberal state. It is a feature of how the liberal state has learned to govern insecurity.
This is where the global conversation must resist the imported script — and recognise that the script is no longer imported at all. It is written simultaneously in every major democracy.
In the United States, Gallup found in June 2026 that 73 per cent of Americans still see immigration as a good thing, and that the share wanting less immigration had fallen from a peak of 55 per cent in 2024 to 30 per cent — yet the political class continues to behave as if the opposite were true.
In Europe, the Transatlantic Trends survey records that 47 per cent of Europeans and 50 per cent of Americans see immigration as more of a problem than an opportunity, with the divide sharpest among those without a secondary education and those who have no personal contact with migrants. In Berlin, where 85 per cent of households rent, advertised rents have nearly doubled since 2014, and the far-right AfD has converted the housing crisis into an argument for restricting immigration, reaching around 17 per cent in city polling.
In Canada, Nanos Research found 52 per cent of respondents favour admitting fewer immigrants and temporary residents, with housing shortages, strained public services and the cost of living cited as the drivers — even as population growth slowed sharply. The proximate grievances are real and material: housing scarcity, wage stagnation, underfunded hospitals and schools.
But the moment those grievances are translated into a cultural threat narrative. These solutions might actually work — denser cities, a functioning care economy, a tax base that funds public infrastructure, sectoral bargaining that lifts wages — are displaced by a politics of exclusion that leaves the underlying failure untouched and the underlying distribution of power intact. The scapegoat is not a misunderstanding of the crisis. It is a substitute for solving it.
READ: France summons Iranian ambassador over alleged disinformation on student protests
The far-right playbook now travels with a translation layer. The Guardian documented nationalist parties from the National Rally to Vox to Chega seizing on the same European unrest, each converting a housing or cost-of-living protest into evidence of “anarchic immigration” or an “uncontrolled influx”. The script is modular. Only the cast changes.
Macron’s own record is compromised. His governments have passed anti-separatism laws that Muslim civil society experienced as a targeted gaze, and his defence of French Muslims against foreign slander sits awkwardly beside domestic policies that have often treated Islamic practice as a problem to be administered. That contradiction matters, because it reveals the deeper trap.
The liberal centre condemns the crudest scapegoating while maintaining a softer, more respectable version of the same logic: integration as cultural erasure, security as a permanent suspicion. The choice is not between Trump’s panic and Macron’s laïcité. It is between a politics that names the real sources of anger and one that keeps looking for a minority to absorb it.
The lesson is not that immigration is costless or that every grievance is economic. It is that the political economy of scapegoating is now more profitable than the political economy of repair. A party that blames a migrant for a hospital queue need not explain why the hospital was starved of capital. A leader who warns of an Islamist takeover need not account for the energy shock, the fiscal squeeze or the algorithmic amplification that turned a local protest into a civilisational melodrama.
The costs of that evasion are not borne by the scapegoater. They are borne by the Muslim family in a Paris banlieue, the asylum seeker in a Mediterranean detention centre, the working-class neighbourhood in Ohio or Saxony told that its neighbours are the cause of its decline. They are borne by every community invited to trade solidarity for suspicion, and by every democracy that discovers, too late, that the anger it mobilised cannot be contained by the institutions it hollowed out.
Macron’s word — stupid — was undiplomatic and precise. It named an intelligence failure disguised as a political strategy. The task for policymakers is to make that strategy expensive. That means provenance and transparency in digital information, so that fabricated images carry a cost. It means fiscal and industrial policy that makes migration’s contribution visible in the public ledger, not merely in think-tank working papers. It means a security architecture capable of distinguishing suspicion from citizenship.
And it means a political language that treats the cost-of-living crisis as a crisis of distribution, not of demography. The scapegoat is a substitute for argument. The only antidote is the argument itself — conducted with the courage to name who actually benefits when the crowd is pointed at the wrong gate.

Israel’s Religious Zionists campaign for more land and war – RT reports (VIDEO)
Politicians advocating for annexation and further military operations could decide Israel’s next government despite holding only a handful of parliamentary seats, RT correspondent Charlotte Dubenskij reports.
With 37 parties competing for the Knesset’s 120 seats on October 27, Israel’s proportional representation system gives smaller factions leverage in coalition negotiations.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud faces rivals including Avigdor Lieberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, Gadi Eisenkot’s centrist Yashar, and Yair Golan’s left-leaning Democrats. In her report, Dubenskij examines the Religious Zionist Party (RZP), which currently holds seven seats and is led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
Smotrich has called for territory as far as the Yellow Line in Gaza and the Litani River in Lebanon to be annexed. His ambitions also extend to the occupied West Bank, which he calls Judea and Samaria.
“I think we need to go to war in Judea and Samaria, do there what we did in Gaza, dismantle the Palestinian Authority, which is a terrorist authority,” he said on a podcast in September.
The minister has also advocated for taking all of Gaza for “Zionist and security reasons” and described withholding food and water from its population until hostages were returned as potentially “just and moral.”
Fellow party candidates Zvi Sukkot and Orit Strook have taken similar positions, advocating for more hostility, expanding Israeli settlements, and taking over territories controlled by the Palestinian Authority.
The election comes amid continuing Israeli attacks in Gaza and southern Lebanon, along with escalating settler violence in the West Bank. Recent olive-harvest attacks have targeted Palestinian farmers, European diplomats, and American photojournalist Heidi Levine.
Dubenskij examines how a party with just seven seats could help shape the next coalition and its policies.

Ukrainians have selected the &quot;landmark publications of independence&quot; — which book took first place, and which won the readers’ choice award
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:22:05 EEST
22:22:05 KST

Ukrainians have selected the "landmark publications of independence" — which book took first place, and which won the readers’ choice award
Kyiv • UNN
Illarion Pavliuk’s psychological thriller won the readers’ vote in a project marking the 35th anniversary of Independence. It received the greatest support among 100 entries.
In Ukraine, the results were announced for the project "Iconic Publications of Independence: 35 Books We Choose Together," dedicated to the 35th anniversary of the restoration of independence. First place in the readers’ vote went to Illarion Pavliuk’s psychological thriller "I See You’re Interested in the Dark," UNN reports, citing the Ukrainian Book Institute.
Details
The voting lasted from September 7 to October 6. Readers selected between 1 and 35 books and publishing series from a longlist of 100 entries, which had previously been compiled by 40 experts in literature, culture, and media.
A total of 168,889 votes were cast based on the results of the voting.
Which books Ukrainians chose as iconic
As reported by the Ukrainian Book Institute, the final list brought together different genres, generations of authors, and ways of reflecting on our shared experience. It included contemporary novels, including genre fiction, works about the war, historical memory, and Ukrainian identity, poetry collections, nonfiction, and foundational editions of classics.
The strong demand for contemporary genre literature is evidenced by the leading position of Illarion Pavliuk’s novel, which ranked first in the readers’ vote. The finalists also included Pavlo Derevianko’s trilogy "The Chronicle of the Gray Order," Maks Kidruk’s series "The New Dark Ages," and Andrii Sem’iankiv’s medical thriller "Dancing with Bones."
Books devoted to Ukrainian history and culture and to rethinking the past occupy a prominent place on the list. These include "The Case of Vasyl Stus" by Vakhtang Kipiani, "The Gates of Europe" by Serhii Plokhii, "Language-Sword" by Yevheniia Kuznietsova, and "Revolt Against the Empire: The Ukrainian Sixtiers" by Radomyr Mokryk.
Readers also placed considerable emphasis on book series that reveal Ukraine’s literary heritage and return important prose and poetic works to cultural circulation. The shortlist included collections of works by Vasyl Stus, Lesia Ukrainka, and Taras Shevchenko, as well as series of Ukrainian classics that bring renewed attention not only to canonical texts but also to works that had not previously been actively published.
Several authors secured more than one place on the shortlist: Serhii Zhadan (3 entries), Oksana Zabuzhko (2 entries as an author and 1 as an editor), Lina Kostenko (2 entries), Yevheniia Kuznietsova (2 entries), and Ivan Malkovych (1 entry as an author and 4 as the editor of book series).

Readers’ Choice Award: How Ukrainians Voted in Diia
A separate component of the project was a poll in the Diia app dedicated to landmark Ukrainian books published in 2022–2026. As part of this nomination, users chose the book that, in their opinion, deserved a special readers’ choice award from among 15 nominated publications.
The winner was “The Colony” by Maksym Kidruk, which received 23% (14,052) of the votes.
In total, 60,596 Diia users cast their votes. The full results are available in the Diia app. The special nomination provided an additional opportunity to engage a broad audience in a conversation about Ukrainian books that appeared during the full-scale war.
In total, 229,485 votes were cast in the two polls.

Context
"Landmark Publications of Independence: 35 Books We Choose Together" — a joint project of MEGOGO BOOKS and the Ukrainian Book Institute dedicated to the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s Independence. During the project’s first stage, 40 experts from the fields of literature, culture, and media compiled a longlist of 100 books and publishing series published between 1991 and 2026. During the second stage, which lasted from September 7 to October 6, Ukrainians voted for publications from the longlist, selecting between 1 and 35 entries. Based on the results of the readers’ vote, a shortlist of 34 publications and publishing series was formed.
Within the project, a book or series was considered landmark if it had a lasting impact on readers or society: becoming a subject of conversations and discussions, helping to rethink history and identity, returning important names and topics to public discourse, influencing the development of the Ukrainian language and culture, or becoming part of the shared experience of an entire generation.

Tsahkna: the stronger Ukraine is, the less leverage Russia has to dictate the terms of peace

“Russia has not abandoned its objectives and continues to attack Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure as the country faces another difficult winter. PURL, or the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List, is a NATO-coordinated initiative through which European Allies and Canada fund the procurement of weapons for Ukraine from the United States. It is one of the most effective ways for Allies to channel financial support towards purchasing weapons Ukraine needs urgently, particularly air defence systems and ammunition. NATO coordinates the delivery of this assistance to Ukraine.

A court in Ohrid has acquitted two men accused of severely beating Hristiyan Pendikov, secretary of a Bulgarian cultural club in the city, ruling that neither their responsibility for the assault nor an ethnic motive had been proven.
The decision by the Basic Court in Ohrid comes more than three years after the attack and follows a ruling by the Court of Appeal in Bitola that sent the case back to the first-instance court.
The hearing lasted around two and a half hours, with no additional evidence presented. The court concluded that the charges against the two defendants, Borche Angelov and Iliya Spaseski, had not been substantiated and that an ethnic motive could not be established.
Pendikov’s legal team strongly criticized the reversal, noting that the same judge had previously sentenced both defendants to eight months in prison for inflicting grievous bodily harm.
“For us, it is indisputable that the act was committed for ethnic reasons. Throughout the entire trial, no other facts or evidence emerged to suggest any other motive,” lawyer Stefan Kamishevski said.
Kamishevski explained that Pendikov’s lawyers cannot appeal the acquittal themselves, leaving the decision to challenge it with the Public Prosecutor’s Office, which is expected to appeal to a higher court.
Pendikov expressed outrage after hearing the verdict.
“I am ashamed of this verdict. To hand down an acquittal in the face of all the video evidence presented is shameful and disgraceful. With this ruling, the court is giving the green light for anyone who identifies as Bulgarian in [North] Macedonia to be beaten with impunity - without anyone facing any consequences,” he said.
Pendikov added that the attack on January 19, 2023, had been followed by three years of daily harassment, insults and slander targeting him and his family. He argued that countries that fail to uphold human dignity and the rule of law have no place in the European Union.
Members of the Bulgarian Parliament attended the hearing to show their support for Pendikov.

The number of Americans filing first-time claims for unemployment benefits fell by 6,000 to 194,000 last week, below market expectations, according to US Labor Department data released Thursday.
Market expectations for initial jobless claims were 200,000 for the week ending Oct. 17.
The previous week’s figure was revised up by 1,000 to 200,000 from 199,000.
The four-week moving average, which smooths out weekly volatility, declined by 1,000 to 197,750.
Continuing claims, which reflect the number of people already receiving unemployment benefits, rose by 25,000 to 1.728 million in the week ending Oct. 10.
The previous week’s continuing claims figure was revised down by 7,000 to 1.703 million.

The seasonally adjusted insured unemployment rate remained unchanged at 1.1% for the week ending Oct. 10.
In September, the US economy added just 29,000 nonfarm jobs, well below forecasts of 90,000, according to an earlier Bureau of Labor Statistics report.
The unemployment rate rose to 4.2% in September from 4.1% in August.

The Ministry of Education and Research is implementing additional security measures starting Thursday in response to critical software vulnerabilities to ensure the security of the Moodle learning platform and the data processed within it.
The Moodle learning platform will be temporarily shut down starting Thursday until the necessary security updates have been installed and their effectiveness verified.
The ministry emphasized that ensuring the security of the learning platform and the data it contains is its top priority.
"The temporary shutdown of Moodle is a preventive measure aimed at avoiding potential data leaks, damage to the learning platform and resulting prolonged disruptions," the Ministry of Education and Research added.
The ministry said it understands that the temporary shutdown may cause inconvenience to users and is working with technical partners to implement the necessary security updates as quickly as possible.
Normal operations will resume once the necessary security updates have been installed and their effectiveness verified. A separate announcement will be made when Moodle reopens.

Trump's approval rating on economy hits all-time low as midterm looms: CNBC survey
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:18:36 UTC
22:18:36 KST

With less than two weeks to go before the congressional elections, Americans are nearly as gloomy about the economy as they were when the nation was emerging from the pandemic, and President Donald Trump's economic approval rating is hitting an all-time low, according to the latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey.
Eight out of 10 Americans rate the economy as fair or poor, the highest number since December 2023 and one of several ominous signs for Republicans in the new polling data released Thursday that show why their candidates are facing an uphill battle in the midterm.
Downbeat views on the economy are most intense among Democrats and independents, but there's been a strong move toward economic pessimism even among Republicans in recent months. Overall, 63% of the public is pessimistic about the current state of the economy and the outlook, up 1 percentage point from the July survey. But that percentage now includes 35% of Republicans, up 6 points from July and the highest level of Republican pessimism of either of Trump's two terms.
"We got there not because of independents or Democrats getting more sour — it's because Republicans have," said Micah Roberts, partner at Public Opinion Strategies, the Republican pollster for the survey. "Since Trump has been president, [Republicans] have held on to a small margin saying that the current economy is either excellent or good. And now that has kind of broken and changed."
The survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1%, found Americans preferring Democratic control of Congress by a 52% to 45% margin. The 7 percentage point Democratic edge represents a 3 percentage point gain for Democrats from the July survey.
The poll contained other foreboding signs for Republicans as well. It showed 72% of Democrats highly interested in the midterm election on Nov. 3, compared with just 62% of Republicans. Women are 10 percentage points more interested in the election than men, and they prefer Democratic control of Congress by 22 points. Independents prefer Democratic control by a wide 49% to 33% margin. And the majority of survey respondents said Democrats would do a better job than Republicans on many of the issues they singled out as their top concerns, including corruption and the cost of food and gas.
Read the full survey results here.
In the eight states with competitive Senate races, respondents prefer Democratic congressional control by 4 percentage points. Trump carried those eight states by a combined 10 points in the 2024 presidential election.
The survey shows "things moving either away from Republicans or toward Democrats, depending how you want to look at it, in a way that would make me very nervous if I was leading Republican campaigns leading into these last two weeks," said Jay Campbell, partner at Hart Associates, the Democratic pollster for the poll.
Despite the economic gloom, Trump's overall approval rating has remained stable, though at just 40% approving and 59% disapproving. His current net approval of -19 percentage points compares with -8 a year ago.
More striking is the sharp 9-point drop in the president's net economic approval rating from just the last survey in July. The president's economic approval fell to 34% from 38% in three months and disapproval rose to 65% from 60%. The net -31 economic approval is the lowest of either of Trump's two terms. The 65% disapproval rating is 1 percentage point higher than former President Joe Biden's worst showing and the highest for any president surveyed by CNBC going back to President Barack Obama.
Government corruption was identified as the top concern by 36% of respondents, and Democrats hold a 4-point lead on addressing the issue. On the cost of food and groceries, the second-most important issue, the Democratic lead widened to +16 from +7 in the July survey. Democrats also topped Republicans on protecting democracy as well as dealing with the high price of gas.
Among those most interested in the election are respondents who identify corruption and protecting democracy as top issues, and they prefer Democratic congressional control by wide margins.
Republicans continued to hold a strong advantage on border security and immigration, but the lead on immigration fell to +9 from +15. Democrats, meanwhile, are seen as better at handling the issues of jobs and unemployment and Iran, which flipped from +2 for Republicans to +5 for Democrats.
The public continued to be skeptical of the value of the Iran war. The survey found just 46% of the public believe the military action was worth it to disrupt development of Iran's nuclear capabilities, down from a 53% majority in April. And just 35% say the military action was worth it given the rise in the price of gasoline.
While the survey showed continued deep divisions by party, there was near unity on the corruption issue. Ninety-three percent said elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, should not be allowed to personally own or trade stocks in individual companies that have contracts with the federal government. And 89% said companies owned by or invested in by a sitting president's immediate family members should not be allowed to receive contracts from the federal government.
While corruption was a top issue, prices are clearly top of mind for registered voters. Taken together, concern about the cost of food, gas and housing is the top concern for 57% of respondents. Eighty percent say prices are rising, up 5 percentage points from a year ago, with 55% saying they are rising faster than usual, also up 5 points. The cost of food actually eclipses gas as a greater concern in the survey 34% to 23%. It's a top worry among most major demographic groups but is most elevated among those making $30,000 or less and supporters of the agenda of Democratic Socialists of America. Yet it's also the top issue for those Republicans who don't count themselves as MAGA supporters.
Both pollsters were cautious about how extensive Democratic gains could be. Roberts from POS said it's a battle between "the map and momentum."
"There are several indications nationally that the electorate is tilting more toward Democrats … but the movement is also fairly concentrated, each party's base is consolidating, and a 'big change' is dependent on Democrats flipping a lot of districts and states that Trump won handily just two years ago," he said.
Campbell doesn't see a "realignment" election like in 1994 and 2008, saying, "This looks like a return to the mean—young voters and voters of color returning to the Democratic fold, bolstered by independents being fed up with Trumpenomics." He adds, "At no point did anyone expect that Democratic candidates would suddenly pull 15% of the Republican vote."

Interpol arrests over 1,400 suspects across Africa in $105M cybercrime crackdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:17:59 UTC
22:17:59 KST

Andrew Wasike 
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Interpol arrested at least 1,462 people across Africa in an operation which led to the recovery of $105 million in illicit funds, it said Thursday.
"Cybercrime networks operate without regard for borders, exploiting technology to target victims on an unprecedented scale," Interpol's Director of Cybercrime Neal Jetton said in a statement.
The criminal activities linked to these individual led to more than $385 million in losses, it said.
The operation, conducted between June 29 and Aug. 31 under the name Serengeti III, involved law enforcement agencies from 21 countries and resulted in the disruption of 10,909 malicious networks.
Nearly 66,000 victims identified
Investigators identified nearly 66,000 victims of cybercriminal activities involving online investment scams, ransomware, digital extortion and fraudulent business communications.
In Uganda, police dismantled two international fraud operations and arrested 365 foreign nationals accused of targeting victims in Asia through elaborate investment and pension scams.
The suspects operated call centers where workers used prepared scripts, counterfeit investment websites and fraudulent trading platforms to convince victims, including pensioners, to invest in nonexistent financial opportunities.
In Angola, authorities shut down two illegal cryptocurrency mining facilities, arrested nine suspects and confiscated more than 2,000 mining devices.
Police also seized six unauthorized electrical installations, with the confiscated power infrastructure alone valued at more than $1 million.
In Nigeria, investigators arrested a suspect accused of operating a large-scale phishing scheme that collected software login credentials and approximately 2.1 million email addresses.
A separate Nigerian investigation uncovered an international investment fraud operation promoted through messaging applications, with investigators tracing more than $2.4 million in suspected criminal proceeds, much of it moved through cryptocurrency transactions.
Authorities also disrupted fraudulent mobile lending operations in Tanzania, an online vehicle import scam in Gabon and a cybercrime network in the Republic of Congo, where 30 suspects were arrested.
 
AI being exploited by cybercriminals
Kenya was among the participating countries, alongside Ghana, South Africa, Rwanda, Cameroon, Zimbabwe and the United States.
Interpol said intelligence sharing and cooperation with technology companies helped investigators identify suspicious online infrastructure and trace criminal activity across borders.
The agency warned that artificial intelligence is increasingly being exploited by cybercriminals, allowing fraudsters to develop more sophisticated schemes and reach larger numbers of victims.
"Operation Serengeti III reinforces a clear message: while cybercrime is increasingly borderless, international cooperation remains one of the most effective tools for disrupting criminal networks, recovering criminal assets and protecting communities from digital harm," Jetton said.
Interpol said several investigations remain underway as authorities pursue additional suspects and examine digital evidence recovered during the operation.

Ukrainian OSINT analyst: Russia’s Yandex data center in Sasovo burned out inside, though its roof shows almost no significant holes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:17:42 UTC
22:17:42 KST

Russian tech giant Yandex's data center in Sasovo burned out from the inside, a Ukrainian OSINT analyst wrote on 22 October. On cloud-free satellite images, he saw almost no significant holes in its roof. Ukrainian drones hit the site overnight on 8 October.
Sasovo was the first strike on a data center in Russia. It came two weeks after Russia destroyed data centers in Kyiv. Drones then hit Yandex sites in Vladimir and Kaluga, a Sber data center, and a VK data center near St. Petersburg, which VK acknowledged. In occupied Donbas, monitoring channels reported hits on buildings housing telecom operators.
What the analyst sees
The analyst, who goes by Harbuz, runs the Ukrainian OSINT channel Dnipro Osint. His roof reading comes from the images. His interior claim comes from what he called available information: he wrote that a fire broke out inside and put part of the equipment out of action.
In an earlier post, Harbuz wrote that a third of the data center had burned out. In the new one, he writes that the building burned out from the inside. He does not say whether he revised the earlier figure.
Russian outlet Agentstvo studied Airbus images from 12 October. It found damage on about a third of the building. Unlike Harbuz, though, Agentstvo described a blackened western roof with damage resembling holes.
What Yandex says
On 8 October, Yandex stated that the attack caused a fire and forced it to suspend operations at the site, which hosts tens of thousands of servers, Reuters reported. Yandex Cloud and the Disk and Documents services that run on it ran with major disruptions that morning, Russian outlet The Bell reported.
Later that day, the company stated: "The scale of the damage to the infrastructure is still being assessed. For the moment, we cannot confirm whether it is possible to restore the data centre equipment in Sasovo." Two of Yandex's three supercomputers, used to develop its AI model, are housed there.
The same day, journalists asked Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy whether Ukraine was targeting Russian data centers. He did not refer specifically to the Yandex strike, Reuters noted, but said: "We always respond in mirror-like fashion."

Istanbul’s vanished historic mosque to rise again after 70 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:16:19 UTC
22:16:19 KST

Aise Humeyra Akgun
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Bostancilar Tabhanesi Mosque, also known as the Yedekciler Mosque, which disappeared from Istanbul’s historic skyline around 70 years ago, is being restored in the city’s Sarayburnu district.
Built during the reign of Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent to serve sick palace gardeners, the mosque was located outside the sea walls of Topkapi Palace, between Sarayburnu and Ahirkapi. It was demolished during coastal road development works in the 1950s.
Restoration efforts led by Fatih Municipality aim to return the structure to Istanbul as part of the city’s historical and cultural heritage.
For centuries, the mosque served as a place of worship and formed part of daily life around the Ottoman palace. Its story also sheds light on the fate of historical buildings lost during Istanbul’s modernization.
Urban development projects carried out between 1956 and 1960, which altered Sarayburnu’s coastline and urban fabric, permanently transformed not only the area’s transport network but also its historic skyline.
Academic studies have also identified the mosque among the structures that disappeared from the coastline during this period and whose former locations have been traced through historical photographs.
 
‘Mosque had completely disappeared by 1950s, 1960s’
Bostancilar Tabhanesi Mosque was the only mosque located immediately outside Istanbul’s sea walls, Fatih Mayor Mehmet Ergun Turan told Anadolu.
“When crossing over to this side from Uskudar or by sea, this was the first mosque whose minaret came into view. However, the structure began falling into disrepair in the 1930s. Its minaret was demolished in the 1940s. By the 1950s and 1960s, when the coastal road was built, the mosque had completely disappeared,” he said.
“Today, we are delighted to restore this mosque to Istanbul’s skyline, perhaps nearly 100 years later. We have photographs of it in numerous documents, its location is marked on maps, and it appears in engravings.”
Underlining that they aimed to restore all lost works of ancestral heritage, he said: “We do not use public funds to build any of the mosques we restore. They are funded by donors. So far, we have completed the reconstruction of eight mosques. We are currently working on the restoration of 10 similar mosques.”

How TIME and Statista Determined America's Growth Leaders of 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:15:59 UTC
22:15:59 KST

The ranking "America’s Growth Leaders 2027" is the result of a comprehensive analysis conducted to identify the top performing publicly listed companies in the US. The analysis is based on three primary dimensions: Growth Performance, Financial Stability and Stock Performance.
Methodology
The first dimension, Growth Performance, was assessed using data from Statista’s revenue database, which contains company growth data for the last five years. To be considered for the evaluation the companies had to be headquartered in the USA, publicly traded and demonstrate strong revenue growth in the last five years. Relative growth and the number of years in which growth was achieved were considered in the evaluation.
The second dimension, Financial Stability, was investigated by analyzing the companies’ profitability as well as using classic metrics such as the Piotroski F-Score and Altman Z-Score, which refer to a company’s overall financial health and the probability to file for bankruptcy. Industry specific KPIs were utilized to portray financial stability of companies within the banking, insurance and REIT sector.
The third dimension, Stock Performance, was evaluated based on multiple KPIs, that underline the companies’ strengths as a stock investment. The analysis process focused on the average annual growth rate, recent returns, a comparison to the overall market and the stocks’ volatility for the past 5 years.
Once the data was collected and evaluated, it was consolidated and weighted within a scoring model. The scores of all three dimensions were added on an equal percentage basis to form the final ranking score of a maximum of 100 points. The 500 companies with the highest score were awarded as “America’s Growth Leaders 2027” by TIME and Statista.

AI continues to dominate American business growth. In TIME’s and Statista’s second annual ranking of America’s Growth Leaders—which highlights the top performing publicly listed companies in the U.S.—Nvidia retains its top ranking from 2025.

Comfort Systems has especially benefitted from having established businesses in Tier 2 cities where data centers tend to be built. Last night, the Russians launched, among other weapons, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads against Kyiv. According to him, one of these missiles struck Pechersk—the historic center of Kyiv—specifically the area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Holy Vvedensky Monastery. The strike damaged monastery buildings, homes, stores, cafes, and other civilian infrastructure in the city.

First known human case of Shamonda virus confirmed in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:14:26 UTC
22:14:26 KST

A nurse pushes a medical bed into the corridor of the emergency medical service next to empty stretchers at Valence hospital, France, October 24, 2024. | Nicolas Guyonnet/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images
France has reported the first ever human case of Shamonda virus, a disease that had so far only affected animals, in a patient that died in early October.
The patient was severely immunocompromized and had been receiving treatment for a serious illness that made them more susceptible to infection and complications, the country’s agriculture, food and health authorities said Thursday.
Brain complications observed in the patient before their death "would most likely be linked to the infection with the Shamonda virus," the authorities said.
Advertisement
They added that this is “an exceptional case in a highly immunocompromized patient,” and that there is “no health risk for the general population.”
Health authorities have highlighted the potential of zoonotic spillover — or the jump of diseases from animals to humans — being behind the next pandemic. Currently, over 60% of emerging infectious disease threats are of zoonotic origin, including Covid-19 and Ebola. As diseases adapt and jump from wild animals to pets to humans, their potential for pandemic threats evolves too. For this reason, scientists have been on high alert for the bird flu.
The Shamonda virus, which spreads between animals through bites from infected midges, was detected in European farm animals for the first time this year. It had previously been found only in countries outside Europe, predominantly in Africa. It is mainly observed in cattle, but there have been cases of infections in horses, sheep, goats and an alpaca.
Since the summer, the virus has been detected in farm animals in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said. In cattle, its symptoms include fever, diarrhea, lethargy, reduced milk production and mild respiratory signs.
It's still not clear whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired, the ECDC said. French authorities said they believe the patient might have been infected by a midge bite while in eastern France, an area where the virus has been circulating in animals since the spring.
The ECDC said it is “carefully monitoring the situation” and is in touch with French authorities and European partners to “investigate the potential public health implications of this first human infection.”

Pentagon and Lockheed have agreed to produce 850 F-35 fighter jets
Kyiv • UNN

Lockheed Martin has reached a preliminary agreement with the U.S. Department of Defense to produce and support at least 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets over the next 10 years, they said on October 22. UNN reports this, citing Reuters.
Details
The Pentagon said the defense contractor would independently finance at least $7 billion in initiatives supporting the F-35 program.
The F-35, built using stealth technology that allows it to avoid detection by the enemy, is considered the most advanced fighter jet in the world and is the backbone of Lockheed’s aeronautics division, which accounts for about 40% of its quarterly revenue.
Under the agreement with the Pentagon, Lockheed aims to maintain annual production at 156 aircraft.
The agreement is not an order but is considered a preliminarily agreed long-term contract.
"If multiyear authorization is provided in the coming months, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will work toward finalizing the contract terms, pricing, and schedule through the formal award of a contract," the company said.
The agreement also covers international orders for the F-35, as well as initial spare parts and modification kits, according to a statement from Lockheed, based in Arlington, U.S.
"We have fundamentally changed our approach to stabilizing the American defense industrial base to ensure rapid and large-scale production," said U.S. Deputy Secretary of Defense Michael Duffy.
"This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we ensure that our military is equipped with the lethal capabilities necessary to fight and win," he said.
Lockheed and its colleagues across the United States have benefited from increased global defense spending amid ongoing geopolitical conflicts, the publication notes.
According to Lockheed’s estimates, the agreement will support 317,000 jobs in the United States and generate nearly $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade. It also expects the arrangement to reduce production costs and ease supply-chain constraints, from raw materials to finished parts.

Nvidia's Jensen Huang says he sees no sign of a 2029 memory glut: 'You can always use more'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:12:38 UTC
22:12:38 KST

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that a surplus of memory supply is unlikely by 2029, despite a sell-off in memory stocks over the past week amid concerns about oversupply and weakening demand.
"One of the things that's really great about memory is that you can always use more of it," Huang told CNBC's Arjun Kharpal in a wide-ranging interview on the sidelines of the company's GTC Berlin conference. He added that HBM, a type of random access memory, or RAM, will be used for years to come.
"We're the first company in the world to put LPDDR memory — what goes into your cell phones — into the world's data centers, and it's enabled us to deliver performance that's twice as energy efficient as anything in the world today, and so we're going to continue to use abundant amounts of them as well," he added.
Memory stocks have taken a battering in the past week after an opinion column published in a prominent South Korean publication on Oct. 15 urged the country's government to brace for a deceleration in the AI boom.
The column cited two experts who said they expect to see a "flood of new supply," which will turn the memory market "into a red ocean" in 2029, per CNBC's translation. "The supercycle could be over, and the industry could enter a downturn," by 2029, they wrote.
Memory is a core component of Nvidia's chips, and a glut of supply could push prices lower and hit profit margins for the companies that make the product, such as SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron.
SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk responded to the article at the time, saying that China "will be making a LOT of RAM in 2028."
The memory selloff was also driven by China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, which announced new design architecture that could lead to greater efficiencies. The announcement added to investor concern that CXMT could take market share from rivals SK Hynix, Samsung, and Micron.
"We're open-minded," Huang said Thursday when asked about whether he plans to partner with CXMT and use its memory product. "We work with Chinese companies; just about the whole world works with Chinese companies in the supply chain somewhere."
"China is incredible at the fundamental infrastructure technology, and no country collectively is better at manufacturing than China, and so we have to take their capabilities very seriously," he added.
U.S. regulation 'accelerated' China's chip advancements
Huang also told CNBC that China's advancements in the semiconductor industry are due to mounting U.S. regulations, which pushed the country to speed up its own chip technology and manufacturing.
The U.S. currently restricts exports of the country's most advanced semiconductors to China, including top-end Nvidia chips. However, some Chinese firms are making use of a loophole to access the product's compute power through data centers in Southeast Asia. Experts say that this has been key to Chinese AI models becoming more capable.
China "definitely accelerated because of all the regulations," he said.
"We've definitely accelerated China's initiatives, its nationalization of semiconductor manufacturing capabilities, and all of the industrial support that has been put into that sector, and so there's no question we've accelerated that," he added.
Huang emphasized that American tech firms are "mighty" and are prepared to take on competition "from anybody."

Elsewhere in France, authorities also prohibited protests planned for Thursday in Lyon, Lille and Grenoble.
The restrictions come after more than half a million people gathered across France on Saturday in a protest that brought together students demanding better conditions in schools and groups denouncing high living costs.
France’s justice minister Gerald Darmanin said on Thursday that at least 2,700 people had been taken into custody after riots broke out in several areas, and shops were looted. Darmanin added that 217 of those arrested had already been convicted and jailed. 1,000 others were being prosecuted.
President Macron blamed Saturday’s riots on what he called “seditious acts” by “ultra-left” groups, whom he accused of trying to “bring down the Republic”.
Speaking from the Elysee Palace on Thursday, Macron said France would ban all “illegitimate” protests in the coming days, while approved demonstrations led by organised groups like unions would be required to take alternative routes outside city centres to protect businesses.
He added that he would convene the country’s defence council on Friday to take further action.
Thursday’s planned protests were seen as a prelude to a large demonstration on Saturday, when activists from the “yellow vest” movement, whose demonstrations over fuel prices shook France in 2018 and 2019, are expected to join.
Some of those protests, including marches in Lyon, will also be banned, local authorities said after hours of “chaos” last weekend when more than 200 shops were looted.
Officials for the Bouche-du-Rhone region covering France’s second-largest city Marseille has also banned all protests there on Saturday citing “obvious reasons of security”.
The French government said the Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in Paris would remain closed on Saturday due to new planned demonstrations.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, a far-left candidate for next year’s presidential election criticised by the government for not strongly condemning the protest violence, blamed authorities’ “non-stop brutal repression” for the unrest.
“On Saturday, the army is guarding buildings instead of the police, and the Paris police prefect is asking shopkeepers to call on private security guards…,” Melenchon said in a post on X.
Meanwhile Marine Le Pen, the far-right leader currently topping opinion polls, accused Macron’s government of being too soft and lacking authority.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu, who met union representatives on Wednesday, said a “massive” security operation was planned for Saturday to prevent a repeat of the violence by small groups of rioters that had exposed shortcomings in security measures.
Meanwhile, Macron held a meeting with intelligence services, Lecornu and ministers on Thursday morning to obtain a detailed account of what went wrong over the weekend and review preparations for upcoming protests.
Union representatives said their meeting with Lecornu did not result in concrete proposals. They are now focusing on another big day of action scheduled for November 5, calling on private and public sector employees to join.
The education demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school in Creteil, southeast of Paris, over a lack of staff.
From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, including in smaller towns.
High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools, dilapidated facilities and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighbourhoods.
The school demonstrations and blockades have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs.

Philippine Energy Security Could Determine the Outcome of a Taiwan Contingency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:12:00 UTC
22:12:00 KST

In March, a U.S. ally declared a “state of energy emergency” after experiencing disruptions to its crude deliveries. After gaining a waiver from Washington, Petron, the Philippines’ only refinery, bought Russian oil. The episode exposed a decades-old vulnerability in U.S. strategy: Philippine fuel insecurity.
Beginning in 2010, across three Pacific tours, I’ve watched China erode regional security through its increased power and aggression. For the United States to deter China from a Taiwan annexation attempt, it requires access to the Philippines and its oil. However, a conflict that draws in the U.S. will likely disrupt the Philippine oil imports that sustain American operations.
The Philippines sits at the Pacific’s crossroads, in the middle of the First Island Chain, connecting Taiwan and the South China Sea. The Philippines’ placement makes it vital to U.S. deterrence. Economically, this region carries 43 percent of global crude shipments and 21 percent of trade. Geographically, control of the Luzon Strait would allow China to isolate Taiwan.
For 20 years, Chinese coercion has revealed Beijing’s desire to control these crossroads, annex Taiwan, and dominate the Pacific. To deter China and sustain American operations 6,500 miles from California, the U.S. needs reliable access to the Philippines and its oil. Yet Manila’s small, nearly import-only oil industry leaves it and U.S. forces vulnerable.
During my last tour in the Pacific, then-Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan. China’s response, and its subsequent isolation “rehearsals,” demonstrated its power and aggression. Several isolation zones extended across the Luzon Strait, and, based on recent events, Beijing intends to contest Philippine sovereignty in these areas.
Luzon is critical to deterring “a conflict over Taiwan” and safeguarding global shipping routes, because it’s within ground-based missile range of Taiwan. For China to annex Taiwan, it must control the Luzon Strait to blockade Taiwan, threaten Philippine sovereignty, and degrade U.S. intervention. However, if the United States can maintain reliable access, it can resupply Taiwan and deny a Chinese annexation operation.
But geography is only one part of the equation. Operations from Luzon depend on reliable Philippine oil. American fuel dependence turns Manila’s energy fragility into a strategic vulnerability.
In 2022, the U.S. Department of Defense required over 73 million barrels for operations, training, and exercises globally, with 48 percent purchased overseas. Unsurprisingly, air and maritime operations account for 91 percent of demand, roughly 66.5 million barrels. Any Sino-American conflict would place enormous pressure on fuel supplies thousands of miles from the U.S. homeland.
The Philippines alone consumes 474,000 barrels per day and maintains only a 40-45 day reserve. Since Caltex and Shell closed their refineries, Petron has capacity to support only a limited share of national demand. Manila relies on imports, with almost 97 percent of crude coming from the Middle East and nearly 95 percent of refined products coming from Asia.
In a crisis, U.S. demands on Philippine oil would rapidly deplete Manila’s reserves. At the same time, Chinese maritime interdiction operations in the South China Sea would disrupt Philippine import routes and constrain American operations. The result would be another “state of energy emergency.”
Proven Philippine oil reserves stand at 139 million barrels, with another 202 million more locked in Bangsamoro’s Liguasan Marsh, which is a historical insurgency hotspot. Developing these resources and expanding refining capacity strengthens Manila’s resiliency. It’s also a mutually beneficial opportunity for Philippine-U.S. commercial cooperation.
Currently, the Pentagon is building extra oil capacity in Davao to “enable U.S. naval vessels to receive fuel.” The new depot is a positive step forward, but its limited capacity and continuous resupply needs mean that storage alone cannot solve the underlying problem.
American security requires more than stockpiles; it requires stronger Philippine extraction and refining capacity. The U.S.-Venezuela framework offers one possible model. This year, several U.S.-based oil companies signed agreements to develop Venezuelan reserves in support of both countries’ interests. The Philippine context differs, but the underlying mechanism, a bilateral agreement to unlock private-sector investment in domestic production, could be adapted to Washington’s and Manila’s needs.
Many existing Philippine-U.S. energy programs cover renewables, nuclear power, energy costs, and critical minerals, but none specifically targets Manila’s weak fuel extraction, refining, and distribution system. The November ASEAN Summit in Manila, where U.S. President Donald Trump and Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. may meet, offers an opportunity.
Washington should create a targeted Philippine oil resilience program directly linked to U.S. strategy. An ideal model to emulate is the Philippines Energy Threshold Program. Both nations’ commercial investment sectors can strengthen Manila’s fuel security and expand its capacity. To be sure, one program cannot address every wartime need, but it will reduce U.S. vulnerabilities.
My proposal benefits both nations’ prosperity, commercial industries, and U.S. strategy. From my tours, I’ve seen how oil underpins strategy. In a Sino-American conflict, we cannot assume fuel will arrive. Both nations should create an oil resilience program now, before the crisis begins.
