Have scientists finally found a way to save the banana from disaster?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:00:05 UTC
22:00:05 KST

Love them or loathe them, bananas are one of the world’s most popular fruit. But a combination of the climate crisis and new killer diseases have had growers concerned over the banana’s threatened extinction, something that would impose a huge toll on farmers in countries from Guatemala to Malawi, alongside eradicating a staple food.
Now researchers say they have made fresh advances in the race to save them from disaster. This month, Yelloway – a research collaboration between Chiquita, the world’s largest banana company, and the crop-improvement company KeyGene – announced it had developed a fully fertile Cavendish banana, meaning it may be possible, through cross-breeding, to create new banana varieties that are commercially viable and resistant to disease.
Second only to the tomato in terms of fruit consumption globally, the world grows about 139m tonnes of bananas a year. While there are more than 1,000 varieties, it is the Cavendish that is now found in most fruit bowls, taking over from the Gros Michel cultivar, which fell victim to Panama disease from the 1950s.
But the Cavendish itself is under threat from diseases including a strain of Panama known as Tropical Race 4 (TR4). Dr Jose De Vega, an expert on crop genomics at the Earlham Institute in Norwich, said TR4 had spread from south-east Asia to Australia, Africa, the Middle East and Latin America.
“The most worrying recent report came in December 2025 from Ecuador, the world’s largest banana exporter,” he said, noting that the disease threatened both global supply chains “and the food security of millions of people in the tropics for whom bananas and plantains are a staple food and a source of income”.
Cavendish bananas have three sets of chromosomes, meaning they are typically sterile. “Combined with the ability to set fruit without pollination, this gives us the seedless banana,” said De Vega.
There are several different types of Cavendish, including dwarf versions, which have arisen as a result of random mutations in the Cavendish genome.
But in each case new plants are grown from offshoots, so they are virtually genetically identical to the plant from which they came. While this results in uniform fruit, it also means they are vulnerable to the same diseases.
Peter Stedman, Chiquita’s sustainability director, said: “We are not trying to preserve Cavendish. We’re trying to replace Cavendish because we believe at the core of any sustainable farming system is biodiversity and genetic diversity.”
Other researchers have taken different approaches. In Australia, a team at Queensland University of Technology led by Prof James Dale has created a genetically modified Cavendish by using a bacterium to introduce a gene from a wild banana that produces resistance to TR4.
The upshot, a type of Cavendish called QCAV-4, has been approved for human consumption in Australia and New Zealand, with researchers confirming that it tastes like the traditional banana.
De Vega, by contrast, is collaborating with other researchers to explore gene-editing techniques. These involve using “molecular scissors” to cut parts of the Cavendish’s DNA and replace them with genes from other banana cultivars.
His team have been sequencing the genomes of banana varieties that have different responses to TR4. “We are looking for the [immune genes] that resistant varieties have and that the Cavendish lacks, carries a broken version of, has too few copies of, or doesn’t switch on strongly enough,” said De Vega.
“Once we identify a candidate gene, the idea is to edit the Cavendish’s own copy so it matches the copy in the resistant cousin. That keeps everything that makes a Cavendish a Cavendish.”
In England and elsewhere in Europe, De Vega added, gene-editing was seen as precision breeding rather than genetic modification.
“That is because the change is one that could happen naturally or through conventional breeding,” he said. “The catch is that with a sterile Cavendish, conventional breeding has never really been an option, which is exactly why editing is so attractive for bananas.”
But Stedman said there were drawbacks to such approaches. “Every time you are editing or improving Cavendish, you’re not creating a new variety, you’re not creating biodiversity – you’re just maintaining a monocrop,” he said, noting that brought susceptibility to disease.
Yelloway’s production of a fully fertile Cavendish line – known as “Yellowdish” – using non-GM technologies potentially opens up a new route.
Dale and De Vega noted that details on exactly how Yellowdish was produced, and with how many chromosomes, had not been revealed – meaning questions remained.
Dale said the approach with Yelloway of crossing a fertile Cavendish with other types of fertile banana resistant to TR4 – and potentially other diseases – could have benefits, including in the regulatory environment and in public perceptions.
But while it may result in disease-resistant progeny, he noted it could also yield a very different type of fruit.
“Whatever they generate is going to be different to Cavendish,” Dale said, pointing out that crosses could produce a huge range of types but any new variety needed not only to be resistant to disease but also produce high yields and taste good.
For Stedman, the challenge boils down to a numbers game. “If you have enough progeny, if you have enough children, the chances of one of them having … the traits that you want is much, much higher,” he said.

This ‘living drug’ could change the course of autoimmune disease
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

This ‘living drug’ could change the course of autoimmune disease
A new CAR T cell therapy may be the first approved treatment for stiff person syndrome
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
Two months before the treatment that would change Lynn Montgomery-Haga’s life, she could barely walk down a hallway.
In a test at the University of Colorado Anschutz, Montgomery-Haga struggled to walk 25 feet, often reaching out to the walls for support. Usually, the 49-year-old relied on her walker or wheelchair. “She had a very stiff, hesitant gait,” says Montgomery-Haga’s neurologist, Amanda Piquet.
For about a decade, Montgomery-Haga had lived with a debilitating autoimmune disease known as stiff person syndrome. The progressive condition can lock up the body’s muscles without warning, leading to falls, broken bones, excruciating pain and difficulty moving. Singer Celine Dion, who returned to the stage in September after years of battling the disease, has said it can feel “like somebody’s strangling you.”
Montgomery-Haga’s own days were marked by dizziness, fatigue and pain. And sudden muscle spasms would send her sprawling. It was like the fainting goat videos popular on the internet, she says. “They get surprised and they fall over, and there’s nothing they can do about it.”
But stiff person syndrome is no joke. It stripped Montgomery-Haga of her accounting job and her ability to drive. She couldn’t sit up in bed unless she had a safety bar to pull on. If she dropped the soap in the shower, it’d take her 10 minutes to pick it up.
Now, Montgomery-Haga hopes those struggles are finally coming to an end. That’s because a clinical trial with an experimental therapy has helped restore mobility for her — and others like her. She can stride through her living room again. She can landscape her front yard. She doesn’t have to brace herself when her dogs jump on her. And she hasn’t fallen once since the treatment. The change has been drastic, she says. “I’m just really excited about the future.”
The treatment, a type of CAR T cell therapy, extracts immune cells from a person’s body and engineers them to attack the very cells causing the disease. First used to fight cancer, CAR T is now also targeting a variety of autoimmune diseases. If given the green light by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Montgomery-Haga’s treatment would be the first such therapy approved for an autoimmune condition — and it would be the first approved treatment for stiff person syndrome.
Stiff person syndrome may be just the beginning, says Carl June, the University of Pennsylvania immunologist and oncologist who spearheaded CAR T cell therapy for cancer decades ago. The “living drug” could herald a new era of therapeutics for autoimmune diseases like lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and even multiple sclerosis. “It’s revolutionary to think how far things have gone,” June says.
But he warns that it’s far too early to know if scientists have definitively cured stiff person syndrome. And there haven’t been enough people treated to get a good handle on all the possible side effects. “There could be long-term complications in autoimmune patients that don’t happen in our cancer patients,” he says. Other researchers urge caution. “It’s very important not to oversell it,” says Marc Scherlinger, a rheumatologist at Strasbourg University Hospital in France.
For Piquet, one crucial question is how long the treatment will last. In Montgomery-Haga’s case, the answer seems to be at least two years. Montgomery-Haga still considers herself disabled, or “disabled-ish,” as she calls it. But when rating how she used to feel on a scale of one to 10, she’d put herself at a zero before treatment, she says. These days, she’s more like a seven.
What’s more, Montgomery-Haga says, “I think I’m still improving.”
No approved therapies
There’s no single symptom that clued Montgomery-Haga in to her disease. In 2014, she started having difficulty picking things up off the floor. Then her boss asked her why she was limping — Montgomery-Haga hadn’t noticed. Her balance was off and her head felt weird, like “I was walking around in a fishbowl,” she says. It got to the point where Montgomery-Haga had difficulty crossing thresholds between rooms.
Montgomery-Haga would startle easily, prompting her body to stiffen up like a board. One time when cooking, she burned her finger, spasmed and collapsed, cracking the back of her head on the cabinets. She lay on the floor crying, but finally managed to right herself. “As soon as you hit the floor,” she says, “your muscles are like, ‘Fine,’ and you can get up again.”
Those unpredictable symptoms capture a slice of what life is like with stiff person syndrome, or SPS. The disease, which affects roughly 2 in 100,000 people in the United States, typically develops in a person’s 30s or 40s. It is about twice as common in women as in men.
Scientists don’t know what sets off the disease. But they think a person’s own antibodies start attacking a neurological network that helps muscles throughout the body relax. And when those tensed muscles are in opposition, like the biceps and triceps, they start fighting one another, Piquet says. That’s when people can end up in a stuck position, leading to stiffness. But because everyone’s immune system is different, patients’ experiences with the disease can vary greatly.
For Tara Zier, a former dentist based in Maryland, SPS started with extreme neck pain, blood pressure spikes, shortness of breath and feelings of impending doom. While some people struggle with mobility, Zier’s difficulties include standing and extreme fatigue. When she holds herself upright, her muscles clamp down on her spine like it’s in a vise. “Have you ever had a charley horse in your calf?” she asks. “Imagine one in your whole body that stops you in your tracks.”
Zier and Montgomery-Haga went years before learning what was behind their symptoms. Their cases mystified doctors — Zier saw 13 specialists and visited the emergency room nine times before getting a diagnosis. When she finally found out she had SPS three years after her first symptoms, Zier says she felt validated, like medicine was confirming what she already knew: “Something’s wrong with me.”
Montgomery-Haga’s 2018 diagnosis put her “over the moon,” she says. For nearly four years, she had gotten sicker and sicker — but doctors couldn’t tell her why. She felt as if they were giving up on her. With the diagnosis, Montgomery-Haga not only learned that SPS existed, she says, “I was told it’s treatable.”
Current treatments include muscle relaxers, anti-seizure medications and Botox injections in body parts that feel especially stiff. Although these off-label therapies can address people’s symptoms, they’re “doing nothing to treat the underlying autoimmune disease,” Piquet says. And some can come with potent side effects, like mental fog.
Zier, who has tried multiple combinations of different meds, remembers frequently losing her train of thought. She has since tapered off all but one drug, a low dose of Valium. “The trade-off,” she says, “is pain.”
People with SPS can also receive intravenous infusions of healthy antibodies, a treatment called IVIG, to decrease muscle spasms and stiffness. Montgomery-Haga found it helpful but time-consuming. She’d go to the clinic every three weeks for an infusion, which could take up to six hours.
“The bottom line is there are no FDA-approved therapies for this disease,” Piquet says. Now, the one most likely to cross the finish line first is something no one would have expected even a few years ago, CAR T pioneer June says. If you told doctors that CAR T cell therapy was going to be FDA approved for an autoimmune disease, he says, “people would have laughed.”
To catch a killer
June may be best known for his work in cancer, but he’s been keenly following the progress in auto-immune therapy. His daughter, now in her 30s, was diagnosed with juvenile rheumatoid arthritis when she was 9 years old. For her, that’s meant over 20 years of treatment with drugs that bring a bundle of side effects, such as fatigue and risk of infections. “It would be much better to be cured,” he says.
In autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and SPS, a person’s own antibodies attack tissues throughout the body, from blood vessels to cartilage to neurons. Wiping out these rogue antibodies can stop the attacks. But CAR T cell therapy doesn’t act on the antibodies themselves. It goes straight to the source, snuffing out the cellular factories that manufacture them.
Those antibody factories are known as B cells. To eliminate them, doctors recruit T cells, which act as the body’s security system and work together to hunt down and destroy problematic cells. In the lab, scientists fine-tune these hunters, outfitting them with a molecular homing device called a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. When infused back into patients’ bodies, the newly-engineered T cells can target the antibody factories directly — like a saboteur told exactly what to destroy.
A new treatment
The CAR T cell therapy Lynn Montgomery-Haga received wipes out B cells, including the ones likely driving her disease. Doctors hope this therapy “resets” her immune system, getting rid of harmful B cells and letting healthy new ones take their place.
“The secret behind CAR T cell therapy is that you completely deplete B cells in the body,” says Georg Schett, a rheumatologist at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg in Germany. Temporarily wiping out a person’s B cells lets the body replace them with fresh, unproblematic ones, Schett says. He calls it an “immune reset.”
CAR T cell therapy got its start in the 2010s, when researchers used engineered T cells to target cancer. In 2017, the FDA approved the first CAR T cell therapies for two blood cancers, acute lymphoblastic leukemia and large B cell lymphoma. Soon after, scientists saw the first tantalizing hints that it might work for autoimmune diseases, too. In some cases, cancer patients with autoimmune disorders reported improvements in both conditions after treatment.
But most researchers didn’t think it could be that easy, Schett says. After all, autoimmune diseases were driven by a complex network of cell types. How could targeting just one of them work?
That thinking underwent a paradigm shift in 2021 when Schett and his team published the first major paper reporting a successful treatment with the therapy. The patient was a 20-year-old woman with a severe case of lupus, a complex, sometimes-fatal illness that can damage the kidneys and other organs. Within five weeks of CAR T cell therapy treatment, signs of her disease began to vanish.
Results like these were “unheard of,” says rheumatologist Maximilian Konig of Johns Hopkins Medicine in Baltimore. Lupus is extremely difficult to treat, and for decades, most drugs tested against it failed. No one had ever seen the kind of improvements that Schett’s patient experienced.
After the paper came out, “everybody was talking about it,” Konig says. Today, more than five years later, the woman’s lupus hasn’t returned, Schett says. “We consider this patient cured,” he says.
The woman’s response was no fluke. The following year, Schett’s team reported similar results in five more lupus patients. All went into remission after CAR T cell therapy.
This was the true tipping point, June says. “It’s rare, very rare, that you get such striking results.”
What followed was an explosion of research around the world. Scientists are now testing CAR T cell therapy in nearly a dozen autoimmune diseases linked to harmful B cells, including lupus, rheumatoid arthritis and a connective-tissue disease known as systemic sclerosis.
Kyverna, the California-based company behind the SPS trial, is also running trials for neurological autoimmune conditions including generalized myasthenia gravis and progressive multiple sclerosis, or MS.
One reason using CAR T cell therapy for neurological conditions excites researchers is because of the cells’ potential to slip past the blood-brain barrier. That means they might be able to access pockets of smoldering inflammation inaccessible to other drugs, says neurologist Rebecca Farber of Columbia University.
That could be a huge help in diseases like MS, in which a person’s antibodies attack the protective sheaths around nerve cells, causing numbness, brain fog and difficulty walking. Still, Farber doubts that CAR T cell therapy could fix existing damage. “We’re not expecting it to repair the nervous system,” she says. But it’s possible the treatment could freeze the disease’s progress. Patients are already asking her team about future treatments.
For Piquet, who cares for roughly 100 people with SPS, Kyverna’s trial offered a compelling opportunity to help her patients. Montgomery-Haga cried when Piquet told her about the trial at one of their regular Zoom appointments. She recalls wondering, is this the treatment that “might help me be normal again?”
The good, the bad and the potentially ugly
Though Montgomery-Haga leapt at the chance to try Kyverna’s treatment, called miv-cel, CAR T cell therapy is no walk in the park. Before starting, doctors sit patients down to “talk about the good, the bad and the potentially ugly,” Piquet says.
That includes the rigorous prep work needed before people receive their engineered T cells. Patients must first get low-dose chemotherapy, which flushes T cells from the body and makes space for the new ones. Chemo can ambush the body with symptoms including hair thinning, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea.
Treatment itself also carries risks. It destroys most B cells in the body — not just the ones that cause disease. That can lead to fever, inflammation and potentially risky infections. In Kyverna’s trial, for example, 15 percent of participants had severely low white blood cell counts after treatment. Such symptoms were expected, Piquet says, and were easily treated.
Other CAR T treatments seem to have fared far worse. In August, the pharmaceutical company Novartis paused clinical trials of its therapy, rap-cel, across a spectrum of autoimmune diseases after three patients died. Bristol Myers Squibb has also paused similar studies after some patients experienced neurological complications, according to the Wall Street Journal. Details of the incidents were slow to emerge and have set the field on edge. “It’s a tragedy,” Konig says. He calls such outcomes an important wake-up call.
But red flags in one trial don’t mean all CAR T products are dangerous, Konig says. That’s because many different designs and manufacturing processes exist, and scientists can’t always predict what will make one product toxic and another safe. Kyverna’s miv-cel, for instance, has been consistently well-tolerated in the more than 100 patients treated, a spokesperson for the company says.
CAR T cell therapies are transformative, Konig says. “They’re going to change the field — but there are risks.”
Another risk is that the once-vanquished disease will return. Doctors don’t know all the genetic and environmental conditions that trigger autoimmune disease. Some researchers wonder whether vulnerable individuals remain vulnerable, even after treatment. But because it often takes multiple insults for someone to tip into a state of disease, Scherlinger says, CAR T cell therapy could buy patients lots of time.
“Now I can”
After 10 days in the hospital for her treatment, Montgomery-Haga returned to recover at home. In the following months, she started to notice some changes. It was easier getting around the house, for one. And she felt her balance and stability improving. She can now kneel down to garden and clean without the days of recovery it used to require. “I can vacuum my house,” she says. “It seems so little, but now I can vacuum!”
Montgomery-Haga can even sit down “crisscross applesauce,” she says. “I couldn’t do that for, like, 10 years.”
Four months after the treatment, Piquet’s team tested Montgomery-Haga’s walking ability. In a hallway at University of Colorado Anschutz’s research building, the team marked out 25 feet with little orange cones. At one end stood Montgomery-Haga. At the other, Piquet watched behind a video camera. This time, Montgomery-Haga’s gait was smooth and her arms were down, not hovering out into the air to catch herself if she fell. “You could see that she was walking with a lot more confidence,” Piquet says.
The team saw similar results in other SPS patients. Some who had difficulty walking before treatment now wanted to run, Piquet says. “It’s incredible to just see those patients speeding down the hallway.” She remembers smiles, high fives and a sense of celebration in the air. Eight of 12 people who had used a walking aid for the initial test didn’t need one for the follow-up, Piquet reported at the American Academy of Neurology meeting in April.
In September, Kyverna reported the trial’s one-year results: Patients maintained mobility improvements, with a third completing their 25-foot walk about as fast as a healthy adult. Additionally, nearly all patients no longer rely on immuno-suppressive drugs to tamp down harmful immune activity. That’s good news because such drugs can bring all sorts of nasty side effects, like vomiting, bleeding and infections.
The results with SPS are “really something to celebrate,” June says. But only time and many more treatments will reveal how safe CAR T really is, he says.
That’s a concern for Zier, who says she wouldn’t feel comfortable trying the therapy at this point. Zier doesn’t know how she’d respond. She’s a single mother with two kids; even a rare side effect could disrupt her life in a way she may not be able to manage. And these days, she’s managing as well as she can. Zier is the founder and CEO of The Stiff Person Syndrome Research Foundation, which supports research for SPS treatments.
Kyverna is in the process of submitting miv-cel for FDA approval. The company is seeking priority review and hopes the treatment might be available to patients in 2027. If SPS is the first autoimmune disease to have an FDA-approved CAR T cell therapy, myasthenia gravis could be the second, says Warner Biddle, Kyverna’s CEO. What’s more, miv-cel also appeared to improve symptoms in six patients with severe cases of rheumatoid arthritis, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.
As for what’s next, the door is wide open. Some scientists are working to make off-the-shelf forms of CAR T that wouldn’t require personalized engineering. Others are trying to reprogram T cells directly inside people’s bodies, rather than in the lab. Still others are trying to make T cells that target only the B cells responsible for disease. In the future, doctors might use such drugs to help patients avoid the cumbersome treatment process that Montgomery-Haga endured.
Montgomery-Haga’s own future looks far different than what she had imagined a few years ago. In 2026, she took a trip to Washington, D.C., to see the monuments. Now she’d like to visit Paris, Scotland and Ireland, too.
For so many years, Montgomery-Haga has looked at trips and activities — and even household chores — that most people take for granted, thinking, “Man, I wish I could do that,” she says. “Now I can.”

Meet Mori, a Cute Robot Mushroom That Doesn’t Really Say (or Do) Anything
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

You've had a long day. You finally get home, fling the door open, plonk on the couch, and let out a big sigh. In the corner of your eye, you notice your mushroom lamp perk up. Its microphone must have heard you come in. Its head raises to reveal round, animated eyes, and a little diamond-shaped nose—which actually houses a camera.
It does a little jiggle because it sees you're back. Its name is Mori.
As you move around the space—maybe it's time to start cooking dinner—the little robot's face follows you, observing your movements and making soft sounds that are a cross between a bird and R2-D2. The day's stress catches up, and you need a moment to relax, so you head over to Mori, touch its head, and its eyes and camera-nose dip back inside its body. It goes back to being a lamp, except now it plays nature soundscapes so you can feel at ease.
That's the pitch from OKA, or One Kind Artifact, a new startup based in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and Shenzhen, China, focusing on experimental technology. CEO Hua Wang tells WIRED he wants his company to create five experimental “Artifacts” over the course of OKA's lifetime. Mori is the first.
“There are certain relationships in this era we want to fix between humans and our surroundings—human with nature, human with one another—every product is an experience trying to reconnect some of those relationships,” Wang says. Before cofounding OKA, he was a general manager at Meipai, a video-sharing app from the Chinese phone brand Meitu. He also cofounded Bondee, a now-defunct social media app that briefly went viral in Asia.
According to the company, the point of Mori, the nearly 12-inch-tall home robot lamp, is to reconnect its owners with nature. It can play nature soundscapes. It will glow different colors—inspired by rain, forests, fire, and wind—while reacting to your movements. It can guide you through a calming breathing session.
It also uses its built-in camera and microphones to serve as a fun little interactive companion in your home. Ask it how your outfit looks, and Mori will jiggle excitedly. If you're playing music or watching TV, Mori can dance to the tunes and react to the action on your TV screen.
It intentionally does not do anything else. Unlike an Amazon Echo, it isn't an assistant: You can't use voice commands to control smart lights or cue up Spotify tracks, and it won't answer if you ask about the weather.
The Founder's Edition is a staggering $649 and is available starting today, though stock is limited to a few hundred units. That price also includes a two-year warranty and two years of Mori's subscription service ($17 per month or $80 a year). If you miss out on the Founder’s Edition, you can still buy a standard edition Mori, but that costs $849 (there's a preorder price of $799), and that higher price shockingly does not include any of the subscription features.
The breathing exercises are free, and you can still access those without a subscription. But if you want the nature soundscapes, you need to subscribe. Otherwise, Mori is just a glorified lamp that dances a little bit while pointing its camera at you and any other people in your home.
Wang says today's home robots have mostly taken on “machine-like” forms that don't mesh well with personal environments, so OKA designed a lamp that blends in, but is also anthropomorphized to make being at home “feel better.”
OKA's AI algorithms (powered by multiple local large language models) let Mori understand the room's context through the camera and microphone, so it knows when to interact and when to stay quiet. The company calls this “Attentive Intelligence.” It has memory, so it remembers you and interacts with you a certain way over time, whereas it might act a little more shy if you bring home a guest. If it doesn't see someone for a month, it will forget them.
It might notice, for example, that you've been on your phone doomscrolling for two hours straight on the couch. Mori might then try to get your attention so you come over, listen to some wind rustling through the leaves, and give your eyes a break. When you're on a phone call, or maybe having an argument with a significant other, it understands what’s happening and goes silent so as not to distract you.
“All gadgets try to capture more of your attention,” Wang says. “Mori gives your attention back to you. It invites you to do meditative experiences. Nature has this restorative power to humans.”
The robot can connect to Wi-Fi, which should give you pause from a security standpoint, but Wang says the internet connection is only used for firmware updates.
Mori processes raw images and audio locally, and then discards the files. Facial feature data—which is collected so it knows to react to you versus a guest—is encrypted on the device, and never uploaded. The camera turns off when the robot retracts into a lamp, and the microphone turns off when you double-tap the top of Mori's head. It is battery-powered, so you can take it from room to room, or just leave it plugged in.
Wang says Mori's skill set is limited for now, though it could expand in the future. He suggests it could connect to your Oura Ring data in the future so it knows exactly when you need some relaxing sounds, or to your Spotify account to play different content. Voice commands could even come later—like asking Mori to play nature sounds instead of having to touch it.
“People feel isolated and want this kind of presence in their home. A lot of people leave their TV on to fill the emptiness of the room,” Wang says, pointing to a time when he was feeling isolated while studying abroad in the US. “It's not particularly for the elderly or children, but for younger generations.”
Cute robot pets that interact with you have been welcomed into our homes before. Chris Harrison, director of the Future Interfaces Group at Carnegie Mellon University, points to Sony's Aibo dog from 1999 as an early digital companion. However, he says the crucial ingredient they have been missing is what artificial intelligence can now provide. These previous robots were too simplistic, but now that the modern versions can understand and react to human actions and emotions, they could become more impactful.
“Humans have always wanted to anthropomorphize everything—they love making things cute,” Harrison says. “We want to make robots cute; we want to put cute little cases on our iPhones.” He points to Meta's new Muse agent, which has a cuddly avatar. “It is almost like a pet, but a hyper-capable pet.”
When I point out that Mori doesn't seem very capable with its limited feature set, Harrison likens it to people owning a goldfish or a hamster.
“Are we holding [Mori] to an unrealistic bar? People do extract a lot of pleasure out of taking care of their pets and snuggling with their pets and interacting with their pets that I wouldn't say are necessarily more sophisticated.”
Whether people will shell out hundreds of dollars for a robotic pet that can’t fetch—or even tell you the time—is up in the air. But if this mushroom-shaped, camera-wielding lamp can fool overstimulated brains into feeling a little less alone at the end of the day, maybe that’s enough.

630 drones, by Moscow’s count

The volatility around the Israeli and US midterm elections is fueling fears of renewed US-Israeli strikes on Iran in a short and intensive military campaign to push Tehran into concessions, with Iran vowing a devastating response against the Gulf nations.
The Gulf countries and the wider Middle East are bracing for a possible resumption of hostilities in the Iran war amid multiple simultaneous warnings and media reports of increasing intensity and detail, coupled with a massive US military build-up in the Gulf and Israeli and Iranian armies placed on high alert, raising fears of an imminent escalation with devastating consequences for the region.
Against the backdrop of growing speculation over the last weeks that the US and Israel may launch a new attack against Iran before or after the mid-term elections in the US and next week’s elections in Israel, a new US Department of State travel alert issued on Wednesday evening was relayed by news agencies and wider media as an urgent signal as to the imminence of war restarting, with the Gulf nations bearing the brunt of a potentially larger conflict.
The US Department of State announced that it ordered non-essential US government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as “the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area.”
Several news outlets reported that families of embassy staff in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar, and Bahrain were also ordered to leave, quoting multiple diplomatic sources.
US Department of State spokesperson Tommy Pigott said these reports were “inaccurate."
“The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only,” as a result of the growing Houthi attacks, Pigott said in a post on X.
The US Saudi warning follows a Middle East-wide red alert issued by Washington on Monday to US citizens in 12 countries across the Middle East, warning their citizens in Israel, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Lebanon, Jordan, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, the UAE, Yemen and Iran, citing risks of potential attacks on US interests.
War vs elections
With days before Israel’s close elections in which prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and ahead of next month’s US midterm elections in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are growing concerns and speculations that US-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.
The US has been rebuilding a massive strike force in the Gulf by sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest US naval and air force in the Middle East since the invasion of Iraq in 2003.
Iran has been warning for weeks that it has reorganised its defence capabilities and that any attack would be matched with what they called a devastating response against US interests and civilian infrastructure across the region, which would be far worse than their previous attacks on the Gulf nations and longer in time too.
Iranian officials and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) are preparing for war, having declared their “100% certainty” that the US and Israel will attack them again.
According to reports in Iran, Tehran activated its so-called Mosaic Defence doctrine by which Iran would operate in a decentralised way, by giving local commanders a list of targets to keep fighting even if the central command is destroyed.
In parallel with the US Department of State alert on Wednesday, the New York Times and other media reported that the US and Israel have developed specific plans for new strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections.
US President Donald Trump declared recently that any considerations for a new attack on Iran would be made after the US midterm elections.
According to the New York Times report, which quoted US officials, targets would likely include Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and arsenals of missiles and drones, with the objective of pushing Iran into a deal to end the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu earlier this week on an unannounced trip in Israel to discuss “the threats in the region.”
Speaking at an IDF officer graduation ceremony on Wednesday night, Netanyahu said that the Tehran regime has to be finally overthrown.
The Israeli premier justified this by stating that Iran's Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei "decided to follow in his father's footsteps (to attempt) once again to develop the bombs of death."’
The younger Khamenei, who has been selected as the new supreme leader following his father Ali Khamenei's killing in the US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in the opening salvo of the war on 28 February, is yet to be seen in public amid continued reports questioning his health condition.
Earlier this week, US media reported that dozens of Israeli fighter jets and refuelling aircraft reportedly flew towards the Iranian border before turning back, calling the sorties a military exercise and a "show of force," according to the Times of Israel newspaper.
According to media reports, US officials have questioned Israel's fighter jet deployment, believing the purpose of the exercise was to test Iranian air defence units and provoke them to open fire.
In parallel, Israeli media reported that Israeli security officials warned the government that an attack on Iran could be perceived as political interference in the election next week.
Israel’s opposition leader Yair Lapid told the Israeli media that “based on the information available to me, there is absolutely no reason to attack Iran or anywhere else before the elections.”
Calls for extreme caution amid uncertainty
Meanwhile on Thursday, seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said, a markedly high number as tensions wind upward over concerns about a return to all-out war.
Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the US over the war.
During his state visit to Qatar, French President Emmanuel Macron issued a stern warning on Wednesday about the Gulf's fragile security situation, urging “extreme caution” to avoid escalating tensions that could reignite conflict, after talks with Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
Macron told the media that he was “very cautious because no one can tell how the situation will evolve in the next days and weeks."
"No one can ignore that we are in a period that despite everything can lead to tensions: elections in Israel, the midterm elections in the United States, and so during this time efforts and initiatives must be doubled to avoid that these tensions don’t result in a resumption of conflict,” the French president explained.
"There is a lot of uncertainty and measures taken by one side and the other that I would not comment on."
Nevertheless, the US-Iran exchanges continue through international mediators, with Qatar and Pakistan leading the efforts to find a diplomatic breakthrough.
The US has previously applied pressure and threats on Iran to push for concessions and reach a deal.
A return to all-out war would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertiliser from the region and likely bring another spike in energy prices around the world.

She moves more and constructs full sentences — how Krista Pike is recovering after a botched execution

Gandhi's nephew asked to remove artwork depicting youth protests
Raihan Vadra, the nephew of Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, was asked to remove a number of photos from an exhibition he was running at a government-run cultural center in New Delhi.
The center, Bikaner House, requested the removal of several pieces of artwork on the grounds that they were "objectionable."
"The photos were of the youth protests in Delhi," Vadra said in a post on social media. "Apparently the content is objectionable."
The Bikaner House Management Society said "certain photographs" from the exhibition were not in line with the center's policies, without elaborating.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's BJP governs Rajasthan state, which is in charge of Bikaner House.
The protest movement has proven to be a major challenge to Modi's power. A recent renewal of the protests, with Rahul Gandhi at its forefront, has seen protesters calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of voter lists.
Amit Shah criticizes opposition over 'vote theft' protests
Union Home Minister Amit Shah criticized Congress and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) on Thursday over allegations of electoral irregularities, saying protests and demonstrations would not help them win elections, the Hindustan Times reported.
Speaking at an event in Delhi, Shah accused the opposition of using allegations of "vote theft" to challenge the Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) electoral victories.
Indian opposition leader Rahul Gandhi has claimed that India's election authority had enabled "vote theft," or manipulation of electoral rolls to favor Modi's BJP in the 2024 general elections.
Currently, the opposition along with the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) and other student organizations are demanding the resignation of the country's controversy-hit Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, after more than 130 million names were removed from draft electoral rolls nationwide.
Meanwhile, separately, BJP spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia accused Gandhi of links with foreign-based organizations that he alleged were amplifying protests in India, the Times of India newspaper reported.
Bhatia alleged that the organizations were part of a wider effort to create unrest and undermine constitutional institutions, and demanded that Gandhi disclose details of his meetings with them, the report said.
One Indian killed, three injured in attacks on Saudi airport, oilfield
One Indian national was killed and two others injured in an attack on Dammam airport in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, while another Indian national was injured in an attack on the Shaybah oil field, the Indian foreign ministry said in a statement on Thursday.
The Wednesday evening attack in the Saudi Arabian city of Dammam killed two people and eight others in total, the country's aviation authority said on Thursday.
In a separate attack on Wednesday, two people were killed by debris from an intercepted drone launched by the Iran-backed Houthis targeting the Shaybah oil field operated by state energy giant Aramco, Saudi media reported.
The US embassy in Riyadh issued a security alert on Wednesday about possible further attacks by the Houthis on Saudi Arabia.
"We strongly condemn the continued attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including the attack on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam and Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field in the Eastern Province on October 21," the Indian foreign ministry statement said.
"These attacks have unfortunately resulted in civilian deaths and injuries," India's foreign ministry said.
Modi meets Polish PM Donald Tusk, discusses bilateral ties
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Polish counterpart Donald Tusk held talks in New Delhi on Thursday to review bilateral ties and explore cooperation in trade, defense and technology, media reports said.
"Our growing economic strength has created new opportunities for the India-Poland partnership. And the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement has made these opportunities even broader," Modi said while addressing the joint press meet with Tusk.
Tusk said the friendship between New Delhi and Warsaw is not based merely on diplomatic relations, but on the "shared heritage of humanity and empathy."
The two leaders oversaw the exchange of several memorandums of understanding.
Tusk is on a two-day trip to India ending on Friday. He is accompanied by Polish Minister of Finance and Economy, Andrzej Domanski, and a business delegation.
On Wednesday, Tusk met Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar where the two discussed ways to deepen bilateral cooperation, according to reports.
Tiger Shroff shooters allegedly surveyed homes of other Bollywood stars
Authorities investigating last week's shooting at actor Tiger Shroff's car said the alleged shooters had conducted reconnaissance at the homes of Bollywood stars Salman Khan, Aamir Khan and Ranbir Kapoor before targeting Shroff, who they believed had less security, the Indian Express newspaper reported.
This comes even as three more people were arrested in connection with the shooting, Mumbai Police said.
The total number of people arrested related to the case has now risen to 10.
Three motorcycle-borne assailants had opened fire at Shroff's car in the western city of Mumbai on October 18. The actor escaped unhurt, while his driver and a bystander were injured.
Three key accused, including the alleged shooters, were caught by the police while trying to escape to Nepal.
Police suspect the attack was carried out at the behest of Anil Pandit, an alleged operative of the Lawrence Bishnoi gang.
The Bishnoi gang, accused of involvement in the 2023 killing of Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in Canada, has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Bishnoi, a jailed Indian gangster, has been accused by US prosecutors of directing murders, extortion and international drug trafficking from inside a prison in Gujarat.
Google, Mozilla, Apple block certificates by Indian company over security flaw
Bengaluru-based digital identity and cybersecurity company eMudhra has revoked eight intermediate certificates after their private keys were found to be weak, prompting Google, Mozilla, Apple and Microsoft to block the affected certificates.
"Eight intermediate (issuing) CAs in our Global TLS business were revoked because their published keys were weak," the company said, adding that it was investigating the issue.
A certificate authority (CA) is an organization that browsers such as Chrome, Firefox and Safari rely on to verify website identities and establish secure connections.
The flaw could have allowed attackers to impersonate legitimate websites using fraudulent certificates and potentially intercept or manipulate supposedly secure online communications. However, no evidence of such misuse has been publicly confirmed.
The flaw originated in a key-generation process in April 2025 that produced weak private keys, the company said.
Media reports citing security researcher Scott Helme said one of the keys was the number four, rather than a cryptographically secure, randomly generated number, while others were also easily guessable.
India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) said it had taken serious note of the incident.
"A special team has been constituted to investigate the matter," the ministry said in a statement on X.
CJP leaders freed after undertaking not to call for protests at Jantar Mantar
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were released from Tihar Jail on Wednesday after a Special Executive Magistrate declined a police request to extend their judicial custody by three more days, reports said.
The two leaders at the forefront of the protests calling for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar following voter-list irregularities, furnished personal bonds and sureties of Rs 50,000 (€470; $530) each.
Their written undertakings promised to maintain peace and not call for protests at Jantar Mantar "till such a time that it is denotified in accordance with law."
The iconic protest site was denotified by Delhi Police earlier in October, months after CJP-led protests culminated in the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Das and Ranka were booked for "trespassing" after entering the Jantar Mantar protest site and raising the Indian flag.
The latest CJP protests have called for Kumar’s resignation over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the deletion of voters' names.

Prime minister: We'll definitely work better with the Social Democrats under Vseviov
Prime Minister and Reform Party Chairman Kristen Michal said his party would certainly have better cooperation with the Social Democratic Party if it were led by Jonatan Vseviov.
Jonatan Vseviov, the longtime secretary general of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and a security expert who has announced he is joining the Social Democrats, criticized the current government and Prime Minister Kristen Michal's leadership at a press conference Thursday, saying they lacked sharpness of mind, intellectual breadth and the courage to assert themselves.
Michal responded to Vseviov's criticism in broader terms.
"I think it's very good that Jonatan has entered politics. When I think about people who want to have a say and contribute, it's very good that they enter politics. It would be rather peculiar if people just wrote poetry and kept it in a drawer — not that there's anything wrong with that. Writing poetry and keeping it in a drawer is fine, too. But if you actually want to engage in politics, you have to do it in politics. So I certainly welcome Jonatan's arrival," Michal said at the government's press conference.
"And I'll add something on a personal note. I understand that he may have been given a few Social Democratic talking points. I think we'll certainly have better cooperation with the Social Democrats led by Jonatan Vseviov. I really do. So I'm genuinely pleased. I understand it might not seem logical for me to be happy about a political rival, but I actually am," Michal said.
SDE head Lauri Läänemets said at the Social Democratic Party's press conference that he would remain the party's leader. Michal's reference to the Social Democrats being led by Vseviov can therefore be interpreted as a jab at the party's current chairman.
"Second, I want to thank him for his work on foreign policy. We've done a great many things together. Some really impressive things. We've shared all the highs and lows of Estonian foreign policy and I want to thank him for that. We've carried that responsibility together," he added.
"And third, I understand that there's one recurring point in the Social Democrats' talking points, which I also noticed during Monday's confidence vote. They say Estonia's economy is on the wrong track. I heard something similar from that press conference, that Estonia's economy is supposedly heading for catastrophe or something along those lines. Well, it isn't. This year, Estonia's economy is growing twice as fast as the European Union average. I think that should be written in the corner at every press conference and we should say: Friends, let's start with that. I'm not just talking about the economy in general — Estonians' incomes have increased, precisely because of what we did with income tax reform: We eliminated the tax hump created by the progressive income tax system introduced by the Social Democrats, the Center Party and Isamaa," Michal said.
Michal added that the Reform Party and the Social Democrats would not find common ground on economic issues, but said cooperation was possible on foreign and security policy.
Both Lauri Läänemets and Vseviov said Estonia needs to do more to assert itself on the international stage and in various discussions concerning security. In their view, the country's current leadership has failed to achieve this.
"After all, we've all worked on foreign policy together. Jonatan, myself, Margus [Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna — ed.] and everyone else, including the presidents. If I look at the issues that matter to us, first of all, Russian assets have been permanently frozen since the end of last year. From our perspective, that's a very good result. Previously, we had to vote on extending the freeze every three or six months. Should our voice be heard? I think it has been. When it comes to the shadow fleet, we took the lead. I even remember criticism at home and I remember going to parliament where I think it was either EKRE or the Center Party trying to argue that we shouldn't be bothering these honest ships sailing to and from Russia. Why were we harassing them? They said the whole thing was suspicious and some even claimed we were about to trigger World War III. But then [French President] Emmanuel Macron came up to me and said they were doing the same thing and they also detained a ship that we had already detained. Then the Americans came along and said, 'Good, let's get to work.' I don't know, is that good or not? I think it is. I'm personally satisfied and I think it was the right thing to do," Michal said.
"Then there are Russian fighters. This is something we're all working on, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is working on, Jonatan has worked hard on it, Margus has worked on it, I've worked on it and I think many others have as well. The result is that European countries are seriously discussing, at the European Council summit I'm attending, how to put an end to Russians vacationing in Europe — the very same people who are killing women and children. We want to stop issuing them visas. Finland has joined us, Petteri Orpo [the Finnish prime minister — ed.] has made such a proposal and many other countries have come on board. I think the countries where Russians go on vacation are clearly moving in that direction as well," Michal said.
"I'm not sure how you would measure that. I also read an article by Lauri Läänemets, again featuring Social Democratic talking points, in which he said Kaja Kallas used to exchange messages with Macron. But here's a candid admission: I exchange messages with Macron more often than I do with Lauri Läänemets. It's actually quite funny," Michal added.

Australia hits North Korean 'shadow bankers' with fresh sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:32:50 UTC
11:32:50 KST

North Korean companies employing fraudulent online workers hit with fresh sanctions
In short:
North Korean companies have been accused of employing workers to launder billions of dollars through cybercrime.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong has announced fresh sanctions and says the "export of labour" violates UN sanctions.
What's next?
Australia continues to call on North Korea to comply with its international obligations.
The federal government has hit two North Korean companies and "shadow bankers" with sanctions for employing fraudulent online workers who help Pyongyang evade UN sanctions and earn cash for its nuclear weapons program.
The US and several other nations have accused North Korea of setting up an international network of IT workers to launder billions of dollars through cybercrime and overseas earnings.
The two men sanctioned by Australia — Sim Hyon Sop and Yu Py Ung — have been identified by US authorities as key financial brokers for the regime.
In 2024 the US Treasury called Yu Pu Ung "a linchpin in the DPRK's illicit financial activities [who] is skilled at employing various schemes to avoid detection".
The year before that the FBI offered a $5 million dollar reward for information to assist with the capture of Sim Hyon Sop, who the agency said helped North Korea evade sanctions.
He "allegedly played a pivotal role in defrauding U.S. banks by remitting U.S. dollar payments to facilitate trade on behalf of North Korea," the FBI said.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong said the sanctioned companies employed North Koreans who impersonated nationals from other countries, worked on online platforms and sent their income to key North Korean government agencies.
Senator Wong said that was "a violation of UN Security Council resolutions that prohibit North Korea's export of labour" and that Australia was acting "in coordination with international partners, including the European Union".
"Australian sanctions reinforce our ongoing efforts, alongside international partners, to disrupt North Korea's illicit revenue-generating networks and increase pressure on the regime to comply with its international obligations and abandon its nuclear and ballistic missile programs," she said.
North Korea has repeatedly denied setting up shadow financial networks and says the allegations against it are fabricated.
But law enforcement and financial institutions from across the world say there is a mountain of evidence to back their accusations.
In July the US, Australia, Japan, South Korea, the UK, Canada and several European nations warned that North Korean workers were employing "increasingly sophisticated methods, including the integration of AI, to obfuscate their identities and expand their activities globally".
They urged countries around the world to "deepen their understanding of North Korean IT worker schemes and implement measures to counter [them]".
New Zealand's cyber authorities also warned in advisory earlier this year that a North Korean operative posing as remote contractor was unwittingly hired by a local business.
Senator Wong said Australia continued to call on North Korea to "comply fully with UN Security Council resolutions and to take concrete steps towards complete, verifiable and irreversible denuclearisation".

MINSK, October 22. /TASS/. The West’s aggressive actions against Russia and Belarus are intensifying, with NATO, the European Union, and the Kiev regime deliberately pursuing a path of escalation, Russian Defense Minister Andrey Belousov said during a joint board meeting of the Russian and Belarusian Defense Ministries.
He emphasized that the North Atlantic Alliance’s military preparations require the armed forces of Russia and Belarus to respond promptly to changes in the military-political situation.
TASS has summarized the defense minister’s key statements.
Aggressive actions by the West
Aggressive actions by the West against Russia and Belarus are on the rise: "Today, the military-political situation surrounding our countries remains complex. We are observing a rapid increase in tensions and aggressive actions by the West against Russia and Belarus."
NATO, the European Union, and the Kiev regime are deliberately pursuing a path of escalation: "NATO, the EU, and the Kiev regime are deliberately pursuing a path of escalation. <…> The accelerated militarization of Europe poses a particular danger, as it is shifting industry toward military production and preparing infrastructure for the rapid deployment of armed forces."
NATO countries are increasing their military presence near the borders of Russia and Belarus: "The coalition’s military presence near our borders is growing."
In 2027, the North Atlantic Alliance plans "to bring eight multinational battalion tactical groups on its ‘eastern flank’ up to brigade strength in 2027."
NATO is also conducting exercises to rehearse offensive scenarios against Russia and Belarus: "The Alliance is conducting drills rehearsing offensive scenarios against our countries."
Need to respond
The North Atlantic Alliance’s military preparations require the armed forces of Russia and Belarus to respond promptly to changes in the military-political situation: "All of this requires us to respond in a timely manner to changes in the military-political situation - to strengthen cooperation in ensuring security and to build up our military capabilities. To this end, we are refining our approaches to the joint use of armed forces."
As part of this response, military personnel from both countries regularly conduct "combat coordination exercises for formations and units assigned to the regional grouping of troops (forces)": "We give priority to joint practical exercises based on best practices from the special military operation."
In September-October, the Center 2026 strategic command and staff exercise took place alongside the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) Rapid Reaction Forces’ Interaction maneuvers held according to a unified plan, the Search intelligence forces and assets exercise, and the Echelon logistical support exercise: "I would like to note the active participation of the Belarusian side in these events."
Cooperation with Belarus
Belarus and Russia are close allies and partners with shared cultural and moral values: "Belarus and Russia are strategic allies and partners, bound not only by treaty obligations but also by shared values, a shared history, and a shared responsibility for security within the Union State."
Russia and Belarus are developing cooperation between the defense-industrial complexes of the two countries: "We continue to pay special attention to cooperation in the military-technical sphere. We are establishing cooperation between the defense-industrial complexes of the two countries."
Russian military universities, he reported, continue to train Belarusian military personnel at the Russian Defense Ministry’s educational institutions: "Currently, 418 Belarusian military personnel are studying at 24 military universities under unified curricula and programs."
Training in the most sought-after specialties is organized at Russia’s joint-force combat training center in Mulino: "Since the start of the special military operation, 1,315 people have undergone training there on behalf of the Armed Forces of the Republic of Belarus."
"We are developing cooperation in the field of culture. In May 2027, we will organize the Avanpost International Festival of Army Culture and Creativity, featuring ensembles from the armed forces of Russia, Belarus, and other friendly nations."
The extensive cooperation achieved between the military departments of Russia and Belarus ensures the prompt fulfillment of tasks aimed at countering the full spectrum of modern challenges and threats to the security of both countries.

Gallery: Tallinn hosts 11 Ukrainian artists' work from international residency

Gallery: Tallinn hosts 11 Ukrainian artists' work from international residency
Three Tallinn locations are showing work by 11 Ukrainian photographers and visual artists, capping a recent international art residency held in Estonia, Finland and Germany.
The four-and-a-half-month "Waves of Creativity" project supported Ukrainian artists whose lives and work have been affected by Russia's war against Ukraine, including two who have spent time on the front.
Residencies took place in Saaremaa, Estonia, Joutsa, Finland and Stuttgart, Germany earlier this year.
The project's final exhibition opened in Tallinn on October 15, with displays at the Vabamu Museum of Occupations and Freedom, Okapi Gallery and the open-air Baltic Station Art Street.
The Tallinn show brings together documentary photography, experimental photo art, video and installations. While not all the works depict war directly, many explore personal experience, memory, home, everyday life, changing surroundings and people's relationships with the world around them.
Three ways to encounter the work
The three participating locations offer three different ways to encounter the work.
Okapi Gallery presents work developed during the residency in a traditional gallery setting, while a pop-up exhibition at Vabamu connects the artists' personal experiences with broader historical and social themes.
An outdoor display along the Art Street at Tallinn's Balti jaam, meanwhile, brings contemporary Ukrainian photography into public space, reaching audiences who may not typically visit galleries.
Curated by Temuri Hvingija and co-curator Andrii Mur, participating artists include Mykyta Bezus, Oxana Chorna, Iryna Klachek, Olia Koval, Herman Krieger, Ievgeniia Kupchan, Valentyn Kuzan, Oleh Pereverziev, Alina Prisich, Olesia Saienko and Elena Subach.
The exhibition runs at Okapi Gallery through November 20 and will remain on display at Baltic Station Art Street through March 30. 2027.

In a different light: How Türkiye is bringing history to life after dark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:49:06 UTC
21:49:06 KST

As night falls, the Istanbul Archaeological Museum takes on a different character.
Artificial lighting illuminates its facades, sculptures, and architectural details, turning daytime grandeur into a more intimate journey where light and shadow bring each feature to life.
This transformation is part of Türkiye's night museum initiative, which allows visitors to explore selected museums and archaeological sites after dark between June and October.
It has attracted visitors like Elif, a 29-year-old Turkish woman who has visited Ephesus and Side at night, two ancient cities on Türkiye's Aegean and Mediterranean coasts, and frequently visits the Nevsehir Open-Air Museum in Cappadocia.
"These places, which we usually explore during the day almost through the eyes of an archaeologist, offer a truly spectacular visual experience at night," she tells TRT Español. "I think they give you a much stronger sense of what it was like to live in that era."
For her, visiting these sites at night offers something that a conventional daytime visit cannot.
"These initiatives breathe life into these places and allow you to experience emotions you haven't felt before."
From one night to a whole summer
While "museum nights" have become established as one-off cultural events across much of Europe, Türkiye has taken the concept a step further, making it a summer-long initiative since 2024.
Ephesus, Hierapolis and Side were among the first major sites to participate.
That year, the programme attracted 395,212 visitors, reflecting growing interest in experiencing the country's cultural heritage in a new light.
In 2025, the initiative expanded to include additional museums and archaeological sites, marking a significant increase in scale.
Speaking to TRT Español, Serkan Geduk, head of the Museums Department at the General Directorate of Cultural Heritage, says the initiative, launched in 2024, aims to preserve cultural heritage, pass it on to future generations, and promote tourism.
"Our goal is to make Türkiye's rich cultural heritage accessible at any time of the day and to reinforce our vision of sustainable tourism," says Geduk.
The 2026 season, which ran from June to October, opened 22 locations to visitors, including 11 museums and 11 archaeological sites.
In Istanbul, the programme includes the Istanbul Archaeological Museums, the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts and Galata Tower.
The latter is an exception, with night visits year-round.
Geduk tells TRT Español that the programme expanded to 27 museums and archaeological sites by 2025, drawing more than one million visitors.
Among the most popular locations, he cites Ephesus, Hierapolis, Galata Tower and the Bodrum Museum of Underwater Archaeology.
The figures point to strong demand. Between June and July 2026, Ephesus welcomed 213,192 visitors during its evening opening hours, with more than 156,000 in July.
For Seda Cicekli Ayyildiz, a researcher at the Faculty of Tourism at Bolu Abant Izzet Baysal University and co-author of one of the first academic studies specifically examining night-time museum experiences in Türkiye, the key is to see the initiative as more than simply an extension of opening hours.
"Visitors no longer want to be passive observers; they want to be part of the experience," Ayyildiz tells TRT Español.
According to the researcher, night visits enhance the sensory experience of museums and archaeological sites, creating a deeper and more memorable connection with cultural heritage.
In Türkiye, where temples, theatres and ancient cities remain part of the landscape, nightfall offers a different perspective on this heritage. Lighting highlights details, the surroundings grow quieter, and history feels much closer to visitors.
Practical reasons also drive this transformation. Many of Türkiye's major archaeological sites are in regions where high summer temperatures make daytime visits difficult, particularly during the hottest hours.
"During the summer months, the high temperatures often make it difficult to visit during the day," says Geduk, adding that evening opening hours allow visitors to explore museums and archaeological sites "in a cooler and more pleasant atmosphere", particularly at Ephesus, Hierapolis and Side.
Ayyildiz believes the initiative has even greater potential: extended opening hours make cultural heritage more accessible, help spread tourist crowds, and link museum visits to evening activities in their destinations.
The ministry shares this view, highlighting the programme's ability to spread tourist activity throughout the day, benefit local economies and strengthen cultural tourism.
What the darkness reveals
But reducing the appeal of night-time museum visits by lowering temperatures and extending opening hours would overlook something more profound.
"At night, a museum or archaeological site becomes a very different place from the one we see during the day," Omer Yilmaz, an architect specialising in tourism design, tells TRT Español.
"During the day, we perceive the whole; at night, our field of vision narrows and we concentrate on what the light shows us."
A column, a wall or a relief can take on prominence that might go unnoticed in uniform daylight. Lighting is no longer simply a means of making a monument visible; it begins to shape how visitors move through and interpret the space.
"In nighttime museology, lighting becomes a fundamental design tool that directly determines how the visitor interprets the space," says Yilmaz.
This means deciding what to illuminate, what to leave in the background and which routes visitors should follow. It also means accepting something that may seem contradictory: not everything needs to be visible.
"We must not forget that darkness is also part of the design," he says.
Ayyildiz agrees that lighting can become a storytelling tool. Through the interplay of light and shadow, it can draw visitors' attention to columns, reliefs and architectural details that might otherwise go unnoticed during the day.
For her, success is simple: "The ideal is not for the visitor to say 'how well lit', but 'I have never seen this place like this'."
She suggests lighting should draw attention to the heritage, not itself.
Canan, 36, who visited the Istanbul Archaeological Museums this summer, highlights another effect of the darkness: silence. Having visited several times during the day, she found the night-time experience "very different".
"Going at night made the atmosphere quieter, and I really liked that. I think that, above all, I enjoyed that feeling of silence," she tells TRT Español.
Night-time visits also offer new possibilities for designing exhibition spaces. Canan, for example, points to the potential for further developing the lighting of artefacts displayed in gardens and outdoor areas.
There is no single approach. A Roman theatre, an archaeological museum, a rock-cut settlement or a hoyuk (a mound formed by successive layers of human settlement) each offers different possibilities.
Each site's character can determine what to illuminate, which routes to create, and what kind of night-time experience to offer.
The experience can also extend beyond the visual. Ayyildiz suggests activities such as archaeology nights under the stars, storytelling sessions, workshops and events incorporating music, literature and gastronomy, allowing visitors to engage with heritage through more than just sight.
When the night ends
The 2026 night museum season concluded this month across much of Türkiye, although some Istanbul sites remain open after dark. While locations such as Ephesus, Side and Goreme extended their opening hours only until mid-to-late October, Galata Tower will continue welcoming visitors at night throughout the year.
The ministry is already looking ahead.
"Our ministry continues to carry out the necessary infrastructure work to more effectively extend night museology throughout the country," says Geduk.
The aim is to include more museums and archaeological sites and gradually expand the programme.
For those who have experienced it, the appeal is clear. Elif says she would return and recommends the experience to others.
"I think it transports you to completely different universes and renews your way of looking."
Canan agrees: "I would repeat the experience. In fact, I would also like to visit Topkapi Palace and Galata Tower at night. I hope that this initiative will continue in the coming years as well".
With visitor numbers more than doubled, the programme is now entering a new phase. The ministry plans to expand its reach by adding sites, using data-driven planning, and developing new experiences tailored to each destination.
For museum specialists, architects, and heritage managers, the challenge is to ensure these experiences respect each site's character.
"The aim should not be to turn a historic space into a set or a place of entertainment," says Yilmaz,
"but to allow the visitor to discover in a different way, at night, spatial and historical features that they might not perceive during the day."
For Ayyildiz, the objective "should not simply be to attract more people, but to encourage more people to establish a quality, conscious and sustainable relationship with cultural heritage".
Perhaps that is the real appeal of night-time museum visits. It is not simply about illuminating historic sites so they can be seen as they are in daylight, but about discovering how nightfall can change the way we experience and understand history.

The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies.
Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades.
During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”.

— Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 22, 2026
Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies.
Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20.
“The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said.
Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.”
Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market.
Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”.
“Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.”
However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals.
The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible".

To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations.
Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people.
The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors.
Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS).

The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year.
