Sanctions-hit ICC wins top EU rights prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:47:09 UTC
21:47:09 KST

A general view of the exterior of the International Criminal Court in The Hague, Netherlands, March 12, 2025. (AP File Photo)
Facing U.S. sanctions, the International Criminal Court was on Oct. 22 awarded the European Union’s top rights prize, in a show of support that risks upsetting President Donald Trump.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” said European Parliament chief Roberta Metsola in announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize “at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges.”
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick,” furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.
The win comes after ex-ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as U.N. rights chief, was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize this month, a choice Trump slammed as “disgraceful,” arguing the award should have gone to him.
The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the U.S. sanctions, which will come into force in six months, and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can keep working.
Set up in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organisations to recognise their fight for human rights or democracy.
The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government.

France confirms first Shamonda virus infection in a human death of 'severely immunocompromised' individual
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:46:00 UTC
21:46:00 KST

France confirms first human infection of Shamonda livestock virus
October 22, 2026
French health officials on Thursday confirmed that they had detected the Shamonda virus in a human — who died early this month — in what they say was the first-ever case of a human contracting the livestock disease.
"Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, the Shamonda virus has never previously been detected in humans," said France's Ministries of Health and of Agriculture in a joint statement.
"No health risk to the general public identified at this time," they said, adding that the human infection appeared to be, "an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient."
The World Health Organization (WHO) said the virus was unlikely to spread.
"Based on current information and knowledge of the transmission of closely related viruses, this is an isolated human case and it is unlikely to lead to wider spread at this time," WHO told Reuters in a statement.
How is Shamonda virus transmitted?
First identified in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, the insect-borne Shamonda virus is a variant of the Orthobunyavirus, a genus that contains 138 species, and primarily affects livestock, particularly cattle.
It is transmitted by culicoides, or biting midges.
The virus has been detected in animals in Africa and Japan for years and has been spreading across Europe this year.
Until now, it was not thought to be transmissible to humans.
According to a press statement on the Ministry of Agriculture's webpage, "At this stage of the investigation, the hypothesis is that the case resulted from vector-borne transmission via the bite of a culicoid midge in eastern France, a region where the virus was reported to be circulating among animals in the spring and summer of 2026."
The ministry said biological, clinical and epidemiological investigations are being carried out by experts in human, animal and environmental health, adding that authorities at the WHO and European Center for Disease Control had been notified of the incident.

Every Moment Is a Life: Gaza in the Time of Genocide
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:44:30 UTC
21:44:30 KST

“To write stories in the heart of an unfolding genocide is to draw ink from the depths of your own heart,” writes Huzama Habayeb, the Arabic editor of Every Moment Is a Life. “To read stories of genocide, while the slaughter rages relentlessly, unceasingly, means that—at the very least—your heart will be crushed.”
She is right. Reading this anthology is a crushing experience. More than once the book has to be put down, and each time the reader picks it up again, because the people who wrote it deserve to be heard to the end.
The collection was compiled by the Palestinian American novelist Susan Abulhawa. It brings together heart-rending true stories by eighteen young writers from Gaza. They wrote in Arabic while Israel’s bombs fell around them, and the book is published in a bilingual Arabic-English edition by Atria/One Signal Publishers, an imprint of Simon & Schuster. All proceeds go to the contributors in Gaza and to the Palestine Writes Literature Festival.
The origin of this compilation has its roots in two journeys made by Abulhawa to Gaza in 2024. On both visits, she crossed into the besieged enclave with as many bags of aid as she could carry. While there, she collected stories from women recovering in hospital. Many wept as they described what they had seen, heard and felt, often exploring those details aloud for the first time, and the sessions became what Abulhawa calls “a kind of Indigenous therapy”.
Two friends, Majeda Saqqa and Maha elRa’ee, asked Abulhawa to run a writing workshop for young people at the Culture and Free Thought Association (CFTA). Every writer included in the collection had been displaced and had lost people they loved. Struck by the writers’ talent for storytelling, Abulhawa decided that the most useful thing she could do was to help Palestinians in Gaza tell their story of living through genocide.
READ: What is life like for Palestinians with disabilities during Israel’s genocide?
The workshops were held on the beach and in the CFTA courtyard, under the constant buzz of Israeli drones. The stories that emerged draw the reader into the heart of their reality: ordinary human moments, buying bread, mending a shoe, sharing a meal, set against what Abulhawa describes as “the first live-streamed genocide”.
Habayeb spent more than three months editing the Arabic stories with the writers entirely over WhatsApp. She calls it an “emotional odyssey”. She would send her notes and then wait, sometimes for days, fearing the worst. One reply read: “I buried my wife yesterday; please bear with me until the mourning period ends.” Another writer apologised for the delay because the family had fled to the sea and still had nowhere to sleep. A third hoped to send the final version at the weekend, adding: “my brother was martyred.”
In Every Moment Is a Life, the story that gives the book its title, Rizq Ahmad describes four families sharing a makeshift nylon shack, which they carry from one so-called “safe zone” to another. They nickname it “The Four Coupons”, after their food-aid vouchers.
There is no mirror in the shack. Anyone wanting to check their appearance turns to Ahmad’s mother, Hanan, who finds them beautiful whatever they look like. Ahmad’s trousers barely stay up, even with a belt wrapped around his waist. As he leaves the shack, his brother calls after him: “Don’t stay out long! I need the pants later.”
Even in these impossible times, Ahmad finds warmth in the family’s life together. They still gather for meals around a rickety table or on a mat on the ground, and lunch turns into lively political debate. They laugh as they squeeze together to sleep, sharing whatever food they have.
“A new intimacy formed among us—no blame, no complaints, no regret,” he writes. “Maybe because every minute of life is a whole life, one that cannot be taken for granted.”
In Ma’rouf, Ghassan Salam tells the story of Sami, who spends a night hiding in a greenhouse after fleeing Khan Younis. Across an open field, a baby is crying in his dead mother’s arms. Sami fears that trying to reach the child will get them both killed. For hours he listens, blaming himself each time the crying fades. After daybreak, he reaches the boy and carries him to safety.
Sami cares for the child as his own and names him Ma’rouf, which means “known”. Later, he finds papers showing that the boy’s real name is Adam and returns him to his uncle. When the uncle’s house is bombed, killing the rest of the family, Sami rushes to the scene and recognises the boy, alive but injured, as medics rescue the casualties.
BOOK REVIEW: How to Sell a Genocide: The Media’s Complicity in the Destruction of Gaza
“I recognized him by his little toes. I had kissed them so many times.”
An aunt later takes the child north to Jabalia. Sitting in a café some time afterwards, Sami watches breaking news of an Israeli air strike there and sees the boy among the bodies in the street. “Ma’rouf was gone. And I was left behind.”
In Khadija Abu-Lebdeh’s The Decision, the narrator, Ghada, has lost both her parents in the genocide and watched her brother Qasim die of illness. She clings to his bed, the last trace of their life together, its headboard covered in his drawings. But the family has burned everything else they own for cooking, and her older brother asks her to give it up.
“Are memories of our departed loved ones more important than those still living?”
Ghada lets it go and watches the fire take Qasim’s drawings. One charred scrap of paper drifts into her lap with just two words left on it: “the living”.
In Coffee by Old Blue, Muhammad Mu’ammar’s narrator takes his morning coffee to the sea he calls Old Blue, his friend since childhood. He had always dreamed of living by the sea. Now he does, in a tent, after being driven from his home and helping gather the remains of thirty or more relatives.
“My dream came true at last, but not as I dreamed.”
The narrator and his wife used to sit there together. Now he sits alone, having buried her with his own hands. “I do not dare call her name now.” He has come back to the sea, he says, “to become like you. An old blue soul. An immensity of silence.”
Umbilical Cord by Maysa Salama is a love story told in sign language. At an Israeli checkpoint, soldiers order the men to fall back. The husband is deaf, and his wife translates the orders for him with her hands. Before they part, he writes their three-year-old daughter’s name on his wife’s hand and ties the girl’s wrist to her mother’s with rope, like a new umbilical cord that might deliver the child safely into the world a second time.
The mother walks on, still bleeding after giving birth only days earlier, the newborn crying at her chest, until she faints. When she comes round, her daughter tells her: “Mama, you were going to fly away if I hadn’t held on to you.”
Not every writer offers the steadfastness the world expects of Palestinians. In For Gaza to Leave Us Something, Nebal Al-Najjar describes being displaced four times and her wish to escape Gaza’s destruction. Abulhawa praises her for daring to write what a world that expects Palestinians to be superheroes may not want to hear.
No review can do justice to this book. It is not one to be read once and put away. In the hospital in Gaza, the women who first spoke of what they had seen, heard and felt found comfort in being listened to. Every Moment Is a Life asks the same of its readers: to sit with these writers, to take in every detail of their loss, and to grieve with them. It is painful, but it can also be healing, the kind of “Indigenous therapy” Abulhawa found among those women. It is a book to be read, and read again.

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:44:23 BST
21:44:23 KST

Ministry of Defence Police: misconduct hearings
Find out about misconduct hearings involving Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) officers and how to attend these public hearings.
Misconduct hearings
To increase openness and transparency in the MDP (and the police service in general), misconduct hearings, special case hearings and police appeals tribunals, involving Police Officers, are held in public.
Misconduct hearings deal with allegations of gross misconduct committed by MDP officers on or off duty. Gross misconduct is defined as ‘a breach of the police standards of professional behaviour (PSPB)’ that is so serious as to justify dismissal’. Misconduct hearings form part of the disciplinary process and are not criminal proceedings.
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings
Accelerated Misconduct Hearings take place when the investigation of allegations of Gross Misconduct, committed by MDP officers on or off duty, identifies that special conditions, such as the following are satisfied:
- that there is sufficient evidence, in the form of written statements or other documents, to establish on the balance of probabilities that the conduct of the officer concerned constitutes Gross Misconduct
- it is in the public interest for the officer concerned to cease to be a member of the MDP without delay
Police Appeals Tribunals
Police Appeals Tribunals deal with appeals submitted by MDP officers, against the findings and/or the outcomes of misconduct hearings (including accelerated misconduct hearings), under the MDP Conduct Regulations, or stage 3 meetings under the Performance Regulations.
The decision to hold misconduct hearings and police appeals tribunals in public was announced by the Home Secretary in 2015. The Ministry of Defence Police followed suit in March 2017 by amendments to the Ministry of Defence Police conduct (2015) and performance (2012) regulations, and by subsequent revision of those Regulations into the new Ministry of Defence Police (Conduct, Performance and Appeals Tribunals) Regulations 2020, which came into effect for all cases assessed as Gross Misconduct after 2 November 2020.
This change of legislation does not affect misconduct meetings, where a breach of PSPB does not amount to gross misconduct. These proceedings will be held in private and the public have no right to observe (except in the case of a complainant or the commission^, where appropriate).
^Director General (IOPC) or Ombudsman (NI) if they conducted or directed the investigation.
What happens at a misconduct hearing
At a misconduct hearing the facts are heard by a panel, often with the help of witnesses, to enable a finding to be made. If an officer is found to have committed misconduct or gross misconduct, depending on the circumstances, the available outcomes are:
- written warning (only if misconduct only found)
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at an Accelerated Misconduct Hearing
An accelerated hearing is heard by the Chief Constable. Due to the evidence being incontrovertible there is no requirement for any witness attendance. If an officer is found to have committed gross misconduct, the available outcomes are:
- final written warning
- reduction in rank
- dismissal without notice
What happens at a Police Appeals Tribunal
Police appeals tribunals are heard by a panel chaired by a person nominated by the Lord Chancellor who satisfies the judicial appointment criteria. The tribunal determines whether the ‘grounds of appeal’ on which the appellant relies, have been made out. On the determination of an appeal, a tribunal may make an order dealing with the appellant in any way in which they could have been dealt with at the original hearing.
Attending a misconduct hearing
Any member of the public or press can request to attend a misconduct hearing, provided that they are aged 18 or over.
When the date of a misconduct hearing is confirmed, the details will be published below. Due to the MDP being a national force the location of the misconduct hearing may vary (dependent upon the case).
Please note the following conditions of entry:
- any member of the public or press wishing to attend must register in advance, by the specified closing date, and using the they must also provide valid photo identification (for example passport or driving licence) upon attendance. (To fill out the misconduct hearing form on a mobile device you must make sure that the PDF is opened in the editable mode.)
- any person who is a witness at the proceedings will not be permitted to attend prior to giving their evidence but, may be permitted to take a seat in the public gallery after this time
- priority will be given to interested parties and attendance will then be granted on a ‘first come, first served’ basis (up to the capacity of the venue)
- any restrictions on reporting will be notified in advance of the hearing
- members of the public and press are to remain silent at all times while the hearing is in session
- no photographs, film or sound recording are permitted; mobile phones and other devices can be retained but must be switched off during the hearing
- any conditions particular to an individual hearing will be published on this page in advance of the hearing
- where a hearing is adjourned for an extended period, attendees may be expected to leave the premises and return at the appointed time; if the hearing is held within an MOD establishment members of the public and press will be escorted from the gate to the venue and back; they will not be permitted to leave the venue except to leave the establishment
- no food or refreshments, with the exclusion of water, will be permitted in the hearing room; however, an area will be set aside for use by members of the public when the panel adjourn for short periods of time
- no refreshments will be provided by the MDP and if held at an MOD establishment, there may be no facilities to purchase food; in this instance, attendees should be self sufficient
- we cannot reimburse any expenses you incur by attending and please note that in some cases a hearing may be cancelled at short notice; in these situations, we will do our best to notify you but, it may not be possible
- members of the public and press, together with any bags, will be subject to a security search as a condition of entry and exit; anything that can be used or adapted to cause injury or damage will not be permitted
If you require disabled access, or have any other reasonable adjustment requirements, please advise us of your requirements on your registration form.
Once all applications to attend have been received and reviewed (after the closing date), your attendance will be confirmed, as applicable, by the means identified on your registration form.
Private hearings
Please note: in exceptional circumstances, the Chair can exclude anyone from all or part of the hearing at his/her discretion and may impose conditions relating to the attendance of any person.
Should the Secretary of State for Defence consider it expedient in the interests of national security, he/she may also give direction that:
- all or part of the hearing must be conducted in private
- a specified person must be excluded from all or part of the hearing
- specific steps are taken to conceal the identity of a witness
- specific information must be excluded from the published notification of misconduct hearings or notification of outcome

"Sometimes there is even heard an opinion at present that LNG overproduction will be in coming years. As long as Novatek deals with LNG, we always hear this phrase. Poll: Yotova Leads Gyurov by 14.5 Points in Bulgaria's Presidential Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:43:11 UTC
21:43:11 KST

Iliaana Yotova and Kiril Valchev lead Bulgaria’s presidential election race with 43.4% support, ahead of Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev at 28.9%, according to a nationally representative survey by polling agency Myara for the Bulgarian National Radio (BNR).
The poll, reflecting voter preferences in mid-October, puts Kostadin Kostadinov and Petar Volgin in third place with 10.2%. Ivelin Mihaylov and Yuliana Mateeva receive 3.1%, followed by Radostin Vasilev and Krasimir Manov with 2.9%, and Ivan Hristanov and Stoyanka Cherkezova with 1.9%.
“These figures represent a snapshot of electoral sentiment as of mid-October. There are hundreds of thousands of eligible Bulgarian voters who have yet to make up their minds,” the sociologists said.
Other candidates, including Georgi Dimov, Ivaylo Simeonov, Rosen Milenov, Volen Siderov, Rumyana Chenalova and Ivanka Tsvetanova-Petkova, have declared support levels of around 1%. Myara said it was too early to determine how much support they would ultimately attract. A further 2.5% of respondents said they would select the option “I do not support anyone.”
Based on respondents’ stated intentions, projected voter turnout stands at 39.4%, apparently slightly above the level recorded in previous surveys.
Myara’s team also found that more than three-quarters of Bulgaria’s adult population consider the person holding the presidency important. The vice president’s role is also significant to respondents, although to a lesser degree, with 57.4% attaching importance to the office. Meanwhile, 67.8% support expanding the powers of Bulgaria’s presidential institution.
“It appears that the presidency, as an institution, is significant to Bulgarian citizens. For more than three-quarters of the country's adult population, the individual holding the office of president is of substantial importance. The same applies to the office of the vice president, though to a lesser extent - 57.4%. Furthermore, a majority of 67.8% agree that the powers of the presidential institution in Bulgaria should be expanded. Naturally, these figures may reflect a certain automatic response, yet this in itself is revealing of broader public instincts,” the Myara team commented.
The poll also examined BNR’s role in informing voters during the presidential campaign. More than one-third of adult Bulgarians rely on the public broadcaster to some extent for information about the candidates and their platforms.
For 8.2% of respondents, BNR is their main source of information about the presidential candidates, while 13% regard it as one of their primary sources. Nearly 15% use the broadcaster as an additional source. Another 9.5% rely on BNR for general news and current affairs, but not specifically for coverage of the presidential election.
More than one-third of respondents said they do not follow BNR during the campaign, while the remaining participants were unable to assess the broadcaster’s role or declined to answer.
The survey was conducted between October 8 and October 19, 2026, through face-to-face tablet-assisted interviews with 1,009 adult Bulgarian citizens. The maximum margin of error is ±3.1% at a 50% share. One percent of the total sample, rather than of the electorate, represents approximately 53,000 people.

WHO was not told that Nigeria's Ebola patient travelled to Congo, official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:41:34 UTC
21:41:34 KST

Ebola patient in Nigeria believed to have contracted disease in Uganda, Switzerland says
DAKAR, Oct 22 - The Ebola patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, is believed to have contracted the disease while travelling in Uganda, a Swiss government statement to Reuters said on Thursday.
Nigeria reported the case, its first Ebola case in more than a decade, on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that was announced in Democratic Republic of Congo in mid-May and has since become the fastest-spreading on record.
Ugandan authorities have said the woman who fell ill in Nigeria had travelled to eastern Congo before transiting through Uganda. But the World Health Organization and Africa's top health agency said on Thursday they had not received confirmed information that the woman had travelled to Congo.
The woman "has been in a private clinic in Abuja for around a week with symptoms. She is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda around two weeks ago," said an emailed statement from the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs.
"Her husband is in isolation; he has not shown any symptoms. He was travelling with his wife when she is believed to have contracted Ebola."
Uganda reported 20 cases in May and June, mostly imported from Congo, but the World Health Organization declared the country Ebola-free in August.
Ugandan government spokesperson Alan Kasujja told Reuters late on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases.
"That's a fact. If we did, as has happened before, we'd be the first to say," he said.
Asked whether the Ugandan government had proof that the woman had travelled to Congo, Kasujja said, "Like what? A passport stamp? Without infringing on the patient’s rights?"
AFRICA CDC, WHO SAY NO INFORMATION THAT PATIENT WENT TO CONGO
Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention official Wessam Mankoula said on Thursday that Nigeria and Uganda were sharing information to establish the patient's movements and possible source of exposure.
"So far, there is no validated information (that) this case traveled to DRC (Democratic Republic of Congo)," Mankoula told an online press conference.
The WHO said information it had received about the case did not include travel outside Uganda.
"The facts which we have received is that the patient returned to Abuja on October 3, being away from September 16 in Uganda," WHO representative to Nigeria Pavel Ursu told the press conference.
Ursu said the focus in Nigeria was now on containing the viral infection and that the patient remained hospitalised, with her biochemical markers improving.
Jean Kaseya, Africa CDC director, told Reuters on Wednesday that the patient had been on a two-week holiday in Uganda.
Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response manager, said on Thursday the source of her infection was still unknown as health authorities were working to piece together her travel history.
One issue under investigation is which health facilities the woman visited in Abuja after the onset of her symptoms and before her hospitalisation 48 hours later, Otim said.
KENYA TRACES ALL CONTACTS OF FIRST CASE
Separately, a senior Kenyan health official said authorities there had now traced all 135 contacts of the country's first Ebola case, which was confirmed on October 6 and after which a further eight cases have been reported.
"We have been able to account for them 100%," health ministry director-general Patrick Amoth said. He said the last contact to be traced was a Ugandan citizen who had arrived in Kenya in early October on the same flight as the index patient but exited by road via the Namanga border post with Tanzania, which meant it took more time to find him.
Africa CDC is investigating whether the Kenyan case may have come into contact with the patient being treated in Nigeria, as both travelled from Uganda's Entebbe airport on the same day, Mankoula said. Transmission between the two was one of the possible scenarios being examined, he said.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.
The rare Ebola species behind the current outbreak kills about half of those infected and has no approved treatment or vaccine.
So far the outbreak is confirmed to have killed about 4,700 people across the four African countries that have reported cases, according to the Africa CDC. REUTERS

US university professor warns China seeks to divide Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:40:15 UTC
21:40:15 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Texas’ University of St. Thomas Professor Yeh Yao-yuan (葉耀元) warned Thursday that China is interfering in elections to deepen political divisions and undermine public trust in democracy, CNA reported.
Speaking at a National Taiwan University Hospital forum on election interference and democratic defense, Yeh said Beijing's main goal was not necessarily to help particular candidates win or lose elections. Instead, he said, China seeks to turn voters against one another and undermine confidence in democracy.
Yeh said China uses disinformation and online influence campaigns to reinforce existing political divisions. He warned that growing distrust could deepen disagreements over national defense and relations with China, leaving Taiwan more vulnerable to outside pressure.
China's interference should not be judged solely by election results, the professor said. The greater concern, Yeh said, is whether people with different political views become increasingly unwilling to accept one another.
The National Security Bureau has also warned of growing Chinese information campaigns ahead of the Nov. 28 local elections. The bureau said that it identified about 2.5 million items of contentious online content from January to September, up from 1.69 million during the same period last year, per Liberty Times.
China uses fake accounts, AI-generated videos, and coordinated online campaigns to spread misleading information, the bureau said. Social media and online forums were among the main platforms used for such activity.
Tsai Ming-yen (蔡明彥), the bureau's director-general, said that Chinese election interference was becoming more targeted. He identified six methods, namely illegal campaign funding, subsidized trips to China, discounted flights, disinformation, illegal betting, and cyberattacks, per SETN.
Yeh called for a foreign agents law to address activities carried out on behalf of foreign governments. He said stronger legal measures were needed to protect Taiwan's democracy from outside interference.
Hung Pu-chao (洪浦釗), director of the University of Taipei's Center for Global Strategy and Democratic Resilience, warned that China could step up election interference. He said Beijing would use the results to assess its efforts to influence Taiwan ahead of the Chinese Communist Party's 21st National Congress in 2027, per CTS News.
Hung said Greater Taipei could be major targets because of their political importance and competitive elections. The director warned that foreign funding and local networks could also be used to influence election campaigns.
He urged national security, law enforcement, and election agencies to share more intelligence and investigate suspicious foreign funding and coordinated online campaigns. Hung also called for tougher penalties to ensure elections are decided by voters.

The Dobrynya Nikitich drone is used to deliver cargo weighing up to 10 kg over distances of up to 12 km.

Macron targets Trump over French riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:38:28 UTC
21:38:28 KST

Macron targets Trump over French riots
French President Emmanuel Macron has slammed as “stupid” and “unacceptable” remarks by foreign leaders about the unrest gripping France, in an apparent swipe at US President Donald Trump, who blamed the violence on Paris’ lax border policies.
France has been rocked by some of its worst riots in years, sparked last month by teacher shortages and crumbling schools before escalating into nationwide protests over inequality, soaring living costs and public service cuts.
Hundreds of thousands took to the streets over the weekend as demonstrations descended into clashes with police, arson and looting. Nearly 2,400 people were arrested, around 1,000 officers injured, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched, with damage estimated at “hundreds of millions of euros.”
Trump pours fuel on the fire
Trump claimed that “migrants, jihadists, and communists” had “conquered, looted, and burned” France, accusing Macron of failing to secure its borders. He urged European leaders to “close their borders,” before seizing on the unrest to rally Republicans ahead of the November 3 midterms, warning that scenes of “burning steeples and raging fires” were “what the Radical Dumocrats want to do to AMERICA” with their own migration agenda.
Macron isn’t amused
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Macron accused outside actors of manipulating information about the events to their gain.
“There was foreign manipulation of information, which gave rise to unacceptable and stupid comments from many people, including foreign leaders,” he said. “We have had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false… These people annoy me.”
Asked whether he was referring to Trump, Macron replied: “Among others.”
President Emmanuel Macron said Wednesday that foreign leaders — including those “on the other side of the Atlantic” — were seeking to exploit France’s tense social climate for political gain following a weekend of street violence and looting.
Protests over soaring living costs… pic.twitter.com/XlitrzVoK6
— The Associated Press (@AP) October 21, 2026
While there is no clear evidence that migrants have played a disproportionate role in the unrest, multiple videos posted online have shown protesters waving Palestinian flags alongside French ones.
They said the riots and destruction in France were about the cost of living and schools.
Then explain the Palestinian flags and keffiyehs.
Allowing mass third-world migration is why France is done. pic.twitter.com/jDr733vcOx
— TaraBull (@TaraBull) October 19, 2026
French authorities have largely blamed the violence on radical far-left groups and opportunistic criminals, without linking its organization to immigrants. Meanwhile, politicians across France’s political spectrum blamed Macron and his government for the unrest, accusing the administration of undermining public services and failing to maintain order.
Macron leaves the building
Macron made his remarks during a Middle East trip that he refused to postpone despite the turmoil at home, leaving his government to deal with the fallout. He tried to defend his decision, insisting that changing his plans would have signaled “nervousness” and that he had given his government a “sufficient roadmap.” Yet with just six months until France’s presidential election and his approval rating at a record-low 15%, the trip has only fueled perceptions of a lame-duck presidency as Macron quite literally left the scene as Paris and other cities burned.
His absence drew criticism of an “absent president” and left rivals Marine Le Pen, who leads first-round polling for April 2027 with 32-36% support, and Jean-Luc Melenchon, to dominate the debate at home.
Meanwhile, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has ordered curfews ahead of fresh protests, with gatherings banned near Paris landmarks including the Louvre and Champs-Elysees for three days. France also plans to deploy 1,000 counterterrorism troops to reinforce police on Saturday, October 24. Lecornu is due to meet mayors of riot-hit cities on Thursday to coordinate efforts to prevent further violence.
Russia, the usual suspect
In his remarks, Macron also dismissed suggestions of foreign interference in the unrest itself, citing a lack of evidence. His remarks followed a flurry of Western media speculation seeking to blame the riots, which spread from France to Belgium, Italy, Portugal and Albania, on outside meddling – with Russia once again cast as the usual suspect.
Outlets such as The Financial Times and the Telegraph, citing “anonymous” sources, reported that several EU governments had asked intelligence agencies to investigate possible Russian involvement. The FT expanded the suspect list to Iran and Algeria, claiming some officials had even demanded a formal EU probe.
European officials also joined the finger-pointing. Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto suggested the riots were part of a “hybrid war” waged through social media by an unidentified actor. Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama went further, accusing Russian and Iranian intelligence services outright.
Yet the allegations have apparently failed to convince even Brussels. According to Euronews, the European Commission has declined to launch an investigation, citing insufficient evidence.
The speculation follows a familiar pattern of EU officials invoking “hybrid warfare” and the alleged “Russian threat” amid domestic turmoil. Just this week, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen accused Moscow and Minsk of “weaponizing migration,” linking them to the summer crisis in Spain’s Ceuta, where an estimated 70,000 migrants crossed from Morocco, sparking a border emergency and political fallout over EU migration policies. However, yet again, she presented no evidence connecting either country to the crisis.
Moscow says look closer to home
Moscow routinely dismisses allegations of interference and claims of a Russian threat as “absurd” fabrications, accusing EU leaders of using the narrative to deflect blame for their own policy failures and distract from mounting domestic crises.
Responding to Rama’s accusations, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told him to look closer to home.
“These are citizens of your own country who took to the streets to protest. Don’t shift your responsibility onto others. Deal with your own domestic problems,” she said.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, meanwhile, described the unrest sweeping the EU as evidence of “a major crisis… bordering on chaos.”

Currency pressure easing on Swiss pharma giant Roche
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:37:58 UTC
21:37:58 KST

Currency pressure easing on Swiss pharma giant Roche
At Roche, the headwinds from currency fluctuations have eased somewhat after nine months. The third quarter, in particular, brought some relief thanks to a weaker Swiss franc. On Thursday, the pharmaceutical group confirmed its previous targets for the full year.
Roche generated sales of CHF46.5 billion ($56.5 billion) between January and September. In the reporting currency, the Swiss franc, this represented an increase of 1%, as Roche announced on Thursday. At constant exchange rates, the increase was 6%. The Group has therefore met its own target, which is based on constant exchange rates.
While Roche had still suffered to some extent from the strong Swiss franc in the first and second quarters, its depreciation in the third quarter provided some tailwind, which was broadly in line with analysts’ expectations. As Roche itself reports, currency effects were slightly positive in the third quarter at +1%, having previously been a clear drag at -11% in the first quarter and -4% in the second.
+ Pharma pushes for higher European drug prices, Trump or no Trump
Of the two business divisions, the larger pharmaceuticals division generated sales of CHF36.2 billion in the first three quarters, an increase of 2%. The five key growth drivers – Xolair, Hemlibra, Ocrevus, Phesgo and Vabysmo – together generated sales of CHF16.8 billion (+12%). Sales of off-patent products (Avastin, Herceptin, MabThera/Rituxan, Lucentis and Actemra/RoActemra) fell by a total of CHF600 million.
In the diagnostics business, Roche generated CHF10.3 billion, which was in line with the previous year’s figure. This indicates that the negative impact of the price reform in China has noticeably eased. Roche had repeatedly emphasised that the impact was expected to diminish as the year progressed. By way of comparison: in the first quarter, revenue had fallen by 7%, and by 3% in the first half of the year.
Roche does not traditionally report profit figures for odd-numbered quarters.
Outlook confirmed
With the figures reported, Roche has largely exceeded analysts’ estimates.
Management, led by CEO Thomas Schinecker, has confirmed its previous guidance for the rest of the financial year. At constant exchange rates, sales are expected to rise by a mid-single-digit percentage. Core earnings per share are expected to grow in the high single-digit percentage range. Furthermore, the Group remains committed to increasing the dividend in Swiss francs.

Türkiye's central bank has reduced its benchmark policy rate by 100 basis points to 36 percent, in line with market expectations, after holding rates steady for five consecutive meetings.
The bank's Monetary Policy Committee, chaired by Governor Fatih Karahan on Thursday, lowered the one-week repo auction rate from 37 percent.
It also reduced the overnight lending rate from 40 percent to 39 percent and the overnight borrowing rate from 35.5 percent to 34.5 percent.
Despite monthly fluctuations, recent inflation figures and leading indicators confirm a slowdown in the underlying inflation trend, the committee said in a statement.
Economic activity data and the limited pass-through of supply shocks to domestic prices indicate that domestic demand remains weak, it added.
However, elevated energy prices stemming from ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to pose an upside risk to the inflation outlook.
Geopolitical developments
The committee said it is closely monitoring the impact of geopolitical developments on inflation through costs, economic activity, and expectations.
“The tight monetary policy stance, which will be maintained until price stability is achieved, will strengthen the disinflation process through demand, exchange rate, and expectation channels,” it said.
Future rate decisions will take into account realised and expected inflation, as well as its underlying trend, to maintain the tightness needed to support the projected disinflation path in line with interim targets.
The size and timing of policy steps will be determined prudently on a meeting-by-meeting basis, with a focus on the inflation outlook.
“In case of a significant and persistent deterioration in the inflation outlook, monetary policy stance will be tightened,” the committee said, reiterating its attention to upside inflation risks.
Additional macroprudential measures will support monetary transmission if unexpected developments emerge in credit and deposit markets, while liquidity management tools will continue to be used effectively.

What’s the PHP coding flaw that could pull down 70 percent of the internet?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:37:34 UTC
21:37:34 KST

What’s the PHP coding flaw that could pull down 70 percent of the internet?
The vulnerability allows a hacker to change a website or extract data, including personal information.
Government websites in Europe and elsewhere have gone offline after news of critical vulnerabilities in a widely used programming language sent website operators scrambling to protect their systems.
Developers of the PHP programming language on Wednesday released urgent new fixes, saying all users were “encouraged to update immediately”.
PHP runs on the servers that host websites, building pages behind the scenes before they reach a visitor’s browser. Most people never see it, but it powers everything from blogs to online shops and government portals.
The vulnerabilities, which had been lurking in the software for years, were uncovered with the help of artificial intelligence. Details about them leaked online on Tuesday before fixes were available, forcing PHP to rush them out.
Experts said they were bracing for a wave of intrusions as hackers jumped to get ahead of the updates.
What is the bug?
Andrew Cullen, a lecturer on AI and cybersecurity at the University of Melbourne, said many devices in the world are connected to one piece of foundational software, which is where the bug was found.
The vulnerability allows a hacker to run code on a website, meaning they could change the website or force it to release personal information collected in a database, Cullen told Al Jazeera.
Both flaws stem from how PHP handles fatal errors, such as running out of memory. Because the problem sits in PHP itself, even the simplest website running an affected version can be vulnerable, and attackers could read passwords and other credentials from a server’s memory, the cloud security company Wiz said. Both flaws scored 9.2 out of 10 on the industry’s standard severity scale, placing them in the “critical” category.
The two flaws, nicknamed PHP2Shell, were found independently by two cybersecurity companies using AI. Calif, working with OpenAI, reported the first on August 11. Wiz, which is owned by Google, reported the second on August 24.
The vulnerabilities remained hidden in the PHP codebase for more than a decade and would have been extraordinarily complicated for a human hacker to take advantage of, Wiz said in a statement.
Calif and Wiz said they had coordinated with each other, the PHP team and OpenAI before making the vulnerabilities public.
However, Amazon security chief CJ Moses said his security team detected an attempt to exploit the vulnerabilities on October 17, four days before the public disclosure.
Moses said it was unclear how the hacker learned of the flaws while Calif’s and Wiz’s reports were still under embargo. Security researchers usually keep details of flaws secret until a fix is ready, so attackers cannot use them in the meantime.
Who can potentially be affected?
PHP, a language that dates back to the early 1990s and initially stood for Personal Home Page, underpins huge parts of the public-facing web and is baked into WordPress, Drupal, Joomla and Magento sites, meaning any critical vulnerability potentially has enormous knock-on consequences.
Calif, Wiz and the web infrastructure company Cloudflare said the flaws affect PHP 5.4 and later versions, more than a decade of releases.
Cullen said the vulnerability was “really unprecedented”, noting that PHP powers more than 70 percent of websites globally, although sites that have been updated are protected.
“There is a real risk to the kind of shared digital infrastructure that we all rely on,” Cullen told Al Jazeera. “There is concern in the cybersecurity community about what the blast radius for this will be, even though the developers of PHP have been very quick to try and develop patches for it.”
Cullen added that while AI was getting better at cybersecurity, it was also getting better at being a hacker. “This means that we are developing systems … that are making the internet safer by helping to fix bugs, but we’re also making it riskier by discovering bugs and creating bugs they’ll be able to hack,” he said.
What has the impact been so far?
In the Netherlands, the Dutch cybersecurity agency itself went offline, saying it had done so as a precaution because of the vulnerabilities. Several organisations followed the example and took public-facing websites offline, including the Port of Rotterdam, government portal Overheid.nl, the national football association KNVB, the websites for the country’s five largest political parties and several hospital websites.
Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten said he was closely monitoring the situation.
Disruptions were even more widespread in Finland, where state IT services provider Valtori said government public network services had been taken offline “as a precautionary measure”.
France’s Ministry of the Interior said it had placed all of its websites into preventive maintenance.
Belgium’s Federal Public Service Foreign Affairs, Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation said it had temporarily taken its websites offline after reports of cyberattacks exploiting the PHP vulnerabilities although the country’s cybersecurity centre said it had not recorded any attacks on Belgian websites.
South Korea’s government raised its private-sector cybersecurity alert level and activated emergency response measures. It issued security guidance to about 28,000 companies with registered chief information security officers and 5,900 members of a government information-sharing network as well as operators of critical infrastructure, web-hosting firms and data centres.
The operator of the online encyclopedia Wikipedia also said it had taken down an unspecified number of systems until they could be safely patched while the Internet Archive, the sprawling online library, said it also briefly went offline to deal with the issue.

On the president’s schedule

On foreign companies’ assets

Hezbollah recruiting convicts in Latin America for revenue, relaxing ideological requirements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:36:53 UTC
21:36:53 KST

Hezbollah is increasingly recruiting convicted felons in Latin America, targeting individuals with financial difficulties who harbor resentment toward the courts – while relaxing its requirements for ideological alignment – according to a new Washington Institute for Near East Policy assessment. The report was written by Lucas Gualtieri, a Brazilian federal prosecutor who specializes in organized crime and Hezbollah’s use of criminal networks.
Operation Trapiche, a counterterrorism operation launched by Brazil’s Federal Police in November 2023 with support from Israel’s Mossad, has shed light on Hezbollah’s efforts to outsource operatives, as well as on criminal revenue generation and financial services in Latin America, building capabilities the terrorist group can plausibly deny if confronted.
Hezbollah has long outsourced operations in Latin America, as illustrated by the 2021 expulsion of two criminals hired by the Iran-backed group to target an Israeli in Bogotá.
The investigation has uncovered what amounts to an assembly line for operatives. Rather than simply contracting hitmen, Hezbollah recruits men with no prior ties to the group, flies them to Lebanon for training, and sends them back to their home countries to scout for potential Israeli and Jewish targets.
Gualtieri said Hezbollah was specifically seeking to recruit financially vulnerable convicted felons with no prior ties to the group or Lebanon. In intercepted audio, recruiters discussed looking for aggrieved individuals who had been “locked up” and felt they “owe the courts,” he said.
By recruiting men without prior ideological or personal ties to Hezbollah or Lebanon, Gualtieri said, the group could deny involvement in attacks, allowing any resulting unrest to be dismissed as hate crimes committed by fringe extremists.
Lucas Passos Lima, whose conviction was reinstated by Brazil’s Superior Court of Justice last month after a federal court ruled that his role in a network targeting Jews and Israelis was motivated by financial gain rather than terrorism, had returned from Lebanon with more than $5,000 in untraceable cash.
Had the court failed to convict Lima of terrorism, Gualtieri said, Brazil could have been viewed as a permissive environment for the group, and individuals who support terrorism for personal gain could have escaped more severe sentencing, despite their knowing involvement in plots.
Hezbollah relying on Latin American criminal network revenue
Hezbollah has also increasingly relied on revenue generated by criminal networks in Latin America, he added, as in, for example, the discovery of Brazilian tobacco shops that helped fund plane tickets for recruits. The shops were initially identified by tax inspectors investigating a tobacco shop in Belo Horizonte’s Mercado Central that was selling banned electronic cigarettes.
The case was referred to counterterrorism police in October 2023 after an FBI warning about a criminal financial network funding Hezbollah raised alarm among Brazilian officials.
Although the shops were registered to an individual identified as Hussain Abdulmajid, investigators found that the real operator was his brother, Mohamad Khir Abdulmajid, a Syrian-born naturalized Brazilian. The FBI memo also flagged Haissam Houssin Diab, a Lebanese-born naturalized Brazilian whose passport and travel bookings were later found in Abdulmajid’s cloud storage.
Abdulmajid is believed to have approached at least five Brazilians through social media and paid for their short trips to Beirut, including stays in upscale hotels. There, they allegedly received operational instruction and training in clandestine communications. This included learning a physical recognition signal and how to use shared email accounts as dead drops, leaving messages unsent in draft folders. They were also instructed to photograph Lebanese tourist sites to support a cover story that they had traveled for leisure.
Lima was among those recruited through Abdulmajid’s network; he was flown to Lebanon twice in 2023.
After his first trip, researchers found that he had geolocated and filmed three synagogues, a Jewish cemetery, the Israeli embassy, and a rabbi in and around Brasília. He had also trained with firearms, purchased untraceable radios and surveillance equipment, and approached a pilot about exfiltration routes that would bypass migration controls.
Hezbollah, IRGC using cryptocurrency for money laundering
Although Hezbollah’s use of criminal enterprises for fundraising is not new, the significance of these cases is that the group did not need to launder its own money to evade sanctions, Gualtieri said.
Dante Felipini, a São Paulo cryptocurrency broker arrested in a separate money-laundering case as part of Operation Colossus, was able to establish three separate cryptocurrency wallets for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Hezbollah. Prosecutors charged him with money laundering, currency evasion, membership in a terrorist organization, and terrorism financing.
Gualtieri said that Felipini’s case showed that Hezbollah views outsourcing as both a tactic and an opportunity for recruitment. After the cryptobroker traveled to Baalbek in January 2023, where he fired rifles in the hills with Hezbollah terrorists, Felipini told a contact that the trip had been his “baptism” into the group.
Gualtieri argued that the cases highlighted the need for authorities to pursue terrorism-related charges alongside other criminal offenses where the evidence supports them. He noted that such charges can lead to longer sentences and that relying solely on formal terrorism charges can understate the extent of Hezbollah’s activities.
He also highlighted a precedent set by Brazil’s Superior Court of Justice, which affirmed that financial motivation does not preclude terrorism liability when suspects knowingly participate in a terrorist plot, even if they do not share the group’s ideological motives.
Finally, he said authorities should strengthen financial monitoring to identify suspicious cryptocurrency transfers and shell companies, continue tracking networks after assets are frozen, and expand national mechanisms for designating terrorist organizations.
While international cooperation was crucial to Operation Trapiche, Gualtieri argued that domestic enforcement tools remained essential to disrupting Hezbollah’s networks and prosecuting those involved. In Spanish, trapiche means “shady business.”

Iran has deployed artillery and more weaponry to its northwest Kurdish regions, which border Iraq, while it has been increasingly cracking down on the Kurdish Iranian opposition group Kurdistan Free Life Party (PJAK). Iran views Kurdish opposition groups as potential regional threat

The situation in the Kurdistan region of Iran is complex. Some Kurds also work with Iran, which has often attempted to recruit Kurds to its units. As such, Rudaw says that the IRGC has also mobilized Kurdish fighters. From the Iranian regime’s point of view, it is preferable to get Kurds to fight one another, not only because Kurds know the terrain but also because any blowback would fall on Kurdish communities, rather than on Tehran.
Iran has also been using drones to attack PJAK forces in Iraq. The group said that drones had been used in the mountainous and forested areas of Marivan “with two suicide drones, followed by more than 30 mortar shells and heavy weapons on Sunday.”

I met Gadi Eisenkot. He did not perform leadership. He practiced it - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:36:22 UTC
21:36:22 KST

I have attended enough political events to recognize the usual performance: the polished entrance, loud promises, and leaders who speak about “the people” while remaining distant from them, but when I observed Gadi Eisenkot in person, I encountered something different—a man who did not appear to be acting like a leader because he seemed too busy listening, standing among Israelis and carrying himself like a servant rather than an owner.
I did not feel that I was watching a political celebrity. I felt that I was meeting one of us.
That judgment is personal, not scientific. One encounter cannot answer every policy question. I am a religious Zionist with convictions about Jewish sovereignty, national security and Israel’s right to defend itself. I surrender those convictions to no politician. But leadership is revealed not only on platforms. It is also revealed in whom a leader notices, whom he brings into the room and whether he treats citizens as partners rather than scenery.
That is why Eisenkot’s inclusion of Yaffa Tabaja in his Yashar party matters to me.
The importance of Yaffa Tabaja
Tabaja is not a professional slogan-maker. She is a builder. She is an Ethiopian Israeli woman from a traditional family of eight children whose parents made aliyah during Operation Moses. Born in Karmiel, she grew up partly among Russian-speaking immigrants and later described herself as a human “gathering of the exiles”: Ethiopian, Russian-speaking, traditional and Israeli. Her parents did not raise her with wealth, political privilege or famous connections. They gave her discipline, dignity, and faith in education.
The first in her family to pursue higher education, she earned degrees in criminology and government, and communications. At Ashkelon Academic College, Tabaja became the first Ethiopian Israeli elected to lead a student union. She served two terms and represented public colleges nationally. Young people from the periphery asked her a question: Is higher education possible for someone like me? Tabaja did not answer with a speech. She answered by working. She later led Ashkelon’s MTech Innovation Center, building a community of thousands and connecting southern entrepreneurs with Google for Startups, Amazon Web Services, Cisco and Nvidia. She wanted technology to become an instrument of social mobility, bringing opportunity to communities too often told to wait.
“If we aren’t given a seat at the decision-making table, we build our own table,” she has said.
That sentence should disturb Israel’s establishment. Parties visit Ethiopian neighborhoods, photograph our elders, and praise our military service.
Yet Ethiopian Israelis are still invited to decorate politics more often than direct it. We provide loyalty, votes and immigration stories, but are seldom trusted with authority over diplomacy, technology, security or the economy. Tabaja represents a different demand. She is not asking to be included simply because she is Ethiopian. She is asking to serve because she has already demonstrated that she can build institutions, create partnerships and turn neglect into opportunity.
Eisenkot deserves credit for recognizing that leadership. Yashar placed Tabaja at No. 21 on its electoral list, a potentially consequential position for a party polling around that range. Representation becomes meaningful only when a candidate has a realistic path to power and is allowed to address the whole nation, not merely “community affairs.” Eisenkot’s story may explain why he recognizes quiet service. From a working-class Moroccan Israeli family, he rose through four military decades to become chief of staff. He also carries a sacrifice no parent should endure: his son and two nephews were killed in the war.
Grief does not qualify anyone automatically to govern, and military rank does not guarantee political wisdom. Israelis must examine Eisenkot’s policies and coalition choices. But his service and sacrifice give moral weight to his call for responsibility after October 7. Israel does not need another messiah. It does not need citizens to worship a leader or pretend one man can save the nation. We have paid too high a price for politics organized around personality. Israel needs servant leadership: leaders who understand that public office is borrowed authority, who can be strong without humiliating others and who place proven workers beside them including women from communities rarely entrusted with national power.
October 7 exposed failures of security, governance and political culture. Israel’s next government must restore border security, establish a credible state commission of inquiry, rebuild international diplomacy, lower living costs and ensure every community contributes to and benefits from the state.
Tabaja offers a practical model. When rockets made Ashkelon appear like a place to escape, she stayed and built. After October 7, her center assisted soldiers, women, businesses, and entrepreneurs. She understood that survival was insufficient; citizens also needed employment and hope. That is Zionism in work clothes.
I was moved by Eisenkot because he appeared simple in the best sense: approachable, disciplined and unpossessed by his importance. I am moved by Tabaja because she reflects the true colors of my community, not merely our struggle, but our competence, faith, endurance, and desire to contribute.
My admiration is not blind. I will challenge them when they are wrong. I will ask whether Eisenkot will give Tabaja and other underrepresented leaders genuine authority, not merely a place on a list. I will ask whether Yashar will bring the periphery into decisions about Israel’s economy, diplomacy, and security. But what I witnessed gave me hope.
In Eisenkot, I saw a leader who still looks like a citizen. In Tabaja, I see a citizen who has already become a leader. Israel will be renewed not by the loudest people in the room, but by those who enter ready to work. Gadi Eisenkot and Yaffa Tabaja may represent that renewal. Now they must prove that servant leadership can become national leadership—and that the table they are building has room for all Israel.

With less than a week until Israelis vote, Benjamin Netanyahu has come back to mainstream television studios carrying a fresh, effusive endorsement from President Trump.
On this episode of The Deep Dive, host Jacob asks Shmuel Rosner, a JPPI senior fellow and Channel 13 election pollster, whether any of that can still move votes. His answer is blunt. After the judicial overhaul fight of 2023, October 7, and the long wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and with Iran, most Israelis already know what they want. Any last-minute shifts will happen inside the political blocs, not across them.
He argues that Netanyahu's late blitz is not a play for 61 seats. It is a defensive move meant to stop the opposition from forming a viable coalition, which would force yet another election in six months, one in which the prime minister might get luckier.
The conversation then turns to the scenarios likely to dominate the morning after. Rosner explains why a minority government backed by a 57–50 split is a very different thing from one resting on 52–51. He also covers how far President Herzog can actually push the rival camps toward the unity government many Israelis say they want. And he describes the one arrangement that could appeal to nearly everyone except one man: a plea deal that lets Netanyahu step aside. He takes on the theory that a post-election flare-up with Iran could be used to herd rivals into an emergency government.
Here, he points out that the opposition has already watched that approach play out twice, first with Benny Gantz and then after October 7. He also offers a clear explanation of Trump's endorsement: it carries no risk for Trump. If Netanyahu wins, Trump can collect on it, and if he loses, the winner will still need Washington.
The last striking moments
The most striking moments come near the end. Asked about warnings over election integrity and comparisons to America's January 6, Rosner defends Israel's voting system as one of the few institutions the public still trusts. He warns that leaders who spread false claims about the count would be creating a dangerous moment for the country's democracy.
He also offers a provocative thought about the stakes. Whether this vote really is the most important in Israel's history, he suggests, depends on its outcome, and the stakes are not equal for both sides. For many opposition voters, he believes, another term for the current coalition would be a crisis of identity and of attachment to the country itself.

Lockheed Martin has entered into an initial production and sustainment agreement with the US Defense Department to deliver at least 850 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets over the next 10 years, the department said Thursday.
The defense contractor will self-fund at least $7 billion in initiatives that support the F-35 program, the department said in a statement.
The F-35, built with stealth technology that helps it evade enemy detection, is considered the world's most advanced fighter jet and sits at the core of Lockheed's aeronautics division, which accounts for nearly 40% of its quarterly revenue.
Under the agreement with the Defense Department, which US President Donald Trump calls the Department of War, Lockheed aims to maintain annual production at 156 aircraft.
The agreement is not an order but is considered a prearranged long-term contract.
"If granted multi-year authority in the coming months, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will work to finalize contract terms, pricing, and schedules through a formal contract award," the company said.
The agreement also covers international orders for the F-35, along with initial spares and modification kits, Arlington-based Lockheed said in a statement.
"We have fundamentally changed how we stabilize the American defense industrial base to produce at speed and scale," said Under Secretary of Defense Michael Duffey.
"This agreement with Lockheed Martin proves it. By aligning financial incentives with actual performance, we are ensuring our warfighters are equipped with the lethal capabilities they need to fight and win."
Lockheed, defense industry, benefit from increased global defense spending
Lockheed and its peers across the US have benefited from increased global defense spending as geopolitical conflicts remain unabated.
Lockheed estimates the agreement will support 317,000 US jobs and generate nearly $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade.
It also expects the arrangement to lower production costs and ease supply-chain constraints from raw materials to finished parts.

Death Just Got Out of This Truck (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:36:06 UTC
21:36:06 KST

“There are, I find, things I want philosophy to do that it cannot. Or that I cannot do with it.”
That’s Amy Olberding, professor of philosophy at the University of Oklahoma, on the limits of philosophy that life sometimes makes vivid.
The guest post by her, below, is an excerpt from her truly remarkable book, Kill All The Chickens, which was published last month, and which you should all buy today (Amazon, Bookshop).
The book is a beautiful example of an academic philosopher breaking free of the standard publishing conventions of the profession (at which she was perfectly adept) to produce writing that is full of wisdom and personality, and that, even as it confronts us with an exploration of life’s difficulties, is nonetheless a pleasure to read.
Death Just Got Out of This Truck
by Amy Olberding
Maybe we should just skip the middle step and throw it all straight in the toilet? This is what I ask my mother as we together stand and consider the overburdened farm table. We are bereaved and so a steady stream of neighbors has come by to deliver casseroles and pies, lunch meats and cookies, chicken and potato salad. If death were an appetite, we’d have the means to satisfy and send him off by now. But he is not an appetite, nor have we any of our own.
Mine are a people of uneasy stomachs. I remember one night spent in the ER alongside some uncles and cousins, waiting to hear what the doctors would make of my grandfather’s alarming stroke-like swoon. That night we shared the TUMS bottle the way others might pass a flask. Bringing food to us bereaved is like giving a dog a pencil. There’s just not much that we can do with it, at least not much that anyone could count useful.
Grief is an affliction physical and material. It roils the gut and stops the sleep. It can put a tremble in the limbs, a quiver in the voice, a restless agitation run all through. It makes the knees want to let go, the body just to sink. It is tired but cannot ever really rest, a breath you cannot really catch. It can make the gaze go vacant, blank. Grief is eyes that see too much, make sense of little. How long have I now stared out the window into nothing, seeing nothing? Grief sets the body all awry. The body wants, but what? Something it can now no longer have, a voice in the ear gone mute, a touch tactile, now but memory. We stare at food; we do not eat it.
My book on death, the one I will not write, was originally going to have a chapter on the body. It seemed to me that one of the troubles with philosophy on grief is that it misses out on bodies. The philosopher’s talk is all of what loss means, what grief can make you think. It speaks to what the mind and heart may feel, but not the stalling, empty mind or trembling heart. It speaks to one who speaks and thinks, not the instinctive, aching animal, not the raw creature all sensation without sense. This is not a novelty where philosophy is concerned—philosophers have long neglected the cruder materiality from which thought transpires. But still, I wanted some way to make philosophy answer not to thought or feeling or meaning, but to the brute stuff upon which all the rest is set. I wanted some way to make loss less like an experience of the mind and thought, to make loss on the page more like itself in life, an experience altogether nauseating. Before the reasoning or meaning, first the gut.
There are, I find, things I want philosophy to do that it cannot. Or that I cannot do with it. There is nothing wrong with thought, with seeking out some sense. But what can be made sense is rarely all there is; it leaves in remainder much, too much. Worse still, even good sense can be misleading. You can get your thoughts in careful order, root out all mistake, prepare to read the vexations of experience with well-honed training pitched to make vexations yield. But all that practiced thought and careful habits of the mind can leave you unready for what comes. Don’t trust them more than they can bear. The body is not a prison, but neither can thought escape its meaty and substantial bonds. I cannot make philosophy bend to this, I think, not in a way that is not all false and false confidence.
Many years ago now, when the farm was still a working dairy and the place was hectic with cows and work, my grandfather hired a milker to come in and help. The milker had a love of the drink and would sometimes cry off work for a hangover, but he was, I suppose, reliable enough that they kept him on. One day, he’d taken the farm’s yellow truck into town to retrieve some feed. At a four-way stop sign, he was briefly bested by a fancy man in a fancy car, the kind of man who didn’t want to wait on a beater truck that got there first and instead just blew the stop sign so he’d get ahead. The milker would have none of this, so he drove that yellow truck right up to and behind the man’s bumper for blocks that soon turned into miles. Finally, the fancy man pulled over in a parking lot, the milker close behind. Both men got out of their vehicles. The fancy man planted his feet wide and bellowed out a caution meant to be severe: I have to warn you that I just got out of karate! The milker didn’t even pause before he answered quietly, Well, I just got out of this yellow truck. Before aught else could happen, the milker’s fist had found that fancy man and laid him flat.
Karate class is fine and so, too, is philosophy. But make no mistake, you can’t really get ahead of it. Loss comes at you like a fist.
“Death Just Got Out of This Truck,” from Kill All The Chickens by Amy Olberding.

Poland Began Receiving Kleszcz Reconnaissance Vehicles to Replace BRDMs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:32:18 UTC
21:32:18 KST

On October 21, the reconnaissance units of the Polish Armed Forces started receiving the first Kleszcz light armored reconnaissance vehicles.
These deliveries are the result of the implementation of the first agreement from August 2024 and will continue until 2028, with the next batch scheduled to arrive by the end of this year, according to the Polish Army’s website.
The project was launched by a framework agreement signed on February 28, 2024, between the Armaments Agency and AMZ-Kutno SA, which provides for the procurement of a total of 286 vehicles by 2035.
The first contract, worth $205 million, covers the delivery of 28 vehicles along with a package of logistical services, training, and investments in expanding production capacity.
The new armored vehicles are intended to completely replace several hundred obsolete Soviet BRDM-2 armored reconnaissance and patrol vehicles.
The Kleszcz (Bóbr-3) is a 4×4 amphibious armored vehicle developed between 2013 and 2022 by AMZ-Kutno SA in collaboration with Polish military research institutes.
Weighing 14–16 metric tons, the vehicle is equipped with a 326 k.s. diesel engine and an Allison automatic transmission, allowing it to reach speeds of up to 100 km/h on the highway and 7 km/h on water.
The vehicle’s ballistic protection meets Level 2a of the STANAG 4569 standard (protection against 7.62×39 mm rounds and a 6 kg explosive charge), with the option to install additional armor panels.
The crew consists of five members: a commander, a driver-mechanic, a reconnaissance and communications systems operator, a weapons operator, and an external equipment operator.
The primary armament is the Kongsberg Protector remotely controlled module, capable of mounting a large-caliber machine gun or an automatic grenade launcher.
As a reminder, Poland received a batch of CGR-080 guided missiles and CTM-290 ballistic missiles for the Homar-K multiple launch rocket systems.
The shipment included CGR-080 missiles with a range of up to 80 km, as well as CTM-290 ballistic missiles with a range of up to 290 km.

According to its interim financial report, Nokia's net sales reached 5.15 billion euros (5.77 billion U.S. dollars) in the July-September period, up from 4.7 billion euros (5.26 billion U.S. dollars) a year earlier. On a constant currency basis, sales grew 9 percent.

Nokia maintained its full-year 2026 outlook, forecasting comparable operating profit of between 2.1 billion and 2.6 billion euros (2.35 billion and 2.91 billion U.S. dollars).

The study examined three economically important estuarine species, yellowfin bream, sand whiting and tarwhine, and found that they were "thermal generalists" capable of tolerating a broad range of temperatures, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's Adelaide University.

Europe still has no clear goal on China

This month alone, Europe has threatened China with a trade “kill switch”, rebuked it in parliament, sent its trade commissioner on a much-trumpeted trip to Beijing and announced three new economic security instruments.
