====================================================================================================

‘Former inmates want to come back to visit’: inside Florida’s prison zoo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:30:04 UTC
21:30:04 KST

At the Monroe County detention center on Stock Island in the Florida Keys, most of the prisoners do the type of work you’d typically imagine people doing in jail. Preparing meals in the kitchens, cleaning the common areas, working in the laundry, and so on.
But for about five prisoners at a time the work looks a little more exotic. They’re working in the jail’s on-site zoo, taking care of animals including a capybara, a kinkajou, a zebu and an ostrich.
The zoo was started in 1994, after a sheriff’s deputy noticed that ducks living near the jail were often getting hit by cars while crossing a highway. He gathered a group of prisoners and relocated the flock to a disused area beneath the jail, which sits on stilts as it is in a hurricane-prone area.
Word of the rescue spread, and people started showing up at the jail to drop off rescued or unwanted animals. “People started bringing in a goat, a pig, a cow, pets they’d gotten that they didn’t want or couldn’t keep,” said Jeanne Selander, the zoo’s supervisor. “We got a blind horse from the Miami area that had been abandoned, and then the sheriff thought, ‘Well, there’s a need for this.’”
The Monroe County detention center is the only correctional facility in the world with its own zoo. There was, briefly, another one. In Venezuela, a gang took over a prison and installed various resort-style amenities for the prisoners, including a pool, night club, and a zoo, with big cats, monkeys and flamingoes. But the Venezuelan government forcefully retook control of that prison a few years ago. Several of the zoo’s animals were reportedly killed in the battle for the prison and the ones that survived were relocated.
According to Selander, all of the animals in her zoo were either rescued, donated or confiscated. Rocky the fox was rescued from a fur farm in Minnesota. Jack the ostrich was donated as a tax write-off by a breeder that was unable to sell him because he’s blind in one eye. Harriet Houdini, a red-tailed boa constrictor, was donated by a school after the teacher that kept her as a class pet retired. “I had some alligators one time that came from a raid on a crack house,” said Selander.
But the zoo doesn’t accept all of the animals it is offered. Selander said she previously declined a camel and a bear as they presented too much of a risk to the residents.
You are unable to see the zoo from the inside as the building’s windows are frosted. Selander said that, when she is upstairs in the jail, the prisoners will ask her about the sounds they can hear coming from outside. She has been told that, from inside the jail, the peacock can sound like a woman screaming.
The prisoners that work on the zoo spend around six hours a day feeding and cleaning the animals, and performing maintenance tasks. Those selected are typically low-level offenders and are not allowed to have charges for violence or animal abuse. “It’s kind of hard to get down [to the zoo] because if you have a high bond or you’re in any way shape or form a risk to run away, they’re not going to let you come outside,” said Peter Faraco, a former inmate who worked on the zoo in 2021.
Inside the jail, prisoners sleep on concrete bunk beds with no pillows. “Stuck in them cells all day, or in the kitchen; it’s not that nice,” said Rodney Cox, who previously worked on the zoo. “There’s no air.”
Boredom is also an issue. “It’s a lot of time,” said Nicholas Sheldrake, a current inmate who is working in the zoo. “It’s just very boring. Watching the same TV shows and movies over and over, hoping a football or baseball game or something comes on.”
The zoo offers a respite for the prisoners that get to work there. “I love it down here,” said Sheldrake. “It makes my time go by fast. Nobody bothers me. I love working with the animals and talking to them.”
“And we can see stuff like birds and trees,” he added.
It is important to Selander that the zoo not look like it is part of a jail, as she hopes to make it appealing to visitors on the zoo’s regular open days. She has planted trees around the property, and had inmates paint murals of animals on the walls and support pillars. “People will come in, they’re like, ‘You don’t even realize you’re at a jail,’” she said.
In the 20 years she has worked there, she said, the number of visitors on open days has grown from about a dozen to more than 300.
Studies have shown that access to animals can have a positive effect on incarcerated people, leading to improvements in mental health, as well as a decrease in reoffending after release.
There are animal programmes of various kinds in prisons around the world. There are prisoners in Chile living alongside cats, and in New Zealand training service dogs, and in the UK receiving equine therapy, and in South Africa raising birds. Selander said that she believes working on the zoo has had a positive effect on the prisoners she has worked with, and has, over the years, received positive feedback from her workers.
She was recently out for brunch and her server was a man who’d worked at the zoo. “He was like, ‘I wanted to thank you, Miss Jeannie … Being able to be on the farm and have peace while I served my time just made it so much easier,’” she said.
Selander said that it’s not uncommon for former incarcerated zoo workers to come back and visit during open days to see the animals. Some will bring their family members. “One of the greatest compliments is that the inmates want to come back to visit,” she said. “What a compliment. Who wants to come back to jail?”

The international community prefers not to address the fact that violence poses a permanent threat to food security and, as a result, to any humanitarian paradigm. On Monday, the World Food Program (WFP) announced that 500,000 Palestinians in Gaza will be left without food support due to funding shortages. For 2026, the WPF received less than half its funding and requires $450 million “to maintain critical operations in the occupied Palestinian territory over the next six months.”
WFP’s announcement broke down the consequences of its funding shortage. Out of 1.6 million Palestinians in Gaza, 1.1 million remain eligible for WFP’s services. Food rations have been but down by half. Hot meals have been reduced from 250,000 to 150,000, while Palestinians living in the vicinities of the Yellow Line can only receive one hot meal on alternate days. The WFP also reduced cash assistance to 75,000 families. Bakeries are, until now, still supported, however the aid only covers one third of the population reached by the bakeries. Unemployment in Gaza is over 80 per cent, and 1.4 million Palestinians are classified as experiencing acute food insecurity.
Meanwhile, for the fifth consecutive year, Israeli arms sales broke another record – from $14.8 billion in 2024 to $19.2 billion in 2025. This means that during the genocide in Gaza, when government were begrudgingly fulfilling their rhetorical duty calling for humanitarian pauses and deploring civilian deaths, arms sales were contributing to the genocide and, as a result food insecurity.
Governments have billions to spend on weapons while $450 million to maintain the WFP’s critical operations are hard to come by.
READ: UN: 950,000 displaced people in Gaza face flood risks this winter
Governments also support humanitarian paradigms, albeit only as a veneer against their complicity in fomenting violence. However, even that veneer can no longer support its own narrative, as the consequences of Israel’s internationally supported genocide in Gaza is further illustrating that humanitarian aid was never designed to be permanent. The budget allocated to humanitarian aid was never on a par with that allocated for war. With that discrepancy, it is likely that a state of permanent colonial violence in Gaza is fast becoming normalised to the point that the lack of humanitarian aid will go the same way.
Just as forced displacement no longer elicits anything but statistical data, so will humanitarian aid follow the same trajectory. Funding deficits are already normalised, and so will food insecurity and starvation.
Calling upon Israel to assume its responsibilities as an occupying power never worked. The humanitarian paradigm failed since its inception. The weakest calls from the international community are for Israel to exercise restraint, while the loudest silence encouraged genocide. It is only here that the international community’s warped logic shines through – it will not contradict its own complicity in genocide by investing more in the humanitarian paradigm. On the contrary, Gaza remains testimony to genocide and the international community’s commitment to it. If Israel and the international community do not carry the humanitarian burden because it contradicts their complicity in genocide, Palestinians then face permanent food insecurity. As things stand, all roads lead to genocide in Gaza, and Israel has already completed the groundwork with the international community’s aid.

Hong Kong’s Vanishing Rainbow Shows How China’s Social Control Travels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:25:00 UTC
21:25:00 KST

China’s growing pressure on LGBTQ communities is increasingly transnational. Chinese nationals who attend Pride events overseas can attract police attention after returning home; overseas Chinese LGBTQ groups remain vulnerable to censorship on Chinese platforms; cultural spaces in Europe can lose access to Chinese social media for promoting transgender films; and mainland writers publishing gay fiction on overseas platforms have faced prosecution at home. Hong Kong offers a particularly revealing entry point because similar pressures are visible there even though same-sex relationships are legal (though not legally recognized as marriages).
In October, the organizing committee of Hong Kong Pride canceled its annual Rainbow Market at Central Market after being told that an administrative error had resulted in double-booking. Organizers had already received confirmation, paid a deposit, and announced the venue.
The cancellation followed a wider pattern. Earlier in 2026, Pink Dot HK, the city’s largest annual LGBTQ carnival, canceled its event after the operator of Stanley Plaza and Murray House withdrew the venues, citing unresolved licensing issues. It was the second consecutive year in which Pink Dot failed to proceed. In 2025, negotiations to hold the event at West Kowloon Cultural District’s Art Park had also collapsed.
Hong Kong Pride itself lost a planned venue at Kwun Tong Promenade in 2025 after organizers had already paid rent and announced the event.
These cases illustrate how LGBTQ public life in Hong Kong is being narrowed through administrative and institutional means rather than formal criminal prohibition. Consensual same-sex conduct remains legal, and LGBTQ organizations continue to exist. But these groups find it harder and harder to organize publicly, retain venues, sustain institutions, and remain visible in civic life.
This is striking because Hong Kong once had one of the most visible LGBTQ communities in East Asia. The city decriminalized consensual homosexual conduct between adult men in 1991, while its courts later expanded legal protections for same-sex couples in areas including immigration, taxation, and public housing. Social acceptance also rose significantly. Survey research published in 2023 found that 69 percent of respondents were “moderately” or “very accepting” of gay men and lesbians, while 60 percent supported same-sex marriage and 71 percent supported anti-discrimination legislation based on sexual orientation.
Hong Kong Pride once drew thousands into the streets, but its last full Pride march took place in 2018. In 2019, police declined permission for a march amid the citywide protests and permitted only a static rally. Pandemic restrictions later pushed Pride activities online, after which organizers shifted toward indoor markets and smaller events. The large public march never returned.
Most LGBTQ organizations in Hong Kong were never primarily political in the conventional sense. Their work focused on discrimination, health, family acceptance, culture, community support, and legal equality. Their shrinking space therefore shows how Hong Kong’s post-2020 transformation has moved beyond suppressing explicit political opposition and into regulating autonomous social life.
The same pattern is visible in mainland China. China decriminalized homosexuality in 1997 and removed homosexuality from its official classification of mental disorders in 2001 (in practice, if not in actual fact). During the 2000s and early 2010s, LGBTQ organizations, university groups, online communities, and cultural events expanded in major cities. Under Xi Jinping, that space has contracted sharply. Shanghai Pride ceased operations in 2020, the Beijing LGBT Center closed in 2023, university LGBTQ groups have faced mounting restrictions, and social media accounts associated with sexual minority organizations have been deleted or suspended.
Foreign connections have become increasingly important to this repression. Chinese authorities often treat independent organizations with international ties as possible channels of foreign influence. LGBTQ groups are especially exposed because contemporary sexual minority advocacy is highly transnational, involving foreign NGOs, embassies, academic institutions, cultural organizations, and legal networks. This allows questions of private identity and social equality to be reframed as questions of sovereignty and political security.
The reach of this logic now extends beyond China’s borders. In 2026, France’s Le Monde reported that Chinese nationals who had participated in Bangkok Pride later received police attention after returning to China. How the authorities identified them remains unclear, but participation in a lawful LGBTQ event in Thailand had become a matter of interest to Chinese police.
This fits within the broader discussion of transnational repression, but LGBTQ communities also reveal a related form of cross-border control that operates through information systems. Chinese platforms and censorship practices increasingly project domestic restrictions into overseas Chinese-speaking communities.
The Chinese Rainbow Network illustrates this problem. The organization operates overseas, yet material on its WeChat public account became inaccessible. Citizen Lab had already shown the structural basis for such control when it found that content exchanged between non-China-registered WeChat accounts could still be subjected to analysis for politically sensitive material. Overseas users can therefore remain inside an information environment shaped by the political requirements of the Chinese party-state.
Recent cases involving the LGBTQ community show how this extends to cultural expression. The Paris-based Chinese-language cultural space 8lithèque reportedly had its Xiaohongshu (RedNote) account banned after promoting a screening of a transgender-themed film. The event was taking place in France, but the organizers remained vulnerable to the content rules of a Chinese platform.
The Haitang Literature City prosecutions show another dimension of this expanding reach. Haitang, a Taiwan-based platform, became popular among mainland Chinese writers of danmei and boys’ love fiction, including sexually explicit material. Chinese authorities later summoned, detained, and prosecuted mainland writers who had published on the platform, citing China’s obscenity laws. The platform was outside mainland China, but the writers were not beyond the reach of Chinese law enforcement.
Taken together, these cases show how China’s control increasingly travels through people, platforms, and language communities. Whether joining a cultural space in Paris, a platform in Taiwan, a Pride parade in Bangkok, or a community organization in North America, Chinese citizens and Chinese-language communities remain exposed to censorship, surveillance, or coercive pressure originating from inside China.
Why should LGBTQ communities matter so much to the party-state?
One reason is autonomous organization. Community centers, university societies, legal aid groups, online networks, cultural organizations, and Pride events create horizontal ties among citizens outside structures supervised by the Communist Party. Chinese authorities have become increasingly suspicious of such organization across many fields, including labor rights, feminism, religion, public health, and environmental activism.
Sexual minority rights also raise broader questions about pluralism. The principle that individuals should retain dignity and rights even when they depart from majority social norms places limits on the authority of the state, family, and society over private identity.
Family structure adds another dimension. Under Xi Jinping, official discourse has placed growing emphasis on marriage, reproduction, family responsibility, and demographic duty. These themes have become more prominent as China confronts low fertility, population decline, delayed marriage, and rapid aging. Women are increasingly encouraged to marry and have children, while official rhetoric emphasizes “good family traditions” and reproductive responsibility.
LGBTQ identities sit uneasily within this model because they challenge the assumption that adult life should culminate in heterosexual marriage and biological reproduction. They also complicate fixed gender roles within the family.
These tensions acquire greater political significance because Xi has tied social order to the broader project of the “great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation.” The Communist Party increasingly presents itself as a guardian of Chinese civilizational continuity and social morality.
This emphasis on tradition also represents a shift in the party’s own ideological history. The early People’s Republic was explicitly revolutionary in its approach to family hierarchy. The 1950 Marriage Law attacked arranged marriage, concubinage, male superiority, and other practices described as remnants of the feudal family system. Maoist discourse framed women’s emancipation as part of the destruction of inherited social hierarchy.
Mao-era China was never sexually liberal, but the contrast shows that the Communist Party’s current appeal to traditional family values is selective rather than timeless. During the revolutionary period, dismantling inherited hierarchies served the party’s claim to be creating a new society. Under Xi, family hierarchy, reproductive responsibility, and civilizational continuity serve a different political purpose by reinforcing social order and distinguishing Chinese values from supposedly foreign liberal influence.
LGBTQ communities therefore sit at the intersection of several Xi-era concerns: autonomous organization, minority rights, gender hierarchy, demographic policy, foreign influence, and individual autonomy.
Repression can be effective at weakening the organizational capacity of such groups. Authorities can close community centers, prevent events, delete accounts, restrict fundraising, discourage international partnerships, and make public participation more risky. But these measures cannot remove the identities and experiences that produced these communities.
That creates a long-term political problem. Concepts such as constitutionalism or representative government can remain abstract for citizens who encounter them mainly through rhetoric. Sexuality and gender are experienced through everyday life. Government policy reaches LGBTQ people through relationships, family formation, public expression, employment, access to community, and the ability to describe oneself openly. Feminists encounter a similar dynamic when state-defined expectations concerning marriage, reproduction, and gender roles collide with their own lives.
Repeated discrimination turns political authority into a personal experience. Not every LGBTQ person or feminist will become politically oppositional, but a state that continually restricts people at the level of identity, family, and bodily autonomy risks creating durable alienation that cannot easily be displaced by nationalism or civilizational rhetoric.
The contraction of LGBTQ space in Hong Kong therefore matters beyond sexual minority rights. It shows how the logic of political control can expand into social life and how Chinese digital platforms, information systems, and law enforcement practices can extend that control across borders.
For LGBTQ communities, the immediate result is the erosion of public and organizational space. For Beijing, the longer-term consequence may be a widening gap between its civilizational narrative and the everyday experience of those whose identities increasingly fall outside the social order it seeks to define.

Bolt and Uber drivers protest low fares in Helsinki
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:22:46 EEST
21:22:46 KST

More than 100 Bolt and Uber taxi drivers gathered outside Helsinki’s Olympic Stadium on Thursday, to protest against low fares, rising fuel costs and commissions charged by ride-hailing platforms. Drivers demanded higher payments, lower company fees and the right to reject trips without facing penalties.
The demonstration began at around 11 am in the stadium’s car park, where drivers parked their vehicles and gathered to express concerns about their earnings.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
According to Helsingin Sanomat, organisers had notified police that between 150 and 350 vehicles were expected. Reports say more than 100 taxis were at the site during the protest.
Drivers called for fares to increase by at least 15% and for the commissions collected by Bolt and Uber to fall to a maximum of 15% of each journey’s price.
Protest organiser Kappa Mahmoud told Iltalehti that platform commissions currently range from 25% to 35%, leaving drivers struggling to cover their expenses.
The drivers also demanded greater transparency over how fares are calculated, higher payments for airport journeys and trips during rush hours, and changes to the way applications handle rejected bookings.
Several drivers described working long hours without earning enough to support their families.
Driver Erdal Karsandi told Iltalehti that refusing too many bookings risked temporary account restrictions. He said some drivers worked 12 to 13 hours a day, raising concerns about fatigue and passenger safety.
Long-distance journeys were another source of dissatisfaction. Drivers said trips to areas outside Helsinki often failed to cover the cost of returning without a passenger.
Finland’s Transport Workers’ Union AKT expressed support for the demonstration, arguing that self-employed platform drivers face financial insecurity and lack employment protections.
AKT chairman Ismo Kokko said in a statement that passengers paying less than €10 for a taxi journey should recognise the effect of such prices on drivers’ earnings.
The union said self-employed drivers must cover their own pension contributions, healthcare and other expenses without the protections available to employees.
AKT vice-chairman Niko Blom attended the demonstration and told Iltalehti that the union wanted to hear drivers’ concerns. He also called for collective negotiations over working conditions.
According to Iltalehti, the union is working with the Finnish Taxi Owners’ Federation on a collective agreement for taxi drivers.

Russia sentences 77-year-old Crimean political prisoner to 18 years over alleged plot to assassinate Kremlin-installed governor
Volodymyr Ananiev, a 77-year-old Crimean political prisoner, has been illegally sentenced to 18 years in prison by a court in Rostov-on-Don. Ananiev is accused of plotting an "assassination attempt" on Sergei Aksyonov, the so-called head of occupied Crimea.
Source: Crimean Tatar Resource Center
Details: Volodymyr Ananiev was detained in Simferopol on 2 February 2024 while he was at an acquaintance's flat.
Russian investigators claim that Ananiev was part of a group that used a hidden camera to monitor Sergei Aksyonov. The group was allegedly preparing a remotely controlled explosive device, which they stored in a rented garage in Simferopol.
Volodymyr Bodnar and Oksana Shevchenko are also implicated in the case. The Russian occupation authorities sentenced them earlier: Bodnar received 13 years in prison and Shevchenko 10 years.
The 77-year-old Ananiev was "tried" by the Southern District Military Court in Rostov-on-Don and sentenced to 18 years in prison. He will spend the first four years in prison and the remainder of his sentence in a maximum-security penal colony.
Ananiev was also ordered to pay a fine of RUB 600,000 (about US$7,300).
"Volodymyr Ananiev is the oldest Crimean political prisoner. He has problems with his eyesight, spine, muscles, kidneys and legs and walks with a cane. He has undergone surgery on both eyes, but his eyesight continues to deteriorate, and glaucoma is developing in one eye. He also suffers from high blood pressure," the Crimean Tatar Resource Center reported.
The centre added that 64 elderly Crimean political prisoners have faced persecution by Russia. Of these, 45 have already been sentenced and 19 are being held in pre-trial detention centres.
Background: Earlier, the condition of 68-year-old Halyna Bekhter from Zaporizhzhia Oblast deteriorated significantly while she was imprisoned in Russia. Bekhter was "sentenced" under Russian occupation for transferring money to support the Ukrainian military.

Nestlé corrects recycling claims on plastic bottles

Nestlé corrects recycling claims on plastic bottles
Swiss firm Nestlé along with Coca-Cola and Danone are amending their recycling claims on plastic bottles. This comes after discussions with the European Commission and EU consumer protection authorities.
The aim is to correct misleading statements regarding recyclability. According to a statement issued by the European Commission on Thursday, companies intend to replace statements on bottle labels such as “This bottle is made from 100% recycled plastic” with phrases such as “This bottle is 100% recycled. Excluding the cap and label”. Labels such as “Recycle me again” are also to be changed to “Recycle me”.
The European Commission and national authorities reviewed the revised claims and found them to be in line with EU consumer protection law. According to the Commission, Coca-Cola and Nestlé have already implemented some of their commitments, such as recycling pledges on digital channels.
+ Nestlé shamed as third-largest plastic polluter
The case was triggered in 2023 by a warning from the European consumer organisation BEUC, which targeted misleading recycling claims on plastic bottles. The European Commission and the national consumer protection authorities subsequently entered into dialogue with the companies.

Africa’s richest man expands fuel empire into Kenya
Africa’s richest man Aliko Dangote has bought a roughly 25% stake in Kenya’s fuel pipeline operator as part of a wider push to expand petroleum distribution across the continent.
The Nigerian industrialist announced the acquisition at the Financial Times Africa Summit in London on Wednesday. Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) operates pipelines and storage facilities supplying Kenya and other regional markets.
“We bought 25% of their pipeline network for the distribution of petroleum products,” Dangote said.
The purchase involved 4.5 billion KPC shares worth $335 million, bought at a slight premium to the last-traded price, the FT reported. Dangote said the acquisition and planned network expansion formed part of a continent-wide fuel distribution strategy. “We are going very aggressively with that,” he said.
Dangote also plans to invest $1.5 billion in expanding the pipeline network as part of a wider African refining, storage, and distribution business, the FT reported.
KPC operates about 1,342 km of pipelines transporting refined petroleum products inland from the port of Mombasa. Its infrastructure supports supplies to Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, and eastern DR Congo.
Kenyan President William Ruto said on Tuesday that private investors had acquired a quarter of KPC from public entities, without identifying the buyers. The government sold a 65% stake through an IPO earlier this year to raise revenue, with the company listing on the Nairobi Securities Exchange in March.
The purchase follows the September 30 groundbreaking for Dangote’s planned 700,000-barrel-per-day refinery in Kenya’s coastal Lamu County. The project is intended to supply the wider East African market and is scheduled for completion in 2030.
Dangote already operates Africa’s largest refinery near Lagos, Nigeria’s commercial capital. The roughly $20 billion facility began commercial operations in 2024, helping the country reduce its reliance on imported fuel. In September, the company launched a $1.6 billion public offering to help finance an expansion intended to double its capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day.

Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE nominee for UN General Secretary?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

Breadcrumb
Who is Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE nominee for UN General Secretary?
The UAE has formally nominated veteran diplomat Lana Nusseibeh to become the next UN secretary-general, placing one of its most experienced international representatives in the race to succeed Antonio Guterres.
The nomination was submitted on Wednesday by UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in a letter to the presidents of the UN General Assembly and Security Council.
Nusseibeh, 48, is a former UAE ambassador to the UN who spent more than a decade in international diplomacy, including during the country's 2022-23 membership of the Security Council.
If successful, she would become the first woman to lead the UN and the second person from the Middle East and North Africa to hold the position, following Egypt's Boutros Boutros-Ghali.
Who is Lana Nusseibeh?
Nusseibeh is the daughter of Zaki Nusseibeh, a senior Emirati presidential adviser who has served successive UAE leaders for decades. However, the Nusseibeh family are originally from Palestine and have longstanding connections to Jerusalem.
Her grandfather, Anwar Nusseibeh, was a prominent Palestinian politician and lawyer who served in senior government positions in Jordan.
She studied history at the University of Cambridge before obtaining a master's degree in Israeli and Jewish Diaspora Studies from the School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) in London.
Nusseibeh founded the UAE foreign ministry's Policy Planning Department in 2009, becoming its first director, and subsequently served as a joint special envoy to Afghanistan and Pakistan.
In September 2013, she became the first Emirati woman appointed as the country's permanent representative to the UN, a position she held until April 2024.
During her tenure, she served as president of the executive board of UN Women in 2017 and as a vice-president of the General Assembly. She also co-chaired negotiations concerning UN institutional reform.
Her most prominent diplomatic role came during the UAE's membership of the Security Council between 2022 and 2023, when she twice presided over the body.
During Israel's war on Gaza, Nusseibeh helped secure Security Council Resolution 2720 in December 2023, establishing a UN mechanism intended to facilitate humanitarian assistance to Palestinians.
She was also involved in securing resolutions condemning the Taliban's restrictions on Afghan women working for the UN and addressing the relationship between hate speech, discrimination and international security.
Following her departure from New York, she continued serving in senior positions within the UAE foreign ministry, becoming a minister of state in September 2025.
Can she become UN secretary-general?
Nusseibeh enters the contest as the organisation confronts financial pressures, questions over its effectiveness in responding to conflicts and growing divisions between major powers.
Her campaign programme, titled 'A United Nations for the Next Eighty Years', advocates strengthening conflict prevention, reducing institutional duplication and improving accountability.
Her extensive diplomatic experience could prove advantageous in a contest where leading candidates have struggled to secure the consensus required for appointment.
Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, head of UN Trade and Development, and Argentina's Rafael Grossi, director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, are among her principal rivals.
However, Nusseibeh's candidacy could encounter geopolitical obstacles.
The UAE has faced serious allegations of supplying weapons and financial support to Sudan's Rapid Support Forces (RSF), whose members and allied militias were determined by the US in January 2025 to have committed genocide.
Amnesty International has documented weapons it believes reached the RSF through the UAE, while Abu Dhabi has consistently denied providing military support to either side in Sudan's war.
The controversy could complicate Nusseibeh's candidacy, although no evidence has been presented implicating her personally in the alleged arms transfers.
Regional rivalries, particularly the UAE's complicated relationship with Saudi Arabia, could also influence the contest, alongside expectations that the next secretary-general should come from Latin America.
Ultimately, her prospects will depend on securing at least nine Security Council votes without facing a veto from any of its five permanent members.
The successful candidate will take office on 1 January 2027, succeeding Guterres after two five-year terms.

The Turkic world: From shared history to a shared future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:16:44 UTC
21:16:44 KST

The Turkic world: From shared history to a shared future
Ahead of the 13th OTS Summit in Ankara and as his tenure as Secretary General draws to a close, H.E. Ambassador Kubanychbek Omuraliev shares his reflections on the progress achieved within the Organization of Turkic States and the road ahead. In his article, he looks back on the key developments of recent years and considers how the Turkic States can build on their shared heritage to deepen cooperation, strengthen connectivity, and create new opportunities for their peoples. Qazinform News Agency offers its readers the full text of the article titled The Turkic world: From shared history to a shared future.
By H.E. Ambassador Kubanychbek OMURALIEV
Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States
Istanbul, October 2026
The Turkic World: From Shared History to a Shared Future
There are critical moments in the life of nations and states when shared history ceases to be merely a memory and becomes a force shaping the future. I believe the Turkic World is living through such a moment today.
Across a vast geography connecting East and West, the Turkic World brings together a population of around 180 million people, bound by deep historical and cultural ties and increasingly connected through trade, transport, investment, education, technology and people-to-people cooperation. What for centuries was sustained through common language, culture, traditions and collective memory is increasingly taking institutional and practical form under the umbrella of the family Organization of Turkic States (OTS).
The transformation has been remarkable. Since its establishment in 2009, the OTS has evolved from a platform focused primarily on political dialogue and cultural affinity into a comprehensive and action-oriented framework of cooperation.
As I approach the completion of my tenure as Secretary General, I see this moment not simply as an occasion to look back at what has been accomplished. More importantly, it is an opportunity to reflect on what makes our cooperation distinctive, what it can offer to our peoples, and what kind of Turkic World we wish to build together in the decades ahead.
A Unity Rooted in Something Deeper
The OTS possesses a quality that is rare among international organizations.
International institutions are often created in response to a particular political challenge, economic necessity or security concern. The foundation of the OTS is different. Our cooperation rests upon something that existed long before the establishment of the Organization itself: centuries of shared history, linguistic affinity, common cultural traditions, values and a profound sense of belonging to the same civilizational space.
Common history, language, identity and culture are not simply references to our past. They provide a foundation of trust upon which strong and sustainable cooperation can be built.
Few, if any, international organizations enjoy such a natural foundation. Yet heritage alone does not guarantee a shared future. The responsibility of our generation is to transform this historical closeness and affinity into opportunities, connectivity and cooperation that respond to the realities and challenges of the 21st century.
There is a simple expression that captures this idea particularly well: “Together, We Are Stronger”.
Remarkably, these words are understood across the Turkic World and require almost no translation, reflecting the deep linguistic and cultural bonds among our peoples. Today, “Together, We Are Stronger” is not merely an expression of solidarity, but a guiding principle for practical cooperation.
From Shared Identity to Institutional Strength
One of the most important transformations of recent years has been the gradual conversion of this natural affinity into institutional capacity.
Today, the OTS continues to make significant strides in strengthening cooperation among its Member States. Currently, 65 cooperation mechanisms exist under OTS umbrella, which range cover– from economy, trade, transport and customs to energy, digitalization, industry, science and technology, health, education, youth, agriculture, labour and social protection, intellectual property, space and many others. Since 2023 alone, 32 new mechanisms have been established – matching the total number created by the end of 2022. This reflects not only the expansion of our agenda but also the growing determination of our Member States and Observers to translate shared priorities into concrete institutional cooperation.
What matters even more than the numbers is a change in how we work together. Political consultations have become more frequent and substantive; ministries and specialized institutions are in closer contact; and our ability to think together, plan together and act together has grown. I would describe this stage of our development in three words: implementation, transformation and institutional deepening.
As Chair of the Coordination Committee of the Turkic Cooperation Organizations, the OTS maintains close and structured cooperation with affiliated and related organizations, including the Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic States (TURKPA), the International Organization of Turkic Culture (TURKSOY), the Turkic Academy, the Turkic Culture and Heritage Foundation, the Turkic Investment Fund (TIF) and the Union of Turkic Chambers of Commerce and Industry (TCCI). Together, these institutions contribute to a multidimensional framework of cooperation, strengthening institutional ties and advancing shared priorities across the Turkic World.
The establishment and operationalization of the Turkic Investment Fund represent an important milestone in this evolution. For the first time, the Turkic States have created a joint financial institution designed to mobilize their economic potential, support investment and entrepreneurship, strengthen small and medium-sized enterprises and facilitate joint projects. The Council of Central Banks, the Turkic Green Finance Council and the Turkic Investment Promotion Network (TurkIPAnet) further reinforce this emerging financial and investment architecture.
Yet among the most encouraging developments I have witnessed during my tenure is the emergence of cooperation networks beyond governmental and formal institutions, including within the private sector and professional communities.
Notaries, auditors, engineers, trade unions and representatives of other professions are establishing contacts, creating networks and exploring institutional forms of cooperation within a broader Turkic framework. This growing cooperation is also reflected in initiatives such as the Union of International Road Transport Associations of the OTS, the Union of Turkic Ski Resorts and the Turkic Red Network, bringing together stakeholders across transport, tourism and humanitarian cooperation. Business communities, universities, young people, experts and professional associations are finding their own reasons – and increasingly their own ways – to connect.
When people and professional communities begin building connections on their own initiative, cooperation acquires a life beyond institutions. It becomes rooted in society itself.
For me, this is one of the clearest signs of the growing maturity of Turkic cooperation.
An Emerging Economic and Strategic Space
The growing importance of the Turkic World is shaped not only by our shared heritage, but also by the scale of our collective economic and strategic potential. According to figures reported for the end of 2025, the combined GDP of OTS Member States and Observers exceeded $2.4 trillion, and their aggregate trade turnover reached approximately $1.27 trillion.
Together, the Turkic States would represent the world’s 11th largest economy and third-largest energy provider. With substantial reserves of oil, natural gas, coal, and critical minerals, including over 40 percent of global uranium production, our countries possess significant energy potential while increasingly investing in renewable energy development.
In a time of rising demand and fast changes in global energy systems, working together is not optional – it is a necessary thing to do. Recent OTS Summits stress the importance of energy security, which depends on connecting pipelines, power grids, storage, and transport routes to ensure stable supply, increase trade, and strengthen economic and geopolitical stability.
The Turkic States are strengthening regional and international energy connectivity through major infrastructure projects, including the Southern Gas Corridor, the Central Asia -Azerbaijan Green Energy Corridor, the Kambarata-1 Hydropower Plant and the Black Sea Submarine Cable. These initiatives reflect the growing role of the Turkic World in enhancing energy security, diversifying supply routes and advancing renewable energy cooperation.
In this regard, the Turkic World Vision-2040 provides an important strategic framework. It calls on us to deepen economic integration, improve connectivity, strengthen institutions, invest in knowledge-based industries, and promote sustainable and inclusive growth.
Perhaps nowhere is this logic more visible than in connectivity.
The Trans-Caspian International East - West Middle Corridor is becoming an increasingly important link between Asia and Europe, with freight volumes potentially reaching 11 million tons by 2030. The China - Kyrgyzstan - Uzbekistan railway, with a projected capacity of up to 15 million tons annually, will further strengthen regional connectivity and expand trade opportunities across Eurasia.
But a modern corridor is more than railway tracks, roads and ports. Goods must cross borders efficiently; information and documentation must move with them.
The OTS is complementing physical infrastructure with customs and digital solutions, including the Simplified Customs Corridor, e-Permit, e-CMR and digital TIR, to facilitate cross-border trade and reduce administrative barriers. The Digital Economy Partnership Agreement and ongoing efforts to conclude a free trade agreement in services and investment will further strengthen economic integration among our countries.
We also welcome the recently established cooperation among competition authorities, financial intelligence units, investment promotion agencies, supreme audit institutions and tax administrations. These partnerships strengthen institutional connectivity and improve economic governance across the Turkic World.
The digital economy remains at the center of this agenda. Digital trade platforms, interoperable e-customs systems, fintech cooperation, secure data exchange, and common approaches to digital regulation can make economic relations more efficient and accessible. Digital transformation is not simply a technical matter. It is one of the foundations of modern economic integration.
The objective is straightforward: to make connectivity work better for those who actually use it.
Taken together, these developments point towards the gradual emergence of a more connected Turkic economic space – one in which infrastructure is reinforced by efficient borders, trade is supported by investment, and the strengths of individual countries increasingly become sources of shared opportunity.
Towards a More Connected Turkic World
For the younger generation, the Turkic World should be a living space of opportunity. The Turkic Universities Union (TURKUNIB) and Orhun Exchange Programme help bring students, academic staff and universities closer together. Youth initiatives, including the Youth Volunteering Educational Programme, the Multilateral Youth Exchange Programme and the International Youth Camp, further promote people-to-people contacts, mutual understanding and a sense of shared identity among young people across the Turkic World. Meanwhile, initiatives under discussion, such as the Turkic ID and Common Museum Card, aim to facilitate travel and access to our shared cultural heritage.
A transport corridor becomes more valuable when businesses use it. Business cooperation becomes stronger when supported by investment. Investment becomes more productive when connected with technology and human capital. And all of these become more sustainable when our societies participate in and benefit from the process.
The future of the OTS therefore lies not simply in expanding the number of areas in which we cooperate, but in bringing existing mechanisms together into a more coherent space of opportunity.
Our strength lies precisely in building upon our unique foundations while remaining open to the wider world.
Our long-term direction is set out in the Turkic World Vision-2040. Deeper connectivity and integration, pursued with full respect for the sovereignty and national priorities of our States, should strengthen our common capacity to address climate change, food and health security, emergencies and other cross-border challenges.
A Turkic World Open to the World
A stronger Turkic World should also mean a more connected and outward-looking Turkic World.
Our geography gives us a natural role in this regard. For centuries, the lands of the Turkic World have connected peoples, cultures, markets and ideas across Eurasia. Today, we have an opportunity to give this historical role a modern meaning.
By improving transport links, facilitating trade, connecting energy networks, encouraging innovation and strengthening contacts among societies, the Turkic States can contribute not only to their own prosperity, but also to greater connectivity and cooperation across the wider Eurasian region.
This approach is reflected in the OTS’s growing engagement with the United Nations system and other international and regional organizations, as well as in the development of the OTS+ format, which provides a flexible platform for cooperation with countries and partners beyond the Organization. Our aim is to develop mutually beneficial, practical partnerships that contribute to peace, stability, connectivity, sustainable development and dialogue.
Our objective is not to build walls around the Turkic World, but to build bridges that connect it with the wider world.
A Turkic World that is more connected within can also be more open, more relevant and more capable of contributing to dialogue, development and shared prosperity beyond its own borders.
The Road Ahead
Over the past years, I have had the privilege of witnessing and making my humble contribution to the Turkic World move closer together in ways that are increasingly diverse and increasingly tangible.
Yet perhaps the most important conclusion I draw from these years is that we are still at the beginning of what is possible.
The foundations have been laid. The commitment of our Member States is strong. The institutional architecture has expanded. Our collective economic and strategic potential is increasingly recognized. And our societies themselves are discovering new ways of connecting with one another.
The forthcoming 13th OTS Summit in Ankara, to be held under the theme “Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed”, which will mark the beginning of Türkiye’s Chairmanship, offers an important opportunity to carry this momentum into the next phase of our common work.
Looking ahead, the success of our cooperation must be measured not only by the agreements we sign or the mechanisms we establish, but by the tangible benefits we deliver to our peoples. Our priority must remain to translate our collective ambitions into meaningful opportunities and lasting progress for future generations.
I remain deeply grateful to the Heads of State of our Member States and Observers for their vision and unwavering support, as well as to our governments, institutions, Permanent Representatives, experts and colleagues at the OTS Secretariat. Their dedication, professionalism and shared commitment have been indispensable to every step of our collective progress.
It has been a great honour to contribute to this journey as Secretary General.
Although my tenure as Secretary General is drawing to a close, my commitment to the unity, cooperation and prosperity of the Turkic World will remain unchanged. I will always regard it as a privilege to have contributed to this common endeavour and will continue to believe in the extraordinary potential of our shared future.
The Turkic World must continue its journey from affinity to connectivity, from potential to capacity, and from cooperation to tangible benefit for its people.
Our ancestors gave us a shared heritage. What we leave to future generations must be more than the memory of that heritage.
It must be a shared future built upon it.
Across our languages and across our geography, the following message should continuously resonate:
Together, We Are Stronger.

‘In 1949, they brought a cardboard box and called it a ballot box’: Veterans recall 77 years of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:16:13 UTC
21:16:13 KST

"I remember the elections to the first Knesset. I was a soldier in the Golani Brigade's 13th Battalion, and I voted in the army. We were out in the field. They brought a cardboard box and called it a ballot box. We voted, and they immediately left."
Seventy-seven years later, Zir Luz can still recall the moment with remarkable clarity. Now 97 and approaching his 98th birthday next month, he was among the Israelis who cast their ballots in the country's first national election in January 1949. Next Tuesday, when Israel returns to the polls, he intends to vote once again.
Luz was born in 1928 at Kibbutz Ein Harod, in northern Israel's Jezreel Valley, to pioneering parents who helped settle the region. Today, he lives at Ein Harod Meuhad, one of two kibbutzim created when the original community split during the political and ideological disputes of the 1950s.
For much of his life, his political identity was shaped by the socialist Labor movement that dominated Israel's early decades. But his voting record also includes one significant break with tradition.
From the Labor movement to a family spanning Israel's political divide
"For years, we were identified with the Labor movement and the Histadrut," Luz says, referring to Israel's powerful labor federation. "In the first Knesset election, I voted for Mapam. Since then, throughout my life, I've voted only for Mapai and the Labor Party, and I intend to vote for the Democrats."
There was one exception: the historic 1977 election, which brought Menachem Begin's Likud to power and ended nearly three decades of Labor-led rule.
"Only in 1977 did I not vote for the Labor Party. I voted for the National Religious Party," Luz recalls. "I felt that Mapai had become corrupt, and I wanted change."
The political landscape of his kibbutz has changed considerably since then. Once firmly associated with the Labor movement, Ein Harod now includes supporters of parties across the political spectrum.
"Today, the vote in Ein Harod is spread among all the parties. That's not how it used to be," he says. "Everyone in the kibbutz knows who I vote for."
The political differences extend into his own family, where views range from the left-wing Democrats to supporters of far-right politicians Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich.
"Everyone in my family knows my opinions, and my family spans the entire spectrum, from the Democrats to Ben-Gvir and Smotrich," Luz says. "I talk to them about political issues, but I don't try to convince them, and they don't try to convince me. Neither of us has a chance."
Despite the ideological divisions, politics remains a familiar subject of conversation rather than something he avoids.
Luz also remembers serving at a polling station during the election to the second Knesset in 1951, this time as a representative of an Arab party affiliated with Mapam.
"I sat at a polling station in an Arab village as the representative of an Arab satellite party of Mapam," he recalls. "It was nice to sit there. If I were younger, I'd do it again today."
As for how many more elections he hopes to participate in, he has a simple answer: "As far as I'm concerned, I intend to vote for as long as I live."
‘I miss hearing Ben-Gurion's voice on the radio’
Pinchas Avhar, 91, was too young to vote in Israel's first election. In 1949, when the country's first Constituent Assembly was elected, he was just 13.
But since reaching voting age, Avhar has not missed a single election. He will celebrate his 92nd birthday in February and still recalls the early years of Israeli democracy with affection.
Like Luz, he grew up in the Jezreel Valley. His parents immigrated from Yemen in 1914, decades before Israel's establishment. After the family's early years in the Neve Tzedek neighborhood of Tel Aviv, Avhar moved to Kibbutz Beit Alfa, not far from Ein Harod.
"I miss that period in the kibbutz very much," he says. "There was a lot of simplicity there, and above all, love between people."
Later, Avhar joined the Working and Learning Youth movement, where he spent 35 years guiding and supporting teenagers who had left school and entered the workforce. He also took an active role in efforts to establish minimum-wage protections for young workers.
His commitment to younger generations has continued into old age. For the past 12 years, he has volunteered at Yizre'elia School in Haifa, mentoring and accompanying students.
At his carefully maintained home in Haifa's Neve Sha'anan neighborhood, Avhar is particular about historical details.
"The state was established in 1948, but the elections to the Constituent Assembly were only held in January 1949," he explains. "I voted for the first time in 1955. That really was the beginning of the state."
He remembers the voting process as far simpler than today's crowded election ballots.
"There was a big curtain, and behind it were just a few party lists. That's where I made my choice."
And which party received his vote?
"Mapai, of course," he replies with a broad smile, referring to the dominant political party led by Israel's founding prime minister, David Ben-Gurion.
"I loved Ben-Gurion very much. I miss hearing his voice on the radio. There weren't advertisements like there are today. Those were leaders of another era: Ben-Gurion, Shapira, Tabenkin, Rokach and Begin."
For Avhar, the contrast with contemporary Israeli politics is striking.
"Today, people will go to the polling stations and be confused about whom to vote for," he says. "There are so many small parties joining together and demanding positions, otherwise there's no government. That really troubles me, election after election."
He remains committed to voting for a party on the political left, but has not yet made his final choice ahead of Tuesday's election.
"The left, as always. Exactly which party? We'll have to see what happens in the coming days, and then I'll make an informed decision," he says.
He also believes the political landscape could shift following Benny Gantz's decision not to run, suggesting that Gadi Eisenkot may attract additional support. But he prefers to wait and see how events unfold before deciding.
‘We have to heal the rift’
Sitting in a large armchair in his living room, beside the balcony, Avhar grows noticeably more serious when discussing the country's current condition.
"I am very, very worried about the state of the country," he says firmly. "There is a deep rift between people, especially after the disaster of October 7, and it hurts me."
For someone who has lived through Israel's entire existence, watched governments rise and fall and taken part in nearly every chapter of its democratic history, the divisions have become deeply personal.
"It hurts me to see my country, where I've lived since its establishment and where I've always voted, in such a state."
The concerns go beyond political disagreements. Avhar points to the cost of living, continuing security pressures and the growing distance between different parts of Israeli society.
"Where are we even heading? It's difficult here, with the cost of living, the internal divisions and the security pressure. But we have to heal the rift," he says.
"It's time for us to live in peace, at least among ourselves. That's my hope at my advanced age, to feel here the way I once did, that we're all united."
Avhar is the father of three children, grandfather of six and great-grandfather of five. This year's election carries particular significance for his family because his grandson Ido, an IDF soldier, will be voting for the first time.
"It's the first time in his life that he'll vote," Avhar says. "I hope he makes the right choice among all those party lists."
The moment marks another chapter in a family whose experience of Israeli elections now spans generations, from a grandfather who remembers the early years of the state to a young soldier casting his first ballot.
For Avhar, who has never missed an opportunity to vote, participating in the democratic process remains as important as it was in 1955.
And despite his concerns about Israel's future, he ends with a message to the public:
"I tell everyone: Go out and vote this coming Tuesday. This is the most important election for our country."

Kazakh schoolers build AI platform to translate sign language in real time
Students at the Nazarbayev Intellectual School in Kyzylorda have developed an AI platform that translates sign language into text and speech in real time, Qazinform News Agency reports.
Aishabibi Yerlankyzy and Gainizhamal Berikkyzy piloted their web platform, QOLDAU AI, at Kyzylorda Specialized Boarding School No. 6 for Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Children.
Requiring only a standard web camera and an internet connection, the system recognizes Kazakh sign language gestures and converts them into text and audio formats, helping hearing-impaired individuals communicate with others without the need to install additional applications.
While testing, children evaluated the platform and shared their impressions. Teachers highlighted the platform's practical benefits, urging developers to add more gestures and noting its potential to support literacy development.
"I thank the girls for creating a useful platform that can become a good assistant for specialists and parents. Some of the sign language elements still need refinement, but they can be improved. In the future, I would like to see more educational materials and video tutorials," said sign language specialist Zukhra Kalzhanova.
NIS Kyzylorda physics teacher Ainur Kurakbayeva and deputy principal Madina Rashitova are supervising the project. Feedback gathered during testing will help the project authors refine the system to suit users' needs.
Alongside the technology demonstration, the NIS students also organized an art contest titled "Kazakhstan is My Pride" for the boarding school pupils ahead of Republic Day.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that a student of the Nazarbayev Intellectual School in Kyzylorda invented a rehabilitation system for stroke survivors.

21:15:57 KST

OpenAI expands ChatGPT ads to 26 more countries
The expansion includes 14 new markets in Latin America, as well as countries across Europe, the Middle East, Africa and Asia. New markets include Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Peru, Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
Advertisers can launch campaigns through OpenAI's Ads Manager or its technology partners, depending on the market.
OpenAI says more than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week to explore ideas, compare options and make decisions. The company aims to place advertisements alongside relevant conversations, allowing businesses to reach users while they consider products and services.
For example, someone planning their first marathon might discuss meal planning with ChatGPT and then see an advertisement for a grocery delivery service.
OpenAI says advertisements will appear only on its Free and Go plans. Users subscribed to Plus, Pro and Enterprise will not see ads, according to the announcement.
The company also says advertisements will be clearly labeled and displayed separately from ChatGPT's answers. OpenAI states that it does not share users' conversations with advertisers or sell their personal data, and that advertisements do not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.
According to OpenAI's advertising guidelines, the system selects ads based on factors such as the current conversation, the user's apparent intent and the advertisement's content. When ad personalization is enabled, the system may also use certain signals from a user's broader interactions with ChatGPT.
Advertisers can pay for impressions or valid clicks and can use supported conversion tracking to measure campaign performance. OpenAI recommends starting with a maximum bid of $3 to $5 per click for campaigns using cost per click pricing.
OpenAI plans to introduce additional advertising formats, campaign objectives, purchasing options and measurement tools as the service expands.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that eight US states sued OpenAI over ChatGPT safety.

Türkiye’s Central Bank cuts policy rate by 100bps to 36 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:15:22 UTC
21:15:22 KST

Data on economic activity indicates that domestic demand remains weak, says the Central Bank.
As widely expected, Türkiye’s Central Bank has reduced its policy rate, the one-week repo auction rate, from 37 percent to 36 percent.
The bank’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), led by Governor Fatih Karahan, convened on Oct. 22 to decide about the key interest rate. Expectations for a rate cut were reinforced by September inflation data. Türkiye’s annual consumer inflation rate stood at 29.73 percent in September, below market expectations of 30.3 percent, marking the first reading below 30 percent since November 2021. Consumer prices rose 1.84 percent month-on-month.
The bank on Oct. 22 also lowered the overnight lending rate from 40 percent to 39 percent and the overnight borrowing rate from 35.5 percent to 34.5 percent.
Despite monthly fluctuations, recent inflation figures and leading indicators confirm the deceleration in the underlying trend of inflation, said the bank in a statement accompanying the rate decision.
Data on economic activity as well as the limited pass-through of supply shocks to domestic prices indicate that domestic demand remains weak, according to the bank.
“On the other hand, elevated energy prices due to ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to pose an upside risk to the inflation outlook. The impact of geopolitical developments on the inflation outlook through the cost channel, economic activity and expectations is closely monitored,” it added.
The tight monetary policy stance, which will be maintained until price stability is achieved, will strengthen the disinflation process through demand, exchange rate and expectation channels, said the bank.
“The committee will determine the policy rate by taking into account realized and expected inflation and its underlying trend in a way to ensure the tightness required by the projected disinflation path in line with the interim targets, it noted.
The size and timing of policy steps will be decided prudently on a meeting-by-meeting basis with a focus on the inflation outlook, the bank reiterated.
The final MPC meeting of 2026 is scheduled for Dec. 10.
“In case of a significant and persistent deterioration in the inflation outlook, monetary policy stance will be tightened,” said the bank, adding that the committee remains highly attentive to upside risks on inflation.
“The committee will make its policy decisions so as to create the monetary and financial conditions necessary to reach the 5 percent inflation target in the medium term,” said the statement, noting that the committee will make its decisions in a predictable, data-driven and transparent framework.

Russian envoy says diesel deal with US to take effect Friday

Elena Teslova
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
A deal between Russia and the US on Russian diesel supplies will be effective from Friday, Russia's special envoy said Thursday.
Speaking in Istanbul on the sidelines of the Verona Eurasian Economic Forum, Kirill Dmitriev, the special envoy for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries, said Russia was also open to diesel supply deals with European nations if requests were made.
“We all know about the diesel deal, it will begin to be implemented literally tomorrow,” he said.
The official added that Moscow and Washington were discussing potential Russian fertilizer supplies to the US market, other energy projects and technological cooperation, including the possible creation of joint artificial intelligence data centers.
Dmitriev said economic cooperation between Russia and the US would continue to expand despite opposition from some European officials, adding that European countries themselves purchased significantly more Russian energy resources than the US.
 
Europe's fuel crisis to 'intensify'
He also predicted that Europe’s fuel crisis would worsen, attributing it to attempts to abandon Russian energy supplies.
“We see a fuel crisis in Europe, and it will only intensify,” he said.
“I have no doubt that the more deals we have with the US, the more European companies will want to join. They will not want to be left out,” he said.
Dmitriev also said European businesses were suffering from high energy prices as a result of the EU’s policies and the shift away from Russian energy supplies.
According to him, European business representatives had approached the Russian delegation at the forum to express support for maintaining dialogue with Moscow.
The Russian envoy also predicted that the Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines would eventually resume operations.
“There is absolutely no doubt that Nord Stream 1 and 2 will operate again at some point. It is inevitable,” he said.
Nord Stream 1 and 2 were designed to deliver Russian gas directly to Germany via the Baltic Sea.
Nord Stream 1 operated from 2011, while Nord Stream 2 was completed in 2021 but never entered service.
Explosions damaged three of the four pipeline lines in September 2022. Germany’s investigation into the sabotage remains ongoing, with a Ukrainian national suspected of coordinating the attack arrested in 2025.

Iran reveals ‘offensive’ doctrine, US issues alert: Is war imminent?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:12:32 UTC
21:12:32 KST

Iran reveals ‘offensive’ doctrine, US issues alert: Is war imminent?
US orders diplomatic staff out of Saudi Arabia amid escalating conflict and reports of potential US and Israeli strikes on Iran.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says renewed attacks by the United States could prompt Tehran to invade neighbouring countries and hit bases used in US military operations as part of its new “offensive” strategy.
The warning on Wednesday came amid escalating attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint, and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to end the nearly eight-month war.
“Our defence doctrine was previously defensive; we used to say that if a country attacks us, we will respond. Now we say that if a country attacks us, we will both respond and launch an offensive,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said.
Washington ordered some diplomatic personnel to leave Saudi Arabia amid attacks from Yemen’s Houthis while US President Donald Trump has signalled that a decision on the conflict could come soon.
According to media reports, the US and Israel are planning potential attacks on Iran in the coming weeks.
As negotiations seem stalled and both sides exchange threats, could the region be heading towards another military escalation?
What is Iran’s new doctrine?
The IRGC on Wednesday announced a shift towards an “offensive and asymmetrical” defence doctrine, threatening to invade countries that launch attacks against it.
Mohebi said Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes.
Mohebi stressed that Iran’s missile stockpile has increased 1.5 times since the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025. He did not provide specific figures.
“The quality of the missiles has improved significantly, and their range, destructive power and accuracy in hitting targets have increased,” the spokesman said.
Moreover, Mohebi said Iranian forces were in the “stage of preparing to unveil the ‘father of all bombs’. This is something new for the enemy.”
Meanwhile, attacks in the Strait of Hormuz continued unabated.
The IRGC’s navy said on Thursday that four vessels it accused of being involved in illegal oil transfers were struck and caught fire in the northern Gulf. Three other vessels hit mines west of the strait, it added.
Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz. While shipments through the strait are still below those levels, oil shipments from the region returned to pre-war levels last month as exporters found alternative ways to ship out their oil and gas, including using pipelines.
However, a flurry of recent attacks in the key waterway and the fighting between Yemen’s Houthis and its Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, which has resulted in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, have once again sent oil prices surging. Brent crude climbed above $110 a barrel on Thursday amid fears of further disruptions to regional energy supplies.
Why the shift?
Iran’s shift towards an offensive military doctrine reflects Tehran’s determination to make future US-Israeli attacks significantly more costly, according to analysts.
Negar Mortazavi, senior fellow at the Centre for International Policy, told Al Jazeera that Tehran was drawing lessons from the wars of 2025 and 2026 after its previous strategy of retaliation failed to prevent repeated attacks.
“Tehran now wants to establish a new equation: Any future attack on Iran will come at a much higher cost for the aggressors,” she told Al Jazeera.
Unable to match conventional US military capabilities, Iran is increasingly relying on asymmetric warfare, including missiles, drones and its leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, Mortazavi explained.
She said Tehran was pursuing a broader strategy aimed at imposing military, economic and political costs on Washington, including potentially influencing the November 3 US midterm elections.
“Iran wants to teach Washington a lesson: Attacking Iran comes with a high price, one that can even cost elections,” Mortazavi said, referring to US surveys that are predicting electoral losses for Trump’s Republican Party.
She added that Iranian officials were closely monitoring the elections, believing the economic fallout from the war could damage the Republican Party’s prospects of retaining control of Congress.
“The long-term objective is to establish deterrence so that future American administrations think twice before daring to attack Iran again,” she said.
Political analyst Rami Khouri said the doctrine was also intended to ensure that the consequences of attacks extend to the US, Israel and regional countries supporting their military operations.
“That’s one part of the strategy, that the suffering and the damage have to be equal and reciprocal,” Khouri, nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center, told Al Jazeera.
Khouri argued that Tehran was also seeking to challenge what it views as longstanding Western domination of the region.
“The Iranians are actually working to try to end the colonial period,” he said.
He added that Iran’s strategy could extend the economic consequences of conflict far beyond the Middle East, affecting energy supplies, transportation, insurance costs and shipments of essential goods.
“The pain is going to go way beyond just the Middle East and Israel and the US and will hurt people in other parts of the world,” Khouri said.
What has the US said about resuming the war?
Trump has offered conflicting signals about Washington’s next steps.
On Wednesday, he said the US was no longer negotiating with Tehran and suggested developments were imminent. “We are going to have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon,” he told reporters.
He also said Washington could end the war immediately but wanted a lasting outcome. “It’ll end very soon. We could leave now, but we want to make sure it lasts for a long time,” Trump said at a campaign rally in South Carolina.
Trump previously pledged not to attack Iran before the November 3 elections.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this week that reaching a peace agreement is extremely difficult and insisted that Iran must stop targeting commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.
In recent weeks, Iran’s enrichment of uranium has re-emerged as a point of contention.
Rubio has maintained that Washington will reject any agreement allowing Iran to develop nuclear weapons, which require highly enriched uranium. “The United States will not support any deal that creates a pathway for Iran to ever have a nuclear weapon,” he said on Wednesday.
Tehran insisted its right to enrichment is guaranteed under the Non-Proliferation Treaty.
Iran has offered a seven-day plan to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for Washington ending its blockade of Iranian ports, easing sanctions and unfreezing Iranian assets.
Meanwhile, the US Department of State on Wednesday ordered nonemergency personnel and their families to leave Saudi Arabia after recent Houthi attacks.
The US embassy in Riyadh has warned of further attacks while American officials told the Reuters news agency that family members could be withdrawn from other Gulf missions.
State Department spokesman Tommy Piggott said departure orders for mission personnel across the Gulf have not been ordered, saying the current orders were for “employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only”.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reiterated on Sunday his pledge to topple Iran’s government, saying it was key to preventing it from rebuilding its nuclear programme and the “axis of resistance”, further raising prospects of an escalation.
Netanyahu made the comments as Israel’s longest-serving prime minister is locked in a tough battle to remain in power in Tuesday’s elections.
Is war imminent?
Analysts warned that renewed US-Israeli attacks on Iran are increasingly possible with both sides preparing for another confrontation despite the continued possibility of diplomacy.
“Another round of war seems to be approaching,” Mortazavi said.
“Both sides appear to be preparing for renewed confrontation while escalating tensions in the Strait of Hormuz increase the risk of a wider conflict,” she said.
Mortazavi added that the elections in the next two weeks in the US and Israel could influence the timing of military action but warned that the current trajectory appeared to favour escalation over negotiations.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, on Wednesday said, “Everyone must know that any action against Iran comes at a cost.”
“If diplomacy can create this understanding, we prefer diplomacy, but if the war continues, Iran has the necessary means to sustain its response,” Rezaei said, according to the IRNA news agency.
Echoing Mortazavi, Khouri warned that another confrontation could be approaching although he said US threats might still be part of a negotiating strategy.
“I think imminent conflict is on the cards, but I don’t know if war is the right word to use,” Khouri told Al Jazeera.
He said renewed strikes could target Iran’s critical infrastructure, including electricity networks, transportation systems, bridges and essential services.
“We’re probably going to get some severe attacks on a few targets that will try to make life in Iran very difficult,” he said.
However, Khouri cautioned that Iran’s ability to withstand another major military offensive while inflicting comparable damage on its adversaries remained uncertain.
“It’s not clear if Iran has the ability to withstand major new assaults against it,” he said, while stressing that Tehran was unlikely to surrender to military pressure.

“Badr Memorandum of Understanding” was signed between the Defense Ministries of Türkiye, Qatar, Indonesia, and Pakistan. (AA Photo)

“Together with the Mecca Defense Alliance and the Badr Memorandum of Understanding, it is a concrete indicator of our country’s effectiveness and strategic cooperation in the international arena,” ministry officials said on Oct. 22.
