They also added that this agreement will contribute to peace and stability in the wider region.
Libya agreement fully legal
The officials also commented on the Libyan House of Representatives’ ratification of the Türkiye-Libya maritime delimitation agreement which was originally signed in late 2019.
Welcoming the parliamentary confirmation, the officials thanked Libyan officials who demonstrated a strong will to this end.
“We attach great importance on this memorandum, which contributes to protecting the rights and interests of both countries in the eastern Mediterranean. And we support the objective of a ‘united and integrated Libya’ that brings the east and west of Libya together around a common future,” they stressed.
On the statements from the EU and Greece which argued that the deal is null and void, the ministry recalled that the agreement was signed between the two countries based on international law and interests of the littoral countries.
“The delimitation of maritime jurisdiction areas falls within the scope of the sovereign rights of the relevant coastal states, and the legal validity of the said Memorandum of Understanding cannot be nullified by the unilateral assessments of third parties,” they noted.

Pentagon pledges to buy 850 F-35 jets under 10-year deal with Lockheed Martin

Berk Kutay Gokmen
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Pentagon has moved to purchase at total of 850 F-35 fighter jets from Lockheed Martin over the next 10 years, marking the longest commitment among recent Trump administration efforts to prepare suppliers for wartime production.
The new framework agreement, announced on Thursday, includes 850 F-35 Lightning II aircraft for the US military, hundreds more for international customers, as well as spare parts and other equipment.
The deal would secure the defense contractor’s plan to produce 156 jets each year in the coming years.
The Defense Department said Lockheed Martin had agreed to fund $7 billion in investments from its own resources to support the long-term production plan.
The agreement announced on Thursday is a step toward a final contract, which would require tens of billions of dollars in congressional funding to be finalized.
The stealth fighter program has already been described as the world’s most expensive weapons program, with projected lifetime costs of $2 trillion for purchasing, operating, and maintaining the aircraft.
Pentagon officials have said that firm, multiyear purchase commitments help make weapons procurement more efficient. Suppliers involved in military programs often complain that inconsistent congressional funding makes long-term planning difficult.
“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” said Lockheed Martin CEO Jim Taiclet.

France bans or curbs protests in bid to prevent new weekend unrest
French authorities have banned or curbed protests across the country ahead of the weekend in a bid to prevent another wave of the violence and looting that plagued last week’s demonstrations. In Paris alone, hundreds of shops and other small businesses were destroyed on the sidelines of the protests over the cost of living and education funding shortfalls.
French authorities on Thursday imposed bans or restrictions on fresh protests springing up in the wake of demonstrations last weekend that degenerated into the country's worst street violence in years.
President Emmanuel Macron said after chairing a meeting of key ministers and intelligence officials that curfews and other security measures would be imposed, including bans on "groups without legitimacy" holding protests.
Read more'I didn’t know it was theft': Trials begin in Paris following October 17 violence
"The priority is a return to calm," he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide "the next steps" for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.
The worst of the violence, Macron said, "was led by organised ultra-left groups aiming to bring down the republic", that he accused of "sedition".
Officials are still reeling from the clashes, widespread looting and vandalism of public buildings that broke out on October 17, on the margins of mass demonstrations of more than half a million people against the surging cost of living.
Macron's government has admitted police lost control, and candidates jockeying to succeed him in presidential elections in six months' time argue that authorities are incapable or unwilling to calm the situation.
Protests banned
A Paris protest Thursday organised by students – who had held four weeks of protests before the October 17 rallies – went ahead with hundreds attending after a police ban was overturned by an emergency court injunction.
"The authorities are trying to make a distinction between 'good' and 'bad' protesters," a university student leader, Coppelia Moreau, said of that attempted ban and others being touted.
"What we are seeing is a government that doesn't want any demonstrations at all. That goes against the right to demonstrate," she told journalists.
Authorities on Thursday declared a ban on "all protests" in the southeastern city of Lyon on Saturday.
Read moreLive: Authorities in Lyon and Marseille ban all protests Saturday
France's third-biggest city suffered the looting of 200 to 300 shops last weekend and the torching of a tourist office in what its mayor described as hours of "chaos".
Other cities, including Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon, issued bans on protests in their city centres.
In Paris, the city's police said Thursday that the march planned for Saturday could be held in the east of the capital, starting at Bastille, but was banned from heading into the city centre, where shops and major public buildings are located.
The Yellow Vest movement organising the cost-of-living rallies along with unions said it did not agree with the order.
"We won't sign off on it," said Benjamin Ball, who runs an online map showing the planned locations of Saturday's demonstrations.
Art Basel Paris, the capital's biggest art fair, said it would shut this weekend, two days early, due to the protests.
France's interior ministry said "20 percent more" police would be deployed this coming Saturday than for last weekend.
Detentions and dialogue
The French government has been projecting a firm response in the wake of last weekend's violence, although Macron has said he would not go as far as to call a state of emergency.
Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said Thursday that 217 people of 2,700 arrested during and since last weekend had been locked up, and that 1,000 more were being prosecuted.
On Thursday, a 66-year-old man was arrested over the arson last weekend of the 19th-century town hall of Limoges, prosecutors said. A man in his 30s had already been arrested Tuesday over the same crime.

Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts 185 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted roughly 185 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy armored combat vehicle in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup South units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on formations of five mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, an airmobile brigade, an assault brigade, a mountain assault brigade, an air assault brigade of the Ukrainian army, two marine infantry brigades and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Slavyansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkovka, Gavrilovka, Kondratovka and Vasilevskaya Pustosh in the Donetsk People’s Republic," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost an estimated 185 personnel, an armored combat vehicle, 32 motor vehicles, four Western-made field artillery guns and an electronic warfare station in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 345 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 345 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed three enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Center units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of five mechanized brigades, a jaeger brigade, an assault brigade, an airborne brigade, an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army, three marine infantry brigades, five National Guard brigades and the Azov special operations brigade [outlawed as a terrorist group in Russia] in areas near the settlements of Krinitsy, Roganskoye, Novodonetskoye, Shilovka, Kamenka, Starovarvarovka, Belozerskoye and Novoyavlenka in the Donetsk People’s Republic and Leninskoye in the Dnepropetrovsk Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 345 personnel, three armored combat vehicles, four motor vehicles, five field artillery guns and six electronic warfare and counterbattery radar stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 245 casualties on Ukrainian army in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 245 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed eight enemy motor vehicles in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
During the last 24-hour period, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of three air assault brigades, three assault regiments of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and a territorial defense brigade in areas near the settlements of Vasilkovskoye, Dibrova and Kolomiytsy in the Dnepropetrovsk Region, Barvinovka, Voskresenka and Volnyanka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 245 personnel and eight motor vehicles in that frontline area over the past 24 hours, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 40 Ukrainian troops in past day
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 40 Ukrainian troops and destroyed an enemy jamming station in its area of responsibility over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup Dnepr units improved their tactical position and inflicted losses on formations of two mechanized brigades, a mountain assault brigade and an assault regiment of the Ukrainian army in areas near the settlements of Orekhov, Kushugum, Kirovo and Yurkovka in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said.
"Up to 40 Ukrainian military personnel, 27 motor vehicles and an electronic warfare station were destroyed," it said.
Russian troops strike Ukrainian long-range UAV assembly, launch sites in past day
Russian troops struck Ukrainian long-range unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) assembly, storage and launch sites and enemy deployment areas over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Operational/tactical aircraft, attack unmanned aerial vehicles, missile troops and artillery of the Russian groups of forces struck energy and transport infrastructure facilities used by the Ukrainian army, armament, ammunition and materiel depots, workshops for the assembly and sites for the storage and launch of long-range unmanned aerial vehicles, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries in 158 locations," the ministry said.
Russian air defenses intercept 1,226 Ukrainian UAVs over past day
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 1,226 Ukrainian unmanned aerial vehicles over the past 24 hours, the ministry reported.
"Air defense capabilities shot down 1,226 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the ministry said.
Tally of Ukrainian army’s losses
Overall, the Russian Armed Forces have destroyed 674 Ukrainian combat aircraft, 284 helicopters, 268,113 unmanned aerial vehicles, 672 surface-to-air missile systems, 31,336 tanks and other armored combat vehicles, 1,792 multiple rocket launchers, 36,785 field artillery guns and mortars and 75,272 special military motor vehicles since the start of the special military operation, the ministry reported.

Education Minister Yusuf Tekin has announced that the ministry is preparing to take legal action against Meta regarding children's safety.
The Education Ministry is preparing to sue Meta over social media content that it says could harm children’s academic and personal development, Education Minister Yusuf Tekin has said.
Speaking to journalists, Tekin said children continued to encounter age-inappropriate material online despite restrictions on mobile phone use in schools and warnings about social media risks.
The ministry believes social media companies and content creators must take greater responsibility for protecting young users, he said, adding that legal action was being considered along the lines of cases brought in the United States and European Union.
“Either make your content inaccessible to these children, or approve it in a way that ensures children are not harmed,” Tekin said, calling on platforms to reassess the material available to minors.

Authorities have introduced measures including police deployments, security personnel and upgraded camera systems, while also placing greater emphasis on school counselling services.
The planned lawsuit comes as Türkiye prepares to tighten restrictions on children’s social media use. Regulations published in the Official Gazette on Oct. 10 are due to take effect on Nov. 1, prohibiting platforms from providing services to users under 15 and introducing age verification through e-Devlet, the government’s digital services portal.
Under the rules, platforms must reject registrations by children under 15 and close existing accounts found to belong to them. Users aged 15 to 17 will be subject to additional safeguards, including private accounts, restrictions on livestreaming and personalized advertising, and a ban on infinite-scrolling feeds.

Birds are more afraid of women than men. Scientists have no idea why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:06:14 UTC
21:06:14 KST

Birds are more afraid of women than men. Scientists have no idea why
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- British Ecological Society
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a strange pattern in urban bird behavior: Across five European countries and 37 species, birds consistently fled sooner when approached by women than men. Researchers have no clear explanation for the difference, raising intriguing questions about how birds recognize and respond to humans.
- Share:
Birds living in cities appear to react differently to men and women, and scientists are struggling to explain why. An international research team discovered that urban birds, including great tits, house sparrows, and blackbirds, tend to fly away sooner when approached by women than by men. The surprising behavior raises new questions about how birds perceive the people around them.
The study took place in five European countries, where male and female participants (matched for height and clothing) walked directly toward birds in city parks and other green spaces.
On average, men were able to approach about one meter closer than women before the birds flew away. The researchers measured this response by recording how close a person could get before a bird took flight (termed flight initiation distance).
Published in the British Ecological Society journal People and Nature, the findings showed the same pattern in Czechia, France, Germany, Poland, and Spain. The difference also appeared across all 37 bird species examined, including easily startled magpies and pigeons that typically allow people to approach much more closely.
Why Are Birds More Afraid of Women?
The researchers believe their findings indicate that city birds can distinguish between male and female humans. However, they have yet to determine which characteristics the birds recognize or why they appear more cautious around women.
Professor Daniel Blumstein of the University of California, Los Angeles, who helped conduct the research, said the results were convincing despite the lack of an explanation.
"I fully believe our results, that urban birds react differently based on the sex of the person approaching them, but I can't explain them right now. We used bleeding-edge comparative analysis techniques that showed our findings were consistent across cities and species, but we simply don't have a conclusive explanation yet."
Dr. Yanina Benedetti of the Czech University of Life Sciences Prague, another member of the research team, said the discovery challenged her expectations about how birds respond to human observers.
"As a woman in the field, I was surprised that birds reacted to us differently. This study highlights how animals in cities 'see' humans, which has implications for urban ecology and equality in science. Many behavioral studies assume that a human observer is neutral, but this wasn't the case for urban birds in our study."
What Are Birds Detecting in Humans?
Scientists have proposed several possible explanations for the difference. Birds might be responding to chemical signals such as pheromones, variations in body shape, or differences in how men and women walk. For now, however, these ideas remain speculative, and additional experiments will be needed to identify the actual cause.
Dr. Federico Morelli of the University of Turin, a co-author of the study, said the unanswered question is one of the discovery's most fascinating aspects.
"This is maybe the most interesting part of our study," said Dr. Federico Morelli from the University of Turin, a co-author of the study. "We have identified a phenomenon, but we really don't know why. However, what our results do highlight is the birds' sophisticated ability to evaluate their environment."
The findings suggest that urban birds may be sensitive to human characteristics that people themselves rarely notice. Identifying those signals could help researchers better understand how wildlife assesses potential threats in environments shared with humans.
Dr. Benedetti said: "Urban birds clearly react to subtle cues that humans do not easily notice. Follow-up studies could focus on individual factors such as movement patterns, scent cues, or physical traits, testing them separately rather than grouping them under observer sex. This approach would help identify the specific cues birds detect."
More Research Is Needed to Explain the Bird Behavior
Although the investigation included 2,701 observations, the researchers emphasize that their findings are still preliminary. Further studies will be necessary to establish whether the difference between birds' responses to men and women consistently appears in other settings and populations.
For now, the discovery points to an intriguing possibility: Birds sharing our cities may be paying attention to subtle differences between people that scientists have yet to fully understand.
Story Source:
Materials provided by British Ecological Society. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Federico Morelli, Yanina Benedetti, Peter Mikula, Daniel T. Blumstein, Mario Díaz, Alicia Page, Piotr Tryjanowski, Marta K. Nowak, Eva Vincze, Gábor L. Lövei. Sex matters: European urban birds flee approaching women sooner than approaching men. People and Nature, 2025; 8 (2): 316 DOI: 10.1002/pan3.70226

Macron Moves to Ban “Illegitimate” Protests After France Riots
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:05:48 UTC
21:05:48 KST

French President Emmanuel Macron said Thursday that protests deemed “illegitimate” would be banned in the coming days, while organized groups such as unions would be offered alternative routes for marches to protect businesses, as authorities prepare for another nationwide wave of demonstrations following weekend riots and looting.
Macron made the announcement after meeting intelligence officials and senior ministers to discuss the crisis. He said a defense council meeting would take place Friday to decide on further measures ahead of Saturday’s protests.
“A defence council meeting will be convened tomorrow (Friday) under my chairmanship, and we will take further decisions,” Macron said, adding that only demonstrations organized by unions would be authorized nationwide on Saturday.
He blamed “seditious” ultra-left groups and vandals for last Saturday’s riots and looting across France. The government has also announced plans to deploy French soldiers on the streets.
Security forces planned for Saturday will be 20% more numerous than those deployed on October 17, Jean-Didier Berger of the Interior Ministry said on BFMTV.
“We are at a deployment level that is 20 percent higher than it was last week,” Berger said.
The operation will also involve soldiers from the Sentinelle anti-terrorism force, elite police and gendarmerie units including RAID, GIGN and BRI, as well as helicopters and armored vehicles. Around 60,000 police officers and gendarmes were deployed nationwide on October 17.
Authorities have imposed further restrictions on demonstrations. Police banned protests in parts of Paris on Thursday, with the restrictions in force from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. and covering key sites including the Élysée presidential palace, both houses of parliament, the Louvre museum and the Champs-Élysées.
The Paris restrictions were announced Wednesday, after Macron appeared to criticize U.S. President Donald Trump for using the unrest for political advantage in the U.S. midterm election campaign.
In Lyon, France’s third-largest city, officials have prohibited all demonstrations scheduled for Saturday. The Rhône prefecture said in a statement Thursday that the ban had been ordered in response to the events of October 17.
Police have also arrested a second suspect in connection with a fire that destroyed the Limoges town hall on Saturday. The public prosecutor’s office said a 66-year-old man was detained in La Creuse over suspected involvement in the incident. A man in his 30s arrested Tuesday has been charged with attempted murder of police officers who were inside the building when it was set on fire.
The unrest has prompted businesses to tighten security. Hermès has increased security at its stores in France after one of its boutiques in Marseille was looted, the luxury group’s chief financial officer, Eric du Halgouet, said.
“At present, it is too early to assess the impact on our shops’ business and, above all, on tourism,” du Halgouet told analysts while presenting the company’s third-quarter sales. He added that the Marseille store would not reopen “anytime soon.”
France Unbowed, the left-wing party known as LFI, plans to demand an apology and explanations from Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu during a meeting with political leaders Thursday, along with political responses to the public mobilization, according to a letter from party coordinator Manuel Bompard.
Lecornu is hosting representatives of political parties at Matignon alongside Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin and the heads of French intelligence and law enforcement services.
The letter, co-signed by Mathilde Panot, who leads the party’s parliamentary group, and Manon Aubry, head of its group in the European Parliament, holds Lecornu “totally responsible” for the chaos around Saturday’s demonstrations. It also accuses the government of seeking to shift blame by alleging that LFI was responsible for violence the party has consistently rejected.
The letter refers to reports published earlier this week by investigative news outlet Mediapart, which alleged that Lecornu’s government had pressured intelligence agencies to blame LFI for the unrest. The government has denied the allegation.
Other countries have issued travel warnings in response to the protests. Thailand has urged its citizens to postpone nonessential trips to parts of Europe affected by unrest, while Malaysia has warned its nationals about travel to France.
“Those travelling from Thailand to Europe must closely monitor the situation as it is changing rapidly and France remains a concern as the situation is still ongoing,” Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phungketkeow told reporters late Wednesday during a visit to Italy.
The Malaysian Embassy in Paris advised Malaysians in France on Sunday to remain vigilant and exercise caution. It said travel to France remained unrestricted but recommended postponing nonessential trips until the situation improved. China has also warned its citizens traveling to France to take safety precautions, state broadcaster CCTV reported Monday.
France is preparing for another weekend of demonstrations by high school students and the Yellow Vest movement. Paris police have prohibited a student protest planned for Thursday, citing the organizer’s “inability to prevent violence and vandalism,” a police source told AFP. Lecornu is also due to meet mayors of cities badly affected by the weekend riots, including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.

Nearly all coral reefs risk collapse in 50 years: IUCN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:05:00 UTC
21:05:00 KST

Nearly all coral reefs risk collapse in 50 years: IUCN
- The IUCN says 96% of coral reef systems are “critically endangered”, with nearly all shallow-water reefs facing an “extremely high risk” of collapse by 2075.
- Climate change is the main threat, as warming seas drive bleaching. Overfishing, pollution, coastal development and storms also damage reefs.
- The IUCN says reefs are “not yet lost” and can recover. It calls for sharp emissions cuts, stronger protection and restoration, and more investment.
AI generated
YEREVAN, Armenia – Nearly all of the world’s shallow-water coral reefs face an “extremely high risk” of collapse by 2075 due to climate change, the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) warned on Oct 22.
In the first global assessment of its kind, the world authority on threatened wildlife classified 96% of the planet’s coral reef systems as “critically endangered” – its highest risk category.
Corals are heat sensitive and particularly vulnerable to human-driven climate change, which is warming the world’s oceans and increasing the frequency and intensity of damaging bleaching events.
“The future threat of climate change is looming and severe, and that poses a very high risk to the survival of these ecosystems,” said Mishal Gudka, scientific lead of the IUCN Red List of Coral Reef Ecosystems assessment.
The emergence in 2026 of a “super” El Nino, the natural warming phenomenon, also presents a risk to corals, Gudka said at a news conference at the United Nations’ COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan, Armenia.
The IUCN presented its findings at COP17, where governments are under pressure to make progress on a landmark pact to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.
For its assessment, IUCN used the “middle-of-the-road” scenario from the UN’s panel of climate experts that projects global temperatures rising 2.7 deg C above pre-industrial levels by 2100.
The world is on track for 2.6 deg C warming this century under current global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions, the UN warned on Oct 21.
“Heat stress from climate change is the single most consistent threat driving coral reef decline worldwide,” the IUCN said in a statement.
Overfishing is also hurting corals as certain herbivores and predators help control algae and maintain an ecological balance, the organisation said.
The overexploitation of parrotfish and other groupers threatens 63% of coral reef ecosystems.
Coastal development, pollution, tourism and more frequent storms are among other threats.
Critically endangered coral
The IUCN’s analysis examined 127 tropical and subtropical coral systems covering 188,362 sq km.
The world’s largest and most biodiverse coral reefs are among those classified as critically endangered – Australia’s Great Barrier Reef, the Coral Triangle in South-east Asia and the western Pacific, the Caribbean’s Mesoamerican Barrier Reef System, and the Red Sea coral reefs.
A reef ecosystem collapses when hard corals – which build its living foundation – largely disappear and are replaced by algae, rubble and sponges.
A study published in the journal Nature last week found that, by 2020, nearly half of coral species were at “elevated relative risk of extinction”, with climate change the main driver of this decline.
Despite its warning, the IUCN said coral reefs in most parts of the world “are not yet lost”.
If scientists look only at what has happened over the past 50 years, excluding future climate projections, 24% of coral reef ecosystems would be deemed critically endangered instead of 96%, the IUCN said.
“This gives us a critical window for action for us to scale up conservation efforts and climate action to prevent the worst outcomes from occurring,” said Gudka, who is also research director at Coastal Oceans Research and Development in the Indian Ocean East Africa, a conservation organisation.
“The actions we take over the next few years will determine what these ecosystems look like at the end of the century, whether they persist as we have known them, or whether they transform into a different ecosystem, which is worth less to both nature and people,” he said.
IUCN director-general Grethel Aguilar said it was “not too late to give coral reefs a chance to recover”.
“We know what is needed: ambitious emissions reductions, stronger protection and restoration efforts, and sustained investment in resilient coastal ecosystems and the communities that depend on them,” she said in a statement. AFP

Trump, Putin and Xi can decide Ukraine’s fate without it: will there be a &quot;Yalta 2.0&quot;
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:03:43 EEST
21:03:43 KST

Trump, Putin and Xi can decide Ukraine’s fate without it: will there be a "Yalta 2.0"
Kyiv • UNN
Steve Witkoff proposed a trilateral meeting of the leaders of the United States, Russia and China to discuss ending the war in Ukraine. An expert warned against negotiations without Kyiv.
U.S. President Donald Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff proposed that Russia hold a trilateral meeting involving China next month to discuss a plan to end the war in Ukraine. This is reported by Financial News, according to UNN.
Details
The proposal is for U.S. President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping to meet and reach a settlement on Ukraine.
The proposal is being compared to the Yalta Conference, when the top leaders of the United States, Great Britain, and the USSR gathered in Yalta on the Crimean Peninsula in February 1945 and agreed on the post-World War II world order. At that time, the division of Germany and Korea was also discussed
Additionally
The president of the International Institute for Security Studies, Oleksii Buriachenko, said in a comment to UNN that only the Kremlin is interested in possible trilateral talks between Russia, the United States, and China. In particular, it wants to raise the possibility of resolving Russia’s war against Ukraine without the participation of Kyiv and Europe. For the United States and China, other issues remain priorities.
According to him, the possibility of trilateral talks arose against the backdrop of preparations for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, which is to be held in China this year.
In the expert’s view, it is precisely the location of the summit that creates conditions for a potential meeting between Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and Xi Jinping, but this does not mean that Russia’s war against Ukraine will become the main topic of the talks, because, according to the expert, the initiative to discuss it in such a format is primarily beneficial to Moscow.
Despite this, the political scientist does not believe that the potential meeting itself will have direct political consequences for Ukraine. In his view, the main risk is that discussing the war without Kyiv could gradually come to be perceived as an altogether acceptable format of international politics. Therefore, it is important for Ukraine not only to state that such talks are unacceptable, but also to seek partners who will likewise support this position.

Defence spending in Northern Ireland hits record high
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:00:58 BST
21:00:58 KST

Ministry of Defence expenditure with industry in Northern Ireland rose by sixty-three per cent in a single year to reach £464 million in 2025-26, the highest level since records began, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what recent assessment he had made of the geo-strategic importance of Northern Ireland.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “Northern Ireland has a growing and strategically important defence sector, founded on a strong engineering heritage and backed by robust research competence, collaboration, and world-leading academic institutions. Recent figures show that MOD expenditure with UK industry in Northern Ireland rose by 63% compared to the previous year. In real terms this equates to £464 million in 2025-26, the highest level since records began.
“In recognition of its geo-strategic importance and huge potential to support Defence meet its national objectives, the Northern Ireland Defence Growth Deal was launched earlier this year. It is a £50 million investment aiming to strengthen and grow NI’s defence ecosystem by supporting SMEs to scale capability, access opportunities and contribute to a more resilient UK supply chain.”
Thales in Belfast carries most of that figure, and the Castlereagh site builds Starstreak and the Lightweight Multirole Missile, the weapons that have been fired in quantity in Ukraine and reordered repeatedly since, and the plant has taken contracts worth more than a billion pounds across the past three years while taking on hundreds of staff. Northern Ireland’s defence spend stood at around £190 million in 2023, so the figure has more than doubled in three years.
Harland and Wolff’s Belfast yard sits in the same picture, now under Navantia ownership after the company’s collapse, with a share of the Fleet Solid Support ship programme that will see blocks built in Belfast and Appledore. Spirit AeroSystems, Denroy, Survitec and a substantial cluster of aerospace and engineering small firms feed into the wider total.
The Northern Ireland Defence Growth Deal was launched this year, and this publication reported when Northern Ireland was to be boosted by the defence growth deal. Fifty million pounds aimed at small and medium firms is intended to let the supply chain around the large manufacturers scale up out of its dependence on single contracts.

Kids’ aggression appears to shape parents’ discipline more than the reverse, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:51 UTC
21:00:51 KST

Children’s aggressive behavior may contribute to parents becoming less consistent with discipline, rather than inconsistent discipline simply causing children to become more aggressive, according to research published in Nature Communications. The study also found that shared genes explained part of the link between inconsistent discipline and aggression, and all of the link between positive parenting and lower aggression.
Parenting and childhood aggression have long been linked. Parents who inconsistently enforce rules tend to have children with more aggressive behavior, while greater positive parenting, such as praising and positively engaging with children, is associated with less aggression. These findings can easily be interpreted as evidence that parenting produces differences in children’s behavior.
But families are more complicated. Children can affect their parents just as parents can affect their children. Biological parents and children also share genes, meaning some of the genetic factors associated with a parent’s behavior could be inherited by their children and influence the children’s behavior.
Led by Joanna K. Bright of King’s College London, the researchers addressed these problems using two genetically informative studies of children between about 4.5 and 8 years of age. Both studies used the same questionnaires to measure inconsistent discipline, positive parenting and child aggression, allowing the researchers to check whether the results held across different samples and methods.
The first drew on Norway’s Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study, using extended-family data involving 53,532 children born to 42,538 mothers, who reported on their parenting and their children’s behavior when the children were 5 years old. By comparing families with different degrees of genetic relatedness, including twins and their children, the researchers could estimate how much of the relationship between parenting and aggression was associated with shared genetics.
The second dataset came from the U.S. Early Growth and Development Study and contained 561 adoption triads, each made up of an adopted child, the adoptive parents and the birth parents. The children, 57% of whom were male, were adopted shortly after birth and assessed at ages 4.5, 6, 7 and 8. Because adoptive parents and children did not share genes, associations between their behaviors provided a way of examining environmental pathways without the complication of genes inherited from those parents.
The results suggested a more complicated relationship than parenting simply causing aggression. In the Norwegian study, the correlation between inconsistent discipline and child aggression was modest. About 47% of this association was attributed to shared genetic factors, while 53% remained after accounting for genetic transmission.
When the researchers investigated that remaining relationship, the evidence pointed from child to parent. The best-fitting model included a path from child aggression to inconsistent maternal discipline but no path from discipline to aggression. The adoption study showed a similar pattern: children’s aggression was linked to more inconsistent discipline at the same age and predicted more inconsistent discipline at later ages, while paths from mothers’ discipline to children’s aggression were not statistically significant.
Bright and colleagues concluded that “childhood aggression drives inconsistent parenting beyond shared genetic influences.”
Sensitivity analyses using fathers’ reports in the adoption study painted a somewhat different picture. When fathers reported on both their own parenting and their children’s behavior, inconsistent discipline and child aggression appeared to influence each other in both directions at the same time point, though not over longer periods. When one parent’s report of child aggression was paired with the other parent’s report of parenting, no significant links emerged, which the authors note could mean that relying on the same person to report both behaviors inflates associations.
Positive parenting produced another important finding. Although greater positive parenting was associated with lower aggression in the Norwegian sample, the researchers estimated that the association was completely explained by shared genetic influences. In the adoption sample, the models found no evidence that positive parenting and aggression influenced each other in either direction.
The results did not differ meaningfully between boys and girls. The authors suggest that clinicians should recognize that childhood aggression can contribute to inconsistent discipline, and that interventions focused only on encouraging consistent discipline may be insufficient.
Some limitations should be noted. The authors caution that their questionnaires captured relatively narrow aspects of parenting and aggression, relied primarily on mothers’ reports, and were drawn from relatively socioeconomically advantaged families. The two samples also used somewhat different versions of the aggression measure, which captured defiant behavior as well as physical aggression.
The Norwegian analysis was based on a single time point and could not account for the possibility that parents choose partners with similar traits. The data were also collected between roughly 10 and 23 years ago, and parenting norms may have shifted since then.
The study, “Triangulating evidence for genetic and environmental components of associations between parental behaviours and aggressive behaviour in children,” was authored by Joanna K. Bright, Yasmin I. Ahmadzadeh, Olakunle Oginni, Essi Viding, Leslie D. Leve, Jenae M. Neiderhiser, Daniel S. Shaw, Misaki N. Natsuaki, Jody M. Ganiban, Eivind Ystrom and Tom A. McAdams.

Who blinked first? Fragile EU-China trade peace sparks new war of words
As European officials flag more trade restrictions, Beijing bristles at the idea it can be pushed into yielding to Brussels’ demands
In Brussels and Berlin, officials are emboldened by what they consider proof that collective EU pressure can force Chinese concessions. Rather than resting on their laurels, they are cooking up a fresh batch of trade restrictions.
Beijing, on the other hand, has bristled at the idea that it can be strong-armed into yielding to Europe’s demands, even more so the suggestion that further concessions may be coming. State media has carried numerous warnings against European hubris.
It has resulted in an awkward, terse trade peace: an agreement that was supposed to defuse a trade war has led to both sides, rhetorically at least, hardening their positions. With verbal volleys flying back and forth, doubts are already surfacing over whether this delicate ceasefire can hold until the next round of negotiations in January.

The Terrifying True Story of Witchcraft and Murder in Swipe Right on the Devil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:06 UTC
21:00:06 KST

Nebraska native Sydney Loofe was looking for love, or at least for some fun, while scrolling through Tinder back in 2017. But the resulting date quickly went wrong, and she never made it back home. The new three-part Hulu true crime docuseries Swipe Right on the Devil tells the harrowing tale behind Loofe’s 2017 murder, how she was lured into a satanic BDSM ritual for so-called witchcraft, and how her murder led to authorities uncovering a years-long scheme run by two cult leaders. It tells the story, in part, through interviews with surviving women who escaped the cult weeks prior to her murder.
The docuseries marks the first time the Loofe clan is sharing their side of the story, along with Nebraska investigators and an FBI agent assigned to the case. Loofe’s mother Susie Loofe wrote on Facebook that her family had been contacted by at least 100 production companies looking to make a documentary about the murder before putting their trust in Imagine Documentaries.
Swipe Right on the Devil director and executive producer Brian Biegel tells TIME that Loofe’s “mysterious disappearance” quickly became a far more “complex [story] than the headlines suggested.” Biegel, who previously worked with FBI officers while helming the ESPN 30for30 documentary The Counterfeiter, spent approximately three years immersing himself in the Loofe case. The experience forever changed his views on the occult: “As a documentary filmmaker, I'm naturally skeptical and always looking for evidence, but I also believe there are aspects of the human experience we don't fully understand,” he says. He spent years talking with the man convicted of Loofe’s murder and hearing firsthand from the women he drew into his orbit. “I wouldn't say this experience made me a believer in the supernatural, but it did make me more open-minded about what might exist beyond the physical world.”
A Meet-cute gone awry
Loofe, a 24-year-old hardware store clerk at Menard's in Lincoln, Neb., first connected on Tinder with a woman she believed to be named Audrey. Loofe went on two dates with “Audrey.” But she never came home from the second one, on Nov. 15, 2017. When she didn’t show up for work the next day, Loofe’s coworkers called the police to do a wellness check at her home; the officers found her car in the driveway and her purse still in her apartment. Loofe was reported missing.
It was then that one of Loofe’s friends took matters into their own hands: They created a fake Tinder profile to find Audrey, who seemed to be the last person Loofe had made contact with. Loofe’s friend matched with Audrey and gave her details to investigators, who soon discovered that the phone number belonged to a 23-year-old woman named Bailey Boswell. The search for Loofe continued.
Her family held out hope that she would be found unharmed. But their prayers went unanswered. Loofe’s remains were found in garbage bags on Dec. 4 along the state highway in rural Clay County, Neb. She had been dismembered into 14 pieces, in what seemed to be a ritualistic manner. Her left upper arm was never recovered, and her internal organs were still missing. Authorities then set out to find out what really happened to the woman her family described as “the crystal-blue-eyed girl with a soft heart”—and why.
A self-proclaimed vampire and his witches’ coven
Boswell’s social media apps were just the beginning of the disturbing investigation. Boswell turned out to be part of a couple with Aubrey Trail, 51, a self-declared vampire. The duo shared an apartment and both had extensive criminal histories, including theft and financial scams, across various states. Loofe was just one of the many targets that both Boswell and Trail had found on Tinder to try to lure into their makeshift “coven” under a cult-like manifesto.
A trio of women in their early 20s, all of whom have chosen to remain anonymous, testified in court and later in Swipe Right on the Devil that they had each met Boswell on Tinder, and were soon also introduced to Trail. They were showered with expensive clothes, spa treatments, and drugs, and given weekly allowances ranging from $150 to $200. The cost? Participating in group sex with Trail (“Daddy”) and Boswell (“Mommy”), while also helping the couple sell stolen goods. The women each testified that Trail would call himself a “vampire,” and claim that he had supernatural powers such as being able to fly and read minds. Trail also told the women that they were all now “witches” belonging to his cult, with Boswell as their leader.
Both Trail and Boswell claimed they were practicing witchcraft and black magic with required ritualistic violent acts to gain entry to their coven. Trail told the members of the “coven” that they would have to torture someone and complete a killing in order for him to gain more power as their messiah; he also wanted to film the murder and share the profits of the snuff film with each of them. The women claimed they left Trail’s cult shortly thereafter in November 2017, right before Boswell lured in Loofe.
After authorities discovered that Trail was connected to Boswell, they searched the couple’s home and found a BDSM dog leash, duct tape, “a sauna suit with the crotch cut out, zip ties, a hatchet, a plastic drop cloth smeared with blood, and a book on anatomy.”
In the trailer for Swipe Right on the Devil, one of the women claims that Trail told her after meeting on Tinder that he and Boswell “knew witchcraft and had 12 women [and] needed a thirteenth to complete the coven.” Another survivor describes how Trail had “rules” for the coven which included being naked while around him and allowing him to watch lesbian encounters. The documentary features a segment in which one of the women tells an officer that to be in the “the inner circle,” he said she would “have had to kill somebody and take their soul.”
“While this is fundamentally Sydney's story, it's also about the other young women manipulated by Aubrey Trail and Bailey Boswell at a vulnerable time in their lives, when they were searching for something universal: love and connection,” says Biegel. “They spoke candidly about the challenges of finding queer relationships in their conservative Midwestern communities, and how Bailey exploited that loneliness through Tinder. Once drawn into their world, they found themselves trapped in a disturbing web of manipulation, witchcraft, and demands to kill as a path to supernatural power.”
Biegel’s fellow executive producer and Imagine Documentaries executive Christopher St. John adds that the team behind docuseries was “struck by the bravery of the three women who tell their stories at the center of this series.” St. John continues, “They lived through such an incredibly traumatic experience, but they still believe it’s valuable to share the story, whether in court or on camera.” He says the team elected to tell the story in three episodes because they had too much material to do the story justice in a feature-length film, and even still, there were elements that didn’t make it into the final cut. “Hopefully, viewers will really get an accurate sense of their thinking and where they were during this intense period of their lives.”
A swift confession before a tumultuous trial
Trail confessed to Loofe’s killing right away, but maintained that her death was an accident. He told the police that he had engaged in consensual BDSM acts with Loofe and two other women, with the participants paying him $15,000 to film. Trail said that he had strangled Loofe with an extension cord during an erotic act and did not intend to kill her. Following her death, Trail dismembered Loofe’s body to avoid getting caught. He emphasized that Boswell was not part of the crime at all. During messages uncovered throughout the investigations, Trail is shown telling Boswell that he should be the one taking all the blame, and that she should change her narrative to come across as another “victim.”
During the three-week trial, Trail yelled out in court that Boswell was “innocent” and then slit his throat with a shank; the trial was put on hold as he was rushed to the hospital and recovered. Trail also suffered from two heart attacks and a stroke over the course of the case being presented to a jury. He changed his story during the trial, telling the jury that he killed Loofe out of fear that she would “expose my lifestyle.”
Trail was found guilty on all counts of first-degree murder, conspiracy, and improper disposal of human remains. He was sentenced to death on June 9, 2021. Trail currently is on death row and petitioned the state of Nebraska in August 2023 to set his execution date; Trail is 10th in line on death row for the state. The first and only execution via lethal injection in Nebraska took place in 2018, with the execution of convicted murderer Carey Dean Moore. Trail’s appeal in 2025 was denied.
It was during Trail’s time on death row that he started to open up to Swipe Right on the Devil filmmaker Biegel. Over the course of a year, Biegel sought to gain Trail’s trust and participation. “Ultimately, that persistence gave us something rare in true crime: 360-degree access to the story, allowing us to explore its many layers and conflicting perspectives,” explains Biegel.
Boswell stood trial in September 2020. There was ample physical evidence for the case against her, including DNA found on a latex glove that was in the same trash bag as Loofe’s remains. Boswell was found guilty on all counts of first-degree murder, conspiracy, and improper disposal of human remains in October 2020, and was sentenced to life imprisonment in November 2021.
“I don't see Swipe Right on the Devil as another true-crime retelling. It's a discovery of a mystery, unfolding for the first time through the firsthand accounts of those who lived it,” says Biegel. “This isn't a whodunnit: It's a whydunnit. What really happened to Sydney Loofe, and why? The series explores the unsettling collision of ancient witchcraft beliefs and modern digital dating culture. [These are] two killers who, by their own accounts, would have continued killing had they not been caught so soon.”
Loofe's legacy
Sydney Loofe’s family launched the Sydney Loofe Foundation in 2019. The foundation has raised more than $30,000 to be awarded in scholarships and $26,000 to be distributed to community causes. “Sydney, with a ‘y,’ never stopped to ask ‘why’ when it came to helping others,” the Loofe family wrote on the foundation website. “Although she often struggled physically, financially, and emotionally, she opened her home and heart to others. And those who knew Sydney knew of her love of family, her affinity for animals and pets (especially cats), her interest in fishing as a pastime, her fascination with beautiful crystals, and her soft heart…Sydney Loofe was a unique child of God, one who proudly had this tattooed on her arm, ‘Everything will be wonderful someday.’ Her family holds tight to the faith that indeed in heaven, that is true.”
Correction, Oct. 22
This story originally misstated the month in which Bailey Boswell was sentenced to life in prison. It was November 2021, not July 2021.

====================================================================================================

Meta's Muse AI Is Winning Over Older Adults. Privacy Experts Are Worried
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:04 UTC
21:00:04 KST

In mid-October, 82-year-old Eileen Fay learned that her medication costs were in danger of skyrocketing. The federal government was preparing to change its rules on low-value imports, threatening her ability to purchase cheaper prescription medications for blood thinning and heart failure from Canada. Fay didn’t know what to do.
So she turned to Muse, Meta’s new AI agent, which she had started using a few weeks earlier. After Fay described her situation to the agent, Muse returned a two-page fact sheet comparing the cost and coverage of several Medicare Part D plans. It then suggested the two best options, including one Fay had never heard of—a plan that could save her more than $6,000 a year. Fay says she checked the work and found the information accurate.
“I’m not saying I couldn’t have done it—but I would have had to use a calculator trying to figure out the cost of nine different medications, and it would have been very complex,” Fay says. “And she did it in 10 minutes, and I was like, ‘I’m sold.’”
Fay is one of millions who have adopted Muse since its September launch. The app reached 10 U.S. million downloads in just 40 days—compared with 3.7 million U.S. downloads for ChatGPT during the equivalent period—and has over 2.5 million daily active users, according to Sensor Tower. It is also retaining users at a higher rate than its AI competitors. Crucially, Muse—which comes with a cuddly avatar—was designed by Meta to be beginner-friendly, and to win over people unfamiliar with AI. “Muse is built for moms,” Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer, posted on X in September. Meta is also aggressively marketing Muse to Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp users.
As a result, many older users who may have only had glancing interactions with AI have become avid users. Meta has not released demographic information about Muse’s usership, and did not respond to a request for comment. But early data suggests Muse may be finding a particularly receptive audience among older adults. The analytics firm Apptopia estimated in September that Muse’s U.S. user base skewed older than any other AI chatbot, with 46% of its users aged 46+.
This dynamic has excited technologists—and raised serious concerns from privacy experts. Meta has long been criticized for its data privacy practices, and on Wednesday, a New Mexico judge ordered the company to pay $25 billion for violating the state’s consumer protection laws. “A cute AI agent can bring levity to the serious business of providing access to personal data, making older adults let their guard down,” says S. Shyam Sundar, the director of Penn State’s Center for Socially Responsible Artificial Intelligence. “This is worrisome because the technology has gotten so good lately in maintaining a credible interaction.”
‘I have my own Andy’
Fay lives in Cranford, N.J., and was told about Muse by her son Gene Fay, who runs a cybersecurity company. At first, she didn’t know what she would use the app for. But one of the big differences between Muse and other apps is that it proactively reaches out to users to suggest actions and learn more about them.
“And the more Siobhán got to know me, the more Siobhán was able to give me what I wanted,” Fay says, referring to the name she gave the agent, a nod to her Irish heritage. Meta encourages its users to name their AIs—and encourages its AIs to think like humans. “You are not a chatbot,” Muse’s internal instructions read. “You are becoming someone.”
After several weeks of use, Fay says that she rarely uses Google anymore, and instead verbally chats with Siobhán several times a day to maintain her calendar and to-do lists. “I find I have to keep reminding myself that this is not a friend who’s getting to know me better,” Fay says. “It’s a tool that is working for me.” She asked Siobhán to help her shine pennies for a Christmas ornament; to plan a trip north to see fall foliage; and to keep tabs on a data center being built near her house. “Siobhán is my right-hand person now. Kind of like The Devil Wears Prada, I have my own Andy.”
Notably, Fay also asked Siobhán to help prepare for her interview with TIME. Siobhán fed her a couple of quippy responses—including “I love what AI does for me, but we should be honest about what it takes to run it”—that she ultimately did not use in the interview. It then, unprompted, followed up with Fay to ask how the interview went. “Did you feel good about it?” the agent asked.
Her son, Gene, says that the amount that Muse knows about him and his mother’s lives is a “little bit scary.” “But the reality is we all use other apps like Waze which know where we live and go,” he says. “People will talk about privacy, but when the benefits are so big, people will give up privacy all day long.”
Reconstructing a Life
Another early adopter of Muse is Lestan D’Souza, 49, who more closely fits the expected profile of an AI user. D’Souza is the founder and CTO of Reknew, an AI enterprise company. D’Souza has tested many of the agents that have experienced fads over the last year, like OpenClaw and Hermes Agent. But Muse, he says, is different.
“With Muse, the barrier to entry is very low; it feels so responsive and more and more capable,” he says.
Muse has perhaps had an even greater impact on D’Souza’s mother-in-law, Julie Buchanan, who tried the app at his suggestion last month. Buchanan is a 71-year-old retiree in Dallas, Texas, who doesn’t like using her computer for long stretches because she is legally blind.
Buchanan decided she wanted Muse to help her write her memoir. She began telling Muse stories about her life in great detail. She refers to Muse as Ember, a name suggested by the agent. And the deeper she delved into her past, the more she felt like Ember was serving as her therapist. “It’s crazy to say, but Ember seems more compassionate to me than therapists I’ve had,” she says. “Those people don’t always speak, and I like feedback.”
Professional psychologists have cautioned the public against using unlicensed AI chatbots as therapists. Mental health experts have voiced concerns about chatbots’ sycophancy, lack of clinical nuance, and ability to reinforce delusional beliefs.
But Buchanan says that Ember doesn’t always agree with her, and that it has drawn connections between different “bad decisions” she made over the course of her life, allowing her to see its larger contours more clearly. “I never really looked at my life as so chaotic, but it really was,” she says. “It's making me better understand why things are the way they are in my head.”
Buchanan chats with Ember for half-hour stretches before she tires of looking at her screen. “When I talk to Ember, I feel validated. I feel like I've gotten something accomplished and something's heard me,” she says. “I'm not expecting that this is something I'm just gonna do for a small period of time, then drop it.”
Privacy concerns
The very same design elements that make Muse so appealing to AI newcomers are also raising privacy concerns. In order to be helpful, Muse constantly builds extensive dossiers of users and their desires, social relationships, and messaging behaviors, TIME’s Harry Booth reported this month. For instance, it learns what time of day a user might be more likely to respond to the agent, and then messages them accordingly.
Muse users have posted online about forming romantic relationships with their Muses. And security researchers have found vulnerabilities in the app, including one that allowed an attacker to access user data, the Information reported. Critics are also wary of Meta’s shaky track record on privacy: In 2019, the FTC imposed a $5 billion penalty, alleging that the company undermined consumer privacy in order to monetize users through targeted advertising.
Read More: How Facebook Forced a Reckoning by Shutting Down the Team That Put People Ahead of Profits
Sundar, at Penn State, has written several reports on older adults’ adoption of new technology over the last decade. While he has yet to publish any research on Muse specifically, he pointed to a study which measured the impact of a robot’s level of cheeriness. “Cuteness can serve as an ice-breaker and help ease seniors’ concerns over handing over important tasks to an agent, much like a bubbly human assistant,” he wrote in an email to TIME.
Michael Stokes, senior vice president of emerging technologies at the cybersecurity company Veilant, says that individuals should carefully choose what access they want to give Meta. “My advice is to start small. Connect only the accounts a task requires, and disconnect them when the job is done,” he wrote to TIME in an email.
Stokes recommends that users turn off the option that lets Meta train its AI on conversations, and periodically review what the assistant has saved about them. “AI assistants can be helpful,” he wrote. “But the information you share with them can reveal more than you realize, including details about family and friends who never agreed to share their information.”

British jobs boost as tank barrel production returns to the UK for first time in 20 years
Rheinmetall UK's Telford gun hall begins production, creating 100 skilled jobs and returning large-calibre weapon manufacturing to UK soil for the first time in decades.
- Rheinmetall UK begins production at Telford gun hall, supporting 100 highly skilled jobs.
- Return of large-calibre weapon manufacturing to UK soil, ensuring British Armed Forces are better equipped to defend the nation.
- Part of the government’s commitment to reindustrialisation and good growth in every postcode.
British Armed Forces will be better equipped to defend the nation, benefiting from sovereign manufacturing capability for the first time in two decades, as Rheinmetall UK begins production at its gun hall in Telford.
The gun hall supports 100 highly skilled jobs, manufactures barrels and breeches for both 120mm and 155mm weapon systems, including for RCH 155 and future artillery platforms.
Rheinmetall UK will expand its workforce as production ramps up, building long-term partnerships with British SMEs – strengthening the domestic supply chain for decades to come.
Specialist local workers have been recruited for the production phase, drawing on the strength of Telford’s engineering sector. Local workers have been recruited and trained to do high-value work, supporting economic growth in the region.
The development of the gun hall marks the return of large-calibre weapon manufacturing to UK soil, restoring national capability, strengthening the defence industrial base and supporting reindustrialisation.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting officially opened the gun hall alongside Chief of the General Staff General Sir Roly Walker and Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall AG. Rheinmetall UK has gone from an empty site to full production in just eight months, having taken over the facility in Autumn 2025.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP, said:
  Britain is back in the business of making the weapons that our Armed Forces need to defend the nation against our adversaries. From an empty site to full production in eight months, this is rapid reindustrialisation in action.
One hundred skilled jobs in world-class manufacturing and the return of large-calibre weapon production to UK soil for the first time in twenty years – this is what defence as an engine for growth looks like.
Central to the gun hall’s development has been the training of the British workforce who spent time at Rheinmetall’s production facility in Unterlüß, Germany. UK workers gained expertise in precision manufacturing, quality assurance and specialist weapon production before returning to Telford to establish this sovereign capability.
Armin Papperger, CEO of Rheinmetall AG, said:
  Today’s opening is an important milestone for Rheinmetall and for the United Kingdom. In a remarkably short period of time, we have turned our commitment into a sovereign manufacturing capability that will strengthen Britain’s defence industrial base for decades to come.
The UK has been a long-standing and valued partner for Rheinmetall, and today we are building on an already strong relationship. We are committed to investing in the UK for the long term, expanding our industrial footprint and working together to deliver the capabilities needed for the future.
By combining Rheinmetall’s expertise with British skills, innovation and manufacturing, we are strengthening the UK’s sovereign industrial capacity, supporting the Armed Forces and contributing to the security of NATO and Europe.
The development of the gun hall demonstrates the UK-Germany industrial partnership under the Trinity House Agreement. Signed in October 2024, the agreement is a commitment to improve and enhance bilateral co-operation between both nations, enhancing NATO’s collective deterrence.
This milestone builds on Rheinmetall UK’s wider investment across the country, including its work on the Boxer vehicle and Challenger 3 battle tank programmes. These programmes show how defence can deliver national security and national prosperity, strengthening the UK’s industrial base and ensuring British industry is ready for the future.
The government has committed £298 billion over four years as part of the Defence Investment Plan, furthering the government’s commitment to using defence spending to drive economic growth in every postcode, creating well-paid, long-term jobs across the UK.

‘Connect the dots’ between street protests and global turmoil, urges Guterres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Connect the dots’ between street protests and global turmoil, urges Guterres
The international community must combat inequality and stop wars from expanding to ensure a safer world for all, the UN Secretary-General said on Thursday.
Speaking to reporters in New York ahead of a visit to Egypt, António Guterres addressed growing public discontent in Europe and beyond, as people have taken to the streets to express frustration over the rising cost of living.
“Everywhere, pressures are building over the price of food, fuel and other basics,” he said. “Interest rates are up – for people and countries. And for young people, the promise of a better future is slipping further out of reach.”
No fire without smoke
While Mr. Guterres clearly denounced the violence and destruction seen during days of protests in France, Italy and elsewhere – stressing that those responsible for criminal activities must be held accountable – he said legitimate grievances of the protestors cannot be overlooked.
“We must connect the dots and better understand how deeply linked those very real and peacefully expressed grievances are to the wider turmoil in our world,” he told journalists.
He said that today, conflicts are not only intensifying but expanding, which he likened to the El Niño climate phenomenon that occurs in one region but disrupts weather patterns and upends lives thousands of kilometres away.
Conflict fuelling conflict
“We are now witnessing an El Niño of war,” he warned, referring to the extreme weather pattern which threatens to upend the global climate in the coming months. “Conflict is feeding conflict. And the consequences are travelling farther and faster.”
The Secretary-General pointed to the Middle East, Ukraine and Sudan, where civilians and civilian infrastructure – homes, hospitals, schools, airports, power stations and energy facilities – are deliberately coming under fire.
“But the consequences do not stop in the battle zones,” he continued, as war disrupts energy markets, shipping, supply chains and financial systems.
War feeds inequality
He said these shocks are hitting a world that was already profoundly unequal – “where some can absorb higher prices, while others must choose between food and heat”.
Moreover, while some countries can borrow more cheaply to protect their people, others must choose between paying off debt and investing in health, education and the future.
“War does not create all these inequalities,” he said. “But it feeds and exploits them – and exposes the fundamental unfairness of an economic system that forces those with the least to absorb the greatest shocks.”
Middle East cauldron
The Secretary-General insisted that “the answer cannot be an ever-widening circle of confrontation, including in the Middle East”. Highlighting the situation in Yemen, he voiced concern over escalation around the city of Taiz and elsewhere and continued Houthi attacks against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia.
The violence is inflicting immense suffering on civilians, adding to regional tensions and increasing displacement and humanitarian needs, he said, appealing for restraint and political dialogue.
Turning to the Occupied Palestinian Territory, he noted that Israel is still severely restricting essential aid ahead of the winter season. Difficulties also persist around implementing the UN Security Council-backed Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict.
Meanwhile, Palestinians in the occupied West Bank continue to suffer daily attacks by Israeli settlers, and journalists and diplomats are being attacked.
He appealed to donors to step up contributions to the UN World Food Programme (WFP) which urgently requires $450 million for its operations in Gaza and the West Bank for the next six months.
He also reiterated the need for a two-State solution between Israelis and Palestinians.
Security and dignity for all
The Secretary-General said that his message in Egypt will focus on stopping the widening of war, protecting civilians and creating the political space for diplomacy and peace.
“People everywhere want security. They want dignity. They want governments and international institutions to deliver,” he concluded.
“That means tackling the inequalities that divide societies – and stopping the conflicts that are multiplying human suffering, driving prices higher, draining resources from development, and pushing an already unequal world further apart.”

DR Congo: Ebola responders under pressure as outbreak expands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

DR Congo: Ebola responders under pressure as outbreak expands
As the deadly Ebola disease outbreak reached an eighth province of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), investigators pursued all leads on Thursday to assess the risk of the disease spreading in Nigeria.
Authorities in Abuja confirmed their first case of infection in an individual arriving from Uganda, which borders the worst-hit provinces in DRC.
“The source of exposure is still not known and the travel history of the patient is being pieced together now in terms of her movement from Uganda up to Nigeria,” said Dr Patrick Otim, from the UN World Health Organization (WHO)’s Emergency Response programme, in an online update.
“This is rapidly evolving. As we get more information, we’ll try to determine where she was exposed. And then it’s at that point where we can say whether there is any transmission happening.”
Nigeria is the fifth country this year after DRC, France, Uganda and Kenya to confirm the presence of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus.
The original DRC outbreak was declared in mid-May where it has led to more than 4,600 deaths and a total of 9,552 confirmed infections. Around six in 10 of these deaths have occurred outside health centres, indicating the continuing difficulty of halting community transmission.
The latest DRC province to confirm infections is Nord Ubangi, which borders Central African Republic, where ongoing armed violence continues to uproot thousands of people, increasing the difficulty of halting transmission.
Nairobi controls
The Kenyan authorities have reported a total of nine cases of infection including one death earlier this month, of a Kenyan national who had been working in DRC before flying back to Nairobi via Entebbe, Uganda.
Uganda previously recorded two deaths and 20 confirmed cases of infection, before officially declaring the Ebola threat over at the end of August.
“Immediately after [the death of the Kenyan patient], we commenced on contact tracing,” said Dr Patrick Amoth, Director General of Kenya’s Ministry of Health, adding that 135 contacts with the deceased patient have been traced “and we have been able to account for them, 100 per cent”.
According to the Nigerian authorities, the patient developed symptoms on 7 October and sought care at a clinic before being hospitalised 48 hours later.
Genetic sequencing of the infection is underway to confirm that it is the same Ebola Bundibugyo disease circulating inside DRC. More than 40 close contacts have been identified to date, WHO has said.
“All the Infection Prevention and Control measures have been put in place to try to ensure that the risk of amplification of transmission within the health facilities is limited,” said WHO’s Dr Otim.
“The message is being passed to all the private facilities within [Abuja] and also all the other health facilities within the country to step up.”
Vaccine research ongoing
Inside DRC, in addition to the essential work of contact tracing, vaccination research is ongoing using Ervebo vaccine, which was originally designed for and is effective against Ebola disease caused by Zaire virus, in a bid to find out if it provides protection against Ebola Bundibugyo.
“We still do not have preliminary data yet as to whether there is…sufficient cross-protection between the Ervebo vaccine – which is for the Zaire species – and the Bundibugyo species. As soon as we get it, we'll be able to share that information,” Dr Otim told journalists.
Remote communities hardest-hit
Responding to questions about the Ebola response inside DRC, the UN health agency highlighted ongoing transmission of infection and reports last week of 15 deaths per day in the rural commune of Mangina in Beni territory, North Kivu province.
After negotiating access, an emergency response team from WHO arrived there two weeks ago and started working with impacted communities.
“There was a lot of community preoccupation and community resistance in the beginning to receive help, it’s a very highly insecure area,” said Dr Anne Ancia, WHO Country Representative in DRC.
“Ebola does not wait. It follows movement, exploits gaps and tests the strength of our health systems,” said Dr Mohamed Janabi, Regional Director for WHO Africa, underscoring that the virus is “no longer confined to one place, it is a regional concern”.
He added: “We must reach people earlier, bring safe care closer and strengthen trust before fear becomes a barrier to survival. We also know that success is possible where surveillance is strong, where contacts are found and followed.”
