France reports world's first documented case of human infection with Shamonda virus
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:51:17 CST
19:51:17 KST

PARIS, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- French health authorities announced Thursday the world's first documented case of human infection with the Shamonda virus. The patient died in early October. No health risk to the general population has been identified to date.
The Shamonda virus is transmitted to animals by biting midges of the genus Culicoides. First detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s, the virus has been sporadically reported in cattle in West, East and Southern Africa, as well as in Japan. Despite circulating in Africa and Asia for several decades, no human infection had been officially documented until now.
According to the statement, the patient, who was severely immunocompromised, was receiving treatment in Lyon, France, for a serious illness. Preliminary investigations indicated that the brain complications observed in the patient before death were very likely linked to the Shamonda virus infection. At this stage, health authorities consider infection through the bite of a virus-carrying midge of the genus Culicoides in eastern France to be the most likely explanation.
The health authorities stressed that this was an exceptional case involving a severely immunocompromised patient. They have also notified the World Health Organization (WHO) and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) of the case. ■

Helsinki to host 2030 European Athletics Championships
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:47:35 EEST
19:47:35 KST

Helsinki has secured the right to host the 2030 European Athletics Championships, defeating Brussels in a vote by European Athletics officials on Thursday. The week-long competition will take place at the Helsinki Olympic Stadium in August 2030, bringing the championships back to the Finnish capital for the fourth time.
The European Athletics Council selected Helsinki during a meeting in Lausanne, Switzerland, following a three-year bidding process. The decision involved 17 voting members, who chose between the Finnish and Belgian capitals through an open show of hands.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Zurich had also entered the bidding process but withdrew before the final decision.
The Finnish Athletics Federation confirmed the result, with its chairwoman, Riikka Pakarinen, welcoming the outcome after three years of preparations.
Pakarinen thanked the City of Helsinki, the Finnish government and the organisations involved in supporting the bid. She said the decision marked the beginning of preparations for the championships and expressed hope that other Finnish sports federations would pursue international events.
The championships will have an estimated budget of €30 million, including €5 million in government support.
The competition will feature seven evening sessions and five morning sessions over one week. Organisers expect ticket sales to begin in 2027.
Helsinki previously hosted the European Athletics Championships in 1971, 1994 and 2012. The 2030 event will make it the first city to stage the championships four times.
The Finnish capital also hosted the World Athletics Championships in 1983 and 2005.
The Olympic Stadium, which underwent a renovation completed in 2020, will serve as the main competition venue.
European Athletics president Dobromir Karamarinov welcomed the selection and expressed confidence in Helsinki's ability to host the championships.
The Finnish bid placed emphasis on the renovated stadium, transport connections and the concentration of competition facilities within the city centre.
Finnish Athletics Federation chief executive Harri Aalto identified the stadium and the event's compact organisation as factors supporting Helsinki's application.
Helsinki Mayor Daniel Sazonov welcomed the decision, describing the championships as an opportunity to bring athletes and spectators from across Europe to the Finnish capital.
The 2030 championships will follow the 2028 edition in Silesia, Poland. Birmingham hosted the competition in 2026.

Twenty-three members of the U.S. House of Representatives have urged President Donald Trump to allow Ukraine to use the Starlink satellite network for military operations inside Russia.
According to The Hill, the lawmakers believe that such authorization would help Ukraine detect Russian missile launchers in a timely manner and strike them on Russian territory.
The initiative was led by Republican Joe Wilson. The letter was signed by 16 Democrats and seven Republicans, who urged Trump to personally contact SpaceX founder Elon Musk to secure the lifting of the relevant restrictions.

The letter also noted that Ukraine had already approached Elon Musk with a request for an exemption from the restrictions preventing the use of Starlink for such operations inside Russia.
The lawmakers believe that Donald Trump could help secure the decision.
In July 2026, during closed-door talks at the White House, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly asked the U.S. President Donald Trump to authorize the use of Starlink to guide long-range drones toward ballistic missile launchers on Russian territory.
In August 2026, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk held talks with former Ukrainian Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
According to reports, the talks proved ‘extremely unsuccessful,’ after which Musk reportedly became firmly inclined to deny Ukraine permission to use Starlink for such operations.
Following his departure from office on August 7, Fedorov said he was continuing negotiations with Musk but did not specify their subject or outcome.

Meta’s Ad Sales Are Suffering Now That Europeans Can Pick Less Personalization
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:43:13 UTC
19:43:13 KST

Meta’s advertising growth in Europe is slowing now that residents have the option for less of their personal data to influence what advertisements they see.
Advertising revenue in Europe continued to decelerate in the three months through September, the company said on Wednesday, underperforming its global figures. In the region, advertising revenue grew 18 percent year-on-year, slowing from the previous two quarters and lagging the 33 percent growth seen in the US and Canada.
Though Meta did not explicitly blame the introduction of the Less-Personalized Ads model on Wednesday, chief financial officer Susan Li had previously warned “we’re seeing the impact of less personalized ads offering in Europe now that it’s fully rolled out, and that may be an additional headwind,” in July’s second quarter results follow-up call. The preceding two quarters had seen advertising growth fall from around 40 percent to 24 percent; in the US and Canada, it had accelerated from 30 percent to 31 percent.
“We believe the EU’s free, personalized advertising option is contributing to the European slowdown,” Dominic Ball, equity research director at market analysis firm Rothschild & Co Redburn, told WIRED.
Meta began to offer Instagram and Facebook users the LPA option at the beginning of this year, after EU regulators ruled that it was breaching its Digital Markets Act obligation to give consumers the choice of an equivalent service that uses less of their personal data and hit the firm with a €200 million fine. Sales growth has slowed in the region since the start of the year, when Meta rolled out the option. The European Commission said that charging EU users who did not want their personal data used for personalized advertising for an ad-free service—a measure Meta introduced in the EU in November 2023—did not satisfy this. Meta does not disclose how many people have chosen each option.
LPA uses 90 percent less data than personalized ads, Meta says, with ads shown based on what a person sees in a particular session on the site, plus some data points like their age, location, and gender. It leads to poorer returns for EU advertisers, it warned in a response to the EU’s ruling. Less-personalized ads are less efficient, leading to fewer transactions, and more ads being closed due to being irrelevant or repetitive, it said. Indeed, the price advertisers were willing to pay per ad in Europe is not growing as fast as in the US and Canada, Wednesday’s results showed.
Li told investors on Wednesday the company has “a lot of runway” to increase ad conversions and efficiency, as it is “continuing to find ways to either enhance the actual performance of the recommendation engine.” Rothschild & Co Redburn’s Ball believes the company will be able to use AI to improve its ad targeting in Europe despite working with fewer personal data signals.
Investors were keen to understand how this fits into Meta’s personal AI agent, Muse, launched last month, questions about which dominated the call. Li said the company is seeing high commercial intent from people using Muse—asking for product recommendations, researching alternatives, and comparing options—which will allow them to eventually tap into the advertising market with that product.

ICC wins EU's top human rights honor while in Trump's crosshair
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:41:00 UTC
19:41:00 KST

The EU awarded its top human rights prize to the International Criminal Court Thursday, defying U.S. President Donald Trump, who recently hit the war crimes tribunal with sweeping sanctions.
"The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions and this prize recognizes the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice," said Roberta Metsola, chief of the European Parliament, announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize "at a time when the court and its officials face unprecedented challenges."
"Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law," said Tomoko Akane, president of the ICC.
This month, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which prosecutes individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has vowed to dismantle the court "brick by brick," furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's prime minister, for war crimes in Gaza.
The win comes after former ICC judge Navi Pillay, who also served as U.N. human rights chief, received the Nobel Peace Prize this month. U.S. President Donald Trump slammed the choice as "disgraceful," arguing the award should have gone to him.
The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of U.S. sanctions, which will come into force in six months and has said it is "ready to take any necessary measures" to make sure the court can continue working.
"The International Criminal Court must be free to pursue its mission independently and without pressure or intimidation," said Ursula von der Leyen, chief of the EU, after the prize was announced.
Brussels hopes to use the delay before the sanctions are applied to try to persuade the U.S. to reconsider, but it is also considering implementing a "blocking statute" to shield the ICC from Washington.
Established in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organizations to recognize their fight for human rights and democracy.
The ICC was among three finalists this year, alongside Tundu Lissu, a Tanzanian opposition leader, and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, who represent those prosecuted by the Iranian government.
The nominees are nominated by the political groups in the EU, and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December.
Lissu, head of Tanzania's opposition Chadema party, was detained on April 9, 2025. He faces a possible death penalty if convicted of treason for allegedly inciting the public to boycott elections last year.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, have been sentenced, respectively, to death and 36 years in prison for taking part in anti-government protests in Iran.
Other recent high-profile winners of the Sakharov Prize have been Maria Corina Machado, a Venezuelan opposition chief; the late Russian Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and the people of Ukraine.

Missing lift fire door frames confined to Taizoom, Hong Kong authorities say
No missing fire-resistant door frames found in lifts maintained by other firms after probe into Taizoom Elevator uncovers citywide omissions
Inspections into lift safety across Hong Kong have found no missing fire-resistant door frames among contractors other than Taizoom Elevator, authorities have said, after 338 buildings served by the firm were confirmed to lack the crucial components.
The Electrical and Mechanical Services Department provided an update on the checks on Thursday after the government pledged to expand the inspection scope to cover lifts handled by other contractors as well to check whether the problem existed across Hong Kong.
Citywide inspections of lifts serviced by Taizoom were launched on October 16 after fire-resistant door frames were found missing from 48 newly installed lifts at two public housing estates.
The department eventually found that 338 buildings under Taizoom’s service lacked crucial components designed to prevent flames and smoke from entering the shaft in the event of a fire.

Evergrande liquidators recover US$435m in asset sales
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:35:10 UTC
19:35:10 KST

China Evergrande Group's liquidators have recovered US$435.9 million from asset sales and loan recoveries so far, highlighting the challenge of repaying creditors with claims of about US$46 billion against the developer.
In their second progress report since a Hong Kong court ordered Evergrande's liquidation in January 2024, the liquidators, Edward Middleton and Tiffany Wong of Alvarez & Marsal, said on Thursday they aimed to make a first interim dividend payment to creditors in the first half of 2027, although the amount has yet to be determined.
Evergrande, once China's top property developer, defaulted on most of its roughly US$300 billion in liabilities.
The liquidators said they had raised the US$435.9 million through the sale of assets including aircraft, artwork and club memberships, as well as the settlement of loan receivables.
They said 96 of the 107 artworks found at Evergrande's Hong Kong headquarters had been sold for US$28.8 million at a loss. The collection included works by Picasso, Monet and Warhol, as well as sculptures by Moore and Hepworth.
Other assets being sold include a private jet expected to fetch about US$12 million in the fourth quarter. The liquidators are also seeking a US$2 million refund from a US university for part of a donation made in 2020. (Reuters)

Peter Thiel Says US Should Not Have Gone to War with Iran
Billionaire technology investor Peter Thiel has voiced opposition to the U.S. war with Iran, saying Washington should not have launched the conflict and putting him at odds with President Donald Trump over a major foreign policy decision of his administration, according to audio obtained by POLITICO’s Decoded.
Thiel made the remarks during a private event on October 12, in his most explicit publicly disclosed comments on the war to date. They came less than two weeks before midterm elections, as Trump’s Republican Party seeks to retain control of Congress.
“I’m skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it,” Thiel said. “There were a lot of mistakes that were made.”
He also questioned whether the United States had sufficient influence to prevail, saying, “Maybe we don’t have the hard power. Maybe we’re going to lose the soft power war.”
During the full lecture, Thiel expressed strong opposition to neoconservatives and wars in the Middle East. Despite criticizing the Iran conflict, he reiterated his support for Trump and indicated that he wanted to protect the president.
His comments nevertheless mark one of the clearest instances so far of a prominent Trump ally expressing serious reservations about the war.
The remarks were made during Thiel’s lecture series in Nashville, which Decoded has been documenting since it began this fall. In his latest lecture, Thiel also warned extensively about what he described as the unchecked power of the International Criminal Court, referring to comments by Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney, figures from the George W. Bush administration.
“I read the Cheney family’s Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [International Criminal Court] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late,” Thiel said. “And I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran.”
Thiel also recounted a meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in early 2024, following the October 7 attack, during which he asked Netanyahu about his plans for Gaza. According to Thiel, the Israeli leader replied, “I can’t just Dresdenize it,” referring to the Allied bombing of Dresden in World War II, which killed approximately 25,000 people.
Thiel was the first major technology investor to support Trump in 2016 and delivered a high-profile speech at the Republican National Convention that year. He was also the largest financial backer of super PACs supporting Vice President JD Vance’s Senate campaign in 2022.
POLITICO reported in March that Vance had been “skeptical” of U.S. strikes against Iran in the period leading up to the start of the war.
Representatives for Thiel and the White House did not respond to requests for comment.

Britain undersells its nuclear contribution to NATO
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:30:38 BST
19:30:38 KST

Britain is unique among allies in declaring its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite nuclear capabilities consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the Ministry of Defence does not maximise the political and economic value of that commitment, according to a report by the Defence Committee.
The committee, chaired by Tan Dhesi, the Labour member for Slough, examined nuclear deterrence in the High North as part of its inquiry.
Dhesi said: “The High North poses a major strategic challenge for the UK’s security. This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage.”
Its conclusion states: “The United Kingdom has committed to acquiring a sub-strategic nuclear capability to enhance deterrence, although how this aligns with the security of the High North is less clear. To ensure the capability is effective it will probably be necessary for the RAF to occasionally rehearse forward deploying the nuclear-capable F-35A aircraft to the High North. Recipient countries will, therefore, need to be fully aligned and supportive of Britain’s extended deterrence strategy. Uniquely, the UK already declares its existing nuclear forces to NATO, but despite consuming over a fifth of the defence budget the MOD does not maximise the political and economic value of this considerable financial and military commitment.”
According to the most recent departmental annual report and accounts cited by the committee, spending on nuclear capabilities accounts for £14.45 billion of the total defence budget of £69.61 billion.
Britain agreed in 2025 to purchase twelve F-35A fighter aircraft for the Royal Air Force, giving it a sub-strategic nuclear capability and joining NATO’s Dual Capable Aircraft programme, with the Defence Investment Plan allocating £2.1 billion up to 2030 for the total British F-35 fleet. The committee notes that while the aircraft will be flown by RAF pilots, approval to use the nuclear weapons carried by those jets would in any crisis remain under American control.
The report asks how Britain will operate the new capability, including whether the aircraft would deploy to allied countries during peacetime to practise their wartime nuclear role, and how concern about the enduring level of American commitment to European security is addressed by carrying a weapon that remains under American sovereign control during any crisis.
France and Britain each hold around three hundred nuclear warheads, against an American stockpile the report puts at around 3,700 operational weapons. Under the July 2025 Northwood Declaration the two countries agreed to create a Nuclear Steering Group to provide political direction and coordinate across nuclear policy, capabilities and operations, and President Macron announced changes to French nuclear doctrine in March 2026 which included moving towards forward deterrence.
That resulted in bilateral agreements with NATO countries including Denmark and Norway in the High North, allowing French nuclear aircraft to deploy temporarily to their territory for exercises and joint missions. French nuclear assets will not be shared and French nuclear decision making will remain sovereign.
The committee records that France has generated considerable publicity around its agreements, strengthening its international profile on security matters and offering a platform to engage on wider issues including defence export sales.
Its recommendation asks the department to provide the committee with a classified briefing on how it intends to enhance nuclear deterrence through the new sub-strategic capability, including any discussions with regional allies on extended deterrence in the High North and the forward deployment of the capability, and states that given the financial burden of operating the deterrent the department should remind allies more frequently of the unique nuclear capability Britain declares to NATO.

Meta Sued in Australia Over Alleged Harm to Children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:30:04 UTC
19:30:04 KST

Social media giant Meta was hit with a class action lawsuit in Australia on behalf of children and teenagers who allegedly suffered harm over the addictive design features and exposure to harmful content on its platforms Facebook and Instagram.
Australian law firm MinterEllison filed the class action in the country’s Federal Court on Oct. 9. The firm announced the suit on Wednesday, saying it seeks to “recover compensation for both current and former users” of the two Meta social media platforms.
The class action, funded by Sydney-headquartered Litigation Lending Services, was brought in the names of eight unnamed lead applicants. Australia’s Federal Court on Monday ordered a gag on reporting any information that could reveal the applicants’ identities and their statements of claim.
“This proceeding raises important questions about the design and operation of social media platforms and their impact on children and teenagers in Australia,” MinterEllison Partner William Nolan said in its press release. “Those questions will now be considered through the Federal Court process.”
TIME reached out to Meta for comment. A spokesperson told Reuters: “We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously.”
The Australian government, which enforced the world’s first social media ban for children under 16, is also set to take action against Meta and other social media companies. In a Bloomberg interview published Tuesday, Communications Minister Anika Wells, a 2026 TIME100 Next honoree, said that the government expects to bring Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, ByteDance’s TikTok, Snapchat, and Google’s YouTube to court for allegedly failing to comply with the country’s laws.
U.S. parallels
The Australian class action follows several civil victories against Meta in the U.S. In March, a Los Angeles jury ordered Meta and Google to pay $6 million in damages to a 20-year-old plaintiff in a bellwether social media addiction trial. In August, a New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay more than $900 million and introduce a slew of reforms to its platforms, including rigorous age verification, time limits for users under 18 years old, and enhanced protection against sextortion and child sexual exploitation. The same month, Meta agreed to pay up to $18 billion to settle a nationwide lawsuit that alleged its platforms were “addictive” by design and harmed children.
Rob Nicholls, a senior researcher at the University of Sydney with expertise on digital regulations, tells TIME in an email that he was “not surprised” with the class action, given the cases in the U.S.
“The U.S. lawsuits were primarily concerned with negligence,” Nicholls tells TIME. “It’s likely that in Australia the suit will be both negligence and the consequences of the supply of an unsafe product.”
Regulatory enforcement
Australia has led the way in trying to rein in social media platforms in the name of child safety. Last year, it enforced a blanket ban on children under 16 from having social media accounts, a move that other countries have followed.
The effort, however, has been criticized by some, including politicians and digital rights advocates, for not being aggressively enough enforced since the ban took effect in December 2025. The latest data from the country’s online regulator, eSafety, shows that 42% of children aged 10 to 15 still own a social media account.
In a podcast published Thursday, Wells, the Communications Minister, said there was a “great initial response” with 5 million accounts deactivated, but that has since “tapered off.” She added that the eSafety Commissioner believes the five platforms in particular could be doing more to comply with the law and the Commission is investigating potential violations.
Asked why there haven’t been any fines yet, Wells said: “Unfortunately, this isn't a police officer on duty pointing a speeding radar at a car and issuing an on-the-spot fine. This is asking the eSafety Commissioner, our independent regulator, to take on some of the biggest, richest, most resourced companies in the world.”
In September, the Australian government increased the fines for noncompliant social media firms. Failing to take “reasonable steps” to prevent underage Australians from creating or keeping accounts could incur a maximum penalty of 109.2 million Australian dollars (around $76 million).
But speaking to Bloomberg, Wells pointed to the multi-billion-dollar settlement Meta agreed to in the U.S. and said, “I’m not convinced that any particular dollar value is going to change it.” For her, the policy should be measured on how it creates cultural change. “And cultural change,” she said, “takes time.”

I Worked for a Whole Day Using Only the iPhone Duo. Here’s How It Went
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

An iPhone 18 Pro is $1,199. An iPad is $449. If you want both—the iPhone as your primary device and the iPad to handle some work when you’re away from your desk—you'll be spending a total dollar amount that’s pretty close to the $1,999 price of Apple’s first folding smartphone, the iPhone Duo.
So can the Duo’s 7.6-inch screen pull double duty as a phone and a workstation? Does it make sense to shell out a few hundred more dollars for a single gadget that can theoretically handle the workload of two devices?
I wrote my entire iPhone Duo review on Apple’s new handset. I used a note-taking app called Bear, which was mercifully optimized for the Duo’s larger screen. (Read my review and you’ll hear about how most apps aren’t optimized; it could take weeks or months for everything to look right.) But surprisingly, I didn’t hate the experience.
I have run this experiment before on Android foldables and even smart glasses with virtual workspaces, but iOS has its own unique hurdles. Notably, iOS doesn’t recognize a Bluetooth mouse or trackpad by default. Instead, you have to go to the phone’s accessibility settings and enable AssistiveTouch—then you’ll get an iPad-like cursor that lets you navigate the Duo’s interface and select text without constantly reaching for the touchscreen.
Even with the cursor, small tasks like pasting hyperlinks into a written piece or quickly Googling topics for additional research are slower and more cumbersome, so I left those for the end when I moved everything into WIRED’s content management system. Even then, I had to switch over to my desktop for the final touches.
Apple also imposes arbitrary multitasking restrictions in iOS because, well, Apple likes to control how people use its devices. For example, if you open two apps in split screen mode, you can only view them in an equal 50-50 split. Unlike most operating systems that let you adjust how much of each app you can see by dragging the border in between the windows, iOS leaves you stuck with a view that gives both apps equal screen space. If you want to use the iPhone in portrait orientation and stack two apps vertically, one on the top part of the screen and the other on the bottom, you’re out of luck. In portrait mode, you can only pin video apps to the top with another app below.
One thing Apple did get right is app pairs. You can “pin” two apps together, and they will live in your Recents, ready when you need them. Say you always want to look at your email and calendar together; you can pair them and find them in Recents whenever you need them. (Tap the bar in the middle to lock and save the pair.)
My keyboard of choice is an old Seenda folding Bluetooth keyboard that is admittedly not very good. I imagine we'll see an array of compact keyboards hitting the market soon—like Nillkin or ProtoArc keyboards already available now—to cater to workaholics who need to work everywhere. I also used one of Apple's cases, the iPhone Duo Folio with Kickstand, to keep the phone propped up. You can use various MagSafe kickstands, tripods, or cases with the Duo.
I typed most of the day, but I also had to juggle between apps to respond to coworkers or hop on a Zoom call. Thankfully, the Slack iOS app updated the day before my testing to fully support the iPhone Duo's larger screen and vertical navigation, making it very easy to bounce between multiple conversations in the two-pane view. I still think Apple should add a feature like the iPad's Slide Over, where you can “hide” a floating app off to the side and bring it back in when you need it. It’d be the perfect spot for messaging apps like Slack, WhatsApp, or Messages, and it wouldn’t interrupt your split screen experience.
Zoom wasn’t optimized for the Duo, though my editor said the video quality from the inner and outer selfie cameras was “really good.” I used the folio kickstand to Zoom on the big 7.6-inch screen until we realized my video was stuck in an awkward portrait orientation, so I laid the phone down on the table and pointed the 5.4-inch outer screen toward my face, which made it feel like a traditional laptop experience.
The app that annoyed me the most was Gmail. Even though Google updated the Google Search app to be compatible with the iPhone Duo early this week, the rest of Google's workspace apps currently look awful on the Duo. I imagine full support will come very soon, if not on Friday, when the Duo officially launches. The two-pane view in Gmail (or any email app) is a game changer for clearing a bunch of emails when you’re on the go.
By 6 pm, battery life was sitting around 45 percent, which is very impressive. That's with around six hours of screen-on time.
You probably won’t want to replace your laptop with the iPhone Duo. And anyone accustomed to the iPad’s larger screen may feel cramped on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas. But with a kickstand and the right portable keyboard? Knocking out focused, light work on the Duo is entirely doable. Things will get even more interesting once Apple Pencil support arrives later this year.
But as I packed up my keyboard, I couldn’t shake a familiar feeling. Maybe we’ll realize a single do-it-all device isn’t as great as it’s chalked up to be. Maybe it is better to kick back with a dedicated MP3 player. Or snap photos with a camera. Or write in a notebook. Or work off a laptop.
Speaking of which, did you hear Apple’s making a touchscreen MacBook?

Kazakhstan eyes localizing satellite manufacturing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Kazakhstan eyes localizing satellite manufacturing
Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov held a series of bilateral meetings with international companies on the sidelines of the ninth Kazakhstan Global Investment Roundtable (KGIR-2026) in Shymkent, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing the government’s press service.
The meetings brought together representatives of Aksa Energy, Carlsberg Kazakhstan, Solico Group and CONTEC. Discussions covered ongoing and prospective investment projects in energy, agribusiness, food production and the space sector.
The parties examined prospects for expanding cooperation, developing processing industries and introducing new technologies in line with the priorities set by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. Increasing the share of local content was also a key focus.
During a meeting with Aksa Energy CEO and Executive Committee Chairman Naci Ağbal, Bektenov discussed the results of the company’s cooperation with Kazakhstan and prospects for new energy projects.
The sides highlighted the launch of a combined-cycle power plant in Kyzylorda, valued at 215 billion tenge. The facility, with an electrical capacity of 240 MW and a thermal capacity of 277 Gcal per hour, entered commercial operation in June 2026. It is designed to meet the region’s growing demand for electricity and heat.
Further investment plans by Aksa Energy in Kazakhstan were also discussed.
At a meeting with Carlsberg Kazakhstan CEO Vyacheslav Maltsev, the discussions focused on food industry development, production localization and export expansion.
Carlsberg Kazakhstan has become the official distributor of PepsiCo products in Kazakhstan. As part of the cooperation between the two companies, a $344 million soft drinks plant was launched in Almaty region on October 1, 2026.
The facility supplies the domestic market and is also intended to serve export markets. It has created 230 permanent jobs.
Local content currently accounts for 71.5% of Carlsberg Kazakhstan’s operations. The meeting also addressed opportunities to expand cooperation with domestic suppliers of raw materials and packaging materials.
Bektenov also met with Alireza Mohammad Rahimi, CEO and Board Member of Solico Group in the CIS countries, to discuss construction of a cheese manufacturing plant in Almaty region.
The project represents an investment of nearly 45 billion tenge and is expected to have an annual production capacity of 41,000 tons. It is projected to create around 450 permanent jobs.
Construction and installation work is ongoing, with the facility scheduled to begin operations in 2029.
The sides also considered prospects for establishing additional processing facilities in Kazakhstan’s agricultural regions. Such projects are expected to support the expansion of exports of domestically produced goods.
During talks with CONTEC founder and CEO Lee Sung-hee, the sides discussed opportunities to expand cooperation in the space industry.
The proposals include joint production of satellites and satellite components in Kazakhstan, development of ground infrastructure and localization of selected manufacturing processes.
The discussions also covered the use of artificial intelligence to process satellite data, cooperation in training Kazakhstani specialists and opportunities to export jointly manufactured products to international markets.
Kazakhstan is seeking to attract new investment and implement projects focused on producing high-value-added goods. Prime Minister Bektenov instructed the relevant ministries and responsible organizations to provide the necessary support for investment projects.
Earlier, Qazinform reported Kazakhstan and Chinese company advance a $1 billion Kuryk port project.

European court faults Switzerland in Brian Keller trial
The European Court of Human Rights has ruled that Switzerland must pay former prisoner Brian Keller CHF5,000 ($6,095) in compensation for procedural irregularities. The court did not address the complaints regarding the conditions of detention.
The judges found that there had been a breach of the right to a fair trial, as set out in the ruling published on Thursday. Keller was not given sufficient opportunity to comment on the matter. However, the Court dismissed Keller’s complaints regarding the harsh conditions of detention and solitary confinement at Pöschwies Prison in Zurich as inadmissible.
+ Zurich court sentences Brian Keller to long prison term
Keller appealed to the Court regarding the conditions during his many years at Pöschwies. He spent 23 hours in solitary confinement. On some occasions, he was also denied his one-hour daily exercise break.
Hardly any contact in prison
He often had contact only with prison staff, with whom he frequently had altercations. These form part of proceedings that are still pending before the Zurich High Court.
Keller was released from prison in November 2023.
Keller is a boxer and once Switzerland’s “most famous inmate”. Since his release, he has come into conflict with the law on several occasions.
Among other things, he knocked out an opponent after the two had provoked each other on social media. This case is also still pending.

Spain Receives Third A330 MRTT Converted From Passenger Airliner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:16:51 UTC
19:16:51 KST

European aircraft manufacturer Airbus has delivered the third A330 MRTT tanker aircraft to the Ministry of Defence of Spain.
The company’s press service announced this.
The aircraft’s delivery on October 20, 2026, completed Spain’s initial order, placed in 2021.
The aircraft will join the Spanish Air and Space Force’s 45th Wing and operate from Torrejón de Ardoz Air Base near Madrid.
In November 2021, the Ministry of Defence of Spain purchased three used A330 passenger aircraft from Iberia. Airbus converted them into multirole military tanker aircraft at its facility in Getafe, near Madrid.
After retiring its last Boeing 707 in 2016, Spain lost its capability for long-range strategic aerial refueling.
Some of these missions were carried out by A400M Atlas aircraft, while the country used C295s and other transport aircraft to carry personnel and cargo.
Spain’s A330 MRTTs are equipped with a hose-and-drogue aerial refueling system. The aircraft can remain airborne for more than 18 hours and cover distances of up to 16,000 kilometers.
They have a fuel capacity of 111 tonnes, allowing them to refuel other aircraft without installing additional fuel tanks. The Spanish aircraft use a hose-and-drogue system rather than a flying boom.
Besides Spain, the United Kingdom and France also operate A330 MRTT in Europe. The UK Royal Air Force operates 14 of these aircraft, while France has received 13 of the 15 ordered.
Another 10 aircraft are operated by NATO’s Multinational Multi-Role Tanker Transport Fleet Programme (MMF), which is shared by nine European countries: Belgium, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Finland, Germany, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Norway, and Sweden. Spain and Poland also plan to jointly procure seven A330 MRTT tanker aircraft, four of which Poland is expected to receive by 2030.
Militarnyi previously reported that the first A330 MRTT multi-role aircraft, designated the CC-330 Husky by Canada, had made its maiden flight at Airbus’s facility in Getafe, Spain.

They Believe 2020 Was Stolen. They Could Be in Charge of Elections in 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

One was central to facilitating the bogus Cyber Ninjas audit of the 2020 vote in Maricopa County that found no evidence of voter fraud but cost taxpayers $4 million. Another is friends with a Covid-denying former boxer turned MAGA influencer who was filmed on the steps of the Capitol on January 6, 2021 shouting “1776.” Another was set to headline a rally with MyPillow founder and election denial funder Mike Lindell.
This is not a list of edgy MAGA influencers sharing hot takes on X, or podcast hosts on Rumble boosting wild conspiracy theories. No, this is a list of some of the Republican candidates running for attorney general in states across the US.
A WIRED review has identified a slate of GOP attorney general candidates in more than half a dozen states, including key swing states, who have repeatedly expressed their belief that the 2020 election was stolen. If elected, several have said, they are willing to relitigate 2020 once again—and all will potentially play a key role in the 2028 presidential election.
“Any attorney general should be dedicated to upholding the rule of law,” Christina Beeler, senior counsel for the Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights, tells WIRED. “The office of attorney general is a powerful office, and it is deeply important that anyone in that role is dedicated to upholding the rule of law and the results of elections.”
The role of attorney general in the administration and protection of elections differs from state to state, but in general, as their state’s chief legal officer they are required to be a check on both the governor and the federal government. The functions of the role have been highlighted in recent months, as attorneys general across the country have repeatedly stood up to President Donald Trump and his administration's efforts to take control of elections, seize ballots, and obtain voter rolls containing sensitive information on US citizens.
Here, WIRED has looked at GOP candidates for attorney general in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, and Kansas, where some have openly espoused baseless allegations about the 2020 election.
Arizona
Warren Petersen, an Arizona state senator, was one of the most vocal supporters of Trump’s baseless claim that the 2020 election was stolen. In 2020, he signed a document that asked Congress to accept 11 alternate electoral votes for Trump, and later signed another demanding the US Senate reject Arizona’s slate of electors.
Petersen was also central to getting the bogus audit in Maricopa County approved, a process run by a firm called Cyber Ninjas. The audit ultimately showed that Joe Biden had won by more votes than originally thought. The whole process cost Arizona taxpayers millions.
Earlier this year, Petersen complied with a grand jury subpoena, handing over files on the Cyber Ninjas audit to the FBI as part of its investigation into the 2020 election in Maricopa.
And the lawmaker has also signaled a possible desire to relitigate the 2020 election if he’s elected, calling for an expansion of the attorney general’s Election Integrity Unit. “People will know we’re serious about it,” Petersen said during his primary campaign in July. “Just like they know the Trump DOJ is serious about it right now.”
Polls show Petersen tied with his Democratic opponent, Kris Mayes.
Georgia
In Georgia, the focus of much of Trumpworld’s conspiracy theories about elections, the GOP’s nominee for attorney general is Brian Strickland. In 2020, as a state senator, Strickland shared a press release that called for officials to consider launching an investigation into “fraudulent activities” in the 2020 election, a forensic audit of the election in Georgia, and new voting laws in the state.
Strickland has also signaled his willingness to fall in line with the Trump administration’s continuing efforts to investigate the 2020 election. When FBI officials raided Fulton County’s election offices earlier this year and seized ballots from the 2020 election, Strickland called it a “transparency” measure. “Fulton County can't run elections,” Strickland wrote on X in February. “That's the simple truth. Every Georgian, regardless of party, should have faith in our election process.”
An Atlanta Journal Constitution poll published this week shows Strickland in a tie with his Democrat opponent Tanya Miller.
Kansas
Unlike the other election deniers on this list, Kris Kobach is already in the position he’s running for in November, having won the attorney general’s race in 2022.
A long-time promoter of baseless conspiracy theories about fraudulent elections, Kobach previously served as Kansas’ secretary of state from 2011 to 2019. During his time in office, Kobach claimed that an estimated 18,000 noncitizens were on the state’s voter rolls based on non-peer reviewed research that initially found six people who may have attemped to register or registered to vote. In 2017, Trump appointed Kobach to the short-lived “election integrity” commission that found no evidence of widespread voter fraud.
In the wake of the 2020 election, Kobach was an adviser to Texas’ effort to overturn the results and assisted a member of the Michigan Board of State Canvassers who tried to rescind her vote to certify Michigan’s 2020 presidential election results. In 2022, Kobach was announced as a headliner at a Kansas rally with prominent election denier Lindell.
Recent polling suggests Kobach is in a tight race with his Democratic opponent, Chris Mann.
Michigan
In Michigan, Eaton County prosecutor Doug Lloyd won the GOP nomination for attorney general earlier this year, in a race that had once included Matt DePerno, a lawyer facing felony charges for undue possession of a voting machine and conspiracy in the wake of the 2020 election. (DePerno pled not guilty to the charges, and the case is still pending in the district court.)
Unlike DePerno, Lloyd is not typically labeled as an election denier, and he has claimed to be more moderate than his Democratic opponent, Eli Savit. But in a recent podcast interview reviewed by WIRED, when asked about “credible concerns raised by voters about the 2020 election,” he signaled his willingness to relitigate the six-year-old issue.
“I believe the attorney general has the ability to actually use their investigative officers within their office or the Michigan State Police to actually go back and look at those items,” Lloyd told the MI True Red podcast. “And so as I look at it, you know, I want to take those things in.”
Recent polling shows Lloyd tied in his race against Lavit.
Nevada
In Nevada, Trump has endorsed lawyer Adriana Guzmán Fralick for the position of attorney general. That may be because she has said she would push for Nevada’s version of the SAVE Act, which Trump has failed to force Congress to approve on a federal level. The act would impose severe restrictions on eligible voters by requiring those registered to produce a passport or birth certificate, documents that tens of millions of Americans readily do not have.
"President Trump is fighting for secure elections—but DC keeps dragging its feet,” Guzmán Fralick wrote on Facebook earlier this year. “Nevada shouldn't have to wait. As your Attorney General, I will push for the SAVE Nevada Act to remove non-citizens from our voter rolls, count all ballots on Election Day, and end universal mail-in voting. What Washington won't finish, Nevada will.”
Experts have repeatedly said the SAVE Act would disenfranchise millions of voters.
Guzmán Fralick has also touted the endorsement of Joey Gilbert, a far-right boxer turned MAGA influencer who gained fame for spreading conspiracy theories about the Covid-19 pandemic. Gilbert, who calls Fralick a “friend,” was also present at the rally at the Capitol on January 6, 2021. While he didn’t enter the building, he was captured on video near serial conspiracy theorist Alex Jones, chanting “1776.”
Recent polling shows Guzmán Fralick trailing her Democratic opponent Nicole Cannizzaro by 8 points.

International Criminal Court wins EU's 2026 Sakharov prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:12:09 UTC
19:12:09 KST

Targeted by Trump, ICC wins Europe’s top human rights prize
- The International Criminal Court won the EU’s Sakharov Prize, a top human rights award, as the European Parliament backed its work on international law and justice.
- The award comes after US sanctions aimed at crippling the ICC. US President Donald Trump has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick”.
- The ICC beat finalists from Tanzania and Iran, and the EU has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to keep the court working.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – Facing US sanctions, the International Criminal Court (ICC) was on Oct 22 awarded the European Union’s top human rights prize in a show of support that risks upsetting US President Donald Trump.
“The European Union is built on respect for multilateralism and international institutions, and this prize recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and justice,” European Parliament President Roberta Metsola said in announcing the award.
The ICC thanked the European Parliament for giving it the Sakharov Prize “at a time when the Court and its officials face unprecedented challenges”.
“Against this backdrop, the Sakharov Prize carries particular significance, reaffirming the importance of independent judicial institutions and of those who work to uphold international law,” ICC President Tomoko Akane said.
Earlier in October, the United States announced sanctions against the ICC aimed at crippling the day-to-day operations of the court, which tries individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
Trump’s administration has vowed to dismantle the court “brick by brick”, furious that judges have issued an arrest warrant for Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged crimes in Gaza.
The win comes after after former ICC judge Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize, a choice Trump slammed as “disgraceful”, arguing the award should have gone to him.
The EU has already thrown its support behind the ICC in the face of the US sanctions, which will come into force in six months, and has said it is “ready to take any necessary measures” to make sure the court can keep working.
Set up in 1988 and named after Soviet dissident Andrei Sakharov, the EU prize is bestowed annually on individuals or organisations to recognise their fight for human rights or democracy.
Three finalists
The ICC was among three finalists, alongside Tanzania opposition leader Tundu Lissu and twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, representing those prosecuted by the Iranian government.
The nominees are put forward by the political groupings in the EU, and the winner is chosen by senior lawmakers. An award ceremony will be held in December.
Lissu, head of Tanzania’s opposition Chadema party, was detained in April 2025. He faces a possible death penalty if convicted of treason for allegedly inciting the public to boycott elections last year.
Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, have respectively been sentenced to death and 36 years in prison for having taken part in anti-government protests in Iran.
Other recent high-profile winners of the Sakharov prize have been Venezuelan opposition chief Maria Corina Machado, deceased Russian Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny and the people of Ukraine.. AFP

In Iowa stronghold, Trump urges Republicans to turn out and vote
SIOUX CITY, Iowa, Oct 22 - President Donald Trump on Thursday tried to galvanize Republican voters in Iowa, a state he won by double digits two years ago but now faces a tougher battle in the November midterm elections due to dissatisfaction with rising prices and the Iran war.
The Midwestern stop is part of Trump's push through states Republicans usually expect to win, but where polling points to some tight races.
Trump held a rally in Sioux City as Republicans defend a Senate seat, three House districts and the governor's office, giving Democrats an opening after years of Republican gains.
"Pretend I'm on the ballot, because if you get out, we're going to win big," Trump told the crowd gathered in an airport hangar.
He has spoken repeatedly with confidence about his connection with voters, though his approval rating has fallen and some Republicans Trump is trying to help have broken with him over the Iran war, as higher fuel and grocery prices deepen voters' economic worries.
Republican Representative Ashley Hinson, who also addressed the Sioux City rally, has called for an "immediate end" to the war, saying Iowans should not bear higher fuel or grocery prices because of it. She is in a close Senate race against Democratic state Representative Josh Turek.
"If we lose this seat here in Iowa, the Democrats will control the US Senate. Mark my words," she said on Thursday.
Republican Representatives Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, facing difficult reelection races, joined Democrats last month in voting to limit Trump's war powers in Iran.
"The only thing is the fuel prices that are hurting him more than anything," said rally attendee Ron Sitzmann, 73, a semi-retired parts and service director for an automotive company in Iowa, adding that he thought prices would drop once the conflict ended.
"I just wish it would happen sooner than later because it’s kind of dragging on," said Sitzmann, who remains a strong Trump supporter.
'PREACHING TO THE CHOIR'
Trump was in Iowa to back his party's candidates but used the platform to attack Democrats from other states, including Somali American Minnesota lawmaker Ilhan Omar, suggesting that she should quit Congress in the wake of a raid by federal agents on her home.
Omar says the government is being weaponized to target her as a political enemy of Trump's, who has been ramping up anti-Somali and anti-Muslim rhetoric in recent weeks.
In the Iowa races, Democrat Rob Sand leads Republican Zach Lahn in recent polling for governor, while Democrats are targeting an open House seat in the state's second congressional district.
Republican losses would be a setback for Trump in a state where his popularity helped the party build a commanding advantage.
The Senate and House races could help decide control of Congress, shaping his ability to advance his agenda during his final two years.
Republicans also worry about rural voters who powered Trump's Iowa victories, with farmers facing higher costs and trade uncertainty.
A Marist poll this month found 42% of likely voters said their finances had worsened over the past year, including more than half of independents. Thirty-five percent viewed their vote as a vote against Trump, versus 21% who saw it as a vote for him.
Trump's Iowa stop follows rallies earlier this week in Kansas for Senator Roger Marshall and South Carolina for Senator Darline Graham, where the Republicans are defending seats.
"We know he’s preaching to the choir," said Harlan Grau, 70, a staunch Trump supporter and pig farmer from Iowa. The rallies encourage supporters to "go out and get them 10 people to go to the polls with us," he added.
Trump's campaign swing comes as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either presidential term, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday. The survey found 68% of Americans disapproved of his handling of the economy.
At recent rallies, his economic message has largely avoided the financial pressures facing many Americans. The Iran war has driven up gas prices, compounding broader cost-of-living concerns, while Trump has repeatedly promised prices will fall when the conflict ends.
Behind the scenes, Trump has questioned campaign spending, criticized redistricting efforts and second-guessed candidate choices, according to people familiar with the matter.
White House spokesman Davis Ingle rejected the people's characterizations, saying they were "armchair experts peddling their baseless speculation." Publicly, Trump has noted the tendency of a president's party to lose seats in midterm elections. REUTERS

But they differ on their positions on settlements in the occupied West Bank, and are likely to rely on different coalition partners to form governments, which could broadly set the country on diverging paths.
Here is a look at the candidates’ views on the conflict with the Palestinians:
West Bank settlements
Hundreds of thousands of Israelis live in the West Bank, settling in territory Israel captured in a 1967 war, a practice nearly all countries consider illegal under international law, although Israel disputes this.
Netanyahu has presided over a rapid expansion of settlements, including small outposts in parts of the West Bank reserved for civil administration by the Palestinian Authority, where settlements are illegal under Israel’s own laws. Settlers have increasingly attacked Palestinians, and critics say the government has turned a blind eye to such violence.
Eisenkot favours settlement in principle, but says that it should comply with Israeli law. He opposes settlements built without authorisation, would dismantle outposts in areas where they are forbidden, and has pledged to prevent violence by settlers against Palestinians.
He also opposes a decision by the Netanyahu government to build in territory known as E1, which would bisect the West Bank and cut it off from East Jerusalem, which settlers say is intended to “bury” the possibility of a Palestinian state.
Palestinian self-rule
In a sign of how far Israeli politics has shifted to the right, Netanyahu and Eisenkot, along with the leaders of nearly all other Jewish-led parties, oppose the establishment of a future independent Palestinian state alongside Israel.
This effectively repudiates the two-state solution that underpinned international peace negotiations for generations.
Netanyahu and Eisenkot both say Israel must retain ultimate security control over all territory between the Jordan River and Mediterranean Sea.
There are, however, differences in their emphasis. Eisenkot’s position on limiting settlements in the West Bank would reserve territory where Palestinians now exercise civil self rule. Netanyahu’s coalition includes parties that openly call for Israel to fully annex occupied Palestinian land.
Gaza
Three years since Hamas-led fighters attacked southern Israel, prompting an Israeli invasion of the Gaza Strip, and a year since a US-brokered ceasefire ended major combat there, Israeli troops now control around two-thirds of the enclave.
Nearly the entire population of more than 2 million Palestinians lives in the remaining third, mainly in tents or damaged buildings, still under the full political control of Hamas. US-brokered talks have so far failed to agree terms for Hamas to disarm, Israel to withdraw and reconstruction to begin under international auspices.
Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu say Israeli troops will not withdraw from Gaza until Hamas is disarmed, and that Israel is prepared to restart fighting to achieve this.
Eisenkot says the continued rule of Hamas in Gaza is a profound failure, and that within 18 months of taking office he would ensure that the Hamas administration had been replaced, either through a US-brokered plan or through military force.
Coalition partners
Netanyahu’s governing coalition now includes far-right Jewish nationalist groups led by settler activists Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who support full annexation of Palestinian land and are under sanctions in several Western countries for promoting settler violence.
Netanyahu also relies on ultra-Orthodox parties that seek exemptions from military service for Jewish religious students.
Opposition parties likely to be courted by Eisenkot for a future coalition to unseat Netanyahu include several right-wing groups, but none with leaders as extreme as Smotrich or Ben-Gvir. His supporters are mainly opposed to the military exemption for religious students, which probably rules out an alliance with the ultra-Orthodox.
To unseat Netanyahu, Eisenkot is likely to require the support of the Democrats, which include the rump of the centre-left Labour Party that dominated Israeli politics for generations but has dwindled as the country has shifted to the right. The Democrats are now the only prominent Jewish-led party that supports a two-state solution.
Eisenkot and Netanyahu have both said they would not form a government with parties primarily representing Israeli citizens of Palestinian descent, who comprise around a fifth of the population. REUTERS

Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:10:23 UTC
19:10:23 KST

Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- Deutsches Primatenzentrum (DPZ)/German Primate Center
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered why common marmosets have unusually small, smooth brains despite starting development much like other primates. The secret lies in subtle changes to brain-building cells that slow neuron production, revealing new clues about how the large, folded human brain evolved.
- Share:
Most primates have relatively large brains covered in distinctive folds and grooves. However, common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) are an unusual exception. These small monkeys have brains that are almost entirely smooth, with very little folding. Scientists at the German Primate Center (DPZ), the Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen, have now identified several cellular processes that help explain this difference.
Using miniature brain structures known as organoids, the researchers discovered that certain neural progenitor cells, which produce neurons, develop differently in marmosets than in humans. These differences involve the cells' structure, the speed at which they divide, and the timing of their development. Together, these changes reduce the number of neurons produced, contributing to the smaller size and smoother surface of the marmoset brain. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide new insights into primate brain evolution and could eventually improve our understanding of human brain development disorders.
Why Some Primate Brains Are Smooth Instead of Folded
Brain size and the extent of surface folding are important features that distinguish different primate species. The human brain, for example, has a highly folded surface resembling the ridges and grooves of a walnut. This arrangement greatly expands the brain's surface area, creating room for billions of neurons that support complex thinking and other advanced mental abilities.
Scientists believe that the common ancestor of modern primates already possessed a moderately sized brain with at least some folding. Yet not all primates living today retain these characteristics.
Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), small monkeys native to South America that are becoming increasingly important in biomedical research, have brains with almost no visible folds. Researchers at the German Primate Center set out to determine why their brains develop so differently from those of humans and other primates.
"We wanted to understand which changes at the cellular level cause the marmoset brain to grow less and form fewer folds," explains Lidiia Tynianskaia, one of the study's two first authors and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution at the DPZ. "At the beginning of development, the common marmoset brain exhibits the typical structure and composition of a large, folded primate brain. As development progresses, processes must therefore occur that effectively slow down the production of nerve cells."
Scientists Discover What Slows Brain Growth
To investigate these developmental differences, the team compared brain organoids grown from human and common marmoset cells. Their attention centered on neural progenitor cells, the cells responsible for generating neurons during brain development.
These progenitor cells play a major role in determining the eventual size and shape of the brain. The more neurons they produce, the greater the potential for the cerebral cortex to expand and develop folds.
The researchers found that the marmoset's smaller, smoother cerebral cortex is not the result of a single developmental change. Instead, several differences involving distinct types of progenitor cells work together to limit neuron production and brain folding.
"Our investigations have shown that certain progenitor cells in the common marmoset divide significantly more slowly than in humans," explains César Mateo Bastidas Betancourt, also a first author of the study and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group. "Other progenitor cells have a simpler structure than their human counterparts, with fewer processes, and are therefore less proliferative. Both of these factors ultimately result in fewer nerve cells, which contributes to a smaller size and less folding of the cerebral cortex in marmosets."
The scientists also identified important differences in when certain progenitor cell characteristics and behaviors emerge during development. Compared with humans, marmosets have a shorter overall period during which these cells can multiply rapidly.
Together, the slower rate of cell division, simpler cell structures, and shorter window for rapid growth help explain why the marmoset brain produces fewer neurons and develops far fewer folds.
Miniature Brains Reveal Important Developmental Clues
Much of the research relied on brain organoids, small, three-dimensional structures grown from cells that reproduce important features of early brain development. These miniature models allowed scientists to investigate developmental changes across multiple samples and compare the timing of key processes.
"The study combines the advantages of in vivo and in vitro methods," says Michael Heide, head of the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution. "Organoids are well-suited for obtaining statistically robust results because such sample sizes are not feasible in primates. We subsequently repeated some key experiments in fetal brain tissue to confirm the results from the organoids."
One particularly important finding involved the relationship between development in organoids and development in actual marmoset brains. The researchers determined that a marmoset brain organoid grown for 50 days closely matches the developmental stage of a natural marmoset brain at day 90.
Establishing this relationship was essential because brain organoids and actual brains do not necessarily develop at the same rate. By identifying corresponding developmental stages, the scientists could make meaningful comparisons and interpret their experimental findings more reliably.
What Smooth Monkey Brains Reveal About Human Brain Evolution
The findings help explain how relatively small differences in the behavior and developmental timing of brain-building cells can contribute to major differences in brain size and folding among primates.
They also offer a potential explanation for how the wide variety of primate brain shapes and sizes emerged over evolutionary time, including why some species developed relatively smooth brains while others possess much larger, heavily folded ones.
Beyond their evolutionary significance, these discoveries provide a foundation for investigating how the human brain develops and what happens when those processes are disrupted. A better understanding of the cellular mechanisms that control neuron production and brain growth could ultimately help researchers study developmental disorders affecting the human brain.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Deutsches Primatenzentrum (DPZ)/German Primate Center. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Lidiia Tynianskaia, Cesar Mateo Bastidas-Betancourt, Esther Marie Grewe, Julia Marie Kniep, Neringa Liutikaite, Nesil Esiyok, İrfan Burak Göloğlu, Sabrina Heide, Nancy Rüger, Dimitri Lindenwald, Charis Drummer, Stoyan Petkov, Nataliya Di Donato, Michael Heide. Coordinated neural progenitor adaptations contribute to primate neocortical downscaling. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (39) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aeg5563

Trump's tax-exempt diesel draws skepticism from farmers, eludes others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:06:52 UTC
19:06:52 KST

Trump's tax-exempt diesel draws skepticism from farmers, eludes others
CHICAGO, Oct 22 - US President Donald Trump signed an executive order this month to expand access to tax-exempt diesel as soaring prices frustrate voters ahead of midterm elections. But farmers say it is too risky to use the fuel on public roads, while some other drivers do not have access to it.
Trump has sought to lower prices and boost his sagging approval ratings through a series of actions focused on fuel, including an $8 billion financial support program he announced on Monday to offset diesel costs for farmers during the autumn harvest.
His administration also relaxed sanctions on Russian fuel shipments, pushed allies to release emergency oil stocks and temporarily lifted restrictions on foreign-flagged vessels moving between US ports. Still, prices remain elevated because of the US-led war with Iran.
Trump said his executive order would temporarily waive an off-road requirement for red-dyed diesel, which is generally sold for use in farm equipment. Red diesel is essentially the same as regular or clear diesel but exempt from highway fuel taxes. It is dyed red to indicate highway taxes have not been paid.
Farmers said potential savings from using dyed diesel in semi-trucks on highways were too small to justify the risk of red residue staying in fuel tanks after the order expires. States have their own taxes and rules for red diesel use, and can fine drivers thousands of dollars if authorities inspect fuel tanks and find signs red diesel was used improperly on public roads.
The Internal Revenue Service said it would not impose a penalty when dyed diesel is used on highways from October 1 to December 31 but that Trump's order had no effect on state taxes and penalties.
"In my mind, it's not anywhere near worth the risk," said Glenn Brunkow, president of the Kansas Farm Bureau, who raises crops and cattle near Wamego, Kansas. "That residue might be in there for years."
FINES UP TO $10,000 IN KANSAS
Farmers use the most diesel during the autumn harvest season, burning dyed fuel in tractors, combines and other machinery. Under Trump's order, they could also use red diesel to haul crops to market in semi-trucks normally fueled by clear diesel, if allowed by states.
Kansas, a major grain producer, prohibits using dyed diesel on public roadways unless it is purchased lawfully outside the state. Violators can be charged with a felony, have their driver's license suspended, and face penalties of $1,000 to $10,000, according to the Kansas Department of Revenue.
Governor Laura Kelly, a Democrat, said the state could not legally implement Trump's order as drafted. The Kansas Highway Patrol was concerned it "would result in law enforcement difficulties once red dye diesel returns to its normal usage restrictions," she said in a statement.
Democrats hope surging farm costs can help revive their support in the Republican heartland in November's midterm elections.
Trump wants lower fuel prices, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said.
"President Trump remains committed to unleashing American energy dominance, cutting costs, and putting more money back in the pockets of hardworking American families," Rogers said.
For Jay Sorg, a fifth-generation farmer in New Richland, Minnesota, the order could save $1,500 to $2,000, but that is not enough to offset higher costs for fuel and other inputs. Like many farmers, he buys diesel in advance to store in tanks.
"In the grand scheme of our business, it's kind of inconsequential, especially when we already have fuel bought and in the tank for highway use," Sorg said. "It's a move to try to win votes."
Ryan Wagner, a farmer in Roslyn, South Dakota, worried that increasing usage of tax-exempt red diesel could drain government funds used to maintain roads.
"It's a very short-sighted plan that could come back and haunt us in the future," he said.
LIMITED ACCESS
For other motorists, it can be hard to get their hands on red diesel.
Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds, a Republican, issued a proclamation that allows vehicles to use dyed diesel on highways until February, but only if they are hauling specific agricultural products.
In Texas, drivers must register with the state to take advantage of a temporary suspension of restrictions on the use of red diesel on highways.
A Reuters reporter visited four sites around Houston that were listed online as selling red diesel by companies that offer fuel cards to commercial operators. Three of the sites sold only commercial diesel, and red diesel pumps at the fourth site were not working. A notice at the fourth site said red diesel was purely for agricultural use and should not be used on roads.
Vincenzo Lasalosi, a firefighter in Houston, said he considered using red diesel in his Ram 2500 truck due to high diesel prices but did not know where to find it.
"Even if I do find it, it's probably too far and not worth the drive to fill it up," he said. REUTERS
