As Trump's support slips, white evangelicals remain his Republican bedrock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:06:33 UTC
19:06:33 KST

As Trump’s support slips, white evangelicals remain his Republican bedrock
BLYTHEWOOD, South Carolina – US President Donald Trump is losing ground among many of the voters who returned him to the White House in 2024. But Reuters/Ipsos polling and interviews with white evangelical Christians show they remain his most reliable constituency and could prove crucial in the Nov 3 midterm elections.
With Republicans on the defensive amid record-low approval ratings for Trump, strong evangelical turnout could help the party limit losses driven by voter frustration over the cost of living and the war in Iran.
That loyalty was on display last week at Village Church, an evangelical congregation in Blythewood, South Carolina, where hundreds of worshippers gathered for a weekly “Bible and Politics” sermon by pastor Erik Estep. The backdrop: an unexpectedly competitive race for a Republican-held US Senate seat.
Speaking in the main worship hall, framed by a giant video screen and concert-style lighting, Estep did not endorse a candidate or party. But as he spoke against gambling, following sermons on abortion and socialism, he urged his predominantly white parishioners to view politics through a biblical lens.
“I believe the church is the bulwark of truth for our nation,” Estep said from the stage. “And it will take people like you and churches like this church to protect this nation spiritually and morally.”
The message resonated with Karen Whiting, a 72-year-old retired pharmaceutical executive who plans to vote for Republican Darline Graham over Annie Andrews, the Democrat. Graham was appointed by the governor to fill the seat of her late brother, Senator Lindsey Graham.
Whiting cited concerns that Democrats would allow transgender girls and women to compete in female sports, echoing other white evangelicals Reuters interviewed in South Carolina last week who prioritised social and religious issues over economic concerns.
“I’m voting for biblical principles, and I do not believe the Democratic Party stands for biblical principles,” Whiting said. “Without God, this country’s going to fail.”
If visitors to Village Church needed more explicit guidance on how to vote, a candidate guide available in the church lobby left little doubt. Produced by the conservative Christian advocacy group Palmetto Family Council and distributed to churches across South Carolina, it awarded Graham green check marks on all seven issues it rated, including restrictions on abortion medication and gender-affirming care, while Andrews received mostly red X’s.
Andrews offered a different reading of evangelical voters’ priorities. In a statement to Reuters, she said she had visited evangelical churches and met voters of various faiths, political persuasions and backgrounds, finding that they were chiefly concerned about the economy. “They’re struggling with the cost of everything. That’s why I’m running,” she said.
Strong bonds
Reuters/Ipsos polling shows Trump’s support among white evangelicals fell to 63% in October from 77% in January 2025. The decline is slightly smaller than his drop among the electorate as a whole, from 47% to 31%, and white evangelicals remain the only major demographic group tracked by Reuters/Ipsos where his support tops 60%.
The thrice-married Trump’s bond with white evangelicals has survived a decade of scandals and investigations, including dozens of allegations of sexual misconduct, which he denies, and a hush-money case involving a porn star. The question for Republicans is whether economic pressures and unhappiness over the Iran war, now in its eighth month, are weakening that bond.
Reuters interviews with 15 people at two South Carolina churches suggested that his hold on white evangelical voters remained strong. At Village Church and Carolina Baptist Church in the city of Spartanburg, about a 90-minute drive from Blythewood, only two of the 15 said they were considering Andrews, and none indicated they were abandoning Trump.
While several voiced frustration with the Iran conflict and rising gas prices, most said they trusted Trump to keep Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon or, like Trump, blamed inflation on policies enacted under Democratic president Joe Biden.
Chad Connelly, an evangelical activist who heads the Christian voter-engagement group Faith Wins, said that while evangelicals “don’t like paying higher prices”, they are equally animated by social issues. Concerns about transgender athletes are “really playing everywhere” across the nearly two dozen states he has visited this election cycle, he said.
White evangelicals’ loyalty to Trump reflects what Robert P. Jones, president of the Public Religion Research Institute, a non-profit organisation that studies religion and politics, calls a “grand bargain” forged during the 2016 election.
Many evangelicals have overlooked his personal conduct in exchange for his commitment to curtail abortion and LGBTQ rights, advance a conservative Christian vision of American life and pursue strict immigration policies that some supporters see as preserving the country’s white Christian identity, Jones said.
“That has proven to be more powerful for this group than what they’re having to pay at the gas pump,” Jones, who has written extensively about the rise of Christian nationalism in American politics, told Reuters.
Why evangelicals matter
White evangelicals make up about 13% of US adults but nearly a third of Trump’s winning coalition in 2024, according to a PRRI survey and a validated-voter analysis by the non-partisan Pew Research Center. More than 80% voted for Trump in each of his three presidential campaigns, according to Pew. They differ sharply from black Protestant evangelicals, who overwhelmingly support Democrats.
Evangelicals’ loyalty could also prove pivotal in Senate races beyond South Carolina that may help determine control of Congress, including in Iowa and Kansas, where white evangelicals make up a significant share of the electorate.
Opinion polls suggest the race in South Carolina is close. This week Trafalgar Group, a Republican-leaning pollster, released a survey showing Andrews trailing Graham by 3 percentage points.
Part of Graham’s challenge stems from lingering unease among some conservatives over her appointment to the Senate seat. Even after a boost from Trump, the political newcomer only narrowly defeated US Representative Ralph Norman in the party’s August run-off, underscoring questions among some Republicans about her experience and conservative credentials.
A spokesperson for the Graham campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Yet even evangelicals lukewarm on Graham, like 53-year-old Kevin Thomas, said they felt they had no choice. Thomas, who attended the Village Church sermon, said he did not trust Andrews on transgender issues, despite a recent campaign ad in which she said she opposed both transgender women competing in women’s sports and gender-affirming surgical operations for minors.
“I’m leaning towards holding my nose and voting for Graham,” said Thomas, who had backed Norman. “I’m not willing to sacrifice six years of having a Democrat representing us in South Carolina.” REUTERS

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Seawater temperature and salinity data collected by the National Academy of Marine Research (NAMR) during a 2024 Arctic scientific expedition have been archived on PANGAEA, an international platform for Earth and environmental sciences.
Fang Ying-chih (方盈智), an associate professor in National Sun Yat-sen University’s oceanography department, and NAMR associate research fellow Fu Ke-hsien (傅科憲) traveled aboard the German research vessel Polarstern from August to October 2024, per Liberty Times. Fu recorded oceanographic data along the route using expendable conductivity-temperature-depth probes to measure seawater temperature and salinity, according to Liberty Times. The measurements were taken between approximately 80 degrees north latitude and the North Pole.
The academy made two datasets publicly available on PANGAEA, covering raw and processed data, Liberty Times reported. It also released a comprehensive report, enabling international researchers to trace the data’s origins, processing procedures, and quality-control methods.
The academy said the Alfred Wegener Institute in Germany and the University of Bremen’s Center for Marine Environmental Sciences jointly operate PANGAEA.

Greenlight Family Hub (2026): Finally, a Digital Wall Calendar With a Voice Assistant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:01:00 UTC
19:01:00 KST

I set up a digital wall calendar at a friend’s house a couple of months ago. Her first question was one I’ve constantly asked myself as I test these devices in my own home: “Does it have a voice assistant?”
It feels like the one thing missing from these devices. Digital wall calendars have been on the rise in popularity this year, driven by the popularity of the Skylight Calendar. After testing multiple models in my own home, I can see why. These devices take any and all of the digital calendars you already have (Google Calendar, iCalendar, Outlook Calendar—you name it) and put them onto a single device in your home.
It’s great if you’re like my husband and me, who live by our Google Calendars but don’t want to be tied to our phones when discussing plans. These devices can also double as household management tools with meal planning, chore trackers, to-do lists, photo screen savers that double as a digital photo frame, and even financial management for your kids if you go with the Greenlight Family Hub.
The Greenlight Family Hub has been an interesting device in the world of digital calendars because of how many features it offers. It not only adds financial management, as the company was originally a banking tool for parents and their teens, but family location tracking, which uses the Greenlight app on a family member’s phone to show their location, or a GPS tracker that you can separately purchase for younger children.
But there’s one feature behind the paywall (a $10-a-month membership) that finally satisfies the thing I’ve always wanted: a voice assistant.
Greenlight’s proprietary voice assistant has been both easy to use and has given smart, thoughtful answers. So why isn’t there a voice assistant in every digital wall calendar? And conversely, why haven’t smart displays that do have smart voice assistants gained features like full-page calendars and chore charts?
Not Just a Calendar
Part of what makes Greenlight’s hub different from other digital calendars is that the company is using the calendar as a starting point for the offerings it already has. That’s also why it’s called the Family Hub instead of just a calendar like most other devices I’ve tested. Greenlight grew from a banking tool to a way to manage chores and money for kids and teens, and has now become a full family management platform where you can track your family’s calendars, chores, kids’ spending, and even family locations.
Greenlight says it noticed the lack of voice support among competitors’ offerings and baked that into its hub intentionally. “Voice assistants have been around for over a decade, yet when building the specs for Family Hub, we noticed that voice support was absent in the digital calendar market," says Sushil Sharma, chief product officer at Greenlight. "Our goal with Hub was to create an all-in-one command center for busy families to engage with technology in a way that feels natural and seamless. By combining a voice assistant feature with a centralized home display, we are able to limit the number of devices families need in their home.”
It’s also smart for families with younger children—Sharma pointed out that not all kids can read and type fluently, and voice support makes it more accessible for them and the rest of the family. But it’s also a way people are expecting to interact with their home devices after years of smart speakers and smartphones offering voice support.
Voice Report
Greenlight’s assistant reminds me of the modern, AI-powered iterations of Alexa and Google because it’s also powered by AI. Greenlight says its family AI assistant uses frontier large language models with Greenlight’s own proprietary safety tools that it designed with family safety in mind. That means the assistant shouldn’t get into sensitive or inappropriate topics (or accidentally tell your child Santa isn’t real) but will both schedule a timer and answer day-to-day questions. You’ll also see a conversation appear on the right-hand side, reminding me a lot of the Alexa+ experience on an Echo Show device.
Greenlight’s Hub is supposed to only wake at its wake phrase, “Hey Greenlight,” but in the days I’ve been testing it, I’ve found it to be a little sensitive and likely to wake at random. It also tends to keep listening, waiting to see if you’ll continue the conversation or give a new command, so if my family is having a general conversation after asking a question, Greenlight will try to pick up a question from that and answer it. I find myself often ordering Greenlight to stop.
That isn’t an issue just for Greenlight. My Google Gemini-powered smart speaker does the same thing, and both my son and I are quick to yell, “Google, stop!” to get it to stop trying to answer a question we didn’t ask. It’s a problem with these AI-powered voice assistants overall, but I’m finding I’d rather say the wake word multiple times than get interrupted.
Big Brother Energy
When I described to my editor the laundry list of features that the Greenlight Family Hub has, she said it sounded like a “Big Brother machine.” I see why, of course—tracking your location and financial information in a device that sounds like a simple calendar might come as a surprise to most people. It was certainly a surprise to me when I went to set up the hub through the app and ended up stuck on the financial pathway (Greenlight says it’s fixing this issue in the app but I had to have support clear my information so I could set up the hub without setting up a bank card for my child).
Still, I like how much it has to offer, even if it might feel a tad Big Brother-y for some. And while it does have a microphone, it doesn’t have a camera like most smart displays have, so in that sense it feels less creepy to me than other devices I’ve had in my home.
I also really like that most of the features are accessible without needing a premium subscription—notably the photo screen saver feature, which Skylight will charge you for. (Skylight’s business model in general has become charging for storage, for both its calendars and digital photo frames.) Greenlight charges instead for its AI assistant and voice interaction, along with family location sharing. If you’re less voice-inclined than I am, you’d be plenty happy with this hub without the premium subscription.
I am hoping we see more digital wall calendars add at least some kind of voice assistance, as well as offering some control of your smart home devices. Maybe I’m biased coming from a background in smart home technology, but it feels like a huge missed opportunity. Smart displays have existed for years (and Apple just announced its first one) but have lacked the key feature that digital wall calendars have to really make them a touch point in the home beyond your voice. I reached out to both Amazon and Skylight to ask why neither has introduced any such model yet, but both companies declined to comment.
Maybe, for a company like Skylight, it’s the cost of creating an assistant that would work with its platform and needing to change its hardware to include a microphone, but Amazon is well positioned to bring something like this to the market (especially since the newest version of Alexa, Alexa+, is already paywalled). I’m hopeful we’ll see the next generation of smart displays at least make some kind of calendar mode an option; I’d certainly rather see my calendar than another ad or piece of screen clutter on my Echo Show.

Ministers restate plan for combined force of 13 Type 26 frigates
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
11:00:57 BST
19:00:57 KST

Ministers have restated that a combined force of thirteen Type 26 frigates with Norway is expected to enter service from the late 2020s, with five Type 31 frigates in service by the early 2030s, and that the Type 23 fleet will go through phased retirement, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Andrew Rosindell, the Reform UK member for Romford, asked the Secretary of State for Defence whether he would make it his department’s policy to increase the lifespan of the Type 23 frigate fleet.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “As set out in the Defence Investment Plan, the Ministry of Defence will be implementing a phased retirement Type 23 Frigates after decades of proud and faithful service.
“The Government is investing in: new autonomous surface vessels; autonomous sub-surface; an amphibious fleet with the Netherlands; future Common Combat Vessels; and delivering a combined force of 13 Type 26 frigates with Norway expected to enter service from the late 2020s; five Type 31 frigates expected to be in service by the early 2030s; and new Fleet Solid Support ships.
“To avoid compromising operational security, the Ministry of Defence does not routinely disclose individual out of service dates or specific in-service dates for warships to avoid revealing elements of the Fleet’s long-term schedule. However, the Royal Navy continues to ensure that it has sufficient assets available to deliver operational outputs.”
Norway selected the Type 26 this year, ordering at least five ships to replace its Fridtjof Nansen class and signing a strategic partnership with Britain that runs beyond the hulls to joint operations, shared support and common training. Britain is building eight at Govan and Scotstoun, and the thirteen figure counts both navies as one force, which is how the partnership has been presented since the Norwegian decision.
The Type 23s are the ships carrying the burden in the meantime. Designed for a sixteen year life in the Cold War, several have served more than thirty years, and the general purpose ships have been leaving as their refits became uneconomic. Westminster and Argyll both went early after surveys found work that could not be justified, and the remaining hulls are the towed array ships that hunt submarines.

10:00:56 UTC
19:00:56 KST

Dansk Folkeparti (DF), the Danish People’s Party, wants a Pakistani man removed from a bill that would grant Danish citizenship to 2,055 foreign nationals next year.
The party’s citizenship spokesperson, Mikkel Bjørn, cited a Facebook post from 2016 that DF claims showed the man supporting an execution carried out under Islamic law.
Bjørn told public broadcaster DR that the government should remove the applicant from the bill or, at minimum, arrange for him to appear before Parliament’s Naturalisation Committee for questioning.
DR contacted the man, who said he could not explain why he had shared the post but denied supporting violence or murder.
“I respect people of all religions, from all backgrounds, and of all genders. I support freedom of speech, mutual respect, and peaceful coexistence,” he wrote in an email.
The dispute follows a similar demand from Liberal Alliance concerning a female citizenship applicant.
The party claims she repeatedly praised Hamas and its former leaders Yahya Sinwar and Ismail Haniyeh. It wants her questioned by the parliamentary committee.
The cases have intensified debate over whether citizenship applicants are adequately screened for attitudes considered incompatible with democratic values.
Denmark typically introduces citizenship bills every six months, following an extensive application process.
The current bill was first debated in Parliament, known as the Folketing, on February 5 but was postponed after Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen called a general election later that month.
Earlier in October, the government announced plans to introduce a screening system to identify potentially anti-democratic attitudes among citizenship applicants.
However, it has decided to proceed with the citizenship bill before the new screening system is ready.

Danish krone loses value against major currencies in 2026
The Danish krone has lost value in 2026, making Danish goods and services cheaper for customers in several foreign markets while making some holidays abroad more expensive.
The krone’s effective exchange rate, a weighted average of its value against the currencies of Denmark’s most important trading partners, has fallen by 2.7 percent since the start of the year. The figures come from a compilation by Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry.
“The weakening of the krone’s value makes Danish goods and services cheaper for customers abroad, which makes it easier for export companies to secure new orders,” Sørensen said.
“It is in both the US, China, Norway, and Japan where the exchange rate means that they now have to pay less money to buy our products,” he added.
The Norwegian krone has risen 12.9 percent against the Danish krone over the past year, while the Chinese yuan has gained 9.8 percent. The US dollar and Japanese yen have each risen 4.8 percent.
However, not all currencies have strengthened against the Danish krone. The Swedish krona and Indian rupee have lost value, making goods from those countries slightly more expensive for Danish importers.
Exchange rates also affect the cost of holidays abroad. When a foreign currency strengthens against the Danish krone, Danish travellers get less for their money.
“For those who love a trip to the snow, a trip to Norway has become significantly more expensive solely as a result of the strengthening of the Norwegian krone,” Sørensen said.
“The weakening of the Swedish krona and low inflation in Sweden, on the other hand, make a ski vacation much more economically affordable in Sweden compared to Norway,” he added.
The Turkish lira has recorded the largest decline among the currencies in the compilation. It now costs 9.7 percent less to buy Turkish currency than it did at the start of the year.
Denmark to get 51 emergency supermarkets stocked for major crises
Shoppers across Denmark will be able to buy essential groceries and household supplies during power outages, cyberattacks and other emergencies under a new initiative by Salling Group.
The Danish retail giant, which operates Bilka, Føtex and Netto, plans to establish 51 emergency-ready supermarkets nationwide by 2027.
The stores will be equipped to operate for at least 48 hours without electricity or external communication systems, ensuring access to basic necessities during major disruptions.
According to Salling Group, the network will include 17 Bilka stores, 32 Føtex stores and two Netto locations.
The stores will be distributed so that up to 80 percent of Denmark’s population lives within 50 kilometers of one.
Each location will maintain emergency stocks of 50 essential products, selected according to Danish authorities’ recommendations for household preparedness.
These include oatmeal, protein bars, canned meatballs in curry, rice cakes, tuna, beans, chickpeas and other foods with long shelf lives.
Nonfood essentials such as batteries, wet wipes and diapers will also be available.
Customers will be able to pay offline using almost all physical payment cards and digital cards stored on smartphones.
Salling Group recently partnered with payment provider Nets to help maintain card transactions during system failures.
CEO Anders Hagh said establishing the emergency stores remains a top priority, with preparations progressing toward the 2027 target.
Meanwhile, competing retailer Coop, which operates Brugsen, SuperBrugsen, 365discount and Kvickly, has not decided whether to establish similar stores.
Coop’s chief risk officer, Ulrik Mester, said the company was discussing crisis preparedness with authorities, including Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed (SAMSIK), Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security.

Several Danish public websites were shut down Wednesday after security vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language used by websites and online services worldwide.

Fake meat ban email tricks 1,200 Danish regional employees in phishing test
A warning about meat disappearing from workplace canteens prompted 1,200 employees in Denmark’s Capital Region to click a suspicious link in an internal cybersecurity test.
The exercise, reported by TV 2 Kosmopol, was designed to assess how well employees recognize phishing attempts, in which scammers impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into clicking links or sharing information.
Of the 13,000 employees who received the fake email, approximately 9 percent clicked the link.
The message claimed that meatballs and roast beef would be removed from workplace canteens and that some would switch to entirely vegan menus, excluding meat, dairy and eggs.
Employees were invited to click a link to find out how the changes would affect their local canteen.
However, the sender’s email address contained a small but important difference: it ended in “reqionh.dk” rather than the Capital Region’s actual domain, “regionh.dk”.
Anna Aaskilde Laursen, the region’s head of security, explained that the email deliberately targeted something employees cared about.
She told TV 2 Kosmopol that emotionally charged messages can prompt people to react without thinking, making it important to pause before clicking.
Laursen confirmed that the 1,200 employees who clicked the link would face no consequences.
Instead, the region intends to use the results to improve its preparedness for genuine cyberattacks.
Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security warns that phishing emails can be difficult to recognize because criminals often imitate official logos and use convincing language.
The agency recommends checking senders’ email addresses carefully and, when uncertain, contacting the supposed sender by telephone to verify whether a message is genuine.

Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey with Danish minister
Denmark’s Queen Mary will travel to Antalya, Turkey, from November 8 to 10 to participate in the United Nations climate summit COP31, the Danish Royal House has announced.

New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.
Venstre and other opposition parties expect to be left out of Denmark’s 2027 budget deal
Venstre does not expect to be included in an agreement with the government on Denmark’s 2027 national budget, party chairman Troels Lund Poulsen said after an introductory meeting on Wednesday.
“There is no willingness to listen to our views. It is a budget that has been agreed upon in advance with the government’s support parties. And that is just how it is,” Lund Poulsen said, according to Danish public broadcaster DR.
The government’s support parties are Enhedslisten, the Red-Green Alliance, and Alternativet, a green political party. Both are expected to reach a budget agreement with the government, particularly as it is the first national budget deal since the general election earlier this year.
Lund Poulsen said Venstre would be willing to attend further negotiations if the government invited the party.
Other opposition parties also expressed doubts about their chances of joining the agreement after meeting with Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard, a member of the Social Democrats, on Wednesday.
Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, does not expect to receive further invitations, according to its finance spokesperson, Anders Vistisen, who spoke to DR.
The same applies to De Konservative, the Conservative People’s Party.
“That is what I think. Because regarding the wishes we have for the budget, we have not been accommodated,” party chairman Mona Juul said.
The Conservatives were the only opposition party included in last year’s budget agreement, when the government consisted of the Social Democrats, Venstre and Moderaterne, the Moderates.
Liberal Alliance also took part in negotiations on Wednesday. Its political leader, Alex Vanopslagh, does not expect the party to be included in the final budget agreement, according to DR.
Danmarksdemokraterne, another opposition party, also attended negotiations on Wednesday.
The budget negotiations follow a setback for the government on Tuesday, when it had to abandon a proposal to tighten the eligibility requirements for senior pensions after failing to secure support from the parties involved in the negotiations.
The decision was welcomed by Pelle Dragsted, Enhedslisten’s political spokesperson.
“We are very happy about that. It was antisocial to cut the opportunities of worn-out workers to be able to retire,” he said on Tuesday.
Under its budget proposal, the government had planned to save 200 million kroner in 2028, 500 million kroner in 2029 and 800 million kroner in 2030 by tightening the requirements for senior pensions.
Enhedslisten and Alternativet held their budget negotiations with the government on Tuesday.
Danish municipalities shut down IT systems after potential security risk
Kombit, the IT organization serving Denmark’s municipalities, has shut down several of its digital services, either fully or partially, after identifying a potential technical security risk.
The shutdown began Wednesday afternoon and affects services including Aula, the digital communication platform used by schools and parents, and the municipal library system, Lars Skov Granerud, Kombit’s press manager, told news agency Ritzau.
“We have been made aware of a potential technical security risk in an underlying element of several of our solutions,” he said.
“Therefore, we decided a short while ago to shut down several of them.”
Kombit does not yet have a complete overview of the situation, Granerud said.
The disruption also affects several municipal systems used by local government employees in their daily work, including systems for processing benefit payments.
Aula has been shut down completely, while the library system is only partially affected, Granerud said.
Kombit has not disclosed which other digital services have been affected.
The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.
“The development in the labor market matches well with the general economic development. Activity is increasing, and it is therefore not surprising that more people are entering employment,” Sørensen said.
There are multiple reasons for the increase in employed people.
One of the main reasons is foreign labor, according to Jesper Grunnet-Lauridsen. He works as chief analyst at 3F, Fagligt Fælles Forbund, which is the United Federation of Danish Workers and the largest trade union in Denmark.
“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.
Energinet to prioritize addressing public service queries as power grid capacity runs short
Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.
The payment company Nets has lost a court case against Konkurrencerådet, the Danish Competition Council, which serves as the public competition authority in Denmark.
The ruling was delivered Wednesday by Sø- og Handelsretten, the Danish Maritime and Commercial Court.
Nets had asked the court to set aside a decision made by the Competition Council. That decision concluded that Nets abused its dominant position in the market for payment solutions between the years 2012 and 2016.
The case involves the company Teller, which was a subsidiary under Nets during that period. Teller offered what were described as exclusivity discounts to a number of large customers. The competition authorities determined that this practice broke legal rules meant to secure free competition, and they made their official decision on the case back in 2018.
The legal process has taken several years. Alongside the civil lawsuit, police have also run an investigation into Nets. That investigation led to criminal charges against the company, with authorities seeking a fine. The criminal case was put on hold to wait for the result of the civil case, and it has not yet gone to trial.
The specific legal reasons behind the court decision are not yet known. In a brief summary published on its website, the Maritime and Commercial Court stated that the full ruling will be released within four weeks.
The court noted that the delay is needed because the text of the ruling may contain business secrets that cannot be made public.
Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.
Denmark warns travelers in France to avoid protests as curfews continue
Denmark’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has advised people in France to stay away from demonstrations and large gatherings because of the risk of violence.
In updated travel advice on its website, the ministry warns that unrest and clashes between protesters and police remain possible in major cities, including Paris.
It also warns that authorities may introduce curfews at short notice.
Curfews were imposed overnight into Tuesday in parts of Paris and the northern French cities of Lille, Douai, Wattignies and Denain.
According to AFP, French police said the Paris curfew began at 11 p.m. Monday. In the other cities, restrictions remain in place Tuesday from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said Tuesday that the curfews had helped restore calm overnight, according to Reuters and AFP.
He added that local authorities could impose further restrictions if necessary.
“Tonight, new curfews will be introduced where the situation requires it. The decisions will be made locally by the prefects in cooperation with the mayors,” Lecornu wrote on X.
The measures follow a weekend of demonstrations that brought hundreds of thousands of people onto the streets across France.
Protesters are demonstrating against the high cost of living and what they see as a lack of economic opportunity and security.
The demonstrations were accompanied by reports of vandalism and looting.
According to the Paris Chamber of Commerce, between 300 and 400 shops were vandalized in the capital.
Nationwide, around 2,000 shops were affected, the French Chamber of Commerce told Reuters.
More than 1,800 people were arrested Saturday following demonstrations across the country.
Plans to tighten Denmark’s senior pension rules dropped after political opposition
The government has abandoned proposed changes to Denmark’s senior pension scheme after failing to secure support from parties behind the existing agreement.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen announced the decision Tuesday following a meeting with the parties involved.
The changes were part of the government’s proposed 2027 budget and were expected to save 200 million DKK in 2028, 500 million DKK in 2029 and 800 million DKK in 2030.
Under the proposal, applicants would have needed to prove that their ability to work was limited to 15 hours a week or less across all types of jobs, rather than just their most recent job.
This would have made qualifying for senior pension more difficult. In 2026, a single person receiving senior pension gets 22,053 DKK per month.
The scheme was introduced through a political agreement in 2019. Its signatories include the Danish People’s Party, the Social Democrats, the Socialist People’s Party, the Moderates and the Social Liberal Party.
Changes to the agreement require approval from all participating parties during the parliamentary term.
Several center-right parties opposed the proposal, while the Red-Green Alliance also rejected changes.
“We respect the agreements we have. It has not been my intention to terminate any agreement,” Halsboe-Jørgensen said.
“On the contrary. The fact that I called the colleagues from the other parties together today was precisely an expression of the fact that I actually wanted to discuss it with them, and that I respect that the agreement we have with each other gives all of them a veto right against changes in this area,” she added.
Dropping the proposal leaves a gap in the government’s budget plans.
Halsboe-Jørgensen said spending priorities would need to change but did not specify where the missing funds would come from.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard will now have to address the shortfall during negotiations on the 2027 Finance Act.
Four Danish opposition parties demand broader tax cuts in government plan
Denmark’s Liberal Party, Liberal Alliance, the Conservative People’s Party and Denmark’s Democrats say they will reject the government’s upcoming tax plan unless it includes cuts for people earning less than 58,000 DKK a month.
The four opposition parties will present their demands during tax negotiations with Minister for Taxation and Growth Jakob Engel-Schmidt later this week.
The government wants to remove the top-top tax and intermediate income tax, benefiting people earning more than approximately 58,000 DKK a month.
It also plans to reduce corporate tax by three percentage points starting in 2030.
The four parties argue that lower-income workers should also benefit.
“It is only fair and reasonable that the police officer, the shop assistant, the electrician, and everyone else with a salary below 58,000 kroner also get a tax cut,” Conservative leader Mona Juul said in a written statement.
Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen said his party supports reducing corporate and intermediate taxes but wants cuts for everyone in employment.
Liberal Alliance leader Alex Vanopslagh said “completely ordinary Danes must get more out of going to work”.
Denmark Democrats leader Inger Støjberg called for tax changes that would help families facing higher fuel, energy and food prices.
The government may need support from the four center-right parties to pass its plan.
Its usual parliamentary allies, The Red-Green Alliance, a left-wing party, and The Alternative, a green progressive party, are not expected to support several of the proposed measures.
Government plan would remove SU from 14,000 students living with parents
About 14,000 higher education students living with their parents would lose their entire state education grant under the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
Another 8,000 students in the same group would receive lower payments, Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said in a parliamentary response.
Denmark’s state education grant is commonly known as SU.
An estimated 31,800 higher education students living at home received SU in 2025.
The government proposes ending payments for students whose parents have a combined annual income above 710,077 DKK. This corresponds to an average monthly income of 29,583 DKK for each parent in a two-parent household.
Payments would gradually decline for students whose parents earn between 419,589 and 710,077 DKK annually. The lowest monthly grant would be 500 DKK before disappearing entirely above the upper threshold.
The government initially estimated that 81,000 students living at home across different education programs would be affected. The later decision to reduce grants gradually for middle-income households means the final number could be higher.
Disability supplements and additional support for single parents would remain available regardless of parental income.
The Socialist People’s Party and Social Liberal Party have faced criticism for supporting the reductions.
SF leader Pia Olsen Dyhr acknowledged that her party had not proposed the measure but said it was part of the compromises required in government.
Minister calls for talks after report finds major employment losses due to stress
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr will convene labor unions, employer organizations and other groups for talks on preventing work-related stress.
The first roundtable discussion will take place Friday following a new report from the Danish Economic Council’s independent economic advisers.
The report estimates that severe work-related stress reduces Denmark’s labor supply by between 16,000 and 39,000 people.
More than one in 10 people affected by severe stress do not return to employment, while more than one in three disability pension recipients receive the benefit after a stress reaction, according to the report.
“Stress makes us poorer,” Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party said. “This applies both to the individual person who becomes ill with stress and their family, but it also matters for our society.”
Chief Economic Adviser Jakob Roland Munch said severe stress has long-lasting effects on people’s connection to the labor market.
However, the report found no evidence that the number of severe stress cases has increased during the past 15 to 20 years.
Dyhr said Denmark must place greater emphasis on preventing stress instead of responding only after people become ill.
The government’s proposed 2027 budget includes 50 million DKK for a prevention fund intended to help people remain healthy and employed.
Dyhr said the government wants stronger evidence about which preventive measures work before deciding how to prioritize future efforts.
The European Commission has made security the main focus of its new Arctic strategy as Russia and China expand their activity in the region.
The approach marks a significant shift from the European Union’s 2021 strategy, which concentrated primarily on international cooperation, climate and environmental protection.
“As Russia and China increase their presence and ambitions, the Arctic has become a frontline in the global power competition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The Commission fears the Arctic could become a major source of conflict with Russia after the war in Ukraine ends.
The strategy proposes expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity and strengthening protection of northern maritime borders and critical undersea infrastructure.
The EU’s 27 countries collectively have about 10 icebreakers, compared with an estimated 40 operated by Russia.
The Commission also proposes creating a maritime security center to monitor activity in the Arctic.
A separate Arctic cable center would monitor, protect and repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. It could later track ships belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which transports sanctioned oil and gas.
Western intelligence services also suspect that Russia has used shadow fleet vessels in hybrid attacks.
The strategy contains no spending figures and must now be discussed with EU governments.
Kallas said Arctic security was a European concern because Denmark, Sweden and Finland are Arctic countries and more than 500,000 EU citizens live in the region.
Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.
Social Democrat warns foreign labor risks creating master-servant society
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek has warned that Denmark risks developing a society divided between those providing low-paid services and those becoming dependent on them.
“What do we become as human beings if we slowly let low-paid Africans and Asians do everything that is not immediately manageable?” Dybvad Bek said Monday during a budget debate in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
He questioned whether Danes lose practical skills and the ability to learn when they rely on foreign workers, delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for routine tasks.
Dybvad Bek referred to German philosopher Georg Hegel’s theory that a master becomes increasingly helpless as a servant performs more of the work.
He said individual consumers were not responsible for the development.
“It is up to us politicians to stop the flow of underpaid labor that forms the basis for these services,” he said.
Dybvad Bek argued that goods and services should be priced at a level that allows workers to earn a living wage.
He also warned that Denmark could create new parallel societies if foreign workers remain socially separated from the people they serve.
The comments came as Dybvad Bek presented a government proposal requiring employers to finance Danish lessons for workers from countries outside the European Union before they arrive.
He said companies should help pay for the integration of workers from whom they profit.
Lego named Denmark’s most valuable brand at 114 billion DKK
Lego has Denmark’s most valuable brand, with an estimated value of 114 billion DKK, according to a report by British consultancy Brand Finance.
The Danish toy company’s brand value increased by 54 percent from the previous year, business newspaper Børsen reported.
Nordea placed second with a brand value of 46.2 billion DKK, while shipping company Maersk ranked third.
“Lego is an exceptional brand, regardless of how you measure it,” Brand Finance Chief Operating Officer Mike Rocha told Børsen.
Brand Finance calculates how much a company would hypothetically have to pay to license its brand if it did not own it.
The consultancy said Lego’s financial performance contributed to the increase in value.
Lego recorded revenue of 83.5 billion DKK in 2025, an increase of 12 percent from the previous year and the highest annual total in the company’s history.
Growth accelerated during the first half of 2026, when Lego’s revenue rose by 21 percent compared with the same period in 2025.
Lego declined to comment to Børsen on the Brand Finance report.
MobilePay launches digital proof of age for use in Danish stores
MobilePay’s nearly 4.8 million Danish users will be able to document their age through the payment app when shopping in physical stores.
The feature will appear under the app’s “Wallet” menu in an update being gradually released from Tuesday, Vipps MobilePay said.
Users can add a passport-style photograph to the digital proof, which displays only their name, photo and age category.
Vipps MobilePay product manager Dennis Kvade said the need to confirm age and identity was increasing both online and in physical stores.
“It is not particularly practical to bring your passport on a night out,” he said, adding that existing age checks can also be vulnerable to fraud.
Supermarket chain Rema 1000 will accept MobilePay’s proof of age. Its employees will receive information about the feature.
However, the MobilePay document is not an official identification card and cannot replace a passport, health insurance card or driving licence.
It is intended for situations in stores and nightlife venues where young people must show they are old enough to purchase restricted products such as alcohol.
Individual businesses can decide whether to accept it, meaning users cannot assume it will be recognized everywhere.
Denmark’s Agency for Digital Government launched AltID earlier in 2026 as the country’s first official digital proof of age and identification app for both online and in-person use.
Pensioners occupy Aarhus rehabilitation center to protest closure
Between 10 and 12 pensioners occupied Rehabiliteringshøjskolen in Risskov on Tuesday and locked staff outside to protest its planned closure.
The demonstration began after the Aarhus City Council decided to close the residential rehabilitation center at the end of 2026, TV2 Østjylland reported.
“The folk high school cannot raise the dead, but it can keep them alive,” read one sign displayed in a window.
The center provides residential stays lasting two to five weeks, during which people receive support and guidance from a healthcare team.
Protester Torben Blom said the program had been crucial after both his legs were amputated.
“It has meant that I have become a human being again,” he said.
The center opened in 2018 but will close because Denmark’s healthcare reform requires Aarhus Municipality to transfer certain responsibilities and buildings to the regional authority.
Health and Care Alderman Metin Lindved Aydin of the Social Liberal Party said the municipality could not afford to build a similar facility during the next four years.
He said the reform required the municipality to save 185 million DKK.
Aydin said other rehabilitation services would remain available but acknowledged that they would differ from the existing program.
He described the occupation as a new form of senior activism and called it “refreshing” and “brave,” while saying he could not encourage illegal occupations.
Aydin said he would not call the police.
Danish home sales fall 12 percent as higher rates slow market
Denmark’s housing market is showing signs of slowing after a strong start to 2026, according to transaction figures from property portal Boligsiden.
A total of 7,709 homes were sold in September, 12 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
Housing transactions during the first nine months of 2026 were three percent below the corresponding period in 2025.
Apartment sales have fallen most sharply. Eight percent fewer apartments have been sold nationwide this year, while Copenhagen has recorded a decline of 23 percent.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said rising mortgage rates could partly explain the slowdown.
Fixed-rate mortgages have recently fluctuated between four and five percent, compared with 3.5 percent at the beginning of the year.
Higher prices for gasoline, natural gas and electricity are also reducing the money households have available, he said.
However, strong employment and rising inflation-adjusted incomes continue to support the housing market.
Sales of houses and terraced homes are also below last year’s level. Holiday home sales, by contrast, have increased by 4.5 percent.
Boligsiden communications director Birgit Daetz said the increase indicates that many households remain financially secure because holiday homes are traditionally purchased during periods of economic strength.
Rising property values and the possibility of rental income may also make such purchases more affordable, she said.
Copenhagen mayor disputes Frederiksen’s claims about meat in nursing homes
Copenhagen Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling of the Socialist People’s Party has accused Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of presenting an inaccurate picture of food policies in the city’s nursing homes.
Frederiksen wrote on Instagram that a Copenhagen proposal could prevent nursing home residents from receiving the meat they want.
“It is a lack of respect for the elderly person’s right to make decisions for themselves,” Frederiksen wrote. “Those people in nursing homes who have toiled and slaved for our country must of course be allowed to eat meat.”
Welling rejected the claim.
“The elderly must naturally have the food they know and like. For many of them, that involves meat,” she wrote.
Welling said individual nursing homes can decide how to plan menus and how much meat to serve. She said residents’ nutritional needs should take priority over climate concerns.
The dispute follows debate over Copenhagen’s food and meal strategy, which aims to make municipal meals more sustainable and reduce purchases of beef.
A consultancy analysis reported that some nursing homes had rejected residents’ birthday requests for beef because of carbon reduction targets.
The study surveyed 200 nursing home residents and 607 people receiving meals at home.
Between 58 and 60 percent were satisfied with the food, while 8 to 13 percent reported little or no satisfaction.
Several nursing home residents criticized meat quality and said beef rarely appeared on menus. The analysis also found that residents wanted greater influence over their meals.
More than half of surveyed Danish teachers feel stressed every week
More than half of teachers in a new union survey said they experience stress daily or weekly, with most attributing it to their working conditions.
The survey by Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, included responses from 1,901 public school teachers and kindergarten class leaders.
Sixteen percent said they felt stressed at work every day, while 36 percent experienced stress weekly and 23 percent monthly.
Nine in 10 of those experiencing stress said workplace conditions were responsible.
“We are facing a working environment problem in the public schools, while at the same time many teachers choose to leave,” union chair Gordon Ørskov Madsen said.
More than one in three respondents said they had taken sick leave from teaching because of stress.
Teachers identified classroom disruption, insufficient preparation time, heavy workloads and difficulty obtaining help for pupils with special needs as major pressures.
Some also reported that parents expected them to resolve conflicts between pupils that occurred outside school.
Nana Vaaben, an associate professor at University College Copenhagen, said teachers can experience moral stress when they know pupils need help but lack the authority to provide it.
Respondents identified fewer teaching hours, more preparation time and better support for pupils with special needs as the measures most likely to reduce stress.
The union plans to raise those proposals in upcoming negotiations with the government and other labor market parties.
