Denmark and Vietnam will establish a strategic partnership during Vietnamese President Tô Lâm’s state visit to Denmark this week.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Lâm are expected to formally enter into the agreement Tuesday, the Prime Minister’s Office said.
The partnership will build on a 2023 agreement covering areas including climate policy, green growth and the transition to cleaner energy.
The Prime Minister’s Office did not provide further details about the new agreement.
“I am pleased that we, here on the 55th anniversary of Denmark’s diplomatic relations with Vietnam, are now further strengthening Danish-Vietnamese cooperation,” Frederiksen said.
“In an unpredictable world, we need strong partnerships. Both for Denmark and for the EU,” she added.
The agreement is being announced during a state visit by Lâm and his spouse, Ngô Phương Ly.
Independent authority to investigate police strikes against photographers
The Independent Police Complaints Authority will investigate reports that police officers struck two press photographers with batons during demonstrations in Copenhagen on Saturday.
The photographers worked for Danish newspapers Politiken and Ekstra Bladet and were involved in separate incidents during demonstrations for and against remigration.
Copenhagen Police referred the cases to the independent authority, known as DUP, following criticism from both newspapers.
“The Copenhagen Police in no way wish to place obstacles in the way of the press carrying out their work,” police said.
Politiken reported that its photographer was struck several times, had his camera smashed and received treatment at an emergency room.
Ekstra Bladet’s photographer said he was struck on the arm with a baton despite carrying cameras and visible press credentials.
Politiken editor-in-chief Christian Jensen described the incident as a serious attack on press freedom.
“The police make the press their adversary by preventing us from doing our job, which is also about witnessing the police’s exercise of their power,” he wrote.
Ekstra Bladet editor-in-chief Knud Brix also called the reported incident “completely unacceptable.”
The Danish Union of Press Photographers and the Danish Union of Journalists have requested a meeting with the national police commissioner.
They want police leadership to explain how similar incidents will be prevented and how journalists will be protected while covering demonstrations.
Delayed UN climate reports could weaken action before COP33, Danish expert warns
Global climate efforts could face serious setbacks if the UN climate panel does not publish its next assessment reports before the COP33 summit in 2028, a Danish climate expert has warned.
“Without the reports, countries will stand on a basis that is less comprehensive. They will lack crucial knowledge,” said Adrian Lema, head of the National Centre for Climate Research at the Danish Meteorological Institute.
He said countries could spend time debating scientific facts instead of agreeing on action.
“The consequence may be that we set climate action back years, and that uncertainty is created about some of the progress we have achieved,” Lema said.
COP33 will include the next major review of countries’ progress under the 2015 Paris Agreement.
A weeklong meeting of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, known as the IPCC, ended Friday without agreement on a budget or timetable for the reports.
Lema attended as Denmark’s lead negotiator and wanted the reports published well before COP33.
Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iran, India and China argued that publication before the summit was unnecessary, he said.
IPCC decisions require consensus rather than majority votes.
Lema said an agreement remained possible but had become more difficult.
“If we can get enough countries to say it loud and clear, then the few who disagree will be under a different pressure,” he said.
Copenhagen begins separate collection of used diapers for recycling
The City of Copenhagen began installing separate waste bins for used diapers in residential courtyards and municipal day-care centers Monday.
Diapers previously had to be placed with residual waste and were incinerated. They will now be processed at Denmark’s first diaper treatment facility.
“There is a major climate benefit in recycling the diapers instead of incinerating them,” Climate, Environment and Technology Mayor Line Barfod of the Red-Green Alliance said.
The city estimates that between 85 and 94 percent of diaper waste, including liquids and feces, can be converted into new materials.
Cellulose and the contents of the diapers will become biofiber used to produce biogas, electricity and district heating.
Plastic components can be recycled into products such as car interiors. Superabsorbent polymers can become binding material for the construction industry.
Collection will expand to municipal nursing homes, senior housing and other city institutions in February 2027.
Residents of detached houses and members of allotment garden associations will also be able to join the program next year. The scheme is expected to be fully implemented in 2029.
The bins will accept diapers for children and adults, incontinence pads, paper-based cloths and wet wipes without plastic or bamboo. Menstrual hygiene products are excluded.
Diaper waste must be placed in an ordinary plastic trash bag sealed with a tight knot.
Study finds misogynistic TikTok content can appear within minutes
Young male TikTok users can encounter misogynistic content within minutes, even when they do not actively search for it, according to a Danish study.
Researchers from the Center for Digital Pedagogy and Analyse & Tal created eight fictional profiles representing men ages 16 to 19 interested in fitness, dating, investing and gaming.
After the profiles interacted with videos about those subjects, researchers allowed them to scroll automatically for one hour.
Content associated with the “manosphere” appeared after an average of three minutes. In one case, it appeared after 21 seconds.
The manosphere refers to online communities and content that degrade women or support restricting their rights and opportunities.
Researchers also examined one year of viewing data provided by 29 men ages 15 to 22. They identified an average of five to six manosphere videos in each participant’s weekly feed.
The researchers said this was a minimum estimate but emphasized that the 29 participants were not representative of all young men.
Employment and Equality Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen of the Social Democrats called for stronger social media regulation and more discussion in schools and homes.
TikTok said it takes the findings seriously.
“We proactively remove 98.1 percent of the videos that violate our rules on hate and hateful behavior,” Nordic communications director Lukasz Lindell said.
TikTok said it was also working to diversify recommendations and interrupt repetitive content patterns.
Government wants employers to fund Danish lessons for foreign workers
The Danish government wants employers to pay for Danish lessons for workers from countries outside the European Union before they arrive in Denmark.
Social Democratic finance spokesperson Kaare Dybvad Bek announced the proposal Monday during the Folketing’s debate on the government’s 2027 budget bill.
“It provides a saving of 100 million DKK, but first and foremost it sends a clear signal that people who come to the country to work must speak Danish,” he said.
Dybvad Bek said the issue concerned Denmark’s understanding of itself as a society.
More foreign workers have entered the restaurant and service industries in recent years, particularly in Copenhagen. This has led to more customers being served in English rather than Danish, he said.
During the debate, Dybvad Bek also argued that Danes risk losing practical skills when they rely on food delivery services such as Wolt and artificial intelligence for manageable tasks.
He also referred to planned restrictions affecting what he called “underpaid African agricultural workers.”
Dybvad Bek further criticized Nepalese and Iranian nationals who, he said, use Denmark’s education system to enter the labor market while avoiding other requirements.
Regional trains suspended between Odense and Fredericia after cable damage
Regional train services between Odense and Fredericia have been suspended until at least 2 p.m. Monday because of a severed cable.
DSB, Denmark’s national rail operator, has ordered rail replacement buses and updated its journey planner.
InterCity and express trains continue to operate on the route, although passengers may experience longer travel times.
“In Odense and Fredericia, there are staff in orange vests who can assist with guidance,” DSB said.
Banedanmark, the state agency responsible for Denmark’s railway infrastructure, is working to repair the damaged cable.
Train services on the route were expected to return to full capacity Monday after several days of disruptions. The cable damage means that this is no longer possible.
Passengers have experienced longer journeys and fewer trains between the two cities since a fire damaged a relay hut near Aarup in western Funen on October 9.
The hut contained electronic equipment used by the railway’s signaling system. The fire caused signal failures between Middelfart and Odense, disrupting services on Funen and across Denmark.
Even after more trains return, services will continue at reduced speeds near Aarup Station, where trains will temporarily be unable to stop.
Sunny Monday to give way to rainy and windy week in Denmark
Denmark can expect sunshine Monday before rain and stronger winds arrive during the rest of the week.
“On Monday, we have a beautiful autumn day in store,” Danish Meteorological Institute meteorologist Marie Timm said. “There will be some high-altitude clouds in the sky, but otherwise it is a beautiful day where there will be sun for everyone.”
After overnight temperatures fell close to freezing in some areas, daytime temperatures will rise to between 9 and 13 degrees Celsius.
Winds will generally be light to moderate, although coastal areas could experience fresher conditions.
Tuesday will begin dry with some sunshine before clouds and rain move across Denmark from the southeast.
The islands will receive rain during the morning and early afternoon, while northern Jutland will be affected later.
Timm said the amount of rain and strength of the wind remained uncertain because forecasts continued to change.
Another weather front will bring rain from the west Wednesday, with only brief dry periods expected.
Widespread rain is also forecast Thursday, followed by stronger southerly winds and further rain Friday.
Daytime temperatures from Tuesday through Friday will range from 8 to 13 degrees, while nighttime temperatures will remain between 5 and 10 degrees.
Timm advised people to bring rainwear rather than umbrellas because of the expected wind.
One in three Danish teachers reports verbal abuse from pupils
One in three Danish public school teachers experienced rude or abusive language from pupils during the previous week, according to a new survey.
Four in 10 teachers said such incidents occurred daily or several times a week, education trade publication Folkeskolen reported.
The survey was completed by 1,901 teachers and kindergarten class leaders between August 26 and September 14, 2026.
Teachers reported comments including “You fucking bad teacher,” “You are a damn idiot” and “You don’t boss me around.”
Lars Peter Sønderbo Andersen, a senior researcher in occupational and environmental medicine at Regional Hospital Gødstrup, said the language damages teachers’ working environment and undermines their authority in classrooms.
He said the problem has worsened in recent years.
In a similar survey conducted almost 10 years ago, one in four teachers reported being called derogatory terms such as “bitch,” “idiot” or “whore” at least once a month.
Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, described the new findings as concerning.
“Some of these statements are quite severe, and we can hear from the inquiries we receive that it affects the teachers when they are spoken to like that,” union representative Thomas Andreasen said.
He called for schools to establish clear, shared rules for acceptable language. He also said having more permanent teachers in classrooms could help.
Denmark contacts more than 25 countries seeking prison spaces
Denmark has contacted more than 25 European countries about potentially renting prison spaces as its correctional system faces record overcrowding.
“The Danish Prison and Probation Service is in a serious situation,” Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen of the Social Democrats said. “We must do everything we can to resolve the capacity challenges in Danish prisons.”
Denmark already has an agreement to rent 300 prison spaces in Kosovo for foreign nationals sentenced to deportation. However, delays mean the renovated prison is not expected to begin accepting inmates until late 2027 or early 2028.
The original plan expected inmates to begin serving sentences there in early 2023.
Wammen called the Kosovo agreement important but said additional measures were needed to relieve Denmark’s prisons.
The Justice Ministry declined to identify the countries it contacted or disclose the correspondence. It said publication could risk damaging Denmark’s foreign policy interests.
Estonia’s Justice Ministry confirmed that Denmark had not entered discussions with it. Estonia is concentrating on an existing agreement under which it began receiving inmates from Sweden in 2026.
At the end of September, Denmark had about 4,650 inmates but only 4,300 prison spaces, according to the Prison Officers’ Union.
The union calculated the average occupancy rate at 105.4 percent, the highest recorded level. It stood at 102.7 percent in 2025.
Denmark rejects Russian proposal for maritime and air security agreement
Russia has urged Denmark to enter into a security agreement intended to prevent incidents at sea and in the air, Danish broadcaster TV 2 reported.
The Russian Embassy in Denmark said Russia had previously made the same proposal.
“Today, one can only note that Russia’s initiative for de-escalation has not been met with understanding,” the embassy wrote.
The appeal follows a September incident in which the Russian frigate Soobrazitelny fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter in international waters near Gedser.
According to the Danish Armed Forces, the flares were fired without warning while the Fennec helicopter was photographing the frigate during a routine mission.
Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, later accused the helicopter of acting “provocatively.”
The embassy said an agreement could provide a legal framework for preventing similar incidents.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats rejected the proposal.
“Russia’s aggressive behavior clearly and deliberately violates the international rules by which the country is already bound,” he said. “As long as that is the case, entering into more agreements that are not complied with does not solve the problem.”
The embassy said Russia had protested through diplomatic channels over similar incidents in 2025 and 2026.
Eight arrested during demonstration and counterprotests in Copenhagen
Eight people were arrested Saturday in connection with a demonstration organized by the movement Det Danske Folk in central Copenhagen.
Three arrests occurred before the demonstration began at 2 p.m. in Kongens Nytorv, Copenhagen Police Deputy Inspector Jakob Hansen said.
Two people were arrested after being “in disagreement about some things,” while another was arrested for refusing to provide their name to police.
Five more people were arrested around 5 p.m. as the demonstration ended at Højbro Plads.
“As the demonstration is dispersed, there are smaller groups that begin putting on masks and initiating confrontations with others,” Hansen said. “We have to prevent that, and that leads to a clash with the police.”
Officers drew their batons during the confrontation.
Police did not disclose why the five people were arrested or how many people were involved. It was also too early to specify possible charges against any of the eight people.
The demonstrators marched from Kongens Nytorv toward Christiansborg Palace Square. Counterprotesters gathered at several locations along the route.
Det Danske Folk promoted the demonstration with slogans supporting what it called “fair and realistic remigration” and opposing Islamization, Sharia law and social control.
The counterprotesters gathered under the slogan “No to remigration.”
Electricity’s share of Danish energy use rises to 23.4 percent
Electricity accounted for 23.4 percent of Denmark’s total energy consumption in 2025, an increase of 1.5 percentage points from the previous year.
Green Power Denmark, an industry organization representing the Danish energy sector, said the increase was driven mainly by electric vehicles and the district heating sector’s use of electric boilers and heat pumps.
The organization said growing electrification is gradually reducing Denmark’s reliance on oil and natural gas.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is happening in the Middle East and American politics,” Green Power Denmark chief executive Kristian Jensen said.
He said Danish energy prices remain affected by developments abroad because the country still relies on prices set by global markets.
Denmark’s electrification rate rose by only 3.8 percentage points in total from 2016 through 2024, making the 1.5-point increase in 2025 significant.
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of total energy consumption by 2035.
Jensen said achieving that target would require industrial companies to replace natural gas with electricity and heat pumps.
He pointed to iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, as examples of industries already using heat pumps.
Such changes could reduce companies’ carbon dioxide emissions and energy costs while improving their competitiveness, Jensen said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available.
The 21-year-old singer has gone from posting piano videos on TikTok to becoming one of Denmark’s biggest pop stars. On Friday, she received the top prize at DR’s annual P3 Guld music awards.
Danish singer Annika has won P3 Prisen, the main award at one of Denmark’s most prominent annual music events, P3 Guld.
The 21-year-old received the award Friday evening at DR Koncerthuset in Copenhagen, a year after being nominated for the same prize but losing out to Danish band Aphaca.
P3 Guld is the annual music awards show organised by P3, the youth-oriented music and entertainment radio station run by Danish public broadcaster DR.
The event celebrates artists who have made a significant impact on Danish music over the past year, with P3 Prisen regarded as its main award.
Annika, whose full name is Annika Wedderkopp, was selected by a P3 jury ahead of fellow nominees Zar Paulo and producer Anton Westerlin, who is also her boyfriend.
“With an authentic foundation in her own life, Annika creates massive hits about breakups and infatuations, about doubt and a steely belief that everything will naturally work out,” the jury said.
From TikTok to the Danish charts
Annika’s rise has been rapid.
She began by posting videos of herself singing at the piano on TikTok before breaking through with “Knuser hjerter” in 2024.
She followed it with several successful releases, including “Så længe jeg er sexy”, and won P3 Talentet, the event’s talent award, that same year.
Last year, she released her debut album “AW”, which includes “Stolt”, a collaboration with Danish rapper Lamin. She also opened Roskilde Festival’s Orange Stage, the festival’s largest and most prestigious stage.
Previous recipients of P3 Prisen include some of Denmark’s best-known contemporary artists, including The Minds of 99, Tobias Rahim, Artigeardit, Lamin, Tina Dickow and Jada.
Other winners
Several other awards were presented at Friday’s ceremony.
Guldimund and Saveus won P3 Lytterhittet – the listeners’ choice award – for their song “Vil du noget?”.
Zar Paulo received P3 Live, an award recognising an artist who has distinguished themselves on Denmark’s live music scene. The award returned this year after previously being presented in 2001 and 2009.
Danish-Faroese artist Friða Saiya won P3’s Næste, a new award that has replaced P3 Talentet and highlights emerging artists.
Criticism over lack of women
This year’s P3 Guld also faced criticism before the ceremony over the gender balance among its performers.
Twelve men and two women were scheduled to perform during the evening.
Ditte Christiane Jensen, head of editorial at DR Ung, defended the lineup in a written response to Ritzau.
“Talent, creativity and artistic quality are not about gender,” she said.
“This year’s lineup was put together based on the artists and bands that have left a significant mark on the music year and in P3’s universe.”

Trump: Greenland deal biggest real estate deal ever
The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.
US President Donald Trump has described a new defence and security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as potentially “the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made”.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.
“It is probably the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made.”
Trump was campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
His comments come after months of tension over Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has repeatedly said that the United States wants control and ownership of Greenland, arguing that the island is crucial to American national security.
Two new US military bases
The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new security and defence agreement on Greenland at the end of September following lengthy negotiations.
The agreement was signed at the United Nations in New York shortly after Trump addressed the UN General Assembly.
It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
Trump’s comments came as Republicans campaign to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Democrats are currently polling more strongly in the race for the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains more uncertain.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.

Indonesia haze: why Jakarta won’t declare wildfires a national disaster
Indonesia resists declaring the wildfires a national disaster despite health crises, facing criticism over political and budget priorities
4-MIN READ4-MIN
 Listen
Resty Woro Yuniarin Jakarta
Indonesia’s government has resisted mounting calls to declare widespread forest and land fires a national disaster, insisting it can handle the crisis alone as residents report worsening health impacts and disaster experts warn that a broader, coordinated response is needed.
Critics suggest the reluctance may stem from concerns that a national declaration could force Jakarta to redirect funds from other political priorities, while exposing the administration to greater scrutiny over its disaster response.
The dispute intensified on Tuesday – the second anniversary of President Prabowo Subianto’s administration – when student protesters across the country demanded a national disaster declaration, the restoration of damaged ecosystems and action against both the rising cost of living and the perceived erosion of democracy.
A similar demand was included in a class-action lawsuit filed by civil society and indigenous groups in West Kalimantan last month, though the government maintains the fires do not warrant such a designation.
“If a national disaster is declared, there will inevitably be those who exploit the situation. Disaster management is now nationally mandated, no longer the responsibility of regional governments,” Dudung Abdurachman, Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs, told reporters on Wednesday.

Hacker attempts to compromise 1,700 accounts at Aarhus University
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:39 UTC
19:00:39 KST

A hacker gained access to a server at Aarhus University and attempted to access and change passwords belonging to approximately 1,700 users, the university has confirmed.
The attempted password changes were unsuccessful after the intrusion was detected Monday, according to a statement published on the university’s internal website.
There is currently no indication that sensitive or confidential information was leaked during the attack. However, the university said further investigations would be carried out in the coming days to establish the full extent of the incident.
The university also clarified that the attack was unrelated to the security vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, a widely used programming language, which prompted temporary shutdowns of several Danish websites Wednesday.
Despite the breach, Aarhus University said students and employees could continue their normal activities without disruption.
However, it urged everyone to remain particularly vigilant about suspicious online activity, including phishing attempts, in which criminals use fraudulent messages to obtain passwords or other personal information.
Anyone noticing unusual activity has been advised to contact the university’s IT support team.
Minister for Societal Security and Emergency Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen, from Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, confirmed that authorities were aware of the incident.
In a written statement, she said the Agency for Societal Security was closely monitoring developments and maintaining contact with the university.
“There is dialogue with Aarhus University, and relevant higher education institutions have already been gathered for a briefing where the Agency for Civil Security has advised,” the minister said.
Danske Bank announces third round of layoffs this year
Danske Bank is cutting 106 jobs, around half of them in Denmark, in its third round of layoffs this year.
The bank announced the cuts in a press release on Thursday, saying they are intended to help create a “more efficient and competitive bank”.
The remaining positions are in the bank’s operations in Finland, Lithuania, Norway, Poland and Sweden.
“We continue to develop Danske Bank to meet our customers’ expectations, strengthen our competitiveness, and realize the ambitions in our Forward ’28 strategy,” Karsten Breum, the bank’s head of human resources, said in the release.
“This means that we continuously simplify the organization, invest in new competencies, and move resources to the areas where we create the greatest value for our customers.
“It is a natural part of running and developing a large company.”
The latest cuts follow two previous rounds of job reductions in 2026.
In February, Danske Bank announced that it would cut 420 positions across the organization. At the time, the bank said it wanted to adapt to customer needs, invest in technology and advisory services, and become more digital.
Three months later, a further 262 positions were affected. The bank gave broadly similar reasons for those cuts.
Both earlier rounds primarily affected employees in Denmark.
Breum acknowledged the impact of the latest decision on employees.
“Decisions like these affect people,” he said in Thursday’s press release.
“For the colleagues who are affected, it is a difficult situation. Therefore, it is important that we implement the changes responsibly and give our affected colleagues the support and respect they deserve throughout the entire process.”
All employees affected by the latest cuts have been notified.
Danske Bank says on its website that it has more than 20,000 employees across its international operations.
Danish krone loses value against major currencies in 2026
The Danish krone has lost value in 2026, making Danish goods and services cheaper for customers in several foreign markets while making some holidays abroad more expensive.
The krone’s effective exchange rate, a weighted average of its value against the currencies of Denmark’s most important trading partners, has fallen by 2.7 percent since the start of the year. The figures come from a compilation by Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry.
“The weakening of the krone’s value makes Danish goods and services cheaper for customers abroad, which makes it easier for export companies to secure new orders,” Sørensen said.
“It is in both the US, China, Norway, and Japan where the exchange rate means that they now have to pay less money to buy our products,” he added.
The Norwegian krone has risen 12.9 percent against the Danish krone over the past year, while the Chinese yuan has gained 9.8 percent. The US dollar and Japanese yen have each risen 4.8 percent.
However, not all currencies have strengthened against the Danish krone. The Swedish krona and Indian rupee have lost value, making goods from those countries slightly more expensive for Danish importers.
Exchange rates also affect the cost of holidays abroad. When a foreign currency strengthens against the Danish krone, Danish travellers get less for their money.
“For those who love a trip to the snow, a trip to Norway has become significantly more expensive solely as a result of the strengthening of the Norwegian krone,” Sørensen said.
“The weakening of the Swedish krona and low inflation in Sweden, on the other hand, make a ski vacation much more economically affordable in Sweden compared to Norway,” he added.
The Turkish lira has recorded the largest decline among the currencies in the compilation. It now costs 9.7 percent less to buy Turkish currency than it did at the start of the year.
Denmark to get 51 emergency supermarkets stocked for major crises
Shoppers across Denmark will be able to buy essential groceries and household supplies during power outages, cyberattacks and other emergencies under a new initiative by Salling Group.
The Danish retail giant, which operates Bilka, Føtex and Netto, plans to establish 51 emergency-ready supermarkets nationwide by 2027.
The stores will be equipped to operate for at least 48 hours without electricity or external communication systems, ensuring access to basic necessities during major disruptions.
According to Salling Group, the network will include 17 Bilka stores, 32 Føtex stores and two Netto locations.
The stores will be distributed so that up to 80 percent of Denmark’s population lives within 50 kilometers of one.
Each location will maintain emergency stocks of 50 essential products, selected according to Danish authorities’ recommendations for household preparedness.
These include oatmeal, protein bars, canned meatballs in curry, rice cakes, tuna, beans, chickpeas and other foods with long shelf lives.
Nonfood essentials such as batteries, wet wipes and diapers will also be available.
Customers will be able to pay offline using almost all physical payment cards and digital cards stored on smartphones.
Salling Group recently partnered with payment provider Nets to help maintain card transactions during system failures.
CEO Anders Hagh said establishing the emergency stores remains a top priority, with preparations progressing toward the 2027 target.
Meanwhile, competing retailer Coop, which operates Brugsen, SuperBrugsen, 365discount and Kvickly, has not decided whether to establish similar stores.
Coop’s chief risk officer, Ulrik Mester, said the company was discussing crisis preparedness with authorities, including Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed (SAMSIK), Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security.

Several Danish public websites were shut down Wednesday after security vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language used by websites and online services worldwide.

Fake meat ban email tricks 1,200 Danish regional employees in phishing test
A warning about meat disappearing from workplace canteens prompted 1,200 employees in Denmark’s Capital Region to click a suspicious link in an internal cybersecurity test.
The exercise, reported by TV 2 Kosmopol, was designed to assess how well employees recognize phishing attempts, in which scammers impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into clicking links or sharing information.
Of the 13,000 employees who received the fake email, approximately 9 percent clicked the link.
The message claimed that meatballs and roast beef would be removed from workplace canteens and that some would switch to entirely vegan menus, excluding meat, dairy and eggs.
Employees were invited to click a link to find out how the changes would affect their local canteen.
However, the sender’s email address contained a small but important difference: it ended in “reqionh.dk” rather than the Capital Region’s actual domain, “regionh.dk”.
Anna Aaskilde Laursen, the region’s head of security, explained that the email deliberately targeted something employees cared about.
She told TV 2 Kosmopol that emotionally charged messages can prompt people to react without thinking, making it important to pause before clicking.
Laursen confirmed that the 1,200 employees who clicked the link would face no consequences.
Instead, the region intends to use the results to improve its preparedness for genuine cyberattacks.
Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security warns that phishing emails can be difficult to recognize because criminals often imitate official logos and use convincing language.
The agency recommends checking senders’ email addresses carefully and, when uncertain, contacting the supposed sender by telephone to verify whether a message is genuine.

Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey with Danish minister
Denmark’s Queen Mary will travel to Antalya, Turkey, from November 8 to 10 to participate in the United Nations climate summit COP31, the Danish Royal House has announced.

Her upcoming visit follows a new report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), published Wednesday, warning that global warming will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.
The report attributes this to decades of insufficient climate action.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries committed to keeping global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius compared with temperatures between 1850 and 1900, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees.

New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.

The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.
“The development in the labor market matches well with the general economic development. Activity is increasing, and it is therefore not surprising that more people are entering employment,” Sørensen said.
There are multiple reasons for the increase in employed people.
One of the main reasons is foreign labor, according to Jesper Grunnet-Lauridsen. He works as chief analyst at 3F, Fagligt Fælles Forbund, which is the United Federation of Danish Workers and the largest trade union in Denmark.
“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.
Energinet to prioritize addressing public service queries as power grid capacity runs short
Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.
The payment company Nets has lost a court case against Konkurrencerådet, the Danish Competition Council, which serves as the public competition authority in Denmark.
The ruling was delivered Wednesday by Sø- og Handelsretten, the Danish Maritime and Commercial Court.
Nets had asked the court to set aside a decision made by the Competition Council. That decision concluded that Nets abused its dominant position in the market for payment solutions between the years 2012 and 2016.
The case involves the company Teller, which was a subsidiary under Nets during that period. Teller offered what were described as exclusivity discounts to a number of large customers. The competition authorities determined that this practice broke legal rules meant to secure free competition, and they made their official decision on the case back in 2018.
The legal process has taken several years. Alongside the civil lawsuit, police have also run an investigation into Nets. That investigation led to criminal charges against the company, with authorities seeking a fine. The criminal case was put on hold to wait for the result of the civil case, and it has not yet gone to trial.
The specific legal reasons behind the court decision are not yet known. In a brief summary published on its website, the Maritime and Commercial Court stated that the full ruling will be released within four weeks.
The court noted that the delay is needed because the text of the ruling may contain business secrets that cannot be made public.
Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.

The government has abandoned proposed changes to Denmark’s senior pension scheme after failing to secure support from parties behind the existing agreement.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen announced the decision Tuesday following a meeting with the parties involved.
The changes were part of the government’s proposed 2027 budget and were expected to save 200 million DKK in 2028, 500 million DKK in 2029 and 800 million DKK in 2030.
Under the proposal, applicants would have needed to prove that their ability to work was limited to 15 hours a week or less across all types of jobs, rather than just their most recent job.
This would have made qualifying for senior pension more difficult. In 2026, a single person receiving senior pension gets 22,053 DKK per month.
The scheme was introduced through a political agreement in 2019. Its signatories include the Danish People’s Party, the Social Democrats, the Socialist People’s Party, the Moderates and the Social Liberal Party.
Changes to the agreement require approval from all participating parties during the parliamentary term.
Several center-right parties opposed the proposal, while the Red-Green Alliance also rejected changes.
“We respect the agreements we have. It has not been my intention to terminate any agreement,” Halsboe-Jørgensen said.
“On the contrary. The fact that I called the colleagues from the other parties together today was precisely an expression of the fact that I actually wanted to discuss it with them, and that I respect that the agreement we have with each other gives all of them a veto right against changes in this area,” she added.
Dropping the proposal leaves a gap in the government’s budget plans.
Halsboe-Jørgensen said spending priorities would need to change but did not specify where the missing funds would come from.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard will now have to address the shortfall during negotiations on the 2027 Finance Act.

About 14,000 higher education students living with their parents would lose their entire state education grant under the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
Another 8,000 students in the same group would receive lower payments, Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said in a parliamentary response.
Denmark’s state education grant is commonly known as SU.

Minister calls for talks after report finds major employment losses due to stress
Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr will convene labor unions, employer organizations and other groups for talks on preventing work-related stress.
The first roundtable discussion will take place Friday following a new report from the Danish Economic Council’s independent economic advisers.
The report estimates that severe work-related stress reduces Denmark’s labor supply by between 16,000 and 39,000 people.
More than one in 10 people affected by severe stress do not return to employment, while more than one in three disability pension recipients receive the benefit after a stress reaction, according to the report.
“Stress makes us poorer,” Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party said. “This applies both to the individual person who becomes ill with stress and their family, but it also matters for our society.”
Chief Economic Adviser Jakob Roland Munch said severe stress has long-lasting effects on people’s connection to the labor market.

Dyhr said Denmark must place greater emphasis on preventing stress instead of responding only after people become ill.
The government’s proposed 2027 budget includes 50 million DKK for a prevention fund intended to help people remain healthy and employed.
Dyhr said the government wants stronger evidence about which preventive measures work before deciding how to prioritize future efforts.
The European Commission has made security the main focus of its new Arctic strategy as Russia and China expand their activity in the region.
The approach marks a significant shift from the European Union’s 2021 strategy, which concentrated primarily on international cooperation, climate and environmental protection.
“As Russia and China increase their presence and ambitions, the Arctic has become a frontline in the global power competition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The Commission fears the Arctic could become a major source of conflict with Russia after the war in Ukraine ends.
The strategy proposes expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity and strengthening protection of northern maritime borders and critical undersea infrastructure.
The EU’s 27 countries collectively have about 10 icebreakers, compared with an estimated 40 operated by Russia.
The Commission also proposes creating a maritime security center to monitor activity in the Arctic.
A separate Arctic cable center would monitor, protect and repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. It could later track ships belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which transports sanctioned oil and gas.
Western intelligence services also suspect that Russia has used shadow fleet vessels in hybrid attacks.
The strategy contains no spending figures and must now be discussed with EU governments.
Kallas said Arctic security was a European concern because Denmark, Sweden and Finland are Arctic countries and more than 500,000 EU citizens live in the region.
Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.

A total of 7,709 homes were sold in September, 12 percent fewer than in the same month last year.

The survey by Danmarks Lærerforening, the Danish Union of Teachers, included responses from 1,901 public school teachers and kindergarten class leaders.
Sixteen percent said they felt stressed at work every day, while 36 percent experienced stress weekly and 23 percent monthly.

Copenhagen begins separate collection of used diapers for recycling
The City of Copenhagen began installing separate waste bins for used diapers in residential courtyards and municipal day-care centers Monday.
Diapers previously had to be placed with residual waste and were incinerated. They will now be processed at Denmark’s first diaper treatment facility.
“There is a major climate benefit in recycling the diapers instead of incinerating them,” Climate, Environment and Technology Mayor Line Barfod of the Red-Green Alliance said.
The city estimates that between 85 and 94 percent of diaper waste, including liquids and feces, can be converted into new materials.
Cellulose and the contents of the diapers will become biofiber used to produce biogas, electricity and district heating.
Plastic components can be recycled into products such as car interiors. Superabsorbent polymers can become binding material for the construction industry.
Collection will expand to municipal nursing homes, senior housing and other city institutions in February 2027.
Residents of detached houses and members of allotment garden associations will also be able to join the program next year. The scheme is expected to be fully implemented in 2029.
The bins will accept diapers for children and adults, incontinence pads, paper-based cloths and wet wipes without plastic or bamboo. Menstrual hygiene products are excluded.
Diaper waste must be placed in an ordinary plastic trash bag sealed with a tight knot.
Study finds misogynistic TikTok content can appear within minutes
Young male TikTok users can encounter misogynistic content within minutes, even when they do not actively search for it, according to a Danish study.
Researchers from the Center for Digital Pedagogy and Analyse & Tal created eight fictional profiles representing men ages 16 to 19 interested in fitness, dating, investing and gaming.
After the profiles interacted with videos about those subjects, researchers allowed them to scroll automatically for one hour.
Content associated with the “manosphere” appeared after an average of three minutes. In one case, it appeared after 21 seconds.
The manosphere refers to online communities and content that degrade women or support restricting their rights and opportunities.
Researchers also examined one year of viewing data provided by 29 men ages 15 to 22. They identified an average of five to six manosphere videos in each participant’s weekly feed.
The researchers said this was a minimum estimate but emphasized that the 29 participants were not representative of all young men.
Employment and Equality Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen of the Social Democrats called for stronger social media regulation and more discussion in schools and homes.
TikTok said it takes the findings seriously.
“We proactively remove 98.1 percent of the videos that violate our rules on hate and hateful behavior,” Nordic communications director Lukasz Lindell said.
TikTok said it was also working to diversify recommendations and interrupt repetitive content patterns.

Green Power Denmark, an industry organization representing the Danish energy sector, said the increase was driven mainly by electric vehicles and the district heating sector’s use of electric boilers and heat pumps.
The organization said growing electrification is gradually reducing Denmark’s reliance on oil and natural gas.
“We are freeing ourselves from what is happening in the Middle East and American politics,” Green Power Denmark chief executive Kristian Jensen said.
He said Danish energy prices remain affected by developments abroad because the country still relies on prices set by global markets.
Denmark’s electrification rate rose by only 3.8 percentage points in total from 2016 through 2024, making the 1.5-point increase in 2025 significant.
Green Power Denmark wants electricity to account for 60 percent of total energy consumption by 2035.
Jensen said achieving that target would require industrial companies to replace natural gas with electricity and heat pumps.
He pointed to iron foundries and food producers, including dairy group Arla, as examples of industries already using heat pumps.
Such changes could reduce companies’ carbon dioxide emissions and energy costs while improving their competitiveness, Jensen said.
Figures for Denmark’s electrification rate in 2026 are not yet available.

Danish singer Annika has won P3 Prisen, the main award at one of Denmark’s most prominent annual music events, P3 Guld.
The 21-year-old received the award Friday evening at DR Koncerthuset in Copenhagen, a year after being nominated for the same prize but losing out to Danish band Aphaca.
P3 Guld is the annual music awards show organised by P3, the youth-oriented music and entertainment radio station run by Danish public broadcaster DR.
The event celebrates artists who have made a significant impact on Danish music over the past year, with P3 Prisen regarded as its main award.

“This year’s lineup was put together based on the artists and bands that have left a significant mark on the music year and in P3’s universe.”

Trump: Greenland deal biggest real estate deal ever
The US president says he “got it for nothing” after signing a new defence agreement with Denmark and Greenland that expands the American military presence on the island.
US President Donald Trump has described a new defence and security agreement with Denmark and Greenland as potentially “the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made”.
Speaking at a Republican campaign rally in Dalton, Georgia, Trump portrayed the agreement as a major achievement for the United States.
“What do you think of the deal I made on Greenland? Got it for nothing,” Trump told supporters.
“It is probably the biggest real estate deal that has ever been made.”
Trump was campaigning ahead of the US midterm elections on November 3.
His comments come after months of tension over Greenland, an autonomous territory within the Kingdom of Denmark. Trump has repeatedly said that the United States wants control and ownership of Greenland, arguing that the island is crucial to American national security.
Two new US military bases
The United States, Denmark and Greenland signed a new security and defence agreement on Greenland at the end of September following lengthy negotiations.
The agreement was signed at the United Nations in New York shortly after Trump addressed the UN General Assembly.
It allows the United States to establish two additional military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, which plays an important role in missile warning, space surveillance and Arctic security.
The new agreement also opens the possibility of deploying parts of the planned US Golden Dome missile defence system in Greenland. The system is intended to protect the United States against threats including missiles and drones.
Despite Trump’s description of the agreement as a “real estate deal”, it does not transfer ownership of Greenland to the United States.
Trump’s comments came as Republicans campaign to retain control of Congress in the November midterm elections. Democrats are currently polling more strongly in the race for the House of Representatives, while control of the Senate remains more uncertain.
Republicans currently hold majorities in both chambers.

Growing security concerns and economic opportunities are shaping the European Union’s proposed Arctic strategy, with Greenland playing a central role in its plans.

Jozef Síkela, the EU commissioner for international partnerships, told Ritzau that the aim was to develop a strategy “together with the Arctic for the Arctic.”
Compared with the EU’s 2021 strategy, the new proposal places greater emphasis on security while maintaining commitments to environmental protection and sustainability.
Síkela identified critical raw materials and emerging shipping routes as potential sources of economic growth.
During a September visit to Greenland, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced investments of 1.5 billion DKK for projects involving renewable energy, sustainable mining, satellite connectivity, tourism and housing.

Síkela acknowledged that growing security concerns were partly driven by Russia’s military activities in the Arctic and its war in Ukraine.
However, he argued that investments in ports, infrastructure protection and maritime monitoring could also benefit local communities.
The Commission is seeking to double financial support for Greenland in the EU’s next long-term budget.
Asked about Greenland potentially joining the EU, Síkela welcomed the possibility but stressed that the decision belonged to Greenlanders.
Greenland withdrew from the European Economic Community in 1985.
Its head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, reiterated in September that Greenland wants closer cooperation with the EU, not membership.

Brain scans suggest first graders don’t engage their control networks like adults when talking to ChatGPT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:26 UTC
19:00:26 KST

A small brain imaging study suggests that young children show less communication within and between the brain networks responsible for self-regulation and focused attention when brainstorming with an artificial intelligence chatbot than adults do. Although first graders and adults scored similarly, relative to their age groups, on a standard test of creative thinking outside the brain scanner, only adults showed a link between higher creativity and stronger coordination among these mental control systems during the conversation. The findings, published in Cerebral Cortex, suggest that young children may not yet have the mature brain wiring needed to actively direct and evaluate a collaborative conversation with generative artificial intelligence.
Generative artificial intelligence programs, such as ChatGPT, are powered by large language models, which are computer systems trained on massive amounts of text to predict how words fit together, allowing them to produce human-like responses and brainstorm ideas in real time. As these tools enter homes and elementary classrooms, children are increasingly using them for storytelling and collaborative problem-solving, a process known as co-creativity. Keeping up with a fast-talking, unpredictable digital partner requires cognitive control, which is the mind’s ability to plan ahead, stay focused on a goal, remember what was already said, and filter out unhelpful distractions.
Generating original and useful ideas relies heavily on how different systems in the brain communicate with one another. For instance, a 2018 neuroimaging study of adults (covered by PsyPost at the time) indicated that people who come up with more original ideas tend to have stronger synchronization among three major brain networks: one involved in spontaneous daydreaming and memory, another that flags important new thoughts, and a third that handles cognitive control and goal-directed planning. Instead of operating separately, these systems team up so a person can both brainstorm freely and judge whether an idea actually makes sense.
In young children, however, the brain networks that manage cognitive control and focused attention are still under construction, only reaching full maturity in a person’s mid-twenties. A 2019 neuroimaging study of young children, conducted by the same research group behind the new study, found that across children ranging from 17 months to nine years old, older children tended to show stronger connections within and between their cognitive control networks while listening to stories. In addition, a neuroimaging study covered by PsyPost in 2023 indicated that the way cognitive control networks relate to creative thinking shifts across development, with stronger connectivity in these control regions linked to higher creativity in adolescents but lower creativity in adults.
First grade, around ages six and seven, is a sensitive developmental window when children are first learning to evaluate text and speech on their own, while still tending to trust perceived experts and technology without much skepticism. The research was led by Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus, an associate professor with the Educational Neuroimaging Group in the Faculty of Education in Science and Technology and the Faculty of Biomedical Engineering at the Technion – Israel Institute of Technology, who is also affiliated with the Kennedy Krieger Institute and Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine.
She and her Technion colleagues Yoed Kenett, Dafna Link-Sourani, Emeel Ashqar, and Rola Farah examined whether first graders engage their cognitive control and attention networks to the same degree as adults when brainstorming with ChatGPT, and how that brain activity relates to their underlying creative ability. Part of the motivation came from a 2025 preprint, which has not been peer reviewed, in which adults who wrote essays with ChatGPT showed less coordinated brain activity than those who used a search engine or no tools at all.
“Generative AI is entering children’s lives, and classrooms, much faster than the evidence about how young brains engage with it,” Horowitz-Kraus told PsyPost. “Studies in adults have suggested that people recruit fewer cognitive resources when they work with ChatGPT, but adults have mature cognitive control systems, and these systems keep developing into the mid-twenties. We focused on first graders (ages 6–7) because this is when formal schooling begins, when executive functions are developing rapidly, and when children tend to place a great deal of trust in sources they perceive as experts. We wanted to know what the brain of a young child is actually doing during a real conversation with ChatGPT, compared with an adult given exactly the same task.”
To investigate this, the researchers recruited 15 first-grade children with an average age of about 6.4 years and 16 adults with an average age of about 38 years. All participants came from average to above-average socioeconomic backgrounds, had no history of neurological or psychiatric conditions, and completed standard tests to confirm typical verbal and nonverbal intelligence. Before entering the brain scanner, each participant took a behavioral creativity test called the Divergent Association Task, which asks a person to name 10 words that are as unrelated in meaning as possible.
Inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) scanner, which measures brain activity by tracking changes in blood flow, participants engaged in a five-minute spoken conversation with ChatGPT. Using a specialized microphone and noise-canceling audio system built for the scanner, both children and adults were given the same open-ended goal: they had to plan the opening of any kind of store they wanted, anywhere and for anyone, by consulting out loud with ChatGPT. Immediately before the scan began, children were told they would be speaking to “the smartest computer in the world,” also known as ChatGPT, whereas adults were simply told they would be speaking to ChatGPT.
“I would also like to note that holding a live spoken conversation with ChatGPT inside an MRI scanner, with six-year-olds, required dedicated infrastructure developed at the Technion Human MRI Research Center,” Horowitz-Kraus noted. “I am very grateful to the children, parents and students who took part.”
The researchers recorded and transcribed every conversation to measure how original and varied the spoken exchanges were. They used a computer model to calculate a “divergent semantic integration” score, which measures how far apart the meanings of all the words in a conversation are from one another; for example, the words “cat” and “democracy” sit much farther apart in meaning than “cat” and “dog.” On the brain scans, the team measured functional connectivity, which reflects how closely different brain regions synchronize their activity over time, across seven major brain networks after statistically controlling for head movement inside the scanner.
These seven systems included the frontoparietal and cingulo-opercular networks, which manage cognitive control and task goals; the dorsal and ventral attention networks, which handle voluntary focus and automatic reactions to new information; the salience network, which acts as a switchboard by detecting important ideas; the default mode network, which supports spontaneous imagination; and the memory retrieval network.
On the word-association creativity test taken outside the scanner, children and adults scored at comparable levels relative to others their age, with average percentile scores of 28.61 and 26.16, respectively, a difference that was not statistically significant. During the actual five-minute conversation with ChatGPT, however, adults produced slightly more diverse and wide-ranging spoken narratives than the children did, scoring an average of 0.82 on the semantic integration measure compared to 0.81 for the first graders, a small difference that was nonetheless statistically reliable.
When the researchers examined the brain scans, they found pronounced differences in how the two age groups engaged their mental control and attention systems while talking to the chatbot. Within individual brain networks, adults showed substantially stronger internal synchronization in the frontoparietal control network, where adults averaged a connectivity score of 0.201 compared to 0.113 in children. Adults also had higher internal connectivity in the salience network (0.289 versus 0.198 in children) and the dorsal attention network (0.211 versus 0.162 in children). Only the frontoparietal difference held up after the researchers adjusted for the number of comparisons they ran.
In contrast, internal connectivity within the default mode network, which handles spontaneous imagination, did not differ between the two groups, averaging 0.187 in adults and 0.181 in children. Communication across different brain networks was also more integrated in adults than in first graders during the AI conversation. After adjusting for multiple statistical comparisons, the most robust difference appeared in how the frontoparietal control network linked up with the dorsal attention network (averaging 0.126 in adults versus 0.039 in children).
Before correcting for multiple comparisons, adults additionally showed stronger cross-network ties linking memory retrieval regions to cognitive control and attention systems, as well as stronger coupling between the default mode network and memory retrieval (0.150 in adults versus 0.111 in children). The researchers then tested whether a person’s baseline creativity score outside the scanner predicted how strongly their brain networks communicated while using ChatGPT.
They found that in adults, higher creativity scores were positively linked to stronger communication between the frontoparietal control network and the salience network during the AI dialog. Among the first graders, however, baseline creativity showed no statistically significant relationship with the strength of these brain network connections. That adult pattern differs from the 2023 study described earlier, which tied stronger connectivity within the executive control network to lower creativity in adults, though that study looked at connections within a single network rather than links between networks.
“Two things” surprised the team, Horowitz-Kraus explained. “First, children and adults looked similar in creative ability on the standard test, yet the neural route they took during the conversation was quite different; the difference lay in how creativity is implemented in the brain, not in baseline capacity. Second, the default mode network, which is central to most models of creativity, did not differ between the groups. One possible explanation is that conversing with ChatGPT in a scanner was novel for everyone, but that needs to be tested directly.”
Taken together, the results suggest that even when young children have age-appropriate creative potential, they engage their control, attention, and memory systems in a less integrated way than adults do during a conversation with generative AI. The authors propose that adults use their salience and frontoparietal networks to filter ChatGPT’s rapid responses and steer the brainstorming toward their goal, a role these networks may not yet play in six- and seven-year-olds.
“Talking to a chatbot looks effortless, but it draws on planning, monitoring, attention and memory systems that are still under construction in a six-year-old, which is why adult guidance matters when young children use these tools,” Horowitz-Kraus said.
“The practical message is that young children should not be left to use generative AI on their own,” she added. “For parents and teachers, this means sitting with the child, asking questions about the answers, and treating the AI as a shared activity instead of an independent tutor. For educators, pediatricians and policy makers, it means that the age at which children start using these tools deserves the same careful attention we already give to screen exposure. This study cannot set a specific ‘safe age’ since it focused on two very distinct age groups, but it is a clear signal that tools designed around adult abilities should not simply be handed to young children.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the study did not include a comparison task where participants brainstormed on their own or talked with a human partner inside the scanner, the design cannot separate general age differences in brain maturity from effects caused specifically by ChatGPT. In other words, the lower network connectivity seen in children may reflect how six-year-old brains handle this kind of complex task in general, rather than showing that ChatGPT actively suppresses or harms their brain activity.
“This study does not show that ChatGPT reduces cognitive control in children or harms their brains,” Horowitz-Kraus emphasized. “We compared children with adults doing the same ChatGPT task; we did not compare children with and without ChatGPT, or ChatGPT with a human conversation partner. So we cannot yet separate what is specific to AI from general developmental differences in how the brain handles this kind of conversation.”
The way the chatbot was introduced may have also influenced how the children behaved. Telling first graders that they were about to talk to “the smartest computer in the world” may have encouraged them to passively accept the machine’s suggestions rather than questioning or evaluating its ideas, which could naturally lower their use of cognitive control networks. Future research will need to give children and adults the exact same instructions, or intentionally test how calling an AI an “expert” changes how critically kids think.
In addition, the sample size of 15 children and 16 adults was relatively small, and the groups were unevenly split by sex, with 11 boys among the 15 children and four men among the 16 adults. The study had enough participants to detect large differences between age groups, but the analyses linking creativity to brain connectivity were exploratory and likely underpowered.
The researchers also did not control for differences in everyday vocabulary size, how fast participants spoke, how many turns they took in the conversation, or how much prior experience they had with ChatGPT before the experiment (and adults likely had far more experience with the tool). Tracking children over several years in larger studies will help educators and pediatricians determine the developmental stage at which kids build the mental control needed to actively collaborate with artificial intelligence tools.
“The next steps are larger samples, a direct comparison of talking with ChatGPT versus talking with a human partner or working without AI, and longitudinal follow-up to identify when in development the control networks begin to engage in an adult-like way and to relate to creativity,” Horowitz-Kraus said. “We also plan to measure children’s familiarity with AI and to test how the perceived authority of the AI shapes their engagement. The long-term goal is to give educators, pediatricians and policy makers evidence for developmentally appropriate use of generative AI, in the same way that guidance exists for screen exposure.”
“Technology can support learning, but it cannot lead it; children learn best alongside an adult who guides and challenges them,” she added.
The study, “Lower engagement of cognitive control in children on ChatGPT,” was authored by Tzipi Horowitz-Kraus, Yoed N. Kenett, Dafna Link-Sourani, Emeel Ashqar, and Rola Farah.
