Press review: Russia-US-Ukraine peace hopes rise as Moscow offers Iran-US mediation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. The prospects for peace and trilateral talks between Russia, the US and Ukraine following the October 21 St. Petersburg meeting; Moscow’s willingness to mediate between Tehran and Washington; and Russia’s potential agreement with the US to start shipping fertilizers alongside diesel. These stories topped Thursday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Chances of peace and Russia-US-Ukraine talks following St. Petersburg meeting
US efforts to end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine have resumed, perhaps the main visible and indisputable outcome of the October 21 talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg. The envoy left Russia with news of the release of an American citizen from a Russian prison and Moscow’s assurances that the proposals he brought would be reviewed. In addition, Putin expressed readiness to launch trilateral talks in the Russia-US-Ukraine format. The talks are scheduled for mid-November, after the US congressional elections, which are likely to bring significant changes.
Witkoff’s visit to St. Petersburg wrapped up a busy diplomatic round, international affairs expert Nikolay Novik told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. The St. Petersburg talks were preceded by consultations in Oslo. Witkoff and Kushner, who participated remotely, met with Zelensky, European leaders, and EU and NATO representatives there, the expert recalled. "It is likely that Witkoff presented an updated plan to end the conflict and a proposal for direct talks involving Trump and Zelensky. There may also have been discussions about a meeting between Putin, Trump, and Xi Jinping in China during the APEC summit on November 18-19: Washington doesn’t need a technical pause, but rather an outcome from the summit that can be presented as a tangible result," Novik said.
At the same time, the package of conditions that the US envoy might have brought - if these were the ones recently mentioned in the Western media - does not suit Russia, Russian International Affairs Council President Dmitry Trenin told Vedomosti. According to the expert, Moscow agreed to discuss not so much the settlement itself as possible ways to establish a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends. "By 2027, we will most likely still be in the midst of ongoing hostilities, though the US administration had certainly hoped to achieve tangible results by the end of this year," Trenin noted. The expert stressed that the future prospects of the negotiation process, including the development of specific terms, will be determined by the actual situation on the battlefield.
The current round of talks differs from previous ones because the agenda will include the issue of security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, an issue that was not included in negotiations with Kiev following the Istanbul consultations, Nikolay Silayev, a leading researcher at the MGIMO Institute of International Relations, said. However, the expert does not expect the upcoming negotiations with Ukraine to conclude any differently from the previous ones. "The main reason for the lack of confidence in a breakthrough is the public statements made by Ukrainian and European officials. Their position remains the same: an unconditional ceasefire," he stressed.
Izvestia: Russia ready to mediate between Tehran and Washington
Moscow is prepared to act as a mediator in settling the conflict between the US and Iran, provided both parties are interested. Talks between Washington and Tehran have reached an impasse, partly due to the unresolved question of Iran’s nuclear program. Russia previously proposed transporting Iran’s enriched uranium to its territory, but this initiative has yet to receive support.
The eight-month conflict between the US and Iran has stalled. Washington’s initial plan to quickly topple the country’s government has failed. Passage through the Strait of Hormuz remains difficult, and diplomats have yet to make progress toward resolving the conflict. Under these circumstances, Russia could assume the role of mediator. Moscow is ready to take such a step, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Andrey Rudenko told Izvestia. "If all parties express interest, then we are ready [to act as mediators]," he noted. "We previously offered our services regarding how the Iranian nuclear program could be resolved, but our proposals have not yet been supported," the senior diplomat said.
Thanks to its good relations with both Iran and Israel, Russia occupies a unique position as a universal intermediary in the Middle East, political analyst Alexander Kargin said. Moreover, Moscow is currently pursuing a negotiating track with the US as well. The expert noted that Pakistan, another potential mediator, has no diplomatic relations with Israel at all, whereas Russia does not face this problem.
Russian mediation would at least help establish a ceasefire, paving the way for a comprehensive resolution of the crisis, Kargin said. The analyst expects that, ultimately, the practical necessity of Moscow’s involvement will prevail, and the parties will bring Russia into the negotiations. At the same time, according to him, the parties to the conflict have diametrically opposed views on the nuclear program. While Russia’s proposal to remove the uranium would be ideal, heightened tensions in the Middle East are preventing the parties from making even the smallest compromises, Kargin stressed.
Izvestia: Russia may begin exporting fertilizers to US alongside diesel
Russia is ready to supply mineral fertilizers and fuel to the US, but expanding fertilizer exports would require a reallocation of shipments: currently, about 69% of fertilizer production is exported, experts said. Russian President Vladimir Putin has discussed the prospect of supplying fertilizers to the US market on a significant scale. In addition, the first shipment of 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel fuel is scheduled to leave for the US on October 22, with other countries set to receive shipments by the end of the year.
During a meeting with US special presidential envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on October 21, Russian President Vladimir Putin said that Moscow could supply fertilizers to the American market in large quantities. However, it is difficult to gauge potential export volumes, since a significant portion of Russian production is already under contract with foreign buyers, Denis Prikhodko, an equity market analyst at Alfa-Capital Asset Management, told Izvestia. According to him, shipments will increase gradually, primarily through the redistribution of export flows among foreign markets rather than through higher production.
Increasing fertilizer and diesel fuel shipments to the US market could help bring down prices for these products both in the US and globally, which is especially important for agricultural producers. Such agreements with Russia would benefit both the Donald Trump administration and the Russian authorities, Igor Yushkov, a leading analyst at the National Energy Security Fund, stressed.
The European factor is also relevant. According to political scientist and German studies expert Yegor Belyachkov, the current leadership of most European countries will likely react negatively to an agreement between Russia and the US on fertilizer supplies, just as they did with the diesel deal. This approach directly reflects European countries' policy in recent years, under which the slightest compromise between Moscow and Washington prompts EU nations to attempt to block such agreements. Brussels could do so by tightening sanctions against Russia and coordinating with American Democrats, the expert said.
Rossiyskaya Gazeta: Possibility of routing Persian Gulf oil around Strait of Hormuz
New pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz and lead to seaports outside the Persian Gulf will address the problem of supplying Middle Eastern oil to the global market. In five years, the strait may become obsolete for oil trade as shipments are redirected along new routes. This is not the first attempt to find alternative ways to deliver oil from Persian Gulf countries. Previously, this idea was also proposed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. According to him, the construction of oil pipelines will render the Strait of Hormuz "a worthless piece of water" in as little as two to three years.
Bypass routes are currently more profitable, not because transporting oil via pipeline is inexpensive, but because of the increased costs linked to transit through the Strait of Hormuz, Maxim Malkov, a Kept partner and head of the firm’s oil and gas practice, told Rossiyskaya Gazeta. Before the crisis, tanker transit cost the same as or less than pipeline transport, while now, that balance has reversed, the expert noted. However, maritime transport is cheaper in peacetime. The cost of pumping oil through a pipeline is up to five times higher than the cost of moving it by oil tanker per kilometer, Oleg Abelev, head of the analytical department at the Rikom-Trust investment company, pointed out.
Existing alternative routes do not resolve the problem because their combined capacity is less than half of the volumes that previously passed through the Strait of Hormuz, Malkov emphasized. Moreover, the Red Sea poses its own risks, such as Houthi attacks, and there are virtually no alternatives to tankers for transporting refined petroleum products, the expert noted. But even if the existing infrastructure that bypasses the Strait of Hormuz is expanded and new oil pipelines are built in parallel, the economic viability of these projects will be questionable, economist Boris Kopeikin stressed. If the situation in the region stabilizes in the long term, oil will once again follow the traditional route, through the Strait of Hormuz, he said.
At the same time, the main advantage of alternative routes is the diversification of risks. They reduce dependence on the Strait of Hormuz and allow exports to continue in the event of shipping restrictions, but they do not guarantee complete supply security, Ivan Timonin, a senior manager at the Implementa consulting firm, said. According to Abelev, pipelines are no safer than maritime transport. They are vulnerable to drone and missile attacks, and protecting them along their entire length is quite difficult. Unlike seagoing vessels, a pipeline is stationary and its location is precisely known. It cannot be replaced or rerouted. Maritime transport offers greater flexibility. Oil pipelines for the Persian Gulf states are an expensive insurance policy, not a cheap alternative, the expert stressed.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: French authorities trying to ease protests with talks and concessions
Ahead of another round of large-scale protests scheduled for the weekend, the authorities are trying to reach a deal with the protesters. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu met with union representatives on October 21. The meeting produced no results; the government did not receive any promises to call off the protests. In fact, a general strike has been announced.
Nevertheless, Lecornu remains undeterred. The government has proposed an aid program for businesses affected by the unrest. Following his trip to the Persian Gulf states, President Emmanuel Macron issued a statement saying that he had secured additional fuel shipments to bring down prices in the country. The authorities are hoping these measures will have a rapid effect.
Rather than resorting to force, the French authorities have decided to address the wave of protests sweeping the country through persuasion. They have chosen to respond to the demonstrators’ main demands. Perhaps there is no other option: last weekend, more than half a million French citizens took to the streets across the country. The protests are no longer limited to schoolchildren and their parents who are dissatisfied with the education system. Labor unions are actively participating in the protests, which are directed against the rising cost of living and ultimately against the economic policies of the current president and government.
At the same time, the situation in the country is gradually returning to normal, although this will take some time, Tatyana Zvereva, a professor at the World Economy and World Politics Faculty of the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. "The composition of the protesters is complex. It includes high school students, members of the ‘Yellow Vests’ movement, and others, including members of fringe political organizations," she noted. According to the expert, the French authorities are pursuing two main lines of action. On the one hand, they are restoring order, which society as a whole expects. The far-right National Rally party has been particularly vocal in demanding this. On the other hand, the authorities are negotiating with moderate protesters.
"The logic is this: the most aggressive protesters must be held accountable, and positive-minded citizens must be reached out to by addressing their socio-economic demands. However, the second point is much more difficult to achieve. Therefore, it seems unlikely that we can expect quick results from the negotiations. But dialogue can help defuse the situation and let off some steam," Zvereva emphasized.

Hugging Face’s New AI Biology Model Lets You Chat With DNA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

The AI platform Hugging Face on Thursday released a new open model for understanding DNA that can run locally on a laptop.
Developed in collaboration with researchers at Zhongguancun Academy in China and the University of Naples Federico II in Italy, the model is trained on genomic sequences and natural language so that people can ask questions about the effects of DNA changes on gene activity and health and get conversational answers in return.
Lewis Tunstall, a senior research scientist at Hugging Face, says the tool is meant to help researchers design new drugs and genetic therapies, and it could potentially aid patients in interpreting their own genomes.
“We've unlocked a new capability in language models, which is fundamentally about being able to chat with DNA,” he says of the new model, dubbed Carbon-X. Using natural language means even nontechnical users “can actually ask questions about DNA that wouldn't be accessible through any other tool.”
Known as essentially GitHub for AI models, Hugging Face provides a library of readymade AI tools and a platform for running primarily open-weight and open-source AI applications for developers, researchers, businesses, and people who want to experiment with AI without building everything from scratch. In September, Nvidia agreed to acquire the company for nearly $13 billion. (Hugging Face was also at the center of a major hack by OpenAI’s models earlier this year.)
DNA is more like computer code than natural language. Instead of 0s and 1s, though, it uses As, Cs, Gs, and Ts to encode information. A human genome contains 6 billion of these letters. While the human genome has been sequenced end to end, scientists still don’t understand how most of it works.
Now, AI models are helping researchers decipher some of those mysteries. Last year, Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome, which predicts the effects of DNA sequences and genetic mutations but does so in a numeric format. It also requires more compute power. Evo 2, a model developed by the Arc Institute and Nvidia, along with academic partners, speaks the language of DNA and can generate entire genomes from scratch.
Carbon-X integrates both DNA and natural language in a conversational interface. Think of it like a ChatGPT for DNA.
The team started with an existing language model and expanded its vocabulary to read DNA in groups of six letters. They then continued training on 300 billion chunks of data, or tokens, that combined DNA sequences, English text, and examples linking DNA to biological descriptions. The DNA sequences came from mammals (including humans), other vertebrates, invertebrates, plants, fungi, and protozoa. Tunstall says the team didn’t train the model on viruses because they didn’t want it to be used for potentially dangerous applications.
Users won’t be able to upload full human genomes. The model was trained to be able to ingest DNA sequences of roughly 50,000 base pairs, so users will only be able to query small parts of the genome at a time.
One of the ways scientists could use Carbon-X is to help understand whether a genetic mutation is benign or disease-causing, a key step in developing a targeted drug or genetic therapy. If an intervention targets the wrong mutation, it could be totally ineffective or, worse, cause unintended harm.
Researchers face restrictions when it comes to uploading identifiable or sensitive patient data to frontier AI models, so Tunstall says his team intentionally designed a small model with 14 billion parameters. That will allow it to run locally on the user’s hardware, rather than rely on cloud-based models. No data is sent to Hugging Face or any other company, he says.
The developers of Carbon-X caution that they haven’t validated the model yet with actual wet lab experiments, so they can’t say how accurate its predictions are.

Bulgarian Watchdog Flags Food Markups of Up to 135%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Consumer Protection Commission Chair Maya Manolova has presented evidence of retail markups of up to 135% on basic food products and outlined potential penalties for large retail chains during an interview on bTV’s “This Morning” (Tazi Sutrin).
Manolova displayed invoices collected during joint inspections by the commission, tax authorities and the Food Safety Agency at retail warehouses across Bulgaria. The commission has forwarded the documentation to the Commission for Protection of Competition, seeking fines of up to 10% of the retailers’ annual turnover.
Packages of butter, fresh milk, yogurt and white brined cheese were displayed in the studio alongside information boards detailing the inspection findings.
“They cooked up this mess with absurdly high prices and left the Bulgarian people to deal with the consequences. We aren't talking about avocados, mangoes, or luxury goods here; we are talking about the staple food products found on the Bulgarian table,” Manolova said.
She argued that the invoices contradict retailers’ public claims that they do not apply excessive markups.
The figures presented showed that a 250-gram package of butter bought for €1.34 excluding VAT was sold for €3.79 including VAT, a markup of 135%. Half a liter of fresh milk cost retailers €0.44 to purchase and €1.07 to sell, representing a 99% markup. Yogurt bought for €0.44 was priced at €0.95, an 80% increase.
A 700-gram block of white brined cheese purchased for €3.79 was sold for €8.18, also an 80% markup. Another producer’s 600-gram package of the cheese cost €2.78 at procurement and retailed for €5.11, a markup of 53%.
“I am presenting these products, not for the sake of Bulgarian citizens, who are well aware of what they pay at the supermarket checkout, but for the retail chains, in light of their claims that such discrepancies do not exist. Here are the facts and the invoices, provided by the retailers themselves during inspections,” Manolova said.
She explained that inspectors began their checks at logistics centers and followed the products through the supply chain to the supermarket shelves.
The commission’s chair also contrasted the prices charged by retailers with the amounts received by Bulgarian farmers. “The purchase price of milk from Bulgarian farmers is 50 euro cents per liter - a figure that has remained unchanged for fifteen years. The Bulgarian farmer operates with zero markup and is, quite literally, being crushed. Meanwhile, the markup applied by retail chains reaches and even exceeds one hundred percent,” she said.
Food processors generally work with margins of 5% to 15%, Manolova added. An example discussed during the broadcast compared imported Gouda cheese, which carries a 25% markup, with Bulgarian kashkaval, or yellow cheese, subject to a commercial margin of 125%, putting domestic products at a disadvantage.
Manolova outlined two legal mechanisms that could be used to penalize retailers. Under consumer protection legislation, fines can be imposed for unjustified price increases compared with the preceding two-month period. The commission has opened 11 proceedings on this basis involving products such as fruits and vegetables, where purchase prices have declined while retail prices have risen. Each established violation can attract a penalty of between €10,000 and €100,000.
She identified Article 37b of the Law on the Protection of Competition, adopted in July, as the main additional instrument for action against unfair commercial practices and discrimination among suppliers. The provision prohibits differences in markups exceeding 10% for similar products within the same category.
“For any price discrepancy exceeding 10 percent for the same product sourced from different suppliers, the potential fine can reach up to 10 percent of the retailer's turnover. Given a turnover of 1.5 billion euros, one can calculate what the penalty for the respective retail chain might be. We have submitted the invoices and supporting evidence to the antitrust authority, and the Commission for Protection of Competition is now taking action,” Manolova said.
The consumer protection regulator has also referred the retail chains to the antitrust authority over alleged abuse of a collective dominant position. Together, the chains account for more than 70% of the market, a position that could provide grounds for penalties over excessively high selling prices. The measures are intended to ease pressure on Bulgarian producers and consumers.
Manolova said retailers’ operating costs typically account for 18% to 28% of turnover, while a markup of up to 31% is sufficient to generate a profit.
“The 'Care Basket' initiative was a wasted opportunity for dialogue; therefore, we are now turning to the law. We are developing a mobile application to help citizens gauge fair market values,” she added.
The commission is also preparing legislation that would impose mandatory markup limits of 15% to 25% on essential food products.
Its oversight activities will extend to other areas of public concern. Commission representatives will take part in Energy and Water Regulatory Commission (EWRC) proceedings on prices for natural gas, district heating, water and electricity.
Upcoming measures include inspections of over-the-counter medicines sold in pharmacies, negotiations with mobile operators to eliminate early termination penalties, and an analysis of bank fees. The regulator is also investigating reports that one-day school excursions in Sofia that do not include meals are being charged at between 45 and 60 leva per student.

South Korea's stranded celebrity shark swims back into canal after rescue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:59:38 UTC
18:59:38 KST

An endangered dusky shark that had been trapped in a canal in South Korea’s southeastern port city of Busan for more than a month returned hours after authorities guided it out to sea, local media reported on Thursday.
The female shark, nicknamed Bukang-i, was spotted on Thursday morning near the entrance to the canal at Busan’s North Port Waterfront Park after crossing a floating barrier late on Wednesday, according to The Korea Herald.
It was the second time the shark had slipped past barriers following rescue attempts.
Authorities had declared Wednesday’s operation successful at around 6.10 pm local time (0910GMT), but the shark was seen crossing the barrier again at around 11.05 pm (1405GMT).
Officials are considering reinforcing the barriers or capturing the shark and transporting it to open waters.
Lee Gwang-seok, an official with the oceans and fisheries ministry, said Bukang-i was unlikely to slip past more barriers and move farther up the canal, considering the density of the nets and the narrow waterway in that section that leaves little room for the shark to squeeze through.
The shark’s repeated returns have puzzled authorities, who remain concerned about its deteriorating health and falling water temperatures.
The National Institute of Fisheries Science has not observed Bukang-i feeding, while apparent injuries and footage showing it striking a canal wall have raised further concerns.
Sharing the Korean name of Busan’s North Port, where it was first spotted in mid-September, Bukang-i has become a major local tourist attraction as it slowly circled the canal, its fins slicing through the water’s surface. It has drawn more than 1.6 million visitors as of Sunday, according to Yonhap News Agency.
Previous rescue attempts on September 29 and October 2 failed. Authorities fear the shark could die if temperatures continue to fall.

Researchers warn of global decline in childhood measles vaccination
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:56:27 CST
18:56:27 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Researchers have warned of a global decline in childhood measles vaccination rates since the COVID-19 pandemic, contributing to a resurgence of the highly contagious disease.
Routine vaccine program disruptions and under-resourced health systems are driving the global decline, with estimated measles cases among children under five rising to 15.6 million worldwide in 2023, a 40 percent increase from 2019, according to a statement released Thursday by Australia's University of Queensland (UQ).
The study, published in Nature Medicine, examined measles cases, deaths and vaccination gaps among children under five across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023.
Associate Professor Benn Sartorius from UQ's Frazer Institute said the resurgence coincided with pandemic-related disruptions to immunization programs, health systems and funding, reversing decades of progress, with measles cases falling nearly 80 percent worldwide between 1990 and 2019.
An estimated 23.7 million infants, or one in five worldwide, missed their first measles vaccine dose in 2023. Sub-Saharan Africa accounted for 50 percent of the missed doses, followed by South Asia at 20 percent, Sartorius said, adding the study's data could help authorities identify under-vaccinated populations to prevent future outbreaks. ■

Xinhua Headlines-Xi Focus: Xi calls for new achievements on new Long March

Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a gathering commemorating the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March held at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 22, 2026. (Xinhua/Yao Dawei)
BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday called for new achievements on the new Long March as China commemorates the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Red Army's Long March.
"Only by remembering history can we create a brighter future," said Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, when addressing a gathering held in Beijing to mark the anniversary.
Under Xi's proposal, all participants stood up and observed a moment of silence for the revolutionary heroes who gave their lives during the Long March and in revolutionary struggles across China.
From October 1934 to October 1936, the Red Army marched through more than 10 provinces during the Long March, opening up a new chapter in the Chinese revolution, Xi said.
"This earth-shattering revolutionary feat holds great significance in the history of our Party, country and military, and has a profound impact on our path toward the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation," he noted.
Xi stressed that the Party's right leadership and the establishment of Mao Zedong's core position were decisive for the victory of the Red Army's Long March.
The Party and the Red Army relied on firm conviction, Xi said, adding that troops with noble ideals and firm beliefs are invincible.
Xi emphasized the importance of integrating the basic tenets of Marxism with China's specific realities in addressing the country's issues and problems.
He further underscored that the people will always be the source of strength and a strong support for the Party and the people's armed forces.
Xi said the great spirit of the Long March demonstrates the power of loyalty, truth, justice and unity. "It will always be a precious treasure and a powerful driving force inspiring us to overcome difficulties and forge ahead courageously."
He said the road of the Long March continues to extend. "On our new journey, we are now committed to realizing the Second Centenary Goal of building China into a great modern socialist country in all respects and advancing the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation on all fronts through a Chinese path to modernization," he said.
To forge ahead on the new Long March, Xi said, it is imperative to stay committed to the Party's ideals, convictions and purpose and rely closely on the people to create new achievements.
He underscored the need to unswervingly advance high-quality development and promote common prosperity for all.
Efforts must be made to better ensure both development and security and seize the historical initiative to overcome difficulties, combat risks and meet challenges, he stressed.
Xi also emphasized the importance of moving more quickly to reinforce the people's armed forces to world-class standards and adhering to the Party's absolute leadership over the military.
It is also vital to uphold the leadership of the Party, strengthen Party building and persevere with full and rigorous Party self-governance, he added.
Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang and Li Xi, who are members of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee, as well as Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, attended the gathering.
Zhao, who presided over the event, said Xi's speech was of immense political, ideological and guiding significance, urging earnest efforts to study and grasp its essence and ensure its effective implementation.
He called on the whole Party, the entire military and the Chinese people of all ethnic groups to rally more closely around the Party Central Committee with Xi at its core and strive to build a great country and advance national rejuvenation on all fronts through Chinese modernization.
Around 3,000 people participated in the gathering at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. ■

18:55:59 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Your first glass of water today comes with an invisible bill.
Behind it is a vast network of life, from forests and wetlands to microscopic organisms, helping keep water supplies clean and reliable.
The United Nations calls this interconnected system the "web of life," on which we depend for food, water, medicine and a stable climate.
Biodiversity is the variety of life that makes up this web.
At the ongoing 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17) in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, countries are grappling with how to halt biodiversity loss and translate pledges into action.
VALUE OF BIODIVERSITY
From bacteria and fungi to forests and coral reefs, the biodiversity we see today is the product of 4.5 billion years of evolution, increasingly shaped by human activity.
Pollinating plants, dispersing seeds, sustaining food webs ... every species has a role to play in nature. Losing a single species can mean losing ecological relationships and genetic resources accumulated over millions of years of evolution.
The scale of the loss is alarming.
The 2026 Living Planet Report of the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) shows that the average size of monitored wildlife populations shrank by 73 percent between 1970 and 2022.
Conservation, meanwhile, is making progress.
In Colombia, conservationists are breeding, reintroducing and monitoring the critically endangered Orinoco crocodile, aiming to restore self-sustaining wild populations rather than simply releasing more animals.
Armenia has applied for funding from the Kunming Biodiversity Fund to cover projects bolstering the biodiversity of Lake Sevan, including the protection of the Sevan trout, an endemic species, said Armenian Environment Minister and COP17 President Hambardzum Matevosyan.
And the projects go beyond saving a particular fish species. They aim to preserve genetic diversity, which helps species adapt to changing conditions.
Such diversity is practically valuable for humans: crop varieties may carry genes for drought or disease resistance, while natural organisms provide compounds used in medicine. According to the WHO, more than half of modern medicines came from nature.
INVISIBLE SERVICES
Scientists call the benefits nature provides -- including water purification, pollination and carbon storage -- "ecosystem services."
They rarely appear on household bills or business balance sheets, but their loss can bring very real costs, from poorer water quality to damaged crops and increased exposure to environmental disasters.
According to the United Nations, more than half the world's gross domestic product is moderately or highly dependent on nature. More than 1 billion people rely on forests for their livelihoods. And land and the ocean absorb more than half of all carbon emissions.
As COP17 opened, forest fires in Indonesia's Kalimantan region had affected more than 57,000 hectares, with haze reaching communities in Malaysia and Singapore, said Theiva Lingam, co-chair of Friends of the Earth International.
She described the fires as "a stark reminder of the deeper biodiversity crisis which is unfolding across the Global South."
The vulnerability of peatlands helps explain why such environmental damage can have consequences far beyond the areas affected.
Peatlands cover only about 3 percent of the world's land but store roughly twice as much carbon as all the forests on Earth. When drained or burned, these ecosystems can release large amounts of stored carbon while losing their ability to regulate water and support wildlife.
FOOTING THE BILL
The economic gains from activities that harm biodiversity are often shared globally, while the environmental and social costs fall disproportionately on developing countries and local communities, Lingam said.
To help redress this imbalance, Article 20 of the Convention on Biological Diversity requires developed countries to provide "new and additional financial resources" to help developing ones cover the agreed costs of implementing the convention.
Likewise, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, adopted in 2022, calls for international biodiversity funding to developing countries to reach at least 20 billion U.S. dollars annually by 2025 and 30 billion dollars by 2030.
Preventing damage is particularly important as extinction is irreversible, while restoring degraded ecosystems can be costly and the outcome uncertain, experts said.
Celine Beaulieu, who works on biodiversity finance at the WWF, said funding must also translate into results, urging countries to "judge biodiversity finance not only by what is being pledged, but by what reaches implementation."
As Armenian Deputy Environment Minister Aram Meymaryan put it, conservation must be judged by results on the ground: Have threats been reduced? Have species' chances of survival improved? Are their populations recovering?
Nature may never send a bill, but the cost of losing the ecosystems behind it is real. Protecting biodiversity is not simply an act of generosity toward nature. It is an investment in the systems that sustain everyone's life. ■

The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported the figures.
The new record surpassed the previous high, which had stood for nearly two years.
According to the General Staff, three of the five highest daily Russian troop loss figures were recorded in September and October this year.
The previous record was set on December 19, 2024, when Russian forces suffered 2,200 casualties in a single day.

In total, drone operators struck 2,353 enemy targets during the day, including nine artillery systems, 14 radar and electronic warfare systems, and 493 drones of various types.
Since the beginning of October, units of the Unmanned Systems Forces have struck more than 45,000 enemy targets and neutralized over 11,000 Russian military personnel.

Finns Party targets immigrant benefits in €9 billion savings plan
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
12:43:06 EEST
18:43:06 KST

Finland’s Finns Party has announced plans for €9 billion in fiscal adjustments during the next parliamentary term, including cuts to pensions, immigration, healthcare funding and state administration. The proposals would also abolish the Ministry of the Environment and several state agencies.
Party leader and Finance Minister Riikka Purra presented the programme on Thursday, arguing that Finland must reduce public spending to meet its debt targets without imposing broad tax increases on workers and businesses.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The package includes approximately €8.06 billion in direct expenditure reductions by 2031, alongside around €1 billion in additional tax revenue and other measures. The party also proposes dissolving the Finnish Innovation Fund Sitra and reallocating approximately €1 billion in assets.
Purra said the government must examine spending across all sectors. She acknowledged that the proposed administrative restructuring would result in public-sector redundancies.
Purra identified middle-management positions among the potential targets and suggested that artificial intelligence and automation would help reduce administrative costs.
The party proposes cutting €1.3 billion from central government administration. It would abolish the Ministry of the Environment, the Finnish National Agency for Education and the Natural Resources Institute Finland, transferring selected responsibilities to other government bodies.
Deputy chairman Joakim Vigelius said the restructuring would include €150 million in agency-related savings. Abolishing the National Agency for Education would account for approximately €10 million.
Public broadcaster Yle would face €200 million in reductions, while its automatic funding increases would end. Parliamentary spending and political party subsidies would also face cuts, including the abolition of funding for parties’ youth organisations.
Immigration and integration programmes would lose approximately €690 million. The party proposes ending Finland’s refugee quota, withdrawing municipal integration subsidies and tightening access to social security for foreign nationals.
Under the proposal, access to several benefits would require ten years of residence. These would include housing allowances, child benefits, student support, parental benefits and unemployment assistance.
Pensions would account for €1.62 billion in projected adjustments. The party proposes restricting inflation-linked increases for pensions exceeding €2,000 monthly between 2028 and 2031.
MP Miko Bergbom said existing pension payments would not fall in nominal terms. Pensions below €2,000 would retain their full index adjustments.
Healthcare regions would face €1 billion in reductions to projected funding increases, while municipalities would lose €600 million.
Social Affairs and Health Minister Wille Rydman said healthcare funding would continue rising annually, although at a slower rate.
The programme would also eliminate €500 million in development cooperation spending. Parliamentary group chairman Jani Mäkelä said assistance to Ukraine would remain unaffected, alongside provisions for emergency humanitarian relief.
Universities and universities of applied sciences would face approximately €340 million in funding adjustments. Students pursuing a second qualification at the same level would pay €2,000 per semester.
Research, development and business subsidies would face further reductions.
The proposed tax measures include a 3% levy on banks’ net interest income, higher electricity taxes for data centres, taxes on added sugar and plastic bags, and restrictions on tax exemptions for foundations.
Newspapers’ value-added tax would rise from 10% to 13.5%.
The proposals follow an agreement among several parliamentary parties to pursue fiscal adjustments estimated at €8 billion to €11 billion during the next parliamentary term.
Purra said the Finns Party would publish its separate economic policy programme in November.

Far-left leader Melenchon in firing line as France blame-game heats up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:41:40 UTC
18:41:40 KST

Far-left leader Melenchon in firing line as France blame-game heats up
PARIS, Oct 22 - Rivals from the centre-left to the far right have turned on Jean-Luc Melenchon and his France Unbowed (LFI) party, accusing them of fuelling France's worst civil unrest in years.
Melenchon, who launched his fourth presidential bid in May and remains the hard left's strongest hope of reaching next year's election run-off, has faced mounting criticism since unrest engulfed several French cities, with opponents saying years of confrontational rhetoric helped fuel tensions now spilling onto the streets.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu sharpened those attacks on Tuesday, telling an LFI lawmaker that the party's "political agenda of instilling violence and chaos in the country was now on full display".
The 75-year-old leader has rejected suggestions that LFI bears responsibility for the unrest, accusing the government instead of failing to address deep-rooted social and economic grievances in France's poorer suburbs.
But criticism has come from across the political spectrum.
Gerard Larcher, the president of the Senate, told Le Figaro this week it was worth considering whether LFI should be banned, a suggestion decried as "authoritarian" by LFI.
Laurent Jacobelli, a spokesperson for Marine Le Pen's National Rally (RN), blamed "the ultra-left, including France Unbowed", as well as what he called uncontrolled immigration, for creating a revolutionary climate.
Marc Fesneau, of centrist party MoDem, said Melenchon had long promoted the idea that "everything must be a battleground".
"When you turn everything into a confrontation, you run serious risks," Fesneau told Reuters.
The attacks underscore both Melenchon's central place in French politics and the unease he provokes as the country heads toward a presidential election expected to pit increasingly strong anti-establishment forces against a weakened political centre.
The unrest has reinforced that contrast, shifting scrutiny onto the hard left while allowing Le Pen to strike a more presidential tone on law and order, an issue that traditionally favours the far right.
Yet with France's political landscape fragmented into three rival blocs and traditional centre-left and centre-right parties struggling, analysts say Melenchon remains a formidable political force.
YOUTH APPEAL AND THE 'NEW FRANCE'
LFI has built its support by mobilising younger voters, many of whom have grown disillusioned with mainstream politics. An IFOP poll for LCI published this month put Melenchon on 16.5%, behind Le Pen's 36% but ahead of all other mainstream candidates.
A Cluster17 poll found nearly half of 18-to-24-year-olds and more than a third of 25-to-34-year-olds would back Melenchon.
That has made him a prominent voice for many students involved in the protest movement and wider unrest that has shaken France in recent weeks.
However, Frederic Dabi, head of pollster IFOP, said the unrest risked reinforcing one of Melenchon's biggest electoral weaknesses: his inability to win over older voters.
"The perception that Jean-Luc Melenchon has been too indulgent towards perpetrators of violence is an absolute red line for a large part of the electorate," Dabi said.
Nevertheless, the party has also built strong support in poorer urban areas and among many voters from immigrant backgrounds who see themselves reflected in Melenchon's vision of a "New France" — a multicultural republic that embraces ethnic and religious diversity and gives greater political representation to communities that often feel overlooked.
Supporters say that reflects social realities rather than identity politics.
"It's the unique synthesis between a programme of revolutionary rupture and the desire to govern the country," LFI lawmaker Hadrien Clouet told Reuters.
Clouet said that meant tackling inequality and reversing a decades-long transfer of wealth towards finance and a narrow oligarchic elite.
Yet critics say LFI often blurs the line between democratic protest and more radical political agitation.
UPRISING LANGUAGE DRAWS SCRUTINY
Melenchon has frequently invoked the language of popular uprising. During the pensions crisis of 2023, he urged supporters to "tear down the citadel" of President Emmanuel Macron's government and has at times spoken favourably of "citizen insurrection" as a democratic force.
Supporters say such language refers to mass political mobilisation, not violence. The party officially advocates non-violent action.
LFI and its allies argue some of the accusations are politically motivated. This week, investigative news outlet Mediapart reported, citing an anonymous intelligence officer, that officials had been instructed to portray LFI as being behind the protest movement despite what the source described as a lack of evidence. The government denied the allegation.
Still, opponents say Melenchon's messaging is often deliberately ambiguous.
"They say they are against vandals, but at the same time they justify masks at demonstrations," said Sylvain Maillard of Macron's Renaissance party. "They never calm things down. They always say it's the police's fault. They want chaos."
Former Socialist President Francois Hollande, however, warned against making Melenchon the sole focus of the debate.
"It is not one political party or one individual that poured fuel on the fire," Hollande told France Inter. While criticising LFI for sometimes drawing an equivalence between rioter violence and police violence, he said: "To fixate on LFI is to fail to see what is happening in the country." REUTERS

Burglaries soar in Switzerland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:38:40 UTC
18:38:40 KST

Burglaries soar in Switzerland
Burglaries are soaring in Switzerland. Thieves are particularly active during the winter months and in French-speaking Switzerland, with the cost per incident reaching record levels, according to an analysis by the Swiss insurance company AXA.
Since 2020, AXA has recorded a steady rise in the number of burglaries per insured household, the insurance company announced on Thursday. In 2025, the company recorded 4% more burglaries than in the previous year and 15% more than in 2022.
The switch to winter time and the resulting earlier onset of darkness contributed to the rise in burglaries. From October to March last year, for example, AXA recorded 45% more offences than during the summer months. December proved to be the month with the highest number of burglaries, followed by November.
More
Geneva super-rich rocked by luxury home burglary spree
On Christmas Eve and New Year’s Eve, the insurance company recorded more than twice as many burglaries as on ordinary days. Burglaries were least frequent between April and June.
The risk of burglary also varied greatly depending on where people lived: between 2019 and 2025, the likelihood of falling victim to a burglary in the canton of Geneva was more than twice as high as the Swiss average. During this period, there were 8.4 burglaries per year per 1,000 households in Geneva. The cantons of Vaud, Basel-City, Basel-Country as well as Jura, Solothurn and Neuchâtel were also affected more frequently than average.
In central and south-eastern Switzerland, however, the risk was significantly lower. In Uri and Graubünden, AXA recorded just one burglary per year per 1,000 households since 2019, while in Glarus the figure was 1.2 burglaries. The Swiss average stood at 3.3 burglaries.
Claims costs at record levels
Average claim costs also rose. Last year, AXA paid out over CHF22 million for burglaries, representing a 9% increase on the previous year and a 60% rise compared with three years earlier. The average claim per incident reached a record high of over CHF7,000 ($8,534) in 2025, making it 30% more expensive than three years earlier.
AXA attributes this trend to several factors. For instance, many people now own increasingly expensive valuables such as smartphones, laptops or e-bikes. Furthermore, these same goods are more expensive than before due to higher prices. Another reason is the significant increase in major claims, i.e. cases costing over CHF30,000. Since 2023, AXA has recorded around twice as many such cases per year as in previous years. Experts at AXA suspect that such complex offences point to organised structures and that professionally executed burglaries and organised crime have increased significantly.

The vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell by Wiz, could allow attackers to take control of affected servers or steal sensitive information without logging in.

The country is also preparing to host several major UEFA events in the coming years. Astana is scheduled to stage the UEFA European Under-19 Futsal Championship in 2027, while the capital’s main football stadium will host the UEFA Super Cup in 2028.
The host of the 2030 European Futsal Championship is scheduled to be announced in September 2027 following a meeting of the UEFA Executive Committee.
It is worth noting that Kazakhstan will also host UEFA’s 51st Congress in Astana on 22 April 2027. The gathering, the organization’s highest governing body, will include elections for the UEFA president and members of its Executive Committee.

This Preamp Costs More Than a Fancy Sports Car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

In the world of hi-fi, there’s “high end,” and then there’s Goldmund. Since 1978, the Swiss manufacturer has produced exquisitely designed, astonishingly high-performance and staggeringly expensive audio equipment. As it nears half a century of proudly uncompromised engineering, its determination to position its products as credible alternatives to jewellery, art, or other pricey indulgences for the superrich shows no sign of abating—quite the opposite.
I was recently invited to Goldmund's headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, to experience the new Mimesis Statement, the company’s flagship analog preamplifier. Goldmund's HQ, incidentally, features the sort of high ceilings, generous use of concrete and glass, and fanatical tidiness that puts me in mind of a Bond villain who's decided to devote their time to audio gratification rather than global tyranny.
In a traditional stereo chain, a preamplifier takes the low-level signals from your source gear, handles volume and input selection, and feeds that clean signal to a power amp to drive your speakers. Most people use an integrated amplifier, one that combines pre-amplification and power amplification in the same box.
Those who want to take things to the next level often separate pre-amplification and power amplification into two boxes—to keep the precious audio signal away from any electrical activity that might compromise its integrity. Goldmund, naturally, is convinced that a preamplifier alone needs to occupy three separate boxes.
The first box, the one with the buttons, dials, and display, houses the pre-amplification electronics. It’s where your source equipment—turntable, network streamer, whatever you fancy—connects using the generous selection of balanced and unbalanced inputs. The other two boxes are external power supplies serving the left and right channels of your stereo signal.
Goldmund reckons this radical separation, along with painstaking internal architecture featuring complete symmetry, voltage regulation stages, and optimized heat dissipation, guarantees signal integrity and utterly consistent operating conditions in all circumstances.
It’s apparently not enough to make a preamplifier with such a low total harmonic distortion figure (0.0002 percent) that it’s extremely difficult to measure in the first place. No, it has to be housed in three chassis with mirrored-glass displays, metal-coated controls, and Goldmund’s signature slender gold-line design flourish to confirm its identity.
In the US, the Goldmund Mimesis Statement analog preamplifier costs $240,000. No, I didn't accidentally add a few zeros. We’re already into “fairly fancy European sports car” territory here, but a preamplifier by itself doesn’t constitute an audio system. For the Mimesis Statement to do its thing, it needs a music input signal, which it will output to a power amplifier. From there, it goes to a pair of speakers.
Thankfully, Goldmund offers plenty of options. During my listen to the Mimesis Statement, it is connected to the company’s Eidos network streamer (yours for $27,000) at one end and a pair of Thelos 9800 power amplifiers (nearly 800 pounds per amplifier, 1,560 watts per channel, an imposing aesthetic, and $500,000 each) at the other. The amplified signal then moves to a pair of Theia Passive four-way floor-standing loudspeakers ($215,000 for two). That’s a total system price of $1,482,000—not so much “sports car” as “very nice apartment, probably with a balcony.” And I haven’t even added in the price of cables.
What does all that money buy you? Well, it most certainly buys a distinctive industrial design language, attention to detail and precision where fit and finish is concerned that’s beyond OCD, hand-soldered circuit boards, military-grade alloys crafted using established Swiss watchmaking techniques, and the sort of overall physical presence that’s more commonly associated with the stuff they build at NASA.
But can a stereo system possibly be worth $1.5 million? The answer has to be “no.” I’ve been a part of the audio equipment appraisal process for over two decades, and I know full well that the law of diminishing returns kicks in long before you’ve spent six figures, let alone seven. But Goldmund isn’t selling you a hi-fi any more than Rolex is selling you a wristwatch—it’s selling you an unmistakable symbol of status, wealth, and success. It’s selling you exclusivity. It’s selling you what it sincerely believes is the pinnacle of artisanal engineering.
And it’s also selling you a serving of detailed, tremendously insightful, and eloquently communicative sound. I am not a prospective Goldmund customer, but if I had the disposable income, I really think I might be.

Stubb and Costa Emerge as Possible EU Negotiators with Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:28:00 UTC
18:28:00 KST

European governments are considering appointing a representative to negotiate directly with Russian President Vladimir Putin on a peace deal for Ukraine, as concerns grow that the United States could reach an agreement without adequately protecting Kyiv’s and Europe’s interests, POLITCO reports.
The debate intensified this week after U.S. presidential envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Russia to propose a three-way summit involving Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in an effort to secure a ceasefire.
Czech President Petr Pavel said in an interview with the Axel Springer Global Reporters’ Network, of which POLITICO is a part, that Putin does not regard the European Union as an authority. “President Putin disregards the European Union as an authority,” Pavel said Tuesday. “He doesn’t want to talk to Ursula von der Leyen, he doesn’t talk to Kaja Kallas. He stopped talking to other European leaders, including Emmanuel Macron.”
Pavel argued that European leaders should agree on a representative or delegation authorized to negotiate on their behalf. “identify a person or a group of people who would speak for Europe. Not necessarily representatives of the EU or NATO, but simply leaders who would be given a mandate by the others to negotiate,” he said.
Trump has unsettled Ukraine and its European allies in recent days by conducting discussions with Putin without them and appearing increasingly inclined to support Russia's position in the war, which is approaching its fifth year. The developments have revived debate in Brussels and elsewhere about establishing a direct European channel to the Kremlin to defend the continent's interests and strengthen Ukraine's ability to reject an unfavorable settlement.
David Lidington, a distinguished fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London, said Europe should consider opening such a channel despite limited prospects for immediate progress. “Much as it sticks in the craw, I do think a channel of some kind to Putin would be a good thing to have,” he said. “I am not optimistic that it would achieve anything much in the short term, but to have a channel which can then be used as and when an opportunity arises is not a bad thing.”
European diplomats and officials remain divided over who should lead the effort. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has negotiated directly with Trump on trade, European Council President António Costa has previously established contact with the Kremlin through his office, and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas is another possible representative of European interests.
However, a diplomat from an EU member country, speaking anonymously about sensitive matters, said European officials must recognize that negotiations involving Putin and Trump would not necessarily follow the bloc's institutional protocols.
“We cannot show up with two or three people all speaking on behalf of the EU,” the diplomat said. “The choice of who ends up representing the EU will be based on what would provide the most value, not personal power struggles or narcissistic preferences.”
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has emerged as a possible candidate from outside the EU's institutional structure. His advantages include what is considered one of the strongest relationships with Trump among EU leaders and Finland's extensive experience dealing with Russia. The two countries share a 1,300-kilometer border and have fought wars against each other in the past.
“Stubb is of interest because of Finnish knowledge of and traditional dialogue with Russia,” one European diplomat said. “They know more than anyone on our side [about] what it takes to feel secure in such a situation.”
Another EU diplomat described Stubb as “the only person who has come forward so far” to demonstrate political leadership at the highest level, suggesting he could represent Europe at a future peace summit. Stubb met with Zelensky and Witkoff in Norway on Tuesday for discussions ahead of the U.S. envoy's trip to Russia. Von der Leyen's senior aide, Bjoern Seibert, also attended the Oslo meeting. Seibert has participated in gatherings of national security advisers within the Coalition of the Willing, which supports Ukraine.
A third European diplomat stressed that the EU as a whole must be represented in negotiations, rather than leaving the process to a handful of major powers such as Germany, France and the United Kingdom.
The diplomat said Seibert and Pedro Lourtie, Costa's senior aide, should both participate in preparatory discussions. EU member states must also receive adequate updates on the negotiations, the diplomat added.
At last week's summit in Brussels, European leaders asked Costa whether he should begin direct talks with Putin, according to a fourth EU diplomat.
“Costa said, no, he’s not going to talk to Putin now,” the diplomat said. “But Costa should start talking to Putin if we want to play a role in the negotiations. By not speaking, we are playing into the hands of our opponents.”
The diplomat argued that Costa would be a more suitable negotiator than von der Leyen or Kallas, whom some regard as too closely aligned with Ukraine to represent the EU effectively in leader-level discussions. Kallas has also been particularly vocal in criticizing Trump. “Costa comes across as more of an honest broker,” the diplomat said.
The European Commission maintains that the EU is already involved in the peace process, pointing to Seibert's participation in Tuesday's meeting in Oslo.
European Commission spokesperson Paula Pinho told reporters on Wednesday that the Oslo discussions sought to determine whether conditions were in place to advance toward talks involving Ukraine and Russia together, potentially in a trilateral or broader multilateral format.
She said the discussions covered territorial questions, security and Ukraine's postwar prosperity. Witkoff is expected to brief Ukrainian and European officials following his meeting with Putin.
“What is very important is that we are sitting at the table, that we are able to present our position, and that we can engage in what is a shared objective to put an end to this horrific war,” Pinho said.

Russia and Türkiye back South Africa in G20 row with US
Russia and Türkiye have called for South Africa’s swift return to G20 activities after the US barred the country from participating during America’s presidency amid tensions over Pretoria’s domestic policies and foreign ties.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Aleksandr Pankin and his Turkish counterpart, Berris Ekinci, discussed the issue during consultations in Moscow, according to a Russian Foreign Ministry statement released on Tuesday. They said any changes to G20 membership must be agreed on by consensus, with greater representation for countries of the Global South and East.
The diplomats also discussed preparations for the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting in Atlanta on October 30-31 and the leaders’ summit in Miami December 14-15. They stressed that the forum should remain a platform for equal dialogue on global economic challenges.
Russia and Türkiye are both members of the G20, which comprises 19 countries, the EU, and the African Union.
US President Donald Trump announced in November 2025 that South Africa would not be invited to the Miami summit, saying it demonstrated that it is “unworthy of membership.”
The Trump administration boycotted the G20 leaders’ summit in Johannesburg that month over allegations that the African country allows “horrific” abuses against its white minority, including killings and land confiscation, which Pretoria denies.
Trump also accused Pretoria of refusing to hand over the G20 presidency to a US Embassy representative. South Africa said it would breach protocol for President Cyril Ramaphosa to hand over to a junior diplomat. The transfer later took place at the Department of International Relations and Cooperation between officials of similar rank.
The South African presidency said US punitive measures are based on “misinformation and distortions.” Prior to the Johannesburg summit, Ramaphosa also rejected US pressure against issuing a joint declaration without Washington’s support. He told reporters on November 20 that South Africa “will not agree to be bullied.”
In December, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio extended the exclusion to all G20 meetings during America’s presidency. South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola rejected the move, saying no single member can unilaterally exclude South Africa, a founding member.
Relations have since deteriorated, with the US announcing visa restrictions in September against officials and people it accuses of enabling racial discrimination, uncompensated land seizures, and inciting violence against minorities in South Africa. US Ambassador Brent Bozell also criticized Pretoria’s ties with Russia, China, and Iran, pledging to challenge its “geostrategic drift” toward America’s competitors.
Ramaphosa warned on Monday that South Africa, which already faces steep US tariffs, must prepare for possible exclusion from America’s preferential trade program for African countries.

Expert sees creation of ‘nuclear belt’ as next step in militarization of the Arctic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:24:32 UTC
18:24:32 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. The next stage of Arctic militarization will likely involve the expansion of nuclear military infrastructure across the region and the emergence of a nuclear belt along Russia’s northern borders, encompassing Northern Europe and Greenland, Alexander Stepanov, a military expert at the RANEPA Institute of Law and National Security, told TASS.
He was commenting on the European Commission’s new Arctic strategy, which, for the first time in more than 30 years, places primary emphasis on military development.
According to Stepanov, the EU’s formal adoption of a militarization agenda, driven in part by efforts to exploit the Arctic’s natural resources, will entail a strengthening of NATO’s northern flank. This trend aligns with the strategic priorities of Northern Europe’s military-industrial complexes, Finland and Sweden’s accession to NATO, and the designation of the Baltic and North seas as priority areas for Europe’s geo-economic and military presence.
"The next step will most likely be the ‘nuclearization’ of the Arctic, specifically through the expansion of nuclear military infrastructure into the region. I envisage a ‘nuclear arc’ stretching from the Baltic Sea to the northern seas. A nuclear belt is taking shape in the areas adjacent to the Arctic along Russia’s borders, encompassing Northern Europe and Greenland, which has recently de facto legalized an expanded US military presence. This will likely involve the deployment of nuclear-capable assets, including US strategic bombers and nuclear-powered submarines," Stepanov said.
He noted that the necessary legal frameworks are already being prepared in several countries. In Finland, steps are being taken to remove restrictions on the potential deployment of nuclear weapons, effectively reversing a policy that had been in place since 1987. A similar trend is evident in Sweden, where the country’s leadership has signaled a possible willingness to host nuclear weapons. Lithuania, meanwhile, has removed restrictions at the constitutional level, effectively opening the way for the deployment of nuclear arsenals.
"The Arctic is becoming a key area of interest not only for the United States but also for the European Union, which urgently needs access to hydrocarbons and rare-earth metals. This creates additional threats to the peaceful development of the Arctic and to the maritime trade routes that are vital to Russia," Stepanov concluded.

FACTBOX: What we know about one of largest Ukrainian drone attacks on Moscow
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:23:14 UTC
18:23:14 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Air defense systems on duty intercepted and destroyed a total of 808 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones overnight over Russian regions, the Defense Ministry said.
A nighttime Ukrainian drone attack injured two people in Moscow and one person in Lipetsk.
Kiev’s attempted drone attack on Moscow on Wednesday evening and overnight became one of the largest since the beginning of this year.
TASS has compiled the main details of the aftermath.
Scale
- Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed a total of 808 fixed-wing Ukrainian drones over Russian regions between 8 p.m. Moscow time (5 p.m. GMT) on October 21 and 8 a.m. Moscow time (5 a.m. GMT) on October 22, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
- The Defense Ministry said the drones were shot down over the Belgorod, Bryansk, Vladimir, Voronezh, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Leningrad, Oryol, Rostov, Ryazan, Smolensk, Tambov, Tver, Tula and Yaroslavl regions, as well as the Moscow Region, the Republic of Crimea and the Black Sea.
- The attempted Ukrainian drone attack on Moscow from Wednesday evening into Thursday morning was one of the largest of the year, according to TASS’s analysis of data published by Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin on the Max messenger.
- Sobyanin said that 630 drones headed toward the Moscow Region between 8:30 p.m. Moscow time (5:30 p.m. GMT) on October 21 and 4:00 a.m. Moscow time (1:00 a.m. GMT) on October 22.
- On-duty air defense systems destroyed most of the drones at long range and intercepted 163 on their approach to Moscow.
- Seventy Ukrainian drones were shot down over the Tula Region in western Russia overnight, regional Governor Dmitry Milyaev reported on Max.
- A total of 44 Ukrainian drones were destroyed over the Voronezh Region in southwestern Russia overnight, regional Governor Alexander Gusev wrote on Max.
- About 20 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the Lipetsk Region in western Russia, regional Governor Igor Artamonov reported on Max.
- Air defense crews downed 17 Ukrainian drones over the Kaluga Region in western Russia overnight, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said on Max.
- Shapsha specified that air defense forces shot down the drones over the Babyninsky, Dzerzhinsky, Zhukovsky, Maloyaroslavetsky, Peremyshlsky, Sukhinichsky, Ulyanovsky, and Ferzikovsky municipal districts, the Kuibyshevsky District, and the outskirts of the city of Kaluga.
- Twelve drones were intercepted over the Oryol Region in western Russia overnight, regional Governor Andrey Klychkov said on Max.
- Ten drones were downed over the Ryazan Region in central Russia overnight, regional Governor Pavel Malkov reported on Max.
Aftermath
- A nighttime drone attack on Moscow injured two people in the capital’s Troitsky Administrative District, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said on Max.
- Medical and emergency personnel are providing the injured with all necessary assistance.
- A drone attack injured a civilian in Lipetsk, a city in western Russia, regional Governor Igor Artamonov reported on Max.
- The injured person is receiving necessary medical care at a hospital.
- Drone strikes also damaged the windows and facades of several private houses and apartment buildings in various parts of Lipetsk.
- Drone debris struck an outpatient clinic on Merkulova Street in Lipetsk. The building was empty at the time, so no one was injured.
- The outpatient clinic on Merkulova Street will remain closed on Thursday, Lipetsk Mayor Mikhail Shcherbakov said on Max.
- The regional government’s press service later clarified that a drone’s unexploded warhead remained on the building’s roof following the nighttime attack.
- Falling drone debris damaged the roofs and facades of several private houses and apartment buildings, as well as one social infrastructure facility, in a municipal district of the Voronezh Region, Governor Alexander Gusev reported on Max.
- A man injured in the large-scale drone attack on Lipetsk underwent surgery and remains under medical supervision, Shcherbakov later added.
- Drone debris also damaged several passenger cars with shrapnel.
- The attack also damaged power supply networks in another district, which now require repairs.
- Emergency response teams are working at the affected sites.
- A drone attack damaged private homes in the Zaoksky District of the Tula Region and in the city of Tula, regional Governor Dmitry Milyaev reported on Max.
- A drone attack damaged four private houses in the Zhukovsky District of the Kaluga Region, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said on Max.
- Drone debris damaged the windows and fence of a private house in the Maloyaroslavetsky District.
- The attack also caused minor damage to a power line serving a settlement in the Dzerzhinsky District.
- Repair crews are carrying out restoration work.

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin signed decrees appoint five new government members.
Their nominations were approved the day before by the Russian State Duma at its meeting. TASS collected key points of new appointments.
Government resignations
Dmitry Grigorenko stepped down from the office of Deputy Prime Minister - Chief of the Government Staff. The Supervisory Board of Sberbank will consider the issue of appointing Grigorenko to the position of the Deputy CEO of the bank, the press service of the credit institution said.
Yury Trutnev was relieved of his duties as the Deputy Prime Minister - Presidential Plenipotentiary in the Far Eastern Federal District by the presidential decree. Trutnev was appointed as the aide to the Russian President by the same decree.
New position in the Cabinet
The position of the Deputy Prime Minister - Minister of Finance was introduced in the Russian Cabinet. The number of deputy prime ministers is now increased to eleven.
Putin appointed Anton Siluanov to this position, who served before as the Finance Minister.
Cabinet reshuffle
Andrey Nikitin, earlier serving as the Minister of Transport, was appointed to the office of the Deputy Prime Minister.
Irina Okladnikova, the ex-first deputy finance minister, became the Deputy Prime Minister - Chief of the Government Staff.
Oleg Kozhemyako, who served before as the Governor of the Primorye Region, was appointed to the position of the Deputy Prime Minister - Presidential Plenipotentiary in the Far Eastern Federal District.
Dmitry Yadrov, the ex-head of the Russian Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, took the post of the Minister of Transport.
The first meeting of the new Cabinet will take place this Thursday, the government’s press service told TASS.

Denmark to Provide €100.5 Million Loan Guarantee for Fire Point Subsidiary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:15:31 UTC
18:15:31 KST

Denmark is providing a state-backed loan guarantee of DKK 750 million (approximately €100.5million) to a subsidiary of Fire Point Rocket Technologies.
According to a press release published by ViaRitzau, the guarantee is intended to help the company secure a loan from a Danish bank.
Because of the war in Ukraine, the company has been unable to obtain financing under normal commercial terms.
Under the guarantee, the Danish state will not provide the loan directly. Instead, it will cover the bank’s losses if the company fails to repay the loan, subject to the guarantee’s terms.
The financing is being arranged through the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark (EIFO), which is currently involved in nearly 40 projects supporting Ukraine and its reconstruction.
Danish Minister for Business and Competitiveness Martin Lidegaard noted that establishing Ukrainian defence production in Denmark promotes knowledge sharing, strengthens Danish industry, and makes Europe more independent.
Meanwhile, Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus stressed that locating production facilities outside Ukraine protects them from Russian strikes and helps ensure reliable supply chains.
In addition, the cooperation gives the Danish armed forces and businesses access to unique technologies and combat experience gained by Ukrainian specialists during the war.
As a reminder, Denmark became the first country to allow a Ukrainian defence company to establish production facilities on its territory, allocating a site in Southern Jutland.
The facility is designed to produce solid rocket propellant.
The project is being carried out by the Danish subsidiary of Fire Point Rocket Technologies, which operates under its parent company in Ukraine.
Construction was initially estimated to cost €50 million. The total project cost has since increased to more than €150 million. The company has already obtained all the necessary permits to begin operations.

Northern Fleet ships hold drills to protect Russian military facilities in Arctic
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
09:14:30 UTC
18:14:30 KST

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. A detachment of the Russian Navy’s Northern Fleet warships has held an exercise to defend Russian military facilities in the Arctic, the fleet’s press service reported.
"A detachment of Northern Fleet warships conducted an exercise with a Northern Fleet tactical group to defend Russian military infrastructure facilities in the Arctic," the press service said.
According to the exercise scenario, a group of simulated enemy ships was preparing to seize military facilities on Alexandra Land Island. After receiving the mission, a battalion of the Bastion coastal missile launcher, stationed on the Franz Josef Land archipelago, moved to its designated area. The Bastion crews carried out simulated missile launches against the naval group. The targets were located 350 kilometers away. The surviving enemy landing forces reached Alexandra Land from assault boats.
Exercise events
A detachment of Northern Fleet warships practiced reinforcing the protection and defense of military infrastructure facilities. The crew of a Ka-29 ship-based helicopter, which took off from the Ivan Papanin patrol ship, delivered a counterterrorism team to the island. During the combat exercise, the simulated enemy forces were destroyed. Mobile air defense teams practiced intercepting unmanned aerial vehicles.
The press service emphasized that the tasks of simulating a missile strike by the Bastion coastal missile launcher crews against a detachment of enemy warships, as well as reinforcing and defending the Northern Fleet’s tactical group, were fully accomplished.
The fleet noted that the exercise was conducted using lessons from the special military operation. The exercise took place in challenging weather conditions, including snowfall and winds reaching speeds of up to 30 meters per second. However, the personnel completed all assigned tasks.
