14:31:30 CST
15:31:30 KST

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 21 (Xinhua) -- Thousands of California state employees staged a one-day statewide strike on Wednesday over pay, healthcare and remote work, marking the first such walkout for California's largest public employees union in its 44-year history.
The Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1000, which represents more than 100,000 working people employed by the State of California, is seeking salary increases totaling 20 percent over three years, higher state healthcare contributions and department-level remote-work policies based on operational needs.
Workers rallied in Sacramento, San Francisco, Oakland and Los Angeles, nonprofit California news outlet CalMatters reported.
"We're making noise on the picket line and sending a clear message to the State: we won't be silenced because state workers deserve fair bargaining NOW!" said the union in a post on Facebook.
Union President Anica Walls said workers needed a contract that would allow them to afford groceries, childcare, rent and other necessities, according to a statement reported by San Francisco public broadcaster KQED.
About 95,000 employees were eligible to strike, while fewer than 5,000 designated essential employees were required to continue working under staffing requirements determined by the labor board, according to the union.
Some motor vehicle offices and state parks had modified or limited operations ahead of the strike, CalMatters reported. The Department of Motor Vehicles had warned that offices could face delays or close early, the outlet reported, citing a department spokesperson.
The union has accused the California state government of negotiating in bad faith, as workers' collective bargaining agreement with the government expired on June 30, according to local media.
The state had sought to stop the walkout, arguing that it put pressure on negotiations and threatened public health and safety, KQED said. ■

Feature: Vietnamese diners develop growing appetite for Chinese cuisine
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
14:30:59 CST
15:30:59 KST

People enjoy hotpot at Chinese hotpot chain Haidilao in Hanoi, Vietnam, Oct. 20, 2026.(Xinhua/Liu Ying)
HANOI, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- The spicy aroma of mala hotpot drifted from the Chinese booth at the second Cultures of the World Festival in Hanoi earlier this month, drawing a long queue of Vietnamese visitors curious to sample its fiery flavors.
The scene was one sign of a growing curiosity about Chinese food in Vietnam, where diners are discovering not only familiar hotpot and dim sum but also the cooking traditions of different Chinese regions.
For some young Vietnamese, the attraction begins with the heat.
Pham Linh Dan, a 19-year-old university student in Hanoi, said she eats at Chinese hotpot chain Haidilao two to three times a week and has also tried several other Chinese-style hotpot restaurants.
Dan, who describes herself as a fan of spicy food, said what draws her to Chinese cuisine is not simply the level of heat, but the way different spices build the flavor.
"Chinese food is not just spicy in an ordinary way. It combines spices such as cinnamon and star anise, which create a kind of spiciness that is different from what we have in Vietnam," she said.
The distinctive taste has also made her curious about the culture behind the food.
"It makes me like Chinese food even more and want to explore more of Chinese culture and cuisine," Dan said, adding that Sichuan would be her first choice if she had the chance to travel to China for food.
That enthusiasm is also reflected in the performance of larger Chinese restaurant brands in Vietnam.
According to data released by Super Hi International, Haidilao generated about 57 million U.S. dollars in revenue in Vietnam in the first half of 2026, up 31 percent year on year and accounting for more than 10 percent of its global revenue.
But the appetite for Chinese flavors is no longer confined to Vietnam's major cities.
In central Vietnam's Nghe An province, a newly opened restaurant specializing in Jiangxi cuisine has also been drawing local diners as well as visitors from neighboring areas curious about Chinese food.
Nguyen Thu Hien traveled about an hour from neighboring Ha Tinh province to Nghe An and took the opportunity to try Chinese food for a change.
"Before trying it, I thought Chinese food was quite spicy and a little oily," Hien said.
After tasting the dishes, however, she said they were less oily than she had expected and thought the flavors had been adjusted for local diners.
Pham Thi Nhu Quynh, who had previously traveled to southwest China's Yunnan Province and eaten Chinese food there, offered a different perspective.
"I think the food is quite authentic, still oily and spicy," Quynh said, adding that it was neither too sweet nor too spicy for her taste.
For Quynh, seeing more Chinese regional cuisines appear in Vietnam also carries meaning beyond the meal itself.
"I think it is also a way to convey culture, especially food culture, and gives Vietnamese people more diverse choices," she said.
For Wang Shixiang from the Jiangxi Chamber of Commerce in Vietnam, the spread of regional Chinese cuisines to more parts of the country carries a broader cultural meaning.
"We hope to use food as a bridge to preserve and promote Chinese culinary culture, bring Chinese cuisine to the world, and help more people learn about China and fall in love with Chinese flavors," Wang said. ■

S. Korea freezes key rate at 3.00 pct to evaluate impact of back-to-back rate hikes

SEOUL, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's central bank froze its key rate on Thursday, pausing its monetary tightening cycle to evaluate the impact of back-to-back rate hikes in July and August.
Bank of Korea (BOK) Governor Shin Hyun-song and other monetary policymakers decided to leave the benchmark seven-day repurchase rate unchanged at 3.00 percent.
The unanimous decision was in line with market expectations. According to a Korea Financial Investment Association survey of 100 fixed-income experts, 93 percent predicted the rate on hold.
Shin told a press conference that the central bank needs to prolong its tightening cycle despite the pause, stating that the consecutive rate hikes in July and August gave the BOK policy room to maneuver according to domestic economic conditions.
Expectations ran high for the BOK to resume its rate-hiking path later this year or early next year amid the still high inflationary pressure and the continuous household debt growth.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 2.9 percent in September from a year earlier, decelerating from an increase of 3.1 percent in August.
The headline inflation, however, stayed above the central bank's mid-term inflation target of 2 percent for 13 straight months.
Petroleum product prices jumped 14.8 percent last month amid the continued Middle East conflicts.
Despite slowing household loan growth, total debt kept an upward trajectory for a seventh consecutive month.
Debt owed by households to deposit-taking banks totaled 1,198.9 trillion won (906.1 billion U.S. dollars) at the end of September, up 0.6 trillion won from a month earlier.
It marked a significant slowdown from the 3.5 trillion won expansion in the previous month, affected by a slump in retail stock investments and a reduction in newly completed housing.
The BOK said in a statement that the domestic economy maintained strong growth led by exports and investment, but it cautioned that inflation remained high at around 3 percent.
The bank explained that housing-related loans continued to increase while the pace of growth in housing prices in Seoul and its surrounding areas accelerated again.
The overall South Korean economy showed a robust recovery thanks to soaring exports of semiconductors used in the artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.
Outbound shipments surged 83.5 percent in September from a year earlier, while the daily average exports more than doubled.
Revised gross domestic product (GDP) data showed that facility investment climbed 6.3 percent year-on-year in the second quarter.
After shrinking 0.1 percent in the fourth quarter of last year, real GDP rebounded 1.8 percent quarter-on-quarter in the first quarter of this year and beat expectations with a 0.6 percent expansion in the second quarter.
The current account surplus from January to August totaled 279.2 billion U.S. dollars, a more than fourfold expansion compared to the same period last year.
Backed by the strong fundamentals, the central bank raised its 2026 growth outlook from 2.6 percent to 3.3 percent in August. ■

====================================================================================================

U.S. Army tests artillery shell that hunts moving tanks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:21:22 UTC
15:21:22 KST

- The U.S. Army fired three prototype XM1180 hit-to-kill 155 mm shells at a tank target at Yuma Proving Ground to test a new image-based seeker.
- The seeker will next undergo GPS-denied testing and be integrated into the XM1230 Extended Range Artillery Projectile, with firings planned within months.
The U.S. Army fired three prototype tank-killing artillery shells at a tank target in the Arizona desert at Yuma Proving Ground. The Army used the tests to check a new seeker that builds an image of the target area and steers the 155 mm round into an armored vehicle, including one that has moved since the shell was fired.
The rounds belong to the XM1180 Cannon-Delivered Area Effects Munition (C-DAEM) Armor program. They were launched from a 39-caliber cannon in different configurations, so the team could evaluate the seeker’s performance on each shot.
Yuma Test Center personnel ran the firings together with Project Manager Combat Ammunition Systems, the U.S. Army’s DEVCOM Armaments Center at Picatinny Arsenal and Raytheon, which builds the GPS-guided M982 Excalibur shell that the XM1180 is based on. Col. Alicia Johnson, who heads the ammunition program office, traveled to Yuma with her leadership team to watch the tests. They were the second phase of a series of guided test vehicle firings meant to prove the shell can find targets on its own.
Lovjoat Singh, a test and evaluation engineer at DEVCOM Armaments Center who planned and ran the firings, explained the two steps of the test.
“It will be an open loop test then following a closed loop test. Open-loop test means the seeker is going to be seeking a target but not actually acting upon it. Then closed loop is actually using the seeker to guide to a target,” said Singh.
The seeker gives the XM1180 a different job from the Excalibur, which flies to a fixed GPS coordinate and was never designed to hit a vehicle on the move. The new shell keeps much of the Excalibur’s design but swaps the payload for an armor-piercing warhead and adds the terminal seeker. As a result, an artillery battery tens of kilometers from the front can attack tanks and armored vehicles that a forward observer can no longer pin to a single grid point.
“It’s a cool new technology that basically creates (an) image of the target area and it’s able to find the target in that area. It should be able to use the image to guide to target,” said Casey Scharenbroich, an evaluator with the U.S. Army Operational Evaluation Command who was on site to judge how mature the technology has become.
“It would be a huge advantage on the battlefield for commanders, allowing them to engage targets that have moved or are on the move with this munition,” Scharenbroich said.
The Army also expects the seeker to reduce collateral damage, because the shell guides onto a specific vehicle instead of saturating an area. That is the main difference from cluster rounds such as the Cold War-era DPICM, which scatter dozens of bomblets and leave unexploded ordnance across the battlefield.
The XM1180 program dates to 2018. The Army fired its first guided test vehicle at Yuma in February 2024, when the shell identified a target and handed guidance over to its seeker, and the program reached Technology Readiness Level 6 ahead of schedule. Army officials have since said they want future rounds to share data with one another, so that several shells fired at a column of vehicles do not all strike the same tank.
The seeker is now headed for a second, newer program. Yuma test officer Ashley Lochetto said the next steps are testing the seeker without satellite navigation and fitting it to the XM1230 Extended Range Artillery Projectile.
“Our intent is to conduct GPS denied testing of the (seeker) along with integrating it into the XM1230 Extended Range Artillery Projectile,” said Lochetto.
The Extended Range Artillery Projectile effort is the U.S. Army’s push for a maneuvering 155 mm shell with deployable wings that can strike moving targets such as self-propelled howitzers, rocket launchers, infantry fighting vehicles and tanks beyond 65 km (40 miles) without a rocket motor. General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems joined General Dynamics Ordnance and Tactical Systems and BAE Systems on the program in June. The Army is aiming for low-rate production in fiscal 2029 and initial operational capability in fiscal 2030. Separately, the service is pursuing a new rocket-assisted 155 mm projectile for the M109 and M777 howitzers.
The C-DAEM Armor guided test vehicle series will continue through fiscal 2027. The first XM1230 firings with the new seeker are scheduled at Yuma Test Center within the next few months.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Taitung County Magistrate Wu Chun-li (吳俊立) was released on NT$5 million (US$153,761) bail Wednesday evening after prosecutors sought his detention over corruption allegations involving a road project serving his family’s resort.
The Taitung District Court granted Wu bail, imposed travel restrictions, and ordered electronic monitoring. It ruled that detention was unnecessary despite finding strong grounds to suspect his involvement in a crime, and said Wu denied wrongdoing.

The case involves a project to widen a road leading to a resort owned by the Wu family. Wu is the brother of Wu Hsiu-hua (吳秀華), the KMT’s candidate for Taitung County magistrate in the November elections.

DPP Legislator Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said one of the witnesses was Wu’s secretary, who also worked as an assistant to Wu Hsiu-hua, per Up Media. He urged prosecutors to investigate whether the aide had helped push for the road project.
Chuang added that seven county councilors had used their discretionary funds to finance the project. Prosecutors did not summon any of them on Tuesday.
Wu Hsiu-hua’s campaign office said it respected the rule of law and the ongoing investigation, and hoped the truth would come to light soon.
Wu Chun-li was elected county magistrate in 2005 but was suspended from his post over a corruption case. He was later acquitted for lack of evidence.
In 2012, however, the Supreme Court upheld a vote-buying conviction against him, carrying a two-year prison sentence.

Brothers manager Hirano Keiichi said the team had emphasized internal competition throughout the season, giving players opportunities while leaving it up to them to prove themselves, per Liberty Times.
“We substituted Yueh Tung-hua (岳東華) the day before. If he performs well, he might start in the next game. But considering the overall situation, we will still start Chang Shih-lun. We have emphasized the importance of competition all year, and that will not waver,” Hirano said.
Chang Shih-lun’s performance was a positive development for the Brothers after a difficult start to the series. Both he and Chang Jen-wei have gained experience in high-pressure championship games.
The victory cut the Brothers’ deficit to 3-1 in the best-of-seven series. The Dragons remain one win away from the championship, while the Brothers must win the remaining three games to become the first team to win the Taiwan Series after falling behind 3-0.

Taiwan legislative hearing discusses abolition of Control Yuan

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Former Control Yuan member Yeh Yi-jin (葉宜津) warned lawmakers Wednesday against paralyzing the Control Yuan before amending the Constitution, arguing that such a move would be unconstitutional.
The legislative hearing focused on the potential transfer of the Control Yuan’s powers and the mechanisms needed to facilitate the change, per CNA. National Taipei University professor Chen Chih-hua (陳志華) proposed transferring its investigative and audit powers to the Legislative Yuan to better fulfill the body's intended functions.
Retired Ming Chuan University professor Chi Chun-chen (紀俊臣) argued that the Control Yuan’s perceived poor performance stemmed from personnel issues rather than structural flaws, per UDN. He suggested adopting Sweden’s parliamentary ombudsman system, under which ombudsmen investigate public authorities and courts nationwide, as a possible way to transfer the Control Yuan’s powers to the legislature if lawmakers proceed with its abolition.
Yeh said she respected lawmakers’ desire to abolish the Control Yuan but argued that paralyzing the institution before its formal abolition would be unconstitutional, per Liberty Times. She said the body had processed 89,791 public complaints, conducted 65,503 disclosures of civil servants’ financial information, and produced 1,484 investigation reports, emphasizing that it continued to carry out its constitutional duties.
Yeh also rejected the ombudsman proposal, arguing that lawmakers were already burdened with existing responsibilities and lacked the capacity to act independently of their political parties. She questioned whether the public would accept having four ombudsmen under the legislature oversee public authorities nationwide.
At a legislative hearing in July, Fu Jen Catholic University professor Yao Meng-chang (姚孟昌) argued that transferring the Control Yuan’s powers to the legislature would concentrate too much power in one branch of government, per CNA. He recommended introducing greater democratic legitimacy to the institution by allowing its members to be elected.
In June, rejected Control Yuan nominee Chen Yung-hsing (陳永興) proposed constitutional amendments to transform Taiwan into a “modern democratic state,” per UDN. He suggested transferring the Control Yuan’s investigative and impeachment powers to the legislature.
KMT lawmaker Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯) previously said that, while investigating the military’s dashcam procurement, she found that the legislature’s lack of investigative powers limited her to requesting information rather than questioning Ministry of National Defense officials, per UDN. She also noted that when Sun Yat-sen (孫中山) conceived of the Control Yuan, its members were elected rather than nominated by the president.

====================================================================================================

Censorship in Pakistan Goes From ‘Pleasant’ to ‘Unpleasant’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:14:00 UTC
15:14:00 KST

The famous Pakistani satirist and playwright, Anwar Maqsood, once said at the Karachi Literature Festival: “The biggest lie in Pakistan is PTV’s weather report. Outside it is scorching hot, but the news announces: ‘The weather across the country is pleasant.'”
The man, a master of puns and wordplay, used the weather analogy to highlight the censorship imposed on the state broadcaster to keep people away from the harsh realities of the country. He used “scorching hot” as a metaphor for unemployment, inflation, poverty and social unrest.
Now, things have gone from “pleasant” to “unpleasant.”
The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (PEMRA) on October 13 directed satellite television channels to refrain from broadcasting or providing live coverage of “unpleasant incidents,” meaning explosions, blasts, firing and terrorist attacks.
“All satellite TV channel licensees are once again hereby directed to refrain from broadcast, re-broadcast and live coverage of any unfortunate/unpleasant incident such as explosion, blast, firing, terrorist attack etc,” the notification said, adding, “Satellite TV channels must broadcast only such verified information, warranted by the concerned department/law enforcement agency.”
The notification also directed channels to “effectively use time delay mechanism” and ensure the constitution of an independent editorial board in accordance with PEMRA laws, a Supreme Court judgment in suo motu case No. 28 of 2018, and an Islamabad High Court order issued on September 5, 2022.
Before the PEMRA notification, Pakistani satellite TV channels had refrained from broadcasting the “most unpleasant” – the name of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan and his image. Following the May 9, 2023, protests triggered by Khan’s arrest, PEMRA asked television licensees to ensure that “hate mongers, rioters, their facilitators and perpetrators” were “completely screened out from media.” Although it did not name Khan, television channels got the message.
Now, TV anchors have devised a new nomenclature while referring to news regarding Khan’s court proceedings. The preferred terms are “chairman Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI)” or “PTI chief.” One TV anchor satirically uses “Kasim ke Abba” (father of Kasim), which is the name of Khan’s elder son.
Recently, Pakistani journalist and author Mohammed Hanif, in his satirical blog on BBC Urdu, said people of his age had seen posters saying, “Please avoid political discussions in Pakistani restaurants.” Hanif says that, though he has not seen any restaurant owner pushing guests out for indulging in political discussion, this rule will now be implemented by Pakistan’s cyber authorities.
Any comment or discussion can be construed as anti-national or as disturbing public peace because the cyber authorities have not specified what constitutes such content. So, even a harmless post can invite the government’s wrath if a comment below it is seen as an attack on a government department. In the end, Hanif suggests that the safest way to avoid the midnight knock on your door is to discuss cooking recipes.

15:14:00 KST

Bulgaria’s budget deficit widened to 4% of gross domestic product in 2025, while government debt climbed to 29.9% of GDP, according to the latest data from the National Statistical Institute (NSI).
The General Government sector reported a deficit of 9.122 billion leva (4.664 billion euros) for the year, alongside public debt totaling 68.057 billion leva (34.797 billion euros).
Central Government accounted for most of the shortfall, with a deficit of 8.891 billion leva, equivalent to 3.9% of GDP. The Local Government sub-sector recorded a deficit of 223 million leva, while Social Security Funds posted a shortfall of 8 million leva.
A comparison of the official notification tables shows that both Bulgaria’s budget deficit and public debt have continued to rise.
The deficit increased from 2% of GDP, or 3.684 billion leva, in 2023 to 3%, or 6.242 billion leva, in 2024, before reaching 4% in 2025. Public debt also rose sharply, climbing by nearly 20 billion leva in one year, from 48.851 billion leva, or 23.8% of GDP, in 2024 to 68.057 billion leva, or 29.9%, in 2025.
In 2022, General Government debt stood at just over 37.8 billion leva. Over the following three years, the country’s liabilities therefore increased by more than 30 billion leva. Bulgaria’s GDP also expanded, reaching 227.949 billion leva in 2025, NSI data show.
The statistics are compiled using a harmonized methodology applied across the European Union. Under the Council Regulation implementing the Protocol on the excessive deficit procedure, Bulgaria, like the other EU member states, must submit preliminary figures to Eurostat by March 31 and final data by September 30 each year.
Despite the increase, Bulgaria’s public debt remains among the lowest in the European Union.
Eurostat, the EU’s official statistical office, reported that Bulgaria’s debt-to-GDP ratio stood at 28.7% in the second quarter of 2026, placing the country among the lowest in both the eurozone and the EU. Only Estonia, at 26.1%, Denmark, at 27.1%, and Luxembourg, at 28.2%, recorded lower ratios.
The highest public debt ratios were registered in Greece at 140.8%, Italy at 139.9%, France at 119.1%, Belgium at 110.2%, and Spain at 101.4%.
Across the eurozone, public debt reached 88.8% of GDP in the second quarter of 2026, up from 88.4% in the first quarter and 87.3% in the second quarter of 2025.
Bulgaria’s debt ratio rose by 0.1 percentage points from 28.6% in the first quarter of 2026 and by 2.4 percentage points from 26.3% in the second quarter of 2025.

U.S. Army tests smoke screen built to blind enemy radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:12:00 UTC
15:12:00 KST

- The U.S. Army has field-tested a portable module that releases coated fibers to hide soldiers and vehicles from enemy millimeter-wave radar.
- DEVCOM CBC handed the radar-blocking smoke system to the Army’s CBRN defense portfolio office for further testing before fielding.
The U.S. Army has developed a smoke screen that hides soldiers and vehicles from enemy radar as well as from enemy eyes. The Millimeter Wave Screening Obscuration Module releases a cloud of coated fibers into the air, and that cloud blurs the radar signature of everything behind it. Engineers at the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command Chemical Biological Center (DEVCOM CBC) at Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, demonstrated the module in live field trials in August. The center then handed it to the Army office that will test it further and prepare it for fielding.
Battlefield smoke has worked the same way for generations: it blocks what the enemy can see. The Army’s Cold War-era generators, such as the M56 Coyote and the vehicle-mounted M58 Wolf, were built to defeat the human eye, optical rangefinders and early infrared sights. Those screens do almost nothing against millimeter-wave radar, the type used in many modern fire-control radars and missile seekers. A platoon hidden in a dense cloud of conventional smoke can still show up clearly on an enemy radar screen.
“Different sensors are designed to operate across distinct regions of the electromagnetic spectrum,” said Dr. Jill Harland, a research scientist at DEVCOM CBC.
Visible-light cameras work on extremely short wavelengths, while thermal imagers and radars operate on progressively longer ones. Particles that block a camera are simply too small to interfere with a radar beam, so the center’s scientists had to rebuild the obscurant around the radar band itself. Their answer is about 30 pounds (13.6 kg) of specially coated fibers, which a portable device releases into the air, where they hang like thousands of tiny shields and scatter the incoming radar energy.
Every vehicle, weapon or soldier gives a radar a distinct signature, a numerical value the radar uses to detect and identify the target. During the August trials, the team set up several targets, watched them on radar and then released the fiber cloud around them to measure how quickly the cloud formed and how far the signatures dropped.
“We used radar to observe the cloud formation and show the degradation of the radar signatures of each of those targets,” said Michael Smith, a mechanical engineer at DEVCOM CBC. “As the cloud formed, the signature dropped and we got our obscuration that way.”
Smith said the moment the team watched those signatures fade on the radar screens during live dissemination was a defining one for the developers.
“Our objective is to buy Soldiers critical time on the battlefield, improving survivability directly accomplishes our core mission,” said Smith.
The radar module comes from the same team at the center’s Smoke and Target Defeat Branch that developed the M75 Screening Obscuration Module. That suitcase-sized smoke generator can be run by one soldier, and the Army has tested it at Dugway Proving Ground in Utah since 2018 as the successor to the Coyote. In November 2025, the center mounted an M75 on an unmanned ground vehicle at Aberdeen to conceal soldiers during a simulated wet gap crossing. At the time, the center said the next generation would add infrared and radar obscurants, and the millimeter-wave module is that radar piece now leaving the lab.
The Army is also looking further ahead. In January, Army Contracting Command at Aberdeen Proving Ground asked industry for ideas on a multispectral version of the module, one infantryman could carry and that would screen troops and combat vehicles from ultraviolet, visible, infrared and radar sensors at the same time. Its stated goal is a cloud that forms within 95 seconds, stretches 204 m (670 feet) long and 12 m (40 feet) high, and holds for 12 minutes.
The Millimeter Wave module now moves to the Portfolio Management Executive for Chemical, Biological, Radiological and Nuclear Defense, which will run the additional testing required before the system is issued to Army units.

What Happened to Gwadar’s Rights Movement?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:04:00 UTC
15:04:00 KST

In November 2021, thousands of people rallied and participated in sit-ins along Gwadar’s Harbor Road, demanding rights for the local Baloch people. What came to be known as the “Haq Do Tehreek” (Give Us Our Rights Movement) began mainly as a movement of the fishing community to address their grievances. But soon, women, children, men, and people from different walks of life joined the protests, making it the largest mass mobilization in the history of Gwadar.
Gwadar is not just another town or port. Located on Pakistan’s Makran coast, it sits near the mouth of the Strait of Hormuz. Its proximity to this strategic waterway through which a significant amount of the world’s oil and gas passes, and China’s investment and foothold at its port, have cemented Gwadar’s role not only in regional trade but also in global maritime geopolitics.
Gwadar port and Balochistan’s mineral wealth have, however, long been points of contention and have contributed to the turbulent political situation in the province.
As the gateway of the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), Gwadar port triggered great expectations in the early days of the port’s construction. Many believed that the fishing town would be transformed into a modern city, bringing prosperity to Gwadar’s residents. But two decades later, most of the expectations are unfulfilled.
In 2021, the Haq Do Tehreek emerged. The movement drew attention to the wide gap between the development and prosperity that Gwadar port promised and the everyday realities that the majority of its residents encountered. It brought people together to demand basic services like water, electricity, economic security, a ban on illegal fishing and trawling, freedom of movement, and relief from excessive security checkpoints, along with a list of other longstanding grievances.
Thus, in 2021, the Haq Do Tehreek became a symbol of resistance, and an example of how collective action and local mass mobilization of people, mainly the fishing community, could bring their long-neglected grievances to the forefront.
One of the reasons for the Haq Do Tehreek’s rapid rise and mass participation was its leadership. Maulana Hidayat-ur-Rehman, the leader of Haq Do Tehreek, was already politically active as a member of the Jamaat-e-Islami (JI). He also belonged to the fishing community, rather than to elite or established political families. This helped him connect with the masses. Consequently, JI activists and fishing communities participated in large numbers in the movement. In December 2022, they participated in large numbers to protest and blockade the entrance to Gwadar port and the East Bay Expressway.
The Haq Do Tehreek began as a peaceful movement. However, it soon escalated and violence erupted. A police constable died from injuries in the unrest; more than 100 people were arrested and restrictions were imposed on public gatherings and telecommunications.
With the government cracking down on the movement, Rehman came under scrutiny, forcing him to go into hiding in December 2022. When he re-emerged weeks later in January 2023 and presented himself before the courts to surrender and seek bail, he was arrested. He denied allegations linking him to the constable’s death and was then granted bail by the Supreme Court in May 2023. Mass support for the Maulana increased after his arrest. In February 2024, Rehman contested provincial elections and won a seat in the Balochistan assembly.
His participation in elections was controversial; while some considered his contesting the election as a route for pursuing the movement’s demands through formal politics, others opposed it, seeing it as a step that would weaken the Haq Do Tehreek. There were doubts whether Rehman, who had built his reputation by challenging the authorities, could deliver results from within the same political system.
Many conspiracy theories circulated at that time. Some believed that Rehman’s political rise and participation in elections were engineered by the state. After all, his entry into the provincial assembly served the government’s interest, as the unrelenting rallies and mass protests that he led were putting pressure on the local police and undermining the law and order situation in an already restive province.
So, has Rehman, as a legislator in the Balochistan assembly, been successful in getting the grievances of Gwardar’s residents addressed? The results are mixed. Illegal fishing and trawling, which were major concerns during the protests, continue unabated, as do the presence of innumerable security checkpoints and shortages of water and electricity.
Although such issues cannot be resolved overnight, the people of Gwadar cannot help but wonder what the movement achieved through its leaders joining formal politics.
The Haq Do Tehreek has transformed over the last couple of years. From a grassroots movement, it has evolved into a political party. Since the 2024 provincial elections, Haq Do Tehreek is listed as a political party with Pakistan’s Election Commission. Maulana’s political party is listed as Haq Do Tehreek on the Balochistan Assembly’s website.
Haq Do Tehreek no longer conducts mass mobilizations, aside from a long march from Quetta to Islamabad in July 2025 that Rehman led to pressure the federal government to address longstanding Baloch grievances, including enforced disappearances, restrictions on border trade, and illegal trawling. Even then, some claimed the march was organized by JI, others described it as the “Haq Do Balochistan Long March.”
The movement also suffered a setback with the death of its secretary-general, Hafeez Kiazai, in a road accident in March 2026.
Rehman is reportedly taking up issues pertaining to the fisherfolk in the provincial assembly. In October 2026, he chaired a meeting of the Balochistan Assembly’s Standing Committee on Fisheries in Gwadar to review the proposed Balochistan Fisheries and Aquaculture Bill 2026. The meeting brought together fishermen and other stakeholders to discuss reforms to protect their livelihoods and marine resources.
However, Gwadar’s Haq Do Tehreek has clearly lost the momentum and energy it once displayed. The massive rallies that were seen in 2021-2023 are no longer visible.
The movement may have handed over its struggle to formal politics, but formal politics also comes with its own constraints. After all, blaming and criticizing the very system one has become a part of is a contradiction in itself.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

IN BRIEF
- A lawsuit is seeking compensation for Facebook and Instagram users who were allegedly exposed to harmful content.
- Meanwhile, a judge in the US state of New Mexico has ordered Meta to pay US$25 billion for misleading consumers.
Meta and its social media platforms Facebook and Instagram are facing a class action lawsuit in Australia over allegations that addictive design features are harming children and teenagers.
The suit filed in the Federal Court on behalf of eight applicants seeks to recover compensation for Facebook and Instagram users who were exposed to harmful content or developed an addiction to social media, law firm Minter Ellison and Litigation Lending said in a statement.
The Federal Court in Sydney issued a suppression order on Monday stopping publication of details of the claim and the identity of the applicants, court documents show.
"We are aware of this claim and we will defend ourselves vigorously," a Meta spokesperson said in a statement.
Litigation Lending Services said it was funding the class action for Australian families who "would have no practical means of pursuing these claims against a global technology giant".
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"This proceeding raises important questions about the design and operation of social media platforms and their impact on children and teenagers in Australia," Minter Ellison partner William Nolan said in a statement.
The lawsuit comes amid rising tensions between Australia and big tech after a world-first ban on social media for children under 16, and newly proposed rules that could let users switch off algorithm-driven content on their feeds.
In August, Meta agreed to pay up to US$17.7 billion (roughly $25 billion) in the United States to settle claims that it deliberately engineered its platforms to hook young users.
Meta ordered to pay US$25 billion in New Mexico
News of the Australian lawsuit came shortly after a judge in the US state of New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay US$25 billion ($35.2 billion) after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in US President Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent.
New Mexico attorney general Raúl Torrez said it was one of the largest, if not the largest, single state verdict against a company in US history.
"Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order following the verdict.
Mathew found that a penalty of more than $219 billion was warranted, based on state law, but he reduced the figure to $25 billion.
In a statement, CJ Mahoney, Meta's chief legal officer, said the company is confident it will win on appeal.
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said.
"At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
The company had previously said a penalty in the billions of dollars risked violating its constitutional rights to due process and protection from excessive fines.

U.S. Air Force tests shipping military cargo by rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
06:02:12 UTC
15:02:12 KST

- The Air Force Research Laboratory flew cargo pods aboard a SpaceX Starfall capsule on Oct. 20 to test rocket delivery of military supplies.
- The pods carried survival gear, medical equipment and trackers, with sensors measuring heat, shock and vibration during launch and reentry.
The U.S. Air Force has sent military-style cargo into space and back aboard a SpaceX Starfall capsule as it tests whether rockets could one day deliver supplies to troops anywhere on Earth within hours.
The Air Force Research Laboratory flew its own cargo pods inside the capsule on a commercial rideshare launch from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 20, packing them with satellite trackers, batteries, survival gear, a water desalinator and emergency medical equipment to see how they would hold up through launch, spaceflight and the plunge back through the atmosphere.
The flight was part of Rocket Cargo, an AFRL project studying whether large commercial rockets can move materiel around the world on tactical timelines, and the capsule carried sensors that recorded the temperature, shock and vibration the cargo experienced along the way. Engineers paid particular attention to how electronics and survival equipment came through the ride, and they also checked whether a UNI-PAC III life raft would fit inside the capsule for future tests, which hints at missions such as dropping rescue kits to downed aircrew or stranded sailors far from any base.
“Any day you launch a rocket is a good day, but today was more than just another big rocket launch,” said Brig. Gen. Douglas P. Wickert, Department of the Air Force Technology Executive Officer and AFRL commander. “Today’s launch was another demonstration of how AFRL is partnering with industry to burn down risk, collect hard data and deliver war-winning technologies for the operational force.”
Starfall is SpaceX’s new uncrewed reentry capsule, a squat disk about 3.1 meters (10 feet) across that weighs roughly 2,100 kg (4,600 pounds) and can bring back up to 1,000 kg (2,200 pounds) of payload under parachutes, with recovery planned in the Pacific Ocean. SpaceX flew the first Starfall demonstration in June, and regulatory documents describe the capsule as a way to support both rapid point-to-point cargo delivery and a commercial market for products made in orbit and returned to Earth.
The Air Force’s ambitions for Rocket Cargo are much bigger than a single capsule, since AFRL says the concept stands apart from other fast-delivery efforts because a large rocket could carry tens of tons per launch to places with no runways or roads. The service has said it wants rocket-delivered cargo to reach almost any point on Earth within about an hour and a half and eventually to move loads comparable to a C-17 transport, and in June it awarded Colorado-based Geneva Technologies $4.3 million to help design the rocket cargo system.
AFRL sees uses ranging from resupplying forces in contested areas and expeditionary operations to rescue missions, disaster relief and responding to chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear incidents, and it is working with a long list of companies to get there, including SpaceX, Blue Origin, Rocket Lab, Sierra Space, Anduril, Inversion Space and Outpost Space. In August, the Air Force expanded Blue Origin’s role in the program with a study contract now worth about $13 million.
“This was a critical achievement to demonstrate the potential of Rocket Cargo delivery for point-to-point rapid global mobility for the Future Force,” said Adam Remaly, director of the AFRL Technology Transition Office.
AFRL plans further tests with commercial rockets and reentry capsules as it gathers data on how cargo survives the trip, and it is also looking at how the military could benefit from commercial investment in capsules built to return products manufactured in space.

Devonport to restart submarine defuelling at 14 Dock
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
07:00:52 BST
15:00:52 KST

Recommissioning 14 Dock at Devonport will allow legacy submarine defuelling to restart, paid for from the £7.1 billion going into the naval base over the next decade under Project Royal Oak, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked what progress the department has made in re-establishing a safe and secure defuelling capability at Devonport Dockyard.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, said: “As part of Project Royal Oak, £7.1 billion will be invested in HMNB Devonport over the next decade. Part of this investment is being used to complete the 14 Dock recommissioning programme, which will enable the recommencement of legacy submarine defueling activity.”
Defuelling at Devonport stopped in 2004, and the submarines that have decommissioned since then have been held afloat with their fuel still aboard, tied up in the Hamoaze and requiring crews, monitoring and maintenance for decades after their operational lives ended. Restarting the capability is the step that unlocks the rest of the dismantling process, since a boat cannot be broken up until its reactor fuel has been removed.
The Submarine Dismantling Project has been running since 2011 and demonstrated the later stages at Rosyth, where Swiftsure was taken apart as the trial vessel and the work was completed last year. The Devonport boats have been waiting on the defuelling step, and the Public Accounts Committee and the National Audit Office have both examined the cost of storing them.
Project Royal Oak is the wider rebuild of the naval base infrastructure that the submarine flotilla depends on, and it covers dock recommissioning, deep maintenance facilities and the shore support the Astute and Dreadnought classes will need through their lives. The programme was mapped out this year at around £26 billion across the naval bases, with Devonport taking the £7.1 billion share.
Devonport’s role is changing as Faslane consolidates the operational submarine flotilla, with the Plymouth base holding deep maintenance, refits and now the disposal pipeline. This publication reported recently that the Navy is looking to accelerate the Devonport submarine upgrades, and that more refit work is being done at Faslane while the Devonport docks are rebuilt.

China moves to set global standards for brain-computer interface technology
As Beijing prioritises development of the technology, a China-led committee aims to dictate how it is built
China has taken a major step in spearheading the standardisation of brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies, as it now chairs the secretariat of a subcommittee jointly overseen by two key international organisations and lists the technology applications as a national development priority.
The China-led subcommittee, known as ISO/IEC JTC 1/SC 43, was set to formulate global standards regarding the communication and interaction between brains and computers that are applicable across application areas, according to abstracts on both websites of the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) and International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC).
The committee, chaired by Yu Yuntao, a former department head with the China Electronics Standardization Institute, has already published several standards, including the BCI vocabulary, data format for non-invasive brain information collection, reference architecture and use cases.
“The [Chinese] government is betting on this industry, among others, as one that has the potential to become the next EV sector,” said Xiaomeng Lu, director of geo-technology at Eurasia Group.

U.S. and Israel prepare for a new war with Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:56:50 UTC
14:56:50 KST

- President Trump said the U.S. is not negotiating with Iran and that “something” will happen “fairly soon,” as plans for renewed strikes take shape.
- U.S. troops are leaving bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait, and Israeli jets flew a mock strike mission to Iran’s border.
The United States and Israel are moving toward a new war with Iran within days, as President Donald Trump said Washington is no longer negotiating with Tehran and that “something” will happen “fairly soon,” while U.S. troops pull out of exposed bases across the Middle East and Israeli fighter jets rehearse a strike on Iran at the edge of its airspace.
The troop withdrawals, embassy staff cuts and large-scale air activity over the region closely resemble the buildup that came just before the war began in late February, and they put the next round of fighting on a timeline measured in days rather than months, with the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections now less than two weeks away.
“No, I think we’re not negotiating… we are going to have something, one way or the other. It’ll happen fairly soon,” said President Donald Trump on Oct. 21.
The remarks mark a sharp turn from Trump’s pledge on Oct. 8 that the United States would not attack Iran before the midterms, and they come as Washington and Jerusalem finalize plans for what officials described to The New York Times as a short but intensive operation against Iran’s energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone arsenals. Options presented to Trump include strikes on tunnel entrances at nuclear sites such as Pickaxe Mountain and on the strategic islands of Kharg, which handles most of Iran’s oil exports, and Qeshm, NBC News reported, while officials quoted by the Times said there is a chance he could order strikes before the end of this month.
On the ground, the U.S. military has quietly moved troops out of bases in Jordan, Qatar and Kuwait in recent days, two U.S. officials and two people familiar with the matter told NBC News, and one official said getting forces out of harm’s way is part of planning as Trump weighs restarting major combat operations. The State Department has ordered staff reductions at the U.S. embassy in Saudi Arabia, citing Houthi attacks on the kingdom including strikes on civilian airports, and chiefs of mission at several other posts across the region have been told to operate with fewer personnel, in moves that sources compared directly with the drawdowns at the start of the war in February.
“We regularly move U.S. service members and assets to optimize mission readiness,” a U.S. Central Command spokesperson said.
Israel has already rehearsed the opening move of a new campaign, sending dozens of fighter jets and refueling aircraft along a route through Syrian and Iraqi airspace consistent with a strike on Iran and turning them back only as they approached the Iranian border, Axios reporter Barak Ravid reported, citing sources who described it as a massive power projection operation. Israel told Washington the flight was an exercise and a show of force, but the sortie was followed overnight by large-scale tactical aircraft activity over the region that defense writer Tyler Rogoway said looked like a dry run for a large integrated operation, in which commanders put much of the real strike force in position to rehearse before the order to execute is given.
Such rehearsals also force Iran to switch on its air defenses as if a full attack were coming, which lets U.S. and Israeli intelligence detect, classify and pinpoint radars and missile sites that would have to be suppressed, destroyed or avoided on the first night of an offensive, Rogoway noted, and that kind of targeting picture is far sharper when Iranian crews are on high alert than during routine surveillance.
Tensions are climbing at sea as well, after the naval arm of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said its forces hit four vessels it accused of illegal oil transfers in the northern Persian Gulf and that three more ships struck mines west of the Strait of Hormuz, warning that continued provocations could bring a wider response against U.S. bases in the region. Iran’s neighbors are bracing for the fallout, with Saudi Arabia already under a sustained Houthi missile and drone campaign that has led Britain to send Royal Air Force Typhoons to guard Saudi cities and Türkiye to prepare forces for deployment to the kingdom under its new defense pact with Riyadh and Pakistan.

DARPA wants smart nuclear reactor for space and bases
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:44:36 UTC
14:44:36 KST

- DARPA awarded SpaceNukes an agreement to ground-test a Kilopower nuclear reactor with active, autonomous control rods under its Fat Cat program.
- The team behind the 2018 KRUSTY reactor test will run the new test with Los Alamos National Laboratory.
The Pentagon’s top research agency wants a nuclear reactor that can run itself, and it has hired the team that built America’s last space reactor to prove it can be done. DARPA has awarded Space Nuclear Power Corporation, a small Los Alamos, New Mexico, company known as SpaceNukes, an agreement to build a Kilopower reactor with self-adjusting control rods and switch it on in a full nuclear ground test, the company announced on Oct. 21.
DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, was created in 1958 after the Soviet Union launched Sputnik, with a mandate to make sure the United States would never again be caught off guard by a rival’s technology. The agency does not build weapons itself; it funds high-risk ideas that the military services and industry consider too uncertain to pay for, and its bets have included the ARPANET network that grew into the internet and early stealth aircraft research. The new work falls under a DARPA program called Fast Capacitance, or Fat Cat, run by program manager Tabitha Dodson in the agency’s Defense Sciences Office, which is looking for ways to let reactors operate on their own for national security missions.
The reactor at the center of the project has already worked once. Between November 2017 and March 2018, engineers from Los Alamos National Laboratory and NASA ran a test called KRUSTY, short for Kilopower Reactor Using Stirling Technology, at the Nevada National Security Site, powering up a reactor built around a solid cast uranium-235 core about the size of a paper towel roll. Sodium heat pipes carried heat from the core to Stirling engines that turned it into electricity, and the reactor ran at full power for about 28 hours while engineers deliberately cut power, shut down engines and disabled heat pipes to see whether it would keep going, which it did.
That test used a passive design, in which the reactor’s own physics kept it stable without moving parts adjusting the reaction. The new version will add active control rods that move to raise or lower the reactor’s output, giving it the ability to change power on demand and respond quickly to shifting needs, which SpaceNukes says opens the technology to a much wider range of missions. A reactor that manages itself matters most in places where no operator can reach it quickly, such as a spacecraft, a base on the Moon or a remote military outpost, where power needs can change suddenly and a human may be minutes or hours away.
“There is no substitute for demonstrated technology when American national security objectives are at stake,” said Andy Phelps, CEO of SpaceNukes. “This award lets us advance the work begun in the KRUSTY program and bring another tested capability forward for the nation.”
SpaceNukes is essentially the KRUSTY team reassembled as a company. Chief technology officer David Poston and chief operating officer Patrick McClure led the reactor work at Los Alamos, chief engineer Marc Gibson ran the program at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, and the company holds a license from Los Alamos for the Kilopower design. Gibson will lead integration of the new test hardware at the company’s workshop in Medina, Ohio, and the program will move through design, procurement and integration stages before the reactor goes critical in a joint test with Los Alamos.
“This award recognizes the maturity and continuity of the team that designed, built, and tested KRUSTY in 2018,” said Patrick McClure, chief operating officer of SpaceNukes.
The project lands as Washington is pushing hard to get reactors into space and onto military bases. A White House policy memo in April directed the Pentagon and NASA to compete designs for space reactors, with an orbital demonstration targeted as early as 2028 and a reactor on the Moon as early as 2030, while on the ground the U.S. Army has committed up to $2.2 billion to build nuclear microreactors at five military bases. The KRUSTY reactor was designed to deliver between 1 and 10 kilowatts of electricity continuously for at least a decade, and the DARPA test will produce flight-relevant hardware that has actually been run on nuclear power, along with the engineering basis for reactors that can control themselves.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:43:45 UTC
14:43:45 KST

Israeli forces and illegal settlers carried out 23 attacks and violations against Palestinian farmers, their lands and crops, as well as solidarity activists, across seven governorates in the occupied West Bank within 12 hours on Wednesday, a Palestinian commission said.
The Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said in a statement that the incidents were recorded between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. local time (0300–1500 GMT), coinciding with the ongoing olive harvest season.
According to the commission, 10 incidents were documented in Nablus, six in Ramallah and Al-Bireh, two each in Salfit and Hebron, and one each in Qalqilya, Jenin and Bethlehem.
The violations included shootings, physical assaults, arrests, preventing farmers from harvesting olives, theft of crops and equipment, and the burning and bulldozing of agricultural land.
The commission said a Palestinian farmer was shot in the hand with live fire while harvesting olives in the village of Osarin in Nablus governorate.
Another farmer suffered severe breathing difficulties after being sprayed with pepper spray in the Wadi Abbas area of Qarawat Bani Hassan in Salfit governorate.
In the town of Nahalin, southwest of Bethlehem, Israeli forces attacked farmers and solidarity activists in the al-Habla area, arresting an elderly woman and several activists, including Brad Lander, a Democratic candidate for the US Congress, according to the commission.
Israeli forces also confiscated harvested olives during the incident.
The commission also reported the arrest of a Russian solidarity activist while participating in the olive harvest in the Christian town of Taybeh in the central West Bank, and a young Palestinian man while harvesting olives in Kafr ad-Dik in the north.
Israeli violence
In Nablus governorate, illegal Israeli settlers set fire to agricultural land in the town of Burqa, while Israeli bulldozers levelled olive-planted land in the Rajmanat area of Madama, the commission said.
Illegal settlers also attacked olive pickers near Jalud School and opened fire towards them before Israeli forces arrived and physically assaulted the farmers.
In Beit Furik, illegal settlers threw harvested olives onto the ground and seized crops at gunpoint, forcing families to leave their fields.
Similar incidents involving the theft of olives and agricultural equipment were reported in Qaryut, Awarta and Tell, while farmers were expelled from the Wadi Abuwayn area of al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya.
The commission said Israeli forces also pursued farmers in the al-Jiza area of Beita, preventing them from harvesting olives and opening fire in their direction.
In Ramallah and Al-Bireh governorate, farmers were prevented from accessing their lands in the al-Harayiq area of Deir Jarir.
Farmers, journalists and commission staff were also expelled from agricultural land in Turmus Ayya after Israeli forces declared the area a closed military zone.
Landowners were prevented from harvesting olives in al-Mughayyir, while illegal settlers brought livestock onto olive-planted land in Burqa and Kafr Malik.
Daily struggle
In the southern Hebron governorate, armed Israeli settlers opened fire towards olive pickers in the Birin area, while farmers and activists were prevented from harvesting in Idhna, according to the commission.
In Qalqilya governorate, illegal settlers cut down olive trees in the town of Farata, east of the city.
Meanwhile, farmers in Deir Abu Daif, east of Jenin, were forced to leave their lands despite having obtained prior coordination and approval to access them.
The commission said the incidents reflected a combination of direct attacks, military closures, arrests and crop confiscations that have turned access to farmland into a daily struggle for Palestinian farmers.
It warned that expelling landowners and targeting solidarity activists and journalists undermines efforts to protect the olive harvest and document violations.
The commission called for effective measures to ensure farmers’ safe and continuous access to their lands and accountability for those responsible for the attacks.
Attacks by illegal Israeli settlers against Palestinians and their agricultural lands have intensified during the olive harvest season, which began in early October and provides a vital source of income for thousands of Palestinian families.
According to Palestinian figures, approximately 750,000 illegal Israeli settlers live in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, across 194 settlements and around 400 settlement outposts.
Israeli settlements built on occupied Palestinian territory are illegal under international law.
Palestinian, Israeli and international human rights organisations have repeatedly accused Israeli authorities of failing to prevent attacks by illegal settlers or hold those responsible accountable, despite repeated assaults on Palestinians, their homes, farmland and property.

Further educational cooperation between China and Central Asia should include more practical, skills-based training programs tailored to local industry needs, she added.
"Such programs can help young people develop professional skills and acquire the qualifications they need for employment," Kalandarova said.
In March, the Confucius Institute at TNU launched a workshop that offers local young people free training in practical skills, including filigree enamel painting and copper bas-relief making.

The document, jointly issued by the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology and other government departments, calls for integrated efforts in technological breakthroughs and their application, addressing weaknesses in China's industrial foundation systematically, and achieving a comprehensive upgrade toward stronger innovation, greater self-reliance and higher quality.
Industrial foundation, the bedrock of manufacturing competitiveness, covers a range of areas including core components, basic materials and foundational software, as well as related talents, market conditions and the policy environment.
While China has built the world's largest and most complete industrial system over the past decades, its industrial foundation remains a weak link, experts said.

Vulnerabilities and risks persist particularly in areas like integrated circuits and industrial software, Zhou noted.
As China pursues high-quality economic development and advances its new industrialization drive, the strengthening and upgrading of its industrial foundation has become increasingly critical.
According to the plan issued on Thursday, the weaknesses in China's industrial foundation will be significantly alleviated by 2030, while China's overall industrial foundation capabilities will reach internationally advanced levels, thereby providing strong support for building a modern industrial system anchored in advanced manufacturing.
A new cohort of single-champion manufacturers and "little giant" specialized enterprises in the industrial foundation sector should also be cultivated by then, the plan says. ■

World Insights: Protests reflect France's economic, fiscal dilemmas
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:42:58 CST
14:42:58 KST

PARIS, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- France has been shaken by a wave of protests that began in classrooms and spilled onto the streets. What started as student anger over crumbling schools, overcrowded classes and chronic staff shortages has escalated into violent unrest in several regions.
Soon other groups, angered by soaring energy bills, a cost-of-living squeeze and deteriorating public services, joined the protests. Beneath the disorder lie deeper, intertwined pressures: feeble growth, shrinking fiscal room for manoeuvre and a welfare model under strain, all of which highlight the acute economic and fiscal challenges confronting France.
COST-OF-LIVING SQUEEZE
Soaring fuel prices are one of the drivers behind this concentrated outburst of public anger.
Buffeted by turbulence in global energy markets, French energy prices have kept climbing. The rise has not merely lifted household bills for transport and everyday living; it has also rippled through supply chains and production costs, pushing up prices across the wider economy and further tightening family budgets.
Data released by the French National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (INSEE) on Oct. 15 showed that France's consumer prices rose by 3.1 percent year-on-year in September, up from 2.4 percent in August. The acceleration was mainly driven by faster increases in energy prices, which surged 21.3 percent year-on-year in September, up from 16.7 percent in August.
For French residents who rely on cars for daily commutes, fuel is an unavoidable routine expense. In 2018, a fuel tax hike triggered the nationwide "yellow vest" movement. Years later, fuel prices becoming the focal point of public discontent once again demonstrates that certain long-standing issues affecting people's livelihoods have not been fundamentally resolved.
Sluggish economic growth has further eroded citizens' ability to cope with the rising cost of living. According to INSEE data, the French economy contracted by 0.2 percent in the first quarter of this year, posted zero growth in the second quarter, and household purchasing power per consumption unit declined by 0.6 percent in the second quarter.
LIVELIHOODS VS FISCAL CONSOLIDATION
High public debt and rising borrowing costs leave the French government with limited fiscal leeway to address social grievances.
INSEE data indicates that by the end of the second quarter of this year, France's public debt stood at 119 percent of its Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
Meanwhile, yields on government bonds have continued to climb. French radio station Europe 1 reported that the yield on France's 10-year government bonds exceeded the symbolic 5 percent threshold on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. Rising financing costs will increase the government's debt servicing burden, squeezing space for other public expenditures.
The French government estimates that interest payments on public debt will rise from 79.2 billion euros (88.96 billion U.S. dollars) this year to 91.2 billion euros next year.
Substantial social protection spending also complicates fiscal consolidation efforts. Data show that in 2024, French social protection benefits expenditure accounted for 31.9 percent of GDP, higher than the European Union average of 27.3 percent. As population aging accelerates, spending on pensions, healthcare and related areas faces sustained pressure.
The French government finds itself in a dilemma: on the one hand, in response to rising energy prices and calls to improve public services, it needs to provide subsidies, adjust taxes, and increase public spending; on the other, heavy debt burdens, rising interest expenses, and pressures for fiscal consolidation constrain its ability to expand expenditure.
UNREST-FUELING ECONOMIC RISKS
The protests and violent riots have damaged shops, public buildings, and infrastructure across France. The government estimates that around 3,000 businesses nationwide have been directly affected, with economic losses likely to reach hundreds of millions of euros.
In the longer run, persistent social unrest could also undermine consumer and investment confidence, dragging down an already fragile French economy. The OFCE, an independent economic research institute affiliated with Sciences Po in Paris, released a report on Oct. 14 forecasting that the French economy would grow by 0.4 percent in 2026 and 0.5 percent in 2027, noticeably below the eurozone average. If social unrest intensifies further, it could place additional strain on economic performance.
At the same time, social turmoil creates greater political headwinds for fiscal consolidation. As the 2027 presidential election approaches, debates over public services, social welfare, fiscal austerity and governance are growing increasingly fierce.
Divergent views among political forces on the root causes of social conflicts and their solutions make it harder for the government to build consensus to cut spending and rein in deficits.
On Oct. 19, Gilles Moec, chief economist at French insurance group Axa, told French daily Le Monde that while France's debt problem was serious but manageable, political instability could significantly aggravate the situation.
The deep-seated economic and social contradictions behind these protests cannot be resolved solely through short-term measures. Striking a balance between easing livelihood pressures, restoring economic growth, and managing public debt remains a long-term challenge for the French government. ■

LONDON, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Government websites throughout Europe became unavailable on Wednesday as operators raced to patch two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a scripting language widely used in website development.

PHP is a widely used, open-source general-purpose scripting language. It runs on servers to generate web content, interact with databases and perform other functions. It is also integrated into a wide range of software products.
Researchers at cybersecurity firms discovered the flaws with the help of artificial intelligence (AI) tools, according to the BBC. The vulnerabilities had reportedly gone undetected for more than a decade.
The incident affected a range of public services. Finland suspended public online government services, while the Dutch cybersecurity agency temporarily shut down its website because of the vulnerabilities.
Britain's Oxford City Council said on Wednesday that its website was temporarily unavailable as a precautionary "because of a worldwide issue affecting the underlying technology."
Britain's National Cyber Security Centre issued an alert on Wednesday, urging organizations to take immediate action to install the available security updates.
The BBC reported that patches were released on Wednesday afternoon.
Dane Knecht, chief technology officer at cloud cybersecurity services company Cloudflare, said on the social platform X that this would not be the last time such vulnerabilities were discovered. AI models, he said, would continue to identify similar flaws in widely used software.
"Maintainers, researchers, providers and governments need a new shared playbook so the response scales with the findings and critical Internet infrastructure gets patched," he said. ■

Colombian frontline police unaware of new AFP anti-drug taskforce

Colombia's frontline anti-drug police unaware of new AFP international taskforce
In short:
Two Colombian National Police departments say they have no evidence of an agreement with the Australian Federal Police for its newly announced anti-drugs taskforce, based in Bogotá.
Five months after the taskforce's announcement, the departments say drug-related intelligence has not been shared and no substance seizures or arrests have been made in cooperation with the AFP.
The AFP says the taskforce is not yet operational, but agreements have been made that would allow it to "focus on transnational organised crime networks".
Two police departments on the frontline of Colombia's fight against cartels say they have no evidence of an agreement with the Australian Federal Police (AFP) for its newly announced anti-drugs taskforce based in the South American nation.
In May, Commissioner Krissy Barrett announced the AFP and New Zealand Police would fund an international joint investigations team (IJIT) "to gather evidence about illicit drug shipments".
The team would include AFP officers in the capital Bogotá, working with Colombian, US, INTERPOL and Mexican authorities to curb the flow of drugs through the Pacific to Australia, the commissioner said.
A joint investigation by the ABC and the Colombian newspaper El Tiempo can reveal the anti-narcotics department of Colombia's National Police (PNC) has no recorded data that shows subscribed "protocols, agreements, or procedures" relating to the IJIT.
In a response to a freedom of information request filed by El Tiempo and shared with the ABC, the department said drug-related intelligence had not been shared with the AFP and no "operational activities" such as illicit substance seizures or arrests had been made in cooperation with Australian police as part of the IJIT.
The department also said there was currently only a "letter of intent" outlining a "framework for cooperation and exchange of information", which the ABC understands was signed jointly by PNC Major General Jesús Alejandro Barrera Peña and the AFP in August.
"The instrument does not identify the so-called 'IJIT', nor does it establish specific functions, responsibilities or procedures for this department in relation to said mechanism," the department said.
The letter made no connection between the IJIT and joint drug seizures, destruction of narcotics production infrastructure, disruption of criminal groups or the identification of international trafficking routes, the department said.
The ABC understands the IJIT agreement was made with — and expected to be overseen by — the PNC's Office of International Relations and Cooperation (ORECI) and not the anti-narcotics department.
ORECI coordinates Colombia's international policing efforts by connecting other PNC departments to global counterparts, such as the AFP.
The department focuses on strategic decision-making and intelligence and sits above the anti-narcotics and criminal investigations agencies, which oversee frontline drug and domestic crime policing operations.
An AFP spokesperson told the ABC the IJIT was not yet operational, but an "annex" agreement was made with the PNC in August in addition to the letter of intent that would allow the taskforce to "focus on transnational organised crime networks".
The AFP did not specify when the IJIT would become operational.
In a separate response shared with the ABC, the PNC's criminal investigations department said it had no data that was able to determine whether the AFP was involved, supported, funded or shared intelligence in 174 drug trafficking investigations conducted between January 1, 2025 and October 6 this year.
The department said those figures were collated based on aggregate numbers of cases and investigations outcomes that did not list specific agencies involved.
But the department also said it had no knowledge of Colombian anti-narcotics intelligence being used to "identify, locate, track, monitor or intercept" suspected drug trafficking vessels in the Pacific Ocean or Caribbean Sea as part of the IJIT.
The revelations follow ABC questions posed to the AFP in June about the IJIT's allocated budget, operational commitments and measure of how it would be deemed successful, as part of a separate Freedom of Information request.
In response, the AFP said it had 60 documents that would answer the questions.
The AFP declined to release them, citing national security and international relations concerns, and said at the time that the IJIT was "still in the negotiation phase".
It also said publishing the information would be harmful to relations between Australia and Colombia, or could divulge confidential details regarding how AFP officers operate.
In this year's federal budget, more than $1.16 million was allocated to the AFP for "ordinary annual services" in policing assistance efforts abroad and on Australian external territories in 2026-27.
That figure is expected to rise to $1.4 million next year, before dropping to $1.01 million and $1.03 million in the following two years.
But the budget does not detail how much is set aside specifically for the IJIT.
Commissioner Barrett said 17 tonnes of illicit drugs, mostly cocaine, have been seized by "local and international" police since January this year and stopped from reaching Australia through the Pacific.
The ABC understands, to July this year, most of the offshore seizures were made in French Polynesia, AFP officers were not physically involved in any interceptions and none were in Australian territorial waters.
The PNC this month announced an Australian-Iranian national, Arash Ebrahimi Far, was detained in Colombia as a subject of an INTERPOL Red Notice for alleged drug trafficking and money laundering, which was not believed to be related to the IJIT.

Pentagon extends Raytheon deal for missile defense radars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
05:33:32 UTC
14:33:32 KST

- The Missile Defense Agency extended Raytheon’s AN/TPY-2 radar sustainment contract by two years, raising its ceiling from $2.6 billion to nearly $3 billion.
- The ordering period now runs to Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million obligated at award.
The Missile Defense Agency has extended Raytheon’s contract to operate and maintain the U.S. military’s AN/TPY-2 missile defense radars for two more years, adding $394 million to the deal and lifting its ceiling to nearly $3 billion, the Department of War announced.
The sole-source modification raises the maximum value of the contract from about $2.6 billion to $2.999 billion and keeps the ordering period open until Oct. 31, 2028, with $112.3 million in fiscal 2027 operations and maintenance, research and development, and procurement funds obligated at the time of award.
The AN/TPY-2 is a transportable X-band radar that sits at the heart of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense system, better known as THAAD, and also serves as a standalone early warning sensor for U.S. ballistic missile defense. The radar can work in two ways: deployed far forward to spot ballistic missiles shortly after launch and pass tracking data to other defenses, or as part of a THAAD battery to track an incoming warhead and guide interceptors to hit it as it descends.
Under the extension, Raytheon will continue to run and support the radars from its facility in Woburn, Massachusetts, and at radar sites in the United States and overseas, where the company’s field teams help keep the sensors operating around the clock. The work combines cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee and firm-fixed-price contract items, and the Missile Defense Agency at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, is also extending the task orders that fund individual radar sites.
The U.S. Army fields eight THAAD batteries, each with one AN/TPY-2 radar, including units at Fort Bliss, Texas, in South Korea and on Guam, while forward-based radars have been stationed at sites including the Shariki area in Japan, Türkiye, Israel and Qatar. The radar is also sold abroad, and in 2020 the Missile Defense Agency awarded Raytheon a production contract worth up to $2.3 billion for seven AN/TPY-2 radars for Saudi Arabia, built with gallium nitride components that extend the radar’s range and sensitivity.
The radars have come under direct fire during the war with Iran this year, and satellite images analyzed by CNN showed that a THAAD radar at Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan was apparently destroyed by an Iranian strike in early March, along with damage at radar sites near Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and in the United Arab Emirates. Each AN/TPY-2 costs hundreds of millions of dollars and takes years to build, which makes keeping the existing fleet working a priority for the Missile Defense Agency while new radars are produced.
The original contract was awarded to Raytheon on a sole-source basis in 2018 as the radar’s designer and builder, and the extension was likewise issued without competition. The new ordering period gives the Missile Defense Agency two more years to keep the current support arrangement in place before it decides how to handle long-term sustainment of the AN/TPY-2 fleet beyond October 2028.
